docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(I\) be an open interval, and let \(f,g\colon I\to\mathbb{R}\text{.}\) At every point where the stated derivatives exist:

  1. If \(f\) is a constant function, then \(f'(x)=0\text{.}\)

  2. If \(f\) is the identity function \(f(x)=x\text{,}\) then \(f'(x)=1\text{.}\)

  3. (Power rule) For a positive integer \(k\text{,}\) if \(f(x)=x^k\) then \(f'(x)=kx^{k-1}\text{.}\) To prove it from the definition, factor \(x^k-x_0^k=(x-x_0)\left(x^{k-1}+x^{k-2}x_0+\cdots+x_0^{k-1}\right)\text{;}\) after dividing by \(x-x_0\text{,}\) the second factor has \(k\) terms, each tending to \(x_0^{k-1}\) as \(x\to x_0\text{.}\)

  4. (Sum and difference rule) If \(f\) and \(g\) are differentiable, then \(f \pm g\) is differentiable, and \((f \pm g)'(x) = f'(x) \pm g'(x)\text{.}\)

  5. (Product rule) If \(f\) and \(g\) are differentiable, then \(f g\) is differentiable, and \((fg)'(x) = f'(x)g(x) + f(x)g'(x)\text{.}\)

  6. If \(f\) is differentiable and \(c\) is a real number, then \(cf\) is differentiable, and \((cf)'(x) = cf'(x)\text{.}\)

  7. If \(g\) is differentiable and \(g(x)\neq0\text{,}\) then \(1/g\) is differentiable at \(x\text{,}\) and \(\displaystyle \left(\frac{1}{g}\right)'(x)=-\frac{g'(x)}{g(x)^2}\text{.}\)

  8. (Quotient rule) If \(f\) and \(g\) are differentiable and \(g(x)\neq0\text{,}\) then \(f/g\) is differentiable at \(x\text{,}\) and

\[ \left(\frac{f}{g}\right)'(x)=\frac{f'(x)g(x)-f(x)g'(x)}{g(x)^2}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Differentiation rules compute derivatives without returning to the difference quotient each time: once the derivatives of a few basic functions are known, the derivative of any expression built from them by sums, products, quotients and constant multiples follows mechanically. Each rule is proved once from the definition of the derivative.

The sum and constant-multiple rules say that differentiation is linear: \((af+bg)'=af'+bg'\) for constants \(a,b\). The product rule is not of this form. Over a small step \(h\), the change in \(fg\) consists of the change in \(f\) times \(g\), plus \(f\) times the change in \(g\), plus the product of the two changes. After division by \(h\) the last term tends to \(0\), which leaves \(f'g+fg'\). The quotient rule follows from the product rule and rule 7 by writing \(f/g=f\cdot(1/g)\).

Repeated use of rules 1 to 6 shows that every polynomial is differentiable on \(\mathbb{R}\), with

\[ (a_nx^n+\cdots+a_1x+a_0)' =na_nx^{n-1}+\cdots+a_1, \]

and the quotient rule extends this to rational functions wherever the denominator is nonzero. Together with the chain rule for compositions, the rules reduce the derivative of any elementary expression to the derivatives of its building blocks.

A common slip is to differentiate a product factor by factor. In general \((fg)'\neq f'g'\): for \(f(x)=g(x)=x\) one has \(f'(x)g'(x)=1\), while \((x^2)'=2x\). In the quotient rule the order in the numerator matters, since \(f'g-fg'\) and \(fg'-f'g\) differ by a sign.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Differentiation rules preserve differentiability under algebraic operations.
  • The product and quotient rules account for interactions between factors.
  • Constant multiples factor out of derivatives.

  • Together with the chain rule, the standard formulas give

    \[ \begin{gathered} (\ln x)'=\frac{1}{x}\;\;(x>0),\\ (b^x)'=b^x\ln b\;\;(b>0),\\ (x^p)'=p\,x^{p-1}\;\;(x>0,\ p\in\mathbb{R}). \end{gathered} \]

    The domain condition \(x>0\) is essential for a general real exponent \(p\text{;}\) for integer powers the power rule holds wherever the expression is defined.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \((x^2+3x)'=2x+3\text{.}\)
  • \((x^2\sin x)'=2x\sin x+x^2\cos x\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The Dirichlet function is the indicator function of the rational numbers, defined by

\[ f(x)=\indicator_{\mathbb{Q}}(x)=\begin{cases} \displaystyle \,1,& \text{if }x\in\mathbb{Q},\\[2pt] \displaystyle \,0,& \text{if }x\notin\mathbb{Q}. \end{cases} \]

If the input \(x\) is a rational number, the output of the Dirichlet function is \(1\text{;}\) otherwise, if the input \(x\) is an irrational number, the output of the Dirichlet function is \(0\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The Dirichlet function provides a fundamental example of extreme irregularity. It sorts real numbers into rational and irrational ones, giving the value \(1\) to the first kind and \(0\) to the second.

The irregularity comes from how the two kinds are mixed: every interval \((a,b)\) with \(a<b\), however short, contains both rational and irrational numbers. So close to any point \(x\), the function takes both values \(0\) and \(1\), and its values never settle down near \(x\). A sketch of the graph as two horizontal lines \(y=0\) and \(y=1\) is misleading: each of these "lines" has gaps between any two of its points.

The function is the indicator function of \(\mathbb{Q}\). Later it serves as the standard example of a function that is continuous at no point, and of a bounded function that is not Riemann integrable.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The Dirichlet function is discontinuous at every point.
  • It is not Riemann integrable on any nondegenerate bounded interval.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• On any nondegenerate interval, rational and irrational inputs are densely interwoven, preventing continuity.
  • Any neighbourhood contains points where the function value jumps between \(0\) and \(1\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Two sets \(A\) and \(B\) are said to be disjoint if they intersect emptily, i.e., \(A\cap B =\varnothing\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Disjoint sets share no common elements: an element of one set is ruled out of the other. The condition concerns only their intersection, not how the sets are described.

In the left panel the discs \(A\) and \(B\) have no common points, so \(A\cap B=\varnothing\). In the right panel the shaded overlap contains points of both sets, so the sets are not disjoint. A single common element is enough to break disjointness, however small the overlap.

Disjointness makes counting additive: for disjoint finite sets, \(|A\cup B|=|A|+|B|\), because no element is counted twice. A set and its complement are always disjoint, and so are \(A\setminus B\) and \(B\). For more than two sets, "pairwise disjoint" means that every two of them are disjoint; this is stronger than an empty common intersection, as \(\{1,2\}\), \(\{2,3\}\) and \(\{1,3\}\) show.

This notion formalizes the idea of mutual exclusivity in probability: events that cannot happen at the same time.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(A\) and \(B\) are disjoint finite sets, then \(|A\cup B|=|A|+|B|\text{.}\)
  • Disjoint sets are distinct, with one exception: \(\varnothing\cap\varnothing=\varnothing\text{,}\) so the empty set is disjoint from itself. It is the only such set, because \(A\cap A=A\text{.}\)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The sets \(\{1,\,2\}\) and \(\{3,\,4\}\) are disjoint.
  • Any set \(A\) and \(\varnothing\) are disjoint.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(f\) be a function defined on some punctured neighbourhood of \(x_0\text{.}\) We say that \(f\) diverges to positive infinity as \(x\to x_0\) and write \(\displaystyle \lim_{x\to x_0} f(x)=+\infty\text{,}\) if for every \(M\in\mathbb{R}\) there exists \(\delta>0\) such that

\[ 0<|x-x_0|<\delta \,\implies\, f(x)>M. \]

Similarly, we say that \(f\) diverges to negative infinity as \(x\to x_0\) and write \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to x_0} f(x)=-\infty\text{,}\) if for every \(M\in\mathbb{R}\) there exists \(\delta>0\) such that

\[ 0<|x-x_0|<\delta \,\implies\, f(x)<M. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Divergence to infinity describes functions whose values grow beyond all bounds near a given point. It is not a limit in the ordinary sense, since \(+\infty\) is not a real number: the notation \(\lim_{x\to x_0}f(x)=+\infty\) records the particular way in which the limit fails to exist.

The figure shows the sequence version from the Key Results, with the index \(n\) in the role of \(x\) and \(n\to\infty\) in place of \(x\to x_0\). For the level \(M\) drawn, all terms from \(N\) onwards lie in the shaded region above \(M\). A single early term above \(M\), here \(a_7\), is not enough, since \(a_8\) and \(a_9\) fall below \(M\) again. The small wiggles do not matter, as long as such an \(N\) exists for every level \(M\).

Raise the level \(M\), then find a \(\delta\) with \(0<|x-x_0|<\delta\implies f(x)>M\). However high \(M\) goes, a small enough \(\delta\) works.

This modifies the definition of a limit at a point: instead of entering every small band about a finite value, the outputs must eventually exceed every real threshold, or fall below every threshold for negative divergence. The quantifiers work as in the \(\varepsilon\)-\(\delta\) definition: the level \(M\) is given first and is arbitrary, and \(\delta\) may depend on it, typically shrinking as \(M\) grows. For \(f(x)=1/|x|\) at \(x_0=0\), the choice \(\delta=1/M\) works for every \(M>0\).

A common slip is to equate "unbounded" with "diverges to infinity". The sequence with \(a_n=n\) for even \(n\) and \(a_n=0\) for odd \(n\) is unbounded, yet it does not diverge to \(+\infty\), because infinitely many terms stay at \(0\). Divergence to infinity, possibly one-sided, is what defines a vertical asymptote.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Divergence to infinity is a form of non-finite limit.
  • Divergence may differ on one-sided neighbourhoods.
  • A sequence \((a_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) diverges to \(+\infty\text{,}\) written \(a_n\to+\infty\text{,}\) if for every \(M\in\mathbb{R}\) there exists \(N\geq1\) such that \(a_n>M\) for all \(n\geq N\text{;}\) divergence to \(-\infty\) is defined with \(a_n<M\text{.}\)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\displaystyle \lim_{x\to 0}1/|x|=+\infty\text{.}\)
  • \(\displaystyle \lim_{x\to 0^-}1/x=-\infty\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The quotient \(x/y\) of two real numbers \(x\) and \(y\neq 0\) is defined as \(x/y = x \times y^{-1}\text{,}\) where \(y^{-1}\) is the reciprocal of \(y\text{.}\) This operation is known as division.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Division undoes multiplication: \(x/y\) is the number that gives \(x\) when multiplied by \(y\). It formalizes the idea of distributing one quantity into equal parts, by means of multiplication with the reciprocal \(y^{-1}\).

The condition \(y\neq0\) cannot be removed. If \(x/0=q\), then \(q\cdot0=x\); for \(x\neq0\) no \(q\) satisfies this, and for \(x=0\) every \(q\) does, so no single value can be assigned. Equivalently, \(0\) has no reciprocal.

The integers are not closed under division, since \(1/2\) is not an integer; the rational numbers are exactly the quotients of integers with nonzero denominator. Besides not being commutative, division is not associative: \((8/4)/2=1\), but \(8/(4/2)=4\).

A common slip is to split a denominator: \(\frac{a}{b+c}\) is not \(\frac{a}{b}+\frac{a}{c}\); for \(a=b=c=1\) the two sides are \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) and \(2\). Only a numerator splits: \(\frac{a+b}{c}=\frac{a}{c}+\frac{b}{c}\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Division is not defined when the divisor is the number zero.
  • Division is not commutative: in general \(x/y\neq y/x\) (for example \(6/3=2\) but \(3/6=1/2\)).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The domain of a function is its specified set of allowed inputs. We call an input \(x\) the independent variable.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The domain specifies which input values are allowed for a function. It is part of the function itself: the same formula on two different domains gives two different functions.

The red interval \([-2,2]\) is the domain of the function in the figure: it contains the inputs where \(f\) is defined and is the projection of the graph onto the \(x\)-axis. For \(|x|>2\) the number \(4-x^2\) is negative, so its square root is not defined.

When a function is given only by a formula, the usual convention is to take as domain the largest set of real numbers on which the formula makes sense. The usual obstacles are division by zero, even roots of negative numbers and logarithms of numbers that are not positive. The domain also has to be checked when functions are combined: a composition \(g\circ f\) needs the values of \(f\) to lie in the domain of \(g\), and choosing a smaller domain can make a function invertible, as \(x^2\) is from \([0,\infty)\) to \([0,\infty)\).

A common slip is to mix up the domain, which collects inputs, with the range, which collects outputs. For \(f(x)=\sqrt{4-x^2}\) the domain is \([-2,2]\), but the range is \([0,2]\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A function is only defined on its domain.
  • Restrictions on the domain may arise from algebraic or analytical conditions.
  • Different domains lead to different functions, even if formulas coincide.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The function \(f(x)=\sqrt{x}\) has domain \([0,+\infty)\text{.}\)
  • The function \(f(x)=1/x\) has domain \(\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}\text{.}\)
  • The function \(f(x)=x^{2/3}=(\sqrt[3]{x})^2\) has domain \(\mathbb{R}\text{,}\) whereas an even root such as \(\sqrt{x}\) requires a nonnegative input.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A set is called the empty set, denoted \(\varnothing\text{,}\) if it contains no elements.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The empty set represents the absence of elements. Among sets it plays a role like that of \(0\) among numbers: it is the answer whenever a condition has no solutions, such as the set of natural numbers that are both even and odd.

Both Key Results follow from the definitions of a subset and of set equality. The statement "every element of \(\varnothing\) lies in \(A\)" has no element to check, so it cannot fail: \(\varnothing\subseteq A\) for every set \(A\). Two empty sets have the same elements, namely none, so they are equal. Under the set operations, \(A\cup\varnothing=A\) and \(A\cap\varnothing=\varnothing\), much like \(a+0=a\) and \(a\cdot0=0\).

A common slip is to confuse \(\varnothing\) with \(\{\varnothing\}\) or with \(\{0\}\). Both of the latter are singleton sets: each has exactly one element, so neither is empty.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The empty set is a subset of every set.
  • There is exactly one empty set.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The solution set of \(x^2+1=0\) in \(\mathbb{R}\) is \(\varnothing\text{.}\)
  • \(\{x\in\mathbb{N}\colon x<0\}=\varnothing\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(a,b\in \mathbb{R}\) be real numbers such that \(a<b\text{.}\) The numbers \(a\) and \(b\) are called the endpoints of the intervals (either \((a,b)\text{,}\) \([a,b]\text{,}\) \((a,b]\) or \([a,b)\)), and any number \(x\) with \(a<x<b\) is called an interior point of the interval. An interval contained between two real endpoints is called a bounded interval.

The real line itself has no endpoints. The symbols \(+\infty\) and \(-\infty\) describe unbounded directions; they are not real numbers and are never elements of an interval.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The endpoints of an interval are the real numbers where it starts and stops. They fix the extent of the interval; whether they belong to it is a separate choice, recorded by the type of bracket.

The figure shows the closed interval \([a,b]\), which contains both endpoints. The intervals \((a,b)\), \((a,b]\) and \([a,b)\) cover the same stretch of the line and differ only at \(a\) and \(b\); all four have the same interior points \(a<x<b\) and the same width \(b-a\).

A bounded interval is one with two real endpoints. A ray such as \([a,+\infty)\) has only one, and \(\mathbb{R}\) has none, because \(\pm\infty\) are not real numbers.

A common slip is to assume that an endpoint belongs to the interval: \(0\) is an endpoint of \((0,1]\), but \(0\notin(0,1]\). In Math III, the endpoints return as the boundary of the interval.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• An interval with two endpoints is bounded.
  • A bounded interval is a specific type of bounded set in \(\mathbb{R}\text{.}\)
  • Bounded intervals have finite length.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \([0,1]\) has endpoints \(0\) and \(1\text{.}\)
  • \((0,1]\) is bounded but does not include its left endpoint.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Euler's number \(\mathrm{e}\) is defined by the standard sequence limit

\[ \mathrm{e}=\lim\limits_{n\to\infty}\left(1+\frac{1}{n}\right)^n, \]

which is an irrational number approximately equal to \(2.71828182846\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Euler's number \(\mathrm{e}\approx2.718\) arises naturally from processes involving continuous growth. If an amount grows by \(100\%\) per period and the growth is credited \(n\) times per period, each time by a fraction \(\tfrac{1}{n}\) of the current amount, the amount is multiplied by \(\left(1+\tfrac{1}{n}\right)^n\); the definition lets \(n\to\infty\).

The right panel shows the defining sequence: \(\left(1+\tfrac{1}{n}\right)^n\) equals \(2\) for \(n=1\), \(2.25\) for \(n=2\) and about \(2.594\) for \(n=10\). The terms increase towards \(\mathrm{e}\), but slowly: crediting more often helps less and less, and the result stays below \(\mathrm{e}\). The left panel looks ahead to the curve \(y=\mathrm{e}^x\), which passes through \((0,1)\) with slope \(1\), touching the line \(y=x+1\) there, and reaches the height \(\mathrm{e}\) at \(x=1\).

Increase \(n\) and watch \(\left(1+\frac1n\right)^n\) creep up towards \(\mathrm{e}\), slowly. Switch to \(\left(1+\frac rn\right)^n\) to see the whole curve approach \(\mathrm{e}^r\).

A common slip is to take the limit of the base first: \(1+\tfrac{1}{n}\to1\) and \(1^n=1\), which suggests the limit \(1\). This is wrong because the base and the exponent change together. The limit laws cover sums, products and quotients of convergent sequences, so they give \(\left(1+\tfrac{1}{n}\right)^k\to1\) for a fixed exponent \(k\), but they say nothing about a power whose exponent grows with \(n\). Later, \(\mathrm{e}\) becomes the base of the exponential function and of the natural logarithm, and it appears in probability, for example in the Poisson distribution.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Euler’s number is irrational; Math I: Calculus uses this fact without proving it.
  • The natural exponential function is defined using \(\mathrm{e}\text{.}\)
  • In Math I: Calculus, this limit is used as the definition of \(\mathrm{e}\text{;}\) proving that the defining sequence converges is optional.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\displaystyle \lim_{x\to 0^+}\left(1+x\right)^{1/x}=\mathrm{e}\text{.}\)
  • \(\displaystyle\lim\limits_{n\to\infty}\left(1+\frac{r}{n}\right)^n=\mathrm{e}^r\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Functions \(f(x)=ab^x\) are called exponential functions, where \(b>0\) is known as the base of the exponential function. One of the most important exponential functions is the natural exponential function \(f\colon \mathbb{R}\to \mathbb{R}\) with \(f(x)=\mathrm{e}^x=\exp(x)\) using exponentiation with a fixed positive base and a varying exponent; its base is Euler's number \(\mathrm{e}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Exponential functions model processes where growth or decay is proportional to the current value. For \(f(x)=ab^x\), increasing \(x\) by \(1\) multiplies the value by \(b\), since \(f(x+1)=b\,f(x)\): equal steps in \(x\) give equal factors, not equal increments.

Both curves pass through \((0,1)\) because \(b^0=1\) for every base. The curve \(y=2^x\) doubles with each unit step to the right, through \(2\), \(4\) and \(8\) at \(x=1,2,3\), and approaches \(0\) far to the left. The curve \(y=\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^x=2^{-x}\) is its mirror image in the \(y\)-axis. Neither curve meets the \(x\)-axis, because \(b^x>0\) for all \(x\).

Change the base \(b\) and the factor \(a\) in \(f(x)=ab^x\): \(b>1\) grows, \(0<b<1\) decays, \(b=1\) is constant, and the sign of \(f\) is always the sign of \(a\).

The base must be positive for \(b^x\) to be defined for every real \(x\): \((-2)^{1/2}\) is not a real number. A base \(b>1\) gives growth, \(0<b<1\) decay and \(b=1\) a constant; the factor \(a=f(0)\) is the starting value and fixes the sign. For \(b\neq1\) the logarithm with base \(b\) is the inverse of \(b^x\), and \(b^x=\mathrm{e}^{x\ln b}\), so every exponential function is a rescaled version of \(\mathrm{e}^x\).

A common slip is to confuse \(2^x\), where the exponent varies, with the power function \(x^2\), where the base varies. The exponential eventually wins: \(2^x>x^2\) for all \(x>4\), although \(2^3=8<9=3^2\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The exponential function \(b^x\) is always positive; a scaled exponential function \(ab^x\) therefore has the sign of \(a\text{.}\)
  • The exponential function is continuous and differentiable everywhere.
  • The natural exponential function is its own derivative.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(f(x)=2^x\) describes exponential growth.
  • \(f(x)=\mathrm{e}^{-x}\) describes exponential decay.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In the expression \(x^\alpha\text{,}\) the number \(x\) is the base, \(\alpha\) is the exponent, and \(x^\alpha\) is a power of \(x\text{.}\) The meaning is introduced in stages:

  • For a positive integer \(n\text{,}\) \(x^n\) is the product of \(n\) factors equal to \(x\text{.}\) We use \(x^0=1\text{;}\) in the algebraic convention of this course, this includes \(0^0=1\text{.}\)
  • If \(x\neq0\) and \(n\) is a positive integer, then \(x^{-n}=1/x^n\text{.}\)
  • If \(x>0\) and \(q=a/b\) is rational with \(a\in\mathbb{Z}\) and \(b\geq1\text{,}\) then \(x^q=(x^{1/b})^a\text{.}\)
  • If \(x>0\) and \(\alpha\) is any real number, then \(x^\alpha\) is defined and obeys the usual exponent laws.

For a negative base, arbitrary real powers are not generally real. When \(q=p/r\) is in lowest terms with odd denominator \(r\text{,}\) the course uses \(x^{p/r}=(\sqrt[r]{x})^p\) for every real \(x\) (and for \(x\neq0\) when \(p<0\)).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
For positive integer exponents, exponentiation describes repeated multiplication: \(x^n\) multiplies \(n\) factors equal to \(x\). Each later stage of the Definition extends this meaning in the only way that keeps the exponent laws true.

The laws determine the extensions. From \(x^nx^0=x^n\) we need \(x^0=1\), and from \(x^nx^{-n}=x^0=1\) we need \(x^{-n}=1/x^n\), the reciprocal of \(x^n\). From \((x^{1/b})^b=x\) we need \(x^{1/b}\) to be the \(b\)-th root of \(x\). An irrational exponent is then approached through rational ones: \(2^{\sqrt{2}}\) is the limit of \(2^{1.4},2^{1.41},2^{1.414},\ldots\).

The domain of a power matters: even roots require nonnegative inputs, odd roots allow negative inputs, and an irrational exponent requires a positive base. This is why the Key Results are stated for \(x,y>0\). For a negative base the laws can fail: with \(x=-8\), \((x^2)^{1/6}=64^{1/6}=2\), whereas \(x^{2\cdot(1/6)}=x^{1/3}=-2\). For the same reason the Definition writes the exponent in lowest terms before it applies a root to a negative base.

Fixing the base and varying the exponent gives the exponential function \(b^x\); fixing the exponent and varying the base gives the power function \(x^k\). The logarithm \(\log_b x\) answers the reverse question: which exponent turns \(b\) into \(x\).

A common slip is to read a negative exponent as a negative number: \(2^{-3}=1/8\), which is positive.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
For positive real numbers \(x,y\) and real exponents \(\alpha,\beta\text{,}\) we have:

  • Product of powers: \(x^\alpha x^\beta=x^{\alpha+\beta}\text{.}\)
  • Power of a power: \((x^\alpha)^\beta=x^{\alpha\beta}\text{.}\)
  • Power of a product: \((xy)^\alpha=x^\alpha y^\alpha\text{.}\)
  • Power of a quotient: \((x/y)^\alpha=x^\alpha/y^\alpha\text{.}\)
  • If \(x>1\text{,}\) then \(x^\alpha>x^\beta\) exactly when \(\alpha>\beta\text{.}\)
  • If \(0<x<1\text{,}\) then \(x^\alpha>x^\beta\) exactly when \(\alpha<\beta\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: We can extend the real number system to include \(+\infty\) and \(-\infty\), resulting in the extended real number system denoted as \(\overline{\mathbb{R}}\text{:}\) it consists of all real numbers together with the two symbols \(-\infty\) and \(+\infty\text{,}\) ordered so that \(-\infty<x<+\infty\) for every real \(x\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The extended real number system augments the real numbers by symbols for positive and negative infinity, placed as a least and a greatest element. This extension allows limits, divergence and unbounded behaviour to be described within a single framework.

The figure draws \(\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) as the real line with two endpoints attached. Every real \(x\) lies strictly between them, \(-\infty<x<+\infty\), and the order of \(\mathbb{R}\) is kept. With these endpoints every nonempty set of real numbers has a supremum and an infimum in \(\overline{\mathbb{R}}\): a set without an upper bound, such as \(\{1,2,3,\ldots\}\) in the Examples, gets the supremum \(+\infty\).

The gain lies in the order, not in arithmetic. A common slip is to treat \(+\infty\) as a very large real number and compute with it. Some operations have a natural value, such as \(x+(+\infty)=+\infty\) for real \(x\), but \((+\infty)-(+\infty)\) has none: \(a_n=n+1\) and \(b_n=n\) both tend to \(+\infty\) with \(a_n-b_n=1\) for every \(n\), while \(a_n=2n\) and \(b_n=n\) give \(a_n-b_n=n\). Likewise, a sequence with limit \(+\infty\) is still called divergent, because convergence asks for a real limit \(L\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Infinities are symbols, rather than big numbers.
  • Many limit statements naturally take values in the extended real numbers.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: The sequence \(a_n=n\) has extended-real limit \(+\infty\), and the set \(\{1,2,3,\ldots\}\) has supremum \(+\infty\) in \(\overline{\mathbb{R}}\). Neither statement makes infinity an ordinary real number: expressions such as \(+\infty-(+\infty)\) are not defined by real arithmetic.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: Let \(a<b\) be real numbers, and let \(f\colon [a, b] \to\mathbb{R}\) be a continuous function on \([a, b]\text{.}\) Then \(f\) attains its global maximum at \(x=x_{\mathrm{max}} \in [a, b]\text{,}\) and also attains its global minimum at \(x=x_{\mathrm{min}} \in [a, b]\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The extreme value theorem guarantees that a continuous function on a closed and bounded interval attains both a largest and a smallest value. It does not say where they are, only that a search for them cannot come back empty.

In the figure the maximum is attained at the interior point \(c\), the highest point of the graph, and the minimum at the endpoint \(b\). Both are values that \(f\) actually takes, \(f(c)\) and \(f(b)\), not merely bounds that it approaches. The theorem allows either kind of location, so the endpoints always have to be checked.

On a closed interval both extreme values are attained. Switch to the open interval \((a,b)\), or to the function with a jump, and watch an extreme value turn into a supremum or infimum that is never reached.

Each hypothesis is needed. On the open interval \((0,1)\) the function \(f(x)=x\) comes arbitrarily close to \(1\) without reaching it, so it has no maximum; on the unbounded interval \([0,+\infty)\) the same function is not even bounded above. Without continuity a jump can remove the extreme value: on \([0,1]\), the function equal to \(x\) for \(x<1\) and to \(0\) at \(x=1\) has supremum \(1\) but never takes the value \(1\). The hypotheses are sufficient, not necessary: \(\sin x\) attains its maximum \(1\) on the open interval \((0,\pi)\), at \(x=\tfrac{\pi}{2}\).

In the language of global extrema, the theorem says that a continuous \(f\) on \([a,b]\) has a global maximum and a global minimum; in particular, \(f\) is bounded there and its supremum is a maximum. Math III extends the theorem from closed bounded intervals to a wider class of sets in the extreme value theorem on compact sets.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The theorem does not apply to open or unbounded intervals.
  • The theorem does not apply to functions that are not continuous.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The function \(f(x)=x^2\) on \([0,1]\) attains the largest value \(1\) and the smallest value \(0\text{.}\)
  • The function \(f(x)=x\) has no maximum on \((0,1)\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(n\) be a natural number. The factorial of \(n\), denoted \(n!\), is the product of all positive natural numbers up to \(n\):

\[ n!=1\times 2\times 3\times \cdots\times (n-1)\times n. \]

In addition, \(0!\) is defined to be \(1\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The factorial counts how many ways distinct objects can be arranged in order. For \(n\) objects there are \(n\) choices for the first position, then \(n-1\) for the second, and so on down to \(1\) for the last; the choices multiply, giving \(n!\).

The definition can also be read recursively: \(0!=1\) and \((n+1)!=(n+1)\cdot n!\), the form used in proofs by mathematical induction. The convention \(0!=1\) fits this recursion, since \(1!=1\cdot0!\), and it fits the counting meaning, since there is exactly one way to arrange no objects.

Factorials grow very fast: each step multiplies by \(n+1\), an ever larger factor, whereas a power \(a^n\) multiplies by the fixed factor \(a\). A common slip is to treat the factorial as if it were linear or multiplicative: \((2n)!\) is neither \(2\cdot n!\) nor \((n!)^2\). For \(n=3\), \(6!=720\), while \(2\cdot3!=12\) and \((3!)^2=36\).

In probability, factorials return whenever outcomes are counted through ordered arrangements or selections.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• There are \(n!\) permutations of \(n\) distinct objects.
  • Factorials appear in binomial coefficients:
\[ \binom{n}{k}=\frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}. \]
  • The factorial function grows faster than any fixed polynomial or exponential function.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(4!=24\).
  • \(10!=3628800\).
  • Three different apples can be assigned to three ordered people in \(3!=6\) ways.
  • A full ordering of 52 distinct cards has \(52!\) possible orders.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Consider a set \(A\text{.}\) We say \(A\) is finite if it has \(n\) distinct elements for some natural number \(n\) and we write \(|A|=n\text{;}\) otherwise, we say \(A\) is infinite.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
This distinction separates sets whose elements fit into a completed finite list \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\) from sets for which no such finite list exists. For a finite set, \(|A|\) is the length of that list.

The list counts distinct elements only, so \(|\{1,1,2\}|=2\). The case \(n=0\) is allowed, which makes the empty set finite. A set is infinite when every finite list misses some of its elements: any list \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\) of natural numbers misses \(a_1+\cdots+a_n+1\), so \(\mathbb{N}\) is infinite.

Infinite sets behave differently when sizes are compared. The even natural numbers form a proper subset of \(\mathbb{N}\), yet \(n\mapsto2n\) pairs every natural number with exactly one even number; a finite set can never be paired in this way with a proper subset of itself. This comparison is the enrichment topic in the note below.

A common slip is to read "infinite" as "very large". A set with \(10^{100}\) elements is finite, however long its list.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A finite set with \(n\) distinct elements has cardinality \(n\text{.}\)
  • The empty set is finite and has cardinality \(0\text{.}\)
  • Every finite set of real numbers is bounded.

Enrichment: sizes of infinite sets

Comparing infinite sets by bijections, and distinguishing countable from uncountable sets, is not part of the assessed Math I: Calculus core in 2026–27.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\{1,\,2,\,3\}\) is finite.
  • \(\mathbb{N}\) is infinite.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A finite sequence is an ordered list with only finitely many entries, \(a_m,\,a_{m+1},\,\ldots,\,a_n\) with integers \(m\le n\) (usually \(m=0\) or \(m=1\)), written \((a_i)_{i=m}^n\text{.}\) It has \(n-m+1\) terms. In contrast, a sequence \((a_n)_{n\ge m}\) never ends.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A finite sequence is an ordered list of numbers with a first and a last term: \(a_m\) comes first, \(a_n\) comes last, and each index in between carries exactly one term.

The figure shows \((a_i)_{i=0}^{5}\): one stick for each index \(0,1,\dots,5\), so \(5-0+1=6\) terms, and nothing after the last term \(a_5\). The position along the axis is the index; the height of the stick is the value of the term.

Order and repetition both matter: \((1,2)\) and \((2,1)\) are different, and \((1,1,2)\) has three terms although the set \(\{1,1,2\}=\{1,2\}\) has two elements. Counting terms is a common slip: \(a_3,\dots,a_7\) has \(7-3+1=5\) terms, not \(4\). Later, the terms of a finite sequence are added up as a finite series.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Finite sequences have a last term.
  • Every finite sequence can be viewed as a function on a finite index set.
  • Finite sequences are always bounded.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \((a_i)_{i=1}^3=(2,\,4,\,6)\) is a finite sequence.
  • \((a_i)_{i=1}^1\) consists of a single term \(a_1\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\) be real numbers. Set \(S_0=0\) and, for \(k=1,\ldots,n\text{,}\) define

\[ S_k=S_{k-1}+a_k. \]

The finite series \(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\) is \(S_n\text{,}\) so that \(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n a_i=a_1+\cdots+a_n\text{.}\) The empty sum is \(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^0 a_i=0\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A finite series represents the sum of the terms of a finite sequence.

The recursion adds one term at a time: the partial sum \(S_k\) is the running total after the first \(k\) terms, so \(S_n\) is the total of all \(n\) terms. Starting from \(S_0=0\) means that a sum with no terms is \(0\).

The index is only a label: \(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\) and \(\sum_{k=1}^n a_k\) are the same number, and so is the shifted form \(\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}a_{i+1}\). Constants can be taken out and sums can be split: \(\sum_{i=1}^n(\alpha a_i+\beta b_i)=\alpha\sum_{i=1}^n a_i+\beta\sum_{i=1}^n b_i\). A common slip is to treat sums like products: \(\sum a_ib_i\) is in general not \(\bigl(\sum a_i\bigr)\bigl(\sum b_i\bigr)\); with \(a_i=b_i=1\) for \(i=1,2\), the first is \(2\) and the second is \(4\). Similarly, \(\sum_{i=1}^n c=nc\), not \(c\).

Infinite series are built from these partial sums, and the arithmetic and geometric series formulas are closed forms for \(S_n\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every finite series has a well-defined sum, obtained by the recursion above.
  • The empty sum equals \(0\text{,}\) which keeps the recursion valid at \(k=1\text{.}\)
  • Finite series do not involve convergence issues.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: Let \(a< b\) be real numbers, and let \(f \colon (a, b) \to \mathbb{R}\) be a function. If \(f\) is differentiable at \(x=x_0\in (a, b)\text{,}\) and \(f\) attains a local maximum or minimum at \(x=x_0\text{,}\) then \(f'(x_0) = 0\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The first-order condition is a necessary criterion for local extrema: at an interior point where \(f\) is differentiable, a local maximum or minimum forces a horizontal tangent, \(f'(x_0)=0\). It turns the search for extrema into solving the equation \(f'(x)=0\).

Slide \(x\) and watch the tangent: at the local extrema of the cubic it is horizontal. \(x^3\) has \(f'(0)=0\) without an extremum, and \(|x|\) has an extremum where \(f'\) does not exist.

The reason is a sign argument. At a local maximum, \(f(x)-f(x_0)\le0\) for all \(x\) near \(x_0\), so the difference quotient \(\frac{f(x)-f(x_0)}{x-x_0}\) is \(\ge0\) for \(x<x_0\) and \(\le0\) for \(x>x_0\). Its left-hand limit is therefore \(\ge0\) and its right-hand limit \(\le0\); both equal \(f'(x_0)\), so \(f'(x_0)=0\). The case of a local minimum is the same with the signs reversed.

Each hypothesis is used. The point must be interior, so that \(x\) can approach \(x_0\) from both sides: \(f(x)=x\) on \([0,1]\) has its minimum at \(0\) and its maximum at \(1\), and its one-sided derivative is \(1\) at both. And \(f\) must be differentiable at \(x_0\); otherwise an extremum can sit at a corner. This is why the candidates for extrema are the critical points together with the boundary points of the domain.

The condition is necessary, not sufficient: it only produces the stationary points as candidates, and each candidate still has to be checked by comparing \(f(x)\) with \(f(x_0)\) nearby. Later tools such as the second-order condition make this check easier, and Math IV uses the same condition for functions of several variables in the unconstrained extrema conditions.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Local extrema of differentiable functions at interior points of the domain occur only at stationary points.
  • The condition is necessary but not sufficient for optimality.
  • Boundary points require separate analysis.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The function \(f(x)=x^2\) satisfies \(f'(0)=0\) at its minimum.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a real number \(x\), the floor of \(x\) is the largest integer less than or equal to \(x\), and the ceiling of \(x\) is the smallest integer greater than or equal to \(x\):

\[ \begin{aligned} \lfloor x\rfloor&=\max\{n\in\mathbb{Z}\colon n\le x\},\\ \lceil x\rceil&=\min\{n\in\mathbb{Z}\colon n\ge x\}. \end{aligned} \]

Equivalently, for an integer \(n\), \(\lfloor x\rfloor=n\) exactly when \(n\le x<n+1\), and \(\lceil x\rceil=n\) exactly when \(n-1<x\le n\). Both are functions from \(\mathbb{R}\) to \(\mathbb{Z}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The floor rounds down and the ceiling rounds up to the nearest integer. On the number line, \(\lfloor x\rfloor\) is the integer at or immediately to the left of \(x\) and \(\lceil x\rceil\) the integer at or immediately to the right.

"Down" means towards \(-\infty\), not towards \(0\). The name integer part usually means \(\lfloor x\rfloor\), but for negative numbers some texts instead mean truncation towards zero, which differs: \(\lfloor-2.5\rfloor=-3\), while truncation gives \(-2\). For the same reason \(\lfloor-x\rfloor\) is not \(-\lfloor x\rfloor\) unless \(x\) is an integer.

The graphs are staircases. On each interval \([n,n+1)\) the floor is constant, so it is continuous at every non-integer; at each integer it jumps up by \(1\). This makes the floor a standard example for one-sided limits and one-sided continuity: the filled dot of each step sits at its left end, so the function agrees with its limit from the right.

The floor (solid blue) has its filled dots at the left ends of the steps; the ceiling (dashed red) is constant on each \((n-1,n]\) and has its filled dots at the right ends, so it is left-continuous instead. At an integer \(n\) both take the value \(n\). The thin grey line \(y=x\) runs between the two staircases, which is the inequality \(\lfloor x\rfloor\le x\le\lceil x\rceil\), and the vertical line at \(x=2.7\) meets the floor at \(2\) and the ceiling at \(3\), as in the first example.

Move \(x\), or type an integer: the floor and ceiling are the integers on either side of \(x\) and coincide only when \(x\) is an integer. For negative \(x\), compare the floor with truncation towards \(0\). The last view shows the fractional part \(x-\lfloor x\rfloor\), which has period \(1\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For every \(x\in\mathbb{R}\), \(x-1<\lfloor x\rfloor\le x\le\lceil x\rceil<x+1\), and the two non-strict inequalities are equalities exactly when \(x\) is an integer.
  • \(\lceil x\rceil-\lfloor x\rfloor\) is \(0\) if \(x\) is an integer and \(1\) otherwise.
  • \(\lceil x\rceil=-\lfloor-x\rfloor\), and \(\lfloor x+n\rfloor=\lfloor x\rfloor+n\) for every integer \(n\). In general the floor is not additive: \(\lfloor x\rfloor+\lfloor y\rfloor\le\lfloor x+y\rfloor\le\lfloor x\rfloor+\lfloor y\rfloor+1\).
  • Both functions are nondecreasing step functions that jump by \(1\) at each integer. At an integer \(n\), \(\lim_{x\to n^-}\lfloor x\rfloor=n-1\) and \(\lim_{x\to n^+}\lfloor x\rfloor=n=\lfloor n\rfloor\), so the two-sided limit does not exist. The floor is right-continuous but not left-continuous at every integer; the ceiling is left-continuous but not right-continuous there.
  • From \(x-1<\lfloor x\rfloor\le x\) and the squeeze theorem, \(\lfloor x\rfloor/x\to1\) as \(x\to\infty\).
  • For \(x\ge0\), \(\lfloor x\rfloor\) counts the positive integers in \([1,x]\).
  • The fractional part \(x-\lfloor x\rfloor\) lies in \([0,1)\) and is periodic with period \(1\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\lfloor2.7\rfloor=2\), \(\lceil2.7\rceil=3\), \(\lfloor-2.7\rfloor=-3\), \(\lceil-2.7\rceil=-2\) and \(\lfloor5\rfloor=\lceil5\rceil=5\).
  • At \(x=1\), \(\lfloor x\rfloor=0\) for \(0\le x<1\) but \(\lfloor1\rfloor=1\), so the left-hand one-sided limit is \(0\neq\lfloor1\rfloor\) while the right-hand limit is \(1\).
  • Additivity fails: \(\lfloor0.5\rfloor+\lfloor0.5\rfloor=0\), but \(\lfloor0.5+0.5\rfloor=1\).
  • The number of multiples of \(3\) in \(\{1,2,\ldots,100\}\) is \(\lfloor100/3\rfloor=33\).
  • In branch-and-bound, a fractional LP value \(x_j=1.25\) is excluded by the two branches \(x_j\le\lfloor1.25\rfloor=1\) and \(x_j\ge\lceil1.25\rceil=2\).
  • In life insurance, the curtate future lifetime is \(K_x=\lfloor T_x\rfloor\), the number of complete future years: a future lifetime \(T_x=23.6\) gives \(K_x=23\), and \(K_x=k\) exactly when \(k\le T_x<k+1\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A function \(f\colon X\to Y\) assigns to every input \(x\in X\) exactly one output \(f(x)\in Y\text{.}\) The phrase "exactly one" is essential: one input cannot be assigned two different outputs, although different inputs may share the same output.

Functions are also called maps. A function is specified by its domain, its codomain, and its assignment rule. Two functions \(f,g\colon X\to Y\) with the same domain and codomain are equal, written \(f=g\text{,}\) if \(f(x)=g(x)\) for every \(x\in X\text{;}\) a formula alone therefore does not determine a function.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A function is a rule that answers one question for each allowed input: which output belongs to it? Every input receives exactly one answer, so the output is completely determined by the input.

In the left diagram every point of \(X\) has exactly one arrow leaving it. Two inputs share the middle output and the top point of \(Y\) is never reached; both are allowed. In the right diagram the top input has two arrows and the middle input has none, so the rule fails in both ways and does not define a function from \(X\) to \(Y\).

The definition therefore makes two demands on every \(x\in X\): at least one output, so the rule must make sense on the whole domain, and at most one output. It demands nothing of the elements of \(Y\). Whether every element of \(Y\) is reached, and whether it is reached only once, are separate questions, answered by surjectivity and injectivity.

A common slip is to identify a function with its formula. The rule \(x\mapsto x^2\) on \(\mathbb{R}\) and the same rule on \([0,+\infty)\) are different functions: the second is injective, the first is not, since \((-1)^2=1^2\). In the same way, \(f\) denotes the function, while \(f(x)\) is a single number, its value at \(x\).

A sequence \((a_n)\) is itself a function: it assigns a term \(a_n\) to each index \(n\). The idea returns in later courses too, for example as linear maps between vector spaces in Math II.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every function has a domain and a codomain.
  • The range of a function is a subset of its codomain.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(f(x) = x^2\) defined on the real numbers \(\mathbb{R}\text{.}\)
  • \(f(x) = \sqrt{x}\) defined on \([0, +\infty)\text{.}\)

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Suppose \(a < b\) are real numbers, \(f\colon [a, b] \to\mathbb{R}\) is a Riemann integrable function, and \(F\colon [a, b] \to\mathbb{R}\) is the function defined as:

\[ F(x)=\int_a^x f(t)\,\mathrm{d}t. \]

Then, \(F\) is continuous on \([a,b]\text{.}\) Moreover, if \(x_0\in(a,b)\) and \(f\) is continuous at \(x=x_0\text{,}\) then \(F\) is differentiable at \(x=x_0\text{,}\) with \(F'(x_0)=f(x_0)\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Integrating \(f\) from \(a\) up to a moving point \(x\) produces a new function \(F\), and this part of the fundamental theorem describes how \(F\) changes: it is always continuous, and where \(f\) is continuous its rate of change is the current value \(f(x)\). In this sense differentiation undoes integration.

The figure shows why. Moving the right edge from \(x\) to \(x+h\) adds the thin red strip, whose area \(F(x+h)-F(x)\) is about \(f(x)\,h\) for small \(h\). Dividing by \(h\) and letting \(h\to0\) gives \(F'(x)=f(x)\). The approximation becomes exact in the limit because \(f\) is continuous at \(x\), so its values on the strip are all close to \(f(x)\).

Move \(x\) and watch \(F(x)=\int_a^x f(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\) being drawn below; its slope at \(x\) is \(f(x)\). Where \(f\) jumps, \(F\) is still continuous but gets a corner.

The two conclusions need different hypotheses. Continuity of \(F\) needs only integrability: a Riemann integrable \(f\) is bounded, say \(|f|\le M\), and then \(|F(x)-F(y)|\le M|x-y|\). The derivative statement needs continuity of \(f\) at \(x_0\). Where \(f\) jumps, \(F\) has a corner and is not differentiable. Even a change at a single point matters: if \(f(1)=1\) and \(f(x)=0\) otherwise on \([0,2]\), then \(F\) is identically \(0\), so \(F'(1)=0\ne f(1)\).

The theorem shows that every continuous function on an interval has an antiderivative, namely \(F\), and part 2 then turns integrals into differences \(F(b)-F(a)\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Integration defines a continuous function.
  • Differentiation recovers the original integrand at points of continuity.
  • The theorem establishes a local connection between integration and differentiation.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(f(x)=x^2\text{,}\) then \(\displaystyle F(x)=\int_0^x t^2\,\mathrm{d}t\) and \(F'(x)=x^2\text{.}\)

  • For variable limits, suppose \(g\) and \(h\) are differentiable at \(x\), their values stay in \([a,b]\) near \(x\), and \(f\) is continuous at both \(g(x)\) and \(h(x)\). Then:

    \[ \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\int_{g(x)}^{h(x)}f(t)\,\mathrm{d}t=h'(x)f(h(x)) -g'(x)f(g(x)). \]

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Suppose \(a < b\) are real numbers, and let \(f\colon [a, b] \to\mathbb{R}\) be a Riemann integrable function. If \(F\colon [a, b] \to\mathbb{R}\) is an antiderivative of \(f\text{,}\) then

\[ \int_a^b f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x =F(x)\big|_{x=a}^{b}=F(b)-F(a). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
This part of the fundamental theorem turns the evaluation of a definite integral into a subtraction. Once an antiderivative \(F\) of \(f\) is known, the limit of Riemann sums equals \(F(b)-F(a)\), and no sums have to be computed.

The left panel shows the area under \(f\) between \(a\) and \(b\); the right panel shows an antiderivative \(F\), which climbs from \(F(a)\) to \(F(b)\). The theorem says that these are the same number: the area accumulated under \(f\) equals the total rise of \(F\). Where \(f\) is large, \(F\) climbs steeply, and where \(f\) is small, \(F\) is nearly flat.

The reason is a telescoping sum. For a partition \(P\), the mean value theorem gives points \(c_i\) with \(F(x_i)-F(x_{i-1})=f(c_i)(x_i-x_{i-1})\). With these tags the Riemann sum is exactly \(F(b)-F(a)\), for every \(P\), so the integral is \(F(b)-F(a)\) as well.

Both hypotheses are needed. The integral must exist: \(F(x)=x^2\sin(1/x^2)\) with \(F(0)=0\) is differentiable on \([0,1]\), but \(F'\) is unbounded near \(0\) and therefore not Riemann integrable. And \(F\) must be an antiderivative on all of \([a,b]\). The function \(-\arctan(1/x)\) has derivative \(\frac{1}{1+x^2}\) for \(x\ne0\), yet its difference between \(x=1\) and \(x=-1\) is \(-\frac{\pi}{2}\), while \(\int_{-1}^{1}\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{1+x^2}=\frac{\pi}{2}\); it jumps at \(0\), so the theorem does not apply to it.

Later, the rules of integration by parts and substitution combine this theorem with the product rule and the chain rule.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Definite integrals can be evaluated using antiderivatives.
  • The result depends only on boundary values.
  • Integration becomes an algebraic operation once antiderivatives are known.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\displaystyle \int_0^1 x^2\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\text{.}\)
  • \(\displaystyle \int_a^b 1\,\mathrm{d}x=b-a\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Self-study material

In 2026-27 the gamma function is the self-study section of Lecture 12. It is worth knowing as an application of improper integrals, but it is not developed in class.

The gamma function \(\Gamma\colon (0,+\infty)\to \mathbb{R}\) is defined by an improper integral:

\[ \Gamma(x)=\int_0^{+\infty} t^{x-1}\mathrm{e}^{-t}\,\mathrm{d}t. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The gamma function extends the factorial from integers to all positive real arguments: \(\Gamma(n)=(n-1)!\) for integers \(n\ge1\), and between the integers \(\Gamma\) is given by the same integral. Because of the shift by one, \(\Gamma(n+1)=n!\).

The red dots are the factorials: \(\Gamma(1)=0!=1\), \(\Gamma(2)=1!=1\), \(\Gamma(3)=2\), \(\Gamma(4)=6\) and \(\Gamma(5)=4!=24\). The curve passes through them and also takes values in between, such as \(\Gamma(\tfrac{1}{2})=\sqrt{\pi}\approx1.77\). It has its minimum between \(1\) and \(2\), about \(0.886\) near \(x\approx1.46\), and grows without bound as \(x\downarrow0\).

The link with factorials comes from integration by parts. For \(x>0\) it gives \(\Gamma(x+1)=x\,\Gamma(x)\), the same recursion as \(n!=n\cdot(n-1)!\), and \(\Gamma(1)=\int_0^\infty\mathrm{e}^{-t}\,\mathrm{d}t=1\); induction then gives \(\Gamma(n)=(n-1)!\). The integral is improper at \(\infty\) and, for \(x<1\), also at \(0\); the domain \((0,+\infty)\) is where it converges. Near \(0\) the integrand behaves like \(t^{x-1}\), which by the \(p\)-test with \(p=1-x\) is integrable exactly when \(x>0\). Near \(\infty\) the factor \(\mathrm{e}^{-t}\) outweighs any power, and comparison with \(t^{-2}\) gives convergence.

A common slip is the shift: \(\Gamma(5)\) is \(4!=24\), not \(5!=120\). The gamma function returns later in probability, in the formula of the gamma distribution.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The gamma function satisfies \(\Gamma(n)=(n-1)!\) for all integers \(n\ge 1\text{.}\)
  • It generalizes factorial growth to real arguments.
  • The domain of the gamma function can be extended further.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
Let \((a_i)_{i=1}^n\) be a finite geometric sequence defined by \(a_i=aq^{i-1}\) where \(a,q\in\mathbb{R}\) and \(q\) is known as the common ratio. The (finite) geometric series formula is given by

\[ \sum_{i=1}^n\left(aq^{i-1}\right)=\begin{cases} \displaystyle \,\frac{a\left(1-q^n\right)}{1-q},& \text{if } q\neq 1,\\[2pt] \displaystyle \,an,&\text{if } q= 1. \end{cases} \]

Taking the limit of the finite partial sums gives the infinite geometric series formula

\[ \sum_{i=1}^\infty aq^{i-1}=\frac{a}{1-q} \qquad\text{when }|q|<1. \]

If \(a\neq0\text{,}\) the series diverges when \(|q|\geq1\text{.}\) If \(a=0\text{,}\) every term is zero and the series converges for every \(q\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A geometric series models repeated proportional change: each term is obtained by multiplying the previous one by the fixed ratio \(q\). It is one of the few infinite series whose convergence behaviour and sum can be described explicitly, which makes it a standard benchmark for other series.

The square has area \(1\). The pieces \(\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{4},\tfrac{1}{8},\ldots\) form the geometric series with first term \(a=\tfrac{1}{2}\) and ratio \(q=\tfrac{1}{2}\). After \(n\) pieces the uncovered part has area \((\tfrac{1}{2})^n\), so the partial sums \(1-(\tfrac{1}{2})^n\) tend to \(1\), in agreement with \(a/(1-q)=1\).

With \(|q|<1\) the partial sums settle at \(\frac{a}{1-q}\); with negative \(q\) they approach it from alternate sides. Push \(|q|\) to \(1\) or beyond and they stop settling.

For a finite series, subtracting \(q\) times the sum from the sum cancels the intermediate terms. This gives \((1-q)S_n=a(1-q^n)\); the finite calculation comes before the limiting argument for an infinite series. Everything then depends on \(q^n\). When \(|q|<1\), \(q^n\to0\) and the sum is \(a/(1-q)\). When \(|q|\ge1\) and \(a\neq0\), the terms do not tend to \(0\) and the series diverges; for \(q=-1\) the partial sums \(a,0,a,0,\ldots\) oscillate.

A common slip concerns the first term. The formula \(a/(1-q)\) is for a series whose first term is \(a\): \(\sum_{i=1}^\infty q^i=q/(1-q)\), not \(1/(1-q)\), because its first term is \(q\). For \(q=\tfrac{1}{2}\) this gives \(1\), against \(2\) for the series in the Examples. Geometric sums return later, for example in the probabilities of the geometric distribution and in the ratio test of Math III.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • If \(a\neq0\text{,}\) the infinite geometric series converges if and only if \(|q|<1\text{.}\) The all-zero series is the only exception.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^4 2^{i-1}=15\text{.}\)
  • \(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^\infty \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{i-1}=2\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A function \(f\) defined on a domain \(X\subseteq \mathbb{R}\) attains its global maximum (aka absolute maximum) at \(x=x_{\mathrm{max}}\text{,}\) if \(f(x_{\mathrm{max}}) \geq f(x)\) for all \(x\in X\text{.}\) Similarly, the function attains its global minimum (aka absolute minimum) at \(x=x_{\mathrm{min}}\text{,}\) if \(f(x_{\mathrm{min}}) \leq f(x)\) for all \(x \in X\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A global extremum describes the largest or smallest value a function attains over its entire domain. Unlike local extrema, which compare \(f(x)\) only with values at nearby inputs, global extrema account for all possible inputs.

On \([a,b]\) the cubic has a local maximum inside the interval, but it is not global: the value at the endpoint \(b\) is larger. The global minimum lies inside the interval, at the bottom of a valley, so it is also a local minimum. The global maximum, by contrast, sits at an endpoint, where the graph is still rising.

Move the interval \([a,b]\): the global maximum and minimum are found among the endpoints and the stationary points inside, and a local extremum need not be global.

The definition separates the location from the value. The point \(x_{\mathrm{max}}\) need not be unique: \(\cos x\) on \(\mathbb{R}\) attains its global maximum \(1\) at every integer multiple of \(2\pi\). The value \(f(x_{\mathrm{max}})\) is unique when it exists, since it is the maximum of the range \(\{f(x)\colon x\in X\}\). It can fail to exist even for a bounded function: \(f(x)=x\) on \((0,1)\) has supremum \(1\) but no maximum. The domain is part of the question, too: \(x^2\) has no global maximum on \(\mathbb{R}\), but on \([-1,2]\) it has one at \(x=2\), with value \(4\).

For a continuous function on a closed bounded interval, the extreme value theorem guarantees that both global extrema exist. Math IV uses the same definition for functions of several variables.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Global extrema may occur at interior points or boundary points of the domain.
  • A global extremum may not exist on unbounded or open domains.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The function \(f(x)=x^2\) has a global minimum at \(x=0\text{.}\)
  • The function \(f(x)=x\) has no global extremum on \(\mathbb{R}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(X\) be a subset of \(\mathbb{R}\text{,}\) and let \(f\colon X\to\mathbb{R}\) be a function. The graph of \(f\) is

\[ \{(x,f(x))\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x\in X\}, \]

which is a subset of the Cartesian product \(X\times\mathbb{R}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The graph turns a function into a picture. It collects the pairs \((x,f(x))\) as points of the plane, so that the behaviour of \(f\) can be read off by eye: the Cartesian coordinate system places each input on the horizontal axis and its output on the vertical axis.

The graph is a set of points with exactly one point above each \(x\) in the domain \(X\). So every vertical line \(x=c\) meets the graph once when \(c\in X\) and not at all when \(c\notin X\). This vertical line test decides which curves in the plane are graphs of functions of \(x\): the unit circle \(x^2+y^2=1\) is not one, since the line \(x=0\) meets it at \((0,1)\) and at \((0,-1)\).

Horizontal lines describe outputs: the line \(y=c\) meets the graph exactly above the inputs with \(f(x)=c\). In particular, the zeros of \(f\) are where the graph meets the \(x\)-axis, the range of \(f\) is the projection of the graph onto the \(y\)-axis, and \(f\) is injective if and only if no horizontal line meets the graph more than once. Likewise, the graph of an increasing monotone function never falls from left to right.

A plot is a guide, not a proof. It shows finitely many sampled points, so a single missing point or very fast oscillation can be invisible, and a claim read off a picture still has to be checked from the formula. The idea returns later for functions of two variables, whose graphs are surfaces in space.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Each input corresponds to exactly one point on the graph.
  • The graph encodes continuity and monotonicity visually.
  • Many analytical properties can be inferred from the graph.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The graph of \(f(x)=x^2\) is a parabola.
  • The graph of \(f(x)=\mathrm{e}^x\) grows rapidly.

The graph of \(f\) is the set of points \((x,f(x))\); the graph of \(f_4\) has two branches, as \(0\) is not in its domain.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The harmonic series is an infinite sum of the reciprocals of positive integers, i.e.,

\[ \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n}\text{.} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The harmonic series is the standard example of an infinite series whose terms tend to zero but whose sum diverges. It shows that vanishing terms are necessary for convergence, but not sufficient.

The terms \(1/n\) shrink towards \(0\), but the partial sums \(H_n\) keep climbing, close to the dashed curve \(\ln n+\gamma\) with \(\gamma\approx0.5772\). The growth is slow, \(H_{30}\approx3.99\) and \(H_{1000}\approx7.49\), but there is no upper bound, so \(H_n\) diverges to infinity. The grouping argument in the Examples proves this: every block of terms between consecutive powers of two adds at least \(\tfrac{1}{2}\).

Push \(N\) up to \(1000\): the terms \(\frac1n\) shrink to \(0\), but the partial sums keep growing, close to \(\ln N+\gamma\text{,}\) where \(\gamma\approx0.5772\) is the Euler–Mascheroni constant.

A common slip is to conclude from \(1/n\to0\), or from partial sums that seem to level off in a computation, that the series converges. The condition that the terms tend to \(0\) can only rule convergence out, never prove it.

The harmonic series is the benchmark on the divergent side: by the comparison test, any series with nonnegative terms at least \(1/n\), such as \(\sum 1/\sqrt{n}\), diverges as well. With alternating signs the picture changes: \(1-\tfrac{1}{2}+\tfrac{1}{3}-\cdots\) converges by the alternating series test, to \(\ln2\). The harmonic series returns as the borderline case \(p=1\) of the \(p\)-series \(\sum 1/n^p\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The harmonic series diverges to infinity.
  • Divergence occurs despite terms decreasing to zero.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Group the terms of the partial sum \(\displaystyle H_{2^m}=\sum_{n=1}^{2^m}1/n\) into blocks ending at powers of two. For each \(j=1,\ldots,m\), the block from \(n=2^{j-1}+1\) to \(n=2^j\) contains \(2^{j-1}\) terms, each at least \(1/2^j\). Thus every block contributes at least \(1/2\), and

\[ H_{2^m}\ge 1+\frac{m}{2}\longrightarrow+\infty. \]

The partial sums are increasing, so the whole sequence of partial sums diverges to infinity, even though \(1/n\to0\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The derivative \(f'\) is itself a function. If \(f'\) is differentiable, its derivative is the second derivative

\[ f''=(f')'=f^{(2)}, \]

and we may continue whenever the next derivative exists, obtaining \(f'''\text{,}\) \(f^{(4)}\text{,}\) and so on. These are the higher-order derivatives of \(f\text{.}\)

Let \(I\subseteq \mathbb{R}\) be an open interval and let \(k\geq 1\) be an integer. A function \(f\colon I\to\mathbb{R}\) is \(k\)-times differentiable on \(I\) if the derivatives \(f'\text{,}\) \(f''\text{,}\) \(\ldots\text{,}\) \(f^{(k)}\) exist at every point of \(I\text{.}\) Recursively, \(f^{(1)}=f'\) and \(f^{(k)}=\left(f^{(k-1)}\right)'\) for \(k\geq 2\text{;}\) we also set \(f^{(0)}=f\text{.}\) A function with derivatives of every order is called infinitely differentiable or smooth.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Higher-order derivatives measure change of change: \(f'\) is the rate of change of \(f\), \(f''\) is the rate of change of \(f'\), and so on. If \(f(t)\) is the position of an object at time \(t\), then \(f'(t)\) is its velocity and \(f''(t)\) its acceleration.

Each curve is the slope of the one before it. Where the red curve \(f'(x)=x^2-1\) crosses \(0\), at \(x=\pm1\) (dashed lines), the graph of \(f(x)=\tfrac{1}{3}x^3-x\) is flat: these are its stationary points. The green line \(f''(x)=2x\) is negative at \(-1\), so \(f'\) is decreasing there and \(f\) has a local maximum; it is positive at \(1\), where \(f\) has a local minimum.

Move \(x\) through the three panels: each is the slope of the one above, so where \(f'\) is positive \(f\) rises, and where \(f''\) is positive \(f'\) rises.

The second derivative tells how the graph bends: \(f''>0\) on an interval makes \(f\) convex there and \(f''<0\) makes it concave. This is the basis of the second-order condition for extrema and of inflection points; in the figure the graph of \(f\) changes from concave to convex at \(0\), where \(f''\) changes sign.

Two slips are common. The brackets in \(f^{(n)}\) matter: \(f^{(2)}=f''\) is the second derivative, while \(f^2=f\cdot f\) is a power; for \(f=\sin\), \(f^{(2)}=-\sin\) but \(f^2=\sin^2\). And a twice differentiable function need not have a continuous second derivative; that stronger property is the differentiability class \(C^2\). Higher derivatives return in Math III as the coefficients \(f^{(k)}(a)/k!\) of the Taylor polynomial.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Higher-order derivatives are defined recursively.
  • Smooth functions admit derivatives of all orders.
  • Second derivatives are particularly important for shape analysis.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(f(x)=x^3\text{,}\) then \(f''(x)=6x\text{.}\)
  • Polynomial functions have derivatives of all orders.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(L\) be a real number. The line \(y=L\) is called a horizontal asymptote of the curve \(y=f(x)\) if either

\[ \lim_{x\to +\infty}f(x)=L\quad \text{or}\quad \lim_{x\to -\infty}f(x)=L. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A horizontal asymptote describes the long-term behaviour of a function as the input grows large in magnitude.

It indicates that the function approaches a constant value.

\(f(x)\to1\) as \(x\to+\infty\) and as \(x\to-\infty\): the line \(y=1\) is a horizontal asymptote.

Pick a band of half-width \(\varepsilon\) around \(L\): from some \(M\) on, the graph stays inside, which is what \(\lim_{x\to+\infty}f(x)=L\) means.

A limit at infinity describes how the outputs behave far along the input axis. In the graph, this says that the vertical distance from the curve to the horizontal line tends to zero, without requiring the curve to stay on one side.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A function may have different horizontal asymptotes as \(x\to+\infty\) and \(x\to-\infty\text{.}\)
  • Horizontal asymptotes may or may not be attained by the function.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The function \(f(x)=1/x\) has horizontal asymptote \(y=0\text{.}\)
  • The function \(f(x)=\arctan x\) (see inverse trigonometric functions) has horizontal asymptotes \(y=\pm\dfrac{\pi}{2}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(X\) be a set. The identity function on \(X\) is the function \(\operatorname{id}_X\colon X\to X\) defined by \(\operatorname{id}_X(x)=x\) for all \(x\in X\text{.}\) That is, a function that always returns its input (argument) unchanged.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The identity function is the function that does nothing: it returns every input unchanged. It matters because it plays the role for composition that the number \(1\) plays for multiplication.

The graph of the identity on \(\mathbb{R}\) is the diagonal line \(y=x\): the marked point \((a,a)\) has equal coordinates. Reflecting the graph of a bijection in this line gives the graph of its inverse.

For \(f\colon X\to Y\), composing with the identity on either side changes nothing: \(f\circ\operatorname{id}_X=f\) and \(\operatorname{id}_Y\circ f=f\). This is why inverses are described by \(f^{-1}\circ f=\operatorname{id}_X\) and \(f\circ f^{-1}=\operatorname{id}_Y\); the subscript matters, since for \(X\neq Y\) these are two different functions. In Math II the identity returns as the identity matrix, which leaves every vector unchanged.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Composing any function with the identity function leaves it unchanged.
  • The identity function is bijective, and it is its own inverse.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For any \(x\in X\text{,}\) \(\operatorname{id}_X(x)=x\text{.}\)
  • For a bijection \(f\colon X\to Y\text{,}\) we have \((f\circ f^{-1})(x)=\operatorname{id}_Y(x)\) and \((f^{-1}\circ f)(x)=\operatorname{id}_X(x)\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An improper integral is an integral over an unbounded interval or one whose integrand becomes unbounded near an endpoint or an interior point. It is defined by one-sided limits of ordinary definite integrals. It converges if every required limit exists as a finite real number; otherwise, it diverges.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Improper integrals extend definite integrals to unbounded intervals and unbounded integrands, where the Riemann sums of a definite integral are not available. The idea is to integrate over a range where everything is ordinary and then let that range grow: the improper integral is the limit, if it exists, of these ordinary integrals.

\(\displaystyle\int_1^b\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{x^2}=1-\frac{1}{b}\) is the dark area. Letting \(b\to\infty\) adds the light tail: \(\displaystyle\int_1^{\infty}\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{x^2}=\lim_{b\to\infty}\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{b}\Bigr)=1\). An infinitely long region can therefore have a finite area, provided the integrand decays fast enough.

Push the limit of integration towards \(\infty\) (or towards \(0\)) and watch whether the area settles. Then change \(p\): the borderline case is \(p=1\) for both types.

An infinite integration boundary is handled by a limit at infinity of truncated integrals. A singularity at a finite boundary is handled by a limit at a point from the allowed side. When there are several problem points, the integral is split so that each piece has only one, and every piece must converge separately.

Two slips come from skipping this step. Applying the antiderivative across an interior singularity gives \(\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{x^2}=\Bigl[-\frac{1}{x}\Bigr]_{-1}^{1}=-2\), a negative value for a positive integrand; in fact both halves diverge. And \(\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x\,\mathrm{d}x\) diverges even though \(\displaystyle\int_{-R}^{R}x\,\mathrm{d}x=0\) for every \(R\): the two tails must converge on their own, not only cancel in a symmetric limit.

The gamma function is defined by an improper integral, and improper integrals return in Probability Theory, where probabilities for quantities with an unbounded range are computed this way.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Improper integrals are defined via limits of definite integrals.
  • Convergence depends on the existence of the defining limit.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\displaystyle\int_1^\infty \frac{1}{x^2}\,\mathrm{d}x\) converges.
  • \(\displaystyle\int_1^\infty \frac{1}{x}\,\mathrm{d}x\) diverges.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The set of all antiderivatives of a function \(f\) is the indefinite integral of \(f\) with respect to \(x\) and denoted by \(\displaystyle \int f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\text{.}\) If \(F\) is an antiderivative of \(f\text{,}\) then we have \(\displaystyle \int f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=F(x)+C\) where \(C\) is any constant.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The indefinite integral collects all antiderivatives of \(f\) in one expression. It is not a number but a family of functions, and on an interval the family is \(F+C\): one antiderivative shifted by every constant \(C\).

The indefinite integral \(\int f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=F(x)+C\) is the whole family drawn here; the constant \(C\) picks one member, and differentiating any member gives back \(f\).

The notation deliberately resembles the definite integral. By the fundamental theorem of calculus, any member of the family evaluates definite integrals, \(\int_a^b f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=F(b)-F(a)\), and the constant \(C\) cancels in the difference. An equation such as \(\int 2x\,\mathrm{d}x=x^2+C\) is an equality of families, and it is checked by differentiating the right-hand side.

Because the answer is a family, correct answers can look different. Both \(\sin^2x+C\) and \(-\cos^2x+C\) are correct for \(\int 2\sin x\cos x\,\mathrm{d}x\): differentiating either gives \(2\sin x\cos x\), and \(\sin^2x-(-\cos^2x)=1\) is a constant.

The single constant \(C\) relies on the domain being an interval. For \(\int\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{x}=\ln|x|+C\) the formula holds on \((-\infty,0)\) and on \((0,\infty)\) separately: the function equal to \(\ln|x|\) for \(x<0\) and to \(\ln|x|+1\) for \(x>0\) also has derivative \(1/x\) at every \(x\ne0\).

Later, the rules of substitution and integration by parts help to find antiderivatives that cannot be read off directly.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Indefinite integrals are defined up to an additive constant.
  • Differentiation recovers the original integrand from any antiderivative.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\displaystyle\int 2x\,\mathrm{d}x = x^2 + C\text{.}\)
  • \(\displaystyle \int \cos x\,\mathrm{d}x = \sin x + C\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
An indeterminate form is a symbolic expression involving \(0\text{,}\) \(1\text{,}\) and \(\infty\) that results from applying limit laws to a limit expression, and which fails to uniquely determine the value or divergence of the limit. There are mainly seven typical indeterminate forms:

\[ \frac{0}{0},\,\frac{\infty}{\infty},\,0\times \infty,\,\infty-\infty,\qquad 0^0,\,1^\infty,\text{ and } \infty^0. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An indeterminate form is a pattern of limits, such as a numerator and a denominator that both tend to \(0\), which the limit laws cannot settle. The word describes the form, not the limit: knowing only that \(f\to0\) and \(g\to0\) does not tell what \(f/g\) does, so further analysis is required, and the limit may well exist.

The same form can lead to any outcome. As \(x\to0^{+}\), the quotients \(x/x\), \(x^2/x\) and \(x/x^2\) all have the form \(0/0\), but tend to \(1\), \(0\) and \(+\infty\). Likewise, \((x+1)-x\to1\) and \(x^2-x\to+\infty\) as \(x\to+\infty\), although both have the form \(\infty-\infty\). By contrast, forms such as \(0/\infty\), \(\infty+\infty\) and \(0^{+\infty}\) are not indeterminate: they always give \(0\), \(+\infty\) and \(0\).

The symbols \(+\infty\) and \(-\infty\) describe divergent quantities, including those arising in limits at infinity; they are not real numbers on which ordinary arithmetic determines the answer. For example, two divergent terms can have a finite, infinite or oscillating difference.

The usual tools are algebra (factorizing, cancelling, multiplying by a conjugate), asymptotic equivalence and L'Hôpital's rule, which handles \(0/0\) and \(\infty/\infty\). The other forms are first rewritten: \(f\cdot g=f/(1/g)\) turns \(0\times\infty\) into a quotient, and \(f^g=\mathrm{e}^{g\ln f}\) turns \(0^0\), \(1^\infty\) and \(\infty^0\) into the form \(0\times\infty\) in the exponent.

A common slip is to read \(1^\infty\) as \(1\). The base tends to \(1\) while the exponent grows, and the two effects compete: \((1+\tfrac{1}{n})^n\to\mathrm{e}\), which is how Euler's number is defined.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• An indeterminate form does not determine the value of a limit.
  • Different expressions with the same symbolic form may have different limits.
  • Resolving indeterminate forms often requires algebraic manipulation.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\displaystyle \lim_{x\to 0}\frac{\sin x}{x}\) has the form "\(\dfrac{0}{0}\)" and it converges to \(1\text{.}\)
  • \(\lim\limits_{x\to +\infty} \mathrm{e}^{-x} x\) has the form "\(0\times \infty\)" and it converges to \(0\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The indicator function is a function that identifies whether an element of a set satisfies a given property. It is denoted as \(\indicator_{A}(x)\) and defined as:

\[ \indicator_{A}(x)= \begin{cases} \displaystyle \,1, & \text{if } x \in A, \\[2pt] \displaystyle \,0, & \text{if } x \notin A. \end{cases} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An indicator function encodes set membership as a number: it answers the question "is \(x\) in \(A\)?" with \(1\) for yes and \(0\) for no.

Here \(A=[1,3]\). The graph is at height \(1\) above \(A\) and at height \(0\) everywhere else, so it jumps at the two endpoints. The filled dots at \((1,1)\) and \((3,1)\) show that the endpoints belong to \(A\) and receive the value \(1\).

Set operations become arithmetic on the values. For all sets \(A\) and \(B\),

\[ \indicator_{A\cap B}=\indicator_A\indicator_B,\quad \indicator_{A^{\complement}}=1-\indicator_A, \]

and \(\indicator_{A\cup B}=\indicator_A+\indicator_B-\indicator_A\indicator_B\); each identity is checked by going through the four cases of whether \(x\) lies in \(A\) and in \(B\). In probability the same idea returns as the indicator random variable, which is \(1\) when an event occurs and \(0\) otherwise.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Indicator functions take only the values \(0\) and \(1\text{.}\)
  • Set operations can be translated into algebraic relations between indicator functions.
  • Indicator functions are widely used in integration and probability.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\indicator_{[0,1]}(x)=1\) for \(x\in[0,1]\) and \(0\) otherwise.
  • \(\indicator_{\mathbb{Q}}(x)\) distinguishes rational from irrational numbers.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
An inequality is a relation which makes a non-equal comparison between two real numbers. There are several different notations used to represent different kinds of inequalities:

  • We say \(a\) is less than \(b\) if \(a-b\) is a negative number, denoted by \(a<b\text{;}\)
  • We say \(a\) is greater than \(b\) if \(a-b\) is a positive number, denoted by \(a>b\text{;}\)
  • We say \(a\) is less than or equal to \(b\) if \(a-b\) is a negative number or zero, denoted by \(a\leq b\text{;}\)
  • We say \(a\) is greater than or equal to \(b\) if \(a-b\) is a positive number or zero, denoted by \(a\geq b\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Inequalities describe the order of the real numbers: \(a<b\) means that \(a\) lies to the left of \(b\) on the number line. The definition reduces every comparison to the sign of one number, the difference \(a-b\).

The figure shows the numbers that satisfy both \(-1<x\) and \(x\le2\), written \((-1,2]\). The open circle at \(-1\) marks a strict inequality, whose boundary point is excluded; the filled dot at \(2\) marks a non-strict one, whose boundary point is included: \(2\le2\) is true, while \(2<2\) is false.

The sign of \(a-b\) explains the rules in the Key Results. Adding \(c\) to both sides leaves the difference unchanged, \((a+c)-(b+c)=a-b\), while multiplying by \(c\) turns it into \((a-b)c\), whose sign flips when \(c<0\). A common slip is to multiply by a quantity of unknown sign, such as \(x\) in \(1/x<2\); the cases \(x>0\) and \(x<0\) must be treated separately.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Inequalities define ordering on the real numbers.
  • Inequalities are preserved under addition.
  • Multiplication by negative numbers reverses inequality direction.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(a<b\text{,}\) then \(a+1<b+1\text{.}\)
  • If \(a<b\) and \(c<0\text{,}\) then \(ac>bc\text{.}\)
