docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(E\subseteq\mathbb{R}\) be nonempty and bounded below. The infimum of \(E\) is its greatest lower bound, denoted by \(\inf E\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The infimum is the greatest value that does not exceed any element of a set: among all lower bounds of \(E\), it is the largest. It provides a precise way to describe how far down a set reaches, even when no minimum exists.

For \(E=\{1,\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{3},\ldots\}\), every number \(\le0\) is a lower bound, and no positive number \(c\) is one, since \(\tfrac{1}{n}<c\) once \(n>\tfrac{1}{c}\). So the shaded lower bounds end exactly at \(0\), and \(\inf E=0\) although \(0\notin E\); the set has no minimum.

Move the candidate \(u\): every number at or below \(\inf E\) is a lower bound, and for every \(\varepsilon>0\) some element of \(E\) lies within \(\varepsilon\) above it.

The definition has two parts, and the interactive figure tests both. A number \(m\) is the infimum of \(E\) if and only if \(m\) is a lower bound of \(E\) and, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), some \(x\in E\) satisfies \(x<m+\varepsilon\). The first part says that \(m\) is low enough; the second says that nothing larger works, because \(m+\varepsilon\) is not a lower bound. This is the usual way to verify an infimum, as for \((0,1)\) in the Examples.

A common slip is to think that the infimum must belong to the set. It does exactly when the set has a minimum, and then \(\inf E=\min E\). Another is to expect an infimum in every number system: in \(\mathbb{Q}\), the set \(\{x\in\mathbb{Q}\colon x>0,\ x^2>2\}\) is bounded below but has no greatest rational lower bound, since its infimum in \(\mathbb{R}\) is \(\sqrt{2}\). The infimum mirrors the supremum: \(\inf E=-\sup(-E)\), where \(-E=\{-x\colon x\in E\}\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• By the greatest-lower-bound property (see real number) of \(\mathbb{R}\text{,}\) every nonempty subset of \(\mathbb{R}\) that is bounded below has a unique infimum.
  • An infimum need not belong to the set; it is a minimum exactly when it is attained.
  • In the extended real numbers, one uses the conventions \(\inf E=-\infty\) for a nonempty set with no lower bound and \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\text{;}\) neither \(+\infty\) nor \(-\infty\) is a real number.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The infimum of \((0,1)\) is \(0\text{.}\)
  • The infimum of \(\{x\in\mathbb{R}\colon x>2\}\) is \(2\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \((a_n)_{n=1}^{\infty}\) be a sequence. For any integer \(N\geq 1\text{,}\) we define the \(N\)-th partial sum, formed by the finite series of the first \(N\) terms, \(S_N\) of this sequence to be a real number \(\displaystyle S_N = \sum_{n=1}^N a_n\text{.}\) 1. If the sequence \((S_N)_{N=1}^\infty\) converges to \(L\in\mathbb{R}\) as \(N\to\infty\text{,}\) then we say that the infinite series \(\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n\) is convergent and converges to \(L\text{.}\) We write \(\displaystyle L=\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n\) and say that \(L\) is the sum of the infinite series. 2. If the sequence \((S_N)_{N=1}^\infty\) diverges, then we say \(\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n\) is divergent.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An infinite series \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n\) adds up infinitely many terms, and the definition gives this a precise meaning: add the first \(N\) terms, an ordinary finite sum, and ask whether these partial sums settle down as \(N\) grows. The sum of the series is the limit of the sequence \((S_N)\), not the result of adding infinitely many numbers one by one.

The figure shows the geometric series with terms \(a_n=\tfrac{1}{2^n}\). The terms (red squares) shrink towards \(0\), while the partial sums \(S_N=1-\tfrac{1}{2^N}\) (blue dots) rise towards the dashed line at \(1\). Each blue dot is the previous one plus the next term, \(S_N=S_{N-1}+a_N\), and the series converges to \(L=1\).

Increase \(N\): a series converges exactly when its partial sums \(S_N\) settle. Compare \(\frac1n\), whose terms shrink but whose sums do not settle, with \((-1)^{n+1}\), whose terms do not shrink at all.

Two sequences are involved and should be kept apart: the terms \((a_n)\) and the partial sums \((S_N)\). Since \(a_N=S_N-S_{N-1}\), a convergent series has \(a_N\to L-L=0\), which is the necessary condition in the Key Results. The converse fails: the terms of the harmonic series \(\sum 1/n\) tend to \(0\), but its partial sums grow past every bound, only slowly.

A common slip is to regroup the terms as if the series were a finite sum. Grouping \((1-1)+(1-1)+\cdots\) suggests the sum \(0\), and \(1+(-1+1)+(-1+1)+\cdots\) suggests \(1\). In fact \(\sum(-1)^{n+1}\) diverges: its partial sums alternate between \(1\) and \(0\).

The same pattern, a limit of finite approximations, returns later in improper integrals.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A necessary condition for an infinite series \(\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n\) to converge is that its terms \(a_n\) tend to zero.
  • A series may still diverge even if its terms tend to zero.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n}\) diverges.
  • \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n^2}\) converges.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Infinity refers to a concept that is unbounded, limitless, and endless. It is denoted by the symbol \(\infty\text{,}\) and it is not a (real) number, but rather an abstract idea used to describe unbounded growth or extent.

In contexts where the direction is implicit, such as limit of a sequence, the notation \(n\to\infty\) is commonly used. However, when a variable may increase or decrease without bound, the direction must be specified explicitly:

  • \(+\infty\) denotes positive infinity, e.g., \(x\to+\infty\text{;}\)
  • \(-\infty\) denotes negative infinity, e.g., \(f(x)\to -\infty\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Infinity describes unbounded growth rather than a numerical value. Writing \(n\to\infty\) says that the index \(n\) eventually passes every bound one names, however large; it does not say that \(n\) reaches a number called \(\infty\).

No real number can play this role, since every real number \(x\) is passed by \(x+1\); and a number with \(\infty+1=\infty\) would give \(1=0\) after subtracting it from both sides. This is why expressions such as \(\infty-\infty\) are given no value. When growth is possible in both directions, the sign must be stated: \(+\infty\) for growth upwards, \(-\infty\) for growth downwards.

For finite and infinite sets, infinity describes the absence of a finite number of elements. This is a different use from unbounded growth: an infinite set, such as \(\{1/n\colon n\ge1\}\), can remain bounded, since all its elements lie between \(0\) and \(1\). Later, the extended real numbers add \(-\infty\) and \(+\infty\) to the number line as two endpoints.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • Infinity is not a real number, only a symbol: it cannot be used in real arithmetic (expressions such as \(\infty-\infty\) or \(\infty/\infty\) are undefined). Order comparisons such as \(1<+\infty\) make sense only in the extended real number system, never as statements about real numbers.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(n\to\infty\) describes unbounded growth of a sequence.
  • \(\displaystyle \lim_{x\to 0^+}\frac{1}{x}=+\infty\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(f\) be defined on an interval, and let \(x_0\) be an interior point of it. The graph point \((x_0,f(x_0))\) is an inflection point if the graph changes from convex to concave, or from concave to convex, at \(x_0\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An inflection point marks a change in the curvature of a function: on one side of it the graph is convex, on the other side concave. It is a statement about the shape on both sides, not about a single value of a derivative.

For \(f(x)=\tfrac{1}{3}x^3-x\), the second derivative \(f''(x)=2x\) is negative to the left of \(0\) and positive to the right, so the graph changes from concave to convex at the inflection point \((0,0)\). The tangent there, \(y=-x\), crosses the graph: on the concave side the graph lies below the tangent, on the convex side above it.

The shading follows the sign of \(f''\). An inflection point needs a change of curvature, not just \(f''=0\): compare the cubic with \(x^4\).

The point lies on the graph of the function, so its coordinates are \((x_0,f(x_0))\). For a differentiable \(f\), convex means that \(f'\) is increasing and concave that \(f'\) is decreasing, so at an inflection point \(f'\) switches from decreasing to increasing or back: \(x_0\) is a local extremum of \(f'\). In the figure, \(f'(x)=x^2-1\) has its minimum at \(0\).

Two slips go in opposite directions. The equation \(f''(x_0)=0\) is not enough: \(x^4\) has \(f''(0)=0\) but is convex on both sides of \(0\). And an inflection point need not satisfy \(f''(x_0)=0\), because \(f''(x_0)\) need not exist: \(x|x|\) is concave on \((-\infty,0]\) and convex on \([0,\infty)\), but has no second derivative at \(0\). So the candidates are the zeros of \(f''\) together with the points where \(f''\) does not exist, and each candidate must be checked for a change of sign of \(f''\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(f\) is twice differentiable at an inflection point \(x_0\text{,}\) then \(f''(x_0)=0\text{.}\)
  • The equation \(f''(x_0)=0\) alone is not sufficient: the convexity must actually change at \(x_0\text{.}\)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The function \(f(x)=x^3\) has an inflection point at \(x=0\text{.}\)
  • The function \(f(x)=x^4\) has no inflection point at \(x=0\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A function \(f\colon X\to Y\) is injective if different elements map to different elements, i.e., for any \(x,y\in X\text{,}\)

\[ x\neq y \;\implies\; f(x)\neq f(y). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An injective function never merges inputs: different inputs always give different outputs. Equivalently, each output comes from at most one input, so the value \(f(x)\) is enough to recover \(x\).

In the left diagram the three inputs go to three different points of \(Y\), so the function is injective; one point of \(Y\) is not reached at all, which injectivity allows. In the right diagram the inputs \(x_2\neq x_3\) share an output, \(f(x_2)=f(x_3)\), and this single collision is enough to make the function not injective.

In proofs the definition is mostly used in its contrapositive form: \(f\) is injective if and only if, for all \(x,y\in X\),

\[ f(x)=f(y)\implies x=y. \]

So to prove injectivity, assume two outputs are equal and show that the inputs are equal; to disprove it, one pair suffices, as \((-1)^2=1^2\) shows for \(x^2\) on \(\mathbb{R}\). For a function on a subset of \(\mathbb{R}\), injectivity means that every horizontal line meets the graph at most once.

Injectivity depends on the domain: \(x^2\) is not injective on \(\mathbb{R}\), but it is injective on \([0,+\infty)\), and there its inverse is \(\sqrt{x}\). Every strictly monotone function is injective, which gives a quick sufficient test. Together with surjectivity, injectivity makes \(f\) a bijection with an inverse.

A common slip is to check the wrong implication. The statement \(x=y\implies f(x)=f(y)\) holds for every function and says nothing about injectivity.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • Injectivity depends on both formula and domain.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(f(x)=x^3\) is injective on \(\mathbb{R}\text{.}\)
  • \(f(x)=x^2\) is not injective on \(\mathbb{R}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The integers are the positive and negative whole numbers together with zero:

\[ \mathbb{Z}=\{\ldots,-3,-2,-1,0,1,2,3,\ldots\}. \]

Every natural number is an integer, so \(\mathbb{N}\subseteq\mathbb{Z}\text{.}\) Math I: Calculus takes \(\mathbb{Z}\) and its usual arithmetic and order as given.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Integers extend the natural numbers by introducing additive inverses \(-1,-2,-3,\ldots\). They make subtraction unrestricted: for example, the equation \(x+5=3\) has no solution in \(\mathbb{N}\) but has the integer solution \(x=-2\).

On the number line the integers are equally spaced points, one unit apart, continuing without end in both directions. The bracket marks \(\mathbb{N}=\{0,1,2,\dots\}\), the integers from \(0\) upwards; the points to the left of \(0\) are the negatives that \(\mathbb{Z}\) adds. There is no integer strictly between two neighbouring integers.

Division remains restricted, since \(1\div2\) is not an integer; removing this limitation is the step to the rational numbers. A common slip concerns the convention for \(\mathbb{N}\): here \(0\in\mathbb{N}\), so the positive integers are \(\mathbb{N}^{+}=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}\), not all of \(\mathbb{N}\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every integer is exactly one of the following: zero, a positive natural number, or the negation of a positive natural number.
  • The set \(\mathbb{Z}\) is closed under addition, subtraction, and multiplication, but not under division.
  • Every integer \(x\) has a unique additive inverse \(-x\) satisfying \(x+(-x)=0\text{.}\)
  • For integers \(x\) and \(y\text{,}\) we have \(x<y\) exactly when \(y=x+n\) for some positive natural number \(n\text{.}\)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(-7,\,0,\) and \(23\) are integers.
  • \(1/2\) is not an integer.
  • The difference \(3-5=-2\) is an integer.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
Let \(f\colon[1,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuous, nonnegative, and nonincreasing. Then

\[ \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}f(n) \quad\text{and}\quad \int_1^{\infty}f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x \]

converge or diverge together. Moreover, the sequence

\[ \left(\sum_{i=1}^n f(i)-\int_1^n f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\right)_{n=1}^{\infty} \]

converges.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The integral test compares a series of nonnegative terms with an improper integral of the same shape. The terms \(f(n)\) are the heights of rectangles of width \(1\) along the graph of \(f\), so the partial sums and the integrals \(\int_1^N f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\) grow together, and one stays bounded if and only if the other does.

For \(f(x)=\frac{1}{x}\) the rectangles have areas \(1,\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{3},\dots\) and lie above the graph, so \(\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{N}\frac{1}{n}\ge\int_1^{N+1}\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{x}\), which tends to \(\infty\).

The rectangles of height \(f(i)\) and the area under \(f\) grow together. Their difference settles for every \(p\), which is why the series and the integral converge or diverge together.

The rectangles give a precise comparison. Since \(f\) is nonincreasing, \(f(n+1)\le f(x)\le f(n)\) for \(x\in[n,n+1]\); integrating over \([n,n+1]\) and adding gives

\[ \sum_{n=2}^{N}f(n)\le\int_1^N f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x \le\sum_{n=1}^{N-1}f(n). \]

Because \(f\ge0\), both the partial sums and the integrals increase with \(N\), so each converges if and only if it is bounded, and the inequalities transfer boundedness in both directions. Without monotonicity the test fails: \(f(x)=\sin^2(\pi x)\) is continuous and nonnegative with \(f(n)=0\) for every \(n\), so the series converges, while \(\int_1^\infty\sin^2(\pi x)\,\mathrm{d}x\) diverges.

The test is how the \(p\)-series are settled from the \(p\)-test. The second statement says more: for \(f(x)=\frac{1}{x}\) the differences \(\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{1}{i}-\ln n\) converge, with limit about \(0.577\), so the partial sums of the harmonic series grow like \(\ln n\).

A common slip is to take the integral as the value of the series. The series \(\sum\frac{1}{n^2}\) and \(\int_1^\infty\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{x^2}\) converge together, but the sum is \(\frac{\pi^2}{6}\approx1.645\) while the integral is \(1\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The test applies only to continuous, nonnegative, nonincreasing functions.
  • Convergence of the improper integral implies convergence of the series.
  • Divergence of the improper integral implies divergence of the series.
  • The test provides a comparison, not the value of the sum.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n^2}\) converges because \(\displaystyle \int_1^\infty \frac{1}{x^2}\,\mathrm{d}x\) converges.
  • The series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n}\) diverges because \(\displaystyle \int_1^\infty \frac{1}{x}\,\mathrm{d}x\) diverges.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Given an integral of the form \(\displaystyle \int_a^b f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\) or \(\displaystyle \int f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\), the function \(f\) is called the integrand of the integral.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The integrand is the function being integrated. In \(\int_a^b f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\) it supplies the heights of the rectangles in each Riemann sum, and the integral adds these heights up, weighted by width. The letter \(x\) in \(f(x)\) is only a placeholder, and \(\mathrm{d}x\) says which variable runs over the interval.

The integrand decides whether the integral exists. An integrand that is continuous or monotone on \([a,b]\) is Riemann integrable, while an unbounded one, such as \(1/\sqrt{x}\) on \((0,1]\), is not; integrals of that kind are treated later as improper integrals.

A common slip is to confuse the integrand with the result. In \(\int_0^1 x^2\,\mathrm{d}x\) the integrand is \(x^2\), an antiderivative is \(x^3/3\), and the value of the integral is \(\tfrac{1}{3}\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • Properties of the integrand influence integrability.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In \(\displaystyle\int_0^1 x^2\,\mathrm{d}x\text{,}\) the integrand is \(x^2\text{.}\)
  • In \(\displaystyle\int \,\mathrm{d}x\text{,}\) the integrand is \(1\text{.}\)

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
Let \(f\) and \(g\) be differentiable functions on \([a, b]\) with \(f'\) and \(g'\) Riemann integrable. Then:

\[ \int_a^b f(x)g'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x =f(b)g(b)-f(a)g(a) -\int_a^b f'(x)g(x)\,\mathrm{d}x, \]

or

\[ \int_a^b f(x)\,\mathrm{d}g(x) =f(b)g(b)-f(a)g(a) -\int_a^b g(x)\,\mathrm{d}f(x). \]

If we consider the indefinite integral, we get:

\[ \int f\,\mathrm{d}g = fg -\int g\,\mathrm{d}f+C. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Integration by parts is the product rule read backwards. Since \((fg)'=f'g+fg'\), integrating gives \(fg\) back, so an integral of \(fg'\) can be traded for an integral of \(f'g\) plus a boundary term. This helps when differentiating \(f\) makes it simpler while \(g'\) is easy to integrate.

Put \(u=f(x)\) and \(v=g(x)\). As \(x\) runs from \(a\) to \(b\), the point \((u,v)\) traces the curve from \((u_1,v_1)\) to \((u_2,v_2)\). The area below the curve is \(\int v\,\mathrm{d}u\) and the area to its left is \(\int u\,\mathrm{d}v\); together they fill the large rectangle minus the small one, so \(\int u\,\mathrm{d}v+\int v\,\mathrm{d}u=u_2v_2-u_1v_1\). With \(u_1=f(a)\), \(u_2=f(b)\) and so on, this is the second form of the formula. The picture assumes increasing positive \(f\) and \(g\); the formula does not.

The differential notation \(\mathrm{d}g=g'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\) rewrites the same product-rule integral. It identifies which factor is differentiated; it does not make \(\mathrm{d}g\) an unrelated integration variable.

The choice of \(f\) and \(g'\) decides whether the method helps. For \(\int x\mathrm{e}^x\,\mathrm{d}x\), taking \(f(x)=x\) turns the new integrand into \(\mathrm{e}^x\). The opposite choice \(f(x)=\mathrm{e}^x\), \(g'(x)=x\) is a common slip: it leads to \(\frac{x^2}{2}\mathrm{e}^x-\int\frac{x^2}{2}\mathrm{e}^x\,\mathrm{d}x\), which is harder than the original.

The same step proves the recursion \(\Gamma(x+1)=x\,\Gamma(x)\) of the gamma function, and in improper integrals it is applied on a bounded interval first, with a limit afterwards, as in the second Example.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Integration by parts follows directly from the product rule.
  • The method can be applied to both definite and indefinite integrals.
  • Appropriate choice of functions is essential for simplification.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Choose \(f(x)=x\) and \(g'(x)=\mathrm{e}^x\). Then \(f'(x)=1\) and \(g(x)=\mathrm{e}^x\), so \(\int x\mathrm{e}^x\,\mathrm{d}x=x\mathrm{e}^x-\mathrm{e}^x+C=(x-1)\mathrm{e}^x+C\).
  • The integral \(\int_0^1x^2\ln x\,\mathrm{d}x\) is improper at zero. Apply integration by parts once on \([\varepsilon,1]\), with \(f(x)=\ln x\) and \(g(x)=x^3/3\):
\[ \int_\varepsilon^1x^2\ln x\,\mathrm{d}x=\left[\frac{x^3\ln x}{3}\right]_\varepsilon^1 -\frac{1}{3}\int_\varepsilon^1x^2\,\mathrm{d}x. \]

Since \(\varepsilon^3\ln\varepsilon\to0\) as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\), the integral equals \(-1/9\).

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
Let \(g\colon[\alpha,\beta]\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuously differentiable, and let \(f\) be continuous on an interval containing the range of \(g\text{.}\) Then

\[ \int_\alpha^\beta {\color{red}f(g(x))}{\color{blue}g'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x} \overset{t=g(x)}{=} \int_{g(\alpha)}^{g(\beta)}{\color{red}f(t)}\,{\color{blue}\mathrm{d}t}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Substitution of type 1 is the chain rule read backwards. When the integrand has the form \(f(g(x))g'(x)\), the inner function \(g(x)\) is renamed \(t\), and the integral becomes \(\int f(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\) in the new variable. It works best when the derivative factor \(g'(x)\) already appears in the integrand.

The colours in the formula show the matching. The red part \(f(g(x))\) becomes \(f(t)\), and the blue part \(g'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\) becomes \(\mathrm{d}t\). As \(x\) runs from \(\alpha\) to \(\beta\), \(t=g(x)\) runs from \(g(\alpha)\) to \(g(\beta)\), so the limits change too and there is no need to return to \(x\) at the end.

The equality concerns Riemann integrals under the stated continuity assumptions. The differential relation \(\mathrm{d}t=g'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\) records the derivative factor and the transformed endpoints. The hypotheses make both sides ordinary integrals of continuous functions, and \(f\) has an antiderivative \(F\) with \((F\circ g)'=f(g(x))g'(x)\). The function \(g\) may go back and forth: for \(g(x)=\sin x\) on \([0,\pi]\), \(g(0)=g(\pi)=0\), so \(\int_0^\pi f(\sin x)\cos x\,\mathrm{d}x=0\) for every continuous \(f\).

A common slip is to substitute when the factor \(g'(x)\) is missing. The substitution \(t=x^2\) turns \(\int 2x\cos(x^2)\,\mathrm{d}x\) into \(\int\cos t\,\mathrm{d}t\), but it does not help with \(\int\cos(x^2)\,\mathrm{d}x\). Another is to change the integrand but keep the old limits \(\alpha,\beta\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The function \(g\) need not be invertible; the formula follows from the chain rule and the fundamental theorem of calculus.
  • The limits of integration must be transformed together with the integrand, from \(\alpha,\beta\) to \(g(\alpha),g(\beta)\text{.}\)
  • If \(F'=f\text{,}\) then the corresponding indefinite identity is \(\displaystyle\int f(g(x))g'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=F(g(x))+C\text{.}\)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\displaystyle \int 2x\cos(x^2)\,\mathrm{d}x\) can be simplified by proposing \(t=x^2\text{.}\)
  • \(\displaystyle\int_1^2 \frac{3x^2+2}{x^3+2x+3}\,\mathrm{d}x\) can be evaluated using \(t=x^3+2x+3\text{.}\)

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
Let \(\varphi\colon[\alpha,\beta]\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuously differentiable, with \(\varphi(\alpha)=a\) and \(\varphi(\beta)=b\text{,}\) and let \(f\) be continuous on an interval containing the range of \(\varphi\text{.}\) Then

\[ \int_a^b {\color{red}f(x)}\,{\color{blue}\mathrm{d}x} \overset{x=\varphi(t)}{=} \int_\alpha^\beta {\color{red}f(\varphi(t))}{\color{blue}\varphi'(t)\,\mathrm{d}t}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Substitution of type 2 starts from the other side: instead of spotting an inner function, it writes the variable as \(x=\varphi(t)\) and replaces \(\mathrm{d}x\) by \(\varphi'(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\). It is useful when no derivative factor appears in the integrand, but an awkward expression such as \(\sqrt{1-x^2}\) becomes simpler in terms of \(t\).

The chain rule differentiates an antiderivative composed with \(\varphi\), producing \(f(\varphi(t))\varphi'(t)\). This proves the Riemann integral identity above; the differential notation \(\mathrm{d}x=\varphi'(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\) records that factor. The two types are therefore one identity read in opposite directions: type 1 goes from the side with \(g'(x)\) to the simpler side, and type 2 deliberately creates the factor \(\varphi'(t)\).

In the Example, \(x=\sin t\) with \(t\) from \(0\) to \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) gives \(\sqrt{1-\sin^2t}=\cos t\) and \(\mathrm{d}x=\cos t\,\mathrm{d}t\), so \(\int_0^1\sqrt{1-x^2}\,\mathrm{d}x=\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^2t\,\mathrm{d}t=\frac{\pi}{4}\), the area of a quarter of the unit disc. The limits only have to satisfy \(\varphi(\alpha)=a\) and \(\varphi(\beta)=b\), and \(f\) must be continuous on an interval containing all values of \(\varphi\), not only those between \(a\) and \(b\).

A common slip is to simplify a square root without checking the sign. In general \(\sqrt{1-\sin^2t}=|\cos t|\). The limits \(t=\pi\) and \(t=\frac{\pi}{2}\) are also valid here, since \(\sin\pi=0\) and \(\sin\frac{\pi}{2}=1\), but on \([\frac{\pi}{2},\pi]\) we have \(\cos t\le0\), and writing \(\cos t\) instead of \(|\cos t|\) gives \(-\frac{\pi}{4}\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The function \(\varphi\) does not need to be invertible.
  • This formula is particularly useful for expressions such as \(\sqrt{a^2-x^2}\text{,}\) where a trigonometric parametrization can simplify the integrand.
  • This formula is often complementary to the \(t=g(x)\) approach, and usually only one of the two is effective for a given integral.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\displaystyle\int_0^1\sqrt{1-x^2}\,\mathrm{d}x\) can be evaluated by setting \(x=\sin t\text{,}\) which changes the limits to \(0\) and \(\pi/2\text{.}\)
  • Trigonometric substitutions are common examples of parametrizations of this form.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: Let \(a < b\) be real numbers, and let \(f\colon [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}\) be continuous. If \(y\) is any number between \(\min\{f(a), f(b)\}\) and \(\max\{f(a), f(b)\}\), then there exists \(c \in [a, b]\) such that \(f(c) = y\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The intermediate value theorem makes precise the picture that the graph of a continuous function on an interval can be drawn without lifting the pen: to get from height \(f(a)\) to height \(f(b)\), the graph has to pass through every height in between.

Every level \(y\) between \(f(a)\) and \(f(b)\) is reached by the continuous \(f\): here \(f(c)=y\) at three points \(c_1,c_2,c_3\) of \([a,b]\). The theorem promises at least one such point; it says nothing about how many there are or where they lie.

Slide the level \(y\) between \(f(a)\) and \(f(b)\): the continuous cubic always reaches it, sometimes at several points \(c\). The function with a jump skips a whole range of levels.

Both hypotheses are needed. Continuity rules out jumps: the signum function on \([-1,1]\) takes the values \(-1\) and \(1\) but never the value \(\tfrac{1}{2}\). The domain must also be a whole interval without gaps: \(f(x)=1/x\) is continuous on \([-1,1]\) with \(0\) removed and takes the values \(-1\) and \(1\), but never the value \(0\).

The theorem is mostly used in its sign-change form from the Examples: if \(f(a)\) and \(f(b)\) have opposite signs, then \(f\) has a zero in \([a,b]\). It proves that an equation has a solution without solving it, and repeatedly halving the interval while keeping the sign change locates that solution numerically. Math III later extends the theorem beyond intervals.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every value between \(f(a)\) and \(f(b)\) is attained on \([a,b]\text{.}\)
  • The theorem ensures existence but not uniqueness.
  • Continuity is essential for the result.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • A continuous function changing sign on an interval must have a root.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The intersection \(A\cap B\) of two sets \(A\) and \(B\) is defined to be the set

\[ \begin{aligned} &A\cap B=\{x\in A\colon x\in B\},\quad \text{or equivalently}\\ &x\in A\cap B\;\iff\; x\in A \text{ and }x\in B \iff \; (x\in A) \land (x\in B). \end{aligned} \]

Thus, \(A\cap B\) consists of all the elements which belong to both \(A\) and \(B\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The intersection of sets captures the elements common to all sets involved. An element of \(A\cap B\) must pass both membership tests at once, so intersection is the set version of the logical "and".

The shaded lens is where the two discs overlap; its points lie in \(A\) and in \(B\). Points in only one of the discs are left out. The lens lies inside each disc, so \(A\cap B\subseteq A\) and \(A\cap B\subseteq B\); if the discs were moved apart, the lens would vanish and the sets would be disjoint.

The form \(\{x\in A\colon x\in B\}\) reads as a filter: start from \(A\) and keep the elements that also lie in \(B\). Although this notation treats \(A\) and \(B\) differently, the result does not depend on the order. If \(A\subseteq B\), the filter removes nothing: \(A\cap B=A\) if and only if \(A\subseteq B\). By associativity, \(A_1\cap\cdots\cap A_n\) needs no brackets.

In probability, \(A\cap B\) returns as the event that both \(A\) and \(B\) happen (see union and intersection of events).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• An element belongs to the intersection if and only if it belongs to each set.
  • Intersection is commutative (i.e., \(A\cap B=B\cap A\)) and associative (i.e., \(A\cap(B\cap C)=(A\cap B)\cap C\)).
  • The intersection with the empty set is empty.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(a,b\in \mathbb{R}\) be real numbers with \(a\leq b\).

  • We define the closed intervals \([a, b]\) and the open intervals \((a,b)\) as follows:
\[ \begin{aligned} &[a,b] = \{x\in \mathbb{R}\colon a\leq x\leq b\},\\ &(a,b) = \{x\in \mathbb{R}\colon a< x< b\}. \end{aligned} \]
  • In the case when \(a<b\text{,}\) we define the half-open intervals \([a, b)\) and \((a, b]\) as follows:
\[ \begin{aligned} &[a,b) = \{x\in \mathbb{R}\colon a\leq x< b\},\\ & (a,b] = \{x\in \mathbb{R}\colon a< x\leq b\}. \end{aligned} \]
  • We define open half-infinite interval as follows:
\[ \begin{aligned} &(-\infty,b)=\{x\in \mathbb{R}\colon x< b\},\\ & (a,+\infty) = \{x\in \mathbb{R}\colon x>a\}. \end{aligned} \]
  • We define closed half-infinite interval as follows:
\[ \begin{aligned} &(-\infty,b]=\{x\in \mathbb{R}\colon x\leq b\},\\ & [a,+\infty) = \{x\in \mathbb{R}\colon x\geq a\}. \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Intervals are exactly the subsets of the real line without gaps: whenever two numbers lie in an interval, every number between them does too. They are the usual domains of the functions studied in this course.

The four number lines show the intervals from \(a\) to \(b\). A filled dot marks an endpoint that belongs to the interval and a hollow dot one that does not: \([a,b]\) has both endpoints, \((a,b)\) neither, and each half-open interval has one. In the notation, a square bracket corresponds to a filled dot and a round bracket to a hollow one.

Each interval is a subset of the real numbers defined by inequalities. Weak inequalities \(\le\) include the endpoint and strict inequalities \(<\) exclude it. The symbols \(-\infty\) and \(+\infty\) are not real numbers, so they always take a round bracket: one writes \([a,+\infty)\), never \([a,+\infty]\). The half-infinite intervals, together with \(\mathbb{R}=(-\infty,+\infty)\) itself, are the unbounded intervals; the others are bounded. The case \(a=b\) is allowed for the closed and open intervals: \([a,a]=\{a\}\) is a singleton and \((a,a)\) is the empty set.

Whether the endpoints belong to the interval often matters: \([0,1]\) has maximum \(1\), while \((0,1)\) has no maximum, although its supremum is still \(1\). A common slip is to read \((a,b)\) as a point of the plane. The same symbols denote an ordered pair of coordinates, and only the context tells which is meant.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Intervals may be open, closed, or half-open.
  • Endpoints determine whether boundary values are included.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \((0,1)\) is an open interval.
  • \([0,1]\) includes both endpoints.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be open intervals in \(\mathbb{R}\), and let \(f\colon X\to Y\) be an invertible function, with inverse \(f^{-1}\colon Y\to X\text{.}\) Suppose that \(x\in X\) and \(y\in Y\) are such that \(f(x)=y\text{,}\) or equivalently, \(x=f^{-1}(y)\text{.}\) If \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\text{,}\) \(f'(x)\neq 0\text{,}\) and \(f^{-1}\) is continuous at \(y\text{,}\) then \(f^{-1}\) is differentiable at \(y\) and

\[ \left(f^{-1}\right)'(y)=\frac{1}{f'(x)}=\frac{1}{f'(f^{-1}(y))}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The inverse function theorem says when the inverse of a differentiable function is again differentiable, and how to find its derivative without a formula for \(f^{-1}\): the slope of \(f^{-1}\) at \(y\) is the reciprocal of the slope of \(f\) at the matching point \(x=f^{-1}(y)\).

The graph of \(f^{-1}\) is the graph of \(f\) reflected in the line \(y=x\), and the reflection swaps rise and run. Here \(f(x)=x^2\) and \(f^{-1}(y)=\sqrt{y}\): the tangent to \(f\) at \((x_0,y_0)\) has slope \(f'(x_0)=2x_0\), and its mirror image, the tangent to \(f^{-1}\) at \((y_0,x_0)\), has slope \(1/(2x_0)\), which is indeed the derivative of \(\sqrt{y}\) at \(y_0=x_0^2\).

Each hypothesis has a role. If \(f'(x)=0\), the tangent of \(f\) is horizontal and its mirror image is vertical, so \(f^{-1}\) has no derivative at \(y\): \(f(x)=x^3\) has \(f'(0)=0\), and the cube root has a vertical tangent at \(0\). Continuity of \(f^{-1}\) at \(y\) makes \(f^{-1}(y+k)\to x\) as \(k\to0\), so that difference quotients of \(f^{-1}\) are reciprocals of difference quotients of \(f\) near \(x\). When \(f\) is continuous on the whole interval \(X\), it is strictly monotone, and then \(f^{-1}\) is automatically continuous.

The formula is easy to remember through the chain rule: differentiating \(f(f^{-1}(y))=y\) gives \(f'(f^{-1}(y))\,(f^{-1})'(y)=1\). This calculation assumes that \((f^{-1})'(y)\) exists; the theorem guarantees it. A common slip is to evaluate \(f'\) at the wrong point: \((f^{-1})'(y)\) is \(1/f'(x)\) with \(x=f^{-1}(y)\), not \(1/f'(y)\). For \(f(x)=\mathrm{e}^x\) this gives \((\ln)'(y)=1/\mathrm{e}^{\ln y}=1/y\), not \(1/\mathrm{e}^{y}\). Math IV extends the theorem to functions of several variables in the multivariable inverse function theorem.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(f'\) is nonzero throughout an open interval, then \(f\) is strictly monotone there and hence invertible onto its range. The theorem itself assumes that \(f\) is invertible and only concerns the differentiability of \(f^{-1}\text{.}\)
  • Differentiability of the inverse depends on continuity assumptions.
  • The derivative of the inverse is determined by the reciprocal of the original derivative.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(f'(x_0)=2\text{,}\) then the derivative of the inverse is \(1/2\) at \(y=f(x_0)\text{.}\)
  • The derivative \(\mathrm{e}^x\) at \(x=1/2\) is the reciprocal of the derivative of \(\ln y\) at \(y=\mathrm{e} ^{1/2}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Where this appears in the course

Lecture 7 states that the derivatives of the inverse trigonometric functions are derived in that week's tutorial (Tutorial 4) rather than in the lecture itself. The functions and their derivatives are still part of the course.

The inverse sine function \(\arcsin \colon [-1,1] \to \left[-\pi/2, \pi/2\right]\) is defined as the inverse of the restriction of the sine function to the interval \(\left[-\pi/2, \pi/2\right]\text{.}\) That is, for each \(x \in [-1,1]\text{,}\) \(\arcsin x\) is the unique number \(y \in \left[-\pi/2, \pi/2\right]\) such that \(\sin y = x\text{.}\)

The inverse cosine function \(\arccos \colon [-1,1] \to [0,\pi]\) is defined as the inverse of the restriction of the cosine function to the interval \([0,\pi]\text{.}\) That is, for each \(x \in [-1,1]\text{,}\) \(\arccos x\) is the unique number \(y \in [0,\pi]\) such that \(\cos y = x\text{.}\)

The inverse tangent function \(\arctan \colon \mathbb{R} \to \left(-\pi/2, \pi/2\right)\) is defined as the inverse of the restriction of the tangent function to the interval \(\left(-\pi/2, \pi/2\right)\text{.}\) That is, for each \(x \in \mathbb{R}\text{,}\) \(\arctan x\) is the unique number \(y \in \left(-\pi/2,\pi/2\right)\) such that \(\tan y = x\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Inverse trigonometric functions recover an angle from the value of its sine, cosine or tangent. The trigonometric functions are periodic, so each value is taken infinitely often; they are therefore first restricted to an interval on which they are injective, and only then inverted. Thus \(\arcsin x\) is the one angle in \([-\pi/2,\pi/2]\) whose sine is \(x\).

Each graph is the reflection in the line \(y=x\) of the restricted sine, cosine or tangent. On \([-1,1]\), \(\arcsin\) increases from \(-\pi/2\) to \(\pi/2\) and \(\arccos\) decreases from \(\pi\) to \(0\); together they satisfy \(\arcsin x+\arccos x=\pi/2\). The function \(\arctan\) is defined on all of \(\mathbb{R}\) and has horizontal asymptotes at \(y=\pm\pi/2\), the mirror images of the vertical asymptotes of \(\tan\) at \(x=\pm\pi/2\).

Switch the restriction off: on all of \(\mathbb{R}\) the level \(c\) is hit infinitely often. Restricted to the standard interval, each function is a bijection and \(\arcsin\), \(\arccos\) and \(\arctan\) are its mirror images.

The restriction fixes which angle is returned. So \(\sin(\arcsin x)=x\) for every \(x\in[-1,1]\), but \(\arcsin(\sin x)=x\) only for \(x\in[-\pi/2,\pi/2]\); for example, \(\arcsin(\sin\pi)=\arcsin 0=0\). The notation \(\sin^{-1}x\) means \(\arcsin x\), not \(1/\sin x\).

The derivatives follow from the inverse function theorem. For \(y=\arcsin x\) with \(-1<x<1\), the angle \(y\) lies in \((-\pi/2,\pi/2)\), where \(\cos y>0\), so \((\arcsin)'(x)=1/\cos y=1/\sqrt{1-x^2}\). In the same way \((\arctan)'(x)=\cos^2 y=1/(1+x^2)\). At \(x=\pm1\) the sine has derivative \(\cos(\pm\pi/2)=0\), and \(\arcsin\) has a vertical tangent there. Math II returns to the arctangent in the 2-argument arctangent, which recovers angles in all four quadrants.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Domain restrictions are essential for defining inverses.
  • Inverse trigonometric functions are continuous on their domains.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\arcsin 0=0\text{.}\)
  • \(\arctan 1=\pi/4\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An irrational number is a real number but not a rational number, i.e., it is an element of the set \(\mathbb{R}\setminus \mathbb{Q}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An irrational number cannot be expressed as a fraction \(p/q\) of two integers. Such numbers arise from ordinary geometry, and they are what the real numbers add to the rationals.

The diagonal of the unit square has length \(\sqrt{2}\), since \(1^2+1^2=2\). Rotating it down onto the number line marks the point \(1.414\ldots\): a length that is easy to construct lands at a point that no fraction reaches. The classical proof is by contradiction. If \(\sqrt{2}=p/q\) in lowest terms, then \(p^2=2q^2\), so \(p\) is even; writing \(p=2k\) gives \(q^2=2k^2\), so \(q\) is even as well, which contradicts lowest terms.

A common slip is to expect the irrationals to be closed under arithmetic. They are not: \(\sqrt{2}+(-\sqrt{2})=0\) and \(\sqrt{2}\cdot\sqrt{2}=2\) are rational. A rational number plus an irrational number, on the other hand, is always irrational.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A real number is rational exactly when it has a decimal expansion that terminates or is eventually periodic. Irrational numbers therefore have non-terminating decimal expansions that are not eventually periodic.
  • Every real number is either rational or irrational, and never both.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\sqrt{2}\) is an irrational number.
  • \(\pi\) and \(\mathrm{e}\) are irrational numbers.
  • It is still unknown if \(\pi+\mathrm{e}\) is irrational or not.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a bounded interval \(I\) represented by \([a, b]\text{,}\) \((a, b)\text{,}\) \([a, b)\text{,}\) or \((a, b]\) where \(a < b\) are real numbers, we define the length of \(I\text{,}\) denoted by \(|I|\text{,}\) as \(|I|=b-a\text{.}\) If \(I\) is a singleton set or the empty set, then \(|I|=0\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The length of an interval measures how much of the real line it covers. For a bounded interval it is the distance \(b-a\) between the endpoints, so it depends only on where the interval starts and ends.

The figure shows the half-open interval \([1,4)\): the filled dot at \(1\) belongs to it, the open dot at \(4\) does not, and the arrow above marks its length \(4-1=3\). The intervals \([1,4]\) and \((1,4)\) have the same length: \([1,4]\) is \([1,4)\) together with the single point \(4\), and a singleton has length \(0\).

The notation \(|I|\) echoes the absolute value: since \(a<b\), \(|I|=b-a=|b-a|\), the distance from \(a\) to \(b\). Lengths are the widths of the rectangles in a Riemann sum, and over a partition of \([a,b]\) the lengths of the subintervals add up to \(b-a\).

A common slip is to count points instead of measuring: \([1,4]\) contains the four integers \(1,2,3,4\), but its length is \(3\), and it contains infinitely many real numbers.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The length depends only on the endpoints.
  • Singletons and empty sets have length zero.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The interval \((2,5)\) has length \(3\text{.}\)
  • The interval \([a,b]\) has length \(b-a\text{.}\)

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(x\) approach \(a\in\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty,+\infty\}\) through an interval. Assume that, sufficiently near \(a\):

  • \(f\) and \(g\) are differentiable, and \(g'(x)\neq0\text{;}\)
  • either \(f(x)\to0\) and \(g(x)\to0\text{,}\) or \(|f(x)|\to\infty\) and \(|g(x)|\to\infty\text{;}\)
  • \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to a}\frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)}=L\text{,}\) where \(L\) may be finite or infinite.

Then

\[ \lim_{x\to a}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}=L. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
L’Hôpital’s rule evaluates limits of quotients that have the indeterminate form \(0/0\) or \(\infty/\infty\) by comparing the rates of change of the numerator and denominator. It replaces the limit of \(f/g\) by the limit of \(f'/g'\), which is often simpler.

\(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}=\lim_{x\to0}\frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)}=\frac{f'(0)}{g'(0)}=\frac{1}{2}\): near \(0\) both functions are close to their tangents (dashed), with slopes \(f'(0)=1\) and \(g'(0)=2\), so the quotient tends to the ratio of the slopes.

Zoom in towards the point: both graphs straighten into lines through \((a,0)\), and the quotient of their values approaches the quotient of their slopes.

Each hypothesis matters. The rule needs an indeterminate form: \(\frac{x+1}{x+2}\to\frac{1}{2}\) as \(x\to0\), while the quotient of the derivatives is \(1\). It also needs the limit of \(f'/g'\) to exist: \(\frac{x+\sin x}{x}\to1\) as \(x\to\infty\), but \(\frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)}=1+\cos x\) has no limit. In such a case the rule gives no information, and the limit of \(f/g\) must be found in another way.

The rule may be applied again as long as the form stays indeterminate: as \(x\to\infty\), the quotient \(x^2/\mathrm{e}^x\) leads to \(2x/\mathrm{e}^x\) and then to \(2/\mathrm{e}^x\to0\). Other indeterminate forms are first rewritten as a quotient of type \(0/0\) or \(\infty/\infty\).

A common slip is to differentiate the quotient \(f/g\) with the quotient rule. The rule differentiates numerator and denominator separately: it uses \(f'/g'\), not \((f/g)'\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• L’Hôpital’s rule applies only to indeterminate forms of type \(0/0\) or \(\infty/\infty\text{.}\)
  • Differentiability of both numerator and denominator is required in a punctured neighbourhood of the point.
  • The rule must not be used to justify limits that are needed to establish the derivatives involved.
  • The rule needs \(\frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)}\) to have a limit \(L\text{,}\) finite or an infinite extended real number; if that limit does not exist, the rule gives no conclusion about \(\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The limit \(\displaystyle \lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{\ln x}{x}=0\) can be evaluated using L’Hôpital’s rule.

  • Although formally applicable, L’Hôpital’s rule cannot be used to justify

    \[ \lim_{x\to 0}\frac{\sin x}{x}=1, \]

    because the derivative of \(\sin x\) depends on this limit itself. This would result in circular reasoning.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}\text{,}\) let \(f\colon X\to\mathbb{R}\) be a function, and let \(x_0\) be a limit point of \(X\text{.}\) We say that \(f\) converges to \(L \in \mathbb{R}\) as \(x\) approaches \(x_0\text{,}\) and write

\[ \lim_{x \to x_0} f(x) = L, \]

if for every \(\varepsilon > 0\) there exists a number \(\delta>0\) such that, for every \(x\in X\text{,}\)

\[ 0 < |x - x_0| < \delta \; \implies \; |f(x) - L| < \varepsilon. \]

Some remarks:

  • The point \(x_0\) must be a limit point of the domain; \(x_0\) itself need not belong to \(X\text{.}\)
  • The condition \(0<|x-x_0|\) excludes \(x=x_0\text{,}\) so the value \(f(x_0)\) is irrelevant to the limit.
  • If the limit exists, it is unique.
  • The \(\varepsilon\)-\(\delta\) definition contains no motion: it is a precise implication between two inequalities. An opponent chooses the output tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\text{;}\) we must answer with a valid input tolerance \(\delta>0\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The limit describes the value that \(f(x)\) approaches as \(x\) gets arbitrarily close to \(x_0\text{,}\) regardless of whether \(f(x_0)\) is defined. The definition turns "approaches" into a test: every output tolerance \(\varepsilon\) around \(L\) must be met by some input tolerance \(\delta\) around \(x_0\).

In the figure the point \(a\) plays the role of \(x_0\), and \(f(x)=x+1\) is drawn with an open circle at \((1,2)\), so the value at \(a=1\) is left out. The horizontal band is \(|y-L|<\varepsilon\) around \(L=2\), the vertical band is \(|x-a|<\delta\). Since \(|f(x)-2|=|x-1|\), the choice \(\delta=\varepsilon\) works for every \(\varepsilon>0\), so \(\lim_{x\to1}f(x)=2\).

Play the opponent's game: pick \(\varepsilon\), then look for a \(\delta\) that keeps every \(x\) with \(0<|x-x_0|<\delta\) inside the \(\varepsilon\)-band. For the jump, no candidate \(L\) survives a small \(\varepsilon\).

The order of the quantifiers matters: \(\varepsilon\) is given first, and \(\delta\) may depend on it. The limit exists only if an answer \(\delta\) exists for every \(\varepsilon>0\), however small. The requirement that \(x_0\) is a limit point of the domain guarantees that there are points \(x\in X\) with \(0<|x-x_0|<\delta\) to test. At an isolated point the implication would hold vacuously for every \(L\), and the limit would not be unique.

The same pattern defines the limit of a sequence, with an index \(N\) in place of \(\delta\), and the limit at infinity, with a bound \(M\). Using only one side of \(x_0\) gives the one-sided limits, and requiring \(L=f(x_0)\) gives continuity. The idea returns later in the derivative, which is defined as a limit of this kind.

A common slip is to compute \(f(x_0)\) and call it the limit. The two agree only when \(f\) is continuous at \(x_0\): \(f(x)=(x^2-1)/(x-1)\) is not defined at \(1\), yet \(\lim_{x\to1}f(x)=2\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Limits, if they exist, are unique.
  • A function may have a limit at a point where it is not defined.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} x^2 = 0\)
  • \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 1\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(X\subseteq \mathbb{R}\) and let \(f\colon X\to \mathbb{R}\) be a function. Assume there exists \(M_0\in\mathbb{R}\) such that \((M_0,+\infty)\subseteq X\text{.}\) We say that \(f\) converges to \(L\in\mathbb{R}\) as \(x\to +\infty\text{,}\) and we write \(\displaystyle \lim_{x\to +\infty} f(x)=L\text{,}\) if for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists \(M\ge M_0\) such that

\[ x>M \, \implies\, |f(x)-L|<\varepsilon. \]

Similarly, assume there exists \(M_0\in\mathbb{R}\) such that \((-\infty,M_0)\subseteq X\text{.}\) We say that \(f\) converges to \(L\in\mathbb{R}\) as \(x\to -\infty\text{,}\) and we write \(\displaystyle \lim_{x\to -\infty} f(x)=L\text{,}\) if for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists \(M\le M_0\) such that

\[ x<M \, \implies\, |f(x)-L|<\varepsilon. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A limit at infinity describes how a function behaves as the input grows without bound: \(f(x)\to L\) as \(x\to+\infty\) means that \(f(x)\) stays as close to \(L\) as we like once \(x\) is large enough. It formalizes long-term or asymptotic behaviour: the line \(y=L\) is then a horizontal asymptote of the graph.

The shaded band is the strip \(|y-L|<\varepsilon\) to the right of the threshold \(M\), and the definition asks that the graph stays inside it for all \(x>M\). The damped oscillation keeps crossing the dashed line \(y=L\): \(f\) need not approach \(L\) monotonically or from one side, only the distance \(|f(x)-L|\) has to become small. A narrower band usually needs a larger \(M\).

Pick \(\varepsilon\), then look for an \(M\) with \(x>M\implies|f(x)-L|<\varepsilon\). For the oscillating example, the smallest working \(M\) jumps as \(\varepsilon\) shrinks.

The bound \(M\) takes over the role of \(\delta\) in the limit at a point: \(\varepsilon\) is given first, and \(M\) may depend on it. The assumption \((M_0,+\infty)\subseteq X\) makes sure that every \(x>M\) belongs to the domain, so the condition says something about \(f\) for all large inputs.

The definition is the continuous counterpart of the limit of a sequence, with \(x>M\) in place of \(n>N\). If \(f(x)\to L\) as \(x\to+\infty\), then also \(f(n)\to L\) as \(n\to\infty\). The converse fails: \(\sin(\pi n)=0\) for every integer \(n\), but \(\sin(\pi x)\) has no limit as \(x\to+\infty\). Limits at infinity return later, for example in improper integrals over unbounded intervals.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Limits at infinity describe behaviour far from any finite region.
  • A function may have different limits at \(+\infty\) and \(-\infty\text{.}\)
  • Limits at infinity may also be infinite: \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to+\infty}f(x)=+\infty\) means that for every \(K\in\mathbb{R}\) there exists \(M\ge M_0\) such that \(x>M\implies f(x)>K\text{;}\) the cases with \(-\infty\) are analogous.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\displaystyle \lim_{x\to+\infty}\frac{1}{x}=0\text{.}\)
  • \(\displaystyle \lim_{x\to-\infty}x^2=+\infty\text{.}\)

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(f\colon X \to\mathbb{R}\) and \(g\colon X \to\mathbb{R}\) be functions that are defined on some punctured neighbourhood of \(x_0\text{.}\) Suppose that \(\lim\limits_{x\to x_0}f(x)=L\text{,}\) and \(\lim\limits_{x\to x_0}g(x)=M\) where \(L\) and \(M\) are real numbers. Then, we have:

\[ \begin{aligned} \lim_{x\to x_0}(f\pm g)(x)&=L\pm M,\\ \lim_{x\to x_0}\max\{f,g\}(x)&=\max\{L, M\},\\ \lim_{x\to x_0}\min\{f,g\}(x)&=\min\{L, M\},\\ \lim_{x\to x_0}(fg)(x)&=LM,\\ \lim_{x\to x_0}(f/g)(x)&=\frac{L}{M}\quad\text{if }M\neq0. \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Limit laws describe how limits at a point interact with algebraic operations on functions: the limit of a sum, difference, product, maximum, minimum or quotient (with a nonzero limit in the denominator) is obtained by applying the same operation to the separate limits. They allow limits of complicated expressions to be evaluated from the limits of simpler components.

In practice the laws are applied step by step. A polynomial is built from constants and \(x\) by sums and products, so \(\lim_{x\to x_0}p(x)=p(x_0)\) for every polynomial \(p\); by the quotient law the same holds for a rational function at every point where its denominator is nonzero. In the language of continuity: sums, products and quotients of continuous functions are continuous wherever they are defined.

The laws work in one direction only. If both limits exist, so does the limit of the combination, but the combination may have a limit when the parts do not: the signum function \(\operatorname{sgn}\) and its negative \(-\operatorname{sgn}\) have no limit at \(0\), yet their sum is the zero function. The laws also do not cover infinite limits; a form such as \(\infty-\infty\) has to be rewritten before any law applies.

A common slip is to apply the quotient law when the denominator tends to \(0\). For \(\lim_{x\to1}\frac{x^2-1}{x-1}\) both parts tend to \(0\), the law does not apply, and \(0/0\) is not a value. Cancelling the factor \(x-1\) first gives \(\lim_{x\to1}(x+1)=2\). Such \(0/0\) cases return later as indeterminate forms.

The same laws hold for one-sided limits and limits at infinity, and they are the function version of the limit laws for sequences.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Limit laws apply only when both limits exist and are real numbers; they do not cover infinite limits or limits that fail to exist.
  • Algebraic combinations preserve convergence.
  • Division requires nonzero limiting denominators.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\displaystyle \lim_{x\to 0}(x^2+\sin x)=0\text{.}\)
  • \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 1}\frac{x^2+1}{x+1}=1\text{.}\)

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \((a_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) and \((b_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) be convergent sequences of real numbers, and let \(x\text{,}\) \(y\) be the real numbers given by \(\displaystyle x=\lim_{n\to\infty}a_n\) and \(\displaystyle y=\lim_{n\to\infty}b_n\text{.}\) Then we have the following laws. In the quotient law, assume \(y\neq0\) and that \(b_n\neq0\) for all sufficiently large \(n\text{.}\)

\[ \begin{aligned} &\lim_{n\to\infty}(a_n\pm b_n)=\lim_{n\to\infty}a_n\pm \lim_{n\to\infty}b_n =x\pm y,\\ &\lim_{n\to\infty}(a_n b_n)=\lim_{n\to\infty}a_n\cdot \lim_{n\to\infty}b_n =xy,\\ &\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{a_n}{b_n}=\frac{\lim\limits_{n\to\infty}a_n}{\lim\limits_{n\to\infty}b_n}=\frac{x}{y}\qquad (\text{if }b_n\text{ and }y\text{ are nonzero}),\\ &\lim_{n\to\infty}\max\{a_n,b_n\} =\max\left\{\lim_{n\to\infty}a_n,\lim_{n\to\infty}b_n\right\} =\max\{x,y\},\\ &\lim_{n\to\infty}\min\{a_n,b_n\} =\min\left\{\lim_{n\to\infty}a_n,\lim_{n\to\infty}b_n\right\} =\min\{x,y\}. \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Limit laws for sequences describe how convergence behaves under algebraic operations: the limit of a sum, product or quotient of convergent sequences is the sum, product or quotient of their limits. They allow limits of complicated sequences to be inferred from simpler ones without returning to the \(\varepsilon\)-\(N\) definition each time.

A typical use is a quotient of polynomials in \(n\), such as

\[ a_n=\frac{3n^2+1}{n^2+2n}. \]

Numerator and denominator both grow without bound, so the quotient law cannot be applied directly. After dividing both by \(n^2\), \(a_n=(3+1/n^2)/(1+2/n)\), and now every part converges: \(3+1/n^2\to3\) and \(1+2/n\to1\ne0\), so \(a_n\to3\).

The hypotheses matter. Every law needs both sequences to converge. If \(a_n\) and \(b_n\) both grow without bound, \(a_n-b_n\) can do anything: \((n+1)-n=1\) for every \(n\), while \(n^2-n\) grows without bound. The quotient law also needs \(y\ne0\): with \(a_n=1\) and \(b_n=1/n\) the quotient \(a_n/b_n=n\) diverges, while with \(a_n=b_n=1/n\) it equals \(1\).

The laws only work in one direction. Convergence of \(a_n+b_n\) does not imply convergence of \(a_n\) and \(b_n\): \((-1)^n+(-1)^{n+1}=0\) for every \(n\). When one factor diverges, the product law gives no information, yet the limit may exist: \((-1)^n\cdot\tfrac{1}{n}\to0\) by the squeeze theorem. The laws for \(\max\) and \(\min\) follow from the others through \(\max\{a,b\}=\tfrac{1}{2}(a+b+|a-b|)\) and \(\min\{a,b\}=\tfrac{1}{2}(a+b-|a-b|)\), since \(|a_n-b_n|\to|x-y|\) by the reverse triangle inequality.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Limit laws apply only to convergent sequences.
  • Algebraic combinations preserve convergence.
  • Division requires nonzero limiting denominators.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(a_n\to 2\) and \(b_n\to 3\text{,}\) then \(a_n+b_n\to 5\text{.}\)
  • If \(a_n\to 1\text{,}\) then \(2a_n\to 2\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(L\in\mathbb{R}\text{.}\) A sequence \((a_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) converges to \(L\) if for every \(\varepsilon >0\text{,}\) there exists an \(N \geq 1\) such that for every \(n\geq N\text{,}\) we have \(|a_n-L|<\varepsilon\text{.}\) In this case, the sequence \((a_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) is called convergent, and \(L\) is called its limit. We write

\[ L=\lim_{n\to\infty} a_n\quad\text{or}\quad a_n\to L\text{ as }n\to\infty. \]

If no such \(L\in\mathbb{R}\) exists, the sequence \((a_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) is called divergent.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The limit of a sequence describes the value approached by its terms as the index increases. The definition formalizes "approached" as eventual closeness: however small a tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\) is chosen, from some index \(N\) on every term lies within \(\varepsilon\) of \(L\).

\(a_n=1/n\to0\): for \(\varepsilon=0.1\), every term with \(n\ge N=11\) (red) lies within \(\varepsilon\) of the limit \(0\), since \(1/n<0.1\) exactly when \(n>10\). A smaller \(\varepsilon\) needs a larger \(N\): for \(\varepsilon=0.01\), \(N=101\) works. The definition asks only that some \(N\) exists for each \(\varepsilon\), not the smallest one.

Shrink \(\varepsilon\) and watch \(N\) grow. Then move the candidate \(L\) away from the limit, or pick \((-1)^n\): no \(N\) keeps every later term in the band.

The order of the quantifiers carries the meaning: first \(\varepsilon\) is given, then \(N\) may be chosen depending on \(\varepsilon\), and the condition must hold for all \(n\ge N\). This last part rules out sequences that only come close now and then. The terms of \((-1)^n\) equal \(1\) infinitely often but also return to \(-1\), so for \(\varepsilon=1\) no \(N\) keeps all later terms within \(\varepsilon\) of any candidate \(L\). Only the tail matters: changing finitely many terms does not change whether the limit exists or what it is.

Two slips are common. "The terms get closer and closer to \(L\)" is not the definition: the terms of \(1/n\) also get closer to \(-1\) at every step, but \(-1\) is not the limit. And the terms need not approach from one side: \((-1)^n/n\) converges to \(0\) while jumping from one side of \(0\) to the other. The same \(\varepsilon\)-idea returns later for limits of functions, as a limit at a point.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Limits of sequences are unique when they exist.
  • Every convergent sequence is bounded.

Enrichment: non-assessable in 2026-27

Every convergent sequence is a Cauchy sequence, and over \(\mathbb{R}\) the converse also holds. The Cauchy criterion is optional enrichment in Math I: Calculus and is not part of the assessable sequence-limit core.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\displaystyle \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}=0\text{.}\)
  • The sequence \((-1)^n\) does not converge.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(f\) be a function defined on a domain \(X\subseteq \mathbb{R}\text{.}\) A point \(x=x_{\mathrm{max}}\) is a local maximum point (aka relative maximum point) of \(f\) if there exists some \(\varepsilon > 0\) such that \(f(x_{\mathrm{max}}) \geq f(x)\) for all \(x \in X\) with \(|x-x_{\mathrm{max}}|<\varepsilon\text{.}\) Similarly, \(x=x_{\mathrm{min}}\) is a local minimum point (aka relative minimum point) of \(f\) if there exists some \(\varepsilon > 0\) such that \(f(x_{\mathrm{min}}) \leq f(x)\) for all \(x \in X\) with \(|x-x_{\mathrm{min}}|<\varepsilon\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A local extremum is a point where a function attains a maximum or minimum relative to nearby values: the comparison is made only with the points of the domain within some distance \(\varepsilon\), not with the whole domain. It captures optimal behaviour in a neighbourhood rather than globally.

The figure shows \(f(x)=x^3-3x\), with a local maximum at \(x_{\max}=-1\), where \(f(-1)=2\), and a local minimum at \(x_{\min}=1\), where \(f(1)=-2\). Inside each shaded strip of half-width \(\varepsilon\), the marked value is the largest, respectively the smallest, value of \(f\). Neither is global: \(f(x)>2\) for \(x>2\) and \(f(x)<-2\) for \(x<-2\).

Grow the neighbourhood radius \(\varepsilon\): the comparison \(f(x_{\max})\ge f(x)\) only has to hold for \(x\) within \(\varepsilon\) of the point, not on the whole domain. A local extremum only needs one \(\varepsilon>0\) that works.

The definition only asks for some \(\varepsilon>0\), and a smaller \(\varepsilon\) can only make the comparison easier. The inequality is not strict, so a constant function has a local maximum and a local minimum at every point. Only points of the domain are compared, which is why an endpoint can be a local extremum: \(f(x)=x\) on \([0,1]\) has a local minimum at \(0\), although its one-sided derivative there is \(1\).

Every global extremum is a local one, but not conversely. To find local extrema at interior points, one first lists the critical points with the first-order condition and then checks each of them by comparing nearby values. The definition returns in Math IV for functions of several variables as a local maximum or minimum.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Under this definition a local extremum may occur at an interior point or at a boundary point of the domain. The first-order condition applies only to interior points where \(f\) is differentiable; boundary points must be examined separately.
  • Local extrema need not be global.
  • Critical points are candidates for local extrema.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The function \(f(x)=x^2\) has a local minimum at \(x=0\text{.}\)
  • The function \(f(x)=x^3\) has no local extremum.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The logarithm of a positive real number \(x\) with respect to base \(b\) (\(b>0\) and \(b\neq 1\)) is the exponent to which \(b\) must be raised to get \(x\text{.}\) In other words, the logarithm of \(x\) to base \(b\) is the solution \(y\) to the equation \(b^y=x\text{.}\) This logarithm is denoted by \(\log_b x\text{.}\) The function \(g(x)=\log_b x\) on \(\mathbb{R}^+\) is called the logarithmic function of \(x\) to base \(b\text{.}\) It is the inverse of the exponential function with base \(b\text{.}\) The logarithm with base \(\mathrm{e}\) is called the natural logarithm, denoted \(\ln x\text{.}\) Without a base, \(\log x\) usually means \(\ln x\) in analysis texts but \(\log_{10}x\) in some other texts, so it is safest to state the base.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The logarithm answers the question "which power?": \(\log_b x\) is the exponent \(y\) with \(b^y=x\). Logarithmic functions therefore measure exponents and invert exponential growth, and they transform multiplicative relationships into additive ones.

\(\ln\) undoes \(\mathrm{e}^x\): the points \((0,1)\), \((1,\mathrm{e})\) on \(y=\mathrm{e}^x\) mirror to \((1,0)\), \((\mathrm{e},1)\) on \(y=\ln x\), so \(\ln 1=0\) and \(\ln \mathrm{e}=1\). The reflection in the dashed line \(y=x\) swaps inputs and outputs, so the logarithm accepts only positive inputs but can return any real number.

Change the base \(b\) and drag across the plot: every point \((x,b^x)\) has a mirror image \((b^x,x)\) on the graph of \(\log_b\), reflected in the line \(y=x\).

The restrictions in the definition come from the exponential function. For \(b>0\) with \(b\neq1\), every value \(b^y\) is positive and every positive number is reached exactly once, so \(\log_b x\) exists only for \(x>0\) and is then unique. The base \(b=1\) is excluded because \(1^y=1\) for every \(y\): the equation \(1^y=x\) has no solution for \(x\neq1\) and infinitely many for \(x=1\). For \(b>1\) the logarithm is negative on \((0,1)\), zero at \(x=1\) and positive beyond.

The product law is the reason logarithms turn growth factors into increments: multiplying \(x\) by \(b\) adds exactly \(1\) to \(\log_b x\). Different bases differ only by a constant factor, \(\log_b x=\ln x/\ln b\), so the natural logarithm, with base Euler's number, is enough in practice.

A common slip is to apply the product law to sums: \(\log_b(x+y)\) is in general not \(\log_b x+\log_b y\). For instance, \(\log_2(1+1)=1\), whereas \(\log_2 1+\log_2 1=0\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Logarithms are defined only for positive inputs.
  • Logarithmic functions are strictly monotone.
  • We have the following results:
    • Product law: \(\displaystyle \log_b(xy)=\log_b x+\log_b y\text{;}\)
    • Quotient law: \(\displaystyle \log_b(x/y)=\log_b x-\log_b y\text{;}\)
    • Power law: \(\displaystyle \log_b\left(x^\alpha\right)=\alpha\log_b x\text{.}\)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\ln\mathrm{e}=1\text{.}\)
  • \(\log_2 8=3\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(E\) be a subset of \(\mathbb{R}\text{,}\) and let \(M\) be a real number. We say that \(M\) is a lower bound for \(E\) if we have \(x \geq M\) for every element \(x\) in \(E\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A lower bound of a set is a value that does not exceed any element of the set: it marks a level that the set never goes below. Lower bounds describe constraints from below without requiring attainability.

Here \(E\) consists of the point \(-1.1\) and the numbers in \((-0.5,2]\). The marked \(m_1\), \(m_2\) and \(m_3\) are lower bounds, and so is every \(m\le-1.1\); the greatest one is \(\inf E=-1.1=\min E\). The number \(-1\) is not a lower bound, because the single element \(-1.1\) lies below it.

The set \(E\) specifies which elements must be compared. The inequality \(M\le x\) must hold for every \(x\in E\); \(M\) need not be an element of \(E\). Lower bounds are never unique: if \(M\) is one, so is every smaller number. The useful question is therefore which lower bound is the largest, and that is the infimum.

A common slip is to negate the definition incorrectly. \(M\) fails to be a lower bound as soon as one element \(x\in E\) satisfies \(x<M\). So \(\mathbb{Z}\) has no lower bound, every nonempty finite set has its smallest element as one, and for the empty set every real number is a lower bound, since there is nothing to compare.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(M\) is a lower bound for \(E\), then so is every \(M'\le M\text{;}\) hence lower bounds are never unique.
  • Lower bounds need not belong to the set.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Both sets \((0,1)\) and \(\{0,1\}\) share the same lower bound \(0\text{.}\)
  • Any number less than \(0\) is also a lower bound of \((0,1)\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(P(n)\) be a statement about a natural number \(n\). The principle of mathematical induction says: if

  1. base case: \(P(0)\) is true, and
  2. inductive step: for every natural number \(k\), \(P(k)\) implies \(P(k+1)\),

then \(P(n)\) is true for every \(n\in\mathbb{N}\).

This is the fifth Peano axiom, where the successor \(S(k)\) is written \(k+1\) once addition is available. A proof by induction checks the base case and proves the inductive step. In the step, \(k\) is an arbitrary but fixed natural number, and the assumption that \(P(k)\) holds is called the inductive hypothesis.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Induction works like a row of dominoes. The base case knocks over the first domino. The inductive step says that whichever domino falls, it knocks over the next one. Together they make every domino fall: \(P(0)\) gives \(P(1)\), \(P(1)\) gives \(P(2)\), and so on through all of \(\mathbb{N}\).

The green arrow is the base case: it pushes \(P(0)\). Each blue arc is one instance of the inductive step, and the arc from \(P(k)\) to \(P(k+1)\) stands for all of them at once, because \(k\) is arbitrary. The green line underneath is the conclusion: \(P(n)\) holds for every natural number \(n\).

Neither part works alone. A step without a base case is a chain of dominoes that nobody pushes, and a base case without a step knocks over only the first domino. Checking \(P(0),P(1),\ldots,P(40)\) one by one is still not a proof for every \(n\).

The inductive step proves an implication. It does not claim that \(P(k)\) is true; it shows that \(P(k+1)\) would follow if \(P(k)\) were true. Assuming "\(P(n)\) for every \(n\)" in the step would assume the very statement to be proved.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Set form. If \(A\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) contains \(0\), and \(k+1\in A\) whenever \(k\in A\), then \(A=\mathbb{N}\). Apply the principle to the statement "\(n\in A\)".
  • Starting at \(n_0\). If \(P(n_0)\) is true and \(P(k)\) implies \(P(k+1)\) for every integer \(k\ge n_0\), then \(P(n)\) is true for every integer \(n\ge n_0\). Apply the principle to \(Q(m)\): "\(P(n_0+m)\)". Statements about positive integers start at \(n_0=1\).
  • Both parts are needed. For \(P(n)\): "\(n^2+n+1\) is even", the step holds, since \((k+1)^2+(k+1)+1=(k^2+k+1)+2(k+1)\). But \(P(0)\) fails, and in fact \(n^2+n+1\) is odd for every \(n\). For \(P(n)\): "\(n^2-n+41\) is prime", the cases \(n=0,1,\ldots,40\) are all true, but \(n=41\) gives \(41^2\).
  • Recursion and induction go together. The factorial is defined recursively: \(0!=1\), and \((k+1)!=(k+1)\times k!\) for every \(k\in\mathbb{N}\). Statements about a recursively defined quantity are proved by induction: the value at \(0\) settles the base case, and the rule from \(k\) to \(k+1\) drives the step. Powers (\(m^0=1\), \(m^{k+1}=m^k m\)) and multiplication on \(\mathbb{N}\) (\(0\cdot m=0\), \(S(n)\cdot m=n\cdot m+m\)) can be built the same way.
  • Several variables. For a statement about \(n\) and \(m\), such as \(n\cdot S(m)=n\cdot m+n\), fix \(m\) and induct on \(n\): the base case is \(n=0\) for that \(m\), and the step goes from \(n\) to \(S(n)\) with the same \(m\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A sum formula. For every \(n\in\mathbb{N}\),

    \[ 0+1+2+\cdots+n=\frac{n(n+1)}{2}. \]

    Base case: for \(n=0\) both sides are \(0\). Inductive step: assume \(0+1+\cdots+k=k(k+1)/2\) for some \(k\in\mathbb{N}\). Then

    \[ 0+1+\cdots+k+(k+1) =\frac{k(k+1)}{2}+(k+1) =\frac{(k+1)(k+2)}{2}, \]

    which is the formula for \(n=k+1\). This is the arithmetic series \(1+2+\cdots+n\).

  • Odd numbers. \(1+3+\cdots+(2n-1)=n^2\) for every integer \(n\ge1\). For \(n=1\), \(1=1^2\). If \(1+3+\cdots+(2k-1)=k^2\), adding the next odd number \(2k+1\) gives \(k^2+2k+1=(k+1)^2\).

  • Divisibility. \(3^{2n}-1\) is divisible by \(8\) for every integer \(n\ge1\). For \(n=1\), \(3^2-1=8\). If \(3^{2k}-1=8m\) for an integer \(m\), then

    \[ \begin{aligned} 3^{2(k+1)}-1&=9\cdot3^{2k}-1\\ &=9(3^{2k}-1)+8\\ &=8(9m+1). \end{aligned} \]

  • An inequality. \(n+1\le2^n\) for every \(n\in\mathbb{N}\). For \(n=0\), \(1\le1\). If \(k+1\le2^k\), then, since \(1\le2^k\),

    \[ (k+1)+1\le2^k+2^k=2^{k+1}. \]

  • From a recursive definition. With multiplication defined by \(0\cdot m=0\) and \(S(n)\cdot m=n\cdot m+m\), the rule \(n\cdot0=0\) needs a proof, because \(0\) stands on the right. For \(n=0\) it is the definition. If \(n\cdot0=0\), then \(S(n)\cdot0=n\cdot0+0=0\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(E\subseteq \mathbb{R}\) be a set. The maximum of \(E\text{,}\) denoted by \(\max E\text{,}\) is the largest element in \(E\) if it exists. That is, \(\max E= x\) if \(x\in E\) and \(x\geq y\) for all \(y\in E\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The maximum of a set is its largest element: a value that belongs to the set and is at least as large as every other element. Not every set has one: a set can be bounded above without any element being on top.

Both sets in the figure lie between \(0\) and \(1\). The closed interval \([0,1]\) contains \(1\), so its maximum is \(1\). The open interval \((0,1)\) has no maximum: for any \(x\in(0,1)\), the midpoint \(\tfrac{1}{2}(x+1)\) also lies in \((0,1)\) and is larger. Its supremum is still \(1\), but \(1\notin(0,1)\).

The definition has two parts. The inequality \(x\ge y\) for all \(y\in E\) says that \(x\) is an upper bound; the condition \(x\in E\) says that this bound is attained. An upper bound outside the set is therefore not a maximum. The two parts also give uniqueness: if \(x\) and \(x'\) are both maxima, then \(x\ge x'\) and \(x'\ge x\).

A set has a maximum if and only if it has a supremum that belongs to the set, and then \(\max E=\sup E\). Every nonempty finite set has a maximum; infinite sets such as \((0,1)\) or \(\mathbb{N}\) may have none. The minimum of a set is the mirror image. Later, the extreme value theorem gives conditions under which the set of values of a function has a maximum.

A common slip is to write \(\max E\) where only \(\sup E\) exists. The set \(\{1-\tfrac{1}{n}\colon n\ge1\}\) has supremum \(1\) but no maximum, since every element is below \(1\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A set can have at most one maximum.
  • The maximum, if it exists, is the least upper bound for the set.
  • A set may have upper bounds without having a maximum.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The set \(\{1,\,2,\,3\}\) has maximum \(3\text{.}\)
  • The interval \((0,1)\) has no maximum.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(a < b\) be real numbers, and consider a function \(f\colon [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}\) that is continuous on \([a, b]\) and differentiable on \((a, b)\text{.}\) Then, we can assert that there exists a \(c \in (a, b)\) such that

\[ \displaystyle f'(c) =\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}\text{.} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The mean value theorem links the average rate of change of \(f\) over an interval with its instantaneous rate of change: somewhere strictly between \(a\) and \(b\), the derivative equals the slope of the secant through \((a,f(a))\) and \((b,f(b))\). If a car covers \(100\) km in one hour, then at some moment its speed is exactly \(100\) km/h.

The figure shows \(f(x)=x^3-x\) on \([-2,2]\). The secant has slope \((f(2)-f(-2))/4=(6+6)/4=3\), and \(f'(c)=3c^2-1=3\) gives \(c=\pm2/\sqrt{3}\approx\pm1.15\). These are the points \(c_1\) and \(c_2\), where the tangents are parallel to the secant. The theorem promises at least one such point; it says nothing about how many there are or where they lie.

Move \(a\) and \(b\): there is always a point \(c\in(a,b)\) where the tangent is parallel to the secant. With \(|x|\) and \(0\in(a,b)\) the hypothesis fails, and so can the conclusion.

Both hypotheses are needed. Without continuity at an endpoint the conclusion can fail: \(f(x)=x\) on \([0,1)\) with \(f(1)=0\) has secant slope \(0\), but \(f'(x)=1\) on \((0,1)\). Without differentiability at a single interior point it can fail too: for \(|x|\) on \([-1,2]\) the secant slope is \(\tfrac{1}{3}\), while the derivative only takes the values \(-1\) and \(1\). Differentiability at the endpoints themselves is not required.

Rolle’s theorem is the special case \(f(a)=f(b)\), and the general theorem follows from it by subtracting the secant line from \(f\). In practice the theorem is used in the form \(f(y)-f(x)=f'(c)(y-x)\) from the Key Results, which turns information about \(f'\) into information about \(f\): the sign of \(f'\) gives monotonicity, and a bound \(|f'|\le M\) on an interval gives \(|f(y)-f(x)|\le M|y-x|\) for all \(x,y\) in it.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The theorem requires continuity on a closed interval and differentiability on the open interval.
  • It justifies the derivative sign test. Applying the theorem on \([x,y]\) gives \(f(y)-f(x)=f'(c)(y-x)\) for some \(c\in(x,y)\text{,}\) so the sign of \(f'\) on the interior determines whether \(f\) is increasing, decreasing, or constant.
  • Two functions with the same derivative. If \(f,g\) are continuous on \([a,b]\) and differentiable on \((a,b)\) with \(f'=g'\) on \((a,b)\text{,}\) then \(f=g+C\) on \([a,b]\) for some constant \(C\text{.}\) The domain has to be an interval for this to hold.
  • The version above is Lagrange's mean value theorem, and it is what "the mean value theorem" means in this course. The two-function version due to Cauchy, which underlies L'Hôpital's rule, is optional and non-assessable.
  • It generalizes the Rolle’s theorem.
  • The conclusion does not specify the location of the point.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(f(x)=x^2\) on \([0,1]\), the secant slope is \((1-0)/(1-0)=1\). Solving \(f'(c)=2c=1\) gives \(c=1/2\).
  • For \(f(x)=3x+2\) on any interval \([a,b]\) with \(a<b\), the secant slope and derivative both equal \(3\), so every \(c\in(a,b)\) satisfies the conclusion.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(E\subseteq \mathbb{R}\) be a set. The minimum of \(E\text{,}\) denoted by \(\min E\text{,}\) is the smallest element in \(E\) if it exists. That is, \(\min E = x\) if \(x\in E\) and \(x\leq y\) for all \(y\in E\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The minimum of a set represents the smallest value that is actually attained within the set.

It formalizes the idea of a smallest element, distinguishing it from lower bounds that may not belong to the set.

The set \(S=\{1,\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{3},\dots\}\) has no minimum. Its elements approach \(0\), but \(0\notin S\), so \(\inf S=0\) is not attained.

The defining inequality compares the proposed minimum with every element, and membership requires that the proposed value actually occur. A lower bound outside the set is therefore not a minimum.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A set can have at most one minimum.
  • The minimum, if it exists, is always the greatest lower bound for the set.
  • A set may have lower bounds without having a minimum.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The set \(\{1,\,2,\,3\}\) has minimum \(1\text{.}\)
  • The interval \((0,1)\) has no minimum.
