docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A point \(x_0\) is called a singularity of a function \(f\) if \(f\) fails to be defined or continuous at \(x=x_0\text{,}\) while being defined and continuous in a punctured neighbourhood of \(x_0\text{.}\)

Lecture 5 classifies these problem points by their one-sided limits:

  • Removable: the finite limit exists, but \(f(x_0)\) is missing or has the wrong value.
  • Jump: both one-sided limits are finite but unequal.
  • Infinite: at least one one-sided limit is \(+\infty\) or \(-\infty\text{.}\)
  • Oscillatory: a one-sided limit fails because of persistent oscillation.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A singularity marks a point where a function fails to behave regularly, although it is defined and continuous at all points close to it. The question is what goes wrong at that single point, and the one-sided limits answer it.

The four types can be read as a sequence of questions. If both one-sided limits are finite and equal, the singularity is removable: defining or redefining \(f(x_0)\) as the common limit makes \(f\) continuous at \(x_0\). If they are finite but different, no value of \(f(x_0)\) helps, and the jump has size \(f(x_0^+)-f(x_0^-)\). If one of them is infinite, the graph has a vertical asymptote at \(x=x_0\). If a one-sided limit fails to exist because the values keep oscillating, the singularity is oscillatory.

A typical removable singularity: \(\frac{\sin x}{x}\) is undefined at \(0\) but has limit \(1\) there, so setting the value \(1\) at \(0\) gives a function that is continuous on all of \(\mathbb{R}\).

A common slip concerns points outside the domain. The function \(1/x\) is continuous at every point of its domain \(\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}\); what fails at \(0\) is that \(1/x\) cannot be extended to a function continuous at \(0\). Calling \(0\) a discontinuity of \(1/x\) should be read in this sense, not as a point of the domain where continuity fails.

The word returns later with improper integrals, where a function that is unbounded near a point, such as \(1/\sqrt{x}\) near \(0\), is integrated by taking a limit.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• At an interior point, \(f\) is continuous if and only if \(f(x_0^-)=f(x_0^+)=f(x_0)\text{;}\) a discontinuity is exactly a failure of this equality.
  • Several distinct things can go wrong at \(x_0\text{:}\) \(f(x_0)\) may be undefined while nearby values behave well; \(f\) may be defined but not continuous; nearby values may become unbounded; or nearby values may oscillate without approaching anything.
  • The word singularity returns in Lecture 12 for improper integrals: an integrand may be unbounded at an interior singularity, and the integral is then split there.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The function \(f(x) = (x^2 - 1)/(x - 1)\) has a removable discontinuity at \(x=1\text{.}\)
  • The piecewise function \(f(x)=x\) for \(x\leq 0\) and \(f(x)=x+1\) for \(x>0\) has a jump discontinuity at \(x=0\text{;}\) so does the signum function at the origin.
  • The function \(f(x)=1/x\) has an infinite discontinuity at \(x=0\text{.}\)
  • The function \(f(x) = \sin(1/x)\) has an oscillatory discontinuity at \(x=0\text{.}\)

The three graphs illustrate singularities at \(x=0\). The first is removable because changing the assigned value \(-1\) to the limit \(0\) restores continuity; the second has unequal one-sided limits \(0.5\) and \(1\); and the third, \(1/x\), has an infinite singularity.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Suppose that \(g(x)\leq f(x)\leq h(x)\) for every \(x\) sufficiently close to \(x_0\), except perhaps at \(x=x_0\) itself. If

\[ \lim_{x\to x_0}g(x)=\lim_{x\to x_0}h(x)=L, \]

then \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to x_0}f(x)=L\text{.}\)

For a one-sided limit, use the inequalities only on that side and replace all three limits by the matching one-sided limits.

The same statement holds for limits as \(x\to+\infty\) or \(x\to-\infty\): the inequalities need only hold for sufficiently large \(|x|\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The squeeze theorem shows that a function inherits its limit from two bounding functions: if \(f\) is trapped between \(g\) and \(h\) near \(x_0\) and both bounds approach the same value \(L\), then \(f\) has no room to do anything else and must approach \(L\) as well. It is useful exactly when \(f\) is hard to analyse directly but easy to bound.

Both parts of the hypothesis are needed. The limits at the point of the lower and upper bounding functions must be the same finite value: \(-1\le\sin(1/x)\le1\) for all \(x\neq0\), but the bounds stay at \(-1\) and \(1\), and \(\sin(1/x)\) has no limit at \(0\). A bound on the values alone does not force a limit. The inequalities only have to hold near \(x_0\), except perhaps at \(x_0\) itself, because the limit ignores the value at \(x_0\) and everything outside a small punctured neighbourhood.

Two forms are used most often. If \(|f(x)-L|\le h(x)\) and \(h(x)\to0\), then \(f(x)\to L\); this is the squeeze with the bounds \(L-h\) and \(L+h\). If \(u\) is a bounded function, \(|u(x)|\le K\), and \(v(x)\to0\), then \(u(x)v(x)\to0\), since \(|u(x)v(x)|\le K|v(x)|\). The squeeze also proves \(\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin x}{x}=1\) from the inequalities \(\cos x\le\frac{\sin x}{x}\le1\) for \(0<|x|<\tfrac{\pi}{2}\).

The theorem is the function version of the squeeze theorem for sequences, and it holds in the same form for one-sided limits and limits at infinity.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The function must be bounded above and below by convergent functions.
  • Equality of the bounding limits forces convergence.
  • The theorem applies even when the middle function is difficult to analyse directly.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\displaystyle \lim_{x\to 0}x^2\sin(1/x)=0\) follows from squeezing between \(\pm x^2\text{.}\)

  • Oscillatory functions can converge when tightly bounded.

Zoom in on \(x_0=0\): however fast \(x^2\sin(1/x)\) oscillates, it stays between \(-x^2\) and \(x^2\), which both tend to \(0\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: Let \((a_n)_{n=1}^\infty\text{,}\) \((b_n)_{n=1}^\infty\text{,}\) and \((c_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) be sequences of real numbers such that \(a_n\leq b_n\leq c_n\) for all \(n \geq 1\text{.}\) Suppose also that \((a_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) and \((c_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) converge to the same limit \(L\text{.}\) Then \((b_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) also converges to \(L\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The squeeze theorem proves convergence by trapping: a sequence caught between two sequences with the same limit has nowhere else to go. It is the standard tool when \(b_n\) is hard to handle directly but easy to bound by simpler sequences.

In the figure, \(c_n\) approaches \(L\) from above and \(a_n\) from below, while the middle sequence \(b_n\) oscillates around \(L\). The oscillation does not matter: \(b_n\) always stays between \(a_n\) and \(c_n\), and the gap between them shrinks to \(0\).

Shrink \(\varepsilon\): from the index where both \(a_n\) and \(c_n\) are inside the band, \(b_n\) is trapped inside too, so it converges to the same \(L\).

Both hypotheses are needed. The outer limits must be equal: \(b_n=1+(-1)^n\) lies between \(a_n=0\) and \(c_n=2\) but alternates between \(0\) and \(2\). Both bounds are needed too: \(b_n=-n\) satisfies \(b_n\le\frac{1}{n}\) with \(\frac{1}{n}\to0\), yet diverges. The inequalities only have to hold from some index on, since finitely many terms do not affect a limit. Unlike the monotone convergence theorem, the theorem needs no monotonicity, and it gives both the existence and the value of the limit.

In practice the theorem is often used in the form \(|b_n-L|\le d_n\) with \(d_n\to0\), which is the theorem with \(a_n=L-d_n\) and \(c_n=L+d_n\). For example, \(\left|\frac{(-1)^n}{n}\right|\le\frac{1}{n}\) gives \(\frac{(-1)^n}{n}\to0\). The same trapping argument returns later for functions in the squeeze theorem for functions.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The middle sequence \((b_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) must lie termwise between two convergent sequences.
  • Equality of outer limits enforces convergence of the middle sequence.
  • The theorem does not require monotonicity.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(-1/n \le b_n \le 1/n\text{,}\) then \(b_n\to 0\text{.}\)
  • \(\lim\limits_{n\to\infty}\left(n \cdot\sin(1/n)\right)= 1\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a differentiable function \(f\colon X\to\mathbb{R}\text{,}\) a stationary point of \(f\) is a point \(x_0\in X\) where its derivative is zero, i.e., \(f'(x_0)=0\text{;}\) the corresponding point \((x_0,f(x_0))\) on the graph of \(f\) is sometimes also called a stationary point.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A stationary point is a point where the derivative is zero: the tangent to the graph is horizontal, and to first order the function is not changing there. Stationary points are the candidates for local extrema of a differentiable function at interior points.

The curve in the figure has three stationary points, each marked with a horizontal tangent: two peaks, which are local maxima, and a valley between them, which is a local minimum. At each of them the curve turns from rising to falling or the other way round, so \(f'\) changes sign there.

Every stationary point has a horizontal tangent. Most here are peaks or valleys, but \(x^3\) shows a stationary point that is neither.

A zero derivative alone does not say what happens nearby: the function may have a peak, a valley or neither, as \(x^3\) at \(0\) shows. Whether a stationary point is a local extremum has to be checked by comparing \(f(x)\) with \(f(x_0)\) for \(x\) near \(x_0\); the second-order condition later gives a shortcut.

Every stationary point is a critical point, but critical points also include points where \(f'\) does not exist; for a differentiable function the two notions coincide.

A common slip is to confuse a stationary point with a zero of \(f\). The condition is \(f'(x_0)=0\), not \(f(x_0)=0\): \(x^2+1\) has a stationary point at \(0\) but no zeros.

Stationary points return for functions of several variables in Math III and Math IV, with the gradient equal to zero in place of \(f'(x_0)=0\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Not every stationary point corresponds to an extremum.
  • Stationary points must be analysed further to determine behaviour.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The function \(f(x)=x^2\) has a stationary point at \(x=0\text{.}\)
  • The function \(f(x)=x^3\) has a stationary point that is not an extremum.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Where this appears in the course

Subsequences are not defined in the 2026-27 lectures. The definition is given inside the tutorial question that uses it (Tutorial 2), and this page records it in the same form.

Let \((a_n)_{n\ge m}\) be a sequence. A subsequence of \((a_n)\) is a new sequence \((a_{n_k})_{k\ge 1}\) obtained by selecting terms of \((a_n)\) along a strictly increasing sequence of indices \((n_k)_{k\ge 1}\) with \(n_k \ge m\):

\[ (a_{n_k})_{k\ge 1} = a_{n_1},\,a_{n_2},\,a_{n_3},\,\dots, \]

where \(m \le n_1 < n_2 < n_3 < \cdots.\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A subsequence is what you get when you thin out a sequence while keeping the original order. You choose infinitely many of its terms, further and further along, and you may not reorder or repeat them.

The figure keeps the even-indexed terms of \(a_n=(-1)^n\left(1+\frac{1}{n}\right)\), so \(n_k=2k\) and \(a_{n_k}=1+\frac{1}{2k}\). These terms, \(a_2=1.5\), \(a_4=1.25\), \(a_6\approx1.17,\dots\), decrease to \(1\), while the skipped odd-indexed terms tend to \(-1\).

Choose the indices \(n_k\): the even and odd subsequences of \(a_n=(-1)^n\left(1+\frac1n\right)\) converge to different limits, which is why the whole sequence diverges.

The condition \(n_1<n_2<\cdots\) makes a subsequence a sequence in its own right. Because the indices are integers that strictly increase, \(n_k\ge k\) when the sequence starts at \(n=1\), so the subsequence runs through the tail of \((a_n)\) as \(k\) grows. This is why every subsequence of a sequence with limit \(L\) also has limit \(L\). Lists such as \(a_1,a_1,a_2,a_3,\dots\) or \(a_2,a_1,a_4,a_3,\dots\) are not subsequences.

Subsequences are the usual tool for proving divergence: two subsequences with different limits, as in the figure, show that \((a_n)\) has no limit. They also return in Math III, where the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem states that every bounded sequence has a convergent subsequence.

A common slip is to run the implication backwards. One convergent subsequence says nothing about the whole sequence: \((-1)^n\) has the constant subsequence \(1,1,1,\dots\) but diverges.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every subsequence of a sequence uses terms from the original sequence, but with a new index set \(n_1<n_2<\cdots\text{.}\)
  • If \(a_n \to L\text{,}\) then every subsequence \(a_{n_k}\) also converges to \(L\text{.}\)
  • Subsequence limits help detect non-convergence: if two subsequences converge to different limits, then the original sequence does not converge.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(a_n = (-1)^n\text{,}\) then \((a_{2k})_{k\ge 1} = 1,1,1,\dots\) and \((a_{2k-1})_{k\ge 1} = -1,-1,-1,\dots\) are subsequences.
  • If \(a_n = \dfrac{1}{n}\text{,}\) then \(a_{2k}=\dfrac{1}{2k}\) is a subsequence, and it still converges to \(0\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(A\text{,}\) \(B\) be sets. We say that \(A\) is a subset of \(B\text{,}\) denoted \(A\subseteq B\text{,}\) if every element of \(A\) is also an element of \(B\text{,}\) i.e.,

\[ \text{for any object }x,\; x\in A \; \implies\; x\in B. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A subset describes containment between collections of objects: \(A\subseteq B\) means that whatever belongs to \(A\) also belongs to \(B\). The definition allows \(A=B\).

In the left panel the disc \(A\) lies entirely inside \(B\), so every \(x\in A\) is also in \(B\). In the right panel \(A\) sticks out of \(B\), and the single marked point \(x\in A\) with \(x otin B\) is enough to show that \(A ot\subseteq B\). To prove \(A\subseteq B\), take an arbitrary \(x\in A\) and show \(x\in B\); to disprove it, one point of \(A\) outside \(B\) suffices.

Since the definition is an implication, there is nothing to check when \(A=\varnothing\), which is why the empty set is a subset of every set. Inclusion in both directions gives equality: \(A\subseteq B\) and \(B\subseteq A\) together mean \(A=B\). A proper subset adds the requirement \(A eq B\).

A common slip is to expect any two sets to be comparable, as any two numbers are under \(\le\): neither \(\{1\}\subseteq\{2\}\) nor \(\{2\}\subseteq\{1\}\) holds.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every set is a subset of itself.
  • Subset relations are transitive, i.e., \(A\subseteq B\) and \(B\subseteq C\) implies \(A\subseteq C\text{.}\)
  • Proper subsets exclude equality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\{1,\,2\}\subseteq\{1,\,2,\,3\}\text{.}\)
  • \(\varnothing\) is a subset of every set.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The operation of subtraction \(x-y\) of two integers \(x\) and \(y\) is defined as

\[ x-y=x+(-y). \]

The result is called the difference between \(x\) and \(y\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The difference \(x-y\) measures how much larger \(x\) is than \(y\): it answers "what must be added to \(y\) to reach \(x\)?", since \(y+(x-y)=x\). Its sign tells which number is larger, and its absolute value \(|x-y|\) is the distance between \(x\) and \(y\) on the number line.

Subtraction is defined using addition and negation, \(x-y=x+(-y)\), to ensure algebraic consistency: every property of subtraction follows from the rules of addition. This also explains why subtraction is less well behaved. It is not commutative, since \(y-x=-(x-y)\), and not associative: \((5-3)-1=1\), but \(5-(3-1)=3\). A minus sign before brackets therefore changes every sign inside, \(x-(y-z)=x-y+z\). The difference set \(A\setminus B\) uses the same word for removing the elements of \(B\) from \(A\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Subtraction is not commutative.
  • The difference \(x-y\) equals \(x+(-y)\text{.}\)
  • Subtraction extends addition within the integers.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(E\subseteq\mathbb{R}\) be nonempty and bounded above. The supremum of \(E\) is its least upper bound, denoted by \(\sup E\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The supremum of a set is its least upper bound: the smallest number that no element of the set exceeds. It describes where a set ends on the right even when no element sits there, that is, even when the set has no maximum.

For \(E=(0,1)\), every number from \(1\) onwards is an upper bound, such as the marked \(1.6\) and \(2.2\); together they form the shaded ray \([1,\infty)\). Its left end is the least upper bound, so \(\sup E=1\), although \(1\notin E\).

Move the candidate \(u\): every number at or above \(\sup E\) is an upper bound, and for every \(\varepsilon>0\) some element of \(E\) lies within \(\varepsilon\) below it, which is what makes it the least one.

Being the least upper bound has two parts: \(u=\sup E\) is an upper bound, and no smaller number is one. The second part is usually checked with an \(\varepsilon\): for every \(\varepsilon>0\) some \(x\in E\) satisfies \(x>u-\varepsilon\). For \((0,1)\) and \(0<\varepsilon<1\), the element \(1-\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}\) lies above \(1-\varepsilon\).

The existence of suprema is the completeness of the real numbers, and several results depend on it: the monotone convergence theorem identifies its limit as a supremum, and the \(n\)-th root is defined as one. The mirror notion is the infimum.

A common slip is to treat \(\sup E\) as the largest element of \(E\). It is the largest element exactly when it belongs to \(E\), and then \(\sup E=\max E\); for \((0,1)\) it does not belong to the set.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A supremum need not belong to the set.
  • By the least-upper-bound property (see real number) of \(\mathbb{R}\text{,}\) every nonempty subset of \(\mathbb{R}\) that is bounded above has a unique supremum.
  • In the extended real numbers, one uses the conventions \(\sup E=+\infty\) for a nonempty set with no upper bound and \(\sup\varnothing=-\infty\text{;}\) neither \(+\infty\) nor \(-\infty\) is a real number.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The supremum of \((0,1)\) is \(1\text{.}\)
  • The supremum of \(\{x\in\mathbb{R}\colon x<2\}\) is \(2\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A function \(f\colon X\to Y\) is surjective if for every \(y \in Y\text{,}\) there exists an \(x \in X\) such that \(f (x) = y\text{.}\) In other words, a function is onto if its codomain is exactly its range.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Surjectivity describes how completely a function covers its codomain: every element of \(Y\) must be the output of at least one input, so no element of the codomain is left unused.

In the left diagram each of the three points of \(Y\) receives at least one arrow, the top one even two, so the function is surjective; sharing an output is allowed. In the right diagram the bottom point of \(Y\), drawn hollow, receives no arrow, so that function is not surjective, even though every input is used.

To prove surjectivity, take an arbitrary \(y\in Y\) and find an \(x\in X\) with \(f(x)=y\), usually by solving this equation for \(x\). For \(f(x)=x^3\) on \(\mathbb{R}\) the solution is \(x=\sqrt[3]{y}\). To disprove it, a single \(y\) without a solution suffices, as \(y=-1\) shows for \(x^2\) on \(\mathbb{R}\). In terms of the range, \(f\) is surjective if and only if its range equals \(Y\); for a function on a subset of \(\mathbb{R}\), every horizontal line \(y=c\) with \(c\in Y\) must meet the graph at least once.

Surjectivity is a property of the rule together with the codomain: with codomain \([0,+\infty)\) instead of \(\mathbb{R}\), the function \(x^2\) becomes surjective. Together with injectivity it makes \(f\) a bijection: surjectivity guarantees at least one solution of \(f(x)=y\), injectivity at most one.

A common slip is to check the inputs instead of the outputs. That every input has an output is true for every function; surjectivity is about every element of the codomain.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A function is surjective if every element of the codomain is attained.
  • Surjectivity depends on both the function rule and the chosen codomain.
  • Changing the codomain may change surjectivity.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The function \(f(x)=x^3\) from \(\mathbb{R}\) to \(\mathbb{R}\) is surjective.
  • The function \(f(x)=x^2\) from \(\mathbb{R}\) to \(\mathbb{R}\) is not surjective.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
For all real numbers \(x\) and \(y\text{,}\)

\[ |x+y|\leq |x|+|y|. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The triangle inequality bounds the size of a sum by the sizes of its parts: \(|x+y|\) is never more than \(|x|+|y|\). It formalizes the idea that direct paths are never longer than indirect ones: walking \(x\) and then \(y\) ends at distance \(|x+y|\) from \(0\), after covering a total length of \(|x|+|y|\).

In the top diagram, \(x\) and \(y\) have the same sign, so \(|x+y|=|x|+|y|\). In the bottom diagram their signs are opposite, so the displacements partly cancel. In general, equality holds precisely when \(xy\ge0\), including the case where either value is zero.

Walk \(x\), then \(y\): when they have the same sign the lengths add up exactly, and when the signs differ part of the walk is undone, so \(|x+y|<|x|+|y|\).

Applied to differences, the inequality becomes a statement about three points on the line. Writing \(x-z=(x-y)+(y-z)\) gives

\[ |x-z|\le|x-y|+|y-z|, \]

so the distance from \(x\) to \(z\) is at most the distance via a third point \(y\). This is the form used most often: to show that two numbers are close, compare both with a third number. Applying the inequality to \(x=(x-y)+y\) and to \(y=(y-x)+x\) also gives the reverse triangle inequality \(\bigl||x|-|y|\bigr|\le|x-y|\).

A common slip is to expect \(|x-y|\le|x|-|y|\); it fails for \(x=0\) and \(y=1\), where it would say \(1\le-1\). The correct bounds are \(\bigl||x|-|y|\bigr|\le|x-y|\le|x|+|y|\). The name becomes literal later, for the side lengths of a triangle formed by vectors in Math II.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Absolute values interact subadditively under addition.
  • The inequality provides fundamental bounds in analysis.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(|3+(-1)|\le |3|+|{-1}|\text{.}\)
  • \(|x-y|\le |x|+|y|\) for all real numbers \(x,y\text{.}\)

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text: For any two real numbers \(x\) and \(y\text{,}\) exactly one of the following is true: \(x<y\text{,}\) \(x=y\text{,}\) or \(x>y\text{.}\) Equivalently, for any real number \(x\text{,}\) exactly one of the following is true: \(x\) is zero, \(x\) is positive, or \(x\) is negative.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Trichotomy says that any two real numbers are comparable; together with transitivity of \(<\) it makes \(\mathbb{R}\) totally ordered. It ensures that comparisons between real numbers are always decisive.

The three number lines show the three possible positions of two points \(x\) and \(y\): \(x\) to the left of \(y\), both at the same point, or \(x\) to the right of \(y\). Every pair of real numbers fits exactly one picture. The two forms in the Proposition are linked by the difference: \(x<y\), \(x=y\) or \(x>y\) exactly when \(x-y\) is negative, zero or positive.

"Exactly one" has two parts: at least one case holds, so there are no incomparable pairs, and at most one holds, so the cases do not overlap. Both are used in proofs by cases. For instance, if \(a<b+\varepsilon\) for every \(\varepsilon>0\), then \(a\le b\): otherwise \(a>b\), and \(\varepsilon=a-b\) would give \(a<a\). A common slip is to negate \(x<y\) as \(x>y\); by trichotomy the negation is \(x\ge y\), which includes \(x=y\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Exactly one of three relations holds between any two real numbers.
  • Trichotomy underpins order-based arguments.
  • Many proofs rely on splitting cases via trichotomy.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • For \(x=\sqrt{2}\) and \(y=1.4\text{,}\) exactly one relation holds, namely \(x>y\text{,}\) because \(1.4^2=1.96<2\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(x \in \mathbb{R}\text{.}\) Consider the point \((\cos x, \sin x)\) on the unit circle \(\{(u,v)\in\mathbb{R}^2 \colon u^2+v^2=1\}\) obtained by rotating the point \((1,0)\) counterclockwise by an angle \(x\) (measured in radians). The functions \(\sin x\) and \(\cos x\) are defined as the second and first coordinates of this point, respectively.

For all \(x \in \mathbb{R}\) such that \(\cos x \neq 0\text{,}\) the tangent function is defined by \(\displaystyle \tan x = \frac{\sin x}{\cos x}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The trigonometric functions turn an angle into coordinates: \(\cos x\) and \(\sin x\) are the horizontal and vertical coordinates of the point reached by turning through the angle \(x\) on the unit circle. Because a full turn of \(2\pi\) brings the point back to where it started, they provide periodic models for oscillatory behaviour.

The point at angle \(x\) on the unit circle is \((\cos x,\sin x)\): \(\cos x\) is its horizontal coordinate (red dashed), \(\sin x\) its vertical one (green dashed), and \(\tan x=\sin x/\cos x\). On the right the same coordinates are plotted against \(x\). The tangent has no value at \(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\) and \(\tfrac{3\pi}{2}\), where \(\cos x=0\); near these dashed lines its graph shoots up or down.

Turn the angle \(x\) (or press play): the coordinates of the point on the unit circle trace out \(\cos x\) and \(\sin x\) on the right. Show \(\tan x\) to see it blow up where \(\cos x=0\).

Standard facts can be read off the circle. The point lies on \(u^2+v^2=1\), so \(\cos^2x+\sin^2x=1\) and both values lie in \([-1,1]\). Turning by \(2\pi\) more gives the same point, so \(\sin(x+2\pi)=\sin x\) and \(\cos(x+2\pi)=\cos x\). Turning by \(-x\) instead of \(x\) reflects the point in the horizontal axis, so \(\cos(-x)=\cos x\) and \(\sin(-x)=-\sin x\). The tangent is the slope of the line from the origin through the point; turning by a further \(\pi\) gives the opposite point on the same line, which is why \(\tan\) has period \(\pi\) rather than \(2\pi\).

A common slip is to measure the angle in degrees. Here \(x\) is in radians, the length of the arc travelled on the unit circle, so a full turn is \(2\pi\), and \(\sin 1\) is the sine of one radian, about \(57^\circ\). In Math II, Euler's formula links sine and cosine to the exponential function.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Sine and cosine are defined for all real numbers.
  • Trigonometric functions are periodic.
  • Tangent is defined only where cosine is nonzero.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\sin 0=0\) and \(\cos 0=1\text{.}\)
  • \(\tan x\) is undefined at \(x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}+\pi k\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Given two sets \(A\) and \(B\text{,}\) the union \(A\cup B\) of \(A\) and \(B\) is a set whose elements consist of all the elements which belong to \(A\) or \(B\) or both,

\[ x\in A\cup B \; \iff \; x\in A \text{ or } x\in B \iff \; (x\in A)\lor (x\in B). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The union of sets combines elements from multiple collections. The "or" in the definition is inclusive: an element that lies in both sets belongs to the union, and it appears there only once. Union is the set version of the logical "or", just as intersection is the set version of "and".

The whole area covered by either disc is shaded. The lens in the middle lies in both \(A\) and \(B\), and it belongs to the union once, not twice. Each disc lies inside the shaded region, so \(A\subseteq A\cup B\) and \(B\subseteq A\cup B\). If \(A\subseteq B\), the union adds nothing new: \(A\cup B=B\) if and only if \(A\subseteq B\).

A common slip is to count elements as \(|A\cup B|=|A|+|B|\). This holds only for disjoint finite sets; in general the overlap is counted twice and must be subtracted once, \(|A\cup B|=|A|+|B|-|A\cap B|\). For \(\{1,2\}\cup\{2,3\}\) this gives \(2+2-1=3\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Elements belong to the union if they belong to at least one set.
  • Union is commutative and associative, i.e., we have \(A\cup B=B\cup A\) and \(A\cup(B\cup C)=(A\cup B)\cup C\text{.}\)
  • The union with the empty set leaves a set unchanged.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(E\) be a subset of \(\mathbb{R}\text{,}\) and let \(M\) be a real number. We say that \(M\) is an upper bound for \(E\) if we have \(x \leq M\) for every element \(x\) in \(E\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An upper bound for a set \(E\) is a number \(M\) that no element of \(E\) exceeds. It controls the set from above without having to belong to it and without having to be close to it.

Here \(E\) consists of the interval \([-2,0.5]\) and the isolated point \(1.1\). Every \(M\ge1.1\) is an upper bound, including the marked \(M_1\), \(M_2\) and \(M_3\), so a set with one upper bound has infinitely many. The least of them, \(\sup E=1.1\), is also \(\max E\), because \(1.1\) belongs to \(E\).

The inequality \(x\le M\) must hold for every \(x\in E\) with the same \(M\). To show that \(M\) is not an upper bound, one element is enough: a single \(x\in E\) with \(x>M\). Equality is allowed, so \(1\) is an upper bound for \((0,1)\) as well as for \([0,1]\). For the empty set the condition holds vacuously, and every real number is an upper bound.

A set with an upper bound is called bounded above; a set with both an upper and a lower bound is bounded. Applied to the terms of a sequence, the same idea gives a bounded sequence. The least upper bound is the supremum, which exists for every nonempty set that is bounded above.

A common slip is to confuse an upper bound with a maximum. An upper bound need not lie in the set and is never unique; the maximum lies in the set and is unique when it exists.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(M\) is an upper bound for \(E\), then so is every \(M'\ge M\text{;}\) hence upper bounds are never unique.
  • Upper bounds need not belong to the set.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The set \((0,1)\) has upper bound \(1\text{.}\)
  • Any number greater than \(1\) is also an upper bound for \((0,1)\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}\text{.}\) The vertical line \(x=x_0\) is called a vertical asymptote of the curve \(y=f(x)\) if at least one of the following holds:

\[ \begin{aligned} \lim_{x\to x_0}f(x)&=+\infty,\\ \lim_{x\to x_0^+}f(x)&=+\infty,\\ \lim_{x\to x_0^-}f(x)&=+\infty,\\[6pt] \lim_{x\to x_0}f(x)&=-\infty,\\ \lim_{x\to x_0^+}f(x)&=-\infty,\\ \lim_{x\to x_0^-}f(x)&=-\infty. \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A vertical asymptote describes unbounded behaviour near a finite input value: as \(x\) approaches \(x_0\) from at least one side, \(f(x)\) tends to \(+\infty\) or to \(-\infty\), and the graph runs along the vertical line \(x=x_0\).

The figure shows \(f(x)=\frac{1}{x-1}+1\). As \(x\to1^+\) the term \(\frac{1}{x-1}\) is large and positive, so \(f(x)\to+\infty\); as \(x\to1^-\) it is large and negative, so \(f(x)\to-\infty\). Either side alone would make the line \(x=1\) a vertical asymptote. The same graph approaches the line \(y=1\) as \(x\to\pm\infty\), a horizontal asymptote.

Shrink \(h\) and watch \(f(x_0-h)\) and \(f(x_0+h)\): the values run off to \(+\infty\) on one side and \(-\infty\) on the other. Change the sign of \(k\) to swap the sides.

Divergence to infinity at a finite input is the analytic condition behind the vertical line. At least one relevant one-sided limit must diverge; the two sides need not have the same sign. Unboundedness alone is not enough: \(\frac{1}{x}\sin\frac{1}{x}\) is unbounded near \(0\), but it swings between large positive and large negative values and has no infinite one-sided limit, so the definition does not apply.

For a rational function \(p/q\) with no common factor, the vertical asymptotes are the lines \(x=x_0\) at the zeros of \(q\). When numerator and denominator share a zero, the point may instead be a removable singularity: \(\frac{x^2-1}{x-1}\) has no vertical asymptote at \(x=1\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Vertical asymptotes arise from divergence at finite points.
  • One-sided divergence is sufficient.
  • Vertical asymptotes are detected using limits.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The function \(f(x)=1/x\) has a vertical asymptote at \(x=0\text{.}\)
  • Rational functions often exhibit vertical asymptotes at zeros of the denominator.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A zero of a function (also called a root or \(x\)-intercept) is any input value that makes the function's output equal to zero.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A zero of \(f\) is an input at which the output is exactly \(0\), so finding the zeros means solving the equation \(f(x)=0\). Graphically, a zero is where the function's graph crosses or touches the \(x\)-axis.

The zeros of \(f\) are the \(x\)-intercepts of its graph: \(f(x_1)=f(x_2)=f(x_3)=0\) for \(f(x)=x^3-3x+1\). These zeros, approximately \(-1.88\), \(0.35\) and \(1.53\), are not easy to find by hand. The values \(f(-2)=-1\), \(f(-1)=3\), \(f(0)=1\), \(f(1)=-1\) and \(f(2)=3\) change sign on \((-2,-1)\), on \((0,1)\) and on \((1,2)\), and the figure shows the graph crossing the axis once in each of these intervals.

Shift the graph with \(c\) and count the zeros: three crossings become a touch and then a single crossing. At a touching zero the graph meets the \(x\)-axis without crossing it.

A zero is an element of the domain, a number \(x\), not a point of the plane: the zeros of \(x^2-1\) are the numbers \(1\) and \(-1\), while the graph meets the axis at the points \((1,0)\) and \((-1,0)\). Solving \(f(x)=g(x)\) is the same as finding the zeros of \(f-g\), so every equation in one unknown can be written as a zero problem.

A common slip concerns quotients. A zero of the denominator is not a zero of the function: \(1/x\) is not defined at \(0\), and it has no zeros at all, since \(1/x=0\) has no solution. Later, the intermediate value theorem turns the sign changes above into a proof that a zero exists.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • A zero of a function is a solution to the equation \(f(x)=0\text{.}\)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The zeros of the quadratic polynomial \(f(x)=x^2-1\) are \(x=1\) and \(x=-1\text{.}\)
  • The function \(f(x)=2^x\) does not have any zeros.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An algorithm is a prescribed sequence of computational rules for solving a problem. In the iterative methods considered in the course, these rules are applied repeatedly; each repetition is an iteration.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An algorithm turns a problem into a list of steps that can be carried out mechanically. In an iterative method the same rule is applied again and again, and a stopping condition says when the work is finished.

The flowchart shows the three parts of an iterative method: a starting point, a rule for one iteration, and a stopping test that ends the method or sends it back for another round. The output box also names what is known about the answer when the method stops.

That guarantee separates an exact method, whose answer is known to be optimal, from a heuristic such as first fit, which guarantees only a feasible answer. "Algorithm" says that the procedure is fully specified, not how good its answer is.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The simplex method, network algorithms, and dynamic programming use different problem structures.
  • An iteration need not strictly improve the objective: a degenerate simplex pivot can leave its value unchanged.
  • A heuristic is a solution procedure without a general guarantee of optimality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Simplex checks its objective-row sign condition; the shortest-path method settles vertices until the destination is reached; flow augmentation stops when no augmenting path remains; dynamic programming advances through stages.

  • A simplex iteration exchanges a basic and a nonbasic variable.
  • A spanning-tree algorithm repeatedly adds an eligible edge.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The ambulance location model selects a minimum number of station towns while ensuring that every town is within 18 minutes of a selected station. Let \(y_j=1\) if a station is placed at town \(j\), and let \(N_i=\{j\colon t_{ij}\le18\}\). Then

\[ \begin{gathered} \min\sum_{j=1}^6y_j,\\ \sum_{j\in N_i}y_j\ge1\ (i=1,\ldots,6),\\ y_j\in\{0,1\}. \end{gathered} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The model answers one question: at how few towns must ambulance stations be placed so that every town has a station within 18 minutes? Each coverage constraint requires at least one sufficiently close station. A station may cover several towns, and a town may be covered by several stations.

The dashed links join each chosen station to the towns it reaches within 18 minutes. The station at town 4 covers towns 1, 2 and 6 as well as itself, and the station at town 5 covers towns 2 and 3 and itself, so all six towns are covered and town 2 is covered twice.

Read \(N_i\) as the set of towns from which town \(i\) can be served in time, always including \(i\) itself. The sum \(\sum_{j\in N_i}y_j\) then counts the stations that serve town \(i\), and the constraint says that this count is not zero. The two constraints in the Examples, \(y_1+y_4\ge1\) and \(y_3+y_5\ge1\), share no variable, so every feasible choice opens at least two stations; the figure shows that two suffice.

This is a binary integer program: each \(y_j\) is a binary variable. The bus scheduling model has the same kind of coverage constraints with integer counts instead.

A common slip is to write the coverage constraints with \(=1\) instead of \(\ge1\). That would forbid any town from being served by two stations, and the choice of towns 4 and 5 would become infeasible because of town 2.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Include the town itself because its travel time to itself is zero.
  • The threshold includes exactly 18 minutes.
  • This is the set-covering structure illustrated by the exercise; no station-capacity limit is specified.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The dashed links indicate travel times at most 18 minutes; the displayed positions are schematic rather than a geographical scale.

  • Town 1 can be covered from towns 1 or 4, giving \(y_1+y_4\ge1\).
  • Town 3 can be covered from towns 3 or 5, giving \(y_3+y_5\ge1\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An artificial variable \(R_i\ge0\) is introduced temporarily into an equality or a converted \(\ge\) constraint to construct an initial basis. It is added with coefficient \(+1\) and initially takes the nonnegative right-hand-side value while the other variables in that row are zero.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An artificial variable is a temporary device for starting the simplex method. It gives a constraint row a ready starting value when neither a slack nor a surplus variable can provide one. It has no practical interpretation and must be driven to zero before the original equations hold.

The figure shows why the surplus alone is not enough. After subtracting \(S_1\), setting \(x_A=x_B=0\) in the first row would give \(S_1=-6\), which violates \(S_1\ge0\), and the equation \(3x_A+x_B=6\) has no added variable at all. Adding \(R_1\) and \(R_2\) with coefficient \(+1\) gives both rows a nonnegative starting value.

A solution with \(R_1>0\) does not satisfy the original row: it gives \(x_A+2x_B-S_1=6-R_1<6\). The original constraints hold exactly when every artificial variable is zero. This is why Phase I of the two-phase method pushes their sum down to zero, and why a positive minimum shows that the original problem is infeasible. A \(\le\) row with a nonnegative right-hand side needs no artificial variable, because its slack already starts at the right-hand side.

Unlike a slack or surplus, which measures a real amount and may stay positive in the final solution, an artificial variable measures nothing and must be zero in any solution of the original problem.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• They differ from slack and surplus variables, which record genuine inequalities.
  • The first phase of the two-phase method maximizes the negative sum of artificial variables.
  • The original constraints are recovered when every artificial variable is zero.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the figure, setting \(x_A=x_B=S_1=0\) gives the initial artificial basis \(R_1=R_2=6\). Minimizing \(R_1+R_2\) is equivalent to maximizing its negative, as used in Phase I.

  • \(2x_1+3x_2=6\) becomes \(2x_1+3x_2+R_1=6\).
  • \(3x_1-x_2\ge4\) becomes \(3x_1-x_2-S_1+R_2=4\).

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text: In a square one-to-one assignment problem, adding a constant \(a_i\) to every cost in row \(i\), or a constant \(b_j\) to every cost in column \(j\), preserves the set of optimal assignments. Every complete assignment's cost changes by the same total \(\displaystyle \sum_i a_i+\sum_j b_j\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Every complete assignment uses each row and each column of the cost table exactly once. Adding a constant to a whole row or column therefore adds it exactly once to every complete assignment: all totals shift by the same amount and the ranking is unchanged.

In the figure only row \(1\) changes: its entries \(4,2,8\) become \(2,0,6\). Whichever task agent \(1\) receives, that one entry is \(2\) lower, so every complete assignment costs \(2\) less, as the table in the Examples confirms for three of them.

The argument needs every row and every column to be used exactly once, which is why it applies to the square assignment problem. In a rectangular table without dummy entries, some agent stays unused, and changing that agent's row alters only the assignments that use the agent, which can change the optimum. Changing a single entry, or multiplying a row by a factor, can also change which assignment is best.

The transformation is the engine of the Hungarian algorithm. If the subtracted constants keep all entries nonnegative, every complete assignment costs at least the total amount subtracted, and an assignment that uses only zero entries reaches this bound, so it is optimal. The transformed totals only rank the assignments; the cost of the chosen assignment is read from the original table.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Subtracting row and column minima is a valid transformation.
  • The Hungarian uncovered-entry adjustment is equivalent to suitable row and column changes.
  • For a maximum-profit assignment, negate profits and add a constant large enough to make the resulting costs nonnegative.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the figure, subtracting \(a_1=2\) from row 1 lowers each complete assignment cost by 2. More generally, subtracting row amounts \(a_i\) and column amounts \(b_j\) changes every complete total by \(\displaystyle -\sum_i a_i-\sum_j b_j\).

Assignment pairs Original total Transformed total \((1,1),(2,3),(3,2)\) \(4+7+1=12\) \(2+7+1=10\) \((1,2),(2,1),(3,3)\) \(2+4+6=12\) \(0+4+6=10\) \((1,3),(2,2),(3,1)\) \(8+3+3=14\) \(6+3+3=12\)
  • If row minima are 2, 5, 6, and 4, subtracting them reduces every assignment cost by 17.
  • Transforming profits \(p_{ij}\) into costs \(M-p_{ij}\) changes a complete assignment objective to \(\displaystyle nM-\sum_i p_{i,\pi(i)}\), where \(\pi(i)\) is the column assigned to row \(i\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The assignment problem pairs \(n\) agents with \(n\) tasks so that each agent receives exactly one task and each task exactly one agent. If \(c_{ij}\) is the cost of assigning agent \(i\) to task \(j\), a binary model is

\[ \min\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^nc_{ij}x_{ij},\qquad \sum_jx_{ij}=1,\qquad \sum_ix_{ij}=1,\qquad x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The assignment problem asks for the cheapest way to pair two equally large groups one-to-one, such as machines with jobs. The choices are coupled: once a task goes to one agent, it is no longer available for the others, so the pairs cannot be chosen one at a time.

The table and the diagram show the same instance. Each green cell of the table is a bold edge in the diagram, and each row and each column of the table contains exactly one green cell. Of the \(3!=6\) complete assignments, three cost \(12\): besides the highlighted one, also \((1,2),(2,1),(3,3)\) and \((1,2),(2,3),(3,1)\). An optimal assignment need not be unique.

In the binary integer program, \(x_{ij}=1\) means that agent \(i\) performs task \(j\). The equation \(\sum_jx_{ij}=1\) gives agent \(i\) exactly one task, and \(\sum_ix_{ij}=1\) gives task \(j\) exactly one agent. Together they describe a perfect matching between agents and tasks, and the objective adds the costs of the chosen pairs. The model is a transportation problem in which every supply and every demand equals \(1\).

Listing all assignments is hopeless beyond small sizes: there are \(n!\) of them, already \(3{,}628{,}800\) for \(n=10\). The Hungarian algorithm exploits the one-per-row, one-per-column structure instead, and dummy entries and forbidden pairs adapt the model to unequal group sizes and excluded pairs.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Costs can represent execution times as well as monetary amounts.
  • Unequal numbers of agents and tasks can be handled with dummy entries.
  • Task quotas can be modelled by duplicating agent rows into separate slots.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The illustrated three-agent instance has \(3!=6\) complete assignments. The highlighted pairs have total cost \(4+7+1=12\), which is optimal. For this assignment formulation with integer data, an integral optimal solution exists even after relaxing the binary restrictions.

  • The main example assigns machines 1, 2, 3, 4 to jobs 1, 4, 2, 3, with cost 20.
  • Machines can be assigned to locations or players to field positions.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The augmented form of the course's initial LP models replaces each \(\le\) functional constraint by an equality with a nonnegative slack variable. For \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\le \boldsymbol{b}\), \(\boldsymbol{x}\ge0\), this gives

\[ \boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{s}=\boldsymbol{b},\qquad \boldsymbol{x}\ge0,\quad \boldsymbol{s}\ge0, \]

with the same objective in the original variables.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The augmented form rewrites each \(\le\) constraint as an equation by giving the unused amount a name, the slack variable. Adding slacks changes the algebraic representation, not the allowed original decisions: each feasible choice of the original variables determines exactly one value of every slack.

The figure applies this to the three constraints of the Giapetto model: every row gets its own slack, and the slacks receive the same nonnegativity requirement as \(x_s\) and \(x_t\). At the production plan \((x_s,x_t)=(20,60)\), for example, the slacks are \(s_1=0\), \(s_2=0\) and \(s_3=20\): finishing and carpentry hours are used up, while the soldier-demand limit has 20 units to spare.

The requirement \(s_i\ge0\) is what keeps the meaning of the inequality: \(s_1=100-2x_s-x_t\ge0\) holds exactly when \(2x_s+x_t\le100\). Without it, the equation could be satisfied by any \(x_s\) and \(x_t\) and would restrict nothing. The objective gives every slack coefficient zero, since unused capacity earns nothing.

Equations are what the simplex method needs: it fixes some variables at zero and solves the equations for the others, which gives a basic solution. Constraints of type \(\ge\) are turned into equations with a subtracted surplus variable instead, and rows without an obvious starting value then receive an artificial variable.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Auxiliary variables count as variables of the equality system from which a basis is chosen.
  • For \(m\) independent equalities in \(n\) augmented variables, a basis contains \(m\) variables.
  • Artificial variables used for other constraint types require a feasibility phase; they cannot simply remain free in the final model.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the figure, \(s_1\) measures unused finishing hours, \(s_2\) unused carpentry hours, and \(s_3\) unused soldier-demand allowance. The three equations contain five variables, so a basis sets two nonbasic variables to zero.

  • Two original variables and two slack variables give four augmented variables.
  • The constraints \(2x_1+x_2+s_1=10\) and \(x_1+3x_2+s_2=15\) have initial solution \((0,0,10,15)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The augmenting path algorithm starts with a feasible flow, initially zero in the course examples. Find a source-to-sink augmenting path, augment by its bottleneck \(\delta\), decrease each traversed residual capacity by \(\delta\), increase the opposite residual capacity by \(\delta\), and repeat. If no augmenting path remains, the current flow is maximum.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The augmenting path algorithm builds a maximum flow step by step: as long as some route from source to sink still has spare capacity, it sends as much as that route allows. The residual network keeps track of the spare capacity and allows both new routing and correction of earlier routing.

The figure runs the algorithm from zero flow on the network of the augmenting path figure. Three paths are found, with bottlenecks \(3\), \(3\) and \(2\), raising the flow value to \(3\), \(6\) and \(8\). At the end both edges into \(F\) are full: \(D-F\) carries \(5\) and \(E-F\) carries \(3\). Every unit reaching \(F\) uses one of them, so no flow can exceed \(8\): the stopping condition has certified a maximum.

The reverse residual directions are not a technicality. Take edges \(S\to A\), \(S\to B\), \(A\to B\), \(A\to T\) and \(B\to T\), all of capacity \(1\). After a first path \(S-A-B-T\), no forward route with spare capacity is left, although the maximum flow is \(2\). The reverse residual \(B\to A\) of the used edge \(A\to B\) gives the path \(S-B-A-T\), which cancels that unit on \(A\to B\) and reaches the maximum.

The final flow value does not depend on which augmenting paths are chosen, although the flows on individual edges can. A common slip is to read the final residual capacities as flows: the flow on an original edge equals its reverse residual.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Maintain flow conservation after every augmentation.
  • The integer capacities in the exercises allow integer augmentations and finite termination.
  • Recover original flows from the final residual values, taking edge directions into account.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
On an original forward edge the augmentation adds \(\delta\) to its flow; on a backward residual edge it subtracts \(\delta\). With integer capacities and an integral starting flow, each augmentation increases the value by at least 1, so only finitely many are possible.

  • The main example augments by \(5,2,1,4,1,2\), totalling 15.
  • The last residual network cannot reach the sink T from the source S through positive residual directions.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
An augmenting path is a source-to-sink path in the residual network with strictly positive residual capacity in every traversed direction. Its residual capacity, or bottleneck, is

\[ \delta=\min_{e\text{ on the path}}r_e. \]

An additional \(\delta\) units of net source-to-sink flow can be assigned along it.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An augmenting path is a route from source to sink along which more flow can still be sent. The smallest remaining capacity on it, the bottleneck \(\delta\), limits the whole path: sending more than \(\delta\) would overload that edge.

Labels are flow/capacity, and the current flow value is \(3+2=5\) out of \(A\). The red path \(A-C-E-F\) has residual capacities \(5-2=3\), \(4-0=4\) and \(3-0=3\), so \(\delta=3\); after sending \(3\) more units, \(A-C\) and \(E-F\) are both full and the value is \(8\). The bottleneck uses residual capacities, not capacities: \(A-C\) has capacity \(5\), but only \(3\) of it is still free.

A path may also use the reverse direction of an original edge, which the residual network offers with residual capacity equal to the current flow on that edge. Traversing it takes back flow sent earlier and reroutes it. Such a backward segment reduces an original flow while still increasing the total source-to-sink value, and flow conservation at every intermediate vertex still holds.

Augmenting paths drive the augmenting path algorithm, which stops when none is left. In the figure, after the augmentation both edges into \(F\) are full and no residual capacity leads into \(F\), so no augmenting path remains and \(8\) is the maximum flow.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• All residual directions on the path must be feasible.
  • Augmenting by the bottleneck saturates at least one residual direction.
  • A path may use both forward and reverse directions relative to original edges.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The illustrated edge labels are flow/capacity. The red path \(A-C-E-F\) has residual capacities \(3,4,3\), so \(\delta=\min(3,4,3)=3\) increases total flow from 5 to 8. A feasible flow is maximum exactly when no source-to-sink augmenting path remains.

  • The first S-A-D-T augmentation in the video has bottleneck 5.
  • A later S-B-E-D-A-C-T path cancels part of the earlier A-D flow and adds two units overall.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A basic feasible solution is a basic solution of an equality-form LP with all its variables nonnegative. A basic solution with a negative variable is a basic infeasible solution.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A basic feasible solution is a corner point of the feasible region written in algebraic form: a basic solution whose values, slacks included, are all nonnegative. The simplex method keeps this combination of structure and feasibility at every step, so it can improve the objective without leaving the allowed region.

The five filled points \((0,0)\), \((40,0)\), \((40,20)\), \((20,60)\) and \((0,80)\) are the corners of the region of the Giapetto model, and these are its basic feasible solutions. The four hollow points are also intersections of two boundary lines, so they are basic solutions, but they lie outside the region: at \((40,40)\), for instance, \(s_1=100-2\cdot40-40=-20\).

Each intersection of two boundaries corresponds to a basic solution. The feasible ones (filled) are the basic feasible solutions; the hollow ones are basic but infeasible.

Two separate tests are involved. A solution is basic when the nonbasic variables are set to zero and the equations are solved for the rest; it is feasible when every resulting value satisfies its nonnegativity constraint. A point strictly inside the region passes the second test but not the first, and a hollow point passes the first but not the second.

Restricting attention to basic feasible solutions loses nothing: by corner point optimality, an LP with a finite optimum has an optimal corner, and simplex moves from one basic feasible solution to a better adjacent one until the optimality test is passed.

A common slip is to check only the decision variables. The hollow point \((50,0)\) has \(x_s,x_t\ge0\), yet \(s_3=40-50=-10\), so it is not feasible.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Nonbasic variables are set to zero; feasibility is checked through the resulting basic values.
  • A basic variable may be zero in a degenerate solution.
  • For the course LPs with a finite optimum, an optimal basic feasible solution exists.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The filled points in the illustrated region \(F\) are its feasible corners; the hollow boundary intersections violate at least one nonnegativity restriction in the augmented system.

  • \((x_1,x_2,s_1,s_2)=(0,0,10,15)\) is basic feasible in the main simplex example.
  • \((0,10,0,-15)\) is basic but infeasible.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For \(m\) independent linear equality constraints in \(n\) variables, a basic solution is obtained by choosing \(n-m\) variables to be nonbasic and setting them to zero, then uniquely solving for the other \(m\) variables.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A basic solution is what one obtains by deciding in advance which variables are zero and solving the equations for the rest. In a two-variable LP each such choice picks two boundary lines, and the basic solution is their intersection point, a candidate for a corner of the feasible region.

Each labelled point is named by its two zero variables. A zero slack places the point on that constraint's boundary line, and a zero decision variable places it on an axis. So \(s_1=s_2=0\) is the intersection \((20,60)\) of the lines \(2x_s+x_t=100\) and \(x_s+x_t=80\), while \(x_t=s_1=0\) gives \((50,0)\), which lies outside the region.

With \(m\) equations in \(n\) variables, setting \(n-m\) variables to zero leaves \(m\) equations in \(m\) unknowns. The choice gives a basic solution only if this smaller system has exactly one solution. In the Giapetto system, setting \(x_s=s_3=0\) turns the third equation into \(0=40\); geometrically, the lines \(x_s=0\) and \(x_s=40\) are parallel and never meet. Of the ten choices of two zero variables, nine therefore give a basic solution.

Only some basic solutions are feasible, as the table in the Examples shows; those with all values nonnegative are the basic feasible solutions that the simplex method moves between. The equation system itself comes from the augmented form, which adds slack or surplus variables to the inequalities.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• There are at most \(\binom{n}{m}\) basis choices.
  • A basic solution may be feasible or infeasible.
  • Different bases can represent the same degenerate solution.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The illustrated system has \(m=3\) equations and \(n=5\) variables:

\[ \begin{aligned} 2x_s+x_t+s_1&=100,\\ x_s+x_t+s_2&=80,\\ x_s+s_3&=40. \end{aligned} \]

Setting two nonbasic variables to zero gives the following basic solutions. The nonnegative solutions are corners of the shaded feasible region; negative slack values identify the red, infeasible points.

Variables set to zero \((x_s,x_t)\) \((s_1,s_2,s_3)\) Feasible? \(x_s,x_t\) \((0,0)\) \((100,80,40)\) Yes \(s_1,s_2\) \((20,60)\) \((0,0,20)\) Yes \(x_t,s_3\) \((40,0)\) \((20,40,0)\) Yes \(s_2,s_3\) \((40,40)\) \((-20,0,0)\) No \(x_t,s_1\) \((50,0)\) \((0,30,-10)\) No

There are at most \(\binom53=10\) basis choices for this system. The figure shows five of their corresponding basic solutions.

  • The four-variable example has at most \(\binom42=6\) bases.
  • Week 2 practice 4 has five variables and two equalities, but only eight basic solutions from ten candidate choices.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A basic variable belongs to the selected basis of an equality-form LP. Its value is obtained from the constraint equations after the nonbasic variables have been set to zero. With \(m\) independent equalities, the basis contains \(m\) variables.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
In a basic solution the variables fall into two groups: the nonbasic variables are fixed at zero, and the basic variables take whatever values the constraint equations then force. Being basic describes a variable's role in the current representation; it does not mean that the variable must be positive.

In this tableau each basic variable, \(x_t\), \(s_3\) and \(x_s\), has a column with a single 1 in its own row and zeros elsewhere, including the \(z\)-row. With the nonbasic \(s_1=s_2=0\), every row therefore reads "basic variable equals right-hand side": \(x_t=60\), \(s_3=20\), \(x_s=20\) and \(z=180\). This is the optimal plan of the Giapetto model, with 20 units of soldier demand left unused.

There are as many basic variables as constraint equations, here three, regardless of how many decision variables the model has, and slack variables can be basic, as \(s_3\) is here. At each simplex pivot the set of basic variables changes by one: the variable chosen by the entering variable rule becomes basic, and the one chosen by the minimum-ratio test becomes nonbasic.

A basic variable may still take the value zero: what makes it basic is that its value is solved from the equations rather than fixed at zero in advance.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• In a canonical tableau, a basic variable has coefficient 1 in its row and 0 in the other rows, including the objective row.
  • A zero-valued basic variable makes the basic feasible solution degenerate.
  • A pivot replaces one member of the basis.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the illustrated canonical tableau, the basic variables are \(x_t,s_3,x_s\). Their unit columns let their values \(60,20,20\) be read from the right-hand side when \(s_1=s_2=0\).

  • The initial simplex example uses the two slacks as basic variables.
  • At the optimal basis, \(x_1=3\) and \(x_2=4\) are basic.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The bin packing problem assigns every item to a container, subject to a common capacity per container, and minimizes the number of containers used. If item \(i\) has weight \(w_i\) and a container has capacity \(C\), the weights assigned to each container must sum to at most \(C\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Bin packing asks how few containers are needed when items of different weights must be grouped without exceeding a common capacity. The difficulty lies in deciding which items share a container: the number of possible groupings grows very quickly with the number of items.

The figure shows a packing of the four items \(15,30,20,35\) into containers of capacity \(C=50\). Both containers are filled exactly to \(50\), and no packing can use fewer: one container holds at most \(50\), while the total weight is \(100\).

The constraints have two parts: every item goes whole to exactly one container, and in each container the assigned weights sum to at most \(C\). If items could be split, the containers could be filled one after another up to capacity, and the ceiling \(\lceil\sum_i w_i/C\rceil\) containers would be enough. This relaxation is why the total-weight bound is a lower bound on the minimum. A heuristic such as first fit builds a feasible packing quickly, and its number of containers is an upper bound; when the two bounds are equal, the packing is optimal.

A common slip is to treat the total-weight bound as the answer. Three items of weight \(30\) with \(C=50\) have total weight \(90\), so the bound is \(\lceil 90/50\rceil=2\), but no two of them fit together because \(60>50\); three containers are needed.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Each item must be packed exactly once without splitting it.
  • Any feasible packing provides an upper bound on the minimum number of containers.
  • The total-weight bound is \(\displaystyle \lceil\sum_i w_i/C\rceil\); it need not be attainable. This follows by aggregating the capacity requirements.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The figure is a separate four-item illustration with weights \(15,30,20,35\) and capacity \(C=50\). Its lower bound is \(\lceil100/50\rceil=2\), attained by the displayed packing \(\{15,35\}\) and \(\{30,20\}\). This proves optimality for the illustrated instance, rather than for the 15-item course exercise.

  • The exercise has 15 items and container capacity 50.
  • First-fit uses five containers, while the solution sheet states that four suffice.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A binary integer program (BIP) is a linear optimization model in which all decision variables are binary. For variables \(y_1,\ldots,y_n\), the domain is \(y\in\{0,1\}^n\) before imposing the remaining constraints.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A binary integer program models a collection of yes-or-no decisions linked by linear constraints: which projects to fund, at which sites to build, which options to accept. Even a moderate number of such choices creates very many combinations.

With two variables the only candidates are the four corners of the unit square. The constraint \(y_1+y_2\le1\) removes \((1,1)\), so at most one of the two alternatives can be chosen, and the feasible set consists of the three dots alone. The shaded triangle contains the points that would be allowed if \(y_1\) and \(y_2\) could take any value between 0 and 1; its other points carry no meaning as decisions.

With \(n\) variables there are \(2^n\) assignments before the constraints are applied: \(2^{10}=1024\), but \(2^{30}\) is already more than a billion, so listing them all is not a practical solution method. Exact methods such as branch-and-bound are built to avoid this.

A binary integer program is the special case of integer linear programming in which every variable is a binary variable. Sums of binary variables count the selected alternatives, so constraints such as \(\sum_jy_j\le k\) or \(\sum_jy_j\ge1\) express "at most \(k\)" and "at least one", as in the project selection and ambulance location models.

A common slip is to allow \(0\le y_j\le1\) and read the answer as a decision. The point \((\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{2})\) satisfies \(y_1+y_2\le1\) but does not say whether either alternative is chosen.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• There are \(2^n\) binary assignments before functional constraints eliminate infeasible combinations.
  • Its LP relaxation replaces each binary restriction by \(0\le y_j\le1\).
  • The objective can count selected alternatives or weight them by costs or returns.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Project selection maximizes the return from projects under yearly budgets.
  • Ambulance location minimizes the number of selected station sites.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A binary variable is a decision variable restricted to \(\{0,1\}\). For a yes-or-no choice \(j\), the course convention is

\[ y_j=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if decision }j\text{ is yes},\\0,&\text{if decision }j\text{ is no}.\end{cases} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A binary variable turns a yes-or-no decision into a number, 1 for yes and 0 for no, so that the decision can appear in linear objectives and constraints. Its practical meaning must be stated explicitly: which decision it describes and which value means yes.

Only the two endpoints are allowed values. The light band between them is the relaxation \(0\le y\le1\), which also admits values such as \(0.4\) that correspond to no decision at all.

The 0–1 coding gives linear expressions a logical meaning. The sum \(\sum_jy_j\) counts the yes decisions, \(\sum_jc_jy_j\) adds up the costs \(c_j\) of the chosen alternatives only, \(y_1+y_2\le1\) allows at most one of two alternatives, and \(y_2\le y_1\) allows alternative 2 only if alternative 1 is chosen.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The continuous bounds \(0\le y_j\le1\) alone do not enforce binarity.
  • Summing binary variables counts the selected decisions.
  • Auxiliary binary variables can activate or relax constraints.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The red points are the allowed values 0 and 1; the shaded interval belongs to the continuous relaxation.

  • A station-location variable is 1 exactly when an ambulance station is built in that town.
  • \(y_1+y_2\le1\) prohibits selecting both alternatives.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A bipartite matching pairs entities from two distinct groups, with each selected pair containing one member of each group and no entity used in more than one pair. A complete one-to-one assignment between equally sized groups is a perfect bipartite matching.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A bipartite matching pairs members of one group with members of another, such as workers with jobs, where every pair crosses between the groups and nobody is used twice. The question is how many pairs can be formed at once, or which complete pairing is cheapest.

The grey edges are the allowed worker-job pairs and the green edges form a matching: no two green edges share an endpoint. With three jobs, no matching can have more than three edges, so this one is as large as possible, even though worker \(4\) stays unmatched. Other largest matchings exist, for example \(4\)–\(a\), \(1\)–\(b\), \(3\)–\(c\).

In network terms, entities are vertices, allowed pairs are edges, and every edge joins the two groups. A matching is perfect when it covers every vertex on both sides, which requires equally many vertices in the two groups. A matching to which no edge can be added is not necessarily largest: in the figure, \(1\)–\(b\) and \(4\)–\(c\) block every remaining edge, yet this matching has only two pairs.

The assignment problem asks for a cheapest perfect matching, which the Hungarian algorithm finds using this bipartite structure. A largest matching can be found as a maximum flow. The odd-vertex pairing of the Chinese postman problem is also a matching, but within one group of vertices, so it is not bipartite.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Agents and tasks form the two groups in an assignment problem.
  • A matching need not use every entity unless completeness is required.
  • Maximum zero-cost matching can be represented as a unit-capacity flow problem.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Grey edges are allowed pairs and green edges form the matching. It contains \(|M|=3\) pairs, equal to the number of jobs, so no larger matching is possible; the fourth worker remains unmatched. A perfect matching would cover every vertex on both sides and requires equal group sizes.

  • A machine-job pair connects the machine group to the job group.
  • The CPP odd-vertex pairing is nonbipartite because all paired vertices belong to one common set.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text: For a maximization integer program with incumbent value \(L\), a branch-and-bound node can be pruned if its LP relaxation is infeasible, its relaxed optimizer satisfies all integer restrictions, or its relaxed upper bound \(U\) satisfies \(U\le L\). In the integral case, update the incumbent if appropriate. For minimization, reverse the bound comparison.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Pruning is how branch-and-bound avoids searching the whole tree: a node is closed as soon as it is certain that its subproblem cannot contain a better integer solution than the incumbent.

The figure shows the outcomes of solving a node's LP relaxation in a maximization problem. If the relaxation is infeasible, the subproblem has no feasible points. If its optimum is integer, it is the best point of the subproblem and replaces the incumbent value \(L\) when it is better. If its bound \(U\) (written \(z_R\) in the figure) satisfies \(U\le L\), no point of the subproblem beats the incumbent. Only a fractional optimum with \(U>L\) leads to further branching.

All three rules rest on the optimization bounds. The integer points of a subproblem are feasible for its relaxation, so in a maximization none of them has a value above \(U\), and branching only adds constraints, so every node further down has a bound of at most \(U\) too. For minimization the roles reverse: a node is pruned when its relaxed lower bound is at least the incumbent value.

Two slips are common. A fractional relaxed optimum is never a reason to prune; it only shows where to branch. And pruning by bound needs a genuine incumbent: comparing with a rounded point that violates a constraint can discard the subproblem containing the true optimum.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For maximization, a valid global upper bound is the maximum of the incumbent value and the LP bounds of active unresolved nodes.
  • At completion the incumbent proves the optimal value.
  • Pruning equality with the incumbent is sufficient to find the optimum value, but can discard other equally optimal solutions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For minimization, prune a node when its relaxed lower bound \(z_R\), the optimal value of its LP relaxation, is at least the incumbent value.

  • A node with upper bound 3.3 can be discarded once the incumbent is 3.4.
  • In week 3 practice 9, the branch \(x_3\ge7\) is infeasible because \(x_2+3x_3\le20\) and \(x_2\ge0\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Branch-and-bound solves an integer program by solving LP relaxations of subproblems, splitting subproblems when restricted variables are fractional, and discarding subproblems whose bounds cannot improve the best feasible integer solution. If \(x_j=v\) is fractional, branch into

\[ x_j\le\lfloor v\rfloor\qquad\text{and}\qquad x_j\ge\lceil v\rceil. \]

For a binary variable these branches fix it to 0 and 1.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Branch-and-bound finds the best integer solution by divide and conquer. It splits the problem into subproblems whose integer solutions together are exactly those of the original, and uses LP relaxations, ordinary linear programs, to decide which subproblems are still worth exploring.

The tree belongs to the model \(\max(3x_1+2x_2)\) with \(2x_1+2x_2\le9.5\) and \(x_1\le3.5\) from the pure integer program page. The root relaxation gives \((3.5,1.25)\) with bound \(13\). Branching on \(x_2\) gives nodes with bounds \(12.5\) and \(12.25\). Under \(x_2\le1\), branching on \(x_1\) gives the integer point \((3,1)\) with \(z=11\), the first incumbent, and an infeasible node, since \(x_1\ge4\) contradicts \(x_1\le3.5\). The node \(x_2\ge2\) has bound \(12.25>11\), so it must still be explored; it contains no integer point better than \(11\), so \((3,1)\) is optimal.

The branches \(x_j\le\lfloor v\rfloor\) and \(x_j\ge\lceil v\rceil\), built with the floor and ceiling functions, together keep every point with integer \(x_j\) and remove only the strip \(\lfloor v\rfloor<x_j<\lceil v\rceil\), which contains the fractional optimum. So no integer solution is lost, and that fractional point cannot reappear. Each relaxation bounds every integer solution below its node, and the pruning rules close nodes that cannot help.

An integer solution found early is a candidate, not yet the answer: the search ends only when every open node is pruned. The order of exploring nodes changes the amount of work, not the optimum finally proved.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Carry all ancestor branching constraints into each child.
  • Prune for infeasibility, an integral relaxed optimum, or an uncompetitive bound.
  • Continue until every remaining possibility is resolved or bounded by the incumbent.
  • Branching choices affect the work required but not the correctly proven optimum.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The figure branches on \(x_2=1.25\), giving \(x_2\le\lfloor1.25\rfloor=1\) or \(x_2\ge\lceil1.25\rceil=2\).

  • A fractional value \(x_1=3.3\) yields branches \(x_1\le3\) and \(x_1\ge4\).
  • The development-project model has optimum 3.4; recompute the LP relaxation at each node rather than copying intermediate values.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The bus scheduling model chooses nonnegative integer counts \(x_i\) of buses starting in each of six consecutive four-hour intervals. Each bus operates for two intervals. With requirements \(d=(4,8,10,7,12,4)\), the cyclic model is

\[ \begin{gathered} \min\sum_{i=1}^6x_i,\\ x_{i-1}+x_i\ge d_i\ (i=1,\ldots,6),\\ x_i\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}, \end{gathered} \]

where \(x_0=x_6\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The model finds the smallest fleet of buses that meets the requirement in every four-hour interval when each bus works two consecutive intervals. The variables count shift starts, while each coverage constraint counts all buses operating in an interval.

The bars show the requirements \(d_1,\ldots,d_6\) and the arrows show shifts. The \(x_1\) buses run from 0 to 8 h and serve intervals 1 and 2, and the \(x_4\) buses serve intervals 4 and 5. The \(x_6\) buses start at 20 h, serve interval 6 and then, after midnight, interval 1 of the next day. Interval 1 is therefore covered by \(x_6+x_1\), which is why the model sets \(x_0=x_6\).

Each variable appears in exactly two constraints, those of its starting interval and the next one. Adding all six constraints gives \(2\sum_ix_i\ge45\), so at least 23 buses are needed. This bound is not attained: enumerating the integer solutions gives a minimum of 26, so the optimal plan covers some intervals with more buses than they require.

Linear program formulation turns shift counts into decision variables and requirements into linear inequalities. Because every variable counts buses, the model is a pure integer program. The ambulance location model has the same coverage structure with yes-or-no variables.

A common slip is to write \(x_i\ge d_i\), reading \(x_i\) as the number of buses on duty in interval \(i\). That ignores the buses that started one interval earlier and asks for more buses than necessary.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Eight-hour operation covers exactly two consecutive four-hour intervals.
  • Coverage may exceed the minimum demand.
  • The repeating daily interpretation is the assumption used to formulate the midnight boundary.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The midnight-to-4 AM constraint is \(x_6+x_1\ge4\).
  • The 4 PM-to-8 PM requirement gives \(x_4+x_5\ge12\).
