docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The course's capacity expansion model uses a binary purchase variable \(y\) to switch additional capacity on or off. If existing capacity is 100 and a new machine supplies 50 more, the restriction is

\[ x_1+x_2\le100+50y,\qquad y\in\{0,1\}. \]

Here \(x_1,x_2\) are the production quantities that share this capacity, and \(y=1\) means the additional machine is purchased.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A capacity expansion model lets the optimization decide whether to invest in extra capacity instead of fixing that choice in advance. One binary variable \(y\) records the investment, and the capacity constraint \(x_1+x_2\le100+50y\) changes with it.

The two lines are the two possible capacity limits. With \(y=0\) only the blue triangle below \(x_1+x_2=100\) is allowed; with \(y=1\) the orange band up to \(x_1+x_2=150\) is added. The point \(A=(50,40)\) uses \(90\) units and fits either way, while \(B=(70,50)\) uses \(120\) units and is allowed only when the machine is bought.

The right-hand side \(100+50y\) is linear in \(y\), so the model stays a mixed integer program: the quantities \(x_1,x_2\) may be continuous while \(y\) is binary. The constraint allows the extra \(50\) units when \(y=1\) but does not force their use. Without a cost attached to \(y\), choosing \(y=1\) is therefore never worse, and nothing in the model discourages buying the machine. The investment cost has to appear in the objective, for example as a term \(-Fy\) in a profit maximization with purchase cost \(F\), or in a budget constraint.

The integrality of \(y\) is essential. In the LP relaxation, \(y=0.4\) would be allowed and would give capacity \(100+50\cdot0.4=120\), as if part of a machine could be bought. The same device, a right-hand side switched by a binary variable, is also used in either-or constraints.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• With \(y=0\), the capacity limit is 100.
  • With \(y=1\), the capacity limit is 150.
  • Any specified acquisition cost must also be represented in the economic objective or budget; the isolated course example only demonstrates the capacity restriction.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The illustrated point \(A=(50,40)\) uses capacity 90 and is allowed with \(y=0\); \(B=(70,50)\) uses 120 and requires \(y=1\).

  • A plan with total production 120 requires \(y=1\).
  • A plan with total production 90 satisfies the capacity restriction with \(y=0\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The Chinese postman problem (CPP) finds a minimum-length closed route traversing every edge at least once in a connected undirected network with nonnegative edge lengths. To solve the course version, find a minimum-cost pairing of the odd-degree vertices using shortest-path distances, duplicate the corresponding paths, and construct an Euler tour in the resulting network.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The Chinese postman problem asks for the shortest closed route that covers every edge at least once, like a postman who must walk every street and return to the post office. Without an Euler tour, which would use every edge exactly once, some edges must be repeated, and the question becomes which repetitions add the least length.

In the figure \(A\) and \(C\) have degree \(3\) and \(B\) and \(D\) degree \(2\), so by the Euler network characterization there is no Euler tour. Duplicating the edge \(A-C\) (dashed) raises both odd degrees to \(4\); now every degree is even, and an Euler tour of the enlarged network covers all edges with length \(14+4=18\).

A closed route leaves every vertex as often as it arrives there, so it uses an even number of edge ends at each vertex, and an odd-degree vertex forces at least one repeated edge. Duplicating a path between two odd vertices makes both endpoints even and leaves the parity of the vertices in between unchanged, so the odd vertices are paired, each pair costing its shortest-path distance. Such a pairing exists because the number of odd vertices is even: each edge adds \(2\) to the sum of all degrees.

The pairs are chosen jointly by a minimum-weight perfect matching, because pairing the closest odd vertices first can give a larger total than the best pairing.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If every vertex already has even degree, any Euler tour is optimal.
  • The optimal cost is the sum of original edge lengths plus the minimum pairing cost.
  • The shortest path between paired vertices can contain intermediate vertices.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the figure, \(A\) and \(C\) are the two odd-degree vertices. Their direct edge costs 4, compared with \(2+3=5\) via \(D\) or \(3+2=5\) via \(B\). Duplicating the direct edge gives route length \(14+4=18\). The dashed edge denotes this extra copy.

  • The five-vertex example has total edge length 25 and minimum pairing cost 7, giving CPP value 32.
  • Pairing A with D duplicates A-C-D, while pairing B with E duplicates B-E.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The classical EOQ model, based on the economic order quantity (EOQ), assumes deterministic constant demand rate \(D>0\), instantaneous batch replenishment, no shortages, fixed setup cost \(K>0\) per order, and holding cost \(h>0\) per unit per unit time. A constant unit purchasing price can be excluded when optimizing. For batch size \(y>0\), relevant total cost per unit time (TCU) is

\[ TCU(y)=\frac{KD}{y}+\frac{hy}{2}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The classical EOQ model is the simplest inventory policy model: demand is steady and known, so stock follows a fixed repeating pattern, and only the batch size \(y\) remains to be chosen. Large batches mean few setups but much stock; small batches mean the reverse.

Stock starts at \(y=22\) and falls with slope \(-D=-2\), reaching zero after \(t_0=y/D=11\) days, when the next batch arrives at once. The dashed line at \(y/2=11\) is the average stock, which fixes the holding cost rate \(hy/2\).

Move \(y\): the setup cost rate \(KD/y\) falls and the holding cost rate \(hy/2\) rises. The right panel shows the inventory sawtooth for this batch size.

Each assumption shapes the picture. Constant demand makes the falling parts straight lines. Instantaneous replenishment makes the jumps vertical. Because shortages are not allowed and ordering earlier would only add holding cost, the next batch arrives exactly when stock reaches zero. A constant unit price adds the same purchasing cost per unit time for every \(y\), so it can be left out of \(TCU(y)\) when choosing \(y\).

Minimizing \(TCU(y)\) gives the economic order quantity. Relaxing one assumption at a time gives the other models of this week: a delay between ordering and delivery in EOQ with lead times, backlogged demand in EOQ with planned shortages, and order-size discounts in EOQ with price breaks. In the last model, \(TCU(y)\) without purchasing cost is no longer enough, since the unit price then depends on \(y\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Average stock is \(y/2\) and ordering cycle length is \(y/D\).
  • The cost is strictly convex for positive \(y\).
  • The model optimizes a continuous order quantity; discrete purchasing units require checking feasible nearby quantities.
  • Using a mean demand to approximate stochastic demand does not incorporate its variability.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The phone data \(D=2\), \(K=605\), \(h=5\) give an optimal batch of 22.
  • The exercise uses average weekly demand 100 while explicitly omitting its standard deviation 10 from the EOQ calculation.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An undirected network is connected if every pair of vertices can be joined by a path. It is disconnected if at least one pair cannot be joined.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A network is connected when it is in one piece: from any vertex one can reach any other along edges. The spanning-tree and undirected routing problems in the course assume this of the network.

Both networks have the same five vertices. On the left every pair is joined by a path, for example \(A-B-D\) or \(A-C-E\). On the right the edges stay within \(\{A,B,C\}\) or within \(\{D,E\}\), so no path joins \(A\) to \(D\); one such pair already makes the network disconnected, although no vertex is isolated.

The condition matters whenever a route or a tree must cover the whole network: a disconnected network has no spanning tree, and vertices in different parts have no shortest path between them.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A disconnected network has no spanning tree covering all its vertices.
  • A tree is connected as well as cycle-free.
  • For a directed flow network, available directed routes must still be checked; undirected connectedness alone does not imply flow to the sink.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A chain of roads linking A to B and B to C connects all three towns.
  • Two groups of towns with no road between the groups are disconnected.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A constraint is a requirement that an allowed decision must satisfy. A linear functional constraint has the form

\[ a_{i1}x_1+\cdots+a_{in}x_n\le b_i, \]

or the corresponding equality or \(\ge\) inequality. The \(a_{ij}\) are constraint coefficients and \(b_i\) is the right-hand side.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Constraints translate capacity limits, demand requirements, and other restrictions into mathematics. Feasibility requires all constraints to hold together.

The objective function \(f(\boldsymbol{x})\) is the quantity to maximize (for example, profit) or minimize (for example, cost). Functional constraints describe what an allowed decision must satisfy, such as resource limits or demand requirements. Domain restrictions specify signs or integrality.

In the diagram, blue identifies decision variables, whose values the model determines; red identifies model parameters, the given data \(c_j\), \(a_{ij}\) and \(b_i\). In general, the model is \(\max/\min\ f(\boldsymbol{x})\) subject to \(\boldsymbol{x}\in F\), where the constraints define the feasible set \(F\). A solution assigns values to all variables.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A capacity limit commonly gives a \(\le\) constraint; a minimum requirement commonly gives a \(\ge\) constraint.
  • An equality represents an exact requirement or balance.
  • Multiplication by a negative number reverses an inequality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(x_s+x_t\le80\) limits carpentry use in the Giapetto production model.
  • \(800x_A+1000x_B\ge8000\) requires enough calories in the diet problem, where \(x_A,x_B\) are the pounds of feeds A and B.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Contingent decisions are binary choices whose admissibility depends on other choices. If decision 2 is allowed only when decision 1 is yes, the implication is represented by

\[ y_2\le y_1,\qquad y_1,y_2\in\{0,1\}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Contingent decisions model the logical rule "decision 2 is only possible if decision 1 is taken", such as building a warehouse only where a factory is built. With binary variables for the two yes-or-no choices, the rule becomes the linear inequality \(y_2\le y_1\).

The table lists all four value pairs of \((y_1,y_2)\). Three of them satisfy \(y_2\le y_1\); only \(y_1=0\), \(y_2=1\) fails, since \(1\le0\) is false. That is exactly the forbidden combination, decision 2 without decision 1. The pair \(y_1=1\), \(y_2=0\) stays allowed, so the inequality does not force decision 2 once decision 1 is taken.

Checking every value combination, as in the table, is the general way to design and verify such constraints. In words, \(y_2\le y_1\) says "if \(y_2=1\) then \(y_1=1\)", or equivalently "if \(y_1=0\) then \(y_2=0\)". If instead decision 2 must be taken whenever decision 1 is, the reverse inequality \(y_1\le y_2\) is needed, and requiring both gives \(y_1=y_2\).

A common slip is to read \(y_2\le y_1\) as a two-way link. It only rules out "2 without 1"; whether decision 2 is taken when decision 1 is depends on the objective and the other constraints. Rules with several conditions are built from several such inequalities, one per condition, as in the Key Results. Mutually exclusive decisions express a different rule, "at most one", with a sum. Both kinds of rule can be added to a project selection model when projects depend on or exclude each other.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If decision 2 must be yes when decision 1 is no, use \(y_1+y_2\ge1\).
  • If decision 3 is allowed only when both decisions 1 and 2 are yes, use \(y_3\le y_1\) and \(y_3\le y_2\).
  • If \(y_1=1\) and \(y_2=0\) must imply \(y_3=0\), use \(y_1-y_2+y_3\le1\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• With binaries \(W_{LA}=1\) if a warehouse is built at location LA and \(F_{LA}=1\) if a factory is built there, \(W_{LA}\le F_{LA}\) requires a local factory before a warehouse can be built.
  • \(y_1+y_2+y_3\le2\) rules out all three yes decisions together.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
For continuous demand with finite mean and CDF \(F\), the newsvendor expected cost \(G(y)\) of ordering \(y\), with underage cost \(b\) and overage cost \(h\), satisfies

\[ G'(y)=(b+h)F(y)-b. \]

If \(F\) is continuous and strictly increasing through \(\beta=b/(b+h)\) and that quantile lies in the allowed quantity domain, the unique optimum is

\[ y^*=F^{-1}(\beta). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The rule says that the best order is a demand level, not the average demand: order the quantity \(y^*\) that demand stays at or below with probability exactly \(\beta\), the critical ratio. Which level is chosen depends on the costs only through \(\beta\).

For meal demand uniform on \([80,120]\) with \(b=3.3\) and \(h=2.2\), the line \(G'(y)=5.5F(y)-3.3\) rises from \(-3.3\) at \(y=80\) to \(2.2\) at \(y=120\). Where it is negative, ordering a little more lowers the expected cost; where it is positive, ordering more raises it. It crosses zero at \(y^*=104\), where \(F(104)=0.6=\beta\).

Where \(G'(y)=(b+h)F(y)-b\) is zero the CDF equals \(\beta\); read \(y^*=F^{-1}(\beta)\) off the right panel.

The formula for \(G'(y)\) compares the two risks of one extra unit. It is left over with probability \(F(y)\), at cost \(h\), and is sold with probability \(1-F(y)\), saving \(b\); the net effect is \(hF(y)-b(1-F(y))=(b+h)F(y)-b\). Because \(F\) never decreases, \(G'\) never decreases either, so \(G\) first falls and then rises and a zero of \(G'\) is a global minimum. Strict increase of \(F\) at \(\beta\) makes the zero unique: if \(F\) stays equal to \(\beta\) on a whole interval, every point of that interval is optimal, so continuity alone is not enough. The quantile must also lie in the allowed range of \(y\); a normal quantile can be negative, and then the best order is \(0\).

The discrete newsvendor rule makes the same comparison for whole units, with a difference \(G(y+1)-G(y)\) instead of a derivative.

docs.text:

  • For the course normal demand approximation \(\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\), it is \(\max\{0,\mu+\sigma\Phi^{-1}(\beta)\}\), where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal CDF.
  • A continuous demand approximation may give a noninteger answer even when actual items are indivisible.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Meal demand uniform on \([80,120]\) with \(\beta=0.6\) gives 104 meals.
  • Normal meal demand with mean 100 and standard deviation 20 gives about 105.07.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
If \(\boldsymbol{x}^{(1)},\ldots,\boldsymbol{x}^{(k)}\) are optimal solutions of the same LP and \(\alpha_j\ge0\) with \(\displaystyle \sum_{j=1}^k\alpha_j=1\), then

\[ \boldsymbol{x}=\sum_{j=1}^k\alpha_j\boldsymbol{x}^{(j)} \]

is also optimal. Such a weighted average is a convex combination.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The proposition says that optimal solutions of a linear program never come as an isolated pair: if two points are optimal, so is every point on the segment between them. A convex combination is a weighted average with nonnegative weights that add up to \(1\), and for two points these averages fill exactly that segment.

With objective \(2x_s+2x_t\) the optimal objective line lies along the edge from \(\boldsymbol{x}^{(1)}=(0,80)\) to \(\boldsymbol{x}^{(2)}=(20,60)\), so both corners have value \(160\). The marked point \((15,65)=\tfrac{1}{4}\boldsymbol{x}^{(1)}+\tfrac{3}{4}\boldsymbol{x}^{(2)}\) lies three quarters of the way from \((0,80)\) towards \((20,60)\), and its value \(2\cdot15+2\cdot65\) is again \(160\).

For any \(\alpha\in[0,1]\) the mixture \(\alpha \boldsymbol{x}^{(1)}+(1-\alpha)\boldsymbol{x}^{(2)}\) of the two optimal corners is feasible and has the same optimal \(z\).

Two facts make this work, shown for weights \(\alpha\) and \(1-\alpha\). If both points satisfy a constraint \(\sum_ja_jx_j\le b\), multiplying the two inequalities by \(\alpha\) and \(1-\alpha\) and adding them shows that the average satisfies it too. This needs nonnegative weights, since multiplying an inequality by a negative number reverses it. And because the objective is linear, the value of the average is the same average of the two values, again the optimum \(z^*\).

Hence an LP has no optimal solution, exactly one, or infinitely many, never exactly two: multiple optimal solutions fill at least a whole segment. The argument needs continuous variables: \(\max(x_1+x_2)\) with \(x_1+x_2\le1\) and binary \(x_1,x_2\) is an integer program with exactly the two optimal solutions \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\), since their midpoint \((\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{2})\) is not allowed.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Weights must be nonnegative and sum to one.
  • For two points use \(\alpha\) and \(1-\alpha\), with \(0\le\alpha\le1\).
  • The property concerns continuous LP feasibility; averaging integer solutions need not preserve integrality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For the illustrated objective \(2x_s+2x_t\), the edge between \((0,80)\) and \((20,60)\) is optimal with value 160. The displayed combination \(\tfrac{1}{4}(0,80)+\tfrac{3}{4}(20,60)=(15,65)\) has the same value. In general, the combined value is \(\displaystyle \sum_j\alpha_jz^*=z^*\).

  • Combining \((5,0)\) and \((3,4)\) gives \((3+2\alpha,4-4\alpha)\), all with value 20.
  • Combining \((2,3)\) and \((0,6)\) gives \((2\alpha,6-3\alpha)\); \(\alpha=1/2\) gives \((1,9/2)\).

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text: For the LPs in the course with a nonempty feasible region in nonnegative variables, if a finite optimum exists, at least one feasible corner point attains it. Consequently, a unique optimal solution must be a feasible corner point. If a bounded feasible region has multiple optimal solutions, at least two of its corner points are optimal.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
This result reduces the search for the optimum of an LP from infinitely many feasible points to finitely many corners: if the best value is attained at all, it is attained at some feasible corner point.

The figure lists the value of \(z=3x_s+2x_t\) at each of the five feasible corners. The largest, \(180\), belongs to \((20,60)\), and the objective line \(3x_s+2x_t=180\) touches the region only there.

Turn the objective with \(c_1\) and \(c_2\): whenever a finite optimum exists, some feasible corner attains it.

The reason is linearity. Along a straight edge between two corners the objective changes at a constant rate, so on that edge it is largest at one of the endpoints, or equal along the whole edge. The hypotheses matter. Without a finite optimum there is nothing to attain: maximizing cost over the unbounded region of the diet problem has no optimum. Without the sign restrictions the region may have no corner at all: maximizing \(x_1+x_2\) subject only to \(x_1+x_2\le1\) has optimal value \(1\), attained along a whole line, but no two boundary lines meet.

The proposition says that some optimal solution is a corner, not that every one is: when an objective line lies along an edge, all points of that edge are optimal. The graphical method uses the result directly, and the simplex method later turns it into an algebraic search from corner to corner.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The existence of a finite optimum is essential.
  • The bounded-region qualification in the multiple-corner statement matters when the feasible region has rays.
  • Every convex combination of optimal corners is optimal.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The figure evaluates \(z=3x_s+2x_t\) at its five feasible corners: the values are \(0,120,160,180,160\). The largest is 180 at \((20,60)\), and the orange line is the objective line through that point.

  • The manufacturing optimum \((2,5)\) is a feasible corner.
  • For the course LP with objective \(4x_1+2x_2\) and boundary \(2x_1+x_2\le11\), an entire feasible boundary segment attains 22.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: In an LP with \(n\) decision variables, a corner point is a point determined by the intersection of constraint boundaries with \(n\) independent boundary equations. At least \(n\) constraints are therefore active there, counting nonnegativity boundaries. A corner point is feasible only if it satisfies all constraints.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Corner points are the points where boundary lines of the constraints cross. In an LP with two variables, a corner is found by turning two constraints into equations and solving them together.

The orange points are the five feasible corners of the Giapetto region, from \((0,0)\) round to \((0,80)\). The point \((50,0)\), where the finishing line \(2x_s+x_t=100\) meets the axis \(x_t=0\), is also a corner point in the sense of the Definition, but it lies outside the region because \(50>40\) violates the demand limit \(x_s\le40\).

Every intersection of two boundaries is a candidate corner. Filled points are feasible corners; hollow ones lie outside the region.

With \(n\) variables, a corner needs \(n\) boundary equations that pin down exactly one point. In two variables these are two different lines that are not parallel: the lines \(x_s=0\) and \(x_s=40\) never meet, and writing the same line twice fixes no point. The five boundary lines of the figure, three constraints and two axes, form \(10\) pairs; one pair is parallel, and of the other nine intersection points only five are feasible.

Corner points matter because an LP that has an optimum attains it at a feasible corner (corner point optimality). The graphical method uses this directly, and the simplex method later finds corners by algebra. A common slip is to treat every corner point as feasible: a corner satisfies its two defining constraints with equality, but the other constraints must still be checked.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• In two dimensions, two nonparallel active boundaries determine a corner.
  • Extra active constraints can occur at a degenerate corner.
  • Not every intersection of boundaries is feasible.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The illustrated feasible corner \((20,60)\) solves \(2x_s+x_t=100\) and \(x_s+x_t=80\). The boundary intersection \((50,0)\) is infeasible because it violates the soldier-demand limit; it is not an extreme point of the feasible set. Feasible corners correspond to basic feasible solutions of the augmented model.

  • The lines \(x_2=5\) and \(2x_1+x_2=9\) intersect at \((2,5)\).
  • The nonnegativity boundaries meet at the origin \((0,0)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For newsvendor selling price \(p\), unit cost \(c\) and salvage value \(s\), with overage cost \(h=c-s>0\) and underage cost \(b=p-c>0\), the critical ratio is

\[ \beta=\frac{b}{b+h}=\frac{p-c}{p-s},\qquad 0<\beta<1. \]

It is the cumulative-demand probability used to select the optimal stock quantile.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The critical ratio turns the two newsvendor costs into one target probability: the optimal stock covers demand with probability \(\beta=b/(b+h)\). It compares what one unit too few costs, the underage cost \(b\), with what one unit too many costs, the overage cost \(h\).

The CDF \(F(y)\) gives the probability that demand is at most \(y\). For meals, \(\beta=3.3/(3.3+2.2)=0.6\); reading across from height \(0.6\) to the CDF and then down gives \(y^*=104\), the quantity that covers demand with probability \(0.6\).

Change \(p\), \(c\) and \(s\): \(\beta=b/(b+h)\) moves, and the optimal stock is the demand quantile where the CDF reaches \(\beta\).

The ratio comes from the last unit ordered. It is unsold with probability \(F(y)\), costing \(h\), and sold with probability \(1-F(y)\), saving \(b\), so ordering it pays while \(b(1-F(y))>hF(y)\), that is, while \(F(y)<b/(b+h)\). A large underage cost pushes \(\beta\) towards \(1\) and the stock up; a large overage cost pushes \(\beta\) towards \(0\). The second form follows from \(b+h=p-s\) and shows the prices directly: a higher selling price or a higher salvage value raises \(\beta\), and a higher unit cost lowers it. How far the price can move before the order changes is the subject of newsvendor price sensitivity.

A common slip is to read \(\beta\) as the fraction of demand that is served on average. It is the probability that all demand is met, not a fraction of demand.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For integer demand, increasing from \(y\) to \(y+1\) helps while \(F(y)<\beta\).
  • For the continuous strictly increasing CDFs used in the examples, the optimum solves \(F(y^*)=\beta\).
  • The ratio is not the expected fraction of demand served.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Newspapers with \(b=1.5\) and \(h=2\) have \(\beta=3/7\).
  • Meals with \(b=3.3\) and \(h=2.2\) have \(\beta=0.6\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: In the course's network terminology, a cycle or tour is a path that starts and ends at the same vertex. Because its path convention requires distinct edges, no edge is repeated within such a cycle.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A cycle is a route that ends where it started. In the course's convention it is a path whose first and last vertices coincide, so no edge is used twice. Cycles describe routes that must return home, and they are excluded when constructing a tree.

The red cycle \(B-D-E-C-B\) uses the four edges \(B-D\), \(D-E\), \(E-C\) and \(C-B\), each once, and returns to \(B\).

Only repeated edges are forbidden, so a cycle may pass through a vertex twice, like a figure of eight. Removing one edge of a cycle keeps the network connected, because the rest of the cycle still joins its two ends; this is why the Kruskal method rejects an edge that closes a cycle and a spanning tree contains none.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• An Euler tour is a closed traversal using every edge exactly once.
  • A tree contains no cycles.
  • In the Chinese postman problem, “tour” is also used for a closed route that may repeat original edges; repeated copies are distinct in the augmented network.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The red cycle in the figure is \(B-D-E-C-B\). An undirected network with no cycles is a forest; when it is also connected, it is a tree.

  • Three edges \(A-B\), \(B-C\), and \(C-A\) form a cycle.
  • Adding an edge between two already connected vertices of a tree creates a cycle.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A decision variable represents a quantity or choice that the model is intended to determine. Its definition specifies its practical meaning, unit, and allowed values. A solution assigns a value to every decision variable.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A clear variable definition connects a mathematical expression to a real decision. It also determines whether fractions, negative values, or only yes-or-no choices make sense.

The objective function \(f(\boldsymbol{x})\) is the quantity to maximize (for example, profit) or minimize (for example, cost). Functional constraints describe what an allowed decision must satisfy, such as resource limits or demand requirements. Domain restrictions specify signs or integrality.

In the diagram, blue identifies decision variables, whose values the model determines; red identifies model parameters, the given data \(c_j\), \(a_{ij}\) and \(b_i\). In general, the model is \(\max/\min\ f(\boldsymbol{x})\) subject to \(\boldsymbol{x}\in F\), where the constraints define the feasible set \(F\). A solution assigns values to all variables.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The number of decision variables is the dimension of the original optimization problem.
  • Input data such as available hours are parameters rather than decisions.
  • Variable restrictions must be stated explicitly.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(x_s\) denotes the number of wooden soldiers to produce in the Giapetto production model.
  • \(x_A\) denotes pounds of feed A in a pig diet problem.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A degenerate basic feasible solution has at least one basic variable equal to zero. A degenerate pivot has a zero step length (the minimum-ratio test gives \(\theta=0\), so the entering variable stays at zero) and can change the basis without changing the solution vector or objective value.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Degeneracy happens when a corner of the feasible region lies on more constraint lines than are needed to fix it. In two variables two lines suffice; when a third passes through the same point, more variables are zero there than a basic solution sets to zero, so some basic variable takes the value \(0\).

At \((20,60)\) the lines \(2x_s+x_t=100\), \(x_s+x_t=80\) and \(x_t=60\) meet, so \(s_1=s_2=s_4=0\). The augmented form has six variables and four equations, so only two variables are nonbasic and at least one of the three zero slacks is basic. Any two of \(s_1,s_2,s_4\) can be the nonbasic pair, and each choice gives the same point: one corner, three bases.

In the simplex method, degeneracy shows up in the minimum-ratio test. A tie means that two basic variables reach zero at the same moment; only one leaves, and the other stays basic with value \(0\). If a later ratio test gives \(\theta=0\), the pivot exchanges variables without moving: the point and \(z\) stay the same.

Being basic is a matter of the chosen basis, not of the value, so a basic variable can be zero. At a degenerate corner the optimality test can even show a negative coefficient although the point is optimal; further degenerate pivots can then reach a basis that passes the test. The real risk is cycling, described in the Examples.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A tie for the minimum ratio can produce a degenerate basic feasible solution.
  • Zero ratios must be considered when the pivot-column coefficient is positive.
  • The basic/nonbasic distinction is determined by the basis, not by whether a value is zero.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
At the illustrated point \((20,60)\), \(s_1=s_2=s_4=0\). The augmented model has two nonbasic variables, so at least one of these three zeros is basic. Without an anti-cycling rule (a tie-breaking rule for the entering and leaving variables, such as Bland's smallest-index rule), repeated degenerate pivots can cause simplex to cycle, that is, return to an earlier basis and repeat indefinitely.

  • With \(x_1-x_2\le1\) and \(2x_1+x_2\le2\), increasing \(x_1\) gives tied ratios of 1.
  • At \((x_1,x_2,s_1,s_2)=(1,0,0,0)\), exchanging \(s_2\) for \(x_2\) leaves the point and \(z=3\) unchanged.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The course's diet problem chooses pounds \(x_A,x_B\) of two feeds to minimize daily feed cost while satisfying calorie, vitamin, and composition requirements:

\[ \begin{aligned} \min\quad &0.4x_A+0.8x_B\\ \text{subject to}\quad &800x_A+1000x_B\ge8000,\\ &140x_A+70x_B\ge700,\\ &2x_A-x_B\le0,\\ &x_A,x_B\ge0. \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The diet problem is a minimum-cost mixture model: choose amounts of the ingredients so that the mixture meets every requirement as cheaply as possible. Where the Giapetto model caps the use of resources with \(\le\) constraints, the diet problem sets minimum requirements with \(\ge\) constraints.

The figure uses the simplified model from the Examples. Both requirements keep the feasible points on or above their lines, so the feasible region is unbounded upwards and to the right. The dashed cost lines become cheaper towards the origin, and the cheapest one that still meets the region touches it at the corner \((1.2,2.4)\), with cost \(9.6\).

The unbounded region causes no difficulty for minimization. Both feeds have a positive price and the amounts are nonnegative, so the cost never falls below zero, and moving the cost line towards the origin eventually leaves the region. Maximizing cost over the same region would have no optimum.

The composition restriction shows how a share requirement becomes linear. "At most one third of the feed is A" reads \(x_A\le\tfrac{1}{3}(x_A+x_B)\); multiplying by \(3\) and collecting terms gives \(2x_A-x_B\le0\). The fraction form \(x_A/(x_A+x_B)\le\tfrac{1}{3}\) is not linear and is undefined when no feed is bought, so in linear program formulation the multiplied-out form is the one to use.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The share constraint follows from \(x_A\le(x_A+x_B)/3\).
  • Nutrient requirements are lower bounds, so their inequalities point toward greater nutrient intake.
  • The optimal solution is \(x_A=20/7\), \(x_B=40/7\), with cost \(40/7\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The figure uses a simplified illustrative diet model, distinct from the course-data formulation above: minimize \(2x_A+3x_B\) subject to \(x_A+2x_B\ge6\), \(3x_A+x_B\ge6\) and \(x_A,x_B\ge0\). The variables still represent pounds of feeds A and B. Sliding the cost line towards the origin gives the illustrated optimum \((1.2,2.4)\) with cost 9.6.

  • The optimal mixture contains exactly one-third feed A.
  • At the optimum the calorie requirement is tight, while vitamin intake is \(800\ge700\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The Dijkstra-Prim method constructs a minimum spanning tree in a connected undirected network with nonnegative edge lengths. Let \(U\) be the set of vertices reached so far; start with \(U\) containing one arbitrary vertex and no selected edges. Repeatedly select a shortest edge joining a vertex in \(U\) to a vertex outside \(U\), add that edge, and add the outside endpoint to \(U\). Stop when every vertex belongs to \(U\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The method grows one connected tree from a start vertex. Each step adds the cheapest edge that brings in a vertex not yet reached, so the selected edges never form a cycle and never fall apart into separate pieces.

The numbers in brackets give the order of selection when the method starts at \(A\): first \(A-C\) (2), then \(C-B\) (1). The oval marks \(U=\{A,B,C\}\) after these two steps. The edges leaving \(U\) are \(B-D\) (5), \(C-D\) (8) and \(C-E\) (10), so \(B-D\) is chosen next; \(A-B\) is no longer a candidate because both its ends are in \(U\). Then \(D-E\) and \(E-F\) follow, for a total length of 13.

Only edges between \(U\) and the rest are compared: an edge inside \(U\) would close a cycle, and an edge with neither end in \(U\) would start a second piece. The cheapest crossing edge is a safe choice: every spanning tree uses at least one edge between \(U\) and the rest, and one can show that a cheapest such edge always belongs to some minimum spanning tree.

The shortest path algorithm grows a set \(U\) in the same way but compares \(d(u)+\ell_{uv}\), the full distance from the origin, instead of the length of the edge \(u-v\) alone. Mixing up the two is a common slip: the Dijkstra-Prim method minimizes the total length of the tree, not the distance from the start vertex.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Compare edges crossing from the whole set \(U\), not only from the last added vertex.
  • Ties can be broken arbitrarily.
  • The starting vertex can change the construction order without changing the minimum total value.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the figure, each green edge label gives its weight and selection step in brackets. After reaching \(U=\{A,B,C\}\), \(BD=5\) is cheaper than \(CD=8\) or \(CE=10\); \(AB\) is ineligible because both endpoints are already in \(U\). The five selected edges have total length 13.

  • In the Euclidean example, starting with \(U=\{1\}\) selects edge \(1-7\) of length \(\sqrt{13}\).
  • The next edge is \(1-4\), of length 5.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A directed network is a network whose edges have specified orientations. An edge \(i\to j\) allows traversal or flow from \(i\) to \(j\); reverse traversal is not implied by its existence.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Direction represents asymmetric connections, such as one-way streets, pipes that carry flow one way, or activities that must happen in a given order. An edge \(i\to j\) says that one can go from \(i\) to \(j\), and nothing about going back.

Every edge in the figure carries an arrow. The red edge \(E\to D\) allows the move from \(E\) to \(D\), but no edge leads from \(D\) to \(E\); since the only edge leaving \(D\) is \(D\to F\) and \(F\) has no outgoing edge, \(E\) cannot be reached from \(D\) at all.

So every route must follow the arrows, and a two-way connection needs two opposite edges \(i\to j\) and \(j\to i\). Direction is essential in the maximum flow problem, where each capacity belongs to one directed edge.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Incoming and outgoing edges have different roles at a vertex.
  • Maximum-flow constraints respect the original edge directions.
  • A backward residual edge cancels assigned flow; it is not necessarily an original directed edge.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The red edge permits \(E\to D\), but there is no edge permitting \(D\to E\). Such orientations can represent one-way streets, pipe flows or activity precedence.

  • The maximum-flow network has outgoing edges at the source and incoming edges at the sink.
  • An activity edge \(i\to j\) points from its preceding event to its following event.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
Let demand be a nonnegative integer-valued random variable with CDF \(F\), finite mean, and newsvendor underage cost \(b>0\) and overage cost \(h>0\). Over nonnegative integer order quantities, a smallest optimal quantity is

\[ \begin{gathered} y^*=\min\{y\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}\colon F(y)\ge\beta\},\\ \beta=\frac{b}{b+h}. \end{gathered} \]

For the expected cost \(G(y)\) of ordering \(y\), the marginal difference is

\[ G(y+1)-G(y)=(b+h)F(y)-b. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
With demand in whole units, the order is raised one unit at a time. Going from \(y\) to \(y+1\) changes the expected cost by \((b+h)F(y)-b\), which is negative exactly when \(F(y)<\beta\). So keep adding units while \(F(y)<\beta\), and stop at the first \(y\) with \(F(y)\ge\beta\), where \(\beta\) is the critical ratio.

The CDF of integer demand is a staircase that jumps at the possible demand values. The level \(\beta=0.75\) lies between \(F(9)=0.70\) and \(F(10)=0.85\). Going from \(9\) to \(10\) still lowers the expected cost, because \(0.70<0.75\), while going from \(10\) to \(11\) raises it, because \(0.85>0.75\); hence \(y^*=10\).

With integer demand, increase \(y\) while \(F(y)<\beta\): the first \(y\) with \(F(y)\ge\beta\) is optimal.

The difference formula compares the two outcomes for unit \(y+1\). It is left over when \(D\le y\), with probability \(F(y)\) and cost \(h\), and it is sold when \(D\ge y+1\), with probability \(1-F(y)\) and saving \(b\). Because \(F\) never decreases, the differences never decrease either, so the first stop is a global optimum and not only a local one. If \(F(y)=\beta\) exactly, the step from \(y\) to \(y+1\) costs nothing and both quantities are optimal; the rule returns the smaller one. Usually no integer \(y\) has \(F(y)=\beta\), which is why the rule uses \(\ge\) instead of solving an equation as the continuous rule does.

A common slip is to stop at the last \(y\) with \(F(y)<\beta\), here \(9\). That quantity still gains from one more unit.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(F(y)=\beta\), quantities \(y\) and \(y+1\) have equal expected cost.
  • All integer optimal quantities satisfy \(F(y-1)\le\beta\le F(y)\), taking \(F(-1)=0\).
  • Compute the expected cost with the actual discrete probabilities, not only the critical ratio.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The drawn CDF steps other than \(F(9)\) and \(F(10)\) are schematic; they do not specify additional probabilities for the dress example.

  • For the newspaper distribution, \(F(16)=0.25<3/7\le F(17)=0.50\), so the smallest optimum is 17; expected cost is 1.975.
  • The dress example has \(\beta=0.75\), optimal quantity 10, and expected cost 138.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A dummy assignment makes a rectangular assignment matrix square by adding fictitious agents or tasks with zero assignment costs. Add dummy agents when there are fewer agents than tasks; add dummy tasks when there are fewer tasks than agents.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A dummy assignment turns an assignment problem with unequal numbers of agents and tasks into a square one: an agent paired with a dummy task stays idle, and a task paired with a dummy agent is left undone.

The original \(3\times2\) table has one agent too many. The zero column \(T_{\mathrm{dummy}}\) makes it square; whichever agent receives it is the idle one. The minimum \(5\) is reached with \(A_2\) idle, as in the Examples, but also with \(A_1\) idle, \(A_2\to T_1\) and \(A_3\to T_2\).

The zero costs say that leaving an entity unused costs nothing, so each complete assignment of the square table costs exactly as much as its real pairs. The Hungarian algorithm can then run on the square table, and the dummy pairs in its result only record who is idle or which task stays open.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Use zero dummy costs under the course assumption that leaving the corresponding entity unused has no additional penalty.
  • A dummy agent leaves its assigned real task unperformed.
  • A real agent assigned to a dummy task remains unused.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the figure, one optimal assignment is \(A_1\to T_2\) at cost 2, \(A_3\to T_1\) at cost 3 and \(A_2\) to the dummy task. Thus \(A_2\) is idle and the total cost is 5.

  • Three agents and four tasks require one dummy-agent row.
  • Five machines and four jobs require one dummy-job column if machines are the rows.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The dynamic lot-size model chooses order quantities over \(n\) discrete periods with known varying demands, no shortages, and no lead time. In the detailed course notation, \(y_i\) is the period-\(i\) order, \(D_i\) demand, \(x_i\) starting stock, \(K_i\) setup cost, \(c_i(y_i)\) the variable ordering cost of \(y_i\) units, and \(h_i\) holding cost per unit carried to the next period. Then

\[ \begin{gathered} x_{i+1}=x_i+y_i-D_i\ge0,\\ C_i(y_i)=\begin{cases}0,&y_i=0,\\K_i+c_i(y_i),&y_i>0.\end{cases} \end{gathered} \]

Minimize \(\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n[C_i(y_i)+h_ix_{i+1}]\), with given \(x_1\) and terminal stock \(x_{n+1}=0\) in the course examples.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The dynamic lot-size model plans orders over a finite number of periods whose demands are known but differ. Each order triggers a setup cost, so it can be cheaper to order once for several periods and carry the surplus, paying holding cost for it.

Each box is one period with its demand, and the arrows on top are orders. The balance \(x_{i+1}=x_i+y_i-D_i\) can be followed from left to right: period \(1\) starts empty, orders \(2\) and uses \(2\), so \(x_2=0\); period \(2\) orders \(2\) but uses only \(1\), so one unit is carried into period \(3\) at cost \(h_2\); period \(3\) orders \(2\), which with the carried unit covers its demand \(3\) and leaves \(x_4=0\).

The constraint \(x_{i+1}\ge0\) forbids shortages, and fixing the final stock at zero stops the plan from ending with useless stock. The cost \(C_i(y_i)\) contains the full setup \(K_i\) as soon as \(y_i>0\), however small the order: this fixed charge is what makes combining orders attractive.

The balance equation is the one of the production-inventory model (there \(I_{t-1}+P_t-d_t=I_t\)). The EOQ is the constant-demand counterpart; here no single formula exists. The best plan can be found period by period with dynamic programming, in the form of the lot-size Bellman recursion, and the Silver-Meal heuristic gives a quick approximate plan.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The course tables enumerate nonnegative integer order and stock quantities.
  • Variable ordering cost \(c_i(y_i)\) may depend nonlinearly on the batch size.
  • The model is introduced in the week 5 overview and developed in week 6.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the illustrated three-period policy, the period-2 order exceeds that period’s demand by one unit. Carrying it into period 3 gives the displayed total cost 79.

  • For demands \((2,1,3)\), the worked optimum orders \((2,2,2)\) at total cost 79.
  • Week 6 practice 2 has two optimal policies, \((4,0,4,0)\) and \((6,0,0,2)\), both costing 31.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Dynamic programming (DP) decomposes an optimization problem into related subproblems and computes their optimal values recursively. A state records the information needed to connect stages, and the optimum for a smaller subproblem becomes an input to the next calculation.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Dynamic programming solves a problem made of a sequence of decisions stage by stage. The cost of the remaining decisions depends only on the current state, not on how that state was reached, so the best value of each state is computed once and reused, instead of once for every complete policy that passes through it.

Each column is a stage, each circle a state, and every route from start to end is one complete policy. Listing routes repeats the same arrow costs many times: with \(m\) stages of three states there are \(3^m\) routes but fewer than \(9m\) arrows. The forward calculation stores one value \(f_1\) per stage-1 state, computes each \(f_2\) from the three arrows entering it, and reaches the end after looking at every arrow once.

A DP model needs a state that contains everything the later stages depend on. In the dynamic lot-size model the stage is the period and the state is the stock carried into the next period, as in the lot-size recursion. If the state leaves out relevant information, histories that should be treated differently are merged and the recursion can give a wrong answer.

The cheapest policy is a cheapest route from start to end through the staged network, which links DP to the shortest path problem. Unlike a heuristic such as the Silver-Meal heuristic, DP guarantees an optimal solution.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Specify the state, decision, transition, cost, boundary conditions, and recursion.
  • Store minimizing decisions as well as costs to reconstruct an optimal policy.
  • Keep every minimizing decision if all optimal policies are required.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For the figure’s forward calculation, each incoming arrow contributes its transition cost plus the preceding state value: \(f_2(\text{state})=\min_{\text{incoming arrows}}\{\text{arrow cost}+f_1(\text{previous state})\}\). The red arrows record the minimizing decisions used to reconstruct the policy.

  • \(f_i(x_{i+1})\) records the least cost through period \(i\) for a specified ending inventory.
  • The three-period calculation finds \(f_3(0)=79\) and then traces decisions backward.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
Under the classical EOQ assumptions with \(D,K,h>0\), the unique order quantity minimizing the total cost per unit time (TCU) \(TCU(y)=KD/y+hy/2\) over \(y>0\) is

\[ y^*=\sqrt{\frac{2KD}{h}},\qquad t_0^*=\frac{y^*}{D}=\sqrt{\frac{2K}{Dh}}. \]

The optimal policy orders \(y^*\) units when stock reaches zero.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The economic order quantity is the batch size at which the setup cost rate \(KD/y\) and the holding cost rate \(hy/2\) of the classical EOQ model are in balance. Larger batches cut the number of setups; smaller batches cut the average stock.

The setup curve \(1210/y\) falls and the holding line \(2.5y\) rises; they cross at \(y=22\), where each equals \(55\). The total cost is lowest exactly there, at \(110\) per day.

Change \(D\), \(K\) and \(h\): the minimum of \(TCU(y)\) sits where the two cost rates are equal, at \(y^*=\sqrt{2KD/h}\).

That the minimum lies at the crossing is no coincidence. The product of the two terms, \(\frac{KD}{y}\cdot\frac{hy}{2}=\frac{KDh}{2}\), does not depend on \(y\), and for two positive numbers \(a+b\ge2\sqrt{ab}\), since \((\sqrt{a}-\sqrt{b})^2\ge0\). Hence

\[ TCU(y)\ge2\sqrt{\frac{KDh}{2}}=\sqrt{2KDh}, \]

with equality if and only if \(KD/y=hy/2\), that is \(y^2=2KD/h\). This inequality gives the same answer as setting the derivative to zero.

The square root makes the answer move slowly with the data: doubling demand raises \(y^*\) only by a factor \(\sqrt{2}\approx1.41\). The cost curve is also flat near its minimum: batches of \(11\) or \(44\) phones instead of \(22\) cost \(137.5\) per day instead of \(110\), so an order size somewhat away from \(y^*\) costs little extra. The same formula reappears with lead times, is corrected by a factor with planned shortages, and serves as a candidate with price breaks.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• At the optimum, \(KD/y^*=hy^*/2\).
  • The minimum relevant cost rate is \(\sqrt{2KDh}\).
  • Increasing demand raises the batch size but shortens the ordering cycle.
  • The formula follows from \(-KD/y^2+h/2=0\) and strict convexity.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For the illustrated phone shop, \(K=605\), \(D=2\) per day and \(h=5\) per unit per day give \(y^*=\sqrt{2\cdot605\cdot2/5}=22\). It orders every \(22/2=11\) days; setup and holding each cost \(55\) per day, giving relevant daily cost \(110\).
  • The snack bar obtains \(y^*=\sqrt{2(50)(10)/(3/7)}\approx48.30\) kilograms.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a repeating EOQ ordering cycle of length \(t_0^*>0\) and fixed lead time \(L\ge0\), the effective lead time is

\[ L_e=L-nt_0^*,\qquad n=\left\lfloor\frac{L}{t_0^*}\right\rfloor. \]

Thus \(0\le L_e<t_0^*\). The course's on-hand reorder level is \(DL_e\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The effective lead time says where in the stock cycle an order must be placed when the delivery delay is longer than one cycle. Whole cycles inside the delay do not change the position in the sawtooth, so only the remainder \(L_e\) matters for the reorder level.

The cycle lasts \(7\) weeks and the delay \(L=20\) weeks. The order placed at week \(1\), when stock has fallen to \(6D\), arrives at week \(21\): it spans the remainder \(L_e=6\) weeks plus \(n=2\) full cycles. Placing the order \(6\) weeks before some stockout is therefore the right moment, even though the stockout it serves lies \(20\) weeks ahead.

Whole cycles inside \(L\) do not matter for the reorder level: only \(L_e=L-nt_0^*\) does. Make \(L\) longer than a cycle to see orders overlap.

The number \(n=\lfloor L/t_0^*\rfloor\) is the floor of \(L/t_0^*\): the number of complete cycles that fit into the delay. Subtracting them leaves \(0\le L_e<t_0^*\), so the reorder level \(DL_e\) is always below the batch size \(y^*\) and is actually reached by the on-hand stock. With \(L<t_0^*\), nothing is subtracted and \(L_e=L\).

A common slip is to use \(DL\) as the reorder level when \(L\) exceeds a cycle: in the figure, \(DL=20D\) is far above the maximum stock \(y^*=7D\), a level the on-hand stock never reaches. The physical delay is still \(L\): \(L_e\) only fixes the ordering moment, and when an order is placed, \(n\) earlier orders are still on their way, as in EOQ with lead times.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For a lead time shorter than a cycle, \(L_e=L\).
  • The quantity \(L_e\) is a cycle remainder, not a shorter physical delivery delay.
  • If the delay is an exact multiple of the cycle, the remainder is zero; ordering and receipt events must be interpreted at that common cycle boundary.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In the figure, time is measured in weeks. A cycle of \(t_0^*=7\) weeks gives \(y^*=7D\). With \(L=20\) weeks, \(n=2\) and \(L_e=20-2\cdot7=6\) weeks, so the reorder level is \(6D\). The order placed at week 1 arrives at week 21; two earlier orders are still in transit when it is placed.
  • The snack bar has \(L=12\) days and \(t_0^*\approx4.83\), giving \(L_e\approx2.34\) days.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
To require at least one of \(\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\le b\) and \(\boldsymbol{d}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\le e\), introduce \(y\in\{0,1\}\) and write

\[ \boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\le b+My,\qquad \boldsymbol{d}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\le e+M(1-y). \]

The finite constant \(M\) must be large enough that the relaxed inequality imposes no unintended restriction over the relevant variable domain.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Either-or constraints require a solution to satisfy at least one of two inequalities. A binary variable \(y\) decides which inequality is enforced, and a large constant \(M\) switches the other one off. Points satisfying both are also allowed, so this is the inclusive "or".

The blue region satisfies \(3x_1+2x_2\le18\), the red region \(x_1+4x_2\le16\), and the allowed set is their union. The point \((1,7)\) gives \(17\le18\) but \(29>16\), so it is allowed with \(y=0\), which enforces the first inequality. The point \((7,1)\) gives \(23>18\) but \(11\le16\), so it needs \(y=1\). The point \((5,5)\) violates both and is excluded whatever \(y\) is.

With \(y=0\) the second inequality becomes \(\boldsymbol{d}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\le e+M\), which should hold for every relevant \(\boldsymbol{x}\) and so restricts nothing; for \(y=1\) the roles swap. Hence \(M\) must cover the largest amount by which the switched-off left-hand side can exceed its right-hand side. If \(M\) is too small, allowed points are cut away; a much larger \(M\) is still correct but weakens the LP relaxation, where \(y\) may be fractional.

The binary variable is needed: the union contains \((7,1)\) and \((1,7)\) but not their midpoint \((4,4)\), since \(20>18\) and \(20>16\). A system of linear inequalities always contains the average of any two of its points (see convex combinations), so none in \(x_1,x_2\) alone describes this set. With several binaries the same device gives K-out-of-N constraints and nonconvex region modelling.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For \(y=0\), the first inequality is enforced; for \(y=1\), the second is enforced.
  • A valid value of \(M\) requires information about bounds on the expressions being relaxed.
  • This is a modelling device; it does not mean multiplying two decision variables.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The blue inequality is enforced when \(y=0\), and the red one when \(y=1\). The illustrated union is nonconvex, so it cannot be represented by one system of continuous linear inequalities in \(\boldsymbol{x}\) alone.

  • \(3x_1+2x_2\le18+My\) and \(x_1+4x_2\le16+M(1-y)\) implement the video example.
  • The week 3 exercise applies the same switch to two inequalities involving four variables.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: In the course's maximization simplex tableau, the entering variable rule selects a nonbasic variable with the most negative coefficient in the objective row. If several coefficients tie for most negative, any tied variable may be chosen.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The rule decides which nonbasic variable to increase next: the one that raises the objective fastest per unit. Because the objective row is written with \(z\) on the left, as \(z+\sum_jq_jx_j=z_0\), a coefficient \(q_j<0\) means that \(z\) rises by \(-q_j\) for every unit increase of \(x_j\), so a more negative coefficient corresponds to a higher improvement rate.

The arrow marks the \(x_s\) column of the initial Giapetto tableau: its coefficient \(-3\) is the most negative, since a soldier adds 3 to \(z\) and a train only 2.

The sign convention is the point to remember. A variable with profit \(c_j\) appears in the first tableau with coefficient \(-c_j\), so negative means improving. If no nonbasic coefficient is negative, no increase can raise \(z\), and the optimality test stops the method. Any variable with a negative coefficient would improve \(z\); choosing the most negative one is a convention that fixes a definite next step.

The rule compares rates, not total gains. How far the entering variable can increase is decided afterwards by the minimum-ratio test. Here \(x_s\) can rise only to 40, a gain of \(3\cdot40=120\), whereas \(x_t\) could rise to 80, a gain of \(2\cdot80=160\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The selected variable defines the pivot column.
  • The greatest improvement rate is not necessarily the greatest total improvement, because allowable step sizes differ.
  • The ratio test determines how far the entering variable can increase while preserving feasibility.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The illustrated row is \(z-3x_s-2x_t=0\), so \(x_s\) has the largest objective improvement rate per unit, \(3>2\), and enters. Choosing the smallest index is one possible tie convention; it is not required by the course rule. A feasible canonical tableau with no negative nonbasic objective-row coefficient is already optimal.

  • From \(z-3x_1-2x_2=0\), choose \(x_1\).
  • From \(z-(1/2)x_2+(3/2)s_1=15\), choose \(x_2\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The EOQ model with lead times retains constant known demand, no shortages, and the classical setup and holding costs, but an order arrives after a fixed delay \(L\ge0\). The optimal quantity remains \(y^*=\sqrt{2KD/h}\). In the course's repeating on-hand-stock convention, order when stock falls to \(DL_e\), where \(L_e\) is the effective lead time.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A lead time is the delay between placing an order and receiving it. With constant known demand, a delay only shifts the moment of ordering: the order is placed early enough that the batch arrives exactly when stock runs out, and the batch size stays the EOQ.

Stock falls from \(y^*=6000\) at \(100\) per day. The order is placed on day \(48\), when stock reaches the reorder level \(DL=1200\), and arrives on day \(60\), just as stock hits zero. The remaining \(1200\) pencils are exactly the demand during the \(12\)-day delay.

Change the lead time \(L\): the batch size stays \(y^*\), but the order must be placed when stock reaches \(DL_e\) (dashed).

The stock pattern over time is the same sawtooth as in the classical EOQ model; only the ordering moments have moved. Setup and holding costs per unit time are therefore unchanged, and so are \(y^*\) and the minimum cost. The trigger has become a stock level instead of the moment stock reaches zero.

The rule \(DL\) assumes that the delay is shorter than an ordering cycle. For longer delays, \(DL\) exceeds \(y^*\), a level that on-hand stock never reaches from below. The effective lead time then removes the full cycles and gives the level \(DL_e\). The reasoning also relies on demand and delay being known exactly: if either were uncertain, stock could run out before the order arrives.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(L<t_0^*\), the reorder stock level is \(DL\).
  • If lead time exceeds an ordering cycle, several orders can be outstanding; use the course effective-lead-time construction.
  • The on-hand trigger describes steady-state cycles, not the initial setup of an empty supply pipeline.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For the illustrated pencil inventory, demand is \(D=100\) per day, each order costs \(K=180\), and holding one pencil costs \(h=0.001\) per day. The optimal order quantity and relevant daily cost are

\[ y^*=\sqrt{\frac{2KD}{h}}=\sqrt{\frac{2\cdot180\cdot100}{0.001}} =6000,\qquad \sqrt{2KDh}=6. \]

The cycle lasts \(t_0^*=y^*/D=60\) days. With a 12-day lead time, the reorder level is \(DL=1200\): place the order on day 48 so that it arrives on day 60, when the stock runs out. The order quantity and cost remain unchanged.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The EOQ model with planned shortages allows all unmet demand to be backordered until instantaneous replenishment. With constant \(D>0\), setup \(K>0\), holding rate \(h>0\), and shortage cost (backlog penalty) \(p>0\), choose batch size \(y>0\) and stock just after replenishment \(0\le s\le y\). Maximum backlog is \(y-s\), and

\[ TCU(y,s)=\frac{KD}{y}+\frac{hs^2}{2y}+\frac{p(y-s)^2}{2y}. \]

The optimum is

\[ \begin{aligned} y^*&=\sqrt{\frac{2KD}{h}}\sqrt{\frac{p+h}{p}},\\ s^*&=\sqrt{\frac{2KD}{h}}\sqrt{\frac{p}{p+h}}. \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
This model lets stock run below zero on purpose: customers who arrive when the shelf is empty wait, and are served as soon as the next batch arrives. Waiting is charged at rate \(p\) per unit per unit time, so the model trades waiting customers against the cost of holding stock.

In the phone example, each batch of \(y^*\approx29.79\) first clears the backlog of about \(13.54\) and leaves \(s^*\approx16.25\) phones on hand. Stock is positive for about \(8.1\) days (blue) and backlogged for about \(6.8\) days (red) of each \(14.9\)-day cycle. The fraction of time with stock is \(s^*/y^*=6/11=p/(p+h)\).

Choose the batch size \(y\) and the stock \(s\) after replenishment. The level curves of \(TCU(y,s)\) (left) surround the optimum; the right panel shows stock and backlog.

Two decisions are made now: the batch size \(y\) and the stock \(s\) left after the backlog is cleared. Holding cost is charged only on the blue triangles, so the average stock over a whole cycle is \(s^2/(2y)\), and shortage cost is charged on the red triangles. Short periods of shortage save holding cost, which is why some backlog pays off whenever \(p\) is finite.

The factor \(\sqrt{(p+h)/p}\) links the model to the classical EOQ: the larger \(p\), the closer the factor is to \(1\). With \(p=600\) instead of \(6\), \(y^*\approx22.09\), almost the classical \(22\), with a tiny backlog. A common slip is to treat backlog as lost sales: here every waiting customer is served, so the ordering cycle is still \(y/D\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Order \(y^*\) when backlog reaches \(y^*-s^*\).
  • Ordering cycle length is \(y^*/D\); the fraction of time without shortage is \(p/(p+h)\).
  • The stock-phase mean \(s/2\) is not the whole-cycle average; the latter is \(s^2/(2y)\).
  • For finite positive \(p\), the optimal batch is larger than the classical EOQ.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In the illustrated phone example, \(D=2\) per day, \(K=605\), \(h=5\) per phone per day and \(p=6\) per backlogged phone per day give \(y^*=22\sqrt{11/6}\approx29.79\) and \(s^*=22\sqrt{6/11}\approx16.25\). Order when the backlog reaches \(y^*-s^*\approx13.54\). The cycle lasts about \(14.9\) days: stock is positive for about \(8.1\) days and backlogged for about \(6.8\) days, with stock-positive fraction \(6/11\).
  • With \(p=h\), the model is out of stock for half the cycle.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The course's EOQ model with price breaks gives an all-unit discount: every ordered unit has price \(c_2<c_1\) when the batch meets a threshold \(q\). Following the “at least” convention of the worked examples,

\[ \begin{gathered} c(y)=\begin{cases}c_1,&0<y<q,\\c_2,&y\ge q,\end{cases}\\ TCU(y)=Dc(y)+\frac{KD}{y}+\frac{hy}{2}. \end{gathered} \]

Holding rate \(h\) is fixed across price levels; demand is constant, replenishment instantaneous, and shortages prohibited.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
With an all-unit discount, ordering at least \(q\) units lowers the price of every unit in the batch. Buying more than the EOQ can then pay off even though it raises the holding cost, so the purchasing cost \(Dc(y)\) must be included in the comparison instead of being left out as in the classical EOQ model.

The blue curve is the total cost at price \(170\), which applies below \(35\) units, and the red curve the total cost at price \(160\) from \(35\) on. The blue curve is lowest at \(y_m=22\), with cost \(450\) per day. The red curve does not apply at \(22\), but at the threshold \(35\) it costs \(442.07\), which is lower, so the optimal order is \(35\).

From the break \(q\) on, every unit costs \(c_2<c_1\), so the total cost curve jumps down. Compare the best quantity on each side of \(q\).

Both curves have the same shape and differ only by the constant \(D(c_1-c_2)\), so each is lowest at \(y_m=\sqrt{2KD/h}\). On the discounted curve, the cheapest quantity that qualifies is \(y_m\) if \(y_m\ge q\), and otherwise \(q\) itself, since that curve rises to the right of \(y_m\). The comparison is therefore between at most two candidates, \(y_m\) at the higher price and \(q\) at the lower price.

The price-break indifference quantity turns this comparison into a threshold rule. A common slip is to take the discounted price at \(y_m=22\), which gives \(430\) per day, but \(22\) units do not qualify for that price.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Let \(y_m=\sqrt{2KD/h}\). If \(y_m\ge q\), order \(y_m\) at the discount price.
  • If \(y_m<q\), compare the full costs at \(y_m\) and \(q\) and choose the cheaper; both are optimal at equality.
  • This page treats \(y=q\) as qualifying for the discount, as the worked examples do; check the convention when a problem states the threshold as \(y>q\).
  • The discount is all-unit, not a discount only on units above the threshold.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For phones, \(y_m=22\): cost at 22 is 450 per day, while cost at the qualifying 35 is about 442.07; order 35.
  • For the snack bar, the 100-kilogram threshold is not worthwhile; the optimal quantity remains about 48.30.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In the course's Euclidean network, cities have plane coordinates \((x_i,y_i)\), an edge may join every pair of cities, and its length is

\[ d_{ij}=\sqrt{(x_i-x_j)^2+(y_i-y_j)^2}. \]

The resulting distances provide the weights for the minimum spanning tree problem.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Coordinates turn a location problem into a complete weighted network: every pair of cities is joined by an edge, and the length of that edge is the straight-line distance between the two points, computed with Pythagoras' theorem. These are straight-line lengths, not road distances or travel times.

The four cities lie at the grid points \((1,1)\), \((4,3)\), \((5,1)\) and \((2,3)\), and all \(6\) pairs are joined. The red edge between cities 1 and 2 spans \(3\) units horizontally and \(2\) vertically, so \(d_{12}=\sqrt{3^2+2^2}=\sqrt{13}\approx3.61\). The coordinates only fix the edge lengths; they add no further connections.

With \(n\) cities there are \(n(n-1)/2\) edges, so the seven-city example already needs 21 distances. Since \(d_{ij}=d_{ji}\), the network is undirected. Straight-line distances also have a useful property: going from \(i\) to \(j\) via a third city is never shorter than the direct edge, so in a Euclidean network the direct edge is always a shortest path between its endpoints.

Many distances are irrational numbers, and different edges can have equal or nearly equal lengths: in the figure, the edges \(1-2\) and \(3-4\) both have length \(\sqrt{13}\). Rounding too early can therefore change the comparison between two close edges. Once the distances are computed accurately, the Dijkstra-Prim and Kruskal methods for a minimum spanning tree apply without change.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Distances are symmetric: \(d_{ij}=d_{ji}\).
  • Use sufficient precision when comparing close distances.
  • The usual spanning-tree algorithms apply once the distance matrix is computed.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The red edge has length \(d_{12}=\sqrt{3^2+2^2}=\sqrt{13}\). Euclidean distances satisfy the triangle inequality and can also be used as routing costs.

  • Between \((13,6)\) and \((15,9)\) the distance is \(\sqrt{13}\approx3.61\).
  • The seven-city example has tree length about 27.29 using the displayed rounded distances.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text: A finite connected undirected network has an Euler tour if and only if every vertex has even degree. Such a network is called an Euler network.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The proposition replaces a search over all possible routes by a check done vertex by vertex: in a connected network, a closed route using every edge exactly once exists exactly when all degrees are even.

In the left network the degrees are \(4,2,2,2,2\), all even, and an Euler tour exists. The right network adds the edge \(B-D\), which raises the degrees of \(B\) and \(D\) to \(3\). Now no Euler tour exists, but a route that starts at \(B\), ends at \(D\) and uses every edge once still does.

Even degree is necessary because a closed route pairs every arrival at a vertex with a departure; at the starting vertex, the first departure pairs with the final arrival. So the route uses the edges at each vertex two at a time. Sufficiency is the harder direction, and the cycle-splicing construction of the Euler tour algorithm establishes it. Connectedness cannot be dropped: two separate triangles have all degrees equal to 2, yet no single route covers both.

With exactly two odd vertices, as on the right, a connected network still has an open route between them that uses every edge once; the Königsberg network, with four odd vertices, has neither kind of route. The Chinese postman problem makes odd degrees even by duplicating paths, after which the proposition applies.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• One odd-degree vertex is enough to rule out an Euler tour.
  • Connectedness is required to traverse all edges in one tour.
  • Parallel copies introduced by the Chinese postman construction are counted as separate edges.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The seven-bridge network violates the even-degree condition.
  • Duplicating suitable paths between odd-degree vertices makes their endpoint degrees even.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a connected undirected Euler network, the course's Euler tour algorithm starts at a vertex \(s\), follows unused edges until returning to \(s\), and calls the resulting cycle \(\Omega\). If unused edges remain, choose a vertex \(v\) on \(\Omega\) incident to an unused edge, build another closed unused-edge traversal \(\Omega_1\) from \(v\), and splice \(\Omega_1\) into \(\Omega\) at \(v\). Repeat until every edge is used.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The method builds a complete tour from smaller cycles: walk along unused edges until you are back at the start, then insert further closed detours at vertices already on the tour. Even degree ensures that every such detour can close at its starting vertex.

Starting at \(s=A\), the first cycle \(\Omega=A-B-C-A\) (blue edges 1 to 3) returns to \(A\) but leaves \(A-D\), \(D-E\) and \(E-A\) unused. The second cycle \(A-D-E-A\) (red edges 4 to 6) starts at \(A\), a vertex of \(\Omega\), and is spliced in there, giving \(A-B-C-A-D-E-A\), which uses all six edges.

A walk can only get stuck at its start. When it arrives at a vertex \(v\ne s\), it has used an odd number of the edges at \(v\), two for each earlier pass and one for this arrival; since the degree of \(v\) is even, an unused edge remains to leave by. A closed walk uses an even number of edges at every vertex, so after removing its edges all remaining degrees are still even and the next detour also closes. Connectedness ensures that, as long as unused edges remain, one of them touches a vertex already on the tour.

The algorithm thus proves the harder half of the Euler network characterization: even degrees suffice. It is also the final step of the Chinese postman problem, where each duplicated copy counts as a separate edge.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Keep track of used edge identities, especially with parallel copies.
  • The splice inserts one closed excursion into another without losing any previously used edge.
  • Arbitrary eligible choices can give different valid Euler tours.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the figure, the first cycle is \(\Omega=A-B-C-A\). The remaining cycle \(A-D-E-A\) is spliced at \(A\), giving \(A-B-C-A-D-E-A\). The even-degree condition permits these closed excursions.

  • The worked example begins its first cycle at A.
  • It later adds a cycle through B and then one through D to include all 12 edges.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An Euler tour is a closed traversal of a network that uses every edge exactly once. Vertices may be revisited. A network possessing an Euler tour is called an Euler network.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An Euler tour is a round trip that uses every edge exactly once. It models a route that must cover every street, for a postman or a street sweeper, without retracing any edge.

The numbers give the order of the edges in the tour \(A-B-C-A-D-E-A\). All six edges are used once and the tour ends where it started. The vertex \(A\), of degree 4, is passed through halfway as well, while each other vertex, of degree 2, is passed through once.

The requirement concerns edges, not vertices: vertices may be revisited, as \(A\) is here. A round trip that visits every vertex exactly once is a different question; in the network of the figure no such trip exists, since a round trip through both triangles must pass through \(A\) twice.

Whether an Euler tour exists is decided by the vertex degrees: a connected undirected network has one if and only if every vertex has even degree, by the Euler network characterization, and the Euler tour algorithm builds one by joining cycles. The network of the Königsberg bridges fails this test. When no Euler tour exists, the Chinese postman problem asks for a shortest closed route that uses every edge at least once.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• At each vertex, arrivals and departures balance.
  • For connected undirected networks, an Euler tour exists exactly when every vertex has even degree.
  • In a weighted Euler network, every Euler tour has length equal to the sum of all edge lengths.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the illustrated Euler network, \(\deg A=4\) and every other degree is 2. The tour returns to its start while using every edge once.

  • The Königsberg bridge network has no Euler tour because its vertices have odd degree.
  • The course weighted Euler example has total edge length 24, so its Euler tours have length 24.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The course's Excel sensitivity report summarizes a solved continuous LP through variable values, reduced costs, objective coefficients and their allowable changes, constraint left-hand-side values, shadow prices, right-hand sides, and their allowable changes. The course obtains this report after solving with Simplex LP.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The sensitivity report answers what-if questions about a solved linear program without solving it again: how far a coefficient may change before the optimal plan changes, and what one more unit of a resource is worth. Every number refers to the final solution of Excel Solver.

The variable table concerns the objective: each variable's final value, reduced cost, objective coefficient and its allowable increase and decrease. Within that range the optimal variable values stay the same, while the optimal objective value moves with the coefficient. The constraint table concerns the right-hand sides: the final value of the left-hand side, the shadow price, the right-hand side and its allowable range. Within that range each extra unit changes the optimal value by the shadow price, while the variable values may change.

The entries are linked. A constraint whose final value differs from its right-hand side is not binding and has shadow price \(0\): more of a resource that is not used up is worth nothing. In the pipes example processing time is used for \(624\) of \(2{,}400\) units, so its shadow price is \(0\).

The ranges need the most care. They are changes relative to the current value, not new totals: a coefficient \(5\) with allowable increase \(2\) may rise to \(7\). Each range also assumes that only that one number changes.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For a constraint, Final Value is the evaluated left-hand side, not its right-hand side.
  • An allowable increase is an increment, not a new total.
  • The report's very large bound notation is used for an effectively unlimited allowable change in these examples.
  • Interpret the ranges for separate single-parameter changes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The pipes plan produces 72 large pipes, 48 small pipes, and no sheets, with profit 816.
  • Processing time used is 624 out of 2,400, leaving 1,776 units of slack.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Excel Solver for linear programming represents the LP's decision variables in changing cells, its objective in a formula cell, and its constraints through formulas and bounds. The course uses the Simplex LP solving method for continuous linear models.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Solver is a numerical tool: it solves exactly the model typed into the spreadsheet, nothing more and nothing less. The spreadsheet must therefore represent the same objective, coefficients, constraints and variable domains as the mathematical model.

Each part of the linear program formulation has a place in the sheet: changing cells for the decision variables, an objective cell with a formula that adds up coefficient times variable, and a formula cell for the left-hand side of each constraint, compared in the Solver dialog with its right-hand side. The Simplex LP method requires these formulas to be linear in the changing cells.

Restrictions that are obvious in words must still be entered: nonnegativity, and integer or binary restrictions as constraints of type int or bin. Solver cannot supply a restriction that was omitted, and a typing error in one coefficient changes the problem without any warning. A message that no feasible solution was found corresponds to an infeasible linear program, and a message that the objective cell values do not converge to an unbounded one.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Use the specified maximization or minimization direction.
  • Integer and binary restrictions must be added explicitly when solving an integer model.
  • A reported solution should be checked against the original constraints.
  • What matters is the model entered and the reported outcome, not the layout of the Solver dialog in a particular Excel version.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Week 2 practice 1(a) has optimum \((14/3,4/3)\) and value \(32/3\).
  • Practice 1(b) has optimum \((4,9,6)\) and value 19.
