docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The feasible region is the set of all feasible solutions of a model:

\[ F=\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{x}\text{ satisfies all constraints}\}. \]

For a two-variable LP it is obtained by intersecting the allowed half-planes and equality lines, including variable-domain restrictions.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The feasible region collects every decision that the constraints allow, before the objective is considered. The objective only chooses among these points; it cannot add new ones.

In the figure, each of the three constraints keeps the points on one side of its line, and \(x_s,x_t\ge0\) keep the first quadrant. The shaded pentagon \(F\) is what remains when all five conditions hold at once: the intersection of the allowed sides. The grey point outside breaks more than one condition, although breaking a single one would already exclude it.

Drag the decision point: it is feasible exactly when it satisfies every constraint, including \(x_s,x_t\ge0\).

Each extra constraint intersects \(F\) with one more allowed side, so it can keep or shrink the region but never enlarge it; this is why a relaxation, which removes constraints, has a feasible region at least as large. Points on a boundary line belong to \(F\) when the constraint is \(\le\) or \(\ge\), and the corner points of \(F\), where boundary lines meet, are where the graphical method finds optima.

The region need not be a bounded shape like this pentagon. The requirements of the diet problem leave an unbounded region, and if the constraints contradict each other the region is the empty set: the model has no feasible solution at all.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Removing a constraint cannot shrink the feasible region.
  • An empty feasible region means the model is infeasible.
  • An unbounded feasible region does not by itself imply an unbounded objective value.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For the illustrated upper-bound model, \(F=\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\le \boldsymbol{b},\ \boldsymbol{x}\ge0\}\). It is an intersection of half-planes in two dimensions, or a convex polyhedron in \(\mathbb{R}^n\); an LP feasible set may be bounded, unbounded or empty.

  • \(x_1,x_2\ge0\) restrict the region to the first quadrant.
  • The diet requirements define the intersection of calorie, vitamin, and feed-share half-planes.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A feasible solution assigns values to all decision variables and satisfies every constraint, including their domain restrictions. A solution violating at least one constraint is infeasible.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Feasibility asks whether a decision is allowed, independently of how good it is. A decision is feasible when it satisfies every constraint of the model, including the restrictions on the values of the variables.

The green points \((15,40)\) and \((40,20)\) are feasible; \((40,20)\) lies on two boundary lines, which is allowed because the constraints are \(\le\). The red point \((30,50)\) fails a single constraint, finishing time, and is therefore infeasible, as is any point with \(x_s<0\).

Drag the point and read each constraint: a single violated inequality makes the decision infeasible, however good its objective value.

All constraints must hold together: one violated inequality is enough to reject a decision, and a large surplus in one constraint does not make up for a violation in another. In the figure, \((30,50)\) would give Giapetto a profit of \(3\cdot30+2\cdot50=190\), more than the best feasible profit \(180\), but it needs \(110\) finishing hours where only \(100\) are available.

The feasible solutions together form the feasible region, and an optimal solution is a feasible solution with the best objective value. A feasible solution without a proof of optimality, for example one found by a heuristic, can still be carried out, and its objective value bounds the optimum.

A common slip is to treat a boundary point as infeasible. Constraints with \(\le\) or \(\ge\) include equality, so a plan that uses a resource exactly is feasible.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• An attractive objective value does not compensate for a violated constraint.
  • An LP-feasible fractional solution may be infeasible after integer restrictions are imposed.
  • Every optimal solution is feasible.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the figure, \((15,40)\) satisfies \(70\le100\), \(55\le80\) and \(15\le40\); \((40,20)\) is also feasible. By contrast, \((30,50)\) requires \(2\cdot30+50=110>100\) finishing hours, and any \(x_s<0\) violates nonnegativity.

  • For \(x_1\le4\), \(x_2\le5\), \(2x_1+x_2\le9\), \(x_1,x_2\ge0\), \((2,5)\) is feasible.
  • In the same model, \((4,5)\) is infeasible because \(2(4)+5=13>9\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A linear expression can be restricted to one of the listed values \(d_1,\ldots,d_N\) by introducing binary variables \(y_i\) and writing

\[ a_1x_1+\cdots+a_nx_n=\sum_{i=1}^Nd_iy_i,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^Ny_i=1,\qquad y_i\in\{0,1\}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A finite-value constraint lets a linear expression take only a few listed values, such as \(x_1+x_2\in\{3,5,8\}\), which linear inequalities alone cannot express. Exactly one indicator selects the allowed value, so no separate alternative constraint is needed for every possible value.

The red points are the three allowed totals, each produced by one selector: \(y_1=1\) gives \(3\), \(y_2=1\) gives \(5\) and \(y_3=1\) gives \(8\), as in the first Example. The light band from \(3\) to \(8\) shows what the right-hand side \(3y_1+5y_2+8y_3\) could reach if the selectors were fractions; \(y_1=y_3=\tfrac{1}{2}\), for instance, gives \(5.5\).

Each part of the formulation has a role. Because the \(y_i\) are binary and sum to \(1\), they are mutually exclusive decisions of the exactly-one type: one \(y_i\) equals \(1\), the others are \(0\), and \(\sum_id_iy_i\) collapses to the single selected value \(d_i\). The values \(d_i\) are fixed data, which keeps every term \(d_iy_i\) linear.

A common slip is to write \(\sum_iy_i\le1\) instead. Then all selectors may be \(0\), and the expression may equal \(0\), a value that is not on the list. The parity constraint can be read as a finite-value constraint with listed values \(0\) and \(2\), written more compactly with one auxiliary variable.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The sum-to-one equality ensures that a value is actually selected.
  • The \(d_i\) are fixed data, so \(d_iy_i\) is linear.
  • Relaxing the indicators to continuous fractions would generally allow values between the listed values.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The light band shows intermediate totals made possible by fractional selector values; the binary selectors permit only the listed totals.

  • For allowed totals 3, 5, or 8, write \(x_1+x_2=3y_1+5y_2+8y_3\).
  • An even number of three yes decisions can take only the values 0 and 2.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The first-fit heuristic processes packing items in their given order. Place the current item into the first previously opened container with enough unused capacity. If no such container exists, open a new container and place the item there. Assume every item individually fits in a container.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
First fit packs the items one at a time and never reconsiders a placement. Each item goes into the earliest opened container that still has room, and a new container is opened only when none has.

The figure follows the order \(15,30,20,35\) with capacity \(50\). Items \(15\) and \(30\) share container 1, leaving \(5\) units free. The \(20\) does not fit there (\(45+20>50\)) and opens container 2. The \(35\) fits neither container 1 (\(45+35>50\)) nor container 2 (\(20+35>50\)) and opens container 3. Two containers suffice for these items, so first fit is not optimal here.

Each part of the rule has a role. "First" means the earliest opened container, not the fullest or the emptiest one; another choice gives a different heuristic. Because an item is only placed where it fits, every intermediate packing respects capacity, and the assumption that each item fits into an empty container guarantees that opening a new container always works. The result depends on the item order: with the order \(35,30,20,15\) the same items need only two containers.

As a heuristic for the bin packing problem, first fit gives a feasible packing and hence an upper bound on the minimum number of containers; comparing it with the total-weight lower bound shows how far from optimal it can be.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every produced packing respects capacity.
  • Its container count is an upper bound, not a proof of optimality.
  • The exercise gives this procedure without a name; first-fit is its conventional search name.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The illustrated order \(15,30,20,35\) with capacity 50 uses three containers under first fit. Two suffice with \(\{15,35\}\) and \(\{30,20\}\), so that first-fit result is not optimal. Reordering the same items as \(35,30,20,15\) makes first fit use two containers here.

  • In the course exercise, items 1, 2, 3, and 9 fill container 1 to weight 49.
  • Items 6, 7, and 8 fill another container to weight 49; the full heuristic packing uses five containers.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A forbidden assignment is an agent-task pair that is not allowed. In the course's Hungarian cost matrix, represent this pair by \(\infty\) and leave that entry infinite during all transformations.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A forbidden assignment excludes one agent-task pair. The infinite cost turns the pair into a prohibition rather than an expensive option: no complete assignment that uses it can compete with one that avoids it.

The entry for \(A_2\to T_2\) is \(\infty\) before and after the row and column reductions, since subtracting a finite number from \(\infty\) leaves \(\infty\). The highlighted optimal assignment avoids that cell: \(A_1\to T_1\), \(A_2\to T_3\), \(A_3\to T_2\) with cost \(2+4+6=12\).

A large finite number \(M\) works only if it is large enough: here the cheapest assignment through \(A_2\to T_2\) costs \(2+M+2\), so \(M\) must exceed \(8\). In the Hungarian algorithm, an infinite entry is never a zero, so it is never selected; in the binary formulation, the same ban is the constraint \(x_{ij}=0\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Do not apply finite row or column adjustments as if they made an infinite entry available.
  • If no complete assignment avoiding forbidden pairs exists, the intended assignment problem is infeasible.
  • In a binary formulation, the equivalent restriction is \(x_{ij}=0\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the figure, prohibiting \((2,2)\) gives the highlighted assignment \(A_1\to T_1\), \(A_2\to T_3\), \(A_3\to T_2\) with cost \(2+4+6=12\). A finite penalty \(M\) represents a prohibition only if it is sufficiently large and an allowed complete assignment exists; \(x_{22}=0\) enforces the ban directly.

  • A machine unable to process job 3 receives an infinite entry in that job's column.
  • A feasible assignment must choose another machine for that job.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The Giapetto production model chooses wooden soldier production \(x_s\) and train production \(x_t\) to maximize profit. With the data in the course, the LP is

\[ \begin{aligned} \max\quad &z=3x_s+2x_t\\ \text{subject to}\quad &2x_s+x_t\le100,\\ &x_s+x_t\le80,\\ &x_s\le40,\\ &x_s,x_t\ge0. \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The Giapetto model is a complete small production-planning LP: two products compete for two shared workshop resources, and one of them also faces a sales limit.

The three constraint lines cut the first quadrant down to a pentagon of possible plans. The orange profit line \(3x_s+2x_t=180\) touches the region only at the corner \((20,60)\), where the finishing and carpentry lines cross; every line with a larger profit misses the region, so \((20,60)\) is the best plan.

The three resource constraints cut out the shaded region of production plans. Slide the profit line \(3x_s+2x_t=\bar z\) to find the best plan.

Each number has a practical reading. The objective coefficients \(3\) and \(2\) are the profits per soldier and per train. In \(2x_s+x_t\le100\) the coefficients are finishing hours per toy and \(100\) is the number of finishing hours available; \(x_s+x_t\le80\) does the same for carpentry, with one hour per toy. The limit \(x_s\le40\) restricts soldiers only. This is linear program formulation at work: data become model parameters, and the choices become decision variables.

The optimum is not obvious from the profits alone. Soldiers earn more per unit, yet the best plan makes three times as many trains as soldiers. Making as many soldiers as allowed, \(x_s=40\), uses \(80\) finishing hours, so at most \(20\) trains remain possible and the profit is \(160<180\). Per finishing hour a soldier earns \(1.5\) and a train \(2\), so the limited finishing time favours trains.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The profit contribution is 3 per soldier and 2 per train.
  • Finishing and carpentry constrain the two products jointly.
  • The soldier demand limit constrains only \(x_s\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
At the illustrated plan \((x_s,x_t)=(20,60)\), the finishing and carpentry restrictions bind, while the soldier-demand restriction has slack because \(20<40\).

  • Producing 20 soldiers and 60 trains uses 100 finishing hours and 80 carpentry hours.
  • Producing 40 soldiers and 40 trains violates the finishing limit because it needs 120 hours.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Graphical integer programming solves a two-variable integer model by plotting its continuous constraints and considering only the lattice points satisfying all restrictions. Evaluate the objective at feasible integer points to identify the best value.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Graphical integer programming solves a two-variable integer problem by looking: draw the continuous feasible region as in the graphical method, mark the lattice points inside it, and find the best of those points. Unlike an LP, the best integer point need not be a corner of the continuous region.

The shaded polygon is cut out by \(2x_1+2x_2\le9.5\) and \(x_1\le3.5\); filled dots are the feasible lattice points and hollow dots are not. The orange lines are objective lines \(3x_1+2x_2=z\) for \(z=6\), \(9\) and \(11\). Moving the line outwards, the last one that still meets a filled dot is \(z=11\), at \((3,1)\), a point inside the polygon rather than at a corner.

Only the lattice points count. The best integer point (ringed) need not be a corner of the continuous region: with the starting objective it lies on an edge, while in the static figure above it is an interior point.

Two habits from the LP case have to be dropped. Checking the corners is not enough: the best corner \((3.5,1.25)\), with value \(13\), is not a lattice point, and rounding it to \((4,1)\) leaves the region. Instead, the objective is compared over the feasible lattice points, which is possible because a bounded two-variable region contains only finitely many of them.

The picture also shows why the LP relaxation gives a bound: the polygon contains every feasible lattice point, so its optimum \(13\) is at least the integer optimum \(11\). With more variables there is no picture, and branch-and-bound replaces this comparison by a systematic search.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Both coordinates must satisfy the stated integrality restrictions.
  • An LP-optimal fractional corner is not an integer-feasible decision.
  • For a small bounded example, explicit comparison of feasible lattice points proves optimality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The figure uses the illustrative model \(\max(3x_1+2x_2)\) subject to \(2x_1+2x_2\le9.5\), \(x_1\le3.5\) and \(\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}^2\). Its best lattice point is \((3,1)\) with value 11; it is not a corner of the continuous polygon.

  • The integer work-order model uses \(3.2T+2.4S\le16\) and \(2T+3S\le15\).
  • Its best integer decision is \((T,S)=(0,5)\), with profit 750.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The graphical method solves a two-variable LP by drawing each constraint boundary, identifying the common feasible region, drawing a constant-objective line, and moving that line in the direction of improvement until the best feasible contact is reached. Intersecting the relevant boundary equations gives exact coordinates.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The method makes feasibility and optimality visible. It also reveals whether the best value is attained at one point or along a segment.

The numbered markers illustrate the method for the objective \(z=3x_s+2x_t\):

  1. Draw the boundaries \(2x_s+x_t=100\), \(x_s+x_t=80\) and \(x_s=40\).
  2. Shade their common feasible region, including the restrictions \(x_s,x_t\ge0\).
  3. Draw a constant-objective line, such as the dashed line \(3x_s+2x_t=90\).
  4. Move the line in the improving direction \((3,2)\) while it still touches the feasible region.
  5. The last contact is the optimum, here the corner \((20,60)\).

Push the objective line \(z=\bar z\) in the direction of the arrow until it last touches the feasible region; press the button to jump there. Here the last contact is the corner \((20,60)\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Determine the allowed side of each boundary from the inequality; do not assume it is always below the line.
  • Check the direction of improvement from the objective, especially with negative coefficients.
  • Also allow for an empty feasible region or an objective that can improve without bound.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Maximizing \(x_1+2x_2\) with \(x_1\le4\), \(x_2\le5\), \(2x_1+x_2\le9\) gives \((2,5)\).
  • For \(z=2x_1-3x_2\), increasing \(z\) moves its objective line downward.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A heuristic is a solution method designed to obtain a good feasible solution without a general guarantee that it is optimal. In this course, a heuristic solution is required to satisfy the original problem's constraints.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A heuristic gives up the guarantee of optimality in exchange for speed or simplicity: a good decision that can actually be carried out is often needed when an exact optimum is too hard or too slow to find.

The figure is drawn for maximization. The heuristic value \(z_H\) lies on the left: the heuristic solution is one of the feasible candidates, so the unknown optimum \(z^*\) is at least as large. The optimal value \(z_R\) of a relaxation lies on the right, and the gap \(z_R-z_H\) is the most that accepting the heuristic answer can lose. For minimization the picture is mirrored, and \(z_H\) is an upper bound.

Feasibility is required: an answer that breaks a constraint is not acceptable, however good its value. "No general guarantee" does not mean a poor answer: first fit may well find an optimal solution, but cannot prove it by itself; a bound from elsewhere equal to \(z_H\) would.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For minimization, a feasible heuristic value is an upper bound on the optimum.
  • For maximization, a feasible heuristic value is a lower bound.
  • A relaxation can supply an opposing bound that measures solution quality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For maximization, improved incumbents raise the feasible lower bound. Resolving branch-and-bound nodes can reduce the global upper bound formed from the incumbent and the remaining open-node relaxation bounds.

  • In the vehicle routing problem, visiting each routing location separately from the depot gives a feasible starting plan.
  • First-fit packs items into the first container with enough remaining capacity.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A holding cost charges for inventory kept in stock. In the continuous-time EOQ model, \(h\) is the cost per unit held per unit of time. With average inventory \(\bar I\), the average holding cost rate is \(h\bar I\). In the discrete-time models, \(h_i\) charges each unit carried from period \(i\) to \(i+1\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Holding cost is the price of keeping goods in stock: space, tied-up money, spoilage. Charged per unit and per unit of time, it penalizes large and early orders and pushes batch sizes down.

The triangle is one cycle of the sawtooth: stock falls from \(y\) to \(0\) in time \(t_0\). Its area \(\tfrac{1}{2}yt_0\) adds up stock multiplied by time, and \(h\) turns it into the holding cost of one cycle, the same as holding the average stock \(y/2\), the dashed line, all the time.

The average stock in the sawtooth is \(y/2\) (dashed line), so the holding cost rate is \(hy/2\). Raise \(h\) to see \(y^*\) fall.

A common slip is to charge \(hy\) per unit time in the classical EOQ model, as if the whole batch stayed in stock. The time unit of \(h\) must match that of the demand rate: in the snack-bar Examples, \(3\) per kilogram per week becomes \(3/7\) per kilogram per day.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The shaded triangle has area \(yt_0/2\). Multiplying by \(h\) gives the holding cost of one cycle, \(hyt_0/2\); dividing by the cycle length \(t_0\) gives the cost rate \(hy/2\). Thus classical EOQ average inventory is \(y/2\).
  • With planned shortages, the full-cycle average positive stock is \(s^2/(2y)\), not \(s/2\).
  • Discrete-time exercises charge end-of-period stock.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The snack bar converts 3 per kilogram per week to \(3/7\) per kilogram per day.
  • The pencil example charges \(1/1000=0.001\) per pencil per day.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The Hungarian algorithm solves the square minimum-cost assignment problem. Subtract each row minimum, then each column minimum. Cover all zeros of the resulting matrix with a minimum number of rows and columns. If \(n\) lines are needed, select \(n\) independent zeros, one per row and column. Otherwise let \(k\) be the smallest uncovered entry, subtract \(k\) from uncovered entries, add \(k\) to doubly covered entries, leave singly covered entries unchanged, and repeat the covering step.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The Hungarian algorithm changes the cost table, without changing which assignment is best, until it contains a complete assignment made of zeros. Since all entries stay nonnegative, such a zero assignment is optimal.

Subtracting the row minima \(2,3,1\) and then the column minima \(1,0,4\) gives the third table, whose zeros can be covered by two lines. Two lines are fewer than three, so no complete zero assignment exists yet. The adjustment by the smallest uncovered entry \(1\) creates the fourth table, where the three green zeros form the optimal assignment with original cost \(4+7+1=12\).

Each step is an assignment cost transformation. The adjustment equals subtracting \(k\) from every uncovered row and adding \(k\) to every covered column: uncovered entries lose \(k\), doubly covered entries gain \(k\), and singly covered entries are unchanged. The constants subtracted in the figure add up to \(6+5+1=12\), exactly the optimal cost: every complete assignment costs at least that total, and the zero assignment attains it.

The number of lines must be the minimum, found by a minimum zero cover: it equals the largest number of zeros with no two in the same row or column, so \(n\) lines mean that a complete zero assignment exists. That largest set of zeros is a largest matching on the zero entries, which can be found as a maximum flow.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The zero cover must use the minimum number of lines.
  • A set of independent zeros has no two in the same row or column.
  • The minimum line-cover size equals the maximum number of independent zero assignments in this construction.
  • Do not add together transformed zero costs to report the original objective value.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the figure, the smallest uncovered entry is 1: subtract 1 from uncovered entries, add 1 at double intersections, and leave singly covered entries unchanged. The final zero assignment \((1,1),(2,3),(3,2)\) has original cost \(4+7+1=12\).

  • The worked four-machine matrix initially needs three covering lines; an adjustment with \(k=2\) enables a complete assignment.
  • The final original cost is \(2+5+6+7=20\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The incumbent solution in branch-and-bound is the best feasible solution of the original integer problem found so far. Its objective value supplies a lower bound for maximization and an upper bound for minimization.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The incumbent is the best solution found so far that can actually be implemented: it satisfies every original restriction, integrality included. In branch-and-bound it is the record to beat. Its value \(L\) is a lower bound for maximization, and every subproblem is judged by whether it could still do better than \(L\).

The blue step line is the incumbent value of a maximization problem. It only rises, from \(L=9\) to \(L=12\) to \(L=13\), because the incumbent is replaced only by a better feasible solution. The red dashed line is the best bound still possible among the unexplored nodes; it can only fall. The orange node has bound \(11\le L=12\): nothing inside it can beat the incumbent, so it is pruned without further branching.

Only a point that satisfies all restrictions may become the incumbent. A fractional optimum of an LP relaxation gives a bound, not an incumbent; an integral relaxed optimum, or a point found by a heuristic and checked for feasibility, does qualify. A good incumbent found early makes the pruning test, node bound at most \(L\), succeed more often.

A common slip is to treat the incumbent as optimal as soon as it is found. It is only the best known value; the gap between the two lines limits how much it could still improve, and only when no unexplored node has a bound above \(L\) is the incumbent proven optimal.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For maximization, replace the incumbent when a feasible solution with a larger value is found.
  • A fractional relaxed optimizer cannot become the incumbent.
  • Without a known feasible solution there is no incumbent value, although an obvious feasible point may already be available.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The graph shows the maximization incumbent value rising in steps and the best remaining bound falling. When valid global bounds meet, the incumbent is proven optimal.

  • Projects 1, 4, and 5 give an incumbent value 3.2.
  • Projects 1, 3, and 4 improve it to 3.4.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An infeasible linear program has no decision vector satisfying all its constraints. Equivalently, its feasible region is empty. In the two-phase method, a negative optimal value of \(\displaystyle r=-\sum_iR_i\) proves infeasibility.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An LP is infeasible when its constraints cannot all hold at once, so the feasible region is the empty set. Conflicting requirements can make a model impossible even when each requirement is sensible on its own, and no choice of objective can resolve the conflict.

The blue triangle contains the points with \(x_1+x_2\le40\) and the red region those with \(x_1+x_2\ge60\). No point can have \(x_1+x_2\) at most 40 and at least 60, so the two regions do not meet.

The two constraints cannot hold together, so no decision is feasible. Lower \(b_2\) until the requirements become compatible.

Infeasibility is a property of the constraints alone. To prove it, combine constraints into a contradiction, as in the Examples, where \(2x_1+x_2\le2\) and nonnegativity force \(3x_1+4x_2\le8\), which contradicts \(3x_1+4x_2\ge12\). In the simplex method it shows up in Phase I of the two-phase method: the artificial variables cannot all be driven to zero.

Do not confuse an infeasible LP with an unbounded one. Both have no optimal solution, but an unbounded LP has feasible points whose objective values grow without limit, while an infeasible LP has no feasible point at all. In an applied model, infeasibility often points to a requirement that is too strict or to a constraint entered with the wrong direction.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• An infeasible model has no optimal feasible solution.
  • A positive remaining artificial variable at the Phase I optimum indicates an unsatisfied original requirement.
  • Infeasibility differs from an unbounded objective, which requires feasible points.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(2x_1+x_2\le2\), \(3x_1+4x_2\ge12\), \(x_1,x_2\ge0\) is infeasible: the first constraint implies \(3x_1+4x_2\le8\).
  • A negative phase-I optimum, such as \(r^*=-4\), cannot be repaired by beginning Phase II.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An integer linear program (ILP) is a linear optimization model in which some or all decision variables must take integer values. The linear objective and functional constraints are retained, with restrictions such as \(x_j\in\mathbb{Z}\) added to the specified variables.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An integer linear program is an LP with the extra requirement that some variables take whole-number values. Integrality represents indivisible decisions, such as numbers of buses, and also allows yes-or-no choices and logical conditions to be modelled. It changes the feasible set and can make the problem substantially harder to solve.

The dashed polygon is the feasible region of the LP; once both variables must be integers, only the dots are feasible. The LP optimum \((3.5,1.25)\) with \(z=13\) is not a dot, and the best dot is \((3,1)\) with \(z=11\). This point lies strictly inside the polygon, so the optimum of an integer program need not be a corner point of the LP region.

Change the objective and compare the LP optimum with the best feasible lattice point.

Dropping the integrality requirement gives a relaxation: it allows more points, so for maximization its optimum is an upper bound on the integer optimum, \(11\le13\) here, as in the optimization bounds. Rounding the LP optimum is no reliable shortcut: rounding \((3.5,1.25)\) to \((4,1)\) violates \(x_1\le3.5\), and in other problems a rounded point can be feasible but not optimal.

The bus scheduling model and the project selection model are integer programs of this kind. An exact method for them, branch-and-bound, works with a sequence of such relaxations.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Pure integer programs require all decision variables to be integer.
  • Mixed integer programs include both integer and continuous variables.
  • Binary integer programs restrict every decision variable to 0 or 1.
  • Rounding an LP solution need not preserve feasibility or optimality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The figure uses the illustrative objective \(3x_1+2x_2\) and restrictions \(2x_1+2x_2\le9.5\), \(x_1\le3.5\), \(x\ge0\). Its continuous optimum \((3.5,1.25)\) has value 13, whereas requiring both variables to be integers gives \((3,1)\) with value 11. Branch-and-bound on LP relaxations is an exact method; arbitrary rounding is not.

  • A bus count must be a nonnegative integer.
  • A warehouse-opening decision uses a binary variable.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An inventory policy specifies when to replenish stock and how much to order. Inventory theory constructs and analyses models to choose these decisions while accounting for demand and relevant costs.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An inventory policy answers two questions: when to order, and how much. Ordering often keeps stock low but triggers many setup costs; larger, less frequent orders save setups but keep more stock on hand. Which policy is best depends on these costs and on what is known about demand.

The three panels show three demand settings. On the left, demand runs at a constant known rate, and the EOQ policy repeats the same order whenever stock reaches zero. In the middle, demand is known but differs per period; orders, marked by arrows, are placed in only two of the four periods, so each order also covers the next period. On the right, demand is uncertain and only one quantity \(y^*\) is chosen before it is observed.

Each setting leads to its own optimization model. The model fixes which decisions are allowed and which costs count: purchasing, setup, holding and, where unmet demand is allowed, shortage costs. The policy is the answer the model returns.

A policy is only complete when both parts are stated. "Order \(22\) units" is not yet a policy without the trigger, such as "when stock reaches zero" in the classical EOQ model or a reorder level once there is a lead time.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The EOQ models use a constant deterministic demand rate.
  • Dynamic lot sizing uses known demand varying by discrete period.
  • The newsvendor model uses stochastic demand for one selling period.
  • A complete policy states both the quantity and the ordering trigger or period.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The left panel shows a classical EOQ policy: order \(y^*\) when stock reaches zero, or at \(DL_e\) when a positive lead time requires ordering ahead.
  • The middle panel shows dynamic lot sizing: order in selected periods to cover consecutive known demands \(D_i+\cdots+D_t\).
  • The right panel shows a newsvendor policy: choose one stock quantity before demand is observed, balancing the cost of having too little stock against the cost of having too much.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The job sequencing model orders jobs on one machine, each processed without interruption once started (nonpreemptive), to minimize total weighted tardiness penalties. Let \(s_i\ge0\) be job \(i\)'s start, \(p_i\) its duration, \(d_i\) its due date, \(T_i\ge0\) its tardiness, and \(w_i\) its penalty rate. Minimize \(\displaystyle \sum_iw_iT_i\) subject to \(T_i\ge s_i+p_i-d_i\). For each pair \(i<j\), impose

\[ s_i+p_i\le s_j+M(1-y_{ij}),\qquad s_j+p_j\le s_i+My_{ij},\qquad y_{ij}\in\{0,1\}. \]

Here \(y_{ij}=1\) means \(i\) precedes \(j\), and \(M\) must be valid for the scheduling horizon.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The job sequencing model decides in which order jobs run on a single machine so that lateness costs as little as possible. Pairwise order choices keep two jobs from occupying the machine at the same time, and tardiness variables charge for finishing after the due date but not for finishing early.

The timeline shows the sequence \(2,1,3\) from the Examples: job 2 runs from \(0\) to \(20\), job 1 from \(20\) to \(25\) and job 3 from \(25\) to \(40\). Job 2 finishes before \(d_2=22\), so \(T_2=0\); job 1 finishes one unit after \(d_1=24\) and job 3 five units after \(d_3=35\), which gives the marked \(T_1=1\) and \(T_3=5\) and the cost \(189\).

For each pair the two order constraints are an either-or pair. If \(y_{ij}=1\), the first says that job \(i\) finishes before job \(j\) starts, and the second is switched off by \(M\); if \(y_{ij}=0\), the roles are swapped. One binary variable per pair suffices because two non-overlapping jobs run in one of only two orders. With continuous start times, the model is a mixed integer program.

The tardiness constraint \(T_i\ge s_i+p_i-d_i\) with \(T_i\ge0\) only bounds \(T_i\) from below. Because the objective minimizes \(\sum_iw_iT_i\) with positive rates \(w_i\), an optimal solution pushes each \(T_i\) down to the larger of \(0\) and \(s_i+p_i-d_i\). Writing \(T_i=s_i+p_i-d_i\) instead is a common slip: an early job would then get negative tardiness, rewarding earliness, or, with \(T_i\ge0\) kept, be ruled out altogether.

docs.text:

  • Nonnegative penalty rates make unnecessary idle time avoidable.
  • The formulation applies the either-or technique to the exercise's three jobs.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
To require at least \(K\) of \(N\) inequalities \(\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\le d_i\), introduce binary relaxation indicators \(y_i\) and impose

\[ \begin{gathered} \boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\le d_i+My_i\quad(i=1,\ldots,N),\\ \sum_{i=1}^Ny_i\le N-K. \end{gathered} \]

Here \(0\le K\le N\) and \(M\) must validly relax each marked inequality. The video's equality \(\displaystyle \sum_i y_i=N-K\) gives the same allowed \(\boldsymbol{x}\) values when such relaxation is valid.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The K-out-of-N construction requires enough conditions from a list to hold, without saying in advance which ones. Each indicator \(y_i\) can release one inequality, at most \(N-K\) inequalities may be released, and so at least \(K\) remain enforced. A released inequality is allowed to hold as well.

Here \(N=4\) and \(K=2\). The switches \(y_2\) and \(y_4\) equal \(1\), so the second and fourth inequalities are released, while \(y_1=y_3=0\) keeps the first and third enforced. The bound \(y_1+y_2+y_3+y_4\le2\) forbids releasing a third one, so at least two of the four inequalities always hold.

Each part has one job. With \(y_i=0\) the term \(My_i\) disappears and \(\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\le d_i\) is enforced; with \(y_i=1\) the right-hand side grows by \(M\), which must be large enough to impose no restriction on the relevant values of \(\boldsymbol{x}\). For \(N=2\) and \(K=1\) this is the either-or construction, where the two indicators are \(y\) and \(1-y\). The counting constraint is the same kind of bound on a sum of binary variables as in mutually exclusive decisions.

Mind the direction: \(y_i=1\) means that inequality \(i\) is released, not that it holds. Read the other way round, \(\sum_iy_i\le N-K\) would seem to say that at most \(N-K\) inequalities hold, the opposite of what is intended. The construction also does not make exactly \(K\) inequalities true, since a released inequality may still be satisfied.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The formulation does not require exactly \(K\) original inequalities to be true.
  • The practice solution uses the inequality version; the video uses equality.
  • For \(K=N\), no constraint may be relaxed.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The figure sets \(N=4\), \(K=2\): the binary bound \(y_1+y_2+y_3+y_4\le2\) allows at most two released inequalities, leaving at least two enforced. The constant \(M\) must be large enough to remove unintended restrictions from every released inequality.

  • At least two of four constraints can be enforced using \(y_1+y_2+y_3+y_4\le2\).
  • At least two of three constraints leave at most one relaxation indicator equal to 1.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The Königsberg bridge problem asks whether a closed walk can cross each of the city's seven bridges exactly once. Represent each land region by a vertex and each bridge by an edge. The resulting four-vertex network asks whether an Euler tour exists.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The Königsberg problem shows how a network model reduces a question to its essentials: land areas become vertices, bridges become edges, and shapes and distances disappear. The impossibility then follows from vertex degrees rather than from testing every possible walk.

The island \(A\) is joined to each bank \(B\) and \(C\) by two parallel bridges and to \(D\) by one, and \(D\) is also joined to \(B\) and to \(C\): seven edges in all. The degrees are \(5,3,3,3\), so all four vertices are odd, while an Euler tour needs every degree to be even.

Parallel bridges must stay separate edges, because each bridge has to be crossed; merging the two bridges between \(A\) and \(B\) into one edge would change both degrees and the question. A single odd vertex would already settle the matter: a closed walk uses the bridges at each land area in pairs, one to arrive and one to leave, and an odd number of bridges cannot be paired.

If the walker may cross some bridges twice, the question becomes a Chinese postman problem. Counting each bridge as length 1, pairing \(A\) with \(B\) and \(C\) with \(D\) needs one extra crossing each, so a closed walk with \(9\) crossings exists, two bridges being crossed twice, and no shorter closed walk crosses every bridge.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Parallel bridges are separate edges between the same vertices.
  • The illustrated degrees are 5, 3, 3, and 3, so the even-degree condition fails.
  • The requested return to the starting point is part of the problem.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The four vertices represent the land areas: island \(A\), banks \(B,C\) and area \(D\). Four odd-degree vertices also rule out an open edge-once trail: such a trail has exactly two odd endpoints, or none if closed. Euler’s 1736 analysis is conventionally regarded as the beginning of graph theory.

  • The central land region has five incident bridge edges.
  • At an odd-degree region, a closed traversal cannot pair all arrivals and departures.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The Kruskal method constructs a minimum spanning tree by starting with no selected edges and repeatedly choosing a shortest unselected edge that does not create a cycle with the already selected edges. Stop once the selected edges connect all vertices.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The Kruskal method builds a minimum spanning tree by always taking the shortest edge that is still allowed. The selected edges may initially form several separate pieces; the method joins those pieces while avoiding unnecessary loops.

The labels give the order in which the edges are considered, by increasing length. The first four, \(B-C\), \(A-C\), \(D-E\) and \(E-F\), are accepted and form two pieces, \(\{A,B,C\}\) and \(\{D,E,F\}\). The fifth edge, \(A-B\), is skipped because \(A\) and \(B\) are already joined through \(C\). The sixth, \(B-D\), joins the two pieces, and with \(6-1=5\) edges the tree is complete, of total length 13.

The test "does this edge create a cycle?" is the same as asking whether its two endpoints already lie in the same piece. An edge between two different pieces merges them; an edge inside one piece adds nothing to connectedness and would close a cycle. Once \(n-1\) edges are accepted, all vertices lie in one piece, so the remaining edges need not be inspected.

Always taking the cheapest available step is often only a heuristic, without a guarantee of optimality; for spanning trees it is exact, which is why the method always ends with a minimum spanning tree. The Dijkstra-Prim method instead grows a single connected tree from a start vertex. Both reach the same minimum total length, possibly with different trees when there are ties.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Equivalently, inspect edges in nondecreasing order and reject any that create a cycle.
  • For \(n\) vertices, a completed tree has \(n-1\) selected edges.
  • Equal-length eligible edges may be chosen in any order.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For the figure, the sorted weights are \(1,2,2,3,4,5,6,8,10\). Accept \(BC,AC,DE,EF\), reject \(AB\) because it closes \(A-B-C-A\), then accept \(BD\). These \(n-1=5\) edges have total length 13.

  • If A-B and B-C are already selected, adding A-C would create a cycle and must be rejected.
  • Week 4 practice 3 has three independent binary tie choices, giving \(2^3=8\) minimum trees.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Linear program formulation converts a practical description into an LP by organizing the data, stating the objective in words, defining decision variables, writing the objective function, and writing all constraints including variable restrictions.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Formulation translates a description in words into a model that can be solved. A good formulation can be read without guessing: every symbol has a stated meaning and unit, and every requirement in the description appears as a constraint.

The five boxes carry out the steps of the Definition for the Giapetto model: collect the data (profits \(3\) and \(2\), hours per toy, limits \(100\), \(80\) and \(40\)), state the goal of maximizing weekly profit in words, define \(x_s\) and \(x_t\) as soldiers and trains per week, and only then write the objective and the constraints. The variables are defined before any formula uses them.

The steps separate what can be chosen from what is given. A model parameter, such as a unit profit or a number of available hours, is fixed data; only the decision variables are left to the optimizer. Each constraint compares quantities in one unit, hours with hours or pounds with pounds.

Two slips are common. One is a vague variable definition such as "\(x_s\) = soldiers", which leaves open whether \(x_s\) counts soldiers per week or in total. The other is leaving out a restriction that is obvious in the description, such as nonnegativity: the optimizer only knows what is written in the model.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• State variable meanings before using them in formulas.
  • Use consistent measurement units in each constraint.
  • A percentage requirement can often be rearranged into a linear inequality.
  • Do not add integrality to a requested LP unless the intended model requires an integer program.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
After solving, translate the variable values and objective back into the practical decisions they represent.

  • A maximum one-third share of feed A in the diet problem becomes \(x_A\le(x_A+x_B)/3\).
  • Tow-bar production uses \(3.5x_t+2.5x_s\le18\) for machine 1.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A linear program (LP) maximizes or minimizes a linear objective function subject to linear equality and/or inequality constraints. Its decision variables are continuous unless additional integer restrictions are imposed. For example,

\[ \begin{gathered} \max z=\sum_{j=1}^n c_jx_j,\\ \sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij}x_j\le b_i\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\\ x_j\ge0. \end{gathered} \]

Other inequality directions and equalities are also allowed in an LP.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A linear program optimizes a linear objective over the decisions allowed by linear constraints. "Linear" means that each variable enters only multiplied by a constant, and the terms are added, as in \(3x_s+2x_t\). This simple form is what makes large planning models tractable.

The figure shows what linearity looks like in two variables. Every constraint boundary is a straight line, so the feasible region is a polygon with straight edges, and every set of points with equal objective value is a straight line; the lines \(z=120\) and \(z=180\) are parallel. The best value \(180\) is reached where the highest objective line still touches the region, at the corner \((20,60)\).

Change the objective coefficients \(c_1,c_2\): the feasible region stays put, and the optimum jumps from corner to corner.

The definition rules out products such as \(x_1x_2\), powers such as \(x_j^2\) and fractions with a variable in the denominator, although some fractions can be multiplied out, as the share constraint of the diet problem shows. Variables are continuous, so \(20.5\) soldiers is an allowed value; indivisible decisions need explicit integer restrictions. The definition does not promise an optimum either: the constraints may contradict each other, or the objective may improve without limit.

Two variables can be handled by the graphical method; larger LPs are solved by the simplex method, which moves from corner to corner of the region.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Products of decision variables and powers such as \(x_j^2\) are not linear.
  • Negative coefficients are allowed.
  • The graphical method is useful for two variables; simplex handles larger models.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The illustrated Giapetto LP has objective \(3x_s+2x_t\) and attains value 180 at \((20,60)\). Its original quantities are continuous; no integrality restriction is included.

  • Giapetto maximizes \(3x_s+2x_t\) under linear labour and demand limits.
  • The diet problem minimizes cost under nutrient and composition requirements.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(f_i(x_{i+1})\) be the minimum cost through period \(i\) of the dynamic lot-size model, including its ending-stock holding cost, conditional on stock \(x_{i+1}\). For given initial stock \(x_1\), the course's forward lot-size recursion is

\[ f_1(x_2)=C_1(D_1+x_2-x_1)+h_1x_2 \]

when the required order is nonnegative, and \(+\infty\) otherwise. For \(i\ge2\),

\[ f_i(x_{i+1}) =\min_{0\le y_i\le D_i+x_{i+1}} \left\{C_i(y_i)+h_ix_{i+1} +f_{i-1}(x_{i+1}+D_i-y_i)\right\}. \]

Use integer states and decisions in the course tables; unreachable predecessor states have value \(+\infty\). The required final value is \(f_n(0)\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The recursion fills a table with one value \(f_i(x_{i+1})\) for each period and ending stock: the cheapest way to meet the demand of periods \(1,\dots,i\) and end period \(i\) with \(x_{i+1}\) units. To compute it, try each order size \(y_i\) in period \(i\). The stock balance then fixes where period \(i\) must have started, \(x_i=x_{i+1}+D_i-y_i\), and the best cost of reaching that starting stock is already known as \(f_{i-1}(x_i)\).

The columns are the stock levels after each period, from \(x_1=0\) to \(x_4=0\), and the arrows join stock levels of consecutive periods. The highlighted route orders \(2\) units in each period, and the stock goes \(0\to0\to1\to0\), which matches the demands \(2\), \(1\) and \(3\). The value \(f_2(1)=53\) is the cheapest cost of ending period 2 with one unit in stock; the last step adds \(C_3(2)=26\) and gives \(f_3(0)=79\), the minimum total cost.

The upper bound \(y_i\le D_i+x_{i+1}\) says exactly that the starting stock \(x_i\) is not negative. The answer is \(f_n(0)\) because the plan must end with \(x_{n+1}=0\).

This is the dynamic programming scheme with periods as stages and stock levels as states. Under the zero-inventory ordering property, only order sizes that are sums of consecutive demands need to be tried.

A common slip is to index \(f_i\) by the starting stock \(x_i\) instead of the ending stock \(x_{i+1}\). The holding cost \(h_ix_{i+1}\) is charged on the stock carried out of period \(i\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The bound on \(y_i\) ensures nonnegative predecessor inventory.
  • Reconstruct from \(x_{n+1}=0\) using stored minimizers and \(x_i=x_{i+1}+D_i-y_i\).
  • In the course examples, states need not exceed the remaining future demand.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The three-period example gives \(f_2(1)=53\) and \(f_3(0)=26+53=79\).
  • Backward reconstruction gives \(y_3=2\), \(x_3=1\), \(y_2=2\), \(x_2=0\), \(y_1=2\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The LP relaxation of an integer linear program removes its integrality requirements and keeps the objective and all other restrictions. In particular, a binary variable becomes a continuous variable satisfying \(0\le x_j\le1\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The LP relaxation asks how good the best decision would be if the integer requirements were dropped. It is an ordinary LP, solvable with the graphical method or the simplex method, and as a relaxation it keeps every integer-feasible point. Its optimum therefore bounds the original integer optimum.

The shaded polygon is the feasible region of the relaxation, and the filled dots are the integer-feasible points inside it. The objective line \(3x_1+2x_2=13\) touches the polygon at the corner \((3.5,1.25)\), the LP optimum with \(z_R=13\), while the best lattice point is \((3,1)\) with \(z^*=11\).

Dropping integrality enlarges the feasible set, so the relaxed optimum \(z_{LP}\) is an upper bound on the integer optimum \(z_{IP}\) for this maximization.

The bound holds because the relaxation chooses among more points, so it can only do at least as well. Its value is an upper bound for maximization and a lower bound for minimization. If the relaxed optimum happens to be integral, it is feasible for the original problem and no integer point can beat it, so it is integer-optimal. A binary variable keeps its bounds \(0\le x_j\le1\): dropping them too still gives a relaxation, but its bound can only become weaker.

The LP relaxation is solved at every node of branch-and-bound and is the starting point of the rounding heuristic. A common slip is to report the relaxed value as the integer optimum. It is only a bound, and it need not be close: in the figure it is \(13\) against the true \(11\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Its value is an upper bound for maximization and a lower bound for minimization.
  • If a relaxed optimizer satisfies every original integrality restriction, it is also integer-optimal.
  • Do not drop binary upper bounds when dropping binarity.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the illustrated model, the relaxed optimum \((3.5,1.25)\) gives value 13. Rounding to \((4,1)\) violates the constraints; \((3,1)\) is feasible and happens to be integer-optimal with value 11. That success does not establish a general rounding rule.

  • The project-selection relaxation allows \(x_3=0.2\) and obtains 3.52 at the root.
  • An integral relaxed solution such as \((1,0,1,1,0)\) is a feasible candidate for the original project model.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For the course network with only outgoing source edges and only incoming sink edges, the maximum flow LP (linear program) uses continuous variables \(x_{ij}\) and solves

\[ \begin{aligned} \max\quad &\sum_jx_{sj}\\ \text{subject to}\quad &\sum_jx_{ji}=\sum_jx_{ij}\quad(i\ne s,t),\\ &0\le x_{ij}\le c_{ij}\quad\text{for every directed edge }(i,j). \end{aligned} \]

Here \(c_{ij}\) is the edge capacity and sums run over existing edges.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The maximum flow LP writes the maximum flow problem as an ordinary linear program: one continuous decision variable per edge, the capacities and the flow balances as linear constraints, and the flow leaving the source as the objective.

Each edge label in the figure is one capacity constraint, such as \(x_{AB}\le4\). Together with \(x_{ij}\ge0\) and one balance equation for each of \(B\), \(C\), \(D\) and \(E\), these constraints form the whole model. The two edges into \(F\) have capacities \(5\) and \(3\), so no feasible flow can deliver more than \(8\); the Examples report that \(8\) is attained.

Each part has its own role. The balance equations say that intermediate vertices pass flow on without creating or losing any. They are not imposed at the source and the sink: the source has only outgoing edges, so balance there would force all its edges to carry zero flow. The objective counts only the flow leaving the source, which equals the flow arriving at the sink once all balances hold.

Because the model is an LP, the simplex method or Excel Solver can solve it, as an alternative to the augmenting path algorithm. The same pattern of conservation equations returns in the shortest path formulation, where one unit of flow is sent from origin to destination.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Source outflow equals sink inflow by summing conservation equations.
  • No binary selection variable is needed: an edge may carry any feasible flow amount.
  • The formulation combines the capacity and flow-conservation conditions of the maximum flow problem.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the figure, maximize \(x_{AB}+x_{AC}\) with the displayed edge capacities. The intermediate balances are

\[ \begin{aligned}x_{AB}&=x_{BC}+x_{BD},\\x_{AC}+x_{BC}&=x_{CD}+x_{CE},\\x_{BD}+x_{CD}&=x_{DF},\\x_{CE}&=x_{EF}.\end{aligned} \]

The optimum is 8. For a maximum-flow formulation with integer capacities, an integral optimal flow exists; this is a property of this network formulation, not of arbitrary LPs with integer data.

  • In the course example network with source \(S\), the objective is \(x_{SA}+x_{SB}\).
  • At vertex \(A\) of that network, conservation is \(x_{SA}=x_{AB}+x_{AC}+x_{AD}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The maximum flow problem assigns nonnegative flow \(x_{ij}\) to the edges of a directed network, subject to capacities \(x_{ij}\le c_{ij}\) and flow conservation (inflow equals outflow) at every intermediate vertex, that is, every vertex other than the source and the sink. The course assumes the source has only outgoing edges and the sink only incoming edges. The objective is to maximize total source outflow, equivalently total sink inflow.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The maximum flow problem asks how much can be sent from a source to a sink through a network of directed connections with limited capacity. Intermediate vertices pass flow on rather than create or consume it.

Each edge is labelled flow/capacity. The source \(A\) sends \(3+5=8\), and every intermediate vertex passes on what it receives; for example, \(D\) receives \(3+2=5\) and sends \(5\) to \(F\). The dashed line separates \(F\) from the other vertices; the only edges crossing it, \(D\to F\) and \(E\to F\), are full and have total capacity \(5+3=8\), so no flow can exceed 8 and the flow shown is maximum.

The capacity constraints \(x_{ij}\le c_{ij}\) bound the flow on each edge, nonnegativity keeps flow in the direction of the edge, and the conservation constraints balance incoming and outgoing flow at intermediate vertices. Without conservation, an intermediate vertex could simply absorb what the source sends, and the source outflow would no longer measure what reaches the sink.

The value of a flow is the source outflow, not the sum of all edge flows: in the figure the edge flows add up to \(24\), while the value is \(8\), since a unit that travels over three edges is counted once.

The augmenting path algorithm finds a maximum flow using the residual network. Later in the course, the same model is written as a linear program.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Flow into each intermediate vertex equals flow out.
  • The same maximum value can have several feasible edge-flow assignments.
  • Residual reverse capacity permits earlier routing choices to be revised.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The illustrated flow has source outflow \(3+5=8\), and each intermediate vertex passes on what it receives (for example, \(C\) receives 5 and sends \(2+3\)). A cut splits the vertices into a source side and a sink side; its capacity is the total capacity of the edges directed from the source side to the sink side, and no feasible flow value exceeds the capacity of any cut. The red dashed cut in the figure separates \(\{A,B,C,D,E\}\) from \(\{F\}\): only \(D\to F\) and \(E\to F\) cross it, with capacity \(5+3=8\), so no feasible flow can exceed 8. Attaining that cut bound certifies maximality.

  • A minimum cut need not be unique: the cut separating \(\{A,B,C,E\}\) from \(\{D,F\}\) is crossed by \(B\to D\), \(C\to D\) and \(E\to F\) and also has capacity \(3+2+3=8\).
  • Week 4 course examples (networks not shown on this page) use source \(S\) and sink \(T\): the main example has maximum flow 15, and Week 4 practice 7 reaches 16, with 9 entering \(T\) from \(D\) and 7 from \(E\).

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text: Over the same feasible set, minimizing \(f(\boldsymbol{x})\) is equivalent to maximizing \(-f(\boldsymbol{x})\). The two problems have the same optimal solution vectors, and their optimal objective values have opposite signs.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Minimizing and maximizing are mirror images: a feasible point where \(f\) is smallest is exactly a point where \(-f\) is largest. The simplex method is presented for maximization, and negating a minimization objective lets the same procedure be used while the constraints stay unchanged.

The red curve \(-f\) is the blue curve \(f\) reflected in the horizontal axis. The lowest point of \(f\) and the highest point of \(-f\) lie above and below the same \(x^\ast\), at heights \(f(x^\ast)\) and \(-f(x^\ast)\).

The reason is a single fact about inequalities: multiplying by \(-1\) reverses the direction, so \(f(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)\le f(\boldsymbol{x})\) holds exactly when \(-f(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)\ge-f(\boldsymbol{x})\). Only the objective is negated; the feasible set stays the same, and the optimal values satisfy \(\min f=-\max(-f)\).

Two slips are common: negating the constraints as well, which changes the feasible set, and forgetting to change the sign back at the end, so that the transformed value 10 is reported instead of the original minimum \(-10\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Negate every objective coefficient.
  • Recover the original optimal value by changing the sign back.
  • Only the objective changes; the allowed decisions remain the same.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a feasible canonical tableau and an entering variable with constraint-column coefficients \(a_{ik}\) and right-hand sides \(b_i\ge0\), the minimum-ratio test selects

\[ \theta=\min_{i\colon a_{ik}>0}\frac{b_i}{a_{ik}}. \]

A row attaining the minimum supplies the leaving basic variable. Zero ratios are eligible; only the denominator must be strictly positive.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Once the entering variable is chosen, the ratio test decides how far it may increase: as far as possible while every basic variable stays nonnegative. The test finds the first basic variable that reaches zero; a larger step would violate nonnegativity, so that variable leaves.

In the figure, each right-hand side is divided by the positive entry of the \(x_s\) column. The smallest ratio, 40 in the \(s_3\) row, is the step length: at \(x_s=40\) the slack \(s_3\) reaches zero while \(s_1=20\) and \(s_2=40\) are still positive. In the graph of the Giapetto model, moving from the origin along the \(x_s\)-axis, the boundary \(x_s=40\) is the first one met, at the corner \((40,0)\).

In row \(i\) the basic variable equals \(b_i-a_{ik}t\) when the entering variable is raised to \(t\), so it reaches zero at \(t=b_i/a_{ik}\) if \(a_{ik}>0\). Rows with \(a_{ik}\le0\) are skipped because their basic variable stays the same or grows. Taking the minimum guarantees that no basic variable becomes negative. If no row has \(a_{ik}>0\), nothing limits the increase, and an improving column then shows that the LP is unbounded.

A common slip is to compute ratios for rows with negative entries: a negative "ratio" would then win the minimum and pick a wrong leaving variable. A ratio of zero, by contrast, is eligible and gives a step of length zero.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Rows with zero or negative pivot-column coefficients do not restrict the increase.
  • A tie may be broken arbitrarily in the course procedure and can lead to degeneracy.
  • If there is no positive coefficient and the objective improves along this column, the objective is unbounded.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the illustrated tableau, increasing \(x_s\) gives \(s_1=100-2x_s\), \(s_2=80-x_s\) and \(s_3=40-x_s\). The limits \(50,80,40\) give step length 40, so \(s_3\) leaves.

  • The initial ratios \(10/2=5\) and \(15/1=15\) make \(s_1\) leave.
  • The next ratios are \(5/(1/2)=10\) and \(10/(5/2)=4\), so \(s_2\) leaves.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Given a connected undirected network with nonnegative edge lengths, a minimum spanning tree is a spanning tree whose total selected edge length is smallest among all spanning trees of that network.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The objective is to connect every location at minimum total construction length, for example the cheapest set of roads or cables that links all sites. It does not minimize the travel distance from one selected origin.

The five green edges reach all six vertices without a cycle and have total length \(1+2+2+3+5=13\); no other spanning tree of this network is shorter. Each grey edge is the longest edge on a cycle whose other edges are green: \(A-B\) (4) closes \(A-B-C-A\) with edges of length 1 and 2, and \(C-D\) (8), \(C-E\) (10) and \(D-F\) (6) close cycles in the same way. Such an edge is never needed: the rest of its cycle already connects its endpoints more cheaply.

Simple rules solve the problem exactly: the Kruskal method accepts the shortest edges that close no cycle, and the Dijkstra-Prim method grows one tree from a start vertex. For many optimization problems, always taking the cheapest next step is only a heuristic; here it is guaranteed to be optimal.

A minimum spanning tree is not a collection of shortest paths. In a triangle with edges \(A-B\) and \(B-C\) of length 2 and \(A-C\) of length 3, the minimum spanning tree uses the two edges of length 2, so \(A\) and \(C\) are \(4\) apart in the tree, although the shortest path between them is the direct edge of length 3.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Both Dijkstra-Prim and Kruskal methods produce a minimum spanning tree.
  • There may be several minimum trees with the same total length.
  • Tie choices may be explored to identify alternative minimum trees.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The green edges in the figure have total length \(1+2+2+3+5=13\). They form a minimum spanning tree.

  • Roads can be selected to connect all cities while minimizing total road length.
  • Week 4 practice 1 has two minimum spanning trees, differing by the choice B-F or F-G.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In the CPP construction, a minimum-weight perfect matching pairs the odd-degree vertices so that each belongs to exactly one pair and the sum of pair costs is minimized. The cost \(d_{ij}\) of a pair is its shortest-path distance. With a binary variable for each unordered pair,

\[ \begin{gathered} \min\sum_{i<j}d_{ij}x_{ij},\\ \sum_{j<i}x_{ji}+\sum_{j>i}x_{ij}=1\quad \text{for each odd vertex }i. \end{gathered} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The matching decides which odd vertices should be linked by duplicated paths in the Chinese postman construction. Each odd vertex needs exactly one partner, and the total extra length should be as small as possible.

The left panel gives the shortest-path distances between the four odd vertices \(P,Q,R,S\). Four vertices can be paired in three ways: \(\{PQ,RS\}\) costs \(4+5=9\), \(\{PS,QR\}\) costs \(6+5=11\), and \(\{PR,QS\}\) costs \(6+7=13\). The middle panel shows the cheapest pairing, of weight 9.

Perfect means that every odd vertex lies in exactly one pair; this is the constraint that sets the sum of the variables at vertex \(i\) equal to \(1\). Minimum-weight refers to the objective \(\sum d_{ij}x_{ij}\). A perfect matching always exists here, because the number of odd-degree vertices is even (see vertex degree). Each pair cost is a shortest-path distance rather than the length of a direct edge, since the duplicated route may pass through other vertices.

Pairing must be optimized jointly, since a locally cheap pair may leave expensive remaining pairs. On a line \(P-Q-R-S\) with edge lengths \(2,1,2\), taking the closest pair \(Q,R\) first (cost 1) forces \(P\) with \(S\) (cost 5), a total of 6, whereas \(\{PQ,RS\}\) costs \(2+2=4\). This is why the choice is written as a binary integer program, as in the Definition. Matchings return later in the course with two separate groups of vertices, in bipartite matching.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Each pair variable is binary.
  • For four odd vertices there are three complete pairings to compare.
  • This is a nonbipartite matching problem because the vertices are not separated into two assignment groups.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For the illustrated four odd vertices, the alternative pairing \(\{PR,QS\}\) costs 13. The minimum-cost pairing determines which shortest paths are duplicated in the CPP construction.

  • The pairings AB/DE, AD/BE, and AE/BD cost 8, 7, and 8.
  • The optimum selects \(x_{AD}=x_{BE}=1\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A minimum zero cover is a smallest set of matrix rows and columns (lines) that together cover all zero entries.

Zeros are independent if no two share a row or a column; a maximum independent zero assignment is a largest set of independent zeros. From such an assignment, a minimum zero cover is found by marking:

  1. Mark every row without an assigned zero.
  2. Mark every column that has a zero in a marked row.
  3. Mark every row whose assigned zero lies in a marked column.
  4. Repeat steps 2 and 3 until nothing new is marked; then cover all marked columns and all unmarked rows.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A minimum zero cover counts how many zeros of the reduced table can be used at the same time. By the matching duality quoted in the Examples, the smallest number of lines covering all zeros equals the largest number of zeros with no two in the same row or column. Fewer than \(n\) lines therefore prove that no complete zero assignment exists yet.

The blue zeros sit in row \(2\) and column \(2\), so these two red lines cover them all. Every zero lies in row \(2\) or column \(2\), and independent zeros can take at most one from each, so at most two exist, for example \((1,2)\) and \((2,1)\). Since \(2<3\), the Hungarian algorithm must adjust the table before it can stop.

The marking procedure must start from a maximum assignment of zeros; one to which no zero can be added is not enough. In the figure, \((2,2)\) alone cannot be extended, since the other zeros all lie in row \(2\) or column \(2\). Starting the marking from it marks rows \(1\) and \(3\), then column \(2\), then row \(2\), and finally all three columns, giving three lines and the false conclusion that a complete zero assignment exists.

A largest set of independent zeros is a largest bipartite matching between rows and columns that uses only zero entries, and the maximum flow construction finds one.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For an \(n\times n\) matrix, \(n\) required covering lines indicate that a complete zero-cost assignment exists.
  • The cover size equals the size of the maximum independent zero assignment.
  • Rows and columns marked during the search are not the same as the final lines: the final rows are the unmarked ones.
  • If fewer than \(n\) lines are needed, subtract the smallest uncovered entry from all uncovered entries and add it to entries at intersections of covering lines. Repeat the assignment and covering steps until \(n\) lines are needed.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In the illustrated matrix, the independent zeros at \((1,2)\) and \((2,1)\) form a maximum assignment of size \(2\). Row 2 and column 2 cover every zero with two lines. Their equal sizes illustrate Kőnig's theorem: the largest number of independent zeros always equals the smallest number of lines covering all zeros (the matrix form of the bipartite matching duality). Since \(2<3\), the matrix still needs adjustment before a complete zero assignment is possible.
  • The marking finds this cover. Row 3 has no assigned zero, so it is marked; its zero in column 2 marks column 2; the zero assigned in column 2 is in row 1, so row 1 is marked; row 1 adds no new column. The cover is the marked column 2 and the unmarked row 2.
  • Course examples (matrices in the course materials, not reproduced here): Week 5 practice 5(b) covers columns 1 and 2 and rows 2 and 3; the ten-job example covers columns 1, 3, 4, 5, 8, 9 and rows 2, 10, eight lines in all.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A mixed integer program (MIP) is an integer linear program containing both integer-restricted decision variables and continuous decision variables. Binary variables may be used for the discrete decisions.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A mixed integer program combines indivisible decisions, such as whether to buy a machine, with divisible quantities, such as how much to produce. A single model can thus select a discrete action and determine continuous quantities that depend on it, which is why the domain of each variable must be stated individually.

Here only \(x_1\) must be an integer, so the feasible set consists of vertical segments at \(x_1=0,1,2,3\), each running up to the line \(2x_1+2x_2=9.5\). On the segment \(x_1=3\) the variable \(x_2\) can rise to \(1.75\), which gives the optimum \((3,1.75)\) with \(z=12.5\).

This value lies between the pure-integer optimum 11 and the LP optimum 13, and the same order holds for any maximization problem with finite optima: requiring integrality of fewer variables allows more points, so the mixed problem is a relaxation of the pure integer program, and the LP is a relaxation of both.

Integer linear programming supplies the integrality restrictions; a mixed model keeps them on some decisions only. A typical pattern pairs a binary variable with continuous quantities, as in \(x_1+x_2\le100+50y\) from the Examples, where buying the machine (\(y=1\)) raises the production limit from 100 to 150.

A common slip is to declare every variable integer by accident. In the figure this would turn the problem into the pure integer program and lower the optimal value from \(12.5\) to \(11\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• An LP relaxation removes integrality only from the restricted variables.
  • Continuous variables should not accidentally be forced to integer values.
  • Logical modelling often introduces auxiliary binary variables alongside quantities.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The figure maximizes \(3x_1+2x_2\) under \(2x_1+2x_2\le9.5\), \(x_1\le3.5\) and \(\boldsymbol{x}\ge0\), with only \(x_1\) integer. Its optimum \((3,1.75)\) has value 12.5, between the pure-integer value 11 and the continuous relaxation value 13.

  • \(x_1+x_2\le100+50y\) combines continuous production with a binary machine-purchase decision.
  • Continuous job start times (as in the job sequencing model) can be combined with binary variables specifying which job comes first.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A model parameter is a given numerical input to the optimization model. In the course's LP notation, parameters include objective coefficients \(c_j\), constraint coefficients \(a_{ij}\), and right-hand sides \(b_i\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Parameters describe the circumstances under which decisions are made. A parameter may be an estimate even though the optimization treats its supplied value as fixed.

The objective function \(f(\boldsymbol{x})\) is the quantity to maximize (for example, profit) or minimize (for example, cost). Functional constraints describe what an allowed decision must satisfy, such as resource limits or demand requirements. Domain restrictions specify signs or integrality.

In the diagram, blue identifies decision variables, whose values the model determines; red identifies model parameters, the given data \(c_j\), \(a_{ij}\) and \(b_i\). In general, the model is \(\max/\min\ f(\boldsymbol{x})\) subject to \(\boldsymbol{x}\in F\), where the constraints define the feasible set \(F\). A solution assigns values to all variables.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Changing parameters can change both the optimal decision and the optimal value.
  • Units must agree within an equation or inequality.
  • Sensitivity analysis investigates the effect of parameter changes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The coefficient \(3\) in \(3x_s+2x_t\) is profit per soldier.
  • The right-hand side \(100\) in \(2x_s+x_t\le100\) is available finishing time.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An optimization problem has multiple optimal solutions if distinct feasible decision vectors attain the same optimal objective value. In an LP, every convex combination of two optimal solutions is also optimal.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Different decisions can be equally good under the stated objective. In a two-variable LP, this often appears as an objective line coinciding with a feasible boundary segment.

The figure and the interactive example both use the feasible region of the Giapetto production model: \(x_s\) wooden soldiers and \(x_t\) trains, with finishing \(2x_s+x_t\le100\), carpentry \(x_s+x_t\le80\) and soldier demand \(x_s\le40\). Only the objective is changed, so that it becomes parallel to one edge.

With \(z=2x_s+2x_t\), every objective line \(x_s+x_t=z/2\) is parallel to the carpentry edge. Pushing the dashed line \(z=100\) outwards, it leaves the region along the whole edge from \((0,80)\) to \((20,60)\), where \(z=160\).

Here the objective is \(z=4x_s+2x_t\), parallel to the finishing line \(2x_s+x_t=100\), so the optimal edge runs from \((40,20)\) to \((20,60)\) with \(z=200\). Move \(\alpha\) along it.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A zero objective-row coefficient for a nonbasic variable in an optimal simplex tableau suggests an alternative optimum.
  • A positive feasible movement in that direction produces a distinct optimum; a zero-length degenerate pivot alone does not establish a different decision vector.
  • Additional requirements can select one point from an optimal segment.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For the illustrated objective \(2x_s+2x_t\), the feasible part of \(x_s+x_t=80\) between \((0,80)\) and \((20,60)\) is optimal. It includes \((10,70)\); every point on the segment has value 160.
  • For the interactive objective \(4x_s+2x_t\), the five corners \((0,0)\), \((40,0)\), \((40,20)\), \((20,60)\), \((0,80)\) give \(0\), \(160\), \(200\), \(200\), \(160\), so the edge from \((40,20)\) to \((20,60)\) is optimal with value 200.
  • Adding the requirement \(x_s=30\) to that problem selects the single point \((30,40)\) of the optimal edge: \(2\cdot30+40=100\) and \(4\cdot30+2\cdot40=200\).
  • With the original Giapetto profit \(3x_s+2x_t\), the corner values are \(0,120,160,180,160\), so the optimum \((20,60)\) is unique.
  • The Week 3 course materials (data not reproduced here) give another LP in which \((5,0)\) and \((3,4)\) both attain \(4x_1+2x_2=20\); in practice exercise 3 of Week 3, imposing \(x_1=1\) selects \((1,9/2)\) from the optimal segment.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For binary variables \(y_1,\ldots,y_k\), mutually exclusive decisions allow at most one variable to equal 1:

\[ \sum_{j=1}^ky_j\le1. \]

If one alternative must be chosen, use \(\displaystyle \sum_{j=1}^ky_j=1\) instead.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Mutually exclusive decisions describe options of which at most one may be chosen, such as building at most one of two warehouses. Because each \(y_j\) is \(0\) or \(1\), the sum \(\sum_jy_j\) counts the yes decisions, and the constraint is a statement about that count.

For two decisions the tables list all four combinations. "At most one", \(y_1+y_2\le1\), forbids only \(y_1=y_2=1\); "exactly one", \(y_1+y_2=1\), also forbids choosing neither. The inequality permits choosing none while the equality requires one choice, so the wording "at most one" or "exactly one" decides which version to use.

The same counting idea gives "at least \(K\) of \(N\)" in K-out-of-N constraints, and the exactly-one version selects a single listed value in a finite-value constraint.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Binarity is essential to interpret the sum as the number of yes decisions.
  • Exactly one implies at most one, but the reverse is false.
  • This restriction concerns decisions, not an either-or condition on continuous inequalities.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• With binaries \(W_{LA}\) and \(W_{SF}\) equal to 1 if a warehouse is built at location LA or SF, \(W_{LA}+W_{SF}\le1\) permits at most one warehouse.
  • \(y_1+y_2+y_3=1\) selects exactly one allowed quantity value.
