docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The negative right-hand-side transformation multiplies an entire constraint by \(-1\) when its right-hand side is negative. An inequality reverses direction; an equality remains an equality.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Multiplying a whole constraint by \(-1\) rewrites it without changing which points satisfy it. The elementary simplex starting construction needs nonnegative right-hand sides, and this transformation provides them while keeping the same feasible decisions.

The shaded half-plane is described by both forms: a point satisfies \(-x_1+x_2\le-3\) exactly when it satisfies \(x_1-x_2\ge3\); for example, \((5,1)\) gives \(-4\le-3\) and \(4\ge3\).

Multiplying both sides of an inequality by a negative number reverses its direction, so \(\le\) becomes \(\ge\) and every coefficient changes sign. Nonnegative right-hand sides matter because the starting solution sets the original variables to zero, so each slack starts at its right-hand side; with \(x_1-x_2+s=-1\) this would give \(s=-1<0\). After the transformation, \(-x_1+x_2\ge1\) receives a surplus and an artificial variable instead.

Changing only the sign of the right-hand side turns \(-x_1+x_2\le-3\) into \(-x_1+x_2\le3\), a different half-plane: the origin satisfies the new constraint but not the original one.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Change every coefficient and the right-hand side.
  • A \(\le\) constraint can become a \(\ge\) constraint and consequently require a surplus and an artificial variable.
  • Changing only the right-hand side would change the problem.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A network consists of a set of vertices and edges connecting specified pairs of vertices. Vertices represent entities or locations; edges represent connections. Depending on the problem, edges may have directions and numerical values such as distances, costs, or capacities.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A network separates the connection structure of a problem from its physical setting: it records only which pairs of objects are joined and, where needed, a number on each connection. The same representation can describe roads between cities, cables between sites or the order of project activities.

The figure has six vertices \(A,\dots,F\) and nine edges, each labelled with its length; only these numbers count, not the lengths on paper.

Edges may be usable in both directions, as in an undirected network, or in one direction only, as in a directed network. An edge value is read in the problem's own units: a distance is added up along a path, while a capacity limits how much can pass through a single edge.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Vertices are also commonly called nodes.
  • An edge may be used only in its specified direction in a directed network.
  • The meaning of an edge value depends on the problem: distance and capacity are different quantities.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The figure has vertices \(\{A,\ldots,F\}\) and edge labels denoting lengths.

  • A road network connects cities by roads.
  • A project network represents activities and their precedence relations.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The newsvendor model chooses a single order quantity \(y\ge0\) before observing random demand \(D\). With unit purchase cost \(c\), selling price \(p>c\), and salvage value \(s<c\), define overage cost \(h=c-s\) and underage cost \(b=p-c\). Minimize

\[ G(y)=h\,\mathbb{E}[(y-D)^+]+b\,\mathbb{E}[(D-y)^+], \]

where \(u^+=\max\{u,0\}\) and the expectations are finite. Sales equal \(\min\{y,D\}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The newsvendor model chooses one stock level before an uncertain demand is seen, for a product that cannot be sold later at full price. Too much stock leaves units that are sold off at the salvage value, costing \(h=c-s\) each; too little misses sales that would have earned \(b=p-c\) each.

In the meal example, demand lies between \(80\) and \(120\) with all values equally likely, and \(h=2.2\), \(b=3.3\). Raising \(y\) increases the expected cost of leftovers (red) and decreases the expected cost of missed sales (green). The sum \(G(y)\) is lowest at \(y^*=104\), with value \(26.4\).

Move \(y\): the expected overage cost rises and the expected underage cost falls. Their sum \(G(y)\) is smallest at the \(\beta\)-quantile of demand (right).

The optimum can be found by asking whether one more unit is worth stocking: it is left over if demand is at most \(y\), costing \(h\), and sells if demand is above \(y\), saving \(b\). Adding it pays off as long as \(b\) times the chance that demand exceeds \(y\) is larger than \(h\) times the chance that it does not. In the example, the chance that demand is at most \(y\) is \((y-80)/40\), and the two sides balance when this chance equals \(b/(b+h)=0.6\), at \(y=104\). The positive part \((y-D)^+\) counts leftovers and \((D-y)^+\) missed sales, so each gets its own unit cost.

Unlike the EOQ models, there is a single period and no setup cost, and unmet demand is lost rather than backlogged. The balance point \(b/(b+h)\) is developed further as the critical ratio.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Salvage value can be zero or negative.
  • \(G(y)\) is convex; an optimum occurs where increasing stock stops reducing expected cost.
  • \(G(y)\) measures overage and underage loss, not gross purchasing expenditure.
  • The model is introduced in the week 5 overview and developed in week 6.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The illustrated meal-demand example is uniform on \([80,120]\) with critical ratio \(\beta=0.6\). Its optimal stock is \(y^*=104\), for which \(F(104)=0.6\).

  • A newsvendor chooses newspaper stock before daily demand is known.
  • A shop chooses seasonal dress inventory; a canteen prepares meals before evening demand.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
For a fixed integer quantity \(y\) and fixed purchase cost \(c\) and salvage value \(s<c\), newsvendor price sensitivity finds selling prices \(p>c\) for which \(y\) remains optimal. The condition is

\[ F(y-1)\le\frac{p-c}{p-s}\le F(y). \]

The endpoints include ties with neighbouring quantities.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The question is how far the selling price can move before a chosen order stops being optimal. The price enters the newsvendor model only through the critical ratio \(\beta=(p-c)/(p-s)\), so the question becomes: for which prices does \(\beta\) stay between the two CDF values that make \(y\) optimal?

With \(c=110\) and \(s=50\), the curve \(\beta(p)=(p-110)/(p-50)\) rises with \(p\). It reaches \(F(9)=0.70\) at \(p=250\) and \(F(10)=0.85\) at \(p=450\), so \(y=10\) is optimal for every price in the shaded interval \([250,450]\). Below \(250\) the target probability drops under \(0.70\) and fewer units are optimal; above \(450\) it exceeds \(0.85\) and more units are optimal.

Fix the quantity \(y\) and vary the price \(p\): \(y\) stays optimal while \(F(y-1)\le\frac{p-c}{p-s}\le F(y)\).

The two inequalities come from the discrete newsvendor rule. The condition \(\beta\le F(y)\) says that adding unit \(y+1\) does not lower the expected cost, and \(F(y-1)\le\beta\) says that removing unit \(y\) does not lower it. At an endpoint one of them holds with equality and a neighbouring quantity is equally good. Since \(\beta=1-(c-s)/(p-s)\) increases with \(p\), the set of prices is an interval, and solving \(\beta(p)=F\) gives each endpoint:

\[ p=\frac{c-Fs}{1-F}. \]

So the optimal quantity, as a function of the price, is constant on intervals and jumps at their endpoints. This is the newsvendor version of sensitivity analysis for linear programs, where a coefficient may move within a range without changing the optimal solution.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The condition is for being an optimum, not necessarily the smallest optimum.
  • At the lower boundary, \(y-1\) can tie with \(y\).
  • This analysis holds the demand distribution fixed, as the exercise does.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
At \(p=250\), quantities 9 and 10 tie; at \(p=450\), quantities 10 and 11 tie. Increasing price past the upper endpoint calls for additional stock, with demand distribution held fixed.

  • The dress solution uses effective unit cost \(c=80+30=110\) and salvage \(s=50\).
  • For \(y=10\), \(F(9)=0.70\) and \(F(10)=0.85\) give \(250\le p\le450\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A nonbasic variable is a variable outside the chosen basis and is set to zero when the associated basic solution is read. For \(m\) independent equations in \(n\) variables, there are \(n-m\) nonbasic variables.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The nonbasic variables are the ones fixed at zero to read off a basic solution; with \(m\) equations in \(n\) variables there are \(n-m\) of them. They are the directions in which the simplex method can move: it raises one nonbasic variable from zero, and the basic values change to keep the equations satisfied.

At the optimal Giapetto plan \((20,60)\) the nonbasic variables are \(s_1\) and \(s_2\), so the finishing and carpentry constraints are both used up. Their columns show what raising each one would do. In particular, the objective row reads \(z+s_1+s_2=180\), so raising either lowers \(z\), which is why this tableau is optimal.

Geometrically, a nonbasic slack at zero means that its constraint holds with equality, and a nonbasic decision variable at zero means that the point lies on an axis. The nonbasic variables therefore name the boundary lines that meet at the current corner. At each pivot, the entering variable is chosen among the nonbasic variables and becomes basic, and the leaving variable becomes nonbasic, so the method moves to a neighbouring corner.

Being nonbasic is a choice made before the equations are solved, not an observation that a value happens to be zero: a basic variable can be zero too.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A zero value alone does not establish that a variable is nonbasic; basic variables can also be zero.
  • The objective row expresses the effect of changing nonbasic variables.
  • The entering variable becomes basic after a pivot.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The illustrated tableau has \(n-m=5-3=2\) nonbasic variables, \(s_1,s_2\). Raising \(s_1\) by 1 changes \(x_t\) and \(s_3\) by \(+1\), \(x_s\) by \(-1\) and \(z\) by \(-1\), while the displayed basis remains feasible.

  • The original decision variables are nonbasic at the initial slack-basis solution.
  • The final two-variable example sets \(s_1=s_2=0\) as its nonbasic variables.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Nonconvex region modelling represents a union of allowed regions using binary variables that select which region's inequalities are enforced. The selected region must satisfy all its defining inequalities; common constraints remain active for every selection.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Some models allow decisions in one of several separate pieces, but not in between. A single system of linear inequalities cannot describe such a region exactly: if two points satisfy a linear inequality, so does every point on the segment between them, so a gap can never be cut out. Binary switches make it possible by enforcing the inequalities of one piece at a time.

The two pieces share \(x_1+x_2\le3\) and \(\boldsymbol{x}\ge\boldsymbol{0}\) but differ in one inequality: \(x_2\le1\) below and \(x_2\ge2\) above. The points \((0,1)\) and \((0,2)\) are both allowed, while their midpoint \((0,1.5)\) lies in the excluded gap \(1<x_2<2\). This is what nonconvex means: a segment between allowed points leaves the region.

In the model of the Examples, \(y\) selects the piece, each inequality that belongs to only one piece receives a big-\(M\) term as in either-or constraints, and the shared restrictions stay outside the switches so that they hold for both choices. With more than two pieces, one indicator per piece and an exactly-one constraint do the selection.

The size of \(M\) matters. If it is too small, a switched-off inequality still cuts off allowed points: with \(M=1\) and \(y=0\), the second inequality becomes \(x_2\ge1\), which together with \(x_2\le1\) leaves only the points of the lower piece with \(x_2=1\). A much larger \(M\) than needed is valid but enlarges the region of the LP relaxation, so its bound can only become weaker.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Use one indicator per region and require exactly one selected region. With only two regions a single binary \(y\) suffices: \(1-y\) and \(y\) act as the two indicators.
  • Relax every inequality belonging only to an unselected region with a valid big-\(M\) constant, as in either-or constraints: \(M\) must be large enough that the relaxed inequality cuts off no point the model allows.
  • Keep nonnegativity and shared boundaries outside the switches.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The illustrated region, the course video example, is \(x_1,x_2\ge0\), \(x_1+x_2\le3\), with either \(x_2\le1\) or \(x_2\ge2\). Its switch is \(x_2\le1+My\), \(x_2\ge2-M(1-y)\), \(y\in\{0,1\}\). With \(y=0\) the lower piece \(x_2\le1\) is enforced and the second inequality becomes \(x_2\ge2-M\); with \(y=1\) the upper piece \(x_2\ge2\) is enforced and the first becomes \(x_2\le1+M\). Because \(0\le x_2\le3\) on the shared region, \(M=2\) is already large enough. The common restrictions \(x_1+x_2\le3\) and \(\boldsymbol{x}\ge\boldsymbol{0}\) remain active for both choices.

  • The practice region additionally selects \(x_1\in[0,1]\), \([2,3]\), or \([4,5]\) under \(2x_1+5x_2\le20\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A nonnegativity constraint requires a decision variable to satisfy \(x_j\ge0\). It excludes negative quantities while permitting zero. For a vector of variables, \(\boldsymbol{x}\ge0\) means \(x_j\ge0\) for every component \(j\). In the course's augmented simplex models, all original and auxiliary variables are nonnegative.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A nonnegativity constraint says that a variable cannot go below zero. Produced or shipped amounts are naturally of this kind, but the model only knows it once \(x_j\ge0\) is written down.

The two axes are the boundaries of \(x_1\ge0\) and \(x_2\ge0\), which together keep the first quadrant. The line \(2x_1+2.4x_2=7.2\), meeting the axes at \((3.6,0)\) and \((0,3)\), cuts off the darker triangle of feasible points; everything with a negative coordinate is excluded.

With two nonnegative variables \(x,y\ge0\) the feasible region lies in the first quadrant. Drag the peak of the objective to the left of the \(y\)-axis: the optimum moves onto the axis and the constraint \(x\ge0\) binds.

Zero is allowed: corners of a feasible region often lie on an axis, such as \((0,80)\) in the Giapetto region. The constraints matter even when they look harmless: without them, maximizing \(x_1\) over the half-plane \(2x_1+2.4x_2\le7.2\) would have no optimum, since \(x_2\) could be made as negative as wanted. A variable that can be a profit or a loss takes either sign; it is left unrestricted or handled by a transformation. A common slip is to read \(x_j\ge0\) as \(x_j>0\), or as "\(x_j\) is a whole number"; it means neither.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Nonnegativity is a constraint, not an automatic consequence of a variable name.
  • With two nonnegative variables, feasible points lie in the first quadrant.
  • Nonnegative continuous variables may still take fractional values.
  • At an optimum a nonnegativity constraint is either slack (\(x_j^\ast>0\)) or binding (\(x_j^\ast=0\)); in nonlinear problems this is what the Kuhn-Tucker conditions with nonnegativity constraints handle.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(x_s\ge0\) prevents negative soldier production.
  • \(s_1\ge0\) ensures that a slack variable represents unused rather than exceeded capacity.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In the course's normal demand approximation, \(D\sim \mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\) with standard deviation \(\sigma>0\). If \(\Phi\) is the standard normal CDF, then

\[ \begin{gathered} F(y)=\Phi\!\left(\frac{y-\mu}{\sigma}\right),\\ y^*=\max\!\left\{0,\mu+\sigma\Phi^{-1}(\beta)\right\}. \end{gathered} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Normal demand is described by two numbers: the mean \(\mu\), the typical demand level, and the standard deviation \(\sigma\), the typical size of deviations from it. The optimal order starts from \(\mu\) and adds a safety amount \(\sigma\Phi^{-1}(\beta)\), which depends on the costs only through the critical ratio.

The bell curve is the demand density, centred at \(\mu=100\) with \(\sigma=20\); areas under it are probabilities. The shaded area to the left of \(y^*\approx105.07\) equals \(\beta=0.6\). Since \(\Phi^{-1}(0.6)\approx0.2533\), the order lies about a quarter of a standard deviation above the mean: \(100+20\cdot0.2533\approx105.07\).

With \(D\sim \mathcal{N}(100,20^2)\) the optimal stock is \(\mu+\sigma\Phi^{-1}(\beta)\): above the mean when \(\beta>1/2\), below it when \(\beta<1/2\).

Standardizing turns the continuous newsvendor rule \(F(y)=\beta\) into \((y-\mu)/\sigma=\Phi^{-1}(\beta)\), a single look-up in the standard normal table, and the quantile is then rescaled. If \(\beta>\tfrac{1}{2}\), the order lies above the mean; if \(\beta<\tfrac{1}{2}\), below it; and \(\beta=\tfrac{1}{2}\) gives \(y^*=\mu\). More uncertainty, a larger \(\sigma\), moves the order further from the mean in the same direction.

A common slip is to use the variance \(\sigma^2\) instead of \(\sigma\): with \(\sigma^2=400\) the meal example would give an order of about \(201\) instead of \(105\). The normal model also gives some probability to negative demand; this hardly matters when \(\mu\) is several standard deviations above \(0\), and if the formula gives a negative quantity the order is \(0\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Use the standard deviation \(\sigma\), not the variance \(\sigma^2\), in the quantile formula.
  • The order quantity must satisfy \(y\ge0\). Use the normal quantile when it is nonnegative; otherwise the constrained optimum is \(y^*=0\).
  • The untruncated normal distribution allows negative values; the course examples retain that approximation.
  • The normal table gives rounded quantiles.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The shaded area in the figure is \(\mathbb{P}(D\le y^*)=0.6\). Table values \(\Phi(0.25)=0.5987\) and \(\Phi(0.26)=0.6026\) bracket the standardized quantile between 0.25 and 0.26.

  • Meal demand with \(\mu=100\), \(\sigma=20\) and \(\beta=0.6\) gives about 105.07.
  • For apples, \(\beta=1.8/2.2\approx0.8182\) and the source table approximation \(z\approx0.91\) gives 82.75 kilograms.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
An objective coefficient range is an interval of values for one objective coefficient over which the current optimal basis remains optimal while all other data stay fixed. A report with coefficient \(c_j\), allowable decrease \(d_j\), and allowable increase \(u_j\) gives

\[ c_j-d_j\le c_j^{\mathrm{new}}\le c_j+u_j. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The objective coefficient range answers how far one profit or cost coefficient may move before a different decision becomes optimal. Within this interval the reported decision stays an optimum; only its objective value changes, because the same quantities now earn a different return per unit.

With objective \(c_1x_s+2x_t\), every objective line has slope \(-c_1/2\). The corner \((20,60)\) stays optimal as long as this slope lies between the slopes of the two constraint lines through it: \(-1\) for carpentry, \(x_s+x_t\le80\), and \(-2\) for finishing, \(2x_s+x_t\le100\). That gives \(1\le c_1/2\le2\), the range \(2\le c_1\le4\) shaded as a fan. At \(c_1=2\) or \(c_1=4\) the objective line lies along an edge of the region, and the whole edge is optimal.

Change the profit per soldier \(c_s\): within the shown range the corner \((20,60)\) stays optimal and only \(z^*\) changes.

The range is a one-at-a-time question of sensitivity analysis, stated in the Excel sensitivity report as an allowable decrease and increase. For a variable that is \(0\) at the optimum, lowering its coefficient never makes it attractive, so the decrease is unlimited; for a nonbasic variable the allowable increase equals the size of its reduced cost.

Separate ranges do not combine. Raising \(c_1\) to \(4\) and lowering the train coefficient from \(2\) to \(1.6\) stays within each range on its own, but together the slope is \(-2.5\), steeper than the finishing line, and the optimum moves to \((40,20)\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For a change \(\Delta c_j\) within the range, the value changes by \(x_j^*\Delta c_j\).
  • At a range endpoint, additional optimal solutions may become available.
  • Separate reported ranges do not justify simultaneous changes automatically.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For the illustrated objective \(c_1x_s+2x_t\), the coefficient \(c_1=3\) may decrease or increase by 1, giving \([2,4]\). The corner \((20,60)\) remains optimal, while its value becomes \(20c_1+120\); endpoint values may admit other optima.

  • The small-pipe profit coefficient 5 has allowable decrease 1 and increase 3, giving \([4,8]\).
  • Changing banana profit by \(-0.03\) with quantity 75 changes total profit by \(-2.25\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The objective function assigns a numerical value to a decision vector. The model specifies whether this value should be maximized or minimized. In an LP it has the form

\[ z=c_1x_1+\cdots+c_nx_n, \]

where the \(c_j\) are given objective coefficients.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The objective expresses the criterion used to compare feasible choices. Profit maximization and cost minimization are common, but the course also considers distance, time, and flow.

The objective function \(f(\boldsymbol{x})\) is the quantity to maximize (for example, profit) or minimize (for example, cost). Functional constraints describe what an allowed decision must satisfy, such as resource limits or demand requirements. Domain restrictions specify signs or integrality.

In the diagram, blue identifies decision variables, whose values the model determines; red identifies model parameters, the given data \(c_j\), \(a_{ij}\) and \(b_i\). In general, the model is \(\max/\min\ f(\boldsymbol{x})\) subject to \(\boldsymbol{x}\in F\), where the constraints define the feasible set \(F\). A solution assigns values to all variables.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• An objective value is a number; an optimal solution is a vector of decisions.
  • In a profit objective, use revenues minus relevant costs.
  • The direction of optimization determines what constitutes an improvement.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Giapetto maximizes \(z=3x_s+2x_t\).
  • The pig diet minimizes \(z=0.4x_A+0.8x_B\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a two-variable linear objective \(z=c_1x_1+c_2x_2\) with at least one nonzero coefficient, an objective line is the set of points giving a fixed value \(z=\bar z\). If \(c_2\ne0\), its slope-intercept form is

\[ x_2=-\frac{c_1}{c_2}x_1+\frac{\bar z}{c_2}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An objective line collects all points with the same objective value. Changing the value moves the line parallel to itself without changing its slope, and this is what the graphical method uses: it slides the line as far as the feasible region allows.

The three lines belong to \(z=3x_s+2x_t\) with values \(60\), \(120\) and \(180\). Each has slope \(-\tfrac{3}{2}\), and raising \(z\) by \(60\) raises the intercept on the \(x_t\)-axis by \(60/2=30\), from \(30\) to \(60\) to \(90\). The arrow \((c_1,c_2)=(3,2)\) shows the direction in which \(z\) increases.

Change \(\bar z\) to translate the line and \(c_1,c_2\) to turn it: all lines for one objective are parallel, with slope \(-c_1/c_2\).

The slope-intercept form in the Definition shows the role of each number. The slope \(-c_1/c_2\) depends only on the coefficients, so all objective lines of one objective are parallel; the value \(\bar z\) enters only through the intercept \(\bar z/c_2\). Moving a point by \(t(c_1,c_2)\) with \(t>0\) changes \(z\) by \(t(c_1^2+c_2^2)>0\), so the direction \((c_1,c_2)\) always improves a maximization, and the opposite direction a minimization.

A common slip is to assume that a larger \(\bar z\) always moves the line upwards. That holds when \(c_2>0\); for \(z=2x_1-3x_2\) the intercept is \(-\bar z/3\), so the line moves down as \(\bar z\) grows. In economics the same lines are called isoprofit or isocost lines.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• All constant-objective lines for a fixed objective are parallel.
  • If \(c_2<0\), a larger objective value lowers the vertical intercept.
  • When \(c_2=0\), the objective lines are vertical.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Translating a line in the direction \((c_1,c_2)\) raises its objective value. When a finite maximum is attained, the last objective line meeting the feasible region identifies it.

  • \(z=x_1+2x_2\) gives \(x_2=-x_1/2+z/2\).
  • \(z=2x_1-3x_2\) gives \(x_2=2x_1/3-z/3\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Operations research (OR) uses mathematical models and analytical solution methods to support optimal, or sufficiently good, decisions in practical situations. The decision problem includes an objective, available choices, and restrictions on those choices.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Operations research applies mathematics to practical decisions, such as how much to produce, how to route vehicles or how to pack goods. The real question is first turned into a model that can be analysed systematically, and the usefulness of the answer depends on how well that model represents the situation.

The cycle shows where the mathematics sits. Only the step from a mathematical model to a solution is pure calculation. The steps before it decide what is simplified and which data are used, and the validation step asks whether the answer makes sense in the real situation. A rejected answer sends the work back to the assumptions, not just to the calculation; the OR study cycle describes these stages.

The definition allows "sufficiently good" decisions as well as optimal ones. When a problem is too hard to solve exactly, a heuristic provides a usable decision, and a relaxation shows how far from optimal it can be. Small examples of both kinds are the Giapetto model and the diet problem, solved exactly, and the bin packing and vehicle routing problems, approached with heuristics. Other names for the field are operational research and management science.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Applications include production, transport, scheduling, maintenance, and inventory management.
  • An optimal model solution must still be checked against the practical situation.
  • Difficult problems may require a heuristic instead of an exact solution method.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Any stage of the OR study cycle can prompt a return to an earlier stage if validation shows that the simplified representation is inadequate.

  • Lecture scheduling allocates teaching activities to times and rooms.
  • A warehouse chooses replenishment quantities and ordering times.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a minimization problem with feasible set \(F\), a feasible vector \(\boldsymbol{x}^*\) is an optimal solution if

\[ f(\boldsymbol{x}^*)\le f(\boldsymbol{x})\quad\text{for every }\boldsymbol{x}\in F. \]

For maximization the inequality is reversed. The number \(z^*=f(\boldsymbol{x}^*)\) is the optimal value.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Optimality compares a feasible decision with every other allowed decision. An optimal solution is at least as good as each of them; it need not be strictly better, so several equally good decisions may exist.

For \(z=3x_s+2x_t\) the dashed lines \(z=60\) and \(z=120\) cross the feasible region, so better plans exist. The line \(z^*=180\) is the last one in the direction of increasing \(z\) that still meets the region, and it touches only at \((20,60)\): this point is the optimal solution, and \(180\) is the optimal value.

Both parts of the Definition matter: \(\boldsymbol{x}^*\) must itself be feasible, and the inequality must hold for every \(\boldsymbol{x}\in F\), not only for the points tried so far. An optimum need not exist, since a model may have no feasible solution or an objective that improves without limit, and need not be unique: when an objective line lies along an edge of the region, every point of that edge is optimal.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A model may have no feasible solution or no finite optimum.
  • The optimal value and the vector attaining it are different objects.
  • An optimum is relative to the specified objective, constraints, and input data.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For the illustrated Giapetto objective, the optimal point \((20,60)\) has value \(3\cdot20+2\cdot60=180\).

  • The manufacturing example has \(x_1^*=2\), \(x_2^*=5\), and \(z^*=12\).
  • The practice LP with objective \(2x_1+2x_2\) has optimum \((3,4)\) and value 14.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
Suppose an optimization problem has a finite optimal value \(z^*\). Let \(z_H\) be the value of a feasible solution and \(z_R\) the finite optimal value of a relaxation with the same objective. Then

\[ z_R\le z^*\le z_H\quad\text{for minimization}, \] \[ z_H\le z^*\le z_R\quad\text{for maximization}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The two bounds trap the unknown optimum between a value that is known to be achievable and a value that cannot be beaten. Their difference measures how much the current feasible solution could still be improved, without knowing the optimum itself.

The figure is drawn for maximization. The value \(z_H\) of a feasible solution lies on the left and the optimal value \(z_R\) of a relaxation on the right; the unknown \(z^*\) lies somewhere between them. The gap \(z_R-z_H\) is the largest possible loss from accepting the feasible solution.

Each inequality has a short reason. The feasible solution is one of the points over which the optimum is taken, so the optimum is at least as good as \(z_H\). The relaxation optimizes the same objective over a larger set \(F_R\supseteq F\), so its optimum is at least as good as \(z^*\). This is why the relaxed value must be an optimal value and the other must come from a feasible point: an infeasible point says nothing about \(z^*\).

The direction words switch with the problem type, but the order does not: the feasible value is always on the worse side and the relaxed value on the better side. For minimization a heuristic gives an upper bound and a relaxation a lower bound; in the vehicle routing problem this gives \(202\le z^*\le214\) miles.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For a minimization problem, \(z_H-z^*\le z_H-z_R\).
  • If the feasible and relaxed values coincide, the feasible solution is proven optimal.
  • A feasible solution of a relaxation alone is not generally an opposing bound; its optimal value is needed.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For maximization, improved incumbents raise the feasible lower bound. Resolving branch-and-bound nodes can reduce the global upper bound formed from the incumbent and the remaining open-node relaxation bounds.

  • The routing example gives \(202\le z^*\le214\), so the remaining improvement is at most 12 miles.
  • A 232-mile route is also an upper bound, but 214 is tighter.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
An optimization model specifies decision variables \(\boldsymbol{x}\), an objective function \(f(\boldsymbol{x})\) to maximize or minimize, and constraints defining the allowed decisions. Writing the feasible set as \(F\), its form is

\[ \min_{\boldsymbol{x}\in F} f(\boldsymbol{x})\qquad\text{or}\qquad\max_{\boldsymbol{x}\in F} f(\boldsymbol{x}). \]

The coefficients and other given inputs are model parameters.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The model states what can be chosen, what counts as better, and which choices are allowed. Solving it selects the best allowed decision according to the chosen objective.

The objective function \(f(\boldsymbol{x})\) is the quantity to maximize (for example, profit) or minimize (for example, cost). Functional constraints describe what an allowed decision must satisfy, such as resource limits or demand requirements. Domain restrictions specify signs or integrality.

In the diagram, blue identifies decision variables, whose values the model determines; red identifies model parameters, the given data \(c_j\), \(a_{ij}\) and \(b_i\). In general, the model is \(\max/\min\ f(\boldsymbol{x})\) subject to \(\boldsymbol{x}\in F\), where the constraints define the feasible set \(F\). A solution assigns values to all variables.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The objective and constraints need not be linear in a general OR model.
  • Some simple models have a closed-form solution; many require an algorithm.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\min\{x^2+bx+c\colon x\ge d\}\), the optimum is \(x^*=\max\{-b/2,d\}\).
  • Giapetto chooses soldier and train production to maximize profit under labour limits.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The OR study cycle moves from a real situation to an assumed representation of it, then to a mathematical model, a solution, validation, and implementation. Validation checks whether the model and its solution adequately represent the practical decision problem.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The OR study cycle describes how a practical decision problem becomes a model, a solution and finally an implemented decision. Its main message is that a mathematically correct answer can still be wrong for the real problem if the model leaves out something essential.

Follow the arrows: the real situation is abstracted into an assumed representation (which simplifications, which data), formulated as a mathematical model, solved and checked. If the answer makes sense it is accepted and implemented; if not, the dashed arrow leads back to the assumptions or the model, not only to the calculation.

Validation is different from checking the computation. A solution can be computed correctly and still be rejected because the model was too simple, for example a route plan based on straight-line distances where the roads are far from straight. Each extra detail makes the model more realistic, but it also needs more data and makes the model harder to solve, so the cycle is often run several times with gradually refined models.

The optimization model is only one stage of the cycle, and an algorithm or software package performs only the solution stage; interpreting, validating and implementing the answer are separate parts of operations research.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Additional detail may improve realism but also increase data requirements and solution difficulty.
  • The required data must be available or obtainable.
  • Validation can reveal a need to revise assumptions before implementation.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Any stage can prompt a return to an earlier stage if validation shows that the simplified representation is inadequate.

  • A route model may initially approximate travel distances by straight lines.
  • Road layout and time-dependent traffic may require a more detailed route model.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In the constant-demand EOQ setting, the ordering cycle length \(t_0\) is the time between consecutive orders. If each order contains \(y\) units and demand occurs at rate \(D>0\), then

\[ t_0=\frac{y}{D}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The ordering cycle is the time one batch lasts. With constant demand, a batch of \(y\) units is used up after \(y/D\) time units, and the next order then starts the same pattern again.

Each tooth of the sawtooth is one cycle: \(6{,}000\) pencils used at \(100\) per day last \(60\) days, so orders arrive at days \(0\), \(60\) and \(120\), marked by the arrows.

One batch of \(y\) units lasts \(t_0=y/D\): change \(y\) or \(D\) and watch the sawtooth's teeth stretch or shrink.

The reciprocal \(D/y\) is the number of orders per unit time, which turns the setup cost per order into the rate \(KD/y\). Demand and time must use the same unit: \(700\) per week is \(100\) per day. The identity also holds with planned backorders, since over a full cycle the batch still equals the cycle's demand. The cycle is the spacing between orders, not the lead time, the delay between placing an order and receiving it.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Orders per unit time equal \(D/y\).
  • Cycle length and lead time are different: one measures spacing of orders, the other order-to-receipt delay.
  • Convert demand and time consistently.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Ordering 22 phones at demand two per day gives an 11-day cycle.
  • In the figure, time is measured in days. Ordering \(6{,}000\) pencils at demand \(D=100\) per day gives a \(60\)-day cycle and \(D/y=1/60\) orders per day.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The overage cost in the newsvendor model is the net loss on one unit ordered but not sold at its regular price:

\[ h=c-s>0, \]

where \(c\) is its unit cost and \(s\) its salvage value. Total expected overage cost at order quantity \(y\) is \(h\mathbb{E}[(y-D)^+]\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The overage cost is what one unsold unit costs in the end: it was bought for \(c\) and brings back only the salvage value \(s\), so the net loss is \(c-s\). It is the price of ordering one unit too many.

The money scale shows the newspaper data: the purchase cost \(c=3.50\) and the salvage value \(s=1.50\) are \(h=2\) apart, the lower gap. The upper gap, from \(c\) to the selling price \(p=5\), is the underage cost \(b=1.50\); together they span \(p-s=3.50\), the denominator of the critical ratio \(\beta=1.5/3.5=3/7\).

Each unsold unit loses \(h=c-s\). A low or negative salvage value \(s\) pushes \(y^*\) down.

Only leftover units are charged, and the positive part \((y-D)^+\) counts them. A higher salvage value lowers \(h\) and raises the optimal order; a negative \(s\), a disposal fee, makes \(h\) larger than \(c\). Unlike the EOQ holding cost, which is charged per unit per unit of time, \(h\) is charged once per leftover unit of the single period.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Only leftover units incur overage loss.
  • Increasing salvage value lowers overage cost.
  • This is a single-period per-unit loss, whereas EOQ holding cost is charged per unit per unit time.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The illustrated newspaper data give overage cost \(h=2\) and underage cost \(b=1.5\), hence critical ratio \(\beta=1.5/3.5=3/7\). These are single-period per-unit losses, rather than EOQ cost rates.

  • Newspapers costing 3.50 and salvaged for 1.50 have \(h=2\).
  • Meals costing 2.20 with zero salvage have \(h=2.20\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For three binary decisions \(y_1,y_2,y_3\), requiring an even number of yes decisions is equivalent to

\[ y_1+y_2+y_3=2x,\qquad x\in\{0,1\}. \]

The sum can therefore be 0 or 2, the only even values possible for three binary decisions.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The parity constraint counts yes decisions and requires the count to be even. Three binary decisions sum to at most \(3\), so the even counts are \(0\) and \(2\), and the auxiliary variable \(x\in\{0,1\}\) in \(y_1+y_2+y_3=2x\) produces exactly these.

The number line shows the four possible counts. The even ones are reached with \(x=0\) (all three no) and \(x=1\) (exactly two yes); the odd counts \(1\) and \(3\) would need \(x=\tfrac{1}{2}\) or \(x=\tfrac{3}{2}\), which are not allowed.

The whole effect comes from \(x\) being an integer: with \(x\) continuous, every count \(c\) is matched by \(x=c/2\) and the restriction disappears. An odd count is required by writing \(2x+1\), and more decisions need a larger integer range for \(x\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• When \(x=0\), all three decisions are no.
  • When \(x=1\), exactly two decisions are yes.
  • Allowing \(x\) to be continuous would remove the parity restriction.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \((y_1,y_2,y_3)=(1,1,0)\) is allowed with \(x=1\).
  • \((1,1,1)\) is excluded because it would require \(x=3/2\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: In the course's terminology, a path is a sequence of distinct edges connecting a starting vertex to an ending vertex, with consecutive edges joined through their shared vertices. For directed edges, traversal respects their directions.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A path describes a route through a network: it starts at one vertex, follows edges that meet end to end, and stops at another vertex. Its length, the sum of the lengths of its edges, is the quantity that route problems compare.

The highlighted path \(A-C-B-D-E-F\) uses five different edges, each sharing a vertex with the next, and its length is \(2+1+5+2+3=13\).

The course definition requires distinct edges, not distinct vertices. In graph theory such a route is usually called a trail, and path is kept for routes that also visit every vertex at most once; this course uses path for the edge-distinct version. So a route that returns to an earlier vertex is still a path, and one that ends where it starts is a cycle.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The length of a weighted path is the sum of the lengths of the traversed edges.
  • The course convention corresponds to what some texts call a trail.
  • A path whose first and last vertices coincide is called a cycle or tour in the terminology video.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The highlighted path is \(A-C-B-D-E-F\), with length \(2+1+5+2+3=13\).

  • In the course introduction network (not shown here), a path follows \(A-D-C-E-G\).
  • The shortest-path example gives \(S-B-A-D-E-T\) with length 12.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a real number \(u\), its positive part is

\[ u^+=\max\{u,0\}=\begin{cases}u,&u\ge0,\\0,&u<0.\end{cases} \]

In the newsvendor model, \((y-D)^+\) is leftover stock and \((D-y)^+\) is unmet demand.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The positive part keeps a number when it is positive and replaces it by \(0\) otherwise. In the newsvendor model it splits one difference \(y-D\) into two counts that cannot be negative: leftover stock and unmet demand.

The graph is flat at height \(0\) for \(u<0\) and follows the line \(u^+=u\) for \(u\ge0\); the dashed piece of the line \(u\) below zero is what the positive part cuts off. Like the absolute value, it has a corner at \(u=0\), and in fact \(u^+=\tfrac{1}{2}(u+|u|)\).

A common slip is to compute \((y-D)^+\) as \(y^+-D^+\). For \(y=10\) and \(D=12\) the leftover is \((-2)^+=0\), not \(10-12=-2\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Both leftover and shortage quantities are nonnegative.
  • For a fixed realized demand, at least one of them is zero.
  • For discrete demand, expectations are computed by probability-weighting the positive parts for every demand outcome.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Defining the negative part by \(u^-=\max\{-u,0\}\) gives the identity \(u=u^+-u^-\).

  • If \(y=10\) and \(D=7\), leftovers are 3 and unmet demand is zero.
  • If \(y=10\) and \(D=12\), leftovers are zero and unmet demand is 2.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
Let \(y_m=\sqrt{2KD/h}\) and \(TCU_j(y)=Dc_j+KD/y+hy/2\), with \(c_1>c_2\). The price-break indifference quantity \(Q>y_m\) solves

\[ TCU_2(Q)=TCU_1(y_m), \]

or equivalently

\[ Q^2+\frac{2(c_2D-TCU_1(y_m))}{h}Q +\frac{2KD}{h}=0. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The indifference quantity answers how far above the EOQ a price-break threshold may lie and still be worth reaching. Up to \(Q\), the purchasing discount on every unit outweighs the extra setup and holding costs of the larger batch; beyond \(Q\) it does not.

The horizontal line at \(450\) is the best cost without discount, \(TCU_1(22)\). The discounted curve \(TCU_2\) lies below it from \(22\) up to \(Q\approx39.86\), where it climbs back to \(450\). A threshold \(q\) in the shaded band, such as \(35\), should be reached; a threshold beyond \(Q\) should not.

\(Q\) is where the discounted cost curve climbs back to the best cost without discount, \(TCU_1(y_m)\). Move \(q\) past \(y_m\) and past \(Q\) to see the three cases.

At \(y_m\) the discount saves \(D(c_1-c_2)=2\cdot10=20\) per day. Moving the batch from \(y_m\) to \(Q\) raises setup and holding cost from \(110\) to \(130\) per day, which uses up exactly that saving. Multiplying \(TCU_2(Q)=TCU_1(y_m)\) by \(2Q/h\) gives the quadratic equation of the Proposition. It has two solutions, for the phones about \(12.14\) and \(39.86\); the smaller one lies below \(y_m\), and a threshold below \(y_m\) needs no comparison, since \(y_m\) itself then qualifies for the discount. Only the larger solution is a useful boundary.

\(Q\) is not an optimal order quantity itself: it is a boundary for the threshold \(q\). In practice it is enough to compare the full costs of the two candidates \(y_m\) and \(q\), as in EOQ with price breaks; \(Q\) shows at once which thresholds are worth reaching.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• With the worked-example convention that \(q\) qualifies, a threshold \(y_m<q<Q\) favours ordering \(q\).
  • For \(q>Q\), retain \(y_m\); for \(q<y_m\), \(y_m\) already receives the discount.
  • At \(q=Q\), the two candidates tie.
  • Directly comparing candidate costs avoids solving for \(Q\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The snack-bar exercise gives \(Q\approx89.07\) kilograms; its threshold 100 is too high.
  • For the phone example, \(Q\approx39.86\), and threshold 35 lies between \(y_m=22\) and \(Q\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A production-inventory model chooses production \(P_t\) and end-of-period stock \(I_t\) to meet known demands \(d_t\) across periods. With given initial stock \(I_0\), unit production costs \(c_t\), and end-of-period holding costs \(h_t\), the course problem is represented by

\[ \min\sum_{t=1}^T(c_tP_t+h_tI_t),\qquad I_{t-1}+P_t-d_t=I_t,\qquad P_t,I_t\ge0. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The model decides when to produce, not only how much. Production in a cheaper month may be stored for a later month at a holding cost, and the inventory balance ensures that every unit sold comes from current production or previously held stock.

Each month in the figure is a balance: stock arriving from the previous month plus production equals demand plus stock carried out. In month 1, \(I_0=0\) and \(P_1=120\) meet \(d_1=100\) and leave \(I_1=20\), which is carried into month 2 at a cost of 8 per window.

The balance \(I_{t-1}+P_t-d_t=I_t\) is what links the months: without it each month would be a separate problem. The nonnegativity of \(I_t\) excludes shortages, so demand must be met on time. The objective then weighs producing early against producing late: a month-3 window made in month 2 costs \(45+8=53\), less than the 55 it costs in month 3, so producing early pays whenever the earlier unit cost plus the holding costs is lower, as long as capacity allows.

Linear program formulation introduces production and inventory decisions, balance equations and capacity restrictions; with continuous \(P_t\) and \(I_t\) the model is an LP. The same balance returns in the dynamic lot-size model, where every order also carries a fixed setup cost.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Nonnegative inventory rules out shortages.
  • The window example charges a holding cost of 8 per window per month on end-of-month inventory.
  • The six-month exercise does not specify initial stock; taking \(I_0=0\) is an explicit modelling assumption.
  • With positive production and holding costs and no required final stock, surplus final inventory is unnecessary.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Month 1 requires 100 windows; producing 120 from zero stock leaves 20.
  • Producing a month-3 window in month 2 costs 45 plus 8 holding, compared with 55 in month 3.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The course's project longest path model uses a directed acyclic activity network with start \(S\) and finish \(T\). Each edge has an activity duration; an outgoing activity may start only after all activities entering its starting vertex finish. Under these precedence rules and without additional resource restrictions, project duration is the length of a longest \(S\)-to-\(T\) path.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The project cannot finish before its longest chain of dependent activities has finished. Activities on different chains can run side by side, but along one chain each activity must wait for the previous one, so the project duration is the length of the longest \(S\)-to-\(T\) path. The model finds it with binary edge-selection variables.

Each node carries its earliest start time: the largest total duration over the paths from \(S\) to that node. Node 3 can start only when both \(C\) and \(D\) are done, at \(\max\{3+4,\,2+5\}=7\), and \(T\) is reached at \(\max\{7+2,\,2+6\}=9\). The red path \(S\to2\to3\to T\) has length \(2+5+2=9\), but so does \(S\to1\to3\to T\) with \(3+4+2=9\): a longest path need not be unique. The path through \(F\) has length \(8\), so activity \(F\) could finish one time unit later without delaying the project.

The formulation reuses the shortest path binary formulation: one unit of flow leaves \(S\), enters \(T\) and is balanced at every other node, but the objective is maximized instead of minimized. This is safe because a precedence network is acyclic, since a cycle would mean that an activity waits for itself; with cycles, maximizing could select an extra cycle that satisfies the balance equations without lying on the \(S\)-to-\(T\) path.

A common slip is to add up all activity durations. Activities on parallel chains overlap in time, so only the durations along one chain count.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Maximize the sum of selected activity durations.
  • Use one unit of source-to-sink binary flow with balance at intermediate vertices.
  • Acyclicity matters: in a general cyclic network, flow balance alone could allow unrelated selected cycles.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the figure, both critical paths, \(S-2-3-T\) with \(2+5+2=9\) and \(S-1-3-T\) with \(3+4+2=9\), have duration 9, compared with 8 for \(S-2-T\). Negating the activity lengths turns this acyclic longest-path calculation into a shortest-path calculation; the lack of cycles permits the negative lengths.

  • In the exercise, \(S-A-D-F-T\) has duration \(5+2+6+4=17\).
  • \(S-B-D-F-T\) has duration \(3+3+6+4=16\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The project selection model chooses complete projects under resource budgets. Let \(y_j=1\) if project \(j\) is selected, \(r_j\) be its return, \(a_{tj}\) its expenditure in year \(t\), and \(B_t\) that year's budget. Then

\[ \begin{gathered} \max\sum_jr_jy_j,\\ \sum_ja_{tj}y_j\le B_t\ \text{for every }t,\\ y_j\in\{0,1\}. \end{gathered} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The model chooses which complete projects to fund so that the total return is as large as possible without exceeding any year's budget. A project uses resources in each relevant year and contributes its full return only when selected; fractional project funding is excluded.

The green columns are the selected projects 1, 3 and 4, with \(y_j=1\). Each year's budget row adds only their expenditures, \(a_{t1}+a_{t3}+a_{t4}\le B_t\), because the unselected projects 2 and 5 have \(y_j=0\) and contribute nothing.

The product \(a_{tj}y_j\) equals \(a_{tj}\) when project \(j\) is selected and 0 otherwise, so \(\sum_ja_{tj}y_j\) is the spending on the selected projects in year \(t\). The same \(y_j\) appears in every year's constraint: a selected project must be paid for in every year it needs money, and the projects compete for the budget of each year. The model is a binary integer program with one binary variable per project.

Ranking projects by return, or by return per unit of cost, and funding them in that order is a heuristic that can miss the optimum. With a single budget of 10, a project costing 6 with return 7 has the best ratio, but after funding it neither of two projects costing 5 with return 5 fits; funding those two instead gives return 10.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A separate budget constraint is needed for each year.
  • The later development-project example uses one capital budget.
  • Relaxing a binary variable to a fraction supplies a bound but not an implementable partial project.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The green columns in the figure represent selected projects, \(y_j=1\); each budget row sums only their expenditures.

  • The week 2 exercise has five projects and a budget of 25 in each of three years.
  • The development-project example has capital 20 and an optimal return of 3.4 from projects 1, 3, and 4.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The purchasing cost is the amount paid per inventory unit, multiplied by the quantity purchased. If its constant unit price is \(c\) and all demand is met at constant rate \(D\), the long-run purchasing cost rate is \(cD\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Purchasing cost is the money paid for the goods themselves, not the fixed charge per order or the cost of keeping stock. If all demand is met, on average \(D\) units are bought per unit of time whatever the batch size, so a constant unit price \(c\) gives the rate \(cD\) for every EOQ policy.

The lines show cumulative purchasing cost over days at \(D=2\) phones per day: slope \(340\) at the price \(c_1=170\), slope \(320\) at the discounted price \(160\). The batch size appears in neither line; it only decides which price applies.

A constant \(cD\) can therefore be left out when choosing the classical EOQ. With quantity discounts the unit price \(c(y)\) depends on the batch size \(y\), and then \(c(y)D\) must be compared together with setup and holding costs.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A constant \(cD\) can be omitted when finding the classical EOQ, but retained when reporting full costs.
  • All-unit price breaks require comparing purchasing cost as well as setup and holding costs.
  • Purchasing cost is different from the fixed cost of initiating an order.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In the figure, time is measured in days. At demand \(D=2\) phones per day and unit price \(c_1=170\), the cumulative purchasing cost has slope \(c_1D=340\) per day.
  • A discounted unit price of 160 reduces that rate to 320 when the order qualifies.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A pure integer program is an integer linear program in which every decision variable is restricted to integer values. Nonnegativity, upper bounds, and other restrictions remain separate model constraints.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A pure integer program fits decisions that are counts, such as numbers of buses or workers, where a fractional answer has no meaning. Its feasible solutions are then only the points with integer coordinates inside the region of the constraints.

The shaded polygon is that region without integrality; the filled dots are the integer points in it. Moving the objective line \(3x_1+2x_2=z\) outwards, the last filled dot it reaches is \((3,1)\) with \(z=11\), while the best point of the polygon is the corner \((3.5,1.25)\) with \(z=13\).

"Pure" only says that every variable is integer-restricted; nonnegativity and upper bounds remain separate constraints. The best integer point need not be a corner of the polygon, and rounding \((3.5,1.25)\) to \((4,1)\) violates \(x_1\le3.5\), so integer programs need their own methods, such as branch-and-bound.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• All \(n\) decision variables are integer-restricted, whereas a mixed integer program restricts only some of them.
  • Binary integer programs are a special case with the additional bounds 0 and 1.
  • Dropping integrality gives its LP relaxation.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The figure uses the illustrative model \(\max(3x_1+2x_2)\) subject to \(2x_1+2x_2\le9.5\), \(x_1\le3.5\) and \(\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}^2\). Its best lattice point is \((3,1)\) with value 11; it is not a corner of the continuous polygon.

  • The bus-scheduling model counts buses beginning each shift.
  • The integer work-order model counts tow bars and stabilizer bars.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: In the course's maximization sensitivity report, the reduced cost of a currently zero-valued variable is the marginal change in the objective when that variable is increased and the other variables adjust through the current basis. If the tableau row is \(z+q_jx_j+\cdots=z_0\), the corresponding reduced cost is \(-q_j\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The reduced cost of an activity that is not used at the optimum says what happens to the objective if one unit of it is forced into the plan while the other variables adjust to keep the constraints satisfied. It is the opportunity cost of that activity: a negative value means that a small forced increase reduces profit.

The line starts at \(z^*=180\) for \(t=0\) and falls by \(1\) for every unit of the product \(x_c\) forced into the plan, so its slope \(-1\) is the reduced cost. As the Example computes, one unit of \(x_c\) earns \(4\) but uses hours worth \(5\) at the current shadow prices.

The sign follows from the tableau. The row \(z+q_jx_j+\cdots=z_0\) gives \(z=z_0-q_jx_j-\cdots\), so raising the nonbasic variable \(x_j\) by one unit changes \(z\) by \(-q_j\). At an optimal tableau of a maximization problem every \(q_j\ge0\) by the optimality test, so the reduced costs of nonbasic variables are at most \(0\) there.

In sensitivity analysis the reduced cost also says how much more profitable an unused activity would have to be: raising its coefficient by the size of the reduced cost makes it break even, so the allowable increase of a nonbasic variable equals that size, as for the sheets in the Examples. A common slip is to read the reduced cost as the profit coefficient itself; it is that coefficient minus the value of the resources the activity uses.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Do not confuse a reported reduced cost with the original objective coefficient.
  • The sign is opposite to the coefficient in the course maximization tableau.
  • The interpretation is local and relies on a feasible basis adjustment.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the figure, a third product \(x_c\) earns 4 and uses 3 finishing and 2 carpentry hours. At shadow prices 1 and 1, its reduced cost is \(4-(3\cdot1+2\cdot1)=-1\). A small forced increase therefore costs 1 unit of profit per unit produced while the basis remains feasible. Raising its profit by 1 removes that marginal disadvantage; a tie need not force it into every optimal solution.

  • Sheets have reported reduced cost -3.3 in the pipes-and-sheets example.
  • Their profit coefficient is 4 and its allowable increase is 3.3 before the current optimal basis can cease to be optimal.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A relaxation retains a problem's objective and removes or weakens constraints to obtain an easier problem. If \(F\) and \(F_R\) are the original and relaxed feasible sets, then \(F\subseteq F_R\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A relaxation keeps the objective but allows more decisions. The relaxed problem is usually easier to solve, and its optimal value is a benchmark that the original problem cannot beat.

Dropping \(x_s\le40\) from the Giapetto region adds the small red triangle \(F_R\setminus F\) to the blue region \(F\). With the objective \(4x_s+x_t\) the original optimum is \((40,20)\) with value \(180\); in the larger region the best point is \((50,0)\) with value \(200\). That point violates \(x_s\le40\), so it is not a solution of the original problem, but it shows that no original solution can exceed \(200\).

The reason is \(F\subseteq F_R\): every original solution is also a relaxed one, so the best over \(F_R\) is at least as good as the best over \(F\). The objective must stay the same, otherwise the two optimal values cannot be compared.

A relaxation does not always change the answer. With Giapetto's own objective \(3x_s+2x_t\), the same relaxation still has its optimum at \((20,60)\) with value \(180\), because \((50,0)\) gives only \(150\); this relaxed optimum is feasible, and therefore optimal for the original problem.

Relaxations supply the second side of the optimization bounds, opposite to a heuristic; removing the 100-mile limit in the vehicle routing problem is an example. Later, integer programs are relaxed by dropping the requirement that the variables be whole numbers.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For minimization, the relaxed optimum is no greater than the original optimum; for maximization, it is no smaller.
  • A relaxed optimum that is also feasible for the original problem is optimal for the original problem.
  • An infeasible relaxed optimizer need not have a strictly better value; equality can occur.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For the illustrated objective \(4x_s+x_t\), dropping \(x_s\le40\) changes the optimum from \((40,20)\) with value 180 to \((50,0)\) with relaxed value 200.

  • Ignore the 100-mile refuelling limit in the routing example.
  • Remove integrality restrictions from an integer program while keeping its other constraints.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For an original directed edge \(i\to j\) with capacity \(c_{ij}\) and assigned flow \(x_{ij}\), its residual capacities are \(c_{ij}-x_{ij}\) in the forward direction and \(x_{ij}\) in the reverse direction. The residual network records these possibilities for increasing or cancelling current flow.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The residual network records, for the current flow, how the flow on each edge can still change: how much more can be sent forward, and how much of the present flow can be cancelled. It is the network in which the augmenting path algorithm searches for improvements.

The original edge carries flow 3 of capacity 4. In the residual version, the forward edge has capacity \(c_{ij}-x_{ij}=1\), the room left, and the backward edge has capacity \(x_{ij}=3\), the flow that could be undone. The two residual capacities always add up to the original capacity, here \(1+3=4\).

Reverse residual capacity is essential because a good final routing may require undoing part of an initially chosen path. Take a source \(S\), a sink \(T\) and vertices \(A\) and \(B\), with edges \(S\to A\), \(S\to B\), \(A\to B\), \(A\to T\) and \(B\to T\), all of capacity 1. If the first augmentation sends one unit along \(S\to A\to B\to T\), no route of forward edges with spare capacity remains. The residual network still has \(S\to B\), the backward direction \(B\to A\) and \(A\to T\); sending one unit this way cancels the flow on \(A\to B\) and reaches the maximum value 2.

A backward residual edge is neither a new connection in the original directed network nor a negative flow. Using it lowers \(x_{ij}\) on the original edge \(i\to j\), and never below \(0\), because the backward capacity is exactly \(x_{ij}\); in the same way the forward capacity keeps \(x_{ij}\le c_{ij}\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The course draws a connection with two directional residual labels; it must not be interpreted as equal capacity in both directions.
  • Only directions with positive residual capacity can be used by an augmenting path.
  • A forward augmentation decreases forward residual capacity and increases reverse residual capacity by the same amount.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
A saturated original edge has no forward residual capacity; its backward residual direction permits cancelling its assigned flow.

  • Capacity 6 and flow 2 on A-B give residual capacities 4 forward and 2 backward.
  • Cancelling one unit changes those residual capacities to 5 forward and 1 backward.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A right-hand-side sensitivity range is the interval for one constraint's right-hand side over which the current optimal basis remains feasible and optimal, with other parameters fixed. Within this range, its shadow price gives the exact linear change in optimal value.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
In sensitivity analysis, the right-hand-side range answers how far the amount of one resource may change before its shadow price stops being valid. Inside the range the same constraints stay binding, so the same basis describes the optimum. The production quantities do change, but the optimal value changes at the constant rate of the shadow price, so a valid shadow price does not imply an unchanged solution.

The finishing constraint \(2x_s+x_t\le b_1\) is drawn for \(b_1=80\), \(100\) and \(120\). As \(b_1\) grows, the optimal corner, where the finishing and carpentry lines cross, slides along the carpentry line \(x_s+x_t=80\) from \((0,80)\) to \((40,40)\), passing \((20,60)\) at \(b_1=100\). Along the way \(z^*=3x_s+2x_t\) grows from \(160\) to \(200\), one unit per added hour, matching the shadow price \(1\).

Change the finishing hours \(b_1\): inside the shaded range the same constraints stay binding, and \(z^*\) grows linearly in \(b_1\) (right).

The endpoints are where the crossing point would leave the feasible region: below \(80\) it would need \(x_s<0\), and above \(120\) it would violate the demand limit \(x_s\le40\). Beyond them another corner is optimal and the rate changes. For \(b_1\le80\) only trains are made and \(z^*=2b_1\), a rate of \(2\) per hour; above \(120\) the optimum stays at \((40,40)\) and extra finishing hours are worth \(0\).

A common slip is to value a large change with the old shadow price. Raising \(b_1\) from \(100\) to \(130\) adds \(30\) hours, but \(z^*\) rises only from \(180\) to \(200\), not to \(210\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Use \(b_i-d_i\le b_i^{\mathrm{new}}\le b_i+u_i\) from the report.
  • A slack resource can often be reduced by its unused amount without affecting the current decision.
  • A change beyond the range cannot generally be valued by multiplying the full change by the old shadow price.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For the illustrated finishing right-hand side (RHS) \(b_1\), the valid range is \([80,120]\). The intersection with \(x_s+x_t=80\) moves from \((0,80)\) to \((40,40)\); at the upper endpoint the demand limit also binds. With the illustrated objective, the shadow price is 1 per added finishing hour throughout the range.

  • The metal RHS is 960, with allowable increase 240 and decrease 360; the range is 600 to 1,200.
  • Milk availability can fall from 200 to 180 in the ice-cream example without changing its plan or value.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A rounding heuristic solves an integer program's LP relaxation and converts fractional variable values to nearby integers. The rounded vector is only a candidate: all original constraints must be checked before accepting it as a feasible solution.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The rounding heuristic is the quickest way from an LP relaxation to an integer candidate: take the relaxed optimum and replace each fractional value by a nearby integer. The result comes with no guarantee: coupled constraints can make the nearest rounded decisions infeasible or substantially worse than an integer optimum.

The LP optimum \((3.5,1.25)\) has two natural roundings. Rounding \(x_1\) up gives \((4,1)\), which violates \(x_1\le3.5\) and \(2x_1+2x_2\le9.5\); rounding it down gives \((3,1)\), which is feasible with \(z=11\). Here \((3,1)\) is even the integer optimum, but that is luck rather than a property of rounding.

The four lattice points around the LP optimum are the rounding candidates. Some violate a constraint, and none needs to be optimal.

Rounding fails because the constraints couple the variables, while rounding treats each coordinate on its own. An equality shows this most clearly: if \(x_1+x_2=3\) and the relaxation gives \((1.5,1.5)\), rounding both values up or both down breaks the equality, and only a mixed choice such as \((2,1)\) works. This is why the method is a heuristic and why every candidate must be checked against all original constraints. Rounding is most reasonable for large quantities, where a change of less than one unit is small compared with the values.

A feasible rounded point is still useful. Its value is a bound from the feasible side, so together with the LP value it encloses the optimum, here \(11\le z^*\le13\) by the optimization bounds, and it can serve as a first incumbent in branch-and-bound.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Rounding up can violate resource upper bounds.
  • Rounding down can violate minimum requirements or equalities.
  • Even a feasible rounded solution need not be optimal.
  • The video's numerical rounding illustration has inconsistent written constraints and a plotted feasible region; its claimed optimum is not used here.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Rounding \((2.6,1.6)\) upward to \((3,2)\) violates \(4x_1+x_2\le12\) because the left-hand side is 14.
  • The nearby vector \((2,2)\) satisfies that capacity inequality, but its objective value alone does not prove optimality.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Sensitivity analysis examines how changes in model parameters affect an LP's optimal solution and optimal value. The course studies changes to objective coefficients and resource right-hand sides using final simplex tableaux and Excel sensitivity reports.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Sensitivity analysis asks how strongly the answer of an LP depends on its input numbers. Inputs may be estimates, and additional resources may be purchasable, so it matters whether the current decision remains suitable after an input changes and how the optimal value responds, without solving the problem again from scratch.

The figure shows a right-hand-side change in the Giapetto model. Raising the finishing hours from \(100\) to \(110\) shifts the finishing line outwards, and the optimum moves from \((20,60)\) to \((30,50)\), where the same two constraints, finishing and carpentry, still cross. The optimal value rises from \(180\) to \(190\): \(1\) per added hour, the shadow price.

The figure changes a right-hand side; here, vary one objective coefficient at a time instead and watch when the optimal corner changes.

The two kinds of change act differently on the picture. An objective coefficient changes only the slope of the objective line; the feasible region stays the same, so the optimal corner stays put until the slope passes that of an edge, as the objective coefficient range describes. A right-hand side moves a constraint line parallel to itself, so the region changes and the optimal point moves, while the same constraints stay binding over the RHS sensitivity range. For variables that are \(0\) at the optimum, the reduced cost gives the cost of forcing them into the plan.

A common slip is to combine several ranges from an Excel sensitivity report as if they still held together: each range assumes that all other data stay fixed.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The reported allowable ranges apply to one parameter change at a time.
  • Changing an objective coefficient can preserve the solution vector while changing profit.
  • Changing a right-hand side can change the solution vector even while the same basis and shadow prices remain valid.
  • Outside a valid range, reoptimization may be needed.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For the illustrated objective with \(c_2>0\), \((20,60)\) remains optimal when \(1\le c_1/c_2\le2\). Changing the finishing right-hand side (RHS) from 100 to 110 instead moves the optimum to \((30,50)\) while preserving the basis. Within the applicable one-parameter range, \(\Delta z=y_i^*\Delta b_i\).

  • A change in banana ice-cream profit from 0.95 to 0.92 leaves the given production plan optimal.
  • Losing three gallons of cream changes the ice-cream quantities and reduces optimal profit by 3.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A setup cost is a fixed charge incurred whenever an order is placed, regardless of the order quantity. In the EOQ model it is denoted by \(K\). With demand rate \(D\) and batch size \(y\), its average rate is

\[ \frac{K}{y/D}=\frac{KD}{y}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A setup cost is paid once per order, whatever its size, so what matters is how often orders are placed. Ordering \(y\) units at demand rate \(D\) gives one order every \(y/D\) time units, the ordering cycle, hence \(D/y\) orders per unit time and the setup cost rate \(KD/y\).

Both panels cover the same \(33\) days at \(D=2\) units per day. Batches of \(y=11\) last \(5.5\) days, so six setups \(K\) are paid; batches of \(y=22\) last \(11\) days and need only three, but each sawtooth starts twice as high, so the average stock doubles.

Each order costs \(K\) and there are \(D/y\) orders per unit time, so setups cost \(KD/y\). Raise \(K\) to make larger batches worthwhile.

The rate \(KD/y\) falls as \(y\) grows while the holding cost rate rises, and the economic order quantity balances the two. A common slip is to charge \(K\) for every unit ordered: a cost proportional to the quantity belongs to the purchasing cost.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The charge is per order, not per inventory unit.
  • A period with no order incurs no setup in the dynamic lot-size model.
  • Increasing \(K\) increases the classical optimal order size.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For the illustrated phone shop, \(K=605\) per order and \(D=2\) per day. The two panels cover the same \(33\) days:

Batch size Number of setups Setup cost per day \(y=11\) (left) \(6\) \(KD/y=1210/11=110\) \(y=22\) (right) \(3\) \(KD/y=1210/22=55\)

Doubling the batch size halves the setup frequency and its cost rate, but doubles average stock.

  • The snack bar pays 50 per order in addition to a per-kilogram purchase price.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The shadow price \(y_i^*\) of resource \(i\) is the rate of change of the optimal objective value when its right-hand side \(b_i\) increases slightly. Within the applicable sensitivity range,

\[ z^*(b_i+\Delta)=z^*(b_i)+y_i^*\Delta. \]

For the course's maximization LPs with \(\le\) resource constraints, it equals the coefficient of slack \(s_i\) in the final objective row.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A shadow price measures the marginal value of a resource: how much the optimal objective value rises per extra unit of it under the current model. Compared with the cost of acquiring the resource, buying more pays off only while the price per unit is below the shadow price.

The figure draws the optimal value \(V(b)\) as a curve in the resource level \(b\). The shadow price is the slope of the line that touches the curve at the current level \(b_0\), written \(\mu\) there and \(y_i^*\) on this page. For an LP the curve is made of straight pieces, so within the sensitivity range the line and the curve coincide and the change \(y_i^*\Delta\) in the Definition is exact rather than approximate.

The slope of \(z^*(b_1)\) on the right is the shadow price \(y_1^*\). It is valid only within the range where the basis stays the same.

For maximization LPs with \(\le\) resource constraints, a shadow price is never negative, since more of a resource can only enlarge the feasible region. A resource with unused slack has shadow price \(0\): extra units of something already left over cannot help. In the Giapetto model, finishing and carpentry hours both have shadow price \(1\), so one extra finishing hour raises the maximum profit from \(180\) to \(181\).

A common slip is to read the shadow price as the value of the whole stock of a resource or to apply it to large changes; it is a rate, valid only over the RHS sensitivity range.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The rate is valid only over its allowable right-hand-side range.
  • At a degenerate optimum the rates for increasing and for decreasing \(b_i\) can differ, so the tableau value is then only a one-sided shadow price.
  • An unused resource has zero marginal value in the illustrated resource-allocation setting.
  • A binding constraint does not by itself guarantee a positive shadow price.
  • The tableau sign interpretation must be adjusted if the model or objective convention changes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Malt and barley have shadow prices 1, while hops has shadow price 0 in the beer-and-ale example.
  • In the drinks example, an additional unit of sugar is worth 0.5 within the valid range.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A shortage cost penalizes unmet demand. In the EOQ model with planned shortages, customers wait for replenishment and the parameter \(p\) charges each outstanding unit per unit of waiting time. With maximum backlog \(y-s\), the average shortage cost rate is

\[ p\frac{(y-s)^2}{2y}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A shortage cost puts a price on making customers wait. A planned backlog lets the shop keep less stock, but every waiting unit is charged \(p\) per unit of time, so the model can trade holding cost against waiting customers.

In one cycle of length \(t_0=y/D\), the stock falls from \(s\) to zero at time \(s/D\) and then becomes negative: the shaded triangle below the axis is the backlog, with depth \(y-s\) and width \((y-s)/D\), so its area \((y-s)^2/(2D)\) adds up units times waiting time.

The cost rate \(p(y-s)^2/(2y)\) is \(p\) times this area divided by the cycle length. In the EOQ model with planned shortages the optimal backlog shrinks as \(p\) grows. This \(p\) is not the selling price \(p\) of the newsvendor model, which charges a lost margin once per unit of unmet demand, not per unit of waiting time.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The red triangle has area \((y-s)^2/(2D)\). Multiplying by \(p\) gives shortage cost \(p(y-s)^2/(2D)\) per cycle; dividing by \(t_0=y/D\) gives the cost rate \(p(y-s)^2/(2y)\).
  • Demand is backordered and later filled: the arriving batch first clears the backlog \(y-s\) and leaves \(s\) units on hand.
  • Use the same time unit for \(p\), \(h\), and \(D\).
  • In the newsvendor notation, \(p\) instead denotes selling price; symbols must be interpreted within their model.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The phone shop compensates waiting customers by 6 per phone per day.
  • The EOQ practice exercise permits planned shortages at 10 per unit per week.
