docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For nonnegative edge lengths, the course's shortest path algorithm sets \(d(s)=0\) and \(U=\{s\}\). Repeatedly choose an edge \(u-v\) with \(u\in U\), \(v\notin U\) minimizing

\[ d(u)+\ell_{uv}. \]

Set \(d(v)\) equal to this value, record predecessor \(u\), and add \(v\) to \(U\). Stop when the destination is added, or continue to obtain distances to all vertices.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Vertices enter the settled set \(U\) in order of their shortest distance from the origin \(s\). A label \(d(v)\) is final as soon as \(v\) enters \(U\), and the recorded predecessors recover the actual route after the distance has been computed.

The labels give the shortest distance from \(A\) to each vertex; the vertices are settled in the order \(A,C,B,D,E,F\), with \(d=0,2,3,8,10,13\). The label of \(B\) is \(3\), via \(C\), not \(4\) via the direct edge: once \(d(C)=2\) is known, the edge \(C-B\) offers \(2+1=3\). The red edges are the recorded predecessor edges, and following them back from \(F\) gives the route \(A-C-B-D-E-F\) of the shortest path problem.

The settled order is correct because lengths are nonnegative. Any other route to the newly chosen vertex \(v\) must leave \(U\) through some edge, so it already costs at least the smallest candidate value \(d(v)\), and further nonnegative edges cannot make it shorter. With a negative length this breaks down: if \(A-B\) has length 2, \(A-C\) length 3 and \(C-B\) length \(-2\), the algorithm settles \(B\) with \(d(B)=2\), yet the route \(A-C-B\) has length 1.

The Dijkstra-Prim method for minimum spanning trees grows its set \(U\) in the same way but compares only the edge length \(\ell_{uv}\), not \(d(u)+\ell_{uv}\). In the figure both rules happen to select the same edges, but in general a shortest-path tree and a minimum spanning tree differ.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Compare complete distances from the origin, not just individual edge lengths.
  • Ties can be broken arbitrarily when one shortest path is sufficient.
  • Backtrack from the destination through predecessors and reverse the sequence.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The figure settles vertices in the order \(A,C,B,D,E,F\). The recorded predecessor edges form a shortest-path tree rooted at \(A\).

  • The worked labels are \(d(B)=2\), \(d(A)=3\), \(d(D)=6\), \(d(C)=7\), \(d(E)=8\), \(d(T)=12\).
  • The predecessor chain \(T,E,D,A,B,S\) recovers the route of length 12.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A shortest path binary formulation assigns \(x_{ij}=1\) if a directed edge is selected. For the undirected course network, create both directed orientations of each edge. With origin \(s\), destination \(t\), and edge lengths \(\ell_{ij}\), use

\[ \begin{gathered} \min\sum_{(i,j)}\ell_{ij}x_{ij},\\ \sum_jx_{ij}-\sum_jx_{ji}=\begin{cases}1,&i=s,\\-1,&i=t,\\0,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}\\ x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}. \end{gathered} \]

Sums include only existing directed orientations.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The formulation writes the shortest path problem as a binary integer program. Each variable \(x_{ij}\) says whether the route uses edge \(i\to j\), and the balance equations force the selected edges to carry one unit from origin to destination; the objective then picks the cheapest such route.

The selected edges \(A\to C\to B\to D\to E\to F\) have \(x=1\) and the grey edges have \(x=0\). At the origin \(A\) one selected edge leaves and none enters (out \(-\) in \(=1\)), at the destination \(F\) one enters and none leaves (\(-1\)), and at an intermediate vertex such as \(D\) one enters and one leaves (\(0\)).

Each undirected edge becomes two directed edges because the route may use it in either direction. The balance equations do not by themselves rule out a closed loop of selected edges, since such a loop also has out \(-\) in \(=0\) at each of its vertices. With strictly positive lengths a loop only adds cost, so an optimal solution contains none; with zero-length edges an optimal solution may contain one, and removing it leaves a shortest path of the same cost.

The shortest path algorithm solves the same problem directly; the formulation is useful because, as an ordinary integer program, it accepts further constraints. The same balance equations reappear in the project longest path model, with the objective maximized, and at the intermediate vertices they are the flow-conservation constraints of the maximum flow LP.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• With strictly positive lengths as in the exercise, an optimum contains no unnecessary cycle.
  • If zero-cost edges are allowed, an optimal binary solution may contain removable zero-cost cycles.
  • The balances alone must not be claimed to prohibit every possible cycle.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For a feasible network with nonnegative edge lengths, the unit-flow LP relaxation admits an integral optimal solution. Removing any zero-cost cycles leaves a shortest path; arbitrary optimal flow representations need not themselves be cycle-free.

  • In the course exercise network (not the figure), the route \(S-B-A-D-E-T\) selects its five directed edges and has cost 12.
  • At \(A\) on that route, \(x_{BA}=x_{AD}=1\) balances one incoming and one outgoing edge.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The course's shortest path problem is defined on a connected undirected network with nonnegative edge lengths, a specified origin, and a specified destination. It asks for a path between those vertices whose sum of edge lengths is minimum.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The shortest path problem asks for the best route between two given vertices of a network. The same formulation can minimize distance, travel time, fuel use, or any other route measure that adds up along the edges.

The highlighted route \(A-C-B-D-E-F\) has length \(2+1+5+2+3=13\). It uses five edges, while \(A-B-D-F\) uses only three but has length \(4+5+6=15\): the shortest path is the one of smallest total length, not the one with the fewest edges, and it may make a detour through extra vertices.

Each part of the definition has a role. The origin and destination fix which paths are compared, and the objective adds the edge lengths along a path. A measure that is not a sum, such as the smallest capacity along a route, does not fit this form. The nonnegative lengths match distances and times, and they are what the shortest path algorithm relies on when it fixes the distances one vertex at a time.

Shortest paths are also building blocks: they supply the pair costs in the Chinese postman problem. A shortest path should not be confused with a minimum spanning tree, which minimizes the total length of a network connecting all vertices rather than the length of one route. Later in the course, the problem is also written as a binary program.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The nonnegative-length assumption supports the course label-setting algorithm.
  • Several different paths can have the same minimum length.
  • The shortest-path tree from one origin and a minimum spanning tree solve different objectives.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the figure, the red \(A-C-B-D-E-F\) path has length 13. The alternatives \(A-B-D-F\), \(A-C-E-F\) and \(A-C-D-F\) have lengths 15, 15 and 16 respectively.

  • The worked route S-B-A-D-E-T has length 12.
  • In the CPP network, the shortest A-D route is A-C-D, of length 5, rather than the direct edge of length 6.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The Silver-Meal heuristic chooses consecutive periods to cover with each order when the variable unit ordering cost is constant and identical across periods. For an order in period \(i\) covering through \(t\), define

\[ \begin{gathered} TC(i,t)=K_i+\sum_{j=i+1}^tD_j\sum_{k=i}^{j-1}h_k,\\ TCU(i,t)=\frac{TC(i,t)}{t-i+1}. \end{gathered} \]

Starting at the first uncovered period, extend coverage while average cost decreases, select the first local minimum, order \(\displaystyle \sum_{j=i}^{t^*}D_j\), and restart at \(i=t^*+1\). Stop at the horizon; on a flat tie, selecting the first local minimum is the convention used here.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The heuristic decides how many periods one order should cover by looking at the average cost per covered period. Covering more periods spreads the setup cost \(K_i\) over more periods but adds holding cost for the units carried forward; the rule stops extending the order when this average starts to rise.

For an order placed in period 1, covering only period 1 costs \(K\) alone, \(50\) per period. Covering periods 1 and 2 lowers the average to \(35\) and covering periods 1 to 3 lowers it to \(30\), but adding period 4 raises it to \(33\). The first local minimum is \(t^*=3\), so the first order covers \(D_1+D_2+D_3\) and the method restarts at period 4.

In \(TC(i,t)\), the demand \(D_j\) of a later period \(j\) is held from period \(i\) until period \(j\), which is why it is multiplied by \(h_i+\dots+h_{j-1}\). Dividing by \(t-i+1\) makes covers of different lengths comparable. Purchasing cost is left out because, with a common unit price, it is the same for every policy that meets all demand.

The rule is greedy: it fixes each order before looking at later periods and stops at the first rise, so this heuristic can miss a cheaper pattern. In the second listed Example it costs \(169\), against \(152\) for the optimum found by dynamic programming. Its orders always arrive at zero stock and cover whole periods, the form described by the zero-inventory ordering property.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Purchasing cost is omitted from the comparisons because the common unit price gives the same total for every complete demand-covering policy.
  • Add that constant purchasing cost when reporting a total that includes it.
  • At the start or end of the horizon, use only available neighbouring average-cost comparisons.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The figure’s first order covers \(D_1+D_2+D_3\); the rule then restarts at period 4. The displayed values are illustrative rather than the complete course exercise data.

  • The six-period video orders \((32,0,0,20,13,25)\), with setup and holding cost 122.
  • Week 6 practice 4 orders \((9,22,0,0)\) and costs 169 including purchases; the exact DP cost is 152.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The simplex method solves an LP by moving between basic feasible solutions through basis exchanges. In the course's maximization tableau convention, start with a feasible basis, test the objective row (optimality test), select an improving entering variable, apply the minimum-ratio test to select a leaving variable, pivot, and repeat until optimality or unboundedness is established.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The simplex method finds an optimal corner of a linear program without listing all corners. It starts at one corner and repeatedly moves to a neighbouring corner with a better objective value, stopping when no neighbour is better. Algebraically, a corner is a basic feasible solution and a move is a pivot of the tableau.

On the Giapetto model, \(\max(3x_s+2x_t)\), the path starts at the origin, where the slacks are basic and \(z=0\). Each arrow runs along an edge of the feasible region to an adjacent corner: \((40,0)\) with \(z=120\), \((40,20)\) with \(z=160\), and \((20,60)\) with \(z=180\), where the optimality test is passed. The corner \((0,80)\) is never visited.

Step through the iterations: starting from the slack basis at the origin, each pivot moves along an edge to a better corner until no improving variable is left.

The entering variable rule picks a nonbasic variable whose increase improves \(z\); the minimum-ratio test determines how far it can increase before a basic variable would turn negative, and that variable leaves. If no variable improves \(z\), the solution is optimal; if an improving variable can increase without limit, the LP is unbounded. Searching corners suffices because a finite optimum is always attained at some corner (corner-point optimality).

The method needs a feasible starting basis; when none is obvious, as with \(\ge\) or \(=\) constraints, the two-phase method finds one. A pivot never lowers \(z\) in a maximization, but with step length zero it changes the basis without moving the point, a case called degeneracy.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The elementary starting form uses equality constraints, nonnegative right-hand sides, and nonnegative variables.
  • A slack basis starts the method for \(\le\) constraints with nonnegative right-hand sides.
  • The two-phase method supplies a feasible basis when one is not immediately available.
  • Degenerate pivots can change the basis without moving the decision vector.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For maximization, a feasible pivot does not decrease the objective. Degenerate pivots may leave it unchanged; an anti-cycling rule is needed to guarantee termination rather than relying only on the finite number of bases.

  • The two-variable example visits \((0,0)\), \((5,0)\), and \((3,4)\), with values 0, 15, and 17.
  • The three-variable example ends at \((0,5,4)\) with value 33.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text: For a maximization LP with a feasible canonical tableau written as \(\displaystyle z+\sum_{j\in N}q_jx_j=z_0\), if \(q_j\ge0\) for every nonbasic variable, the current basic feasible solution is optimal. Here \(N\) is the nonbasic index set and every variable is nonnegative.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The optimality test tells the simplex method when to stop. It checks whether increasing any nonbasic variable from zero could raise \(z\); if none could, the current basic feasible solution is optimal, and the tableau itself is the proof.

In the final Giapetto tableau the nonbasic variables are the slacks \(s_1\) and \(s_2\), both with objective-row coefficient \(1\). Read as an equation, the row says \(z=180-s_1-s_2\). Since slacks are nonnegative, no feasible solution has \(z>180\), and the current solution with \(s_1=s_2=0\) reaches this bound.

Each condition has a role. The objective row comes from the original equations by row operations, so it holds for every feasible solution, not only the current one; this turns a sign check into a proof. Canonical form makes the row express \(z\) through the nonbasic variables only, so \(z_0\) is the current value and \(q_j\) is the effect of increasing \(x_j\) alone. Feasibility is needed because the row only gives the bound \(z\le z_0\), and this bound is the optimum only because a feasible point attains it.

With the objective on the left, \(z+q_jx_j=\ldots\) means that \(z\) falls by \(q_j\) per unit of \(x_j\). A negative \(q_j\) therefore signals possible improvement, which is why the entering variable rule looks for the most negative coefficient. A coefficient \(q_j=0\) means \(x_j\) could increase without changing \(z\), which often points to multiple optimal solutions.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The sign test depends on the course objective-row convention.
  • Feasibility and canonical form are required before applying the test.
  • A negative coefficient calls for further simplex analysis; degeneracy means it does not alone prove that a strictly better feasible vector exists.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the figure, \(z=180-s_1-s_2\) and \(s_1,s_2\ge0\) certify \(z\le180\). Setting both nonbasic slacks to zero gives \(x_s=20\), \(x_t=60\), \(s_3=20\), attaining 180. A zero nonbasic objective coefficient can indicate an alternative optimum, but a distinct solution requires a positive feasible movement; a degenerate zero-length pivot is insufficient.

  • \(z+(7/5)s_1+(1/5)s_2=17\) proves \(z\le17\).
  • \(z-(1/2)x_2+(3/2)s_1=15\) still has a negative coefficient to investigate.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A simplex pivot replaces the leaving basic variable with the entering variable. Divide the selected pivot row by the nonzero pivot element, then subtract appropriate multiples of that normalized row from every other row, including the objective row, so that the pivot column is a unit column.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A pivot is the algebra behind one step of the simplex method: one variable becomes basic, another becomes nonbasic, and the equations are rewritten so that the tableau is again in canonical form. The rewritten equations have exactly the same solutions as before; only their form changes.

In the Giapetto example \(x_s\) enters and \(s_3\) leaves, so the pivot element is the \(1\) in row \(s_3\), column \(x_s\). Afterwards the \(x_s\) column is a unit column with its \(1\) in the row now labelled \(x_s\). With \(x_t=s_3=0\) the new tableau gives \(x_s=40\), \(s_1=20\), \(s_2=40\) and \(z=120\): the solution has moved from the origin along an edge to the corner \((40,0)\). The \(-2\) under \(x_t\) shows that \(x_t\) enters next.

Each pivot exchanges one basic variable for another; geometrically it moves to an adjacent corner of the feasible region.

Each row operation divides an equation by a nonzero number or adds a multiple of one equation to another. Both steps can be undone, so no solution is gained or lost; the objective row is treated like any other equation. The pivot row must be the one chosen by the minimum-ratio test, because that keeps every right-hand side nonnegative. Pivoting on the row of \(s_1\) instead, with ratio \(50\), would set \(x_s=50\) and give \(s_3=40-50=-10\), an infeasible point.

The same elimination steps return in Linear Algebra as Gauss-Jordan elimination.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The pivot element is the intersection of the entering column and leaving row.
  • Update all coefficients and the right-hand side during each row operation.
  • Update the basic-variable label as well as the numerical entries.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the illustrated Giapetto pivot, the row operations are

\[ \begin{aligned}R_{s_3}&\leftarrow R_{s_3}/1,\\R_z&\leftarrow R_z+3R_{s_3},\\R_{s_1}&\leftarrow R_{s_1}-2R_{s_3},\\R_{s_2}&\leftarrow R_{s_2}-R_{s_3}.\end{aligned} \]

The new point is \((x_s,x_t)=(40,0)\) with \(z=120\); the next entering variable is \(x_t\).

  • Take the objective row \(z-3x_1-2x_2=0\) with the constraints of the augmented-form example. Then \(x_1\) enters and the minimum-ratio test picks the row of \(s_1\), so divide the pivot row \(2x_1+x_2+s_1=10\) by 2.
  • Add three times that normalized row to \(z-3x_1-2x_2=0\) to eliminate \(x_1\) from the objective row.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A simplex tableau records the variable coefficients, right-hand sides, and basic-variable labels of the current simplex equations. In the course convention, the first row writes the objective as

\[ z+\sum_jq_jx_j=z_0. \]

In canonical form (also called proper form), basic-variable columns form unit columns and have zero objective-row coefficients.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A simplex tableau is the bookkeeping of the simplex method: it writes the current equations as a table of coefficients, one row per equation, with the objective as an extra equation on top. The table makes the row operations of a pivot, and reading off the current solution, mechanical.

This is the starting tableau of the Giapetto model. The orange row is the objective \(z-3x_s-2x_t=0\), with all variable terms on the left. The highlighted entries show that the columns of \(s_1\), \(s_2\) and \(s_3\) are unit columns, each with its \(1\) in a different row, so these slacks are the basic variables named in the first column.

A canonical tableau is read in two directions. Down a column: a unit column with its \(1\) in some row marks the basic variable of that row, and the right-hand side of that row is its value, because the other variables in the row are nonbasic and zero. Along the objective row: the right-hand side is the current value \(z_0\), and the entry \(q_j\) under a nonbasic variable means that \(z\) changes by \(-q_j\) per unit increase of \(x_j\), which is what the optimality test reads.

The signs cause most slips. The row \(z-3x_s-2x_t=0\) means \(z=3x_s+2x_t\), so the negative entries mark profitable directions, not losses. Writing the objective as \(z=z_0-\sum_jq_jx_j\) shows the same information with opposite signs.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Set nonbasic variables to zero and read basic values from the solution column.
  • The objective-row right-hand side is the current objective value.
  • A negative nonbasic coefficient indicates an improving direction for maximization.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The illustrated system is \(2x_s+x_t+s_1=100\), \(x_s+x_t+s_2=80\), \(x_s+s_3=40\), with objective \(z-3x_s-2x_t=0\). The orange objective row places coefficients on the left, and the blue basic columns form an identity matrix. Setting \(x_s=x_t=0\) gives \(s_1=100\), \(s_2=80\), \(s_3=40\), \(z=0\).

  • \(z-3x_1-2x_2=0\) gives initial objective coefficients \(-3,-2\).
  • The final main-example row is \(z+(7/5)s_1+(1/5)s_2=17\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a constraint \(\displaystyle \sum_ja_{ij}x_j\le b_i\), a slack variable \(s_i\) converts it into

\[ \sum_ja_{ij}x_j+s_i=b_i,\qquad s_i\ge0. \]

Thus \(\displaystyle s_i=b_i-\sum_ja_{ij}x_j\) measures the unused allowance in the inequality.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A slack variable measures how much of an allowance is left unused: the gap between the limit \(b_i\) and the amount \(\sum_ja_{ij}x_j\) actually used. Adding it turns the inequality into an equation, the form the simplex method works with, without changing which decisions are allowed.

Each constraint line of the Giapetto model carries its slack equation. At the interior point \((20,20)\) all three slacks are positive: \(s_1=40\), \(s_2=40\), \(s_3=20\). At the optimal corner \((20,60)\) the first two constraints are binding, \(s_1=s_2=0\), while \(s_3=20\).

Drag the decision point: \(\displaystyle s_i=b_i-\sum_j a_{ij}x_j\) is the unused amount of resource \(i\). A slack of \(0\) means the constraint is binding.

The nonnegativity constraint \(s_i\ge0\) carries the direction of the original inequality: a negative slack would put the point outside the feasible region. With nonnegative right-hand sides the slacks give the first basic feasible solution, at the origin. A \(\ge\) constraint needs a surplus variable, subtracted instead.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A zero slack means the constraint is binding at that solution.
  • The introduced slack has zero coefficient in the original objective.
  • With nonnegative right-hand sides, slack variables can form an initial feasible basis.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(2x_1+x_2\le10\) becomes \(2x_1+x_2+s_1=10\).
  • At \((x_1,x_2)=(3,4)\) this slack equals zero.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A spanning tree of a connected undirected network contains every original vertex and a subset of its edges that forms a tree. If the network has \(n\) vertices, every spanning tree has \(n-1\) edges.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A spanning tree keeps all locations connected but removes enough edges to eliminate every cycle. It is a smallest set of edges that still connects everything: with \(n\) vertices it always has \(n-1\) edges, and different edge selections can produce different spanning trees.

Both highlighted edge sets reach all six vertices with \(5\) edges and contain no cycle, so both are spanning trees of the same network. Their total lengths differ a lot: \(2+1+5+2+3=13\) for the first and \(4+2+10+8+6=30\) for the second. The number of edges is fixed; the total length depends on which edges are chosen.

The word spanning refers to the vertices: every vertex of the original network must belong to the tree, while many edges are left out. The tree \(A-C-B\) alone is a tree but not a spanning tree. A spanning tree exists if and only if the network is connected: removing an edge that lies on a cycle never disconnects a network, so a connected network can be thinned out to a spanning tree, while a disconnected one lacks the edges to join its parts.

Comparing total lengths is the minimum spanning tree problem; the first tree in the figure, of length 13, is a minimum one.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Spanning refers to including all vertices, not all edges.
  • Adding another original edge to a spanning tree creates a cycle.
  • The minimum spanning tree problem compares the total lengths of spanning trees.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A network with seven vertices needs six edges in each spanning tree.
  • The Euclidean example selects \(1-7\), \(1-4\), \(4-3\), \(3-6\), \(6-2\), and \(6-5\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A surplus variable \(S_i\ge0\) transforms a lower-bound constraint into an equality:

\[ \sum_ja_{ij}x_j\ge b_i \Longleftrightarrow \sum_ja_{ij}x_j-S_i=b_i,\quad S_i\ge0. \]

It measures the excess of the left-hand side over the required minimum.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A surplus variable measures by how much a minimum requirement is exceeded: the amount \(\sum_ja_{ij}x_j\) achieved minus the required \(b_i\). Subtracting it turns a \(\ge\) constraint into an equation, just as an added slack does for a \(\le\) constraint.

The figure shows \(x_A+2x_B\ge6\) written as \(x_A+2x_B-S=6\). The point \((4,3)\) gives \(10\), so \(S=4\); the point \((2,2)\) lies on the line with \(S=0\); the point \((1,1)\) gives only \(3\) and would need \(S=-3\), which the sign restriction forbids, so it is infeasible.

The minus sign follows from what is measured, and the nonnegativity constraint \(S_i\ge0\) carries the original direction; writing \(+S_i\) by mistake gives the opposite requirement \(\sum_ja_{ij}x_j\le b_i\). Unlike a slack, a surplus cannot start the simplex method, since at the origin it would be \(-b_i<0\); such rows therefore also receive an artificial variable.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The course uses capital \(S_i\) for surplus and lower-case \(s_i\) for slack.
  • A surplus variable alone generally does not produce an initial feasible slack-style basis.
  • An artificial variable may be added for the first simplex phase.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(2x_1+x_2\ge4\) becomes \(2x_1+x_2-S_1=4\).
  • At \((x_1,x_2)=(3,0)\), this surplus is 2.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In task quota assignment, each task is assigned to exactly one agent and agent \(i\) must receive exactly \(q_i\) tasks. For binary assignment variables \(x_{ij}\) and times or costs \(c_{ij}\), the model is

\[ \min\sum_i\sum_jc_{ij}x_{ij},\qquad \sum_ix_{ij}=1,\qquad \sum_jx_{ij}=q_i,\qquad x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}. \]

The quotas sum to the number of tasks.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Task quota assignment divides tasks among agents when each agent has a fixed workload: every task is done by exactly one agent, and agent \(i\) does exactly \(q_i\) tasks. Among all divisions that respect these numbers, the objective picks one with the least total cost or time.

In the left diagram \(A_1\) has quota \(q_1=2\) and \(A_2\) has \(q_2=1\). The thick edges give \(A_1\) the tasks \(T_1,T_2\) and \(A_2\) the task \(T_3\): each task has one thick edge, and each agent as many as its quota. The right diagram replaces \(A_1\) by two copies \(A_1'\) and \(A_1''\) with the same costs; each copy takes exactly one task, so the quota model becomes a one-to-one pairing.

The model is a binary integer program with two families of equations. For each task \(j\), \(\sum_ix_{ij}=1\) says the task is done once; for each agent \(i\), \(\sum_jx_{ij}=q_i\) fixes the workload. Adding the task equations and adding the agent equations both count all assignments, so the model is feasible only when the quotas add up to the number of tasks.

The objective adds up all task times, so it minimizes total effort, not the time at which the last person finishes. With every quota equal to \(1\) the model becomes the one-to-one case that returns later as the assignment problem, and the copying trick reduces the quota version to it.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• In the later Hungarian-method treatment, duplicate each agent row \(q_i\) times to represent its available task slots.
  • Each task remains assigned exactly once.
  • Minimizing summed execution time is different from minimizing the latest completion time.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The transportation problem chooses shipments \(x_{ij}\ge0\) from plants \(i\) to distribution centres \(j\) to minimize total transport cost. With unit costs \(c_{ij}\), plant capacities \(s_i\), and required deliveries \(d_j\), a formulation is

\[ \begin{gathered} \min\sum_i\sum_j c_{ij}x_{ij},\\ \sum_jx_{ij}\le s_i\ \text{for every }i,\\ \sum_ix_{ij}=d_j\ \text{for every }j. \end{gathered} \]

The demand constraints can also be written as \(\sum_ix_{ij}\ge d_j\): when every unit cost \(c_{ij}\) is positive, an optimal plan never delivers more than required, so both versions have the same optimal solutions.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The transportation problem decides how much to send along each route from origins with limited supply to destinations with given demand, so that the total transport cost is as small as possible. Each decision variable \(x_{ij}\) is the amount on one route, and every unit on that route costs \(c_{ij}\).

The plants \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) have supplies \(30\) and \(20\), and the customers need \(15\), \(20\) and \(15\). The thick edges are the routes in use, labelled amount @ unit cost: \(P_1\) sends \(15\) to \(C_1\) and \(15\) to \(C_3\), and \(P_2\) sends \(20\) to \(C_2\), for a total cost of \(125\). Each customer receives exactly its demand, and the thin routes carry nothing.

Every variable appears in exactly two constraints, the supply constraint \(\sum_jx_{ij}\le s_i\) of its origin and the demand constraint of its destination. Supplies use \(\le\) because a plant need not use all of its capacity. Adding the demand constraints shows that a feasible plan needs total supply at least total demand, and since every route may be used, this is also enough. When capacity exceeds demand, as in the week 2 data in the Examples, some capacity stays unused.

The model is an ordinary linear program, solvable with the simplex method or Excel Solver. The same bookkeeping returns later in the assignment problem, where every supply and every demand equals \(1\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The decision variables are shipment quantities on routes.
  • Plant capacities are upper bounds rather than mandatory production amounts.
  • With positive unit costs, allowing deliveries above demand (\(\ge d_j\) instead of \(=d_j\)) cannot improve the optimum.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The diagram is a separate balanced illustration with total supply and demand both 50. Its unit costs are \(2,3,1\) from \(P_1\) to \(C_1,C_2,C_3\) and \(5,4,8\) from \(P_2\). Green-edge labels mean shipment quantity @ unit cost; their total is \(15\cdot2+15\cdot1+20\cdot4=125\). The plan is optimal: moving one unit of a customer's delivery from \(P_2\) to \(P_1\) saves \(5-2=3\) for \(C_1\), \(4-3=1\) for \(C_2\) and \(8-1=7\) for \(C_3\), so \(P_1\)'s 30 units go to \(C_3\) (15) and then \(C_1\) (15), and \(P_2\) supplies \(C_2\). Because total supply equals total demand, every plant here also ships its full supply. For a feasible transportation LP with integer supplies and demands, an integral optimal shipment plan exists.

  • Week 2 course data: three plants with capacities 5,000, 6,000 and 2,500 (13,500 in total) serve destinations whose demands total 12,000, so at least 1,500 units of capacity stay unused; with the course's unit costs the optimal cost is 35,000.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A tree is a connected undirected network containing no cycles. In the course, a tree can be formed by choosing a subset of the vertices and edges of a larger network.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A tree connects its vertices without any redundant edge: there is a route between every two vertices, and no cycle offers a second one. This makes it the basic structure for minimum-cost connection problems.

The five blue edges join all six vertices without a cycle, so they form a tree with \(6-1=5\) edges. The dashed edge \(A-B\) shows what one more edge does: \(A\) and \(B\) are already joined through \(C\), so it closes the cycle \(A-B-C-A\).

A tree sits exactly between two failures: removing any of its edges leaves it no longer connected, and adding any edge between two of its vertices creates a cycle. This is why the Kruskal method rejects every edge that would close a cycle when it builds a spanning tree.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A finite tree with \(n\) vertices has \(n-1\) edges.
  • There is exactly one path between any two distinct vertices of a tree.
  • A spanning tree additionally includes every vertex of the original network.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The edges A-B and B-C form a tree on three vertices.
  • A tree on 77 vertices has 76 edges, as reinforced by the final-week statements exercise.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The two-phase method initializes and solves an LP using artificial variables \(R_i\ge0\). Phase I maximizes

\[ r=-\sum_iR_i \]

subject to the augmented constraints. If its optimum is negative, the original LP is infeasible. If its optimum is zero, restore the original objective, remove artificial variables from the working model, put the objective row in canonical form for the resulting feasible basis, and apply simplex in Phase II.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The two-phase method splits a difficult start into two easier problems. Phase I only asks whether the constraints can be satisfied at all and, if so, finds a basic feasible solution; Phase II then runs the ordinary simplex method from there with the real objective.

The flowchart starts from an LP with \(\ge\) or \(=\) rows, where no slack basis is available. Phase I adds artificial variables \(R_i\) and maximizes \(r=-\sum_iR_i\). If \(r^*=0\), all \(R_i\) are zero, so the solution satisfies the original constraints and Phase II continues from it. If \(r^*<0\), every feasible solution of the Phase I problem has some \(R_i>0\), so the original LP is infeasible.

The Phase I objective is chosen so that its optimum answers the feasibility question: since every \(R_i\ge0\), always \(r\le0\), and \(r=0\) exactly when all artificial variables vanish. The artificial variables only make a start possible: each has a unit column and starts at the right-hand side of its row, and a solution with some \(R_i>0\) means nothing for the real problem.

Phase I ignores the real objective, so its solution need not be optimal: in the Examples it reaches \((0,25/3)\), where \(3x_1+2x_2=50/3\), and Phase II improves this to \(25\) at \((5,5)\). Before Phase II, the real objective row must be restored and put in canonical form for the new basis; only then can the optimality test be read from it.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Eliminate basic artificial variables from the initial Phase I objective row before pivoting.
  • The phase-I objective can never exceed zero.
  • A zero-valued artificial variable still in the basis needs basis cleanup before its column is removed; the supplied worked example avoids this case.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(x_1+x_2\le10\) and \(2x_1+3x_2=25\), Phase I finds \((0,25/3)\).
  • Phase II for objective \(3x_1+2x_2\) reaches \((5,5)\) and value 25.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A maximization LP has an unbounded objective if feasible solutions attain objective values greater than any prescribed finite bound. For minimization, feasible values can be arbitrarily negative. In a feasible maximization tableau, an improving entering column with no strictly positive constraint coefficient certifies unboundedness.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An unbounded linear program has feasible solutions but no optimal one: whatever objective value is reached, another feasible solution does better. In an applied model this is a signal to check whether a restriction, such as a limit on demand or capacity, is missing.

The shaded region, given by \(2x_1+x_2\ge40\) and \(x_1,x_2\ge0\), is open towards the upper right. The dashed objective lines \(x_1+x_2=40\), \(70\) and \(100\) all meet the region, and moving the line further out never leaves it, so \(z=x_1+x_2\) can be made as large as desired.

The region is open towards the upper right, and \(z=x_1+x_2\) keeps improving along it. Change the objective or add a constraint to get a finite optimum.

The simplex method detects this in the tableau. The minimum-ratio test normally limits how far an improving entering variable \(x_k\) can increase before a basic variable reaches zero. A coefficient \(a_{ik}\le0\) in the entering column means that the basic variable of row \(i\) does not decrease as \(x_k\) grows. If the whole column has no positive entry, \(x_k\) can grow without limit while all basic variables stay nonnegative, and \(z\) grows with it.

Unboundedness is a property of the objective on the region, not of the region alone. An unbounded feasible region can still have a finite optimum: minimizing \(x_1+x_2\) over the region in the figure gives the optimum \(20\) at \((20,0)\). An unbounded LP should also not be confused with an infeasible one, which has no feasible solution at all.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• An unbounded feasible region can still have a finite optimum for a particular objective.
  • The simplex certificate requires an improving objective coefficient and an unrestricted feasible increase together.
  • Do not confuse unboundedness with infeasibility.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The figure maximizes \(x_1+x_2\) subject to \(2x_1+x_2\ge40\) and \(\boldsymbol{x}\ge0\). Taking \(x_1=t\), \(x_2=0\) for \(t\ge20\) gives feasible values growing without bound. In an applied model, such a result can indicate a missing restriction rather than automatically proving a modelling error.

  • In week 2 practice 1(c), \(x_1=0\), \(x_2=t\ge0\) satisfies \(3x_1-2x_2\le8\) and gives \(z=t\).
  • In the week 3 example, \(x_1=x_2=t\) is feasible and yields \(2x_1+x_2=3t\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The underage cost in the newsvendor model is the foregone margin on one unit of demand that cannot be served:

\[ b=p-c>0, \]

where \(p\) is selling price and \(c\) is unit cost. Expected underage cost is \(b\mathbb{E}[(D-y)^+]\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The underage cost is what one unit of unmet demand costs: the sale is lost, and with it the margin \(p-c\) that the unit would have earned. It is the price of ordering one unit too few.

On the money scale for newspapers, the upper gap between the purchase cost \(c=3.50\) and the selling price \(p=5\) is \(b=1.50\); the lower gap, down to the salvage value \(s=1.50\), is the overage cost \(h=2\). Here \(b<h\): running short is the cheaper mistake, and the critical ratio \(\beta=1.5/3.5=3/7\) is below \(\tfrac{1}{2}\).

Each unit of unmet demand loses the margin \(b=p-c\). Raise \(p\) and watch \(y^*\) move up.

The loss is the margin, not the full price, because the purchase cost \(c\) of a unit never bought is saved; using \(p\) as the underage cost is a common slip. The positive part \((D-y)^+\) counts the units of unmet demand, and \(b\) is charged once for each of them, unlike the EOQ shortage cost, which is charged per unit of waiting time.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Only demand above the available quantity contributes to underage loss.
  • Increasing selling price increases underage cost when unit cost is fixed.
  • The course assumes no additional per-unit stockout penalty beyond the lost margin.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The illustrated newspaper data give overage cost \(h=2\) and underage cost \(b=1.5\), hence critical ratio \(\beta=1.5/3.5=3/7\). These are single-period per-unit losses, rather than EOQ cost rates.

  • Newspapers sold for 5 and purchased for 3.50 have \(b=1.50\).
  • Meals sold for 5.50 and costing 2.20 have \(b=3.30\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An undirected network is a network in which edges have no prescribed orientation. An edge joining vertices \(i\) and \(j\) may be traversed in either direction.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An undirected network represents connections whose availability is symmetric, such as two-way roads or cables. The edge between \(i\) and \(j\) is an unordered pair: it can be written \(\{i,j\}\), and \(\{i,j\}=\{j,i\}\).

The figure shows the network of this week's examples without lengths: six vertices and nine edges, each of which can be travelled both ways, as the red arrow indicates. Each edge still counts once, so the network has nine edges, not eighteen.

The course uses undirected networks for spanning trees, Euler tours, the Chinese postman problem and shortest paths. Several of these first require the network to be connected, meaning that a path joins every pair of vertices.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The pair \(i-j\) describes one undirected connection.
  • A path can traverse its edges in either direction.
  • Connectedness requires a path between every pair of vertices.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
An undirected edge may be written \(\{i,j\}\); roads, cables and other symmetric links provide examples. The degree counts incident edge ends.

  • A two-way road connects two towns.
  • A cable connecting two sites can be selected as part of a spanning tree.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The course's uniform demand model assumes \(D\) is uniformly distributed on a known interval \([a,u]\), with \(0\le a<u\). Its CDF inside the interval is \(F(y)=(y-a)/(u-a)\), with values 0 below \(a\) and 1 above \(u\). Thus the continuous newsvendor quantity is

\[ y^*=a+(u-a)\beta. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Uniform demand says that every demand level in \([a,u]\) is equally likely: only the range is known. The probability that demand is at most \(y\) then grows in proportion to \(y-a\), so the critical quantile is found by a linear interpolation between the two endpoints.

The density is flat at height \(1/40\) between \(a=80\) and \(u=120\), so the shaded rectangle from \(80\) to \(y\) has area \((y-80)/40\), which is \(F(y)\). Setting this equal to \(\beta=0.6\) gives width \(24\) and \(y^*=104\): the order lies \(60\%\) of the way from \(a\) to \(u\).

With demand uniform on \([50,150]\) the optimal stock interpolates linearly: \(y^*=a+(u-a)\beta\).

In \(y^*=a+(u-a)\beta\), the lower endpoint \(a\) is demand that is certain to occur, \(u-a\) is the uncertain part, and the critical ratio \(\beta\) is the fraction of the uncertain part worth covering. With \(\beta=\tfrac{1}{2}\) the order is the midpoint; with \(\beta\) near \(1\) it is close to \(u\), and with \(\beta\) near \(0\) close to \(a\). Since \(0<\beta<1\), the order always lies inside \([a,u]\), so the continuous newsvendor rule needs no boundary case here.

A common slip is to compute \(u\beta\) instead of \(a+(u-a)\beta\). For the meals this gives \(120\cdot0.6=72\), below the smallest possible demand; the two formulas agree only when \(a=0\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The distribution is used as an application of probability prerequisites; the course does not develop a general distribution theory.
  • For \(\beta=1/2\), the quantity is the midpoint.
  • The quantile lies within the demand interval.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For meal demand on \([80,120]\) and \(\beta=0.6\), order 104.
  • For that same interval, \(F(100)=0.5\) and \(F(104)=0.6\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
An unrestricted variable \(x_j\) can be replaced everywhere by the difference of two nonnegative variables:

\[ x_j=x_j^+-x_j^-,\qquad x_j^+,x_j^-\ge0. \]

If \(x_j\le0\) is required, use \(x_j=-x_j^-\) with \(x_j^-\ge0\) instead.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The simplex method works with nonnegative variables only, but some decisions can be negative, for example a change in stock level. The transformation writes such a free variable as the difference of two nonnegative parts, so the model again has only nonnegative variables while the original variable keeps its full range.

On the number line, \(x=2.5\) is written with \(x^+=2.5\) and \(x^-=0\), and \(x=-3\) with \(x^+=0\) and \(x^-=3\). One part carries the size of the number and the other is zero, so \(x=x^+-x^-\) holds with both parts nonnegative.

The substitution has to be made in the objective and in every constraint; afterwards \(x_j\) no longer appears, and its value is recovered as \(x_j^+-x_j^-\). The representation is not unique: \(x=2\) can also be written as \(5-3\). This does no harm: the objective and constraints depend on the two parts only through their difference, so all representations of the same \(x_j\) are equally feasible and give the same objective value. Both parts stay linear terms, so the model remains a linear program.

When the sign is known, splitting is unnecessary: for \(x_j\le0\) the single substitution \(x_j=-x_j^-\) is enough, and a variable that already satisfies a nonnegativity constraint needs no change. With the negative RHS transformation and the minimization-to-maximization transformation, it is one of the steps that bring a model into the form the simplex method starts from.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Apply the substitution to both the objective and every constraint.
  • The difference representation is not unique; it is not necessary to impose a nonlinear restriction preventing both parts from being positive.
  • The optimal original variable is the difference of the computed parts.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The two replacement columns are opposites: the column of \(x_j^-\) is \(-1\) times the column of \(x_j^+\). They cannot both be basic in the same basic solution, although a feasible solution that is not basic may have both parts positive.

  • \(x_2^+=0\) and \(x_2^-=10\) give \(x_2=-10\).
  • The other-model-forms exercise transforms its nonpositive \(x_1\) as \(-x_1^-\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The vehicle routing problem asks for a minimum-distance set of vehicle routes that start and end at a depot, visit every required location, and respect the vehicle's restrictions. In the course example, one depot serves eight required locations. The vehicle can travel at most 100 miles between refuelling stops, and refuelling is possible only at the depot.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The vehicle routing problem plans trips from a depot so that every required location is visited and the total distance is as small as possible. The range limit makes it harder than a single round trip: the locations may have to be split over several trips, and both the split and the order within each trip are decisions.

The figure shows the structure of a feasible plan: two round trips, each starting and ending at the depot and each within the 100-mile limit, together visit all eight locations. Every plan of this form is a feasible solution; the question is which one is shortest.

Serving every location by its own trip from the depot is feasible here, and joining successive visits while keeping each trip within range shortens the plan; such heuristic plans give upper bounds on the minimum distance. Dropping the range limit is a relaxation: its optimum is a lower bound, but its route may be too long for the vehicle. With the distances of the Examples, this traps the optimum between \(202\) and \(214\) miles (optimization bounds).

A common slip is to take the relaxed route as the answer: it is shorter only because it ignores refuelling, so it is a bound, not a plan that can be driven.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every required location must be visited and every trip must respect the fuel limit.
  • Joining successive visits can improve a plan if feasibility is retained.
  • Removing the fuel limit gives a lower bound, not automatically a feasible route for the original problem.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Separate visits from the depot produce the stated 232-mile heuristic plan.
  • The improved plan has length 214; the relaxed optimum has length 202.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The degree of a vertex in the undirected networks considered in the course is the number of edges incident to it. Parallel edges are counted separately. A vertex has even or odd degree according to the parity of that count.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The degree counts how many edge ends meet at a vertex, that is, how many ways there are to enter or leave it. Its parity, even or odd, decides whether a closed route can use every edge at that vertex exactly once.

Each vertex in the figure is labelled with its degree: \(A\) and \(F\) have degree 2, \(C\) and \(D\) degree 4, and \(B\) and \(E\) degree 3. The degrees add up to \(18\), twice the number of edges, because every edge has two ends.

Parallel edges are counted separately because each one is a separate way in or out: in the Königsberg network, two bridges between the same pair of land areas add \(2\) to the degree of each. Parity matters because of pairing: each time a closed route passes through a vertex it uses two of its edges, one to arrive and one to leave, so at a vertex of odd degree one edge is always left over.

Since the degrees sum to twice the number of edges, the number of odd-degree vertices is always even. This is what makes the Chinese postman construction work: the odd vertices can always be split into pairs, and a minimum-weight perfect matching chooses the cheapest pairing. In a connected network, whether an Euler tour exists is settled by degrees alone, see the Euler network characterization.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• At a vertex on an Euler tour, arrivals and departures pair the incident edges.
  • Duplicating a path reverses degree parity at its endpoints and preserves it at internal vertices.
  • Odd-degree vertices are the vertices matched in the Chinese postman construction.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the figure, the degrees sum to \(\displaystyle \sum_v\deg v=2|E|=18\), since each of the nine edges contributes two ends. Thus the number of odd-degree vertices is even; the illustrated odd vertices are \(B\) and \(E\).

  • In the course introduction network (not shown here), \(A\) has degree 3 and \(C\) has degree 5.
  • In the five-vertex Chinese postman example, A, B, D, and E are odd-degree vertices.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The Weibull demand distribution in the exercise has shape \(k>0\), scale \(\lambda>0\), and nonnegative support. For \(x\ge0\),

\[ \begin{gathered} F(x)=1-\mathrm{e}^{-(x/\lambda)^k},\\ f(x)=\frac{k}{\lambda}\left(\frac{x}{\lambda}\right)^{k-1}\mathrm{e}^{-(x/\lambda)^k}. \end{gathered} \]

For the newsvendor critical ratio \(0<\beta<1\), inversion gives

\[ y^*=\lambda[-\ln(1-\beta)]^{1/k}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
With Weibull demand, the newsvendor answer is still the demand level at which the CDF equals the critical ratio. Because this CDF has an explicit formula, the equation \(1-\mathrm{e}^{-(y/\lambda)^k}=\beta\) can be solved by hand with a logarithm, without a table: it gives \((y/\lambda)^k=-\ln(1-\beta)\), which is positive because \(0<1-\beta<1\).

For bananas, \(k=2\) and \(\lambda=50\) kilograms, and \(\beta=1.3/(1.3+0.2)=13/15\). The density starts at \(0\), peaks before \(\lambda\) and has a long right tail. The shaded area to the left of \(y^*\approx70.97\) is \(13/15\approx0.867\): here \(-\ln(2/15)\approx2.015\), its square root is about \(1.419\), and \(50\cdot1.419\approx70.97\).

The scale \(\lambda\) has the units of demand and stretches the distribution: doubling \(\lambda\) doubles every quantile, including \(y^*\). The shape \(k\) changes the form of the curve, but \(F(\lambda)=1-\mathrm{e}^{-1}\approx0.632\) for every \(k\), so \(\lambda\) is always the demand level that is not exceeded with probability about \(0.632\). As in the continuous newsvendor rule, the CDF is strictly increasing on \([0,\infty)\), so the order is unique.

A common slip is to write \(\ln\beta\) instead of \(\ln(1-\beta)\). For the bananas, \(50\sqrt{-\ln(13/15)}\approx18.9\); this is the level where \(F\) equals \(2/15\), not \(13/15\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Use the given shape and scale parametrization.
  • The CDF is zero below zero.
  • The scale parameter has the same units as demand.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Bananas have \(k=2\), \(\lambda=50\), \(b=1.3\), \(h=0.2\), so \(\beta=13/15\).
  • The optimum is \(50\sqrt{-\ln(2/15)}\approx70.97\) kilograms.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: To obtain a maximum zero-cost matching, create a source \(S\), one vertex for each matrix row, one for each column, and a sink \(T\). Add source-to-row edges, row-to-column edges exactly where the matrix entry is zero, and column-to-sink edges. Give every edge capacity 1 and compute an integral maximum flow.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
After the reductions of the Hungarian algorithm, the question is how many zeros can be chosen with no two in the same row or column. This construction answers it with a maximum flow: each unit of flow from \(S\) to \(T\) passes through one row and one column joined by a zero, so it selects one zero-cost pair.

Rows \(r_1\) and \(r_3\) have a zero only in column 2, so both need \(c_2\), which can pass on at most one unit to \(T\). The green flow uses \(r_1\to c_2\) and \(r_2\to c_1\) and has value \(2\). A flow of value \(3\) would need all three rows, so it does not exist. Only two independent zeros can be selected, fewer than the three needed for a complete assignment.

Capacity \(1\) on each edge \(S\to r_i\) lets every row send at most one unit, so no row is used twice; capacity \(1\) on each edge \(c_j\to T\) does the same for the columns. These are exactly the conditions of a bipartite matching. To read the flow as a set of pairs, every edge must carry \(0\) or \(1\); the augmenting path algorithm started from zero flow guarantees this for integer capacities.

When the flow value is smaller than the number of rows, the Hungarian algorithm needs a minimum zero cover. It uses as many lines as there are independent zeros, here \(2\), and tells which entries to adjust next.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The maximum flow value is the maximum number of simultaneous zero-cost assignments.
  • Read selected pairs from row-to-column edges carrying flow 1.
  • The augmenting path algorithm starting at zero preserves integrality for these integer capacities.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The figure’s zero pairs are \((1,2),(2,1),(2,2),(2,3),(3,2)\). Its integral maximum flow is 2, so only two independent zeros can be assigned, fewer than the three required for a complete assignment. The minimum cut also determines a minimum zero cover; further Hungarian adjustment is needed.

  • The five-job practice matrix admits four zero-cost pairs.
  • One such matching is jobs 1, 2, 3, 4 to machines 1, 4, 3, 2.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
In the course's uncapacitated dynamic lot-size special case, assume no shortages or lead time, nonincreasing marginal production and holding costs, and zero initial inventory. There exists an optimal policy with

\[ y_ix_i=0\qquad(i=1,\ldots,n). \]

Thus a positive order is placed only when starting stock is zero, and it covers the exact demand of one or more consecutive periods.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The property says that, under its cost assumptions, there is an optimal policy in which no order is placed while stock is still on hand. Each order then covers the full demand of a run of consecutive periods, so instead of every integer order size, only the sums \(D_i+\dots+D_t\) need to be considered.

The first order, \(61\), is placed at zero stock and lasts exactly through period 1. The order of \(116\) covers periods 2 and 3, with demands \(62\) and \(54\), so period 3 orders nothing (\(y_3=0\)) and starts with \(54\) units. The last order, \(67\), follows when stock is zero again. Every order sits at a red dot at zero stock, so \(y_ix_i=0\) in every period.

The assumptions matter: when ordering costs rise faster than the quantity, splitting a quantity over two orders can be cheaper, and then an optimal policy may carry stock into a period that orders. With ordering cost \(y_i^2\) and no setup cost, for instance, two orders of \(2\) cost \(8\), while one order of \(4\) costs \(16\).

Under the property, the lot-size recursion only needs order sizes that are sums of consecutive demands, and the Silver-Meal heuristic builds its orders the same way, without the guarantee of optimality. A common slip is to read the property as a statement about every optimal policy: it guarantees one optimal policy of this form, and tied optima may look different.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The statement guarantees an optimal policy of this form; it need not describe every tied optimum.
  • The special case is not justified for increasing marginal ordering costs, as in the general example.
  • The course handles positive initial stock by subtracting it from successive demands until exhausted.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In the four-period example, initial stock 15 reduces first-period demand from 76 to 61.
  • The optimal orders \((61,116,0,67)\) cover period 1, periods 2-3, and period 4, at total cost 860.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The 2-argument arctangent, denoted as \(\operatorname{atan2}\), is a function defined by

\[ \operatorname{atan2}(y,x)= \begin{cases} \displaystyle \,\arctan(y/x),& x>0,\\[2pt] \displaystyle \,\arctan(y/x)+\pi,& x<0 \text{ and }y\geq 0,\\[2pt] \displaystyle \,\arctan(y/x)-\pi,& x<0 \text{ and }y< 0,\\[2pt] \displaystyle \,\pi/2,& x=0 \text{ and }y> 0,\\[2pt] \displaystyle \,-\pi/2,& x=0 \text{ and }y< 0,\\[2pt] \displaystyle \,\text{undefined},&x=0 \text{ and }y= 0. \end{cases} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The function \(\operatorname{atan2}\) answers the question: in which direction does the point \((x,y)\) lie, seen from the origin? It returns the angle in \((-\pi,\pi]\) measured from the positive \(x\)-axis, which is the principal argument of the complex number \(x+\mathrm{i}y\).

The blue point \((x,y)\) lies in the second quadrant, with \(x<0\) and \(y>0\). The grey point \((-x,-y)\) has the same ratio \(y/x\), so the inverse tangent gives both points the same angle in \((-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2})\), namely the direction of the grey point. For the blue point the definition adds \(\pi\), half a turn, which gives the correct direction.

Drag the point \((x,y)\) into the left half-plane: \(\arctan(y/x)\) only sees the slope, while \(\operatorname{atan2}(y,x)\) adds or subtracts \(\pi\) to give the true direction.

Each case of the definition repairs one defect of \(\arctan(y/x)\). For \(x>0\) the point lies in the right half-plane, where the range \((-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2})\) of \(\arctan\) is already correct. For \(x<0\) the angle is shifted by \(\pi\), upwards when \(y\ge0\) and downwards when \(y<0\), so that the result stays in \((-\pi,\pi]\); points on the negative \(x\)-axis get \(\pi\), not \(-\pi\). For \(x=0\) the ratio \(y/x\) is not defined, and the angle \(\pm\tfrac{\pi}{2}\) is read off directly. At the origin there is no direction at all, so no value is assigned.

In practice, \(\operatorname{atan2}\) is how the polar form of \(x+\mathrm{i}y\) is found: \(r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\) and \(\varphi=\operatorname{atan2}(y,x)\). Python provides it as math.atan2(y, x). Note the order of the arguments: \(y\) comes first, as in the ratio \(y/x\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The range of \(\operatorname{atan2}(y, x)\) is \((-\pi, \pi]\), covering all four quadrants.
  • \(\operatorname{atan2}(y, x)\) is continuous at every point \((x, y) \neq (0, 0)\) that does not lie on the negative real axis. Crossing the negative real axis (\(x<0\), \(y=0\)), it jumps by \(2\pi\): just below the axis its values are close to \(-\pi\), on and just above the axis they are close to \(\pi\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\operatorname{atan2}(1, -1) = 3\pi/4\) (second quadrant).
  • \(\operatorname{atan2}(-1, -1) = -3\pi/4\) (third quadrant, within range \((-\pi, \pi]\)).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An Abelian group is a group whose operation is commutative.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An Abelian group is a group in which the order of the two elements never matters: \(a\star b=b\star a\) for all \(a,b\). Identity and inverses still come from the group axioms; commutativity is the only extra condition.

Many familiar groups are Abelian: \((\mathbb{Z},+)\), \((\mathbb{R},+)\) and the nonzero real numbers under multiplication. The symmetric group \(S_3\) is not: swapping the first two of three objects and then the last two gives a different permutation from the same swaps in the other order.

Abelian groups are often written additively, with \(+\) for the operation, \(0\) for the identity and \(-a\) for the inverse of \(a\). The name honours Niels Henrik Abel; the alias commutative group says the same. Later, the addition of a vector space makes it an Abelian group.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • Every Abelian group is a group, but not every group is Abelian.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \((\mathbb{R},+)\) is an Abelian group.
  • The permutations of \(\{1,2,3\}\) under composition form the symmetric group \(S_3\), which is not Abelian: the swaps \((1\,2)\) and \((2\,3)\) do not commute.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The adjugate matrix \(\operatorname{adj}(\boldsymbol{A})\) is the transpose of the cofactor matrix of a square matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The adjugate collects all cofactors \(C_{ij}\) of a square matrix in one matrix, transposed, so that multiplying it with \( oldsymbol{A}\) gives the determinant times the identity:

\[ oldsymbol{A}\operatorname{adj}( oldsymbol{A})=\det( oldsymbol{A}) oldsymbol{I}. \]

The same holds for \(\operatorname{adj}( oldsymbol{A}) oldsymbol{A}\), and dividing by \(\det( oldsymbol{A}) eq0\) gives the inverse formula in the Key Results.

The transpose is what makes this work. Entry \((i,j)\) of \( oldsymbol{A}\operatorname{adj}( oldsymbol{A})\) is \(\sum_k a_{ik}C_{jk}\). For \(i=j\) this is the cofactor expansion of \(\det( oldsymbol{A})\) along row \(i\). For \(i eq j\) it is the expansion of the determinant of the matrix obtained from \( oldsymbol{A}\) by replacing row \(j\) with row \(i\), which is \(0\) because that matrix has two equal rows. For a \(2 imes2\) matrix with \(ad-bc eq0\) this gives \( oldsymbol{A}^{-1}= rac{1}{ad-bc} egin{pmatrix}d&-b\-c&a\end{pmatrix}\).

The formula is mainly of theoretical use: it shows that every entry of \( oldsymbol{A}^{-1}\) is a ratio of determinants, and applied to \( oldsymbol{x}= oldsymbol{A}^{-1} oldsymbol{b}\) it gives Cramer's rule. For larger matrices, computing all \(n^2\) cofactors is far more work than Gauss-Jordan elimination on \(( oldsymbol{A}\mid oldsymbol{I})\). A common slip is to forget the transpose or the signs \((-1)^{i+j}\): for a \(2 imes2\) matrix the untransposed cofactor matrix is \( egin{pmatrix}d&-c\-b&a\end{pmatrix}\), not the adjugate.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is nonsingular, then \(\boldsymbol{A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{\det(\boldsymbol{A})}\operatorname{adj}(\boldsymbol{A})\).
  • The adjugate is defined for every square matrix, even if the inverse does not exist.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\boldsymbol{A}=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}\), \(\operatorname{adj}(\boldsymbol{A})=\begin{pmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{pmatrix}\).
  • If \(\boldsymbol{A}=\boldsymbol{I}_n\), then \(\operatorname{adj}(\boldsymbol{A})=\boldsymbol{I}_n\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Aleph null, denoted \(\aleph_0\), is the cardinality of the natural numbers:

\[ \aleph_0=\operatorname{card}(\mathbb{N}). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
\(\aleph_0\) is the name for the size of the set of natural numbers. A set has this size exactly when its elements can be listed as a sequence \(a_0,a_1,a_2,\ldots\) in which every element appears exactly once, that is, when it is countably infinite.

The figure pairs each natural number \(n\) with \(2n\). Every natural number gets exactly one partner and every even number is hit exactly once, so \(n\mapsto2n\) is a bijection from \(\mathbb{N}\) onto the even numbers \(2\mathbb{N}\). Hence \(2\mathbb{N}\) also has cardinality \(\aleph_0\), although it is a proper subset of \(\mathbb{N}\) that misses every odd number. For infinite sets, being a part does not mean being smaller.

The same listing idea explains the cardinal arithmetic \(\aleph_0+1=\aleph_0+\aleph_0=\aleph_0\cdot\aleph_0=\aleph_0\). Adding one element \(x\) to \(\mathbb{N}\) still gives a list \(x,0,1,2,\ldots\). Two disjoint countably infinite sets can be listed together by taking elements from each in turn, and \(\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}\) can be listed along the finite diagonals \(i+j=0,1,2,\ldots\). Ideas of this kind show that \(\mathbb{Z}\) and \(\mathbb{Q}\) have cardinality \(\aleph_0\) as well.

Not every infinite set has this size: by Cantor's diagonal argument the real numbers cannot be listed, and the cardinality of the continuum is strictly larger. So \(\aleph_0\) is one particular infinite size, not the same as the symbol \(\infty\) from calculus, which describes unbounded growth rather than the size of a set.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A set has cardinality \(\aleph_0\) exactly when it is countably infinite.
  • A bijection is the main tool for proving that two sets have the same cardinality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • \(\mathbb{N}\), \(\mathbb{Z}\), and \(\mathbb{Q}\) all have cardinality \(\aleph_0\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
If the characteristic polynomial factors as \(c(\lambda-\lambda_1)^{k_1}\cdots(\lambda-\lambda_l)^{k_l}\) with distinct \(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_l\), then \(k_i\) is the algebraic multiplicity of the eigenvalue \(\lambda_i\), written \(\operatorname{am}(\lambda_i)\).

The geometric multiplicity of an eigenvalue \(\lambda\) is the maximal number of linearly independent eigenvectors associated with \(\lambda\), written \(\operatorname{gm}(\lambda)\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Each eigenvalue comes with two counts. Algebraic multiplicity counts how often it appears as a root of the characteristic polynomial; geometric multiplicity counts how many independent eigendirections it actually has. The first is read from a formula, the second from the eigenvectors.

For \(\boldsymbol{A}=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0\\0&1&0\\0&0&3\end{pmatrix}\), \(p(\lambda)=\det(\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda\boldsymbol{I})=(1-\lambda)^2(3-\lambda)\). The plotted \((\lambda-1)^2(\lambda-3)/2\) differs from it by the constant factor \(-\tfrac{1}{2}\) and has the same roots. It touches the axis at the double root \(1\), where the factor \((\lambda-1)^2\) does not change sign, and crosses it at the simple root \(3\), so \(\operatorname{am}(1)=2\) and \(\operatorname{am}(3)=1\). Yet \(\boldsymbol{A}-\boldsymbol{I}\) has rank \(2\), so its kernel is one-dimensional and \(\operatorname{gm}(1)=1\).

The geometric multiplicity is the dimension of the eigenvectors for \(\lambda\) together with \(\boldsymbol{0}\): \(\operatorname{gm}(\lambda)=\dim\ker(\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda\boldsymbol{I})=n-\operatorname{rank}(\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda\boldsymbol{I})\), by the fundamental theorem of linear maps. It is at least \(1\), because every eigenvalue has an eigenvector, and never exceeds the algebraic multiplicity. Over \(\mathbb{C}\) the algebraic multiplicities add up to \(n\), by the fundamental theorem of algebra.

Comparing the two counts decides diagonalizability: every eigenvalue needs as many independent eigenvectors as its algebraic multiplicity. When \(\operatorname{gm}(\lambda)<\operatorname{am}(\lambda)\), the missing directions are supplied by generalized eigenvectors, and \(\operatorname{gm}(\lambda)\) is the number of Jordan blocks for \(\lambda\) in the Jordan normal form.

A repeated eigenvalue does not by itself prevent diagonalization. The identity \(\boldsymbol{I}_2\) has the double eigenvalue \(1\) with \(\operatorname{gm}(1)=\operatorname{am}(1)=2\), because every nonzero vector is an eigenvector; only \(\operatorname{gm}<\operatorname{am}\) is a problem.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For every eigenvalue of an \(n\times n\) matrix, \(1\leq \operatorname{gm}(\lambda)\leq \operatorname{am}(\lambda)\leq n\).
  • A matrix is diagonalizable if and only if \(\operatorname{gm}(\lambda)=\operatorname{am}(\lambda)\) for every eigenvalue, the eigenvalues being taken in \(\mathbb{C}\) so that the characteristic polynomial factors completely. A real matrix is diagonalizable over \(\mathbb{R}\) only if, in addition, all its eigenvalues are real.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \((\lambda-2)^3(\lambda+1)\), eigenvalue \(2\) has algebraic multiplicity \(3\).
  • For \(\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\), eigenvalue \(1\) has algebraic multiplicity \(2\) but geometric multiplicity \(1\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An algebraic structure consists of a set together with one or more operations on that set.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An algebraic structure packages a set with rules for combining its elements. The set gives the objects; each binary operation, a rule \(A\times A\to A\), says how two objects combine into a third.

The figure reads from top to bottom, each arrow adding one requirement: an associative operation gives a semigroup, an identity element a monoid, inverses a group, and commutativity an Abelian group. A ring adds a second operation that is associative and distributes over \(+\), and a field also asks this multiplication to be commutative, with an identity \(1\neq0\) and inverses for all nonzero elements. Down to the field, each structure is also every structure above it. The last box is different: a vector space is an Abelian group \((V,+)\) whose elements can be multiplied by scalars from a field.

One set can carry several structures. With \(\mathbb{N}=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\), \((\mathbb{N},+)\) is a monoid but not a group, since \(1\) has no additive inverse in \(\mathbb{N}\). \((\mathbb{Z},+)\) is an Abelian group, and \((\mathbb{Z},+,\cdot)\) is a ring but not a field, since \(2\) has no multiplicative inverse in \(\mathbb{Z}\). \(\mathbb{Q}\), \(\mathbb{R}\) and \(\mathbb{C}\) with ordinary addition and multiplication are fields.

This is why the abstract names are worth learning: a fact proved once for all groups, such as the uniqueness of inverses, holds at once for real numbers under addition, nonzero real numbers under multiplication and permutations under composition.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The properties of the operations determine what kind of algebraic structure we have.
  • Associativity, identity elements, and inverse elements determine which algebraic structure is present.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • \((\mathbb{Z},+)\) and \((\mathbb{R},+,\cdot)\) are algebraic structures.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A field \(\mathbb{F}\) is algebraically closed if every nonconstant polynomial in \(\mathbb{F}[x]\) (that is, with coefficients in \(\mathbb{F}\)) has a root in \(\mathbb{F}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A field is algebraically closed when polynomial equations never force us to leave it: every equation \(p(x)=0\) with \(p\) a nonconstant polynomial with coefficients in \(\mathbb{F}\) already has a solution in \(\mathbb{F}\).

The definition asks for one root, but this gives all of them. If \(p(\lambda)=0\), then polynomial long division by \(x-\lambda\) leaves remainder \(0\), so \(p(x)=(x-\lambda)q(x)\) with \(\deg q=\deg p-1\). If \(q\) is nonconstant, it has a root as well, and repeating the step splits \(p\) completely. So over an algebraically closed field, a polynomial of degree \(n\ge1\) is a constant times a product of \(n\) linear factors \(x-\lambda_1,\ldots,x-\lambda_n\), where some \(\lambda_i\) may coincide.

The word closed does not refer to the field operations; every field is closed under addition and multiplication. It refers to solving equations: in \(\mathbb{R}\) the equation \(x^2+1=0\) has no solution, and in \(\mathbb{Q}\) the equation \(x^2-2=0\) has none either. Enlarging \(\mathbb{R}\) by \(\mathrm{i}\) is enough to repair this for every polynomial at once, which is the content of the fundamental theorem of algebra: the complex numbers form an algebraically closed field.

This is one reason why complex numbers appear in linear algebra. Later, the eigenvalues of a square matrix turn out to be roots of a polynomial, so over \(\mathbb{C}\) they always exist, even when the matrix has only real entries.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The complex numbers \(\mathbb{C}\) are algebraically closed (see the fundamental theorem of algebra).
  • The real numbers \(\mathbb{R}\) are not algebraically closed.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(x^2+1\) has no root in \(\mathbb{R}\), but has roots \(\mathrm{i}\) and \(-\mathrm{i}\) in \(\mathbb{C}\).
  • \(\mathbb{Q}\) is not algebraically closed: \(x^2-2\) has no rational root.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: For nonzero vectors \(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the angle \(\theta\) between them satisfies \(\boldsymbol{x}\cdot \boldsymbol{y}=\|\boldsymbol{x}\|\|\boldsymbol{y}\|\cos\theta\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The angle formula turns the algebraic inner product into geometry. Dividing \(\boldsymbol{x}\cdot \boldsymbol{y}\) by the Euclidean norms \(\|\boldsymbol{x}\|\) and \(\|\boldsymbol{y}\|\) removes the lengths and leaves only the information about direction, \(\cos\theta\).

For the vectors drawn, \(\cos\theta=\dfrac{\boldsymbol{x}\cdot \boldsymbol{y}}{\|\boldsymbol{x}\|\,\|\boldsymbol{y}\|}=\dfrac{4+3}{\sqrt{17}\sqrt{10}}\approx0.54\), so \(\theta\approx57.5^\circ\). Two nonzero vectors are perpendicular when their inner product is zero and parallel when their angle is \(0\) or \(180^\circ\).

Drag \(\boldsymbol{x}\) and \(\boldsymbol{y}\) and read \(\theta\) from \(\cos\theta=\dfrac{\boldsymbol{x}\cdot \boldsymbol{y}}{\|\boldsymbol{x}\|\|\boldsymbol{y}\|}\). The sign of \(\boldsymbol{x}\cdot \boldsymbol{y}\) tells acute from obtuse.

In \(\mathbb{R}^2\) and \(\mathbb{R}^3\) the formula follows from the law of cosines in the triangle with sides \(\boldsymbol{x}\), \(\boldsymbol{y}\) and \(\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{y}\). In \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with \(n>3\) there is no picture to measure in, and the formula is used to define \(\theta\in[0,\pi]\) as the inverse cosine of the quotient. This definition makes sense because the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality guarantees that the quotient lies between \(-1\) and \(1\).

Because of the normalization, changing the length of one vector does not change the angle: replacing \(\boldsymbol{x}\) by \(2\boldsymbol{x}\) doubles both \(\boldsymbol{x}\cdot \boldsymbol{y}\) and \(\|\boldsymbol{x}\|\). A negative multiple is different: replacing \(\boldsymbol{x}\) by \(-\boldsymbol{x}\) changes the sign of \(\cos\theta\) and turns \(\theta\) into \(\pi-\theta\). Since the cosine is positive on \([0,\pi/2)\) and negative on \((\pi/2,\pi]\), the sign of \(\boldsymbol{x}\cdot \boldsymbol{y}\) alone tells acute from obtuse.

The formula needs nonzero vectors. For \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{0}\) the quotient is undefined and no angle is assigned, although \(\boldsymbol{0}\cdot \boldsymbol{y}=0\) makes the zero vector orthogonal to every vector.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(\boldsymbol{x}\cdot \boldsymbol{y}>0\), the angle is acute.
  • If \(\boldsymbol{x}\cdot \boldsymbol{y}=0\), the angle is right and the vectors are orthogonal.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\) have angle \(\pi/2\).
  • \((1,0)\) and \((1,1)\) have a positive inner product, so their angle is acute.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The argument of a nonzero complex number \(z\), denoted \(\arg z\), is the angle between the positive real axis and the line joining the origin and \(z\). It is a multivalued function due to the periodicity of the angle in the polar coordinate system. The principal argument, denoted as \(\operatorname{Arg} z\), is the unique value of the argument that lies in the interval \((-\pi, \pi].\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The argument records the direction of a nonzero complex number \(z\), as the modulus records its length; together they are the polar coordinates of \(z\). Because a full turn brings a point back to itself, if \(\varphi\) is one argument of \(z\), then \(\varphi+2\pi k\) is another for every integer \(k\).

Both points lie on the same circle around the origin, so only their directions differ. For \(z_1\) the angle \(\varphi_1\) is measured anticlockwise from the positive real axis. For \(z_2\) in the lower half-plane the principal argument is measured clockwise and is negative, \(\varphi_2=-130^\circ\). The anticlockwise angle \(\varphi_2+2\pi\), that is \(230^\circ\), is also an argument of \(z_2\), but not the principal one, since it lies outside \((-\pi,\pi]\).

Drag \(z\) and change \(k\): \(\operatorname{Arg} z\) is the angle in \((-\pi,\pi]\), and adding whole turns \(2\pi k\) gives the other values of \(\arg z\).

The principal argument picks one value, so that \(\operatorname{Arg}\) is a genuine function on the nonzero complex numbers. The interval \((-\pi,\pi]\) is half-open so that every direction gets exactly one value: the negative real axis gets \(\pi\), not \(-\pi\). The price is a jump there: points just above the negative real axis have \(\operatorname{Arg}\) close to \(\pi\), points just below it close to \(-\pi\).

A common slip is to compute \(\operatorname{Arg}(a+\mathrm{i}b)\) as \(\arctan(b/a)\). This is correct only for \(a>0\): for \(-1-\mathrm{i}\) it gives \(\pi/4\), the direction of \(1+\mathrm{i}\), while \(\operatorname{Arg}(-1-\mathrm{i})=-3\pi/4\). The 2-argument arctangent handles all quadrants. The many values of \(\arg z\) are also why the complex logarithm has many values.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Each nonzero complex number has a unique principal argument. The argument of \(0\) is undefined.
  • For \((a,b)\ne(0,0)\), the principal argument of \(a+\mathrm{i} b\) is \(\operatorname{atan2}(b,a)\), where \(\operatorname{atan2}\) is the 2-argument arctangent.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\operatorname{Arg} \mathrm{i}=\pi /2\).
  • \(\operatorname{Arg}(1-\mathrm{i})=-\pi/4\).
