docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A binary operation \(\star\) on \(A\) is associative if

\[ (a\star b)\star c=a\star(b\star c) \]

for all \(a,b,c\in A\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Associativity says that in a chain \(a\star b\star c\) it does not matter which pair is combined first. Repeating this rule shows that every way of placing brackets in \(a_1\star a_2\star\cdots\star a_n\) gives the same element, so expressions such as \(a+b+c+d\) or \(a\star a\star a\) have a meaning without brackets.

Associativity is about grouping, not about order: the elements keep their places, unlike in commutativity. An operation can be associative without being commutative. Composition of functions is associative, but for \(f(x)=x+1\) and \(g(x)=2x\) one has \((g\circ f)(x)=2x+2\) and \((f\circ g)(x)=2x+1\). Subtraction is not associative: \((5-3)-2=0\), but \(5-(3-2)=4\).

Associativity is the first requirement in the chain semigroup, monoid, group. It returns later with the product of matrices, which is associative but not commutative.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Associativity is required in semigroups, monoids, and groups.
  • Associativity, identity elements, and inverse elements determine which algebraic structure is present.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Addition and multiplication of real numbers are associative. Subtraction is not associative.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The augmented matrix of a linear system \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{b}\) is the matrix formed by adjoining the right-hand side vector \(\boldsymbol{b}\) to the coefficient matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}\), often written \((\boldsymbol{A}\mid \boldsymbol{b})\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An augmented matrix is a linear system with the names of the unknowns, the plus signs and the equals signs removed: each row is one equation, each column to the left of the bar belongs to one unknown, and the last column holds the right-hand sides. It contains all numerical information needed to solve the system.

The figure turns the system \(2x_1+x_2-x_3=8\), \(-3x_1-x_2+2x_3=-11\), \(-2x_1+x_2+2x_3=-3\) into a \(3\times4\) matrix. The shaded \(3\times3\) block is the coefficient matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}\), copied equation by equation, and the column after the bar is \(\boldsymbol{b}=(8,-11,-3)\).

Writing the system this way makes row operations convenient: an operation on equations becomes an operation on rows, and because \(\boldsymbol{b}\) is part of every row, the right-hand sides change together with the coefficients. After reduction to row echelon form the solution set can be read off; a row \((0\;\cdots\;0\mid c)\) with \(c\neq0\) stands for the equation \(0=c\), so the system has no solution. This test is later restated in terms of rank.

A missing unknown must be entered as \(0\) in its column, so that every column stays with one unknown. The name should also not be confused with the augmented form of a linear program in OR Modelling, which adds slack variables to the model rather than a column to a matrix.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Elementary row operations on the augmented matrix correspond to elementary operations on the equations.
  • Gauss-Jordan elimination is performed on augmented matrices.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(2x+y=3\), \(x-y=1\), the augmented matrix is \(\begin{pmatrix}2&1&3\\1&-1&1\end{pmatrix}\).
  • The vertical bar in \((\boldsymbol{A}\mid \boldsymbol{b})\) is visual; the augmented matrix is still a matrix.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A basis of a vector space \(V\) is a collection of vectors that is linearly independent and spans \(V\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A basis of \(V\) is a list of vectors that is just right: it spans \(V\), so every vector can be built from it, and it is linearly independent, so none of its vectors can be built from the others. Together the two conditions mean that every vector of \(V\) is a linear combination of the basis vectors in exactly one way. The coefficients of that combination are the coordinates of the vector.

The two basis vectors \(\boldsymbol{b}_1\) and \(\boldsymbol{b}_2\) draw a slanted grid in the plane. The vector \(\boldsymbol{w}\) is reached by going twice along \(\boldsymbol{b}_1\) and once along \(\boldsymbol{b}_2\), so \(\boldsymbol{w}=2\boldsymbol{b}_1+\boldsymbol{b}_2\) and its coordinates in \(\mathcal{B}=(\boldsymbol{b}_1,\boldsymbol{b}_2)\) are \([\boldsymbol{w}]_{\mathcal{B}}=(2,1)\). Because \((\boldsymbol{b}_1,\boldsymbol{b}_2)\) is a basis, every vector of \(\mathbb{R}^2\) has such a pair of coordinates, and no other pair gives the same vector.

Drag \(\boldsymbol{w}\): it is reached in exactly one way as \(c_1\boldsymbol{b}_1+c_2\boldsymbol{b}_2\). Drag \(\boldsymbol{b}_1\) and \(\boldsymbol{b}_2\) to make a new grid, and line them up to see the basis fail.

Each condition prevents a different failure. Without spanning, some vectors have no coordinates at all: \((1,0)\) alone spans only the horizontal axis of \(\mathbb{R}^2\). Without independence, coordinates are not unique: with the list \(((1,0),(0,1),(1,1))\), the vector \((1,1)\) is both \(1\cdot(1,0)+1\cdot(0,1)\) and \(1\cdot(1,1)\). So a basis is a spanning list that cannot be shortened, and an independent list that cannot be extended.

A vector space has many bases: the standard basis \(((1,0),(0,1))\) of \(\mathbb{R}^2\) is convenient, but the grid in the figure works just as well. In a finite-dimensional space all bases have the same length, the dimension.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every vector in \(V\) can be written uniquely as a linear combination of basis vectors.
  • Any two bases of a finite-dimensional vector space have the same length.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • The standard basis of \(\mathbb{R}^2\) is \(((1,0),(0,1))\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A binary operation \(\star\) on a set \(A\) is a function

\[ \star\colon A\times A\to A. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A binary operation combines two elements of a set into an element of the same set. Writing it as a function \(\star\colon A\times A\to A\) makes this precise.

The domain \(A\times A\) is the Cartesian product: the input is an ordered pair \((a,b)\), and \(a\star b\) is short for \(\star(a,b)\). Because the pair is ordered, \(a\star b\) and \(b\star a\) can differ. Because \(\star\) is a function, every pair has exactly one output. The codomain \(A\) expresses closure: the result never leaves the set.

Whether a rule is a binary operation therefore depends on the set. Subtraction is a binary operation on \(\mathbb{Z}\) but not on \(\mathbb{N}\), and division is one on the nonzero rational numbers but not on \(\mathbb{Q}\), where \(a/0\) has no value.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Closure is built into the definition: \(a\star b\in A\) for all \(a,b\in A\).
  • Associativity, identity elements, and inverse elements determine which algebraic structure is present.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Addition on \(\mathbb{R}\) is a binary operation. Subtraction on \(\mathbb{N}\) is not a binary operation on \(\mathbb{N}\) because the result may be negative.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A block matrix is a matrix viewed as being partitioned into smaller matrices called blocks or submatrices.

A block diagonal matrix is a square block matrix of the form

\[ \begin{pmatrix} \boldsymbol{A}_1&\boldsymbol{0}&\cdots&\boldsymbol{0}\\ \boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{A}_2&\cdots&\boldsymbol{0}\\ \vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\ \boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}&\cdots&\boldsymbol{A}_k \end{pmatrix}, \]

where \(\boldsymbol{A}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{A}_k\) are square matrices.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Block notation treats a large matrix as a small matrix whose entries are themselves matrices. As long as the sizes fit, calculations can then be done with the blocks as if they were numbers, which keeps the structure of the matrix visible.

Cutting the \(3\times5\) matrix after row \(2\) and after column \(2\) gives four blocks: \(\boldsymbol{A}_{11}\) is \(2\times2\), \(\boldsymbol{A}_{12}\) is \(2\times3\), \(\boldsymbol{A}_{21}\) is \(1\times2\) and \(\boldsymbol{A}_{22}\) is \(1\times3\). Blocks in the same block row have the same number of rows, and blocks in the same block column have the same number of columns.

When the column partition of \(\boldsymbol{A}\) matches the row partition of \(\boldsymbol{B}\), block multiplication uses the same row-by-column rule as matrix multiplication; for example, the top-left block of \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{B}\) is \(\boldsymbol{A}_{11}\boldsymbol{B}_{11}+\boldsymbol{A}_{12}\boldsymbol{B}_{21}\). The order of the factors must be kept, since the blocks are matrices and \(\boldsymbol{A}_{11}\boldsymbol{B}_{11}\) differs in general from \(\boldsymbol{B}_{11}\boldsymbol{A}_{11}\).

Block diagonal matrices describe parts that do not interact. If \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is block diagonal with blocks \(\boldsymbol{A}_1,\boldsymbol{A}_2\) and \(\boldsymbol{x}\) is split accordingly into \(\boldsymbol{x}_1,\boldsymbol{x}_2\), then \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\) consists of \(\boldsymbol{A}_1\boldsymbol{x}_1\) and \(\boldsymbol{A}_2\boldsymbol{x}_2\), so the system \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{b}\) splits into two smaller systems. Powers, and inverses when every block is invertible, are likewise computed block by block, and the determinant is the product of the blocks' determinants. A diagonal matrix is the special case with \(1\times1\) blocks.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: Cantor's diagonal argument shows that there is no bijection between \(\mathbb{N}\) and the interval \([0,1]\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
If a list claimed to contain every binary expansion in \([0,1]\), one can construct a new sequence by flipping the diagonal entries. This new sequence differs from the \(i\)th listed sequence in its \(i\)th digit, so it cannot be on the list. Strictly, a few numbers have two binary expansions (\(0.0111\ldots=0.1000\ldots\)), which is why each 0-1 sequence corresponds to a unique number, but not quite conversely. Every number has at most two expansions, so a list of all numbers in \([0,1]\) would still give a list of all 0-1 sequences, and the conclusion stands.

The decimal illustration highlights diagonal digits \(3,7,1,0,3\), which can be changed to \(4,8,2,1,4\), giving a new number with prefix \(0.48214\ldots\). At every subsequent position, choose either \(1\) or \(2\) so that the chosen digit differs from the corresponding diagonal digit. The resulting expansion is neither eventually all \(0\) nor eventually all \(9\), so it avoids the ambiguity of two decimal representations. It therefore represents a number different from every \(r_i\) in the proposed list.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The interval \([0,1]\) is uncountable.
  • The real numbers have strictly larger cardinality than the natural numbers.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • From a list \(s_1,s_2,s_3,\ldots\), define \(s^*\) by making its \(i\)th digit different from the \(i\)th digit of \(s_i\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Cantor's theorem states that for every set \(A\),

\[ \operatorname{card}(A)<\operatorname{card}(2^A), \]

where \(2^A\) is the power set of \(A\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Cantor's theorem says that a set always has more subsets than elements: no function from \(A\) to its power set \(2^A\), also written \(\mathcal{P}(A)\), can reach every subset. This holds for infinite sets too.

For \(A=\{a,b\}\) the power set has \(2^2=4\) elements. The map \(x\mapsto\{x\}\) is injective, which shows \(\operatorname{card}(A)\le\operatorname{card}(2^A)\), but it hits only \(\{a\}\) and \(\{b\}\), never \(\varnothing\) or \(\{a,b\}\). For a finite set with \(n\) elements the theorem is just \(n<2^n\); its content is that no other map does better, even for infinite sets.

The reason is a diagonal construction. Given any \(f\colon A\to2^A\), form \(D=\{x\in A\colon x\notin f(x)\}\). If \(D=f(d)\) for some \(d\in A\), then \(d\in D\) exactly when \(d\notin f(d)=D\), which is impossible. So \(D\) is missed and no \(f\) is surjective, in particular no \(f\) is a bijection. In the figure every \(x\) lies in \(\{x\}\), so \(D=\varnothing\), one of the two missed subsets.

Applied to \(\mathbb{N}\), the theorem gives the uncountable set \(2^{\mathbb{N}}\), whose cardinality is the cardinality of the continuum. Applied again and again it gives \(\aleph_0<2^{\aleph_0}<2^{2^{\aleph_0}}<\cdots\), so there is no largest infinite size. The argument has the same shape as Cantor's diagonal argument for the real numbers.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• There is an infinite staircase of larger and larger infinities: \(A,2^A,2^{2^A},\ldots\).
  • A bijection is the main tool for proving that two sets have the same cardinality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • For \(A=\mathbb{N}\), the power set \(2^{\mathbb{N}}\) has larger cardinality than \(\mathbb{N}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The cardinality of the continuum, often denoted \(\mathfrak{c}\), is the cardinality of the real numbers:

\[ \mathfrak{c}=\operatorname{card}(\mathbb{R}). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
\(\mathfrak{c}\) is the size of the real line. It is an infinite size strictly larger than \(\aleph_0\), the size of \(\mathbb{N}\) (see aleph null): by Cantor's diagonal argument the real numbers cannot be listed as a sequence, so \(\mathbb{R}\) is uncountable.

On the open interval \((-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2})\) the graph of \(\tan\) is continuous and increasing, with a vertical asymptote at each end, so every real height is reached exactly once. Hence \(\tan\colon(-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2})\to\mathbb{R}\) is a bijection, and this short interval has as many points as the whole real line: length plays no role in cardinality. In the same way \(x\mapsto a+(b-a)x\) maps \((0,1)\) bijectively onto any open interval \((a,b)\) with \(a<b\).

Less obviously, \(\mathfrak{c}=2^{\aleph_0}\), the cardinality of the power set of \(\mathbb{N}\). Roughly, a number in \([0,1]\) has a binary expansion \(0.b_1b_2b_3\ldots\), which corresponds to the set \(\{n\colon b_n=1\}\) of positions with digit \(1\). Even \(\mathbb{R}^n\) has no more points than \(\mathbb{R}\).

Between any two real numbers lies a rational number, yet \(\mathbb{Q}\) only has cardinality \(\aleph_0\). So the extra points are the irrational numbers: if they formed a countable set, \(\mathbb{R}\) would be countable too. Whether some set has a size strictly between \(\aleph_0\) and \(\mathfrak{c}\) is the continuum hypothesis.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\operatorname{card}(2^{\mathbb{N}})=2^{\aleph_0}=\operatorname{card}(\mathbb{R})=\mathfrak{c}\).
  • A bijection is the main tool for proving that two sets have the same cardinality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • The interval \([0,1]\) has cardinality \(\mathfrak{c}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Two sets \(A\) and \(B\) have the same cardinality, written

\[ \operatorname{card}(A)=\operatorname{card}(B), \]

if there exists a bijection \(f\colon A\to B\text{.}\)

The empty set has cardinality \(0\text{.}\) A set \(A\) has finite cardinality \(n\) if it has the same cardinality as \(\{1,2,\ldots,n\}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Cardinality measures the size of a set through one-to-one correspondence. For finite sets this reproduces ordinary counting; for infinite sets it provides a precise way to compare sizes.

Each element of \(A\) is joined to exactly one element of \(B\), and every element of \(B\) is reached once, so the lines form a bijection and \(\operatorname{card}(A)=\operatorname{card}(B)=3\). No counting is needed to see that the sets are equally large: the pairing itself shows it, just as a room has as many chairs as people when everyone sits on a chair and no chair is empty.

Because the definition compares sets instead of counting them, it also works for infinite sets, with some surprising answers. \(\mathbb{N}\) and the even natural numbers have the same cardinality, although one is a proper subset of the other, because \(n\mapsto2n\) pairs them. To show that two sets do not have the same cardinality, one failed attempt is not enough: one must show that no bijection exists at all, as Cantor's diagonal argument does for \(\mathbb{N}\) and \(\mathbb{R}\).

The infinite sizes have their own names: aleph null, \(\aleph_0\), for the countably infinite sets such as \(\mathbb{N}\), \(\mathbb{Z}\) and \(\mathbb{Q}\), and the cardinality of the continuum, \(\mathfrak{c}\), for \(\mathbb{R}\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Having equal cardinality is an equivalence relation on sets.
  • A finite set with \(n\) distinct elements has cardinality \(n\text{.}\)
  • Infinite sets can have the same cardinality even when one is a proper subset of the other.
  • Cantor's theorem shows that every set has strictly smaller cardinality than its power set; here \(\operatorname{card}A<\operatorname{card}B\) means that there is an injection \(A\to B\) but no bijection.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\{1,2,3\}\) and \(\{a,b,c\}\) have the same cardinality.
  • \(\mathbb{N}\) and the even natural numbers have the same cardinality because \(n\mapsto 2n\) is a bijection.
  • \(\mathbb{N}\), \(\mathbb{Z}\), and \(\mathbb{Q}\) are countably infinite, whereas \(\mathbb{R}\) is uncountable.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The Cartesian product of two sets \(A\) and \(B\) is the set of all ordered pairs whose first component comes from \(A\) and whose second component comes from \(B\):

\[ A \times B = \{(a,b) \colon a \in A,\ b \in B\}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The Cartesian product \(A\times B\) collects every possible pairing of an element of \(A\) with an element of \(B\), recorded as an ordered pair with the element of \(A\) first.

With \(A=\{a,b,c\}\) along the top and \(B=\{1,2\}\) along the side, each cell of the grid holds one pair: one column for each element of \(A\) and one row for each element of \(B\), so \(A\times B\) has \(3\cdot2=6\) elements.

Order matters in two ways. Within a pair, \((a,1)\) and \((1,a)\) are different objects. Between the factors, \(A\times B\) and \(B\times A\) are different sets unless \(A=B\) or one of the sets is empty; here \((a,1)\in A\times B\) but \((a,1)\notin B\times A\).

The Cartesian coordinate system is the case \(\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}=\mathbb{R}^2\), where every point of the plane is a pair \((x,y)\) of real numbers, and the sample space of two dice is \(\{1,\ldots,6\}\times\{1,\ldots,6\}\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(A\) and \(B\) are finite, then \(\operatorname{card}(A\times B)=\operatorname{card}(A)\operatorname{card}(B)\).
  • Cartesian products are used to define binary operations, since a binary operation on \(A\) is a function from \(A\times A\) to \(A\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(A=\{1,2\}\) and \(B=\{x,y\}\), then \(A\times B=\{(1,x),(1,y),(2,x),(2,y)\}\).
  • The set \(\mathbb{R}^2\) can be understood as \(\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}\), the set of all ordered pairs of real numbers.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: For vectors \(\boldsymbol{x}\) and \(\boldsymbol{y}\) in an inner product space, the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality states \(|\langle\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}\rangle|\leq\|\boldsymbol{x}\|\|\boldsymbol{y}\|\); in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with the dot product this reads \(|\boldsymbol{x}\cdot \boldsymbol{y}|\leq\|\boldsymbol{x}\|\|\boldsymbol{y}\|\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The inner product of two vectors can never exceed the product of their lengths in absolute value. Equivalently, for nonzero vectors the quotient \(\dfrac{\boldsymbol{x}\cdot \boldsymbol{y}}{\|\boldsymbol{x}\|\,\|\boldsymbol{y}\|}\) always lies between \(-1\) and \(1\).

The figure drops a perpendicular from the tip of \(\boldsymbol{y}\) onto the line of the nonzero vector \(\boldsymbol{x}\). The green segment from the origin to its foot has length \(\dfrac{|\boldsymbol{x}\cdot \boldsymbol{y}|}{\|\boldsymbol{x}\|}\), and as a side of a right triangle with hypotenuse \(\boldsymbol{y}\) it ends inside the arc of radius \(\|\boldsymbol{y}\|\). Multiplying \(\dfrac{|\boldsymbol{x}\cdot \boldsymbol{y}|}{\|\boldsymbol{x}\|}\le\|\boldsymbol{y}\|\) by \(\|\boldsymbol{x}\|\) gives the inequality; equality holds when \(\boldsymbol{y}\) already lies on the line of \(\boldsymbol{x}\), so that the segment reaches the arc.

Drag \(\boldsymbol{x}\) and \(\boldsymbol{y}\): \(|\boldsymbol{x}\cdot \boldsymbol{y}|\) never exceeds \(\|\boldsymbol{x}\|\|\boldsymbol{y}\|\), because the shadow of \(\boldsymbol{x}\) on the line of \(\boldsymbol{y}\) is never longer than \(\boldsymbol{x}\). Equality holds exactly when the vectors lie on one line.

The inequality holds for all vectors, including \(\boldsymbol{0}\), where both sides are \(0\). Equality holds if and only if one vector is a multiple of the other, that is, when both lie on one line through the origin. The absolute value matters: \(\boldsymbol{x}\cdot(-\boldsymbol{x})=-\|\boldsymbol{x}\|^2\) is very negative for long \(\boldsymbol{x}\); only the size of the inner product is bounded.

The inequality is what makes the angle between vectors well defined in \(\mathbb{R}^n\), since a cosine must lie in \([-1,1]\), and it is the key step in proving the triangle inequality \(\|\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{y}\|\le\|\boldsymbol{x}\|+\|\boldsymbol{y}\|\). Its proof uses only the defining properties of an inner product, so it holds for every inner product with \(\|\boldsymbol{x}\|=\sqrt{\langle\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}\rangle}\). It returns later in a version for random variables.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Cauchy-Schwarz justifies the formula for the angle between vectors.
  • It can be used to prove the triangle inequality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For orthogonal vectors, the left side is \(0\).
  • For \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{y}\), equality holds.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a square matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}\), the characteristic polynomial is \(\det(\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda \boldsymbol{I})\), viewed as a polynomial in \(\lambda\). The equation \(\det(\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda \boldsymbol{I})=0\) is called the characteristic equation.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The characteristic polynomial turns the search for eigenvalues into a polynomial equation. A number \(\lambda\) is an eigenvalue when \(\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda\boldsymbol{I}\) sends some nonzero vector to \(\boldsymbol{0}\), and the determinant detects exactly this: it is zero when the matrix is singular.

For \(\boldsymbol{A}=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}\), \(\det(\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda\boldsymbol{I})=(2-\lambda)^2-1=\lambda^2-4\lambda+3\). The parabola crosses the horizontal axis at \(\lambda=1\) and \(\lambda=3\), and these roots are the eigenvalues of \(\boldsymbol{A}\), with eigenvectors \((1,-1)\) and \((1,1)\).

Change the entries of \(\boldsymbol{A}\): the roots of \(\det(\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda \boldsymbol{I})\) on the right are the eigenvalues, and their eigenvector lines are dashed on the left.

The identity matrix is needed because \(\lambda\) is a number and \(\boldsymbol{A}\) a matrix: \(\lambda\boldsymbol{I}\) subtracts \(\lambda\) from the diagonal entries only. Expanding the determinant gives a polynomial of degree \(n\); for a \(2\times2\) matrix it is \(\lambda^2-\operatorname{tr}(\boldsymbol{A})\lambda+\det\boldsymbol{A}\), with the trace as a coefficient. Some texts use \(\det(\lambda\boldsymbol{I}-\boldsymbol{A})\) instead, which differs by the factor \((-1)^n\) and has the same roots.

For a real matrix the polynomial has real coefficients, so the results on polynomials apply. By the fundamental theorem of algebra it has \(n\) complex roots counted with multiplicity, and nonreal roots come in conjugate pairs. The quarter-turn rotation \(\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\) has characteristic polynomial \(\lambda^2+1\) and eigenvalues \(\pm\mathrm{i}\), but no real eigenvalue. The multiplicity of a root is the algebraic multiplicity of that eigenvalue.

A common slip is to subtract \(\lambda\) from every entry, or to compute \(\det\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda\). Only the diagonal is shifted, and the determinant is taken after the shift.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The eigenvalues of \(\boldsymbol{A}\) are exactly the roots of the characteristic polynomial, equivalently the solutions of the characteristic equation.
  • For an \(n\times n\) matrix, the characteristic polynomial has degree \(n\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\boldsymbol{A}=\begin{pmatrix}a&0\\0&b\end{pmatrix}\), the characteristic polynomial is \((a-\lambda)(b-\lambda)\).
  • For \(\boldsymbol{I}_n\), the characteristic polynomial is \((1-\lambda)^n\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
For a square matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}\), let \(\boldsymbol{A}_{ij}\) be the matrix obtained by deleting row \(i\) and column \(j\). The number \(\det(\boldsymbol{A}_{ij})\) is the minor of entry \((i,j)\), and

\[ C_{ij}=(-1)^{i+j}\det(\boldsymbol{A}_{ij}) \]

is the corresponding cofactor.

The determinant can be computed by expanding along any row or column:

\[ \det(\boldsymbol{A})=\sum_k a_{ik}C_{ik} \]

for expansion along row \(i\), or

\[ \det(\boldsymbol{A})=\sum_k a_{kj}C_{kj} \]

for expansion along column \(j\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Cofactor expansion reduces the determinant of an \(n\times n\) matrix to \(n\) determinants of size \((n-1)\times(n-1)\), each multiplied by an entry of the chosen row or column and by a sign. Repeating the step ends at \(1\times1\) determinants; the determinant itself is defined this way, along the first row.

Expanding a \(3\times3\) matrix along row \(1\) gives \(\det \boldsymbol{A}=a_{11}C_{11}+a_{12}C_{12}+a_{13}C_{13}\). Deleting row \(1\) and column \(1\) (shaded) leaves the white \(2\times2\) block \(\boldsymbol{A}_{11}\), whose determinant is the minor of \(a_{11}\). The sign \((-1)^{i+j}\) of each cofactor is read off the checkerboard on the right: \(+\) on the main diagonal, alternating along every row and column.

Since every row and every column gives the same value, the choice is purely practical: an entry \(a_{ik}=0\) removes the term \(a_{ik}C_{ik}\) without computing its minor. A full expansion of an \(n\times n\) determinant produces \(n!\) products, so for larger matrices one first creates zeros, for example by adding a multiple of one row to another, which does not change the determinant, and then expands along the sparse row or column.

For \(3\times3\) matrices the expansion gives the same six products as Sarrus' rule, and the cofactors are the entries of the adjugate matrix, which gives a formula for the inverse.

A common slip is to drop the sign: \(C_{12}=-\det(\boldsymbol{A}_{12})\). The sign depends only on the position \((i,j)\), not on the sign of the entry \(a_{ij}\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Cofactor expansion can be performed along any row or column.
  • Choosing a row or column with many zeros makes the computation shorter.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For a \(3\times3\) matrix, expanding along the first row gives three \(2\times2\) determinants.
  • For a diagonal matrix, expanding along sparse rows quickly gives the product of diagonal entries.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A binary operation \(\star\) on \(A\) is commutative if

\[ a\star b=b\star a \]

for all \(a,b\in A\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Commutativity says that the order of the two inputs does not matter: swapping \(a\) and \(b\) gives the same result.

Commutativity is about order, associativity about grouping, and neither implies the other. Subtraction has neither property. Composition of functions is associative but not commutative: for \(f(x)=x+1\) and \(g(x)=2x\), \((g\circ f)(x)=2x+2\) while \((f\circ g)(x)=2x+1\). The average \(a\star b=\tfrac{1}{2}(a+b)\) is commutative but not associative: \((0\star0)\star4=2\), while \(0\star(0\star4)=1\).

Commutativity is the condition that turns a group into an Abelian group, and both operations of a field are commutative. Without it, calculations need more care: the equations \(a\star x=b\) and \(x\star a=b\) may have different solutions. This returns later with the product of matrices, which is generally not commutative.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • An Abelian group is a group whose operation is commutative.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Addition of real numbers is commutative. Matrix multiplication is generally not commutative.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Given a complex number \(z=a+\mathrm{i}b\) where \(a,b\in\mathbb{R}\), the absolute value or modulus of \(z\), denoted \(|z|\), is the real number \(|z| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}.\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The modulus \(|z|\) measures the length of \(z\): its distance from \(0\) in the complex plane. The square root in the definition is the nonnegative root, so \(|z|\ge0\), with \(|z|=0\) only for \(z=0\).

The arrow from \(0\) to \(z=a+b\mathrm{i}\) is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with a horizontal side of length \(a\) and a vertical side of length \(b\), so by Pythagoras its length is \(\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\). In another quadrant the sides have lengths \(|a|\) and \(|b|\), which gives the same formula, since \(|a|^2=a^2\).

Drag \(z\): \(|z|\) is its distance from \(0\), the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs \(|a|\) and \(|b|\).

For a real number \(z=a\) the formula gives \(\sqrt{a^2}=|a|\), so the modulus extends the absolute value of real numbers, and the same notation is used. As for real numbers, \(|z-w|\) is the distance between \(z\) and \(w\).

A common slip is to compute \(|z|^2\) as \(z^2\). The correct identity uses the conjugate, \(|z|^2=z\overline{z}\): for \(z=\mathrm{i}\) one has \(z^2=-1\) but \(|z|^2=1\).

The modulus is multiplicative, \(|zw|=|z|\,|w|\), so multiplying by \(w\) stretches lengths by the factor \(|w|\). Together with the argument, the modulus gives the polar form of \(z\). The same Pythagorean length later measures vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^n\), as the Euclidean norm.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• While it is true that \(|z| = \sqrt{z^2}\) when \(z\) is a real number, it does not hold whenever \(z\) is a non-real complex number, i.e., \(|z| \neq \sqrt{z^2}\) for \(z\in (\mathbb{C}\setminus \mathbb{R})\).
  • The modulus is multiplicative, \(|zw|=|z|\,|w|\), and \(|z|^2=z\bar z\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(|1+\mathrm{i}|=\sqrt{2}\).
  • \(|z|=1\) represents a unit circle in the complex plane.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Given two complex numbers \(z=a+\mathrm{i}b\) and \(w=c+\mathrm{i}d\) where \(a,b,c,d\in\mathbb{R}\), the sum of complex numbers \(z\) and \(w\) is defined as \(z+w=(a+c)+\mathrm{i}(b+d).\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Complex numbers are added part by part: real parts with real parts and imaginary parts with imaginary parts. Nothing beyond the addition of real numbers is needed.

Draw \(z\) and \(w\) as arrows from \(0\). A copy of the arrow \(w\) placed at the tip of \(z\) ends at \(z+w\), since real parts and imaginary parts add separately. The two arrows and their copies form the dashed parallelogram, and \(z+w\) is its diagonal from \(0\).

Drag \(z\) and \(w\): real parts add, imaginary parts add, just like vector addition.

Because the addition works coordinate by coordinate, it is commutative and associative, \(0\) is the identity and the negation \(-z\) is the inverse of \(z\), so \((\mathbb{C},+)\) is an Abelian group. Adding a fixed \(w\) shifts every point of the plane by the same arrow; multiplication instead rotates and stretches. The parallelogram rule returns later for the addition of vectors.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The additive identity for complex numbers is \(0_\mathbb{C} = 0 + 0\mathrm{i},\) which is the real number \(0.\)
  • Complex addition has commutativity: \(z_1 + z_2 = z_2 + z_1.\)
  • Complex addition has associativity: \((z_1 + z_2) + z_3 = z_1 + (z_2 + z_3)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \((2+\mathrm{i}) + (3+4\mathrm{i}) = 5+5\mathrm{i}\).
  • \((1-\mathrm{i})+(-1+\mathrm{i}) = 0_{\mathbb{C}}=0\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: If \(P\) is a polynomial in one variable with real coefficients, and \(a + \mathrm{i} b\) is a root of \(P\) with \(a\) and \(b\) being real numbers, then its complex conjugate \(a - \mathrm{i} b\) is also a root of \(P\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
For a polynomial with real coefficients, the non-real roots come in pairs \(a\pm\mathrm{i}b\): whenever \(a+\mathrm{i}b\) is a root, so is its mirror image in the real axis.

The four plotted points are the roots of \(p(z)=z^4+2z^3+2z^2+10z+25\), a polynomial with real coefficients. They form the two conjugate pairs \(1\pm2\mathrm{i}\) and \(-2\pm\mathrm{i}\), and each dashed segment joins a root to its mirror image. Each pair gives a real quadratic factor: \(p(z)=(z^2-2z+5)(z^2+4z+5)\).

With real coefficients the roots are mirrored in the real axis. Give \(a_0\) an imaginary part and the symmetry breaks: the theorem needs real coefficients.

The proof uses that conjugation respects sums and products, \(\overline{z+w}=\overline{z}+\overline{w}\) and \(\overline{zw}=\overline{z}\,\overline{w}\), and leaves real numbers unchanged. If \(P(z)=c_nz^n+\cdots+c_1z+c_0\) with real \(c_k\) and \(P(\lambda)=0\), then \(P(\overline{\lambda})=\overline{P(\lambda)}=\overline{0}=0\). The step \(\overline{c_k}=c_k\) is where real coefficients are needed; without them the pairing can fail, as the polynomial \(x-\mathrm{i}\) in the Examples shows.

For a non-real root \(\lambda\), the product \((z-\lambda)(z-\overline{\lambda})=z^2-2\operatorname{Re}(\lambda)z+|\lambda|^2\) is a real quadratic factor of \(P\), so non-real roots can be split off in pairs. Together with the fundamental theorem of algebra, this shows that every real polynomial is a product of real linear and real quadratic factors, and that a real polynomial of odd degree has a real root, as the Key Results state. The theorem returns later for eigenvalues: the non-real eigenvalues of a real matrix also come in conjugate pairs.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If the degree of a real polynomial is odd, it must have at least one real root.
  • Any real \(n\times n\) square matrix with \(n\) odd (so its characteristic polynomial has odd degree \(n\)) has at least one real eigenvalue.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(x^2-2x+5\) has real coefficients and the root \(1+2\mathrm{i}\), so \(1-2\mathrm{i}\) is also a root.
  • \(x-\mathrm{i}\) has the root \(\mathrm{i}\) but not \(-\mathrm{i}\): its coefficients are not all real, so the theorem does not apply.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Given a complex number \(z=a+\mathrm{i}b\) where \(a,b\in\mathbb{R}\), the conjugate of the complex number \(z\) is defined as \(\overline{z}=a-\mathrm{i}b.\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Conjugation keeps the real part of \(z\) and changes the sign of its imaginary part. Geometrically, it reflects \(z\) in the real axis.

The point \(\overline{z}=a-b\mathrm{i}\) lies straight below \(z=a+b\mathrm{i}\), at the same distance from the real axis. A reflection keeps lengths, so \(|\overline{z}|=|z|\) for the modulus, and reverses angles, so the argument \(\varphi\) becomes \(-\varphi\).

Drag \(z\): \(\overline z\) is its mirror image in the real axis, with the angle \(-\varphi\).

Conjugation is useful because it produces real numbers: \(z+\overline{z}=2a\) and \(z\overline{z}=a^2+b^2=|z|^2\). The second identity is behind division: multiplying numerator and denominator by \(\overline{w}\) makes the denominator the real number \(|w|^2\). Also \(z\) is real if and only if \(\overline{z}=z\), and conjugating twice gives \(z\) back. Because conjugation respects sums and products (Key Results), it sends a root of a polynomial with real coefficients to another root: the complex conjugate root theorem.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• We have \(\overline{z + w} = \overline{z} + \overline{w},\) \(\overline{-z} = -\overline{z},\) and \(\overline{zw} = \overline{z} \cdot \overline{w}.\)
  • \(z\) and \(\overline z\) are symmetric about the real axis.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\overline{1+\mathrm{i}}=1-\mathrm{i}\).
  • \(\overline{-2-3\mathrm{i}}=-2+3\mathrm{i}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For any two complex numbers \(z\) and \(w\) (where \(w \neq 0\)), the quotient of complex numbers \(z/w\) is defined as \(z/w = z \cdot w^{-1} = \dfrac{z\overline{w}}{|w|^2}.\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Dividing by \(w\) means multiplying by its reciprocal \(w^{-1}\), the number with \(w\,w^{-1}=1\). In practice one multiplies numerator and denominator by the conjugate \(\overline w\), which turns the denominator into the real number \(w\overline w=|w|^2\).

In the figure \(z=3\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}4\pi/9}\) has length \(3\) and angle \(80^\circ\), and \(w=1.5\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}5\pi/18}\) has length \(1.5\) and angle \(50^\circ\). The quotient has length \(3/1.5=2\) and angle \(80^\circ-50^\circ=30^\circ\), so \(z/w=2\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi/6}\): moduli divide and arguments subtract modulo \(2\pi\), the reverse of complex multiplication.

Drag \(z\) and \(w\): the lengths divide and the angles subtract.

The condition \(w\neq0\) is needed just as for real numbers: \(0\cdot v=0\neq1\) for every \(v\), so \(0\) has no reciprocal. Every other complex number has one, which is what makes \(\mathbb{C}\) a field.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(|z/w|=|z|/|w|\).
  • \(\overline{z/w}=\overline z /\overline w\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • \((1+\mathrm{i})/(2-\mathrm{i})=\dfrac{(1+\mathrm{i})(2+\mathrm{i})}{(2-\mathrm{i})(2+\mathrm{i})}=\dfrac{1+3\mathrm{i}}{5}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(z\in\mathbb{C}\). The complex exponential function \(\mathrm{e}^z\) is defined as

\[ \mathrm{e}^z=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{z^n}{n!}=1+z+\frac{z^2}{2!}+\frac{z^3}{3!}+\cdots, \]

where \(z^n\) denotes the \(n\)-fold complex product of \(z\) with itself (with \(z^0=1\)), which can be evaluated in polar form by De Moivre's formula.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
For real inputs the series agrees with the real exponential function. Allowing complex inputs preserves the real exponential growth through \(|\mathrm{e}^{x+\mathrm{i} y}|=\mathrm{e}^x\).

The complex exponential is defined based on the Taylor series of the real exponential, extending its definition using powers of complex numbers.

The modulus \(\mathrm{e}^{x}\) comes from the real part and the angle \(y\) from the imaginary part, because \(\mathrm{e}^{x+\mathrm{i}y}=\mathrm{e}^{x}\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}y}\) with \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}y}=\cos y+\mathrm{i}\sin y\) by Euler's formula: the line \(x=c\) wraps onto the circle of radius \(\mathrm{e}^{c}\), once per height \(2\pi\) (dashed), and the green point \(c+\mathrm{i}\theta\) lands at \(\mathrm{e}^{c+\mathrm{i}\theta}\). So \(\mathrm{e}^{z}\) is \(2\pi\mathrm{i}\)-periodic and never \(0\).

Drag \(z\) and raise \(N\): the terms \(z^n/n!\) are laid tip to tail, and the partial sums spiral into \(\mathrm{e}^z\) (ringed).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • The series converges for all \(z \in \mathbb{C}\) (infinite radius of convergence).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • \(\displaystyle \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}}=1+\mathrm{i}-\frac{1}{2!}-\frac{\mathrm{i}}{3!}+\frac{1}{4!}+\frac{\mathrm{i}}{5!}+\cdots\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(z\neq 0\) and \(w\) be complex numbers. The complex power \(z^w\) is defined as \(\mathrm{e}^{w \log z}\), where the complex logarithm \(\log z\) is a multivalued function. The principal value of the complex exponentiation \(z^w\) is \(\mathrm{e}^{w \operatorname{Log}z}\), where \(\operatorname{Log}z\) denotes the principal value of the complex logarithm.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
For real numbers, \(x^y=\mathrm{e}^{y\ln x}\) when \(x>0\). The complex power uses the same recipe: take a logarithm of the base, multiply it by the exponent \(w\), and apply the complex exponential function. Because \(\log z\) has infinitely many values, \(z^w\) can have many values too.

For an integer exponent nothing new happens. The figure shows \(z,z^2,z^3,z^4\) for \(z=r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\varphi}\) with \(r=1.25\) and \(\varphi=\pi/6\): each further factor \(z\) stretches the length by \(1.25\) and turns by \(\pi/6\), so the points move outwards along a spiral. This is De Moivre's formula: \(z^n\) has modulus \(r^n\) and argument \(n\varphi\).

\(z^{1/n}\) has \(n\) values, evenly spaced on a circle of radius \(|z|^{1/n}\). The highlighted one is the principal value \(\mathrm{e}^{\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{Log}z}\).

The values of \(\log z\) differ by multiples of \(2\pi\mathrm{i}\), so the values of \(z^w\) differ by factors \(\mathrm{e}^{2\pi\mathrm{i}kw}\) with \(k\in\mathbb{Z}\). How many different values arise depends only on \(w\). For an integer \(w\) all these factors equal \(1\), and \(z^w\) is single-valued. For \(w=1/n\) with \(n\) a positive integer there are \(n\) factors \(\mathrm{e}^{2\pi\mathrm{i}k/n}\), giving the \(n\) different \(n\)-th roots of \(z\). For an irrational or non-real \(w\), the values are all different, so there are infinitely many, as for \(\mathrm{i}^{\mathrm{i}}\) in the Examples.

The usual rules for powers need care. With principal values, \((z^a)^b=z^{ab}\) can fail: for \(z=-1\), \(a=2\) and \(b=\tfrac{1}{2}\), the left side is \(1^{1/2}=1\), but \(z^{ab}=-1\). For positive real \(z\) and real \(w\), the principal value agrees with the real power.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • Complex exponentiation is generally multivalued. For an integer exponent \(m\), changing \(\log z\) by \(2\pi\mathrm{i} k\) multiplies the result by \(\mathrm{e}^{2\pi\mathrm{i} km}=1\), so \(z^m\) is single-valued.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The square roots of \(\mathrm{i}\): for \(k\in\mathbb{Z}\),

    \[ \mathrm{i}^{1/2}=\left(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}(\pi/2+2\pi k)}\right)^{1/2} =\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}(\pi/4+\pi k)}, \]

    so \(\mathrm{i}^{1/2}\) has the two values \(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\mathrm{i}\) and \(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\mathrm{i}\).

  • \(\displaystyle \mathrm{i}^\mathrm{i} = \left(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}(\pi/2+2\pi k) }\right)^\mathrm{i} = \mathrm{e}^{-\pi/2-2k\pi}\in\mathbb{R},\) where \(k\in\mathbb{Z}.\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A complex logarithm of a nonzero complex number \(z\) is any complex number \(w\) for which \(\mathrm{e}^{w}=z\). Such a number \(w\) is denoted by \(\log z\). If \(z\) is given in polar form as \(z=r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\varphi}\), where \(r>0\) and \(\varphi\) are real numbers, then \(\ln r+\mathrm{i} \varphi\) is one logarithm of \(z\), and all the complex logarithms of \(z\) are exactly the numbers of the form \(\ln r+\mathrm{i}\left(\varphi +2\pi k\right)\) for integers \(k.\) For each nonzero complex number \(z\), the principal value of the complex logarithm \(\operatorname{Log} z\) is the logarithm whose imaginary part lies in the interval \((-\pi ,\pi].\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A logarithm of \(z\) answers the question: to which power must \(\mathrm{e}\) be raised to give \(z\)? For a real \(x>0\) there is exactly one answer, the natural logarithm \(\ln x\). For a complex \(z\ne0\) there are infinitely many, because the complex exponential function is \(2\pi\mathrm{i}\)-periodic, \(\mathrm{e}^{w+2\pi\mathrm{i}}=\mathrm{e}^{w}\), and therefore not injective.

For \(z=r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\varphi}\) one has \(\mathrm{e}^{\ln r+\mathrm{i}\varphi}=r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\varphi}=z\): the real part \(\ln r\) of a logarithm records the modulus of \(z\), the imaginary part an argument. In the figure all logarithms of \(z\) lie on the vertical line with real part \(\ln r\) in the \(w\)-plane, spaced \(2\pi\) apart, one for each argument \(\varphi+2\pi k\). The marked middle value, with imaginary part in \((-\pi,\pi]\), is \(\operatorname{Log}z\).

Drag \(z\): its logarithms (right) lie on one vertical line, \(2\pi\) apart. \(\operatorname{Log} z\) is the one in the shaded strip; move \(z\) across the negative real axis and it jumps.

So \(\operatorname{Log}z=\ln|z|+\mathrm{i}\operatorname{Arg}z\) is a function, and for a positive real \(z\) it is the real \(\ln z\). It inherits the jump of \(\operatorname{Arg}\): crossing the negative real axis from above to below changes its imaginary part from nearly \(\pi\) to nearly \(-\pi\). For the same reason, the real rule \(\ln(xy)=\ln x+\ln y\) holds for the multivalued \(\log\) only as an equality of sets of values; for \(\operatorname{Log}\) it can fail by \(2\pi\mathrm{i}\), as the Key Results show.

The logarithm is what defines complex powers, \(z^w=\mathrm{e}^{w\log z}\), and its many values are the source of the many values of \(z^w\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • For nonzero \(z,w\), the identity \(\operatorname{Log}(zw)=\operatorname{Log}z+\operatorname{Log}w\) is not valid in general: the sum of principal arguments may lie outside \((-\pi,\pi]\). For example, taking \(z=w=-1\) gives \(\operatorname{Log}(zw)=0\), whereas \(\operatorname{Log}z+\operatorname{Log}w=2\pi\mathrm{i}\). For positive real \(z,w\), the identity does hold.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\log 1=2\pi\mathrm{i} k\) while \(\operatorname{Log} 1=0.\)
  • \(\log (-1)=\mathrm{i} (\pi+2\pi k)\) while \(\operatorname{Log} (-1)=\mathrm{i}\pi.\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Given two complex numbers \(z=a+\mathrm{i}b\) and \(w=c+\mathrm{i}d\) where \(a,b,c,d\in\mathbb{R}\), the product of complex numbers \(z\) and \(w\) is defined as \(zw = (a+\mathrm{i}b)(c+\mathrm{i}d) = (ac-bd) + \mathrm{i}(ad+bc).\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Multiplying two complex numbers works like multiplying two binomials: expand \((a+\mathrm{i}b)(c+\mathrm{i}d)\) term by term and replace \(\mathrm{i}^2\) by \(-1\). The term \(\mathrm{i}b\cdot\mathrm{i}d=-bd\) moves into the real part, which is why the real part of the product is \(ac-bd\).

In the figure \(z\) has length \(2\) and angle \(30^\circ\), and \(w\) has length \(1.5\) and angle \(50^\circ\). The product \(zw\) has length \(2\cdot1.5=3\) and angle \(30^\circ+50^\circ=80^\circ\): the arc \(\varphi\) is the angle of \(z\), and the arc \(\psi\) on top of it is the angle of \(w\), added on. In general complex multiplication multiplies the moduli, \(|zw|=|z|\,|w|\), and for nonzero \(z\) and \(w\) the arguments add modulo \(2\pi\). So multiplying by \(w\) stretches by the factor \(|w|\) and rotates by the angle of \(w\).

Drag \(z\) and \(w\): the length of \(zw\) is the product of the lengths, and its angle is the sum of the angles.

The two descriptions suit different tasks. The Cartesian formula is the quickest way to compute a product such as \((1+2\mathrm{i})(2-\mathrm{i})=4+3\mathrm{i}\); the polar form shows what multiplication does to the picture and leads to De Moivre's formula for powers. Multiplying by the imaginary unit, which has length \(1\) and angle \(90^\circ\), is a quarter turn; multiplying by a real number \(c>0\) is a pure stretch.

A common slip is to multiply part by part, as in complex addition: \((a+\mathrm{i}b)(c+\mathrm{i}d)\) is not \(ac+\mathrm{i}bd\). For \(z=w=1+\mathrm{i}\) that rule would give \(1+\mathrm{i}\), but \((1+\mathrm{i})^2=1+2\mathrm{i}+\mathrm{i}^2=2\mathrm{i}\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The multiplicative identity for complex numbers is \(1_\mathbb{C} = 1 + 0\mathrm{i},\) which is the real number \(1.\)
  • Complex multiplication has commutativity, associativity, and distributivity over complex addition.
  • In polar form, complex multiplication combines stretching, because \(|zw|=|z|\,|w|\), with rotation, because arguments add modulo \(2\pi\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \((1+2\mathrm{i})(2-\mathrm{i})=4+3\mathrm{i}=(2-\mathrm{i})(1+2\mathrm{i})\).
  • \((3+4\mathrm{i})1_\mathbb{C}=(3+4\mathrm{i})(1+0\mathrm{i})=3+4\mathrm{i}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Given a complex number \(z=a+\mathrm{i}b\) where \(a,b\in\mathbb{R}\), the negation of the complex number \(z\) is defined as \(-z=-a-\mathrm{i}b.\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Negating a complex number changes the sign of both its real and its imaginary part: real negation is applied separately to \(a\) and \(b\). Then \(z+(-z)=(a-a)+\mathrm{i}(b-b)=0\), so \(-z\) is the additive inverse of \(z\).

The arrows to \(z\) and \(-z\) have the same length and point in opposite directions: \(-z\) is the mirror image of \(z\) through the origin, reached by the half-turn marked \(+\pi\). This matches complex multiplication: \(-z=(-1)z\), and \(-1\) has length \(1\) and angle \(\pi\), so multiplying by it rotates by \(\pi\) without stretching.

Drag \(z\): \(-z\) is its mirror image through the origin.

Negation should not be confused with the complex conjugate \(\bar z=a-\mathrm{i}b\), which changes only the sign of the imaginary part and reflects \(z\) in the real axis. For \(z=1-\mathrm{i}\) one has \(-z=-1+\mathrm{i}\) but \(\bar z=1+\mathrm{i}\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • \(z\) and \(-z\) are symmetric about the origin in the complex plane.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(-(0+2\mathrm{i}) = 0-2\mathrm{i}\).
  • \(-(1-\mathrm{i}) = -1+\mathrm{i}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A complex number is of the form \(a + \mathrm{i}b\), where \(a\) and \(b\) are real numbers, and \(\mathrm{i}\) is the imaginary unit. The number \(a\) is the real part of the complex number \(a + \mathrm{i}b\) and is denoted by \(a = \operatorname{Re}(a+\mathrm{i}b)=\Re(a+\mathrm{i}b)\). Similarly, \(b\) is the imaginary part and is represented as \(b = \operatorname{Im}(a+\mathrm{i}b)=\Im(a+\mathrm{i}b).\) If the real part of a complex number \(a+\mathrm{i}b\) is zero, we term the number \(0+\mathrm{i}b\) as a purely imaginary number. The set of all complex numbers is denoted by \(\mathbb{C}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Essentially, a complex number is an ordered pair of two real numbers, its real part \(a\) and its imaginary part \(b\). Writing it as \(a+\mathrm{i}b\) lets one calculate as with ordinary algebraic expressions, using the extra rule \(\mathrm{i}^2=-1\).

The point \(z=a+\mathrm{i}b\) lies \(a\) units along the horizontal axis and \(b\) units up the vertical axis, so the two parts are its coordinates. The marked points \(1\) and \(\mathrm{i}\) are the units of the two axes: the real numbers fill the horizontal axis and the purely imaginary numbers \(0+\mathrm{i}b\) the vertical one. This picture is the complex plane.

Drag \(z\): the real part \(a\) is measured along the horizontal axis and the imaginary part \(b\) along the vertical one.

Both parts are real numbers: for \(2-3\mathrm{i}\) the imaginary part is \(-3\), not \(-3\mathrm{i}\). A real number \(a\) is the complex number \(a+0\mathrm{i}\), which is how \(\mathbb{R}\subset\mathbb{C}\) should be read, and two complex numbers are equal if and only if their real parts are equal and their imaginary parts are equal.

What is gained is solvability: \(x^2+1=0\) has no real solution but the two solutions \(\pm\mathrm{i}\) in \(\mathbb{C}\), and by the fundamental theorem of algebra every nonconstant polynomial has a root in \(\mathbb{C}\). What is lost is order. No order on \(\mathbb{C}\) follows the rules of the order on \(\mathbb{R}\), since in such an order every square would be at least \(0\), while \(\mathrm{i}^2=-1\). Sizes are compared through the modulus \(|z|\) instead.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Complex numbers do not have trichotomy, e.g., we cannot say \(1-\mathrm{i}> 0\) or \(1-\mathrm{i} < 0.\)
  • Complex numbers extend the real numbers by adding a solution of \(x^2=-1\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(2-3\mathrm{i}\) is a complex number.
  • Any real number is a special complex number, but not every complex number is real, i.e., \(\mathbb{R}\subset \mathbb{C}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The complex plane or \(z\)-plane is the plane formed by the complex numbers, with a Cartesian coordinate system such that the horizontal \(x\)-axis, called the real axis, is formed by the real numbers, and the vertical \(y\)-axis, called the imaginary axis, is formed by the purely imaginary numbers. The form \(a+\mathrm{i} b\) is called the Cartesian form of a complex number.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The complex plane draws each complex number \(a+\mathrm{i}b\) as the point \((a,b)\) of the Cartesian plane. It can therefore be seen as the plane \(\mathbb{R}^2\) equipped with additional structure, such as complex multiplication.

Each plotted point is read off the grid: \(2+\mathrm{i}\) lies \(2\) to the right and \(1\) up, \(-1+2\mathrm{i}\) lies \(1\) to the left and \(2\) up, and \(-2-\mathrm{i}\) and \(1.5-1.5\mathrm{i}\) lie below the real axis because their imaginary parts are negative. The label \(\mathrm{i}\) on the vertical axis marks the number \(0+1\mathrm{i}\), one unit up; its coordinate is the real number \(1\).

Each complex number \(a+\mathrm{i}b\) is the point \((a,b)\). Drag \(z\) along the axes to see the real and the purely imaginary numbers.

The two axes separate the parts of a number: the real axis holds the numbers with \(b=0\), the imaginary axis those with \(a=0\), and they meet at \(0\). Operations that work part by part have simple pictures here. Complex addition shifts a point by an arrow, the conjugate reflects it in the real axis, and the modulus \(|a+\mathrm{i}b|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\) is its distance from \(0\) by Pythagoras, for example \(|3+4\mathrm{i}|=5\).

Multiplication has no such simple description in coordinates. It becomes clear in the polar form, which describes the same point by its distance from \(0\) and its angle. The Cartesian form is the natural one for adding, the polar form for multiplying.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Each complex number \(a+\mathrm{i} b\) corresponds to unique coordinates \((a,b)\).
  • In the Cartesian coordinate system, the addition of complex numbers can be visualized as vector addition.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(1+\mathrm{i}\) and \(2-\mathrm{i}\) are elements in the complex plane \(\mathbb{C}\).
  • For \(z=3+4\mathrm{i}\), the real part is \(3\), the imaginary part is \(4\), and \(|z|=5\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The polar coordinate system for complex numbers specifies each complex number by its modulus \(r\) and polar angle \(\varphi\) (known as the argument). The form \(z=r(\cos \varphi+\mathrm{i}\sin\varphi)\) is called the polar form of a complex number.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The polar form describes a complex number by its distance from \(0\) and the angle it makes with the positive real axis, instead of by its real and imaginary parts.

The arrow to \(z\) has length \(r=|z|\) and makes the angle \(\varphi=\arg z\) with the real axis. The dashed lines meet the axes at \(r\cos\varphi\) and \(r\sin\varphi\), by the trigonometric functions on a circle of radius \(r\). These are the real and imaginary parts of \(z\), which is why \(z=r(\cos\varphi+\mathrm{i}\sin\varphi)\). The label also shows the short form \(r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\varphi}\) given by Euler's formula.

Set the modulus \(r\) and the angle \(\varphi\), or drag \(z\): \(z=r(\cos\varphi+\mathrm{i}\sin\varphi)\).

Going back uses \(r=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\) and an angle with \(\cos\varphi=a/r\) and \(\sin\varphi=b/r\). For \(3+4\mathrm{i}\) this gives \(r=5\) and \(\varphi=\operatorname{atan2}(4,3)\approx0.927\), about \(53.1^\circ\). The angle has to be found from the signs of both \(a\) and \(b\), not from \(b/a\) alone: \(1+\mathrm{i}\) and \(-1-\mathrm{i}\) have the same ratio but the angles \(\pi/4\) and \(-3\pi/4\), and the 2-argument arctangent takes care of this.

The modulus of a nonzero point is unique, the angle is not: adding \(2\pi k\), \(k\in\mathbb{Z}\), gives the same point, and the principal argument picks the value in \((-\pi,\pi]\). For \(z=0\) one has \(r=0\) and no angle is singled out. The polar form is made for multiplication: lengths multiply and angles add (complex multiplication), so powers follow from De Moivre's formula. For addition the Cartesian form is simpler.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • Complex multiplication in polar form combines stretching (multiplying moduli) with rotation (adding arguments).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The complex number \(1+\mathrm{i}\) has polar coordinates \((\sqrt{2}, \pi/4)\).
  • The complex number \(3+4\mathrm{i}\) has polar coordinates \((5, \operatorname{atan2}(4,3))\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The reciprocal of the complex number \(z\neq 0\) is defined as \(z^{-1} = |z|^{-2} \overline{z}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The reciprocal \(z^{-1}\) is the number that gives \(1\) when multiplied by \(z\). Since the product of \(z\) with its conjugate is \(z ar z=|z|^2\), a positive real number for \(z eq0\), dividing \( ar z\) by the square of the modulus does this: \(z\cdot ar z/|z|^2=1\).

In the figure \(z\) has length \(2\) and angle \(40^\circ\); its conjugate \( ar z\) (dashed) has the same length and the angle \(-40^\circ\), and dividing by \(|z|^2=4\) shrinks it along the same ray to length \( frac{1}{2}\). In general \(1/z\) has the direction of \( ar z\) and modulus \(1/|z|\), so points outside the unit circle are sent inside it and nonzero points inside are sent outside.

Drag \(z\): \(z^{-1}\) lies on the ray of \(\overline z\) at distance \(1/|z|\), inside the unit circle when \(z\) is outside it.

The condition \(z eq0\) is needed because \(0\cdot w=0 eq1\) for every \(w\). Every other complex number has a reciprocal, which is what makes \(\mathbb{C}\) a field, and dividing by \(w\) means multiplying by \(w^{-1}\) (complex division). Reciprocals are not taken part by part: \(1/(1+\mathrm{i})\) is \( frac{1}{2}(1-\mathrm{i})\), not \(1+1/\mathrm{i}\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • We have \(|z^{-1}|=1/|z|\) and \(\arg(z^{-1})=-\arg z\) modulo \(2\pi\). For the principal argument, \(\operatorname{Arg}(z^{-1})=-\operatorname{Arg}z\) unless \(z\) is a negative real number, in which case both equal \(\pi\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • The reciprocal of \(z = 1 + 2\mathrm{i}\) is \(\displaystyle z^{-1} = \frac{1}{5} - \frac{2}{5}\mathrm{i}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Given two complex numbers \(z\) and \(w\), the difference of complex numbers \(z\) and \(w\) is defined as \(z-w=z+(-w).\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Subtracting \(w\) means adding its negative: first take the complex negation \(-w\), then use complex addition to add it to \(z\). Both steps work part by part, so the real parts and the imaginary parts are subtracted separately.

For \(z=a+b\mathrm{i}\) and \(w=c+d\mathrm{i}\) this gives \(z-w=(a-c)+(b-d)\mathrm{i}\). In the figure it is the green arrow from the tip of \(w\) to the tip of \(z\), since \(w+(z-w)=z\); the dashed arrow is the same arrow started at \(0\), so its tip is the point \(z-w\). Its length \(|z-w|\) is the distance between the points \(z\) and \(w\) (see modulus).

\(z-w=z+(-w)\), and the same arrow runs from \(w\) to \(z\). Drag both points.

Subtraction is not commutative: \(w-z=-(z-w)\) is the arrow from \(z\) back to \(w\), with the same length and the opposite direction. For example, \((1+2\mathrm{i})-(2-\mathrm{i})=-1+3\mathrm{i}\), while \((2-\mathrm{i})-(1+2\mathrm{i})=1-3\mathrm{i}\). The same arrow picture returns later for the subtraction of vectors.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • We have \(z-z=0_{\mathbb{C}}\) for any \(z\in\mathbb{C}\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • \((1+2\mathrm{i})-(2-\mathrm{i})=-1+3\mathrm{i}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(z\in\mathbb{C}\). The complex sine function \(\sin z\) and the complex cosine function \(\cos z\) are defined as

\[ \begin{aligned} \sin z&=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^{n} z^{2 n+1}}{(2 n+1) !}\\ &=z-\frac{z^3}{3!}+\frac{z^5}{5!}-\cdots,\\ \cos z&=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^{n} z^{2 n}}{(2 n) !}\\ &=1-\frac{z^2}{2!}+\frac{z^4}{4!}-\cdots, \end{aligned} \]

where the powers \(z^n\) are defined by repeated complex multiplication and can be evaluated in polar form by De Moivre's formula.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The complex sine and cosine extend the real trigonometric functions to complex inputs. A complex number has no point on the unit circle to read the values from, so the definition uses infinite series instead: each power \(z^n\) is computed by complex multiplication, and the terms are added up.

The sine series contains only odd powers and the cosine series only even powers, with alternating signs and factorials in the denominators. Both series converge for every \(z\in\mathbb{C}\). For a real input \(x\) the two sums are the familiar \(\sin x\) and \(\cos x\), so nothing changes on the real axis: the definitions extend sine and cosine rather than replace them.

Off the real axis they behave differently, and the bound \(|\sin x|\le1\) from the unit circle is lost. On the imaginary axis, \((\mathrm{i}y)^{2n}=(-1)^ny^{2n}\) cancels the alternating signs, so \(\cos(\mathrm{i}y)=1+\frac{y^2}{2!}+\frac{y^4}{4!}+\cdots\) for real \(y\). This is larger than \(1\) for every \(y\neq0\) and grows without bound; the Examples show the same for \(\sin\mathrm{i}\).

A common slip concerns Euler's formula. The identity \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}z}=\cos z+\mathrm{i}\sin z\) holds for every complex \(z\), but for non-real \(z\) the numbers \(\cos z\) and \(\sin z\) are in general not real, so they are not the real and imaginary parts of \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}z}\). For \(z=\mathrm{i}\), \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\cdot\mathrm{i}}=\mathrm{e}^{-1}\) is real, while \(\sin\mathrm{i}\approx1.1752\,\mathrm{i}\neq0\).

Why the real sine and cosine are given by exactly these series is explained later by Taylor series.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The complex sine and cosine functions remain periodic with period \(2\pi\).
  • The algebraic identities of real trigonometry, such as \(\sin^2z+\cos^2z=1\) and the addition formulas, continue to hold for complex arguments.
  • By Euler's formula, \(\cos z=\dfrac{\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}z}+\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}z}}{2}\) and \(\sin z=\dfrac{\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}z}-\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}z}}{2\mathrm{i}}\).
  • Unlike the real functions, \(\sin z\) and \(\cos z\) are unbounded on \(\mathbb{C}\): \(|\sin z|\) can be larger than \(1\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Since \(\mathrm{i}^3=-\mathrm{i}\) and \(\mathrm{i}^5=\mathrm{i}\), the signs in the series for \(\sin\mathrm{i}\) all turn positive:

\[ \begin{aligned} \sin\mathrm{i}&=\mathrm{i}+\frac{\mathrm{i}}{3!}+\frac{\mathrm{i}}{5!}+\cdots\\ &=\mathrm{i}\left(1+\frac{1}{3!}+\frac{1}{5!}+\cdots\right)\\ &=\mathrm{i}\,\frac{\mathrm{e}-\mathrm{e}^{-1}}{2}\approx1.1752\,\mathrm{i}. \end{aligned} \]

So \(|\sin\mathrm{i}|\approx1.1752>1\), which no real sine value can reach. The same value follows from Euler's form: \(\sin\mathrm{i}=\dfrac{\mathrm{e}^{-1}-\mathrm{e}}{2\mathrm{i}}=\mathrm{i}\,\dfrac{\mathrm{e}-\mathrm{e}^{-1}}{2}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: If \(\boldsymbol{A}\in\mathcal{L}(V,W)\) and \(\boldsymbol{B}\in\mathcal{L}(U,V)\), the product \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{B}\in\mathcal{L}(U,W)\) is the composition defined by \((\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{B})(\boldsymbol{u})=\boldsymbol{A}(\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{u})\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The product \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{B}\) of two linear maps is their composition as functions: first apply the map on the right, \(\boldsymbol{B}\), then the map on the left, \(\boldsymbol{A}\). It is written as a product because, for matrices, composition is exactly matrix multiplication.

The figure reads from left to right: \(\boldsymbol{B}\) takes \(\boldsymbol{u}\in U\) to \(\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{u}\in V\), and \(\boldsymbol{A}\) takes that vector on to \(\boldsymbol{A}(\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{u})\in W\). The curved arrow is the single map \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{B}\colon U\to W\) that does both steps at once. The middle space must match: \(\boldsymbol{B}\) has to land in \(V\), where \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is defined, otherwise \(\boldsymbol{A}(\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{u})\) has no meaning.

\(\boldsymbol{B}\) turns \(\boldsymbol{u}\) by \(\theta\), then \(\boldsymbol{A}\) acts: \((\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{B})\boldsymbol{u}=\boldsymbol{A}(\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{u})\). Show \(\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{A}\) as well to see that the order usually matters.

The composition is again linear: \(\boldsymbol{B}\) turns \(\boldsymbol{u}+\boldsymbol{v}\) into \(\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{u}+\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{v}\), and \(\boldsymbol{A}\) turns that into \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{u}+\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{v}\); scalar multiples pass through both maps in the same way. For matrices, \([\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{B}]=[\boldsymbol{A}]\,[\boldsymbol{B}]\), and the matching middle space becomes the size condition: \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is \(m\times n\) and \(\boldsymbol{B}\) is \(n\times k\). Composition is associative, since \((\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{B})\boldsymbol{C}\) and \(\boldsymbol{A}(\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{C})\) both mean "first \(\boldsymbol{C}\), then \(\boldsymbol{B}\), then \(\boldsymbol{A}\)".

A common slip is to apply \(\boldsymbol{A}\) first because it is written first. The order matters: on \(\mathbb{R}^2\), let \(\boldsymbol{A}(x_1,x_2)=(x_1,0)\) and let \(\boldsymbol{B}(x_1,x_2)=(x_2,x_1)\) swap the coordinates. Then \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{B}(x_1,x_2)=(x_2,0)\) but \(\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{A}(x_1,x_2)=(0,x_1)\), so \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{B}\neq\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{A}\), just as composition of functions is not commutative.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The product of compatible linear maps is linear.
  • Matrix multiplication represents composition of linear maps.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(\boldsymbol{B}\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}^2\) and \(\boldsymbol{A}\colon\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}\), then \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{B}\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\).
  • For matrices, \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{A}(\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{x})\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The continuum hypothesis is the hypothesis that there is no set whose cardinality is strictly between \(\aleph_0\) and \(\mathfrak{c}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Aleph null, \(\aleph_0\), is the size of the natural numbers; the cardinality of the continuum, \(\mathfrak{c}\), is the size of the reals. These are the two endpoints between which the hypothesis rules out an intermediate cardinality.

It asks whether there is an intermediate size of infinity between the natural numbers and the real numbers.

Equivalently, the continuum hypothesis states \(\mathfrak{c}=\aleph_1\), where \(\aleph_1\) is the smallest cardinality larger than \(\aleph_0\) (see aleph null). Assuming the standard axioms of Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory with the axiom of choice (ZFC) are consistent, they can neither prove nor refute this hypothesis (Gödel, 1940; Cohen, 1963).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• In symbols, it denies the existence of a set \(A\) such that \(\aleph_0<\operatorname{card}(A)<\mathfrak{c}\).
  • A bijection is the main tool for proving that two sets have the same cardinality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • The question compares the size of \(\mathbb{N}\) with the size of \(\mathbb{R}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In \(\mathbb{R}^n\), if

\[ \boldsymbol{v}=(v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_n), \]

then \(v_i\) is called the \(i\)th coordinate of \(\boldsymbol{v}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The \(i\)th coordinate of \(\boldsymbol{v}=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)\) is the number in position \(i\) of the tuple: it says how far to go along the \(i\)th axis. Coordinates are the individual entries of a vector in real coordinate space, and two vectors of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) are equal if and only if all their coordinates agree.

The figure shows that coordinates depend on the chosen basis. In the standard basis \(\mathcal{E}=(\boldsymbol{e}_1,\boldsymbol{e}_2)\), the dashed grey lines drop from \(\boldsymbol{w}\) to \(3.8\) on the \(x_1\)-axis and to \(2\) on the \(x_2\)-axis, so \([\boldsymbol{w}]_{\mathcal{E}}=(3.8,2)\) and \(\boldsymbol{w}=3.8\boldsymbol{e}_1+2\boldsymbol{e}_2\). Along the dashed blue path, the same vector is \(\boldsymbol{w}=2\boldsymbol{b}_1+\boldsymbol{b}_2\), so in the basis \(\mathcal{B}=(\boldsymbol{b}_1,\boldsymbol{b}_2)\) it has coordinates \([\boldsymbol{w}]_{\mathcal{B}}=(2,1)\).

Drag \(\boldsymbol{v}\) and watch \(v_1\) and \(v_2\): each coordinate is the step taken along one axis.

In a general vector space the vectors need not be tuples, and coordinates are defined through a basis: they are the coefficients of the unique linear combination of the basis vectors that gives the vector. The standard basis of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) makes those coefficients exactly the entries \(v_i\), since \(\boldsymbol{v}=v_1\boldsymbol{e}_1+\cdots+v_n\boldsymbol{e}_n\). For polynomials of degree at most \(2\) with the basis \((1,x,x^2)\), the coordinates of \(3-x+4x^2\) are \((3,-1,4)\). In the plane, the Cartesian coordinates of a point are the coordinates of the arrow from the origin to that point in the standard basis.

A coordinate is a number, not a vector: \(v_1\) is a scalar, while \(v_1\boldsymbol{e}_1\) is the vector that goes \(v_1\) steps along the first axis.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • A vector in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) has exactly \(n\) coordinates.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • For \(\boldsymbol{v}=(3,-1,4)\), the second coordinate is \(-1\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A set is countably infinite if it has the same cardinality as the natural numbers, equivalently if there is a bijection between the set and \(\mathbb{N}\text{.}\)

A set is countable if it is finite or countably infinite. A set that is not countable is called uncountable.

Course convention

In Math II: Linear Algebra, countable includes finite sets. Use countably infinite when the set must be infinite and in bijection with \(\mathbb{N}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A countable set is one whose elements can be listed as a first, a second, a third element and so on, with every element appearing somewhere. An uncountable set is too large for this: every sequence indexed by the natural numbers misses some of its elements.

The zigzag runs through the pairs \((i,j)\) along the diagonals on which \(i+j\) is constant. The pair \((1,1)\) gets the number \(1\), the pairs \((2,1)\) and \((1,2)\) get \(2\) and \(3\), the diagonal with \(i+j=4\) gets \(4\), \(5\) and \(6\), and so on. Each diagonal is finite, so every pair receives a number, and different pairs receive different numbers. This is a bijection between the numbers \(1,2,3,\ldots\) and the pairs, so \(\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}\) is countably infinite, although it looks larger than \(\mathbb{N}\).

Repeated entries in a list can be skipped: reading \((i,j)\) as the fraction \(i/j\) and skipping repeats such as \(2/2=1/1\), the zigzag lists every positive rational number; adding \(0\) and the negatives shows that \(\mathbb{Q}\) is countable. Uncountability is harder to show, since every possible list must fail: Cantor's diagonal argument builds, from any list of numbers in \([0,1]\), a number not on it.

A common slip is to treat infinite and uncountable as the same. \(\mathbb{N}\), \(\mathbb{Z}\) and \(\mathbb{Q}\) are infinite but countable, of size aleph null; \(\mathbb{R}\) is strictly larger and has the cardinality of the continuum.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every finite set is countable.
  • Every subset of a countable set is countable.
  • \(\mathbb{N}\), \(\mathbb{Z}\), and \(\mathbb{Q}\) are countably infinite.
  • Cantor's diagonal argument shows that \([0,1]\) and \(\mathbb{R}\) are uncountable.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\{1,2,3\}\) is countable because it is finite.
  • The even natural numbers are countably infinite: \(n\mapsto 2n\) gives a bijection from \(\mathbb{N}\).
  • The real interval \([0,1]\) is uncountable.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: If \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is a nonsingular \(n\times n\) matrix, then the unique solution of \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{b}\) is given by \(x_j=\frac{\det(\boldsymbol{B}_j)}{\det(\boldsymbol{A})}\), where \(\boldsymbol{B}_j\) is obtained from \(\boldsymbol{A}\) by replacing column \(j\) with \(\boldsymbol{b}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Cramer's rule expresses each unknown of a square linear system with a nonsingular coefficient matrix as a quotient of two determinants. The denominator is always \(\det(\boldsymbol{A})\); the numerator is the determinant of \(\boldsymbol{A}\) with the column of \(x_j\) replaced by the right-hand side \(\boldsymbol{b}\).

For the illustrated system \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{b}\), \(\boldsymbol{A}=(\boldsymbol{a}_1\ \boldsymbol{a}_2)=\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\boldsymbol{b}=\begin{pmatrix}7\\4\end{pmatrix}\). The blue parallelogram spanned by \(\boldsymbol{a}_1,\boldsymbol{a}_2\) has area \(5\), the red one spanned by \(\boldsymbol{b},\boldsymbol{a}_2\) has area \(10\), so \(x_1=\dfrac{\det(\boldsymbol{b},\boldsymbol{a}_2)}{\det(\boldsymbol{a}_1,\boldsymbol{a}_2)}=2\); similarly \(x_2=\dfrac{\det(\boldsymbol{a}_1,\boldsymbol{b})}{\det(\boldsymbol{a}_1,\boldsymbol{a}_2)}=\dfrac{5}{5}=1\). Replacing \(\boldsymbol{a}_1\) by \(\boldsymbol{b}=x_1\boldsymbol{a}_1+x_2\boldsymbol{a}_2\) multiplies the area by \(x_1\), while the \(\boldsymbol{a}_2\) component only shears it.

Each unknown is a ratio of determinants: \(x_j=\det(\boldsymbol{B}_j)/\det(\boldsymbol{A})\), where \(\boldsymbol{B}_j\) has \(\boldsymbol{b}\) in column \(j\). Make \(\det(\boldsymbol{A})=0\) and the rule breaks down.

The same argument works in general. The determinant is linear in each column and is zero when two columns are equal, so replacing column \(j\) by \(\boldsymbol{b}=x_1\boldsymbol{a}_1+\cdots+x_n\boldsymbol{a}_n\) leaves only the term \(x_j\det(\boldsymbol{A})\). The hypothesis \(\det(\boldsymbol{A})\neq0\) cannot be dropped: then the system has no solution or infinitely many, so there is no single value of \(x_j\) to give, and elimination is needed to decide which case occurs.

Cramer's rule is convenient for \(2\times2\) and small \(3\times3\) systems, or when only one unknown is needed; an \(n\times n\) system needs \(n+1\) determinants, while Gauss-Jordan elimination needs one reduction. The rule is the formula \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{A}^{-1}\boldsymbol{b}\) written out with the adjugate matrix.

A common slip is to replace a row of \(\boldsymbol{A}\) by \(\boldsymbol{b}\). It must be column \(j\), the column holding the coefficients of \(x_j\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Cramer's rule applies only when \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is nonsingular.
  • It gives an explicit formula for the unique solution of \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{b}\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For a \(2\times2\) nonsingular system, \(x_1=\det(\boldsymbol{B}_1)/\det(\boldsymbol{A})\) and \(x_2=\det(\boldsymbol{B}_2)/\det(\boldsymbol{A})\).
  • If \(\det(\boldsymbol{A})=0\), Cramer's rule cannot be used.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
For any integer \(n\) and nonzero complex number \(z = r(\cos\varphi + \mathrm{i}\sin\varphi)\), with \(r>0\), it holds that:

\[ z^n = r^n(\cos(n\varphi) + \mathrm{i}\sin(n\varphi)). \]

For positive integers \(n\), the identity also holds at \(z=0\). Negative powers require \(z\ne0\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
To raise a complex number in polar form to an integer power \(n\), raise its modulus to the power \(n\) and multiply its angle by \(n\).

The figure shows the case \(r=1\): the powers of \(\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta\) stay on the unit circle, and each multiplication adds the same angle \(\theta\), so the first, second and third powers lie at the angles \(\theta\), \(2\theta\) and \(3\theta\). For \(r>1\) the powers also move outwards and for \(r<1\) inwards, which gives the spiral in the interactive version.

Drag \(z\) and change \(n\): each power multiplies the modulus by \(r\) and adds \(\varphi\) to the angle, so the powers lie on a spiral.

The formula follows from complex multiplication, which multiplies moduli and adds angles: multiplying \(z\) by itself \(n\) times gives modulus \(r^n\) and angle \(n\varphi\). For negative \(n\) one uses reciprocals, since \(z^{-1}\) has modulus \(1/r\) and angle \(-\varphi\); this is why \(z\neq0\) is required there. In the Examples, \(1+\sqrt{3}\mathrm{i}\) has modulus \(2\) and angle \(\pi/3\), so its eighth power has angle \(8\pi/3\), the same direction as \(2\pi/3\) after subtracting \(2\pi\), and equals \(256(-\tfrac{1}{2}+\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\mathrm{i})=-128+128\sqrt{3}\,\mathrm{i}\).

The formula is stated for integers \(n\) only. Used with \(n=\tfrac{1}{2}\), it gives different answers for different angles of the same number: \(1\) has the angles \(0\) and \(2\pi\), and halving them gives \(1\) and \(-1\), the two square roots of \(1\). This is why fractional powers of complex numbers have several values. With Euler's formula the theorem reads \((r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\varphi})^n=r^n\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}n\varphi}\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The formula converts integer powers of a complex number into powers of its modulus and multiples of its argument.
  • It is closely related to Euler's formula.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \((1+\sqrt{3}\mathrm{i})^8=2^8(\cos(8\pi/3)+\mathrm{i}\sin(8\pi/3))\).
  • \((-1+\mathrm{i})^4=(\sqrt{2})^4(\cos(3\pi)+\mathrm{i}\sin(3\pi))=-4\).
