docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\boldsymbol{A}\) be a real symmetric matrix. The definiteness of \(\boldsymbol{A}\) classifies the sign of the quadratic form \(\boldsymbol{x}^{\top} \boldsymbol{A} \boldsymbol{x}\):

  • Positive definite: \(\boldsymbol{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}>0\) for every nonzero vector \(\boldsymbol{x}\).
  • Positive semidefinite: \(\boldsymbol{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\ge 0\) for every vector \(\boldsymbol{x}\).
  • Negative definite: \(\boldsymbol{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}<0\) for every nonzero vector \(\boldsymbol{x}\).
  • Negative semidefinite: \(\boldsymbol{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\le 0\) for every vector \(\boldsymbol{x}\).
  • Indefinite: \(\boldsymbol{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\) takes both positive and negative values.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Definiteness tells whether the quadratic form determined by a symmetric matrix is always positive, always nonnegative, always negative, always nonpositive, or changes sign. It is the matrix version of the sign of \(a\) in \(ax^2\).

The four panels show the curves on which \(\boldsymbol{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\) is constant, its level curves, for \(\operatorname{diag}(1,2)\), \(\operatorname{diag}(-1,-2)\), \(\operatorname{diag}(0,1)\) and \(\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\). For a diagonal matrix the form is \(d_1x_1^2+d_2x_2^2\), so its signs can be read off the diagonal. The first two give ellipses, the first form positive and the second negative in every direction. The third form, \(x_2^2\), gives horizontal lines and is zero along the whole \(x_1\)-axis: nonnegative but not positive, so positive semidefinite. The fourth, \(x_1^2-x_2^2\), gives hyperbolas and takes both signs.

Positive definite means \(\boldsymbol{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}>0\) for every \(\boldsymbol{x}\neq\boldsymbol{0}\): the curve on the right stays above \(0\). Try the examples, and look for directions where the form vanishes.

A positive definite \(\boldsymbol{A}\) gives a bowl, a negative definite one a cap, and an indefinite one a saddle; the eigenvalues are shown below.

The definition quantifies over all nonzero \(\boldsymbol{x}\), not only the axes. Testing the standard basis vectors gives \(\boldsymbol{e}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{e}_i=a_{ii}\), so a positive definite matrix has positive diagonal entries. The converse fails: \(\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}\) has a positive diagonal, but the value \(1-4+1=-2\) at \(\boldsymbol{x}=(1,-1)\), so it is indefinite. The categories overlap: every positive definite matrix is also positive semidefinite, and the zero matrix is both positive and negative semidefinite.

In one variable, the second-order condition reads the sign of \(f''(x_0)\) at a stationary point. For functions of several variables, a symmetric matrix of second derivatives takes the place of \(f''(x_0)\), and its definiteness separates local minima, maxima and saddle points.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A symmetric matrix is positive definite if and only if all its eigenvalues are positive.
  • A symmetric matrix is positive semidefinite if and only if all its eigenvalues are nonnegative.
  • A symmetric matrix is negative definite if and only if all its eigenvalues are negative.
  • A symmetric matrix is negative semidefinite if and only if all its eigenvalues are nonpositive.
  • A symmetric matrix is indefinite if and only if it has both positive and negative eigenvalues.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\boldsymbol{I}_n\) is positive definite, while \(-\boldsymbol{I}_n\) is negative definite.
  • \(\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\) is positive semidefinite, and \(\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}\) is indefinite.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: For a real symmetric matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}\), definiteness is completely determined by the signs of the eigenvalues: positive definite means all eigenvalues are positive, positive semidefinite means all are nonnegative, negative definite means all are negative, negative semidefinite means all are nonpositive, and indefinite means both positive and negative eigenvalues occur.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Eigenvalues reveal the sign behaviour of a symmetric matrix's quadratic form. The theorem replaces a condition on all nonzero vectors \(\boldsymbol{x}\) by a check of \(n\) numbers.

The figure shows the ellipse \(\boldsymbol{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}=1\) for a symmetric matrix with eigenvalues \(\lambda_1=3\) and \(\lambda_2=1\). Its axes lie along the unit eigenvectors \(\boldsymbol{p}_1\) and \(\boldsymbol{p}_2\), which are orthogonal, and have half-lengths \(1/\sqrt{3}\) and \(1\). The larger eigenvalue gives the shorter axis, because the form grows faster in that direction.

On the unit circle \(\boldsymbol{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\) runs between the two eigenvalues, reached along the eigenvectors. Their signs decide the definiteness.

For a unit eigenvector \(\boldsymbol{p}\) with \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{p}=\lambda\boldsymbol{p}\), the form takes the value \(\boldsymbol{p}^{\top}\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{p}=\lambda\,\boldsymbol{p}^{\top}\boldsymbol{p}=\lambda\), so a negative eigenvalue rules out positive definiteness. A real symmetric matrix has real eigenvalues and mutually orthogonal unit eigenvectors, which form the columns of an orthogonal matrix \(\boldsymbol{Q}\), with \(\boldsymbol{Q}^{\top}\boldsymbol{Q}=\boldsymbol{I}\) and \(\boldsymbol{A}=\boldsymbol{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\boldsymbol{Q}^{\top}\). In the coordinates \(\boldsymbol{c}=\boldsymbol{Q}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\) the form becomes \(\lambda_1c_1^2+\cdots+\lambda_nc_n^2\), and its signs can be read from the \(\lambda_i\).

Symmetry matters. The non-symmetric \(\begin{pmatrix}1&4\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\) has the single eigenvalue \(1\), yet \(\boldsymbol{x}=(1,-1)\) gives \(\boldsymbol{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}=-2\). The test must be applied to the symmetric matrix of the form, here \(\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}\), whose eigenvalues \(3\) and \(-1\) show that the form is indefinite.

For a \(2\times2\) symmetric matrix the eigenvalues need not be computed: their product is \(\det\boldsymbol{A}\) and their sum is the trace, so \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is positive definite if and only if \(\det\boldsymbol{A}>0\) and \(\operatorname{tr}(\boldsymbol{A})>0\). A test with determinants of upper-left submatrices for every \(n\) returns later as Sylvester's criterion.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• This theorem converts a quadratic-form problem into an eigenvalue problem.
  • It applies to real symmetric matrices.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A diagonal matrix with diagonal entries \(2\) and \(3\) is positive definite.
  • A diagonal matrix with diagonal entries \(2\) and \(-3\) is indefinite.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The determinant of a square matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}=(a_{ij})\) of size \(n\times n\), denoted \(\det(\boldsymbol{A})\) or \(|\boldsymbol{A}|\), is the scalar defined recursively by \(\det(a)=a\) for a \(1\times1\) matrix and, for \(n\geq2\),

\[ \det(\boldsymbol{A})=\sum_{j=1}^{n}(-1)^{1+j}a_{1j}\det(\boldsymbol{A}_{1j}), \]

where \(\boldsymbol{A}_{1j}\) is the \((n-1)\times(n-1)\) matrix obtained from \(\boldsymbol{A}\) by deleting row \(1\) and column \(j\) (cofactor expansion along the first row). It detects invertibility and encodes the volume scaling of the associated linear transformation.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The determinant condenses a square matrix into one number that answers two questions at once: by what factor the linear map \(\boldsymbol{x}\mapsto\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\) scales areas (in \(\mathbb{R}^2\)) or volumes (in \(\mathbb{R}^3\)), and whether the map can be undone. A nonzero determinant means exactly that \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is invertible.

The unit square of area \(1\) is mapped onto the parallelogram spanned by the columns \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{e}_1\) and \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{e}_2\) of \(\boldsymbol{A}=\begin{pmatrix}2&0.5\\0.5&1.5\end{pmatrix}\). Its area is \(|\det(\boldsymbol{A})|=|2\cdot1.5-0.5\cdot0.5|=2.75\). A negative determinant would reverse the orientation, while a zero determinant would collapse the parallelogram to zero area and make the matrix singular.

The unit square becomes a parallelogram of area \(|\det(\boldsymbol{A})|\). It flips colour when \(\det(\boldsymbol{A})<0\) (orientation reversed) and collapses when \(\det(\boldsymbol{A})=0\).

The sign records orientation: swapping the two columns of \(\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}\) turns \(ad-bc\) into \(bc-ad\), the same area with the opposite sign. The product rule \(\det(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{B})=\det(\boldsymbol{A})\det(\boldsymbol{B})\) fits the picture too: applying \(\boldsymbol{B}\) and then \(\boldsymbol{A}\) scales areas first by one factor and then by the other.

In practice determinants are computed by cofactor expansion along a convenient row or column, or by Sarrus' rule for \(3\times3\) matrices. They give Cramer's rule for square systems, and the test whether a determinant is zero returns later in the course, when eigenvalues are computed.

A common slip is to treat the determinant as additive. In general \(\det(\boldsymbol{A}+\boldsymbol{B})\neq\det(\boldsymbol{A})+\det(\boldsymbol{B})\): for \(\boldsymbol{A}=\boldsymbol{B}=\boldsymbol{I}_2\) the left side is \(\det(2\boldsymbol{I}_2)=4\) and the right side is \(2\). Likewise \(\det(c\boldsymbol{A})=c^n\det(\boldsymbol{A})\) for an \(n\times n\) matrix, not \(c\det(\boldsymbol{A})\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A square matrix is invertible if and only if \(\det(\boldsymbol{A})\neq0\).
  • \(\det(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{B})=\det(\boldsymbol{A})\det(\boldsymbol{B})\) for square matrices of the same size.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\boldsymbol{A}=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}\), \(\det(\boldsymbol{A})=ad-bc\).
  • \(\det(\boldsymbol{I}_n)=1\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A diagonal matrix is a square matrix whose off-diagonal entries are all zero.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A diagonal matrix acts on each coordinate separately: \(\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{x}\) multiplies the \(i\)-th coordinate of \(\boldsymbol{x}\) by the \(i\)-th diagonal entry and never mixes coordinates.

The matrix \(\boldsymbol{D}=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&\tfrac{1}{2}\end{pmatrix}\) stretches \(\boldsymbol{e}_1\) to \(2\boldsymbol{e}_1\) and shrinks \(\boldsymbol{e}_2\) to \(\tfrac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{e}_2\), so the unit square becomes a rectangle twice as wide and half as tall. The axes keep their directions, and the area \(2\cdot\tfrac{1}{2}=1\) is the product of the diagonal entries, the determinant.

A diagonal matrix scales each axis on its own: \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{e}_1=a_{11}\boldsymbol{e}_1\) and \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{e}_2=a_{22}\boldsymbol{e}_2\). Allow off-diagonal entries to see the axes turn.

Calculations reduce to calculations with numbers: products and powers are taken entry by entry on the diagonal, here \(\boldsymbol{D}^k=\operatorname{diag}(2^k,2^{-k})\), and a diagonal matrix is invertible if and only if no diagonal entry is \(0\), with the reciprocals as inverse. Zeros on the diagonal are allowed, so the zero matrix is diagonal too. Later in the course this simplicity is the reason to bring a matrix into diagonal form where possible.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The determinant of a diagonal matrix is the product of its diagonal entries.
  • The product and sum of diagonal matrices of the same size are diagonal.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}\) is diagonal.
  • \(\boldsymbol{I}_n\) and \(\boldsymbol{0}_n\) are diagonal.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Over a chosen field \(\mathbb{F}\) (here \(\mathbb{R}\) or \(\mathbb{C}\)), a square matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is diagonalizable if there exists an invertible matrix \(\boldsymbol{P}\) such that \(\boldsymbol{P}^{-1}\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{P}\) is diagonal, with \(\boldsymbol{A}\) and \(\boldsymbol{P}\) both having entries in \(\mathbb{F}\).

A square matrix without an eigenbasis over \(\mathbb{F}\) is non-diagonalizable over \(\mathbb{F}\). When its characteristic polynomial splits into linear factors over that field, it is called defective if it does not have enough linearly independent eigenvectors to form an eigenbasis. Jordan normal form is the tool used for such defective matrices over a field in which the characteristic polynomial splits. For example, a real planar rotation can fail to be diagonalizable over \(\mathbb{R}\) while being diagonalizable over \(\mathbb{C}\); this is not defectiveness.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A diagonalizable matrix becomes diagonal after changing to a suitable basis. A diagonal matrix only scales each coordinate; a diagonalizable matrix does the same once coordinates are measured along its eigenvectors.

On the left, \(\boldsymbol{A}=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}\) has two independent eigenvectors, \(\boldsymbol{p}_1\) for the eigenvalue \(3\) and \(\boldsymbol{p}_2\) for the eigenvalue \(1\). With these as the columns of \(\boldsymbol{P}\), \(\boldsymbol{P}^{-1}\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{P}=\operatorname{diag}(3,1)\). On the right, the shear \(\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\) has the double eigenvalue \(1\), but all its eigenvectors lie on the horizontal axis: \(\boldsymbol{e}_2\) is sent to \((1,1)\), off its own line. One direction is too few for a basis of \(\mathbb{R}^2\), so the shear is not diagonalizable.

Choose the examples: two eigenvector lines give an eigenbasis; a shear has only one, and a rotation has none over \(\mathbb{R}\).

Being diagonalizable is the same as having an eigenbasis: the columns of \(\boldsymbol{P}\) are eigenvectors, and the diagonal of \(\boldsymbol{P}^{-1}\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{P}\) holds their eigenvalues. In terms of the multiplicities, every eigenvalue needs \(\operatorname{gm}=\operatorname{am}\); the shear fails with \(\operatorname{am}(1)=2\) and \(\operatorname{gm}(1)=1\). Having \(n\) distinct eigenvalues is a sufficient shortcut, but not a necessary one, as \(\boldsymbol{I}_n\) shows. The field matters too: the quarter-turn rotation \(\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\) has no real eigenvalues, so it is not diagonalizable over \(\mathbb{R}\), but it is diagonalizable over \(\mathbb{C}\), with eigenvalues \(\pm\mathrm{i}\).

Diagonalization finds \(\boldsymbol{P}\) and the diagonal matrix; where it fails, Jordan normal form is the nearest substitute.

Diagonalizable and invertible are unrelated properties. The diagonal matrix \(\operatorname{diag}(1,0)\) is diagonalizable but singular, and the shear is invertible, with determinant \(1\), but not diagonalizable.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A matrix is diagonalizable if it has enough linearly independent eigenvectors to form a basis.
  • If an \(n\times n\) matrix has \(n\) distinct eigenvalues in \(\mathbb{F}\), it is diagonalizable.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Every diagonal matrix is diagonalizable.
  • \(\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\) is not diagonalizable.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Diagonalization is the process of finding an invertible matrix \(\boldsymbol{P}\) and a diagonal matrix \(\boldsymbol{D}\) such that \(\boldsymbol{A}=\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{P}^{-1}\), equivalently \(\boldsymbol{P}^{-1}\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{P}=\boldsymbol{D}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Diagonalization rewrites a linear transformation in an eigenbasis, where its action is simple coordinate-wise scaling.

The diagram shows two routes from \(\boldsymbol{v}\) to \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v}\). The top arrow applies \(\boldsymbol{A}\) directly. The detour first computes the eigen-coordinates \(\boldsymbol{c}=\boldsymbol{P}^{-1}\boldsymbol{v}\), then scales each coordinate by its eigenvalue with \(\boldsymbol{D}=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)\), and finally returns to standard coordinates with \(\boldsymbol{P}\). Both routes give the same vector, which is the equation \(\boldsymbol{A}=\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{P}^{-1}\) read from right to left.

Move \(t\): the grid drawn along the eigenvectors \(\boldsymbol{p}_1,\boldsymbol{p}_2\) keeps its directions and only stretches, by \(\lambda_1\) along \(\boldsymbol{p}_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) along \(\boldsymbol{p}_2\). That is \(\boldsymbol{A}=\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{P}^{-1}\) read in the basis \(\boldsymbol{p}_1,\boldsymbol{p}_2\).

In practice, find the eigenvalues as roots of the characteristic polynomial, find a basis of each kernel \(\ker(\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda\boldsymbol{I})\), and put these eigenvectors as the columns of \(\boldsymbol{P}\), with the eigenvalues in the same order on the diagonal of \(\boldsymbol{D}\). This succeeds exactly when there are \(n\) independent eigenvectors. The result is not unique: reordering or rescaling the eigenvectors, with the eigenvalues following, gives another valid pair.

The payoff is in powers. The inner factors cancel in \(\boldsymbol{A}^k=\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{P}^{-1}\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{P}^{-1}\cdots\), leaving \(\boldsymbol{A}^k=\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{D}^k\boldsymbol{P}^{-1}\), where \(\boldsymbol{D}^k\) raises each eigenvalue to the power \(k\). For \(\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}\), with eigenvalues \(3\) and \(1\), this gives \(\tfrac{1}{2}(3^k+1)\) on the diagonal of \(\boldsymbol{A}^k\) and \(\tfrac{1}{2}(3^k-1)\) off it. Powers of matrices return later in Math V, in linear difference systems.

A common slip is the order of the factors. With the eigenvectors as columns of \(\boldsymbol{P}\), the formula is \(\boldsymbol{A}=\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{P}^{-1}\), not \(\boldsymbol{P}^{-1}\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{P}\). Checking \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{P}=\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{D}\) column by column, which says \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{p}_i=\lambda_i\boldsymbol{p}_i\), settles it.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(\boldsymbol{A}=\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{P}^{-1}\), then \(\boldsymbol{A}^k=\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{D}^k\boldsymbol{P}^{-1}\).
  • The columns of \(\boldsymbol{P}\) are eigenvectors of \(\boldsymbol{A}\), and the diagonal entries of \(\boldsymbol{D}\) are the corresponding eigenvalues.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A diagonal matrix is already diagonalized with \(\boldsymbol{P}=\boldsymbol{I}\).
  • If \(\boldsymbol{A}\) has a basis of eigenvectors, then it is diagonalizable.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The dimension of a finite-dimensional vector space is the length of any basis of that vector space. It is denoted by \(\dim(V)\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Dimension counts how many independent directions are needed to describe every vector in the space: it is the number of vectors in a basis, and so the number of coordinates each vector gets. The definition makes sense because in a finite-dimensional vector space all bases have the same length.

The figure shows the three cases inside \(\mathbb{R}^3\). One nonzero arrow spans a line through the origin, of dimension \(1\). Two arrows that do not lie on one line span a plane through the origin, of dimension \(2\). Three independent arrows are needed for all of \(\mathbb{R}^3\), of dimension \(3\). The line and the plane are subspaces of \(\mathbb{R}^3\) with their own dimension, not the dimension \(3\) of the surrounding space.

Dimension can be read in two equivalent ways: it is the largest number of linearly independent vectors in \(V\), and the smallest number of vectors in a spanning list of \(V\). So in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) any three vectors are linearly dependent, and no single vector spans \(\mathbb{R}^2\). In the same way, a subspace never has a larger dimension than the space that contains it.

Dimension is not the number of vectors in the space: the line in the figure contains infinitely many vectors but has dimension \(1\). The zero space \(\{\boldsymbol{0}\}\) is the only space of dimension \(0\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Any two bases of a finite-dimensional vector space have the same length.
  • Every basis of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) contains exactly \(n\) vectors.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{R}^2\) has dimension \(2\).
  • The vector space of polynomials of degree at most \(2\) has dimension \(3\), with basis \((1,x,x^2)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(V_1,V_2,\ldots,V_m\) be subspaces of \(V\), and let \(W=V_1+V_2+\cdots+V_m\). If every \(\boldsymbol{w}\in W\) can be written in exactly one way as

\[ \boldsymbol{w}=\boldsymbol{v}_1+\boldsymbol{v}_2+\cdots+\boldsymbol{v}_m, \]

with \(\boldsymbol{v}_i\in V_i\), then \(W\) is the direct sum of the subspaces, denoted

\[ W=V_1\oplus V_2\oplus\cdots\oplus V_m. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A direct sum is a sum of subspaces in which every vector of the sum has only one decomposition: knowing \(\boldsymbol{w}\) determines each piece \(\boldsymbol{v}_i\in V_i\). The subspaces do not overlap in a way that would allow a vector to be split in two different ways.

In the figure, \(V_1\) and \(V_2\) are two different lines through the origin of \(\mathbb{R}^2\). The parallelogram rule writes \(\boldsymbol{w}\) as \(\boldsymbol{v}_1+\boldsymbol{v}_2\) with \(\boldsymbol{v}_1\) on \(V_1\) and \(\boldsymbol{v}_2\) on \(V_2\), and because the two lines meet only at \(\boldsymbol{0}\), there is no other way to do it. Every vector of the plane can be split like this, so \(\mathbb{R}^2=V_1\oplus V_2\).

For two subspaces, uniqueness is equivalent to \(V_1\cap V_2=\{\boldsymbol{0}\}\). If a nonzero \(\boldsymbol{u}\) lay in both, then \(\boldsymbol{0}+\boldsymbol{0}\) and \(\boldsymbol{u}+(-\boldsymbol{u})\) would be two different decompositions of \(\boldsymbol{0}\). Conversely, if \(\boldsymbol{v}_1+\boldsymbol{v}_2=\boldsymbol{v}_1'+\boldsymbol{v}_2'\), then \(\boldsymbol{v}_1-\boldsymbol{v}_1'=\boldsymbol{v}_2'-\boldsymbol{v}_2\) lies in both subspaces, so it is \(\boldsymbol{0}\) and the two decompositions agree. The idea is the same as in linear independence: uniqueness everywhere follows from uniqueness for \(\boldsymbol{0}\).

For three or more subspaces, checking the intersections in pairs is not enough. In \(\mathbb{R}^2\), the lines spanned by \((1,0)\), \((0,1)\) and \((1,1)\) meet pairwise only in \(\boldsymbol{0}\), yet \((1,1)\) is both \((1,0)+(0,1)+\boldsymbol{0}\) and \(\boldsymbol{0}+\boldsymbol{0}+(1,1)\), so their sum is not direct.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • For two subspaces, \(V_1+V_2\) is direct exactly when \(V_1\cap V_2=\{\boldsymbol{0}\}\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The \(x\)-axis and \(y\)-axis form a direct sum equal to \(\mathbb{R}^2\).
  • Let \(V_1=\{(a,0)\colon a\in\mathbb{R}\}\) and \(V_2=\{(0,b)\colon b\in\mathbb{R}\}\). The vector \((3,-2)\) has the decomposition \((3,0)+(0,-2)\). Any decomposition \((a,0)+(0,b)=(3,-2)\) forces \(a=3\) and \(b=-2\), so it is unique.

docs.title: Distance Between a Point and a Line
Definition
docs.text: The distance between a point \(\boldsymbol{A}\) and a line \(\boldsymbol{\ell}(t)\) is the shortest distance between \(\boldsymbol{A}\) and all points on the line.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The distance from a point to a line is the length of the shortest route from the point to the line. That shortest route is the perpendicular segment: the closest point on the line is the foot \(\boldsymbol{F}\) of the perpendicular from \(\boldsymbol{A}\).

The line passes through \(\boldsymbol{B}=\boldsymbol{\ell}(0)\) in the nonzero direction \(\boldsymbol{v}\). The vector \(\boldsymbol{A}-\boldsymbol{B}\) splits into a part along \(\boldsymbol{v}\) (dashed, from \(\boldsymbol{B}\) to \(\boldsymbol{F}\)) and a part perpendicular to \(\boldsymbol{v}\) (green, from \(\boldsymbol{F}\) to \(\boldsymbol{A}\)), and the distance is the length \(d=\|\boldsymbol{A}-\boldsymbol{F}\|\) of the second part, where

\[ \boldsymbol{F}=\boldsymbol{B}+\frac{(\boldsymbol{A}-\boldsymbol{B})\cdot \boldsymbol{v}}{\boldsymbol{v}\cdot \boldsymbol{v}}\,\boldsymbol{v}. \]

Move \(t\) along the line through \(\boldsymbol{B}\): the distance from \(\boldsymbol{A}\) to \(\boldsymbol{\ell}(t)\) (right panel) is smallest at the foot \(\boldsymbol{F}\) of the perpendicular.

The foot is the closest point because of Pythagoras. For any other point \(\boldsymbol{P}\) on the line, \(\boldsymbol{A}-\boldsymbol{F}\) is orthogonal to \(\boldsymbol{F}-\boldsymbol{P}\), so

\[ \|\boldsymbol{A}-\boldsymbol{P}\|^2=\|\boldsymbol{A}-\boldsymbol{F}\|^2+\|\boldsymbol{F}-\boldsymbol{P}\|^2, \]

which is larger than \(\|\boldsymbol{A}-\boldsymbol{F}\|^2\) when \(\boldsymbol{P}\neq\boldsymbol{F}\). The same answer comes from minimizing the quadratic function \(t\mapsto\|\boldsymbol{\ell}(t)-\boldsymbol{A}\|^2\) with a derivative. Both arguments work in every \(\mathbb{R}^n\). In \(\mathbb{R}^3\) there is also the formula \(d=\dfrac{\|(\boldsymbol{A}-\boldsymbol{B})\times \boldsymbol{v}\|}{\|\boldsymbol{v}\|}\), where \(\boldsymbol{a}\times \boldsymbol{b}=(a_2b_3-a_3b_2,\,a_3b_1-a_1b_3,\,a_1b_2-a_2b_1)\) is the cross product.

For a plane in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) through \(\boldsymbol{B}\) the roles swap: the distance from \(\boldsymbol{A}\) to the plane is the length of the part of \(\boldsymbol{A}-\boldsymbol{B}\) along a normal vector, not the part perpendicular to a direction.

A common slip is to take \(\|\boldsymbol{A}-\boldsymbol{B}\|\), the distance to the given point \(\boldsymbol{B}\) of the line. It is only an upper bound for \(d\), reached when \(\boldsymbol{B}\) happens to be the foot.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The distance is zero if and only if the point lies on the line.
  • In coordinates, the distance can be found by minimizing \(\|\boldsymbol{\ell}(t)-\boldsymbol{A}\|\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\boldsymbol{\ell}(t)=(1+t,2t,-1,2-t)\), a point on the line gives minimum distance \(0\).
  • A point not on the line has positive distance.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: Fix a field \(\mathbb{F}\). If \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is a linear operator with distinct eigenvalues \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n\in\mathbb{F}\) and corresponding eigenvectors \(\boldsymbol{v}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{v}_n\), then \((\boldsymbol{v}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{v}_n)\) is linearly independent.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Different eigenvalues produce genuinely different eigendirections. An eigenvector for \(\lambda_1\) is scaled by \(\lambda_1\) and one for \(\lambda_2\) by a different factor, so neither can be built as a linear combination of eigenvectors with other eigenvalues.

For two eigenvectors the argument is short. Suppose \(c_1\boldsymbol{v}_1+c_2\boldsymbol{v}_2=\boldsymbol{0}\). Applying \(\boldsymbol{A}\) gives \(c_1\lambda_1\boldsymbol{v}_1+c_2\lambda_2\boldsymbol{v}_2=\boldsymbol{0}\), and subtracting \(\lambda_2\) times the first equation leaves \(c_1(\lambda_1-\lambda_2)\boldsymbol{v}_1=\boldsymbol{0}\). Since \(\lambda_1\neq\lambda_2\) and the eigenvector \(\boldsymbol{v}_1\) is nonzero, \(c_1=0\), and then \(c_2=0\). The general case repeats this step, removing one eigenvector at a time.

Distinctness is exactly what the argument uses. Two eigenvectors for the same eigenvalue can be dependent, such as \(\boldsymbol{v}\) and \(2\boldsymbol{v}\), so the theorem takes one eigenvector per eigenvalue. It does not say that a repeated eigenvalue forces dependence: for \(\boldsymbol{I}_2\), the double eigenvalue \(1\) has the independent eigenvectors \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\).

The main use is the first Key Result. An \(n\times n\) matrix with \(n\) distinct eigenvalues in \(\mathbb{F}\) has \(n\) independent eigenvectors, which form a basis of \(\mathbb{F}^n\), an eigenbasis, so the matrix is diagonalizable. For example, \(\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}\) has the eigenvalues \(3\) and \(1\), so its eigenvectors \((1,1)\) and \((1,-1)\) form a basis of \(\mathbb{R}^2\) without further checking.

The condition is sufficient, not necessary. When an eigenvalue is repeated, the matrix may or may not be diagonalizable, and the algebraic and geometric multiplicities decide.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• An \(n\times n\) matrix with \(n\) distinct eigenvalues in \(\mathbb{F}\) is diagonalizable over \(\mathbb{F}\).
  • The theorem is a main reason eigenvectors can form useful bases.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A \(2\times2\) diagonal matrix with diagonal entries \(2\) and \(3\) has two independent eigenvectors.
  • A \(3\times3\) matrix with three distinct eigenvalues has three independent eigenvectors.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\star\) and \(\circ\) be binary operations on a set \(A\). The operation \(\star\) is left distributive over \(\circ\) if

\[ a\star(b\circ c)=(a\star b)\circ(a\star c) \]

for all \(a,b,c\in A\), and right distributive over \(\circ\) if

\[ (a\circ b)\star c=(a\star c)\circ(b\star c) \]

for all \(a,b,c\in A\). It is distributive over \(\circ\) if it is both left and right distributive.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Distributivity is the rule for multiplying out brackets, and read backwards, for factoring out a common factor. It is the law that connects two operations, whereas associativity and commutativity each concern a single operation.

The figure reads the first example, \(3(4+5)=3\cdot4+3\cdot5=27\), as areas. A rectangle of height \(3\) and width \(4+5=9\) has area \(3(4+5)\); cutting it where the width \(4\) ends splits it into rectangles of areas \(3\cdot4=12\) and \(3\cdot5=15\). Multiplying out the brackets is this cut, and factoring out the common factor \(3\) is gluing the two rectangles back together.

Drag \(\boldsymbol{x}\) and \(\boldsymbol{y}\) and change the scalars. Adding first and then scaling lands on the same point as scaling first and then adding: these are the two distributive laws of a vector space.

If \(\star\) is commutative, left and right distributivity are equivalent. For a non-commutative operation such as the matrix product of Week 3, both laws must be stated.

The order of the two operations matters: "\(\star\) distributes over \(\circ\)" is a different statement from "\(\circ\) distributes over \(\star\)". Multiplication of real numbers distributes over addition, but addition does not distribute over multiplication. Many algebra slips come from applying a distributive law that does not hold, such as splitting \(c/(a+b)\) into \(c/a+c/b\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A ring, and therefore a field, requires multiplication to be distributive over addition. Distributivity is the only ring axiom that links the two operations.
  • In any ring, \(a\cdot0=0\): distributivity gives \(a\cdot0=a\cdot(0+0)=a\cdot0+a\cdot0\), and adding \(-(a\cdot0)\) to both sides leaves \(0=a\cdot0\). The same argument on the right gives \(0\cdot a=0\).
  • In any ring, \((-a)b=-(ab)\): by distributivity \(ab+(-a)b=(a+(-a))b=0\cdot b=0\), so \((-a)b\) is the additive inverse of \(ab\). In particular \((-a)(-b)=ab\).
  • Repeated use gives the general laws \(a(b_1+\cdots+b_n)=ab_1+\cdots+ab_n\) and \((a+b)(c+d)=ac+ad+bc+bd\); the second needs both the left and the right law.
  • The vector space axioms of Week 2 contain two distributive laws for scalar multiplication: \(\alpha(\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{y})=\alpha\boldsymbol{x}+\alpha\boldsymbol{y}\) and \((\alpha+\beta)\boldsymbol{x}=\alpha\boldsymbol{x}+\beta\boldsymbol{x}\). Here the operations combine elements of two different sets, scalars and vectors.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Multiplication of real numbers distributes over addition: \(3(4+5)=3\cdot4+3\cdot5=27\).
  • Complex multiplication distributes over complex addition, which is how products are expanded: \((1+\mathrm{i})(2+3\mathrm{i})=2+3\mathrm{i}+2\mathrm{i}+3\mathrm{i}^2=-1+5\mathrm{i}\).
  • For sets, intersection distributes over union and union distributes over intersection: \(A\cap(B\cup C)=(A\cap B)\cup(A\cap C)\) and \(A\cup(B\cap C)=(A\cup B)\cap(A\cup C)\).
  • Addition of real numbers does not distribute over multiplication: \(1+(2\cdot3)=7\), but \((1+2)\cdot(1+3)=12\).
  • A one-sided law: on \(\mathbb{R}\) define \(a\star b=a\). Then \((a+b)\star c=a+b=(a\star c)+(b\star c)\), so \(\star\) is right distributive over \(+\); but \(1\star(1+1)=1\) while \((1\star1)+(1\star1)=2\), so it is not left distributive.
  • Division is right distributive over addition, \((a+b)/c=a/c+b/c\) for \(c\neq0\), but not left distributive: \(1/(1+1)=\tfrac{1}{2}\), whereas \(1/1+1/1=2\).
  • For powers of positive reals, \((ab)^c=a^cb^c\), so exponentiation is right distributive over multiplication; but \(2^{1\cdot1}=2\), whereas \(2^1\cdot2^1=4\).
  • For matrices of compatible sizes, the matrix product distributes over matrix addition on both sides: \(\boldsymbol{A}(\boldsymbol{B}+\boldsymbol{C})=\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{B}+\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{C}\) and \((\boldsymbol{B}+\boldsymbol{C})\boldsymbol{D}=\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{D}+\boldsymbol{C}\boldsymbol{D}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An eigenbasis is a basis of a vector space consisting entirely of eigenvectors of a linear operator.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An eigenbasis is a choice of coordinate directions in which the operator does nothing but stretch: each basis vector is sent to a multiple of itself. In an eigenbasis, the matrix of the operator is therefore diagonal, with the eigenvalues on the diagonal.

The left grid is drawn along the eigenvectors \(\boldsymbol{p}_1\) and \(\boldsymbol{p}_2\) of \(\boldsymbol{A}=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}\), with eigenvalues \(3\) and \(1\). After applying \(\boldsymbol{A}\), the grid is stretched three times in the \(\boldsymbol{p}_1\) direction and unchanged in the \(\boldsymbol{p}_2\) direction. The vector \(\boldsymbol{v}=\boldsymbol{p}_1+\boldsymbol{p}_2\) has coordinates \((1,1)\) in this basis and is sent to \(3\boldsymbol{p}_1+\boldsymbol{p}_2\), with coordinates \((3,1)\); in this basis the matrix of \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is \(\operatorname{diag}(3,1)\).

In the eigenbasis \(\boldsymbol{p}_1,\boldsymbol{p}_2\) the map only scales each basis vector, so its matrix is diagonal.

In general, if \(\boldsymbol{v}=c_1\boldsymbol{p}_1+\cdots+c_n\boldsymbol{p}_n\), then \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v}=\lambda_1c_1\boldsymbol{p}_1+\cdots+\lambda_nc_n\boldsymbol{p}_n\): each coordinate is multiplied by its own eigenvalue. Linear independence rules out several eigenvectors on one line, which cannot supply distinct coordinate directions, and the eigenvectors must span the whole space, so that every vector has such coordinates.

An eigenbasis exists exactly when the matrix is diagonalizable, and its vectors are the columns of \(\boldsymbol{P}\) in diagonalization. The distinct eigenvalues theorem guarantees one when an \(n\times n\) matrix has \(n\) distinct eigenvalues. Not every matrix has one: the eigenvectors of the shear \(\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\) all lie on the horizontal axis.

An eigenbasis is not unique. Each eigenvector may be rescaled and the order may change, and for \(\boldsymbol{I}_n\) every basis is an eigenbasis.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A matrix is diagonalizable exactly when an eigenbasis exists.
  • The change-of-basis matrix \(\boldsymbol{P}\) in diagonalization has eigenbasis vectors as its columns.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The standard basis is an eigenbasis for a diagonal matrix.
  • If two independent eigenvectors span \(\mathbb{R}^2\), they form an eigenbasis.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a linear operator or square matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}\), a nonzero vector \(\boldsymbol{p}\) and scalar \(\lambda\) satisfying \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{p}=\lambda \boldsymbol{p}\) give an eigenvector \(\boldsymbol{p}\) and corresponding eigenvalue \(\lambda\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
For a real eigenvector with a real eigenvalue, the line it spans is invariant under the transformation. A positive eigenvalue preserves its direction, a negative eigenvalue reverses it, and a zero eigenvalue maps it to the zero vector. The equation \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{p}=\lambda \boldsymbol{p}\) also defines eigenvectors and eigenvalues over the complex numbers.

\(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{p}=\lambda \boldsymbol{p}\) with \(\boldsymbol{p}\neq\boldsymbol{0}\): \(\boldsymbol{A}\) only rescales \(\boldsymbol{p}\), by the eigenvalue \(\lambda\). Here \(\boldsymbol{A}=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}\) has \(\lambda_1=3\) on \(\boldsymbol{p}_1=\binom{1}{1}\) and \(\lambda_2=1\) on \(\boldsymbol{p}_2=\binom{1}{-1}\); a vector \(\boldsymbol{v}\) off these lines is turned.

Turn the unit vector \(\boldsymbol{x}\) with \(\varphi\): usually \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\) points elsewhere, but on the dashed eigenvector lines \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}=\lambda \boldsymbol{x}\). A quarter turn has no real eigenvector.

The vector space supplies both the vectors and the scalar multiplication in \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{p}=\lambda\boldsymbol{p}\); this equation compares two vectors in that same space.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The zero vector is excluded from being an eigenvector.
  • Eigenvalues of triangular or diagonal matrices are their diagonal entries.
  • For a real-valued matrix, nonreal complex eigenvalues and eigenvectors occur in complex conjugate pairs.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\boldsymbol{A}=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}\), \((1,0)\) is an eigenvector with eigenvalue \(2\).
  • For the same matrix, \((0,1)\) is an eigenvector with eigenvalue \(3\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: For any square matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}\) with entries in a field \(\mathbb{F}\), the eigenvalues of \(\boldsymbol{A}\) are exactly the roots in \(\mathbb{F}\) of its characteristic polynomial \(\det(\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda \boldsymbol{I})\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The theorem makes eigenvalues computable. The definition \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{p}=\lambda\boldsymbol{p}\) involves the unknown vector \(\boldsymbol{p}\) as well as \(\lambda\); the theorem removes \(\boldsymbol{p}\) and leaves one equation in \(\lambda\) alone, \(\det(\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda\boldsymbol{I})=0\).

The proof is a chain of equivalences. Using the identity matrix, \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{p}=\lambda\boldsymbol{p}\) becomes \((\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda\boldsymbol{I})\boldsymbol{p}=\boldsymbol{0}\). So \(\lambda\) is an eigenvalue if and only if this system has a solution \(\boldsymbol{p}\neq\boldsymbol{0}\), if and only if the kernel of \(\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda\boldsymbol{I}\) is not \(\{\boldsymbol{0}\}\), if and only if this square matrix is singular, if and only if its determinant is \(0\).

The phrase "roots in \(\mathbb{F}\)" matters. For \(\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}\) the characteristic polynomial is \(\lambda^2-2\lambda+5\), with roots \(1\pm2\mathrm{i}\). Over \(\mathbb{C}\) these are eigenvalues; over \(\mathbb{R}\) the matrix has none, since no real \(\lambda\) makes \(\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda\boldsymbol{I}\) singular.

In practice the theorem splits the eigenvalue problem into two steps: first find the roots of the characteristic polynomial, then, for each root, solve the homogeneous system \((\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda\boldsymbol{I})\boldsymbol{p}=\boldsymbol{0}\), for instance by Gauss-Jordan elimination, to find the eigenvectors. The number of times a root is repeated is its algebraic multiplicity.

The determinant step gives only \(\lambda\), not the eigenvectors. And the homogeneous system always has the solution \(\boldsymbol{p}=\boldsymbol{0}\), which does not count: if elimination finds no other solution, the value of \(\lambda\) was not a root after all.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\lambda\) is an eigenvalue if and only if \(\det(\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda \boldsymbol{I})=0\).
  • Every eigenvalue has at least one corresponding eigenvector.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For a diagonal matrix, the roots are precisely the diagonal entries.
  • For \(\boldsymbol{A}=\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}\), the eigenvalues are \(1\pm2\mathrm{i}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An elementary row operation is one of three reversible operations on a system or matrix: adding a multiple of one row to another, interchanging two rows, or multiplying a row by a nonzero scalar.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Elementary row operations are the steps used to solve equations by hand, written for the rows of a matrix: swap two equations, multiply an equation by a nonzero number, or add a multiple of one equation to another. They transform a system without changing its solution set.

Each row of the figure applies one operation to the same matrix. Swapping \(\boldsymbol{R}_1\) and \(\boldsymbol{R}_2\) only reorders the rows; \(\boldsymbol{R}_2\to\tfrac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{R}_2\) turns \((4,5,6)\) into \((2,2.5,3)\); and \(\boldsymbol{R}_3\to\boldsymbol{R}_3-7\boldsymbol{R}_1\) turns \((7,8,9)\) into \((0,-6,-12)\), creating a zero below the first entry.

Replace \(\boldsymbol{R}_2\) by \(\boldsymbol{R}_2+k\boldsymbol{R}_1\): the second line swings about the solution, which never moves. The button picks the \(k\) that eliminates \(x_1\).

The solutions are kept because every operation can be undone by one of the same kind: a swap by the same swap, scaling by \(c\) by scaling by \(1/c\), and adding \(k\boldsymbol{R}_1\) to \(\boldsymbol{R}_2\) by adding \(-k\boldsymbol{R}_1\), so the two systems are equivalent. The scalar must be nonzero: multiplying a row by \(0\) replaces an equation by \(0=0\), which cannot be undone and can add solutions. Each operation can also be written as multiplication on the left by an elementary matrix, obtained by applying the same operation to the identity matrix.

The same operations drive the simplex pivot in OR Modelling. A common slip is to change two rows at once from the old rows: replacing \(\boldsymbol{R}_1\) by \(\boldsymbol{R}_1-\boldsymbol{R}_2\) and at the same time \(\boldsymbol{R}_2\) by \(\boldsymbol{R}_2-\boldsymbol{R}_1\) gives two rows that are negatives of each other, so one equation is lost.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Elementary row operations preserve equivalence of systems.
  • Gauss-Jordan elimination consists of applying elementary row operations until reduced row echelon form is reached.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Replace \(\boldsymbol{R}_2\) by \(\boldsymbol{R}_2-3\boldsymbol{R}_1\).
  • Swap \(\boldsymbol{R}_1\) and \(\boldsymbol{R}_3\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
An equivalence relation on a set \(A\) is a relation \(\sim\) on \(A\) such that, for all \(a,b,c\in A\), it is:

  1. reflexive: \(a\sim a\);
  2. symmetric: if \(a\sim b\), then \(b\sim a\);
  3. transitive: if \(a\sim b\) and \(b\sim c\), then \(a\sim c\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An equivalence relation formalizes when different objects should be treated as the same for a particular purpose, for example integers that leave the same remainder after division by \(3\), or sets of the same cardinality.

In the figure \(x\sim y\) if and only if \(x\) and \(y\) leave the same remainder after division by \(3\), on the set \(A=\{0,1,\ldots,8\}\), labelled \(X\) in the figure. The relation sorts the nine numbers into the three equivalence classes \([0]=\{0,3,6\}\), \([1]=\{1,4,7\}\) and \([2]=\{2,5,8\}\), where \([x]=\{y\in A\colon y\sim x\}\). The classes partition \(A\): every element lies in exactly one class, and \([x]=[y]\) if and only if \(x\sim y\).

Each property has a job. Reflexivity puts \(x\) into its own class \([x]\), so no element is left out. Symmetry and transitivity prevent classes from overlapping without being equal: if \(z\) lies in both \([x]\) and \([y]\), then \(x\sim z\) and \(z\sim y\), so \(x\sim y\) and the two classes coincide. Without one of them this breaks down. The relation \(\le\) on \(\mathbb{R}\) is reflexive and transitive but not symmetric, and "differ by at most \(1\)" is reflexive and symmetric but not transitive: \(0\) is related to \(1\) and \(1\) to \(2\), but \(0\) is not related to \(2\).

Equal cardinality is another example: it relates two sets when there is a bijection between them.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • Equal cardinality is an equivalence relation on sets.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Congruence modulo \(n\) is an equivalence relation on integers.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Two systems of equations are equivalent if they have the same solution set.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Two systems are equivalent when they have exactly the same solutions, so they contain the same mathematical information even if their equations look different. Solving a system means replacing it by ever simpler equivalent systems until the solutions can be read off.

On the left, the lines \(x_1+x_2=3\) and \(x_1-x_2=1\) meet at \((2,1)\). The row operation \(\boldsymbol{R}_2\to\boldsymbol{R}_2-\boldsymbol{R}_1\) gives \(-2x_2=-2\), scaling by \(-\tfrac{1}{2}\) gives \(x_2=1\), and \(\boldsymbol{R}_1\to\boldsymbol{R}_1-\boldsymbol{R}_2\) then gives \(x_1=2\). On the right these two equations are a vertical and a horizontal line: different lines, but they meet in the same point, so the solution set \(\{(2,1)\}\) is unchanged.

Every \(k\) gives a different-looking system with the same solution set: the systems are equivalent.

The definition compares only solution sets; the number of equations, their order and their coefficients may all differ. Adding the equation \(2x_1=4\), the sum of the two original equations, gives a system of three equations that is still equivalent to the original two. Elementary row operations produce equivalent systems because each can be undone. Steps that cannot be undone may change the solution set: \(x=1\) has solution set \(\{1\}\), but after squaring, \(x^2=1\) has solution set \(\{-1,1\}\).

Because "having the same solution set" is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, equivalence of systems is an equivalence relation. Note that any two systems without solutions are equivalent, since both have the empty set as solution set, even if they share no equation.

docs.text:
• Elementary row operations produce equivalent systems.
  • Solving a system by elimination means replacing it by easier equivalent systems.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(x+y=2\), \(x-y=0\) is equivalent to \(x=1\), \(y=1\).
  • Swapping the order of equations gives an equivalent system.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The Euclidean distance between two points \(\boldsymbol{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) and \(\boldsymbol{y}=(y_1,\ldots,y_n)\) in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is \(d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})=\|\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{y}\|=\sqrt{(x_1-y_1)^2+\cdots+(x_n-y_n)^2}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Euclidean distance is the ordinary straight-line distance, inherited from the Euclidean norm: the distance between two points is the length of the vector from one to the other.

From \(\boldsymbol{P}=(1,1)\) to \(\boldsymbol{Q}=(4,3)\) the coordinates change by \(3\) horizontally and \(2\) vertically. These differences are the legs of a right triangle, so by Pythagoras \(d(\boldsymbol{P},\boldsymbol{Q})=\sqrt{3^2+2^2}=\sqrt{13}\). In \(\mathbb{R}^n\) the formula adds one squared difference per coordinate.

Drag the points \(\boldsymbol{x}\) and \(\boldsymbol{y}\): the distance is the length of \(\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{y}\), the hypotenuse of a right triangle with the coordinate differences as legs.

The squares remove the signs, so \(d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})=d(\boldsymbol{y},\boldsymbol{x})\), and \(d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})=0\) only when \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{y}\). For \(n=1\) the formula reduces to \(|x_1-y_1|\), the distance on the real line given by the absolute value. A detour is never shorter: \(d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{z})\le d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})+d(\boldsymbol{y},\boldsymbol{z})\) is the triangle inequality for the norm. OR Modelling uses these distances as edge lengths in a Euclidean network.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The distance between two points is the length of the vector connecting them.
  • The distance from a point to a line is the minimum Euclidean distance from the point to points on the line.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A Euclidean space is a pair \((V,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)\) of a real vector space \(V\) with \(\dim V<\infty\) and an inner product \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\colon V\times V\to\mathbb{R}\); in other words, a finite-dimensional real inner product space.

The standard example, and the one meant by the Euclidean space \(\mathbb{R}^n\), is the real coordinate space \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with the dot product \(\boldsymbol{x}\cdot \boldsymbol{y}=x_1y_1+\cdots+x_ny_n\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Euclidean space is the setting for ordinary geometry in linear algebra. A vector space on its own only knows how to add and scale vectors; the inner product adds the measurements, namely lengths, distances and angles.

In \(\mathbb{R}^2\) with the dot product, every quantity in the figure comes from the inner product: the length \(\|\boldsymbol{x}\|=\sqrt{4^2+1^2}=\sqrt{17}\), the inner product \(\langle\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}\rangle=4\cdot1+1\cdot3=7\), the angle through \(\cos\theta=\dfrac{7}{\sqrt{17}\sqrt{10}}\), so \(\theta\approx57.5^\circ\), and the distance between the tips, \(d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})=\|(3,-2)\|=\sqrt{13}\).

Each part of the definition has a role. The space is real because lengths and angles are real numbers. It is finite-dimensional, which makes every Euclidean space look like \(\mathbb{R}^n\), as the Key Results explain. And the inner product is part of the data: the same vector space \(\mathbb{R}^2\) with the inner product \(2x_1y_1+x_2y_2\) from the Examples has different lengths and angles, so its unit circle is an ellipse in the usual picture.

In \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with the dot product, the Euclidean norm, the Euclidean distance, the angle between vectors and orthogonality all come from this one inner product, and so does the description of planes and hyperplanes by normal vectors.

A common slip is to identify Euclidean space with the set \(\mathbb{R}^n\). The set alone carries no geometry; it becomes the Euclidean space \(\mathbb{R}^n\) together with the dot product.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The inner product induces the norm \(\|\boldsymbol{x}\|=\sqrt{\langle \boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}\rangle}\) and the distance \(d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})=\|\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{y}\|\); on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with the dot product these are the Euclidean norm and the Euclidean distance.
  • The inner product also defines the angle between vectors and orthogonality.
  • Every \(n\)-dimensional Euclidean space is isomorphic to \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with the dot product by a linear bijection that preserves the inner product: write each vector in coordinates with respect to an orthonormal basis, a basis of mutually orthogonal unit vectors.
  • Lines, planes, and hyperplanes are geometric objects in Euclidean spaces.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{R}^2\) with the dot product is the Euclidean plane; \(\mathbb{R}^3\) with the dot product is ordinary three-dimensional Euclidean space.
  • \(\mathbb{R}^2\) with \(\langle \boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}\rangle=2x_1y_1+x_2y_2\) is also a Euclidean space; its unit circle \(\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\langle \boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}\rangle=1\}\) is an ellipse in the usual picture of the plane.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: For any \(z\in\mathbb{C}\), we have \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}z}=\cos z+\mathrm{i}\sin z.\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Euler's formula connects the complex exponential with trigonometry. For a real angle \(\theta\) it says that \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}=\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta\) is the point of modulus one and angle \(\theta\) in the polar coordinates of the complex plane.

The point \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}\) lies on the unit circle at the angle \(\theta\) from the positive real axis, and the dashed lines meet the axes at its real part \(\cos\theta\) and its imaginary part \(\sin\theta\). As \(\theta\) grows the point runs anticlockwise round the circle: \(\theta=0,\pi/2,\pi,3\pi/2\) give the marked points \(1\), \(\mathrm{i}\), \(-1\) and \(-\mathrm{i}\). So \(|\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}|=1\) for every real \(\theta\): multiplying by \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}\) is a rotation by \(\theta\), not a stretch.

Move the real angle \(\theta\): \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}\) runs round the unit circle, with real part \(\cos\theta\) and imaginary part \(\sin\theta\).

The reason lies in the series defining the complex exponential and the complex sine and cosine. Substitute \(\mathrm{i}z\) into the exponential series. The powers of \(\mathrm{i}\) repeat in the cycle \(1,\mathrm{i},-1,-\mathrm{i}\), so the even terms contain no \(\mathrm{i}\) and alternate in sign, which gives the cosine series, while the odd terms all contain a factor \(\mathrm{i}\) and give \(\mathrm{i}\) times the sine series.

With the formula, the polar form becomes \(z=r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\varphi}\), and De Moivre's formula becomes \((\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\varphi})^n=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}n\varphi}\); the angle \(\pi\) gives Euler's identity. The unit-circle reading is for real angles only. The formula holds for every complex \(z\), but then \(\cos z\) and \(\sin z\) need not be real and \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}z}\) need not lie on the unit circle: for \(z=\mathrm{i}\), \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\cdot\mathrm{i}}=\mathrm{e}^{-1}\approx0.37\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• We have \(|\mathrm{e}^z| = \mathrm{e}^{\operatorname{Re}(z)}\) and \(\arg(\mathrm{e}^z) = \operatorname{Im}(z) + 2\pi k .\)
  • We have \(\cos\theta = \dfrac{\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta} + \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\theta}}{2}\) and \(\sin\theta = \dfrac{\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta} - \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\theta}}{2\mathrm{i}}.\)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • When \(z=\pi\), we get the well-known Euler's identity.

docs.title: Corollary
docs.text: Setting \(z=\pi\) in Euler's formula gives \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi}+1=0.\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Euler's identity is Euler's formula at the angle \(\pi\). For a real angle \(\theta\), \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}=\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta\) is the point on the unit circle at angle \(\theta\), and \(\theta=\pi\) is half a turn.

The red arc runs anticlockwise from \(1=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}0}\) through \(\mathrm{i}=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi/2}\) and ends at \(-1\): since \(\cos\pi=-1\) and \(\sin\pi=0\), the imaginary part vanishes and \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi}=-1\). Adding \(1\) to both sides gives \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi}+1=0\).

At \(\theta=\pi\) the point \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}\) has made half a turn from \(1\) to \(-1\), so \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi}+1=0\).

Read as multiplication, the identity says that multiplying by \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi}=-1\) is a half-turn about \(0\), that is, negation; two half-turns give \(\mathrm{e}^{2\pi\mathrm{i}}=1\). The identity is famous for joining the constants \(0\), \(1\), \(\pi\), \(\mathrm{e}\) and \(\mathrm{i}\) in one short equation, but mathematically it is just a special case of Euler's formula.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Euler's identity involves three basic arithmetic operations exactly once: addition, multiplication, and exponentiation.
  • It also links five fundamental mathematical constants: the additive identity \(0\), the multiplicative identity \(1\), the fundamental circle constant \(\pi\), the base of the natural exponential \(\mathrm{e}\), and the imaginary unit \(\mathrm{i}\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Substitute \(\theta=\pi\) into Euler's formula: \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi}=\cos\pi+\mathrm{i}\sin\pi=-1+\mathrm{i}\cdot0=-1\). Adding \(1\) gives \(0\). Thus multiplication by \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi}\) sends \(z=2+3\mathrm{i}\) to \((-1)(2+3\mathrm{i})=-2-3\mathrm{i}\), a half-turn about the origin.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A field is an algebraic structure \((F,+,\cdot)\) in which addition and multiplication behave like ordinary arithmetic: addition makes \(F\) an Abelian group, multiplication is associative and commutative and has an identity \(1\neq0\), every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse, and multiplication distributes over addition.

When a vector space is defined over a field \(F\), the elements of \(F\) are called scalars.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A field is a number system in which the four basic operations work as for the real numbers: one can add, subtract, multiply, and divide by any nonzero element. Equivalently, a field is a commutative ring with an identity \(1 e0\) in which every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse.

Each part of the definition supplies one operation. The Abelian group \((F,+)\) provides \(0\) and negatives \(-a\), hence subtraction \(a-b=a+(-b)\). The multiplicative inverses provide division, \(a/b=a\cdot b^{-1}\) for \(b eq0\). Distributivity is the only rule that links the two operations, and familiar facts such as \(0\cdot a=0\) and \((-1)\cdot a=-a\) follow from it.

\(\mathbb{Q}\), \(\mathbb{R}\) and \(\mathbb{C}\) are fields; \(\mathbb{Z}\) is not, since \(2x=1\) has no integer solution. Fields can also be finite. The set \(\{0,1\}\), with sums and products replaced by their remainders after division by \(2\), is a field. The same construction with remainders after division by \(4\) is not, because \(2\cdot x\) leaves the remainder \(0\) or \(2\) for every integer \(x\), never \(1\).

A common slip is to read the inverse condition as applying to all elements. It is required only for nonzero elements, and \(0\) never has a multiplicative inverse, because \(0\cdot b=0 eq1\) for every \(b\). So division by zero is undefined in every field.

Fields supply the scalars of vector spaces, most often \(\mathbb{R}\) or \(\mathbb{C}\); \(\mathbb{C}\) has the advantage of being algebraically closed.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• In a vector space over \(F\), scalar multiplication uses elements of \(F\).
  • The real numbers and complex numbers are fields; the integers are not a field because most nonzero integers do not have integer multiplicative inverses.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{R}\) with ordinary addition and multiplication is a field.
  • \(\mathbb{C}\) with ordinary addition and multiplication is a field.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A vector space \(V\) over a field \(\mathbb{F}\) is finite-dimensional if it has a finite spanning list: there are vectors \(\boldsymbol{v}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{v}_n\in V\) such that

\[ V=\operatorname{span}(\boldsymbol{v}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{v}_n). \]

Equivalently, every \(\boldsymbol{v}\in V\) is a linear combination \(\boldsymbol{v}=a_1\boldsymbol{v}_1+\cdots+a_n\boldsymbol{v}_n\) with coefficients in \(\mathbb{F}\). The zero vector space is included and has dimension zero. A vector space that is not finite-dimensional is called infinite-dimensional.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A vector space is finite-dimensional when finitely many vectors are enough to build every vector in it by linear combinations. This does not mean that the space contains only finitely many vectors: \(\mathbb{R}^2\) contains infinitely many vectors, but the two coordinate directions \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\) span it.

The condition lets the theory work with finite lists. A finite spanning list can be reduced to a basis by removing redundant vectors one at a time, and every basis then has the same finite length, the dimension. So each vector is described by a fixed, finite number of coordinates. The spaces \(\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(\mathbb{C}^n\) are finite-dimensional, and so is the space of polynomials of degree at most \(m\), which is spanned by \((1,x,\ldots,x^m)\).

Infinite-dimensional spaces exist as well. All real polynomials, of any degree, form a vector space. The polynomials in a finite list have degree at most some number \(d\), and so has every linear combination of them; the polynomial \(x^{d+1}\) is never reached. Hence no finite list spans this space.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A finite spanning list can be reduced to a basis.
  • Relative to a basis, every vector has a unique expression as a linear combination of the basis vectors.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The coordinate vectors \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\) span \(\mathbb{R}^2\).
  • The space \(\mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R})\) of polynomials of degree at most two is spanned by \((1,x,x^2)\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: The fundamental theorem of algebra states that every nonconstant polynomial with complex number coefficients has at least one root in \(\mathbb{C}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The theorem says that \(\mathbb{C}\) is large enough to solve all nonconstant single-variable polynomial equations over \(\mathbb{C}\). In \(\mathbb{R}\), by contrast, \(x^2+1=0\) has no solution.

The figure shows the roots of \(z^5-1\), that is, the solutions of \(z^5=1\). By De Moivre's formula a solution must have modulus \(1\), since \(|z|^5=1\), and an angle \(\varphi\) for which \(5\varphi\) is a multiple of \(2\pi\). This gives five points on the unit circle, \(2\pi/5\) apart. Only \(z=1\) is real: over \(\mathbb{R}\) the polynomial has one root, over \(\mathbb{C}\) it has five, as many as its degree.

Change the coefficients, even to complex ones: a polynomial of degree \(n\) always has exactly \(n\) roots in \(\mathbb{C}\), counted with multiplicity.

The theorem guarantees only one root, but that is enough to find all of them. If \(\lambda\) is a root, polynomial long division by \(z-\lambda\) leaves remainder \(0\) and a quotient of one degree lower, which again has a root if it is nonconstant. Repeating the step splits a polynomial of degree \(n\ge1\) into \(n\) linear factors, so it has exactly \(n\) roots counted with multiplicity; \(x^3\) has the single root \(0\), counted three times.

The word nonconstant is needed, since a nonzero constant polynomial has no root. The theorem says that roots exist, not how to compute them. For polynomials with real coefficients the non-real roots come in pairs by the complex conjugate root theorem, and in the language of fields the theorem says that \(\mathbb{C}\) is algebraically closed.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every complex polynomial of degree \(n\geq1\) has exactly \(n\) roots when counted with multiplicity.
  • Every complex polynomial of degree \(n\geq1\) can be factored into linear factors over \(\mathbb{C}\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(x^2+1\) has roots \(\mathrm{i}\) and \(-\mathrm{i}\) in \(\mathbb{C}\).
  • \(x^3\) has the root \(0\) with multiplicity \(3\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional vector space and let \(\boldsymbol{A} \in \mathcal{L}(V,W)\) be a linear map. Then

\[ \dim(\ker \boldsymbol{A}) + \dim(\operatorname{range} \boldsymbol{A}) = \dim V. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A linear map splits the dimension of its domain into directions lost to the kernel and directions that survive in the range. The kernel collects the input vectors sent to \(\boldsymbol{0}\); the dimension of the range counts the independent output directions that can actually be reached. The theorem says that these two counts always add up to \(\dim V\).

The map in the figure projects \(\mathbb{R}^3\) vertically onto the shaded plane, as \(\boldsymbol{v}\) drops onto \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v}\). The whole vertical line is sent to \(\boldsymbol{0}\), so \(\dim(\ker \boldsymbol{A})=1\), and the outputs fill the plane, so \(\dim(\operatorname{range}\boldsymbol{A})=2\): \(1+2=3=\dim\mathbb{R}^3\).

However you set \(\boldsymbol{A}\), \(\dim(\ker \boldsymbol{A})+\dim(\operatorname{range}\boldsymbol{A})=2\): what the kernel takes away, the range loses.

For an \(m\times n\) matrix, read as a map \(\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\), \(\dim V=n\) is the number of columns, \(\dim(\operatorname{range}\boldsymbol{A})\) is the rank, the number of pivots, and \(\dim(\ker \boldsymbol{A})\) is the number of free variables of the homogeneous system \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{0}\). The theorem is then the count "pivot columns plus free columns equals all columns".

If \(\dim V=\dim W\), a linear map is injective if and only if it is surjective: a kernel of dimension \(0\) leaves a range of full dimension. If \(\dim V>\dim W\), the range has dimension at most \(\dim W\), so the kernel is nonzero; for example, a homogeneous system with more unknowns than equations always has a nonzero solution.

A common misreading is to picture kernel and range as two pieces of \(V\). The kernel lies in \(V\), but the range lies in \(W\); only their dimensions add up.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The theorem is also called the rank-nullity theorem: the rank of \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is \(\dim(\operatorname{range}\boldsymbol{A})\) and its nullity is \(\dim(\ker \boldsymbol{A})\).
  • It connects injectivity, surjectivity, and dimension for finite-dimensional vector spaces.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(\boldsymbol{A}\colon\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R}^2\) has a one-dimensional kernel, then its range has dimension \(2\).
  • If \(V\) is finite-dimensional, \(\boldsymbol{A}\in\mathcal{L}(V)\) and \(\ker \boldsymbol{A}=\{\boldsymbol{0}\}\), then \(\dim(\operatorname{range}\boldsymbol{A})=\dim V\), so \(\operatorname{range}\boldsymbol{A}=V\) and \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is bijective.

docs.title: Algorithm
docs.text: Gauss-Jordan elimination is the algorithm that applies elementary row operations to an augmented matrix until it reaches reduced row echelon form.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Gauss-Jordan elimination solves linear systems by transforming them into equivalent systems whose solutions can be read off directly. It works column by column: create a pivot, use it to clear the entries below it, and finally clear the entries above the pivots as well.

The forward elimination uses the row additions \(\boldsymbol{R}_2+\tfrac{3}{2}\boldsymbol{R}_1\), \(\boldsymbol{R}_3+\boldsymbol{R}_1\), and \(\boldsymbol{R}_3-4\boldsymbol{R}_2\). Scaling the pivots to \(1\) and clearing the entries above them gives reduced row echelon form, from which \(\boldsymbol{x}=(2,3,-1)\) can be read without back substitution. Stopping at row echelon form and then solving by back substitution is called Gaussian elimination.

The final reduced row echelon form shows the type of solution set. A row \((0\;\cdots\;0\mid c)\) with \(c\neq0\) means that there is no solution. Otherwise each column without a pivot gives a free variable that can be chosen as a parameter, and the solution is unique if and only if every column of the coefficient part has a pivot, as in the figure. If the entry in the pivot position is \(0\), a lower row with a nonzero entry in that column is swapped up first; if there is none, the column gets no pivot.

The same steps appear in OR Modelling: a simplex pivot divides the pivot row by the pivot and subtracts multiples of it from all other rows of the tableau, which is one Gauss-Jordan step.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Gauss-Jordan elimination preserves the solution set of the system.
  • If the coefficient side of an augmented matrix becomes the identity matrix, the right side gives the unique solution.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The system \(3x+y-z=-4\), \(x+z=0\), \(3x-2y=-3\) reduces to \(x=-1\), \(y=0\), \(z=1\).
  • Gauss-Jordan elimination can also be used to compute inverse matrices by augmenting with \(\boldsymbol{I}_n\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A generalized eigenvector of a square matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}\) for eigenvalue \(\lambda\) is a nonzero vector \(\boldsymbol{v}\) such that \((\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda \boldsymbol{I})^k \boldsymbol{v}=\boldsymbol{0}\) for some positive integer \(k\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The identity matrix makes \(\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda\boldsymbol{I}\) subtract \(\lambda\boldsymbol{v}\) from the image of \(\boldsymbol{v}\). The defining equation places \(\boldsymbol{v}\) in the kernel of a power of this shifted matrix, even when it is not in the kernel of the first power.

Generalized eigenvectors replace missing ordinary eigenvectors for defective matrices.

A nonzero vector \(\boldsymbol{v}\) is a generalized eigenvector for \(\lambda\) if \((\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda \boldsymbol{I})^k\boldsymbol{v}=\boldsymbol{0}\) for some positive integer \(k\). The vector \(\boldsymbol{v}_1\) is an ordinary eigenvector, while the chain \(\boldsymbol{v}_3\to \boldsymbol{v}_2\to \boldsymbol{v}_1\to\boldsymbol{0}\) supplies further basis vectors for the defective matrix.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every ordinary eigenvector is a generalized eigenvector with \(k=1\).
  • Generalized eigenvectors are used to construct Jordan normal form.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \((\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda \boldsymbol{I})\boldsymbol{v}=\boldsymbol{0}\), then \(\boldsymbol{v}\) is an eigenvector and a generalized eigenvector.
  • If \((\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda \boldsymbol{I})^2\boldsymbol{v}=\boldsymbol{0}\) but \((\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda \boldsymbol{I})\boldsymbol{v}\neq\boldsymbol{0}\), then \(\boldsymbol{v}\) is generalized but not ordinary.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A group is a set \(A\) together with a binary operation \(\star\) such that:

  1. \(\star\) is associative;
  2. \(\star\) has an identity element;
  3. every element has an inverse element.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Associativity allows parentheses to move in \(a\star b\star c\) without changing the result. This makes repeated group operations unambiguous; it does not allow the factors to be reordered.

Groups capture the algebra of reversible operations.

The table shows addition modulo \(4\), which is associative and has identity \(0\). Each row contains a green \(0\), exhibiting an additive inverse; for example, \(1+3=0\) and \(2+2=0\). Each row and column is a permutation of \(\{0,1,2,3\}\). The symmetry of the table also shows that this group is Abelian.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every group is a monoid.
  • If the operation is also commutative, the group is Abelian.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • \((\mathbb{Z},+)\) is a group. \((\mathbb{N},+)\) is not a group because positive natural numbers do not have additive inverses in \(\mathbb{N}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Over \(\mathbb{R}\) or \(\mathbb{C}\), a linear system \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{b}\) is homogeneous if \(\boldsymbol{b}=\boldsymbol{0}\). It is inhomogeneous if \(\boldsymbol{b}\neq \boldsymbol{0}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The standard matrix form gathers all equations into \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{b}\). Homogeneity is the special choice in which the right-hand side is the zero vector, so the zero vector is automatically a solution.

A homogeneous system asks which vectors are mapped to zero. An inhomogeneous system asks which vectors are mapped to a specified nonzero right-hand side.

\(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{0}\) (here \(x_1+2x_2=0\)): the solutions form the subspace \(\ker \boldsymbol{A}\), so \(\boldsymbol{0}\) is always a solution and solutions can be added and scaled; for \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{b}\) (here \(x_1+2x_2=3\)) the solution set is \(\boldsymbol{x}_p+\ker \boldsymbol{A}\), for any one particular solution \(\boldsymbol{x}_p\), or empty.

With \(\boldsymbol{b}=\boldsymbol{0}\) both lines pass through the origin, so \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{0}\) always solves the system. Make the rows parallel for infinitely many solutions, or switch \(\boldsymbol{b}\) on.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A homogeneous system always has at least the trivial solution \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{0}\).
  • If a homogeneous system has more than one solution, then it has infinitely many solutions.
  • An inhomogeneous system may have no solution, one solution, or infinitely many solutions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{0}\) is homogeneous.
  • \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{b}\) with \(\boldsymbol{b}\neq \boldsymbol{0}\) is inhomogeneous.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(V\) be a vector space of dimension \(n\ge1\).

  • A linear hyperplane of \(V\) is a subspace \(H\) of dimension \(n-1\).
  • An affine hyperplane of \(V\) is a translate \(\boldsymbol{p}+H=\{\boldsymbol{p}+\boldsymbol{h}\colon \boldsymbol{h}\in H\}\) of a linear hyperplane \(H\), where \(\boldsymbol{p}\in V\).

In \(\mathbb{R}^n\) the affine hyperplanes are exactly the sets

\[ \{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\colon a_1x_1+\cdots+a_nx_n=d\}\quad \text{with }\boldsymbol{a}=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\neq\boldsymbol{0}, \]

and such a hyperplane is linear exactly when \(d=0\), that is, when it passes through the origin. Used without a qualifier in \(\mathbb{R}^n\), "hyperplane" usually means an affine hyperplane; some linear algebra texts reserve it for linear hyperplanes, so the qualifier is worth stating.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A hyperplane in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is the solution set of one nontrivial linear equation \(a_1x_1+\cdots+a_nx_n=d\). One equation removes one dimension, so a hyperplane has dimension \(n-1\); it generalizes lines in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) and planes in \(\mathbb{R}^3\).

In \(\mathbb{R}^2\) the linear hyperplane \(H=\{ oldsymbol{x}\colon oldsymbol{a}\cdot oldsymbol{x}=0\}\) with \( oldsymbol{a}=(-1,2)\) is the line \(-x_1+2x_2=0\) through the origin. The vector \( oldsymbol{a}\) is perpendicular to it: every vector along \(H\), such as \((2,1)\), has \( oldsymbol{a}\cdot oldsymbol{x}=0\). Changing the right-hand side to \(c eq0\) shifts the line parallel to itself, giving an affine hyperplane (dashed). The dashed line lies on the side away from \( oldsymbol{a}\), so there \(c<0\).

In \(\mathbb{R}^2\) the hyperplane \(a_1x_1+a_2x_2=d\) is a line with normal vector \( oldsymbol{n}=(a_1,a_2)\). Change \(d\) to shift it; drag \( oldsymbol{x}\) to see which side it is on.

The dimension count is the fundamental theorem of linear maps: \(H\) is the kernel of the linear map \( oldsymbol{x}\mapsto oldsymbol{a}\cdot oldsymbol{x}\) from \(\mathbb{R}^n\) to \(\mathbb{R}\), whose range is all of \(\mathbb{R}\) when \( oldsymbol{a} eq oldsymbol{0}\), so \(\dim H=n-1\). The condition \( oldsymbol{a} eq oldsymbol{0}\) matters: for \( oldsymbol{a}= oldsymbol{0}\) the equation reads \(0=d\) and describes all of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) or the empty set. The normal vector \( oldsymbol{a}\) fixes the direction of the hyperplane and \(d\) its position.

The inequality \( oldsymbol{a}\cdot oldsymbol{x}\le d\) describes a half-space, the hyperplane together with one side of it. The constraints of a linear program are such half-spaces and hyperplanes, so its feasible region is an intersection of them.

A common slip is to expect a line in \(\mathbb{R}^3\): there a hyperplane is a plane, and a line needs two independent equations.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The vector \(\boldsymbol{a}=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\) is a normal vector of the hyperplane \(a_1x_1+\cdots+a_nx_n=d\): it is orthogonal to every difference \(\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{y}\) of two of its points.
  • An affine hyperplane \(\boldsymbol{a}\cdot \boldsymbol{x}=d\) divides \(\mathbb{R}^n\) into the two closed half-spaces \(\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon \boldsymbol{a}\cdot \boldsymbol{x}\le d\}\) and \(\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon \boldsymbol{a}\cdot \boldsymbol{x}\ge d\}\), which meet exactly in the hyperplane.
  • The hyperplanes of \(\mathbb{R}^2\) are the lines and those of \(\mathbb{R}^3\) are the planes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(x+y=1\) is an affine hyperplane of \(\mathbb{R}^2\) that is not linear, since it misses the origin.
  • \(x+y+z=0\) is a linear hyperplane of \(\mathbb{R}^3\).
  • The \(xy\)-plane \(\{(x,y,z)\colon z=0\}\) is a linear hyperplane of \(\mathbb{R}^3\).
