docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
An idempotent matrix, or projection matrix, is a real square matrix \(\boldsymbol{P}\) satisfying \(\boldsymbol{P}^2=\boldsymbol{P}\).

Such a matrix projects onto its range: it maps every vector into the subspace \(\operatorname{range}(\boldsymbol{P})\) and leaves every vector of that subspace unchanged. A projection matrix that is also symmetric, \(\boldsymbol{P}^{\top}=\boldsymbol{P}\), is an orthogonal projection matrix; the others are oblique projections. In statistics and econometrics "projection matrix" usually means the orthogonal case, such as the hat matrix \(\boldsymbol{X}(\boldsymbol{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{X})^{-1}\boldsymbol{X}^{\top}\) of least squares, for \(\boldsymbol{X}\) of full column rank.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The square \(\boldsymbol{P}^2\) is a matrix product, representing two successive applications of the same linear map. Idempotence says this composition equals one application.

Applying an idempotent matrix twice has the same effect as applying it once: projecting a vector that already lies in the subspace leaves it where it is.

\(\boldsymbol{A}^2=\boldsymbol{A}\): \(\boldsymbol{A}(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v})=\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v}\), so vectors of \(\operatorname{range}\boldsymbol{A}\) stay fixed (\(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{w}=\boldsymbol{w}\)) and \(\ker \boldsymbol{A}\) is killed (\(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{k}=\boldsymbol{0}\)). Every \(\boldsymbol{v}\) splits as \(\boldsymbol{w}+\boldsymbol{k}\) with \(\boldsymbol{w}\in\operatorname{range}\boldsymbol{A}\), \(\boldsymbol{k}\in\ker \boldsymbol{A}\) (a direct sum). The eigenvalues are \(0\) and \(1\) only; the projection need not be orthogonal (here it is oblique).

For every \(a\) and direction \(d\) the matrix \(\boldsymbol{P}\) satisfies \(\boldsymbol{P}^2=\boldsymbol{P}\). The orthogonal case is also symmetric; the oblique one is not.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The zero square matrix and identity matrix are idempotent.
  • If an idempotent matrix is invertible, then it equals the identity matrix.
  • If \(\boldsymbol{P}\) is idempotent, then every vector splits as \(\boldsymbol{v}=\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{v}+(\boldsymbol{v}-\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{v})\) with \(\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{v}\in\operatorname{range}(\boldsymbol{P})\) and \(\boldsymbol{v}-\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{v}\in\ker(\boldsymbol{P})\), so the space is the direct sum \(\operatorname{range}(\boldsymbol{P})\oplus\ker(\boldsymbol{P})\): \(\boldsymbol{P}\) projects onto its range along its kernel.
  • If \(\boldsymbol{P}\) is idempotent, so is \(\boldsymbol{I}-\boldsymbol{P}\); it projects onto \(\ker(\boldsymbol{P})\) along \(\operatorname{range}(\boldsymbol{P})\).
  • The only possible eigenvalues of an idempotent matrix are \(0\) and \(1\).
  • An orthogonal projection matrix is symmetric and idempotent; then \(\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{v}\) is the point of \(\operatorname{range}(\boldsymbol{P})\) closest to \(\boldsymbol{v}\), and \(\boldsymbol{v}-\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{v}\) is orthogonal to \(\operatorname{range}(\boldsymbol{P})\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\boldsymbol{I}_n^2=\boldsymbol{I}_n\), so \(\boldsymbol{I}_n\) is idempotent: it projects every vector onto the whole space.
  • \(\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\) is idempotent and symmetric: the orthogonal projection onto the \(x\)-axis.
  • \(\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\) is idempotent but not symmetric: an oblique projection onto the \(x\)-axis along the line spanned by \((1,-1)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
An identity element for a binary operation \(\star\) on \(A\) is an element \(e\in A\) such that

\[ a\star e=e\star a=a \]

for all \(a\in A\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The identity element leaves every element unchanged under the operation: combining it with any \(a\), on either side, gives \(a\) back. Which element this is depends on the operation: \(0\) for addition, \(1\) for multiplication, and the function \(x\mapsto x\) for composition of functions from a set to itself.

Both sides matter. For subtraction on \(\mathbb{Z}\), \(a-0=a\) but \(0-a=-a\), so \(0\) works only on the right and subtraction has no identity element. Addition on \(\{1,2,3,\ldots\}\) has none on either side.

If an identity exists, it is unique: for identities \(e\) and \(e'\), \(e\star e'=e\) because \(e'\) is an identity and \(e\star e'=e'\) because \(e\) is one, so \(e=e'\). This is why one speaks of the identity and can define inverse elements with respect to it; the identity matrix plays this role later for matrix multiplication.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If an identity element exists, it is unique.
  • Associativity, identity elements, and inverse elements determine which algebraic structure is present.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • \(0\) is the identity for addition; \(1\) is the identity for multiplication.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The identity matrix \(\boldsymbol{I}_n\) is the \(n\times n\) matrix with \(1\) on the main diagonal and \(0\) everywhere else.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The identity matrix acts like the number \(1\) for matrix multiplication: multiplying by it changes nothing. Its columns are the standard basis vectors \(\boldsymbol{e}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{e}_n\) of \(\mathbb{R}^n\).

The left part shows \(\boldsymbol{I}_3\) with its ones on the main diagonal shaded. The right part shows the map \(\boldsymbol{v}\mapsto\boldsymbol{I}\boldsymbol{v}\) in the plane, given by \(\boldsymbol{I}_2\): the square and the vector \(\boldsymbol{v}\) stay where they are, since \(\boldsymbol{I}\boldsymbol{v}=\boldsymbol{v}\). As a linear map, \(\boldsymbol{I}\) is the identity function.

The reason is visible in the row-times-column rule: row \(i\) of \(\boldsymbol{I}\) has a single \(1\), in position \(i\), so multiplying it with a column picks out the \(i\)th entry of that column and nothing else. In the language of algebraic structures, \(\boldsymbol{I}_n\) is the identity element for multiplication of \(n\times n\) matrices. The subscript gives the size and is dropped when the size is clear from the product; for a non-square \(\boldsymbol{A}\), the identity on the left and the one on the right have different sizes.

The identity matrix is also the target of Gauss-Jordan elimination: when the coefficient part of an augmented matrix has become \(\boldsymbol{I}\), the system has a unique solution, which stands in the last column. Elementary matrices are obtained from \(\boldsymbol{I}\) by one row operation. The identity matrix returns later in the definition of the inverse matrix, \(\boldsymbol{A}^{-1}\boldsymbol{A}=\boldsymbol{I}\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For every \(m\times n\) matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}\), \(\boldsymbol{I}_m\boldsymbol{A}=\boldsymbol{A}\) and \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{I}_n=\boldsymbol{A}\).
  • The identity matrix is diagonal, symmetric, triangular, idempotent, and a permutation matrix.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\boldsymbol{I}_2=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\).
  • \(\boldsymbol{I}_3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The imaginary unit, symbolized as \(\mathrm{i}\), is characterized by its square being \(-1\), i.e., \(\mathrm{i}^2 = -1.\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Integer powers mean repeated multiplication, so \(\mathrm{i}^2=-1\) implies \(\mathrm{i}^3=-\mathrm{i}\) and \(\mathrm{i}^4=1\). Higher powers therefore repeat in a cycle of length four.

The imaginary unit \(\mathrm{i}\) is a solution, not the solution, to the equation \(x^2+1=0\) since \(-\mathrm{i}\) is also a solution.

The choice of \(\mathrm{i}\) over \(-\mathrm{i}\) as the "principal" square root of \(-1\) is largely a matter of convention, similar to how we choose the positive square root of a positive number as its principal square root.

\(\mathrm{i}^2=-1\): multiplying by \(\mathrm{i}\) is a rotation by \(90^\circ\), so four multiplications return to the start (\(\mathrm{i}^4=1\)).

Drag \(z\): multiplying by \(\mathrm{i}\) turns it a quarter turn, and doing it twice gives \(\mathrm{i}^2z=-z\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Complex numbers extend the real numbers by adding a solution of \(x^2=-1\).
  • The complex numbers form a field, so they can be used as scalars in complex vector spaces.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\mathrm{i}^3 = \mathrm{i}^2 \cdot\mathrm{i} = (-1) \cdot \mathrm{i} = -\mathrm{i}, \quad \mathrm{i}^4 = \mathrm{i}^3 \cdot \mathrm{i} = (-\mathrm{i})\cdot \mathrm{i} = 1, \quad \mathrm{i}^5 = \mathrm{i}^4 \cdot \mathrm{i} =\mathrm{i}.\)
  • The roots of \(x^2+x+1=0\) are \(x_{1,2}=\dfrac{-1\pm\sqrt{3}\mathrm{i}}{2}\).
  • For \(z=3+4\mathrm{i}\), the real part is \(3\), the imaginary part is \(4\), and \(|z|=5\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For vectors \(\boldsymbol{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) and \(\boldsymbol{y}=(y_1,\ldots,y_n)\) in \(\mathbb{R}^n\), the dot product, or standard inner product, is

\[ \boldsymbol{x}\cdot \boldsymbol{y}=x_1y_1+x_2y_2+\cdots+x_ny_n. \]

More generally, an inner product on a real vector space \(V\) is a function \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\colon V\times V\to\mathbb{R}\) that is

  • symmetric: \(\langle \boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}\rangle=\langle \boldsymbol{y},\boldsymbol{x}\rangle\);
  • linear in the first argument, \(\langle \alpha \boldsymbol{x}+\beta \boldsymbol{y},\boldsymbol{z}\rangle=\alpha\langle \boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{z}\rangle+\beta\langle \boldsymbol{y},\boldsymbol{z}\rangle\), and hence, by symmetry, in the second;
  • positive definite: \(\langle \boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}\rangle>0\) for every \(\boldsymbol{x}\neq\boldsymbol{0}\).

The dot product is an inner product on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), and it is the one meant when Math II speaks of the inner product of two vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^n\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The inner product combines two vectors into one number that measures how much they point in the same direction. Length, distance, angle and orthogonality are all defined from it.

Dropping a perpendicular from the tip of \(\boldsymbol{y}\) onto the line of \(\boldsymbol{x}\) gives the green segment of signed length \(\|\boldsymbol{y}\|\cos\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the angle between the vectors and \(\|\cdot\|\) the Euclidean norm. The dot product is \(\|\boldsymbol{x}\|\) times this signed length, \(\boldsymbol{x}\cdot \boldsymbol{y}=\|\boldsymbol{x}\|\,\|\boldsymbol{y}\|\cos\theta\): positive for an acute angle as drawn, zero for a right angle, and negative for an obtuse angle, when the foot falls on the other side of the origin.

Drag \(\boldsymbol{x}\) and \(\boldsymbol{y}\): \(\boldsymbol{x}\cdot \boldsymbol{y}\) is positive when they point roughly the same way, zero at a right angle and negative when they point apart. The thick segment is the shadow of \(\boldsymbol{x}\) on the line of \(\boldsymbol{y}\).

Each property in the general definition has a role: symmetry says the order does not matter; linearity lets inner products be expanded like products of numbers, as in \(\|\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{y}\|^2=\|\boldsymbol{x}\|^2+2\,\boldsymbol{x}\cdot \boldsymbol{y}+\|\boldsymbol{y}\|^2\); positive definiteness gives every nonzero vector a positive length.

The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality and the triangle inequality follow from these properties alone, so they hold for every inner product. Dot products are also hidden in every matrix product: entry \((i,j)\) of \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{B}\) is the dot product of row \(i\) of \(\boldsymbol{A}\) with column \(j\) of \(\boldsymbol{B}\).

A common slip is to multiply entry by entry and stop there: the inner product is a number, not a vector, so \((1,2)\cdot(3,4)=11\), not \((3,8)\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\boldsymbol{x}\cdot \boldsymbol{x}\geq0\), and \(\boldsymbol{x}\cdot \boldsymbol{x}=0\) if and only if \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{0}\).
  • For real vectors, \(\boldsymbol{x}\cdot \boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{y}\cdot \boldsymbol{x}\).
  • Together with linearity, these are the defining properties of an inner product, so everything proved from them alone, such as the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, holds for every inner product.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \((1,2)\cdot(3,4)=11\).
  • \((1,0)\cdot(0,1)=0\), so the vectors are orthogonal.
  • \(\langle \boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}\rangle=2x_1y_1+x_2y_2\) is an inner product on \(\mathbb{R}^2\) different from the dot product.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(\boldsymbol{A}\in\mathcal{L}(V)\) be a linear operator. A subspace \(U\subseteq V\) is an invariant subspace under \(\boldsymbol{A}\) if \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{u}\in U\) for every \(\boldsymbol{u}\in U\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An invariant subspace is a part of the vector space that the operator never sends outside itself.

The figure uses \(\boldsymbol{A}=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&3\end{pmatrix}\). The horizontal axis \(U=\operatorname{span}(\boldsymbol{e}_1)\) is invariant: a vector \(\boldsymbol{u}\) on it is sent to \(2\boldsymbol{u}\), which stays on the axis. The vertical axis is not, since \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{e}_2=(1,3)\) leaves it. The \(0\) in the lower left entry of \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is what keeps \(U\) invariant: it says that \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{e}_1\) has no \(\boldsymbol{e}_2\)-component.

A line \(\operatorname{span}(\boldsymbol{p})\) with \(\boldsymbol{p}\neq\boldsymbol{0}\) is invariant if and only if \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{p}=\lambda\boldsymbol{p}\) for some \(\lambda\), that is, if and only if \(\boldsymbol{p}\) is an eigenvector. So the one-dimensional invariant subspaces are exactly the eigenvector lines. Besides the horizontal axis, the figure's matrix has the invariant line through \((1,1)\), which it sends to \((3,3)\). The kernel is invariant because its vectors go to \(\boldsymbol{0}\), and the range because every \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{u}\) lies in it.

If the first \(k\) vectors of a basis span an invariant subspace, the first \(k\) columns of the matrix in that basis have zeros below row \(k\), a block upper triangular shape; \(\boldsymbol{A}\) above is the case \(k=1\). The span of a Jordan chain is invariant as well, which is why the Jordan normal form splits into separate blocks.

Invariant does not mean unchanged: \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{u}\) must stay in \(U\) but may differ from \(\boldsymbol{u}\), as \(2\boldsymbol{u}\) does in the figure.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\{\boldsymbol{0}\}\), \(V\), \(\ker \boldsymbol{A}\), and \(\operatorname{range}\boldsymbol{A}\) are basic invariant subspaces.
  • If \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{p}=\lambda \boldsymbol{p}\), then \(\operatorname{span}(\boldsymbol{p})\) is invariant under \(\boldsymbol{A}\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For a diagonal matrix, each coordinate axis is invariant.
  • The kernel of any linear operator is invariant under that operator.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\star\) be a binary operation on \(A\) with identity element \(e\). An inverse element of \(a\in A\) is an element \(a^{-1}\in A\) such that

\[ a\star a^{-1}=a^{-1}\star a=e. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An inverse undoes the effect of an element with respect to the operation: combining \(a\) with \(a^{-1}\), in either order, gives the identity element \(e\). The definition therefore only makes sense once an identity exists.

The notation \(a^{-1}\) has to be read according to the operation: under addition the inverse of \(a\) is \(-a\), under multiplication it is \(1/a\), and for a bijection from a set to itself under composition it is the inverse function. Some elements have none: \(0\) has no multiplicative inverse, and in \(\mathbb{Z}\) under multiplication only \(1\) and \(-1\) have one.

When the operation is associative, an inverse is unique: if \(b\) and \(c\) are both inverses of \(a\), then \(b=b\star(a\star c)=(b\star a)\star c=c\). Associativity also gives \((a\star b)^{-1}=b^{-1}\star a^{-1}\), with the order reversed, as when undoing "socks, then shoes"; for permutations under composition the order matters. Inverses are what turn a monoid into a group.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A right inverse satisfies \(a\star a^{-1}=e\).
  • A left inverse satisfies \(a^{-1}\star a=e\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Under addition, the inverse of \(a\) is \(-a\). Under multiplication, the inverse of nonzero \(a\) is \(1/a\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a square matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}\), an inverse matrix is a matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}^{-1}\) such that

\[ \boldsymbol{A}^{-1}\boldsymbol{A}=\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{A}^{-1}=\boldsymbol{I}. \]

If such a matrix exists, then \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is invertible, nonsingular, or nondegenerate. If no inverse exists, then \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is singular, non-invertible, or degenerate.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An inverse matrix undoes the action of a linear map: if \(\boldsymbol{A}\) sends \(\boldsymbol{v}\) to \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v}\), then \(\boldsymbol{A}^{-1}\) sends \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v}\) back to \(\boldsymbol{v}\). Singular matrices are precisely those whose action cannot be undone: they send some nonzero vector to \(\boldsymbol{0}\), so different inputs share an output.

\(\boldsymbol{A}\) maps the unit square onto the parallelogram spanned by its columns and \(\boldsymbol{v}\) onto \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v}\); the arrow labelled \(\boldsymbol{A}^{-1}\) leads back, \(\boldsymbol{A}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v})=\boldsymbol{v}\) for every \(\boldsymbol{v}\). This is possible because the parallelogram is not flattened: \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is invertible if and only if \(\det \boldsymbol{A}\neq0\).

\(\boldsymbol{A}^{-1}\) sends \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\) back to \(\boldsymbol{x}\) (ringed). Choose the singular example: two different vectors go to the same place, and no inverse exists.

The defining equalities use matrix products, which represent composition of linear maps, and the identity matrix, which leaves every vector unchanged. So \(\boldsymbol{A}^{-1}\boldsymbol{A}=\boldsymbol{I}\) says that first \(\boldsymbol{A}\) and then \(\boldsymbol{A}^{-1}\) changes nothing, and \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{A}^{-1}=\boldsymbol{I}\) says the same in the other order. For square matrices either equality already implies the other, and an inverse, when it exists, is unique.

An inverse makes every system \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{b}\) uniquely solvable, with \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{A}^{-1}\boldsymbol{b}\). To compute it, row-reduce \((\boldsymbol{A}\mid\boldsymbol{I})\) by Gauss-Jordan elimination to \((\boldsymbol{I}\mid\boldsymbol{A}^{-1})\), or use the cofactor formula of the adjugate matrix.

Two slips are common. The inverse of a product reverses the order, \((\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{B})^{-1}=\boldsymbol{B}^{-1}\boldsymbol{A}^{-1}\): to undo "first \(\boldsymbol{B}\), then \(\boldsymbol{A}\)", undo \(\boldsymbol{A}\) first. And \(\boldsymbol{A}^{-1}\) is not the matrix of reciprocals \(1/a_{ij}\): \(\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\) has a zero entry, yet its inverse is \(\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(\boldsymbol{A}\) and \(\boldsymbol{B}\) are invertible, then \((\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{B})^{-1}=\boldsymbol{B}^{-1}\boldsymbol{A}^{-1}\).
  • A square matrix is invertible if and only if its determinant is nonzero, if and only if it has full rank.
  • If \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is invertible, then \((\boldsymbol{A}^{\top})^{-1}=(\boldsymbol{A}^{-1})^{\top}\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\) is its own inverse.
  • \(\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}\) is singular because its rows are dependent.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A Jordan block \(\boldsymbol{J}(\lambda)\) is a square matrix with eigenvalue \(\lambda\) on the main diagonal, \(1\)s immediately above the diagonal, and \(0\)s elsewhere.

A Jordan chain for eigenvalue \(\lambda\) of a square matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is a sequence of generalized eigenvectors connected by

\[ \boldsymbol{v}_{r-1}=(\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda \boldsymbol{I})\boldsymbol{v}_r, \]

ending with an ordinary eigenvector and then \(\boldsymbol{0}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Jordan blocks are the building pieces of Jordan normal form. A Jordan block of size at least \(2\) is the simplest kind of matrix that is not diagonalizable: it has a single eigenvalue but only one independent eigenvector. Jordan chains explain where those blocks come from and how the generalized eigenvectors are ordered.

The figure shows \(\boldsymbol{J}(\lambda)\) of size \(3\) next to a Jordan chain \(\boldsymbol{v}_3\to\boldsymbol{v}_2\to\boldsymbol{v}_1\to\boldsymbol{0}\) under \(\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda\boldsymbol{I}\). Only \(\boldsymbol{v}_1\) is an eigenvector; the others satisfy \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v}_2=\lambda\boldsymbol{v}_2+\boldsymbol{v}_1\) and \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v}_3=\lambda\boldsymbol{v}_3+\boldsymbol{v}_2\). In the basis \((\boldsymbol{v}_1,\boldsymbol{v}_2,\boldsymbol{v}_3)\) the columns of the matrix of \(\boldsymbol{A}\) are the coordinates of these images, \((\lambda,0,0)\), \((1,\lambda,0)\) and \((0,1,\lambda)\), which is exactly \(\boldsymbol{J}(\lambda)\). Each \(1\) above the diagonal records one step along the chain.

Subtracting \(\lambda\boldsymbol{I}\) leaves only the \(1\)s above the diagonal, and \(\boldsymbol{J}(\lambda)-\lambda\boldsymbol{I}\) shifts: it sends the third basis vector to the second, the second to the first and the first to \(\boldsymbol{0}\). Hence \((\boldsymbol{J}(\lambda)-\lambda\boldsymbol{I})^3=\boldsymbol{0}\) for a block of size \(3\). Its kernel is one-dimensional, so a block of size \(k\) has algebraic multiplicity \(k\) but geometric multiplicity \(1\). A block of size \(1\) is just \((\lambda)\), with an ordinary eigenvector.

The order of the chain matters. Listing the basis as \((\boldsymbol{v}_3,\boldsymbol{v}_2,\boldsymbol{v}_1)\) instead puts the \(1\)s below the diagonal; the convention here starts the basis with the eigenvector.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A Jordan block is upper triangular and has one eigenvalue on its diagonal.
  • The length of a Jordan chain corresponds to the size of the associated Jordan block.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\begin{pmatrix}4&1\\0&4\end{pmatrix}\) is a \(2\times2\) Jordan block.
  • If \((\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda \boldsymbol{I})\boldsymbol{v}_2=\boldsymbol{v}_1\) and \((\boldsymbol{A}-\lambda \boldsymbol{I})\boldsymbol{v}_1=\boldsymbol{0}\), then \((\boldsymbol{v}_1,\boldsymbol{v}_2)\) is a Jordan chain of length \(2\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A Jordan normal form of a square matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is a block diagonal matrix \(\boldsymbol{J}_{\boldsymbol{A}}=\boldsymbol{P}^{-1}\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{P}\) whose diagonal blocks are Jordan blocks, where \(\boldsymbol{P}\) is invertible and its columns are chains of generalized eigenvectors of \(\boldsymbol{A}\). Every square matrix has a Jordan normal form over \(\mathbb{C}\) (more generally, whenever its characteristic polynomial splits into linear factors); it is unique up to the order of the blocks.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Jordan normal form is an almost diagonal form that still works when a matrix is not diagonalizable. It keeps the eigenvalues on the diagonal and uses \(1\)s just above the diagonal to record where eigenvectors are missing.

The figure shows a \(5\times5\) Jordan normal form with three Jordan blocks: \(\boldsymbol{J}_2(\lambda_1)\) from the chain \(\boldsymbol{v}_2\to\boldsymbol{v}_1\to\boldsymbol{0}\), \(\boldsymbol{J}_1(\lambda_1)\) from a lone eigenvector \(\boldsymbol{v}_3\), and \(\boldsymbol{J}_2(\lambda_2)\) from the chain \(\boldsymbol{v}_5\to\boldsymbol{v}_4\to\boldsymbol{0}\). Here \(\lambda_1\) has algebraic multiplicity \(3\) and geometric multiplicity \(2\), while \(\lambda_2\) has algebraic multiplicity \(2\) and geometric multiplicity \(1\).

In general, the number of blocks for an eigenvalue is its geometric multiplicity, their total size is its algebraic multiplicity, and the block sizes are the lengths of the Jordan chains. The matrix is diagonalizable exactly when every block has size \(1\). The form exists over \(\mathbb{C}\) for every square matrix, but not always over \(\mathbb{R}\): the quarter-turn rotation \(\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\) has no real eigenvalues.

Each block acts on the span of its own chain, an invariant subspace. Over \(\mathbb{C}\), two square matrices \(\boldsymbol{A}\) and \(\boldsymbol{B}\) have the same Jordan normal form, up to the order of the blocks, exactly when \(\boldsymbol{B}=\boldsymbol{P}^{-1}\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{P}\) for some invertible \(\boldsymbol{P}\); Math V calls such matrices similar.

The two multiplicities do not always fix the form. With \(\operatorname{am}(\lambda)=4\) and \(\operatorname{gm}(\lambda)=2\), the block sizes can be \(2+2\) or \(3+1\); deciding between them needs the lengths of the chains.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Jordan normal form is upper triangular with eigenvalues on the diagonal and possible \(1\)s above the diagonal.
  • If a matrix is diagonalizable, its Jordan normal form is diagonal.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\begin{pmatrix}\lambda&1\\0&\lambda\end{pmatrix}\) is a \(2\times2\) Jordan block.
  • A diagonal matrix is already in Jordan normal form.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(\boldsymbol{A}\in\mathcal{L}(V,W)\) be a linear map. The kernel or null space of \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is \(\ker \boldsymbol{A}=\{\boldsymbol{v}\in V\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v}=\boldsymbol{0}\}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The kernel contains all input vectors that the linear map sends to the zero vector. It measures what the map loses: two inputs have the same image exactly when their difference lies in the kernel, since \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{u}=\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v}\) if and only if \(\boldsymbol{A}(\boldsymbol{u}-\boldsymbol{v})=\boldsymbol{0}\).

The matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\) flattens the plane onto the \(x_1\)-axis: \(\boldsymbol{w}\) goes straight down to \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{w}\), and every vector on the \(x_2\)-axis, such as \(\boldsymbol{v}\), goes to \(\boldsymbol{0}\). So \(\ker \boldsymbol{A}=\{\boldsymbol{v}\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v}=\boldsymbol{0}\}=\operatorname{span}(\boldsymbol{e}_2)\), the whole \(x_2\)-axis.

Drag \(\boldsymbol{x}\) onto the dashed line: there \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{0}\). The kernel is \(\{\boldsymbol{0}\}\) only when \(\det(\boldsymbol{A})\neq0\).

For a matrix, finding the kernel means solving the homogeneous system \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{0}\) by row reduction. Each free variable contributes one basis vector, so the dimension of the kernel is the number of free variables. The kernel also describes every other solution set: if \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}_p=\boldsymbol{b}\), the solutions of \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{b}\) are exactly \(\boldsymbol{x}_p\) plus a vector of the kernel.

In particular, a linear map is injective if and only if its kernel is \(\{\boldsymbol{0}\}\), and the fundamental theorem of linear maps links the dimension of the kernel to that of the range.

A common slip is to conclude "the kernel is \(\{\boldsymbol{0}\}\)" after checking only that \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{0}=\boldsymbol{0}\). The zero vector lies in every kernel; the question is whether any other vector does. Note also that the kernel is a subspace of the domain \(V\), not of \(W\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The kernel of a linear map is a subspace of the domain.
  • A linear map is injective exactly when its kernel is \(\{\boldsymbol{0}\}\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\boldsymbol{A}(x,y)=(x,0)\), the kernel is \(\{(0,y)\colon y\in\mathbb{R}\}\).
  • The kernel of the identity map is \(\{\boldsymbol{0}\}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \((\boldsymbol{v}_1,\boldsymbol{v}_2,\ldots,\boldsymbol{v}_k)\) be a collection of vectors and let \(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\ldots,\alpha_k\) be scalars. A linear combination is a vector of the form

\[ \alpha_1\boldsymbol{v}_1+\alpha_2\boldsymbol{v}_2+\cdots+\alpha_k\boldsymbol{v}_k. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A linear combination is built by scaling vectors and adding the results: scalar multiplication forms each \(\alpha_i\boldsymbol{v}_i\), and vector addition combines these scaled vectors into a single vector of the same space. These are the only two operations a vector space provides, so the linear combinations are exactly the vectors that can be made from \(\boldsymbol{v}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{v}_k\).

The figure builds \(2\boldsymbol{v}_1+1.5\boldsymbol{v}_2\) in two stages. First \(\boldsymbol{v}_1\) is doubled and \(\boldsymbol{v}_2\) is stretched by \(1.5\); then the two scaled vectors are added tip to tail, so the result is the diagonal of the parallelogram they form. Other coefficients give other points. Since \(\boldsymbol{v}_1\) and \(\boldsymbol{v}_2\) do not lie on one line, every point of the plane is reached by some choice of \(\alpha_1\) and \(\alpha_2\).

Choose \(\alpha_1\) and \(\alpha_2\): the combination \(\alpha_1\boldsymbol{v}_1+\alpha_2\boldsymbol{v}_2\) is reached by walking \(\alpha_1\boldsymbol{v}_1\) and then \(\alpha_2\boldsymbol{v}_2\). Drag \(\boldsymbol{v}_1\) and \(\boldsymbol{v}_2\) to change the grid.

The coefficients may be any scalars, including \(0\) and negative numbers: \(\boldsymbol{v}_1-\boldsymbol{v}_2\) and \(0\boldsymbol{v}_1+0\boldsymbol{v}_2=\boldsymbol{0}\) are linear combinations of \(\boldsymbol{v}_1\) and \(\boldsymbol{v}_2\) as well. In \(\mathbb{R}^n\), deciding whether a vector is a linear combination of given vectors means finding coefficients that satisfy one linear equation per coordinate. For example, \((3,5)=\alpha_1(1,1)+\alpha_2(1,2)\) means \(\alpha_1+\alpha_2=3\) and \(\alpha_1+2\alpha_2=5\), so \(\alpha_2=2\) and \(\alpha_1=1\).

Linear combinations are the common language of the next definitions: the span is the set of all of them, linear independence asks whether \(\boldsymbol{0}\) is reached only with all coefficients zero, and a basis reaches every vector in exactly one way.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Linear combinations are the building blocks of span, linear dependence, and bases.
  • Many questions about the concept reduce to solving equations involving linear combinations.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • \(2\boldsymbol{v}_1-3\boldsymbol{v}_2\) is a linear combination of \(\boldsymbol{v}_1\) and \(\boldsymbol{v}_2\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A collection \((\boldsymbol{v}_1,\boldsymbol{v}_2,\ldots,\boldsymbol{v}_k)\) of vectors is linearly dependent if there exist scalars \(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_k\), not all zero, such that

\[ \alpha_1\boldsymbol{v}_1+\alpha_2\boldsymbol{v}_2+\cdots+\alpha_k\boldsymbol{v}_k=\boldsymbol{0}. \]

The collection is linearly independent if this can only happen when

\[ \alpha_1=\alpha_2=\cdots=\alpha_k=0. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Linear dependence means that at least one vector is redundant because it can be written using the others. Linear independence means that no vector in the collection is redundant: the only combination that gives \(\boldsymbol{0}\) is the one with all coefficients zero.

In the left panel, \(\boldsymbol{v}_1\) and \(\boldsymbol{v}_2\) point in different directions, so \(\alpha_1\boldsymbol{v}_1+\alpha_2\boldsymbol{v}_2\) can only return to \(\boldsymbol{0}\) when \(\alpha_1=\alpha_2=0\). In the right panel, \(\boldsymbol{v}_3=\boldsymbol{v}_1+\boldsymbol{v}_2\) is the diagonal of the parallelogram, so \(\boldsymbol{v}_1+\boldsymbol{v}_2-\boldsymbol{v}_3=\boldsymbol{0}\) is a combination with nonzero coefficients \(1\), \(1\) and \(-1\), and the three vectors are dependent.

Drag \(\boldsymbol{v}_2\) onto the line through \(\boldsymbol{v}_1\) (or press the button): then a combination with coefficients not all zero gives \(\boldsymbol{0}\), and the collection is dependent.

The two readings agree. If \(\alpha_1\boldsymbol{v}_1+\cdots+\alpha_k\boldsymbol{v}_k=\boldsymbol{0}\) with some \(\alpha_j\ne0\), then dividing by \(\alpha_j\), which is possible because the scalars come from a field, writes \(\boldsymbol{v}_j\) as a combination of the others. Conversely, writing \(\boldsymbol{v}_j\) as a combination of the others gives such a relation with coefficient \(-1\) at \(\boldsymbol{v}_j\). Dependence does not mean that every vector is redundant: in \(((1,0),(2,0),(0,1))\), the vector \((0,1)\) is not a combination of the others, yet the list is dependent because \((2,0)=2(1,0)\).

Independence is what makes representations unique: if \(\sum_i\alpha_i\boldsymbol{v}_i=\sum_i\beta_i\boldsymbol{v}_i\), then \(\sum_i(\alpha_i-\beta_i)\boldsymbol{v}_i=\boldsymbol{0}\), so \(\alpha_i=\beta_i\) for every \(i\). This is why a basis must be independent. Two vectors are dependent if and only if one is a scalar multiple of the other, and three vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) are dependent if and only if they lie in one plane through the origin.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A collection is linearly independent if and only if every vector in its span has a unique expression as a linear combination of the collection.
  • Any collection containing the zero vector, a repeated vector, or a scalar multiple of another vector is linearly dependent.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In \(\mathbb{R}^2\), \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\) are linearly independent.
  • In \(\mathbb{R}^2\), \((1,0)\) and \((2,0)\) are linearly dependent, since \((2,0)=2(1,0)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(\mathbb{F}\) be a field, and let \(V\) and \(W\) be vector spaces over \(\mathbb{F}\). A linear map \(\boldsymbol{A}\colon V\to W\) is a function satisfying additivity \(\boldsymbol{A}(\boldsymbol{u}+\boldsymbol{v})=\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{u}+\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v}\) and homogeneity \(\boldsymbol{A}(\lambda \boldsymbol{u})=\lambda \boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{u}\) for all \(\boldsymbol{u},\boldsymbol{v}\in V\) and \(\lambda\in\mathbb{F}\). The set of all linear maps from \(V\) to \(W\) is denoted \(\mathcal{L}(V,W)\).

docs.title: Basic linear maps and operations
docs.text:
Two canonical examples are the zero map \(\boldsymbol{0}\colon V\to W\), defined by \(\boldsymbol{0}(\boldsymbol{v})=\boldsymbol{0}_W\), and the identity map \(\boldsymbol{I}\colon V\to V\), defined by \(\boldsymbol{I}(\boldsymbol{v})=\boldsymbol{v}\). If \(\boldsymbol{A},\boldsymbol{B}\in\mathcal{L}(V,W)\) and \(\lambda\in\mathbb{F}\), then the sum and scalar multiple of linear maps are defined by

\[ \begin{aligned} (\boldsymbol{A}+\boldsymbol{B})(\boldsymbol{v})&=\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v}+\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{v},\\ (\lambda \boldsymbol{A})(\boldsymbol{v})&=\lambda(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v}). \end{aligned} \]

These operations make \(\mathcal{L}(V,W)\) itself a vector space.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A linear map preserves the linear structure of a vector space: it respects vector addition and scalar multiplication. It does not matter whether vectors are first combined and then mapped, or first mapped and then combined: \(\boldsymbol{A}(\lambda\boldsymbol{u}+\mu\boldsymbol{v})=\lambda\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{u}+\mu\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v}\).

The square grid of \(V\), with \(\boldsymbol{e}_1\), \(\boldsymbol{e}_2\) and \(\boldsymbol{v}=\boldsymbol{e}_1+\boldsymbol{e}_2\), is mapped to a slanted grid. By additivity, \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v}=\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{e}_1+\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{e}_2\): the diagonal of the unit square goes to the diagonal of the parallelogram formed by \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{e}_1\) and \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{e}_2\). The grid lines stay straight, parallel and evenly spaced, and \(\boldsymbol{0}\) stays at \(\boldsymbol{0}\). A linear map is determined by its images of a basis; here \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{e}_1\) and \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{e}_2\) are the matrix columns.

Drag the images \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{e}_1\) and \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{e}_2\) of the basis vectors: they decide where the whole grid goes, and \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}=x_1\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{e}_1+x_2\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{e}_2\). Move \(t\) to slide from the identity to \(\boldsymbol{A}\).

Every linear map sends \(\boldsymbol{0}\) to \(\boldsymbol{0}\), because \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{0}=\boldsymbol{A}(0\cdot\boldsymbol{0})=0\cdot\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{0}=\boldsymbol{0}\). This gives a quick test: \(g(x,y,z)=x-y+2z+1\) from the Examples fails it. Fixing the origin is not enough, though: \(x\mapsto x^2\) on \(\mathbb{R}\) sends \(0\) to \(0\), but \((1+1)^2=4\neq1^2+1^2\), so additivity fails.

The two conditions are differentiation rules already known from Math I: \((f+g)'=f'+g'\) and \((cf)'=cf'\), which is why differentiation is a linear map. A common slip comes from the everyday name "linear function" for \(f(x)=ax+b\): it is a linear map only when \(b=0\); for \(b\neq0\) its graph is a line that misses the origin.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A linear map is completely determined by what it does to a basis of its domain.
  • The set \(\mathcal{L}(V,W)\) of all linear maps from \(V\) to \(W\) is itself a vector space.
  • A function \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^k\) is linear if and only if \(\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x})=\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\) for some \(k\times n\) matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}\), and then \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is unique: its \(j\)-th column is \(\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{e}_j)\). In particular a linear map sends \(\boldsymbol{0}\) to \(\boldsymbol{0}\), so a function \(\boldsymbol{x}\mapsto \boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{b}\) with \(\boldsymbol{b}\ne\boldsymbol{0}\) is not linear but affine.
  • Linear map and linear transformation are synonyms. A linear map from a space to itself is also called a linear operator.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The zero map \(\boldsymbol{0}(\boldsymbol{v})=\boldsymbol{0}\) is linear.
  • The derivative map \(\boldsymbol{D}(p)=p'\) on polynomials is linear.
  • \(f(x,y)=x+y\) is a linear map \(\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}\); \(g(x,y,z)=x-y+2z+1\) is not, since \(g(0,0,0)=1\ne0\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A linear operator is a linear map from a vector space to itself, so it has the form \(\boldsymbol{A}\colon V\to V\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A linear operator is a linear map that stays inside one space: input and output are vectors of the same vector space \(V\). This makes repeated application meaningful, because the operator can be applied again to its own output.

The illustrated operator rotates every vector of the plane by \(30^\circ\) about the origin and is represented by \(\boldsymbol{A}=\begin{pmatrix}\cos30^\circ&-\sin30^\circ\\\sin30^\circ&\cos30^\circ\end{pmatrix}\). The triangle \(S\) and the vector \(\boldsymbol{v}\) are moved to \(\boldsymbol{A}(S)\) and \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v}\) in the same plane. Its domain and codomain are the same space, so powers represent repeated application: \(\boldsymbol{A}^2\) rotates by \(60^\circ\), and \(\boldsymbol{A}^{12}\) rotates by \(360^\circ\), which is the identity.

The only difference with a general linear map lies in the codomain. For \(\boldsymbol{A}\colon V\to W\) with \(W\neq V\), the composition \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{A}\) makes no sense, since \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is not defined on \(W\). In matrix terms, an operator on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is given by a square \(n\times n\) matrix, and powers \(\boldsymbol{A}^k\) exist only for square matrices.

The same formula can give an operator or not, depending on the codomain: \((x_1,x_2)\mapsto(x_1,0)\) is an operator on \(\mathbb{R}^2\), while \((x_1,x_2)\mapsto x_1\), from \(\mathbb{R}^2\) to \(\mathbb{R}\), is not. Questions such as which vectors an operator only stretches, or whether its effect can be undone, are asked for operators and return later as eigenvectors and inverses.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The set of linear operators on \(V\) is denoted \(\mathcal{L}(V)=\mathcal{L}(V,V)\).
  • Eigenvalues, determinants, inverses, and diagonalization are concepts for linear operators or their square matrix representations.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The identity map \(\boldsymbol{I}(\boldsymbol{v})=\boldsymbol{v}\) is a linear operator on \(V\).
  • The derivative \(\boldsymbol{D}\colon p\mapsto p'\) is a linear operator on the vector space of polynomials.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The linear span of a collection \(\mathcal{V}=(\boldsymbol{v}_1,\boldsymbol{v}_2,\ldots,\boldsymbol{v}_k)\) is the set of all linear combinations of vectors in the collection, with scalars from the field \(\mathbb{F}\) of the vector space:

\[ \operatorname{span}(\mathcal{V})=\Big\{\sum_{i=1}^{k}\alpha_i\boldsymbol{v}_i\colon \alpha_i\in\mathbb{F}\Big\}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The span is everything that can be reached from the given vectors with linear combinations, that is, by scaling them and adding the results. It answers the question which vectors can be built from \(\boldsymbol{v}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{v}_k\).

The figure shows the two typical shapes in \(\mathbb{R}^3\). The multiples \(\alpha_1\boldsymbol{v}_1\) fill the dashed line through the origin, \(\operatorname{span}(\boldsymbol{v}_1)\). Adding all multiples of \(\boldsymbol{v}_2\), which points out of that line, fills the shaded plane \(\operatorname{span}(\boldsymbol{v}_1,\boldsymbol{v}_2)\). Both contain \(\boldsymbol{0}\), the combination with all coefficients zero.

Animate \(\alpha_1\) and \(\alpha_2\) to see which points are reached. One vector spans a line; two vectors span the whole plane unless they lie on one line.

The span is always a subspace, and it is the smallest subspace containing \(\boldsymbol{v}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{v}_k\): a subspace that contains these vectors is closed under addition and scalar multiplication, so it contains all their linear combinations. The span depends on what the vectors can produce, not on how many there are: the lists \(((1,0),(0,1),(1,1))\) and \(((1,0),(0,1))\) both span \(\mathbb{R}^2\), because \((1,1)\) adds no new direction. When the span is the whole space \(V\), the collection is a spanning list of \(V\).

A common slip is to confuse the span with the collection itself. The collection has \(k\) vectors, while the span of one nonzero vector over \(\mathbb{R}\) already contains infinitely many. And since every span contains \(\boldsymbol{0}\), a line or plane that misses the origin is never a span.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The span of any collection of vectors is a vector space.
  • A collection spans \(V\) if its span equals \(V\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • The span of one nonzero vector in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) is a line through the origin.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An LU decomposition factors a matrix, after possible row permutations, as \(\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{A}=\boldsymbol{L}\boldsymbol{U}\), where \(\boldsymbol{P}\) is a permutation matrix, \(\boldsymbol{L}\) is lower triangular, and \(\boldsymbol{U}\) is upper triangular.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
LU decomposition records the forward phase of Gaussian elimination (row reduction to row echelon form) as a matrix factorization: \(\boldsymbol{U}\) is the echelon form that elimination produces, and \(\boldsymbol{L}\) stores the multipliers used to get there.

The figure factors

\[ \boldsymbol{A}=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&1\\4&3&3\\-2&1&3\end{pmatrix}. \]

Subtracting \(2\) times row 1 from row 2, adding row 1 to row 3 (multiplier \(-1\)), and then subtracting \(2\) times the new row 2 from row 3 leaves \(\boldsymbol{U}\); the multipliers \(2\), \(-1\), \(2\) fill \(\boldsymbol{L}\) below its diagonal of ones.

Multiplying \(\boldsymbol{L}\boldsymbol{U}\) undoes the elimination and rebuilds \(\boldsymbol{A}\) row by row. For instance, row 3 of \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is \(-1\) times row 1 of \(\boldsymbol{U}\), plus \(2\) times row 2, plus row 3: \(-(2,1,1)+2(0,1,1)+(0,0,2)=(-2,1,3)\). Since \(\boldsymbol{L}\) and \(\boldsymbol{U}\) are triangular, the factorization also gives the determinant: \(\det\boldsymbol{A}=\det\boldsymbol{L}\det\boldsymbol{U}=2\cdot1\cdot2=4\).

To solve \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{b}\), first solve \(\boldsymbol{L}\boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{b}\) by forward substitution, then \(\boldsymbol{U}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{y}\) by back substitution. The elimination is done once, so each further right-hand side costs only these two triangular solves. Row swaps are needed when a zero appears in a pivot position: \(\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\) has no decomposition \(\boldsymbol{A}=\boldsymbol{L}\boldsymbol{U}\), since its first pivot would be \(0\), but swapping its rows gives \(\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{A}=\boldsymbol{I}=\boldsymbol{I}\boldsymbol{I}\). When no row swaps are needed, \(\boldsymbol{P}=\boldsymbol{I}\).

A common slip concerns the signs in \(\boldsymbol{L}\). Its entries are the multipliers \(m\) in "subtract \(m\) times row \(j\) from row \(i\)", so adding row 1 to row 3 enters \(\boldsymbol{L}\) as \(-1\), not \(+1\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If no row interchanges are needed, the factorization is \(\boldsymbol{A}=\boldsymbol{L}\boldsymbol{U}\).
  • LU decomposition helps solve \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{b}\) efficiently by forward and back substitution.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\boldsymbol{A}=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&1\\2&4&8\\3&9&27\end{pmatrix}\), subtract \(2\) and \(3\) times row 1 from rows 2 and 3, then \(3\) times the new row 2 from row 3. This gives \(\boldsymbol{U}=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&1\\0&2&6\\0&0&6\end{pmatrix}\), the multipliers fill \(\boldsymbol{L}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\2&1&0\\3&3&1\end{pmatrix}\), and \(\boldsymbol{A}=\boldsymbol{L}\boldsymbol{U}\).
  • \(\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{A}=\boldsymbol{L}\boldsymbol{U}\) includes pivoting through the permutation matrix \(\boldsymbol{P}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For an \(m\times n\) matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}=(a_{ij})\):

  • the main diagonal consists of the entries \(a_{ii}\) with \(i\le\min(m,n)\);
  • the anti-diagonal of a square matrix (\(m=n\)) consists of the entries \(a_{n+1-i,i}\);
  • the off-diagonal entries are all entries \(a_{ij}\) with \(i\neq j\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The main diagonal runs from the top-left entry downwards to the right, through the entries whose row and column index agree. The anti-diagonal of a square matrix runs from bottom-left to top-right; the off-diagonal entries are all the others.

In the \(3\times4\) matrix shown, the main diagonal (shaded) is \(a_{11},a_{22},a_{33}\). It stops after \(\min(3,4)=3\) entries, so a non-square matrix has a main diagonal too, but it does not end in the bottom-right corner.

Diagonal matrices have zeros everywhere off the main diagonal and triangular matrices on one side of it. The transpose mirrors a matrix in it, so the diagonal entries stay in place.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Diagonal entries are central in definitions of diagonal matrices, triangular matrices, and the trace.
  • A square matrix is diagonal exactly when all off-diagonal entries are zero.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In \(\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}\), the main diagonal is \((1,4)\) and the anti-diagonal is \((3,2)\).
  • In \(\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&4\end{pmatrix}\), all off-diagonal entries are zero.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: If \(\boldsymbol{A}=(a_{ij})\) and \(\boldsymbol{B}=(b_{ij})\) have the same size, their sum is the matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}+\boldsymbol{B}=(a_{ij}+b_{ij})\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Matrix addition works entry by entry: the entry in row \(i\) and column \(j\) of \(\boldsymbol{A}+\boldsymbol{B}\) is \(a_{ij}+b_{ij}\). That is why both matrices must have the same size: a \(2\times3\) and a \(3\times2\) matrix have no matching positions to pair.

Because each entry is an ordinary sum in the field, the rules of addition carry over: besides the Key Results, the zero matrix is neutral and \(-\boldsymbol{A}\) cancels \(\boldsymbol{A}\), so the \(m\times n\) matrices form an abelian group under addition. For maps, \((\boldsymbol{A}+\boldsymbol{B})\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{x}\), which matches the sum of linear maps. Entry-by-entry thinking does not carry over to multiplication: the matrix product is not computed entry by entry.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Matrix addition is defined only for matrices of the same size.
  • Matrix addition is associative and commutative.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1&3\\4&4\end{pmatrix}\).
  • A matrix plus the zero matrix of the same size equals itself.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: If \(\boldsymbol{A}\) has size \(m\times n\) and \(\boldsymbol{B}\) has size \(n\times k\), the matrix product \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{B}\) is the \(m\times k\) matrix with entries \(\displaystyle (\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{B})_{ij}=\sum_{r=1}^n a_{ir}b_{rj}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Matrix multiplication combines rows of the left matrix with columns of the right matrix and represents composition of linear maps: \((\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{B})\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{A}(\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{x})\). The row-times-column rule is exactly what makes this hold.

The entry \(c_{22}=a_{21}b_{12}+a_{22}b_{22}+a_{23}b_{32}\) is obtained by multiplying row \(2\) of \(\boldsymbol{A}\) by column \(2\) of \(\boldsymbol{B}\). Both have three entries, which is why the inner sizes of the \(2\times3\) and \(3\times2\) matrices must agree; the outer sizes give the \(2\times2\) size of the product.

A second reading uses columns. If \(\boldsymbol{a}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{a}_n\) are the columns of \(\boldsymbol{A}\), then \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}=x_1\boldsymbol{a}_1+\cdots+x_n\boldsymbol{a}_n\) is a linear combination of these columns, and column \(j\) of \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{B}\) is \(\boldsymbol{A}\) times column \(j\) of \(\boldsymbol{B}\). In the second Example, \(3\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}+4\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}11\\4\end{pmatrix}\). With this reading, a linear system \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{b}\) asks for a combination of the columns of \(\boldsymbol{A}\) that equals \(\boldsymbol{b}\).

The order of the factors matters. When \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{B}\) is defined, \(\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{A}\) may not be, and even for square matrices the two usually differ: for \(\boldsymbol{A}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\boldsymbol{B}=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\), \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{B}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\) but \(\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{A}=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\). A common slip is to multiply matrices entry by entry, as for matrix addition; that is a different operation.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The product \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{B}\) is defined only when the number of columns of \(\boldsymbol{A}\) equals the number of rows of \(\boldsymbol{B}\).
  • Matrix multiplication is associative and distributive, but not generally commutative.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A \(2\times3\) matrix times a \(3\times4\) matrix gives a \(2\times4\) matrix.
  • \(\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}3\\4\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}11\\4\end{pmatrix}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The scalar multiple \(\alpha \boldsymbol{A}\) of a matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}=(a_{ij})\) is the matrix whose entries are \((\alpha a_{ij})\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Multiplying a matrix by a scalar \(\alpha\) multiplies every entry by the same number, so \(\alpha\boldsymbol{A}\) has the same size as \(\boldsymbol{A}\). For \(\alpha=2\) every entry doubles, for \(\alpha=-1\) every sign flips, and for \(\alpha=0\) the result is the zero matrix.

This is the scalar multiplication of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) applied to all entries of the array; together with matrix addition it makes the \(m\times n\) matrices a vector space. For the map \(\boldsymbol{x}\mapsto\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\) it scales every output, \((\alpha\boldsymbol{A})\boldsymbol{x}=\alpha(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x})\), which matches the scalar multiple of linear maps. Do not confuse it with the row operation that multiplies a single row: \(\alpha\boldsymbol{A}\) scales all rows at once.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Scalar multiplication distributes over matrix addition.
  • \(0\boldsymbol{A}\) is the zero matrix and \(1\boldsymbol{A}=\boldsymbol{A}\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(2\begin{pmatrix}1&3\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}2&6\\0&-2\end{pmatrix}\).
  • \(-\boldsymbol{A}\) is the additive inverse of \(\boldsymbol{A}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A matrix is a rectangular array of elements of a field, arranged in rows and columns. A matrix with \(m\) rows and \(n\) columns has size \(m\times n\).

Two matrices are equal if and only if they have the same size and all corresponding entries are equal. A square matrix is a matrix with the same number of rows and columns.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Matrices store coefficients, describe linear maps in coordinates, and organize data in a way that supports algebraic operations. A matrix is a table of numbers in which the position of each entry carries meaning: its row and its column.

The figure shows a \(3\times4\) matrix: \(m=3\) rows and \(n=4\) columns, always counted in that order. The green entry \(a_{23}\) lies where row \(2\) crosses column \(3\); the first index gives the row and the second the column, so \(a_{32}\) would be a different position. The size is read "\(3\) by \(4\)".

What rows and columns mean depends on the use. In a linear system in standard form, each row holds the coefficients of one equation and each column belongs to one unknown. For the map \(\boldsymbol{x}\mapsto\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\) from \(\mathbb{R}^n\) to \(\mathbb{R}^m\), column \(j\) is the image of the \(j\)th standard basis vector, so the number of columns is the number of input coordinates. In a data table, rows often correspond to observations and columns to variables.

A common slip is to treat a matrix as just a collection of numbers. The arrangement matters: \(\begin{pmatrix}1&2\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}\) contain the same numbers but are different matrices, of sizes \(1\times2\) and \(2\times1\). Special shapes are studied on their own pages, such as the identity matrix and symmetric matrices, which equal their transpose.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Rows are listed first and columns second: an \(m\times n\) matrix has \(m\) rows and \(n\) columns.
  • A matrix can be viewed as a list of vertical or horizontal vectors; an \(n\times1\) matrix is a column vector and a \(1\times n\) matrix is a row vector.
  • Matrices of different sizes cannot be equal; matrices of the same size are equal exactly when their corresponding entries match.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}\) is a \(2\times2\) square matrix.
  • \(\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\4&5&6\end{pmatrix}\) is a \(2\times3\) matrix and is not square.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A monoid is a set \(A\) together with a binary operation \(\star\) that is associative and has an identity element.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A monoid is a semigroup with a neutral element: a set with an associative operation and an identity element \(e\). Inverses are not required, which is what separates a monoid from a group.

Associativity makes repeated products \(a\star a\star\cdots\star a\) unambiguous and the identity gives the empty product a value, so powers \(a^n\) are defined for every integer \(n\ge0\), with \(a^0=e\). Negative powers need inverses and exist only in a group.

Typical monoids are \((\mathbb{N},+)\) with identity \(0\) (so \(0\in\mathbb{N}\), as in the Examples), \((\mathbb{Z},\cdot)\) with identity \(1\), and the functions from a set \(A\) to itself under composition, with the identity function \(x\mapsto x\). None of these is a group: in \((\mathbb{Z},\cdot)\) the element \(2\) has no inverse, and a function that is not bijective cannot be undone. The invertible functions, the permutations of \(A\), do form a group.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every group is a monoid.
  • Associativity, identity elements, and inverse elements determine which algebraic structure is present.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • \((\mathbb{N},+)\) is a monoid with identity \(0\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A normal vector to a plane is a nonzero vector perpendicular to every direction vector in the plane.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A normal vector records which way a plane faces. The direction vectors say how one can move inside the plane; the normal vector points straight out of it, so it fixes the tilt of the plane but not its position.

In the figure, \(\boldsymbol{n}\) stands at a right angle to both direction vectors at the point \(\boldsymbol{A}\), so \(\boldsymbol{n}\cdot\boldsymbol{v}=\boldsymbol{n}\cdot\boldsymbol{w}=0\). Every displacement inside the plane is a linear combination \(s\boldsymbol{v}+t\boldsymbol{w}\), and \(\boldsymbol{n}\cdot(s\boldsymbol{v}+t\boldsymbol{w})=s\,\boldsymbol{n}\cdot\boldsymbol{v}+t\,\boldsymbol{n}\cdot\boldsymbol{w}=0\). Checking the two independent directions is therefore enough to be perpendicular to the whole plane.

To find a normal vector \(\boldsymbol{n}=(a,b,c)\), solve \(\boldsymbol{n}\cdot\boldsymbol{v}=0\) and \(\boldsymbol{n}\cdot\boldsymbol{w}=0\), as in the second example of the point-normal equation. In \(\mathbb{R}^3\) one can also take the cross product \(\boldsymbol{n}=\boldsymbol{v}\times\boldsymbol{w}=(v_2w_3-v_3w_2,\,v_3w_1-v_1w_3,\,v_1w_2-v_2w_1)\). Any nonzero multiple of a normal vector is again normal, and in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) all normals of one plane are multiples of each other.

Two planes in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) are parallel or equal exactly when their normals are multiples of each other. The same idea gives the normal \((a_1,\ldots,a_n)\) of a hyperplane \(a_1x_1+\cdots+a_nx_n=d\) in \(\mathbb{R}^n\).

A common slip is to expect the normal vector to be orthogonal to the points of the plane. It is orthogonal to differences \(\boldsymbol{B}-\boldsymbol{A}\) of points, as in the Key Results; \(\boldsymbol{n}\cdot\boldsymbol{B}\) itself is the same for every point \(\boldsymbol{B}\) of the plane, and it is \(0\) only when the plane passes through the origin.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A point and a normal vector determine a plane in \(\mathbb{R}^3\).
  • If \(\boldsymbol{n}\) is normal to a plane and \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is a point of the plane, then \(\boldsymbol{n}\cdot(\boldsymbol{B}-\boldsymbol{A})=0\) for every point \(\boldsymbol{B}\) on the plane.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For the \(xy\)-plane, \((0,0,1)\) is a normal vector.
  • If a plane has direction vectors \(\boldsymbol{v},\boldsymbol{w}\), then a normal vector is orthogonal to both \(\boldsymbol{v}\) and \(\boldsymbol{w}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The origin of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is the vector whose coordinates are all zero:

\[ \boldsymbol{0}=(0,0,\ldots,0). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The origin is the point of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with all coordinates equal to zero, the point where the coordinate axes cross. As a vector, it is the zero vector of the real coordinate space \(\mathbb{R}^n\): adding it to any vector changes nothing.

As a point, the origin is the reference point of the Cartesian coordinate system: the coordinates of any other point say how far, and in which direction, it lies from the origin along each axis. Position vectors are drawn as arrows starting there. Every subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) contains the origin, so lines and planes that miss it are not subspaces.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • Position vectors are often drawn as arrows starting at the origin.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • In \(\mathbb{R}^2\), the origin is \((0,0)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Two vectors \(\boldsymbol{x}\) and \(\boldsymbol{y}\) are orthogonal if their inner product is zero: \(\boldsymbol{x}\cdot \boldsymbol{y}=0\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Orthogonal vectors meet at a right angle in Euclidean geometry. The inner product turns this geometric condition into a computation: instead of measuring an angle, multiply matching coordinates, add, and check whether the result is \(0\).

The vectors \(\boldsymbol{x}=(3,1)\) and \(\boldsymbol{y}=(-1,3)\) in the figure satisfy \(\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{y}=3\cdot(-1)+1\cdot3=0\), so the angle between them is \(90^\circ\). Here \(\boldsymbol{y}\) is \(\boldsymbol{x}\) turned a quarter turn; in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) the vectors \((a,b)\) and \((-b,a)\) are always orthogonal. Pythagoras holds as well: \(\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{y}=(2,4)\) has \(\|\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{y}\|^2=20=10+10=\|\boldsymbol{x}\|^2+\|\boldsymbol{y}\|^2\).

Turn \(\boldsymbol{y}\) until \(\boldsymbol{x}\cdot \boldsymbol{y}=0\), or press the button: the shadow of \(\boldsymbol{x}\) on \(\boldsymbol{y}\) disappears and the vectors meet at a right angle.

The link with Pythagoras holds in every dimension. Expanding gives \(\|\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{y}\|^2=\|\boldsymbol{x}\|^2+2\,\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{y}+\|\boldsymbol{y}\|^2\), so the Euclidean norms add in squares exactly when \(\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{y}=0\). The definition also covers the zero vector: it is orthogonal to every vector, and it is the only vector orthogonal to itself, because \(\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{x}=\|\boldsymbol{x}\|^2\). A right angle only makes sense for nonzero vectors.

Orthogonality defines the normal vector of a plane, and the shortest distance from a point to a line is measured along the perpendicular. It returns later in orthonormal bases, bases of mutually orthogonal vectors of length \(1\).

Orthogonal should not be confused with linearly independent. Nonzero vectors that are pairwise orthogonal are always independent, but independent vectors need not be orthogonal: \((1,0)\) and \((1,1)\) are independent, with inner product \(1\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Orthogonality is equivalent to a \(90^\circ\) angle for nonzero real vectors.
  • If \(\boldsymbol{y}\) has unit length, then \(\boldsymbol{x}\cdot \boldsymbol{y}\) gives the signed length of the projection of \(\boldsymbol{x}\) onto \(\boldsymbol{y}\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\) are orthogonal.
  • \((1,1)\) and \((1,-1)\) are orthogonal.

docs.title: Parametric Representations of Lines and Planes
Definition
docs.text:
A parametric representation of a line in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) has the form

\[ \boldsymbol{\ell}(t)=\boldsymbol{A}+t\boldsymbol{v}, \]

where \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is a point on the line, \(\boldsymbol{v}\neq\boldsymbol{0}\) is a direction vector, and \(t\in\mathbb{R}\).

A parametric representation of a plane has the form

\[ \boldsymbol{P}(s,t)=\boldsymbol{A}+s\boldsymbol{v}+t\boldsymbol{w}, \]

where \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is a point on the plane and \(\boldsymbol{v},\boldsymbol{w}\) are linearly independent direction vectors.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Scalar multiplication turns the parameters into displacements \(t\boldsymbol{v}\), \(s\boldsymbol{v}\) and \(t\boldsymbol{w}\). Their linear combinations, added to the starting point \(\boldsymbol{A}\), trace out the line or plane.

The parameters describe movement from a starting point along one direction for a line, or along two independent directions for a plane.

In \(\boldsymbol{\ell}(t)=\boldsymbol{A}+t\boldsymbol{v}\), \(t\in\mathbb{R}\), the point \(\boldsymbol{A}=\boldsymbol{\ell}(0)\) lies on the line and \(\boldsymbol{v}\ne\boldsymbol{0}\) is its direction. Equally spaced parameter values give equally spaced points. Choosing another point on the line or a nonzero multiple of \(\boldsymbol{v}\) gives another representation of the same line.

Move \(t\): \(\boldsymbol{\ell}(t)=\boldsymbol{A}+t\boldsymbol{v}\) walks along the line, through \(\boldsymbol{A}\) at \(t=0\) and \(\boldsymbol{A}+\boldsymbol{v}\) at \(t=1\). Drag \(\boldsymbol{A}\) and the tip of \(\boldsymbol{v}\) to move the line.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A point lies on the line or plane exactly when it is obtained for some parameter value or parameter pair.
  • Two distinct points determine a line, while three non-collinear points determine a plane.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\boldsymbol{\ell}(t)=(4,2)+t(1,1)\) represents a line through \((4,2)\).
  • \(\boldsymbol{P}(s,t)=(1,0,0)+s(1,1,0)+t(0,1,1)\) represents a plane in \(\mathbb{R}^3\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A permutation matrix is a square matrix with exactly one entry equal to \(1\) in each row and each column, and all other entries equal to \(0\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A permutation matrix reorders: multiplying by it permutes the entries of a vector, or the rows or columns of a matrix, without changing any value. It is the identity matrix with its rows put in a different order.

Row \(1\) of the figure's \(\boldsymbol{P}\) has its \(1\) in column \(2\), so the first entry of \(\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{x}\) is \(x_2\); rows \(2\), \(3\) and \(4\) pick \(x_4\), \(x_1\) and \(x_3\). Row \(i\) says which entry of \(\boldsymbol{x}\) is copied into position \(i\), and column \(j\) says where \(x_j\) goes: column \(1\) has its \(1\) in row \(3\), so \(x_1\) moves to position \(3\).

The matrix product \(\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{A}\) applies the same reordering to the rows of \(\boldsymbol{A}\), and \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{P}\) reorders its columns. A reordering is undone by the transpose: \(\boldsymbol{P}^{\top}\boldsymbol{P}=\boldsymbol{I}\), so the inverse is \(\boldsymbol{P}^{-1}=\boldsymbol{P}^{\top}\). The determinant is \(1\) when the reordering can be made with an even number of swaps and \(-1\) otherwise; the figure's \(\boldsymbol{P}\) is three swaps, so its determinant is \(-1\).

The \(n\times n\) permutation matrices correspond to the \(n!\) elements of the symmetric group \(S_n\). Swapping two rows, an elementary row operation, is multiplication on the left by a permutation matrix; the LU decomposition \(\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{A}=\boldsymbol{L}\boldsymbol{U}\) records its row swaps this way.

A common slip is to take \(\boldsymbol{P}^{-1}=\boldsymbol{P}\). This holds for a single swap such as \(\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\), but applying the figure's \(\boldsymbol{P}\) twice gives \((x_4,x_3,x_2,x_1)\), not \(\boldsymbol{x}\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The identity matrix is a permutation matrix.
  • The product of two permutation matrices is a permutation matrix.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\) swaps two rows when multiplied on the left.
  • \(\boldsymbol{I}_3\) represents the permutation that changes nothing.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A permutation of a set \(A\) is a bijective function

\[ \pi\colon A\to A. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A permutation rearranges the elements of a set without losing or duplicating any element: each element is moved to a place in the same set, and each place receives exactly one element.

The arrows send \(1\mapsto3\), \(2\mapsto1\), \(3\mapsto4\) and \(4\mapsto2\), and every number on the right is hit by exactly one arrow, which is bijectivity. In two-row notation, \(\pi=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3&4\\3&1&4&2\end{pmatrix}\) lists the images in the bottom row. Following the arrows from \(1\) gives the cycle \(1\mapsto3\mapsto4\mapsto2\mapsto1\), written \((1\,3\,4\,2)\). Reversing every arrow gives the inverse \(\pi^{-1}=(1\,2\,4\,3)\), which undoes \(\pi\).

Bijectivity has two halves. Injective means that no two elements land in the same place, so nothing is duplicated; surjective means that every place is filled, so nothing is lost. On a finite set either half implies the other, since \(n\) elements land in \(n\) places. On an infinite set they differ, as the map \(n\mapsto2n\) on \(\mathbb{N}\) in the Examples shows.

To count the permutations of an \(n\)-element set, choose the image of the first element in \(n\) ways, that of the second in \(n-1\) ways, and so on, which gives \(n!\) (factorial). This is the same count as for ordered arrangements of \(n\) distinct objects. Under composition the permutations of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) form the symmetric group \(S_n\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The composition of two permutations is again a permutation.
  • A finite set with \(n\) elements has \(n!\) permutations.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Swapping two elements and leaving the rest fixed is a permutation.
  • On \(A=\{1,2,3\}\), the map \(\pi(1)=2\), \(\pi(2)=3\), \(\pi(3)=1\) is a permutation. The map \(f(n)=2n\) on \(\mathbb{N}\) is injective but not surjective, so it is not a permutation of \(\mathbb{N}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A pivot of a nonzero row is the first nonzero entry in that row.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A matrix arranges the coefficients into rows and columns; finding the first nonzero entry of a row identifies its pivot position and the corresponding column.

Pivots mark the leading variables and structure of an echelon form.

Blue columns hold a pivot: \(x_1,x_3,x_4\) are basic (pivot) variables; the orange column has none: \(x_2\) is a free variable, which can take any value, and the basic variables are then determined by it. The number of pivots is the rank; in echelon form each pivot sits to the right of the one above.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• In row echelon form, each pivot lies to the right of the pivot in the row above.
  • In reduced row echelon form, every pivot is a leading \(1\) and is the only nonzero entry in its column.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In \((0,0,5,2)\), the pivot is \(5\).
  • In \((1,3,0)\), the pivot is \(1\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A plane is a two-dimensional geometric object described by a point \(\boldsymbol{A}\) and two linearly independent direction vectors \(\boldsymbol{v},\boldsymbol{w}\) as \(\boldsymbol{P}(s,t)=\boldsymbol{A}+s\boldsymbol{v}+t\boldsymbol{w}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A plane is a flat two-dimensional surface: from a starting point one can move in two independent directions, and every point is reached by choosing how far to go in each. The parameters \(s\) and \(t\) are these two amounts, and the displacement \(s\boldsymbol{v}+t\boldsymbol{w}\) is a linear combination of the direction vectors.

In the figure the plane passes through \(\boldsymbol{A}\) and contains the directions \(\boldsymbol{v}\) and \(\boldsymbol{w}\). The choice \(s=t=1\) gives the corner \(\boldsymbol{P}(1,1)=\boldsymbol{A}+\boldsymbol{v}+\boldsymbol{w}\) of the dashed parallelogram. Other values of \(s\) and \(t\), negative ones included, fill the rest of the plane.

The parametrization needs linearly independent \(\boldsymbol{v}\) and \(\boldsymbol{w}\). If \(\boldsymbol{w}\) is a multiple of \(\boldsymbol{v}\), the formula only moves along one direction and describes a line. The description is not unique: \(\boldsymbol{A}\) may be any point of the plane, and \(\boldsymbol{v},\boldsymbol{w}\) any two independent vectors in it. A plane through the origin is the span of \(\boldsymbol{v}\) and \(\boldsymbol{w}\), a two-dimensional subspace; any other plane is such a subspace shifted by \(\boldsymbol{A}\).

In \(\mathbb{R}^3\) a plane can also be described by a single equation, the point-normal equation with a normal vector. In \(\mathbb{R}^n\), the one-equation description gives a hyperplane.

A common slip is to read \(\boldsymbol{v}\) and \(\boldsymbol{w}\) as points of the plane. They are directions: \(\boldsymbol{A}+\boldsymbol{v}\) and \(\boldsymbol{A}+\boldsymbol{w}\) lie on the plane, while \(\boldsymbol{v}\) itself does so only when the plane passes through the origin.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Three non-collinear points determine a plane.
  • If two direction vectors are scalar multiples, they do not determine a unique plane.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\boldsymbol{P}(s,t)=(0,0,0)+s(1,0,0)+t(0,1,0)\) is the \(xy\)-plane.
  • The plane through three non-collinear points \(\boldsymbol{A},\boldsymbol{B},\boldsymbol{C}\) can be written \(\boldsymbol{P}(s,t)=\boldsymbol{A}+s(\boldsymbol{B}-\boldsymbol{A})+t(\boldsymbol{C}-\boldsymbol{A})\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The point-normal equation of a plane through \((x_0,y_0,z_0)\) with normal vector \(\boldsymbol{n}=(a,b,c)\) is \(a(x-x_0)+b(y-y_0)+c(z-z_0)=0\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The point-normal equation describes a plane by a test rather than a recipe: a point \(\boldsymbol{P}=(x,y,z)\) lies on the plane exactly when the displacement \(\boldsymbol{P}-\boldsymbol{P}_0\) from the fixed point is orthogonal to the normal vector \(\boldsymbol{n}\).

In the figure the displacement \(\boldsymbol{P}-\boldsymbol{P}_0\) lies in the plane and \(\boldsymbol{n}=(a,b,c)\) stands perpendicular to it. Writing this with the inner product and expanding the coordinate sum gives the defining equation: \(\boldsymbol{n}\cdot(\boldsymbol{P}-\boldsymbol{P}_0)=a(x-x_0)+b(y-y_0)+c(z-z_0)=0\). For a point off the plane, the displacement has a component along \(\boldsymbol{n}\) and the left-hand side is nonzero.

Expanding further gives \(ax+by+cz=d\) with \(d=\boldsymbol{n}\cdot\boldsymbol{P}_0\). The coefficients of \(x,y,z\) form the normal vector, and the constant fixes the position: changing \(d\) while keeping \((a,b,c)\) shifts the plane parallel to itself. One equation in three unknowns leaves two free variables, matching the two parameters of the parametric description. For the plane \(3x-7y+z=0\) of the Examples, \(z=-3x+7y\); choosing \(x=s\) and \(y=t\) gives \(s(1,0,-3)+t(0,1,7)\), which recovers \(\boldsymbol{B}\) and \(\boldsymbol{C}\) as direction vectors.

The same pattern in \(\mathbb{R}^2\), \(a(x-x_0)+b(y-y_0)=0\), describes a line with normal \((a,b)\), and in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) a hyperplane. In linear programming, the boundary of a constraint \(a_1x_1+a_2x_2+a_3x_3\le d\) is such a plane, with the coefficient vector as its normal.

A common slip is to treat the equation as unique. Multiplying by a nonzero number, as in \(6x-14y+2z=0\), describes the same plane, because the normal vector is only fixed up to a nonzero multiple.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• It can be rewritten as \(ax+by+cz=d\), where \(d=ax_0+by_0+cz_0\).
  • The normal vector is read from the coefficients of \(x,y,z\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A plane through \((0,0,0)\) with normal \((0,0,1)\) has equation \(z=0\).
  • For \(\boldsymbol{A}=(0,0,0)\), \(\boldsymbol{B}=(1,0,-3)\) and \(\boldsymbol{C}=(0,1,7)\), a normal \(\boldsymbol{n}=(a,b,c)\) satisfies \(\boldsymbol{n}\cdot(\boldsymbol{B}-\boldsymbol{A})=a-3c=0\) and \(\boldsymbol{n}\cdot(\boldsymbol{C}-\boldsymbol{A})=b+7c=0\). Taking \(c=1\) gives \(\boldsymbol{n}=(3,-7,1)\) and the plane \(3x-7y+z=0\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The polar coordinate system specifies a given point in the plane \(\mathbb{R}^2\) (see Cartesian coordinate system) by using two coordinates:

  • the point's distance from a reference point called the pole,
  • the point's direction from the pole relative to the direction of the polar axis, a ray drawn from the pole.

The distance from the pole is called the radius, and the angle is called the polar angle.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The Cartesian product \([0,\infty)\times\mathbb{R}\) supplies pairs \((r,\theta)\); different angle values can represent the same point. The trigonometric functions convert the radius and direction to Cartesian coordinates through \(x=r\cos\theta\) and \(y=r\sin\theta\).

The polar coordinate system locates a point on a plane by saying how far away it is from a centre point and what angle it makes from a fixed direction.

Using the 2-argument arctangent for the angle, for the nonzero point in the figure, \(r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\) and \(\theta=\operatorname{atan2}(y,x)\). Constant \(r\) gives a circle and constant \(\theta\) gives a ray of the polar grid.

Set the radius \(r\) and the polar angle \(\theta\), or drag the point: \(x=r\cos\theta\) and \(y=r\sin\theta\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Conversion to Cartesian coordinates: \(x = r \cos \theta\), \(y = r \sin \theta.\)
  • Conversion from Cartesian coordinates: \(r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\), \(\theta = \operatorname{atan2}(y, x).\)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• With \(r\ge0\), \(\theta=\pi/4\) describes the ray from the pole at angle \(\pi/4\) to the polar axis: \((x,y)=(r/\sqrt{2},r/\sqrt{2})\).
  • \(r = 1\) is a unit circle centred at the pole.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A greatest common divisor (GCD) of two polynomials \(a(x)\) and \(b(x)\), not both zero, is a polynomial of greatest possible degree that divides both \(a(x)\) and \(b(x)\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A greatest common divisor of \(a(x)\) and \(b(x)\) is a common factor that is as large as possible, with size measured by degree, just as the GCD of two integers is the largest integer that divides both.

The polynomial GCD can be found with the Euclidean algorithm. Polynomial long division gives \(a=qb+r\) with \(r=0\) or \(\deg r<\deg b\). Every common divisor of \(a\) and \(b\) divides \(r=a-qb\), and every common divisor of \(b\) and \(r\) divides \(a=qb+r\), so the pairs \((a,b)\) and \((b,r)\) have the same common divisors. The algorithm keeps replacing the pair by divisor and remainder. The degrees of the remainders strictly decrease, so the remainder eventually becomes zero, and the pair is then \((g,0)\), whose common divisors are exactly the divisors of \(g\). Hence the last nonzero remainder \(g\) is a GCD, and every common divisor of \(a\) and \(b\) divides it.

Since only the degree counts, a nonzero constant multiple of a GCD is again a GCD: both \(x-1\) and \(2x-2\) are GCDs of \(x^2-1\) and \(x-1\). Choosing the monic one makes the answer unique.

Because \(\lambda\) is a root of a polynomial exactly when \(x-\lambda\) divides it, the common roots of \(a\) and \(b\) are the roots of their GCD. In the Examples, \(x^3-1\) and \(x^2-1\) have the GCD \(x-1\), and \(1\) is their only common root.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The last nonzero remainder is a GCD.
  • The GCD is often normalized to be monic (leading coefficient \(1\)), which makes it unique.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The GCD of \(x^2-1\) and \(x-1\) is \(x-1\).
  • Euclidean algorithm: \(x^3-1=x\,(x^2-1)+(x-1)\) and \(x^2-1=(x+1)(x-1)+0\), so the last nonzero remainder \(x-1\) is the GCD of \(x^3-1\) and \(x^2-1\).
