docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(n,k\in\mathbb{N}\) with \(0\le k\le n\). The binomial coefficient \(\binom nk\) is the number of ways to form a combination of \(k\) objects from \(n\) distinct objects without regard to order, and is given by

\[ \binom nk=\frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The binomial coefficient \(\binom nk\), read "\(n\) choose \(k\)", counts the subsets with \(k\) elements of a set with \(n\) elements: the number of ways to choose \(k\) objects when only which objects are chosen matters, not their order.

Row \(n\) of Pascal's triangle lists \(\binom n0,\binom n1,\ldots,\binom nn\) from left to right. The highlighted entry is \(\binom52=\binom41+\binom42=4+6=10\), and this sum has a counting reason: fix one of the five objects; a pair either contains it, and then one partner is chosen from the other four, or it does not, and then both are chosen from the other four. Each row also sums to \(2^n\), here \(1+5+10+10+5+1=32\), because every element is either in a subset or not, which gives \(2^n\) subsets of all sizes together.

The formula reads as "order, then forget the order": \(n!/(n-k)!\) counts the ordered selections, the \(k\)-permutations, and each unordered group of \(k\) objects appears among them \(k!\) times, so dividing by \(k!\) leaves the number of combinations. The symmetry \(\binom nk=\binom n{n-k}\) is the left-right symmetry of each row.

A common slip is to stop at \(n!/k!\) or at \(n!/(n-k)!\); only the full formula counts unordered groups. Binomial coefficients are the basic tool of naive probability when the outcomes are hands, committees or samples, and they owe their name to the expansion of \((a+b)^n\) in the Key Results.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\binom nk=\binom n{n-k}\), since choosing \(k\) objects is equivalent to leaving out \(n-k\) objects.
  • \(\binom n0=\binom nn=1\) and \(\binom n1=n\).
  • Binomial coefficients use factorials and appear in the expansion \(\displaystyle (a+b)^n=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk a^k b^{n-k}\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• From \(10\) applicants, the number of possible interview groups of size \(3\) is \(\binom{10}{3}\).
  • The number of ways to choose \(5\) cards from a \(52\) card deck is \(\binom{52}{5}\).
  • In a binomial distribution, \(\binom nk\) counts the number of ways to choose which \(k\) of the \(n\) trials are successes, which is why it appears in \(\mathbb{P}(X=k)=\binom nk p^k(1-p)^{n-k}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(n\) be a nonnegative integer, \(0\le p\le1\) and \(q=1-p\). A discrete random variable \(X\) has a binomial distribution with parameters \(n\) and \(p\), written \(X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,p)\), if

\[ \begin{gathered} \mathbb{P}(X=k)=\binom{n}{k}p^kq^{n-k},\\ k=0,1,\ldots,n, \end{gathered} \]

and the PMF is zero elsewhere. Equivalently, \(X\) is the sum of \(n\) i.i.d. Bernoulli variables with success probability \(p\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A binomial variable counts the successes in a fixed number \(n\) of independent trials that each succeed with the same probability \(p\).

The figure shows \(X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(10,0.3)\), the number of successes in ten trials with success probability \(0.3\). The bars give \(\mathbb{P}(X=k)=\binom{10}{k}0.3^k0.7^{10-k}\) for \(k=0,\ldots,10\). The tallest bar is at \(k=3\), with probability about \(0.27\), and the bars for \(k\ge8\) are nearly invisible: together they have probability about \(0.0016\). The marked value \(np=3\) is the mean of the distribution: in ten trials with success probability \(0.3\), about three successes are typical.

Change \(n\) and \(p\): the bars sit around \(\mathbb{E}X=np\) with spread \(\sqrt{npq}\). Use \(c\) and \(d\) to add up \(\mathbb{P}(c\le X\le d)\), and hover over a bar for its formula.

The PMF has two factors. Each trial is a Bernoulli trial, and by independence any one fixed sequence with \(k\) successes and \(n-k\) failures, such as \(k\) successes followed by \(n-k\) failures, has probability \(p^kq^{n-k}\). The binomial coefficient \(\binom nk\) counts how many such sequences there are, one for each choice of the \(k\) positions of the successes. Forgetting it is a common slip: for three fair tosses, \(\mathbb{P}(X=2)=\binom32\cdot\tfrac{1}{8}=\tfrac{3}{8}\), not \(\tfrac{1}{8}\).

All three conditions matter. When the draws are made without replacement from a small population, the trials are not independent and the count is hypergeometric instead. When the number of trials is not fixed but one waits for the first success, the first success distribution applies.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{E}X=np\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=np(1-p)\).
  • MGF \(M_X(t)=(1-p+p\mathrm{e}^t)^n\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For three fair tosses, \(\mathbb{P}(X=2)=\binom32(1/2)^3=3/8\).
  • For \(n=10\), \(p=0.2\), the count has mean \(2\), variance \(1.6\), and no-success probability \(0.8^{10}\).

docs.title: Further Properties
docs.text: The binomial count is a sum of independent Bernoulli trials. In the rare-event limit \(n\to\infty\), \(p_n\to0\), and \(np_n\to\lambda\), its distribution converges to \(\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)\).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Consider a group of \(n\) people and assume that each person's birthday is independently and uniformly distributed over \(365\) possible days. The birthday problem asks for the probability that at least two people in the group share a birthday.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The birthday problem shows that coincidences can happen much sooner than intuition suggests. It is usually easier to solve by first finding the chance that no match occurs.

Under the model of independent birthdays uniformly distributed over 365 days, the probability of a shared birthday among \(n\le365\) people is \(1-365\cdot364\cdots(365-n+1)/365^n\). With 23 people there are \(\binom{23}{2}=253\) pairs that could match, and the probability exceeds one half.

Move \(n\): the chance of no shared birthday is a product of fractions that shrinks quickly, and a match becomes more likely than not from \(23\) people on.

Naive probability counts equally likely birthday assignments. The complement event has distinct birthdays, so count assignments without repetition and divide by all \(365^n\) assignments before subtracting from one.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Computing the complement usually gives the simplest formula for at least one match.
  • For \(n\) draws from \(m\) equally likely labels, the no-match probability is \(\frac{m(m-1)\cdots(m-n+1)}{m^n}\).
  • The same calculation applies to hash collisions, repeated IDs, and sampled labels.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In a group of \(23\) people, the probability of at least one shared birthday is already above one half under the usual simplified assumptions.
  • If \(1000\) IDs are sampled with replacement from a million possible IDs, the collision probability can be found from the no-repeat probability.
  • A database using short random codes faces a birthday-type collision risk.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(A\) be a finite set with \(n\) elements, and let \(k\le n\). A combination is a selection of \(k\) elements from \(A\) in which order is not taken into account.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A combination records only which objects are chosen, not in which order: choosing \(A\) then \(B\) gives the same combination as choosing \(B\) then \(A\). A \(k\)-combination of a set is therefore simply a subset with \(k\) elements: rearranging the chosen objects gives no new outcome.

The figure counts pairs from the four letters \(A,B,C,D\) in two steps. First the order is kept: \(4\cdot3=12\) ordered pairs. Then the boxes put each pair together with its reversal, such as \(AB\) with \(BA\), and each box becomes one unordered pair. Every unordered pair appears exactly \(2!=2\) times among the ordered ones, so there are \(\binom42=12/2=6\) of them.

The same argument works in general. There are \(n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)\) ordered selections of \(k\) distinct objects (\(k\)-permutations), and each group of \(k\) objects can be ordered in \(k!\) ways, so the number of combinations is the binomial coefficient \(\binom nk=n!/(k!\,(n-k)!)\).

To decide which count applies, ask whether swapping two chosen objects changes the result: for a committee it does not, for a president and a secretary it does. Combinations here use each object at most once; when repetition is allowed, unordered selections are counted with stars and bars. In naive probability, numerator and denominator must be counted the same way, both ordered or both unordered; mixing the two gives a wrong ratio.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Combinations ignore order, while permutations count order.
  • The number of \(k\)-combinations from \(n\) distinct objects is \(\binom nk\).
  • Combinations are used in sampling without regard to sequence.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Choosing three committee members from twelve people is a combination problem.
  • A five-card poker hand is counted as a combination because the order of the cards in the hand does not matter.
  • Selecting two spare parts from a box of ten distinct parts is counted by \(\binom{10}{2}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(A\) be an event in a sample space \(S\). The complement of \(A\), denoted \(A^c\), is the event

\[ A^c=\{\omega\in S\colon\omega\notin A\}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The complement \(A^c\) is the event "\(A\) does not happen". It contains exactly the outcomes of the sample space that are not in \(A\), so every outcome lies in exactly one of \(A\) and \(A^c\).

The shaded region outside the disc is \(A^c\). It and the disc do not overlap and together fill the rectangle \(S\), so the axioms of probability give \(\mathbb{P}(A)+\mathbb{P}(A^c)=\mathbb{P}(S)=1\), the rule in the Key Results.

The rule pays off for "at least one" events. In four rolls of a fair die, "no six" happens in \(5^4=625\) of the \(6^4=1296\) equally likely ordered outcomes, so \(\mathbb{P}(\text{at least one six})=1-\tfrac{625}{1296}\approx0.52\), with no case split over the number of sixes, as in the birthday problem.

A common slip is to negate the wrong word: the complement of "all four rolls show a six" is "at least one roll is not a six", not "no roll shows a six".

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{P}(A^c)=1-\mathbb{P}(A)\).
  • \(A\cup A^c=S\) and \(A\cap A^c=\varnothing\).
  • The complement method is useful for events described by 'at least one'.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The complement of 'at least one machine fails' is 'no machine fails'.
  • The complement of rolling an even number on a die is rolling an odd number.
  • In the birthday problem, the complement of a shared birthday is that all birthdays are different.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(A\) be an event with \(\mathbb{P}(A)>0\) and let \(Y\) be integrable. Its conditional expectation given \(A\) is the average under the conditional probability model:

\[ \mathbb{E}[Y\mid A]=\frac{\mathbb{E}[Y\indicator_A]}{\mathbb{P}(A)}. \]

For discrete \(Y\), this equals \(\displaystyle \sum_y y\,\mathbb{P}(Y=y\mid A)\). When the conditional law has a density \(f_{Y\mid A}\), it equals \(\int_{\mathbb{R}}y f_{Y\mid A}(y)\,\mathrm{d}y\). Conditioning on an event gives a number; conditioning on a random variable gives a random variable and is treated separately in Probability Distributions (conditional expectation given a random variable).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The conditional expectation \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid A]\) is the average value of \(Y\) when only the outcomes in an event \(A\) that is known to have occurred are considered. It is computed like an ordinary expectation, with the conditional probabilities given \(A\) as weights.

In the figure \(X\) takes the values \(1,2,3,4\) with probabilities \(0.1,0.2,0.3,0.4\), so \(\mathbb{E}[X]=3\). Given \(B=\{X\ge3\}\), with \(\mathbb{P}(B)=0.7\), the values \(1\) and \(2\) drop out, and the masses \(0.3\) and \(0.4\) are rescaled to \(3/7\) and \(4/7\) so that they again add up to \(1\). The conditional mean \(\mathbb{E}[X\mid B]=3(3/7)+4(4/7)=25/7\approx3.57\) lies to the right of \(3\) because only the large values remain.

In the formula \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid A]=\mathbb{E}[Y\indicator_A]/\mathbb{P}(A)\), the indicator sets \(Y\) to zero on the outcomes outside \(A\), so the numerator adds up \(Y\) only over \(A\); dividing by \(\mathbb{P}(A)\) renormalizes those weights to total one. In the figure \(\mathbb{E}[X\indicator_B]=3(0.3)+4(0.4)=2.5\) and \(2.5/0.7=25/7\). The condition \(\mathbb{P}(A)>0\) is needed because the division is otherwise undefined. A common slip is to stop at \(\mathbb{E}[Y\indicator_A]\): here \(2.5\) is smaller than every value \(X\) takes on \(B\), so it cannot be the average over \(B\).

Conditioning on \(A\) and on its complement and averaging the two results with weights \(\mathbb{P}(A)\) and \(\mathbb{P}(A^c)\) gives back \(\mathbb{E}[Y]\), the expectation version of the law of total probability. In the figure \(\mathbb{E}[X\mid X\le2]=0.5/0.3=5/3\), and \(0.7\cdot\tfrac{25}{7}+0.3\cdot\tfrac{5}{3}=2.5+0.5=3\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid A]=\mathbb{E}[Y\indicator_A]/\mathbb{P}(A)\).
  • For constants \(a,b\) and integrable \(Y,Z\), \(\mathbb{E}[aY+bZ\mid A]=a\mathbb{E}[Y\mid A]+b\mathbb{E}[Z\mid A]\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For a fair die conditioned to be even, the mean is \((2+4+6)/3=4\).
  • For \(Y\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) conditioned on \(Y>1/2\), the mean is \(\int_{1/2}^12y\,\mathrm{d}y=3/4\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(A\), \(B\), and \(C\) be events with \(\mathbb{P}(C)>0\). The events \(A\) and \(B\) are conditionally independent given \(C\) if

\[ \mathbb{P}(A\cap B\mid C)=\mathbb{P}(A\mid C)\mathbb{P}(B\mid C). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Conditional independence means two events stop influencing each other once certain information is known. It is a statement about independence inside a restricted situation.

The diagram chooses a fair coin or a coin with head probability \(0.9\), each with probability \(1/2\), and tosses the chosen coin twice. Given its identity \(C\), the two heads events are independent. Without this conditioning, \(\mathbb{P}(H_1\cap H_2)=\frac{1}{2}(0.25)+\frac{1}{2}(0.81)=0.53\), whereas \(\mathbb{P}(H_1)\mathbb{P}(H_2)=0.7^2=0.49\).

Conditional probability first restricts the model to \(C\). The factorization for independent events is then applied inside that restricted model; ordinary independence before conditioning does not automatically imply it.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Conditional independence is not the same as ordinary independence.
  • Two variables can be dependent marginally but conditionally independent after a common cause is known.
  • Conditional independence is central in graphical and hierarchical probability models.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Two symptoms may be dependent overall but conditionally independent given the disease status.
  • Two students' answers may become conditionally independent once their preparation levels are known.
  • Machine failures in different locations may be conditionally independent given the weather condition.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(A,B\) be events with \(\mathbb{P}(B)>0\). The conditional probability of \(A\) given \(B\) is

\[ \mathbb{P}(A\mid B)=\frac{\mathbb{P}(A\cap B)}{\mathbb{P}(B)}. \]

This definition restricts and renormalizes the probability model to \(B\). It is not defined when \(\mathbb{P}(B)=0\), because the quotient would divide by zero.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Conditioning asks how likely \(A\) is once we know that \(B\) has happened. The outcomes outside \(B\) are discarded, and the probabilities of the outcomes in \(B\) are rescaled so that they sum to one again.

Before conditioning, the whole rectangle \(S\) counts. After learning \(B\), only the disc \(B\) remains as the new sample space, and of \(A\) only the part \(A\cap B\) is still possible. \(\mathbb{P}(A\mid B)\) is the share of the probability of \(B\) that lies in \(A\cap B\).

Knowing that \(B\) happened keeps only the outlined region. \(\mathbb{P}(A\mid B)\) is the share of that region taken up by \(A\).

Each part of the formula has a role. The numerator is \(\mathbb{P}(A\cap B)\), not \(\mathbb{P}(A)\), because outcomes of \(A\) outside \(B\) have been ruled out. Dividing by \(\mathbb{P}(B)\) makes the new probabilities add up to one, and it requires \(\mathbb{P}(B)>0\): the formula does not define conditioning on an event of probability zero. With equally likely outcomes, as in naive probability, the formula becomes counting inside \(B\): \(\mathbb{P}(A\mid B)=|A\cap B|/|B|\). For two fair dice, \(\mathbb{P}(\text{at least one six})=\tfrac{11}{36}\), but among the six pairs with sum \(7\) exactly two contain a six, so \(\mathbb{P}(\text{at least one six}\mid\text{sum}=7)=\tfrac{2}{6}=\tfrac{1}{3}\).

A common slip is to swap the roles of \(A\) and \(B\): in general \(\mathbb{P}(A\mid B)\ne\mathbb{P}(B\mid A)\), and Bayes' rule converts one into the other; confusing them is the prosecutor's fallacy. When \(\mathbb{P}(A\mid B)=\mathbb{P}(A)\), learning \(B\) changes nothing, which is the idea of independent events. The law of total probability builds \(\mathbb{P}(A)\) back from the conditional probabilities given the cases of a partition.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{P}(A\cap B)=\mathbb{P}(A\mid B)\mathbb{P}(B)\).
  • For fixed \(B\) of positive probability, \(A\mapsto\mathbb{P}(A\mid B)\) is a probability measure.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For a fair die, \(\mathbb{P}(X=6\mid X\text{ is even})=(1/6)/(3/6)=1/3\).
  • If \(\mathbb{P}(A\cap B)=0.12\) and \(\mathbb{P}(B)=0.4\), then \(\mathbb{P}(A\mid B)=0.3\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(X\) be a random variable and let \(B\) be an event with \(\mathbb{P}(B)>0\). The conditional variance of \(X\) given \(B\) is

\[ \operatorname{Var}(X\mid B)=\mathbb{E}[(X-\mathbb{E}[X\mid B])^2\mid B], \]

provided the conditional expectations exist.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Conditional variance measures how much uncertainty about \(X\) remains once the event \(B\) is known to have occurred. It is the variance of \(X\) computed with the conditional probabilities given \(B\), around the conditional mean \(\mathbb{E}[X\mid B]\).

In the figure \(X\) takes the values \(1,2,3,4\) with probabilities \(0.1,0.2,0.3,0.4\), and \(B=\{X\ge3\}\) leaves the values \(3\) and \(4\) with conditional probabilities \(3/7\) and \(4/7\) and conditional mean \(25/7\). The arrows show the deviations \(3-\tfrac{25}{7}=-\tfrac{4}{7}\) and \(4-\tfrac{25}{7}=\tfrac{3}{7}\); squaring them and weighting with the conditional probabilities gives

\[ \operatorname{Var}(X\mid B)=\frac{3}{7}\Big(\frac{4}{7}\Big)^2+\frac{4}{7}\Big(\frac{3}{7}\Big)^2=\frac{12}{49}\approx0.24. \]

This is much smaller than \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=1\), because only two neighbouring values remain.

Conditioning on \(B\) gives a new probability model, so every rule for variance holds after conditioning. In particular \(\operatorname{Var}(X\mid B)=\mathbb{E}[X^2\mid B]-(\mathbb{E}[X\mid B])^2\); here \(\mathbb{E}[X^2\mid B]=9\cdot\tfrac{3}{7}+16\cdot\tfrac{4}{7}=13\) and \(13-\tfrac{625}{49}=\tfrac{12}{49}\). The centre must be the conditional mean: centring at \(\mathbb{E}[X]=3\) instead would give \(\tfrac{3}{7}\cdot0+\tfrac{4}{7}\cdot1=\tfrac{4}{7}\), which is not the conditional variance.

Conditioning does not always reduce spread. Given \(\{X=1\}\cup\{X=4\}\), the two remaining values lie far apart, and the conditional variance is \(1.44\), larger than \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=1\). Averaged over the events of a partition, however, conditional variances never exceed \(\operatorname{Var}(X)\); this returns later in the law of total variance.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Conditional variance measures spread after conditioning on information.
  • The law of total variance decomposes total variability into within-condition and between-condition parts.
  • Conditional variance is zero when the condition determines the random variable exactly.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Delivery time may have smaller variance after conditioning on the shipping method.
  • Exam score variability may differ between students who studied and students who did not.
  • In a mixture distribution, each component can have its own conditional variance.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Under the course's absolutely continuous convention, a real-valued random variable \(X\) is continuous if it has a nonnegative integrable density \(f_X\) such that

\[ \mathbb{P}(X\in A)=\int_A f_X(x)\,\mathrm{d}x \]

for every interval \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}\). Necessarily \(\int_{\mathbb{R}}f_X(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=1\). A continuous CDF by itself does not guarantee the existence of a density.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A continuous random variable has its probability spread over intervals rather than concentrated on single values. Probabilities are areas under its density \(f_X\), and every single value has probability zero.

In the figure the shaded region between \(a\) and \(b\) has area \(\mathbb{P}(a\le X\le b)\), the integral of \(f_X\) from \(a\) to \(b\). At the point \(c\) the vertical line under the curve has no width and therefore no area: \(\mathbb{P}(X=c)=0\), although \(f_X(c)\) is positive.

Two consequences follow. Endpoints do not matter, so \(\mathbb{P}(a<X<b)=\mathbb{P}(a\le X\le b)\). And \(f_X(x)\) is not a probability: it is probability per unit length, and it may exceed \(1\); the uniform distribution on \((0,\tfrac{1}{2})\) has density \(2\) there. Where \(f_X\) is continuous, a short interval of length \(h\) starting at \(x\) has probability approximately \(f_X(x)\,h\).

Compared with a discrete random variable, sums of masses become definite integrals of a density: the PMF value \(p_X(x)\) is a probability, while \(f_X(x)\) is not. The normal distribution is another standard example. Probability zero does not mean impossible: in each experiment \(X\) takes some value, although every single value had probability zero.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{P}(X=x)=0\) for every real \(x\).
  • Its CDF is absolutely continuous and equals the integral of its density.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A uniform variable on \((0,1)\) has density \(1\) there and no atom at \(1/2\).
  • An exponential waiting time has \(\mathbb{P}(a<X<b)=\int_a^b\lambda \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda x}\,\mathrm{d}x\) for \(0\le a<b\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(A\) be a finite set. Counting is the process of determining the number of elements of \(A\), usually by using systematic rules such as addition, multiplication, permutations, or combinations.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Counting methods help determine how many outcomes are possible. They are essential when probabilities are based on equally likely outcomes.

The diagram pairs each of two shirts with each of three pairs of trousers, giving \(2\cdot3=6\) outfits. Multiplying the numbers of choices counts these ordered combinations; whether order matters determines when permutations or combinations are appropriate.

Finite and infinite sets distinguishes a finite outcome count from an unbounded or countably infinite collection. Cardinality is the number being computed; the counting rules provide ways to find it without listing every element.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The counting multiplication rule multiplies the number of choices at successive stages: if every first-stage choice has \(m\) second-stage choices and there are \(n\) first-stage choices, there are \(nm\) ordered outcomes.
  • The addition rule counts alternatives that do not overlap: for disjoint finite sets, \(|A\cup B|=|A|+|B|\). Overlapping alternatives need the inclusion–exclusion principle.
  • Counting arguments support naive probability models when outcomes are equally likely.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A password with two letters followed by three digits has \(26^2\cdot10^3=676{,}000\) possibilities when all 26 letters and 10 digits are allowed at each position and repetition is permitted.
  • If a menu offers either a soup or a salad but not both, the addition rule counts the first-course choices.
  • Counting favourable poker hands and total poker hands gives a naive probability.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a real-valued random variable \(X\), its cumulative distribution function is

\[ F_X(x)=\mathbb{P}(X\le x),\qquad x\in\mathbb{R}. \]

It is nondecreasing and right-continuous, with \(\lim_{x\to-\infty}F_X(x)=0\) and \(\lim_{x\to\infty}F_X(x)=1\). These limits describe the notation \(F_X(-\infty)=0\) and \(F_X(\infty)=1\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The CDF answers the question "what is the probability that \(X\) is at most \(x\)?" for every threshold \(x\) at once. It collects probability from the left and describes the distribution of any real-valued random variable, whether its values form a list or a whole range.

The left panel is a staircase for \(X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(3,\tfrac{1}{2})\), the number of heads in three fair tosses. \(F_X\) is flat between the possible values \(0,1,2,3\) and jumps there by \(\tfrac{1}{8},\tfrac{3}{8},\tfrac{3}{8},\tfrac{1}{8}\), reaching the levels \(\tfrac{1}{8},\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{7}{8},1\); each jump is the probability of that value, so \(\mathbb{P}(X=1)=\tfrac{3}{8}\). The right panel is the CDF of the standard normal distribution, which rises without any jump and has \(F_X(1)\approx0.84\).

Move \(x\): \(F_X(x)\) collects all probability at or below \(x\). Masses give a staircase, a density a smooth curve, and the mixed example both a jump and a smooth rise.

Each property in the Definition has a probabilistic reason. \(F_X\) is nondecreasing because \(\{X\le x\}\subseteq\{X\le y\}\) for \(x<y\). The limits \(0\) and \(1\) hold because \(\{X\le x\}\) shrinks to the impossible event as \(x\to-\infty\) and grows to the whole sample space as \(x\to\infty\). Right-continuity holds because "\(\le\)" includes the threshold itself, so at a jump the value is the top of the step: in the left panel \(F_X(1)=\tfrac{1}{2}\), not \(\tfrac{1}{8}\).

A common slip is to ignore the difference between \(\le\) and \(<\). In the example \(\mathbb{P}(X<1)=\tfrac{1}{8}\) while \(\mathbb{P}(X\le1)=\tfrac{1}{2}\); for discrete variables the endpoints matter, hence the half-open interval \(a<X\le b\) in the Key Results. For a discrete random variable, \(F_X(x)\) is the sum of the PMF \(p_X(t)\) over all values \(t\le x\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{P}(a<X\le b)=F_X(b)-F_X(a)\).
  • \(\mathbb{P}(X=x)=F_X(x)-F_X(x-)\), where \(F_X(x-)\) is the left limit.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\operatorname{Bern}(0.3)\), the CDF is \(0\) for \(x<0\), \(0.7\) for \(0\le x<1\), and \(1\) for \(x\ge1\).
  • For \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\), \(F_X(0.4)=0.4\) and \(\mathbb{P}(0.2<X\le0.4)=0.2\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A real-valued random variable \(X\) is discrete if there is a finite or countably infinite set \(D\) such that \(\mathbb{P}(X\in D)=1\). Its distribution is determined by the masses \(p_X(x)=\mathbb{P}(X=x)\) on this set.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A discrete random variable puts all its probability on a list of values, finitely many or countably many \(x_1,x_2,\ldots\). The probability of any statement about \(X\) is found by adding the masses of the values for which the statement is true.

Here \(X\) is the number of heads in two fair tosses. The labels under the bars show which outcomes give each value: \(\{TT\}\) gives \(0\), \(\{HT,TH\}\) gives \(1\) and \(\{HH\}\) gives \(2\), so the masses are \(\tfrac{1}{4}\), \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) and \(\tfrac{1}{4}\), and they sum to \(1\). A probability such as \(\mathbb{P}(X\ge1)=\tfrac{1}{2}+\tfrac{1}{4}=\tfrac{3}{4}\) is a sum of bars, as in the second Key Result.

The list of values may be infinite as long as it is countable. The number of tosses of a fair coin up to and including the first head takes the values \(1,2,3,\ldots\) with masses \(\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{4},\tfrac{1}{8},\ldots\), which sum to \(1\) as a geometric series (first success distribution). Discrete does not mean integer-valued: a variable that takes only the values \(0.5\) and \(2.5\) is discrete too.

The PMF \(p_X\) stores the whole distribution, and the CDF is a staircase that jumps by \(p_X(x)\) at each value \(x\). A quantity spread over a whole interval, such as an exactly measured waiting time, where every single value has probability zero, is not discrete; such variables are treated later as continuous random variables.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• There is a countable set \(D\) with \(\mathbb{P}(X\in D)=1\).
  • For any set \(A\), \(\displaystyle \mathbb{P}(X\in A)=\sum_{x\in A\cap D}p_X(x)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A fair die has values \(1,\ldots,6\), each with probability \(1/6\).
  • A Poisson count has possible values \(0,1,2,\ldots\), so a discrete support need not be finite.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(A=\{a_1,\ldots,a_n\}\) be a nonempty finite set of distinct real values. A variable is discrete uniform on \(A\) if \(p_X(a_i)=1/n\) for each \(i\) and its PMF is zero outside \(A\).

The course's integer-range case has \(A=\{a,a+1,\ldots,b\}\), where \(a\le b\) are integers, and

\[ p_X(k)=\frac{1}{b-a+1},\qquad k=a,\ldots,b. \]

The mean and variance formulas below apply to this consecutive-integer case; for an arbitrary finite set, average its listed values and squared deviations.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A discrete uniform variable picks one value from a finite set, with every value equally likely. It is the random-variable form of naive probability, as for a fair die or a random integer from a range.

The figure shows a fair die, \(A=\{1,\ldots,6\}\): six bars of equal height \(\tfrac{1}{6}\). The dashed line at \(3.5\) marks the mean from the Key Results; it lies at the centre because the bars are placed symmetrically, and it is not itself a possible value. The variance \(35/12\) in the figure is the formula \((n^2-1)/12\) with \(n=6\) values.

Move the ends \(a\) and \(b\): every value gets the same mass \(1/(b-a+1)\), and the mean \((a+b)/2\) sits in the middle.

Only the number of values matters for the probabilities: each mass is \(1/n\), and the probability of a set of values is the number of points of \(A\) in that set divided by \(n\). For the integer range \(a,\ldots,b\) there are \(n=b-a+1\) values, which is where the denominator in the PMF comes from; a common slip is to count \(b-a\) values, but \(\{3,\ldots,7\}\) has \(5\) values, not \(4\).

A sum of uniform variables is not uniform: the total of two fair dice takes the \(11\) values \(2,\ldots,12\), but \(7\) arises from six of the \(36\) equally likely pairs and \(2\) only from \((1,1)\) (see sum of independent random variables). The uniform distribution on an interval is the continuous counterpart, spreading probability evenly over an interval instead of over finitely many points.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{E}X=(a+b)/2\).
  • \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=((b-a+1)^2-1)/12\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A fair die has mean \(3.5\) and variance \(35/12\).
  • A uniform integer on \(\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}\) has \(\mathbb{P}(X\ge1)=2/5\) and mean \(0\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(A\) and \(B\) be events. The events \(A\) and \(B\) are disjoint or mutually exclusive if

\[ A\cap B=\varnothing. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Disjoint events have no outcome in common, so they cannot happen on the same run of the experiment: once one of them occurs, the other is ruled out.

The two discs do not overlap, so their intersection is the empty set, and by the third axiom of probability their probabilities add: for a fair die, \(A=\{1,2\}\) and \(B=\{6\}\) are disjoint and \(\mathbb{P}(A\cup B)=\tfrac{2}{6}+\tfrac{1}{6}=\tfrac{1}{2}\).

Disjointness is a property of the events as sets, not of their probabilities. For more than two events it means pairwise disjoint: \(\{1,2\}\), \(\{2,3\}\) and \(\{1,3\}\) have no outcome common to all three, yet no two of them are disjoint.

A common slip is to read "disjoint" as "unrelated": knowing that \(A\) occurred tells you that \(B\) did not. This differs from independence, where knowing that one event occurred does not change the probability of the other.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Disjoint events have empty intersection.
  • For disjoint events, \(\mathbb{P}(A\cup B)=\mathbb{P}(A)+\mathbb{P}(B)\).
  • Disjoint events \(A\) and \(B\) are independent only if \(\mathbb{P}(A)=0\) or \(\mathbb{P}(B)=0\), because \(\mathbb{P}(A\cap B)=0\) must then equal \(\mathbb{P}(A)\mathbb{P}(B)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• On one die roll, rolling a one and rolling a six are disjoint events.
  • Drawing a red card and drawing a black card on a single draw are disjoint.
  • Passing and failing the same exam attempt are mutually exclusive outcomes.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(X\) be a random variable on a probability space \((S,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})\): a sample space \(S\), a collection \(\mathcal{F}\) of events, and a probability function \(\mathbb{P}\) on \(\mathcal{F}\). The distribution of \(X\) is the probability measure on \(\mathbb{R}\) defined by assigning to each suitable set \(B\) the probability

\[ \mathbb{P}(X\in B). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The distribution of \(X\) records where the probability of \(X\) lies on the real line: for every set \(B\) of values it gives the probability that \(X\) lands in \(B\). It forgets the sample space and keeps only what can be said about the values of \(X\).

In the figure probability is spread continuously along the line, and for the interval \(B=[-1,1.5]\) the probability \(\mathbb{P}(X\in B)\approx0.77\) is the shaded area under the curve; the whole area under the curve is \(1\). Such a curve is called a density.

Read \(\mathbb{P}(X\in B)\) as the probability of the generated event \(\{\omega\in S\colon X(\omega)\in B\}\): the distribution carries the probabilities from \(S\) over to sets of real numbers. It is again a probability assignment, now on sets of values: all probabilities are nonnegative, \(\mathbb{P}(X\in\mathbb{R})=1\), and probabilities of disjoint sets add.

In practice a distribution is not written out set by set. A discrete random variable is described by its PMF, the probability of each single value, and every real random variable by its CDF \(F_X(x)=\mathbb{P}(X\le x)\), which already determines all probabilities \(\mathbb{P}(X\in B)\). Named families such as the Bernoulli and binomial distributions are distributions in this sense.

Having the same distribution is weaker than being equal. For one fair coin toss, the indicator of heads and the indicator of tails both take the values \(0\) and \(1\) with probability \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) each, yet they never take the same value.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The distribution of a real-valued random variable is uniquely determined by its CDF.
  • Different random variables can have the same distribution.
  • Discrete, continuous, and mixed distributions describe different ways probability can be allocated.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Two independent fair coin indicators have the same Bernoulli distribution but are not the same random variable.
  • The distribution of a delivery time describes the probabilities of different time intervals.
  • A mixture of customer types can create a distribution with several peaks.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(S\) be a sample space. An event is a subset \(A\subseteq S\) whose occurrence can be assigned a probability.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An event is a yes-or-no statement about the result of an experiment, written as the set of outcomes for which the answer is yes. It occurs exactly when the realized outcome belongs to it.

In the figure, "the roll is even" is the subset \(A=\{2,4,6\}\) of \(S=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}\): a roll of \(4\) makes \(A\) occur, a roll of \(3\) does not, and with equally likely faces \(\mathbb{P}(A)=\tfrac{3}{6}=\tfrac{1}{2}\).

Words become set operations: "\(A\) or \(B\)" is the union, "\(A\) and \(B\)" the intersection, "not \(A\)" the complement. The empty set never occurs and \(S\) itself always occurs.

A common slip is to confuse the outcome \(4\) with the event \(\{4\}\): only events, which are sets, are given probabilities.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Events are subsets of the sample space.
  • Events can be combined using union, intersection, and complement.
  • A probability function assigns probabilities to events, not to informal statements outside the model.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In a die roll, the event 'roll an even number' is the set of outcomes two, four, and six.
  • In a reliability model, the event 'system fails before noon' is a subset of possible histories.
  • In a survey, the event 'respondent is under thirty' collects all outcomes with that property.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For an integrable real-valued random variable \(X\), its expectation is the probability-weighted mean. The formulas are

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}X&=\sum_x x\,p_X(x) \quad\text{for discrete }X,\\ \mathbb{E}X&=\int_{\mathbb{R}}x f_X(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\quad \text{when }X\text{ has a density}. \end{aligned} \]

Finite expectation requires \(\mathbb{E}|X|<\infty\): respectively \(\displaystyle \sum_x|x|p_X(x)<\infty\) or \(\int_{\mathbb{R}}|x|f_X(x)\,\mathrm{d}x<\infty\). More generally, write \(X=X^+-X^-\) with positive part \(X^+=\max(X,0)\) and negative part \(X^-=\max(-X,0)\); the extended expectation is defined if at least one of \(\mathbb{E}X^+\) and \(\mathbb{E}X^-\) is finite. If both are infinite, \(\mathbb{E}X\) is undefined.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Expectation describes the centre of a distribution by weighting each outcome by its probability. Sums and integrals express the same idea for discrete variables and variables with densities.

For the illustrated masses, the mean is \(\mathbb{E}[X]=1(0.1)+2(0.2)+3(0.3)+4(0.4)=3\). This probability-weighted average is the balance point of the masses and the long-run average of i.i.d. draws.

Treat the probabilities as weights on a seesaw and move the fulcrum \(c\): it balances exactly at \(\displaystyle c=\mathbb{E}X=\sum_x x\,p_X(x)\).

For a discrete variable, the probability mass function supplies the weight attached to each possible value in the expectation sum. These are probability weights, not equal weights unless the distribution is uniform.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For nonnegative \(X\), expectation is well-defined in \([0,\infty]\), even when it is not finite.
  • For \(X\ge0\), \(\mathbb{E}X=\int_0^\infty\mathbb{P}(X>t)\,\mathrm{d}t\), possibly \(+\infty\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For a fair die, \(\mathbb{E}X=(1+2+3+4+5+6)/6=3.5\).
  • If \(f_X(x)=2x\) for \(0<x<1\) and zero elsewhere, then \(\mathbb{E}X=\int_0^1 2x^2\,\mathrm{d}x=2/3\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\lambda>0\). A continuous random variable \(X\) has an exponential distribution with rate \(\lambda\), written \(X\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)\), if its density is

\[ \begin{aligned} f_X(x)&=\lambda \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda x}\quad(x>0),\\ f_X(x)&=0\quad(x\le0). \end{aligned} \]

The parameter \(\lambda\) is a rate, not a scale: \(\mathbb{E}X=1/\lambda\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=1/\lambda^2\). Assigning any nonnegative density value at \(x=0\) does not change the distribution.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The exponential distribution is the standard model for a waiting time without memory: the time until the next arrival, failure or decay, when having waited for a while does not change the outlook for the remaining wait. Its rate \(\lambda\) is the inverse of the mean waiting time.

Both densities start at height \(\lambda\) at \(x=0\) and then decrease. The red curve with \(\lambda=2\) starts twice as high and falls faster, so its probability is concentrated on short waits and its mean is \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) instead of \(1\). Each density is highest at \(0\), so an interval of a given length near \(0\) carries more probability than one further out, even though the mean is \(1/\lambda\).

Raise the rate \(\lambda\): the density starts higher and falls faster, and the mean waiting time \(1/\lambda\) shrinks.

The tail probability \(\mathbb{P}(X>x)=\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda x}\) is the formula to remember (later courses call it the survivor function). Each extra unit of time multiplies it by the same factor \(\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda}\), which is the memoryless property: having waited \(s\), the remaining wait is again \(\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)\). The geometric distribution is the discrete counterpart, with \(\mathbb{P}(G\ge n)=(1-p)^n\).

The parameter is a rate, not a mean: \(\operatorname{Exp}(2)\) has mean \(\tfrac{1}{2}\), not \(2\). Some books parametrize by the mean instead, so the convention has to be checked before using a formula.

In a Poisson process with rate \(\lambda\) the times between arrivals are independent \(\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)\) variables; the minimum of independent exponentials is exponential with the rates added; and the half-life \(\ln 2/\lambda\) is its median.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For \(x\ge0\), \(F_X(x)=1-\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda x}\) and \(\mathbb{P}(X>x)=\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda x}\).
  • \(\mathbb{E}X=1/\lambda\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=1/\lambda^2\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\lambda=2\), the mean is \(1/2\) and \(\mathbb{P}(X>1)=\mathrm{e}^{-2}\).
  • At rate \(\lambda=1/5\) per minute, the mean wait is \(5\) minutes and \(\mathbb{P}(X\le5)=1-\mathrm{e}^{-1}\).

docs.title: Further Properties
docs.text: In a homogeneous Poisson process with rate \(\lambda\), interarrival times are independent \(\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)\) variables.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(0<p\le1\) and \(q=1-p\). A discrete random variable \(T\) has a first success distribution with parameter \(p\), written \(T\sim\operatorname{FS}(p)\), if \(T\) counts the trial on which the first success occurs in independent trials with success probability \(p\):

\[ \mathbb{P}(T=k)=q^{k-1}p,\qquad k=1,2,\ldots. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The first success distribution answers the question: in a sequence of independent trials with success probability \(p\), on which trial does the first success occur? The successful trial itself is counted, so \(T\) takes the values \(1,2,\ldots\).

In the figure \(p=0.3\): the first bar is \(\mathbb{P}(T=1)=p=0.3\), and each later bar is \(0.7\) times the previous one, \(0.21\), \(0.147\), and so on. The bars decrease from the start, so the most likely trial for the first success is always the first one, although the mean \(1/p\approx3.33\) given in the figure lies further to the right.

The same shape as the geometric distribution, moved one step to the right because the successful trial is counted: \(\mathbb{E}T=1/p\).

The formula reads as a story: \(T=k\) happens if and only if the first \(k-1\) trials fail and trial \(k\) succeeds. Each trial is a Bernoulli variable, and by independence these \(k\) results have probability \(q^{k-1}p\). In the same way \(\mathbb{P}(T>k)=q^k\), since \(T>k\) means that the first \(k\) trials all fail. The masses sum to \(1\) by the geometric series \(p(1+q+q^2+\cdots)=p/(1-q)=1\), so a success eventually occurs with probability one.

Conventions differ between books and software. This page counts trials, while the geometric distribution \(\operatorname{Geo}(p)\) counts the failures before the first success, so \(T=G+1\); check which version a formula refers to, because the means differ by exactly one, \(1/p\) against \(q/p\). Waiting for the \(r\)-th success instead of the first leads to the negative binomial distribution, which is the first success distribution when \(r=1\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(G\sim\operatorname{Geo}(p)\), then \(T=G+1\) has the first success distribution.
  • \(\mathbb{E}T=1/p\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(T)=(1-p)/p^2\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(p=1/2\), \(\mathbb{P}(T=3)=1/8\).
  • For \(p=0.2\), the expected trial number of the first success is \(5\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(Y\) be a normally distributed random variable. The random variable \(X=|Y|\) has a folded normal distribution.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A folded normal distribution is obtained by reflecting negative normal values to the positive side. It is useful when only the magnitude of a normally distributed quantity matters.

The illustrated calculation gives \(X=|Y|\). The sign is lost, so the density of \(Y\) on the negative side is folded onto the positive side and all mass lands on \([0,\infty)\).

Move \(\mu\) towards \(0\): more of the normal density of \(Y\) lies below zero and gets reflected, and the density of \(X=|Y|\) is the sum of the two dashed curves.

The normal distribution supplies the original variable \(Y\). Folding by absolute value combines the probability near a positive value with the probability near its negative, giving a nonnegative transformed variable.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A folded normal variable is the absolute value of a normal variable.
  • Its support is nonnegative.
  • When the underlying normal mean is zero, it is called a half-normal distribution: \(X=|Y|\) then has density \(2f_Y(x)\) for \(x\ge0\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The absolute measurement error from a normally distributed error has a folded normal distribution.
  • The distance from zero of a one-dimensional normal displacement is folded normal.
  • Quality-control deviations recorded only by magnitude can follow a folded normal model.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(X\) be a random variable and let \(g\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) be a Borel-measurable function, meaning that preimages of Borel sets are Borel sets. Continuous and piecewise continuous functions satisfy this condition. The function of a random variable determined by \(g\) is the random variable \(Y=g(X)\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A function of a random variable is a new quantity computed from the value of \(X\). On each outcome \(\omega\) it takes the value \(g(X(\omega))\), so \(Y=g(X)\) is the composition of \(X\) and \(g\).

In the figure \(X\) is uniform on \(\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}\), each value with probability \(\tfrac{1}{5}\), and \(Y=X^2\). The values \(-1\) and \(1\) are both sent to \(1\), and \(-2\) and \(2\) both to \(4\), so their probabilities add: \(\mathbb{P}(Y=0)=\tfrac{1}{5}\), \(\mathbb{P}(Y=1)=\tfrac{2}{5}\) and \(\mathbb{P}(Y=4)=\tfrac{2}{5}\). \(X\) is discrete uniform, but \(Y\) is not. In general, for discrete \(X\),

\[ \mathbb{P}(Y=y)=\sum_{x\colon g(x)=y}\mathbb{P}(X=x). \]

Apply \(g\) to a fair die: when several faces are sent to the same value, their probabilities add up in the distribution of \(Y=g(X)\).

For a discrete \(X\) this is the whole recipe: list the values of \(g\), and for each value \(y\) add the masses of all \(x\) with \(g(x)=y\). If \(g\) is one-to-one, no masses merge, and \(Y\) has the same masses as \(X\), placed at new values. In general \(\{Y\in B\}\) is the event \(\{X\in C\}\), where \(C\) is the set of \(x\) with \(g(x)\in B\); the condition on \(g\) in the Definition guarantees that \(\{X\in C\}\) is an event, so that it has a probability.

Indicators are functions of this kind: the indicator of \(\{X>10\}\) is \(g(X)\) with \(g(x)=1\) for \(x>10\) and \(g(x)=0\) otherwise. When only the average of \(g(X)\) is needed, LOTUS skips finding the distribution of \(Y\): in the figure \(\mathbb{E}[Y]=0\cdot\tfrac{1}{5}+1\cdot\tfrac{2}{5}+4\cdot\tfrac{2}{5}=2\).

A common slip is to apply \(g\) to the probabilities instead of the values. The masses of \(Y=X^2\) are not the squares of the masses of \(X\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(X\) is a random variable and \(g\) is Borel measurable, then \(g(X)\) is again a random variable. For a discrete \(X\), any real-valued assignment on its finite or countable set of values gives a random variable.
  • The distribution of \(g(X)\) may differ substantially from the distribution of \(X\).
  • LOTUS can compute expectations of \(g(X)\) without first deriving the full distribution of \(g(X)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(X\) is temperature in Celsius, then a linear function of \(X\) gives temperature in Fahrenheit.
  • If \(X\) is a return, then \(X^2\) measures squared return magnitude.
  • If \(X\) is a waiting time, then an indicator of whether it exceeds ten minutes is a function of \(X\).

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
For any event \(A\), let \(\indicator_A\) equal one on \(A\) and zero outside \(A\). The fundamental bridge is

\[ \mathbb{E}[\indicator_A]=\mathbb{P}(A). \]

The expectation always exists because the indicator is bounded.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The fundamental bridge says that the probability of an event equals the expected value of its indicator. It lets every probability be written as an expectation, and every expected count as a sum of probabilities.

In the figure \(\mathbb{P}(A)=0.3\): the indicator equals \(0\) with probability \(0.7\), when \(A\) did not occur, and \(1\) with probability \(0.3\), when it did. Treating the two bars as weights, their balance point, the expectation, lies at \(0\cdot0.7+1\cdot0.3=0.3=\mathbb{P}(A)\).

The proof is one line, since \(\indicator_A\) is a Bernoulli variable with parameter \(\mathbb{P}(A)\). The identity becomes useful together with linearity of expectation: if \(X=\indicator_{A_1}+\cdots+\indicator_{A_n}\) counts how many of the events occur, then \(\mathbb{E}[X]=\mathbb{P}(A_1)+\cdots+\mathbb{P}(A_n)\), whether or not the events are independent. For \(n\) tosses with heads probability \(p\) this gives the binomial mean \(np\). If \(n\) letters are put into \(n\) envelopes at random, letter \(i\) lands in its own envelope with probability \(1/n\), so the expected number of correctly placed letters is \(n\cdot\tfrac{1}{n}=1\) for every \(n\), although these events are dependent.

The bridge does not say that \(\indicator_A\) equals \(\mathbb{P}(A)\). The indicator only takes the values \(0\) and \(1\); \(\mathbb{P}(A)\) is its average value, and it is usually not a value the indicator takes.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{E}[\indicator_A]=1\mathbb{P}(A)+0\mathbb{P}(A^c)=\mathbb{P}(A)\).
  • \(\displaystyle \mathbb{E}[\sum_i\indicator_{A_i}]=\sum_i\mathbb{P}(A_i)\) for finitely many events, without independence.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For an even result on a fair die, \(\mathbb{E}[\indicator_A]=1/2\).
  • For \(10\) components each failing with probability \(0.02\), the expected failure count is \(0.2\), even if failures are dependent.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(X\colon S\to\mathbb{R}\) be a random variable and let \(B\subseteq\mathbb{R}\) be a Borel set: a set built from open intervals using complements and countable unions, such as any interval or finite set. The event generated by \(X\) and \(B\) is

\[ \{\omega\in S\colon X(\omega)\in B\}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A generated event turns a statement about the value of a random variable into an event in the original sample space: "\(X\) lies in \(B\)" becomes the set of outcomes \(\omega\) with \(X(\omega)\in B\).

In the figure the two outcomes inside the shaded oval are sent into the interval \(B\), and the two outcomes outside it are sent to points outside \(B\). The shaded set, labelled \(X^{-1}(B)\), is the generated event: exactly the outcomes whose arrows end in \(B\). The notation does not require \(X\) to have an inverse function; it only names the set of outcomes sent into \(B\).

The usual shorthand drops the outcome: \(\{X\in B\}\), \(\{X\le x\}\) and \(\{X=x\}\) are sets of outcomes, and \(\mathbb{P}(X\in B)\) is the probability of such a set. Different sets \(B\) can generate the same event: for a die roll \(X\), the sets \(\{2,4,6\}\) and \(\{2,4,6,7.5\}\) both generate "an even number is rolled", because no outcome is sent to \(7.5\). Operations on sets of values carry over to events, for example \(\{X\in B\}^c=\{X\notin B\}\) and \(\{X\in B\}\cap\{X\in C\}=\{X\in B\cap C\}\), so the rules for complements and intersections of events apply directly.

Generated events connect a random variable to its distribution, which is defined by the probabilities \(\mathbb{P}(X\in B)\), and to its CDF, built from the events \(\{X\le x\}\). Math III later studies the same construction for general functions under the name preimage.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Generated events are preimages of numerical sets under a random variable.
  • Statements such as \(X\le x\) are events in the original sample space.
  • The distribution of a random variable is defined through probabilities of generated events.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(X\) is a die roll, the event generated by \(X\) and the set of even numbers is rolling an even value.
  • If \(X\) is waiting time, the statement 'wait at most five minutes' is a generated event.
  • If \(X\) is a test score, the event 'score at least seventy' is generated by an interval of scores.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(0<p\le1\) and \(q=1-p\). A discrete random variable \(X\) has a geometric distribution with parameter \(p\), written \(X\sim\operatorname{Geo}(p)\), if \(X\) counts the failures before the first success in independent trials with success probability \(p\):

\[ \mathbb{P}(X=k)=q^kp,\qquad k=0,1,2,\ldots. \]

At \(p=1\) the first trial is a success, so \(X=0\) with probability \(1\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The geometric distribution counts how many failures happen before the first success in independent trials with success probability \(p\). A value of zero means that the first trial succeeds.

In the figure \(p=0.3\): the bar at \(0\) is \(\mathbb{P}(X=0)=p=0.3\), and each next bar is \(0.7\) times the previous one, so the bars decrease like the terms of a geometric series, which gives the distribution its name. The most likely value is \(0\), while the mean \(q/p=0.7/0.3\approx2.33\) given in the figure lies further to the right because of the long tail.

Each bar is \(q\) times the one before, starting at \(\mathbb{P}(X=0)=p\). A smaller \(p\) means a longer wait: \(\mathbb{E}X=q/p\).

Each trial is a Bernoulli variable, and \(X=k\) means \(k\) failures followed by a success, with probability \(q^kp\) by independence. The masses sum to \(1\) because \(p\sum_{k\ge0}q^k=p/(1-q)=1\). The tail formula in the Key Results, \(\mathbb{P}(X\ge m)=q^m\), has an equally direct reading: at least \(m\) failures occur exactly when the first \(m\) trials all fail. It also shows that waiting does not help: given \(m\) failures so far, the conditional probability of at least \(n\) more is \(q^{m+n}/q^m=q^n\), the memoryless property.

Books and software use the name "geometric" for two versions. This page counts failures, with values \(0,1,2,\ldots\); the first success distribution counts trials including the success, \(T=X+1\), with values \(1,2,\ldots\). Before using a formula, check which values it starts from.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{E}X=(1-p)/p\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=(1-p)/p^2\).
  • For integers \(m\ge0\), \(\mathbb{P}(X\ge m)=(1-p)^m\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(p=1/2\), \(\mathbb{P}(X=2)=1/8\).
  • For \(p=1/4\), the expected failure count is \((3/4)/(1/4)=3\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(X\) be a nonnegative random variable with survival function \(S_X(t)=\mathbb{P}(X>t)\), also written \(\overline F_X(t)\). A half-life is a time \(h\) such that

\[ S_X(h)=\frac{1}{2}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The half-life is the time by which half of a population of lifetimes has ended: a lifetime exceeds \(h\) with probability \(\tfrac{1}{2}\), so \(h\) is a median of \(X\). For a decaying quantity it is the time after which half of the initial amount is left.

The curve is \(S_X(t)=\mathrm{e}^{-t}\), an exponential lifetime with rate \(\lambda=1\). It reaches \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) at \(h=\ln 2\approx0.69\), then \(\tfrac{1}{4}\) at \(2h\) and \(\tfrac{1}{8}\) at \(3h\): equal steps in time halve the survival probability each time. In formulas, for integers \(k\ge0\),

\[ S_X(kh)=\big(\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda h}\big)^k=2^{-k}. \]

Change the rate \(\lambda\): the half-life \(h=\ln 2/\lambda\) is where survival drops to \(\frac{1}{2}\), and each further \(h\) halves it again.

Solving \(\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda h}=\tfrac{1}{2}\) with the natural logarithm gives \(h=\ln 2/\lambda\). It is shorter than the mean lifetime \(1/\lambda\) by the factor \(\ln 2\approx0.69\): a few very long lifetimes pull the mean up, while the half-life, being a median, does not depend on how long the longest lifetimes last.

The repeated halving is the memoryless property at work: of the lifetimes that last beyond \(h\), half also last a further \(h\). For a lifetime that is not exponential, the Definition still makes sense, but the halving pattern fails: the time from \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) to \(\tfrac{1}{4}\) need not equal \(h\). If \(S_X\) stays at \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) on a whole interval, every time in it solves the equation, which is why the Definition speaks of a half-life.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For exponential decay with rate \(\lambda\), the half-life is \(\ln 2/\lambda\).
  • Half-life is a median survival time in exponential waiting models.
  • Shorter half-life corresponds to faster decay or faster event occurrence.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If a drug concentration decays exponentially, the half-life is the time until the concentration is halved.
  • In radioactive decay, half-life summarizes how quickly unstable atoms decay.
  • For an exponential component lifetime, the half-life is the time by which half of components are expected to have failed.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let a population contain \(N\) objects, of which \(K\) are successes (\(0\le K\le N\)), and suppose \(n\) objects (\(0\le n\le N\)) are drawn without replacement. A random variable \(X\) has a hypergeometric distribution if \(X\) counts the number of successes in the draw, with

\[ \begin{gathered} \mathbb{P}(X=k)=\frac{\binom Kk\binom{N-K}{n-k}}{\binom Nn},\\ \max(0,\,n-N+K)\le k\le\min(n,K), \end{gathered} \]

and \(\mathbb{P}(X=k)=0\) for all other \(k\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A hypergeometric distribution counts successes when sampling without replacement. The trials are dependent because each draw changes what remains.

The diagram counts successes in a sample of \(n=6\) objects drawn without replacement from \(N=20\) objects, of which \(K=8\) are successes. The PMF is \(\mathbb{P}(X=k)=\binom8k\binom{12}{6-k}/\binom{20}6\) for \(0\le k\le6\). Its mean is \(6\cdot\tfrac{8}{20}=2.4\), and its variance \(1.44\cdot\tfrac{14}{19}\approx1.061\) is smaller than the variance \(6(0.4)(0.6)=1.44\) of \(\operatorname{Bin}(6,0.4)\), the corresponding model with replacement.

Change \(N\), \(K\) and \(n\): drawing without replacement gives mean \(nK/N\), like the binomial, but a smaller variance because each draw changes what remains.

A combination counts an unordered selection without replacement. Counting the chosen successes and failures separately and dividing by all samples gives the hypergeometric probabilities.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The hypergeometric distribution models sampling without replacement.
  • Unlike the binomial distribution, the trials are dependent.
  • Its mean is \(nK/N\) when \(K\) successes are in a population of size \(N\) and \(n\) items are drawn.

  • Its variance is

    \[ \operatorname{Var}(X)=n\frac{K}{N}\left(1-\frac{K}{N}\right)\frac{N-n}{N-1}. \]

    This is the binomial variance with \(p=K/N\) times the finite population correction \(\frac{N-n}{N-1}\), which is below \(1\) when \(n\ge2\) and close to \(1\) when the population is much larger than the sample.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The number of aces in a five-card hand has a hypergeometric distribution.
  • The number of defective items in a sample drawn without replacement from a shipment is hypergeometric.
  • The number of red balls drawn from an urn without replacement is hypergeometric.

docs.title: Independent and Identically Distributed Random Variables
Definition
docs.text: A sequence \(X_1,X_2,\ldots\) is independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) if it is mutually independent and all its variables have the same distribution.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Being i.i.d. means that the observations share one distribution and do not influence each other probabilistically. Both requirements are needed in the course’s weak and strong laws of large numbers and CLT.

Each variable in the diagram has the PMF of a fair die. Independence gives \(\mathbb{P}(X_1=a,X_2=b,X_3=c)=\mathbb{P}(X_1=a)\mathbb{P}(X_2=b)\mathbb{P}(X_3=c)\), so these rolls form an i.i.d. sample.

A random variable assigns numerical values to outcomes. Saying that several such variables are identically distributed concerns their individual laws, while independence concerns their joint law; neither condition alone implies the other.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For i.i.d. \(X_i\), \(\mathbb{P}(X_1\in A_1,\ldots,X_n\in A_n)=\prod_{i=1}^n\mathbb{P}(X_i\in A_i)\) for every finite collection.
  • Identical marginal distributions alone do not imply independence; pairwise independence alone does not establish mutual independence.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Repeated independent fair die rolls are i.i.d., all with the discrete uniform law on \(\{1,\ldots,6\}\).
  • If \(X_1=X_2=Z\) with \(Z\sim\operatorname{Bern}(1/2)\), the margins match but the observations are not i.i.d.: \(\mathbb{P}(X_1=1,X_2=0)=0\) rather than \(1/4\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(A\) and \(B\) be events. The inclusion-exclusion principle for two events states that

\[ \mathbb{P}(A\cup B)=\mathbb{P}(A)+\mathbb{P}(B)-\mathbb{P}(A\cap B). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The probability that \(A\) or \(B\) occurs is not simply \(\mathbb{P}(A)+\mathbb{P}(B)\) when the events overlap: the outcomes in both are counted twice, so the overlap is subtracted once. Inclusion-exclusion is this correction for double counting.

The labels show how many times each region is counted by \(\mathbb{P}(A)+\mathbb{P}(B)+\mathbb{P}(C)\). Subtracting the three pairwise intersections makes the regions labelled \(2\times\) count once, but the centre lies in all three pairwise intersections and is now counted \(3-3=0\) times, so the triple intersection is added back. This gives

\[ \reflow \begin{aligned} &\mathbb{P}(A\cup B\cup C)\\ &=\mathbb{P}(A)+\mathbb{P}(B)+\mathbb{P}(C)\\ &\quad-\mathbb{P}(A\cap B)-\mathbb{P}(A\cap C)\\ &\quad-\mathbb{P}(B\cap C)+\mathbb{P}(A\cap B\cap C). \end{aligned} \]

Grow the overlap: \(\mathbb{P}(A)+\mathbb{P}(B)\) counts \(A\cap B\) twice, so it is subtracted once to give \(\mathbb{P}(A\cup B)\).

The two-event formula follows from additivity of the probability function on disjoint pieces: \(A\cup B\) is the disjoint union of \(A\) and the part of \(B\) outside \(A\), and \(\mathbb{P}(B)\) is the probability of that part plus \(\mathbb{P}(A\cap B)\). For disjoint events the correction term is zero and the ordinary addition rule remains. In general \(\mathbb{P}(A\cup B)\le\mathbb{P}(A)+\mathbb{P}(B)\).

For a heart or a face card from a standard deck, \(\tfrac{13}{52}+\tfrac{12}{52}-\tfrac{3}{52}=\tfrac{22}{52}=\tfrac{11}{26}\); the three heart face cards would otherwise be counted twice. The same formula counts elements of finite sets, \(|A\cup B|=|A|+|B|-|A\cap B|\). For more events the signs keep alternating: subtract all pairwise intersections, add all triple ones, subtract all quadruple ones, and so on. A common slip is to stop after the pairwise terms.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For two events, inclusion-exclusion subtracts the overlap once.
  • For three events, the triple overlap must be added back after pairwise overlaps are subtracted.
  • The principle works for both counting and probability.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• To count students taking mathematics or statistics, add both course counts and subtract students taking both.
  • In card problems, the probability of drawing a heart or a face card requires subtracting heart face cards once.
  • To compute the chance of at least one of several alarms sounding, inclusion-exclusion adjusts for simultaneous alarms.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Events \(A\) and \(B\) are independent if

\[ \mathbb{P}(A\cap B)=\mathbb{P}(A)\mathbb{P}(B). \]

For a collection of events, mutual independence requires the product identity for every finite subcollection; pairwise independence alone is insufficient.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Two events are independent when knowing that one of them happened leaves the probability of the other unchanged. In formula form, the probability that both happen is the product of the two probabilities.

The square \(S\) has area \(1\), the band \(A\) has width \(0.6\) and the band \(B\) has height \(0.5\), so the overlap has area \(\mathbb{P}(A\cap B)=0.6\cdot0.5=0.3=\mathbb{P}(A)\mathbb{P}(B)\). Equivalently, \(\mathbb{P}(A\mid B)=0.3/0.5=0.6=\mathbb{P}(A)\): inside \(B\), the band \(A\) still takes up \(60\%\), just as it does in the whole square.

Make \(B\) fill the same share of \(A\) as of its complement: then \(\mathbb{P}(A\cap B)=\mathbb{P}(A)\mathbb{P}(B)\) and the events are independent.

The product form is the definition because it is symmetric in \(A\) and \(B\) and also makes sense when \(\mathbb{P}(B)=0\); the form \(\mathbb{P}(A\mid B)=\mathbb{P}(A)\) from the Key Results needs \(\mathbb{P}(B)>0\). Independence is a property of the probability function, not of the sets: on a fair die, \(A=\{1,2\}\) and \(B=\{2,4,6\}\) overlap, yet \(\mathbb{P}(A\cap B)=\tfrac{1}{6}=\tfrac{1}{3}\cdot\tfrac{1}{2}\), so they are independent; on a loaded die the same sets need not be.

Two slips are common. Disjoint events with positive probabilities are never independent, since \(\mathbb{P}(A\cap B)=0<\mathbb{P}(A)\mathbb{P}(B)\). And for three or more events, pairwise independence is not enough: for two fair coin tosses, "first toss heads", "second toss heads" and "both tosses equal" are pairwise independent, but all three together have probability \(\tfrac{1}{4}\), not \(\tfrac{1}{8}\). The same idea is later applied to random variables.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(\mathbb{P}(B)>0\), independence is equivalent to \(\mathbb{P}(A\mid B)=\mathbb{P}(A)\).
  • Independence of \(A,B\) implies independence of \(A^c,B\) and of \(A^c,B^c\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Heads on two independent fair tosses have intersection probability \(1/4=(1/2)(1/2)\).
  • On one fair die, \(\{1\}\) and \(\{2\}\) are disjoint but not independent: \(0\ne(1/6)(1/6)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Real-valued random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent if

\[ \mathbb{P}(X\in A,Y\in B) =\mathbb{P}(X\in A)\mathbb{P}(Y\in B) \]

for every pair of intervals \(A,B\); equivalently, for every pair of Borel sets \(A,B\). For a finite family, mutual independence requires the analogous product formula for every selection of intervals (one for each variable) and every subfamily, rather than merely for pairs.

For discrete variables with a joint PMF, this is equivalent to \(p_{X,Y}(x,y)=p_X(x)p_Y(y)\) for every \(x,y\). For a pair with a joint density, it is equivalent to \(f_{X,Y}(x,y)=f_X(x)f_Y(y)\) for all \((x,y)\) except possibly on a set of zero area, for example along finitely many lines. In either case, conditional laws agree with the corresponding marginal laws wherever the conditioning denominator is positive (with density identities allowed to fail on a set of zero length or area).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Independent variables supply separate sources of randomness: learning one variable does not change the distribution of the other. PMF and PDF factorization are two ways to check the same property.

Every cell is the product of its row and column marginal, e.g. \(\mathbb{P}(X=1,Y=1)=0.5\cdot0.6=0.30\): \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent, \(\mathbb{P}(X\in A,\,Y\in B)=\mathbb{P}(X\in A)\mathbb{P}(Y\in B)\) for all \(A,B\); knowing \(Y\) does not change the distribution of \(X\).

The threshold events generated by the variables must be independent events for every selection of thresholds. This condition factors the joint law, rather than comparing only the marginal distributions or one pair of events.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For arbitrary real-valued \(X,Y\), independence is equivalent to \(F_{X,Y}(x,y)=F_X(x)F_Y(y)\) for every \(x,y\).
  • If \(X,Y\) are independent and integrable, then \(XY\) is integrable and \(\mathbb{E}[XY]=\mathbb{E}X\,\mathbb{E}Y\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Two independent fair dice have \(p_{X,Y}(i,j)=1/36=(1/6)(1/6)\) for all \(i,j\in\{1,\ldots,6\}\).
  • The joint density \(2\) on \(0<x<y<1\) has marginals \(f_X(x)=2(1-x)\) and \(f_Y(y)=2y\) on \((0,1)\). At \((x,y)=(1/4,3/4)\) their product is \(9/4\), rather than \(2\), and this discrepancy persists on a whole neighbourhood, which has positive area; hence the density does not factor.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For an event \(A\), the indicator random variable \(\indicator_{A}\) equals \(1\) if \(A\) occurs and \(0\) otherwise.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An indicator turns an event into a numerical yes-or-no observation: \(\indicator_A\) is \(1\) on the outcomes in \(A\) and \(0\) on all others. Counting how many events occur becomes adding random variables: the number of the events \(A_1,\ldots,A_n\) that occur is \(\indicator_{A_1}+\cdots+\indicator_{A_n}\), whether or not the events are independent.

In the figure the outcomes \(\omega_1\) and \(\omega_2\) lie in \(A\) and are sent to \(1\), while \(\omega_3\) and \(\omega_4\) are sent to \(0\). So \(\indicator_A\) takes only the values \(0\) and \(1\), with \(\mathbb{P}(\indicator_A=1)=\mathbb{P}(A)\): a Bernoulli variable with parameter \(\mathbb{P}(A)\), as in the Key Results.

Operations on events become arithmetic: \(\indicator_A\indicator_B=1\) exactly when both \(A\) and \(B\) occur, \(1-\indicator_A=1\) exactly when \(A\) fails, and \(\indicator_{A\cup B}=\indicator_A+\indicator_B-\indicator_A\indicator_B\) is the indicator form of the inclusion-exclusion principle. Combined with the fundamental bridge \(\mathbb{E}[\indicator_A]=\mathbb{P}(A)\), a sum of indicators turns an expected count into a sum of probabilities.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\indicator_A\sim\operatorname{Bern}(\mathbb{P}(A))\).
  • \(\indicator_{A\cap B}=\indicator_A\indicator_B\) and \(\indicator_{A^c}=1-\indicator_A\).
  • A sum of indicators counts the number of events that occur, even when those events are dependent.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A fair-toss heads indicator is \(1\) on heads and \(0\) on tails.
  • The number of heads in three tosses is \(\indicator_{A_1}+\indicator_{A_2}+\indicator_{A_3}\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(\{B_i\}\) be a finite or countable partition of the sample space into events. For every event \(A\),

\[ \mathbb{P}(A)=\sum_{i\colon\mathbb{P}(B_i)>0}\mathbb{P}(A\mid B_i)\mathbb{P}(B_i). \]

Null partition events contribute zero to \(\mathbb{P}(A)\) and are omitted so that no undefined conditional probability is used.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Compute a probability by conditioning on each possible case and weighting by how likely that case is.

The diagram splits \(A\) into the disjoint pieces \(A\cap B_1\), \(A\cap B_2\) and \(A\cap B_3\). Their probabilities add to \(\mathbb{P}(A)\); each positive-probability case contributes \(\mathbb{P}(A\mid B_i)\mathbb{P}(B_i)\).

Split the sample space into three cases and set \(\mathbb{P}(A\mid B_i)\) in each: \(\mathbb{P}(A)\) is the total shaded area, a weighted average of the three.

A partition of a set divides the sample space into disjoint blocks covering every outcome. Additivity of the probability function sums the contributions from \(A\) within those blocks, and conditional probabilities express each contribution as a block probability times a within-block probability.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\displaystyle \mathbb{P}(A)=\sum_i\mathbb{P}(A\cap B_i)\) for a countable partition.
  • Only terms with \(\mathbb{P}(B_i)>0\) need conditional probabilities; zero-probability cases contribute zero.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:

  • For a fair die, conditioning on odd or even gives \(\mathbb{P}(X=6)=0(1/2)+(1/3)(1/2)=1/6\).

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
For integrable random variables \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) and real constants \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\), linearity of expectation states

\[ \mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^n a_iX_i\right]=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\mathbb{E}X_i. \]

Independence is not required. In particular, \(\mathbb{E}[aX+bY]=a\mathbb{E}X+b\mathbb{E}Y\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The average of a finite linear combination is the same linear combination of averages. Dependence does not affect this rule.

The independent variables shown have means \(2\) and \(4\), so their sum has mean \(6\). Here the sum takes the values \(3\), \(5\), \(7\) and \(9\), each with probability \(1/4\); the identity for the means itself does not require independence.

Addition and sum forms the finite weighted sum of the variables. Expectation then averages it: distributing the probability weights across its summands explains why taking this average commutes with the finite sum.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For integrable \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\), \(\displaystyle \mathbb{E}[\sum_ia_iX_i]=\sum_ia_i\mathbb{E}X_i\).
  • \(\mathbb{E}[a+bX]=a+b\mathbb{E}X\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(\mathbb{E}X=2\) and \(\mathbb{E}Y=5\), then \(\mathbb{E}[3X-Y]=1\) regardless of dependence.
  • If \(Y=X\) and \(\mathbb{E}X=4\), then \(\mathbb{E}[X+Y]=8\) despite perfect dependence.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(Y\) be normally distributed with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\). The random variable \(X=\mathrm{e}^Y\) has a lognormal distribution with parameters \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A lognormal variable is a positive quantity whose logarithm is normal. It suits quantities that change by percentages rather than by fixed amounts, such as prices or incomes: a multiplicative change in \(X\) is an additive change in \(\ln X\).

The figure shows \(X=\mathrm{e}^Y\) with \(Y\sim\mathcal{N}(0,0.5^2)\). All probability lies on \(x>0\), and the density has a long right tail. The three dashed lines are, from left to right, the mode \(\mathrm{e}^{\mu-\sigma^2}\approx0.78\), the median \(\mathrm{e}^{\mu}=1\) and the mean \(\mathrm{e}^{\mu+\sigma^2/2}\approx1.13\), the usual order for a right-skewed density.

Change \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\) of the underlying normal \(Y\): the density of \(X=\mathrm e^Y\) is skewed to the right, and more so as \(\sigma\) grows.

Because the exponential function is strictly increasing, \(X\le x\) if and only if \(Y\le\ln x\). Hence, for \(x>0\),

\[ F_X(x)=\Phi\left(\frac{\ln x-\mu}{\sigma}\right), \]

and every lognormal probability is a standard normal probability. Quantiles carry over in the same way, which is why the median of \(X\) is \(\mathrm{e}^{\mu}\): the median of \(Y\) is \(\mu\). The density itself follows from the transformation formula with \(g(y)=\mathrm{e}^y\).

The mean does not carry over like this: \(\mathbb{E}[X]=\mathrm{e}^{\mu+\sigma^2/2}\) is larger than \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathbb{E}[Y]}=\mathrm{e}^{\mu}\). The parameters \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\) are the mean and variance of \(\ln X\), not of \(X\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A lognormal random variable is always positive.
  • If \(X\) is lognormal, then \(\log X\) is normal.
  • Lognormal models often arise from products of many positive random factors.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Household income is often modelled with a lognormal-type distribution.
  • Multiplicative investment growth can lead to lognormal returns over time.
  • Repair times that are positive and right-skewed may be approximated by a lognormal model.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(g\) be a Borel-measurable real function (preimages of Borel sets are Borel sets), so that \(g(X)\) is a random variable. If \(\mathbb{E}|g(X)|<\infty\), the law of the unconscious statistician (LOTUS) gives

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}[g(X)]&=\sum_x g(x)p_X(x)\quad \text{for discrete }X,\\ \mathbb{E}[g(X)]&=\int_{\mathbb{R}}g(x)f_X(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\quad \text{when }X\text{ has a density}. \end{aligned} \]

The formulas also hold as extended nonnegative expectations when \(g\ge0\). A finite signed result requires absolute integrability; no distribution of \(g(X)\) has to be computed first.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
To average a transformed variable, apply the transformation to each possible value and weight using the original distribution. This avoids deriving a new distribution merely to compute an expectation.

For the transformation \(g(x)=x^2\) shown, \(\mathbb{E}[g(X)]=1(0.1)+0(0.3)+1(0.4)+4(0.2)=1.3\). The values of \(g\) are weighted by the PMF of \(X\), without deriving the PMF of \(g(X)\).

A function of a random variable changes the value on each outcome from \(X\) to \(g(X)\). LOTUS averages those transformed values using the original law of \(X\), avoiding a separate derivation of the distribution of \(g(X)\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Choosing \(g(x)=x^k\) computes the \(k\)th moment when it exists; in particular \(g(x)=x^2\) gives the second moment.
  • Choosing \(g(x)=\indicator_{\{x\in A\}}\) gives \(\mathbb{P}(X\in A)\) by a sum or an integral.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For a fair die, \(\mathbb{E}[X^2]=(1+4+9+16+25+36)/6=91/6\).
  • For \(X\sim\operatorname{Exp}(2)\), \(\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{e}^{-X}]=\int_0^\infty2\mathrm{e}^{-3x}\,\mathrm{d}x=2/3\).
