docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(X\) be a random variable with distribution function \(F_X\). A median of \(X\) is a real number \(m\) such that

\[ \mathbb{P}(X\le m)\ge \frac{1}{2}\quad\text{and}\quad \mathbb{P}(X\ge m)\ge \frac{1}{2}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A median is a central value that splits the distribution into two halves. Unlike the mean, it depends only on the order of the values, not on how far out the extreme ones lie.

The density is \(f(x)=x\mathrm{e}^{-x}\) for \(x\ge0\), with CDF \(F(x)=1-(1+x)\mathrm{e}^{-x}\). The solid line at \(m\approx1.68\), the solution of \(F(m)=\tfrac{1}{2}\), cuts the area into two parts of \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) each, and the dashed line marks the mean \(2\). The long right tail pulls the mean outwards but does not move the halfway point.

Move the candidate \(m\) and check both conditions. For the skewed density the median is unique; for \(\operatorname{Bin}(3,\frac12)\) every \(m\in[1,2]\) is a median.

The Definition uses two inequalities rather than the equation \(F_X(m)=\tfrac{1}{2}\), because that equation can have many solutions or none. For \(\operatorname{Bin}(3,\tfrac{1}{2})\) the CDF equals \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) on all of \([1,2)\), and every \(m\in[1,2]\) satisfies both conditions. For \(\operatorname{Bern}(0.3)\) the CDF jumps from \(0\) to \(0.7\) at \(0\), so the equation has no solution, yet \(0\) is the unique median. For a continuous, strictly increasing CDF the median is simply the quantile at level \(\tfrac{1}{2}\).

Because only the order of the values matters, medians move along with increasing transformations: if \(m\) is a median of \(Y\) and \(g\) is strictly increasing, then \(g(m)\) is a median of \(g(Y)\). This gives the median \(\mathrm{e}^{\mu}\) of the lognormal distribution. For a symmetric distribution, the centre of symmetry is a median.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A median need not be unique: the medians of a distribution form an interval, which contains more than one point exactly when the CDF equals \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) on a whole stretch (for a fair die, every point of \([3,4]\) is a median). If the CDF jumps from below \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) to above \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) at a point, that point is the unique median.
  • For a continuous strictly increasing CDF, the median is the point where the CDF equals one half.
  • The median is robust to extreme values compared with the mean.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The median of a symmetric normal distribution is its centre.
  • For waiting times, the median is the time by which half of cases have occurred.
  • In income data, the median can better describe a typical person than the mean when there are extreme high incomes.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A nonnegative waiting time is memoryless if, once it has lasted a certain time, the time still to wait has the same distribution as the original waiting time. For a nonnegative integer-valued \(G\) this means that for all nonnegative integers \(m,n\)

\[ \mathbb{P}(G\ge m+n\mid G\ge m)=\mathbb{P}(G\ge n). \]

For an absolutely continuous nonnegative \(T\) it means that for all \(s,t\ge0\)

\[ \mathbb{P}(T>s+t\mid T>s)=\mathbb{P}(T>t). \]

The conditioning events must have positive probability. The property also works in reverse. Suppose the waiting time is finite with probability \(1\) and all its tail probabilities are positive. Then a memoryless \(G\) has a \(\operatorname{Geo}(p)\) distribution for some \(0<p<1\) (counting the failures before the first success), and a memoryless \(T\) has an \(\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)\) distribution for some \(\lambda>0\). For the first-success distribution, which counts trials and takes the values \(1,2,\dots\), the same condition is written with strict tails: \(\mathbb{P}(X>m+n\mid X>m)=\mathbb{P}(X>n)\) for all nonnegative integers \(m,n\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A memoryless waiting time does not age: having waited for a while says nothing about how much longer the wait will be. A working component with a memoryless lifetime is as good as new.

The blue curve is the survival probability \(\mathbb{P}(T>u)=\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda u}\) of an exponential waiting time. The red dashed curve is the conditional probability of survival given \(T>s\): it starts at \(1\) at time \(s\) and is an exact copy of the blue curve shifted to the right by \(s\). Its height at \(s+t\) equals the height of the blue curve at \(t\):

\[ \mathbb{P}(T>s+t\mid T>s) =\frac{\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda(s+t)}}{\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda s}}=\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda t}=\mathbb{P}(T>t). \]

After waiting \(s\), the wide pale band shows the conditional survival of the remaining wait, shifted back to \(0\): it coincides with the original curve. The discrete version does the same for \(G\).

Since \(\{T>s+t\}\) is contained in \(\{T>s\}\), the condition can be written without conditioning as \(\mathbb{P}(T>s+t)=\mathbb{P}(T>s)\,\mathbb{P}(T>t)\): the survival probability turns sums of times into products, and that is what forces the exponential form. The discrete version reads the same way: \(\{G\ge m\}\) means that the first \(m\) trials all failed, and given this the number of further failures is again \(\operatorname{Geo}(p)\), since the trials are independent.

Most lifetimes with wear do not have it: for \(T\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\), \(\mathbb{P}(T>0.75\mid T>0.5)=0.5\) while \(\mathbb{P}(T>0.25)=0.75\). The property also does not say that a long wait makes an end "due": after ten failures in independent trials, a success is no more likely than before. It is what makes the Poisson process start afresh at every moment: from any fixed time, the wait for the next arrival is again \(\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For \(G\sim\operatorname{Geo}(p)\) counting failures, \(\mathbb{P}(G\ge m+n\mid G\ge m)=(1-p)^n\) for admissible nonnegative integers \(m,n\).
  • For \(T\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)\), \(\mathbb{P}(T>s+t\mid T>s)=\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda t}\) for \(s,t\ge0\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(G\sim\operatorname{Geo}(1/4)\), \(\mathbb{P}(G\ge5\mid G\ge2)=(3/4)^3=27/64\).
  • For \(T\sim\operatorname{Exp}(2)\), \(\mathbb{P}(T>4\mid T>3)=\mathrm{e}^{-2}=\mathbb{P}(T>1)\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: Let \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) be independent exponential random variables with rates \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n\). Then \(\min(X_1,\ldots,X_n)\) is exponentially distributed with rate \(\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_n\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The minimum is the time at which the first of several independent clocks rings. Each running clock is another chance for an early ring, so the rates add up.

The blue and red curves are the survival probabilities \(\mathrm{e}^{-t}\) and \(\mathrm{e}^{-2t}\) of two independent clocks with rates \(1\) and \(2\). The green curve is their product \(\mathrm{e}^{-3t}\), the survival probability of the minimum. It lies below both, because the minimum survives past \(t\) only if both clocks do: its mean is \(\tfrac{1}{3}\), against \(1\) and \(\tfrac{1}{2}\).

Multiply the survival curves: the minimum survives only if both clocks do, which gives rate \(\lambda_1+\lambda_2\). The simulation agrees with the exponential density.

For \(t\ge0\) the proof is one line:

\[ \mathbb{P}(\min(X_1,\ldots,X_n)>t) =\mathbb{P}(X_1>t)\cdots\mathbb{P}(X_n>t) =\mathrm{e}^{-(\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_n)t}. \]

The first step uses that the minimum exceeds \(t\) if and only if every \(X_i\) does, and independence to factor the probability. Without independence it can fail: if \(X_2=X_1\), the minimum is just \(X_1\) with rate \(\lambda_1\). The second step uses the exponential form, since a product of exponential tails is again an exponential tail. For other distributions the type usually changes: for two independent \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) variables, \(\mathbb{P}(\min>t)=(1-t)^2\) on \([0,1]\), which is not the tail of a uniform distribution.

Which clock rings first is also simple: clock \(i\) wins with probability \(\lambda_i/(\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_n)\), which is \(\tfrac{1}{3}\) for the rate-\(1\) clock in the figure. In two independent Poisson processes, the wait until the next arrival in either one is such a minimum, so the combined arrivals come at rate \(\lambda_1+\lambda_2\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The minimum of independent exponentials is exponential with rate equal to the sum of the rates.
  • The probability that a particular clock is first is its rate divided by the total rate.
  • This result connects competing risks with Poisson process arrivals.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If two repair teams respond independently, the first response time can be modelled as the minimum of two exponential times.
  • In competing failure modes, the first failure time has rate equal to the sum of mode-specific rates.
  • If buses from two routes arrive independently, the next bus time can be the minimum of the two route waiting times.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(Z\) be a random index taking finitely or countably many values, and let the conditional distribution of \(X\) given \(Z=i\) be specified for each \(i\) with \(\mathbb{P}(Z=i)>0\). The distribution of \(X\) is a mixture distribution if it is obtained by averaging these conditional distributions using the probabilities of the values of \(Z\). A continuous mixing index instead requires integration against its mixing distribution.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A mixture describes a population made of hidden groups. To draw \(X\), first pick a group \(Z\) at random, then draw \(X\) from that group's distribution; the distribution of \(X\) is the weighted average of the group distributions, with the group probabilities as weights.

The figure has two groups with weights \(\mathbb{P}(Z=1)=0.4\) and \(\mathbb{P}(Z=2)=0.6\). The dashed curves are the group curves \(f_1\) and \(f_2\), centred at \(-1.5\) and \(1.5\) and already multiplied by their weights; the solid curve is their sum \(0.4f_1+0.6f_2\). These curves are densities: areas under them are probabilities. Each group curve has one peak, but the mixture has two, because the groups lie far apart compared with their spread.

Change the weight and the two group means: the mixture density is the weighted average of the group densities, and its mean is the weighted average of their means.

The averaging is the law of total probability for the partition of the sample space by the value of \(Z\): for every set \(B\) of values,

\[ \mathbb{P}(X\in B)=\sum_i\mathbb{P}(Z=i)\,\mathbb{P}(X\in B\mid Z=i). \]

Each conditional probability \(\mathbb{P}(X\in B\mid Z=i)\) describes one group. A discrete example: a coin is fair with probability \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) and two-headed with probability \(\tfrac{1}{2}\); for one toss of this coin, with \(X=1\) for heads, \(\mathbb{P}(X=1)=\tfrac{1}{2}\cdot\tfrac{1}{2}+\tfrac{1}{2}\cdot1=\tfrac{3}{4}\).

A mixture is not a sum of random variables. \(X\) comes from one group, chosen at random, whereas a sum adds a value from each group. In the figure the mixture puts its probability near \(-1.5\) and near \(1.5\); adding one value from each group would instead give values near \(0\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A mixture distribution is a weighted average of component distributions.
  • The weights are nonnegative and sum to one.
  • Mixtures can produce multimodal shapes even when each component is unimodal.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Customer spending can be modelled as a mixture of business and leisure customer distributions.
  • Machine lifetime may be a mixture of lifetimes from old and new machines.
  • Exam scores can form a mixture if two preparation groups are present.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(X\) be a random variable. A mode of \(X\) is a value at which the probability mass function or probability density function attains its maximum.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A mode is the most likely value of a discrete distribution, or the value where a density is highest, that is, where values are most concentrated. On a graph it is the location of the highest peak.

In the left panel the density \(f(x)=x\mathrm{e}^{-x}\) peaks at \(x=1\), where \(f'(x)=(1-x)\mathrm{e}^{-x}\) is zero. For this density the median is about \(1.68\) and the mean is \(2\), so the three centres differ. In the right panel the \(\operatorname{Pois}(3)\) PMF has two equally high bars, \(\mathbb{P}(X=2)=\mathbb{P}(X=3)=\tfrac{9}{2}\mathrm{e}^{-3}\approx0.224\), so both \(2\) and \(3\) are modes.

For the lognormal density, change \(\sigma\) and watch mode, median and mean drift apart. For the Poisson distribution, set \(\lambda\) to a whole number to get two modes.

For a density, finding the mode is a maximization problem from calculus: look for a stationary point or an endpoint of the support. A mode of a continuous distribution has probability \(0\) like every value; it is where short intervals of a fixed length carry the most probability. For the Poisson distribution with a whole-number rate \(\lambda\), the ratio \(\mathbb{P}(X=k)/\mathbb{P}(X=k-1)=\lambda/k\) equals \(1\) at \(k=\lambda\), which explains the two modes \(\lambda-1\) and \(\lambda\).

A mode need not be unique or lie near the middle. Every face of a fair die is a mode, and the exponential density has its mode at \(0\), the smallest possible value. A density with several local peaks is called multimodal, even when only the highest peak is a mode in the strict sense.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A mode is a maximizer of the mass function or density function.
  • A distribution may have more than one mode.
  • For continuous distributions, density height is not itself probability.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A fair die has every face as a mode because all faces are equally likely.
  • A normal distribution has one mode at its centre.
  • A mixture of two separated normal distributions can be bimodal, with two peaks; both peaks are modes in the strict sense only when they have equal height.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be random variables with finite expectations. If \(X\le Y\) almost surely (that is, \(\mathbb{P}(X\le Y)=1\)), then monotonicity of expectation states that

\[ \mathbb{E}[X]\le \mathbb{E}[Y]. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Monotonicity says that if one random variable is never larger than another, its average is not larger either: taking expectations preserves the inequality \(X\le Y\).

Write \(D=Y-X\). The hypothesis says that \(D\ge0\) with probability one, and an average of nonnegative values cannot be negative; by linearity of expectation, \(\mathbb{E}[Y]-\mathbb{E}[X]=\mathbb{E}[D]\ge0\). An event of probability zero cannot affect any average, which is why the comparison need only hold with probability one. The converse fails: for a fair die roll \(X\) and \(Y=7-X\) the means are equal, yet \(X>Y\) whenever \(X\ge4\).

The theorem is mostly used to bound an expectation by a simpler one. If \(X\le c\) for a constant \(c\), then \(\mathbb{E}[X]\le c\). For \(X\ge0\) and \(c>0\), the inequality \(c\,\indicator_{\{X\ge c\}}\le X\) together with the fundamental bridge gives \(c\,\mathbb{P}(X\ge c)\le\mathbb{E}[X]\): a nonnegative variable with a small mean rarely takes large values.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(X\le Y\) almost surely, then \(\mathbb{E}[X]\le \mathbb{E}[Y]\) when expectations exist.
  • Strict inequality is not guaranteed unless the ordering is strict with positive probability.
  • Monotonicity is often used to bound expectations.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If a premium service always costs at least as much as a basic service, its expected cost is at least as large.
  • If one policy always pays no more than another, its expected payout is no larger.
  • Truncating losses from above produces a random variable with no larger expectation.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Consider a compound experiment made of two stages. If the first stage has \(a\) possible outcomes and, for each of them, the second stage has \(b\) possible outcomes, then the compound experiment has

\[ a\cdot b \]

possible outcomes. This is the multiplication rule for counting. For \(k\) successive stages with \(n_1,n_2,\ldots,n_k\) choices it gives \(n_1n_2\cdots n_k\) ordered outcomes; in set notation, \(|A\times B|=|A|\,|B|\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The multiplication rule counts ordered outcomes stage by stage: in a tree diagram, the number of leaves is the product of the numbers of branches at each level. The same tree carries probabilities, and multiplying along a path gives the probability of that path.

Counting the ordered outcomes gives \(52\cdot51=2652\) ordered draws, \(4\cdot3=12\) of them two aces, so \(\tfrac{12}{2652}=\tfrac{1}{221}\). Probabilities multiply along a path in the same way: \(\mathbb{P}(A\cap B)=\mathbb{P}(A)\,\mathbb{P}(B\mid A)\).

The Cartesian product records an ordered choice from each stage. If every first-stage choice permits the same \(b\) second-stage choices, counting the pairs gives \(|A\times B|=|A||B|\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The number of choices at a stage must not depend on the outcomes of earlier stages, although the choices themselves may.
  • Probability version: for events \(A\) and \(B\) with \(\mathbb{P}(A)>0\), \(\mathbb{P}(A\cap B)=\mathbb{P}(A)\mathbb{P}(B\mid A)\); for several events the rule becomes a product of successive conditional probabilities.
  • For independent events, the conditional factor reduces to the marginal probability.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A code of two letters followed by three digits can be formed in \(26^2\cdot10^3=676\,000\) ways.
  • Two dice give \(6\cdot6=36\) ordered outcomes, and \(n\) distinct objects can be ordered in \(n(n-1)\cdots1=n!\) ways.
  • Two cards drawn without replacement are both aces with probability \(\frac{4}{52}\cdot\frac{3}{51}=\frac{1}{221}\): the chance of the first ace times the conditional chance of the second. In counts, \(4\cdot3=12\) of the \(52\cdot51=2652\) ordered draws.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(S\) be a finite sample space whose outcomes are equally likely. For an event \(A\subseteq S\), the naive probability of \(A\) is

\[ \mathbb{P}(A)=\frac{|A|}{|S|}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
When a finite sample space has equally likely outcomes, the probability of an event is the share of outcomes that belong to it. Probability then becomes counting: count the favourable outcomes, count all outcomes, and divide.

The grid lists all \(36\) ordered pairs \((i,j)\), with \(i\) the first die and \(j\) the second; for fair dice each cell is equally likely. The six shaded cells \((1,6),(2,5),\ldots,(6,1)\) have sum \(7\), so \(\mathbb{P}(\text{sum}=7)=\tfrac{6}{36}=\tfrac{1}{6}\). The pairs \((1,6)\) and \((6,1)\) are different cells: recording which die shows which number is what makes all outcomes equally likely.

The equal-likelihood assumption belongs to the model, not to the question, and the choice of outcomes decides whether it holds. Taking the eleven possible sums \(2,\ldots,12\) as outcomes and dividing by \(11\) gives \(\mathbb{P}(\text{sum}=7)=\tfrac{1}{11}\), which is wrong, because a sum of \(7\) arises in six ways and a sum of \(2\) in only one. The sample space must also be finite: infinitely many outcomes cannot all have the same positive probability, since their probabilities would add up to more than \(1\).

The formula satisfies the axioms of probability, because the number of elements (cardinality) of a union of disjoint sets is the sum of their numbers of elements. The multiplication rule, permutations and combinations are the tools for computing \(|A|\) and \(|S|\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Naive probability applies only when all outcomes in the sample space are equally likely.
  • It is computed as favourable outcomes divided by total outcomes.
  • Counting errors in either numerator or denominator lead directly to probability errors.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The probability of rolling an even number on a fair die is three favourable faces out of six.
  • The probability of drawing an ace from a well-shuffled deck is four favourable cards out of fifty-two.
  • If a random PIN is chosen uniformly from all four-digit PINs, naive probability can compute the chance of a repeated digit pattern.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(r\) be a positive integer and \(p\in(0,1]\). A random variable \(X\) has a negative binomial distribution if \(X\) counts the number of trials needed to obtain the \(r\)th success in independent Bernoulli trials with success probability \(p\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
In this trial-count convention, a negative binomial distribution generalizes the first success distribution. Instead of waiting for the first success, it waits for a fixed later success.

The diagram uses \(r=3\) and \(p=0.4\). For \(k\ge r\), \(\mathbb{P}(X=k)=\binom{k-1}{r-1}p^r(1-p)^{k-r}\): the first \(k-1\) trials have \(r-1\) successes, and trial \(k\) is the \(r\)th success.

Change \(r\) and \(p\): the distribution of the trial of the \(r\)th success starts at \(r\) and has mean \(r/p\). With \(r=1\) it is the first success distribution.

Independent random variables describe the successive trial results. Their probabilities multiply for any fixed success-and-failure sequence, after which counting the sequences that place the final success at the specified trial gives the mass function.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• It counts waiting time until a fixed number of successes.
  • For \(r=1\), \(X\) has the first success distribution. The shifted variable \(X-1\) has the geometric distribution used in this course.
  • The failure-count convention uses \(X-r\) instead of \(X\). For \(k=r,r+1,\ldots\), the trial-count probability is \(\mathbb{P}(X=k)=\binom{k-1}{r-1}p^r(1-p)^{k-r}\); the final trial is a success, and the preceding \(k-1\) trials contain exactly \(r-1\) successes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The number of sales calls needed to close five sales can be negative binomial.
  • The number of coin tosses needed to obtain three heads follows a negative binomial model.
  • The number of inspected items until the tenth defective item can be modelled this way under independent constant defect probability.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\mu\in\mathbb{R}\) and \(\sigma>0\). A continuous random variable \(X\) has a normal distribution with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\), written \(X\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\), if its density is

\[ f_X(x)=\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\left(-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A normal distribution is the familiar bell-shaped distribution. It is widely used because many sums and averages of independent variables behave approximately normally, by the central limit theorem.

The curve is symmetric about its mean \(\mu\), and its variance is \(\sigma^2\). Approximately \(68\%\) of its probability lies within \(\mu\pm\sigma\), and \(95\%\) lies within \(\mu\pm2\sigma\).

Move \(\mu\) to shift the bell and \(\sigma\) to widen it. The interval \((\mu-\sigma,\mu+\sigma)\) always holds about \(68\%\) of the probability.

As a continuous random variable, the normal variable assigns probabilities by areas under the density. The exponential function applied to the negative squared standardized deviation gives its bell-shaped decay.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A normal distribution is determined by its mean and variance.
  • Standardizing a normal random variable gives a standard normal random variable.
  • Sums of independent normal random variables are normal.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Measurement error is often approximated by a normal distribution.
  • The average of many small independent effects is often modelled as normal.
  • Manufacturing deviations from a target dimension are frequently modelled with a normal distribution.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) be random variables and let \(X_{(1)}\le\cdots\le X_{(n)}\) be the ordered values. The random variable \(X_{(k)}\) is called the \(k\)th order statistic.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Order statistics describe a sample by rank rather than by the order in which the values were drawn: \(X_{(k)}\) is the \(k\)th smallest value. The most used ones are the minimum \(X_{(1)}\), the maximum \(X_{(n)}\) and, for odd \(n\), the sample median.

The upper row shows five values in the order in which they were drawn; the lower row shows the same five points renamed by rank. No point moves: the minimum \(X_{(1)}\) is \(X_2\), the median \(X_{(3)}\) is \(X_4\) and the maximum \(X_{(5)}\) is \(X_3\). Which draw gets which rank varies from run to run, so each \(X_{(k)}\) is a random variable.

Sort a uniform sample and pick the \(k\)th smallest. Over many samples \(X_{(k)}\) clusters around \(k/(n+1)\): the minimum near \(0\), the maximum near \(1\).

Even when \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) are i.i.d., the order statistics are neither independent nor identically distributed, since \(X_{(1)}\le X_{(2)}\) always holds. The extremes are still easy to handle through the CDF \(F\) of one observation: the maximum is at most \(x\) exactly when every observation is, and the minimum exceeds \(x\) exactly when every observation does, so independence gives

\[ \mathbb{P}(X_{(n)}\le x)=F(x)^n,\qquad \mathbb{P}(X_{(1)}>x)=(1-F(x))^n. \]

A middle order statistic needs a counting argument instead: \(X_{(k)}\le x\) means that at least \(k\) of the \(n\) observations are at most \(x\), and the number of such observations has the binomial distribution with parameters \(n\) and \(F(x)\).

The brackets matter: \(X_{(k)}\) is the \(k\)th smallest value, while \(X_k\) is the \(k\)th draw. For exponential observations the minimum formula returns as the minimum of independent exponentials.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The first order statistic is the sample minimum and the last is the sample maximum.
  • Order statistics are functions of a sample.
  • They are central in quantile estimation and reliability calculations.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The smallest of five component lifetimes is the first order statistic.
  • The median of a sample of odd size \(n\) is the middle order statistic \(X_{((n+1)/2)}\); for \(n=5\) it is \(X_{(3)}\).
  • The maximum daily demand in a month is the largest order statistic of the daily demands.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(S\) be a sample space. An outcome is an element \(\omega\in S\) representing one possible result of the random experiment.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An outcome is one complete result of the experiment, described at the level of detail that the model records. Each run of the experiment produces exactly one outcome.

The figure shows the sample space of a die roll with the realized outcome \(\omega=4\). The event \(\{2,4,6\}\) occurs because it contains \(4\); the event \(\{1,2\}\) does not.

How much detail an outcome carries is a modelling choice: for two coin tosses an outcome can be the ordered pair, such as \(HT\), or only the number of heads. For fair coins the four ordered pairs are equally likely, while the three counts are not, since one head arises from both \(HT\) and \(TH\).

An outcome \(\omega\) is an element of \(S\), while an event is a set of outcomes. Later, a random variable attaches a number to each outcome.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• An outcome is a single element of the sample space.
  • The level of detail in an outcome depends on how the experiment is modelled.
  • Events are collections of outcomes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For one die roll, the outcome can be the face that appears.
  • For two coin tosses, an outcome can record the ordered pair of heads and tails.
  • For a customer-order experiment, an outcome might include purchase amount, item type, and delivery time.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A partition of a set \(E\) is a family \(\{B_i\colon i\in I\}\) of nonempty subsets satisfying

\[ B_i\cap B_j=\varnothing\quad(i\ne j),\qquad\bigcup_{i\in I}B_i=E. \]

In probability, take \(E=S\), the sample space, and require the blocks to be events. The elementary total-probability sums use finite or countable partitions. A nonempty event can still have probability zero; omit such blocks from formulas that divide by their probability.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A partition splits a set into nonempty blocks that do not overlap and together cover everything, so every element lands in exactly one block. In probability, a partition of the sample space is a complete list of cases without overlaps: every outcome belongs to exactly one case.

The four strips \(B_1,\ldots,B_4\) satisfy \(B_i\cap B_j=\varnothing\) for \(i\neq j\) and \(B_1\cup\cdots\cup B_4=S\), so additivity gives \(\mathbb{P}(B_1)+\cdots+\mathbb{P}(B_4)=1\). Any event \(A\) is cut by the strips into the pieces \(A\cap B_i\), which are again disjoint with union \(A\), so \(\mathbb{P}(A)=\sum_i\mathbb{P}(A\cap B_i)\): a question is split into cases.

Both conditions are needed for this sum. If two blocks overlapped, outcomes in the overlap would be counted twice; if the blocks did not cover the whole sample space, outcomes outside all blocks would be missed and the sum would be too small. The simplest partition is \(\{B,B^c\}\) for one event \(B\) with its complement; others are the six values of a die or the possible numbers of defective items in a batch.

Writing \(\mathbb{P}(A\cap B_i)=\mathbb{P}(A\mid B_i)\mathbb{P}(B_i)\) turns the sum into the law of total probability, which in turn supplies the denominator of Bayes' rule. In Math II, the equivalence classes of an equivalence relation form a partition of the set, and every partition arises in this way.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every outcome belongs to exactly one partition event.
  • For any event \(A\), the events \(A\cap B_i\) are disjoint and have union \(A\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For a fair die, the odd and even outcomes partition \(\{1,\ldots,6\}\).
  • For an integer-valued count \(N\), the events \(\{N=0\},\{N=1\},\ldots\) partition the outcomes if \(N\) takes finite nonnegative integer values.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(A\) be a finite set with \(n\) elements and let \(0\le k\le n\). A \(k\)-permutation of \(A\) is an ordered selection \((a_1,\ldots,a_k)\) of \(k\) distinct elements of \(A\). For \(k=n\) it is an ordering of all of \(A\), which corresponds to a bijection \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\to A\); when \(A=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) this is a permutation of \(A\) in the Math II sense of a bijection from \(A\) onto itself.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A \(k\)-permutation is an ordered selection: the same objects in a different order count as a different selection. It counts rankings, arrangements in a row and assignments of objects to labelled positions. Counting texts often say permutation for both the full arrangement and the partial selection; the \(k\) makes clear which one is meant.

The figure lists all \(3!=6\) arrangements of \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\). They are found by filling the positions from left to right: \(3\) choices for the first letter, \(2\) for the second and \(1\) for the last, so \(3\cdot2\cdot1=6\) by the multiplication rule.

The same reasoning for \(k\) positions and \(n\) objects gives \(n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)\): each factor is one smaller than the previous one because an object that has been used cannot be chosen again. For a podium of three among eight runners this is \(8\cdot7\cdot6=336\). The form \(n!/(n-k)!\) gives \(n!/0!=n!\) for \(k=n\), which is one reason for the convention \(0!=1\). Dividing by the \(k!\) orders of each group turns the count into the number of combinations.

A common slip is to use this count when repetition is allowed. Four-digit PIN codes may repeat digits, so there are \(10^4=10\,000\) of them, not \(10\cdot9\cdot8\cdot7=5040\); see sampling with and without replacement. The full case \(k=n\) with \(A=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) is what Math II calls a permutation.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The number of \(k\)-permutations of \(n\) distinct objects is \(n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)=n!/(n-k)!\).
  • In particular there are \(n!\) orderings of \(n\) distinct objects.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The number of possible podium finishes among eight runners is a permutation count.
  • Arranging five books on a shelf uses full permutations.
  • Assigning three distinct tasks to three ordered time slots is a permutation problem.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A distribution has a point mass, or atom, at \(a\in\mathbb{R}\) when \(p_a=\mathbb{P}(X=a)>0\). Here \(X\) is a real-valued random variable with that distribution. The CDF has a jump of size \(p_a\) at \(a\):

\[ p_a=F_X(a)-F_X(a^-),\qquad F_X(a^-)=\lim_{x\uparrow a}F_X(x). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A point mass is a single value that carries positive probability on its own. On the CDF it shows up as a jump: just to the left of \(a\) the CDF approaches \(F_X(a^-)\), at \(a\) it equals \(F_X(a)\), and the height of the step is exactly \(\mathbb{P}(X=a)\).

Because \(F_X\) is right-continuous, the mass at \(a\) is included in \(F_X(a)=\mathbb{P}(X\le a)\), while the left limit \(F_X(a^-)\) equals \(\mathbb{P}(X<a)\). With atoms present, a strict and a non-strict inequality can therefore give different probabilities.

Every value with positive PMF of a discrete random variable is a point mass, and these masses add up to one. A point mass can also be only one part of a distribution: in the Example, \(0.3\) sits at zero and the remaining \(0.7\) is spread by a density, a mixture of a discrete and a continuous part. An atom at \(a\) therefore does not mean that all probability sits at \(a\).

A continuous random variable has a CDF without jumps, so \(\mathbb{P}(X=a)=0\) for every \(a\), even where the density is large: density height is not point probability.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Suppose \(X=0\) with probability \(0.3\) and, with probability \(0.7\), \(X\) is drawn from the uniform distribution on \((0,1)\). Then \(F_X(0^-)=0\) and \(F_X(0)=0.3\): there is a point mass \(0.3\) at zero. The remaining probability is spread over the interval.

This differs from a constant random variable, for which the point mass at its only possible value is one. An absolutely continuous distribution has no point masses.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\lambda>0\). A discrete random variable \(X\) has a Poisson distribution with parameter \(\lambda\), written \(X\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)\), if, for \(k=0,1,2,\ldots\),

\[ \mathbb{P}(X=k)=\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!}, \]

and the PMF is zero elsewhere. The extension \(\lambda=0\) gives the constant-zero distribution.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A Poisson variable models a count of events in a fixed period, such as arrivals or claims, when there is no fixed upper limit on the count. Its single parameter \(\lambda\) is the mean count.

The figure shows \(\operatorname{Pois}(3)\). The bars at \(2\) and \(3\) are equally high, \(\tfrac{9}{2}\mathrm{e}^{-3}\approx0.224\), and the bars fall off quickly on both sides: the values above \(10\) have total probability below \(0.001\). The mean \(\lambda=3\) is marked.

Change \(\lambda\): it is both the mean and the variance. Small \(\lambda\) piles the mass near \(0\); large \(\lambda\) gives a wider, more symmetric hump.

The ratio of neighbouring masses explains the shape: \(\mathbb{P}(X=k)/\mathbb{P}(X=k-1)=\lambda/k\), so the bars increase while \(k<\lambda\) and decrease once \(k>\lambda\). When \(\lambda\) is an integer, as here, the two bars at \(\lambda-1\) and \(\lambda\) are equal. The factorial makes the masses eventually shrink faster than any geometric sequence, and they add up to \(1\) because \(\sum_{k\ge0}\lambda^k/k!=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda}\), the series of the exponential function.

The Poisson distribution approximates the binomial distribution with many trials and a small success probability: for large \(n\), \(\operatorname{Bin}(n,\lambda/n)\) is close to \(\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)\), as the Further Properties state. This is why it fits counts of rare events among many independent opportunities. The same distribution describes the number of arrivals in an interval of a Poisson process.

The parameter is also the variance, so a Poisson model fixes the spread once the mean is known. Count data whose variance is clearly larger than the mean are therefore not well described by a single Poisson distribution.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{E}X=\operatorname{Var}(X)=\lambda\).
  • MGF \(M_X(t)=\exp(\lambda(\mathrm{e}^t-1))\) for every real \(t\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\lambda=2\), \(\mathbb{P}(X=0)=\mathrm{e}^{-2}\) and \(\mathbb{P}(X=1)=2\mathrm{e}^{-2}\).
  • A Poisson count with mean \(5\) has variance \(5\) and standard deviation \(\sqrt{5}\).

docs.title: Further Properties
docs.text: Independent Poisson counts add to a Poisson count with the sum of their parameters. A binomial model converges to this law when the number of trials tends to infinity and the success probabilities shrink so that their product tends to a fixed parameter.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\lambda>0\). A process \(\{N_t\colon t\ge 0\}\) with \(N_0=0\), in which \(N_t\) counts the arrivals in \([0,t]\), is a Poisson process with rate \(\lambda\) if it has independent increments (arrival counts in disjoint time intervals are independent) and

\[ N_{t+s}-N_s\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda t) \]

for all \(s,t\ge 0\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A Poisson process models random arrivals over time. It assumes arrivals occur independently and at a constant average rate.

The count \(N_t\) records arrivals in \([0,t]\). For a Poisson process of rate \(\lambda\), \(N_{t+s}-N_s\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda t)\) and disjoint increments are independent. The interarrival times, that is, the waiting times between consecutive arrivals, are i.i.d. exponential \(\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)\) variables, with \(\lambda\) expected arrivals per unit time.

Each press of the button draws new arrivals at rate \(\lambda\). The number in the window \((s,s+t]\) varies from draw to draw like a \(\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda t)\) variable.

A stochastic process consists of variables indexed by time. The Poisson distribution specifies each interval count, while independent random variables describe counts on disjoint intervals; both properties are needed to specify the process, not just its one-time law.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A Poisson process has independent increments.
  • The number of arrivals in an interval depends only on the interval length.
  • Interarrival times in a Poisson process are independent exponential random variables.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Customer arrivals to a store can be approximated by a Poisson process during a stable period.
  • Particle emissions from a radioactive source are often modelled as a Poisson process.
  • Requests to a server may be modelled as a Poisson process over short intervals.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A probability density function of an absolutely continuous \(X\) is a nonnegative integrable function satisfying

\[ \begin{gathered} \mathbb{P}(X\in A)=\int_Af_X(x)\,\mathrm{d}x,\\ \int_{\mathbb{R}}f_X(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=1. \end{gathered} \]

Densities that agree except possibly on a set of zero length, for example at finitely many points, describe the same distribution. This qualification is called almost everywhere here: values on the exceptional set do not affect the integrals. It does not require two densities to agree at every point.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A density describes how probability is spread over the real line: probabilities are areas under its graph, not heights.

The shaded region between \(a\) and \(b\) has area \(\int_a^bf_X(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=\mathbb{P}(a\le X\le b)\), the first formula of the Definition with \(A=[a,b]\), and the whole area under the curve is \(1\). Moving \(b\) to the right adds the area of a thin strip. A strip of zero width has zero area, so \(\mathbb{P}(X=a)=0\) and it does not matter whether the endpoints are included.

Probabilities are areas under the density. The narrow uniform density reaches height \(2\), which is fine: only areas, never heights, are probabilities.

The height \(f_X(x)\) is probability per unit length. For a short interval of length \(h\) starting at a point \(x\) where \(f_X\) is continuous, \(\mathbb{P}(x<X\le x+h)\approx f_X(x)\,h\). This is why a height above \(1\) is allowed, as for the uniform density of height \(2\) on \((0,\tfrac{1}{2})\), and why changing \(f_X\) at finitely many points changes no probability: no area changes. The definite integral measures these areas; for the piecewise continuous densities in the examples, Riemann integral calculations evaluate them.

For a continuous random variable the density plays the role that the PMF plays for a discrete one, with sums replaced by integrals. Integrating the density up to \(x\) gives the CDF, and by the fundamental theorem of calculus differentiating the CDF gives back \(f_X(x)\) at every point where \(f_X\) is continuous. Density height itself is never a point probability.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{P}(a<X\le b)=\int_a^bf_X(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\).
  • \(F_X(x)=\int_{-\infty}^xf_X(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\), so \(F_X'=f_X\) except possibly on a set of zero length.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(f_X(x)=2x\) on \((0,1)\) and zero elsewhere, \(\mathbb{P}(X\le1/2)=1/4\).
  • The uniform density on \((0,1/2)\) has height \(2\), total area \(1\), and \(\mathbb{P}(X=1/4)=0\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(S\) be a sample space and let \(\mathcal{F}\) be a sigma-algebra of events, that is, a collection of events containing \(S\) and closed under complements and countable unions. A probability function is a function \(\mathbb{P}\colon\mathcal{F}\to[0,1]\) that assigns probabilities to events and satisfies the axioms of probability.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A probability function is the rule that assigns to each event a number between \(0\) and \(1\) saying how likely it is. Together with the sample space and the collection of events, it forms the probability model.

The figure maps events of a fair die roll to \([0,1]\): \(\varnothing\mapsto0\), \(\{6\}\mapsto\tfrac{1}{6}\), \(\{2,4,6\}\mapsto\tfrac{1}{2}\), \(\{1,3,6\}\mapsto\tfrac{1}{2}\) and \(S\mapsto1\). The event \(\{1,3,6\}\) is the union of the disjoint events \(\{1,3\}\) and \(\{6\}\), so its probability is \(\tfrac{1}{3}+\tfrac{1}{6}=\tfrac{1}{2}\). The events \(\{2,4,6\}\) and \(\{1,3,6\}\) show that different events can have the same probability: the function need not be injective.

The input of \(\mathbb{P}\) is an event, a set of outcomes, not an outcome: strictly one writes \(\mathbb{P}(\{6\})\), and \(\mathbb{P}(6)\) is a common shorthand. The axioms restrict which functions are allowed, but they do not choose one; that is a modelling decision. A fair die and a loaded die have the same sample space and the same events, but different probability functions. On a finite sample space, the probability function is determined by the probabilities of the single outcomes, since by additivity \(\mathbb{P}(A)\) is the sum of \(\mathbb{P}(\{\omega\})\) over the outcomes \(\omega\in A\).

Naive probability is the special case in which all single outcomes get the same probability. Conditioning on an event \(B\) with \(\mathbb{P}(B)>0\) produces a new probability function, \(A\mapsto\mathbb{P}(A\mid B)\) (conditional probability).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A probability function assigns numbers to events according to the probability axioms.
  • The full sample space has probability one.
  • Disjoint unions are handled by adding probabilities.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For a fair die, the probability function assigns probability one sixth to each single-face event.
  • In a reliability model, the probability function assigns a probability to the event that the system fails.
  • For a deck of cards, the probability function assigns probabilities to events such as drawing a heart.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(X\) be a discrete random variable. The probability mass function of \(X\) is the function \(p_X\) defined by

\[ p_X(x)=\mathbb{P}(X=x). \]

It is zero except on the countable set of values that \(X\) can take.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A PMF lists, for each possible value of a discrete random variable, the probability that the variable takes exactly that value. It describes the whole distribution of such a variable as a table or a bar chart.

The diagram shows \(X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(3,1/2)\), the number of heads in three fair tosses, with masses \(1/8\), \(3/8\), \(3/8\) and \(1/8\), which sum to \(1\). The two red bars give \(\mathbb{P}(X\ge2)=3/8+1/8=1/2\).

Each bar is a value of \(p_X(x)=\mathbb{P}(X=x)\); together they add up to \(1\). Set \(c\) and \(d\) to add the masses of a range of values.

Each mass is the probability of a generated event \(\{X=x\}\). These events are disjoint for different values and together make up the whole sample space, so the masses are nonnegative, add up to \(1\), and the probability of any set \(B\) of values is the sum of the masses in \(B\); summing up to a threshold \(t\) gives the CDF, as in the Key Results.

The argument of \(p_X\) is a value, not an outcome: in the figure, \(p_X(1)=3/8\) collects the three outcomes \(HTT\), \(THT\) and \(TTH\). The PMF is \(0\) away from the possible values, for example \(p_X(1.5)=0\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(p_X(x)\ge0\) and \(\displaystyle \sum_xp_X(x)=1\).
  • \(\displaystyle F_X(t)=\sum_{x\le t}p_X(x)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For a fair die, \(p_X(3)=1/6\) and \(\mathbb{P}(X\le3)=3/6\).
  • If \(p_X(0)=0.7\) and \(p_X(1)=0.3\), then \(\mathbb{P}(X>0)=0.3\).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The prosecutor's fallacy is the error of confusing the probability of observing evidence under a hypothesis with the probability that the hypothesis is true given the evidence.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The prosecutor's fallacy swaps the two sides of a conditional probability. It reads \(\mathbb{P}(\text{evidence}\mid\text{innocent})\), which says how surprising the evidence would be if the suspect were innocent, as \(\mathbb{P}(\text{innocent}\mid\text{evidence})\), which is the quantity a court needs. This can make evidence sound much stronger than it is.

In a population of \(1\,000\,000\) people there is one culprit, who matches, and \(999\,999\) innocent people, each matching with probability \(10^{-5}\), so about \(10\) of them match by chance. Among the roughly \(11\) people who match, only one is the culprit. Thus \(\mathbb{P}(\text{innocent}\mid\text{match})\approx\tfrac{10}{11}\approx0.91\), although \(\mathbb{P}(\text{match}\mid\text{innocent})=10^{-5}\).

A tiny chance of an innocent match, spread over a large population, still produces several innocent matches. Compare \(\mathbb{P}(\text{match}\mid\text{innocent})\) with \(\mathbb{P}(\text{innocent}\mid\text{match})\).

Bayes' rule shows what the fallacy leaves out. Writing \(I\) for "innocent" and \(M\) for "match", it gives \(\mathbb{P}(I\mid M)=\mathbb{P}(M\mid I)\,\mathbb{P}(I)/\mathbb{P}(M)\). The tiny \(10^{-5}\) is divided by \(\mathbb{P}(M)\), which by the law of total probability is itself only about \(1.1\cdot10^{-5}\), because nearly all matches come from innocent people. The answer therefore depends on how many other people could have produced the evidence. If other information had narrowed the suspects down to \(10\) people, about \(9\cdot10^{-5}\) innocent matches would be expected and \(\mathbb{P}(\text{innocent}\mid\text{match})\) would be below \(10^{-4}\).

The same reasoning applies to a positive test for a rare disease: a test that rarely errs can still produce mostly false positives when the disease itself is rare.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The fallacy confuses \(\mathbb{P}(E\mid H)\) with \(\mathbb{P}(H\mid E)\).
  • Bayes' rule shows that posterior probabilities require prior probabilities and alternative explanations.
  • Rare evidence is not automatically decisive if it can also occur under competing hypotheses.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A rare DNA match probability is not the same as the probability that a defendant is innocent.
  • A rare disease test result is not the same as the probability of disease without considering prevalence.
  • A suspicious transaction pattern must be compared against both fraud and non-fraud explanations.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a CDF \(F\) and \(0<u<1\), its generalized inverse is

\[ F^{-1}(u)=\inf\{x\in\mathbb{R}\colon F(x)\ge u\}. \]

It need not be an ordinary inverse: \(F\) can have flat portions or jumps. Endpoint values at \(u=0,1\) are irrelevant when using a continuous uniform input.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The quantile function answers the reverse question of the CDF. The CDF asks for the probability of being at most \(x\); the quantile function asks for the threshold below which a fraction \(u\) of the probability lies. It converts a probability level into a value of \(X\).

To read the figure, start at the level \(u=0.8\) on the vertical axis, move right until the curve is reached, then move down to the horizontal axis: the value found there is \(Q(0.8)\), about \(1.39\) for this CDF. Here \(Q\) is the \(F^{-1}\) of the Definition; when \(F\) is continuous and strictly increasing, as here, it is the ordinary inverse, and \(F(Q(u))=u\).

Pick a level \(u\) and read the CDF backwards. At a jump many levels share one quantile, and where \(F\) is flat the infimum picks the left end.

The infimum handles the two cases in which no ordinary inverse exists. If \(F\) jumps over the level \(u\), no \(x\) has \(F(x)=u\), and \(F^{-1}(u)\) is the location of the jump. If \(F\) equals \(u\) on a whole interval, many \(x\) have \(F(x)=u\), and the infimum picks the left end. In the \(\operatorname{Bern}(0.3)\) example the two cases together give \(F^{-1}(u)=0\) for \(0<u\le0.7\). By right-continuity of \(F\), \(F^{-1}(u)\) is the smallest \(x\) with \(F(x)\ge u\).

Special levels have their own names: \(F^{-1}(\tfrac{1}{2})\) is a median, and \(F^{-1}(0.25)\) and \(F^{-1}(0.75)\) are the lower and upper quartiles. Feeding a uniform input into \(F^{-1}\) produces a variable with CDF \(F\), the universality of the uniform used to simulate a distribution.

Despite the notation, \(F^{-1}\) is an inverse function, not the reciprocal \(1/F\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For \(0<u<1\), \(F^{-1}(u)\le x\) if and only if \(u\le F(x)\).
  • Consequently, if \(U\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\), \(\mathbb{P}(F^{-1}(U)\le x)=F(x)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\operatorname{Exp}(2)\), \(F^{-1}(u)=-\log(1-u)/2\).
  • For \(\operatorname{Bern}(0.3)\), \(F^{-1}(u)=0\) for \(0<u\le0.7\) and \(1\) for \(0.7<u<1\).

docs.title: Further Properties
docs.text: The median is a quantile at probability level \(1/2\). Other probability levels define percentiles. The generalized inverse is useful even when an ordinary inverse does not exist.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(A\) and \(B\) be random variables with \(A\le B\). A random interval is an interval whose endpoints are random, such as \([A,B]\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A random interval is an interval whose position and length depend on the outcome of the experiment. Before the experiment is run, \([A,B]\) is unknown; afterwards it is an ordinary interval of numbers.

Each horizontal segment is the interval \([A,B]\) obtained in one run, and the dashed vertical line is a fixed number \(\theta\) that is the same in every run. Five of the six segments contain \(\theta\); the orange one lies entirely to its right. The randomness sits in the endpoints, not in \(\theta\).

The basic event is that the interval covers \(\theta\):

\[ \{A\le\theta\le B\}=\{A\le\theta\}\cap\{B\ge\theta\}. \]

Its probability \(\mathbb{P}(A\le\theta\le B)\) is the coverage probability. Because \(A\le B\), the interval can miss \(\theta\) in two disjoint ways, lying entirely to the right (\(A>\theta\)) or entirely to the left (\(B<\theta\)), so the complement rule gives

\[ \mathbb{P}(A\le\theta\le B) =1-\mathbb{P}(A>\theta)-\mathbb{P}(B<\theta). \]

The fraction \(5/6\) in the figure is what happened in six runs, not the coverage probability itself.

The probability statement is about the procedure before the run. After one run, \([A,B]\) is a fixed interval that either contains the fixed \(\theta\) or does not. A natural example is the interval \([X_{(1)},X_{(n)}]\) between the smallest and the largest order statistic of a sample. The idea returns in statistics as the confidence interval, a random interval constructed so that its coverage probability takes a chosen value such as \(0.95\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A random interval has endpoints that are random variables.
  • Events can be formed from statements about whether a fixed value lies inside the interval.
  • Random intervals are useful for uncertainty bands and coverage statements.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A confidence interval computed from data is a random interval before the data are observed.
  • The interval between two random arrival times is random.
  • A forecast range with random lower and upper bounds is a random interval.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(S\) be a sample space. A random variable is a function \(X\colon S\to\mathbb{R}\) that assigns a real number to each outcome in \(S\), subject to the measurability condition that \(\{\omega\in S\colon X(\omega)\le x\}\) is an event for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A random variable attaches a number to every outcome of an experiment. Once outcomes are numbers, probability questions can be asked about values and ranges of values, and answered with functions and distributions.

The diagram counts heads in two independent fair coin tosses: \(X(HH)=2\), \(X(HT)=X(TH)=1\) and \(X(TT)=0\). Two outcomes are sent to the same value \(1\), which is allowed for a function. Each outcome has probability \(\tfrac{1}{4}\), so \(\mathbb{P}(X=1)=\mathbb{P}(\{HT,TH\})=\tfrac{1}{2}\) and \(\mathbb{P}(X=0)=\mathbb{P}(X=2)=\tfrac{1}{4}\).

The usual notation hides the outcome: \(\{X\le x\}\) is shorthand for the event \(\{\omega\in S\colon X(\omega)\le x\}\). The condition in the Definition asks exactly that these sets are events, so that they have probabilities. On a finite sample space in which every subset is an event, the condition holds automatically and every function \(S\to\mathbb{R}\) is a random variable.

Several random variables can live on the same sample space; in the coin example, the number of tails \(2-X\) is another one. Indicators, sums and functions of a random variable build new random variables from old ones, and the CDF \(F_X(x)=\mathbb{P}(X\le x)\) collects the probabilities of the events in the Definition.

Despite its name, a random variable is neither random nor an unknown: it is a fixed function. The randomness lies in which outcome \(\omega\) occurs, and \(X(\omega)\) is a number once \(\omega\) is known.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A random variable is a function from outcomes to real numbers.
  • Random variables generate events such as threshold events.
  • The distribution of a random variable describes probabilities of its numerical values or ranges.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For a die roll, the displayed face is a random variable.
  • For a customer order, the order value is a random variable.
  • For a machine, the time until failure is a random variable.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\sigma>0\). A continuous random variable \(X\) has a Rayleigh distribution with parameter \(\sigma\) if its density is

\[ f_X(x)=\frac{x}{\sigma^2}\exp\left(-\frac{x^2}{2\sigma^2}\right), \]

for \(x\ge 0\), and \(f_X(x)=0\) for \(x<0\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The Rayleigh distribution describes a nonnegative distance: typically the distance from the origin of a random point \((Y_1,Y_2)\) in the plane whose two coordinates are independent and normal with mean \(0\) and the same variance \(\sigma^2\). The Euclidean distance \(X=\sqrt{Y_1^2+Y_2^2}\) then has the density of the Definition.

The figure shows the density for \(\sigma=1\), with the horizontal axis in multiples of \(\sigma\). It starts at \(0\), because a distance near \(0\) requires both coordinates to be near \(0\). It rises to its peak at \(x=\sigma\) (the green line, labelled mode) and then falls quickly, because of the factor \(\exp(-x^2/(2\sigma^2))\). The red line marks the mean \(\sigma\sqrt{\pi/2}\approx1.25\sigma\), to the right of the peak, since the right side of the curve is longer than the left side.

Change \(\sigma\): the density peaks at \(x=\sigma\) and the mean sits a little further out, at \(\sigma\sqrt{\pi/2}\).

Unlike the normal density, this density can be integrated by hand: \(x/\sigma^2\) is, up to sign, the derivative of the exponent, so substitution gives, for \(x\ge0\),

\[ F_X(x)=1-\exp\left(-\frac{x^2}{2\sigma^2}\right). \]

So \(\mathbb{P}(X>x)=\exp(-x^2/(2\sigma^2))\), and probabilities are density integrals over nonnegative intervals, as for any continuous random variable. The parameter \(\sigma\) only sets the scale: \(X/\sigma\) has the Rayleigh distribution with parameter \(1\). Note that \(\sigma\) is the standard deviation of each coordinate \(Y_i\), not of \(X\) itself.

In one dimension the corresponding distance \(|Y_1|\) from the origin has a folded normal distribution.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The Rayleigh distribution is supported on nonnegative values.
  • It arises as the magnitude of a two-dimensional random vector with independent, centred normal components of equal variance.
  • Its density starts at zero, rises to a peak, and then decays.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Wind speed magnitude can sometimes be modelled with a Rayleigh distribution.
  • The distance error from two independent normal coordinate errors can be Rayleigh.
  • Signal envelope amplitudes in some noise models follow a Rayleigh distribution.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let a random experiment be specified. The sample space \(S\) is the set of all possible outcomes of that experiment.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The sample space lists everything that can happen in the model: each run of the experiment produces exactly one of its elements. Events are subsets of \(S\), so \(S\) has to be fixed before any probability can be discussed.

The left panel is one die roll, \(S=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}\). The right panel is two coin tosses, \(S=\{HH,HT,TH,TT\}\), where the order of the tosses is recorded, so \(HT\) and \(TH\) are different outcomes; by the multiplication rule there are \(2\cdot2=4\) of them.

Choosing \(S\) is part of modelling. For two coin tosses, \(\{0,1,2\}\) (the number of heads) is also a valid sample space, but its outcomes are not equally likely, and "the first toss is heads" cannot be expressed in it. \(S\) need not be finite: tossing a coin until the first head gives \(\{1,2,3,\ldots\}\). Some texts write \(\Omega\) instead of \(S\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The sample space must include every possible outcome in the model.
  • Different modelling choices can lead to different sample spaces for the same real situation.
  • Events are subsets of the sample space.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For one coin toss, the sample space can be heads and tails.
  • For two dice, the sample space can be ordered pairs of die faces.
  • For a waiting-time experiment, the sample space can be all nonnegative times.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(A\) be a finite set of \(n\) distinct objects, and draw \(k\) of them one at a time.

  • With replacement: each drawn object is put back before the next draw, so the same object can be drawn more than once.
  • Without replacement: drawn objects are removed, so all \(k\) drawn objects are distinct and \(k\le n\).

A sample is ordered if the order of the draws is recorded, and unordered if only which objects were drawn (with their multiplicities) matters.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The two choices give four counting problems. Ordered samples are counted with the multiplication rule; an unordered sample without replacement is a combination, obtained from the ordered count by dividing out the \(k!\) orders of the same \(k\) objects.

The table places the four counts of the first example, \(k=3\) draws from \(n=10\) tickets, in a grid: the columns say whether drawn tickets are put back, the rows whether the order is recorded. Only in the column without replacement does every unordered sample come from exactly \(3!=6\) ordered ones, so dividing \(720\) by \(3!\) gives \(\binom{10}{3}=120\). With replacement the same division fails, because \(1000/3!\) is not even an integer: a sample with repeats has fewer than \(3!\) orders, which is why the \(220\) unordered samples with replacement are not equally likely.

With replacement, every draw faces the same \(n\) objects, so the history of earlier draws changes nothing; in the language of Week 2, the draws are independent with the same distribution. Without replacement, each draw changes what remains, so the draws are dependent: after a red ball is removed, a second red ball is less likely.

Draw \(n\) balls from an urn with \(N\) balls, \(K\) of them white, and count the white balls drawn. Both counts have mean \(nK/N\), but without replacement the variance carries the extra factor \((N-n)/(N-1)\). Make \(N\) large compared with \(n\) and the two distributions merge.

Two common slips are worth naming. First, "without replacement" does not by itself mean "unordered": dealing cards one by one is ordered sampling without replacement, and a hand of cards is the unordered version of the same experiment. Second, the unordered samples with replacement must not be treated as equally likely, as the Key Results explain.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
The number of possible samples of size \(k\) from \(n\) distinct objects is:

  • ordered, with replacement: \(n^k\);
  • ordered, without replacement: \(n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)=n!/(n-k)!\), the number of \(k\)-permutations; it is \(0\) when \(k>n\);
  • unordered, without replacement: the binomial coefficient \(\binom{n}{k}\);
  • unordered, with replacement: \(\binom{n+k-1}{k}\), by stars and bars.

In the first three cases every sample is equally likely when each draw is uniform, so naive probability applies. The unordered samples with replacement are not equally likely, so probabilities should be computed from ordered samples instead.

  • Each ordered sample without replacement corresponds to exactly \(k!\) orderings of one unordered sample, so \(\binom{n}{k}=\dfrac{n!}{k!\,(n-k)!}\).
  • Without replacement, the \(j\)th draw on its own is still uniform over all \(n\) objects: by symmetry, as many ordered samples have a given object in place \(j\) as in place \(1\). Only the joint behaviour of the draws differs from sampling with replacement.
  • A particular object is included in the sample with probability \(k/n\) without replacement and \(1-(1-1/n)^k\) with replacement; the latter is smaller for \(k\ge2\), because repeats waste draws.
  • With replacement, all \(k\) draws are distinct with probability \(n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)/n^k\), the ratio of the two ordered counts.

Looking ahead to Week 3: if \(n\) balls are drawn from an urn with \(N\) balls, \(K\) of them white, the number of white balls drawn has the binomial distribution \(\operatorname{Bin}(n,K/N)\) with replacement and the hypergeometric distribution without replacement. Both have mean \(nK/N\); sampling without replacement has the smaller variance, and the two are close when \(N\) is large compared with \(n\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Choosing \(3\) of \(10\) numbered tickets gives \(10^3=1000\) ordered samples with replacement, \(10\cdot9\cdot8=720\) ordered samples without replacement, \(\binom{10}{3}=120\) unordered samples without replacement, and \(\binom{12}{3}=220\) unordered samples with replacement.
  • In the same setting, ticket number \(7\) is among the three draws with probability \(3/10=0.3\) without replacement, and \(1-0.9^3=0.271\) with replacement.
  • An urn holds \(20\) balls, \(8\) of them red, and \(6\) are drawn. The probability of no red ball is \(0.6^6\approx0.0467\) with replacement, but \(\binom{12}{6}/\binom{20}{6}=924/38760\approx0.0238\) without replacement.
  • From the same urn, two balls are drawn without replacement. Of the \(20\cdot19=380\) ordered pairs, \(8\cdot7=56\) are red–red and \(12\cdot8=96\) are non-red–red, so the second ball is red with probability \(152/380=0.4=8/20\), the same as the first.
  • Two draws with replacement from \(\{1,2\}\) give the \(\binom{3}{2}=3\) unordered samples \(\{1,1\}\), \(\{1,2\}\) and \(\{2,2\}\), but with probabilities \(\tfrac{1}{4},\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{4}\): the mixed sample arises from the two ordered samples \((1,2)\) and \((2,1)\).
  • In the birthday problem, assigning birthdays to \(k\) people is ordered sampling with replacement from \(365\) days (\(365^k\) outcomes), and all birthdays distinct is ordered sampling without replacement. Hence
\[ \mathbb{P}(\text{no match})=\frac{365!/(365-k)!}{365^k}. \]

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A random variable \(Z\) has the standard normal distribution, written \(Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)\), if its density is \(\phi\); its CDF is \(\Phi\):

\[ \phi(z)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\mathrm{e}^{-z^2/2},\qquad \Phi(z)=\int_{-\infty}^z\phi(t)\,\mathrm{d}t. \]

In \(\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\) the second parameter is the variance.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The standard normal distribution is the single reference bell curve, centred at \(0\) with variance \(1\). Every normal probability can be read from its CDF \(\Phi\), because any normal variable becomes standard normal after standardization: a value is then measured in standard deviations from the mean.

The shaded area is everything to the left of \(z=1\), that is \(\Phi(1)=\mathbb{P}(Z\le1)\approx0.841\), the first Example. The unshaded right tail has area \(1-\Phi(1)\approx0.159\). Since \(\phi\) is symmetric about \(0\), the left tail below \(-1\) has the same area, so \(\Phi(-1)=1-\Phi(1)\) and \(\mathbb{P}(-1\le Z\le1)=2\Phi(1)-1\approx0.683\).

Move \(c\) and \(d\) and read probabilities as differences \(\Phi(d)-\Phi(c)\); try \(c=-1.96\), \(d=1.96\).

The density \(\phi\) has no antiderivative in terms of elementary functions, so \(\Phi\) is evaluated numerically, by a table or software. A table for \(z\ge0\) suffices: symmetry gives \(\Phi(-z)=1-\Phi(z)\), and interval probabilities are differences \(\Phi(d)-\Phi(c)\). The value \(1.96\) suggested in the manipulate prompt satisfies \(\Phi(1.96)\approx0.975\), so \(\mathbb{P}(-1.96\le Z\le1.96)\approx0.95\).

For \(Y\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\), the variable \((Y-\mu)/\sigma\) is standard normal, so \(\mathbb{P}(Y\le y)=\Phi\big((y-\mu)/\sigma\big)\); the second Example uses this with \(\mu=10\) and \(\sigma=2\). A common slip is to divide by the variance: in \(\mathcal{N}(10,4)\) the second parameter is \(\sigma^2=4\), so the divisor is \(\sigma=2\). Later, sums of many independent variables are approximated by this distribution after standardization, in the central limit theorem.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{E}Z=0\), \(\operatorname{Var}(Z)=1\), and \(\Phi(-z)=1-\Phi(z)\).
  • If \(Y\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\) with \(\sigma>0\), then \((Y-\mu)/\sigma\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)\).
  • Quantiles transform the same way: the \(p\)-quantile of \(Y\) is \(\mu+\sigma\Phi^{-1}(p)\). Printed normal tables list the left-tail probabilities \(\Phi(z)\), so a quantile is read off the table in reverse and then transformed back.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{P}(Z\le1)=\Phi(1)\approx0.8413\).
  • For \(Y\sim\mathcal{N}(10,4)\), \(\mathbb{P}(Y\le12)=\Phi((12-10)/2)=\Phi(1)\approx0.8413\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(X\) be a random variable with mean \(\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sigma>0\). The standardization of \(X\) is

\[ Z=\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Standardization expresses a value relative to its mean and spread. It makes variables with different units or scales easier to compare.

The illustrated calculation gives \(Z=\dfrac{X-\mu}{\sigma}\). Subtracting \(\mu\) centres the distribution at \(0\) and dividing by \(\sigma\) rescales the spread to \(1\), so \(\mathbb{E}[Z]=0\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Z)=1\). The \(z\)-score measures the distance from the mean in units of \(\sigma\).

Change \(\mu\), \(\sigma\) and \(x\): the standardized value \(z=(x-\mu)/\sigma\) cuts off exactly the same probability under the standard normal.

Expectation supplies the centring value \(\mu\). Subtracting that value gives mean zero; dividing by the positive standard deviation then gives variance one without asserting that the transformed law is normal.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Standardization subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation.
  • The standardized variable has mean zero and variance one when the original mean and variance exist.
  • For normal variables, standardization produces a standard normal variable.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A student's score can be standardized relative to the class mean and standard deviation.
  • A product weight can be standardized to see how many standard deviations it lies from the target.
  • Standardizing normal measurement errors allows probabilities to be computed from a standard normal table.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Let \(n,k\in\mathbb{N}\). Stars and bars is a counting method for the number of ways to distribute \(k\) identical objects among \(n\) distinct boxes, often by representing objects as stars and dividers as bars.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Stars and bars turns a problem of distributing identical objects among boxes into an arrangement problem. It is useful when objects are identical and only the counts in each box matter.

The six stars and two bars in the figure represent \((x_1,x_2,x_3)=(2,1,3)\). Every arrangement of six stars and two bars corresponds to one nonnegative integer solution of \(x_1+x_2+x_3=6\). Choosing the two bar positions among eight positions gives \(\binom{8}{2}=28\) distributions. In the general notation below, \(k\) objects and \(n\) boxes require \(n-1\) bars.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Stars and bars counts nonnegative integer solutions to \(x_1+\cdots+x_n=k\).
  • The number of such solutions is \(\binom{k+n-1}{n-1}\).
  • Positive integer solutions can be counted by first giving one object to each box.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The number of ways to distribute ten identical candies among four children is a stars-and-bars count.
  • The number of nonnegative solutions to \(x_1+x_2+x_3=8\) is counted by stars and bars.
  • Allocating identical spare parts among labelled warehouses can use stars and bars.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(T\) be an index set. A stochastic process is a collection of random variables \(\{X_t\colon t\in T\}\) defined on a common probability space, that is, one sample space with one probability function.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A stochastic process describes randomness that develops over time, or over another index. Instead of one random value, it is a whole family of random values \(X_t\), one for each index \(t\), all driven by one random experiment.

The two zigzag lines are sample paths for two outcomes \(\omega_1\) and \(\omega_2\); at each step the value moves up or down by \(1\). Fixing the outcome \(\omega\) gives a function of time, \(t\mapsto X_t(\omega)\). The vertical line at \(t=6\) does the opposite: fixing the time gives the random variable \(X_6\), which takes the value \(2\) on the blue path and \(-2\) on the red one.

Defining all \(X_t\) on one probability space is what makes statements about several times at once meaningful, such as \(\mathbb{P}(X_5>0\text{ and }X_6>0)\) or the probability that a path reaches level \(4\) before time \(10\). The distributions of the single \(X_t\) do not determine such probabilities; the dependence between different times matters as well.

With \(T=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\) the process runs in discrete time and each path is a sequence, as in the figure. With \(T=[0,\infty)\) it runs in continuous time, like the count \(N_t\) of a Poisson process, whose paths are staircases that rise by one at each arrival.

A process is not a single random variable that changes over time: each \(X_t\) is a separate random variable, and a path is one realization of the whole family, not the process itself.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A stochastic process is a family of random variables indexed by time or another set.
  • The index set may be discrete or continuous.
  • Sample paths describe how one realization of the process evolves across the index set.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Daily demand over a year can be modelled as a discrete-time stochastic process.
  • The number of arrivals up to time \(t\) in a queue is a continuous-time stochastic process.
  • Stock prices observed over time form a stochastic process.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be independent random variables. The sum of independent random variables is the random variable \(X+Y\), whose distribution is determined by combining the distributions of \(X\) and \(Y\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The sum \(X+Y\) of independent random variables combines two separate sources of randomness, such as two dice, two service stages or two claims. Its distribution is determined by the distributions of \(X\) and \(Y\) alone, because independence fixes how their values combine.

The figure compares one fair die, six bars of height \(\tfrac{1}{6}\), with the sum of two independent fair dice. The sum takes the values \(2,\ldots,12\) with masses rising from \(\tfrac{1}{36}\) to \(\tfrac{6}{36}\) and falling back to \(\tfrac{1}{36}\). The value \(7\) is the most likely: six of the \(36\) equally likely pairs give it, from \((1,6)\) to \((6,1)\), while only \((1,1)\) gives \(2\).

Add dice one at a time: each new distribution is a convolution of the previous one with a single die. Means and variances add, and the shape becomes bell-like.

For discrete variables, the sum is found by adding over all ways to reach the total \(s\):

\[ \mathbb{P}(X+Y=s)=\sum_x\mathbb{P}(X=x)\,\mathbb{P}(Y=s-x), \]

where independence turns the probability that \(X=x\) and \(Y=s-x\) into a product. Without independence the two distributions alone do not determine the sum: for a fair die \(X\), the variable \(7-X\) is again a fair die, yet \(X+(7-X)=7\) always, while \(X+X\) takes only even values.

Means always add, by linearity of expectation, so the sum of two dice has mean \(3.5+3.5=7\). Independence also makes variances add: one die has variance \(35/12\), so the sum of two independent dice has variance \(35/6\). A sum of \(n\) independent Bernoulli variables with the same \(p\) has the binomial distribution. The sum formula above later gets the name convolution.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The distribution of a sum of independent variables is obtained by convolution in many common settings.
  • Means add whenever expectations exist.
  • Variances add for independent variables with finite variances.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The total number of heads from two independent sets of tosses is a sum of independent binomial variables.
  • The total waiting time for independent service stages is a sum of waiting-time variables.
  • The total claim amount from independent claims is a sum of independent losses.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(X\) be a random variable with a distribution. Summary measures of a distribution are numerical quantities, such as centre, spread, and shape measures, that describe important features of that distribution.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Summary measures condense a distribution into a few numbers that answer simple questions: where is it centred, how spread out is it, and what is its shape? They allow distributions to be compared without listing every probability.

The figure annotates the density \(f(x)=x\mathrm{e}^{-x}\) for \(x\ge0\). Three measures of centre are marked: the mode \(1\) at the peak, the median \(\approx1.68\) that halves the area, and the mean \(2\). The arrow shows one standard deviation \(\sigma=\sqrt{2}\approx1.41\) on each side of the mean, from about \(0.59\) to \(3.41\). The density is right-skewed, with a long right tail, and mode, median and mean appear in that order from left to right.

Measures of location answer different questions and can disagree, as here. The mean is the balance point and reacts to extreme values; the median depends only on the order of the values; the mode marks where values are most concentrated. Spread measures, such as the standard deviation or the distance between the quartiles, measure how far values typically lie from the centre. Shape measures describe symmetry and the number of peaks, the modality.

A summary always loses information. \(\operatorname{Unif}(-\sqrt{3},\sqrt{3})\) and \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\) both have mean \(0\) and variance \(1\), yet one is flat on a bounded interval and the other is a bell curve on the whole line. Numerical measures of shape, skewness and kurtosis, follow later.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Location measures describe centre.
  • Spread measures describe variability.
  • Shape measures describe asymmetry, tail weight, or modality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Mean and median summarize the centre of delivery times.
  • Variance and standard deviation summarize variability in demand.
  • Skewness and kurtosis summarize shape features of a loss distribution.
