docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The course uses \(\{x\colon p_X(x)>0\}\) for a discrete support and a positive-density region for standard continuous models. The topological support, which depends only on the distribution, is

\[ \operatorname{supp}(X)=\{x\colon{}\mathbb{P}(|X-x|<\varepsilon)>0\quad \text{ for every }\varepsilon>0\}. \]

For the usual continuous densities, this is the closure of the positive-density region. If a density has been changed on a set of zero length, for example at finitely many points, use the neighbourhood definition: such changes do not change the support.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The support is the set of values a random variable can actually take, as far as probability can tell. For a discrete random variable it is the set of values with positive mass, \(\{x\colon p_X(x)>0\}\).

The left panel shows \(\operatorname{Bin}(3,\tfrac{1}{2})\): the circled points \(0,1,2,3\) form the support, the only values with positive mass. The right panel shows a continuous example, the exponential distribution with rate \(1\), whose density is \(0\) to the left of \(0\) and positive from \(0\) on; its support is the half-line \([0,\infty)\), marked in red.

The support tells where formulas apply: a mass formula such as \(\binom{3}{k}/8\) is meant only for \(k=0,1,2,3\), and sums over the values of \(X\) only need the values in the support.

The topological definition asks that every small interval \((x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)\) around \(x\) has positive probability. For a discrete variable with finitely many values this gives the same set as the positive masses; it differs only in edge cases, such as adding the endpoints \(0\) and \(1\) for \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\), as in the Examples. A value outside the support is not merely unlikely: a whole interval around it has probability zero, and the CDF is constant there.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The course discrete support is \(\{x\colon p_X(x)>0\}\).
  • The topological support consists of points whose every open neighbourhood has positive probability, including boundary and accumulation points.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\operatorname{Bern}(p)\) with \(0<p<1\), the support is \(\{0,1\}\).
  • For \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\), a positive-density region is \((0,1)\), while the topological support is \([0,1]\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(X\) be a random variable and let \(a\in\mathbb{R}\). The distribution of \(X\) is symmetric about \(a\) if \(X-a\) and \(a-X\) have the same distribution.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A distribution is symmetric about \(a\) when deviations below \(a\) behave exactly like deviations above \(a\): \(X\) is as likely to fall at least a distance \(t\) below \(a\) as at least a distance \(t\) above it. The graph of the PMF or density is then a mirror image in the vertical line at \(a\).

The density in the figure is symmetric about \(a\), so \(f_X(a-t)=f_X(a+t)\) for every \(t\), and the two shaded tails \(\mathbb{P}(X\le a-t)\) and \(\mathbb{P}(X\ge a+t)\) have the same area. This holds for every distance \(t\), not just the one drawn.

Pick a centre \(a\) and a distance \(t\): the distribution is symmetric about \(a\) when the two tails match for every \(t\). The exponential distribution fails for every \(a\).

In the Definition, \(X-a\) is the deviation above \(a\) and \(a-X\) the deviation below it; symmetry says that the two have the same distribution. An equivalent condition is \(\mathbb{P}(X\le a-t)=\mathbb{P}(X\ge a+t)\) for all \(t\). With \(a=0\) and the standard normal distribution, this is the identity \(\Phi(-z)=1-\Phi(z)\).

Symmetry fixes the centre. The point \(a\) is a median: \(\mathbb{P}(X\le a)=\mathbb{P}(X\ge a)\), and the two add up to at least \(1\), so each is at least \(\tfrac{1}{2}\). If the mean exists, it equals \(a\), since linearity gives \(\mathbb{E}[X-a]=\mathbb{E}[a-X]=-\mathbb{E}[X-a]\), so \(\mathbb{E}[X-a]=0\).

The converse fails: mean and median can coincide for a distribution that is not symmetric. Symmetry is also not special to the normal distribution; the uniform distribution on \((a-c,a+c)\) and a fair die, symmetric about \(3.5\), are symmetric too.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Symmetry about a centre means left and right deviations have the same distribution.
  • If the distribution is symmetric about \(a\), then \(a\) is a median, and the mean equals \(a\) whenever it exists.
  • A symmetric distribution need not be normal.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A normal distribution is symmetric about its mean.
  • A fair die distribution is symmetric around three and a half.
  • A two-point distribution with equal mass at negative one and one is symmetric about zero.

docs.title: Transformation of a Continuous Random Variable
Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(X\) have a density on an interval \(I\). Suppose \(g\colon I\to J\) is a continuously differentiable bijection with \(g'(x)\ne0\) on \(I\). For the transformed variable \(Y=g(X)\) and \(y\in J\),

\[ f_Y(y)=f_X(g^{-1}(y))\left|\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}y}g^{-1}(y)\right|, \]

and the density is zero outside \(J\). Density values at endpoints do not affect probabilities. The absolute derivative accounts for interval stretching; non-strict monotonicity alone is insufficient for this formula. For transformations with suitable monotone branches, add the contributions from each inverse branch.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A monotone transformation changes a density by stretching or compressing intervals. The absolute inverse derivative compensates for this change of scale.

In the illustrated example, \(f_Y(y)=f_X\big(g^{-1}(y)\big)\Big|\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}y}g^{-1}(y)\Big|=1\cdot\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt y}\) on \((0,1]\) for \(g(x)=x^2\). The derivative factor rescales the density so that each strip keeps its probability and the total area stays \(1\).

A small interval of \(X\) and its image under \(g\) carry the same probability. Where \(g\) stretches intervals, the density of \(Y\) drops by the factor \(\left|\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dy}g^{-1}(y)\right|\).

A continuous random variable assigns probabilities through a probability density function. Integration by substitution type 1 transfers those probabilities through the change of variable. Derivative and differentiability describes local interval stretching, and the inverse function theorem gives the reciprocal derivative of the inverse when the derivative of \(g\) is nonzero.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(Y=a+bX\) with \(b\ne0\), then \(f_Y(y)=f_X((y-a)/b)/|b|\).
  • For a suitable finite collection of monotone branches, sum \(f_X(x)/|g'(x)|\) over the preimages \(g(x)=y\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(X\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) and \(Y=2X+1\), then \(f_Y(y)=1/2\) on \((1,3)\).
  • If \(X\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) and \(Y=X^2\), then \(f_Y(y)=1/(2\sqrt y)\) on \((0,1)\).

docs.title: Further Properties
docs.text: The transformed density integrates to one. In higher-dimensional transformations, a Jacobian determinant provides the corresponding volume adjustment.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For real numbers \(a<b\), a random variable \(X\) has the uniform distribution on \((a,b)\), written \(X\sim\operatorname{Unif}(a,b)\), if its density is

\[ f_X(x)=\begin{cases}1/(b-a),&a<x<b,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} \]

Including the endpoints in the density interval does not change the distribution.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The uniform distribution on \((a,b)\) models a value that lies between \(a\) and \(b\) with no part of that interval favoured: the probability of a subinterval is proportional to its length.

With \(a=1\) and \(b=4\) the density is flat at height \(1/(b-a)=1/3\) and zero outside the interval, so the rectangle under it has area \(3\cdot\tfrac{1}{3}=1\). The shaded strip from \(2\) to \(3\) has length \(1\) and hence probability \(\tfrac{1}{3}\); every other strip of length \(1\) inside \((1,4)\) has the same probability, wherever it is placed.

Widen or narrow \((a,b)\): the density height \(1/(b-a)\) adjusts so that the total area stays \(1\), and equal-length subintervals get equal probability.

The mean \((a+b)/2\) is the midpoint of the interval, and the variance \((b-a)^2/12\) depends only on the length, so shifting the interval moves the mean and leaves the variance unchanged. Height and width trade off: a short interval forces a tall density, and for \(b-a<1\) the height exceeds \(1\), which is allowed because heights of a continuous random variable are not probabilities. For the same reason each single value has probability \(0\); "uniform" means equal probability for equal lengths.

\(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) is the basic building block. If \(U\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\), then \(a+(b-a)U\sim\operatorname{Unif}(a,b)\), and by the universality of the uniform a suitable function of \(U\), its quantile function, has any prescribed distribution; this is how random numbers with other distributions are simulated. The discrete uniform distribution is the counterpart for finitely many equally likely values.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{E}X=(a+b)/2\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=(b-a)^2/12\).
  • For \(a\le c\le d\le b\), \(\mathbb{P}(c<X<d)=(d-c)/(b-a)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(X\sim\operatorname{Unif}(2,6)\), \(\mathbb{P}(3<X<5)=2/4=1/2\).
  • For \(X\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\), \(\mathbb{E}X=1/2\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=1/12\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A distribution is unimodal if its probability mass function or density function has a single peak (one local maximum), and multimodal if it has several separated peaks; with two peaks it is called bimodal. Here every peak is called a mode, although only the highest peak is a mode in the strict sense of a global maximizer.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Modality counts the peaks of a PMF or density. A unimodal distribution has one peak; a multimodal one has several separated peaks, which often signals that the population consists of several groups, each with its own typical value.

The left panel is a bell-shaped density with a single peak, marked in red. The right panel shows two peaks of different heights with a dip between them. Both count as modes in the sense of this page, although only the higher, left peak is a mode in the strict sense of a global maximizer; the right peak is a local maximum.

Pull the two group means apart, or shrink \(\sigma\): at some point a single peak splits into two.

A mixture of two groups shows two peaks only when the groups are far enough apart compared with their spread. If the group means are close, the two bells overlap and add up to a single, wider peak. For an equal-weight mixture of two normal distributions with the same standard deviation \(\sigma\), the density has two peaks exactly when the means are more than \(2\sigma\) apart.

Modality matters for summaries. For a bimodal distribution the mean can fall in the dip between the peaks, a region where few values lie, so a single measure of centre describes it poorly. Bimodal does not require equally high peaks, and a single peak does not imply symmetry: the exponential distribution is unimodal but far from symmetric.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A unimodal distribution has a single peak, which is then its mode.
  • A multimodal distribution has several peaks; they need not be equally high.
  • Mixtures can create multimodal distributions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A normal distribution is unimodal.
  • A mixture of weekday and weekend demand distributions may be bimodal.
  • Exam scores from two very different preparation groups can form a multimodal distribution.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(A\) and \(B\) be events in a sample space. The union \(A\cup B\) is the event that at least one of \(A\) or \(B\) occurs, and the intersection \(A\cap B\) is the event that both \(A\) and \(B\) occur.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The union combines events by allowing either event to happen. The intersection focuses only on outcomes shared by both events.

Adding the probabilities of the two discs counts their overlap twice, so its probability must be subtracted once. De Morgan's identities relate these operations to complements: \((A\cup B)^c=A^c\cap B^c\) and \((A\cap B)^c=A^c\cup B^c\).

Union of sets collects outcomes belonging to at least one of the events. Intersection of sets retains only outcomes shared by both; treating those sets as events connects set operations with probabilistic statements.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(A\cup B\) occurs when at least one of the events occurs.
  • \(A\cap B\) occurs when both events occur.
  • Inclusion-exclusion connects the probability of a union to the probabilities of the two events and their intersection.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The event 'draw a heart or a king' is a union of two events.
  • The event 'draw a red king' is an intersection of two events.
  • The event that a customer buys online and uses a coupon is an intersection.

docs.title: Universality of the Uniform and CDF Realizability
Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(F\colon\mathbb{R}\to[0,1]\) be nondecreasing and right-continuous, with \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to-\infty}F(x)=0\) and \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to\infty}F(x)=1\). Let \(U\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) and define \(Q(u)=\inf\{x\colon F(x)\ge u\}\) for \(0<u<1\). Then \(X=Q(U)\) satisfies

\[ \mathbb{P}(X\le x)=F(x)\quad\text{for every }x. \]

Thus every function satisfying the CDF conditions is realizable as a distribution, and a uniform input can generate that distribution. The construction allows jumps and flat portions of \(F\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A uniform draw selects a probability level; the quantile function converts it into an outcome. This both proves that valid CDFs describe genuine random variables and provides inverse transform simulation.

The equally spaced probability levels map to quantiles \(x=Q(u)\). These quantiles are closer together where \(F\) is steep, illustrating how a uniform input produces the target distribution.

Press the button to draw uniform levels \(U\): pushed through \(Q\), they produce a sample whose histogram follows the target distribution, including the jumps of a discrete one.

The uniform distribution on \((0,1)\) assigns probability \(v\) to the interval \((0,v]\). The quantile construction turns \(\{Q(U)\le x\}\) into \(\{U\le F(x)\}\), so that probability becomes \(F(x)\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The monotonicity, right-continuity, and endpoint-limit conditions are necessary and sufficient for a function to be a CDF.
  • For \(0<u<1\), \(Q(u)\le x\) exactly when \(u\le F(x)\), so \(\mathbb{P}(Q(U)\le x)=\mathbb{P}(U\le F(x))=F(x)\).
  • Conversely, if \(X\) has a continuous CDF \(F\), then \(F(X)\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\); this direction is the probability integral transform. It fails when \(F\) has jumps, because \(F(X)\) then takes some values with positive probability.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For the step CDF \(F(x)=0\) when \(x<c\) and \(F(x)=1\) when \(x\ge c\), \(Q(u)=c\) and the construction gives \(X=c\) almost surely, that is, with probability \(1\).
  • For \(F(x)=0\) when \(x<0\) and \(F(x)=1-\mathrm{e}^{-2x}\) when \(x\ge0\), the construction gives \(X=-\log(1-U)/2\sim\operatorname{Exp}(2)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(X\) be a random variable with \(\mathbb{E}[X^2]<\infty\), and let \(\mu=\mathbb{E}X\). The variance of \(X\) is

\[ \operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb{E}[(X-\mu)^2]=\mathbb{E}[X^2]-\mu^2, \]

and the standard deviation is \(\sigma_X=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Variance measures how far the values of \(X\) typically lie from the mean \(\mu=\mathbb{E}X\): it is the probability-weighted average of the squared distance \((X-\mu)^2\). The standard deviation, its square root, measures the same spread in the original units of \(X\).

The figure shows two bell-shaped distributions with the same mean \(\mu\). The narrow curve has standard deviation \(1\) and the wide one standard deviation \(2\); the arrows run from \(\mu\) to \(\mu+\sigma\) for each curve. Doubling the standard deviation multiplies the variance by four, from \(1\) to \(4\), because variance is measured in squared units.

Spread the mass out and the variance grows; shift the whole distribution and it hardly changes. Darker bars contribute more to \(\mathbb{E}[(X-\mu)^2]\).

Each part of \(\mathbb{E}[(X-\mu)^2]\) has a role. Centring at \(\mu\) makes the measure ignore location: adding a constant to \(X\) moves \(\mu\) by the same amount, so \(\operatorname{Var}(a+X)=\operatorname{Var}(X)\). Squaring makes deviations on both sides count as positive and weights large deviations heavily. The second formula in the definition, \(\mathbb{E}[X^2]-\mu^2\), is usually quicker: for a Bernoulli variable \(X^2=X\), so \(\mathbb{E}[X^2]=p\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=p-p^2=p(1-p)\).

Scaling does not act linearly on variance: \(\operatorname{Var}(bX)=b^2\operatorname{Var}(X)\), while the standard deviation is multiplied by \(|b|\), so \(-X\) has the same variance as \(X\). For independent variables the variances add, as on the page on sums of independent random variables, but the standard deviations do not. Dividing \(X-\mu\) by the standard deviation gives a variable with mean \(0\) and variance \(1\), which returns later as standardization.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\operatorname{Var}(a+bX)=b^2\operatorname{Var}(X)\).
  • \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=0\) if and only if \(X=\mathbb{E}X\) almost surely, that is, \(\mathbb{P}(X=\mathbb{E}X)=1\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\operatorname{Bern}(0.3)\), the variance is \(0.3(0.7)=0.21\).
  • If \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=4\), then \(\operatorname{Var}(5-3X)=36\) and its standard deviation is \(6\).

docs.title: Accumulation Point in a Metric Space
Definition
docs.text:
Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space and let \(E\subseteq X\). A point \(x\in X\) is called an accumulation point (or cluster point, limit point) of \(E\) if every metric ball around \(x\) contains a point of \(E\) different from \(x\), i.e.,

\[ \forall \varepsilon>0,\quad \left(B_d(x,\varepsilon)\setminus\{x\}\right)\cap E\neq\varnothing. \]

Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space and let \((x_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\) be a sequence in \(X\). A point \(x\in X\) is called an accumulation point (or cluster point) of \((x_n)\) if, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist infinitely many \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) such that \(x_n\in B_d(x,\varepsilon)\), i.e., for every \(\varepsilon>0\),

\[ \left|\{n\in\mathbb{N}\colon x_n\in B_d(x,\varepsilon)\}\right|=\infty. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An accumulation point of a set is a location you can approach arbitrarily closely using other points from the set. For a sequence, it is a point to which the sequence returns again and again: however small the ball around it, infinitely many terms lie in that ball.

Both definitions ask something of every \(\varepsilon>0\), so only small balls matter. For a set, the words "different from \(x\)" rule out counting \(x\) itself, and \(x\) need not belong to \(E\): for \(E=(0,1)\) in \(\mathbb{R}\), every point of \([0,1]\) is an accumulation point, including \(0\) and \(1\). For a sequence, indices \(n\) are counted, not distinct values. The constant sequence \(x_n=c\) has \(c\) as an accumulation point, although the set \(\{c\}\) of its terms has none.

The accumulation points of a sequence in a metric space are exactly the limits of its convergent subsequences, which is the form in which they appear in the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem. For a bounded real sequence, the limit superior and limit inferior are its largest and smallest accumulation points. The accumulation points of a set are what a closed set must contain: a set is closed if and only if it contains all its accumulation points, and its closure is the set together with them.

A common slip is to treat a single accumulation point as a limit. The sequence \(0,1,0,2,0,3,\dots\) has \(0\) as its only accumulation point, yet it does not converge, because it is unbounded.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • A limit point can be characterized as an adherent point that is not an isolated point (a point \(x\in E\) such that some ball \(B_d(x,\varepsilon)\) meets \(E\) only in \(x\)).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(E=\{1,\,1/2,\,1/3,\,\dots\}\), the only accumulation point is \(0\). Each point \(1/n\) is isolated.
  • The sequence \(a_n=(-1)^n\) has accumulation points 1 and -1. It does not converge.

  • Consider the sequence \((a_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) that is defined by \(a_n=\sin n\). We can show that any number \(A\in[-1,1]\) is an accumulation point of this sequence.

    Among the first \(50\) terms, four lie in the band \([0.4,0.6]\) (red); infinitely many terms fall in every band around \(0.5\), so \(0.5\) is an accumulation point.

docs.title: Adherent Point and Closure of a Set
Definition
docs.text: Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space and let \(E\) be a subset of \(X\). A point \(x_0\) in \(X\) is termed an adherent point of \(E\) if, for every \(\varepsilon > 0\), the ball \(B(x_0, \varepsilon)\) intersects \(E\) nonemptily. The set of all adherent points of \(E\) constitutes the closure of \(E\), denoted as \(\overline{E}\) or \(\operatorname{cl}E\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An adherent point of a set is one that you can get arbitrarily close to from inside the set: every ball around it, however small, contains a point of the set. The closure is the original set together with all such points: everything you can touch or approach.

In the figure, the point inside \(E\) is adherent because it belongs to \(E\) itself; every point of \(E\) is adherent. The point \(x_0\) on the edge is adherent as well: each ball around it contains points outside \(E\) but still meets \(E\). The grey point outside is not adherent, since one ball around it misses \(E\); it is an exterior point.

An adherent point has every ball meeting \(E\): the points of the closed disc and the isolated point \(\boldsymbol p\). Switching the metric does not change the answer.

Adherent points can be described with sequences: \(x_0\in\overline{E}\) if and only if \(x_0\) is the limit of a sequence in \(E\). If \(x_0\) is adherent, pick \(x_n\in B(x_0,\tfrac{1}{n})\cap E\), so that \(x_n\to x_0\); conversely, if \(x_n\to x_0\) with all \(x_n\in E\), every ball around \(x_0\) contains some \(x_n\).

The closure is the smallest closed set containing \(E\), and the points it adds are exactly the boundary points not already in \(E\). In Probability Theory, the support of a random variable with one of the usual densities is the closure of the region where the density is positive.

A common slip is to think that an adherent point must lie on the edge of \(E\) or outside it. Every point of \(E\) is adherent, including an isolated point such as \(\boldsymbol{p}\) in the interactive example, so \(E\subseteq\overline{E}\) always.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• We have \(\overline{E} = \operatorname{int}E \cup \partial E = E \cup \partial E = X \setminus \operatorname{ext}E.\)
  • A set is closed if and only if it contains all its adherent points.
  • The closure of a set \(E\) is the intersection of all closed sets which contain \(E\), or equivalently, the smallest closed set that contains \(E\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The closure of \((0,1)\) in \(\mathbb{R}\) is \([0,1]\). The endpoints \(0\) and \(1\) are adherent points even though they are not in the open interval.
  • If \(E = \{1/n \colon n \in \mathbb{N}^+\}\) in \(\mathbb{R}\), the closure is \(E \cup \{0\}\). Zero is an adherent point approached by the sequence.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(n,\,k \in\mathbb{N}^+\). A function \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon \mathbb{R}^n\to \mathbb{R}^k\) is an affine map (or affine transformation) if there are a \(k\times n\) real matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}\) and a vector \(\boldsymbol{b}\in\mathbb{R}^k\) such that

\[ \boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x})=\boldsymbol{A} \boldsymbol{x}+ \boldsymbol{b}\qquad\text{for all }\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n. \]

A real-valued affine map \(f\colon \mathbb{R}^n\to \mathbb{R}\) (\(k=1\)) is an affine function:

\[ f(x_1,\,x_2,\,\dots,\,x_n) =a_1x_1+a_2x_2+\cdots+a_nx_n+b. \]

An affine map is a linear map exactly when \(\boldsymbol{b}=\boldsymbol{0}\), that is, when \(\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{0})=\boldsymbol{0}\).

Terminology

The Math III lecture notes, like much of economics and calculus, call an affine function a linear function and reserve linear transformation for the case \(\boldsymbol{b}=\boldsymbol{0}\). In linear algebra linear always means \(\boldsymbol{b}=\boldsymbol{0}\), so this wiki says affine for the general case.

As a Function between Spaces, the map assigns one output vector to each input vector. The Vector Space operations make the expression \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{b}\) meaningful: first apply the matrix, then add the translation vector.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An affine map is a linear map followed by a shift: if one argument is increased by \(c\) units, the value changes by \(c\) times a fixed vector, wherever the starting point is.

The blue linear map \(f(x)=2x\) passes through the origin. The red affine map \(g(x)=f(x)+1\) is shifted upwards by \(1\), so \(g(0)=1\) rather than \(0\). Both lines have slope \(2\): the matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}\), here the number \(2\), sets the slope, and \(\boldsymbol{b}\) only moves the graph.

Both parts can be read off from \(\boldsymbol{f}\): \(\boldsymbol{b}=\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{0})\), and \(\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x})-\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{y})=\boldsymbol{A}(\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{y})\), so a change in the output depends only on the change in the input. Affine maps keep affine combinations: \(\boldsymbol{f}(\lambda\boldsymbol{x}+(1-\lambda)\boldsymbol{y})=\lambda\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x})+(1-\lambda)\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{y})\) for every real \(\lambda\). Hence they map lines to lines or points, and midpoints to midpoints. The image of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is the range of \(\boldsymbol{x}\mapsto\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\), shifted by \(\boldsymbol{b}\).

A common slip comes from the terminology in the note. \(g(x)=2x+1\) is called a linear function in calculus, but it is not a linear map: \(g(1+1)=5\), while \(g(1)+g(1)=6\).

This idea returns later: a differentiable function of several variables is one that is approximated near a point by an affine map, just as a differentiable function of one variable is approximated by its tangent line.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The graph \(\{(\boldsymbol{x},f(\boldsymbol{x}))\colon\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\}\) of an affine function on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is an affine hyperplane of \(\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\); it passes through the origin exactly when \(b=0\text{.}\)
  • The level sets \(\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon f(\boldsymbol{x})=c\}\) of a non-constant affine function are parallel affine hyperplanes of \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
  • A composition of affine maps is affine.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(f(x,y) = x + 2y - 1\) is affine but not linear, since \(f(0,0)=-1\); \(x+2y\) is both.
  • \(g(x,y) = x + xy\) and \(h(x,y) = 2^x + \sin y\) are not affine.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Consider two functions \(f\colon \mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) and \(g\colon \mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\text{.}\) Let \(a\in[-\infty,+\infty]\).

  • We say that \(f(x)\) is big-\(O\) of \(g(x)\) as \(x\) tends to \(a\text{,}\) and write \(f(x)=O(g(x))\) as \(x\to a\text{,}\) if there is a constant \(M>0\) such that \(|f(x)|\le M\,|g(x)|\) for all \(x\) near \(a\text{:}\) for \(0<|x-a|<\delta\) (a punctured neighbourhood of \(a\)) when \(a\) is finite, for \(x>N\) when \(a=+\infty\text{,}\) and for \(x<-N\) when \(a=-\infty\text{,}\) for some \(\delta>0\) or \(N\text{.}\)
  • Assume that \(g(x)\neq0\) for all \(x\) near \(a\) in the same sense. We say that \(f(x)\) is little-\(o\) of \(g(x)\) as \(x\) tends to \(a\text{,}\) and write \(f(x)=o(g(x))\) as \(x\to a\text{,}\) if \(\displaystyle \lim\limits_{x\to a}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}=0\text{.}\)

The constant \(M\) gives an Upper Bound on the relative size of \(f\) near \(a\). For little-\(o\), use a Limit at a Point when \(a\) is finite and a Limit at Infinity when \(a=\pm\infty\) to test whether \(f/g\) tends to zero.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Big-\(O\) and little-\(o\) compare the sizes of two functions near a point \(a\) while ignoring constant factors. \(f(x)=O(g(x))\) means that near \(a\) the size of \(f\) is at most a constant multiple of the size of \(g\); \(f(x)=o(g(x))\) means that \(f\) is negligible compared with \(g\) near \(a\). When \(g\to0\), this reads: \(f\) goes to zero at least as fast as \(g\) (big-\(O\)), or faster than \(g\) (little-\(o\)).

The constant \(M\) in big-\(O\) is fixed but may be large, so big-\(O\) only records an order of magnitude: \(3x^2=O(x^2)\) and \(x^2=O(3x^2)\) as \(x\to0\). Little-\(o\) allows no fixed constant: \(f/g\to0\) means that for every \(\varepsilon>0\) the bound \(|f(x)|\le\varepsilon\,|g(x)|\) holds for all \(x\) near \(a\). Both notations depend on where \(x\) goes: \(x^2=o(x)\) as \(x\to0\), but \(x=o(x^2)\) as \(x\to+\infty\).

The main use is the remainder in Taylor's theorem: the error of the \(k\)-th order Taylor expansion is \(o((x-a)^k)\) as \(x\to a\), small even compared with the last term kept. Comparing leading terms in this way also gives limits of quotients, alongside L'Hôpital's rule.

A common slip is to read the equals sign in \(f(x)=O(g(x))\) as an equation. It is one-way shorthand for "\(f\) is bounded by a constant multiple of \(|g|\) near \(a\)". From \(x^2=O(x)\) and \(x^3=O(x)\) as \(x\to0\) one cannot conclude \(x^2=x^3\), and the reversed form \(O(g(x))=f(x)\) is not used.

The notation returns in Life Insurance, in the force of mortality, for the probability of dying within a very short time.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The little-\(o\) notation makes a stronger assertion than the big-\(O\) notation: every function that is little-\(o\) of \(g\) is also big-\(O\) of \(g\text{,}\) but not all functions that are big-\(O\) of \(g\) are little-\(o\) of \(g\text{.}\)
  • If \(f(x)\) and \(g(x)\) are asymptotically equivalent as \(x\) tends to \(a\text{,}\) i.e., \(f(x)\sim g(x)\) as \(x\to a\text{,}\) then we have \(f(x)=O(g(x))\) and \(g(x)=O(f(x))\text{,}\) as \(x\to a\text{.}\)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• As \(x\to 0\), \(x^2\) is both \(O(x)\) and \(o(x)\) since \(\displaystyle \lim\limits_{x \to 0}\frac{x^2}{x} = 0\).
  • As \(x\to 0\), \(\sin (x^2)\) is \(O(x^2)\) but not \(o(x^2)\) since \(\displaystyle \lim\limits_{x \to 0}\frac{\sin(x^2)}{x^2} = 1\).

  • In the following graph, we have \(g(x)=o(f(x))\) and \(g(x)=o(h(x))\) as \(x\to 0\):

    Near \(0\) the parabola \(g\) is much flatter than \(f\) and \(h\): \(g(x)/f(x)\to0\) and \(g(x)/h(x)\to0\) as \(x\to0\).

Zoom in towards \(0\): \(f=O(g)\) when some \(M\) keeps \(|f|\le M|g|\) near \(0\); \(f=o(g)\) when the ratio \(f/g\) (right) tends to \(0\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Each bounded sequence in the Euclidean space \((\mathbb{R}^n,d_2)\) has a convergent subsequence.

Equivalently, a subset \(E\) of the Euclidean space is sequentially compact if and only if it is both closed and bounded.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Even if a sequence wanders around without settling down, as long as it stays within a bounded region you can always pick out a subsequence that homes in on some point.

All terms lie in the band \(|a_n|\le M\), yet the sequence does not converge: its terms keep jumping between the two halves of the band. The even-indexed terms, in red, form a subsequence that converges to \(1\), while the odd-indexed terms stay below the axis. The theorem promises at least one such subsequence; it does not say where its limit lies.

In \(\mathbb{R}\) the reason is repeated halving. One of the two halves of \([-M,M]\) contains terms \(a_n\) for infinitely many \(n\), one half of that half again, and so on; the nested intervals shrink to a point, and one term from each interval gives a subsequence converging to it. In \(\mathbb{R}^n\) the argument runs coordinate by coordinate.

Both parts of the setting are needed. Without boundedness the conclusion fails: \(x_n=n\) has no convergent subsequence. Without the Euclidean metric it can fail too: under the discrete metric every set is bounded, but a sequence of distinct points has no convergent subsequence.

The limits of convergent subsequences are the accumulation points of the sequence, so a bounded sequence in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) has at least one accumulation point. In the second form, closedness keeps the limit inside \(E\), so closed and bounded sets are sequentially compact; with the equivalence of compactness and sequential compactness in metric spaces, this gives the Heine-Borel theorem.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The limit of a convergent subsequence is an accumulation point of the original sequence.
  • In \(\mathbb{R}^n\), every Cauchy sequence is bounded, so by Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem it has a convergent subsequence. A Cauchy sequence with a convergent subsequence must itself converge. This gives another proof that \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is complete.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The sequence \(x_n = (-1)^n\) in \(\mathbb{R}\) is bounded between \(-1\) and \(1\). It does not converge, but it has two convergent subsequences: the even terms \(x_{2n}=1\) converge to \(1\), and the odd terms \(x_{2n-1}=-1\) converge to \(-1\).
  • The sequence \(x_n = 1/n\) in \(\mathbb{R}\) is bounded in \([0,1]\). It already converges to \(0\), so every subsequence also converges to \(0\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a metric space \((X,d)\text{,}\) and a subset \(E \subseteq X\text{,}\) a point \(x_0\) is a boundary point of \(E\) if it's neither an interior nor an exterior point of \(E\text{.}\) We denote the set of boundary points of \(E\) as \(\partial E\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The boundary is the dividing line between inside and outside: it consists of the points that \(E\) neither surrounds nor avoids. Relative to \(E\), every point of \(X\) is of exactly one of three kinds: interior, exterior or boundary.

Each ball around the point \(x_0\) in the figure, however small, contains points of \(E\) and points of \(X\setminus E\), so no ball fits inside \(E\) and no ball avoids \(E\). The boundary consists of points that are neither interior nor exterior: \(\partial E=\overline{E}\setminus\operatorname{int}(E)\), the adherent points that are not interior.

On the unit circle, and at the isolated point \(\boldsymbol p\), every ball meets both \(E\) and its complement, however small \(\varepsilon\) is.

The condition is symmetric in \(E\) and its complement, so \(\partial E=\partial(X\setminus E)\). A boundary point may belong to \(E\) or not, and this is what separates the kinds of sets: \(E\) is closed exactly when it contains its whole boundary, and open exactly when it contains none of it.

Boundary points matter in optimization. A global extremum on a domain can lie at an interior point, where a derivative test applies, or at a boundary point, which has to be checked separately.

A common slip is to picture the boundary as a thin curve around the set. It depends on the set and on the metric: in the plane, an isolated point of \(E\) such as \(\boldsymbol{p}\) in the interactive example is a boundary point, while with the discrete metric every set has empty boundary, because the ball of radius \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) around any point contains only that point.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A boundary point \(x_0\) of \(E\) may or may not be in \(E\text{.}\)
  • For a boundary point \(x_0\) of \(E\text{,}\) any balls centred at \(x_0\) will contain points both inside and outside \(E\text{.}\)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The boundary of \((0,1)\) is \(\{0,1\}\). Every neighbourhood around \(0\) contains points in \((0,1)\) and points not in \((0,1)\).
  • The boundary of \(\mathbb{Q}\) in \(\mathbb{R}\) is all of \(\mathbb{R}\).

docs.title: Bounded Set in a Metric Space
Definition
docs.text: Given a metric space \((X,d_{X})\text{,}\) a set \(E\subseteq X\) is termed bounded if there exists \(M>0\) such that the ball \(B_{(X,d_{X})} (x,M)\) contains \(E\text{.}\) Here, \(x\) can be any point in \(X\) (usually chosen to be the origin or a particular point in \(E\)).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A bounded set is one that fits entirely inside some large enough ball, so that no two of its points are arbitrarily far apart. It extends the notion of a bounded set of real numbers to any metric space.

The whole set \(E\) lies inside the dashed ball of radius \(M\) around \(x_0\), so \(E\subseteq B(x_0,M)\). The ball is only a witness: it need not be small or centred in \(E\), and any larger radius works as well.

The choice of centre does not matter. If \(E\subseteq B(x,M)\) and \(y\) is any other point, then for every \(z\in E\) the triangle inequality gives \(d(z,y)\le d(z,x)+d(x,y)<M+d(x,y)\), so \(E\subseteq B(y,M+d(x,y))\); only the radius changes. Equivalently, as in the Key Results, a nonempty set is bounded if and only if its diameter \(\sup_{x,y\in E}d(x,y)\) is finite.

In \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with the Euclidean distance, a set is bounded if and only if all coordinates of its points are bounded. Boundedness is one of the two conditions in the Heine-Borel theorem, and a bounded sequence in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) has a convergent subsequence by the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem.

Boundedness depends on the metric, not only on the set. Under the discrete metric every set, including \(\mathbb{R}\) itself, is bounded, because all distances are at most \(1\). For this reason "closed and bounded" implies compact in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) but not in a general metric space.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A nonempty set is bounded if and only if \(\displaystyle \sup_{x,y\in E} d_{X}(x,y)\) is finite.
  • Any subset of a bounded set is bounded.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A unit sphere \(\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb{R}^3\colon x^2+y^2+z^2=1\}\) is bounded.
  • A parabola curve \(\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon y=x^2\}\) is unbounded.

docs.title: Cauchy Sequence in a Metric Space
Definition
docs.text: A sequence of points \((x_i)_{i=1}^\infty\) in a metric space \((X,d)\) is called a Cauchy sequence if, for every \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists an integer \(N\geq 1\) such that the distance \(d(x_j,x_k)<\varepsilon\) for all \(j, k \geq N\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A Cauchy sequence is one whose terms eventually all lie close to each other. It is the same idea as a Cauchy sequence of real numbers, but with the absolute value replaced by a general metric. Unlike the definition of convergence, it never mentions a limit, so it can be checked using the terms alone.

From some index \(N\) on, all terms in the figure lie inside the small dashed circle, close enough that \(d(x_j,x_k)<\varepsilon\) for all \(j,k\ge N\). The terms get closer to each other, but a Cauchy sequence need not converge to a point of \(X\) unless the space is complete.

Raise \(N\) until all tail points lie within \(\varepsilon\) of each other, without using the limit at all.

The condition concerns all pairs \(j,k\ge N\), not only consecutive terms. The partial sums \(x_k=1+\tfrac{1}{2}+\cdots+\tfrac{1}{k}\) of the harmonic series have \(|x_{k+1}-x_k|=\tfrac{1}{k+1}\to0\), yet \(x_{2k}-x_k\ge k\cdot\tfrac{1}{2k}=\tfrac{1}{2}\) for every \(k\), so they are not Cauchy.

Every convergent sequence is Cauchy, by the triangle inequality \(d(x_j,x_k)\le d(x_j,x)+d(x,x_k)\). The converse holds exactly in complete metric spaces, such as \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with any \(p\)-metric, and fails in \(\mathbb{Q}\), as the Examples show. Being Cauchy depends on the metric, but strongly equivalent metrics have the same Cauchy sequences, because \(d_q(x_j,x_k)\le b\,d_p(x_j,x_k)\) and \(d_p(x_j,x_k)\le\tfrac{1}{a}\,d_q(x_j,x_k)\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • While all convergent sequences are Cauchy, not every Cauchy sequence converges because a sequence can cluster together (Cauchy property) around a limit that does not exist within the current space.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Take the rational numbers \(\mathbb{Q}\) with the usual metric \(d(x,y)=|x-y|\). The sequence \(a_n=\left(1+\dfrac{1}{n}\right)^n\) consists of rational numbers and converges in \(\mathbb{R}\) to \(\mathrm{e}\), so it is Cauchy. Since \(\mathrm{e}\) is irrational, it does not converge to any point of \(\mathbb{Q}\): the space \((\mathbb{Q},d)\) is not complete.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a metric space \((X,d)\), a point \(x_0\) in \(X\), and \(r > 0\), the closed metric ball \(\overline{B}_{(X,d)}(x_0,r)\) in \(X\), centred at \(x_0\) with radius \(r\) in metric \(d\), is defined as the following set:

\[ \overline{B}_{(X,d)}(x_0,r) = \{x \in X \colon d(x, x_0) \leq r\}. \]

The ball is a subset of the ambient space \(X\): its members are selected by the distance condition, not by adding new points to \(X\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A closed metric ball is the set of all points whose distance from the centre \(x_0\) is at most the radius \(r\): the open ball together with the points at distance exactly \(r\). In \(\mathbb{R}\) with \(d(x,y)=|x-y|\) it is the closed interval \([x_0-r,x_0+r]\).

The disc is drawn with a solid rim. The green point on the rim has \(d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}_0)=r\) and is included, because the definition uses \(\le\). In the Euclidean plane the rim is the boundary of the disc, and containing it is what makes the closed ball a closed set.

The closed ball also contains its sphere \(\{d(\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol x_0)=r\}\). Drag \(\boldsymbol x\) onto the boundary to see the difference.

Closedness holds in every metric space, by the triangle inequality. If \(d(y,x_0)>r\), put \(s=d(y,x_0)-r>0\); every \(z\) with \(d(z,y)<s\) has \(d(z,x_0)\ge d(y,x_0)-d(y,z)>r\). So the complement of \(\overline{B}(x_0,r)\) is open.

A common slip comes from the notation: \(\overline{B}(x_0,r)\) looks like the closure of \(B(x_0,r)\). The closure is always contained in the closed ball, and in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with a \(p\)-metric the two coincide, but in general they differ. With the discrete metric, \(B(x,1)=\{x\}\) is already closed, while \(\overline{B}(x,1)\) is the whole space.

This idea returns later: closed balls in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) are standard examples of compact sets, on which a continuous real-valued function attains a largest and a smallest value.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The closed metric ball is a closed set.
  • In a normed vector space, in particular in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with any \(p\)-metric, the closed metric ball is the closure of the open metric ball with the same centre and radius. This can fail for a metric that is merely topologically equivalent to these, such as \(\min(|x-y|,1)\) on \(\mathbb{R}\) with radius \(1\).
  • In a general metric space, the closed ball \(\overline{B}_{(X,d)}(x_0,\varepsilon)\) need not equal \(\overline{B_{(X,d)}(x_0,\varepsilon)}\), the closure of the open ball.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • In \(\mathbb{R}^2\) with the usual distance, \(\overline{B}((0,0),1)\) is the closed disc of radius \(1\) centred at the origin. Points with \(x^2 + y^2 \leq 1\) are elements of this ball.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Consider a space \(X\) in which open sets are defined. A subset \(E\) of \(X\) is called compact if every open cover of \(E\) has a finite subcover.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Compactness is a finiteness property for sets that may contain infinitely many points: however a compact set is covered by open sets, finitely many of them already do the job. Arguments that are easy for finitely many objects, such as taking the largest of finitely many numbers or the smallest of finitely many radii, can therefore be carried over to a compact set.

The figure shows the two ways compactness fails in \(\mathbb{R}^2\). The open unit disc is covered by the open discs of radius \(1-\tfrac{1}{n}\) around the centre, \(n\ge2\), but finitely many of them only cover the largest one used, so points near the rim are always missed. The strip is covered by the open discs of radius \(n\) around the origin, and finitely many of them stay inside one bounded disc. In \(\mathbb{R}^n\) these are the only two obstructions: by the Heine-Borel theorem a set is compact if and only if it is closed and bounded.

Compactness is what makes optimal points exist. By the extreme value theorem on compact sets, a continuous function on a nonempty compact set attains its maximum and minimum, which is why later optimization problems check that the feasible set is compact before looking for a global maximum or minimum. In metric spaces, compactness can equivalently be checked with sequences: a set is compact exactly when it is sequentially compact.

Two slips are common. The definition asks for a finite subcover of every open cover; one finite cover is not enough, since the whole space alone covers any set. And "closed and bounded" characterizes compactness in \(\mathbb{R}^n\), but is not the definition: in \(\mathbb{R}\) with the discrete metric, the whole space is closed and bounded, yet the open balls \(B(x,\tfrac{1}{2})=\{x\}\) cover it without a finite subcover.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The set \(E\subseteq \mathbb{R} ^n\) is compact if and only if it is both closed and bounded.
  • Let \(E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\text{,}\) \(\boldsymbol{f} \colon E \to \mathbb{R}^k\) be a function, and \(X \subseteq E\) be a compact set. If \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is continuous on \(X\text{,}\) then the image \(\boldsymbol{f}(X)\) is also compact. This result is known as continuity preserves compactness.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The closed unit ball \(\{\boldsymbol{x}\in \mathbb{R}^n\colon \|\boldsymbol{x}\|\leq 1\}\) is compact.
  • Any finite set in any metric space is compact. You can always pick one open set for each point; finitely many suffice.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A metric space \((X, d)\) is termed complete if each Cauchy sequence contained within converges in \((X, d)\). When a complete normed vector space is encountered, it's also referred to as a Banach space.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A complete metric space is one with no "missing points": every Cauchy sequence, a sequence that looks as if it should converge, actually has a limit inside the space.

The displayed Cauchy sequence converges to \(\sqrt{2}\) in \(\mathbb{R}\). It has no limit in \(\mathbb{Q}\) because \(\sqrt{2}\notin\mathbb{Q}\), illustrating the incompleteness of the rational numbers.

Completeness lets one prove that a limit exists without knowing it in advance: it is enough to show that the sequence is Cauchy. For \(\mathbb{R}\) it comes from the supremum property, which \(\mathbb{Q}\) lacks: \(\{q\in\mathbb{Q}\colon q^2<2\}\) is bounded above but has no least upper bound in \(\mathbb{Q}\).

Completeness depends on the metric, not only on which sequences converge. On \((-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2})\), the metric \(d_{\tan}(x,y)=|\tan x-\tan y|\) has the same convergent sequences as \(|x-y|\), because \(\tan\) and its inverse are continuous. Yet \(d_{\tan}\) is complete, since \(\tan\) matches it with \(\mathbb{R}\) and its usual distance, while \(|x-y|\) is not: \(x_k=\tfrac{\pi}{2}-\tfrac{1}{k}\) is Cauchy for \(|x-y|\) without a limit in the interval.

Every finite-dimensional real normed space, in particular \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with any norm, is complete, so the term Banach space matters mainly for spaces of functions: the bounded functions on a set, with the uniform norm, form a Banach space.

A common slip is to link completeness with boundedness. \(\mathbb{R}\) is unbounded and complete, while the bounded interval \((0,1)\) is not complete.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • In any metric space every convergent sequence is a Cauchy sequence; in a complete metric space the converse also holds, so a sequence converges if and only if it is Cauchy.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The Euclidean space \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is a complete normed vector space.
  • The open interval \((0,1)\) with the usual metric \(d(x,y)=|x-y|\) is not complete: \((1/n)_{n\ge2}\) is a Cauchy sequence whose limit \(0\) does not belong to \((0,1)\text{.}\)
  • The \(n\)-dimensional real coordinate space equipped with the discrete metric is complete: a Cauchy sequence is eventually constant, because \(d(\boldsymbol{x}_j,\boldsymbol{x}_k)<\tfrac{1}{2}\) forces \(\boldsymbol{x}_j=\boldsymbol{x}_k\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Consider a space \(X\) in which openness is defined. A subset \(E \subseteq X\) is called disconnected if it has an open cover \(\{V,W\}\) such that \(E \subseteq V\cup W\) and the intersections \(E\cap V\) and \(E\cap W\) are disjoint and nonempty. Thus \(E\cap V\cap W=\varnothing\); the ambient sets \(V\) and \(W\) may overlap outside \(E\). If \(E\) is nonempty and not disconnected, it is connected.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A set is disconnected if it can be split into two nonempty pieces, each cut out by an open set, with no point of the set in both. A set is connected if it comes in one piece, so that no such split exists.

On the left, the dark set \(E\) lies in the union of the open sets \(V\) and \(W\). It meets both, and no point of \(E\) lies in both, so it is disconnected. The right-hand set cannot be split in this way: whenever two open sets cover it and each meets it, they share a point of the set, so it is connected.

A common slip is to read "split" as "the pieces do not touch". The set \((0,1)\cup(1,2)\) is disconnected, with \(V=(0,1)\) and \(W=(1,2)\), although its two pieces come arbitrarily close at \(1\). On the other hand, \((0,1]\) and \((1,2)\) are disjoint pieces of the connected set \((0,2)\): every open set containing \(1\) also contains points of \((1,2)\), so no open set cuts out \((0,1]\).

In \(\mathbb{R}\) the connected sets are exactly the intervals, which is why the intermediate value theorem of Math I is stated on intervals; Math III extends it to the intermediate value theorem on connected sets. Connectedness is often proved through path-connectedness, which implies it and is easier to check.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The only type of connected subsets of \(\mathbb{R}\) is interval.
  • Consider metric spaces \((X,d_{X})\) and \((Y,d_{Y})\text{.}\) Let \(f\colon X\to Y\) be a continuous function, and let \(E\) be a connected subset of \(X\text{.}\) Then \(f(E)\) is a connected subset of \(Y\text{.}\) This result is known as continuity preserves connectedness.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Any singleton set is connected.
  • \(\mathbb{Q}\) is a disconnected subset of \(\mathbb{R}\).
  • In a discrete metric space, any set with at least two points is disconnected because each singleton is open.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Consider two metric spaces \((X,d_{X})\) and \((Y,d_{Y})\text{,}\) and a function \(f\colon E\to Y\) where \(E\subseteq X\text{.}\) Let \(x_0\in X\text{.}\) Assume there exists an \(r>0\) such that \(B_{(X,d_{X})}(x_0,r)\subseteq E\text{.}\) We say that \(f\) is continuous at \(x=x_0\) if, for any \(\varepsilon > 0\text{,}\) there exists a \(0<\delta \leq r\) such that whenever \(d_{X}(x,x_0)<\delta\text{,}\) we have \(d_{Y}(f(x),f(x_0))<\varepsilon\text{.}\)

We say that \(f\) is continuous on \(E\) (or simply continuous) if it is continuous at every point of \(E\text{.}\) At a point \(x_0\in E\) that has no such ball inside \(E\) (a boundary point of \(E\)), the same condition is required only for \(x\in E\text{.}\)

The condition says that the intersection of the domain with a sufficiently small open metric ball around \(x_0\) is mapped into the \(\varepsilon\)-ball around \(f(x_0)\). With the usual real distance \(|x-y|\), this is the familiar definition of continuity.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A function is continuous at a point if you can make the outputs as close as you want to the value at that point by taking inputs sufficiently close to it. In metric spaces, "close" is measured by the metrics: \(d_{X}\) for the inputs and \(d_{Y}\) for the outputs.

On the left is the open ball \(B(x_0,\delta)\) in \(X\); on the right, its image \(f(B(x_0,\delta))\) lies entirely inside the ball \(B(f(x_0),\varepsilon)\) in \(Y\). This inclusion is the definition restated: every \(x\) with \(d_{X}(x,x_0)<\delta\) satisfies \(d_{Y}(f(x),f(x_0))<\varepsilon\). The order of choice matters. The tolerance \(\varepsilon\) on the outputs comes first, and \(\delta\) is chosen in response; a smaller \(\varepsilon\) usually forces a smaller \(\delta\).

The \(\delta\) may depend on both \(\varepsilon\) and the point \(x_0\). If one \(\delta\) works at all points at once, \(f\) has the stronger property of uniform continuity, known from real functions. The bound \(\delta\le r\) only keeps the \(\delta\)-ball inside the domain \(E\), so that \(f(x)\) is defined there.

With \(X=Y=\mathbb{R}\) and the distance \(|x-y|\), this is the \(\varepsilon\)-\(\delta\) continuity of Math I. Continuity depends on the metrics: if \(X\) carries the discrete metric, every function on \(X\) is continuous, because \(B(x_0,\tfrac{1}{2})=\{x_0\}\). Descriptions by sequences and by preimages of open sets are given in the equivalent formulation of continuity.

A common slip is to fix \(\delta\) first and then look for an \(\varepsilon\). That reversed condition holds for every bounded function, including the discontinuous signum function at \(0\), where \(\varepsilon=2\) works for every \(\delta\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(f(x)\) tends to two different values as \(x\) approaches \(x_0\) in two different ways (for example along two different lines, or along two sequences converging to \(x_0\)), then the limit of the function at that point does not exist, so the function is not continuous there. More generally, if for some sequence \(x_k\to x_0\) the values \(f(x_k)\) do not tend to \(f(x_0)\text{,}\) then \(f\) is not continuous at \(x_0\text{.}\)
  • A vector-valued function into \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with its usual Euclidean metric is continuous if and only if each real component function is continuous.
  • Most properties of real-valued functions of one real variable are preserved under continuity. In particular, continuity is preserved under addition, subtraction, multiplication, division (where the denominator is nonzero), as well as taking the maximum, minimum, and composition of functions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • \(f(x,y)=x^2+y^2\) on \(\mathbb{R}^2\). At \((0,0)\), if you want \(f\) within \(\varepsilon\) of \(0\), choose \(\delta=\sqrt{\varepsilon}\). Then \(\sqrt{x^2+y^2}<\delta\) gives \(x^2+y^2<\varepsilon\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Given a metric space \((X, d)\), a sequence \((x_{i})_{i=1}^\infty\) and a point \(x\) in \(X\), the sequence is said to converge to \(x\) under metric \(d\) if \(\displaystyle \lim_{i\to\infty}d(x_i, x) = 0\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A sequence converges to \(x\) when its distance to \(x\) tends to \(0\). This is just like convergent sequences of real numbers, but with a general notion of distance: the definition reduces convergence in any metric space to the convergence of the real numbers \(d(x_i,x)\) to \(0\).

Written out, the definition says that for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there is an \(N\) with \(d(x_i,x)<\varepsilon\) for all \(i\ge N\). In the figure the terms spiral in towards \(x\); the shaded disc of points within distance \(\varepsilon\) of \(x\) misses some early terms such as \(x_1\) and \(x_2\), but holds every term from some index \(N\) on. A smaller \(\varepsilon\) may require a larger \(N\).

For each \(\varepsilon\) there is an \(N\) after which every \(\boldsymbol x_i\) lies in the \(\varepsilon\)-ball around the limit. Change the metric: \(N\) changes, the limit does not.

A limit, when it exists, is unique: if \(x_i\to x\) and \(x_i\to y\), the triangle inequality gives \(d(x,y)\le d(x,x_i)+d(x_i,y)\to0\), so \(x=y\). Whether a sequence converges depends on the metric. Under the discrete metric, \(d_{\mathrm{disc}}(x_i,x)<1\) forces \(x_i=x\), so only sequences that are eventually constant converge; \(x_i=1/i\) converges to \(0\) for \(|x-y|\) but not for \(d_{\mathrm{disc}}\). Strongly equivalent metrics, such as the Euclidean and taxicab metrics in the Examples, have the same convergent sequences.

A common slip is to confuse converging with terms getting close to each other. The latter is the Cauchy property, and in a space with missing points, such as \(\mathbb{Q}\), a Cauchy sequence need not converge.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • A convergent sequence in a metric space must be a Cauchy sequence.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The sequence \((\boldsymbol{x}_{i})_{i=1}^\infty\) where \(\boldsymbol{x}_i = (1/i, 1/i)\) in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) converges to \((0,0)\) under the Euclidean metric \(d_2\).
  • The sequence \((\boldsymbol{x}_{i})_{i=1}^\infty\) where \(\boldsymbol{x}_i = (1/i, 1/i)\) in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) also converges to \((0,0)\) under the taxicab metric \(d_1\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Consider a power series \(\displaystyle f(x)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n (x-a)^n\) with a radius of convergence \(R > 0\text{.}\) For any chosen \(r\) such that \(0 < r < R\):

  • The series converges pointwise on the open interval \((a-R, a+R)\text{.}\)
  • It converges uniformly on the closed interval \([a-r, a+r]\text{.}\)
  • The limit function \(f\) is differentiable on \((a-R, a+R)\text{.}\)
  • The derivative series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty nc_n (x-a)^{n-1}\) converges uniformly to the derivative, \(f'\text{,}\) on \([a-r, a+r]\text{.}\)

The smaller closed Interval \([a-r,a+r]\) stays strictly inside the convergence interval, which is why one uniform tail estimate works there; the endpoints \(a\pm R\) need separate tests.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Inside its radius of convergence a power series can be handled almost like a polynomial: it may be differentiated term by term, and the differentiated series converges to the derivative of the sum. The price is that uniform convergence is only guaranteed on closed intervals strictly inside \((a-R,a+R)\).

The open interval \((a-R,a+R)\) is where the series converges pointwise; the closed interval \([a-r,a+r]\), with \(0<r<R\), is where the convergence is uniform. The gap between \(r\) and \(R\) cannot be removed in general: the geometric series \(\sum_n x^n\) has \(a=0\) and \(R=1\), but it does not converge uniformly on \((-1,1)\), since its remainder \(x^{N+1}/(1-x)\) is unbounded as \(x\to1^-\).

On every closed interval \([a-r,a+r]\) with \(r<R\) the partial sums approach the sum uniformly; near the ends of the interval they need many more terms.

The uniform convergence on \([a-r,a+r]\) comes from the Weierstrass \(M\)-test: for \(|x-a|\le r\) we have \(|c_n(x-a)^n|\le|c_n|r^n\), and \(\sum_n|c_n|r^n\) converges because \(r<R\). The derivative series has the same radius \(R\), so the same argument applies to it, and the termwise differentiation result for an infinite series of functions gives \(f'\). Every \(x\) in \((a-R,a+R)\) lies in some interval \([a-r,a+r]\), so \(f\) is differentiable at every point of the open interval although the convergence need not be uniform on all of it.

The theorem says nothing about the endpoints \(a\pm R\). There the series and its derivative series can behave differently: \(\sum_{n\ge1}x^n/n^2\) converges at \(x=1\), while its derivative series \(\sum_{n\ge1}x^{n-1}/n\) is the harmonic series at \(x=1\) and diverges.

Repeating the argument shows that \(f\) is infinitely differentiable on \((a-R,a+R)\), and differentiating \(n\) times at \(a\) gives \(c_n=f^{(n)}(a)/n!\). This formula for the coefficients is the starting point of the Taylor series.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Term-by-term differentiation is valid inside the radius of convergence.
  • Locally (on \([a-r,a+r]\)), a power series behaves like a polynomial: it is smooth and uniformly controlled.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty n(-2)^n (x-3)^n\) with \(R = 1/2\) centred at \(a = 3\text{,}\) converges pointwise on \((5/2, 7/2)\) and uniformly on any closed interval within it.
  • The series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty 2^{n^2} (x+2)^n\) with \(R = 0\) centred at \(a = -2\text{,}\) converges solely at its centre \(x = -2\text{.}\)
  • The series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty 2^{-n^2} (x+2)^n\) with \(R = +\infty\) centred at \(a = -2\text{,}\) converges pointwise over the entire real line \(\mathbb{R}\text{.}\) It converges uniformly on every closed interval \([-2-r,-2+r]\), but not on \(\mathbb{R}\): for \(n\ge1\) the term \(2^{-n^2}(x+2)^n\) is unbounded on \(\mathbb{R}\), while uniform convergence would force the terms to tend to \(0\) uniformly.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Consider a (topological) space \(X\text{.}\) Let \(E\) be a subset of \(X\text{,}\) and let \(\mathcal{C}=\{G_i\colon i\in I\}\) be a collection of subsets \(G_i\) of \(X\) indexed by an arbitrary index set \(I\text{.}\) The collection \(\mathcal{C}\) is called a cover of \(E\) if \(\displaystyle E \subseteq \bigcup_{i\in I} G_i\text{.}\)

  • An open cover is a cover where each "patch" \(G_i\) is open.
  • A finite cover consists of a collection \(\{G_i\colon i\in I\}\) where \(I\) is finite. A cover is called a countable cover when \(I\) is a countable set, e.g., \(\mathbb{N}\text{.}\)
  • A subcover is a cover that is a subset of another cover.

The Union of Sets collects all points lying in at least one patch \(G_i\); the inclusion requires every point of \(E\) to occur in that union.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A cover is just a collection of sets that together contain the set you care about. Think of it as laying patches over the set so that every point is under at least one patch; the patches may overlap and may stick out beyond the set.

Five open intervals \(G_1,\dots,G_5\) lie over \(E=[0,1]\), and every point of the segment is under at least one of them. The outer two reach beyond \(0\) and \(1\), as they must: an open interval containing \(0\) also contains points to the left of \(0\). Since each \(G_i\) is open and there are finitely many, this is a finite open cover.

The index set \(I\) only labels the patches and may be infinite. A subcover keeps some of the patches, but it must still cover \(E\): patches can be dropped only as long as no point of \(E\) is left uncovered.

Covers matter because of compactness: a set is compact if every open cover has a finite subcover. The first Example shows how this fails for \((0,1)\). The intervals \((\tfrac{1}{n},1-\tfrac{1}{n})\) increase with \(n\), so finitely many of them cover only the largest one, \((\tfrac{1}{N},1-\tfrac{1}{N})\), and no finite subcover exists. For \([0,1]\), by contrast, every open cover can be reduced to finitely many patches, as the Heine-Borel theorem guarantees.

A common slip is to read "every open cover has a finite subcover" as "some finite open cover exists". The second is always true, because the space \(X\) itself covers \(E\), as the Key Results note.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • Any set \(E\subseteq X\) is covered by the space \(X\). So covers always exist.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The set \((0,1)\) in \(\mathbb{R}\) can be covered by the collection of open sets \(\{(1/n,1-1/n)\colon n\geq 3\}\). This is an infinite open cover.
  • The set \(\{1,2,3\}\) is covered by the three singletons \(\{1\}\), \(\{2\}\), \(\{3\}\). That is a finite cover.
  • The set of rational numbers \(\mathbb{Q}\) in \(\mathbb{R}\) can be covered by open intervals centred at each rational with radius \(1\). That's a countable cover because \(\mathbb{Q}\) is countable.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Consider a subset \(E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\) and a function \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon E\to\mathbb{R}^k\). Let \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) be an interior point of \(E\) and \(\boldsymbol{v}\) be a unit vector in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) (note: some authors only require \(\boldsymbol{v}\) to be a nonzero vector). If the limit

\[ \lim_{t\to 0^+}\frac{\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0+t\boldsymbol{v})-\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)}{t} \]

exists, then \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is said to be differentiable in the direction \(\boldsymbol{v}\) at \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{x}_0\). This limit is termed the directional derivative and is denoted by \(\mathrm{D}_{\boldsymbol{v}} \boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\).

Here unit length is measured by the Euclidean Norm, \(\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_2=1\). Equivalently, the Inner Product satisfies \(\langle\boldsymbol{v},\boldsymbol{v}\rangle=1\), so \(t\) measures distance travelled along the chosen direction.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The directional derivative measures the instantaneous rate of change of a function as you move from a point in a specific direction.

It generalizes the one-sided derivative to functions of several variables by looking at how the function changes along a straight line in that direction.

For a differentiable \(f\) and a unit direction \( oldsymbol{v}\), the directional derivative is \(D_{ oldsymbol{v}}f( oldsymbol{x}_0)= oldsymbol{ abla} f( oldsymbol{x}_0)\cdot oldsymbol{v}\). For the nonzero gradient drawn, it is largest when the direction follows the gradient and zero in a tangent direction to the level curve.

Turn the direction \( oldsymbol v\) with \( heta\): the slope of \(f\) along \( oldsymbol v\) is \( oldsymbol{ abla} f( oldsymbol x_0)\cdot oldsymbol v\), largest along the gradient and zero along the level curve.

Turn \( oldsymbol v\): the slice of the graph through \( oldsymbol x_0\) in direction \( oldsymbol v\) has slope \(\mathrm{D}_{ oldsymbol v}f( oldsymbol x_0)= oldsymbol{ abla} f( oldsymbol x_0)\cdot oldsymbol v\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is totally differentiable at \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\text{,}\) then the directional derivative \(\mathrm{D}_{\boldsymbol{v}}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\) exists for every direction \(\boldsymbol{v}\) and equals the total derivative at \(\boldsymbol{v}\text{,}\) \(\mathrm{D} \boldsymbol{f}_{\boldsymbol{x}_0}(\boldsymbol{v})\text{.}\)
  • A function is totally differentiable at a point implies that this function is directionally differentiable in any direction. The converse is incorrect.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • For the function \(\boldsymbol{f}(x,y)=(x^2,y^2)\), consider \(\boldsymbol{x}_0=(1,2)\) and \(\boldsymbol{v}=(3/5,4/5)\). We have \(\displaystyle \mathrm{D}_{\boldsymbol{v}}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0) =\left(\frac{6}{5},\frac{16}{5}\right)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Consider the space \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with its elements \( oldsymbol{x}\) and \( oldsymbol{y}\). We define a discrete metric \(d_{\mathrm{disc}}\) as:

\[ d_{\mathrm{disc}}( oldsymbol{x}, oldsymbol{y}) = egin{cases} \displaystyle \;1, & ext{if } oldsymbol{x} eq oldsymbol{y}, \[2pt] \displaystyle \;0, & ext{if } oldsymbol{x} = oldsymbol{y}. \end{cases} \]

Although the example uses the Real Coordinate Space \(\mathbb{R}^n\), the same formula works on any set. It satisfies the Metric and Metric Space axioms: in particular, if \(x e z\), at least one of \(x e y\) and \(y e z\) holds, giving the triangle inequality.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The discrete metric is the simplest possible distance: distinct points are always exactly \(1\) apart, and a point is \(0\) from itself. It treats every pair of different points as equally far, so it only records whether two points are equal.

Every line between two of the four points has length \(1\), however the points are drawn. The red circle of radius \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) around \(\boldsymbol{x}\) contains no other point: under this metric no point has neighbours closer than \(1\).

The discrete metric is mainly a test case: it satisfies every metric axiom, yet little of the behaviour of the Euclidean distance carries over. Since \(d_{\mathrm{disc}}(\boldsymbol{x}_i,\boldsymbol{x})<1\) forces \(\boldsymbol{x}_i=\boldsymbol{x}\), a sequence converges only if it is eventually constant. In the same way, \(d_{\mathrm{disc}}(\boldsymbol{x}_j,\boldsymbol{x}_k)<\tfrac{1}{2}\) forces \(\boldsymbol{x}_j=\boldsymbol{x}_k\), so every Cauchy sequence is eventually constant and the space is complete.

The metric also shows that a metric need not come from a norm: a norm would give \(\|2\boldsymbol{x}\|=2\|\boldsymbol{x}\|\), while \(d_{\mathrm{disc}}(2\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{0})=d_{\mathrm{disc}}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{0})=1\) for \(\boldsymbol{x}\ne\boldsymbol{0}\). Points that are very close in the Euclidean distance are at discrete distance \(1\), so no bound \(d_{\mathrm{disc}}\le b\,d_2\) holds, which is why the discrete metric is not strongly equivalent to the \(p\)-metrics.

The discrete metric returns later in the course as a standard counterexample for open and closed sets.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • The discrete metric is not strongly equivalent to any of the \(p\)-metrics.

docs.text: • \(d_{\mathrm{disc}}(2,5)=1\) since \(2\neq 5\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \((X,d_{X})\) and \((Y,d_{Y})\) be metric spaces, and let \(f\colon X\to Y\) be a function. The following statements are equivalent:

  • \(f\) is continuous.
  • For every \(x_0\in X\) and every convergent sequence \((x_i)_{i=1}^\infty\) in \((X,d_{X})\) converging to \(x_0\), its image under \(f\), \(f(x_i)_{i=1}^\infty\), also converges to \(f(x_0)\).
  • The preimage of any open set in \((Y,d_{Y})\) is open in \((X,d_{X})\).
  • The preimage of any closed set in \((Y,d_{Y})\) is closed in \((X,d_{X})\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The theorem gives three tests for continuity that avoid \(\varepsilon\) and \(\delta\). A function is continuous if and only if it preserves limits of sequences, and if and only if the preimage operation preserves openness, or equivalently closedness.

In \(X\) the points \(x_i\) approach \(x_0\), and in \(Y\) their images \(f(x_i)\) approach \(f(x_0)\): this is the sequential condition. The dashed sets show the open-set condition. \(V\) is an open set around \(f(x_0)\), and its preimage \(f^{-1}(V)\), the set of all points that \(f\) sends into \(V\), is an open set around \(x_0\). The two conditions fit together: since \(x_i\to x_0\) and \(f^{-1}(V)\) is open, the \(x_i\) eventually lie in \(f^{-1}(V)\), so the \(f(x_i)\) eventually lie in \(V\).

The conditions concern preimages, not images: a continuous function need not send open sets to open sets, as the Examples show. Preimages behave well because they respect complements, \(f^{-1}(Y\setminus V)=X\setminus f^{-1}(V)\), which is why the open-set and closed-set versions are equivalent.

One sequence \(x_i\to x_0\) with \(f(x_i)\not\to f(x_0)\) proves discontinuity. The preimage forms prove that sets are open or closed: the open unit disc \(\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x^2+y^2<1\}\) is the preimage of the open set \((-\infty,1)\) under the continuous \(f(x,y)=x^2+y^2\), so it is open, and every level set of a continuous real-valued function is closed.

The open-set form uses no distances at all. That is why it serves as the definition of continuity in a topological space, and why replacing a metric by a topologically equivalent one, which has the same open sets, does not change which functions are continuous.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • At a fixed point \(x_0\text{,}\) the sequential condition is equivalent to continuity at \(x_0\text{.}\) In metric spaces it is often the easiest to work with when proving discontinuity. To show \(f\) is not continuous at a point, find one sequence converging to that point whose image does not converge to the function value.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A continuous function \(f\) might map an open set \(V\) to a non-open set \(f(V)\). For example, let \(V=(0,1)\) with \(f(x)=1\) for all \(x\in\mathbb{R}\). Then \(f(V)=\{1\}\) isn't open under usual metrics.
  • A continuous function \(f\) might map a closed set \(F\) to a non-closed set \(f(F)\). For example, let \(F=[1,+\infty)\) and \(f(x)=1/x\) for all \(x>0\). Then \(f(F)=(0,1]\) isn't closed under usual metrics.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Two norms \(\|\cdot\|_p\) and \(\|\cdot\|_q\) on a vector space \(V\) (the subscripts are just labels for two arbitrary norms, not necessarily \(p\)-norms) are termed equivalent if there exist constants \(a, b > 0\) such that for every \(\boldsymbol{v} \in V\), we have:

\[ a \|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p \leq \|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q \leq b \|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p. \]

For example, the Euclidean Norm and maximum norm on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfy \(\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_\infty\le\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_2\le\sqrt n\,\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_\infty\). These constants show precisely how their lengths are comparable.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Equivalent norms are different ways of measuring length that agree up to fixed scaling factors: a vector that is short in one norm is short in the other, and the constants \(a\) and \(b\) say by how much the two lengths can differ. Geometrically, the unit circle of one norm fits between two scaled copies of the unit circle of the other.

On \(\mathbb{R}^2\), the illustrated norms satisfy \(\|\boldsymbol{x}\|_\infty\le\|\boldsymbol{x}\|_2\le\sqrt{2}\,\|\boldsymbol{x}\|_\infty\), so they are equivalent. In the figure, the Euclidean unit circle lies inside the square \(\|\boldsymbol{x}\|_\infty=1\), which is the left inequality, and outside the dashed square \(\|\boldsymbol{x}\|_\infty=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\), which is the right inequality.

Pick \(p\) and \(q\): the \(q\)-circles of radius \(a\) and \(b\) squeeze the \(p\)-unit circle between them, so \(a\|\boldsymbol v\|_p\le\|\boldsymbol v\|_q\le b\|\boldsymbol v\|_p\).

The constants must not depend on \(\boldsymbol{v}\). This uniformity is what makes equivalent norms interchangeable in analysis: the metrics \(\|\boldsymbol{v}-\boldsymbol{w}\|\) they define are strongly equivalent, so they have the same convergent sequences and the same Cauchy sequences. On \(\mathbb{R}^n\), where all norms are equivalent, the choice between the Euclidean, taxicab and maximum norm is a matter of convenience; the constants usually depend on \(n\), as in \(\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_2\le\sqrt{n}\,\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_\infty\).

A common slip is to take equivalence of all norms for granted in every vector space. It is a finite-dimensional fact. For continuous functions on \([0,1]\), the uniform norm and \(\int_0^1|f(x)|\,\mathrm{d}x\) are both norms, but \(f_n(x)=x^n\) has uniform norm \(1\) while the integral \(\tfrac{1}{n+1}\) tends to \(0\), so no constant \(a>0\) gives \(a\|f_n\|_\infty\le\int_0^1|f_n(x)|\,\mathrm{d}x\) for all \(n\).

docs.text: • Any two norms \(\|\cdot\|_p\) and \(\|\cdot\|_q\) on a finite-dimensional vector space \(V\) are equivalent.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a metric space \((X,d)\text{,}\) and a subset \(E \subseteq X\text{,}\) a point \(x_0\) is an exterior point of \(E\) if \(B(x_0,\varepsilon) \cap E = \varnothing\) for some \(\varepsilon > 0\text{.}\) We denote the set of exterior points of \(E\) as \(\operatorname{ext} E\text{.}\)

The Open Metric Ball is a neighbourhood that avoids \(E\); the empty Intersection of Sets expresses that no point lies in both the neighbourhood and \(E\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An exterior point of \(E\) is a point that is not only outside \(E\) but keeps some distance from it: a small open ball around it misses \(E\) completely. The exterior collects the points that are clearly outside \(E\), as opposed to outside points that \(E\) still touches.

In the figure the shaded region is \(\operatorname{int}E\), the red curve is \(\partial E\), and the rest of the rectangle \(X\) is \(\operatorname{ext}E\). The marked point \(x_0\) has a ball that does not meet \(E\), exactly as the definition requires. The radius may be as small as needed, so a point close to the red curve but not on it is still exterior, only with a smaller ball.

Outside the closed disc (and away from \(\boldsymbol p\)) a small enough ball misses \(E\) entirely.

The condition \(B(x_0,\varepsilon)\cap E=\varnothing\) says the same as \(B(x_0,\varepsilon)\subseteq X\setminus E\), so the exterior points of \(E\) are the interior points of its complement: \(\operatorname{ext}E=\operatorname{int}(X\setminus E)\). Every point of \(X\) is of exactly one of three kinds, so \(X\) is the disjoint union \(\operatorname{int}E\cup\partial E\cup\operatorname{ext}E\). The points that are not exterior are precisely the adherent points of \(E\), which is why the closure is \(\overline{E}=X\setminus\operatorname{ext}E\).

A common slip is to take every point outside \(E\) as exterior. For \(E=(0,1)\) in \(\mathbb{R}\), the point \(0\) is not in \(E\), but every interval \((-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\) contains points of \(E\), so \(0\) is a boundary point. For \(E=\mathbb{Q}\) in \(\mathbb{R}\) there are no exterior points at all, since every interval contains rational numbers.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • An exterior point \(x_0\) of \(E\) can never be in \(E\text{.}\)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(E = (0,1) \subseteq \mathbb{R}\), the point \(x = 2\) is an exterior point. A small ball around \(2\), say \((1.9,2.1)\), avoids \((0,1)\).
  • For \(E = \{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x^2 + y^2 \leq 1\}\), the point \((3,0)\) is an exterior point. A small disc around it stays entirely outside the unit disc.
