docs.title: Extreme Value Theorem on Compact Sets
Theorem
docs.text: Let \(E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\text{,}\) \(f \colon E \to \mathbb{R}\) be a function, and \(X \subseteq E\) be a nonempty compact set. If \(f\) is continuous on \(X\text{,}\) then \(f\) attains both its maximum and minimum on \(X\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A continuous function on a compact set cannot sneak off to infinity or skip its highest and lowest values: it attains both a maximum and a minimum on that set.

The level sets of \(f\) are parallel lines, so \(f\) increases steadily in one direction across the disc \(X\). The maximum \(M\) is attained where the disc reaches furthest in that direction and the minimum \(m\) on the opposite side. The image \(f(X)\) is the closed interval \([m,M]\): along the segment from the minimum point to the maximum point, \(f\) takes every value in between by the intermediate value theorem.

Each hypothesis is needed. On the set \((0,1)\), which is not closed, \(f(x)=x\) has neither a maximum nor a minimum; on the unbounded set \([0,\infty)\) it has no maximum. Without continuity, \(f\) can approach a value without reaching it: on \([0,1]\), the function with \(f(x)=x\) for \(x<1\) and \(f(1)=0\) has supremum \(1\) but no maximum.

The proof combines two facts: the continuous image of a compact set is compact, and a nonempty compact subset of \(\mathbb{R}\) contains its supremum and infimum. For \(X=[a,b]\) this is the extreme value theorem of Math I.

The theorem guarantees existence only. The extreme points need not be unique or interior; as in the figure, they may lie on the boundary, where setting derivatives equal to zero does not find them. The theorem returns in Math IV as the existence argument for a global maximum and minimum on a compact feasible set.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If the domain is not compact, the conclusion may fail. For example, \(f(x)=1/x\) on \((0,1)\) is continuous but has no maximum (it blows up as \(x\to0^+\)) and no minimum (its values decrease towards \(1\) as \(x\to1^-\text{,}\) but \(1\) is never attained, since \(1\notin(0,1)\)).
  • This theorem is used to prove existence of solutions in optimization problems.
  • Together with the intermediate value theorem, it gives a complete picture of the range of a continuous real-valued function on a connected compact set: the range is the closed interval \([m,M]\) between the minimum \(m\) and the maximum \(M\). (In \(\mathbb{R}\), a connected compact set is itself a closed bounded interval.)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • The function \(f(x,y)=x+y\) on the closed unit disc \(\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x^2+y^2\leq 1\}\) attains maximum \(\sqrt{2}\)​ at \((1/\sqrt{2},1/\sqrt{2})\) and minimum \(-\sqrt{2}\)​ at \((-1/\sqrt{2},-1/\sqrt{2})\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Consider a function \(f\colon X \to Y\) where \(X\) is a set in an \(n\)-dimensional space (e.g., \(\mathbb{R}^n\)) and \(Y\) is a set in a \(k\)-dimensional space (e.g., \(\mathbb{R}^k\)). We have the following terminologies:

  • it is called a univariate function (also known as single variable function, function of one variable) if \(n=1\);
  • it is called a bivariate function (also known as function of two variables) if \(n=2\);
  • it is called a multivariable function (also known as multivariate function, function of several variables) if \(n\geq 2\);
  • it is called a real-valued function if its codomain is a subset of \(\mathbb{R}\);
  • it is called a vector-valued function if \(k\geq 2\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A function is classified by how many numbers go in and how many come out: \(n\) counts the input variables and \(k\) the output components. These names describe only the shape of the inputs and outputs; they say nothing about the rule itself.

The rows of the figure separate \(n=1\) from \(n\ge2\), and the columns separate \(k=1\) from \(k\ge2\). Each type is drawn in its own way. A univariate real-valued function has a graph in the plane. A function \(\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}^2\) is drawn as the curve traced by its outputs. A function \(\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}\) is drawn by its level sets. A function \(\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}^2\) is drawn as a vector field, with an output arrow attached at each input point. The graph of \(f\colon\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^k\) lies in \(\mathbb{R}^{n+k}\), so it can be drawn directly only when \(n+k\le3\).

A vector-valued function \(\boldsymbol{f}=(f_1,\dots,f_k)\) is the same as \(k\) real-valued functions of the same input; it is written in bold because its values are vectors. For example, \(\boldsymbol{f}(t)=(\cos t,\sin t)\) from \(\mathbb{R}\) to \(\mathbb{R}^2\) traces the unit circle, and each component is an ordinary function of one variable from Math I.

A common slip is to mix up the two counts. "Multivariable" refers to the inputs and "vector-valued" to the outputs: \(f(x,y)=x^2+y^2\) is multivariable but real-valued, and \(\boldsymbol{f}(t)=(\cos t,\sin t)\) is vector-valued but univariate.

This idea returns later: the derivative of \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^k\) is a \(k\times n\) matrix, the Jacobian matrix, with one row per output and one column per input.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • A multivalued function (a rule that may assign several outputs to one input, such as \(x\mapsto\pm\sqrt{x}\)) is not a function in the sense used here, so it is neither a multivariable function nor a vector-valued function.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2\) from \(\mathbb{R}^2\) to \(\mathbb{R}\) is a bivariate real valued function.
  • \(\boldsymbol{F}(x,y) = (x+y, x-y, xy)\) from \(\mathbb{R}^2\) to \(\mathbb{R}^3\) is a multivariable vector valued function.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(E\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(f \colon E \to \mathbb{R}\) be a real-valued function. If \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) is an interior point of \(E\) and all first partial derivatives exist there, the gradient \(\boldsymbol{\nabla} f (\boldsymbol{x}_0)\) of \(f\) at \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{x}_0\) is given as the \(n\)-dimensional column vector:

\[ \boldsymbol{\nabla} f (\boldsymbol{x}_0) = \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1}(\boldsymbol{x}_0),\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_2}(\boldsymbol{x}_0), \ldots,\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_n}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\right)^{\top}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The gradient collects the first partial derivatives of a real-valued function into one vector. For a totally differentiable \(f\) it points in the direction in which \(f\) increases fastest, and its length is that fastest rate of increase.

The figure shows level curves of \(f(x,y)=x^2+2y^2\) for the values \(2\), \(4\) and \(6\), with \( oldsymbol{ abla} f(x,y)=(2x,4y)^{ op}\). The arrows start at four points of the level curve \(f=4\), such as \((2,0)\) and \((0,\sqrt{2})\); each is perpendicular to that curve and points outwards, towards larger values of \(f\). The gradients there are \((4,0)^{ op}\) and \((0,4\sqrt{2})^{ op}\): \(f\) rises faster along the \(y\)-axis, where the level curves lie closer together.

The gradient arrows point uphill, perpendicular to the level curves, and are longer where the curves are close together. Drag \( oldsymbol x_0\) to a stationary point.

The red path climbs the surface along \( oldsymbol{ abla} f\); on the floor it crosses the level curves at right angles.

When \( oldsymbol{ abla} f ( oldsymbol{x}_0)= oldsymbol{0}\), we say that \( oldsymbol{x}_0\) is a stationary point of \(f\) (possibly a local extremum point). At an interior local extremum every partial derivative that exists is \(0\), but a stationary point need not be an extremum: \(f(x,y)=x^2-y^2\) has \( oldsymbol{ abla} f(0,0)= oldsymbol{0}\), yet takes both larger and smaller values than \(f(0,0)\) near the origin.

When \(f\) is totally differentiable at \( oldsymbol{x}_0\) and \( oldsymbol{ abla} f ( oldsymbol{x}_0) eq oldsymbol{0}\), the gradient gives two things: the direction \( oldsymbol{u}= oldsymbol{ abla} f( oldsymbol{x}_0)/\| oldsymbol{ abla} f( oldsymbol{x}_0)\|\) of steepest ascent, and the maximal rate of increase \(\| oldsymbol{ abla} f( oldsymbol{x}_0)\|=\max_{\| oldsymbol{u}\|=1}\mathrm{D}_{ oldsymbol{u}}f( oldsymbol{x}_0) ext{,}\) by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. Along a level curve \(f\) does not change, so the directional derivative in a tangent direction is \(0\); this is why the gradient is perpendicular to the level curves.

A common slip is to draw the gradient on the graph of \(f\). It is a vector in the domain \(\mathbb{R}^n\), drawn in the same plane as the level curves.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(f\) is totally differentiable at \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\text{,}\) the gradient is the vector whose dot product with any unit vector \(\boldsymbol{v}\) equals the directional derivative of \(f\) at \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{x}_0\) along \(\boldsymbol{v}\), i.e.,
\[ \boldsymbol{\nabla} f (\boldsymbol{x}_0) \cdot \boldsymbol{v} = \mathrm{D}_{\boldsymbol{v}}f(\boldsymbol{x}_0). \]
  • The existence of the gradient (all partial derivatives at \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\)) alone does not guarantee this formula.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Let \(f(x,y) = \mathrm{e}^{x+y}\). Then \(\displaystyle \boldsymbol{\nabla} f(x,y) = \begin{pmatrix} \mathrm{e}^{x+y} \\ \mathrm{e}^{x+y} \end{pmatrix}\).
  • Let \(f(x,y) = x^2 y + y^3\). Then \(\boldsymbol{\nabla} f(x,y) = \begin{pmatrix} 2xy \\ x^2 + 3y^2 \end{pmatrix}\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: Let \(E\) be a subset of the Euclidean space \(\mathbb{R}^n\text{.}\) The set \(E\) is compact if and only if it is both closed and bounded.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A set in Euclidean space is compact exactly when it contains all its limit points and stays within some finite distance from the origin. Closedness keeps the boundary in, boundedness keeps it from running off to infinity. The theorem turns the condition on all open covers into two properties that are easy to check.

The closed disc \(E\) is drawn with nine small open discs over it, standing for a finite subcover. Since \(E\) is closed and bounded, every open cover of \(E\) can be reduced to finitely many of its sets.

Both conditions are needed, and each failure has a cover to show it. The bounded but not closed set \((0,1)\) is covered by the open intervals \((\tfrac{1}{n},1)\), \(n\ge2\), and finitely many of them cover only \((\tfrac{1}{N},1)\) for the largest \(N\) used. The closed but unbounded set \([0,\infty)\) is covered by the intervals \((-1,n)\), \(n\ge1\), and finitely many of them miss every point beyond the largest \(n\).

The theorem is special to \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with its usual metric. In every metric space a compact set is closed and bounded, but the converse can fail: with the discrete metric, \(\mathbb{R}\) is closed and bounded but not compact.

Together with the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem, which makes closed and bounded sets in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) sequentially compact, the theorem shows that the three properties coincide there. In practice it is how compactness is checked, for instance for the extreme value theorem on compact sets: the triangle \(\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x\ge0,\ y\ge0,\ x+y\le1\}\) is closed and bounded, hence compact.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The continuous image of a compact set is compact. This yields the extreme value theorem.
  • Any closed subset of a compact set in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is itself compact.
  • Finite unions of compact sets are compact. The intersection of any nonempty family of compact subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is compact; the intersection itself may be empty.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A closed metric ball \(\overline{B}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,r) = \{\boldsymbol{x} \in X \colon d_2(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{x}_0) \leq r\}\) in the Euclidean space is closed and bounded, so compact.
  • Any finite set \(\{\boldsymbol{x}_1,\dots,\boldsymbol{x}_k\}\subset \mathbb{R}^n\) is closed (finite sets are closed) and bounded, so compact.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: Let \(a < b\) be real numbers, and consider a function \(f\colon [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}\) that is continuous on \([a, b]\text{.}\) Then, \(f\) is uniformly continuous on \([a, b]\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Continuity of \(f\) at each point gives, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), a \(\delta\) that may depend on the point. The Heine-Cantor theorem says that on a closed bounded interval this dependence can be removed: one \(\delta\) works at every point of \([a,b]\) at once. The function cannot become steeper and steeper towards an edge, because the endpoints belong to the interval and \(f\) is continuous there as well.

The figure takes \(f(x)=\tfrac{1}{2}x^2\) with \(a=0\) and \(b=2\). Each rectangle has width \(2\delta\) and height \(2\varepsilon\) and is centred on a point of the graph, and the graph stays inside every rectangle over its whole width. Since \(|f'(x)|=|x|\le2\) on \([0,2]\), the mean value theorem gives \(|f(x_1)-f(x_2)|\le2|x_1-x_2|\), so \(\delta=\varepsilon/2\) works everywhere.

Both properties of the domain matter. On the open interval \((0,1)\) the continuous function \(1/x\) is not uniformly continuous: it becomes arbitrarily steep near the missing endpoint \(0\). On the closed but unbounded interval \([0,\infty)\) the function \(x^2\) fails too: the points \(x\) and \(x+\tfrac{\delta}{2}\) are closer than \(\delta\), yet their values differ by \(x\delta+\tfrac{\delta^2}{4}\), which exceeds any \(\varepsilon\) for large \(x\). The theorem gives a sufficient condition only, as the Examples show.

The theorem is the usual step in showing that continuous functions on \([a,b]\) are Riemann integrable: one \(\delta\) controls the variation of \(f\) on every subinterval of a partition at once.

"Uniform" does not mean that \(\delta\) is independent of \(\varepsilon\). It still depends on \(\varepsilon\), only no longer on the point.

The theorem returns later with \([a,b]\) replaced by more general closed and bounded sets, the compact sets.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• This theorem has a generalized version if \([a,b]\) is replaced by a compact set.
  • This theorem does not imply that uniform continuity holds only on closed intervals.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The function \(f(x)=\dfrac{x^2+\sin x}{\mathrm{e}^x}\) is uniformly continuous on any closed interval since we know it is continuous everywhere.
  • The function \(g(x)=x\) is uniformly continuous on \((0,1)\) though \((0,1)\) is not a closed interval. This does not contradict the theorem since the "closed interval" condition is sufficient but not necessary.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(n,\,k \in\mathbb{N}^+\) and \(m\in \mathbb{Z}\). A function \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon \mathbb{R}^n\to \mathbb{R}^k\) is homogeneous of degree \(m\) if

\[ \boldsymbol{f}(cx_1,\dots,cx_n)=c^m \boldsymbol{f}(x_1,\dots,x_n) \]

for every \((x_1,\,x_2,\,\dots,\,x_n)\) and \(c\neq 0\). In economics one often uses the variant with domain \(\mathbb{R}^n_{++}=(0,+\infty)^n\), only \(c>0\), and any real degree \(m\); for example, \(f(x,y)=x^{1/2}y^{1/2}\) is homogeneous of degree \(1\) in this sense.

The definition treats \(\boldsymbol{f}\) as a Function between Spaces: scaling an input vector changes its assigned output by the prescribed scalar factor.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
If all arguments of a homogeneous function are multiplied by the same scalar \(c\), the value is multiplied by the fixed power \(c^m\) of that scalar. The degree \(m\) measures how strongly the function responds when all inputs are scaled together.

Along the ray through \(\boldsymbol{0}\) and \(\boldsymbol{x}\), the values are fixed by the single value \(f(\boldsymbol{x})\): at \(2\boldsymbol{x}\) the function equals \(2^mf(\boldsymbol{x})\), and at \(3\boldsymbol{x}\) it equals \(3^mf(\boldsymbol{x})\). For the figure's example \(f(x_1,x_2)=x_1^2+x_2^2\), with \(m=2\), these are \(4f(\boldsymbol{x})\) and \(9f(\boldsymbol{x})\). Away from the origin, a homogeneous function is therefore determined by its values at one point of each ray.

Scale the point by \(c\): the value is multiplied by \(c^m\), so the level curves are scaled copies of each other along rays from the origin.

The same factor \(c\) must multiply every argument: scaling only \(x_1\) says nothing about homogeneity. Degree \(1\) means that doubling all inputs doubles the value, as for \(x^{1/2}y^{1/2}\); in economics this is called constant returns to scale. Degree \(0\) means \(f(c\boldsymbol{x})=f(\boldsymbol{x})\), so only the ratios of the inputs matter, as for \(x_1/x_2\) on \(\mathbb{R}^2_{++}\).

A linear map is homogeneous of degree \(1\), and a homogeneous polynomial of degree \(k\), such as a quadratic form, is homogeneous of degree \(k\).

A common slip is to add a constant: \(x^2+y^2+1\) is not homogeneous, because the constant term does not scale with \(c^2\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(f\) is homogeneous of degree \(m\) and differentiable, then each partial derivative is homogeneous of degree \(m-1\).
  • The sum of two functions that are homogeneous of the same degree \(m\) is homogeneous of degree \(m\text{;}\) the product of functions homogeneous of degrees \(m\) and \(\ell\) is homogeneous of degree \(m+\ell\text{,}\) and the composition of functions homogeneous of degrees \(m\) and \(p\) is homogeneous of degree \(mp\text{.}\) A sum of homogeneous functions of different degrees, such as \(xy+x\text{,}\) is not homogeneous.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2 + xy\) is homogeneous as \(f(cx, cy) = c^2 f(x,y)\).
  • \(g(x,y) = xy + x\) is said to be inhomogeneous.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A polynomial on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is called homogeneous of degree \(k\) if all of its nonzero terms have degree \(k\). Such a polynomial is also called a (algebraic) form.

Every degree-\(k\) monomial acquires the same factor \(c^k\) when its variables are scaled by \(c\). Their sum therefore satisfies the defining identity of a Homogeneous Function.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A homogeneous polynomial is a polynomial in which every nonzero term has the same total degree \(k\). Scaling all variables by \(c\) then multiplies every term, and hence the whole polynomial, by \(c^k\):

\[ P(cx_1,\dots,cx_n)=c^kP(x_1,\dots,x_n). \]

So a homogeneous polynomial of degree \(k\) is a homogeneous function of degree \(k\). Conversely, a polynomial that satisfies this identity for every \(c\neq0\) is homogeneous of degree \(k\), so for polynomials the two notions agree.

To check homogeneity, add the exponents in each nonzero term: \(x^2y+y^3\) is homogeneous of degree \(3\), while \(x^2+y\) has terms of degrees \(2\) and \(1\) and is not homogeneous. Every polynomial on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) splits uniquely into homogeneous parts by grouping its terms by total degree; for example, \(x^2+2xy+y^2+x+1\) has the parts \(x^2+2xy+y^2\), \(x\) and \(1\).

The forms of low degree are familiar from linear algebra. Forms of degree \(1\) are the linear functions \(a_1x_1+\cdots+a_nx_n\), that is, the linear maps \(\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\). Forms of degree \(2\) are the quadratic forms \(\boldsymbol{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\).

A common slip is to compare the degree of each variable instead of the total degree. The terms \(x^3\) and \(xy^2\) look different, but both have total degree \(3\), so \(x^3-3xy^2\) is homogeneous of degree \(3\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The sum of two homogeneous polynomials of the same degree is homogeneous of that degree.
  • The product of a homogeneous polynomial of degree \(k\) and one of degree \(\ell\) is homogeneous of degree \(k+\ell\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(P(x) = 2x^5\) is a homogeneous polynomial of degree 5.
  • \(P(x,y) = x^2 + xy + y^2\) is homogeneous of degree 2. Each term has total degree 2.

docs.title: Image and Preimage of a Set
Definition
docs.text:
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be sets (in this course usually subsets of metric spaces), and let \(f\colon X\to Y\) be a function. Let \(C\) be a subset of the domain \(X\), the image of \(C\) under \(f\) is defined as:

\[ f(C)=\{y\in Y\colon \text{there exists some } x\in C \text{ such that } y=f(x)\}. \]

Let \(V\) be a subset of the codomain \(Y\), the preimage of \(V\) under \(f\) includes all points in the domain that give results in \(V\):

\[ f^{-1}(V)=\{x\in X\colon f(x)\in V\}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The image pushes a set of inputs forward: \(f(C)\) collects the outputs obtained from inputs in \(C\). The preimage pulls a set of outputs back: \(f^{-1}(V)\) collects all inputs whose output lands in \(V\).

The three marked points of \(C\) are sent to only two points of \(f(C)\), so this \(f\) is not injective. Going back, \(f^{-1}(V)\) contains every point of \(X\) that is mapped into \(V\), wherever it lies in \(X\).

A common slip is to read \(f^{-1}(V)\) as requiring an inverse function. The preimage is defined for every function. For \(f(x)=x^2\) on \(\mathbb{R}\), \(f^{-1}(\{4\})=\{-2,2\}\) and \(f^{-1}(\{-1\})=\varnothing\). Only for a bijection does \(f^{-1}(V)\) coincide with the image of \(V\) under the inverse function. The same \(f\) shows that the inclusions in the Key Results can be strict: for \(C=[0,1]\) we get \(f^{-1}(f(C))=[-1,1]\), and for \(V=[-1,1]\) we get \(f(f^{-1}(V))=[0,1]\).

Preimages behave well with set operations: they preserve unions, intersections and complements. Images preserve unions, but in general only \(f(C_1\cap C_2)\subseteq f(C_1)\cap f(C_2)\) holds.

The range of \(f\) is the image of the whole domain, and a level set is the preimage of a single value. In probability, the event generated by a random variable and a set \(B\subseteq\mathbb{R}\) is the preimage of \(B\) under the random variable.

This idea returns later: continuity can be characterized by preimages of open sets being open, whereas images of open sets need not be open.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(V\) only needs to be a part of the codomain of \(f\). This means there might be some \(y\) in \(V\) that doesn't match any \(x\) in the domain \(X\).
  • We have \(C \subseteq f^{-1}(f(C))\) and \(f(f^{-1}(V)) \subseteq V\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Let \(f\colon\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}\) be \(f(x,y)=x+y\). Image of the unit square \([0,1]\times[0,1]\) under \(f\) is \([0,2]\). Preimage of \(\{0\}\) under \(f\) is the line \(y=-x\).
  • Let \(f\colon \mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}\) be \(f(x,y)=x\). Image of the disc \(\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x^2+y^2 \leq 1\}\) under \(f\) is \([-1,1]\). Preimage of \([2,3]\) under \(f\) is the vertical strip \([2,3]\times\mathbb{R}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Consider a sequence of functions \((f_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) from \(X\) to \(\mathbb{R}\text{.}\) If the sequence of partial sums \(\displaystyle S_N(x) = \sum_{n=1}^N f_n(x)\) converges to \(f\colon X \to \mathbb{R}\) pointwise or uniformly on \(X\) as \(N \to \infty\text{,}\) then we say the infinite series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n\) converges pointwise/uniformly to \(f\) on \(X\text{,}\) denoted as \(\displaystyle f(x) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n(x)\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A series of functions is defined through its partial sums: each \(S_N\) is an ordinary finite sum of functions, and the series converges to \(f\) when the sequence \((S_N)\) does. Every question about a series of functions is therefore a question about the sequence of partial sums, and the results on pointwise and uniform convergence of sequences apply directly.

The figure shows the partial sums with \(1\), \(2\), \(4\) and \(10\) terms of \(\sum_{n\ge1}\sin(nx)/n^2\) on \([0,2\pi]\). Each new term changes the curve less, and the later sums are almost indistinguishable. Since \(|\sin(nx)/n^2|\le1/n^2\) for every \(x\), the sum with \(10\) terms differs from the full sum by at most \(\sum_{n>10}1/n^2\approx0.095\) at every point at once; this is the bound used in the Weierstrass \(M\)-test.

Raise \(N\): the partial sums \(\displaystyle S_N(x)=\sum_{n=1}^N f_n(x)\) settle on the limit function (dashed).

Pointwise convergence at \(x\) is convergence of the numerical infinite series \(\sum_n f_n(x)\), so the tests for numerical series apply for each fixed \(x\). Uniform convergence asks more: the largest error \(\sup_{x\in X}|f(x)-S_N(x)|\) must tend to \(0\). A finite sum can always be differentiated and integrated term by term; for an infinite sum, the Key Results need uniform convergence. Without it, a sum of continuous functions can be discontinuous: \(\sum_{n\ge0}x^2/(1+x^2)^n\) equals \(1+x^2\) for \(x\ne0\) and \(0\) at \(x=0\).

Power series are the most important special case, and normal convergence is the usual way to show that a series converges uniformly.

A common slip is to differentiate term by term because the series itself converges uniformly. The condition is on the derivative series: \(\sum_n\sin(nx)/n^2\) converges uniformly, but its derivative series \(\sum_n\cos(nx)/n\) is the harmonic series at \(x=0\) and diverges.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(f_n\)'s are (continuously) differentiable, \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n \rightarrow f\text{,}\) and \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty f'_n\rightrightarrows g\) on \((a,b)\text{,}\) then \(f\) is (continuously) differentiable on \((a, b)\) with \(f' = g\text{,}\) i.e., for every \(x_0\in(a,b)\),
\[ \sum_{n=1}^\infty f'_n(x_0)=\left(\sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n\right)'(x_0). \]
  • On a finite closed interval \([a,b]\) with \(a<b\), if every \(f_n\) is Riemann integrable and \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n\) converges uniformly, then its sum is Riemann integrable and
\[ \int_a^b \left(\sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n(x)\right) \, \mathrm{d}x = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \int_a^b f_n(x) \, \mathrm{d}x. \]

The finite interval matters: the integral of a uniform error is at most \((b-a)\) times that error. Uniform convergence alone does not provide this bound for an improper integral on an unbounded interval.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The series \(\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^\infty x^n/n!\) converges uniformly (by the Weierstrass \(M\)-test) on every fixed interval \([-R,R]\), where \(R>0\): \(|x^n/n!|\le R^n/n!\), and \(\displaystyle \sum_n R^n/n!=\mathrm{e}^R\). It converges pointwise on \(\mathbb{R}\), but not uniformly there; for each finite partial sum, the difference from \(\mathrm{e}^x\) is unbounded as \(x\to+\infty\).
  • The geometric series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty x^n\) converges uniformly on \([-r,r]\) for every fixed \(0<r<1\), because \(|x^n|\le r^n\) and \(\displaystyle \sum_n r^n<\infty\). On \((-1,1)\) it converges pointwise to \(1/(1-x)\), but not uniformly: the remainder \(x^{N+1}/(1-x)\) is unbounded as \(x\to1^-\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a metric space \((X,d)\text{,}\) and a subset \(E \subseteq X\text{,}\) a point \(x_0\) is an interior point of \(E\) if there exists some \(\varepsilon > 0\) such that \(B(x_0,\varepsilon) \subseteq E\text{.}\) We denote the set of interior points of \(E\) as \(\operatorname{int} E\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An interior point of \(E\) is a point that lies in \(E\) with room to spare: some ball around it, however small, stays inside \(E\). From an interior point one can move a little in every direction without leaving the set.

The green ball lies entirely inside \(E\), so its centre \(x_0\) is an interior point. Every ball around the red edge point leaves \(E\), however small its radius, so that point is not interior but a boundary point. This does not depend on whether the edge point itself belongs to \(E\).

\(E\) is the open unit disc together with one extra point \(p\). Drag \(x_0\) and shrink \(\varepsilon\): an interior point has some ball inside \(E\).

The radius \(\varepsilon\) may depend on the point. In \(E=(0,1)\) the point \(0.01\) is interior, but only balls of radius at most \(0.01\) fit around it; what matters is that some positive radius works. Collecting all interior points gives the largest open subset of \(E\), and \(E\) is open if and only if \(E=\operatorname{int}E\). Interior points of the complement are the exterior points of \(E\).

A common slip is to forget the ambient space. As a subset of \(\mathbb{R}\), \(E=[0,1]\) has interior \((0,1)\). As a subset of the metric space \(X=[0,1]\) with \(d(x,y)=|x-y|\), every point is interior, because there \(B(0,\tfrac{1}{2})=[0,\tfrac{1}{2})\subseteq E\).

This idea returns later: derivatives of functions of several variables, such as the gradient, are taken at interior points of the domain, where the function is defined in every direction around the point.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• An interior point \(x_0\) of \(E\) is always in \(E\) since balls centred at \(x_0\) include \(x_0\text{.}\)
  • The interior of \(E\) is the largest open subset of \(E\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(E = (0,1) \subseteq \mathbb{R}\), every point in \((0,1)\) is interior. Pick a small enough interval around any point and it stays inside \((0,1)\).
  • For \(E = \{1,2,3\} \subseteq \mathbb{R}\), no point is interior. Any ball around \(1\) contains numbers other than \(1,2,3\).

docs.title: Intermediate Value Theorem on Connected Sets
Theorem
docs.text: Let \(f\colon \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}\) be a continuous real-valued function. Let \(E\) be any connected subset of \(\mathbb{R}^n\text{,}\) and let \(\boldsymbol{a}\) and \(\boldsymbol{b}\) be any two points in \(E\text{.}\) If \(y\) is a real number between \(f(\boldsymbol{a})\) and \(f(\boldsymbol{b})\text{,}\) then there exists a \(\boldsymbol{c} \in E\) such that \(f(\boldsymbol{c}) = y\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A continuous function on a connected set cannot skip values: if it takes two different numbers, it must also take every number in between. The connected set \(E\) takes over the role of the interval \([a,b]\) in the one-variable intermediate value theorem, and connectedness replaces "no gaps".

The points \(\boldsymbol{a}\) and \(\boldsymbol{b}\) of the connected region \(E\) are sent to \(f(\boldsymbol{a})\) and \(f(\boldsymbol{b})\) on the real line. For the level \(y\) between these values, the theorem gives a point \(\boldsymbol{c}\in E\) with \(f(\boldsymbol{c})=y\). The curve from \(\boldsymbol{a}\) to \(\boldsymbol{b}\) through \(\boldsymbol{c}\) shows the idea of the proof for path-connected sets in the Key Results: along a path, \(f\) becomes a continuous function on \([0,1]\).

In general, the proof uses that the image \(f(E)\) of a connected set is connected, and the connected subsets of \(\mathbb{R}\) are the intervals. An interval that contains \(f(\boldsymbol{a})\) and \(f(\boldsymbol{b})\) contains every number between them.

Both hypotheses are needed. On the disconnected set \(E=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon |x|\ge1\}\), the continuous function \(f(x,y)=x\) takes the values \(-1\) and \(1\) but never \(0\). On the connected plane, the discontinuous function that equals \(1\) for \(x\ge0\) and \(-1\) for \(x<0\) also skips \(0\).

A typical use is a sign change: if a continuous \(f\) takes a negative and a positive value on a connected set \(E\), then the level set \(\{\boldsymbol{x}\in E\colon f(\boldsymbol{x})=0\}\) is nonempty. Similarly, a continuous function on a connected set that takes only integer values is constant.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Continuous image of a connected set is connected.
  • If \(E\) is path‑connected, the theorem can be proved by composing \(f\) with a path and applying the one‑dimensional intermediate value theorem.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Let \(E\) be the closed unit disk in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) and \(f(x,y)=x^2+y^2\)​. The image is \([0,1]\) which is also a connected set.
  • Let \(E\) be the unit sphere in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) and \(f(x,y,z)=z\) (height). The image is \([-1,1]\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Suppose \(E\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\), and \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) is an interior point of \(E\). For a function \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon E\to\mathbb{R}^k\) that each of its partial derivatives exists at \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{x}_0\), the following \(k\times n\) matrix

\[ \begin{aligned} \boldsymbol{\mathrm{J}}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)&=\begin{pmatrix} \frac{\partial f_1}{\partial x_1}(\boldsymbol{x}_0) & \cdots & \frac{\partial f_1}{\partial x_n}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\\[8pt] \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\[4pt] \frac{\partial f_k}{\partial x_1}(\boldsymbol{x}_0) & \cdots & \frac{\partial f_k}{\partial x_n}(\boldsymbol{x}_0) \end{pmatrix}\\[10pt] &=\begin{pmatrix} \boldsymbol{\nabla} f_1 (\boldsymbol{x}_0)^{\top}\\ \vdots\\ \boldsymbol{\nabla} f_k (\boldsymbol{x}_0)^{\top} \end{pmatrix}\\[10pt] &=\left(\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial x_1}(\boldsymbol{x}_0),\,\cdots,\,\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial x_n}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\right) \end{aligned} \]

is called the derivative matrix or the Jacobian matrix.

Each row is the Gradient of one scalar component \(f_i\). When the function is totally differentiable, multiplying this matrix by an increment gives the Linear Map that approximates the output change; the existence of partial derivatives alone does not guarantee that approximation.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The Jacobian matrix stacks all the partial derivatives of a vector-valued function, showing how each output changes with each input: the entry in row \(i\) and column \(j\) is \(\partial f_i/\partial x_j\). When \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is totally differentiable, it is the matrix of the linear map that best approximates \(\boldsymbol{f}\) near \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\).

The small square at \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) with sides along \(\boldsymbol{e}_1\) and \(\boldsymbol{e}_2\) is sent to the small parallelogram at \(\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\) spanned by \(\boldsymbol{\mathrm{J}}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\boldsymbol{e}_1\) and \(\boldsymbol{\mathrm{J}}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\boldsymbol{e}_2\), the two columns of the matrix, in line with \(\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0+\boldsymbol{h})\approx\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)+\boldsymbol{\mathrm{J}}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\boldsymbol{h}\). The curved grid on the right shows that this is only a first-order picture.

Row \(i\) is the transposed gradient of the component \(f_i\): how one output responds to all inputs. Column \(j\) is \(\partial\boldsymbol{f}/\partial x_j\): how all outputs respond to one input. The matrix is \(k\times n\), outputs by inputs, so for \(k=1\) it is the row vector \(\boldsymbol{\nabla} f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)^{\top}\), and for \(n=k=1\) it is the \(1\times1\) matrix \(f'(x_0)\).

For a totally differentiable \(\boldsymbol{f}\) with \(n=k\), the absolute value of the determinant of the Jacobian is the factor by which \(\boldsymbol{f}\) scales small areas or volumes near \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\), as \(|\det\boldsymbol{A}|\) does for the linear map \(\boldsymbol{h}\mapsto\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{h}\). This factor appears in the transformation of densities of random vectors.

A common slip is to treat the Jacobian as the derivative whenever it exists. All partial derivatives can exist while \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is not totally differentiable, and then the approximation above can fail. In Math IV, Jacobians return in the multivariable chain rule, where the matrices of composed functions are multiplied.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The total derivative of a differentiable function is represented by the Jacobian matrix: the Jacobian is the matrix of this linear map with respect to the standard bases.
  • The existence of the Jacobian matrix does not necessarily imply the total differentiability of the function.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Let \(\boldsymbol{f}(x,y) = (x^2, xy)\). Then \(\dfrac{\partial \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial x} = (2x, y)\), \(\dfrac{\partial \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial y} = (0, x)\), so
\[ \boldsymbol{\mathrm{J}}\boldsymbol{f}(x,y) = \begin{pmatrix} 2x & 0 \\ y & x \end{pmatrix}. \]

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(f\colon X \to \mathbb{R}\) be a real-valued function defined on a set \(X\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\). A level set is defined as the preimage of a singleton set \(\{k\}\), i.e.,

\[ L_k(f)=f^{-1}(\{k\}) =\{(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)\in X\colon f(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)=k\}. \]

When the number of independent variables is two, a level set is called a level curve, also known as contour line.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A level set collects all inputs at which \(f\) takes one prescribed value \(k\): it answers the question "where is \(f\) equal to \(k\)?". For a function of two variables these sets are usually curves in the plane, like contour lines on a map, where all points on one line have the same height.

As the preimage of \(\{k\}\), the level set \(L_k(f)\) lies in the domain \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), not on the graph. For \(n=2\) it is the horizontal cut of the graph at height \(z=k\), projected onto the plane of the inputs. Despite the name, a level set need not be a curve: it is empty when \(k\) is not a value of \(f\), a single point for \(x^2+y^2=0\), and all of \(X\) when \(f\) is constant and \(k\) is its value.

A family of level curves can be read like a contour map. For equally spaced values of \(k\), level curves that lie close together mean that \(f\) changes quickly there. For \(f(x,y)=x^2+y^2\) the curves for \(k=1,2,3,4\) are circles with radii \(1,\sqrt{2},\sqrt{3},2\), so the gaps \(0.41\), \(0.32\), \(0.27\) shrink as \(f\) grows faster further out.

In economics, indifference curves of a utility function and isoquants of a production function are level curves. This idea returns later in optimization with an equality constraint \(g(\boldsymbol{x})=c\): the feasible points form a level set of \(g\) (method of Lagrange).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • Different level sets for distinct values are disjoint, and the union over all possible values covers the entire domain where the function is defined.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Let \(f\colon \mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}\) be \(f(x,y)=x^2+y^2\). Level sets are circles centred at the origin for \(k>0\), a single point \((0,0)\) for \(k=0\), and empty for \(k<0\).

    The level curves \(x^2+y^2=k\) are circles of radius \(\sqrt k\) for \(k>0\). They appear in red on the graph of \(f\) and in blue in the \(xy\)-plane.

  • Let \(f\colon \mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}\) be \(f(x,y)=x+y\). Level sets are straight lines of slope \(-1\): \(x+y=k\). All level sets are parallel lines.

Move \(k\) to highlight the level curve \(L_k(f)\). Drag \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) to read off \(f\); nearby level curves crowd together where \(f\) changes fast.

Move \(k\): the plane \(z=k\) cuts the graph along the level curve \(L_k(f)\), drawn again on the floor.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \((a_n)_{n=0}^{\infty}\) be a sequence. For each \(N\in\mathbb{N}\text{,}\) consider the supremum and infimum of the terms from \(a_N\) onward: \(\displaystyle s_N = \sup_{n\geq N} a_n\) and \(\displaystyle i_N = \inf_{n\geq N} a_n\text{.}\) The limit superior and limit inferior of \((a_n)_{n=0}^{\infty}\) are defined as:

\[ \begin{aligned} \limsup_{n\to \infty}a_n &:= \lim_{N\to\infty} s_N = \inf_{N\geq 0} s_N\\ &=\inf_{N\geq 0}\sup_{n\geq N} a_n, \\ \liminf_{n\to \infty}a_n &:= \lim_{N\to\infty} i_N = \sup_{N\geq 0} i_N\\ &=\sup_{N\geq 0}\inf_{n\geq N} a_n. \end{aligned} \]

Apply the definition of a Limit of a Sequence to the tail suprema \(s_N\) and infima \(i_N\). Their monotonicity ensures extended-real limits; if the original sequence has an ordinary limit, both tail limits equal it.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The limit superior and limit inferior describe where a sequence ends up in the long run, also when it does not converge: they are the eventual upper and lower bounds of its terms. Only the tail counts, so changing finitely many terms changes neither of them.

The figure shows \(a_n=(-1)^n(1+\tfrac{2}{n})\). The tail suprema \(s_N\) form the upper step line and decrease towards \(1\); the tail infima \(i_N\) form the lower one and increase towards \(-1\). So \(\limsup a_n=1\) and \(\liminf a_n=-1\), although no term equals either value: the even terms \(1+\tfrac{2}{n}\) lie above \(1\) and the odd terms lie below \(-1\).

Move \(N\): \(s_N=\sup_{n\ge N}a_n\) can only decrease and \(i_N=\inf_{n\ge N}a_n\) can only increase. Their limits are \(\limsup a_n\) and \(\liminf a_n\).

The tail supremum \(s_N\) is taken over fewer terms as \(N\) grows, so it can only decrease, and a monotone sequence always has a limit in the extended reals. For a bounded sequence there are two equivalent readings. First, \(\limsup a_n\) is the largest limit of a convergent subsequence, and \(\liminf a_n\) is the smallest. Second, if \(L=\limsup a_n\), then for every \(\varepsilon>0\) the terms satisfy \(a_n<L+\varepsilon\) for all large \(n\), and \(a_n>L-\varepsilon\) for infinitely many \(n\).

These quantities appear wherever a sequence of interest need not converge. The root test uses \(\limsup\sqrt[n]{|a_n|}\), and the radius of convergence of a power series is \(1/\limsup|c_n|^{1/n}\).

Two slips are common. The limit superior is not the supremum of the sequence: above, \(\sup_n a_n=a_2=2\), while \(\limsup a_n=1\). And it does not behave like a limit under addition: for \(a_n=(-1)^n\) and \(b_n=-(-1)^n\), \(\limsup(a_n+b_n)=0\), while \(\limsup a_n+\limsup b_n=2\). In general only \(\limsup(a_n+b_n)\le\limsup a_n+\limsup b_n\) holds, when the right-hand side is defined.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The limit superior and limit inferior of a real sequence always exist in the extended real numbers \([-\infty,+\infty]\).
  • A sequence converges if and only if its \(\limsup\) and \(\liminf\) are equal and finite; otherwise, it's divergent.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(a_n = (-1)^n\): \(\limsup\limits_{n\to \infty}a_n = 1\text{,}\) \(\liminf\limits_{n\to \infty}a_n = -1\text{.}\)
  • For \(a_n = 1/2^n\): \(\limsup\limits_{n\to \infty}a_n = \liminf\limits_{n\to \infty}a_n = 0\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The maximum norm of \(\boldsymbol{x}=(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)\) in an \(n\)-dimensional real coordinate space \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with fixed Cartesian coordinate system is:

\[ \|\boldsymbol{x}\|_\infty=\max_{1\leq i\leq n}|x_i|. \]

Correspondingly, the Chebyshev distance between \(\boldsymbol{x}=(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)\) and \(\boldsymbol{y}=(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_n)\) is calculated as:

\[ d_\infty(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})=\max_{1\leq i\leq n}|x_i-y_i|. \]

This is a norm because it is zero only at the zero vector, scales with absolute scalar size, and obeys the triangle inequality coordinate by coordinate. The induced distance is a metric distance. Comparison with the Euclidean Norm gives \(\|\boldsymbol{x}\|_\infty\le\|\boldsymbol{x}\|_2\le\sqrt n\,\|\boldsymbol{x}\|_\infty\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The maximum norm measures a vector by its largest coordinate in absolute value; the other coordinates do not matter as long as they are smaller. It is the limiting case of the \(p\)-norm as \(p\to+\infty\).

The square is the closed unit ball \(\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\|\boldsymbol{x}\|_\infty\le1\}\): a point lies in it exactly when both coordinates lie in \([-1,1]\). The marked point \(\boldsymbol{x}=(0.6,-1)\) lies on the edge because its largest coordinate in absolute value is \(|-1|=1\); the coordinate \(0.6\) does not change the norm. The dashed Euclidean unit circle lies inside the square, which is the inequality \(\|\boldsymbol{x}\|_\infty\le\|\boldsymbol{x}\|_2\).

With \(\|\boldsymbol x\|_\infty=\max(|x_1|,|x_2|)\) the unit circle is a square. Drag \(\boldsymbol x\) and compare the three norms.

The Chebyshev distance \(d_\infty(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})\) is small if and only if every coordinate of \(\boldsymbol{x}\) is close to the corresponding coordinate of \(\boldsymbol{y}\). This makes it convenient in proofs: \(d_\infty(\boldsymbol{x}_k,\boldsymbol{x})\to0\) says exactly that each coordinate sequence converges, and since the maximum norm is equivalent to the Euclidean norm, convergence in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is the same as convergence of each coordinate.

For functions, taking the largest absolute value becomes the uniform norm \(\|f\|_\infty=\sup_x|f(x)|\): the values \(f(x)\) play the role of the coordinates, and the maximum becomes a supremum because there may be infinitely many of them.

A common slip is to take the maximum of the signed coordinates. The absolute values come first: \(\|(-3,2)\|_\infty=3\), not \(2\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The closed unit ball in the maximum norm is an axis-aligned hypercube
\[ \overline{B}_{d_\infty}(\boldsymbol{0},1)=[-1,1]^n. \]

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A metric space \((X, d)\) consists of a set of points \(X\) and a distance function (or metric) \(d\colon X \times X \to [0,+\infty)\) that maps pairs of points to nonnegative real values. The metric adheres to the following properties:

  1. Nonnegativity: \(d(x,y) \geq 0\) for any \(x, y \in X\text{.}\)
  2. Identity of indiscernibles: \(d(x,y) = 0\) if and only if \(x=y\text{.}\)
  3. Symmetry: \(d(x,y) = d(y,x)\) for any \(x, y \in X\text{.}\)
  4. Triangle inequality: \(d(x,z) \leq d(x,y) + d(y,z)\) for any \(x, y, z \in X\text{.}\)

The Triangle Inequality requires a direct distance to be no greater than a journey through an intermediate point. The absolute-value inequality \(|x-z|\le|x-y|+|y-z|\) is its real-line instance.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A metric space is a set of points with a clear and reasonable rule for measuring the distance between any two of them. The axioms keep only what every sensible notion of distance has in common, so that one definition of convergence covers numbers, vectors and even functions.

The figure shows the triangle inequality for three points: the red direct distance \(d(x,z)\) is at most the sum \(d(x,y)+d(y,z)\) of the two blue distances through the intermediate point \(y\). A detour through another point is never shorter than the direct route.

Each axiom has a job. Identity of indiscernibles makes distinct points distinguishable, which is why a convergent sequence has only one limit. Symmetry makes "\(x\) is close to \(y\)" a mutual relation. The triangle inequality lets small distances be chained, which is what arguments with \(\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}\) use. Nonnegativity even follows from the other three: \(0=d(x,x)\le d(x,y)+d(y,x)=2\,d(x,y)\).

On \(\mathbb{R}\) the usual metric is \(d(x,y)=|x-y|\), built from the absolute value, and on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) it is the Euclidean distance from Math II. Every norm gives a metric \(d(x,y)=\|x-y\|\), but a metric needs no vector structure: the discrete metric works on any set.

A common slip is to treat a metric space as just a set. The same set can carry several metrics, such as the Euclidean and the taxicab metric on \(\mathbb{R}^2\), and statements about convergence or completeness depend on which one is meant. That is why a metric space is written as the pair \((X,d)\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Metrics are always nonnegative. The only point at a zero distance from a point \(x\) is \(x\) itself.
  • Metrics are symmetric and adhere to the triangle inequality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The Euclidean distance in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is defined as \(\displaystyle d(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{y}) = \left(\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - y_i)^2\right)^{1/2}\text{.}\)
  • The complex numbers \(\mathbb{C}\) with the distance function (based on modulus) \(d(z,w) = |z-w|\) form a metric space.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A monomial on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is a function from \(\mathbb{R}^n\) to \(\mathbb{R}\) given by a product of real coefficients and variables raised to nonnegative integer powers, i.e., a monomial has the general expression

\[ f(x_1,x_2,\dots,x_n) = a x_1^{k_1} x_2^{k_2} \cdots x_n^{k_n}, \]

with constant \(a \in \mathbb{R}\) and exponents \(k_1,\, \dots,\, k_n \in \mathbb{N}\). The total degree of a monomial on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is the sum of the exponents of all variables appearing in that monomial, i.e., \(k_1+\cdots+k_n\).

For \(n=1\) this is the usual Monomial; for several variables it is a Function between Spaces from an input tuple to one real output.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A monomial on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is the simplest building block of a polynomial in several variables: a constant times a product of powers of the variables, such as \(-2x^2y\). Its total degree counts the variable factors in that product with repetition, so \(x^2y=x\cdot x\cdot y\) has total degree \(3\).

The exponent tuple \((k_1,\dots,k_n)\) records how often each variable occurs, and an exponent \(0\) means that the variable is absent: on \(\mathbb{R}^3\), \(x_1^4\) is the monomial with exponents \((4,0,0)\). The total degree differs from the degree in a single variable: \(x^2y\) has degree \(2\) in \(x\), degree \(1\) in \(y\), and total degree \(3\). Scaling all variables by \(c\) shows why the total degree matters:

\[ a(cx_1)^{k_1}\cdots(cx_n)^{k_n}=c^{k_1+\cdots+k_n}\,ax_1^{k_1}\cdots x_n^{k_n}, \]

so the total degree is the degree of homogeneity (Key Results).

A common slip is to allow other exponents. The exponents must be nonnegative integers, so \(x^{1/2}y^{1/2}\) and \(x^{-1}y\) are not monomials, although on \((0,\infty)^2\) they are homogeneous functions of degrees \(1\) and \(0\).

For \(n=1\) a monomial is the familiar monomial \(ax^k\). Finite sums of monomials are the polynomials on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), and sums of monomials of one total degree are homogeneous polynomials. The monomials of total degree \(2\) are the multiples \(ax_ix_j\) of the products of two variables, the terms of a quadratic form.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The product of two monomials is again a monomial. The exponents add componentwise, and the constant multiplies.
  • Every monomial is a homogeneous function whose degree equals its total degree.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(f(x,y)=-2x^2y\)  is a monomial with exponents \(k_1=2\), \(k_2=1\), total degree \(3\).
  • The monomial \(f(x,y)=x^4\) has \(k_1=4\), \(k_2=0\), total degree \(4\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A norm on a vector space \(V\) over the scalar field \(\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{R}\) or \(\mathbb{C}\) (in this course \(\mathbb{R}\)) is a function \(\|\cdot\|\colon V\to[0,+\infty)\) that adheres to the following criteria:

  1. Nonnegativity and definiteness: For any \(\boldsymbol{x} \in V\), \(\|\boldsymbol{x}\| \geq 0\), and \(\|\boldsymbol{x}\| = 0\) if and only if \(\boldsymbol{x} = \boldsymbol{0}\).
  2. Absolute homogeneity (absolute scalability): For any scalar \(c \in \mathbb{F}\) and any \(\boldsymbol{x} \in V\), \(\|c\boldsymbol{x}\| = |c|\cdot\|\boldsymbol{x}\|\), where \(|c|\) is the absolute value (modulus) of \(c\).
  3. Triangle inequality: For any \(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{y} \in V\): \(\|\boldsymbol{x} + \boldsymbol{y}\| \leq \|\boldsymbol{x}\| + \|\boldsymbol{y}\|\).

A normed vector space \((V, \|\cdot\|)\) is a vector space \(V\) over \(\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{R}\) or \(\mathbb{C}\), equipped with a norm \(\|\cdot\|\).

The norm version of the Triangle Inequality bounds the length of a sum by the sum of the lengths. The Euclidean Norm \(\|\boldsymbol{x}\|_2=\sqrt{x_1^2+\cdots+x_n^2}\) is the standard example satisfying all three axioms.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A norm is a rule that assigns a length to every vector in a way that fits the vector-space operations. A normed vector space is a vector space in which every vector has such a length, and scaling or adding vectors changes lengths as one would expect.

The upper part of the figure shows the triangle inequality: \(\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{y}\) is the diagonal of the parallelogram spanned by \(\boldsymbol{x}\) and \(\boldsymbol{y}\), and its length is at most \(\|\boldsymbol{x}\|+\|\boldsymbol{y}\|\). The lower part shows absolute homogeneity: stretching \(\boldsymbol{x}\) by the factor \(3\) multiplies its length by \(3\).

Each \(p\ge1\) gives a norm on \(\mathbb R^2\) with its own unit circle; all of them are convex and symmetric about \(\boldsymbol 0\).

Absolute homogeneity also covers negative scalars, so \(\|-\boldsymbol{x}\|=\|\boldsymbol{x}\|\): a vector and its opposite have the same length. Together the three axioms make \(d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})=\|\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{y}\|\) a metric, and a metric of this form has two properties that a general metric lacks: it does not change under translation, \(d(\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{y}+\boldsymbol{z})=d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})\), and it scales, \(d(c\boldsymbol{x},c\boldsymbol{y})=|c|\,d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})\). The discrete metric does not scale, since \(d_{\mathrm{disc}}(2\boldsymbol{x},2\boldsymbol{y})=1\) for \(\boldsymbol{x}\ne\boldsymbol{y}\), so it comes from no norm.

The Euclidean norm from Math II is one norm among many. The \(p\)-norms, including the taxicab norm and the maximum norm, are others on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), and the uniform norm measures bounded functions.

Norms return in Math V, where the largest singular value of a matrix serves as a length for matrices.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • Given a normed vector space \((V, \|\cdot\|)\), one can define the metric as \(d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}) = \|\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{y}\|,\) making \((V, d)\) inherently a metric space.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The real line \(\mathbb{R}\) with the absolute-value norm forms a normed vector space over \(\mathbb{R}\).
  • The plane \(\mathbb{R}^2\) with the Euclidean norm is similarly a normed vector space. Using the taxicab norm, \(\mathbb{R}^2\) remains a normed vector space.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \((f_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) be a sequence of bounded functions on \(X\). We say the series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n(x)\) is normally convergent if the series of uniform norms of the terms of the series converges, i.e., \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \|f_n\|_\infty<+\infty.\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Normal convergence asks that the worst-case sizes \(\|f_n\|_\infty\) of the terms form a convergent numerical series. Instead of studying \(\sum_n f_n(x)\) at every \(x\), one attaches a single number to each term, its uniform norm; if these numbers are summable, the series of functions is controlled everywhere at once.

In the figure, \(\|f_n\|_\infty=1/n^2\). The bars are the norms, decreasing to \(0\), and the partial sums of the norms increase towards \(\pi^2/6\approx1.645\). Because the series of norms converges, its tail bounds the error everywhere: after \(N\) terms, the partial sum of the function series differs from its limit by at most \(\sum_{n>N}1/n^2\) at every \(x\), less than \(0.1\) for \(N=10\).

\(\displaystyle \sum_n\|f_n\|_\infty=\sum_n 1/n^2\) converges, so the partial sums stay within the shrinking band around the limit.

The condition involves only numbers, so it is checked with the tests for numerical series, such as comparison with a \(p\)-series. Normal convergence is exactly the hypothesis of the Weierstrass \(M\)-test, which turns it into uniform convergence; at each fixed \(x\) it also gives absolute convergence of \(\sum_n f_n(x)\), since \(|f_n(x)|\le\|f_n\|_\infty\). The name refers to the norm.

The implications in the Key Results go one way only. The Examples give a series that converges absolutely and uniformly but not normally. A uniformly convergent series also need not converge absolutely: the constant functions \(f_n(x)=(-1)^n/n\) form a uniformly convergent alternating series, while \(\sum_n\|f_n\|_\infty\) is the harmonic series. Normal convergence is a convenient sufficient condition, not a description of all uniformly convergent series.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Normal convergence implies uniform absolute convergence (the series \(\sum_n|f_n(x)|\) converges uniformly), which in turn implies uniform convergence, which in turn implies pointwise convergence, i.e.,
\[ \begin{aligned} \sum_{n=1}^\infty \|f_n\|_\infty<+\infty &\implies \sum_{n=1}^\infty |f_n(x)|\rightrightarrows g\\ &\implies \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n(x)\rightrightarrows f\\ &\implies \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n(x)\to f. \end{aligned} \]

Here \(g\) is the sum of the absolute series; it differs from \(f\) unless every \(f_n\ge0\text{.}\)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Uniform absolute convergence does not imply normal convergence. On \(X=\mathbb{N}\), consider

\[ f_n(x)=\begin{cases} 1/n, &x=n,\\[2pt] 0, &x\neq n. \end{cases} \]

The absolute series converges uniformly: its tail after the first \(N\) terms has supremum \(1/(N+1)\), which tends to zero. However, \(\|f_n\|_\infty=1/n\), so the series of uniform norms is the harmonic series and diverges.

docs.title: Open and Closed Sets in a Metric Space
Definition
docs.text:
For a metric space \((X,d)\) and its subset \(E\):

  • \(E\) is closed if it includes all of its boundary points, i.e., \(\partial E \subseteq E\).
  • \(E\) is open if it doesn't include any of its boundary points, i.e., \(\partial E \cap E = \varnothing\).
  • \(E\) is neither open nor closed if it includes some but not all of its boundary points.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Openness and closedness are decided by the boundary of a set. Open sets keep their boundary points out, closed sets keep them in, and sets that include some boundary points but not others are neither open nor closed.

All three discs in the figure have the same boundary, the circle. A dashed rim means that the circle is excluded, as for the open disc \(\{d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}_0)<r\}\); a solid rim means it is included, as for the closed disc \(\{d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}_0)\le r\}\). The third disc contains half of its rim, so it fails both conditions.

The Key Results give two working descriptions. A set is open if and only if every point of it is an interior point: around each point there is a ball inside the set, so one cannot reach the outside by a small step. A set is closed if and only if it contains the limits of its convergent sequences, so one cannot leave it by passing to a limit. Since \(E\) is open exactly when its complement is closed, every statement about open sets has a mirror statement about closed sets.

A common slip is to treat "open" and "closed" as opposites. The interval \([0,1)\) in \(\mathbb{R}\) is neither, while \(\varnothing\) and \(X\) are always both. Showing that a set is not open therefore does not show that it is closed.

Open sets are also the raw material of a topology, which keeps the open sets and forgets the distances; later, continuity and compactness are expressed through open sets as well.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A set \(E\) is open if and only if \(E = \operatorname{int}E\).
  • A set \(F\) is closed if and only if every convergent sequence \((x_i)_{i=1}^{\infty}\) within \(F\) converges to a limiting point lying in \(F\).
  • A set \(E\) is open if and only if its complement \(E^\complement=X\setminus E\) is closed.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a metric space \((X,d)\), a point \(x_0\) in \(X\), and \(r > 0\), the open metric ball \(B_{(X,d)}(x_0,r)\) in \(X\), centred at \(x_0\) with radius \(r\) in metric \(d\), is defined as the following set:

\[ B_{(X,d)}(x_0,r) = \{x \in X \colon d(x, x_0) < r\}. \]

If the context is clear, we'll abbreviate this as \(B_d(x_0,r)\) or simply \(B(x_0,r).\)

A ball is a subset of \(X\) selected by the distance condition; the ambient space matters, so a real-line ball and a plane ball have different members.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An open metric ball is the set of all points whose distance from the centre \(x_0\) is strictly less than the radius \(r\). In \(\mathbb{R}\) with \(d(x,y)=|x-y|\) it is the open interval \((x_0-r,x_0+r)\), and in the plane with the Euclidean distance it is an open disc.

The green point satisfies \(d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}_0)<r\) and belongs to the ball. The red point on the dashed rim has \(d=r\) exactly and is excluded, because the inequality in the definition is strict.

Change the centre, the radius \(r\) and the metric: the ball contains the points at distance less than \(r\). Points on the dashed sphere are not included.

The strict inequality is what makes the ball an open set. If \(d(x,x_0)<r\), put \(s=r-d(x,x_0)>0\). By the triangle inequality, every \(y\) with \(d(y,x)<s\) has \(d(y,x_0)<s+d(x,x_0)=r\), so \(B(x,s)\subseteq B(x_0,r)\): every point of the ball has a smaller ball around it that still fits inside.

"Ball" refers to the distance condition, not to a round shape. In \(\mathbb{R}^2\) the unit ball is a diamond for the taxicab metric and the open square \((-1,1)^2\) for the distance of the maximum norm; here the centre is the origin.

Open balls are the basic building block of analysis in metric spaces: interior points and open sets are defined with them, and convergence \(x_i\to x\) means that every ball \(B(x,\varepsilon)\) contains all but finitely many terms. On the real line, \(B(a,\delta)\) is the set \(|x-a|<\delta\) familiar from the absolute value and the \(\varepsilon\)-\(\delta\) definitions of Math I. Later, continuity between metric spaces is phrased with balls in the same way.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Open balls are open sets.
  • A subset of a metric space is open if and only if it can be written as a union of open balls.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In \(\mathbb{R}^2\) with the usual distance, \(B((0,0),1)\) is the open disc of radius \(1\) centred at the origin. Points with \(x^2 + y^2 < 1\) are elements of this ball.
  • In \(\mathbb{R}^2\) with the taxicab metric \(d_1\), \(B((0,0),1)\) is a diamond shape with vertices at \((\pm1,0)\) and \((0,\pm1)\).
  • In any set with the discrete metric, \(B(x,1) = \{x\}\) and \(B(x,0.5) = \{x\}\), but \(B(x,2)\) is the whole space.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\boldsymbol{x}=(x_1,x_2, \ldots,x_n)\in\mathbb{R}^n\). For \(p\in[1,+\infty)\), the \(p\)-norm, denoted \(\|\cdot\|_p\), is defined on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) by:

\[ \|\boldsymbol{x}\|_p = \left(\sum_{i=1}^n |x_i|^p\right)^{\frac{1}{p}}. \]

For \(p=+\infty\) one sets \(\|\boldsymbol{x}\|_\infty=\max\limits_{1\le i\le n}|x_i|\), which is the limit of \(\|\boldsymbol{x}\|_p\) as \(p\to+\infty\).

Correspondingly, the \(p\)-metric \(d_p\) is defined as \(d_p(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})=\|\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{y}\|_p\), that is,

\[ \begin{aligned} d_p(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})&=\left(\sum_{i=1}^n |x_i-y_i|^p\right)^{\frac{1}{p}}\qquad (1\le p<+\infty),\\ d_\infty(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})&=\max_{1\le i\le n}|x_i-y_i|. \end{aligned} \]

The formula uses Exponentiation and Power twice: raise the coordinate magnitudes to \(p\), then take the \(1/p\) power of their sum. The value \(+\infty\) is an Extended Real Number indexing the separate maximum-norm limit, not a finite exponent to substitute directly. Setting \(p=2\) recovers the Euclidean Norm.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The \(p\)-norm is a way of measuring the size of a vector by raising each coordinate's absolute value to the \(p\)-th power, summing them, and taking the \(p\)-th root. The exponent decides how much weight the large coordinates get: \(p=1\) adds all coordinates equally, \(p=2\) gives the Euclidean length, and as \(p\to+\infty\) only the largest coordinate counts.

The figure compares the unit balls \(\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\|\boldsymbol{x}\|_p\le1\}\) for \(p=1,2,4,\infty\). As \(p\) increases, these balls expand from the diamond towards the square, because \(\|\boldsymbol{x}\|_q\le\|\boldsymbol{x}\|_p\) whenever \(p\le q\). All four boundaries pass through \((\pm1,0)\) and \((0,\pm1)\): a vector with a single nonzero coordinate has the same \(p\)-norm for every \(p\).

Move \(p\): the unit circle \(\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\|\boldsymbol{x}\|_p=1\}\) swells from the diamond at \(p=1\) through the circle at \(p=2\) towards the square at \(p=\infty\). Drag \(\boldsymbol{x}\) to compare its norms.

The restriction \(p\ge1\) is needed for the triangle inequality. For \(p=\tfrac{1}{2}\) the formula gives \(\|(1,0)\|_{1/2}=\|(0,1)\|_{1/2}=1\) but \(\|(1,1)\|_{1/2}=(1+1)^2=4>1+1\). Geometrically, the set \(\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\|\boldsymbol{x}\|_{1/2}\le1\}\) is pinched inwards between the axes: it contains \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\), but not the midpoint \((\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{2})\), whose value is \(2\).

Different \(p\) give different distances but the same analysis: from \(\|\boldsymbol{x}\|_\infty\le\|\boldsymbol{x}\|_p\le n^{1/p}\|\boldsymbol{x}\|_\infty\), all \(p\)-norms on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) are equivalent, and the \(p\)-metrics are strongly equivalent, with the same convergent sequences.

A common slip is to drop the outer root and use \(\sum_i|x_i|^p\) as the norm. For \(p>1\) this is not a norm: it scales like \(|c|^p\) instead of \(|c|\), so absolute homogeneity fails.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • The smallest permissible value for \(p\) in the \(p\)-norm is \(1\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The Euclidean distance \(d_2\) is a particular \(p\)-metric when \(p=2\).
  • The taxicab distance \(d_1\) is a particular \(p\)-metric when \(p=1\).
  • The maximum norm \(\|\cdot\|_\infty\) is a particular \(p\)-norm when \(p=+\infty\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\) and consider a function \(\boldsymbol{f} \colon E \to \mathbb{R}^k\). For an interior point \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) of \(E\) and an integer \(1 \leq j \leq n\), the partial derivative of \(\boldsymbol{f}\) with respect to the \(x_j\)-variable at \(\boldsymbol{x} = \boldsymbol{x}_0\), denoted by \(\displaystyle \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial x_j}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\), is given by

\[ \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial x_j}(\boldsymbol{x}_0) = \lim_{{t\to0}} \frac{\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0 + t\boldsymbol{e}_j) - \boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)}{t} = \left.\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0 + t\boldsymbol{e}_j)\,\right|_{t=0}, \]

where \(\boldsymbol{e}_j\) represents the unit vector in the positive direction of the \(j\)-th coordinate, provided the limit exists.

The partial derivative changes only the \(j\)th coordinate, so it is the Directional Derivative along the coordinate vector \(\boldsymbol{e}_j\) when the corresponding two-sided limit exists.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The partial derivative measures how the function changes when you nudge only one coordinate while keeping all others fixed. It is an ordinary derivative of the one-variable function \(t\mapsto\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0+t\boldsymbol{e}_j)\) at \(t=0\), as the second line of the Definition shows.

The vertical plane \(x_2=b\) cuts the graph of \(f\) in the red curve \(x_1\mapsto f(x_1,b)\), which is the graph of a function of \(x_1\) alone. Its tangent line at \((a,b)\) has slope \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1}(a,b)\). Cutting with the plane \(x_1=a\) instead gives a curve in the \(x_2\)-direction, and its slope at \((a,b)\) is \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_2}(a,b)\).

Choose \(j\): along the line \(\boldsymbol x_0+t\boldsymbol e_j\) the function becomes a one-variable function (right), and \(\partial f/\partial x_j\) is its slope at \(t=0\).

Freeze one variable: the graph is cut along a line through \(\boldsymbol x_0\), and \(\partial f/\partial x_j\) is the slope of that slice. Edit \(f\) to try your own function.

In practice, one treats every other variable as a constant and differentiates with the one-variable rules, as in the Example. For a vector-valued \(\boldsymbol{f}\), the partial derivative is a vector in \(\mathbb{R}^k\), computed component by component. These vectors are the columns of the Jacobian matrix, and for a real-valued \(f\) the partial derivatives form the gradient.

A common slip is to expect partial derivatives to describe the function in every direction. They only look along the coordinate axes. The function with \(f(x,y)=xy/(x^2+y^2)\) for \((x,y)\neq(0,0)\) and \(f(0,0)=0\) vanishes on both axes, so both partial derivatives at the origin are \(0\). Yet it is not even continuous there, since \(f(t,t)=\tfrac{1}{2}\) for every \(t\neq0\). Existence of partial derivatives is therefore weaker than total differentiability; the Key Results give a sufficient condition, continuity of the partial derivatives, that closes the gap.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The partial derivative \(\displaystyle \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial x_j}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\) exists if and only if both \(\mathrm{D}_{\boldsymbol{e}_j}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\) and \(\mathrm{D}_{-\boldsymbol{e}_j}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\) exist and are negatives of each other. In such a scenario, we have \(\displaystyle \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial x_j}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)=\mathrm{D}_{\boldsymbol{e}_j}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0).\)
  • If \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is totally differentiable at \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\text{,}\) then for every unit vector \(\displaystyle \boldsymbol{v} = (v_1,\,\ldots,\,v_n)= \sum_{j=1}^n v_j\boldsymbol{e}_j\) we have \(\displaystyle \mathrm{D}_{\boldsymbol{v}}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0) = \sum_{j=1}^n v_j \frac{\partial }{\partial x_j}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0).\) Without total differentiability this can fail even when all partial derivatives exist.
  • If all the partial derivatives are both existent within a neighbourhood and continuous at the centre, then \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is totally differentiable at this point.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • The partial derivative of \(f(x,y) = 3x^2y^2 + 4xy^3 + 7y\) with respect to the first variable is \(\dfrac{\partial }{\partial x}f(x,y) = 6xy^2 + 4y^3.\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: In the metric space \((X, d_{X})\text{,}\) a nonempty subset \(E\) is termed path-connected if, for any two distinct points \(a, b \in E\text{,}\) a path \(p\colon [0,1] \to E\) exists such that \(p(0) = a\) and \(p(1) = b\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
You can walk from any point to any other point in a path-connected set without ever leaving the set: there is a path inside \(E\) that joins them. It is a constructive way of saying that a set is in one piece.

The path must lie in \(E\) for every \(t\in[0,1]\), not only at its endpoints; a straight segment between two points of \(E\) that leaves \(E\) on the way does not count. Restricting the definition to distinct points loses nothing, since a constant path joins a point to itself.

To show that a set is path-connected, one writes down paths. In a set that contains the straight segment between any two of its points, such as a disc, a box or \(\mathbb{R}^n\) itself, the segment \(p(t)=(1-t)a+tb\) always works. Other sets need bent paths: the annulus \(\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon 1\le\|\boldsymbol{x}\|\le2\}\) is path-connected, because any two of its points can be joined by an arc of a circle followed by a radial segment.

Every path-connected set is connected, as the Key Results state, and path-connectedness is usually the easiest way to prove connectedness. In \(\mathbb{R}\) the two notions coincide, since both describe the intervals, and for open subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) they coincide as well.

A common slip is to assume that the converse holds in general. The two Examples are connected sets with a point that no path inside the set reaches: one oscillates and the other crowds towards that point, so the set stays in one piece without being traversable.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • In the metric space \((X, d_{X})\text{,}\) any path-connected subset of \(X\) is connected.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The topologist's sine curve is connected but not path-connected:

    \[ \{(0,0)\}\cup\{(x,\sin(1/x))\colon x>0\}. \]

    As \(x\to0^+\) the graph oscillates ever faster between \(-1\) and \(1\); the set is connected, but no path inside it reaches \((0,0)\).

  • The collection of line segments joining the origin to points \((1, 1/n)\) for all positive integers \(n\), together with the point \((1,0)\) is also connected but not path-connected.

    Segments from the origin to \((1,1/n)\) crowd towards the missing segment to \((1,0)\); only its endpoint \((1,0)\) belongs to the set, and no path inside the set reaches it.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: In a metric space \((X, d_{X})\), a path is a continuous function \(p\colon [0,1] \to X\). If for two points \(a, b \in X\), the path \(p\) satisfies \(p(0) = a\) and \(p(1) = b\), it is termed as a path from \(a\) to \(b\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A path is a continuous journey from one point to another within the space: the parameter \(t\) runs through \([0,1]\) like time, and \(p(t)\) is the position at time \(t\). It is like drawing a curve without lifting your pencil, with the curve entirely contained in the space.

The interval \([0,1]\) on the left is the domain of \(p\), and the red curve in \(X\) is its image. The start \(p(0)=a\) and the end \(p(1)=b\) are the endpoints of the curve, and an intermediate time \(t\) is sent to the point \(p(t)\) on the way. Continuity of \(p\) means that close times give close positions, so the curve has no jumps.

A path is the function \(p\), not only the curve it traces. Different paths can trace the same curve: \(t\mapsto p(t^2)\) runs through the same points as \(p\), at a different speed. A path may also stop, run back over itself or be constant, and it may have corners, since only continuity is required, not differentiability.

Paths define path-connectedness, and they reduce questions about a set to questions on \([0,1]\): for a continuous real-valued \(f\), the composition \(f\circ p\) is a continuous function of one variable. This is how the intermediate value theorem on connected sets can be proved for path-connected sets. Math IV studies differentiable curves through their velocity vectors and the chain rule on a curve.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(p\) is a path from \(a\) to \(b\) and \(q\) is a path from \(b\) to \(c\), then it is possible to construct a path from \(a\) to \(c\) using \(p\) and \(q\). This is called the concatenation.
  • For any path \(p\) from \(a\) to \(b\), the reverse path \(p(1-t)\) is a path from \(b\) to \(a\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In Euclidean space, the function \(\boldsymbol{p}(t)=(1-t)\boldsymbol{a}+t\boldsymbol{b}\) is a path from \(\boldsymbol{a}\) to \(\boldsymbol{b}\).
  • The function \(\boldsymbol{p}(t)=(\cos(2\pi t),\sin(2\pi t))\) is a path from \((1,0)\) back to itself (a loop).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \((f_n)_{n=1}^{\infty}\) be a sequence of functions \(f_n\colon X\to \mathbb{R}\) and \(f\colon X \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) be another function. We say that \((f_n)_{n=1}^{\infty}\) converges pointwise to \(f\) on \(X\) and write \(f_n\to f\text{,}\) if for every \(x \in X\text{,}\) \(\displaystyle \lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} f_n(x) = f(x)\text{.}\)

Each \(f_n\) is a Function, so fixing \(x\) gives an ordinary numerical sequence \(f_n(x)\). Its Limit of a Sequence is \(f(x)\); the required index may depend on this fixed \(x\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Pointwise convergence means that for each fixed point \(x\in X\), the numbers \(f_n(x)\) form an ordinary sequence that tends to \(f(x)\) as \(n\to\infty\). The functions are compared with the limit one point at a time, and nothing is required about how the points relate to each other.

Written out with quantifiers: for every \(x\in X\) and every \(\varepsilon>0\) there is an \(N\) such that \(|f_n(x)-f(x)|<\varepsilon\) for all \(n>N\). The index \(N\) may depend on both \(\varepsilon\) and \(x\). If one \(N\) can be chosen for all \(x\) at once, the convergence is uniform; the two notions differ only in this order of quantifiers.

Because the required \(N\) may grow without bound as \(x\) moves, properties of the \(f_n\) need not survive in the limit, as the Key Results state. The functions \(x^n\) on \([0,1]\) are continuous, but their pointwise limit is \(0\) on \([0,1)\) and \(1\) at \(x=1\), so it is not continuous. Integrals are not preserved either: on \([0,1]\), let \(f_n=n\) on \((0,\tfrac{1}{n})\) and \(f_n=0\) elsewhere. Then \(f_n(x)\to0\) at every \(x\), while \(\int_0^1 f_n(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=1\) for every \(n\).

A common slip is to let the point move with \(n\). Pointwise convergence fixes \(x\) first and only then lets \(n\to\infty\). For \(x^n\), the values \((1-\tfrac{1}{n})^n\) tend to \(\mathrm{e}^{-1}\), not to \(0\); this does not contradict pointwise convergence to \(0\) on \([0,1)\), but it does show that the convergence is not uniform.

The same idea returns in probability: almost-sure convergence of random variables is pointwise convergence on the sample space outside a set of probability zero.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Pointwise convergence guarantees that the limit exists at each individual point.
  • Pointwise convergence does not preserve boundedness, limits/continuity, differentiability, or integrals.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(f_n(x) = \dfrac{n}{nx + 1}\) converges pointwise to \(f(x)=1/x\) on \((0,+\infty)\text{.}\)
  • \(f_n(x)=\dfrac{x^2}{\sqrt{x^2+1 / n}}\) converges pointwise to \(f(x)=|x|.\)

For each fixed \(x\), \(f_n(x)\to|x|\); at \(x=-1\) the values \(f_n(-1)\) (dots) increase to \(f(-1)=1\).

Point at a value \(x\): the numbers \(f_n(x)\) (right) enter the \(\varepsilon\)-band from some \(N(x)\) on. For \(x^n\) that \(N(x)\) grows without bound as \(x\to1\).
