docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A polynomial on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is a real-valued function that is a finite sum of monomials on \(\mathbb{R}^n\). The degree of a polynomial on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is defined as the maximum, over all its monomials with nonzero coefficient, of the total degree of each monomial (the zero polynomial is usually left without a degree).

With one variable this reduces to an ordinary Polynomial; with several variables the same finite-sum construction uses multivariate monomials.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A polynomial in several variables is a finite sum of monomials. Its degree is the highest total degree among the monomials that appear with nonzero coefficient.

The plotted polynomial \(p(x_1,x_2)=x_1^3-3x_1x_2^2\) is the sum of two monomials, each of total degree \(3\). In polar coordinates \(p=r^3\cos3\theta\), so around the origin the surface rises and falls three times. Along the \(x_1\)-axis it is the cubic \(x_1^3\), which takes both signs near \(0\), so the surface has neither a peak nor a pit at the origin.

Drag the picture to turn it. \(x_1^3-3x_1x_2^2\) has degree \(3\); compare it with the degree-\(2\) examples, whose graphs are bowls and saddles.

The degree counts total degree, not the largest single exponent: \(x^2y^2\) has degree \(4\), although no variable appears with a power above \(2\). In a sum, top-degree terms can cancel, so \((x^2+y)+(-x^2)=y\) has degree \(1\); this is why the Key Results give only an upper bound for the degree of a sum.

Low degrees give familiar functions. The polynomials of degree at most \(1\), together with the zero polynomial, are exactly the affine functions \(a_1x_1+\cdots+a_nx_n+b\). A polynomial whose terms all have degree \(2\) is a quadratic form. Grouping the terms by total degree writes every polynomial as a sum of homogeneous polynomials.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The degree of the sum of two polynomials is at most the maximum of their degrees. The degree of the product of two polynomials is the sum of their degrees.
  • Polynomials are infinitely differentiable. All partial derivatives of all orders exist and are themselves polynomials (or zero).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(f(x,y) = x^2 + 2xy + y^2 + x + 1\) is a polynomial of degree 2. Its highest total degree comes from \(x^2\), \(xy\), and \(y^2\), all degree 2.
  • \(f(x,y) = x^3 + xy + y^2\) has degree 3 from the \(x^3\) term.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(a \in \mathbb{R}\text{.}\) A power series centred at \(a\) is expressed as \(\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n (x-a)^n\text{,}\) where \((c_n)_{n=0}^\infty\) is a sequence of real numbers, independent of \(x\text{.}\) We refer to \(c_n\) as the \(n\)-th coefficient of the power series.

Viewed as an Infinite Series of Functions, its \(n\)th summand is \(x\mapsto c_n(x-a)^n\). Convergence asks whether the partial sums of these functions have a limit at the chosen \(x\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A power series is an infinite sum of power functions \(c_n(x-a)^n\), a polynomial of unlimited degree centred at \(a\). For each fixed \(x\) it is a numerical series that may or may not converge; the definition itself does not say for which \(x\) it does.

The figure takes \(a=0\) and \(c_n=1\) for all \(n\), the geometric series \(\sum_n x^n\), and shows its partial sums with \(2\), \(4\) and \(8\) terms next to \(1/(1-x)\). On the shaded interval \((-1,1)\) the partial sums approach \(1/(1-x)\); outside it the terms \(x^n\) do not tend to \(0\), and the partial sums move away. The function \(1/(1-x)\) exists for \(x<-1\) as well, but the series does not represent it there.

Raise \(N\): inside the shaded interval of convergence the partial sums settle on the sum; outside they run away.

The centre \(a\) and the coefficients \(c_n\) determine the series. At \(x=a\) every term with \(n\ge1\) vanishes and the sum is \(c_0\); here \((x-a)^0\) is read as \(1\) even at \(x=a\). Away from the centre, convergence depends on the distance \(|x-a|\), which is measured by the radius of convergence. Within that radius the sum is a differentiable function that can be differentiated term by term, by the theorem on convergence of power series.

Power series are how many standard functions are defined or computed. The series \(1+x+\tfrac{x^2}{2}+\tfrac{x^3}{6}+\cdots\) in the Examples has sum \(\mathrm{e}^x\), the exponential function. A function that equals a power series near each point of an open interval is real analytic; the series is then built from the derivatives of the function at the centre, which returns later as the Taylor series.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • The definition is formal: it does not say for which \(x\) the series converges. Every power series has a radius of convergence \(R\in[0,+\infty]\): it converges absolutely for \(|x-a|<R\) and diverges for \(|x-a|>R\text{.}\)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Any polynomial is a special case of a power series, since the coefficients \(c_n\) are allowed to be zero.
  • \(1+x+\dfrac{x^2}{2}+\dfrac{x^3}{6}+\cdots\) is a power series.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a given power series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n (x-a)^n\text{,}\) its radius of convergence \(R\) is a nonnegative real number or \(+\infty\) such that the series converges if \(|x-a|<R\) and diverges if \(|x-a|>R\text{.}\) The interval of convergence is the set of all values of \(x\) for which the series converges.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The radius of convergence tells how far from the centre \(a\) a power series converges. Apart from the boundary, only the distance \(|x-a|\) matters: the series converges at every \(x\) within distance \(R\) of the centre and diverges at every \(x\) further away.

The figure shows the open interval \((a-R,a+R)\) where the series converges (absolutely), the radius \(R\) as an arrow from the centre, and divergence outside. The endpoints \(a\pm R\) are drawn as open circles because the radius says nothing about them. The interval of convergence is \((a-R,a+R)\) together with those endpoints at which the series converges. For \(a=0\) and \(R=1\) all four cases occur: \(\sum_n x^n\) converges on \((-1,1)\), \(\sum_{n\ge1}x^n/n\) on \([-1,1)\), \(\sum_{n\ge1}(-x)^n/n\) on \((-1,1]\), and \(\sum_{n\ge1}x^n/n^2\) on \([-1,1]\).

Each series converges for \(|x-a|<R\) and diverges for \(|x-a|>R\); what happens at the endpoints differs from series to series.

Every power series has such an \(R\in[0,+\infty]\). The extreme cases are \(R=0\), where the series converges only at its centre, and \(R=+\infty\), where it converges for every real \(x\). In practice \(R\) is computed with the ratio test, \(R=\lim_{n\to\infty}|c_n/c_{n+1}|\) when this limit exists, or with the root test, \(R=1/\limsup|c_n|^{1/n}\), which always applies.

Inside the radius, the series converges uniformly on every closed interval \([a-r,a+r]\) with \(r<R\), and its sum can be differentiated term by term, as shown in convergence of power series.

Two slips are common. The interval is centred at \(a\), not at \(0\): for \(\sum_n n(-2)^n(x-3)^n\) in the Examples, \(R=\tfrac{1}{2}\) and the interval is \((\tfrac{5}{2},\tfrac{7}{2})\). And the endpoints must be tested separately, with tests for numerical series; their behaviour cannot be read from \(R\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • The convergence of \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n (x-a)^n\) at \(x=a-R\) and \(x=a+R\) is to be determined case-by-case.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty n(-2)^n (x-3)^n\) with \(R = 1/2\) centred at \(a = 3\), converges pointwise on \(\left(5/2, 7/2\right)\) and uniformly on any closed interval within it. Its convergence interval is \(\left(5/2, 7/2\right)\) since the series diverges at both endpoints.
  • The series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty 2^{n^2} (x+2)^n\) with \(R = 0\) centred at \(a = -2\), converges solely at its centre \(x = -2.\)

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
Consider the series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n\) where \(a_n\in\mathbb{R}\) and \(a_n\ne0\) for all sufficiently large \(n\). Let \(\displaystyle L=\lim_{n \to \infty} \left| \dfrac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} \right|\) when this limit exists (possibly as \(+\infty\)). Then:

  • If \(L < 1\text{,}\) the series converges. Moreover, \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty |a_n|\) also converges.
  • If \(L > 1\text{,}\) the series diverges.
  • If \(L = 1\) or the limit does not exist, the test is inconclusive.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The ratio test compares a series with a geometric series. If consecutive terms eventually shrink by a factor close to \(L<1\), the terms decay at least as fast as a geometric sequence with a ratio between \(L\) and \(1\), and the series converges absolutely. If \(L>1\), the terms eventually grow in absolute value, so they do not tend to \(0\) and the series diverges.

The figure shows \(a_n=n/2^n\). Here \(\dfrac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}=\dfrac{n+1}{2n}\to L=\tfrac{1}{2}<1\). For \(n\ge3\), \(a_{n+1}\le\tfrac{2}{3}a_n\), so \(a_n\le a_3(\tfrac{2}{3})^{n-3}\): the dashed geometric curve lies above the terms from \(n=3\) on, and \(\displaystyle \sum a_n\) converges by comparison.

Move \(x\): the ratios \(|a_{n+1}/a_n|\) (right) settle at \(L=|x-a|/R\). The series converges for \(L<1\) and diverges for \(L>1\).

The test only looks at the limit \(L\), so the case \(L=1\) gives no information: the Examples show that \(\sum_n1/n\) diverges and \(\sum_n1/n^2\) converges, and both have \(L=1\). The test also says nothing when the limit does not exist; the root test then often still works, and whenever the ratio limit exists, the root test gives the same \(L\).

Applied to a power series, the ratio of consecutive terms is \(\left|\dfrac{c_{n+1}}{c_n}\right||x-a|\), which tends to \(|x-a|/R\) with \(R=\lim_{n\to\infty}|c_n/c_{n+1}|\). The series converges for \(|x-a|<R\) and diverges for \(|x-a|>R\), which is how the Key Result finds the radius of convergence. Ratios are convenient for terms with factorials and powers, as in \(\sum_n x^n/n!\).

A common slip is to conclude convergence because every ratio is below \(1\). For the harmonic series, \(a_{n+1}/a_n=n/(n+1)<1\) for every \(n\), yet the series diverges: the ratios tend to \(1\), so they are not bounded by a fixed number below \(1\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • For the power series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n (x - a)^n\) with eventually nonzero coefficients, the radius of convergence \(R\) can be found using \(\displaystyle R = \lim_{n \to \infty} \left| \dfrac{c_{n}}{c_{n+1}} \right|\) if the limit exists or tends to infinity.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{n}{\mathrm{e}^n}\) is convergent since \(\displaystyle L=\lim_{n \to \infty} \left| \dfrac{(n+1)/\mathrm{e}^{n+1}}{n/\mathrm{e}^n} \right| =\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{e}}<1\text{.}\)
  • \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{2^n}{n}\) diverges since \(\displaystyle L=\lim_{n \to \infty} \left| \dfrac{2^{n+1}/(n+1)}{2^n/n} \right| =2>1\text{.}\)
  • When \(L=1\text{,}\) both convergent and divergent series exist, e.g., \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n}\) diverges while \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n^2}\) converges.
  • \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n!}\) converges for all \(x\in\mathbb{R}\) since \(\displaystyle R=\lim_{n \to \infty} \left| \dfrac{(n+1)!}{n!} \right|=+\infty\text{.}\)
  • \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty 2^n(x-3)^n\) converges for \(|x-3|<1/2\) since \(\displaystyle R=\lim_{n \to \infty} \left| \dfrac{2^{n}}{2^{n+1}} \right|=\dfrac{1}{2}\text{.}\)
  • \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty n!(x+1)^n\) diverges for all \(x\) except \(x=-1\) since \(\displaystyle R=\lim_{n \to \infty} \left| \dfrac{n!} {(n+1)!}\right|=0\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(f\colon E \to \mathbb{R}\) be a function where \(E \subseteq \mathbb{R}\text{.}\) We say:

  • \(f\) is real analytic at \(x=a\) if \(a\) is an interior point of \(E\) and there exists a power series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n (x-a)^n\) centred at \(a\) and an open interval \((a-r, a+r) \subseteq E\) (for some \(r > 0\)) where this series converges to \(f\text{.}\)
  • \(f\) is real analytic on \(E\) if \(E\) is an open set and \(f\) is real analytic at every point \(a \in E\text{.}\)

The results on Convergence of Power Series justify differentiating the local representation term by term inside its radius. Analyticity requires the resulting series to equal \(f\), not merely to exist formally.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A function is real analytic at a point \(a\) if near \(a\) it equals the sum of a power series centred at \(a\): not only approximated by it, but equal to it on a whole open interval \((a-r,a+r)\).

The point \(a\) must be an interior point of \(E\) so that such an interval fits inside the domain, and "real analytic on \(E\)" is defined for an open set \(E\) so that every point has room for its own interval. Once a series represents \(f\) near \(a\), its coefficients are forced: by convergence of power series the series can be differentiated term by term, and evaluating the \(n\)-th derivative at \(a\) gives \(c_n=f^{(n)}(a)/n!\). So \(f\) is real analytic at \(a\) if and only if \(f\) is infinitely differentiable near \(a\) and the series \(\sum_n f^{(n)}(a)(x-a)^n/n!\) converges to \(f\) on some interval around \(a\).

One series need not serve the whole domain, which is why the definition asks for a series at every point. The function \(1/(1+x^2)\) is real analytic on \(\mathbb{R}\), yet its power series at \(0\), the geometric series \(\sum_n(-1)^nx^{2n}\), has radius \(1\) and represents it only on \((-1,1)\); around other centres, other series take over.

A common slip is to think that an infinitely differentiable function is automatically real analytic. The function in the Examples is infinitely differentiable, but all its derivatives at \(0\) vanish, so the series built from them is the zero series: it converges, but to \(0\) rather than to \(f\). The series built from the derivatives returns later as the Taylor series.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The power series converges to \(f\) pointwise on \((a-r,a+r)\) and uniformly on every closed subinterval \([a-s,a+s]\) with \(0<s<r\).
  • Sums, products, and compositions of real analytic functions are also real analytic.
  • A real analytic function is always infinitely differentiable, and all of its higher-order derivatives are real analytic.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Polynomials, \(\mathrm{e}^x\), \(\sin x\) and \(\cos x\) are real analytic on \(\mathbb{R}\), and \(\ln x\) is real analytic on \((0,+\infty)\).
  • An infinitely differentiable function need not be real analytic. The function \(f\) with \(f(x)=0\) for \(x\le0\) and \(f(x)=\mathrm{e}^{-1/x}\) for \(x>0\) is infinitely differentiable on \(\mathbb{R}\) but not real analytic at \(0\).

Every derivative of \(f\) at \(0\) is \(0\), so its Taylor series at \(0\) is the zero series, yet \(f(x)>0\) for \(x>0\), so that series does not represent \(f\) on any interval around \(0\).

A real analytic function equals its Taylor series near each point \(a\). Move \(a\): the interval of convergence moves and changes size with it.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
Consider the series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n\) where \(a_n \in \mathbb{R}\text{.}\) Let \(\displaystyle L = \limsup_{n \to \infty} \sqrt[n]{|a_n|}\), then:

  • If \(L < 1\text{,}\) the series converges. Moreover, \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty |a_n|\) also converges.
  • If \(L > 1\text{,}\) the series diverges.
  • If \(L = 1\text{,}\) the test is inconclusive.

The \(n\)-th Root measures the geometric size of each term. The Limit Superior and Limit Inferior framework uses the largest limiting tail sizes, so the test can apply even when the root sequence has no ordinary limit.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The root test compares a series with a geometric series directly: it compares the limit superior of the \(n\)-th root of the terms' absolute values with \(1\). If \(\sqrt[n]{|a_n|}\) eventually stays below some \(q<1\), then \(|a_n|\le q^n\) for those \(n\), and the series converges absolutely by comparison.

The figure shows \(\sqrt[n]{a_n}=\sqrt[n]{n}/2\) for \(a_n=n/2^n\). The values rise from \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) at \(n=1\) to about \(0.72\) at \(n=3\) and then decrease towards \(L=\tfrac{1}{2}\), because \(\sqrt[n]{n}\to1\). Since \(L<1\), the series converges: from \(n=15\) on all values lie below \(0.6\), so \(a_n\le0.6^n\) there.

The \(n\)th roots \(|a_n|^{1/n}\) (right) approach \(L=|x-a|/R\); compare with \(1\).

The limit superior is used because the root sequence need not converge. Take \(a_n=2^{-n}\) for even \(n\) and \(a_n=3^{-n}\) for odd \(n\). The roots alternate between \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) and \(\tfrac{1}{3}\), so \(L=\tfrac{1}{2}\) and the series converges, while the ratios \(a_{n+1}/a_n\) tend to \(0\) along even \(n\) and to \(\infty\) along odd \(n\), so the ratio test gives no answer. Whenever the ratio limit exists, the root test gives the same \(L\), so the root test applies in more cases. If \(L>1\), then \(|a_n|>1\) for infinitely many \(n\), the terms do not tend to \(0\), and the series diverges.

For a power series, \(\limsup\sqrt[n]{|c_n(x-a)^n|}=|x-a|\limsup|c_n|^{1/n}\), which gives the formula for the radius of convergence in the Key Results, also known as the Cauchy-Hadamard formula.

A common slip is to conclude convergence because every root is below \(1\). For the harmonic series, \(\sqrt[n]{1/n}<1\) for all \(n\ge2\), but the roots tend to \(1\) and the series diverges.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The ordinary limit used in the ratio test may not exist. The root test above uses a limit superior, which always exists in \([0,+\infty]\), even when the root sequence has no ordinary limit.
  • The radius of convergence of a power series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n (x-a)^n\) is given by
\[ R=\frac{1}{\limsup\limits_{n\to\infty} |c_n|^{1/n}}. \]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{n}{\mathrm{e}^n}\) is convergent since \(\displaystyle L=\limsup_{n \to \infty} \sqrt[n]{\left| \frac{n}{\mathrm{e}^n} \right|} = \frac{1}{\mathrm{e}}<1\text{.}\)
  • \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{2^n}{n}\) diverges since \(\displaystyle L=\limsup_{n \to \infty} \sqrt[n]{\left|\frac{2^n}{n} \right|} = 2>1\text{.}\)
  • When \(L=1\text{,}\) both convergent and divergent series exist, e.g., \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n}\) diverges while \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n^2}\) converges.
  • \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty n(-2)^n (x-3)^n\) is convergent for \(|x-3|<\dfrac{1}{2}\) since \(R = \dfrac{1}{\limsup\limits_{n \to\infty}|n\left(-2\right)^{n}|^{1/n}} = \dfrac{1}{2}\text{.}\)
  • \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty 2^{n^2} (x+2)^n\) is divergent except at \(x=-2\) since \(R= \dfrac{1}{\limsup\limits_{n \rightarrow \infty}|2^{n^{2}}|^{1/n}}= 0\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \((X,d_{X})\) be a metric space. A subset \(E\) of \(X\) is termed sequentially compact if for every sequence \((x_i)_{i=1}^\infty\) with each \(x_i \in E\text{,}\) there exists a convergent subsequence \((x_{i_j})_{j=1}^\infty\) that converges to a point \(x \in E\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A set is sequentially compact if every sequence drawn from it has a subsequence that converges to a point still inside the set. Sequences in the set cannot escape, neither to infinity nor to a missing point at its edge.

In the closed disc, the red subsequence converges to a point of \(E\). In the open disc, the illustrated sequence approaches a missing rim point, and every subsequence has that same limit outside \(E\), so the open disc is not sequentially compact.

Two requirements are packed into the definition: a convergent subsequence must exist, and its limit must lie in \(E\). The first fails for unbounded sets, as \(x_i=i\) in \(\mathbb{R}\) shows; the second fails for sets that are not closed, as for the open disc. The whole sequence need not converge: \(x_i=(-1)^i\) in \(E=\{-1,1\}\) does not, but its even-indexed terms do.

In \(\mathbb{R}^n\), the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem shows that the sequentially compact sets are exactly the closed and bounded ones. In every metric space, sequential compactness is equivalent to compactness, so either description can be used. Sequences are often more convenient in proofs, such as showing that a continuous function attains its maximum, while the definition with open covers also makes sense where no metric is available.

A common slip is to think of sequential compactness as being "closed under limits". That describes closed sets, and it is not enough: \(\mathbb{R}\) is closed, but \(x_i=i\) has no convergent subsequence.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • In any metric space, a set is compact if and only if it is sequentially compact. This gives two equivalent ways to think about compactness: open covers or convergent subsequences.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The closed unit ball \(\{\boldsymbol{x}\in \mathbb{R}^n\colon \|\boldsymbol{x}\|\leq 1\}\) is sequentially compact. This fails in infinite dimensions.
  • Any finite set in any metric space is sequentially compact: some point is taken by infinitely many terms of a sequence in it, which gives a constant subsequence.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(X\) be a metric space. The metrics \(d_p\) and \(d_q\) on \(X\) (two arbitrary metrics; the subscripts are only labels) are termed strongly equivalent, denoted \(d_p\approx d_q\), if positive constants \(a\) and \(b\) exist such that for any \(x,y \in X\),

\[ a \cdot d_p(x,y) \leq d_q(x,y) \leq b \cdot d_p(x,y). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Strongly equivalent metrics measure distances on different scales, but the ratio between the two distances is bounded above and below by fixed constants. A distance that is small in one metric is therefore small in the other, uniformly over all pairs of points.

On \(\mathbb{R}^2\), the illustrated Euclidean and taxicab distances satisfy \(d_2\le d_1\le\sqrt{2}\,d_2\). In the figure, the diamond of points with \(d_1\)-distance less than \(r\) from \(\boldsymbol{x}\) lies inside the disc of points with \(d_2\)-distance less than \(r\), and it contains the smaller disc of \(d_2\)-radius \(r/\sqrt{2}\). Being close to \(\boldsymbol{x}\) in one metric therefore forces being close in the other, so the two metrics have the same convergent sequences.

The constants \(a\) and \(b\) must work for all \(x,y\) at once. Because of this uniformity, strongly equivalent metrics share more than convergent sequences: they have the same Cauchy sequences, so one of them is complete if and only if the other is. For metrics that come from norms, strong equivalence is the same as equivalence of the norms, so any two \(p\)-metrics on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) are strongly equivalent.

Having the same convergent sequences is not enough for strong equivalence. On \((-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2})\), the metric \(d_{\tan}(x,y)=|\tan x-\tan y|\) has the same convergent sequences as \(|x-y|\), but the ratio \(d_{\tan}(x,y)/|x-y|\) is unbounded near \(\pm\tfrac{\pi}{2}\), and \(x_k=\tfrac{\pi}{2}-\tfrac{1}{k}\) is Cauchy for \(|x-y|\) and not for \(d_{\tan}\), since \(\tan x_k\to+\infty\). Such metrics return later in the course as topologically equivalent metrics.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The strong equivalence relation possesses symmetry (\(d_p\approx d_q\) if and only if \(d_q\approx d_p\)), reflexivity (\(d_p\approx d_p\)) and transitivity (if \(d_p\approx d_q\) and \(d_q\approx d_r\), then \(d_p\approx d_r\)).
  • Strongly equivalent metrics induce the same notion of convergence.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Any two \(p\)-metrics on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) are strongly equivalent.
  • The discrete metric, \(d_{\mathrm{disc}}\), is not strongly equivalent to any of the \(p\)-metrics.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The taxicab distance between points \(\boldsymbol{x}=(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)\) and \(\boldsymbol{y}=(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_n)\) in an \(n\)-dimensional real coordinate space \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with fixed Cartesian coordinate system is:

\[ d_1(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}|y_i-x_i|. \]

The taxicab norm, or known as \(\ell^1\) norm, of \(\boldsymbol{x}=(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)\) is calculated as:

\[ \|\boldsymbol{x}\|_1=\sum_{i=1}^{n}|x_i|. \]

The coordinate sum defines a norm length, and subtracting two points gives a metric distance. Its triangle inequality follows by adding \(|x_i-z_i|\le|x_i-y_i|+|y_i-z_i|\) over the coordinates.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The taxicab distance represents the distance a taxi would travel between two points when restricted to cardinal directions (north, south, east, west) without moving diagonally or in any other curved path. It adds the coordinate differences instead of combining them by Pythagoras, so it is the \(p\)-metric with \(p=1\).

The red staircase has taxicab length \(d_1(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})=5+4=9\). Any monotone staircase between the points has the same length, whereas the blue straight segment has Euclidean length \(d_2(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})=\sqrt{5^2+4^2}\approx6.4\).

In the taxicab norm \(\|\boldsymbol x\|_1=|x_1|+|x_2|\) the unit circle is a diamond. Drag \(\boldsymbol x\): the \(1\)-norm is always at least the Euclidean norm.

The diamond-shaped unit circle shows how the taxicab norm weighs directions: the point \((\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{2})\) has taxicab norm \(1\), the same as \((1,0)\), although it is closer to the origin in the Euclidean sense. In general \(d_2\le d_1\le\sqrt{n}\,d_2\) on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), the upper bound by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. In the figure, \(9\le\sqrt{2}\cdot\sqrt{41}\approx9.06\), close to equality because the two coordinate differences are almost equal. These bounds make the two metrics strongly equivalent: they give different numbers but the same convergent sequences.

A common slip is to think that the taxicab distance depends only on the geometry of the plane. It depends on the chosen axes, which is why the definition fixes a Cartesian coordinate system: the vectors \((1,0)\) and \((\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}},\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}})\) have the same Euclidean length \(1\), one being a rotation of the other, but taxicab norms \(1\) and \(\sqrt{2}\).

docs.text: • The closed unit ball in the taxicab norm is an \(n\)-dimensional cross-polytope, e.g., a diamond in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) and a regular octahedron in \(\mathbb{R}^3\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(k\geq0\) be an integer and let the function \(f\) be \(k\) times differentiable at \(x=a\). The \(k\)-th order Taylor polynomial of \(f\) at \(x=a\) is the polynomial

\[ P_{k}(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x-a) + \cdots + \frac{f^{(k)}(a)}{k !}(x-a)^{k}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The \(k\)-th order Taylor polynomial is the polynomial of degree at most \(k\) that imitates \(f\) as closely as possible near \(x=a\). Its coefficients are chosen so that \(P_k\) has the same value and the same first \(k\) derivatives at \(a\) as \(f\): differentiating \((x-a)^j\) exactly \(j\) times leaves the constant \(j!\), which the factorial in the coefficient \(f^{(j)}(a)/j!\) cancels.

Read term by term, \(P_0\) is the constant \(f(a)\), and \(P_1(x)=f(a)+f'(a)(x-a)\) is the tangent line, whose slope is the derivative \(f'(a)\). Each further term corrects what the previous ones miss, starting with the curvature. If \(f\) is \(k\) times differentiable at \(a\), then \(P_k\) is the unique polynomial of degree at most \(k\) with \(f(x)-P_k(x)=o\big((x-a)^k\big)\) as \(x\to a\) (in little-\(o\) notation); in this sense it is the best polynomial approximation of order \(k\) near \(x=a\).

The \(k\)-th order Taylor polynomial consists of the first \(k+1\) terms of the Taylor series centred at the same point, when that series exists.

A common slip is to expect that a higher order always gives a better approximation at a fixed \(x\) far from \(a\). The guarantee is local. For \(f(x)=1/x\) at \(a=1\), \(P_k(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{k}(-1)^j(x-1)^j\), so \(P_k(3)=1-2+4-\cdots+(-2)^k\) moves further away from \(f(3)=\tfrac{1}{3}\) as \(k\) grows.

The same idea returns for functions of several variables in Math IV, in multivariate Taylor approximations.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The \(k\)-th order Taylor polynomial and the function \(f\) have the same value and the same derivatives up to order \(k\) at \(x=a\text{:}\) \(P_k^{(j)}(a)=f^{(j)}(a)\) for \(j=0,1,\dots,k\text{.}\) Away from \(a\) they generally differ.
  • One can write a Taylor polynomial for a function just from its first few derivatives, but the full Taylor series exists if the function is smooth, and the full series converges to the function on a neighbourhood of \(a\) if and only if the function is real analytic at \(a\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The 3rd order Taylor polynomial of \(\sin x\) around \(x=0\) is \(P_3(x) = x - \dfrac{x^3}{3!}\).

    The two panels compare Taylor polynomials of \(\sin x\) about \(0\). The cubic \(P_3\) on the right follows \(\sin x\) over a wider interval than the linear polynomial \(P_1\) on the left.

  • The 1st order Taylor polynomial of \(1/x\) around \(x = 1\) is \(P_1(x)=2-x\).

Raise the order \(k\) and move the centre \(a\): \(P_k\) matches \(f\) and its first \(k\) derivatives at \(a\), and fits over a wider range.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
Let \(a\) be an interior point of \(E\subseteq \mathbb{R}\text{,}\) and let \(f\colon E\to\mathbb{R}\) be real analytic at \(x=a\text{.}\) Then, for some \(r>0\) with \((a-r,a+r)\subseteq E\), \(f\) has the power series expansion around \(x=a\):

\[ f(x) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{f^{(n)}(a)}{n!} (x-a)^n\quad \text{for all } x \in (a-r,a+r), \]

known as the Taylor series of \(f\) around \(x=a\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
If a function is so smooth that it behaves exactly like an infinite polynomial near a point, then that polynomial is built entirely from its derivatives at that point. The Taylor series makes this precise: for a real analytic \(f\), knowing \(f(a),f'(a),f''(a),\dots\) determines \(f\) on a whole interval around \(a\).

The figure shows the partial sums \(P_1,P_3,P_5,P_7\) of the Taylor series of \(\sin x\) at \(0\); only odd powers occur, because the even derivatives of \(\sin\) vanish at \(0\). Each partial sum is a Taylor polynomial and follows \(\sin x\) over a wider interval than the previous one: \(P_7\) stays within \(0.08\) of \(\sin x\) on all of \([-\pi,\pi]\). Further out, every partial sum leaves the band \(-1\le y\le1\), but for each fixed \(x\) the partial sums converge to \(\sin x\) as the degree grows.

For \(\ln(1+x)\) and \(1/(1-x)\) the Taylor polynomials converge to \(f\) inside the shaded interval and not beyond it; for \(\mathrm{e}^x\) and \(\sin x\) everywhere.

Real analyticity is the hypothesis that makes the series equal \(f\). Being smooth is enough to write the series down, but not for it to converge to \(f\), as the smooth function in the Key Results shows. Even for an analytic function the equality is limited by the interval of convergence: \(\ln(1+x)\) is defined for all \(x>-1\), but its Taylor series at \(0\) converges only for \(-1<x\le1\).

Taylor series are how exponentials and trigonometric functions are handled as sums. The Poisson distribution has total probability \(1\) because \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\lambda^k/k!=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda}\). The exponential series returns in Math V, where the same sum with a square matrix in place of the number defines the matrix exponential.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The Taylor series centred at the origin is called the Maclaurin series.
  • For any smooth function you can write down its Taylor series around \(a\), but it need not converge to the function: it equals \(f\) on a neighbourhood of \(a\) if and only if \(f\) is real analytic at \(a\text{.}\) For example, \(f(x)=\mathrm{e}^{-1/x^2}\) for \(x\neq0\), \(f(0)=0\), is smooth, but its Taylor series at \(0\) is identically \(0\text{.}\)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The Taylor series of the natural exponential function at the origin:
\[ \displaystyle \mathrm{e}^x = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n!} = 1 + x + \dfrac{x^2}{2!} + \dfrac{x^3}{3!} + \cdots. \]
  • The generalized binomial expansion (binomial series) at the origin, which extends the binomial theorem to real exponents, valid for \(|x|<1\) and any real exponent \(\alpha\) (and for all \(x\) when \(\alpha\) is a nonnegative integer, since the series then terminates):
\[ (1+x)^\alpha = \sum_{i=0}^\infty \binom{\alpha}{i} x^i = 1 + \alpha x + \frac{\alpha(\alpha-1)}{2}x^2 + \frac{\alpha(\alpha-1)(\alpha-2)}{6}x^3 + \cdots, \]

where \(\displaystyle\binom{\alpha}{i}=\frac{\alpha(\alpha-1)\cdots(\alpha-i+1)}{i!}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(k \geq 1\) be an integer and assume that the function \(f\colon \mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) is \(k\)-times differentiable (not necessarily real analytic) at \(x=a\text{.}\) There exists a function \(\displaystyle h_k \colon \mathbb{R} \to\mathbb{R}\) such that \(\displaystyle \lim_{x\to a} h_k(x) = 0\) and

\[ f(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x-a) + \cdots + \frac{f^{(k)}(a)}{k !}(x-a)^k + R_k(x) \]

where \(R_k(x)= h_k(x)(x-a)^k\) is called the Peano form of the remainder.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Taylor's theorem says that a function which is \(k\) times differentiable at \(a\) is, near \(a\), a polynomial plus a small error. The polynomial is the Taylor polynomial of order \(k\), and the error \(R_k(x)=h_k(x)(x-a)^k\) is small even compared with the last term kept, because the factor \(h_k(x)\) tends to \(0\) as \(x\to a\).

The figure takes \(f(x)=\mathrm{e}^x\) and \(a=0\), with the second-order Taylor polynomial \(P_2(x)=1+x+\tfrac{x^2}{2}\). The two curves touch at \(0\); at the marked point \(x\) the green arrow is the remainder \(R_2(x)=f(x)-P_2(x)\). As \(x\) moves towards \(0\) this gap shrinks faster than \(x^2\), which is the statement \(h_2(x)=R_2(x)/x^2\to0\).

The right panel shows \(h_k(x)=R_k(x)/(x-a)^k\): it tends to \(0\) as \(x\to a\), which is the Peano form of the remainder.

The hypothesis is weak: only \(f^{(k)}(a)\) has to exist, and \(f\) need not be smooth or real analytic. In return, the conclusion only concerns the limit \(x\to a\), not the error at a fixed \(x\). The order of the expansion is limited by the number of derivatives: \(f(x)=x|x|\) has \(f'(0)=0\) and \(f(x)=0+0\cdot x+x|x|\) with \(h_1(x)=|x|\to0\), but \(f''(0)\) does not exist and \(x|x|\) has no expansion \(c_0+c_1x+c_2x^2+o(x^2)\), since \(x|x|/x^2=\operatorname{sgn}(x)\) has no limit at \(0\).

In little-\(o\) notation, the theorem turns limits of quotients into a comparison of leading terms, an alternative to L'Hôpital's rule: from \(\sin x=x-\tfrac{x^3}{6}+o(x^3)\) one reads off \((x-\sin x)/x^3\to\tfrac{1}{6}\) as \(x\to0\).

The theorem returns for functions of several variables in Math IV, in multivariate Taylor approximations.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Using the little-\(o\) notation, the statement in Taylor's theorem reads as \(R_k(x)=o((x-a)^k)\text{,}\) as \(x\to a\text{.}\) In this case, we have the \(k\)-th order Taylor expansion, whose polynomial part is the Taylor polynomial \(P_k(x)\):
\[ f(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x-a) + \cdots + \frac{f^{(k)}(a)}{k !}(x-a)^{k} + o((x-a)^{k}). \]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\mathrm{e}^x=1+x+\dfrac{x^2}{2}+h_2(x)x^2\), where \(\displaystyle h_2(x)=\sum_{n=3}^\infty \dfrac{x^{n-2}}{n!}\).
  • \(\dfrac{1}{1-x}=1+x+x^2+h_2(x) x^2\), where \(\displaystyle h_2(x)=\sum_{n=3}^\infty x^{n-2}\), for \(|x|<1\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Two metrics \(d_p\) and \(d_q\) on a space \(X\) are termed (topologically) equivalent if they produce identical topology (the set of open subsets of \(X\)) on \(X\), i.e., a subset \(E \subseteq X\) is open with respect to \(d_p\) if and only if it's open under \(d_q\). This relationship is expressed as \(d_p \sim d_q.\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Two metrics are topologically equivalent if they determine the same collection of open sets. They may measure distances differently, but they agree on which sets are open, and therefore on every notion that is defined through open sets.

In the left panel, the round \(d_p\)-ball \(B_{d_p}(\boldsymbol{x},r)\) is \(d_p\)-open, and around its point \(\boldsymbol{y}\) fits a diamond-shaped \(d_q\)-ball \(B_{d_q}(\boldsymbol{y},\delta)\), so \(\boldsymbol{y}\) is an interior point of that ball for \(d_q\) as well. The right panel does the same with the roles swapped. If this works around every point of every ball, a set is \(d_p\)-open if and only if it is \(d_q\)-open: the two metrics give the same topology.

The radius \(\delta\) may depend on the point and on \(r\); no fixed ratio between the metrics is required. This is the difference from strongly equivalent metrics: there \(d_q\le b\,d_p\) gives \(B_{d_p}(x,r/b)\subseteq B_{d_q}(x,r)\) with the same factor everywhere, which is why strong equivalence implies topological equivalence. On \(\mathbb{R}^n\) all \(p\)-metrics are strongly equivalent, so "open" in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) does not depend on which of them is used.

Topologically equivalent metrics have the same convergent sequences. A common slip is to assume that they also agree on how large distances are. On \(\mathbb{R}\), \(\min(|x-y|,1)\) gives the same open sets as \(|x-y|\), although under it no two points are more than \(1\) apart. Similarly, \(x_n=\tfrac{\pi}{2}-\tfrac{1}{n}\) is a Cauchy sequence for \(|x-y|\) on \((-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2})\) but not for \(d_{\tan}\) from the Examples.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • If two metrics are strongly equivalent, then they are topologically equivalent.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• On the interval \((-\pi/2,\pi/2)\text{,}\) the metric \(d_{\tan}(x,y)=|\tan x-\tan y|\) is topologically equivalent to the absolute value metric, but they are not strongly equivalent: the ratio \(|\tan x-\tan y|/|x-y|\) is unbounded near \(\pm\pi/2\text{.}\)
  • The discrete metric is not topologically equivalent to any \(p\)-metrics.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A topology on a set \(X\), often denoted by \(\tau\), is a collection of subsets of \(X\) that satisfies the following properties:

  1. Both the empty set and the entire set \(X\) belong to \(\tau\).
  2. Any union of elements in \(\tau\) also belongs to \(\tau\).
  3. The intersection of any finite number of elements in \(\tau\) remains in \(\tau\).

The pair \((X,\tau)\) is called a topological space.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A topology on \(X\) is a choice of which subsets count as open. It describes which points are close to which without using a distance: instead of balls of radius \(\varepsilon\) one works with the open sets directly, and the three axioms keep the properties that open sets of a metric space always have.

\(\tau=\{\varnothing,\{a\},\{a,b\},X\}\) is a topology on \(X=\{a,b,c\}\): it contains \(\varnothing\) and \(X\) and is closed under unions and finite intersections, e.g. \(\{a\}\cup\{a,b\}=\{a,b\}\) and \(\{a\}\cap\{a,b\}=\{a\}\). The members of \(\tau\) are the open sets. The only open set containing \(c\) is \(X\), so in this topology \(c\) cannot be separated from \(a\) or \(b\) by an open set.

Arbitrary unions are allowed, but only finite intersections, because infinitely many open sets can shrink to a set that is not open: in \(\mathbb{R}\) the intersection of the open intervals \((-\tfrac{1}{n},\tfrac{1}{n})\) is \(\{0\}\), whose boundary point \(0\) belongs to it. Formally, \(\tau\) is a subset of the power set of \(X\), not a subset of \(X\).

Every metric space gives a topology (Key Results), but not every topology comes from a metric. In a metric space every one-point set is closed, but in the figure \(\{a\}\) is not closed, since its complement \(\{b,c\}\) is not in \(\tau\).

This idea returns later: two metrics that give the same open sets are called topologically equivalent, and notions such as compactness are defined using open sets only.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • Metric spaces are topological spaces. Every metric space induces a topology where open sets are unions of open metric balls.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • The trivial topology is the topology with the least possible number of open sets, namely the empty set and the entire space, i.e., \(\tau=\{\varnothing, X\}\).

docs.title: Total Derivative as a Linear Map
Definition
docs.text:
Let \(E\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\), let \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon E\to\mathbb{R}^k\) be a function, let \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\in\operatorname{int}E\), and let \(\boldsymbol{L}\colon \mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^k\) be a linear transformation. We say that \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is (totally) differentiable at \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{x}_{0}\) with (total) derivative \(\boldsymbol{L}\) if, as \(\boldsymbol{x}\to\boldsymbol{x}_0\),

\[ \frac{\|\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x})-\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)-\boldsymbol{L}(\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{x}_0)\|}{\|\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{x}_0\|}\to0. \]

The limit must hold however \(\boldsymbol{x}\) approaches \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\), that is, along every convergent sequence \(\boldsymbol{x}_j\to\boldsymbol{x}_0\) with \(\boldsymbol{x}_j\neq\boldsymbol{x}_0\), not just along coordinate lines. It says that the relative error in the linear approximation tends to zero.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Total differentiability means the function can be approximated near the point by a linear transformation, with the error shrinking to zero faster than the distance to the point. The linear map \(\boldsymbol{h}\mapsto\boldsymbol{L}\boldsymbol{h}\) is also called the differential of \(\boldsymbol{f}\) at \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\); for \(n=k=1\) it is \(h\mapsto f'(x_0)h\), the one-variable differential \(\mathrm{d}y=f'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\).

It is the multidimensional version of the one-variable fact that \(f\) is differentiable at \(x_0\) if and only if \(f(x_0+h)=f(x_0)+f'(x_0)h+o(h)\) as \(h\to0\) (sometimes called Newton's approximation).

The first-order approximation is \(\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0+\boldsymbol{h})=\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)+\boldsymbol{L}\boldsymbol{h}+o(\|\boldsymbol{h}\|)\), where \(\boldsymbol{L}=\boldsymbol{Df}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\). Locally, \(\boldsymbol{f}\) acts like this linear map, so small squares become approximate parallelograms.

Move \(\boldsymbol x_0\) and zoom in: near \(\boldsymbol x_0\) the graph is almost the plane \(f(\boldsymbol x_0)+\mathrm{D}f_{\boldsymbol x_0}(\boldsymbol h)\), with an error that shrinks faster than \(\|\boldsymbol h\|\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For the function \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon \mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^k\) at \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{x}_0\), its derivative, \(\mathrm{D} \boldsymbol{f}_{\boldsymbol{x}_0}\), is a \(k\times n\) matrix or an equivalent linear transformation from \(\mathbb{R}^n\) to \(\mathbb{R}^k\).
  • \(\mathrm{D} \boldsymbol{f}_{\boldsymbol{x}_0}(\boldsymbol{h})\), where \(\boldsymbol{h}\) is an infinitesimal vector, provides an approximation of the shift in \(\boldsymbol{f}\) (a vector in \(\mathbb{R}^k\)) arising from the change \(\boldsymbol{h}\) in \(\boldsymbol{x}\) around \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{x}_0\) (a vector in \(\mathbb{R}^n\)).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The function \(\boldsymbol{f}(x,y) = (x^2,y^2)\) is differentiable at \(\boldsymbol{x}=(1,2)\) with the derivative \(\boldsymbol{L}(x,y) = (2x,4y)\).
  • The function \(f(x,y) = \sin(x^2+y)\) is differentiable at \((x,y)=(0,0)\) and the derivative is \(L(x,y)=y\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Consider metric spaces \((X,d_{X})\) and \((Y,d_{Y})\), and a function \(f\colon X\to Y\). We say \(f\) is uniformly continuous on \(X\) if, for any \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists a \(\delta > 0\) such that for all \(x_1,x_2\in X\) with \(d_{X}(x_1,x_2)<\delta\), it holds that \(d_{Y}(f(x_1),f(x_2))<\varepsilon\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Uniform continuity asks for one \(\delta\) that works at every point of \(X\) at once: inputs within \(\delta\) of each other, wherever they lie, have outputs within \(\varepsilon\) of each other. This is the general form of uniform continuity, with possibly different metrics on different spaces.

For a given \(\varepsilon>0\), the three green balls in \(X\) all have the same radius \(\delta\), and each is mapped inside the \(\varepsilon\)-ball around its centre's image. The same \(\delta\) serves at every other point of \(X\).

The difference from continuity lies in the order of the quantifiers. For continuity, \(\delta\) is chosen after the point and may depend on it; for uniform continuity, \(\delta\) depends on \(\varepsilon\) alone. Every uniformly continuous function is therefore continuous, but not conversely. The function \(f(x)=1/x\) on \((0,1)\) is continuous, yet for \(\varepsilon=1\) no \(\delta\) works: for \(0<x<\min\{2\delta,1\}\) the points \(x\) and \(x/2\) are less than \(\delta\) apart, while \(|f(x)-f(x/2)|=1/x>1\).

Compactness removes the difference: a continuous function on a compact set is uniformly continuous, as the Key Results state, and for \([a,b]\) this is the Heine-Cantor theorem. Uniform continuity is what is needed when one estimate must hold over a whole domain, for example in the proof that a continuous function on \([a,b]\) is Riemann integrable.

A common slip is to speak of uniform continuity at a point. Uniform continuity is a property of a function on a set, since it compares all pairs of points of that set; at a single point there is only continuity.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • Any continuous function defined on a compact set is uniformly continuous.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Every constant function is uniformly continuous regardless of the metrics.
  • Every function from a discrete space is uniformly continuous.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A function \(f\colon X \to \mathbb{R}\) with \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}\) is said to be uniformly continuous if, for every \(\varepsilon >0\text{,}\) there exists a \(\delta >0\) such that for all pairs of points \(x_1, x_2\in X\) with \(|x_1-x_2|<\delta\text{,}\) it holds that \(|f(x_1)-f(x_2)|<\varepsilon\text{.}\)

The same \(\delta\) controls all input pairs of the Function \(f\), rather than being selected separately for each point.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Uniform continuity means that one rule for "how close is close enough" works everywhere: for each \(\varepsilon>0\) there is a single \(\delta\) that serves every pair of points of \(X\), wherever they lie. Ordinary continuity only asks for a \(\delta\) at each point separately, and that \(\delta\) may shrink from point to point.

Both rectangles in the figure have the same height, so they correspond to the same \(\varepsilon\). Near \(x=1\) the graph of \(1/x\) is flat enough for a wide rectangle; near \(0\) the graph is so steep that only a very narrow one fits. At a point \(x_0>0\) the largest \(\delta\) that works for \(1/x\) is \(\delta=\varepsilon x_0^2/(1+\varepsilon x_0)\), which tends to \(0\) as \(x_0\to0\), so no positive \(\delta\) serves all points of \((0,1)\).

For a fixed \(\varepsilon\) the right panel shows the largest admissible \(\delta\) at each \(x_0\). Uniform continuity means one positive \(\delta\) works everywhere; for \(1/x\) the admissible \(\delta\) shrinks to \(0\) near \(0\).

In the definition both points \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) are free, and \(\delta\) may depend on \(\varepsilon\) only. Uniform continuity is therefore a property of \(f\) on the whole set \(X\), not at a single point: the same function \(1/x\) is uniformly continuous on \((1,2)\) and not on \((0,1)\), as in the Examples. A simple way to obtain it is a bound \(|f(x_1)-f(x_2)|\le C|x_1-x_2|\) for all \(x_1,x_2\in X\), as for \(\sin x\); then \(\delta=\varepsilon/C\) works.

On a closed bounded interval nothing extra is needed: by the Heine-Cantor theorem, every continuous function on \([a,b]\) is uniformly continuous.

A common slip is to say that \(f\) is "uniformly continuous at \(x_0\)". The phrase has no meaning: uniformity is about all points of \(X\) at once.

The definition returns later for functions between more general spaces, with a general distance in place of \(|x_1-x_2|\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every uniformly continuous function is continuous, the converse doesn't necessarily hold.
  • \(f\) is uniformly continuous on \(X\) if and only if given two equivalent sequences \((x_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) and \((y_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) in \(X\) (that is, \(|x_n-y_n|\to0\) as \(n\to\infty\)), the sequences \((f(x_n))_{n=1}^\infty\) and \((f(y_n))_{n=1}^\infty\) are also equivalent.
  • A continuous function \(f\) is uniformly continuous on \((a, b)\) if and only if the right limit \(\displaystyle f(a^+)\) and the left limit \(\displaystyle f(b^-)\) both exist and are finite. In particular, a continuous function that is unbounded on a bounded interval \((a,b)\) is not uniformly continuous there; a bounded function can fail too, for example \(\sin(1/x)\) on \((0,1)\), which has no right limit at \(0\).
  • A differentiable function \(f\) is uniformly continuous on \((a,b)\) if \(f'\) is bounded. Boundedness of \(f'\) is sufficient, not necessary: \(\sqrt{x}\) is uniformly continuous on \((0,1)\) although its derivative is unbounded there. A typical failure on an unbounded domain is \(f(x)=x^2\) on \(\mathbb{R}\text{,}\) whose slope is unbounded.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The function \(f(x)=1/x\) is uniformly continuous on \((1,2)\), but not uniformly continuous on \((0,1)\).
  • The function \(g(x)=\sin x\) is uniformly continuous on all of \(\mathbb{R}\) (hence on any interval), since \(|\sin x_1-\sin x_2|\le|x_1-x_2|\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \((f_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) be a sequence of functions defined on \(X \subseteq \mathbb{R}\) and \(f\colon X \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) be another function. We say that \((f_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) converges uniformly to \(f\) on \(X\) and write \(f_n\rightrightarrows f\text{,}\) if for every \(\varepsilon > 0\text{,}\) there exists a positive integer \(N\) such that for all \(n > N\text{,}\) the inequality \(|f_n(x) - f(x) | < \varepsilon\) holds for all \(x \in X\text{.}\)

The objects converging are Function values on a common domain. A single index \(N\) must control the error at every input, which distinguishes uniform convergence from separate numerical limits.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Uniform convergence means that the function values get close to the limit at the same rate at all points, not one point at a time. A single index \(N\), chosen for a given \(\varepsilon\), must work for every \(x\) in the domain at once.

Uniform convergence \(f_n\to f\) means that for every \(\varepsilon>0\), the graph of \(f_n\) lies in the \(\varepsilon\)-tube around \(f\) for all sufficiently large \(n\). Thus \(|f_n(x)-f(x)|<\varepsilon\) holds for all \(x\) at once, equivalently \(\sup_x|f_n(x)-f(x)|\to0\).

Uniform convergence asks for one \(n\) that puts the whole graph of \(f_n\) inside the \(\varepsilon\)-band. Compare \(\sin(nx)/n\) with \(x^n\) and the moving bump.

The difference with pointwise convergence lies only in the order of the quantifiers: pointwise, \(N\) may depend on both \(\varepsilon\) and \(x\); uniformly, \(N\) depends on \(\varepsilon\) alone. The functions \(x^n\) on \([0,1]\) show why this matters. They converge pointwise to the function that is \(0\) on \([0,1)\) and \(1\) at \(x=1\), but \(\sup_{0\le x<1}x^n=1\) for every \(n\), so the convergence is not uniform. The limit is discontinuous although every \(x^n\) is continuous.

Uniform convergence is exactly the control needed to pass continuity and integrals to the limit, as the Key Results state. The quantity \(\sup_x|f_n(x)-f(x)|\) later gets its own name, the uniform norm, and the same idea is used to show that series of functions, such as power series, converge uniformly.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Uniform convergence implies pointwise convergence.
  • Uniform convergence preserves boundedness and continuity (uniform limit theorem). On a closed bounded interval \([a,b]\) it preserves Riemann integrability and allows \(\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_a^b f_n=\int_a^b f\text{.}\) It does not preserve differentiability: for that, the derivatives \(f_n'\) must converge uniformly as well.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The sequence \(f_n(x) = x/n\) converges uniformly to \(f(x)=0\) on every bounded interval \([-R,R]\) (since \(|x/n|\le R/n\)), but only pointwise on \(\mathbb{R}\text{.}\)
  • The functions \(f_n(x) = \dfrac{n}{nx + 1}\) on \((0,1]\) converge pointwise, but not uniformly, to \(f(x)=1/x\text{,}\) because \(|f_n(x)-1/x|=\dfrac{1}{x(nx+1)}\) is unbounded near \(0\) for every \(n\text{.}\) (On \([0,1]\) there is no pointwise limit at all, since \(f_n(0)=n\to\infty\text{.}\))

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
On a nonempty set \(X\), the uniform norm \(\|f\|_\infty\) of a bounded function \(f\colon X\to\mathbb{R}\) is defined as:

\[ \|f\|_\infty = \sup_{x \in X} |f(x)|. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The uniform norm measures the size of a bounded function by its worst case: the supremum of the absolute value \(|f(x)|\) over the whole set \(X\). Applied to a difference, \(\|f-g\|_\infty\) is the largest vertical gap between the graphs of \(f\) and \(g\), and it serves as the distance between the two functions.

The dashed lines in the figure are at \(\pm\|f\|_\infty\), and the dot marks where \(|f|\) reaches its supremum. The green arrow marks where the vertical gap between \(f\) and \(g\) is largest; its length is \(\|f-g\|_\infty\). That gap is longer than \(\|f\|_\infty\) itself, because \(g\) is negative where \(f\) is large, so the norm of a difference cannot be read off from the norms of \(f\) and \(g\) alone.

The red segment marks the largest gap between \(f_n\) and \(f\): that is \(\|f_n-f\|_\infty\). Uniform convergence means it tends to \(0\).

Boundedness of \(f\) makes the supremum finite. The supremum need not be attained: for \(f(x)=\mathrm{e}^{-x}\) on \((0,+\infty)\) in the Examples, \(\|f\|_\infty=1\) while \(|f(x)|<1\) everywhere. It behaves like a length on the bounded functions: \(\|f\|_\infty=0\) only for the zero function, \(\|\lambda f\|_\infty=|\lambda|\,\|f\|_\infty\), and the triangle inequality \(\|f+g\|_\infty\le\|f\|_\infty+\|g\|_\infty\) holds because \(|f(x)+g(x)|\le\|f\|_\infty+\|g\|_\infty\) for every \(x\).

The norm turns uniform convergence into convergence of numbers, as in the Key Results. It also appears in normal convergence, in the Weierstrass \(M\)-test and in the Weierstrass approximation theorem.

A common slip is to confuse \(\|f_n-f\|_\infty\to0\) with \(f_n(x)\to f(x)\) at every \(x\). On \([0,1)\) the functions \(x^n\) tend to \(0\) at every point, yet \(\|x^n\|_\infty=1\) for every \(n\).

These three properties return later as the definition of a norm; for vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) the same recipe gives the maximum norm.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A sequence of functions \((f_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) converges uniformly to a function \(f\) on \(X\) if and only if:
\[ \lim_{n \to \infty} \|f_n - f\|_\infty = 0. \]
  • For possibly unbounded functions, the same supremum of the error \(|f_n-f|\) may be \(+\infty\); it is an extended error measure rather than a norm on the space of all functions. Uniform convergence means these errors eventually become finite and tend to zero.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For the function \(f\colon (0,+\infty) \to \mathbb{R}\) defined by \(f(x) = \mathrm{e}^{-x}\), we have \(\|f\|_\infty = 1.\)
  • For the function \(g\colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) defined by \(g(x) = \sin x\), we have \(\|g\|_\infty = 1.\)

docs.title: Union and Intersection of Closed Sets
Proposition
docs.text: For a metric space \((X,d)\) and a collection of closed subsets \((E_i)_{i=1}^\infty\) of \(X\), the countable intersection \(\displaystyle\bigcap_{i=1}^\infty E_i\) and the finite union \(\displaystyle \bigcup_{i=1}^k E_i\) are also closed.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Closed sets are preserved under finite unions and arbitrary intersections. Infinite unions can break closedness, because a limit of points from infinitely many sets need not lie in any one of them.

Each \(F_n=[\tfrac{1}{n},1]\) is closed, and their union over all \(n\) is \((0,1]\). The left endpoints \(\tfrac{1}{n}\) all lie in the union and converge to \(0\), but \(0\) lies in no \(F_n\), so the union misses a limit of its own points and is not closed. Finitely many \(F_n\) never do this: \(F_1\cup\dots\cup F_k=[\tfrac{1}{k},1]\) is closed.

Both statements can be read through sequences, since a set is closed if and only if it contains the limits of its convergent sequences. A convergent sequence in \(\bigcap_i E_i\) lies in every \(E_i\), so its limit does too. A sequence in \(E_1\cup\dots\cup E_k\) has infinitely many terms in one \(E_j\); this subsequence has the same limit, which therefore lies in \(E_j\). With infinitely many sets no single set need contain a whole subsequence, as in the figure.

The proposition is also the mirror image of the union and intersection of open sets: taking complements turns intersections into unions and closed sets into open sets. Arbitrary intersections are why the intersection of all closed sets containing \(E\) is itself closed; it is the closure of \(E\).

A common slip is to read the figure as "infinite unions of closed sets are never closed". They may or may not be: the union of all \([n,n+1]\) with \(n\in\mathbb{Z}\) is \(\mathbb{R}\), which is closed. And \((0,1]\) is not open either.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Both \(X\) and \(\varnothing\) are always closed (and also open).
  • In fact any intersection of closed sets, not just countably many, is closed. This holds for uncountable families as well.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In \(\mathbb{R}\), \(\displaystyle \bigcap_{n=1}^\infty [-1/n, 1/n] = \{0\}\) is closed. Shrinking closed intervals collapse to a single closed point.
  • In \(\mathbb{R}\), \(\displaystyle \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty [0, 1-1/n] = [0,1)\) is not closed. It is missing the endpoint \(1\).

docs.title: Union and Intersection of Open Sets
Proposition
docs.text: For a metric space \((X,d)\) and a collection of open subsets \((E_i)_{i=1}^\infty\) of \(X\), the countable union \(\displaystyle\bigcup_{i=1}^\infty E_i\) and the finite intersection \(\displaystyle \bigcap_{i=1}^k E_i\) are also open.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Open sets are preserved under arbitrary unions and finite intersections. Infinite intersections can break openness, because the balls that fit inside the individual sets may shrink to nothing.

The point \(0\) is interior to every \(G_n=(-\tfrac{1}{n},\tfrac{1}{n})\), but the largest ball around \(0\) inside \(G_n\) has radius \(\tfrac{1}{n}\), and these radii tend to \(0\). No single ball around \(0\) fits inside all \(G_n\), and indeed \(\bigcap_{n\ge1}G_n=\{0\}\) is not open in \(\mathbb{R}\).

The proof is a statement about radii, using that a set is open if and only if all its points are interior points. A point of a union lies in some \(E_j\), and a ball around it inside \(E_j\) also lies inside the union. A point of \(E_1\cap\dots\cap E_k\) has balls of radius \(\varepsilon_i\) inside each \(E_i\), and the smallest of finitely many positive radii, \(\min_i\varepsilon_i>0\), gives one ball inside all of them. With infinitely many sets the radii can have infimum \(0\), as in the figure.

Together with the openness of \(\varnothing\) and \(X\), these two properties are the axioms of a topology. Taking complements gives the union and intersection of closed sets.

A common slip is to read the figure as "infinite intersections of open sets are never open". They may or may not be: \(\bigcap_{n\ge1}(-n,n)=(-1,1)\) is open. The proposition only says that openness is not guaranteed.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Both \(X\) and \(\varnothing\) are always open (and also closed).
  • In fact any union of open sets, not just countably many, is open. This holds for uncountable families as well.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In \(\mathbb{R}\), \(\displaystyle \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty (0, 1-1/n) = (0,1)\) is open. Even though each interval misses the right endpoint, the union still does not include 1.
  • In \(\mathbb{R}\), \(\displaystyle \bigcap_{n=1}^\infty (-1/n, 1+1/n) = [0,1]\) is closed. The intersection includes the endpoints 0 and 1, which are not interior points.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: For a continuous function \(f\colon [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}\) and any \(\varepsilon > 0\text{,}\) there exists a polynomial \(P\colon [a, b]\to\mathbb{R}\) such that \(\|P-f\|_\infty < \varepsilon\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Any continuous function on a closed bounded interval can be approximated as closely as desired by a polynomial, uniformly on the whole interval: for each tolerance \(\varepsilon\) there is a polynomial whose graph stays within \(\varepsilon\) of the graph of \(f\) at every point of \([a,b]\).

The figure approximates \(f(x)=|x|\) on \([-1,1]\), which has a corner at \(0\) and is not differentiable there, by even polynomials \(p_2\), \(p_4\) and \(p_8\). Their largest errors \(\|f-p_n\|_\infty\) in the uniform norm are about \(0.19\), \(0.12\) and \(0.07\), and in each case the largest error sits at the corner. The errors shrink as the degree grows, which is what the theorem promises.

Raise the degree \(n\) of the Bernstein polynomial until it lies within \(\varepsilon\) of \(f\) on all of \([0,1]\), even at the kink of \(|x-\tfrac12|\).

Both hypotheses are needed. A polynomial is continuous, and a uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous, so a function with a jump cannot be approximated uniformly by polynomials. The interval must be closed and bounded as well: every polynomial is bounded on \((0,1]\), so none stays within \(\varepsilon\) of the unbounded function \(1/x\) there, and on \(\mathbb{R}\) even \(\mathrm{e}^x\) cannot be approximated, as in the Examples.

The approximating polynomials are not partial sums of one power series. The sum of a power series is differentiable inside its interval of convergence, so \(|x|\) is not such a sum around \(0\), yet it is a uniform limit of polynomials; in the figure even the constant term changes from one \(p_n\) to the next. The theorem guarantees existence only; Bernstein polynomials, used in the interactive scene, are one explicit construction. It differs from the Taylor polynomials met later, which are built from derivatives at a single point.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • Equivalently, every continuous function \(f\) on \([a,b]\) is a uniform limit of polynomials: there are polynomials \(P_n\) with \(\|P_n-f\|_\infty\to0\) in the uniform norm.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• On \([0,1]\), the polynomials \(P_n(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}x^k/k!\) approximate \(f(x)=\mathrm{e}^x\) uniformly: \(\mathrm{e}^x-P_n(x)=\sum_{k>n}x^k/k!\) is largest at \(x=1\), so \(\|f-P_n\|_\infty=\sum_{k>n}1/k!\to0\). For \(n=3\) the error is \(\mathrm{e}-\tfrac{8}{3}\approx0.052\).
  • Continuous functions, e.g., \(f(x)=\mathrm{e}^x\), over the entirety of \(\mathbb{R}\) aren't always uniformly approximable by polynomials.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The Weierstrass function is defined as

\[ f(x) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty a^n \cos(b^n x) \]

where \(0<a<1\) and \(ab>1\text{.}\)

Each summand uses a Trigonometric Functions cosine with increasing frequency. The Infinite Series of Functions converges uniformly (by the Weierstrass \(M\)-test) because \(|a^n\cos(b^nx)|\le a^n\) and the geometric series converges for \(0<a<1\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The Weierstrass function is one of the best-known examples of a function that is continuous everywhere but differentiable nowhere. It shows that continuity, however it is pictured, does not force a graph to have a tangent at even a single point.

The figure plots the finite partial sum \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^{8}a^n\cos(b^nx)\) with \(a=1/2\) and \(b=3\). The right panel magnifies the red window and illustrates the repeated roughness; the claim about the infinite limit function is stated above.

With \(0<a<1\) and \(ab>1\), add terms and zoom in: the graph keeps its wiggles at every scale, so it has no tangent anywhere.

The two conditions on \(a\) and \(b\) play opposite roles. The condition \(0<a<1\) makes the amplitudes \(a^n\) summable, so the Weierstrass \(M\)-test gives uniform convergence, and the uniform limit of the continuous partial sums is continuous. The condition \(ab>1\) concerns slopes: the \(n\)-th term has derivative \(-(ab)^n\sin(b^nx)\), so each new term is smaller in height but steeper, and the steepness keeps increasing at ever smaller scales. The terms of the differentiated series reach size \((ab)^n\to\infty\), so that series does not converge uniformly and term-by-term differentiation is not available; this explains why differentiability can fail, although the proof that it fails at every point takes more work. If instead \(0<ab<1\), the derivative series converges uniformly by the \(M\)-test and \(f\) is differentiable.

In Weierstrass's original paper the function is \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty a^n\cos(b^n\pi x)\) with \(0<a<1\), \(b\) a positive odd integer and \(ab>1+\tfrac{3\pi}{2}\). Riemann's series \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty\sin(n^2x)/n^2\) is sometimes mentioned in the same context; it is continuous by the same \(M\)-test argument, but it is differentiable at some points, so it is not a nowhere differentiable function.

A common slip is to read the plotted curve as the function itself. Any plot shows a finite partial sum, which is differentiable everywhere; the roughness at every scale belongs only to the infinite sum.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The Weierstrass function is continuous everywhere as long as \(0<a<1\text{.}\)
  • The Weierstrass function is nowhere differentiable if \(ab>1\text{.}\)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • \(\displaystyle f(x) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{2^n} \cos(3^n x)\) is a particular Weierstrass function.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Suppose \((f_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) is a sequence of bounded functions on \(X\) such that the series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \|f_n\|_\infty\) converges. Then, the series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n(x)\rightrightarrows f\text{.}\)

The Uniform Norm \(\|f_n\|_\infty\) is the smallest common upper bound on \(|f_n(x)|\) over all \(x\). Summability of these bounds is what makes the tail estimate independent of the input.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The \(M\)-test reduces uniform convergence of a series of functions to convergence of one numerical series. Bound each term by a constant \(M_n\) that is valid at every \(x\in X\); if \(\sum_n M_n\) converges, the series of functions converges uniformly. The smallest such constant is \(\|f_n\|_\infty\), so the theorem is stated with the uniform norms, and any larger summable bounds \(M_n\) work by comparison.

Each panel shows one term \(f_n\) inside a band of half-width \(M_n\), and the bands shrink from panel to panel. The band bounds the whole graph of \(f_n\), not just its value at one point, which is what makes the estimate below independent of \(x\).

Here \(|f_n(x)|\le M_n=1/n^2\) for every \(x\). The tail bound \(\displaystyle \sum_{n>N}M_n\) is one band width for all \(x\) at once, which gives uniform convergence.

For partial sums \(\displaystyle S_N=\sum_{n=1}^N f_n\) and \(K>N\), the same bounds control every tail:

\[ |S_K(x)-S_N(x)|\le\sum_{n=N+1}^{K}M_n. \]

The right-hand side tends to zero independently of \(x\). For each fixed \(x\), the partial sums therefore form a Cauchy sequence of real numbers, so by the Cauchy criterion they converge, which gives a pointwise limit \(f\). Letting \(K\to\infty\) gives \(|f(x)-S_N(x)|\le\sum_{n>N}M_n\) for all \(x\), so the convergence is uniform.

The hypothesis is normal convergence. The test is the standard tool for proving that a power series converges uniformly on closed intervals inside its radius, and that the Weierstrass function is continuous.

A common slip is to use a bound that depends on \(x\). On \((-1,1)\), \(|x^n|\le|x|^n\) with \(\sum_n|x|^n<\infty\) for each fixed \(x\), but this gives only pointwise convergence, and the geometric series is indeed not uniformly convergent there. The test is also sufficient, not necessary: the constant functions \((-1)^n/n\) form a uniformly convergent series, although \(\sum_n 1/n\) diverges.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The limit function \(f\) is also bounded on \(X\).
  • Due to the uniform limit theorem, if each \(f_n\) is continuous, then the limit function \(f\) is continuous.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• On \(X=\mathbb{R}\), take \(f_n(x)=2^{-n}\cos(3^nx)\). Since \(|\cos(3^nx)|\le1\) for every real \(x\), the bound \(|f_n(x)|\le M_n=2^{-n}\) holds simultaneously for all \(x\). The numerical series of bounds sums to \(1\), so the function series converges uniformly on \(\mathbb{R}\):
\[ \sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}}|f(x)-S_N(x)|\le\sum_{n=N+1}^\infty 2^{-n}=2^{-N}. \]

For example, \(N=10\) makes the error at most \(2^{-10}=1/1024\) at every real \(x\), using the same number of terms everywhere.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For an inequality constraint written as \(g_i(\boldsymbol{x})\le b_i\), the constraint is binding at a feasible point \(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast\) if

\[ g_i(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)=b_i. \]

It is nonbinding or slack at \(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast\) if

\[ g_i(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)<b_i. \]

The same idea applies to constraints written in other equivalent sign conventions.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A binding constraint is tight at the chosen point. A nonbinding constraint still has room left and does not directly limit the current choice.

At the illustrated optimum, \(g_1(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)=3.9\) binds and has multiplier \(\lambda_1>0\), while \(g_2(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)=2.2<3\) is slack and has \(\lambda_2=0\). In this example, relaxing the first constraint increases the maximum, whereas relaxing the second does not change it.

The constraint is binding when the optimum lies on the line \(x+y=b\) and slack when the peak is already feasible.

The function \(g_i\) evaluates the constrained quantity at the chosen point. Comparing that value with \(b_i\) through the defining inequality distinguishes equality at the boundary from strict slack inside the allowed region.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Only binding inequality constraints can carry nonzero multipliers in standard Kuhn-Tucker conditions.
  • The set of binding constraints is often called the active set.
  • Changing a nonbinding constraint slightly usually does not change the optimum locally.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(x\le 10\) and the optimum has \(x=10\), the constraint is binding.
  • If \(x+y\le 5\) and the chosen point is \((1,2)\), the constraint is nonbinding because \(1+2<5\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For an equality-constrained problem with Lagrangian \(L(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{\lambda})\) and constraint Jacobian \(\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{g}(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)\), the bordered Hessian matrix is the block matrix

\[ \begin{pmatrix} \boldsymbol{0} & \boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{g}(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)\\ \boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{g}(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)^{\top} & \boldsymbol{H}_xL(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast,\boldsymbol{\lambda}^\ast) \end{pmatrix}, \]

with the exact block orientation depending on whether gradients are written as rows or columns.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The bordered Hessian packages the constraint linearization and the curvature of the Lagrangian into one matrix. Its leading principal minors tell whether \(L\) bends down or up along the directions that keep the constraints satisfied to first order.

The figure shows the block layout: an \(m\times m\) zero block, the constraint Jacobian \(\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{g}(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)\) (\(m\times n\)) and its transpose as the border, and the \(n\times n\) Hessian of \(L\) with respect to \(\boldsymbol{x}\) in the corner, \((m+n)\times(m+n)\) in total. This is the matrix of the bordered matrix test, with \(\boldsymbol{B}=\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{g}(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)\) and \(\boldsymbol{A}\) the Hessian of \(L\).

The constraint gradient borders the Hessian block; the determinant of the bordered matrix carries the second-order constrained test.

The Hessian of \(L\), not of the objective, is needed because the bending of the constraint matters too. When \(x+y\) is maximized on the circle \(x^2+y^2=1\), the objective has zero Hessian and says nothing. With \(L=x+y+\lambda(1-x^2-y^2)\), the candidate \((1/\sqrt{2},1/\sqrt{2})\) has \(\lambda^\ast=1/\sqrt{2}\), the Hessian of \(L\) is \(-\sqrt{2}\boldsymbol{I}\), and the bordered Hessian has determinant \(4\sqrt{2}>0\), the sign \((-1)^{m+1}=+1\) that the Key Results require for a strict local maximum. Writing a constraint as \(-g\) instead of \(g\) flips the sign of a border row and the matching column together, which leaves every leading minor unchanged.

A common slip is to inspect all leading minors. The first \(2m\) do not depend on the Hessian block, so they say nothing about curvature; only the last \(n-m\) count, as in the second-order sufficient conditions.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The \(m\times m\) zero block corresponds to the multiplier variables; the \(m\times n\) border contains the constraint gradients.
  • The \(n\times n\) Hessian block is taken with respect to the choice variables, so the full matrix has size \((m+n)\times(m+n)\).
  • Determinants of selected bordered submatrices are used in bordered matrix tests.
  • For \(m<n\) equality constraints with independent gradients at a first-order candidate, the second-order sufficient conditions inspect the last \(n-m\) leading principal minors. Alternating signs starting with \((-1)^{m+1}\) give a strict local maximum; signs all equal to \((-1)^m\) give a strict local minimum. These tests check the curvature of \(L\) along directions tangent to the constraints.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For one constraint \(g(x,y)=0\), a common bordered Hessian has first row and column built from \(g_x\) and \(g_y\).
  • For two equality constraints in three variables, the bordered Hessian has a \(2\) by \(2\) zero block and a \(3\) by \(3\) Hessian block.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(Q(\boldsymbol{x})=\boldsymbol{x}^{\top} \boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\) with \(\boldsymbol{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) symmetric, and let the independent linear constraint set be \(\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{x}=0\) with \(\boldsymbol{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(\operatorname{rank}(\boldsymbol{B})=m\). The bordered matrix is

\[ \boldsymbol{H}= \begin{pmatrix} \boldsymbol{0}_m & \boldsymbol{B}\\ \boldsymbol{B}^{\top} & \boldsymbol{A} \end{pmatrix}. \]

Ignore the first \(2m\) leading principal minors. For \(k=2m+1,\ldots,m+n\):

  • If \((-1)^m\det(\boldsymbol{H}_k)>0\) for all relevant \(k\), then \(Q\) is positive definite on the constraint set.
  • If \((-1)^{k-m}\det(\boldsymbol{H}_k)>0\) for all relevant \(k\), then \(Q\) is negative definite on the constraint set.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The bordered matrix test checks the sign of a quadratic form only along the directions that linear constraints leave free (definiteness on the constraint set). It is the constrained version of Sylvester's criterion, again read from determinant signs.

The figure shows the blocks of \(\boldsymbol{H}\): an \(m\times m\) zero block (grey), the constraint matrix \(\boldsymbol{B}\) and its transpose as a border (red), and the matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}\) of the form (blue). \(\boldsymbol{H}_k\) is the top-left \(k\times k\) submatrix. The first \(2m\) leading minors do not depend on \(\boldsymbol{A}\), which is why they are ignored; the remaining \(n-m\) are as many as the dimension of the constraint set \(\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{0}\}\).

With one constraint in two variables, the sign of \(\det(\boldsymbol{H}_3)\) decides definiteness on the constraint set, matching the sign of the form along the highlighted line \(T\).

For \(x_1^2-x_2^2\) on the line \(x_1=2x_2\) from the Examples, \(\boldsymbol{B}=\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\boldsymbol{A}=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\), so \(\det\boldsymbol{H}=-3\) and \((-1)^1\det\boldsymbol{H}>0\); indeed \(Q(2t,t)=3t^2>0\) for \(t\neq0\).

The rank condition says that the \(m\) constraints are independent, so they remove exactly \(m\) directions. Without it the test breaks down: if the rows of \(\boldsymbol{B}\) are dependent, some \(\boldsymbol{w}\neq\boldsymbol{0}\) has \(\boldsymbol{B}^{\top}\boldsymbol{w}=\boldsymbol{0}\), then \(\boldsymbol{H}\) sends \((\boldsymbol{w},\boldsymbol{0})\) to \(\boldsymbol{0}\), and \(\det\boldsymbol{H}=0\) whatever \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is.

A common slip is to expect positive determinants for a positive definite form. With one constraint, positive definiteness on the constraint set shows up as negative minors, as in the example; the factor \((-1)^m\) tells which sign to look for. The test returns later in the course, with a Lagrangian's Hessian as \(\boldsymbol{A}\), as the bordered Hessian.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Definiteness on the whole space can change after restricting to a constraint set.
  • For positive definiteness, all relevant signs match \((-1)^m\).
  • For negative definiteness, relevant signs alternate and the full determinant has sign \((-1)^n\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The form \(x_1^2-x_2^2\) is indefinite on \(\mathbb{R}^2\) but positive on the line \(x_1=2x_2\).
  • When \(n=2\) and \(m=1\), there is just one relevant minor: \(\det \boldsymbol{H}<0\) gives positive definiteness of \(Q\) on the constraint line.
  • When \(n=3\) and \(m=1\), inspect \(\det(\boldsymbol{H}_3)\) and \(\det(\boldsymbol{H}_4)\) after ignoring the first two leading minors.
