docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(I\subseteq\mathbb{R}\) be an interval and let \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}\colon I\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be a differentiable curve. Its velocity at \(t_0\) is

\[ \boldsymbol{\gamma}'(t_0)= \begin{pmatrix} \gamma_1'(t_0)\\ \vdots\\ \gamma_n'(t_0) \end{pmatrix}. \]

If \(B\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is an open set containing \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(I)\) and \(f\colon B\to\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable at \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t_0)\in B\), then

\[ \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(f\circ\boldsymbol{\gamma})(t_0) =\boldsymbol{D}f(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t_0))\boldsymbol{\gamma}'(t_0) =\boldsymbol{\nabla} f(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t_0))^{\top}\boldsymbol{\gamma}'(t_0). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A curve describes motion through a multivariable state space. The chain rule says the value changes by combining the system's velocity with the local sensitivity of the function of several variables.

The chain rule gives \(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}f(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t))\big|_{t=t_0}=\boldsymbol{\nabla} f(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t_0))\cdot\boldsymbol{\gamma}'(t_0)\). In the figure, the velocity has a positive component along the gradient, so \(f\) increases along the curve at \(t_0\). The grey circles are level sets of \(f\).

Move \(t\): the rate of change of \(f(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t))\) (right) equals \(\boldsymbol{\nabla} f(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t))^\top\boldsymbol{\gamma}'(t)\), the gradient dotted with the velocity.

A path assigns a position to each parameter value. Composing it with \(f\) restricts \(f\) to that motion; differentiating the composition pairs the derivative of \(f\) with the path velocity.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The derivative of \(f(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t))\) is the total derivative of \(f\) applied to the velocity of \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}\).
  • If the velocity is a unit vector, the formula is a directional derivative.
  • The curve case is the one-dimensional input version of the multivariable chain rule.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(f(x,y)=x^2+y^2\) and \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t)=(t,2t)\), then \((f\circ\boldsymbol{\gamma})'(t)=10t\).
  • If \(f(x,y)=xy\) and \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t)=(\mathrm{e}^t,t^2)\), then \((f\circ\boldsymbol{\gamma})'(t)=\mathrm{e}^t(t^2+2t)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For an inequality constraint written as \(c_i(\boldsymbol{x})\le 0\) (for example \(c_i=g_i-b_i\) for a constraint \(g_i(\boldsymbol{x})\le b_i\)) with multiplier \(\lambda_i\ge 0\), complementary slackness is the condition

\[ \lambda_i c_i(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)=0. \]

Equivalently, either the constraint is binding or its multiplier is zero.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Complementary slackness says that a constraint can matter through its multiplier only when it is actually tight.

On the left, the binding constraint holds back the maximum, with \(\boldsymbol{\nabla} f=\lambda\boldsymbol{\nabla} c\), \(\lambda>0\), and \(c=0\). On the right, the optimum lies in the interior and the multiplier is zero. The grey curves are objective level sets and the blue region is feasible.

Move \(b\) and the peak: either the constraint binds, or its multiplier is \(0\), so the product \(\lambda\,(b-g(\boldsymbol{x}^*))\) is always \(0\).

The inequality fixes the sign of the slack. A strictly negative constraint value forces its multiplier to zero because their product must vanish; equality permits a nonzero multiplier.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(c_i(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)<0\), then \(\lambda_i=0\).
  • If \(\lambda_i>0\), then \(c_i(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)=0\).
  • The condition is part of the Kuhn-Tucker system for inequality-constrained optimization.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(x\le 4\) is written as \(x-4\le 0\) and the optimum has \(x=3\), then the multiplier must be \(0\).
  • If a multiplier for \(x\le 4\) is positive, then the optimum must satisfy \(x=4\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex. A function \(f\colon C\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex if for all \(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}\in C\) and all \(\lambda\in[0,1]\),

\[ f(\lambda \boldsymbol{x}+(1-\lambda)\boldsymbol{y}) \le\lambda f(\boldsymbol{x})+(1-\lambda)f(\boldsymbol{y}). \]

It is concave if the inequality is reversed.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A convex function lies below the straight interpolation of its values. A concave function lies above that interpolation.

The two graphs illustrate the segment test: on a convex domain \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), apply the defining inequality to every segment joining \(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}\in C\). Reversing the inequality gives concavity; equivalently, \(f\) is concave if and only if \(-f\) is convex. For a twice continuously differentiable function on an open convex domain, the Hessian test checks positive semidefiniteness for convexity and negative semidefiniteness for concavity.

Along the segment from \(\boldsymbol{y}\) to \(\boldsymbol{x}\) (right), a convex function stays below the chord and a concave one above it.

Drag \(\boldsymbol{x}\) and \(\boldsymbol{y}\): for a convex \(f\) the surface along the segment stays below the chord between \(f(\boldsymbol{x})\) and \(f(\boldsymbol{y})\).

A convex domain keeps the interpolated input inside the domain, so its function value is defined. The convexity inequality then compares this output with the same weighted interpolation of the endpoint outputs.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For convex functions, every local minimum is a global minimum.
  • For concave functions, every local maximum is a global maximum.
  • If \(f\) is strictly convex, it has at most one minimizer on \(C\); if \(f\) is strictly concave, it has at most one maximizer on \(C\text{.}\)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The function \(f(x,y)=x^2+y^2\) is convex on \(\mathbb{R}^2\).
  • The function \(u(x,y)=\log x+\log y\) is concave on \((0,\infty)^2\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is convex if for every \(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}\in C\) and every \(\lambda\in[0,1]\),

\[ \lambda \boldsymbol{x}+(1-\lambda)\boldsymbol{y}\in C. \]

Equivalently, the whole line segment between any two points of \(C\) lies inside \(C\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A convex set contains, with any two of its points, the whole straight segment between them. In optimization terms: moving in a straight line from one feasible point to another never leaves the feasible region.

In the left set the segment from \(\boldsymbol{x}\) to \(\boldsymbol{y}\) stays inside, and \(\boldsymbol{z}\) is one of its points \(\lambda\boldsymbol{x}+(1-\lambda)\boldsymbol{y}\). The right set has a dent, and part of the drawn segment runs outside it. One such segment proves that a set is not convex; convexity needs every pair of points.

Drag \(\boldsymbol{x}\) and \(\boldsymbol{y}\) inside the set and move \(\lambda\): a set is convex when every such segment stays inside. Find a segment that leaves the L-shape.

As \(\lambda\) runs from \(1\) to \(0\), the point \(\lambda\boldsymbol{x}+(1-\lambda)\boldsymbol{y}\) moves along the segment from \(\boldsymbol{x}\) to \(\boldsymbol{y}\) (parametric representation of a line); the two weights are nonnegative and add up to \(1\). If \(\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\le b\) and \(\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\le b\), then \(\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}(\lambda\boldsymbol{x}+(1-\lambda)\boldsymbol{y})\le\lambda b+(1-\lambda)b=b\), so a half-space is convex, and so is every intersection of half-spaces, such as the feasible region of a linear program. Unions behave differently: two disjoint discs together are not convex.

In \(\mathbb{R}\) a segment is an interval \([x,y]\), which is why convexity of a function was defined on an interval. A convex function on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) needs a convex domain for the same reason: \(f(\lambda\boldsymbol{x}+(1-\lambda)\boldsymbol{y})\) must be defined.

Convex sets need not be closed or bounded: an open ball, a half-space and \(\mathbb{R}^n\) itself are convex.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Intersections of convex sets are convex.
  • Euclidean open balls, closed balls, half-spaces, and affine subspaces are convex. The same ball conclusion holds for norm-induced metrics, but not for arbitrary metrics.
  • A feasible region described by linear equality and weak linear inequality constraints is convex.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The set \(\{(x,y)\colon x+y\le 1\}\) is convex because it is a half-space.
  • The unit disk \(\{(x,y)\colon x^2+y^2\le 1\}\) is convex, but the unit circle \(\{(x,y)\colon x^2+y^2=1\}\) is not.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
In a parametric problem, the value function is the optimized objective value

\[ F(\boldsymbol{\alpha})=f(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(\boldsymbol{\alpha});\boldsymbol{\alpha}), \]

where \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(\boldsymbol{\alpha})\) is an optimizer. For equality constraints, define

\[ L(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{\mu};\boldsymbol{\alpha})=f(\boldsymbol{x};\boldsymbol{\alpha})+\sum_j\mu_jh_j(\boldsymbol{x};\boldsymbol{\alpha}). \]

If smooth optimizer and multiplier functions satisfy the first-order conditions, then

\[ \frac{\partial F}{\partial\alpha_\ell}(\boldsymbol{\alpha})=\frac{\partial L}{\partial\alpha_\ell}\big(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}),\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}(\boldsymbol{\alpha});\boldsymbol{\alpha}\big). \]

For mixed constraints, the same formula holds with the Lagrangian including the binding inequalities and equality constraints, provided the relevant bordered Hessian is nonsingular and the active set is smooth. In the special equality case \(h_j(\boldsymbol{x};\boldsymbol{\alpha})=\alpha_j-\widetilde h_j(\boldsymbol{x})\) with \(f\) independent of \(\boldsymbol{\alpha}\), the multiplier is the shadow price:

\[ \frac{\partial F}{\partial\alpha_j}(\boldsymbol{\alpha})=\widetilde\mu_j(\boldsymbol{\alpha}). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The envelope theorem computes how the best attainable value changes when a parameter changes. It avoids separately differentiating every movement of the optimizer.

In the illustrated example, the feasible choices do not depend on \(\alpha\), and the value function \(V(\alpha)=\max_x f(x;\alpha)\) (written \(F\) in the theorem above) is the upper envelope of the grey curves obtained by fixing \(x\). At \(\alpha_0\), it touches the curve for \(x^\ast(\alpha_0)\) and shares its slope: \(V'(\alpha_0)=\frac{\partial f}{\partial\alpha}(x^\ast(\alpha_0);\alpha_0)\). The theorem above gives the corresponding formula when the constraints depend on the parameter.

The derivative of the optimal value \(F(\alpha)\) equals the partial derivative of the Lagrangian with respect to \(\alpha\) at the optimum, here the multiplier \(\mu\).

The equality-constraint Lagrange method supplies the stationarity equations. Applying the implicit function theorem to those equations and the constraints can give locally smooth optimizer and multiplier functions when the relevant bordered Hessian is nonsingular. The chain-rule terms involving optimizer movements then cancel by stationarity and differentiated feasibility.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The value function records the optimum as a function of parameters.
  • The envelope derivative is the direct parameter derivative of the Lagrangian at the optimal solution.
  • A shadow price is the marginal value of relaxing a constraint in the stated equality-constraint setup.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(f(x;\alpha)=\alpha x-x^2\), the envelope derivative is \(x^\ast(\alpha)\).
  • In utility maximization with income as a parameter, the multiplier on the budget equation measures marginal utility of income.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In an equation system \(\boldsymbol{F}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})=0\), the variables in \(\boldsymbol{x}\) are called exogenous variables if they are treated as freely chosen inputs. The variables in \(\boldsymbol{y}\) are called endogenous variables if the equation system is used to solve for them as functions of \(\boldsymbol{x}\).

When possible, the implicit function theorem gives a local function \(\boldsymbol{g}\) such that

\[ \boldsymbol{F}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{g}(\boldsymbol{x}))=0. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Exogenous variables are the knobs set from outside the system. Endogenous variables are the quantities the system determines in response.

The model takes the exogenous variables as inputs and solves for the endogenous variables. Under the local invertibility assumptions of the implicit function theorem, \(m\) equations determine \(m\) endogenous variables locally once the inputs are fixed. The split is a modelling choice: prices are endogenous in an equilibrium model but exogenous for a price-taker.

The local function assigns endogenous outputs to exogenous inputs. The partial Jacobian with respect to the endogenous variables is the block whose invertibility lets the implicit function theorem solve for those outputs.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The distinction depends on how the equation system is being used, not only on the symbols.
  • The implicit function theorem requires the partial Jacobian with respect to the endogenous variables to be invertible in the square case.
  • Comparative statics studies how endogenous variables change when exogenous variables are perturbed, that is, the derivatives of the local function \(\boldsymbol{g}\) above.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In \(x+y=10\), if \(x\) is chosen externally, then \(y=10-x\) is endogenous.
  • In supply and demand equilibrium, a tax can be exogenous while price and quantity are endogenous equilibrium variables.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be open, and let \(f,g_i,h_j\) be continuously differentiable on \(A\). For minimization, write the inequalities as \(g_i(\boldsymbol{x})\le0\); for maximization, write them as \(g_i(\boldsymbol{x})\ge0\). With equalities \(h_j(\boldsymbol{x})=0\), define the generalized Lagrangian

\[ \Lambda(\boldsymbol{x},\lambda_0,\boldsymbol{\lambda},\boldsymbol{\mu}) = \lambda_0 f(\boldsymbol{x})+\sum_i\lambda_i g_i(\boldsymbol{x}) +\sum_j\mu_j h_j(\boldsymbol{x}). \]

If \(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast\) is a local constrained optimum, then there exist multipliers with \(\lambda_0\in\{0,1\}\), \(\lambda_i\ge0\), and \((\lambda_0,\boldsymbol{\lambda},\boldsymbol{\mu})\neq0\) such that stationarity, feasibility, and complementary slackness hold.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
This method avoids a separate regularity check by adding a multiplier on the objective itself. The extra case captures points where the active constraints are degenerate.

The illustrated feasible arc satisfies \(h(\boldsymbol{x})=c\) and \(g(\boldsymbol{x})\le3.1\). Both constraints bind at \(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast\), where the objective gradient is a combination of the active constraint gradients with the appropriate multiplier signs. The theorem above specifies the normalization and regularity requirements for the multipliers.

The mixed-constraint method is recovered when the objective multiplier can be normalized to one. The nondegenerate constraint qualification rules out an abnormal candidate with zero objective multiplier: independence of the active constraint gradients would then force every multiplier to vanish.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(\lambda_0=1\), the regular first-order necessary conditions are recovered.
  • If \(\lambda_0=0\), the condition signals linear dependence among active constraint gradients.
  • The method keeps nonregular feasible points inside the theorem.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For a regular optimum, choosing \(\lambda_0=1\) gives the usual Lagrangian conditions.
  • If active constraint gradients are linearly dependent, a solution may appear with \(\lambda_0=0\) and nonzero constraint multipliers.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(f\colon A\to\mathbb{R}\), and let \(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast\in A\).

  • \(f(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)\) is a global maximum if \(f(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)\ge f(\boldsymbol{x})\) for all \(\boldsymbol{x}\in A\).
  • \(f(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)\) is a global minimum if \(f(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)\le f(\boldsymbol{x})\) for all \(\boldsymbol{x}\in A\).

The extremum is strict if the inequality is strict for all \(\boldsymbol{x}\in A\setminus\{\boldsymbol{x}^\ast\}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A global extremum compares the candidate with every feasible point. Strictness means there is no other feasible point with the same optimal value.

In the figure, the global minimum occurs at the boundary point \(0\) and the global maximum at \(c\). The points \(a\) and \(b\) are only a local maximum and minimum, respectively, because their comparisons use a neighbourhood rather than the whole feasible set.

On the square \([-2,2]^2\) the largest and smallest values may sit on the boundary rather than at a critical point.

The extreme value theorem on compact sets gives an existence condition: a continuous function on a nonempty compact feasible set attains both extrema. The definition itself does not guarantee attainment on an arbitrary set.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A strict global maximum or minimum has a unique optimizer.
  • A continuous function on a compact feasible set attains both a global maximum and a global minimum.
  • A global extremum is automatically local when neighbourhoods inside the feasible set are considered.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(f(x,y)=-(x^2+y^2)\) on \(\mathbb{R}^2\), \((0,0)\) is a strict global maximizer.
  • For \(f(x,y)=x^2\) on \(\mathbb{R}^2\), every point with \(x=0\) is a global minimizer.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(f\colon E\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be a scalar-valued function whose second-order partial derivatives exist at \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\in E\). The Hessian matrix of \(f\) at \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) is

\[ \boldsymbol{H}_f(\boldsymbol{x}_0) =\begin{pmatrix} \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_1^2}(\boldsymbol{x}_0) & \cdots & \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_1\partial x_n}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\ \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_n\partial x_1}(\boldsymbol{x}_0) & \cdots & \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_n^2}(\boldsymbol{x}_0) \end{pmatrix}. \]

The entry in row \(i\) and column \(j\) is the second partial derivative with respect to \(x_i\) and \(x_j\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The Hessian collects all second-order bending information of a scalar function at one point. It is the multivariable analogue of the second derivative in one-variable calculus.

The blue diagonal entries are the pure second partials, measuring curvature along the coordinate axes. The mixed partials appear in symmetric pairs when \(f\) is \(C^2\). When \(f\) is \(C^2\) on an open neighbourhood of \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\), the second-order approximation is \(f(\boldsymbol{x}_0+\boldsymbol{h})=f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)+\boldsymbol{\nabla} f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\cdot \boldsymbol{h}+\frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{h}^{\top} \boldsymbol{H}_f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\boldsymbol{h}+o(\|\boldsymbol{h}\|^2)\). At a stationary point, positive or negative definiteness gives a strict local minimum or maximum, and an indefinite Hessian gives a saddle; semidefinite cases can be inconclusive.

Drag \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\): the Hessian collects the second-order partial derivatives there, and its eigenvalues describe how the level curves bend.

Move \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) and read \(\boldsymbol{H}_f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\): at the marked critical points its definiteness matches the shape of the surface.

Arranging the second derivatives in a matrix makes curvature along a displacement accessible through the quadratic form \(\boldsymbol{h}^{\top}\boldsymbol{H}_f\boldsymbol{h}\). For a \(C^2\) function, this is the second-order term in the local Taylor approximation, up to its factor \(1/2\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
For the second-order tests below, assume \(f\) is \(C^2\) on an open neighbourhood of \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) and \(\boldsymbol{\nabla}f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)=\boldsymbol{0}\). Mere existence of the Hessian at one point is insufficient.

  • If \(f\) is \(C^2\) near \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\), then the Hessian is symmetric.
  • At a critical point (for differentiable \(f\) the same as a stationary point, \(\boldsymbol{\nabla}f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)=\boldsymbol{0}\)), a positive definite Hessian gives a strict local minimum.
  • At a critical point, a negative definite Hessian gives a strict local maximum.
  • At a critical point, an indefinite Hessian gives a saddle point.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(f(x,y)=x^2+2xy+3y^2\), the Hessian is \(\begin{pmatrix}2&2\\2&6\end{pmatrix}\) at every point.
  • For \(f(x,y)=x^3+2xy^2-y^3\), the Hessian at \((1,1)\) is \(\begin{pmatrix}6&4\\4&-2\end{pmatrix}\).

docs.title: Hessian Test for Convexity and Concavity
Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex and open, and let \(f\colon C\to\mathbb{R}\) be twice continuously differentiable.

Then \(f\) is convex on \(C\) if and only if \(\boldsymbol{H}_f(\boldsymbol{x})\) is positive semidefinite for every \(\boldsymbol{x}\in C\).

The function \(f\) is concave on \(C\) if and only if \(\boldsymbol{H}_f(\boldsymbol{x})\) is negative semidefinite for every \(\boldsymbol{x}\in C\).

If \(\boldsymbol{H}_f(\boldsymbol{x})\) is positive definite for every \(\boldsymbol{x}\in C\), then \(f\) is strictly convex. If \(\boldsymbol{H}_f(\boldsymbol{x})\) is negative definite for every \(\boldsymbol{x}\in C\), then \(f\) is strictly concave.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The Hessian test turns the geometric question of bending upward or downward into a matrix definiteness check at every point of the domain. It extends the one-variable criterion that a twice-differentiable function on an open interval is convex if and only if \(f''\ge0\) there (convexity and concavity).

The bowl \(x_1^2+x_2^2\) has Hessian \(2\boldsymbol{I}\) at every point, positive definite, so it is strictly convex; the dome \(-x_1^2-x_2^2\) has \(-2\boldsymbol{I}\) and is strictly concave. The saddle \(x_1^2-x_2^2\) has the indefinite Hessian \(\operatorname{diag}(2,-2)\): along the \(x_1\)-axis the graph bends up, along the \(x_2\)-axis down, so it is neither.

For \(-x^2-xy-y^2\) the Hessian is negative definite everywhere, so the function is strictly concave. Other examples fail the test somewhere.

The test reduces to one variable. On the segment from \(\boldsymbol{x}\) to \(\boldsymbol{y}\), put \(\boldsymbol{d}=\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{x}\) and \(g(t)=f(\boldsymbol{x}+t\boldsymbol{d})\); the chain rule, applied twice, gives

\[ g''(t)=\boldsymbol{d}^{\top}\boldsymbol{H}_f(\boldsymbol{x}+t\boldsymbol{d})\boldsymbol{d}, \]

and \(f\) is convex exactly when every such \(g\) is. So the condition must hold at every point of \(C\), and \(C\) must be convex, or segments leave the domain: \(1/x^2\) has \(f''>0\) on \(\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}\), but the segment from \(-1\) to \(1\) crosses the gap, so convexity there is not even defined. Definiteness at a general point is checked with Sylvester's criterion: for \(-x^2-xy-y^2\) in the interactive example the leading minors are \(-2\) and \(3\) everywhere.

The strict statement only goes one way: \(x^4+y^4\) is strictly convex, but its Hessian \(\operatorname{diag}(12x^2,12y^2)\) is only positive semidefinite at the origin. The test pays off in optimization, because for a convex function every local minimum is a global minimum.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Positive semidefinite Hessian everywhere is equivalent to convexity under the stated smoothness and convex-domain assumptions.
  • Negative semidefinite Hessian everywhere is equivalent to concavity under the same assumptions.
  • Positive definiteness everywhere is sufficient for strict convexity, but not necessary in every case.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(f(x,y)=x^2+y^2\), \(\boldsymbol{H}_f=2\boldsymbol{I}\), so \(f\) is strictly convex.
  • For \(f(x,y)=-(x^2+y^2)\), \(\boldsymbol{H}_f=-2\boldsymbol{I}\), so \(f\) is strictly concave.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A higher-order partial derivative is obtained by differentiating a partial derivative again with respect to one or more variables. For example, for \(f\colon A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\),

\[ f_{x_i x_j x_k}(\boldsymbol{a})= \frac{\partial}{\partial x_i} \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial x_j} \left( \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_k} \right) \right)(\boldsymbol{a}) \]

is a third-order partial derivative, when all indicated derivatives exist. In this notation the derivative written closest to \(f\) (here \(\partial/\partial x_k\)) is taken first; many texts instead read subscripts from left to right, so that \(f_{xy}=(f_x)_y\text{.}\) For \(C^3\) functions both readings give the same value.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Higher-order partial derivatives measure how earlier rates of change themselves change as one moves in chosen coordinate directions. They play the role that \(f''\) and \(f'''\) play for a function of one variable (higher-order derivative).

Each arrow differentiates once more, in \(x\) to the left and in \(y\) to the right, so the rows hold the \(2\), \(4\) and \(8\) partial derivatives of order \(1\), \(2\) and \(3\). In \(n\) variables there are \(n^k\) ordered partials of order \(k\). As in the Definition, the new variable is written on the left, so \(f_{yx}\) is obtained from \(f_x\).

Texts that read subscripts from left to right write these labels in reverse order. For \(C^k\) functions the two readings agree, because then the order of differentiation does not matter (higher-order symmetry of partials). The eight third-order partials of a \(C^3\) function of \((x,y)\) then take at most four values, \(f_{xxx}\), \(f_{xxy}\), \(f_{xyy}\) and \(f_{yyy}\). Without continuity the order can matter: for \(f(x,y)=xy(x^2-y^2)/(x^2+y^2)\) with \(f(0,0)=0\), the two mixed second partials at the origin are \(1\) and \(-1\).

The second-order partials of a scalar function form its Hessian matrix, the third-order ones fill the third-order derivative tensor, and both supply the higher terms of multivariate Taylor approximations.

A common slip is to read \(f_{xx}\) as \((f_x)^2\). For \(f(x,y)=x^2y^3\) from the Examples, \(f_x=2xy^3\), so \(f_{xx}=2y^3\), while \((f_x)^2=4x^2y^6\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Second-order partial derivatives form the Hessian matrix when they exist.
  • Third-order partial derivatives can be arranged in a three-dimensional array.
  • Continuity assumptions are usually needed before changing the order of differentiation.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(f(x,y)=x^2y^3\), \(f_{xy}=6xy^2\) and \(f_{xyy}=12xy\).
  • For \(f(x,y,z)=xyz^2\), \(f_{xyz}=2z\) and \(f_{xzz}=2y\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(f\) have continuous partial derivatives up to order \(k\) on an open neighbourhood of \(\boldsymbol{a}\). Then any two \(k\)th-order partial derivatives that differentiate with respect to the same variables the same number of times are equal at \(\boldsymbol{a}\).

For third-order derivatives this means, for example,

\[ \begin{aligned} f_{xyz}(\boldsymbol{a})&=f_{xzy}(\boldsymbol{a})\\ &=f_{yxz}(\boldsymbol{a})=f_{yzx}(\boldsymbol{a})\\ &=f_{zxy}(\boldsymbol{a})=f_{zyx}(\boldsymbol{a}) \end{aligned} \]

whenever the required third-order partial derivatives are continuous near \(\boldsymbol{a}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
When the function is smooth enough, only the number of times each direction is used matters, not the order in which the differentiations are performed.

The top row shows the eight formal third-order partials in two variables. For a \(C^3\) function, they fall into four groups according to how often each variable is used, for example \(f_{xxy}=f_{xyx}=f_{yxx}\). More generally, symmetry reduces the \(n^k\) ordered partials of a \(C^k\) function to at most \(\binom{n+k-1}{k}\) distinct values.

The differentiability class \(C^k\) packages the hypothesis that all partial derivatives through order \(k\) exist and are continuous. This regularity permits repeated interchange of the order of differentiation; existence of derivatives alone is insufficient.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The second-order case is the usual symmetry of mixed partial derivatives.
  • For a sufficiently smooth scalar function, the third derivative tensor is symmetric under permutations of its indices.
  • Without the needed continuity assumptions, mixed partials can fail to agree.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(f(x,y,z)=x^2yz^3\), the derivatives \(f_{xyz}\), \(f_{xzy}\), and \(f_{zyx}\) agree because \(f\) is a polynomial.
  • For \(f(x,y)=\mathrm{e}^{xy}\), \(f_{xxy}=f_{xyx}=f_{yxx}\) at every point because all partial derivatives are continuous.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
In a system \(\boldsymbol{G}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})=0\), the variables \(\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\) are treated as exogenous and \(\boldsymbol{y}\in\mathbb{R}^m\) as endogenous. For \(\boldsymbol{G}\colon A\to\mathbb{R}^m\), define the partial Jacobians \(\boldsymbol{D}_x\boldsymbol{G}\) and \(\boldsymbol{D}_y\boldsymbol{G}\) by differentiating with respect to the \(\boldsymbol{x}\)-block and \(\boldsymbol{y}\)-block.

Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+m}\) be open and let \(\boldsymbol{G}\colon A\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be \(C^1\). Suppose \((\boldsymbol{x}_0,\boldsymbol{y}_0)\in A\), \(\boldsymbol{G}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,\boldsymbol{y}_0)=0\), and

\[ \det(\boldsymbol{D}_y\boldsymbol{G}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,\boldsymbol{y}_0))\neq 0. \]

Then there is a neighbourhood \(B\) of \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) and a \(C^1\) function \(\boldsymbol{\varphi}\colon B\to\mathbb{R}^m\) such that \(\boldsymbol{\varphi}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)=\boldsymbol{y}_0\) and \(\boldsymbol{G}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{\varphi}(\boldsymbol{x}))=0\) for all \(\boldsymbol{x}\in B\). After shrinking \(B\) if necessary, there is a neighbourhood \(W\) of \(\boldsymbol{y}_0\) such that, for each \(\boldsymbol{x}\in B\), \(\boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{\varphi}(\boldsymbol{x})\) is the only solution of \(\boldsymbol{G}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})=0\) in \(W\). Moreover,

\[ \boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{\varphi}(\boldsymbol{x}_0) =-(\boldsymbol{D}_y\boldsymbol{G}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,\boldsymbol{y}_0))^{-1}\boldsymbol{D}_x\boldsymbol{G}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,\boldsymbol{y}_0). \]

For one equation in two variables, this reduces to \(\varphi'(x_0)=-G_x(x_0,y_0)/G_y(x_0,y_0)\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The theorem says that a regular system of equations can locally be solved for the variables that must adjust. It also gives the local response of those adjusting variables when the chosen variables change.

For the circle \(G(x,y)=x^2+y^2-1=0\), the point \((x_0,y_0)=(0,1)\) has \(G_y(x_0,y_0)=2\ne0\). In a neighbourhood of that point, the circle is the graph \(y=g(x)=\sqrt{1-x^2}\), and \(g'(x)=-x/y\). The theorem above gives the corresponding derivative formula for systems of equations.

Move along \(x^2+y^2=1\): wherever \(D_yG\ne0\) the curve is locally a graph \(y=\varphi(x)\) with slope \(-D_xG/D_yG\). At \(y=0\) this fails.

The Jacobian contains the first-order effects of the equation variables. Its endogenous block must be invertible to solve locally for changes in the endogenous variables; a singular block does not meet the theorem's hypothesis.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The determinant condition says the endogenous block is locally pinned down by the equations.
  • The theorem gives local existence, differentiability, and a derivative formula.
  • The one-equation case is the familiar slope formula for an implicit curve.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(G(x,y)=y-x^2\), the theorem gives \(y=\varphi(x)=x^2\) because \(D_yG=1\).
  • For \(G(x,y)=x^2+y^2-1\) near \((0,1)\), the theorem gives the upper circle locally as a function of \(x\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A linear constraint system

\[ \boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{b} \]

with \(\boldsymbol{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) has independent constraints if the rows of \(\boldsymbol{A}\) are linearly independent, equivalently

\[ \operatorname{rank}\boldsymbol{A}=m. \]

For nonlinear equality constraints \(g_1(\boldsymbol{x})=0,\ldots,g_m(\boldsymbol{x})=0\), the corresponding local condition at \(\boldsymbol{a}\) is that the gradients \(\boldsymbol{\nabla} g_1(\boldsymbol{a}),\ldots,\boldsymbol{\nabla} g_m(\boldsymbol{a})\) are linearly independent.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Independent constraints each remove a genuinely new direction. Dependent constraints repeat information and can make multiplier tests misleading.

On the right, the rows of \(\boldsymbol{A}\) are dependent and \(\operatorname{rank}\boldsymbol{A}=1\). The corresponding parallel lines either have no common solution or coincide along a whole line. On the left, the two independent constraints have rank \(2\) and meet at one point.

The rank counts independent rows. Equality to \(m\) means that no constraint equation is an algebraic consequence of the others; for nonlinear constraints the same check applies to their gradients at the chosen point.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For \(m\) independent equality constraints in \(\mathbb{R}^n\), the linearized feasible directions (the null space of the constraint matrix or Jacobian) form an \((n-m)\)-dimensional space, by the rank-nullity theorem.
  • Independence is a rank condition on the constraint Jacobian.
  • Nondegenerate constraint qualification is the nonlinear optimization version of this idea.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The constraints \(x+y=1\) and \(2x+2y=2\) are dependent because the second repeats the first.
  • The constraints \(x+y=1\) and \(x-y=0\) are independent because the matrix \(\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}\) has rank \(2\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be continuously differentiable near \(\boldsymbol{a}\), and write \(\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{a})\) for its \(m\times n\) Jacobian matrix at \(\boldsymbol{a}\).

If \(\operatorname{rank}\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{a})=n\) and \(n\le m\), then \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is locally injective near \(\boldsymbol{a}\).

If \(\operatorname{rank}\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{a})=m\) and \(m\le n\), then \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is locally surjective near \(\boldsymbol{a}\).

If \(n=m\) and \(\det \boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{a})\neq 0\), then \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is locally bijective near \(\boldsymbol{a}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Full rank of the Jacobian tells which local behaviour survives under linearization: no collapsing for full column rank, no missing nearby outputs for full row rank, and a local inverse in the square case.

In the top example, \(n=1\le m=2\) and \(\operatorname{rank}\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{f}=1\). Distinct nearby inputs have distinct images, illustrating local injectivity.

In the bottom example, \(m=1\le n=2\) and \(\operatorname{rank}\boldsymbol{D}f=1\). The map covers a whole interval of nearby target values, illustrating local surjectivity.

Local injectivity and surjectivity describe neighbourhoods, rather than the entire domain and codomain. Full column rank prevents nearby inputs from sharing an output; full row rank permits every sufficiently nearby output to be reached.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The square case is the multivariable inverse function theorem.
  • Full column rank gives a locally one-to-one parametrized surface or curve.
  • Full row rank means nearby target values can be reached by nearby inputs.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\boldsymbol{f}(t)=(t,t^2)\), \(\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{f}(t)=(1,2t)^{\top}\) has rank \(1\), so the curve is locally injective.
  • For \(f(x,y)=x+y\), \(\boldsymbol{D}f=(1\ 1)\) has rank \(1\), so the map is locally surjective onto \(\mathbb{R}\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be open and let \(f\) and the finitely many constraint functions \(g_i\) be \(C^1\) on \(A\). For the maximization problem

\[ \begin{aligned} &\max_{\boldsymbol{x}\in A} f(\boldsymbol{x})\\ &\text{subject to}\quad g_i(\boldsymbol{x})\le b_i,\qquad x_h\ge0, \end{aligned} \]

define the Kuhn-Tucker Lagrangian

\[ \widetilde L(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{\lambda})=f(\boldsymbol{x})+\sum_i\lambda_i(b_i-g_i(\boldsymbol{x})). \]

Assume the nondegenerate constraint qualification holds for all active inequalities, including the active bounds \(-x_h\le0\): their gradients at the candidate point are linearly independent. At such a regular local maximum, there exists \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}^\ast\ge0\) such that

\[ \frac{\partial \widetilde L}{\partial x_h}(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast,\boldsymbol{\lambda}^\ast)\le0,\qquad x_h^\ast\frac{\partial \widetilde L}{\partial x_h}(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast,\boldsymbol{\lambda}^\ast)=0,\qquad x_h^\ast\ge0, \]

and

\[ \frac{\partial \widetilde L}{\partial \lambda_i}(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast,\boldsymbol{\lambda}^\ast)\ge0,\qquad \lambda_i^\ast\frac{\partial \widetilde L}{\partial \lambda_i}(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast,\boldsymbol{\lambda}^\ast)=0,\qquad \lambda_i^\ast\ge0. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Nonnegative variables can be either interior or stuck at the boundary. The Kuhn-Tucker conditions encode that boundary logic together with ordinary inequality slackness.

In this maximization example, \(x_1^\ast>0\) gives \(\partial L/\partial x_1=0\), while \(x_2^\ast=0\) gives \(\partial L/\partial x_2\le0\) and \(x_2^\ast(\partial L/\partial x_2)=0\). The inequality \(g(\boldsymbol{x})\le b\) is slack, so its multiplier is \(\lambda=0\); only the nonnegativity of \(x_2\) binds. The objective would increase by moving below the \(x_1\)-axis, but that move is infeasible.

At a corner two constraints bind at once, each with its own nonnegative multiplier.

These conditions specialize the inequality-constrained maximization method to coordinate restrictions. Treating \(x_h\ge0\) as inequalities gives a zero derivative for a positive coordinate and a nonpositive derivative at a coordinate fixed at zero, with the stated maximization convention.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(x_h^\ast>0\), the derivative condition for that variable becomes equality.
  • If a multiplier is positive, the corresponding ordinary inequality constraint is binding.
  • The conditions are necessary at regular local maxima.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(x_h^\ast>0\), then \(x_h^\ast\partial\widetilde L/\partial x_h=0\) forces \(\partial\widetilde L/\partial x_h=0\).
  • If \(\lambda_i^\ast>0\), then \(\partial\widetilde L/\partial\lambda_i=0\), so the constraint is binding.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For an optimization problem with equality constraints \(h_i(\boldsymbol{x})=0\) and inequality constraints \(g_j(\boldsymbol{x})\le 0\), a Kuhn-Tucker Lagrangian is an expression of the form

\[ L(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{\lambda},\boldsymbol{\mu}) = f(\boldsymbol{x}) +\sum_i \lambda_i h_i(\boldsymbol{x}) +\sum_j \mu_j g_j(\boldsymbol{x}), \]

with sign restrictions such as \(\mu_j\ge 0\) or \(\mu_j\le 0\) depending on the maximization or minimization convention.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The Kuhn-Tucker Lagrangian brings the objective and all active constraint pressures into one stationarity expression.

At the illustrated constrained maximum, the gradient points outwards, towards the infeasible unconstrained maximum. Writing the constraints as \(g_i( oldsymbol{x})\le b_i\) and using the maximization convention \(L=f-\sum_i\lambda_i(g_i-b_i)\) with \(\lambda_i\ge0\), the multipliers satisfy \(\displaystyle oldsymbol{ abla} f( oldsymbol{x}^\ast)=\sum_i\lambda_i oldsymbol{ abla} g_i( oldsymbol{x}^\ast)\), \(\lambda_i\ge0\), and \(\lambda_i(g_i( oldsymbol{x}^\ast)-b_i)=0\). Any slack inequality has multiplier zero.

At the optimum \( oldsymbol{ abla} f\) is a nonnegative multiple of the gradients of the binding constraints.

This extends the Lagrangian function by including inequality residuals. Their multiplier signs depend on how the residual and optimization direction are written; complementary slackness prevents a strictly slack constraint from contributing a nonzero multiplier.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Equality multipliers are usually unrestricted in sign.
  • Inequality multipliers have sign restrictions tied to the chosen convention.
  • Complementary slackness connects each inequality multiplier to whether its constraint is binding.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For maximizing \(f(x)\) subject to \(g(x)\le 0\), one common convention uses \(L=f-\mu g\) with \(\mu\ge 0\).
  • For a nonnegativity condition \(x_i\ge 0\), the Kuhn-Tucker system may include a multiplier attached to that boundary condition.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A Lagrange multiplier is an auxiliary variable attached to a constraint in a Lagrangian. For equality constraints \(h_j(\boldsymbol{x})=c_j\), a typical course convention writes

\[ L(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{\mu})=f(\boldsymbol{x})+\sum_{j=1}^m\mu_j(c_j-h_j(\boldsymbol{x})). \]

At a regular constrained optimum, the multipliers make the gradient of the objective a linear combination of the gradients of the active constraints.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A multiplier records how a constraint enters the first-order trade-off at a candidate optimum. In parameterized problems, it can also measure the marginal value of relaxing a constraint.

At the illustrated optimum, \( oldsymbol{ abla} f( oldsymbol{x}^\ast)=\mu oldsymbol{ abla} h( oldsymbol{x}^\ast)\), so the level set of \(f\) is tangent to the constraint curve. The figure maximizes \(f( oldsymbol{x})=-(x_1-3)^2-(x_2-2.5)^2\), whose level sets are circles about \((3,2.5)\), subject to \(x_1+x_2=3\). The optimum is \( oldsymbol{x}^\ast=(1.75,1.25)\), where \( oldsymbol{ abla} f( oldsymbol{x}^\ast)=(2.5,2.5)=2.5\, oldsymbol{ abla} h( oldsymbol{x}^\ast)\), so \(\mu=2.5\). Under the sensitivity assumptions stated for the envelope theorem, \(\mu=\mathrm{d}V/\mathrm{d}c\) measures the marginal value of changing the constraint level. In the figure, the optimal value for level \(c\) is \(V(c)=- frac{1}{2}(5.5-c)^2\), and \(V'(3)=2.5=\mu\).

Move the point until the arrows \( oldsymbol{ abla} f\) and \( oldsymbol{ abla} h\) line up (both are drawn to the same scale). The factor between them is the multiplier \(\mu\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Equality multipliers may be positive, negative, or zero.
  • Inequality multipliers have sign restrictions under the course convention.
  • In the envelope theorem, some multipliers can be interpreted as shadow prices.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Maximize \(xy\) subject to \(x+y=10\). With \(L(x,y,\mu)=xy+\mu(10-x-y)\), stationarity gives \(y-\mu=0\) and \(x-\mu=0\), so \(x=y=\mu\); the constraint then gives \(x=y=5\) and \(\mu=5\), with maximum \(25\). Raising the budget from \(10\) to \(11\) raises the maximum to \(5.5^2=30.25\), an increase of \(5.25\approx\mu\): the multiplier is the marginal value of the budget.
  • Minimize \(x^2+y^2\) subject to \(x+y=1\). For \(L(x,y,\mu)=x^2+y^2+\mu(1-x-y)\), stationarity gives \(2x-\mu=0\) and \(2y-\mu=0\), so \(x=y=\mu/2\). The constraint gives \(\mu=1\) and \(x=y=\tfrac{1}{2}\), with minimum value \(\tfrac{1}{2}\). For level \(c\) the minimum is \(c^2/2\), whose derivative at \(c=1\) is \(1=\mu\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a constrained optimization problem with objective \(f\) and equality constraints \(h_j(\boldsymbol{x})=c_j\), a Lagrangian function is an auxiliary function that combines the objective and the constraints with multiplier variables. Under the course convention for equality constraints,

\[ L(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{\mu})=f(\boldsymbol{x})+\sum_{j=1}^m \mu_j(c_j-h_j(\boldsymbol{x})). \]

For inequality constraints, the same idea is used with sign conventions chosen so that multiplier restrictions match the direction of the inequality.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The Lagrangian rewrites a constrained problem as one expression whose stationary points encode both the objective trade-off and the constraint equations.

At the illustrated candidate \(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast\), the gradients of \(f\) and \(h\) are parallel. At the orange point they are not, so moving along \(h(\boldsymbol{x})=c\) can improve \(f\). The differentiability and rank assumptions for the multiplier test are stated in the equality-constraint method.

Setting all partial derivatives of \(L(x,y,\mu)\) to zero recovers both the tangency condition and the constraint itself.

The Lagrangian is a function of both the decision variables and the multipliers. Partial differentiation with respect to a multiplier recovers its constraint residual; differentiation with respect to a decision variable gives the corresponding stationarity equation.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Differentiating with respect to the multiplier variables recovers the constraints.
  • Differentiating with respect to the choice variables gives the first-order balance between objective gradients and constraint gradients.
  • Changing the sign convention changes multiplier signs, but not the underlying candidate points when handled consistently.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\max xy\) subject to \(x+y=10\), one convention uses \(L(x,y,\mu)=xy+\mu(10-x-y)\).
  • For \(\min x^2+y^2\) subject to \(x+y=1\), one can use \(L(x,y,\mu)=x^2+y^2+\mu(1-x-y)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(f\colon A\to B\) be a function. A left inverse of \(f\) is a function \(\ell\colon B\to A\) such that

\[ \ell\circ f=\operatorname{id}_A. \]

A right inverse of \(f\) is a function \(r\colon B\to A\) such that

\[ f\circ r=\operatorname{id}_B. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A left inverse undoes the function after the function is applied. A right inverse gives a way to hit every target value.

The left inverse sends each image point back to its original input; it can take arbitrary values on unused points of \(B\). The right inverse chooses one preimage for every point of \(B\).

The equations use composition: applying \(\ell\) after \(f\) must recover the identity function on the input set for a left inverse. A right inverse instead makes applying \(f\) after \(r\) recover the identity on the output set.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A function has a left inverse only if it is injective.
  • A function has a right inverse only if it is surjective. Conversely, a surjective function has a right inverse, obtained by choosing one preimage for every output.
  • A two-sided inverse is both a left inverse and a right inverse.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The inclusion \(\boldsymbol{i}\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}^2\), \(\boldsymbol{i}(t)=(t,0)\), has a left inverse \(\ell(x,y)=x\).
  • The projection \(p\colon\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}\), \(p(x,y)=x\), has a right inverse \(\boldsymbol{r}(t)=(t,0)\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon A\to\mathbb{R}^m\), and let \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\in\operatorname{int}(A)\) with \(\boldsymbol{b}_0=\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\).

  • \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is locally injective at \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) if nearby equations \(\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x})=\boldsymbol{b}\) have at most one nearby solution.
  • \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is locally surjective at \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) if nearby equations \(\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x})=\boldsymbol{b}\) have at least one nearby solution.
  • \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is locally bijective at \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) if nearby equations \(\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x})=\boldsymbol{b}\) have exactly one nearby solution.

If \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is \(C^1\), then (see the Jacobian rank theorem) full column rank of \(\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\) implies local injectivity, full row rank implies local surjectivity, and square full rank implies local bijectivity.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
These local properties ask what happens when the equation \(\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x})=\boldsymbol{b}\) is solved for \(\boldsymbol{b}\) close to \(\boldsymbol{b}_0\), looking only at \(\boldsymbol{x}\) close to \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\): at most one solution (injective), at least one (surjective), or exactly one (bijective).

The function \(f(x)=x^2\) is locally bijective near \(x_0=1\), where \(f'(1)=2\neq0\): inside the green band the line at height \(1.2\) meets the graph once, at \(x=\sqrt{1.2}\approx1.10\). At the fold \(x_0=0\), where \(f'(0)=0\), the level \(0.25\) has two preimages \(\pm0.5\) close to \(0\) and the level \(-0.5\) has none, so \(f\) is neither locally injective nor locally surjective there.

The rank conditions transfer facts about linear maps to \(\boldsymbol{f}\). The linear map \(\boldsymbol{h}\mapsto\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\boldsymbol{h}\) is injective if and only if its kernel is \(\{\boldsymbol{0}\}\), which means full column rank, and surjective if and only if its range is all of \(\mathbb{R}^m\), which means full row rank. By the Jacobian rank theorem, a \(C^1\) map inherits the property of its Jacobian near \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\). The rank conditions are sufficient, not necessary: \(f(x)=x^3\) is bijective although \(f'(0)=0\).

Injectivity goes with a left inverse and surjectivity with a right inverse (left and right inverses). The square case \(n=m\) is the multivariable inverse function theorem.

A common slip is to conclude a global property from local ones. The map \((x,y)\mapsto(\mathrm{e}^x\cos y,\mathrm{e}^x\sin y)\) has Jacobian determinant \(\mathrm{e}^{2x}\neq0\), so it is locally bijective at every point, yet \((x,y)\) and \((x,y+2\pi)\) have the same image.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Full column rank gives local uniqueness of nearby solutions.
  • Full row rank gives local existence of nearby solutions.
  • If \(n=m\) and \(\det(\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0))\neq0\), the function is locally bijective at \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The map \(f(x,y)=x\) is locally surjective from \(\mathbb{R}^2\) to \(\mathbb{R}\) at every point.
  • The map \(\boldsymbol{f}(x,y)=(x,y,x+y)\) is locally injective because its Jacobian has full column rank.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(f\colon A\to\mathbb{R}\), and let \(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast\in A\).

  • \(f(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)\) is a local maximum if there is a neighbourhood \(U\) of \(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast\) such that \(f(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)\ge f(\boldsymbol{x})\) for all \(\boldsymbol{x}\in U\cap A\).
  • \(f(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)\) is a local minimum if there is a neighbourhood \(U\) of \(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast\) such that \(f(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)\le f(\boldsymbol{x})\) for all \(\boldsymbol{x}\in U\cap A\).

The extremum is strict if the inequality is strict for all nearby feasible points other than \(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A local extremum is best only against nearby feasible alternatives. It may or may not be globally best.

The red level sets decrease in value as one moves away from the local maximum, while the blue ones increase away from the local minimum. Only nearby feasible points in \(U\cap A\) are compared. An interior local extremum of a \(C^1\) function is stationary, but the Hessian may be inconclusive when it is semidefinite.

The marked critical points are classified by their Hessians: with the colours of the legend for minima, maxima and saddles.

Marked points are critical points, classified by the Hessian; move \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) onto one and the tangent plane becomes horizontal.

An open metric ball can specify the neighbourhood: choose a radius \(r>0\) and compare the candidate only with feasible points less than \(r\) away. Intersecting the ball with the feasible set also covers candidates on its boundary.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Interior local extrema of differentiable unconstrained problems must satisfy a first-order necessary condition.
  • Second-order conditions use the Hessian to classify critical points when possible.
  • Local extrema need not be unique and need not be global.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(f(x,y)=x^2+y^2\), \((0,0)\) is a strict local minimum.
  • For \(f(x)=x^3-3x\), \(x=-1\) is a local maximum and \(x=1\) is a local minimum.

docs.title: Method of Lagrange for Constrained Minimization
Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be open, and let the objective \(f\) and all constraint functions \(g_i,h_j\) be continuously differentiable on \(A\). For

\[ \begin{aligned} &\min_{\boldsymbol{x}\in A} f(\boldsymbol{x})\\ &\text{subject to}\quad g_i(\boldsymbol{x})\ge b_i,\quad h_j(\boldsymbol{x})=c_j, \end{aligned} \]

the course convention writes the inequality part as \(b_i-g_i(\boldsymbol{x})\le0\) and defines

\[ L(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{\lambda},\boldsymbol{\mu})=f(\boldsymbol{x})+\sum_i\lambda_i(b_i-g_i(\boldsymbol{x})) +\sum_j\mu_j(c_j-h_j(\boldsymbol{x})). \]

If \(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast\) is a local constrained minimizer, then either nondegenerate constraint qualification (NDCQ) fails or there are multipliers satisfying

\[ \begin{gathered} \boldsymbol{\nabla}_xL=0,\quad \lambda_i^\ast(g_i(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)-b_i)=0,\\ g_i(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)\ge b_i,\quad h_j(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)=c_j,\quad \lambda_i^\ast\ge0. \end{gathered} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
For minimization, the inequality is written so the same nonnegative multiplier convention can be used. The resulting conditions are still only a candidate filter.

In the illustrated minimization problem, \(g_i( oldsymbol{x})\ge b_i\) and the nonnegative multipliers satisfy \(\displaystyle oldsymbol{ abla} f( oldsymbol{x}^\ast)=\sum_i\lambda_i oldsymbol{ abla} g_i( oldsymbol{x}^\ast)+\sum_j\mu_j oldsymbol{ abla} h_j( oldsymbol{x}^\ast)\) and \(\lambda_i(g_i( oldsymbol{x}^\ast)-b_i)=0\). At the boundary optimum, the gradient points into the feasible side. Equivalently, one can maximize \(-f\) under the same constraints.

For \(\min x^2+y^2\) on \(x+y=c\) the smallest level circle touching the line marks the optimum, with \( oldsymbol{ abla} f=\mu oldsymbol{ abla} h\) there.

The mixed-constraint method separates equality multipliers from signed inequality multipliers. Passing from maximization to minimization requires the residual convention written above; multiplier signs cannot be copied without checking that convention.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The sign of the inequality term in the Lagrangian depends on the feasible side of the constraint.
  • Nonbinding inequalities have zero multipliers.
  • Equality multipliers remain unrestricted.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\min \mathrm{e}^{x-y}\) subject to \(x^2+y^2\ge4\), use \(L=\mathrm{e}^{x-y}+\lambda(4-x^2-y^2)\).
  • If \(x+y>1\) at a local minimizer subject to \(x+y\ge1\), complementary slackness forces the multiplier on that constraint to be zero.

docs.title: Method of Lagrange for Equality Constraints
Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be open. Consider

\[ \begin{aligned} &\max_{\boldsymbol{x}\in A} f(\boldsymbol{x})\\ &\text{subject to}\quad h_j(\boldsymbol{x})=c_j,\ j=1,\ldots,m, \end{aligned} \]

with \(C^1\) data and \(m<n\). Define

\[ L(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{\mu})=f(\boldsymbol{x})+\sum_{j=1}^m\mu_j(c_j-h_j(\boldsymbol{x})). \]

If \(f(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)\) is a local maximum or minimum subject to the constraints, then either nondegenerate constraint qualification (NDCQ) fails at \(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast\) or there exists \(\boldsymbol{\mu}^\ast\in\mathbb{R}^m\) such that

\[ \boldsymbol{\nabla} L(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast,\boldsymbol{\mu}^\ast)=0. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A regular equality-constrained optimum must be a critical point of the Lagrangian. The reason is that \(f\) cannot be improved to first order by moving along the constraint set, which happens exactly when \( oldsymbol{ abla} f\) is a linear combination of the constraint gradients.

The grey circles are level curves of \(f\) around its unconstrained maximum, and the blue line is the constraint \(h( oldsymbol{x})=c\). At \( oldsymbol{x}^\ast\) the level curve of the highest value that still meets the line just touches it, and the gradients of \(f\) and \(h\) are parallel: \( oldsymbol{ abla} f( oldsymbol{x}^\ast)=\mu oldsymbol{ abla} h( oldsymbol{x}^\ast)\). At the orange point \( oldsymbol{ abla} f\) has a component along the line, so moving along \(h( oldsymbol{x})=c\) still increases \(f\).

Slide the point along \(x+y=c\): \(f\) is largest where its level curve touches the line, which is where \( oldsymbol{ abla} f\) is a multiple \(\mu oldsymbol{ abla} h\) of the constraint normal.

Only points on the line \(x+y=c\) count: the red curve is \(f\) restricted to the constraint, and its highest point is the constrained maximum.

The equations \(\partial L/\partial x_i=0\) say \( oldsymbol{ abla} f( oldsymbol{x}^\ast)=\sum_j\mu_j^\ast oldsymbol{ abla} h_j( oldsymbol{x}^\ast)\), and \(\partial L/\partial\mu_j=0\) gives back \(h_j( oldsymbol{x}^\ast)=c_j\): \(n+m\) equations for \(n+m\) unknowns. NDCQ is needed for the multipliers to exist. Minimizing \(x\) on the curve \(x^3-y^2=0\) shows why: the minimizer is the origin, where \( oldsymbol{ abla} h=(3x^2,-2y)\) is \( oldsymbol{0}\), and no \(\mu\) gives \((1,0)=\mu oldsymbol{0}\). Such points are kept as separate candidates, and all candidates still have to be compared, since the conditions are only necessary.

The method optimizes the restriction of \(f\) to the constraint set; without constraints it reduces to \( oldsymbol{ abla} f= oldsymbol{0}\) (unconstrained extrema conditions). The multiplier returns later as a shadow price: for \(\max xy\) subject to \(x+y=10\) from the Examples, the solution is \(x=y=\mu^\ast=5\); with \(10\) replaced by \(c\) the best value \(c^2/4\) grows at rate \(c/2=5\) at \(c=10\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The theorem gives necessary, not sufficient, conditions.
  • Stationarity in the multiplier variables recovers the equality constraints.
  • Equality constraints can be written on either side because they have no direction.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Maximizing \(xy\) subject to \(x+y=10\) gives \(L=xy+\mu(10-x-y)\).
  • Minimizing \(x^2+y^2\) subject to \(x+y=1\) uses the same equality-constrained stationarity method.

docs.title: Method of Lagrange for Inequality-Constrained Maximization
Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be open, and let \(f,g_1,\ldots,g_k\colon A\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuously differentiable. Consider

\[ \begin{aligned} &\max_{\boldsymbol{x}\in A} f(\boldsymbol{x})\\ &\text{subject to}\quad g_i(\boldsymbol{x})\le b_i,\ i=1,\ldots,k. \end{aligned} \]

The course convention writes \(b_i-g_i(\boldsymbol{x})\ge0\) and defines

\[ L(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{\lambda})=f(\boldsymbol{x})+\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i(b_i-g_i(\boldsymbol{x})). \]

If \(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast\) is a local constrained maximizer, then either nondegenerate constraint qualification (NDCQ) fails or there exists \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}^\ast\) such that

\[ \boldsymbol{\nabla}_xL(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast,\boldsymbol{\lambda}^\ast)=0,\qquad \lambda_i^\ast(g_i(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)-b_i)=0,\qquad \lambda_i^\ast\ge0,\qquad g_i(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)\le b_i. \]

The condition \(\lambda_i^\ast(g_i(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)-b_i)=0\) is complementary slackness.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Inequality constraints are directional, so multiplier signs and slackness matter. At a maximizer each constraint is either slack, and plays no role nearby, or binding, and acts as a one-sided equality. The sign condition \(\lambda_i\ge0\) and complementary slackness handle both cases.

The unconstrained maximum of \(f\), the centre of the grey level circles, lies outside the shaded feasible side of \(x_1+x_2\le3.8\), so the constrained maximum \( oldsymbol{x}^\ast\) lies on the line. There the gradient \( oldsymbol{ abla} f( oldsymbol{x}^\ast)\) and \( oldsymbol{ abla} g=(1,1)\) point the same way, outwards towards the infeasible peak, so \( oldsymbol{ abla} f( oldsymbol{x}^\ast)=\lambda oldsymbol{ abla} g( oldsymbol{x}^\ast)\) with \(\lambda>0\): \(f\) could only increase outside the feasible set.

Drag the peak of \(f\): if it is feasible the constraint is slack and \(\lambda=0\); otherwise the optimum sits on the line and \( oldsymbol{ abla} f=\lambda oldsymbol{ abla} g\) with \(\lambda>0\).

The sign condition encodes this direction. If \( oldsymbol{ abla} f( oldsymbol{x}^\ast)\) were a negative multiple of \( oldsymbol{ abla} g_i( oldsymbol{x}^\ast)\), it would point into the feasible set, and a small step inwards would increase \(f\). Complementary slackness says that each constraint is binding or has \(\lambda_i^\ast=0\). NDCQ is checked for the binding constraints only.

The conditions are necessary only. For \(\max xy\) subject to \(x+y\le10\) from the Examples, both \((0,0)\) with \(\lambda=0\) and \((5,5)\) with \(\lambda=5\) satisfy them. The first is a saddle point of \(xy\). The second is a local maximizer but not a global one: \(xy=t^2\) grows without bound along the feasible points \(x=y=-t\), \(t o\infty\).

Compared with equality constraints, whose multipliers may have either sign, these two conditions are new. Linear programming shows the same pattern: a resource with unused slack has shadow price \(0\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A binding constraint satisfies \(g_i(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)=b_i\).
  • A nonbinding constraint has zero multiplier by complementary slackness.
  • The theorem gives necessary, not sufficient, conditions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\max xy\) subject to \(x+y\le10\), the Lagrangian is \(xy+\lambda(10-x-y)\).
  • If no inequality is binding at a local maximum, all inequality multipliers are zero and the unconstrained stationarity condition returns.

docs.title: Method of Lagrange for Mixed Constraints
Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be open, and let the objective \(f\) and all constraint functions \(g_i,h_j\) be continuously differentiable on \(A\). Consider

\[ \begin{aligned} &\max_{\boldsymbol{x}\in A} f(\boldsymbol{x})\\ &\text{subject to}\quad g_i(\boldsymbol{x})\le b_i,\quad h_j(\boldsymbol{x})=c_j. \end{aligned} \]

The course convention defines

\[ L(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{\lambda},\boldsymbol{\mu}) =f(\boldsymbol{x})+\sum_i\lambda_i(b_i-g_i(\boldsymbol{x})) +\sum_j\mu_j(c_j-h_j(\boldsymbol{x})). \]

If \(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast\) is a local constrained maximizer and the binding inequalities are indexed by \(i_1,\ldots,i_\ell\), then either

\[ \operatorname{rank}\boldsymbol{D}(g_{i_1},\ldots,g_{i_\ell},h_1,\ldots,h_m)(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast) <\ell+m, \]

or there exist multipliers satisfying stationarity, complementary slackness, inequality feasibility, equality feasibility, and \(\lambda_i^\ast\ge0\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Mixed problems combine exact equations with one-sided restrictions. The first-order candidate conditions combine equality stationarity with inequality sign and slackness rules.

The illustrated feasible arc satisfies \(h(\boldsymbol{x})=c\) and \(g(\boldsymbol{x})\le3.1\). Both constraints bind at \(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast\), where the objective gradient is a combination of the active constraint gradients with the appropriate multiplier signs. The theorem above specifies the normalization and regularity requirements for the multipliers.

The equality-constraint method contributes unrestricted multipliers for the equalities. The inequality-constrained maximization method contributes nonnegative multipliers and complementary slackness for the inequalities. Both kinds enter the same stationarity equation.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Only inequalities require nonnegative multipliers.
  • Only binding inequalities are included in the active NDCQ matrix.
  • All equality constraints must hold exactly.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\max xy\) subject to \(x+y\le10\) and \(x-y=0\), the method uses one nonnegative multiplier and one unrestricted multiplier.
  • If an inequality is nonbinding at the solution, its multiplier is zero and it is not part of the active rank test.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), \(B\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\), let \(\boldsymbol{g}\colon A\to B\), and let \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon B\to\mathbb{R}^k\). If \(\boldsymbol{g}\) is differentiable at \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\in\operatorname{int}(A)\), \(\boldsymbol{g}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\in\operatorname{int}(B)\), and \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is differentiable at \(\boldsymbol{g}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\), then \(\boldsymbol{f}\circ \boldsymbol{g}\) is differentiable at \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) and

\[ \boldsymbol{D}(\boldsymbol{f}\circ \boldsymbol{g})(\boldsymbol{x}_0)=\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{g}(\boldsymbol{x}_0))\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{g}(\boldsymbol{x}_0). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Local changes pass through the inner map first and then through the outer map. This is why the derivative matrices multiply in the same order as the composition acts on changes.

The local linear approximations compose in the same order as the maps. Near \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\), the derivative of \(\boldsymbol{f}\circ \boldsymbol{g}\) is the product of the \(k\times m\) matrix \(\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{g}(\boldsymbol{x}_0))\) and the \(m\times n\) matrix \(\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{g}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\); reversing that order is generally invalid.

The Jacobian matrices represent the derivatives as linear maps. Their ordered product first applies the derivative of the inner function and then the derivative of the outer function; reversing the order is generally invalid and can even give incompatible dimensions.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(\boldsymbol{g}\colon\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) and \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}^k\), then the product has size \(k\times n\).
  • If both maps are continuously differentiable near the relevant points, their composition is continuously differentiable near \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(\boldsymbol{g}(x,y)=(x+y,xy)\) and \(f(u,v)=u^2+v\), then \(\boldsymbol{D}(f\circ \boldsymbol{g})=\boldsymbol{D}f(\boldsymbol{g})\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{g}\).
  • If \(\boldsymbol{g}(t)=(t,t^2)\) and \(f(x,y)=x+y\), the formula gives the curve derivative \(1+2t\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be open, let \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon A\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be \(C^1\), and let \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\in A\) with \(\boldsymbol{y}_0=\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\). If

\[ \det(\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0))\neq0, \]

then there exists an open neighbourhood \(V\subseteq A\) of \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) such that \(\boldsymbol{f}|_V\colon V\to \boldsymbol{f}(V)\) is bijective. The image \(\boldsymbol{f}(V)\) is an open neighbourhood of \(\boldsymbol{y}_0\). Its inverse is \(C^1\) and

\[ \boldsymbol{D}(\boldsymbol{f}|_V^{-1})(\boldsymbol{y}_0)=\left(\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\right)^{-1}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An invertible Jacobian makes the function locally reversible: if the linear approximation of \(\boldsymbol{f}\) at \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) can be undone, so can \(\boldsymbol{f}\) itself near \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\), and the inverse is again \(C^1\).

The square \(V\) around \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) is sent onto a curved region \(\boldsymbol{f}(V)\) around \(\boldsymbol{y}_0\); every point of that region comes from exactly one point of the square. The arrow back is the local inverse, defined only on the curved region.

The determinant condition is the square full-rank condition: \(n\) equations in \(n\) unknowns. The \(C^1\) hypothesis keeps the Jacobian invertible near \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\); differentiability alone is not enough. For \(f(x)=x+2x^2\sin(1/x)\) with \(f(0)=0\), \(f'(0)=1\), yet \(f'\) takes the values \(-1\) and \(3\) arbitrarily close to \(0\), so \(f\) is not injective on any interval around \(0\). If \(\det\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)=0\), the theorem is silent: \((x^2,y)\) has no local inverse at the origin, but \((x^3,y)\) has one.

Differentiating \(\boldsymbol{f}|_V^{-1}(\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}))=\boldsymbol{x}\) with the multivariable chain rule gives \(\boldsymbol{D}(\boldsymbol{f}|_V^{-1})(\boldsymbol{y}_0)\,\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)=\boldsymbol{I}\), the derivative formula of the Theorem. For \(n=1\) it is the rule \((f^{-1})'(y)=1/f'(x)\) of the one-variable inverse function theorem.

The conclusion is local bijectivity of a restricted map, not a global inverse on the original domain. For \((\mathrm{e}^x\cos y,\mathrm{e}^x\sin y)\) from the Examples the determinant \(\mathrm{e}^{2x}\) is never \(0\), yet \((x,y)\) and \((x,y+2\pi)\) have the same image.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The determinant condition is the square full-rank condition.
  • The derivative of the local inverse is the inverse matrix of the original derivative.
  • The theorem can be derived from the implicit function theorem and vice versa.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\boldsymbol{f}(x,y)=(\mathrm{e}^x\cos y,\mathrm{e}^x\sin y)\), the determinant is \(\mathrm{e}^{2x}\), so the map is locally invertible everywhere.
  • For \(\boldsymbol{f}(x,y)=(x^2,y)\) at \((0,0)\), the determinant is \(0\), so the theorem does not apply there.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(f\colon\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be sufficiently smooth near \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) and let \(\boldsymbol{h}\) be a small displacement. The first-order Taylor approximation is

\[ f(\boldsymbol{x}_0+\boldsymbol{h})\approx f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)+\boldsymbol{D}f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\boldsymbol{h}. \]

If \(f\) is \(C^2\) near \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\), the second-order approximation is

\[ f(\boldsymbol{x}_0+\boldsymbol{h})\approx f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)+\boldsymbol{D}f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\boldsymbol{h} +\frac{1}{2} \boldsymbol{h}^{\top} \boldsymbol{H}_f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\boldsymbol{h}. \]

The first correction uses local slope, and the second correction uses local curvature.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Taylor approximations replace a complicated function near a point by simpler local information. The linear term estimates the immediate change, and the quadratic term corrects for bending.

The figure follows the line \(\boldsymbol{x}_0+t\boldsymbol{h}\) for a fixed direction \(\boldsymbol{h}\). Its first-order approximation is \(f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)+t\boldsymbol{D}f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\boldsymbol{h}\); the second-order approximation adds \(\frac{1}{2}t^2\boldsymbol{h}^{\top}\boldsymbol{H}_f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\boldsymbol{h}\). As \(t\to0\), the errors are \(o(|t|)\) under differentiability and \(o(t^2)\) under the \(C^2\) hypothesis.

Compare both approximations along a line through \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) (right). Under the smoothness assumptions, the Hessian term improves the order of the local error as the displacement tends to zero.

Compare the first-order approximation (the tangent plane) with the second-order one, \(f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)+\boldsymbol{D}f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\boldsymbol{h}+\tfrac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{h}^{\top}\boldsymbol{H}_f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\boldsymbol{h}\), near \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\).

The Jacobian of a scalar-valued function is a row matrix, so multiplying it by the displacement gives the first-order scalar change. The Hessian contributes the quadratic correction when the \(C^2\) hypothesis holds.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For a real-valued function, \(\boldsymbol{D}f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\boldsymbol{h}=\boldsymbol{\nabla} f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)^{\top} \boldsymbol{h}\).
  • If \(f\) is \(C^2\), then the Hessian is symmetric and the second-order term is a quadratic form.
  • At a critical point, the quadratic term is the first potentially nonzero correction. It may also vanish, in which case higher-order information is needed.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(f(x,y)=x^2+xy+y^2\) at \((0,0)\), the second-order approximation is exact.
  • For \(f(x,y)=\mathrm{e}^{x+y}\) at \((0,0)\), the second-order approximation is \(1+x+y+\frac{1}{2}(x+y)^2\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Write the constraint map as \(\boldsymbol{h}=(h_1,\ldots,h_m)\). For equality constraints \(h_1(\boldsymbol{x})=c_1,\ldots,h_m(\boldsymbol{x})=c_m\), the nondegenerate constraint qualification is satisfied at \(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast\) if

\[ \operatorname{rank}(\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{h}(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast))=m. \]

With inequality constraints, the same rank condition is applied to the gradients of the binding inequality constraints together with the equality constraints.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
NDCQ says the active constraints are locally independent. If it fails, some constraint may be redundant or the feasible set may have a singular shape.

On the left, the constraints cross transversally and \(\operatorname{rank}\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{h}(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)=2=m\), so the qualification holds. On the right, they touch with parallel gradients and \(\operatorname{rank}\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{h}(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast)=1<m\), so it fails.

The Jacobian collects the constraint gradients as rows. Its rank equals the number of active constraints exactly when these rows are independent, excluding a nonzero linear relation between their first-order effects.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• When NDCQ holds, the regular Lagrange necessary conditions apply at a constrained local optimum.
  • If NDCQ fails, the point remains a candidate that must be checked separately.
  • For inequality problems, nonbinding inequalities are not included in the active rank check.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(h(x,y)=x+y\), NDCQ holds at every point because the gradient is nonzero.
  • For \(h_1(x,y)=x+y\) and \(h_2(x,y)=2x+2y\), NDCQ fails because the gradients are dependent.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A parametric constrained optimization problem is an optimization problem whose objective, constraints, or feasible set depend on a parameter. A typical equality-constrained maximization problem has the form

\[ \begin{aligned} &V(s)=\max_{\boldsymbol{x}} f(\boldsymbol{x},s)\\ &\text{subject to}\quad g(\boldsymbol{x},s)=0. \end{aligned} \]

The parameter \(s\) is not optimized over; it changes the problem being solved.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A parametric problem asks how the best choice and best value move when outside conditions change.

In the figure, the parameter \(s\) sets the constraint level \(h(\boldsymbol{x})=s\), and \(V(s)=\max\{f(\boldsymbol{x})\colon h(\boldsymbol{x})=s\}\). The blue lines show different feasible sets, the grey circles are level sets of \(f\), and the dashed path follows the corresponding optima \(\boldsymbol{x}^\ast(s)\).

The parameter \(c\) is not chosen by the optimizer: changing it changes the problem, and the optimum moves along with it.

At a fixed parameter value, the equality-constraint Lagrange method handles the equality example. If inequalities are present, the inequality-constrained maximization method also imposes multiplier signs and complementary slackness. Only after solving each fixed-parameter problem does one study how its optimizer and value change.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The optimal value as a function of the parameter is the value function.
  • Envelope theorems give derivatives of the value function without fully differentiating the optimizer.
  • Constraint multipliers often measure the marginal value of relaxing parameterized constraints.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A firm may maximize profit over inputs while the wage rate is a parameter.
  • A consumer may maximize utility over bundles while income is a parameter in the budget constraint.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\boldsymbol{F}\colon A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{p+q}\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be differentiable, and write the variables as \((\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})\) with \(\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^p\) and \(\boldsymbol{y}\in\mathbb{R}^q\). The partial Jacobians of \(\boldsymbol{F}\) are the blocks

\[ \boldsymbol{D}_x\boldsymbol{F}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times p},\qquad \boldsymbol{D}_y\boldsymbol{F}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times q}. \]

Together they form the full Jacobian:

\[ \boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{F}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}) =\begin{pmatrix}\boldsymbol{D}_x\boldsymbol{F}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})&\boldsymbol{D}_y\boldsymbol{F}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})\end{pmatrix}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A partial Jacobian isolates how an equation system responds to one chosen block of variables while the other block is held fixed. It is the matrix version of a partial derivative.

Each row of the Jacobian belongs to one component \(F_i\) and each column to one variable. In the figure \(m=3\), \(p=2\) and \(q=3\): the two blue columns, derivatives with respect to \(x_1\) and \(x_2\), form \(\boldsymbol{D}_x\boldsymbol{F}\) (\(3\times2\)), and the three red columns form \(\boldsymbol{D}_y\boldsymbol{F}\) (\(3\times3\)). So the full Jacobian is split by columns, \(\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{F}=(\boldsymbol{D}_x\boldsymbol{F}\mid\boldsymbol{D}_y\boldsymbol{F})\), never by rows.

The split matters when the two blocks play different roles. In the implicit function theorem, \(\boldsymbol{x}\) is exogenous and \(\boldsymbol{y}\) is solved for. If \(\boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{g}(\boldsymbol{x})\) satisfies \(\boldsymbol{F}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{g}(\boldsymbol{x}))=\boldsymbol{0}\), the multivariable chain rule gives \(\boldsymbol{D}_x\boldsymbol{F}+\boldsymbol{D}_y\boldsymbol{F}\,\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{g}=\boldsymbol{0}\), so \(\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{g}=-(\boldsymbol{D}_y\boldsymbol{F})^{-1}\boldsymbol{D}_x\boldsymbol{F}\) when the block \(\boldsymbol{D}_y\boldsymbol{F}\) is square and invertible. Square means \(q=m\), as many unknowns as equations, as in the figure. For the circle \(F(x,y)=x^2+y^2-1\) from the Examples this gives \(g'(x)=-x/y\) where \(y\neq0\); at \((1,0)\) the block \(D_yF=0\), and indeed near that point \(y\) is not a function of \(x\).

A common slip is to reverse the product. \((\boldsymbol{D}_y\boldsymbol{F})^{-1}\) is \(q\times q\) and \(\boldsymbol{D}_x\boldsymbol{F}\) is \(q\times p\), so \(\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{g}\) is \(q\times p\): one row for each endogenous variable and one column for each exogenous one. In the other order the sizes do not match unless \(p=q\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Partial Jacobians are the matrix version of holding some variables constant in partial differentiation.
  • The implicit function theorem uses the partial Jacobian with respect to the variables being solved for.
  • Block notation makes comparative statics formulas easier to write and remember.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(F(x,y)=x^2+y^2-1\), \(D_xF=2x\) and \(D_yF=2y\).
  • For \(\boldsymbol{F}(x_1,x_2,y)=(x_1+y,x_2y)\), \(\boldsymbol{D}_x\boldsymbol{F}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&y\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\boldsymbol{D}_y\boldsymbol{F}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\x_2\end{pmatrix}\).
