docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(Y\) be a continuous random variable and \(A\) an event with \(\mathbb{P}(A)>0\). The conditional CDF of \(Y\) given \(A\) is

\[ \begin{aligned} F_{Y\mid A}(y)=\mathbb{P}(Y\leq y\mid A). \end{aligned} \]

Where the derivative exists, the conditional density of \(Y\) given \(A\) is

\[ \begin{aligned} f_{Y\mid A}(y)=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}y}F_{Y\mid A}(y). \end{aligned} \]

Equivalently, by Bayes' rule,

\[ \begin{aligned} f_{Y\mid A}(y)=\frac{\mathbb{P}(A\mid Y=y)f_Y(y)}{\mathbb{P}(A)}. \end{aligned} \]

Here \(\mathbb{P}(A\mid Y=y)\) is the conditional probability given the value \(y\), determined except possibly on a set of values \(y\) of probability zero, where it may be chosen arbitrarily; it is not an elementary ratio, whose denominator \(\mathbb{P}(Y=y)\) would be zero.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Conditioning on an event \(A\) reweights the original density of \(Y\) by how compatible each value \(y\) is with \(A\), and then divides by \(\mathbb{P}(A)\) so that the total area is again \(1\).

In the illustrated example, \(Y\sim\operatorname{Exp}(2)\) and \(A=\{Y>1\}\), with \(\mathbb{P}(A)=\mathrm{e}^{-2}\approx0.14\). Keep the shaded part of the density on \(A\) and divide by \(\mathbb{P}(A)\): \(f_{Y\mid A}(y)=2\mathrm{e}^{-2y}/\mathrm{e}^{-2}=2\mathrm{e}^{-2(y-1)}\) for \(y>1\) and \(0\) elsewhere. The red curve is the original density shifted one unit to the right, the memoryless property.

Move \(c\): on \(A=\{Y>c\}\) the density is divided by \(\mathbb{P}(A)\), and outside \(A\) it is \(0\). For \(\operatorname{Exp}(2)\) the result is the same density shifted to start at \(c\).

The Bayes form of the definition covers two kinds of event. If \(A=\{Y\in B\}\) is decided by \(Y\) itself, then \(\mathbb{P}(A\mid Y=y)\) is \(1\) on \(B\) and \(0\) outside it, and conditioning simply cuts the density to \(B\) and rescales it. If \(A\) also depends on other randomness, \(\mathbb{P}(A\mid Y=y)\) lies between \(0\) and \(1\) and the density is reweighted smoothly. For example, let \(Y\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) and let \(A\) be the event that a coin with success probability \(Y\) shows heads; then \(\mathbb{P}(A\mid Y=y)=y\), \(\mathbb{P}(A)=1/2\) and \(f_{Y\mid A}(y)=2y\) on \((0,1)\).

With this density, the conditional expectation given an event from Probability Theory is \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid A]=\int y\,f_{Y\mid A}(y)\,\mathrm{d}y\); in the figure it equals \(1+1/2=3/2\). Conditioning on the value of another variable, which has probability zero, needs the conditional PDF instead.

Cutting without rescaling is a common slip: the cut density \(2\mathrm{e}^{-2y}\) on \(y>1\) integrates to \(\mathrm{e}^{-2}\), not \(1\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(A=\{Y\in B\}\), then \(f_{Y\mid A}(y)=\indicator_{B}(y)f_Y(y)/\mathbb{P}(Y\in B)\) except possibly on a set of zero length.
  • The conditional density \(f_{Y\mid A}\) integrates to one whenever \(\mathbb{P}(A)>0\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(Y\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) and \(A=\{Y>1/2\}\), the conditional density is \(2\) on \((1/2,1)\).
  • For \(Y\sim\operatorname{Exp}(2)\) and \(A=\{Y>1\}\), the conditional density is \(2\mathrm{e}^{-2(y-1)}\) for \(y>1\).

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text: Let \(\mathbb{E}|Y|<\infty\). If \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent (\(X\perp Y\)), then \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]=\mathbb{E}[Y]\) almost surely.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
If the response \(Y\) is independent of the observed variable \(X\), observing \(X\) cannot change the expected value of \(Y\): the best prediction of \(Y\) given \(X\) is the constant \(\mathbb{E}Y\).

The red lines show \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x]\). For independent fair dice this equals \(3.5\) in every column. A constant conditional mean does not imply independence: if \(Y\sim\operatorname{Unif}(-1,1)\) and \(X=Y^2\), then given \(X=x\) the values \(\pm\sqrt{x}\) are equally likely, so \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]=0\) almost surely, yet \(X\) and \(Y\) are dependent.

Under independence the conditional distribution of \(Y\) given \(X=x\) is the unconditional distribution of \(Y\), for every \(x\), so its mean is \(\mathbb{E}Y\). This gives more than the mean: \(\mathbb{E}[h(Y)\mid X]=\mathbb{E}[h(Y)]\) for every integrable \(h(Y)\). The words almost surely are needed because \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]\) is only determined up to events of probability zero.

The proposition is the first step of a chain: independence implies a constant conditional mean, which implies zero covariance when the variances are finite. The second step uses taking out what is known and Adam’s law: \(\mathbb{E}[XY]=\mathbb{E}[X\,\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]]=\mathbb{E}X\,\mathbb{E}Y\). Neither step can be reversed. The figure shows the first; for the second, \(X\sim\operatorname{Unif}(-1,1)\) and \(Y=X^2\) are uncorrelated, but \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]=X^2\) is not constant.

Note the direction: the proposition is about \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]\). In the right panel \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]=0\) is constant, but \(\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y]=Y^2\) is not, which already shows the dependence.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Independence gives \(\mathbb{E}[h(Y)\mid X]=\mathbb{E}[h(Y)]\) for every integrable \(h(Y)\).
  • The converse fails: a constant conditional mean \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]=\mathbb{E}Y\) does not by itself imply independence.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For independent fair dice \(X,Y\), \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]=3.5\).
  • For \(Y\sim\operatorname{Unif}(-1,1)\) and \(X=Y^2\), symmetry gives \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]=0=\mathbb{E}Y\), yet \(X\) and \(Y\) are dependent.

docs.title: Conditional Expectation Given a Random Variable
Definition
docs.text:
For integrable \(Y\) (that is, \(\mathbb{E}|Y|<\infty\)), the conditional expectation \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]\) is a function \(g(X)\) of \(X\) satisfying the averaging identity \(\mathbb{E}[Y\indicator_{\{X\in B\}}]=\mathbb{E}[g(X)\indicator_{\{X\in B\}}]\) for every event \(\{X\in B\}\) determined by \(X\). When a conditional PMF or PDF exists,

\[ g(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x]=\begin{cases}\sum_y y\,p_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x), & Y\text{ discrete},\\[4pt] \int_{\mathbb{R}}y\,f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)\,\mathrm{d}y, & Y\text{ has a conditional density}.\end{cases} \]

The sum or integral is selected by the conditional law of \(Y\), not by whether the conditioning variable \(X\) is discrete or continuous.

The Expectation calculation averages the possible values of \(Y\) under its conditional law. In the continuous case, the weighting function is the Conditional Probability Density Function, not the marginal PDF of \(Y\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Conditioning on a variable produces a new random variable: \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]\) is the average of \(Y\) predicted from the value of \(X\), and it changes with the value observed. Evaluating it at a fixed value \(x\) gives an ordinary number.

In the illustrated triangular model, with density \(2\) on \(0<y<x<1\), the vertical slice at \(X=x\) shows that the conditional distribution of \(Y\) given \(X=x\) is uniform on \((0,x)\), with mean \(g(x)=x/2\); at \(x=0.7\) this is the red point at height \(0.35\). Evaluating this function at the random \(X\) gives \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]=g(X)=X/2\).

Each value of \(X\) has its own conditional mean \(g(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x]\) (right); \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]=g(X)\) is a random variable.

For each fixed \(x\), compute the number \(g(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x]\) from the conditional PMF or density, as in the Definition; then substitute the random \(X\). The averaging identity explains what the result is: over every event determined by \(X\), the variable \(g(X)\) has the same average as \(Y\). With \(B=\mathbb{R}\) it gives \(\mathbb{E}[g(X)]=\mathbb{E}Y\), which is Adam’s law. In the triangle, \(\mathbb{E}[X/2]=\tfrac{1}{2}\cdot\tfrac{2}{3}=\tfrac{1}{3}\), which is indeed \(\mathbb{E}Y\).

For discrete \(X\), the random variable \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]\) takes the value \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x]\) on the event \(\{X=x\}\), so it collects the numbers \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid A]\) of conditional expectation given an event into one random variable. Its working rules are taking out what is known and the independent case.

Keep three objects apart: \(\mathbb{E}Y\) is a number, \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x]\) is a number for each \(x\), and \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]\) is a random variable, a function of \(X\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]=g(X)\) is determined up to almost-sure equality.
  • For every interval \(B\), \(\mathbb{E}[Y\indicator_{\{X\in B\}}]=\mathbb{E}[g(X)\indicator_{\{X\in B\}}]\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(Y\mid X=x\sim\operatorname{Pois}(x)\) with \(X\ge0\) integrable, then \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]=X\).
  • For joint density \(2\) on \(0<y<x<1\), \(Y\mid X=x\) is uniform on \((0,x)\), so \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]=X/2\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) have joint density \(f_{X,Y}\), and let \(y\) satisfy \(0<f_Y(y)<\infty\). The conditional PDF of \(X\) given \(Y=y\) is

\[ \begin{aligned} f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=\frac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_Y(y)}. \end{aligned} \]

The denominator is the density \(f_Y(y)\), not \(\mathbb{P}(Y=y)=0\). On a set of conditioning values \(y\) of probability zero, for example finitely many points, conditional laws may be chosen arbitrarily.

The Marginal Probability Density Function in the denominator is obtained by integrating the joint density over the other coordinate. Dividing by it makes the conditional density integrate to one.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A conditional density describes one variable after a continuous value of another is observed. It uses a ratio of densities, rather than dividing by the probability of a zero-probability event: the slice of the joint density at \(Y=y\) is rescaled by \(f_Y(y)\) so that it has total area \(1\).

The joint density equals \(2\) on the triangle \(0<x<y<1\). Along the horizontal slice at height \(y\) it equals \(2\) on \(0<x<y\), a segment of length \(y\), so the marginal density is \(f_Y(y)=2y\). Dividing gives \(f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=2/(2y)=1/y\) on \((0,y)\): given \(Y=y\), \(X\) is uniform on \((0,y)\).

Move \(y\): the slice \(f_{X,Y}(\cdot,y)\) divided by \(f_Y(y)\) is the conditional density, with total area \(1\). On the triangle it is uniform on \((0,y)\).

The formula mirrors the conditional PMF \(p_{X,Y}(x,y)/p_Y(y)\), with densities in place of masses. Heuristically, conditioning on a thin strip \(y<Y\le y+h\), which has positive probability, produces a factor \(h\) in both the joint and the marginal probability; it cancels, leaving the ratio of densities. Like any density, \(f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)\) is not a probability and can exceed \(1\): in the triangle it equals \(4\) when \(y=\tfrac{1}{4}\). Changing the conditional density for a set of \(y\)-values of probability zero changes no probability, which is why the definition allows arbitrary choices there.

Multiplying back, \(f_{X,Y}=f_{X\mid Y}f_Y\) builds a joint model in two stages, and integrating over \(y\) gives the continuous law of total probability. For independent \(X\) and \(Y\) the conditional density is simply \(f_X\), and integrating \(f_{X\mid Y}\) up to \(x\) gives the conditional CDF.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For every \(y\) with \(0<f_Y(y)<\infty\), \(\int f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)\,\mathrm{d}x=1\).
  • \(f_{X,Y}(x,y)=f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)f_Y(y)\) except possibly on a set of zero area.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For joint density \(2\) on \(0<x<y<1\), \(f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=1/y\) on \(0<x<y\): a uniform conditional law.
  • For independent \(X\sim\operatorname{Exp}(2)\) and \(Y\sim\operatorname{Exp}(3)\), \(f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=2\mathrm{e}^{-2x}\) for \(x>0\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For discrete random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) and a value \(y\) with \(p_Y(y)>0\), the conditional PMF of \(X\) given \(Y=y\) is

\[ \begin{aligned} p_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=\frac{p_{X,Y}(x,y)}{p_Y(y)}, \quad p_Y(y)>0. \end{aligned} \]

The numerator is the Joint Probability Mass Function, and the denominator is its Marginal Probability Mass Function for \(Y\). This is the ordinary Conditional Probability rule applied to \(\{X=x\}\) and \(\{Y=y\}\) when the latter has positive probability.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A conditional PMF rescales the part of a joint table consistent with the observed discrete value. Once \(Y=y\) is known, only the pairs with that value of \(y\) remain possible, and their masses are divided by \(p_Y(y)\) so that they again add up to \(1\), just as in conditional probability for events.

In the diagram the column \(Y=1\) holds the masses \(0.2\) and \(0.4\), with total \(p_Y(1)=0.6\). Dividing by \(0.6\) gives \(p_{X\mid Y}(0\mid1)=\tfrac{1}{3}\) and \(p_{X\mid Y}(1\mid1)=\tfrac{2}{3}\). Unconditionally \(\mathbb{P}(X=1)=0.3+0.4=0.7\), so learning \(Y=1\) lowers the probability of \(X=1\) slightly.

Here \(y\) runs up the vertical axis. Fix \(Y=y\): keep that row of masses and divide by \(p_Y(y)\) so that they sum to \(1\).

For each fixed \(y\) with \(p_Y(y)>0\), \(x\mapsto p_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)\) is an ordinary PMF: nonnegative and summing to \(1\). Dividing by one number keeps the relative sizes of the masses, so the conditional PMF has the shape of the selected column. As a function of \(y\) for fixed \(x\) it is not a PMF: in the table, \(p_{X\mid Y}(1\mid0)+p_{X\mid Y}(1\mid1)=0.75+\tfrac{2}{3}\neq1\). When \(p_Y(y)=0\) the conditional PMF is not defined.

Independence of \(X\) and \(Y\) means that every conditional PMF equals the marginal \(p_X\): observing \(Y\) changes nothing. Multiplying back, \(p_{X,Y}(x,y)=p_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)p_Y(y)\), which is how two-stage models are built, as in the chicken–egg theorem, where \(N\) is Poisson and the count given \(N=n\) is binomial. Summing over \(y\) gives the law of total probability in PMF form, \(p_X(x)=\sum_yp_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)p_Y(y)\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For \(p_Y(y)>0\), \(\displaystyle \sum_xp_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=1\).
  • \(p_{X,Y}(x,y)=p_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)p_Y(y)\).

docs.title: Conditional Variance Given a Random Variable
Definition
docs.text:
For \(\mathbb{E}[Y^2]<\infty\), conditional variance is

\[ \operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X) =\mathbb{E}[(Y-\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X])^2\mid X] =\mathbb{E}[Y^2\mid X]-(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X])^2. \]

These identities hold almost surely.

Apply the definition of Variance and Standard Deviation within the law conditional on \(X\): subtract the Conditional Expectation Given a Random Variable and average its squared residual under that same conditional law.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Conditional variance measures how much spread in \(Y\) remains once the value of \(X\) is known. Like the conditional expectation \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]\), it is itself a random variable: a function of \(X\), not a single number.

The diagram shows \(Y\mid X=x\sim\operatorname{Pois}(x)\). The band around the conditional mean line \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x]=x\) has half-width \(\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X=x)}=\sqrt{x}\): \(\pm1\) at \(x=1\) and \(\pm2\) at \(x=4\), so larger \(x\) gives more spread. Evaluating at the random \(X\) gives the random variable \(\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X)=X\), as in the first Example.

\(\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X=x)\) is the spread within group \(x\) (right); averaged over \(X\) it gives \(\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X)]\).

Read the definition in two steps. First fix \(X=x\) and compute an ordinary variance under the conditional distribution of \(Y\) given \(X=x\): for discrete \(X\) this is the conditional variance given the event \(\{X=x\}\), a number \(v(x)\); for continuous \(X\) the conditional PDF takes over this role. Then substitute the random \(X\) to get \(\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X)=v(X)\). The squared deviations are measured from \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]\), the centre of each group, not from the overall mean \(\mathbb{E}Y\). The second formula is the familiar "mean of the square minus square of the mean", applied inside the conditional distribution.

Averaging \(v(X)\) over \(X\) gives \(\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X)]\), the within-group part of Eve's law. A common slip is to expect \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X)]\): this misses the spread of the group centres themselves, \(\operatorname{Var}(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X])\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X)\ge0\) almost surely.
  • For real constants \(a,b\), \(\operatorname{Var}(a+bY\mid X)=b^2\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(Y\mid X\sim\operatorname{Pois}(X)\) with \(\mathbb{E}[X^2]<\infty\), then \(\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X)=X\).
  • If \(Y\mid X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,X)\) with \(0\le X\le1\), then \(\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X)=nX(1-X)\).

docs.title: Method
docs.text: When \(Y\) has a natural conditional structure, for example \(Y\mid X=x\sim\operatorname{Pois}(x)\), compute \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)\) by decomposing it with Eve's law (total variance). This is a calculation method rather than a separate theorem; it needs \(\mathbb{E}[Y^2]<\infty\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
When the distribution of \(Y\) is awkward but \(Y\) becomes simple once another variable \(X\) is known, compute its mean and variance in two layers: first for fixed \(X\), then over \(X\), combined by total variance. This avoids finding the marginal distribution of \(Y\).

The figure shows the two cases of the first Example: \(X\) equals \(1\) or \(3\) with probability \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) each, and \(Y\mid X\sim\operatorname{Pois}(X)\). The average conditional variance, the spread within each bar chart, is \((1+3)/2=2\). The variance of the conditional means \(1\) and \(3\), the spread between the charts, is \(1\). The total variance is therefore \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)=2+1=3\).

The method has three steps. Name the variable \(X\) that makes \(Y\) simple; write down \(m(X)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]\) and \(v(X)=\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X)\), here the Poisson mean and variance; then compute \(\mathbb{E}[v(X)]\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(m(X))\) from the distribution of \(X\) alone. The last step needs only the mean and variance of \(X\), which is why the Key Result \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\mathbb{E}X+\operatorname{Var}(X)\) holds for every \(X\) with finite second moment. The mean is the same calculation with Adam's law.

The second term is easy to forget. Here \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)=3\) exceeds \(\mathbb{E}Y=2\), although every conditional Poisson law has variance equal to its mean: the randomness of the rate adds variance. This idea returns later in insurance, where a Poisson claim count with a random rate explains claim counts whose variance exceeds their mean (overdispersion).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Compute \(m(X)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]\) and \(v(X)=\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X)\) first; then \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\mathbb{E}[v(X)]+\operatorname{Var}(m(X))\).
  • For \(Y\mid X\sim\operatorname{Pois}(X)\) with finite second moment of \(X\), \(\mathbb{E}Y=\mathbb{E}X\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\mathbb{E}X+\operatorname{Var}(X)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(X\) is equally likely to be \(1\) or \(3\) and \(Y\mid X\sim\operatorname{Pois}(X)\), then \(\mathbb{E}Y=2\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)=2+1=3\).
  • If \(X\sim\operatorname{Bern}(1/2)\) and \(Y\mid X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(4,0.2+0.6X)\), the within variance is \(0.64\), the conditional-mean variance is \(1.44\), and total variance is \(2.08\).

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
When approximating \(\mathbb{P}(X\leq k)\) for an integer-valued random variable \(X\) by a normal distribution with mean \(\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sigma>0\), use

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb{P}(X\leq k)\approx\Phi\!\left(\frac{k+1/2-\mu}{\sigma}\right) \end{aligned} \]

(and similarly for \(\geq\)). The half-unit shift is an approximation rule, not an exact identity.

Here \(\Phi\) is the CDF of the Standard Normal Distribution. Subtracting \(\mu\) and dividing by \(\sigma\) converts the shifted boundary to its standard-normal scale.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An integer-valued probability is a sum of bar heights, and the bar for the value \(k\) has width \(1\) and covers \([k-\tfrac{1}{2},k+\tfrac{1}{2}]\). A normal area approximates those bars best when it covers the same half-unit cells around the included integers.

The figure shows \(X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(100,0.5)\) with the \(\mathcal{N}(50,25)\) density. The highlighted bars \(45,\ldots,55\) together cover \([44.5,55.5]\), so the normal area is taken between these endpoints: \(\mathbb{P}(45\le X\le55)\approx\Phi(1.1)-\Phi(-1.1)\approx0.7287\), which agrees with the exact value to four decimals. Without the correction, \(\Phi(1)-\Phi(-1)\approx0.6827\) leaves out half of each end bar.

The bars for \(X\le k\) end at \(k+\tfrac12\), not at \(k\). Compare both normal answers with the exact probability.

The direction of the shift depends on which integers the event includes. \(\mathbb{P}(X\le k)\) includes the bar at \(k\), so the area ends at \(k+\tfrac{1}{2}\); \(\mathbb{P}(X<k)=\mathbb{P}(X\le k-1)\) ends at \(k-\tfrac{1}{2}\); \(\mathbb{P}(X\ge k)\) starts at \(k-\tfrac{1}{2}\). Write the event as a range of integers first, then extend it by half a unit at both ends. For a single value, the uncorrected normal answer to \(\mathbb{P}(X=k)\) would be \(0\), while the corrected one uses the width of the bar, as in the first Example.

The correction matters most when \(\sigma\) is small, because half a unit is then a large fraction of a standard deviation. It is used with the normal approximation to the binomial and, more generally, with the central limit theorem for integer-valued sums such as totals of die rolls.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{P}(X\ge k)\approx1-\Phi((k-1/2-\mu)/\sigma)\).
  • For integers \(a\le b\), \(\mathbb{P}(a\le X\le b)\approx\Phi((b+1/2-\mu)/\sigma)-\Phi((a-1/2-\mu)/\sigma)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(100,0.5)\), \(\mathbb{P}(X=50)\approx\Phi(0.1)-\Phi(-0.1)\approx0.0797\).
  • For the same \(X\), \(\mathbb{P}(45\le X\le55)\approx\Phi(1.1)-\Phi(-1.1)\approx0.7287\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
For continuous random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) and an observed value \(x\) with \(0<f_X(x)<\infty\),

\[ \begin{aligned} f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)=\frac{f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)\,f_Y(y)}{f_X(x)}. \end{aligned} \]

Equalities between conditional densities may fail on a set of zero length, for example at finitely many points.

The Continuous Law of Total Probability computes the normalizing marginal density by averaging the likelihood against the conditioning variable’s density. That normalizer makes the reversed conditional density integrate to one.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Bayes’ rule for densities turns a model of how the observation depends on the unknown into a statement about the unknown. The likelihood \(f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)\) times the prior density \(f_Y(y)\), normalized by the marginal density \(f_X(x)\) of the observation, gives the posterior density \(f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)\).

The illustrated joint density equals \(2\) on \(0<x<y<1\). For the observation \(X=0.4\), the prior density \(f_Y(y)=2y\) and the likelihood \(f_{X\mid Y}(0.4\mid y)=1/y\) for \(0.4<y<1\) have the constant product \(2\); dividing by \(f_X(0.4)=2(1-0.4)=1.2\) gives the flat red posterior of height \(5/3\). The posterior is uniform on \((0.4,1)\), in line with the first Example.

Observe \(x\): the prior \(f_Y\) is reweighted by \(f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)\) and divided by \(f_X(x)\), giving the posterior \(f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)\).

Read the formula with \(x\) fixed. The denominator \(f_X(x)\) does not depend on \(y\): it is only the constant that makes the posterior integrate to one, computed by the continuous law of total probability, so one may find the shape first and normalize at the end. The condition \(0<f_X(x)<\infty\) replaces the discrete requirement that the observed event has positive probability: \(\{X=x\}\) itself has probability zero, so a ratio of densities replaces a ratio of probabilities.

It is the discrete rule from Probability Theory with probabilities replaced by densities; the mixed discrete and continuous versions are on Bayes and Total Probability: Four Forms.

The posterior is a density in \(y\), but the likelihood \(f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)\), read as a function of \(y\), need not be one: in the figure, \(\int_{0.4}^1(1/y)\,\mathrm{d}y=\ln2.5\approx0.92\), not \(1\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The normalizing density is \(f_X(x)=\int f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)f_Y(y)\,\mathrm{d}y\).
  • For fixed \(x\), \(f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)\) is proportional in \(y\) to likelihood times prior.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For density \(2\) on \(0<x<y<1\), \(f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)=1/(1-x)\) on \(x<y<1\).
  • For independent \(X,Y\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\), likelihood and marginal cancel, so the posterior density of \(Y\) remains \(1\) on \((0,1)\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
For continuous random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) for which the conditional density \(f_{X\mid Y}\) exists,

\[ \begin{aligned} f_X(x)=\int f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)\,f_Y(y)\,\mathrm{d}y \end{aligned} \]

for every \(x\) except possibly on a set of zero length, for example at finitely many points.

The left side is the Marginal Probability Density Function of the response. It is recovered by averaging the conditional densities over the other variable’s marginal law.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The continuous law of total probability describes a two-stage model: first \(Y\) is drawn, then \(X\) is drawn from the conditional density \(f_{X\mid Y}(\cdot\mid y)\). The unconditional density of \(X\) is then a weighted mixture of the conditional densities, with the density of \(Y\) as the weight.

For \(X\mid Y=y\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,y)\), each conditional density is a rectangle of height \(1/y\) on \((0,y)\): heights \(4\), \(2\), \(4/3\) and \(1\) for \(y=1/4,1/2,3/4,1\). A point \(x\) lies under the rectangles with \(y>x\) only, so with \(f_Y(y)=2y\) on \((0,1)\) the average is \(f_X(x)=\int_x^1(1/y)2y\,\mathrm{d}y=2(1-x)\) for \(0<x<1\). Values near \(1\) lie under few rectangles, so the red marginal decreases.

Cut the range of \(Y\) into \(m\) slices: each contributes \(f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y_j)f_Y(y_j)\Delta y\). Raise \(m\) and the sum becomes \(f_X\).

The formula is the law of total probability \(\mathbb{P}(A)=\sum_i\mathbb{P}(A\mid B_i)\mathbb{P}(B_i)\) with the cases \(B_i\) replaced by the values \(y\), the sum by an integral and \(\mathbb{P}(B_i)\) by \(f_Y(y)\,\mathrm{d}y\); the slider above shows exactly this limit of sums. Since \(f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)f_Y(y)=f_{X,Y}(x,y)\), it is also the computation of a marginal density from the joint density.

The same integral is the normalizing denominator in the continuous Bayes rule, and the same averaging applied to means returns as Adam’s law.

The integration range is easy to get wrong: \(f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)\) is zero unless \(y>x\), so the integral runs from \(x\) to \(1\). Integrating over all of \((0,1)\) would give the constant \(2\), which integrates to \(2\) rather than \(1\); checking that the result integrates to one catches such errors.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The event form is \(\mathbb{P}(X\in A)=\int\mathbb{P}(X\in A\mid Y=y)f_Y(y)\,\mathrm{d}y\).
  • Integrating the conditional density mixture over \(x\) gives total probability one.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For density \(2\) on \(0<x<y<1\), \(f_X(x)=\int_x^1(1/y)(2y)\,\mathrm{d}y=2(1-x)\) for \(0<x<1\).
  • If \(Y\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) and \(X\mid Y=y\sim\operatorname{Bern}(y)\), then \(\mathbb{P}(X=1)=\int_0^1y\,\mathrm{d}y=1/2\), using the event form.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A sequence of random variables \(X_n\) converges in distribution to \(X\) if the CDFs of the \(X_n\) converge to the CDF of \(X\) wherever the latter is continuous:

\[ \begin{aligned} F_{X_n}(x)\to F_X(x) \end{aligned} \]

for every point \(x\) at which \(F_X\) is continuous. This is written as \(X_n\xrightarrow{d}X\). Convergence at the jump points of \(F_X\) is not required, and the variables may be defined on different probability spaces (different sample spaces with their own probability functions), because only their CDFs are compared.

For each continuity point of the limiting CDF, take an ordinary Limit of a Sequence of numbers \(F_{X_n}(x)\). The input \(x\) stays fixed while the random-variable index grows.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Convergence in distribution says that probabilities computed from \(X_n\) approach those computed from \(X\): \(\mathbb{P}(X_n\le x)\approx\mathbb{P}(X\le x)\) for large \(n\). Only the distributions are compared, through their CDFs; the values of \(X_n\) need not approach the values of \(X\) along any sample path.

The figure shows the CDFs of the constants \(X_n=1/n\) for \(n=1,2,4\), each a step from \(0\) to \(1\) at \(1/n\). The steps move towards the step at \(0\) of the limit \(X=0\), so \(F_{X_n}(x)\to F_X(x)\) for every \(x\ne0\). At the jump point \(x=0\) itself, \(F_{X_n}(0)=0\) for every \(n\) while \(F_X(0)=1\).

Raise \(n\) and watch the CDF of \(Z_n\) close in on \(\Phi\). For a discrete start the CDF keeps its jumps, yet the largest gap still shrinks.

This example explains why the definition only asks for convergence where \(F_X\) is continuous. The numbers \(1/n\) certainly approach \(0\), and any reasonable notion of convergence should allow it; demanding convergence at the jump as well would exclude this example. For a continuous limit such as \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\) every point is a continuity point, so the CDFs must converge everywhere, which is the form used in the central limit theorem.

Convergence in distribution is the weakest of the three modes of convergence on these pages. In the second Example, \(X_n=(-1)^nZ\) has the law of \(Z\) for every \(n\), so it converges in distribution to \(Z\), yet \(X_n\) keeps switching between \(Z\) and \(-Z\). A statement \(X_n\xrightarrow{d}X\) therefore says nothing about \(X_n-X\) being small, except when the limit is a constant, where it implies convergence in probability.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Convergence in probability implies convergence in distribution.
  • Convergence in distribution to a constant \(c\) implies convergence in probability to \(c\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(X_n=1/n\), its CDF converges to the CDF of the constant \(0\) at every continuity point \(x\ne0\), so \(X_n\xrightarrow{d}0\).
  • For \(Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)\) and \(X_n=(-1)^nZ\), every \(X_n\) has the law of \(Z\), so \(X_n\xrightarrow{d}Z\), but \(X_n\) does not converge in probability to \(Z\): odd-index differences are \(2|Z|\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(X_1,X_2,\ldots\) and \(X\) be random variables on a common probability space. The sequence converges in probability to \(X\), written \(X_n\xrightarrow{P}X\), if for every \(\varepsilon>0\),

\[ \mathbb{P}(|X_n-X|>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0\quad\text{as }n\to\infty. \]

The Sequence consists of random variables \(X_n\). For each fixed positive tolerance, the Limit of a Sequence is instead taken for the numbers \(\mathbb{P}(|X_n-X|>\varepsilon)\), which must tend to zero.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Convergence in probability asks, for each fixed tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), whether the probability of an error larger than \(\varepsilon\) tends to zero. It makes a statement about each sample size \(n\) separately, not about how a single sample path behaves as \(n\) grows.

The figure shows the density of \(X_n\) for a small and a large \(n\), both centred at \(c\), with the band from \(c-\varepsilon\) to \(c+\varepsilon\) marked. The shaded area outside the band is \(\mathbb{P}(|X_n-c|>\varepsilon)\), and it is much smaller for the narrow large-\(n\) density. Convergence in probability to \(c\) means that this area tends to \(0\) as \(n\to\infty\), however narrow the band is chosen.

Here \(X_n=\bar X_n\) and \(X=\mu\). Pick any \(\varepsilon\): the probability of an error larger than \(\varepsilon\) tends to \(0\), which is exactly the definition.

Two steps are involved: first \(\varepsilon\) is fixed, then the limit of the numbers \(\mathbb{P}(|X_n-X|>\varepsilon)\) is taken. Small errors are allowed at every \(n\); only the probability of errors above the tolerance must vanish. Most uses have a constant limit, as in the weak law of large numbers. A quick proof for a constant limit uses the Chebyshev inequality: if \(\mathbb{E}X_n=c\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X_n)\to0\), then \(\mathbb{P}(|X_n-c|\ge\varepsilon)\le\operatorname{Var}(X_n)/\varepsilon^2\to0\).

A common slip is to conclude that expectations converge as well. If \(X_n=n\) with probability \(1/n\) and \(X_n=0\) otherwise, then \(X_n\xrightarrow{P}0\), yet \(\mathbb{E}X_n=1\) for every \(n\): a rare but large error does not count in the definition. The stronger almost-sure convergence additionally requires almost every path to converge.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Almost-sure convergence implies convergence in probability.
  • Convergence in probability implies convergence in distribution; the converses generally fail.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(X_n=1/n\), then for every \(\varepsilon>0\), \(\mathbb{P}(|X_n|>\varepsilon)=0\) for sufficiently large \(n\), so \(X_n\xrightarrow{P}0\).
  • If \(X_n\sim\operatorname{Bern}(1/n)\), then for \(0<\varepsilon<1\), \(\mathbb{P}(|X_n|>\varepsilon)=1/n\to0\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
For independent continuous random variables \(X\) and \(Y\), the density of \(X+Y\) is the convolution of their densities; independence is what lets the joint density factor into the two marginal densities:

\[ \begin{aligned} f_{X+Y}(t)=\int f_X(x)\,f_Y(t-x)\,\mathrm{d}x. \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A sum can reach a value in many ways. For \(X+Y\) to be near \(t\), \(X\) takes some value \(x\) and \(Y\) must take the matching value \(t-x\); convolution adds up all these splits, each weighted by \(f_X(x)f_Y(t-x)\).

For independent \(X,Y\sim\operatorname{Exp}(1)\), the product \(\mathrm{e}^{-x}\mathrm{e}^{-(2-x)}=\mathrm{e}^{-2}\) is constant for \(0<x<2\), so the green region is a rectangle of height \(\mathrm{e}^{-2}\approx0.135\) and width \(2\). Its area \(f_{X+Y}(2)=2\mathrm{e}^{-2}\approx0.27\) is the height of the red point. More generally, \(f_{X+Y}(t)=t\mathrm{e}^{-t}\) for \(t>0\).

Move \(t\): \(f_Y(t-x)\) is \(f_Y\) flipped and shifted, and the area of its product with \(f_X\) is \(f_{X+Y}(t)\), traced on the right.

Independence is what turns the joint density \(f_{X,Y}(x,t-x)\) into the product \(f_X(x)f_Y(t-x)\). Without it the formula fails: for \(X\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) and \(Y=X\), the sum \(2X\) is uniform on \((0,2)\) with density \(1/2\), whereas the convolution of two uniform densities gives the triangular density. The integral only runs over the \(x\) for which both factors are positive, which for exponentials is \(0<x<t\).

The discrete version is the sum used for two dice in Probability Theory (sum of independent random variables). Moment generating functions give a second route: by the MGF of an independent sum, \(M_{X+Y}=M_XM_Y\), which avoids the integral when the product is a recognizable MGF. The density \(t\mathrm{e}^{-t}\) found here is the Gamma distribution with shape \(2\) and rate \(1\).

Adding values is not adding densities: \(f_X+f_Y\) has total integral \(2\), and the product \(f_X(t)f_Y(t)\) is not a density of the sum either.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For independent discrete variables, \(\displaystyle p_{X+Y}(t)=\sum_xp_X(x)p_Y(t-x)\).
  • For independent variables with densities, the integral is over \(x\) for which both density factors are nonzero.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For independent \(\operatorname{Exp}(1)\) variables, \(f_{X+Y}(t)=\int_0^t\mathrm{e}^{-x}\mathrm{e}^{-(t-x)}\,\mathrm{d}x=t\mathrm{e}^{-t}\) for \(t>0\).
  • For independent fair Bernoulli variables, the sum has masses \(1/4,1/2,1/4\) at \(0,1,2\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) with \(0<\operatorname{Var}(X)<\infty\) and \(0<\operatorname{Var}(Y)<\infty\), the correlation of \(X\) and \(Y\) is

\[ \operatorname{Corr}(X,Y)=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)\operatorname{Var}(Y)}} \in[-1,1]. \]

Correlation is undefined if either variance is zero.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Correlation is the covariance of the two variables after each has been standardized to mean \(0\) and variance \(1\). It is therefore unit-free, lies between \(-1\) and \(1\), and measures how closely the pair follows a straight line. Zero correlation rules out linear association but can coexist with dependence.

The left panel shows the exact decreasing relation \(Y=5-2X\), with correlation \(-1\). The middle panel shows a positive but imperfect linear association, with correlation about \(0.74\). In the right panel, \(X\sim\operatorname{Unif}(-1,1)\) and \(Y=X^2\) are uncorrelated but dependent, illustrating that correlation measures linear association only.

Change the slope and the noise: the correlation measures how tightly the points follow a line. With \(Y=X^2\) it is \(0\), although \(Y\) depends on \(X\).

Dividing by the standard deviations removes the units: measuring \(X\) in cents instead of euros multiplies the covariance by \(100\) but leaves the correlation unchanged. In general \(\operatorname{Corr}(a+bX,c+dY)=\operatorname{Corr}(X,Y)\) when \(bd>0\), and the sign flips when \(bd<0\). The values \(\pm1\) occur only for an exact linear relation.

There is a useful picture from linear algebra: covariance behaves like an inner product of the centred variables, variance like a squared length, and correlation like the cosine of the angle between them. The bound \(|\operatorname{Corr}(X,Y)|\le1\) is then the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, which returns for random variables later in this course (Cauchy–Schwarz for random variables).

Correlation is not the slope of the line: \(Y=5-2X\) and \(Y=5-0.1X\) both have correlation \(-1\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(-1\le\operatorname{Corr}(X,Y)\le1\).
  • Absolute correlation is \(1\) exactly when \(Y=a+bX\) almost surely for constants \(a,b\) with \(b\ne0\); its sign is the sign of \(b\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(Y=5-2X\) and \(X\) has positive finite variance, the correlation is \(-1\).
  • For \(X\sim\operatorname{Unif}(-1,1)\) and \(Y=X^2\), symmetry gives \(\mathbb{E}X=\mathbb{E}[X^3]=0\), so correlation is \(0\) although \(Y\) is determined by \(X\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For square-integrable \(X,Y\), covariance is

\[ \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\mathbb{E}[(X-\mathbb{E}X)(Y-\mathbb{E}Y)] =\mathbb{E}[XY]-\mathbb{E}X\,\mathbb{E}Y. \]

Independence implies zero covariance; the converse generally fails.

Expanding the product of centred variables and using Linearity of Expectation gives \(\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\mathbb{E}[XY]-\mathbb{E}X\,\mathbb{E}Y\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Covariance measures whether two variables tend to deviate from their means in the same direction: it is positive when large values of \(X\) tend to go with large values of \(Y\), and negative when they tend to go with small values. It also accounts for dependence in the variance of a sum.

Points in the green quadrants contribute positive products of deviations, while points in the red quadrants contribute negative products. Covariance averages these products, taking both their magnitudes and probabilities into account.

Points where \(X\) and \(Y\) are on the same side of their means count positively, the others negatively; the covariance averages these products.

The first formula in the Definition carries the meaning; the second, \(\mathbb{E}[XY]-\mathbb{E}X\,\mathbb{E}Y\), is the shortcut for computing, with \(\mathbb{E}[XY]\) found from a joint PMF or density by two-dimensional LOTUS (continuous version). Taking \(Y=X\) gives \(\operatorname{Cov}(X,X)=\operatorname{Var}(X)\). Shifts do not matter, but rescaling does: covariance carries the product of the units of \(X\) and \(Y\), so only its sign is directly interpretable. Correlation divides by the standard deviations to remove the units.

In \(\operatorname{Var}(X+Y)=\operatorname{Var}(X)+\operatorname{Var}(Y)+2\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)\), positive covariance means the deviations reinforce each other and negative covariance means they partly cancel. For independent variables the covariance is zero and the variances simply add, as in Probability Theory. Counts that compete for a fixed total have negative covariance, as in the multinomial distribution.

Zero covariance does not imply independence: for \(X\sim\operatorname{Unif}(-1,1)\) and \(Y=X^2\), \(\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\mathbb{E}[X^3]-\mathbb{E}X\,\mathbb{E}[X^2]=0\), although \(Y\) is a function of \(X\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\operatorname{Cov}(a+bX,c+dY)=bd\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)\).
  • \(\operatorname{Var}(X+Y)=\operatorname{Var}(X)+\operatorname{Var}(Y)+2\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(Y=2X\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=3\), then \(\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=6\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X+Y)=27\).
  • For independent fair Bernoulli variables, \(\mathbb{E}[XY]=1/4\) and \(\mathbb{E}X\mathbb{E}Y=1/4\), so covariance is zero.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) be i.i.d. continuous random variables with PDF \(f\) and CDF \(F\), let \(X_{(1)}\le\cdots\le X_{(n)}\) be their order statistics, and write \(\bar F=1-F\). For \(1\le k\le n\), the \(k\)th order statistic has density

\[ f_{X_{(k)}}(x)= n f(x) {\binom{n-1}{k -1}} \times F(x)^{k-1} \bar F(x)^{n-k}. \]

The formula holds for every \(x\) except possibly on a set of zero length, for example at finitely many points.

The i.i.d. assumption makes the probabilities of falling below a threshold equal and independent. It produces the binomial count underlying the order-statistic CDF and density.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An order statistic is a sorted observation. Its density combines the chance of an observation near a value with the chances that the required numbers of observations fall below and above it.

For three i.i.d. \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) observations, the \(k\)th order statistic has density \(f_{X_{(k)}}(x)=3\binom{2}{k-1}x^{k-1}(1-x)^{3-k}\) for \(0<x<1\) and \(k=1,2,3\): the minimum \(3(1-x)^2\) peaks at \(0\), the median \(6x(1-x)\) peaks at \(1/2\) and the maximum \(3x^2\) peaks at \(1\). The dashed line is the density of a single observation.

Change \(n\) and \(k\): the \(k\)th smallest of \(n\) draws has density \(nf(x)\binom{n-1}{k-1}F(x)^{k-1}\bar F(x)^{n-k}\), moving right as \(k\) grows.

For \(X_{(k)}\) to lie in a short interval of length \(\Delta x\) at \(x\), one of the \(n\) observations must lie there (factor \(n\), probability about \(f(x)\Delta x\)), and of the remaining \(n-1\), exactly \(k-1\) must fall below \(x\). That count is binomial with \(n-1\) trials and success probability \(F(x)\), which gives \(\binom{n-1}{k-1}F(x)^{k-1}\bar F(x)^{n-k}\). The i.i.d. assumption gives every observation the same probability \(F(x)\) and makes the trials independent; continuity makes ties have probability zero, so exactly one observation sits near \(x\). For discrete observations ties occur and the formula does not apply.

For \(k=n\) and \(k=1\) the formula is the derivative of the CDFs \(F(x)^n\) and \(1-\bar F(x)^n\) from Order Statistic, with \(\bar F\) the survivor function.

The factor \(n\) is easy to forget. Without it the density of the maximum of three uniforms would be \(x^2\), which integrates to \(1/3\) instead of \(1\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For the maximum of three i.i.d. \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) variables, the density is \(3x^2\) on \((0,1)\) and \(\mathbb{P}(X_{(3)}\le1/2)=1/8\).
  • The minimum of four independent \(\operatorname{Exp}(2)\) variables has tail \(\mathrm{e}^{-8x}\) for \(x\ge0\), hence distribution \(\operatorname{Exp}(8)\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
For random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) with \(\mathbb{E}[Y^2]<\infty\),

\[ \operatorname{Var}(Y)=\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X)] +\operatorname{Var}(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]). \]

Consequence: the residual \(Y-\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]\) is uncorrelated with every function \(h(X)\) that has \(\mathbb{E}[h(X)^2]<\infty\) (or satisfies another assumption that makes the products integrable):

\[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Cov}(Y-\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X],\,h(X))=0. \end{aligned} \]

The first term averages the Conditional Variance Given a Random Variable; the second is the ordinary Variance and Standard Deviation of the conditional mean. To derive the identity, apply Adam’s Law: Total Expectation to \(Y^2\) and expand both variances as second moment minus squared mean.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Total spread consists of average spread within conditional groups plus spread between their conditional means. Knowing \(X\) splits the variance of \(Y\) into a part that \(X\) explains, how much the group centres move, and a part that remains, how much \(Y\) varies inside a group.

The figure groups values of \(Y\) by \(X=1,2,3\). The short red lines are the group means \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x]\) and the dashed line is the overall mean \(\mathbb{E}Y\). The first term, \(\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X)]\), averages the spread of the points around their own red line (the arrow "within"). The second term, \(\operatorname{Var}(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X])\), measures how far the red lines lie from the dashed line (the arrow "between").

Move the group means and spreads: \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)\) is the average spread within the groups plus the spread of the group means.

Two extreme cases show what each term means. If \(Y\) is a function of \(X\), every group is a single point, the first term is \(0\) and all variance lies between groups. If \(Y\) is independent of \(X\), every group mean equals \(\mathbb{E}Y\) by conditional expectation and independence, so the second term is \(0\) and \(X\) explains nothing. Both terms are nonnegative, which gives the Key Result \(\operatorname{Var}(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X])\le\operatorname{Var}(Y)\): replacing \(Y\) by its conditional mean can only reduce variance.

The practical form of the identity is the conditioning trick for variance. A frequent slip is to drop one of the two terms, or to write the first term as the random variable \(\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X)\) instead of its average \(\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X)]\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\operatorname{Var}(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X])\le\operatorname{Var}(Y)\).
  • The residual \(R=Y-\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]\) has mean zero and \(\operatorname{Cov}(R,h(X))=0\) for every square-integrable \(h(X)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(X\sim\operatorname{Exp}(2)\) and \(Y\mid X\sim\operatorname{Pois}(X)\), then \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\mathbb{E}X+\operatorname{Var}(X)=1/2+1/4=3/4\).
  • If \(X\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) and \(Y\mid X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,X)\), then \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)=n/6+n^2/12=n(n+2)/12\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
For every real \(x\),

\[ \lim_{n\to\infty}\left(1+\frac{x}{n}\right)^n = \mathrm{e}^x. \]

Here \(1+x/n>0\) for all sufficiently large \(n\), which the usual logarithm argument needs.

For each fixed \(x\), the Limit of a Sequence of the powers \(\left(1+x/n\right)^n\) equals the value of the Exponential Function at that same \(x\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Many small multiplicative changes combine into an exponential. Growing by the factor \(1+x/n\) in each of \(n\) steps gives the total factor \((1+x/n)^n\), and as the steps become smaller and more numerous this total approaches \(\mathrm{e}^x\). The same limit explains how rare-event binomial probabilities approach Poisson probabilities.

The curves \((1+x/n)^n\) for \(n=1,2,5,20\) lie below the red dashed curve \(\mathrm{e}^x\) and move up towards it as \(n\) grows. At \(x=2\) they take the values \(3\), \(4\), about \(5.38\) and about \(6.73\), against \(\mathrm{e}^2\approx7.39\): for each fixed \(x\) the gap shrinks, but slowly where \(x\) is far from \(0\).

Raise \(n\): the curve \((1+x/n)^n\) approaches \(\mathrm{e}^x\) for every \(x\). Point at the plot to compare the values at one \(x\).

Taking the logarithm shows why the limit is \(\mathrm{e}^x\): \(n\ln(1+x/n)\) is close to \(n\cdot x/n=x\), because \(\ln(1+u)\approx u\) for small \(u\). This is also why the statement needs \(1+x/n>0\): the logarithm requires a positive argument, which holds for all large \(n\) even when \(x\) is negative.

With \(x=-\lambda\) the limit reads \((1-\lambda/n)^n\to\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda}\). For \(X_n\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,\lambda/n)\) this is \(\mathbb{P}(X_n=0)\): in many trials with a small success probability and mean \(\lambda\), the chance of no success approaches \(\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda}\), the Poisson probability of zero. Applied to the MGF of \(X_n\), the limit gives \((1+\lambda(\mathrm{e}^t-1)/n)^n\to\mathrm{e}^{\lambda(\mathrm{e}^t-1)}\), the MGF of \(\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For fixed \(x\), \(\lim_{n\to\infty}(1+x/n)^n=\mathrm{e}^x\).
  • For fixed \(\lambda>0\), \(\lim_{n\to\infty}(1-\lambda/n)^n=\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda}\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \((1+1/n)^n\to \mathrm{e}\).
  • If \(X_n\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,3/n)\) for \(n\ge3\), then \(\mathbb{P}(X_n=0)=(1-3/n)^n\to \mathrm{e}^{-3}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For shape \(r>0\) and rate \(\lambda>0\), \(X\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(r,\lambda)\) has density

\[ f_X(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{\lambda^r}{\Gamma(r)}x^{r-1}\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda x},&x>0,\\0,&x\le0.\end{cases} \]

The Gamma Function in the denominator normalizes the density: substituting \(z=\lambda x\) makes the unnormalized integral equal to \(\Gamma(r)\), which cancels the denominator.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The gamma family extends exponential waiting times. For a positive integer shape \(r\), \(\operatorname{Gamma}(r,\lambda)\) is the distribution of a sum of \(r\) independent \(\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)\) waits, for example the time until the \(r\)-th arrival in a Poisson process with rate \(\lambda\).

The figure shows three densities with rate \(\lambda=1\). For \(r=1\) the density \(\mathrm{e}^{-x}\) is the exponential one, largest at \(0\). For \(r=2\) and \(r=3\) the factor \(x^{r-1}\) pushes the density down to \(0\) at the origin, giving a hump with its peak at \(x=r-1\). The means \(r/\lambda=2\) and \(3\) move to the right, and the spread grows with the variance \(r/\lambda^2\).

Change the shape \(r\) and the rate \(\lambda\). At \(r=1\) the density is \(\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)\); integer \(r\) gives the waiting time for \(r\) exponential events.

The shape \(r\) sets the form of the density through the power \(x^{r-1}\), and the rate \(\lambda\) only sets the scale: if \(X\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(r,1)\), then \(X/\lambda\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(r,\lambda)\). Non-integer shapes are allowed because the gamma function normalizes the density for every \(r>0\); they no longer count exponential waits, but the formulas for mean, variance and MGF stay the same.

The MGF \((\lambda/(\lambda-t))^r\) is the \(r\)-th power of the exponential MGF, so the MGF of an independent sum and MGF uniqueness prove the sum property. The same argument shows that independent \(\operatorname{Gamma}(r,\lambda)\) and \(\operatorname{Gamma}(s,\lambda)\) variables add to \(\operatorname{Gamma}(r+s,\lambda)\), provided the rates agree. Some texts use a scale parameter \(\theta=1/\lambda\) instead, with mean \(r\theta\); check the convention before using a formula.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• In shape-rate notation, \(\mathbb{E}X=r/\lambda\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=r/\lambda^2\).
  • \(M_X(t)=(\lambda/(\lambda-t))^r\) for \(t<\lambda\); shape \(r=1\) gives the exponential law.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For shape \(r=2\) and rate \(\lambda=1\), the density is \(x\mathrm{e}^{-x}\) on \(x>0\), the mean is \(2\), and the variance is \(2\).
  • The sum of three independent \(\operatorname{Exp}(2)\) waits has \(\operatorname{Gamma}(3,2)\) distribution, with mean \(3/2\) and variance \(3/4\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(f\) be nonnegative and nondecreasing on a domain containing the values of \(X\) and the threshold \(a\). If \(f(a)>0\) and \(\mathbb{E}[f(X)]<\infty\), then

\[ \mathbb{P}(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb{E}[f(X)]}{f(a)}. \]

This follows from \(f(X)\ge f(a)\indicator_{\{X\ge a\}}\). For the ordinary Markov inequality \(\mathbb{P}(X\ge a)\le\mathbb{E}[X]/a\), take \(f(x)=x\) on \([0,\infty)\) and require \(X\ge0\), \(a>0\).

The Inequality gives an upper bound, not an exact tail probability: the event where a nonnegative variable exceeds \(a>0\) contributes at least \(a\) times its probability to the expectation.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A nonnegative variable with a small average cannot often be large. With mean \(10\), at most a fifth of the probability can lie at \(50\) or above, because that part alone would contribute at least \(50\,\mathbb{P}(X\ge50)\) to the mean. The generalized version applies the same reasoning to \(f(X)\) instead of \(X\).

The figure compares \(f\) with the step function \(f(a)\indicator_{\{x\ge a\}}\), which is \(0\) below \(a\) and \(f(a)\) from \(a\) onwards. Both \(f(x)=x\) and the steeper dashed \(f(x)=x^2/a\) have the value \(a\) at \(x=a\) and lie on or above the step everywhere. Taking expectations of \(f(X)\ge f(a)\indicator_{\{X\ge a\}}\) gives \(\mathbb{E}[f(X)]\ge f(a)\,\mathbb{P}(X\ge a)\), which is the theorem.

Compare \(\mathbb{P}(X\ge a)\) with \(\mathbb{E}[f(X)]/f(a)\) for \(f(x)=x\) and \(f(x)=x^2\): a faster-growing \(f\) can give a sharper bound, depending on the distribution and threshold. Compare both bounds rather than assuming one is always better.

Each hypothesis is used in that one comparison: nonnegativity of \(f\) covers \(x<a\), where the step is \(0\), and monotonicity covers \(x\ge a\), where \(f(x)\ge f(a)\). Without nonnegativity the bound fails: if \(X\) takes the values \(-1\) and \(1\) with probability \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) each, then \(\mathbb{E}X/1=0\) but \(\mathbb{P}(X\ge1)=\tfrac{1}{2}\).

Different choices of \(f\) give the other tail bounds: \(f(x)=x^2\) applied to \(|X-\mu|\) gives the Chebyshev inequality, and \(f(x)=\mathrm{e}^{tx}\) gives the Chernoff bound. No single choice is always best. For \(X\sim\operatorname{Exp}(1)\), with \(\mathbb{E}X=1\) and \(\mathbb{E}[X^2]=2\), the first-moment bound \(1/a\) is smaller for \(a<2\) and the second-moment bound \(2/a^2\) is smaller for \(a>2\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For \(X\ge0\) and \(a>0\), \(\mathbb{P}(X\ge a)\le\mathbb{E}X/a\).
  • For \(X\ge0\) and \(r>0\), \(\mathbb{P}(X\ge a)\le\mathbb{E}[X^r]/a^r\) whenever the moment is finite.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A nonnegative loss with mean \(10\) satisfies \(\mathbb{P}(X\ge50)\le10/50=0.2\).
  • If \(X\ge0\) and \(\mathbb{E}[X^2]=9\), then \(\mathbb{P}(X\ge6)\le9/36=1/4\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(X\) be an integrable random variable taking values in an interval on which \(g\) is convex. If \(\mathbb{E}[g(X)]\) exists (in the finite-valued form, \(\mathbb{E}|g(X)|<\infty\)), then

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}[g(X)]\geq g(\mathbb{E} X). \end{aligned} \]

The inequality reverses for concave \(g\).

The Expectation is the weighted average in this result. Convexity compares the function evaluated at that average with the average of the function values.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
For a convex function, averaging before applying the function gives no larger a value than applying it first and then averaging: \(g(\mathbb{E}X)\le\mathbb{E}[g(X)]\). In general an expectation cannot be moved through a nonlinear function, and convexity tells in which direction the error goes.

In the figure \(X\) takes two values \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) with probability \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) each, so \(\mathbb{E}X\) is their midpoint. The chord joins the points of the graph of \(g(x)=x^2\) above \(x_1\) and \(x_2\); above \(\mathbb{E}X\) its height is the average \(\mathbb{E}[g(X)]\), while the curve has height \(g(\mathbb{E}X)\). A convex graph lies below its chords, so \(g(\mathbb{E}X)\le\mathbb{E}[g(X)]\). For a variable with two values this is exactly the definition of convexity, with the probabilities as weights; Jensen's inequality extends it to every distribution.

\(X\) takes two values; \(\mathbb{E}[g(X)]\) lies on the chord and \(g(\mathbb{E}X)\) on the curve. Convex \(g\) puts the chord above, concave \(g\) below.

With \(g(x)=x^2\), Jensen gives \((\mathbb{E}X)^2\le\mathbb{E}[X^2]\), that is \(\operatorname{Var}(X)\ge0\), as in the first Example. For the concave \(\log\) the inequality reverses, \(\mathbb{E}[\log X]\le\log\mathbb{E}X\).

A common slip is to replace \(\mathbb{E}[g(X)]\) by \(g(\mathbb{E}X)\) for a nonlinear \(g\). For positive \(X\), \(g(x)=1/x\) is convex on \((0,\infty)\), so \(\mathbb{E}[1/X]\ge1/\mathbb{E}X\); if \(X\) is \(1\) or \(3\) with equal probability, these are \(\tfrac{2}{3}\) and \(\tfrac{1}{2}\). This idea returns later in insurance: with a concave utility, the expected utility of an uncertain wealth is at most the utility of its expected value.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For a concave function, the inequality reverses.
  • If \(g\) is strictly convex and both sides are finite, equality holds exactly when \(X\) is constant almost surely.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(g(x)=x^2\) and \(X\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\), \(g(\mathbb{E}X)=1/4\le\mathbb{E}[X^2]=1/3\).
  • For \(X=1\) or \(3\) with equal probability, concavity of \(\log\) gives \(\mathbb{E}\log X=\frac{1}{2}\log3\le\log2=\log\mathbb{E}X\).

docs.title: Joint CDF of Continuous Random Variables
Definition
docs.text:
The joint CDF of a random pair \((X,Y)\) is

\[ \begin{aligned} F_{X,Y}(x,y)=\mathbb{P}(X\leq x,Y\leq y). \end{aligned} \]

It exists for every random pair, including pairs without a joint PDF. This page develops its form for pairs with a joint density; the discrete form is on Joint CDF of Discrete Random Variables.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The joint CDF \(F_{X,Y}(x,y)\) is the probability that the pair lands in the lower-left quadrant \(\{(u,v)\colon u\le x,\ v\le y\}\) of the plane. This one function determines the whole joint distribution, and a joint density allows it to be calculated by a double integral.

For independent uniforms, probability is spread evenly over the square, so \(F(0.4,0.5)\) is the area \(0.4\cdot0.5=0.2\). For \(Y=X\), all probability lies on the diagonal, and the quadrant contains the diagonal piece up to \((0.4,0.4)\), so \(F(0.4,0.5)=\mathbb{P}(X\le0.4)=0.4\). Both pairs have \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) marginals, so the marginals alone do not determine the joint CDF.

As a function of two variables, \(F_{X,Y}\) is nondecreasing in each argument, tends to \(0\) when either argument tends to \(-\infty\), and tends to the marginal CDF \(F_X(x)\) when \(y\to\infty\). Where it is smooth enough, the joint density is recovered as the mixed partial derivative \(\partial^2F_{X,Y}/\partial x\,\partial y\); for independent uniforms, \(F(x,y)=xy\) on the unit square and this derivative is \(1\). Moreover, \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent if and only if \(F_{X,Y}(x,y)=F_X(x)F_Y(y)\) for all \(x,y\).

The definition is the same as for discrete pairs; only the way of computing it changes, from a double sum of a joint PMF to a double integral of a joint density.

The upper-right quadrant is not the complement of the lower-left one: \(\mathbb{P}(X>x,Y>y)=1-F_X(x)-F_Y(y)+F_{X,Y}(x,y)\), not \(1-F_{X,Y}(x,y)\). For independent uniforms at \((0.4,0.5)\) this is \(0.3\), not \(0.8\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• With a joint density, \(F_{X,Y}(x,y)=\int_{-\infty}^x\int_{-\infty}^yf_{X,Y}(u,v)\,\mathrm{d}v\,\mathrm{d}u\).
  • Rectangle probabilities follow by inclusion-exclusion: \(F(b,d)-F(a,d)-F(b,c)+F(a,c)\) for \((a,b]\times(c,d]\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For independent \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) variables, \(F_{X,Y}(0.4,0.5)=0.2\).
  • If \(Y=X\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\), then \(F_{X,Y}(0.4,0.5)=0.4\); this pair has no joint PDF.

docs.title: Joint CDF of Discrete Random Variables
Definition
docs.text:
The joint CDF of a random pair \((X,Y)\) is

\[ \begin{aligned} F_{X,Y}(x,y)=\mathbb{P}(X\leq x,Y\leq y). \end{aligned} \]

The definition applies to any random pair; this page develops its discrete form, and Joint CDF of Continuous Random Variables develops the form with a joint density.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The joint CDF measures the probability that two variables simultaneously lie below specified thresholds: \(F_{X,Y}(x,y)\) is the probability that \(X\) is at most \(x\) and \(Y\) is at most \(y\). For a discrete pair it is the sum of the joint masses in the lower-left corner below \((x,y)\).

For two fair dice the highlighted corner \(\{X\le2,\,Y\le3\}\) contains \(2\cdot3=6\) of the \(36\) equally likely outcomes, so \(F_{X,Y}(2,3)=6/36=\tfrac{1}{6}\). Because the dice are independent, this also equals \(F_X(2)F_Y(3)=\tfrac{2}{6}\cdot\tfrac{3}{6}\).

The joint CDF is defined at every point \((x,y)\) of the plane, not only at possible values. Between possible values it is constant, so for the dice \(F_{X,Y}(2.5,3.7)=F_{X,Y}(2,3)\). It is nondecreasing in each argument, and letting \(y\to\infty\) removes the condition on \(Y\) and leaves the CDF of \(X\). In general the joint CDF is not the product of the two marginal CDFs; it is for independent variables. For \(X=Y\sim\operatorname{Bern}(0.4)\), \(F_{X,Y}(0,0)=0.6\), not \(0.6^2\).

Probabilities of rectangles follow from four corner values by inclusion–exclusion: for \(x_1<x_2\) and \(y_1<y_2\),

\[ \reflow \begin{aligned} &\mathbb{P}(x_1<X\le x_2,\,y_1<Y\le y_2)\\ &=F_{X,Y}(x_2,y_2)-F_{X,Y}(x_1,y_2)\\ &\quad-F_{X,Y}(x_2,y_1)+F_{X,Y}(x_1,y_1). \end{aligned} \]

For the dice, \(F_{X,Y}(2,3)-F_{X,Y}(1,3)-F_{X,Y}(2,2)+F_{X,Y}(1,2)=(6-3-4+2)/36=\tfrac{1}{36}=\mathbb{P}(X=2,Y=3)\). The joint CDF of continuous variables has the same definition, with the sum replaced by an integral of a joint density.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\displaystyle F_{X,Y}(x,y)=\sum_{u\le x}\sum_{v\le y}p_{X,Y}(u,v)\).
  • \(F_X(x)=\lim_{y\to\infty}F_{X,Y}(x,y)\) and similarly for \(Y\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For independent fair dice, \(F_{X,Y}(2,3)=(2/6)(3/6)=1/6\).
  • If \(X=Y\) is Bernoulli with parameter \(0.4\), then \(F_{X,Y}(0,0)=0.6\), rather than \(0.6^2\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A random pair \((X,Y)\) is jointly continuous with joint PDF \(f_{X,Y}\) if, for every Borel region \(B\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2\), such as a rectangle, a disc or a half-plane,

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb{P}((X,Y)\in B)=\iint_B f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y. \end{aligned} \]

Continuous marginals alone do not guarantee a joint density: with \(Y=X\) both marginals can be continuous while all the probability lies on a line.

The double Definite Integral adds density over a rectangle or other region in the joint support, giving the probability that the pair falls there.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A joint density describes how probability is spread over the plane: \(f_{X,Y}(x,y)\) is probability per unit area near \((x,y)\), and the probability of a region is the volume under the surface above it.

The illustrated density has height \(2\) over the triangle \(0<x<y<1\) of area \(1/2\), so its total volume is \(2(1/2)=1\). The red part of the triangle below \(y=1/2\) has area \(1/8\), so \(\mathbb{P}(Y<1/2)=2\cdot1/8=1/4\).

Choose \(a\) and \(b\): \(\mathbb{P}(X\le a,Y\le b)\) is the volume under \(f_{X,Y}\) over the shaded rectangle. Try the course examples.

Any nonnegative function with total integral \(1\) is a joint density. The value \(f_{X,Y}(x,y)\) is not itself a probability and may exceed \(1\), as the height \(2\) shows. For a small rectangle with sides \(\Delta x\) and \(\Delta y\) around \((x,y)\), the probability is approximately \(f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,\Delta x\,\Delta y\). Points and curves have area zero and hence probability zero, which is why the pair \(Y=X\), whose probability lies on a line, has no joint density.

This is the one-variable density from Probability Theory with area in place of length, and the continuous counterpart of the joint PMF, with double integrals in place of double sums. From it follow marginal and conditional densities and expectations by two-dimensional LOTUS. For independent variables the joint density is the product \(f_X(x)f_Y(y)\).

The region where the density is positive fixes the integration limits. For \(\mathbb{P}(Y<1/2)\) on the triangle, \(x\) runs from \(0\) to \(y\), not from \(0\) to \(1\); \(0\) to \(1\) would give probability \(1\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(f_{X,Y}\ge0\) and \(\iint_{\mathbb{R}^2}f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y=1\).
  • A region of planar area zero has probability zero under a joint density.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For density \(1\) on \((0,1)^2\), \(\mathbb{P}(X<1/2,Y<1/3)=1/6\).
  • For density \(2\) on \(0<x<y<1\), \(\mathbb{P}(Y<1/2)=\int_0^{1/2}\int_0^y2\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y=1/4\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For discrete random variables \(X\) and \(Y\), the joint PMF is

\[ \begin{aligned} p_{X,Y}(x,y)=\mathbb{P}(X=x,Y=y). \end{aligned} \]

This is the Probability Mass Function of the pair: it assigns a mass to each possible ordered outcome, and summing those masses over an event gives its probability.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A joint PMF assigns probability to each pair of discrete values and describes how the variables behave together: the probability of any event about the pair \((X,Y)\) is the sum of the masses in that event.

Each disc sits at a pair \((x,y)\), and its size shows the mass \(p_{X,Y}(x,y)\). On the left the four masses \(0.1\), \(0.2\), \(0.3\) and \(0.4\) add up to \(1\). On the right \(X=Y\sim\operatorname{Bern}(\tfrac{1}{2})\): all mass lies on the diagonal, \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) at \((0,0)\) and \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) at \((1,1)\), and the pairs \((0,1)\) and \((1,0)\) have mass \(0\).

Each disc is a mass \(p_{X,Y}(x,y)\). Choose \(a\) and \(b\) and add the masses in the corner to get \(\mathbb{P}(X\le a,Y\le b)\).

The joint PMF holds more information than the two separate PMFs. In the right panel each of \(X\) and \(Y\) is \(\operatorname{Bern}(\tfrac{1}{2})\), exactly as for two independent fair coins, where each of the four pairs has mass \(\tfrac{1}{4}\); only the joint PMF tells the two situations apart. The separate PMFs are recovered as marginal PMFs by summing over the other variable, and independence means that every joint mass is the product of the two marginal masses.

Several notions are built directly on the joint PMF: the conditional PMF rescales the masses with one fixed value of \(Y\), the joint CDF adds the masses in a lower-left corner, and two-dimensional LOTUS averages a function \(g(X,Y)\) against them. For pairs of continuous variables, the joint density plays the same role, with sums replaced by integrals.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(p_{X,Y}(x,y)\ge0\) and \(\displaystyle \sum_x\sum_yp_{X,Y}(x,y)=1\).
  • For a set \(B\) of pairs, \(\displaystyle \mathbb{P}((X,Y)\in B)=\sum_{(x,y)\in B}p_{X,Y}(x,y)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Two independent fair dice have \(p_{X,Y}(i,j)=1/36\) for \(i,j=1,\ldots,6\).
  • If \(X=Y\sim\operatorname{Bern}(1/2)\), the masses at \((0,0)\) and \((1,1)\) are \(1/2\), and all other masses are zero.

docs.title: Law of Total Expectation over a Partition
Theorem
docs.text:
If \(\{A_i\}\) is a finite or countable partition of the sample space and \(Y\) is integrable, then

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}[Y]=\sum_i\mathbb{E}[Y\mid A_i]\,\mathbb{P}(A_{i}), \end{aligned} \]

where terms with \(\mathbb{P}(A_i)=0\) are omitted. The law of total probability (LOTP) is the special case \(Y=\indicator_B\) of this partition form of the law of total expectation; the random-variable form \(\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]]=\mathbb{E}[Y]\) is Adam’s Law.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The overall average is a weighted average of the averages within disjoint cases: split the sample space into cases, find the mean of \(Y\) in each case, and weight each case mean by the probability of the case.

In the diagram, the two cases have probabilities \(0.3\) and \(0.7\), drawn as bar widths, and conditional means \(10\) and \(2\), drawn as bar heights. Each term \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid A_i]\mathbb{P}(A_i)\) is the area of a bar, \(3\) and \(1.4\). The dashed level \(4.4\) has the same total area.

The cases must be disjoint so that no outcome is counted twice, and must cover the sample space so that none is missed; that is what a partition guarantees. A case with \(\mathbb{P}(A_i)=0\) has no conditional mean, but it also contributes nothing, so it is left out.

The theorem is useful when the cases make \(Y\) simple. For the number \(N\) of tosses up to and including the first head, with head probability \(p\), condition on the first toss; after a tail the count starts afresh, so \(\mathbb{E}N=p\cdot1+(1-p)(1+\mathbb{E}N)\), giving \(\mathbb{E}N=1/p\), the mean of the first success distribution. With \(Y=\indicator_B\) the theorem becomes the law of total probability, and with the cases \(\{X=x\}\) for a discrete \(X\) it becomes Adam’s law.

The weights are the case probabilities, not equal weights: the unweighted average \((10+2)/2=6\) is wrong.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For a partition \(\{A_i\}\), \(\displaystyle \mathbb{E}Y=\sum_{i\colon\mathbb{P}(A_i)>0}\mathbb{E}[Y\mid A_i]\mathbb{P}(A_i)\).
  • Putting \(Y=\indicator_B\) gives the law of total probability.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If two equally likely customer groups have mean spending \(20\) and \(50\), overall mean spending is \(35\).
  • If \(\mathbb{P}(A)=0.3\), \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid A]=10\), and \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid A^c]=2\), then \(\mathbb{E}Y=0.3(10)+0.7(2)=4.4\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
For a jointly continuous pair \((X,Y)\) and a Borel-measurable function \(g\) with \(\iint |g(x,y)|f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y<\infty\),

\[ \mathbb{E}[g(X,Y)] =\iint g(x,y)\,f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y. \]

For \(g\ge0\) the formula also holds without this assumption, as an extended (possibly infinite) expectation.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Two-dimensional LOTUS computes the mean of a function \(g(X,Y)\) of a continuous pair directly from the joint density: weight each value \(g(x,y)\) by \(f_{X,Y}(x,y)\) and integrate over the plane. The distribution of the new random variable \(g(X,Y)\) is never needed, and the pair need not be independent.

On the unit square the density is \(1\), so \(\mathbb{E}[g(X,Y)]\) is simply the average of \(g\) over the square. Along each blue level curve \(xy=c\) the function \(g\) has the constant value \(c\), and most of the square lies where \(xy\) is small. Here \(\mathbb{E}[XY]=\displaystyle\int_0^1\!\!\int_0^1xy\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y=\tfrac{1}{4}\), without finding the distribution of \(XY\).

The theorem is the LOTUS of Probability Theory with a double integral instead of a single one, and the continuous counterpart of the discrete two-dimensional version. The integrability condition makes the integral a well-defined finite number; for \(g\ge0\) it may be dropped if an infinite answer is allowed. Choosing \(g\) gives the standard quantities: \(g(x,y)=xy\) gives \(\mathbb{E}[XY]\) for the covariance, \(g(x,y)=x+y\) gives \(\mathbb{E}X+\mathbb{E}Y\) for any dependence, and an indicator of a region gives its probability.

For the dependent pair with density \(2\) on \(0<x<y<1\), \(\mathbb{E}[XY]=\int_0^1\int_0^y2xy\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y=1/4\), while \(\mathbb{E}X=1/3\) and \(\mathbb{E}Y=2/3\). So \(\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=1/4-2/9=1/36\). For independent variables the double integral factors and \(\mathbb{E}[XY]=\mathbb{E}X\,\mathbb{E}Y\).

In general \(\mathbb{E}[g(X,Y)]\ne g(\mathbb{E}X,\mathbb{E}Y)\): for the triangle, \(\mathbb{E}[XY]=1/4\) but \(\mathbb{E}X\,\mathbb{E}Y=2/9\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For \(g(x,y)=xy\), the integral gives \(\mathbb{E}[XY]\).
  • For an indicator of a region \(B\), it gives \(\mathbb{P}((X,Y)\in B)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For independent uniform coordinates on \((0,1)\), \(\mathbb{E}[XY]=\int_0^1\int_0^1xy\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y=1/4\).
  • For density \(2\) on \(0<x<y<1\), \(\mathbb{E}X=\int_0^1\int_0^y2x\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y=1/3\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
For a discrete pair \((X,Y)\) and a function \(g\) with \(\displaystyle \sum_{x,y}|g(x,y)|p_{X,Y}(x,y)<\infty\),

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}[g(X,Y)]=\sum_x\sum_y g(x,y)\,p_{X,Y}(x,y). \end{aligned} \]

For \(g\ge0\) the formula also holds without this assumption, as an extended (possibly infinite) expectation.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A function of two variables can be averaged directly using their joint PMF, even when the variables are dependent: each pair \((x,y)\) contributes the value \(g(x,y)\) times its mass. There is no need to work out the distribution of \(g(X,Y)\) first.

For two fair dice, take \(g(x,y)=1\) if \(x+y=7\) and \(g(x,y)=0\) otherwise, the indicator of the event \(\{X+Y=7\}\). It equals \(1\) on the six red pairs of the anti-diagonal and \(0\) on the other \(30\) pairs. Each pair has mass \(\tfrac{1}{36}\), so \(\mathbb{E}[g(X,Y)]=6\cdot\tfrac{1}{36}=\tfrac{1}{6}\), which is \(\mathbb{P}(X+Y=7)\): the expectation of an indicator is the probability of its event.

This is LOTUS with the pair \((X,Y)\) in place of a single variable, so the weights are joint masses, not the two marginal PMFs. The difference matters: for \(X=Y\sim\operatorname{Bern}(\tfrac{1}{2})\), \(\mathbb{E}[XY]=\mathbb{E}[X^2]=\tfrac{1}{2}\), while for independent fair Bernoulli variables, with the same marginals, \(\mathbb{E}[XY]=\tfrac{1}{4}\). The summability condition guarantees that the double sum has the same finite value in any order of summation.

Choosing \(g\) gives familiar rules. With \(g(x,y)=x+y\) the double sum splits into \(\sum_xx\,p_X(x)+\sum_yy\,p_Y(y)\), which is linearity of expectation, \(\mathbb{E}[X+Y]=\mathbb{E}X+\mathbb{E}Y\), without any independence assumption, provided both means exist. For independent \(X\) and \(Y\) the joint PMF factorizes, and \(g(x,y)=xy\) gives \(\mathbb{E}[XY]=\mathbb{E}X\,\mathbb{E}Y\). The continuous version replaces the sums by an integral against a joint density.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Choosing \(g(x,y)=xy\) gives \(\mathbb{E}[XY]\).
  • Choosing \(g(x,y)=\indicator_{\{x+y\le c\}}\) gives \(\mathbb{P}(X+Y\le c)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For independent fair Bernoulli variables, \(\mathbb{E}[XY]=1(1/4)=1/4\).
  • For independent fair dice, \(\mathbb{E}[\indicator_{\{X+Y=7\}}]=6(1/36)=1/6\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a jointly continuous pair \((X,Y)\) with joint density \(f_{X,Y}\), the marginal PDF of \(X\) is

\[ \begin{aligned} f_X(x)=\int f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}y, \end{aligned} \]

where the integral runs over the values allowed for the other coordinate; the density is zero outside the joint support.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The marginal density of \(X\) is the density of \(X\) on its own, ignoring \(Y\). Integrating out the other coordinate of the joint density collapses the probability in the plane onto the \(x\)-axis.

For the illustrated triangular density, the red vertical slice at \(x\) runs from \(y=x\) to \(y=1\) and has length \(1-x\), so \(f_X(x)=\int_x^1 2\,\mathrm{d}y=2(1-x)\) for \(0<x<1\). The green horizontal slice at \(y\) has length \(y\), so \(f_Y(y)=\int_0^y2\,\mathrm{d}x=2y\) for \(0<y<1\).

Move \(x\): integrating the joint density along the vertical slice gives \(f_X(x)\). For the triangle example this is \(2(1-x)\).

The value \(f_X(x)\,\Delta x\) approximates the probability of a thin vertical strip of width \(\Delta x\) at \(x\), which is the volume under the joint density over that strip. When the support is not a rectangle, the limits of the inner integral depend on \(x\), as in the triangle. This is the continuous version of adding up a row of a joint PMF table to get a marginal PMF.

Marginal densities are the denominator of a conditional density, and the continuous law of total probability rewrites the same integral with conditional densities. The marginals do not determine the joint density: on the unit square, both \(f(x,y)=1\) and \(f(x,y)=1+(1-2x)(1-2y)\) have \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) marginals. The joint density is the product of the marginals exactly in the independent case.

Ignoring the support is the usual error: integrating \(2\) over \(y\in(0,1)\) gives the constant \(2\), which integrates to \(2\) in \(x\), so it cannot be a density.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(f_Y(y)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}x\).
  • Each marginal integrates to one, since the joint density does.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(f_{X,Y}(x,y)=2\) on \(0<x<y<1\), then \(f_X(x)=2(1-x)\) for \(0<x<1\).
  • For the same triangle, \(f_Y(y)=\int_0^y2\,\mathrm{d}x=2y\) for \(0<y<1\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a discrete random pair \((X,Y)\) with joint PMF \(p_{X,Y}\), the marginal PMF of \(X\) is

\[ \begin{aligned} p_X(x)=\sum_y p_{X,Y}(x,y), \end{aligned} \]

where the sum runs over all possible values \(y\) of \(Y\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A marginal PMF describes one component of a random pair after the other component has been summed out. Summing over all values \(y\) is the law of total probability for the partition formed by the events \(\{Y=y\}\): \(\mathbb{P}(X=x)=\sum_y\mathbb{P}(X=x,Y=y)\).

In the table the rows are the values of \(X\) and the columns the values of \(Y\). The row sums \(0.1+0.2=0.3\) and \(0.3+0.4=0.7\) give \(p_X\); the column sums \(0.1+0.3=0.4\) and \(0.2+0.4=0.6\) give \(p_Y\). The name comes from writing these sums in the margins of the table.

Move \(x\): here \(x\) runs along the horizontal axis, so \(p_X(x)\) adds the masses in the vertical strip \(X=x\) (a row of the table above).

Going from the joint PMF to the marginals loses information: the marginals do not determine the joint PMF. The pair \(X=Y\sim\operatorname{Bern}(\tfrac{1}{2})\) and a pair of independent fair coins have the same marginals but different joint PMFs. Only for independent variables is the joint PMF the product \(p_X(x)p_Y(y)\); the table above is not of this kind, since \(p_X(0)p_Y(0)=0.3\cdot0.4=0.12\neq0.1\).

The marginal of \(Y\) is the denominator of the conditional PMF of \(X\) given \(Y=y\). For pairs with a joint density, the marginal density is found in the same way, with the sum replaced by an integral.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\displaystyle p_X(x)=\sum_yp_{X,Y}(x,y)\) and \(\displaystyle p_Y(y)=\sum_xp_{X,Y}(x,y)\).
  • Marginalization preserves normalization: \(\displaystyle \sum_xp_X(x)=1\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If the masses at \((0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1)\) are \(0.1,0.2,0.3,0.4\), then \(p_X(0)=0.3\) and \(p_Y(1)=0.6\).
  • For independent fair dice, summing the six masses \(1/36\) in a row gives \(p_X(i)=1/6\).
