docs.title: Location and Scale Property of the MGF
Proposition
docs.text:
For real constants \(a\) and \(b\) (no positivity is needed for \(b\)),

\[ \begin{aligned} M_{a+bX}(t)=\mathrm{e}^{a t}M_X(b t) \end{aligned} \]

for every \(t\) at which \(M_X(bt)\) is finite.

Starting from the Moment Generating Function definition, \(\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{e}^{t(a+bX)}]=\mathrm{e}^{at}\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{e}^{(bt)X}]\). The deterministic shift comes outside the expectation and the scale changes the MGF argument.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A shift contributes an exponential factor to an MGF, while a scale changes its argument. Both follow from \(\mathrm{e}^{t(a+bX)}=\mathrm{e}^{at}\,\mathrm{e}^{(bt)X}\): the constant factor \(\mathrm{e}^{at}\) moves outside the expectation, and the scale \(b\) stays inside, where it multiplies \(t\).

The figure turns the standard normal \(Z\) into \(5+2Z\): the density is first spread wider by the factor \(2\) and then shifted to centre \(5\). In MGF terms, \(M_Z(t)=\mathrm{e}^{t^2/2}\) gives \(M_{5+2Z}(t)=\mathrm{e}^{5t}M_Z(2t)=\mathrm{e}^{5t+2t^2}\). This is the MGF \(\mathrm{e}^{\mu t+\sigma^2t^2/2}\) of \(\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\) with \(\mu=5\) and \(\sigma^2=4\).

Change \(a\) and \(b\): \(M_{a+bX}(t)=\mathrm{e}^{at}M_X(bt)\), and the slope at \(0\) becomes \(a+b\,\mathbb{E}X\).

The expression \(a+bX\) means scaling by \(b\) first and shifting by \(a\) second. Because the scale enters through \(M_X(bt)\), the formula holds only where \(M_X(bt)\) is finite: for \(X\sim\operatorname{Exp}(1)\), \(M_{2X}(t)=1/(1-2t)\) is finite only for \(t<\tfrac{1}{2}\). A negative \(b\) reflects the distribution, and the formula covers that case without change.

Differentiating at \(t=0\) recovers the familiar rules \(\mathbb{E}[a+bX]=a+b\,\mathbb{E}X\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(a+bX)=b^2\operatorname{Var}(X)\), as in moments from the MGF. Combined with uniqueness, the property shows that \(a+bZ\sim\mathcal{N}(a,b^2)\) for every \(b\neq0\), which is the basis of standardization.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The formula is valid where \(M_X(bt)\) is finite.
  • For \(b=0\), \(M_{a+bX}(t)=\mathrm{e}^{at}\), the MGF of the constant \(a\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(X\sim\operatorname{Bern}(p)\), \(M_{2+3X}(t)=\mathrm{e}^{2t}(1-p+p\mathrm{e}^{3t})\).
  • For \(Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)\), \(M_{5+2Z}(t)=\mathrm{e}^{5t+2t^2}\), so \(5+2Z\sim\mathcal{N}(5,4)\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
If \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent (\(X\perp Y\)), then for every \(t\) at which both MGFs are finite,

\[ \begin{aligned} M_{X+Y}(t)=M_X(t)\cdot M_Y(t). \end{aligned} \]

Independence is essential.

Use the Moment Generating Function definition to write \(M_{X+Y}(t)=\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{e}^{tX}\mathrm{e}^{tY}]\). Independence factors this expectation into the two MGFs.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Adding independent variables corresponds to multiplying their MGFs. Since an MGF that is finite near zero determines the distribution, this often identifies the distribution of a sum directly, without working out its PMF or density value by value.

The figure shows \(X\sim\operatorname{Pois}(2)\), an independent \(Y\sim\operatorname{Pois}(3)\) and their sum, which lies further right and is more spread out. Multiplying the Poisson MGFs gives \(\mathrm{e}^{2(\mathrm{e}^t-1)}\mathrm{e}^{3(\mathrm{e}^t-1)}=\mathrm{e}^{5(\mathrm{e}^t-1)}\), the MGF of \(\operatorname{Pois}(5)\), so by uniqueness the sum is \(\operatorname{Pois}(5)\).

For independent \(X\) and \(Y\) the MGF of \(X+Y\) is the product of the two curves, which identifies the distribution of the sum.

The product comes from \(\mathrm{e}^{t(X+Y)}=\mathrm{e}^{tX}\mathrm{e}^{tY}\): for independent \(X\) and \(Y\) the factors \(\mathrm{e}^{tX}\) and \(\mathrm{e}^{tY}\) are independent, and the expectation of a product of independent variables is the product of the expectations. Without independence this step fails. For \(Y=X\) with \(X\sim\operatorname{Bern}(\tfrac{1}{2})\), the sum \(2X\) has MGF \(\tfrac{1}{2}(1+\mathrm{e}^{2t})\), whereas \(M_X(t)^2=\tfrac{1}{4}(1+\mathrm{e}^t)^2\); the difference is \((\mathrm{e}^t-1)^2/4\), which is positive for every \(t\neq0\).

For i.i.d. variables the product becomes a power. Thus \(n\) independent \(\operatorname{Bern}(p)\) variables give \((1-p+p\mathrm{e}^t)^n\), the MGF of the binomial distribution, and \(r\) independent \(\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)\) variables give \((\lambda/(\lambda-t))^r\) for \(t<\lambda\), the MGF of the gamma distribution with shape \(r\) and rate \(\lambda\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For independent \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\), \(\displaystyle M_{\sum_iX_i}(t)=\prod_iM_{X_i}(t)\).
  • For i.i.d. variables, \(\displaystyle M_{\sum_iX_i}(t)=M_{X_1}(t)^n\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The sum of independent Poisson variables with parameters \(2\) and \(3\) has MGF \(\exp(5(\mathrm{e}^t-1))\), so it is \(\operatorname{Pois}(5)\).
  • The sum of two independent \(\operatorname{Exp}(1)\) variables has MGF \((1-t)^{-2}\) for \(t<1\), identifying \(\operatorname{Gamma}(2,1)\) in rate notation.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
If the MGFs of \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite and equal, \(M_X(t)=M_Y(t)\), on an open interval around \(0\), then \(X\) and \(Y\) have the same distribution.

A Moment Generating Function is the exponential expectation \(M_X(t)=\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{e}^{tX}]\). Its finiteness on a neighbourhood of zero is essential to the uniqueness conclusion; matching a finite number of derivatives is not enough.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Two MGFs that are finite and agree on an open interval around zero identify the same distribution. Once an MGF has been computed, it is therefore enough to recognize it as the MGF of a known distribution; this is how independent sums and shifted and scaled variables are identified.

The Poisson and normal laws shown both have mean \(3\) and variance \(3\), so their MGFs have the same value and the same first two derivatives at \(t=0\), where the curves touch. Away from \(0\) they separate: at \(t=1\) the \(\operatorname{Pois}(3)\) MGF is \(\mathrm{e}^{3(\mathrm{e}-1)}\approx173\) and the \(\mathcal{N}(3,3)\) MGF is \(\mathrm{e}^{4.5}\approx90\). Already the third derivatives at \(0\) differ, since \(\mathbb{E}[X^3]=57\) for the Poisson law and \(54\) for the normal law. Agreement of a few derivatives is not enough; the whole function near \(0\) must match.

Both parts of the hypothesis matter. Equality at \(t=0\) alone is automatic, since every MGF equals \(1\) there. The MGFs must also be finite near zero: for the lognormal distribution the MGF is infinite for every \(t>0\), and then the theorem gives no information.

The theorem concerns distributions only. Equal MGFs do not make the variables equal as outcomes, nor independent: for \(X\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)\), the variable \(-X\) has the same MGF \(\mathrm{e}^{t^2/2}\), yet \(-X\neq X\) whenever \(X\neq0\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Equality on an open interval containing zero is sufficient; equality only at zero is not.
  • Matching a computed MGF to a known MGF identifies the distribution under the same finiteness condition.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(M_X(t)=\exp(3(\mathrm{e}^t-1))\) near zero, then \(X\sim\operatorname{Pois}(3)\).
  • If \(M_X(t)=\mathrm{e}^{2t+9t^2/2}\) near zero, then \(X\sim\mathcal{N}(2,9)\), with variance \(9\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The moment generating function (MGF) of a random variable \(X\) is

\[ \begin{aligned} M_X(t)=\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{e}^{tX}]. \end{aligned} \]

The course assumes it is finite on a neighbourhood of \(t=0\): there is \(\delta>0\) with \(\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{e}^{tX}]<\infty\) for every \(|t|<\delta\). Finiteness only at \(t=0\), where \(M_X(0)=1\) always, is not enough for the moment and uniqueness theorems.

The Exponential Function supplies the transform \(x\mapsto \mathrm{e}^{tx}\). Applying LOTUS computes its expectation by a sum or integral against the law of \(X\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An MGF encodes a distribution through exponential averages: for each real \(t\), \(M_X(t)\) is the expectation of \(\mathrm{e}^{tX}\). One function of \(t\) then carries the whole distribution, and when it is finite near zero it can generate moments and identify distributions.

Both curves pass through \((0,1)\), since \(M_X(0)=\mathbb{E}[1]=1\) for every \(X\). The \(\operatorname{Bern}(\tfrac{1}{2})\) MGF \(\tfrac{1}{2}(1+\mathrm{e}^t)\) is finite for every \(t\), because \(X\) takes only the values \(0\) and \(1\). The exponential MGF \(1/(1-t)\) is finite only for \(t<1\) and grows without bound as \(t\) approaches \(1\): for \(t\ge1\) the factor \(\mathrm{e}^{tx}\) outweighs the density \(\mathrm{e}^{-x}\) and the integral diverges. It is finite on \((-\infty,1)\), which contains a neighbourhood of \(0\), and that is all the definition asks for.

Move \(t\) along the curve \(M_X(t)=\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{e}^{tX}]\). Every MGF passes through \((0,1)\); for \(\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)\) it is finite only for \(t<\lambda\).

The parameter \(t\) sets the weighting. For \(t>0\), \(\mathrm{e}^{tX}\) gives the largest values of \(X\) the most weight, so a heavy right tail makes \(M_X(t)\) large or infinite; for \(t<0\) the left tail matters. Finiteness at \(t=0\) alone says nothing, as \(M_X(0)=1\) always. Near \(t=0\), \(\mathrm{e}^{tX}\approx1+tX+t^2X^2/2\), which is why the derivatives at zero give the moments.

Two further rules make the MGF practical: independent sums multiply MGFs, and equal MGFs near zero mean equal distributions. Together they identify sums such as merged Poisson counts without summing over all the ways in which each total can arise.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(M_X(0)=1\).
  • Discrete variables use \(\displaystyle M_X(t)=\sum_x\mathrm{e}^{tx}p_X(x)\); density models use \(M_X(t)=\int \mathrm{e}^{tx}f_X(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\operatorname{Bern}(p)\), \(M_X(t)=1-p+p\mathrm{e}^t\).
  • For \(\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)\), \(M_X(t)=\lambda/(\lambda-t)\) for \(t<\lambda\); it is infinite for \(t\ge\lambda\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(X\) be a random variable and let \(r\ge1\) be a natural number. If \(\mathbb{E}|X|^r<\infty\), the \(r\)th moment (or raw moment, moment about the origin) of \(X\) is

\[ \mathbb{E}[X^r]. \]

Writing \(\mu=\mathbb{E}X\) for the first moment, the \(r\)th central moment (moment about the mean) is

\[ \mathbb{E}[(X-\mu)^r]. \]

If \(\mathbb{E}|X|^r=\infty\), the \(r\)th moment does not exist. Both moments are expectations of a function of \(X\), so by LOTUS they are computed from the PMF as \(\sum_x x^r p_X(x)\) or from the PDF as \(\int x^r f_X(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\), and similarly with \((x-\mu)^r\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Moments summarize a distribution through averages of powers. Raw moments are measured from \(0\); central moments are measured from the mean, so they describe the shape of the distribution around its centre and do not change when \(X\) is shifted. Higher powers give large deviations more weight, so higher moments are increasingly sensitive to the tails.

For \(X\) taking the values \(1,2,3\) with probabilities \(0.5,0.3,0.2\):

  • raw moments: \(\mathbb{E}X=1.7\), \(\mathbb{E}[X^2]=0.5+1.2+1.8=3.5\) and \(\mathbb{E}[X^3]=0.5+2.4+5.4=8.3\);
  • central moments: the deviations from \(\mu=1.7\) are \(-0.7,0.3,1.3\), so the second central moment is \(0.5(0.49)+0.3(0.09)+0.2(1.69)=0.61\) and the third is \(0.5(-0.343)+0.3(0.027)+0.2(2.197)=0.276\).

The positive third central moment reflects the long right tail: the single large deviation \(1.3\) outweighs the more likely deviation \(-0.7\) once it is cubed.

Choose the order \(r\) and measure from \(0\) or from \(\mu\). Each lower bar is one contribution \(x^r p_X(x)\) or \((x-\mu)^r p_X(x)\), and the moment is their sum. Shift every value to see that only the raw moments change.

The order of operations matters. The second moment \(\mathbb{E}[X^2]\) averages the squares, whereas \((\mathbb{E}X)^2\) squares the average; here \(3.5\) against \(1.7^2=2.89\). Their difference is the second central moment, \(3.5-2.89=0.61\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
The first moment is the expectation, and the first central moment is always \(0\). The second central moment is the variance; expanding the power and using linearity of expectation expresses central moments through raw moments:

\[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Var}(X)&=\mathbb{E}[(X-\mu)^2]\\ &=\mathbb{E}[X^2]-\mu^2,\\ \mathbb{E}[(X-\mu)^3]&=\mathbb{E}[X^3]-3\mu\,\mathbb{E}[X^2] +2\mu^3. \end{aligned} \]

The cross terms do not cancel: the third central moment is not \(\mathbb{E}[X^3]-\mu^3\). The third central moment divided by \(\sigma^3\), where \(\sigma\) is the standard deviation, is the skewness, a measure of asymmetry.

  • Since a variance is never negative, \(\mathbb{E}[X^2]\ge(\mathbb{E}X)^2\), with equality exactly when \(X\) is constant almost surely.
  • For constants \(a,b\), the \(r\)th central moment of \(a+bX\) is \(b^r\) (not \(|b|^r\)) times that of \(X\). In particular, shifting by \(a\) leaves all central moments unchanged, and the odd central moments change sign when \(b=-1\). Raw moments are not shift-invariant: \(\mathbb{E}[(a+bX)^2]=a^2+2ab\,\mathbb{E}X+b^2\,\mathbb{E}[X^2]\).
  • If the \(s\)th moment exists, so does every \(r\)th moment with \(r\le s\), because \(|x|^r\le1+|x|^s\). The converse fails: moments can fail to exist for heavy-tailed distributions even when lower moments are finite.
  • If \(X\) is bounded, say \(|X|\le c\), every moment exists and \(|\mathbb{E}[X^r]|\le c^r\).
  • For an indicator random variable \(I_A\), \(I_A^r=I_A\), so every moment equals \(\mathbb{P}(A)\).
  • If the moment generating function is finite on an open interval around \(0\), all moments exist and \(\mathbb{E}[X^n]=M_X^{(n)}(0)\) (moments from the MGF).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For a fair die, \(\mathbb{E}X=21/6=3.5\) and \(\mathbb{E}[X^2]=(1+4+9+16+25+36)/6=91/6\), so \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=91/6-49/4=35/12\).
  • For \(X\sim\operatorname{Bern}(p)\) (Bernoulli distribution), \(X^r=X\), so \(\mathbb{E}[X^r]=p\) for every \(r\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=p-p^2=p(1-p)\).
  • For \(X\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\), \(\mathbb{E}[X^r]=\int_0^1 x^r\,\mathrm{d}x=1/(r+1)\), so \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=1/3-1/4=1/12\).
  • For \(X\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)\), \(\mathbb{E}[X^n]=n!/\lambda^n\); the second central moment is \(2/\lambda^2-1/\lambda^2=1/\lambda^2\).
  • For the three-point \(X\) above and \(Y=2X+1\), \(\mathbb{E}Y=2(1.7)+1=4.4\), the second central moment of \(Y\) is \(2^2(0.61)=2.44\) and the third is \(2^3(0.276)=2.208\).
  • If \(X\) has a symmetric distribution about its mean, every odd central moment that exists is \(0\): the deviations \(X-\mu\) and \(\mu-X\) have the same distribution.
  • The density \(f(x)=2x^{-3}\) for \(x\ge1\) has finite mean \(\mathbb{E}X=\int_1^\infty 2x^{-2}\,\mathrm{d}x=2\), but \(\mathbb{E}[X^2]=\int_1^\infty 2x^{-1}\,\mathrm{d}x=\infty\), so its variance does not exist.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
If the MGF \(M_X\) is finite on an open interval containing \(0\), then all moments of \(X\) are finite and, for every nonnegative integer \(n\),

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}[X^n]=M_X^{(n)}(0), \end{aligned} \]

where \(M_X^{(n)}\) denotes the \(n\)th derivative of \(M_X\). The assumption is what justifies differentiating under the expectation.

The Moment Generating Function is an exponential expectation. Taking its Higher-Order Derivative brings down a power of \(X\) each time, and evaluating at zero leaves \(\mathbb{E}[X^n]\). The finiteness assumption justifies moving those derivatives under the expectation.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Differentiating the MGF at zero extracts the moments of the random variable one at a time: the first derivative gives \(\mathbb{E}X\), the second gives \(\mathbb{E}[X^2]\), and so on.

For \(X\sim\operatorname{Exp}(1)\), \(M_X(t)=1/(1-t)\) for \(t<1\). The tangent line \(1+t\) at \(t=0\) has slope \(M_X'(0)=\mathbb{E}X=1\), and the parabola \(1+t+t^2\), written \(1+t+\tfrac{2}{2!}t^2\) in the legend, matches the second derivative \(M_X''(0)=\mathbb{E}[X^2]=2\). Hence \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=2-1^2=1\).

The tangent at \(t=0\) has slope \(\mathbb{E}X\), and the parabola \(1+\mathbb{E}X\,t+\mathbb{E}[X^2]\,t^2/2\) hugs the curve near \(0\).

The reason is the expansion \(\mathrm{e}^{tX}=1+tX+t^2X^2/2!+\cdots\). Taking expectations term by term gives \(M_X(t)=1+\mathbb{E}[X]\,t+\mathbb{E}[X^2]\,t^2/2!+\cdots\) near \(0\), so, as for any Taylor series, \(\mathbb{E}[X^n]\) is the \(n\)th derivative at \(0\), equivalently \(n!\) times the coefficient of \(t^n\). For \(1/(1-t)=1+t+t^2+\cdots\), a geometric series for \(|t|<1\), every coefficient is \(1\), so \(\mathbb{E}[X^n]=n!\). Finiteness of \(M_X\) on an open interval around \(0\) is what justifies the term-by-term step; without it \(M_X\) may be infinite on one side of \(0\), and then its derivatives at \(0\) are not defined.

The MGF delivers raw moments; the variance and other central moments then follow, as in \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=M_X''(0)-(M_X'(0))^2\). A common slip is to forget to set \(t=0\): \(M_X'(t)\) at some \(t\neq0\) is not a moment of \(X\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{E}X=M_X'(0)\) and \(\mathbb{E}[X^2]=M_X''(0)\).
  • \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=M_X''(0)-(M_X'(0))^2\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(M_X(t)=1-p+p\mathrm{e}^t\), the first two derivatives at zero both equal \(p\), giving variance \(p-p^2\).
  • For \(M_X(t)=\lambda/(\lambda-t)\), the first two moments are \(1/\lambda\) and \(2/\lambda^2\), giving variance \(1/\lambda^2\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(n\ge0\) be an integer and \(\boldsymbol{p}=(p_1,\dots,p_k)\) with \(p_j\ge0\) and \(\displaystyle \sum_{j=1}^kp_j=1\). A random vector \(\boldsymbol{X}=(X_1,\dots,X_k)\) has a multinomial distribution, written \(\boldsymbol{X}\sim\operatorname{Mult}(n,\boldsymbol{p})\), if for all integers \(n_j\ge0\) with \(\displaystyle \sum_jn_j=n\)

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb{P}(\boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{n})=\frac{n!}{n_1!\cdots n_k!}p_1^{n_1}\cdots p_k^{n_k}, \end{aligned} \]

with \(0^0=1\) when a category probability is zero; the PMF is zero otherwise. The margins are binomial: \(X_j\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,p_j)\).

The displayed formula is the Joint Probability Mass Function of all category counts. Each single count has a Binomial Distribution, since each trial either lands in that category or does not.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A multinomial vector counts outcomes in several categories across a fixed number of independent trials. Its category counts must add to the fixed total.

The diagram uses \(n=3\) trials with category probabilities \((1/2,1/4,1/4)\). Each disc represents a count vector \((n_1,n_2,n_3)\) whose entries sum to \(3\), and its area is proportional to the probability given by the PMF above. The red disc marks \((1,1,1)\), with probability \(3/16\), calculated in the first example below. The counts are dependent because their total is fixed.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(X_j\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,p_j)\), so \(\mathbb{E}X_j=np_j\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X_j)=np_j(1-p_j)\).
  • For \(i\ne j\), \(\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j)=-np_ip_j\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(n=3\) and category probabilities \((1/2,1/4,1/4)\), \(\mathbb{P}(\boldsymbol{X}=(1,1,1))=6(1/2)(1/4)(1/4)=3/16\).
  • For \(n=10\) and probabilities \((0.2,0.3,0.5)\), \(\mathbb{E}X_1=2\) and \(\operatorname{Cov}(X_1,X_2)=-0.6\).

docs.title: Approximation
docs.text:
For \(X_n\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,p)\) with fixed \(p\in(0,1)\), as \(n\to\infty\),

\[ \begin{aligned} \frac{X_n-np}{\sqrt{np(1-p)}}\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal{N}(0,1). \end{aligned} \]

For a finite \(n\) the normal approximation can be inaccurate when \(np\) or \(n(1-p)\) is small; there is no universal finite-\(n\) accuracy guarantee.

A Binomial Distribution count is a sum of i.i.d. Bernoulli indicators. The Central Limit Theorem applied to that sum gives the stated normal limit after centring and scaling.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A binomial count with many trials is approximately normal with the same mean \(np\) and variance \(np(1-p)\). The reason is that \(\operatorname{Bin}(n,p)\) is the distribution of a sum of \(n\) i.i.d. Bernoulli indicators, so the central limit theorem applies to it.

The figure compares \(X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(100,0.2)\) with \(\mathcal{N}(20,16)\): mean \(np=20\), variance \(np(1-p)=16\), standard deviation \(4\). The highlighted tail has exact probability \(\mathbb{P}(X\ge25)\approx0.131\). With the continuity correction, the normal tail from \(24.5\) gives \(1-\Phi(1.125)\approx0.130\), while starting at \(25\) would give \(1-\Phi(1.25)\approx0.106\).

Change \(n\) and \(p\): once \(np(1-p)\) is large the bars follow the normal density with mean \(np\) and variance \(np(1-p)\).

The limit statement keeps \(p\) fixed while \(n\) grows. For a finite \(n\), the approximation is poor when \(np\) or \(n(1-p)\) is small: the binomial is then skewed and piled up near \(0\) or \(n\), while the normal curve is symmetric and puts probability below \(0\) or above \(n\). Standardizing the count gives the displayed form; dividing it by \(n\) instead gives the proportion of successes \(X/n\), a sample mean of indicators, which is approximately \(\mathcal{N}(p,p(1-p)/n)\).

A common slip is to use \(np\) as the variance, or to forget the square root in the standard deviation \(\sqrt{np(1-p)}\). In the figure the standard deviation is \(4\), not \(16\) or \(20\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For fixed \(0<p<1\), \(X_n\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,p)\) has \(\mathbb{E}X_n=np\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X_n)=np(1-p)\).
  • For a finite-\(n\) threshold \(k\), a continuity-corrected approximation is \(\mathbb{P}(X_n\le k)\approx\Phi((k+1/2-np)/\sqrt{np(1-p)})\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(100,0.5)\), \(\mathbb{P}(X\le60)\approx\Phi(2.1)\approx0.9821\).
  • For \(X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(100,0.2)\), \(\mathbb{P}(X\ge25)\approx1-\Phi((24.5-20)/4)\approx0.1303\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
If \(X\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda_1)\) and \(Y\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda_2)\) are independent, then \(X+Y\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)\). Independence is needed: Poisson marginals alone do not make the sum Poisson.

The Poisson Distribution has MGF \(\mathrm{e}^{\lambda(\mathrm{e}^t-1)}\). Multiplying the MGFs of the independent counts adds their parameters, identifying the law of the total.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Independent Poisson sources combine into a Poisson total whose parameter is the sum of the source parameters. Counting two independent streams of events together gives a count of the same kind, with the means added.

Over one time unit, the blue arrivals form a \(\operatorname{Pois}(3)\) count and the red arrivals an independent \(\operatorname{Pois}(7)\) count. Placing both on one line gives the merged count \(X+Y\sim\operatorname{Pois}(10)\); in this sample there are \(3+7=10\) arrivals. The merged line no longer records which source an arrival came from.

Two independent Poisson sources together give \(\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)\).

The proof is a short MGF computation: multiplying the MGFs gives \(\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_1(\mathrm{e}^t-1)}\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_2(\mathrm{e}^t-1)}=\mathrm{e}^{(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)(\mathrm{e}^t-1)}\), and uniqueness identifies \(\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)\). A direct check sums over the ways to split a total \(n\) into \(k\) and \(n-k\); the binomial theorem then gives

\[ \sum_{k=0}^n\frac{\lambda_1^k}{k!}\,\frac{\lambda_2^{n-k}}{(n-k)!}=\frac{(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)^n}{n!}. \]

Independence is essential. If \(X\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)\) and \(Y=X\), both counts are Poisson, but \(X+Y=2X\) takes only even values, so it is not Poisson. Merging and Poisson splitting describe the same situation from two sides: given the total \(X+Y=n\), each of the \(n\) items comes from the first source with probability \(\lambda_1/(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)\), independently, which is the binomial statement in the Key Results.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For finitely many independent Poisson variables, \(\displaystyle \sum_iX_i\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\sum_i\lambda_i)\).
  • For \(X\) and \(Y\) as in the theorem, \(X\mid X+Y=n\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,\lambda_1/(\lambda_1+\lambda_2))\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Independent arrival counts with means \(3\) and \(7\) combine to a \(\operatorname{Pois}(10)\) count.
  • Two independent counts with means \(2\) and \(4\) have total-zero probability \(\mathrm{e}^{-2}\mathrm{e}^{-4}=\mathrm{e}^{-6}\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(N\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)\), and give each of the \(N\) items a label, independently of each other and of \(N\): type 1 with probability \(p\) and type 2 with probability \(q=1-p\). Then the numbers of type-1 and type-2 items are independent, with distributions \(\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda p)\) and \(\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda q)\).

This is the Chicken–Egg Theorem applied to independently assigned labels: conditional on \(N=n\), the type-1 count is binomial, and averaging over the Poisson total gives the two independent Poisson counts.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Independent labels divide a Poisson count into independent Poisson category counts. Each category receives the share of the mean that matches its label probability, \(\lambda p\) for type 1 and \(\lambda q\) for type 2.

In the figure, \(N\sim\operatorname{Pois}(20)\) arrivals are each marked urgent with probability \(p=0.1\), independently. The urgent arrivals form a \(\operatorname{Pois}(2)\) count and the others a \(\operatorname{Pois}(18)\) count; in this sample there are \(2\) urgent and \(18\) other arrivals. By independence, knowing how many urgent arrivals occurred says nothing about the number of other arrivals.

Each item is type 1 with probability \(p\). The two counts are independent, with distributions \(\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda p)\) and \(\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda q)\); press New sample to see them vary.

This is the chicken–egg theorem phrased in terms of labels, and both of its conditions matter. The labels must be independent of each other and of \(N\). The total must also be Poisson: for a fixed total \(n\), the type-1 count is \(\operatorname{Bin}(n,p)\) and the type-2 count is \(n\) minus it, so the two are dependent, and with a random total of another distribution they are in general dependent as well.

A common misreading is that the type-1 count is binomial and therefore tied to the type-2 count. It is binomial only conditionally on \(N=n\); averaged over the Poisson total it is \(\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda p)\) and independent of the other count. Splitting reverses Poisson merging, which adds the two counts back into \(N\). For a fixed number of items, the counts of several label types follow the multinomial distribution instead, and they are dependent.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The two parameters add to the original parameter: \(\lambda p+\lambda(1-p)=\lambda\).
  • For \(k\) independent categorical labels with probabilities \(p_i\), the category counts are independent \(\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda p_i)\) variables.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A Poisson arrival count of mean \(20\), labelled urgent with probability \(0.1\), yields independent counts of means \(2\) and \(18\).
  • For mean \(12\) and label probabilities \(1/6,1/3,1/2\), the three counts are independent Poisson variables of means \(2,4,6\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For random variables \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) and \(n\ge1\), their sample mean is

\[ \bar X_n=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i. \]

The sum adds the \(n\) observations before dividing by \(n\). No independence assumption is needed to define this arithmetic average.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The sample mean summarizes \(n\) observations by their arithmetic average. Before the data are observed, \(\bar X_n\) is a random variable with its own expectation, variance and sampling distribution; the observed average \(\bar x_n\) is one realized number.

The figure marks eight observations on a number line. Their mean \(\bar x=(2.1+3.4+3.9+4.6+5.0+5.8+6.7+8.5)/8=5.0\) is the balance point: the deviations to the left and right cancel, \(\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)=0\). A single far-away observation moves the balance point; replacing \(8.5\) by \(16.5\) raises the mean by \(1\) to \(6.0\).

For independent observations with common mean \(\mu\) and finite variance \(\sigma^2\), the sample mean has its own distribution: centred at \(\mu\), with variance \(\sigma^2/n\). Raise \(n\) to see it narrow.

Two properties make \(\bar X_n\) a useful estimate of the population mean \(\mu\). It is centred correctly, \(\mathbb{E}\bar X_n=\mu\), which needs only linearity of expectation. With independent observations of common variance \(\sigma^2\), its variance \(\sigma^2/n\) shrinks, so the standard deviation \(\sigma/\sqrt n\) halves when the sample size is multiplied by four. Without independence the second property can fail: if all \(X_i\) equal \(X_1\), then \(\bar X_n=X_1\) has variance \(\sigma^2\) for every \(n\).

These two properties lead to the weak and strong law of large numbers, which say that \(\bar X_n\) approaches \(\mu\), and to the central limit theorem, which describes the shape of the remaining error. A common confusion is between \(\bar X_n\) and \(\mu\): the sample mean is computed from data and varies from sample to sample, while \(\mu\) is a fixed property of the distribution.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If every \(X_i\) has mean \(\mu\), then \(\mathbb{E}\bar X_n=\mu\) without independence.
  • If the observations are independent with common variance \(\sigma^2\), then \(\operatorname{Var}(\bar X_n)=\sigma^2/n\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For observations \(2,4,9\), the observed sample mean is \((2+4+9)/3=5\).
  • For \(100\) i.i.d. \(\operatorname{Exp}(2)\) observations, the sample mean has expectation \(1/2\) and variance \(1/(4\cdot100)=1/400\).

docs.title: Further Properties
docs.text: For realized observations \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), the observed average is \(\displaystyle \bar x_n=n^{-1}\sum_i x_i\). A sample proportion is the sample mean of success indicators.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(X_1,X_2,\ldots\) be i.i.d. with \(\mathbb{E}|X_1|<\infty\) and mean \(\mu=\mathbb{E}X_1\). Then the sample mean \(\displaystyle \bar X_n=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\) satisfies

\[ \begin{aligned} \bar X_n\xrightarrow{a.s.}\mu. \end{aligned} \]

The i.i.d. assumption gives one common integrable law and independence. The conclusion is Almost-Sure Convergence: outside one probability-zero exceptional set, the entire sequence of sample averages tends to \(\mu\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The running average of an integrable i.i.d. sequence settles at the population mean with probability one. Fix one outcome and follow the whole sequence of averages \(\bar X_1,\bar X_2,\ldots\): for almost every outcome this sequence of numbers converges to \(\mu\).

The figure shows three simulated sequences of fair die rolls, so \(\mu=3.5\). Each line is one sample path \(n\mapsto\bar X_n\). Early on the paths wander, because a single roll still moves the average noticeably: after the first roll the three averages are \(1\), \(3\) and \(4\). After a few hundred rolls each path stays close to \(3.5\). The strong law says that on almost every path the average does not only come close but converges to \(3.5\).

Each path is one sequence of draws. Almost every path eventually enters the band \(\mu\pm\varepsilon\) and stays there; show more steps or narrow the band to test it.

The hypotheses are an i.i.d. sequence and \(\mathbb{E}|X_1|<\infty\); finite variance is not needed, as the second Example shows. Independence cannot simply be dropped: if every \(X_i\) equals the first die roll \(X_1\), the variables are identically distributed but \(\bar X_n=X_1\) for every \(n\), which never approaches \(3.5\). Without a finite mean there is no \(\mu\) to converge to.

Almost-sure convergence implies convergence in probability, so the strong law implies the weak law. Applied to indicators \(\indicator_A\) of independent repetitions of an experiment, it says that the relative frequency of \(A\) converges to \(\mathbb{P}(A)\) almost surely. This justifies reading probabilities as long-run frequencies.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Finite \(\mathbb{E}|X_1|\) is sufficient; finite variance is not required.
  • The almost-sure conclusion also implies \(\bar X_n\xrightarrow{P}\mu\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For i.i.d. fair die rolls, the running average converges almost surely to \(3.5\).
  • For i.i.d. variables with density \(f(x)=\frac{3}{2}x^{-5/2}\) for \(x\ge1\) and zero elsewhere, the mean is \(3\) and the second moment is infinite; the running average still converges almost surely to \(3\).

docs.title: Sum of Two IID Uniform Variables
Proposition
docs.text:
If \(X,Y\) are independent \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) variables, then \(S=X+Y\) has density

\[ f_S(s)=\begin{cases}s,&0<s\le1,\\2-s,&1<s<2,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} \]

The density peaks at \(s=1\).

Each Uniform Distribution on \((0,1)\) has density one there. The Convolution of Independent Random Variables integral reduces to the length of the overlap between \((0,1)\) and \((s-1,s)\), producing \(s\) for \(0<s\le1\) and \(2-s\) for \(1<s<2\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Two independent uniform values have more ways to add up near the centre than near either endpoint. Their sum therefore has a triangular density on \((0,2)\) with its peak at \(1\).

The red triangle on \((0,1/2]\) has base \(1/2\) and height \(1/2\), so \(\mathbb{P}(S\le1/2)=1/8\); by symmetry the right tail has the same probability, and the middle part from \(1/2\) to \(3/2\) carries the remaining \(3/4\), as in the Examples.

Move \(s\): \(f_S(s)\) is the length of the overlap of \((0,1)\) and \((s-1,s)\), which grows to \(1\) at \(s=1\) and then shrinks.

The result can also be read in the unit square, where the pair \((X,Y)\) is uniform. The event \(\{S\le s\}\) is the part of the square below the line \(x+y=s\); for \(0<s\le1\) it is a triangle of area \(s^2/2\), which is the CDF, and its derivative \(s\) is the density. The density is symmetric about \(1\) because \((1-X)+(1-Y)=2-S\) has the same distribution as \(S\). Mean and variance follow without the density: \(\mathbb{E}S=1/2+1/2=1\), and by independence \(\operatorname{Var}(S)=1/12+1/12=1/6\).

This is the continuous counterpart of the triangular distribution of the sum of two dice, which peaks at \(7\). Adding more independent uniforms makes the shape smoother and more bell-shaped, an effect that returns later as the central limit theorem.

The sum of two uniforms is not uniform on \((0,2)\): that would give \(\mathbb{P}(S\le1/2)=1/4\), twice the correct value \(1/8\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{E}(X+Y)=1\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X+Y)=1/6\).
  • The CDF is \(s^2/2\) on \(0<s\le1\) and \(1-(2-s)^2/2\) on \(1<s<2\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a random variable \(X\) with CDF \(F\), the survivor function is

\[ \begin{aligned} \overline{F}(x) = 1 - F(x) = \mathbb{P}(X > x). \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The survivor function gives the probability of exceeding a threshold. For a lifetime or a waiting time \(X\), \(\overline F(x)\) is the probability of still waiting, or still working, at time \(x\); it is useful for reliability and tail probabilities.

The illustrated \(\operatorname{Exp}(1)\) distribution has survivor function \(\overline F(x)=\mathrm{e}^{-x}\) for \(x\ge0\). At \(x=1\) the two curves take the values \(F(1)\approx0.63\) and \(\overline F(1)\approx0.37\), which add up to \(1\), as they do at every \(x\). For rate \(\lambda>0\), the survivor function becomes \(\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda x}\).

Move \(x\): \(\overline F(x)=\mathbb{P}(X>x)\) is the shaded tail. For a discrete variable the strict inequality matters at the jumps.

Many waiting-time facts are simplest in terms of the tail. The memoryless property of the exponential distribution reads \(\overline F(s+t)=\overline F(s)\overline F(t)\), and for independent variables the minimum exceeds \(x\) exactly when every variable does, so its survivor function is the product of theirs, as for the minimum of independent exponentials.

The inequality is strict: \(\overline F(x)=\mathbb{P}(X>x)\). For continuous variables this equals \(\mathbb{P}(X\ge x)\), but for discrete variables the two differ by \(\mathbb{P}(X=x)\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\overline{F}(x)=1-F(x)\) is nonincreasing and right-continuous.
  • For a discrete variable, \(\mathbb{P}(X\ge x)=1-F(x-)\), which can differ from \(\overline{F}(x)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\operatorname{Exp}(3)\), \(\overline{F}(2)=\mathrm{e}^{-6}\).
  • For \(\operatorname{Bern}(0.4)\), \(\mathbb{P}(X>0)=0.4\) but \(\mathbb{P}(X\ge0)=1\).

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
Let \(h\) be a Borel-measurable function, and let \(Y\) and \(h(X)Y\) be integrable (for example, \(h\) bounded). Then, almost surely,

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}[h(X)\,Y\mid X]=h(X)\,\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]. \end{aligned} \]

Inside the Conditional Expectation Given a Random Variable, fixing \(X=x\) fixes \(h(X)=h(x)\). It therefore acts as a constant in the conditional sum or integral, subject to the stated integrability assumptions.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Once \(X\) is observed, any function \(h(X)\) of it is a known number, so it acts as a constant inside the conditional average. The rule is the conditional version of \(\mathbb{E}[cY]=c\,\mathbb{E}Y\).

In the illustrated example, \(Y\mid X\sim\operatorname{Pois}(X)\), so the blue line is \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x]=x\), and \(h(x)=x\). At \(x=2\) the blue value \(2\) is multiplied by the known factor \(h(2)=2\) to give the red value \(4\) of \(\mathbb{E}[XY\mid X=x]=x^2\). In general \(\mathbb{E}[h(X)Y\mid X]=h(X)\,\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]\); here \(\mathbb{E}[XY\mid X]=X\cdot X=X^2\).

At a fixed value \(x\), the rule is ordinary linearity of expectation with the constant \(h(x)\); substituting the random \(X\) afterwards gives the stated identity. The integrability assumptions make both sides well defined, which is automatic when \(h\) is bounded.

Combined with Adam’s law, the rule gives \(\mathbb{E}[h(X)Y]=\mathbb{E}[h(X)\,\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]]\), a standard way to compute mixed moments in two-stage models. In the Poisson example, \(\mathbb{E}[XY]=\mathbb{E}[X^2]\), so \(\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\mathbb{E}[X^2]-(\mathbb{E}X)^2=\operatorname{Var}(X)\). The same step shows that independence implies zero covariance, see conditional expectation and independence.

Only functions of the conditioning variable come out. A function of \(Y\) is not known given \(X\): \(\mathbb{E}[Y^2\mid X]\) is in general not \((\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X])^2\), and in the Poisson example it equals \(X+X^2\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{E}[h(X)\mid X]=h(X)\) when \(h(X)\) is integrable.
  • Combining the rule with Adam’s law gives \(\mathbb{E}[h(X)Y]=\mathbb{E}[h(X)\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]]\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(Y\mid X\sim\operatorname{Pois}(X)\) and \(\mathbb{E}[X^2]<\infty\), then \(\mathbb{E}[XY\mid X]=X^2\).
  • If \(A=\{X>0\}\), then \(\mathbb{E}[\indicator_AY\mid X]=\indicator_A\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(C\) be an event with \(\mathbb{P}(C)>0\) and \(\{B_i\}\) a finite or countable partition, and write \(\mathbb{P}(A\mid B_i,C)\) for \(\mathbb{P}(A\mid B_i\cap C)\). Then, omitting the terms with \(\mathbb{P}(B_i\cap C)=0\),

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb{P}(A\mid C)=\sum_i\mathbb{P}(A\mid B_i,C)\,\mathbb{P}(B_i\mid C). \end{aligned} \]

Analogous versions hold for expectations, PMFs, and PDFs.

Apply the Law of Total Probability within the probability law conditional on \(C\). Its case weights are \(\mathbb{P}(B_i\mid C)\) rather than the unconditional weights.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Case-by-case probability calculations remain valid after some background information \(C\) is fixed. Conditioning on \(C\) gives a new probability function \(\mathbb{P}(\,\cdot\mid C)\), and the ordinary law of total probability holds for it as for any other.

The tree in the figure lies entirely inside the box "given \(C\)". The first branches carry the case weights \(\mathbb{P}(B_1\mid C)=0.7\) and \(\mathbb{P}(B_2\mid C)=0.3\), the second branches the delay probabilities \(\mathbb{P}(A\mid B_1,C)=0.2\) and \(\mathbb{P}(A\mid B_2,C)=0.5\). Multiplying along the two delay paths gives \(0.14\) and \(0.15\), and adding them gives \(\mathbb{P}(A\mid C)=0.29\), as in the first Example.

Both factors in each term must carry \(C\). The weights \(\mathbb{P}(B_i\mid C)\) can differ from the unconditional \(\mathbb{P}(B_i)\): on rainy days a traveller may choose route \(B_1\) more often than usual. Likewise \(\mathbb{P}(A\mid B_i,C)\) is the delay probability on that route on a rainy day, not on an average day. Mixing the two, as in \(\sum_i\mathbb{P}(A\mid B_i,C)\,\mathbb{P}(B_i)\), is the typical slip; it is a valid rule only when every \(B_i\) is independent of \(C\), so that \(\mathbb{P}(B_i\mid C)=\mathbb{P}(B_i)\).

The same pattern extends to the other conditioning rules: Bayes' rule with \(C\) added to every term reads \(\mathbb{P}(B_i\mid A,C)=\mathbb{P}(A\mid B_i,C)\,\mathbb{P}(B_i\mid C)/\mathbb{P}(A\mid C)\), and the version for expectations is Adam's law with extra conditioning.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{P}(B_i\mid C)=\mathbb{P}(B_i\cap C)/\mathbb{P}(C)\).
  • Only cases with \(\mathbb{P}(B_i\cap C)>0\) need conditional probabilities \(\mathbb{P}(A\mid B_i\cap C)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Within known rainy days \(C\), suppose \(\mathbb{P}(B_1\mid C)=0.7\), with delay probabilities \(0.2\) and \(0.5\) in the two routes. Then \(\mathbb{P}(A\mid C)=0.7(0.2)+0.3(0.5)=0.29\).
  • For a fair die conditioned to be even, partition into \(B_1=\{X\le3\}\) and \(B_2=\{X>3\}\). Then \(\mathbb{P}(X=6\mid C)=0(1/3)+(1/2)(2/3)=1/3\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(X_1,X_2,\ldots\) be independent and identically distributed, with \(\mathbb{E}|X_1|<\infty\) and mean \(\mu\). Then their sample mean satisfies

\[ \bar X_n=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\xrightarrow{P}\mu. \]

Probability Distributions uses the sufficient finite-variance case \(\operatorname{Var}(X_1)=\sigma^2<\infty\), which admits the explicit Chebyshev proof below. Finite variance is not required for the more general integrable i.i.d. statement.

The conclusion is Convergence in Probability, so it asks whether each fixed-tolerance error probability tends to zero. In the finite-variance case, Chebyshev Inequality bounds that probability by \(\sigma^2/(n\varepsilon^2)\), which does tend to zero.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
For a large i.i.d. sample with a finite mean, the sample mean is close to the population mean with high probability: for every fixed tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), \(\mathbb{P}(|\bar X_n-\mu|>\varepsilon)\to0\). Finite variance additionally supplies a quantitative bound through the Chebyshev inequality.

The figure shows the distribution of \(\bar X_n\) for \(n=1\), \(4\) and \(16\) with \(\sigma=1\). Since \(\operatorname{Var}(\bar X_n)=\sigma^2/n\), the standard deviation \(\sigma/\sqrt n\) halves each time \(n\) is multiplied by four: \(1\), \(\tfrac{1}{2}\), \(\tfrac{1}{4}\). The probability outside the band \(\mu\pm\varepsilon\) therefore shrinks, and by Chebyshev it is at most \(\sigma^2/(n\varepsilon^2)\to0\).

For a fixed \(\varepsilon\), \(\mathbb{P}(|\bar X_n-\mu|>\varepsilon)\) (right) falls to \(0\) as \(n\) grows, always below the Chebyshev bound \(\sigma^2/(n\varepsilon^2)\) used in the proof.

The finite-variance proof uses two facts: \(\mathbb{E}\bar X_n=\mu\) by linearity of expectation, and \(\operatorname{Var}(\bar X_n)=\sigma^2/n\), because variances of independent terms add. Independence matters: if every \(X_i\) equals \(X_1\), then \(\bar X_n=X_1\) and its spread never shrinks. The bound also shows how the sample size must grow when the tolerance shrinks: halving \(\varepsilon\) requires four times as many observations for the same bound.

A common misreading is that the sum \(S_n=n\bar X_n\) gets close to \(n\mu\). It does not: \(S_n-n\mu\) has standard deviation \(\sigma\sqrt n\), which grows. Only the average is pinned down. The central limit theorem describes the size and shape of the remaining error \(\bar X_n-\mu\) on the scale \(\sigma/\sqrt n\), and the strong law strengthens the conclusion to almost-sure convergence.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\operatorname{Var}(\bar X_n)=\sigma^2/n\).
  • Chebyshev gives \(\mathbb{P}(|\bar X_n-\mu|\ge\varepsilon)\le\sigma^2/(n\varepsilon^2)\to0\) for each \(\varepsilon>0\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For i.i.d. \(\operatorname{Bern}(0.4)\) variables, the proportion of successes converges in probability to \(0.4\).
  • For i.i.d. \(\operatorname{Exp}(2)\) variables and \(n=1000\), the probability that the sample mean differs from \(0.5\) by at least \(0.1\) is at most \(0.25/(1000(0.1)^2)=0.025\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(V\) be a real vector space, \(W\subseteq V\) a subspace and \(\boldsymbol{v}\in V\). The set

\[ \{\boldsymbol{v}\}+W=\{\boldsymbol{v}+\boldsymbol{w}\colon\boldsymbol{w}\in W\} \]

is an affine subspace of \(V\). The subspace \(W\) is its direction space, and the dimension of the affine subspace is defined as \(\dim W\). Some texts also count the empty set as affine; here an affine subspace is always nonempty.

Equivalently, a nonempty set \(S\subseteq V\) is affine if and only if it contains every affine combination of its points: \(\lambda\boldsymbol{x}+(1-\lambda)\boldsymbol{y}\in S\) for all \(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}\in S\) and all \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An affine subspace is a subspace shifted away from the origin: a point, a line, a plane or a higher-dimensional flat that need not pass through \(\boldsymbol{0}\). It is "flat" because the whole line through any two of its points stays inside it.

The figure draws the line from the second example. The dashed red line is the direction space \(W=\operatorname{span}\{(2,1)^{\top}\}\) through \(\boldsymbol{0}\); the blue line is \(\{\boldsymbol{v}\}+W\) with \(\boldsymbol{v}=(1,2)^{\top}\), the same line shifted off the origin. It contains \((1,2)^{\top}\) and \((3,3)^{\top}\), and also the affine combination \(2(1,2)^{\top}-(3,3)^{\top}=(-1,1)^{\top}\) with \(\lambda=2\), which lies outside the segment between them. Since \(\boldsymbol{0}\) is not on the blue line, \(\{\boldsymbol{v}\}+W\) is not a subspace.

The condition \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\) matters. Requiring only \(\lambda\in[0,1]\) gives a convex set, so a line segment is convex but not affine.

The most common source of affine subspaces is linear systems. A consistent system of linear equations \(A\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{b}\) with \(\boldsymbol{b}\neq\boldsymbol{0}\) has a solution set that is not a subspace (it misses \(\boldsymbol{0}\)), yet it is one particular solution plus the kernel \(\operatorname{Null}(A)\). Affine subspaces are exactly the nonempty level sets of affine maps.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The direction space is unique: \(W=\{\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{y}\colon\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}\in S\}\). The base point is not unique: \(\{\boldsymbol{v}\}+W=\{\boldsymbol{v}'\}+W\) if and only if \(\boldsymbol{v}-\boldsymbol{v}'\in W\).
  • An affine subspace \(\{\boldsymbol{v}\}+W\) is a linear subspace if and only if \(\boldsymbol{0}\in\{\boldsymbol{v}\}+W\), that is, if and only if \(\boldsymbol{v}\in W\).
  • If \(A\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{b}\) is consistent and \(\boldsymbol{x}_p\) is any solution, its solution set is \(\{\boldsymbol{x}_p\}+\operatorname{Null}(A)\), of dimension \(n-\operatorname{rank}A\) for an \(m\times n\) matrix \(A\).
  • A nonempty intersection of affine subspaces is affine; the image of an affine subspace under a linear map is affine.
  • In \(\mathbb{R}^n\) the affine subspaces of dimension \(n-1\) are the hyperplanes \(\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}=c\}\) with \(\boldsymbol{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
A plane in \(\mathbb{R}^3\). The solution set of \(x_1+x_2+x_3=1\) contains \(\boldsymbol{x}_p=(1,0,0)^{\top}\). The direction space is the null space of \(\begin{pmatrix}1&1&1\end{pmatrix}\), spanned by \((-1,1,0)^{\top}\) and \((-1,0,1)^{\top}\). Hence

\[ S=\{(1,0,0)^{\top}\} +\operatorname{span}\{(-1,1,0)^{\top},(-1,0,1)^{\top}\}, \]

an affine subspace of dimension \(2\). It is not a subspace, since \(0+0+0\neq1\).

A line in \(\mathbb{R}^2\). The line through \((1,2)^{\top}\) and \((3,3)^{\top}\) is \(\{(1,2)^{\top}\}+\operatorname{span}\{(2,1)^{\top}\}\). The affine combination with \(\lambda=2\), \(2(1,2)^{\top}-(3,3)^{\top}=(-1,1)^{\top}\), is the point with parameter \(t=-1\), so it lies on the line, as it must.

Non-examples. The union of two distinct lines through \(\boldsymbol{0}\) and the unit circle are not affine: in each case the line through two suitable points leaves the set.

docs.title: Basis of Solutions of a Difference Equation
Definition
docs.text:
Consider the homogeneous linear difference equation of order \(k\) with constant coefficients and \(a_0\ne0\),

\[ x_{t+k}+a_{k-1}x_{t+k-1}+\cdots+a_0x_t=0. \]

Its solutions form a subspace \(S\) of the vector space of real sequences. A basis of solutions (fundamental set) is a list of solutions \(y^{(1)},\ldots,y^{(k)}\) that is a basis of \(S\): the sequences are linearly independent, and every solution can be written uniquely as

\[ x_t=c_1y^{(1)}_t+\cdots+c_ky^{(k)}_t. \]

This expression with arbitrary constants \(c_1,\ldots,c_k\) is the general solution.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Linearity makes sums and scalar multiples of solutions again solutions, so the solution set is a vector space. Its dimension is \(k\) because a solution is fixed by its \(k\) initial values: the map \(x\mapsto(x_0,\ldots,x_{k-1})\) is a linear bijection from \(S\) onto \(\mathbb{R}^k\). A basis therefore gives coordinates \((c_1,\ldots,c_k)\) for every possible trajectory, and fitting initial values means solving a \(k\times k\) linear system.

The figure uses the first example, \(x_{t+2}-3x_{t+1}+2x_t=0\). Its basis solutions are the constant sequence \(y^{(1)}_t=1\) and \(y^{(2)}_t=2^t\). The initial values \(x_0=5\), \(x_1=7\) fix the coordinates \(c_1=3\), \(c_2=2\), and the green trajectory \(x_t=3y^{(1)}_t+2y^{(2)}_t=3+2^{t+1}\) follows: \(5,7,11,19\). Other initial values give other coordinates for the same two basis sequences.

Change \(x_0\) and \(x_1\): every solution of \(x_{t+2}-3x_{t+1}+2x_t=0\) is a combination \(c_1\cdot1+c_2\cdot2^t\) of the two basis solutions, and the two initial values fix the coefficients uniquely.

The standard basis comes from the characteristic polynomial. A common error is to take fewer than \(k\) sequences, for example only \(r^t\) for a double root \(r\); the list then spans a proper subspace and cannot match all initial values. Another is to take \(k\) sequences that are multiples of each other, such as \(2^t\) and \(3\cdot2^t\), which are dependent.

The inhomogeneous equation has no basis of solutions: its solution set is the affine subspace "particular solution \(+\,S\)".

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\dim S=k\); any \(k\) linearly independent solutions form a basis.
  • \(k\) solutions form a basis if and only if their vectors of initial values \(\big(y^{(j)}_0,\ldots,y^{(j)}_{k-1}\big)\), \(j=1,\ldots,k\), are linearly independent, that is, the \(k\times k\) matrix with these vectors as columns has nonzero determinant.
  • If the roots \(r_1,\ldots,r_k\) are distinct, \(r_1^t,\ldots,r_k^t\) is a basis (the matrix of initial values is a Vandermonde matrix).
  • A root \(r\) of multiplicity \(m\) contributes \(r^t,tr^t,\ldots,t^{m-1}r^t\); a nonreal pair \(\rho \mathrm{e}^{\pm\mathrm{i}\theta}\) may be replaced by \(\rho^t\cos(\theta t),\ \rho^t\sin(\theta t)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Fitting initial values. For \(x_{t+2}-3x_{t+1}+2x_t=0\) the roots are \(1\) and \(2\), so \(y^{(1)}_t=1\), \(y^{(2)}_t=2^t\), and the matrix of initial values has \(\det\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}=1\ne0\). For \(x_0=5\), \(x_1=7\): \(c_1+c_2=5\), \(c_1+2c_2=7\), so \(c_2=2\), \(c_1=3\) and \(x_t=3+2^{t+1}\). Check: \(x_2=11=3\cdot7-2\cdot5\).

Repeated root. For \(x_{t+2}-4x_{t+1}+4x_t=0\) take \(2^t\) and \(t\,2^t\). Their matrix of initial values has \(\det\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\2&2\end{pmatrix}=2\ne0\), so they form a basis.

Not a basis. \(2^t\) and \(3\cdot2^t\) both solve the previous equation, but \(\det\begin{pmatrix}1&3\\2&6\end{pmatrix}=0\): they are dependent and cannot produce the solution with \(x_0=0\), \(x_1=1\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\mathcal{F}=(\boldsymbol{f}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{f}_n)\) be an ordered basis of \(\mathbb{R}^n\), the new basis, and let \(\boldsymbol{e}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{e}_n\) be the standard basis. The transformation matrix of \(\mathcal{F}\) is the \(n\times n\) matrix whose columns are the new basis vectors,

\[ F=\begin{pmatrix}\boldsymbol{f}_1&\cdots&\boldsymbol{f}_n\end{pmatrix}. \]

\(F\) transforms the standard basis into the new basis, \(F\boldsymbol{e}_i=\boldsymbol{f}_i\), and \(F^{-1}\) transforms it back. It is invertible because its columns form a basis.

The coordinate vector of \(\boldsymbol{x}\) with respect to \(\mathcal{F}\) is the vector \(\boldsymbol{y}=[\boldsymbol{x}]_{\mathcal{F}}\) of the unique scalars with \(\boldsymbol{x}=y_1\boldsymbol{f}_1+\cdots+y_n\boldsymbol{f}_n\). In matrix form,

\[ \boldsymbol{x}=F\boldsymbol{y},\qquad \boldsymbol{y}=F^{-1}\boldsymbol{x}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The vector \(\boldsymbol{x}\) does not move; only its description changes. The columns of \(F\) say where the new basis vectors are, so multiplying new coordinates by \(F\) rebuilds the vector in standard coordinates, and \(F^{-1}\) finds the new coordinates of a vector given in standard coordinates.

The figure shows the first example. The green arrow \(\boldsymbol{x}=(3,1)^{\top}\) is one fixed vector. Along the standard axes it is \(3\boldsymbol{e}_1+\boldsymbol{e}_2\); along the tilted grid of \(\mathcal{F}\) it is \(2\boldsymbol{f}_1+\boldsymbol{f}_2\). Changing basis only changes which grid the vector is read on, so its coordinates change from \((3,1)^{\top}\) to \([\boldsymbol{x}]_{\mathcal{F}}=F^{-1}\boldsymbol{x}=(2,1)^{\top}\).

Drag \(\boldsymbol{x}\), \(\boldsymbol{f}_1\) or \(\boldsymbol{f}_2\): the arrow stays the same while its description changes, from \((3,1)^{\top}\) in the standard basis to \([\boldsymbol{x}]_{\mathcal{F}}=F^{-1}\boldsymbol{x}=(2,1)^{\top}\) along the grid of \(\mathcal{F}\). Switch on the operator \(A\) to follow \(A\boldsymbol{x}\) as well.

The direction is the usual source of errors. \(F\) takes the standard basis vectors to the new ones, but on coordinates it works the other way round: it turns new coordinates \(\boldsymbol{y}\) into standard coordinates \(\boldsymbol{x}=F\boldsymbol{y}\). Going from standard to new coordinates needs the inverse \(F^{-1}\). Other textbooks call such a matrix a change-of-basis or transition matrix and may attach it to either direction, so check which direction is meant.

Changing basis also changes the matrix representation of a linear map. For an operator on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) the result is a similarity transformation; choosing an eigenbasis makes the matrix diagonal.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every invertible \(n\times n\) matrix is the transformation matrix of the basis formed by its columns.
  • If \(A\) is the matrix of a linear operator in standard coordinates, its matrix in the new basis is \([A]_{\mathcal{F}}=F^{-1}AF\): translate new coordinates to standard ones with \(F\), apply \(A\), translate back with \(F^{-1}\).
  • Between two new bases \(\mathcal{F}\) and \(\mathcal{G}\) with transformation matrices \(F\) and \(G\): \([\boldsymbol{x}]_{\mathcal{G}}=G^{-1}F[\boldsymbol{x}]_{\mathcal{F}}\).
  • If \(\mathcal{F}\) is orthonormal, then \(F^{-1}=F^{\top}\) and \(y_i=\boldsymbol{f}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Coordinates. In \(\mathbb{R}^2\) let \(\boldsymbol{f}_1=(1,1)^{\top}\) and \(\boldsymbol{f}_2=(1,-1)^{\top}\), so

\[ F=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad F^{-1}=\tfrac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}. \]

For \(\boldsymbol{x}=(3,1)^{\top}\),

\[ [\boldsymbol{x}]_{\mathcal{F}}=F^{-1}\boldsymbol{x}=\tfrac{1}{2}(4,2)^{\top}=(2,1)^{\top}, \]

and indeed \(2(1,1)^{\top}+1(1,-1)^{\top}=(3,1)^{\top}\).

An operator. Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}\) in standard coordinates. Then \(AF=\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\3&-1\end{pmatrix}\) and

\[ [A]_{\mathcal{F}}=F^{-1}AF =\tfrac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}6&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}. \]

In the new basis the map stretches the first coordinate by \(3\) and leaves the second alone: \(\mathcal{F}\) is an eigenbasis, and this is a diagonalization of \(A\).

docs.title: Characteristic Equation for a Differential Equation
Definition
docs.text:
Consider the homogeneous linear differential equation with constant real coefficients

\[ x^{(n)}(t)+a_{n-1}x^{(n-1)}(t)+\dots +a_1x'(t)+a_0x(t)=0, \]

where \(x'(t)=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}(t)\) and \(x^{(k)}\) is the \(k\)-th derivative. Its characteristic polynomial is

\[ p(r)=r^n+a_{n-1}r^{n-1}+\dots+a_1r+a_0, \]

and \(p(r)=0\) is its characteristic equation. The equation is obtained by substituting the trial solution \(x(t)=\mathrm{e}^{rt}\): since \(\frac{\mathrm{d}^k}{\mathrm{d}t^k}\mathrm{e}^{rt}=r^k\mathrm{e}^{rt}\), the left-hand side becomes \(p(r)\mathrm{e}^{rt}\), which vanishes for all \(t\) if and only if \(p(r)=0\). For a second-order differential equation \(x''+ax'+bx=0\) the characteristic equation is \(r^2+ar+b=0\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The substitution turns a differential equation into an algebraic one: each root of the polynomial \(p\) gives an exponential "mode" \(\mathrm{e}^{rt}\) of the exponential function. Writing the equation as a first-order system with a companion matrix, \(p\) is exactly the characteristic polynomial of that matrix, so the roots are its eigenvalues.

The figure follows the complex-roots example \(x''+2x'+5x=0\). Its characteristic equation \(r^2+2r+5=0\) has the roots \(r=-1\pm2\mathrm{i}\), marked on the left in the complex plane. Through \(\mathrm{e}^{rt}\) and Euler's formula they give the real mode \(\mathrm{e}^{-t}\cos2t\) on the right: the real part \(-1\) fixes the shrinking envelope \(\pm \mathrm{e}^{-t}\), and the imaginary part \(2\) fixes how fast the solution oscillates inside it.

Move \(a\) and \(b\) across \(a^2=4b\): two real roots give two exponentials, a repeated root needs the extra factor \(t\), and a complex pair \(\alpha\pm\mathrm{i}\beta\) gives \(e^{\alpha t}(c_1\cos\beta t+c_2\sin\beta t)\).

The discrete-time analogue is the characteristic polynomial for a difference equation, where the trial solution is \(\lambda^t\) instead of \(\mathrm{e}^{rt}\). The two are linked by \(\lambda=\mathrm{e}^{r}\): sampling \(\mathrm{e}^{rt}\) at integer times gives \((\mathrm{e}^{r})^t\).

Common errors: forgetting that a repeated root needs the extra factor \(t\); writing \(\mathrm{e}^{(\alpha\pm\mathrm{i}\beta)t}\) as the final real answer instead of converting it with Euler's formula; and applying the method to equations with non-constant coefficients, where \(\mathrm{e}^{rt}\) is generally not a solution.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• By the fundamental theorem of algebra, \(p\) has \(n\) complex roots counted with multiplicity.
  • A real root \(r\) of multiplicity \(m\) gives the \(m\) solutions \(\mathrm{e}^{rt},\,t\mathrm{e}^{rt},\,\dots,\,t^{m-1}\mathrm{e}^{rt}\).
  • Since the coefficients are real, nonreal roots come in pairs \(\alpha\pm\mathrm{i}\beta\) (\(\beta\neq0\)) by the complex conjugate root theorem. Each pair gives the real solutions \(\mathrm{e}^{\alpha t}\cos\beta t\) and \(\mathrm{e}^{\alpha t}\sin\beta t\), because \(\mathrm{e}^{(\alpha+\mathrm{i}\beta)t}=\mathrm{e}^{\alpha t}(\cos\beta t+\mathrm{i}\sin\beta t)\); a pair of multiplicity \(m\) gives these two functions multiplied by \(1,t,\dots,t^{m-1}\).
  • The \(n\) functions obtained this way form a basis of the solution space, so the general solution is their linear combination.
  • For \(n=2\), \(r^2+ar+b=0\) has discriminant \(a^2-4b\): positive gives two real roots, zero a double root \(-a/2\), negative a complex pair \(-\frac{a}{2}\pm\mathrm{i}\frac{\sqrt{4b-a^2}}{2}\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Distinct real roots. \(x''-x'-6x=0\): \(r^2-r-6=(r-3)(r+2)\), so \(x(t)=c_1\mathrm{e}^{3t}+c_2\mathrm{e}^{-2t}\).

Complex roots. \(x''+2x'+5x=0\): \(r=\frac{-2\pm\sqrt{4-20}}{2}=-1\pm2\mathrm{i}\), so \(x(t)=\mathrm{e}^{-t}(c_1\cos2t+c_2\sin2t)\), a damped oscillation.

Double root, checked. \(x''+2x'+x=0\): \((r+1)^2=0\). For \(x=t\mathrm{e}^{-t}\): \(x'=(1-t)\mathrm{e}^{-t}\), \(x''=(t-2)\mathrm{e}^{-t}\), and \(x''+2x'+x=(t-2+2-2t+t)\mathrm{e}^{-t}=0\).

Triple root. \(x'''-3x''+3x'-x=0\): \(r^3-3r^2+3r-1=(r-1)^3\), so \(x(t)=(c_1+c_2t+c_3t^2)\mathrm{e}^{t}\).

docs.title: Characteristic Polynomial for a Difference Equation
Definition
docs.text:
For the homogeneous linear difference equation of order \(k\) with constant coefficients and \(a_0\ne0\),

\[ x_{t+k}+a_{k-1}x_{t+k-1}+\cdots +a_1x_{t+1}+a_0x_t=0, \]

the characteristic polynomial is

\[ p(r)=r^k+a_{k-1}r^{k-1}+\cdots+a_1r+a_0, \]

and \(p(r)=0\) is the characteristic equation. Its roots \(r_1,\ldots,r_k\) (real or complex, counted with multiplicity) are the characteristic roots.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Substituting the trial solution \(x_t=r^t\) with \(r\ne0\) gives \(r^t\,p(r)=0\). So the geometric sequence \(r^t\) solves the equation exactly when \(r\) is a characteristic root, and the problem of solving a recurrence reduces to finding the roots of one polynomial.

The figure takes the complex-roots example \(x_{t+2}-x_{t+1}+x_t=0\). The roots of \(p(r)=r^2-r+1\) lie on the unit circle at the angles \(\pm\pi/3\) (left). Because \(|r|=1\) the solutions neither grow nor shrink, and because each step turns by \(\pi/3\) they return after \(6\) steps: the solution from \(x_0=x_1=1\) (right) is \(1,1,0,-1,-1,0\) repeated.

Move \(a_1\) and \(a_0\) until the roots of \(p(r)\) leave the real axis: a complex pair \(\rho e^{\pm\mathrm{i}\theta}\) gives an oscillation of size \(\rho^t\), which dies out for \(\rho<1\), persists on the unit circle and explodes for \(\rho>1\).

The polynomial is read off the equation by replacing \(x_{t+j}\) with \(r^j\). Its coefficients are those of the equation written with every term on the left; with \(x_{t+2}=x_{t+1}+x_t\) one must first rewrite \(x_{t+2}-x_{t+1}-x_t=0\) to get \(p(r)=r^2-r-1\).

The name is not a coincidence. The equation is equivalent to \(\boldsymbol{y}_{t+1}=C\boldsymbol{y}_t\) for the companion matrix \(C\) of a higher-order equation, and \(p(\lambda)=\det(\lambda I-C)\), which is the characteristic polynomial \(\det(C-\lambda I)\) of that matrix up to the factor \((-1)^k\). Characteristic roots are therefore the eigenvalues of \(C\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(r^t\) is a solution if and only if \(p(r)=0\); since \(a_0\ne0\), \(0\) is never a root.
  • A root \(r\) of multiplicity \(m\) gives the \(m\) solutions \(r^t,\,t\,r^t,\,\ldots,\,t^{m-1}r^t\); together over all roots these form a basis of solutions.
  • Real coefficients make nonreal roots appear in conjugate pairs \(\rho \mathrm{e}^{\pm\mathrm{i}\theta}\); the pair can be replaced by the real solutions \(\rho^t\cos(\theta t)\) and \(\rho^t\sin(\theta t)\).
  • Vieta: the roots sum to \(-a_{k-1}\) and multiply to \((-1)^k a_0\).
  • \(p(1)=1+a_{k-1}+\cdots+a_0\); if \(p(1)\ne0\), the equation with constant right-hand side \(b\) has the equilibrium \(x^*=b/p(1)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Distinct roots. \(x_{t+2}-3x_{t+1}+2x_t=0\) has \(p(r)=r^2-3r+2=(r-1)(r-2)\), so \(x_t=c_1+c_2\,2^t\).

Repeated root. \(x_{t+2}-4x_{t+1}+4x_t=0\) has \(p(r)=(r-2)^2\). Besides \(2^t\), \(t\,2^t\) is a solution: \((t+2)2^{t+2}-4(t+1)2^{t+1}+4t\,2^t=2^t(4t+8-8t-8+4t)=0\). Hence \(x_t=(c_1+c_2t)2^t\).

Complex roots. \(x_{t+2}-x_{t+1}+x_t=0\) has \(p(r)=r^2-r+1\) with roots \(\tfrac{1}{2}\pm\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\mathrm{i}=\mathrm{e}^{\pm\mathrm{i}\pi/3}\). So \(x_t=c_1\cos(\pi t/3)+c_2\sin(\pi t/3)\), a solution of period \(6\); from \(x_0=x_1=1\) the recursion gives \(1,1,0,-1,-1,0,1,\ldots\)

Fibonacci. \(p(r)=r^2-r-1\) has roots \(\varphi=\tfrac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}\) and \(\psi=\tfrac{1-\sqrt{5}}{2}\); with \(x_0=0\), \(x_1=1\) this gives \(x_t=(\varphi^t-\psi^t)/\sqrt{5}\).

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
Let \(A\) be a real \(n\times n\) matrix and let \(\lambda=a+b\mathrm{i}\) with \(a,b\in\mathbb{R}\), \(b\ne0\), be an eigenvalue of \(A\) with eigenvector \(\boldsymbol{p}\in\mathbb{C}^n\). Then the complex conjugate \(\bar\lambda=a-b\mathrm{i}\) is also an eigenvalue of \(A\), with eigenvector \(\bar{\boldsymbol{p}}\) (entrywise conjugate), and \(\lambda\) and \(\bar\lambda\) have the same algebraic multiplicity.

Proof. Conjugating \(A\boldsymbol{p}=\lambda\boldsymbol{p}\) and using \(\bar{A}=A\) gives \(A\bar{\boldsymbol{p}}=\bar\lambda\bar{\boldsymbol{p}}\), and \(\bar{\boldsymbol{p}}\ne\boldsymbol{0}\). The multiplicity statement holds because the characteristic polynomial has real coefficients, so its factorization is invariant under conjugation.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The characteristic polynomial \(\det(A-\lambda I)\) of a real matrix has real coefficients, so this is the complex conjugate root theorem from Math II applied to eigenvalues. The hypothesis that \(A\) is real is essential: the \(1\times1\) complex matrix \((\mathrm{i})\) has eigenvalue \(\mathrm{i}\) but not \(-\mathrm{i}\).

The figure uses the numerical matrix from the examples, \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\1&3\end{pmatrix}\). On the left its eigenvalues \(\lambda=2+\mathrm{i}\) and \(\bar\lambda=2-\mathrm{i}\) are reflections of each other in the real axis, with the same modulus \(\rho=\sqrt{5}\) and opposite angles \(\pm\theta\). On the right are the real and imaginary parts \(\boldsymbol{u}=(-1,1)^{\top}\) and \(\boldsymbol{w}=(1,0)^{\top}\) of the eigenvector \(\boldsymbol{p}\): the image \(A\boldsymbol{u}=(-3,2)^{\top}=2\boldsymbol{u}-\boldsymbol{w}\) stays in the plane of \(\boldsymbol{u}\) and \(\boldsymbol{w}\) rather than on the line through \(\boldsymbol{u}\).

Change the entries of \(A\): once the discriminant is negative the eigenvalues form a pair \(\lambda,\bar\lambda\) mirrored in the real axis, and \(A\) acts on the plane of \(\boldsymbol{u}=\operatorname{Re}\boldsymbol{p}\) and \(\boldsymbol{w}=\operatorname{Im}\boldsymbol{p}\) as a rotation by \(\theta\) combined with scaling by \(\rho=|\lambda|\).

A nonreal eigenvalue has no real eigenvector, so it does not describe a stretched line. Instead the pair acts on a real plane: writing \(\boldsymbol{p}=\boldsymbol{u}+\mathrm{i}\boldsymbol{w}\) with real \(\boldsymbol{u},\boldsymbol{w}\), the plane \(\operatorname{span}\{\boldsymbol{u},\boldsymbol{w}\}\) is mapped into itself, and in the coordinates given by \(\boldsymbol{u},\boldsymbol{w}\) the matrix acts as a rotation combined with a scaling. With \(\lambda=\rho \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}\) in polar form, \(\rho=\lvert\lambda\rvert\) is the scaling factor and \(\lvert\theta\rvert\) the rotation angle per application of \(A\).

The pair matters for linear difference equations: for \(\boldsymbol{x}_{t+1}=A\boldsymbol{x}_t\) it produces oscillating terms \(\rho^t\cos(\theta t)\) and \(\rho^t\sin(\theta t)\), which decay exactly when \(\rho=\lvert\lambda\rvert<1\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Nonreal eigenvalues of a real matrix come in pairs, so their number (with multiplicity) is even; a real \(n\times n\) matrix with \(n\) odd has at least one real eigenvalue.
  • If \(\boldsymbol{p}=\boldsymbol{u}+\mathrm{i}\boldsymbol{w}\) is an eigenvector for \(a+b\mathrm{i}\), \(b\neq0\), then \(\boldsymbol{u},\boldsymbol{w}\) are linearly independent and \(A\boldsymbol{u}=a\boldsymbol{u}-b\boldsymbol{w}\), \(A\boldsymbol{w}=b\boldsymbol{u}+a\boldsymbol{w}\), i.e. \(A\,[\boldsymbol{u}\ \boldsymbol{w}]=[\boldsymbol{u}\ \boldsymbol{w}]\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\-b&a\end{pmatrix}\).
  • The pair contributes \(\lambda\bar\lambda=a^2+b^2=\lvert\lambda\rvert^2>0\) to \(\det A\) and \(2a\) to \(\operatorname{tr}A\).
  • A \(2\times2\) real matrix has a nonreal pair if and only if \((\operatorname{tr}A)^2-4\det A<0\).
  • By De Moivre's formula, \(\lambda^t=\rho^t\big(\cos(\theta t)+\mathrm{i}\sin(\theta t)\big)\), so \(\lambda^t\to0\) if and only if \(\rho<1\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
A numerical matrix. For \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\1&3\end{pmatrix}\), \(\operatorname{tr}A=4\) and \(\det A=5\), so \(\lambda^2-4\lambda+5=0\) and \(\lambda=2\pm\mathrm{i}\). From the second row of \(A-(2+\mathrm{i})I\), namely \(p_1+(1-\mathrm{i})p_2=0\), an eigenvector is \(\boldsymbol{p}=(-1+\mathrm{i},\,1)^{\top}\); hence \((-1-\mathrm{i},\,1)^{\top}\) belongs to \(2-\mathrm{i}\). Here \(\boldsymbol{u}=(-1,1)^{\top}\), \(\boldsymbol{w}=(1,0)^{\top}\), and indeed \(A\boldsymbol{u}=(-3,2)^{\top}=2\boldsymbol{u}-\boldsymbol{w}\). Both eigenvalues have modulus \(\sqrt{5}\).

Rotation. \(R_\theta=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}\) has characteristic polynomial \(\lambda^2-2\cos\theta\,\lambda+1\) and eigenvalues \(\mathrm{e}^{\pm\mathrm{i}\theta}\), with eigenvectors \((1,-\mathrm{i})^{\top}\) and \((1,\mathrm{i})^{\top}\). For \(\theta\) not a multiple of \(\pi\) they are nonreal and have modulus \(1\).

Odd dimension. A real \(3\times3\) matrix cannot have eigenvalues \(\mathrm{i},1,2\): the conjugate \(-\mathrm{i}\) would be a fourth eigenvalue.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A difference equation of order \(k\ge1\) for a sequence \((x_t)_{t\ge0}\) is a relation

\[ x_{t+k}=f\big(t,\,x_t,\,x_{t+1},\,\ldots,\,x_{t+k-1}\big), \]

for \(t=0,1,2,\ldots\), in which \(x_t\) actually occurs; the order is the gap between the largest and the smallest time index. A solution is a sequence satisfying the relation for every \(t\ge0\).

The equation is linear if it has the form

\[ x_{t+k}+a_{k-1}(t)\,x_{t+k-1}+\cdots +a_1(t)\,x_{t+1}+a_0(t)\,x_t=g_t, \]

with \(a_0(t)\ne0\) for all \(t\). It is homogeneous if \(g_t=0\) for all \(t\), and has constant coefficients if no \(a_i\) depends on \(t\). A constant solution \(x_t=x^*\) is an equilibrium (steady state).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A difference equation is a rule that produces the next value of a quantity from the current and a few past values, as in a savings balance, a price, or a population observed once per period. Time is discrete; the continuous-time counterpart is a differential equation, studied from Week 3.

The figure runs the Fibonacci example \(x_{t+2}=x_{t+1}+x_t\). The two shaded initial values \(x_0=0\), \(x_1=1\) are given; every later box is filled by the rule from the two boxes before it, so \(x_2=x_1+x_0=1\) and, further on, \(x_5=x_4+x_3=5\). Because the equation has order \(2\), exactly two starting values are needed, and changing them produces a different solution.

The name comes from the forward difference \(\Delta x_t=x_{t+1}-x_t\): the equation \(\Delta x_t=0.1x_t\) is the same as \(x_{t+1}=1.1x_t\). Any relation between \(x_t\) and its differences can be rewritten with shifted terms.

The order counts how many consecutive past values the rule needs, not the largest index. In \(x_{t+3}=x_{t+1}\) the smallest index is \(t+1\), so with \(s=t+1\) it reads \(x_{s+2}=x_s\), an equation of order \(2\). For a homogeneous linear equation the solution set is a vector space (for an inhomogeneous one it is a shifted copy of that space, not a vector space), which is why linear algebra applies.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For an equation in the explicit form above, any choice of the \(k\) initial values \(x_0,\ldots,x_{k-1}\) determines exactly one solution, computed recursively.
  • The solutions of a homogeneous linear equation of order \(k\) form a \(k\)-dimensional subspace of the space of real sequences; see basis of solutions.
  • For a linear equation, every solution equals one particular solution plus a solution of the homogeneous equation.
  • An equilibrium of \(x_{t+1}=f(x_t)\) is a fixed point, \(x^*=f(x^*)\).
  • A linear equation of order \(k\) can be rewritten as a first-order system in \(\mathbb{R}^k\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
First order. \(x_{t+1}=2x_t\) with \(x_0=3\) gives \(x_t=3\cdot2^t\): \(3,6,12,24,\ldots\)

Fibonacci. \(x_{t+2}=x_{t+1}+x_t\) is linear, homogeneous, of order \(2\) with constant coefficients. With \(x_0=0\), \(x_1=1\) the recursion gives \(0,1,1,2,3,5,8,\ldots\); other initial values give other solutions.

Nonlinear. The logistic map \(x_{t+1}=r\,x_t(1-x_t)\) has order \(1\) but is not linear. Its equilibria solve \(x^*=r x^*(1-x^*)\), so \(x^*=0\) or \(x^*=1-1/r\) (for \(r\ne0\)).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(x\) be an unknown real-valued function of time \(t\), and write \(x'(t)=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}(t)\) for its derivative and \(x^{(k)}(t)\) for its \(k\)-th higher-order derivative. An ordinary differential equation (ODE) of order \(n\) is a relation

\[ F\big(t,\,x(t),\,x'(t),\,\dots,\,x^{(n)}(t)\big)=0, \]

in which \(x^{(n)}\) actually occurs. A solution on an interval \(I\) is an \(n\) times differentiable function \(x\colon I\to\mathbb{R}\) that satisfies the relation for every \(t\in I\).

The equation is linear if it has the form \(x^{(n)}+a_{n-1}(t)x^{(n-1)}+\dots+a_0(t)x=g(t)\), homogeneous (linear case) if \(g\equiv0\), and autonomous if \(t\) does not appear explicitly, as in \(x'=f(x)\). An initial value problem adds conditions \(x(t_0)=x_0,\ x'(t_0)=x_1,\dots,x^{(n-1)}(t_0)=x_{n-1}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A differential equation describes continuous-time change: it states how the rate of change of a quantity depends on time and on the current state. It is the continuous-time counterpart of a difference equation, where the state jumps from \(x_t\) to \(x_{t+1}\).

The figure draws the exponential-growth example \(x'(t)=3x(t)\). Each short grey segment has slope \(3x\), the rate of change the equation prescribes at state \(x\). The grey curves are the solutions \(C\mathrm{e}^{3t}\) for \(C=-2,-1,0,1,3\); each follows the segments everywhere. The initial condition \(x(0)=2\) picks out one member of this family, the blue curve \(2\mathrm{e}^{3t}\).

Move \(x(0)\) to pick one curve \(Ce^{at}\) from the family that follows the slope segments, and change \(a\) to switch between growth (\(a>0\)) and decay (\(a<0\)).

The unknown is a whole function, not a number. An equation without initial conditions therefore has a family of solutions, usually indexed by \(n\) free constants; the \(n\) initial conditions select one member of that family.

A common misunderstanding is to treat "solution" as a formula valid for all \(t\). A solution lives on an interval, and for nonlinear equations it can cease to exist after finite time (see the last example).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The order is the highest derivative that occurs; \(x''+(x')^3=0\) has order 2, not 3.
  • The simplest case \(x'(t)=g(t)\) with \(g\) continuous is solved by any antiderivative: \(x(t)=x(t_0)+\int_{t_0}^t g(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\).
  • For a linear equation with continuous coefficients \(a_k(t)\) and \(g(t)\) on \(I\), every initial value problem has exactly one solution, defined on all of \(I\).
  • For a homogeneous linear equation, sums and scalar multiples of solutions are solutions, so the solutions form a vector space.
  • A nonlinear equation can have solutions that exist only on a bounded interval.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Exponential growth. For \(x'(t)=3x(t)\), every function \(x(t)=C\mathrm{e}^{3t}\) is a solution, since \(x'(t)=3C\mathrm{e}^{3t}\). The condition \(x(0)=2\) gives \(C=2\), so \(x(t)=2\mathrm{e}^{3t}\).

Second order. For \(x''(t)=6t\), integrating twice gives \(x'(t)=3t^2+c_1\) and \(x(t)=t^3+c_1t+c_2\): two free constants for an equation of order 2. With \(x(0)=1\), \(x'(0)=0\) we get \(x(t)=t^3+1\).

Finite-time blow-up. For the nonlinear equation \(x'(t)=x(t)^2\) with \(x(0)=1\), the function \(x(t)=\dfrac{1}{1-t}\) satisfies \(x'(t)=\dfrac{1}{(1-t)^2}=x(t)^2\). It is a solution only on \((-\infty,1)\) and tends to \(+\infty\) as \(t\to1^-\).
