docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Consider the autonomous first-order differential equation

\[ x'(t)=f\big(x(t)\big), \]

where \(x'(t)=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}(t)\) and \(f\) is a given real function. A number \(x^*\) is an equilibrium (steady state) if \(f(x^*)=0\). Equivalently, the constant function \(x(t)\equiv x^*\) is a solution.

For a vector equation \(\boldsymbol{x}'(t)=\boldsymbol{f}\big(\boldsymbol{x}(t)\big)\) with \(\boldsymbol{x}(t)\in\mathbb{R}^n\), an equilibrium is a vector \(\boldsymbol{x}^*\) with \(\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}^*)=\boldsymbol{0}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
At an equilibrium the rate of change is zero, so a system that starts there stays there for ever. Finding equilibria is an algebraic task: they are the zeros of \(f\); no differential equation needs to be solved.

The figure shows the logistic example \(x'=x(1-x)\). On the left, the equilibria are the zeros \(0\) and \(1\) of \(f(x)=x(1-x)\), and the arrows on the axis form the phase line: to the right where \(f>0\), to the left where \(f<0\). On the right, the equilibria appear as constant solutions (dashed). The solution from \(x(0)=0.2\) rises towards \(1\), and a solution from \(x(0)=1.5\) falls towards \(1\); neither crosses an equilibrium line.

Choose \(f\) and drag \(x(0)\): the equilibria are the zeros of \(f\) and appear as constant solutions on the right, and the sign of \(f\) between them decides whether \(x(t)\) rises or falls. For \(f(x)=1+x^2\) there is no equilibrium at all.

The sign of \(f\) between consecutive equilibria shows the direction of motion: where \(f(x)>0\) solutions increase, where \(f(x)<0\) they decrease. This one-dimensional picture is called the phase line. Whether nearby solutions approach the equilibrium is a separate question, treated in stability of an equilibrium.

Two misunderstandings occur often. An equilibrium is a value of the state \(x\), not a time \(t\). And an equilibrium need not be reached: in \(x'=-x\) the solution \(x_0\mathrm{e}^{-t}\) approaches \(0\) but never equals it when \(x_0\neq0\). For a non-autonomous equation \(x'=f(t,x)\), a constant \(x^*\) is a solution only if \(f(t,x^*)=0\) for every \(t\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Equilibria of \(x'=f(x)\) are exactly the constant solutions.
  • For \(x'=ax+b\) with \(a\neq0\) there is a unique equilibrium \(x^*=-b/a\), and every solution satisfies \(x(t)-x^*=\mathrm{e}^{at}\big(x(0)-x^*\big)\).
  • For \(x'=ax+b\) with \(a=0\): every point is an equilibrium if \(b=0\); there is none if \(b\neq0\).
  • If \(f\) is continuously differentiable, solutions cannot cross or touch an equilibrium (uniqueness of solutions), so a solution starting between two equilibria stays between them and is monotone.
  • For \(\boldsymbol{x}'=A\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{b}\) with \(A\) invertible, the unique equilibrium is \(\boldsymbol{x}^*=-A^{-1}\boldsymbol{b}\), using the inverse matrix.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Linear. \(x'=4-2x\): \(f(x^*)=0\) gives \(x^*=2\). The solution with \(x(0)=5\) is \(x(t)=2+3\mathrm{e}^{-2t}\).

Logistic equation. \(x'=x(1-x)\) has equilibria \(0\) and \(1\). Since \(f(x)>0\) on \((0,1)\), a solution with \(x(0)=0.2\) increases and stays in \((0,1)\); it tends to \(1\). For \(x>1\), \(f(x)<0\) and solutions decrease towards \(1\).

No equilibrium. \(x'=1+x^2\) has \(f(x)\geq1>0\) for every \(x\), so there is no equilibrium and every solution is strictly increasing.

Vector case. For \(A=\begin{pmatrix}-1&1\\0&-2\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\boldsymbol{b}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\4\end{pmatrix}\), solve \(A\boldsymbol{x}^*=-\boldsymbol{b}\): the second row gives \(-2x_2^*=-4\), so \(x_2^*=2\); the first row gives \(-x_1^*+2=-1\), so \(x_1^*=3\). Thus \(\boldsymbol{x}^*=(3,2)^{\top}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A first-order differential equation is a differential equation in which only the unknown function \(x(t)\) and its first derivative \(x'(t)=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}(t)\) occur. In explicit form,

\[ x'(t)=f\big(t,x(t)\big) \]

for a given function \(f\) of two variables. Three standard classes:

  • linear: \(x'(t)+p(t)x(t)=q(t)\), with \(p,q\) given functions of \(t\); with constant coefficients this is \(x'(t)=ax(t)+b\);
  • autonomous: \(x'(t)=f\big(x(t)\big)\), where the right-hand side does not depend on \(t\);
  • separable: \(x'(t)=g(t)\,h\big(x(t)\big)\).

An initial value problem adds one condition \(x(t_0)=x_0\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The equation prescribes the slope of the solution curve at every point \((t,x)\). Starting from \(x_0\) at time \(t_0\), the solution follows these slopes; one initial value is enough because the equation has order 1.

The figure draws the separable example \(x'(t)=2t\,x(t)\). Each grey segment has the slope \(f(t,x)=2tx\) prescribed at its point; it depends on both \(t\) and \(x\), flat on the line \(t=0\) and steeper further out. The blue curve is the solution \(\mathrm{e}^{t^2}\) fixed by the single initial value \(x(0)=1\). The grey curves are other solutions \(C\mathrm{e}^{t^2}\) (here \(C=2\), \(0.5\), \(-0.5\)). The dashed line is the constant solution \(x\equiv0\), which division by \(x\) loses.

Move \(x(0)\) to pick one curve from the family \(x(t)=3+Ce^{-2t}\) of \(x'=-2x+6\). Then change \(a\) and \(b\). For \(a<0\) every solution approaches the equilibrium \(-b/a\); for \(a>0\) solutions move away from it.

The constant-coefficient case \(x'=ax\) is the continuous-time analogue of the first-order linear difference equation \(x_{t+1}=ax_t\): the factor \(a^t\) there becomes \(\mathrm{e}^{at}\) here. The sign of \(a\), not whether \(|a|<1\), decides growth or decay.

A frequent error is to drop the constant solutions of a separable equation. Dividing by \(h(x)\) is only allowed where \(h(x)\neq0\); each zero \(c\) of \(h\) gives the constant solution \(x(t)\equiv c\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(x'(t)=ax(t)\) has general solution \(x(t)=C\mathrm{e}^{at}\); the initial value problem with \(x(t_0)=x_0\) has the unique solution \(x(t)=x_0\mathrm{e}^{a(t-t_0)}\). This uses the exponential function and \(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathrm{e}^{at}=a\mathrm{e}^{at}\).
  • For \(a\neq0\), \(x'(t)=ax(t)+b\) has general solution \(x(t)=-\dfrac{b}{a}+C\mathrm{e}^{at}\); the constant \(-b/a\) is its equilibrium.
  • If \(p,q\) are continuous on an interval \(I\), the linear equation \(x'+px=q\) has a unique solution on all of \(I\) for each \(x(t_0)=x_0\); it is found with an integrating factor.
  • Separable equations are solved by \(\int \frac{\mathrm{d}x}{h(x)}=\int g(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\) wherever \(h(x)\neq0\); the chain rule justifies this step.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Continuous compounding. A balance with interest rate \(r=0.05\) per year satisfies \(B'(t)=0.05\,B(t)\). With \(B(0)=1000\), \(B(t)=1000\mathrm{e}^{0.05t}\), so \(B(10)=1000\mathrm{e}^{0.5}\approx1648.72\).

Constant forcing. For \(x'(t)=-2x(t)+6\) with \(x(0)=1\): here \(a=-2\), \(b=6\), so \(x(t)=3+C\mathrm{e}^{-2t}\) and \(C=1-3=-2\). Hence \(x(t)=3-2\mathrm{e}^{-2t}\). Check: \(x'(t)=4\mathrm{e}^{-2t}\) and \(-2x(t)+6=-6+4\mathrm{e}^{-2t}+6=4\mathrm{e}^{-2t}\). The solution tends to the equilibrium \(3\).

Separable. For \(x'(t)=2t\,x(t)\) with \(x(0)=1\): for \(x>0\), \(\int\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{x}=\int2t\,\mathrm{d}t\) gives \(\ln x=t^2+c\), so \(x(t)=\mathrm{e}^{t^2}\). Check: \(x'(t)=2t\mathrm{e}^{t^2}=2t\,x(t)\). The function \(x\equiv0\) is the constant solution excluded by the division.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A first-order linear difference equation with constant coefficient is

\[ x_{t+1}=a\,x_t+g_t,\qquad t=0,1,2,\ldots, \]

where \(a\ne0\) is a real constant and \((g_t)_{t\ge0}\) is a given forcing sequence. It is homogeneous if \(g_t=0\) for all \(t\). For every initial value \(x_0\) the unique solution is

\[ x_t=a^t x_0+\sum_{s=0}^{t-1}a^{\,t-1-s}\,g_s. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The next state is the current state scaled by \(a\) plus an external input. The solution formula is obtained by substituting the equation into itself: the initial value is multiplied by \(a\) once per period, and the input \(g_s\) received at time \(s\) has been multiplied by \(a\) for the remaining \(t-1-s\) periods.

The figure shows two solutions with constant input, both starting at \(x_0=10\) and both with the equilibrium (constant solution) \(x^*=6\), dashed. The blue path is the convergent example \(x_{t+1}=0.5x_t+3\), that is \(x_t=6+4(0.5)^t\), which falls monotonically (\(10,8,7,6.5,\ldots\)). The red path is \(x_{t+1}=-0.5x_t+9\), which has the same equilibrium \(9/1.5=6\); here \(x_t=6+4(-0.5)^t\) alternates (\(10,4,7,5.5,\ldots\)). Both transients shrink by the factor \(\lvert a vert=0.5\) per period.

Move \(a\), \(b\) and \(x_0\): for \(|a|<1\) the path settles on the dashed equilibrium \(x^*=b/(1-a)\), monotonically when \(a>0\) and alternating around \(x^*\) when \(a<0\). At \(a=1\) with \(b e0\) there is no equilibrium and the path grows linearly.

With a constant input \(g_t=b\) and \(a e1\), the constant \(x^*=b/(1-a)\) is the unique equilibrium, and the deviation \(x_t-x^*\) satisfies the homogeneous equation. Hence \(x_t=x^*+a^t(x_0-x^*)\): an equilibrium plus a transient. The size of \(\lvert a vert\) decides whether the transient dies out (see stability of a scalar difference equation), and the sign of \(a\) decides whether the path is monotone (\(a>0\)) or alternates around \(x^*\) (\(a<0\)).

The case \(a=1\) is different: there is no equilibrium when \(b e0\), and \(x_t=x_0+bt\) grows linearly. Forgetting this case, and dividing by \(1-a=0\), is a common error.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Homogeneous case: \(x_t=a^t x_0\), a geometric sequence.
  • Constant input \(b\), \(a\ne1\): \(x_t=\dfrac{b}{1-a}+a^t\Big(x_0-\dfrac{b}{1-a}\Big)\); by the geometric series formula, \(\sum_{s=0}^{t-1}a^{t-1-s}b=b\,\dfrac{1-a^t}{1-a}\).
  • Constant input \(b\), \(a=1\): \(x_t=x_0+bt\).
  • If \(\lvert a\rvert<1\) and \(g_t=b\), then \(x_t\to b/(1-a)\) for every \(x_0\); if \(\lvert a\rvert>1\), the path diverges unless \(x_0=x^*\).
  • \(a=-1\) gives a two-cycle \(x_t=x^*+(-1)^t(x_0-x^*)\) around \(x^*=b/2\) (a constant path if \(x_0=x^*\)).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Convergent case. \(x_{t+1}=0.5x_t+3\), \(x_0=10\). The equilibrium is \(x^*=3/(1-0.5)=6\), so \(x_t=6+4(0.5)^t\). Check: \(x_1=0.5\cdot10+3=8=6+4\cdot0.5\), and \(x_t\to6\).

Savings account. A balance earning \(5\%\) per period with a deposit of \(100\) at the end of each period satisfies \(B_{t+1}=1.05B_t+100\), \(B_0=0\). Here \(x^*=100/(1-1.05)=-2000\), so \(B_t=2000(1.05^t-1)\). Check: \(B_1=100\) and \(B_2=2000\cdot0.1025=205=1.05\cdot100+100\). The equilibrium is negative and unstable: it only describes the path, not a long-run level.

Time-varying input. \(x_{t+1}=2x_t+t\), \(x_0=0\): the formula gives \(x_3=2^2\cdot0+2^1\cdot1+2^0\cdot2=4\), matching the recursion \(x_1=0\), \(x_2=1\), \(x_3=2\cdot1+2=4\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(A\) be a real \(m\times n\) matrix of rank \(r\). Its four fundamental subspaces are

  • the row space \(\operatorname{Row}(A)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and the null space (kernel) \(\operatorname{Null}(A)=\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon A\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{0}\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\);
  • the column space (range) \(\operatorname{Col}(A)=\{A\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) and the null space of \(A^{\top}\), \(\operatorname{Null}(A^{\top})=\{\boldsymbol{y}\colon A^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{0}\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\).

Then, with respect to the dot product,

  1. (dimensions) \(\dim\operatorname{Row}(A)=r\), \(\dim\operatorname{Null}(A)=n-r\), \(\dim\operatorname{Col}(A)=r\), \(\dim\operatorname{Null}(A^{\top})=m-r\);
  2. (orthogonality) \(\operatorname{Null}(A)=\operatorname{Row}(A)^\perp\) and \(\operatorname{Null}(A^{\top})=\operatorname{Col}(A)^\perp\).

Consequently \(\mathbb{R}^n=\operatorname{Row}(A)\oplus\operatorname{Null}(A)\) and \(\mathbb{R}^m=\operatorname{Col}(A)\oplus\operatorname{Null}(A^{\top})\), both direct sums of mutually orthogonal subspaces. Math II writes \(\ker A\) and \(\operatorname{range}A\) for \(\operatorname{Null}(A)\) and \(\operatorname{Col}(A)\). The course gives the fourth subspace, \(\operatorname{Null}(A^{\top})\), no separate name; some textbooks call it the left null space.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Part 1 combines the Fundamental Theorem of Linear Maps (rank–nullity, \(\dim\operatorname{Null}(A)+\dim\operatorname{Col}(A)=n\)) with the fact that row rank equals column rank, applied to both \(A\) and its transpose.

In the figure the domain \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is split into the row space (dimension \(r\)) and the null space (dimension \(n-r\)), and the codomain \(\mathbb{R}^m\) into the column space (dimension \(r\)) and the null space of \(A^{\top}\) (dimension \(m-r\)); the right-angle marks stand for the orthogonality in Part 2. The matrix \(A\) carries the row space one-to-one onto the column space and sends the whole null space to \(\boldsymbol{0}\). In the example below, \(r=1\), \(n=2\), \(m=3\), so the four dimensions are \(1,1,1,2\).

Part 2 is almost a one-line proof. \(A\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{0}\) says that every row of \(A\) has dot product \(0\) with \(\boldsymbol{x}\), so \(\boldsymbol{x}\) is orthogonal to all rows and hence to their span; this is exactly membership of the orthogonal complement of the row space. Applying the same argument to \(A^{\top}\) gives the second identity.

The pairs live in different spaces: row space and null space in the domain \(\mathbb{R}^n\), column space and \(\operatorname{Null}(A^{\top})\) in the codomain \(\mathbb{R}^m\). Row space and column space have the same dimension \(r\). For a non-square matrix they lie in different spaces, and even for a square matrix they are in general neither equal nor orthogonal.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Since \(\operatorname{Col}(A)=\operatorname{Null}(A^{\top})^\perp\), \(A\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{b}\) is solvable if and only if \(\boldsymbol{y}^{\top}\boldsymbol{b}=0\) for every \(\boldsymbol{y}\) with \(A^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{0}\).
  • Every \(\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\) splits uniquely as \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{x}_r+\boldsymbol{x}_n\) with \(\boldsymbol{x}_r\in\operatorname{Row}(A)\), \(\boldsymbol{x}_n\in\operatorname{Null}(A)\), and \(A\boldsymbol{x}=A\boldsymbol{x}_r\).
  • \(A\) restricted to the row space is a bijection onto the column space.
  • Full column rank (\(r=n\)) holds if and only if \(\operatorname{Null}(A)=\{\boldsymbol{0}\}\); full row rank (\(r=m\)) holds if and only if \(\operatorname{Null}(A^{\top})=\{\boldsymbol{0}\}\), if and only if \(A\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{b}\) is solvable for every \(\boldsymbol{b}\).
  • \(\operatorname{Null}(A^{\top}A)=\operatorname{Null}(A)\), so \(\operatorname{rank}(A^{\top}A)=\operatorname{rank}A\); this is what makes the normal equations of least squares work.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Let

\[ A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&4\\3&6\end{pmatrix}, \]

so \(m=3\), \(n=2\) and \(r=1\).

  • Row space: \(\operatorname{span}\{(1,2)^{\top}\}\), dimension \(r=1\).
  • Null space: \(x_1+2x_2=0\), so \(\operatorname{span}\{(-2,1)^{\top}\}\), dimension \(n-r=1\); indeed \((1,2)\cdot(-2,1)=0\).
  • Column space: \(\operatorname{span}\{(1,2,3)^{\top}\}\), dimension \(r=1\).
  • Null space of \(A^{\top}\): \(y_1+2y_2+3y_3=0\), spanned by \(\boldsymbol{y}_1=(-2,1,0)^{\top}\) and \(\boldsymbol{y}_2=(-3,0,1)^{\top}\), dimension \(m-r=2\); both are orthogonal to \((1,2,3)^{\top}\).

Solvability: for \(\boldsymbol{b}=(1,0,0)^{\top}\), \(\boldsymbol{y}_1^{\top}\boldsymbol{b}=-2\neq0\), so \(A\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{b}\) has no solution. For \(\boldsymbol{b}=(2,4,6)^{\top}\), \(\boldsymbol{y}_1^{\top}\boldsymbol{b}=\boldsymbol{y}_2^{\top}\boldsymbol{b}=0\), and \(\boldsymbol{x}=(2,0)^{\top}\) solves it.

docs.title: General Solution of a Linear ODE
Proposition
docs.text:
Let \(a_0,\dots,a_{n-1}\) and \(g\) be continuous on an interval \(I\), write \(x'(t)=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}(t)\), and let

\[ L[x]=x^{(n)}+a_{n-1}(t)x^{(n-1)}+\dots +a_1(t)x'+a_0(t)x. \]
  1. The solutions of the homogeneous equation \(L[x]=0\) on \(I\) form a vector space \(S_0\) of dimension \(n\).
  2. If \(x_p\) is a particular solution of \(L[x]=g\), then the set of all solutions of \(L[x]=g\) is \(\{x_p\}+S_0\).

Hence, for any basis \(x_1,\dots,x_n\) of \(S_0\), the general solution of the linear ordinary differential equation (ODE) \(L[x]=g\) is

\[ x(t)=x_p(t)+c_1x_1(t)+\dots+c_nx_n(t), \]

where \(c_1,\dots,c_n\in\mathbb{R}\), and \(n\) initial conditions \(x(t_0),x'(t_0),\dots,x^{(n-1)}(t_0)\) determine \(c_1,\dots,c_n\) uniquely.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The map \(L\) is linear, so \(S_0\) is its kernel and the solution set of \(L[x]=g\) is a shifted copy of that kernel. This is the same structure as for homogeneous and inhomogeneous systems \(A\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{b}\) in Math II, and the solution set is an affine subspace, not a subspace, when \(g\not\equiv0\).

The figure plots the second-order example \(x''+3x'+2x=4t\) with \(x(0)=x'(0)=0\). The green solution \(x(t)=4\mathrm{e}^{-t}-\mathrm{e}^{-2t}+2t-3\) is the dashed particular solution \(x_p=2t-3\) plus the blue element \(4\mathrm{e}^{-t}-\mathrm{e}^{-2t}\) of \(S_0\). The constants \(c_1=4\), \(c_2=-1\) are fitted to the full sum, which is why \(x\) starts at \(0\) with zero slope while \(x_p\) starts at \(-3\). As the homogeneous part decays, \(x(t)\) approaches \(x_p(t)\).

Change \(x(0)\) and \(x'(0)\): only the homogeneous part \(c_1e^{r_1t}+c_2e^{r_2t}\) changes, while the dashed particular solution \(x_p=2t-3\) stays fixed. With roots in the left half-plane every solution approaches it.

The proof of part 2 is one line: if \(L[x]=g\) then \(L[x-x_p]=g-g=0\), so \(x-x_p\in S_0\). The dimension count in part 1 uses uniqueness of solutions: the map sending a solution to its initial data \(\big(x(t_0),\dots,x^{(n-1)}(t_0)\big)\in\mathbb{R}^n\) is a linear bijection.

Common errors: fitting the initial conditions to the homogeneous part before adding \(x_p\) (the constants must be fitted to the full sum); and assuming the sum of two particular solutions is again a particular solution (it solves \(L[x]=2g\)).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(n\) solutions \(x_1,\dots,x_n\) of \(L[x]=0\) form a basis of \(S_0\) if and only if their initial-data vectors \(\big(x_i(t_0),x_i'(t_0),\dots,x_i^{(n-1)}(t_0)\big)\) are linearly independent for one (equivalently every) \(t_0\in I\).
  • For constant coefficients, the roots of the characteristic equation supply such a basis.
  • The same structure holds for systems: all solutions of \(\boldsymbol{x}'=A\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{b}(t)\) are \(\boldsymbol{x}_p\) plus the \(n\)-dimensional solution space of \(\boldsymbol{x}'=A\boldsymbol{x}\); see linear vector ODE.
  • For constant \(A\), the general solution is \(\boldsymbol{x}(t)=\mathrm{e}^{A(t-t_0)}\boldsymbol{x}(t_0)+\int_{t_0}^{t}\mathrm{e}^{A(t-s)}\boldsymbol{b}(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\), using the matrix exponential.

Beyond the course

Many differential-equations textbooks test this independence with the Wronskian, the determinant of the matrix whose columns are the initial-data vectors at \(t\). Math V does not use it: checking the initial-data vectors at one \(t_0\) is enough.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Second-order initial value problem. \(x''+3x'+2x=4t\), \(x(0)=0\), \(x'(0)=0\). Homogeneous basis from \(r^2+3r+2=(r+1)(r+2)\): \(\mathrm{e}^{-t}\), \(\mathrm{e}^{-2t}\). A particular solution is \(2t-3\). So \(x=c_1\mathrm{e}^{-t}+c_2\mathrm{e}^{-2t}+2t-3\). The conditions give \(c_1+c_2=3\) and \(-c_1-2c_2+2=0\), hence \(c_2=-1\), \(c_1=4\):

\[ x(t)=4\mathrm{e}^{-t}-\mathrm{e}^{-2t}+2t-3. \]

Check: \(x(0)=4-1-3=0\) and \(x'(0)=-4+2+2=0\).

Independence check. At \(t_0=0\) the initial-data vectors of \(\mathrm{e}^{-t}\) and \(\mathrm{e}^{-2t}\) are \((1,-1)\) and \((1,-2)\), which are linearly independent, so \(\mathrm{e}^{-t},\mathrm{e}^{-2t}\) form a basis of \(S_0\).

First order. \(x'=-2x+6\): \(S_0=\{C\mathrm{e}^{-2t}\}\) has dimension 1 and \(x_p=3\), so \(x(t)=3+C\mathrm{e}^{-2t}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(A\) be a real \(m\times n\) matrix. A generalized inverse of \(A\) is any \(n\times m\) matrix \(A^{I}\) satisfying

\[ AA^{I}A=A. \]

The matrix products are defined because \(A^{I}\) has the shape of \(A^{\top}\). No condition on \(m\), \(n\) or the rank of \(A\) is imposed.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An inverse matrix exists only for square nonsingular matrices. The condition \(AA^{I}A=A\) keeps only what is needed to solve equations: whenever \(\boldsymbol{b}=A\boldsymbol{x}\) is reachable, \(A^{I}\boldsymbol{b}\) is a vector that \(A\) maps back to \(\boldsymbol{b}\), because \(A(A^{I}A\boldsymbol{x})=A\boldsymbol{x}\).

Because one equation is a weak requirement, a generalized inverse is in general far from unique, and the notation \(A^{I}\) means "some generalized inverse". Adding the three further Penrose conditions singles out one of them, the Moore-Penrose inverse \(A^+\). A common mistake is to assume properties of \(A^+\), such as symmetry of \(AA^{I}\), for an arbitrary \(A^{I}\).

One-sided inverses are special cases: if \(LA=I_n\) (left inverse, full column rank) then \(ALA=A\); likewise for a right inverse.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Existence: every matrix has a generalized inverse. If \(A=P\begin{pmatrix}I_r&O\\O&O\end{pmatrix}Q\) with \(P,Q\) invertible, then the generalized inverses are exactly \(Q^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}I_r&X\\Y&Z\end{pmatrix}P^{-1}\) with \(X,Y,Z\) arbitrary.
  • Uniqueness: \(A^{I}\) is unique if and only if \(A\) is square and invertible, and then \(A^{I}=A^{-1}\).
  • \(AA^{I}\) and \(A^{I}A\) are idempotent, \(\operatorname{rank}(AA^{I})=\operatorname{rank}(A^{I}A)=\operatorname{rank}A\), and \(\operatorname{rank}A^{I}\ge\operatorname{rank}A\).
  • Consistency: \(A\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{b}\) has a solution if and only if \(AA^{I}\boldsymbol{b}=\boldsymbol{b}\).
  • General solution: if the system is consistent, its solutions are exactly \(\boldsymbol{x}=A^{I}\boldsymbol{b}+(I_n-A^{I}A)\boldsymbol{z}\), \(\boldsymbol{z}\in\mathbb{R}^n\), an affine subspace.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\) (rank \(1\), singular).

Two different generalized inverses. For \(G=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\): \(AG=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\) and \(AGA=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}=A\). The matrix \(G'=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\) works too, and so does \(\tfrac{1}{4}A\), since \(A^3=4A\). Note that \(AG\) is idempotent but not symmetric.

Solving a system. For \(\boldsymbol{b}=(2,2)^{\top}\): \(AG\boldsymbol{b}=(2,2)^{\top}=\boldsymbol{b}\), so the system is consistent. With \(I-GA=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\),

\[ \boldsymbol{x}=G\boldsymbol{b}+(I-GA)\boldsymbol{z} =(2,0)^{\top}+z_2(-1,1)^{\top}, \]

which is the line \(x_1+x_2=2\). For \(\boldsymbol{b}=(1,0)^{\top}\): \(AG\boldsymbol{b}=(1,1)^{\top}\neq\boldsymbol{b}\), so there is no solution.

The figure draws the consistent example with \(\boldsymbol{b}=(2,2)^{\top}\). The two generalized inverses \(G\) and \(G'\) give different particular solutions, \(G\boldsymbol{b}=(2,0)^{\top}\) and \(G'\boldsymbol{b}=(0,2)^{\top}\), but both lie on the same line \(x_1+x_2=2\). Adding \((I-GA)\boldsymbol{z}=z_2(-1,1)^{\top}\) moves along that line, so the choice of \(A^{I}\) changes the starting point, never the solution set.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
Input: linearly independent vectors \(\boldsymbol{a}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{a}_k\) in a real inner product space \(V\) (in \(\mathbb{R}^n\): the dot product).

Steps: for \(j=1,\ldots,k\),

\[ \boldsymbol{v}_j=\boldsymbol{a}_j-\sum_{i=1}^{j-1}\frac{\boldsymbol{a}_j\cdot\boldsymbol{v}_i}{\boldsymbol{v}_i\cdot\boldsymbol{v}_i}\,\boldsymbol{v}_i,\qquad \boldsymbol{q}_j=\frac{\boldsymbol{v}_j}{\|\boldsymbol{v}_j\|}. \]

Output: orthogonal vectors \(\boldsymbol{v}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{v}_k\) and orthonormal vectors \(\boldsymbol{q}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{q}_k\) such that, for every \(j\),

\[ \operatorname{span}\{\boldsymbol{q}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{q}_j\}=\operatorname{span}\{\boldsymbol{a}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{a}_j\}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Each step removes from \(\boldsymbol{a}_j\) its orthogonal projection onto the span of the earlier vectors; what is left, \(\boldsymbol{v}_j\), is the component of \(\boldsymbol{a}_j\) in the orthogonal complement of that span. Dividing by the norm \(\|\boldsymbol{v}_j\|=\sqrt{\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot\boldsymbol{v}_j}\) (the Euclidean norm in \(\mathbb{R}^n\)) then gives a unit vector. Since the \(\boldsymbol{q}_i\) are already orthonormal, the update can equally be written \(\boldsymbol{v}_j=\boldsymbol{a}_j-\sum_{i<j}(\boldsymbol{a}_j\cdot\boldsymbol{q}_i)\boldsymbol{q}_i\).

The figure shows the second step of the example below, drawn in the plane spanned by \(\boldsymbol{a}_1=(1,1,0)^{\top}\) and \(\boldsymbol{a}_2=(1,0,1)^{\top}\) with true lengths. The projection of \(\boldsymbol{a}_2\) onto \(\boldsymbol{v}_1=\boldsymbol{a}_1\) is \(\tfrac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{v}_1\), since \((\boldsymbol{a}_2\cdot\boldsymbol{v}_1)/(\boldsymbol{v}_1\cdot\boldsymbol{v}_1)=\tfrac{1}{2}\). Removing it leaves \(\boldsymbol{v}_2=\boldsymbol{a}_2-\tfrac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{v}_1=(\tfrac{1}{2},-\tfrac{1}{2},1)^{\top}\), the dashed perpendicular moved to the origin, which is orthogonal to \(\boldsymbol{v}_1\).

Step through \(j=1,2,3\): each \(\boldsymbol{v}_j\) is \(\boldsymbol{a}_j\) minus its projections onto the earlier \(\boldsymbol{v}_i\), so it is perpendicular to all of them. Edit an \(\boldsymbol{a}_j\) to make the vectors dependent and watch \(\boldsymbol{v}_j\) shrink to \(\boldsymbol{0}\).

Linear independence is what guarantees \(\boldsymbol{v}_j\neq\boldsymbol{0}\), so that the division is allowed. The output depends on the order of the input: reordering the \(\boldsymbol{a}_j\) generally gives a different orthonormal basis of the same space.

A frequent slip is to project onto the original \(\boldsymbol{a}_i\) instead of the new \(\boldsymbol{v}_i\); the \(\boldsymbol{a}_i\) are not orthogonal, so their projections overlap and the result is wrong.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\boldsymbol{v}_j=\boldsymbol{0}\) occurs exactly when \(\boldsymbol{a}_j\in\operatorname{span}\{\boldsymbol{a}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{a}_{j-1}\}\); run on any list, the algorithm detects dependence, and discarding such \(\boldsymbol{a}_j\) yields an orthonormal basis of the span of the list.
  • Every finite-dimensional inner product space has an orthonormal basis, and every orthonormal list extends to one.
  • In floating-point arithmetic the classical version loses orthogonality; the modified version, which subtracts projections one at a time from the updated vector, is the numerically preferred form.

Beyond the course

Many textbooks collect the Gram-Schmidt output in a factorization \(A=QR\) of a matrix with independent columns, with \(Q\) having orthonormal columns and \(R\) upper triangular. This QR decomposition is not part of Math V.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Three vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^3\). Take \(\boldsymbol{a}_1=(1,1,0)^{\top}\), \(\boldsymbol{a}_2=(1,0,1)^{\top}\), \(\boldsymbol{a}_3=(0,1,1)^{\top}\).

  • \(\boldsymbol{v}_1=(1,1,0)^{\top}\), \(\|\boldsymbol{v}_1\|^2=2\).
  • \(\boldsymbol{a}_2\cdot\boldsymbol{v}_1=1\), so \(\boldsymbol{v}_2=(1,0,1)^{\top}-\tfrac{1}{2}(1,1,0)^{\top}=(\tfrac{1}{2},-\tfrac{1}{2},1)^{\top}\), \(\|\boldsymbol{v}_2\|^2=\tfrac{3}{2}\).
  • \(\boldsymbol{a}_3\cdot\boldsymbol{v}_1=1\) and \(\boldsymbol{a}_3\cdot\boldsymbol{v}_2=\tfrac{1}{2}\), so \(\boldsymbol{v}_3=(0,1,1)^{\top}-\tfrac{1}{2}(1,1,0)^{\top}-\tfrac{1}{3}(\tfrac{1}{2},-\tfrac{1}{2},1)^{\top}=(-\tfrac{2}{3},\tfrac{2}{3},\tfrac{2}{3})^{\top}\).

Check: \(\boldsymbol{v}_3\cdot\boldsymbol{v}_1=0\) and \(\boldsymbol{v}_3\cdot\boldsymbol{v}_2=-\tfrac{1}{3}-\tfrac{1}{3}+\tfrac{2}{3}=0\). Normalizing,

\[ \boldsymbol{q}_1=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1,1,0)^{\top},\qquad \boldsymbol{q}_2=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(1,-1,2)^{\top},\qquad \boldsymbol{q}_3=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(-1,1,1)^{\top}. \]

Detecting dependence. For \(\boldsymbol{a}_1=(1,2)^{\top}\), \(\boldsymbol{a}_2=(2,4)^{\top}\): \(\boldsymbol{v}_2=(2,4)^{\top}-\tfrac{10}{5}(1,2)^{\top}=\boldsymbol{0}\), so \(\boldsymbol{a}_2\) is a multiple of \(\boldsymbol{a}_1\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A linear difference equation of order \(k\) with constant coefficients is

\[ x_{t+k}+a_{k-1}x_{t+k-1}+\cdots +a_1x_{t+1}+a_0x_t=g_t, \]

for \(t=0,1,2,\ldots\), with real constants \(a_0,\ldots,a_{k-1}\), \(a_0\ne0\), and a given sequence \((g_t)\). With the state vector \(\boldsymbol{y}_t=(x_t,x_{t+1},\ldots,x_{t+k-1})^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^k\) it is equivalent to the first-order system

\[ \begin{aligned} \boldsymbol{y}_{t+1}&=C\boldsymbol{y}_t+g_t\boldsymbol{e}_k,\\ C&=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&\cdots&0\\\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\0&0&\cdots&1\\-a_0&-a_1&\cdots&-a_{k-1}\end{pmatrix}, \end{aligned} \]

where \(C\) is the companion matrix and \(\boldsymbol{e}_k\) the last standard basis vector.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The second-order equation generalizes directly: the next value uses the \(k\) most recent values, so \(k\) initial values \(x_0,\ldots,x_{k-1}\) are needed. The homogeneous equation is solved by the roots of the characteristic polynomial \(p(r)=r^k+a_{k-1}r^{k-1}+\cdots+a_0\), now of degree \(k\), so for \(k\ge3\) the roots may be harder to find and a factor is often guessed first (with integer coefficients, every integer root divides \(a_0\)).

The companion form shows why difference equations belong to linear algebra. The first \(k-1\) rows of \(C\) only shift the window forward one period; the last row is the equation itself. Iterating is repeated matrix multiplication, \(\boldsymbol{y}_t=C^t\boldsymbol{y}_0\) in the homogeneous case, and \(\det(\lambda I-C)=p(\lambda)\), so the characteristic roots are the eigenvalues of \(C\).

A common slip is to write the last row of \(C\) with \(+a_i\) instead of \(-a_i\): the signs flip because \(x_{t+k}\) is isolated on the left.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every choice of \(x_0,\ldots,x_{k-1}\) gives exactly one solution; the homogeneous solutions form a \(k\)-dimensional space with a basis of solutions built from the characteristic roots.
  • A root \(r\) of multiplicity \(m\) contributes \(r^t,tr^t,\ldots,t^{m-1}r^t\).
  • General solution = particular solution + general homogeneous solution; for \(g_t=b\) and \(p(1)\ne0\) the equilibrium \(x^*=b/p(1)\) is a particular solution.
  • \(\det C=(-1)^k a_0\ne0\), so \(C\) is invertible.
  • All solutions converge to \(x^*\) if and only if every characteristic root has modulus less than \(1\) (stability).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Third order, distinct roots. \(x_{t+3}-6x_{t+2}+11x_{t+1}-6x_t=0\) has \(p(r)=r^3-6r^2+11r-6=(r-1)(r-2)(r-3)\), so \(x_t=c_1+c_2 2^t+c_3 3^t\). For \(x_0=0\), \(x_1=1\), \(x_2=5\):

\[ c_1+c_2+c_3=0,\qquad c_1+2c_2+3c_3=1,\qquad c_1+4c_2+9c_3=5, \]

giving \(c_1=0\), \(c_2=-1\), \(c_3=1\) and \(x_t=3^t-2^t\). Check: \(x_3=19=6\cdot5-11\cdot1+6\cdot0\). The companion matrix is \(C=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\0&0&1\\6&-11&6\end{pmatrix}\), with eigenvalues \(1,2,3\).

The state \(\boldsymbol{y}_t\) is a window of three consecutive values. In the figure, \(\boldsymbol{y}_0=(0,1,5)^{\top}\) is bracketed above the row and \(\boldsymbol{y}_1=C\boldsymbol{y}_0=(1,5,19)^{\top}\) below it: the first two rows of \(C\) copy \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) one place forward, and the last row produces the new value \(x_3=6\cdot5-11\cdot1+6\cdot0=19\). Repeating the step gives \(x_4=65=3^4-2^4\).

Triple root. \(x_{t+3}-3x_{t+2}+3x_{t+1}-x_t=0\) has \(p(r)=(r-1)^3\), so \(x_t=c_1+c_2t+c_3t^2\): exactly the sequences whose third differences vanish.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
Consider the linear first-order differential equation

\[ x'(t)+p(t)\,x(t)=q(t),\qquad t\in I, \]

with \(p,q\) continuous on an interval \(I\) and \(x'(t)=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}(t)\).

  1. Choose an antiderivative \(P\) of \(p\) and set \(\mu(t)=\mathrm{e}^{P(t)}\), the integrating factor.
  2. Multiply the equation by \(\mu(t)\). Since \(\mu'(t)=p(t)\mu(t)\), the left-hand side becomes an exact derivative: \(\mu x'+\mu p x=(\mu x)'\).
  3. Integrate \((\mu x)'=\mu q\): \(\ \mu(t)x(t)=\int\mu(t)q(t)\,\mathrm{d}t+C\).
  4. Divide by \(\mu(t)>0\): \(\ x(t)=\mathrm{e}^{-P(t)}\Big(\int \mathrm{e}^{P(t)}q(t)\,\mathrm{d}t+C\Big)\), and fix \(C\) from an initial condition.

With \(x(t_0)=x_0\) and \(P(t_0)=0\) this gives the closed form

\[ x(t)=\mathrm{e}^{-P(t)}x_0 +\int_{t_0}^{t}\mathrm{e}^{-(P(t)-P(s))}\,q(s)\,\mathrm{d}s. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The left-hand side \(x'+px\) is not a derivative of anything simple; multiplying by \(\mu\) turns it into the derivative of the product \(\mu x\). Step 2 uses the product rule from differentiation rules and the chain rule for \(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathrm{e}^{P(t)}=P'(t)\mathrm{e}^{P(t)}\).

The two terms of the closed form have a meaning: \(\mathrm{e}^{-P(t)}x_0\) solves the homogeneous equation \(x'+px=0\), and the integral is a particular solution that starts at \(0\), so the solution is homogeneous part plus particular part, as in the general solution of a linear ODE. For constant \(p=-a\) the formula reads \(x(t)=\mathrm{e}^{a(t-t_0)}x_0+\int_{t_0}^t \mathrm{e}^{a(t-s)}q(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\), the scalar form of the variation-of-constants formula that returns in Week 4 with the matrix exponential.

Common slips: forgetting to write the equation with coefficient \(1\) in front of \(x'\) before reading off \(p\); using \(\mathrm{e}^{-P}\) instead of \(\mathrm{e}^{P}\); adding the constant \(C\) after dividing by \(\mu\) instead of before.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mu(t)=\mathrm{e}^{P(t)}\) is never zero, so multiplying by it neither loses nor creates solutions.
  • Any antiderivative of \(p\) can be used: replacing \(P\) by \(P+k\) multiplies \(\mu\) by \(\mathrm{e}^{k}\), which cancels.
  • If \(p,q\) are continuous on \(I\), the method yields the unique solution of each initial value problem on all of \(I\).
  • For constant \(p\neq0\) and constant \(q\) the solution tends to \(q/p\) when \(p>0\); this limit is the equilibrium.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Constant coefficients. \(x'+2x=1\), \(x(0)=0\). Take \(\mu=\mathrm{e}^{2t}\): \((\mathrm{e}^{2t}x)'=\mathrm{e}^{2t}\), so \(\mathrm{e}^{2t}x=\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{e}^{2t}+C\) and \(x=\tfrac{1}{2}+C\mathrm{e}^{-2t}\). From \(x(0)=0\), \(C=-\tfrac{1}{2}\): \(x(t)=\tfrac{1}{2}(1-\mathrm{e}^{-2t})\).

The figure plots the general solution \(x=\tfrac{1}{2}+C\mathrm{e}^{-2t}\) for \(C=1\), \(C=-\tfrac{1}{2}\) and \(C=-1\). The constant \(C\) only shifts the decaying homogeneous part \(C\mathrm{e}^{-2t}\), so every curve approaches the equilibrium \(x=\tfrac{1}{2}=q/p\); the initial condition \(x(0)=0\) picks out the highlighted curve with \(C=-\tfrac{1}{2}\).

Move \(x(0)\) to change the constant \(C\) in \(x=q/p+C\mathrm{e}^{-pt}\): for \(p>0\) every solution approaches the dashed level \(q/p\). Then change \(p\) and \(q\).

Variable coefficient. \(x'+\frac{1}{t} x=t\) on \(t>0\). Here \(P(t)=\ln t\) and \(\mu=t\): \((tx)'=t^2\), so \(tx=\tfrac{t^3}{3}+C\) and \(x(t)=\tfrac{t^2}{3}+\tfrac{C}{t}\). Check: \(x'+\frac{x}{t}=\tfrac{2t}{3}-\tfrac{C}{t^2}+\tfrac{t}{3}+\tfrac{C}{t^2}=t\).

With integration by parts. \(x'-x=t\). Here \(\mu=\mathrm{e}^{-t}\) and \((\mathrm{e}^{-t}x)'=t\mathrm{e}^{-t}\). Integration by parts gives \(\int t\mathrm{e}^{-t}\,\mathrm{d}t=-t\mathrm{e}^{-t}-\mathrm{e}^{-t}+C\), so \(x(t)=-t-1+C\mathrm{e}^{t}\). Check: \(x'=-1+C\mathrm{e}^t\) and \(x+t=-1+C\mathrm{e}^t\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(A=(a_{ij})\) be an \(m\times n\) matrix and \(B\) a \(p\times q\) matrix. The Kronecker product \(A\otimes B\) is the \(mp\times nq\) block matrix

\[ A\otimes B=\begin{pmatrix}a_{11}B&\cdots&a_{1n}B\\\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\a_{m1}B&\cdots&a_{mn}B\end{pmatrix}, \]

whose \((i,j)\) block is the scalar multiple \(a_{ij}B\). No compatibility of sizes is required.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Unlike the ordinary matrix product, the Kronecker product is defined for matrices of any sizes, and the dimensions multiply: every entry of \(A\) is replaced by a whole copy of \(B\). Entry by entry, \((A\otimes B)_{(i-1)p+k,\,(j-1)q+l}=a_{ij}b_{kl}\).

The figure uses \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}\) and \(B=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\) from the examples. In \(A\otimes B\) each entry \(a_{ij}\) becomes the block \(a_{ij}B\); in \(B\otimes A\) each entry \(b_{kl}\) becomes \(b_{kl}A\). Both are \(4\times4\) with the same entries, but arranged differently, so the product is not commutative.

It is the natural tool for linear maps acting on matrices or on two indices at once.

The product is not commutative: \(A\otimes B\) and \(B\otimes A\) have the same size and the same entries, but in a different arrangement. They differ by a reordering of rows and columns (they are similar via a permutation matrix when both factors are square).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Bilinear and associative: \((A+A')\otimes B=A\otimes B+A'\otimes B\), \((cA)\otimes B=c(A\otimes B)\), \((A\otimes B)\otimes C=A\otimes(B\otimes C)\).
  • Mixed product: \((A\otimes B)(C\otimes D)=(AC)\otimes(BD)\) whenever \(AC\) and \(BD\) are defined.
  • \((A\otimes B)^{\top}=A^{\top}\otimes B^{\top}\); if \(A,B\) are invertible, \((A\otimes B)^{-1}=A^{-1}\otimes B^{-1}\).
  • For \(A\) (\(n\times n\)) with eigenvalues \(\lambda_i\) and \(B\) (\(p\times p\)) with eigenvalues \(\mu_k\), the eigenvalues of \(A\otimes B\) are the \(np\) products \(\lambda_i\mu_k\); if \(A\boldsymbol{x}=\lambda\boldsymbol{x}\) and \(B\boldsymbol{y}=\mu\boldsymbol{y}\) then \((A\otimes B)(\boldsymbol{x}\otimes\boldsymbol{y})=\lambda\mu\,(\boldsymbol{x}\otimes\boldsymbol{y})\).
  • Hence the determinant and trace satisfy \(\det(A\otimes B)=(\det A)^p(\det B)^n\) and \(\operatorname{tr}(A\otimes B)=\operatorname{tr}A\cdot\operatorname{tr}B\). For any sizes, the rank satisfies \(\operatorname{rank}(A\otimes B)=\operatorname{rank}A\cdot\operatorname{rank}B\).

Beyond the course

Econometrics texts often pair the Kronecker product with the vec operator, which stacks the columns of a matrix into one long vector. The vec operator is not part of Math V.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
A \(4\times4\) product. For \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}\) and \(B=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\),

\[ A\otimes B=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0&2\\1&0&2&0\\0&3&0&4\\3&0&4&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad B\otimes A=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&1&2\\0&0&3&4\\1&2&0&0\\3&4&0&0\end{pmatrix}. \]

The two differ. Checks: the trace is \(0=\operatorname{tr}A\cdot\operatorname{tr}B=5\cdot0\), and \(\det(A\otimes B)=(-2)^2(-1)^2=4\).

Vectors. For \(\boldsymbol{x}=(1,2)^{\top}\) and \(\boldsymbol{y}=(3,4,5)^{\top}\), \(\boldsymbol{x}\otimes\boldsymbol{y}=(3,4,5,6,8,10)^{\top}\): the block \(1\cdot\boldsymbol{y}\) followed by the block \(2\cdot\boldsymbol{y}\).

Block diagonal. \(I_2\otimes B=\begin{pmatrix}B&O\\O&B\end{pmatrix}\), whereas \(B\otimes I_2\) replaces each entry \(b_{kl}\) by the block \(b_{kl}I_2\); here that is \(\begin{pmatrix}O&I_2\\I_2&O\end{pmatrix}\).

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
Let \(A\) be a real \(m\times n\) matrix and \(\boldsymbol{b}\in\mathbb{R}^m\). A least-squares solution of \(A\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{b}\) is a vector \(\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}\in\mathbb{R}^n\) such that, for all \(\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\),

\[ \|\boldsymbol{b}-A\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}\|\le\|\boldsymbol{b}-A\boldsymbol{x}\|, \]

where \(\|\cdot\|\) is the Euclidean norm. To find it, solve the normal equations

\[ A^{\top}A\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}=A^{\top}\boldsymbol{b}. \]

The vector \(\boldsymbol{b}-A\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}\) is the residual.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
When \(\boldsymbol{b}\) is not in the column space \(\operatorname{Col}(A)\) (the range of \(A\)), the system has no solution, typically because there are more equations than unknowns. Least squares replaces \(\boldsymbol{b}\) by the closest attainable vector, the orthogonal projection \(\boldsymbol{p}\) of \(\boldsymbol{b}\) onto \(\operatorname{Col}(A)\), and solves \(A\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}=\boldsymbol{p}\).

The normal equations say that the residual is orthogonal to every column, since the rows of the transpose are the columns of \(A\): \(A^{\top}(\boldsymbol{b}-A\hat{\boldsymbol{x}})=\boldsymbol{0}\), that is, the residual lies in \(\operatorname{Null}(A^{\top})=\operatorname{Col}(A)^\perp\) given by the Fundamental Theorem of Linear Algebra. The same equations follow from setting the gradient of \(\|\boldsymbol{b}-A\boldsymbol{x}\|^2\), namely \(2A^{\top}A\boldsymbol{x}-2A^{\top}\boldsymbol{b}\), to zero.

Misunderstandings to avoid: the fitted vector \(A\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}\) is always unique, but \(\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}\) need not be; and the formula \((A^{\top}A)^{-1}A^{\top}\boldsymbol{b}\) is valid only when the columns of \(A\) are linearly independent.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The normal equations are always consistent, and their solution set equals the set of least-squares solutions.
  • Since \(\operatorname{Null}(A^{\top}A)=\operatorname{Null}(A)\), the least-squares solutions form the affine subspace \(\{\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}\}+\operatorname{Null}(A)\).
  • The solution is unique if and only if \(A\) has full column rank \(n\); then \(\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}=(A^{\top}A)^{-1}A^{\top}\boldsymbol{b}\) and \(\boldsymbol{p}=H\boldsymbol{b}\) with the symmetric idempotent matrix \(H=A(A^{\top}A)^{-1}A^{\top}\).
  • In general, \(\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}^+=A^+\boldsymbol{b}\), with \(A^+\) the Moore-Penrose inverse, is the unique least-squares solution of minimum norm; it is the one lying in the row space \(\operatorname{Row}(A)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Fitting a line. Fit \(y=c_0+c_1t\) to the points \((0,1),(1,2),(2,2)\). Then

\[ A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix},\quad \boldsymbol{b}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\2\end{pmatrix},\qquad A^{\top}A=\begin{pmatrix}3&3\\3&5\end{pmatrix},\quad A^{\top}\boldsymbol{b}=\begin{pmatrix}5\\6\end{pmatrix}. \]

Solving \(3c_0+3c_1=5\), \(3c_0+5c_1=6\) gives \(c_1=\tfrac{1}{2}\), \(c_0=\tfrac{7}{6}\). The fitted values are \((\tfrac{7}{6},\tfrac{5}{3},\tfrac{13}{6})^{\top}\), the residual is \((-\tfrac{1}{6},\tfrac{1}{3},-\tfrac{1}{6})^{\top}\), whose entries sum to \(0\) and are orthogonal to \((0,1,2)^{\top}\), and the minimal sum of squares is \(\tfrac{1}{6}\).

In the figure, the residuals are the vertical gaps between the data and the fitted line, \(-\tfrac{1}{6}\), \(\tfrac{1}{3}\) and \(-\tfrac{1}{6}\). Their squares add up to \(\tfrac{1}{6}\), and no other line does better. Seen in \(\mathbb{R}^3\), the fitted values \((\tfrac{7}{6},\tfrac{5}{3},\tfrac{13}{6})^{\top}\) are the orthogonal projection of \(\boldsymbol{b}\) onto \(\operatorname{Col}(A)\), and the residual vector is orthogonal to both columns of \(A\).

Switch on your own line and move \(c_0\) and \(c_1\): its sum of squared residuals never drops below that of the least-squares line \(y=\tfrac76+\tfrac12t\). Add a fourth point to see the fit move.

Rank-deficient case. For \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\), \(\boldsymbol{b}=(1,3)^{\top}\): the normal equations reduce to \(x_1+x_2=2\), so every \((2-t,t)^{\top}\) is a least-squares solution, with fitted vector \((2,2)^{\top}\), the projection of \(\boldsymbol{b}\) onto \(\operatorname{span}\{(1,1)^{\top}\}\). The minimum-norm solution is \((1,1)^{\top}=A^+\boldsymbol{b}\), using \(A^+=\tfrac{1}{4}A\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A linear vector ODE (ordinary differential equation) with constant coefficients is a system of differential equations of the form

\[ \boldsymbol{x}'(t)=A\boldsymbol{x}(t), \]

where \(\boldsymbol{x}(t)\in\mathbb{R}^n\) is the state vector, \(\boldsymbol{x}'(t)\) is its componentwise derivative \(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\boldsymbol{x}(t)\), and \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is a constant matrix. The inhomogeneous form is \(\boldsymbol{x}'(t)=A\boldsymbol{x}(t)+\boldsymbol{b}(t)\). An initial value problem fixes \(\boldsymbol{x}(0)=\boldsymbol{x}_0\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The scalar equation \(x'=ax\) has solution \(\mathrm{e}^{at}x_0\). The vector equation behaves the same way along each eigenvector: if \(A\boldsymbol{v}=\lambda\boldsymbol{v}\) (an eigenvalue and eigenvector pair), then \(\boldsymbol{x}(t)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda t}\boldsymbol{v}\) is a solution, because \(\boldsymbol{x}'=\lambda \mathrm{e}^{\lambda t}\boldsymbol{v}=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda t}A\boldsymbol{v}=A\boldsymbol{x}\). With an eigenbasis, every solution is a combination of such modes.

The figure uses the triangular example below, \(A=\begin{pmatrix}-2&1\\0&-3\end{pmatrix}\), with eigenvectors \(\boldsymbol{v}_1=(1,0)^{\top}\) (\(\lambda=-2\)) and \(\boldsymbol{v}_2=(1,-1)^{\top}\) (\(\lambda=-3\)). The solution from \(\boldsymbol{x}_0=(1,2)^{\top}\) is \(3\mathrm{e}^{-2t}\boldsymbol{v}_1-2\mathrm{e}^{-3t}\boldsymbol{v}_2\). Both modes decay, so the curve runs into the origin; the \(\boldsymbol{v}_2\)-mode dies out faster, so the curve arrives along the slower direction \(\boldsymbol{v}_1\).

Change the entries of \(A\) and watch its eigenvalues against the shaded half-plane: while every eigenvalue has negative real part, all solutions tend to \(\boldsymbol{0}\); complex eigenvalues make the orbits spiral.

Each eigenvalue \(\lambda=\alpha+\mathrm{i}\beta\) contributes the size factor \(|\mathrm{e}^{\lambda t}|=\mathrm{e}^{\alpha t}\) and, if \(\beta\neq0\), a rotation with angular speed \(\beta\). Hence the real parts decide long-run behaviour. This is the continuous-time rule; for difference equations \(\boldsymbol{x}_{t+1}=A\boldsymbol{x}_t\) the rule is \(|\lambda|<1\) instead (see stability of a system of linear difference equations). Confusing the two is a common error.

The origin \(\boldsymbol{0}\) is always an equilibrium of \(\boldsymbol{x}'=A\boldsymbol{x}\); stability is meant in the sense of stability of an equilibrium.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Existence and uniqueness: the initial value problem has the unique solution \(\boldsymbol{x}(t)=\mathrm{e}^{At}\boldsymbol{x}_0\), with the matrix exponential.
  • If \(\boldsymbol{v}_1,\dots,\boldsymbol{v}_n\) is an eigenbasis with eigenvalues \(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n\), then \(\boldsymbol{x}(t)=\sum_{i=1}^n c_i\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_it}\boldsymbol{v}_i\), with \(\boldsymbol{c}\) solving \(\sum_ic_i\boldsymbol{v}_i=\boldsymbol{x}_0\).
  • A real matrix with eigenvalue \(\alpha+\mathrm{i}\beta\), \(\beta\neq0\), and eigenvector \(\boldsymbol{v}\) (its conjugate is then also an eigenvalue, see complex conjugate pair of eigenvalues) gives the two real solutions \(\operatorname{Re}\big(\mathrm{e}^{\lambda t}\boldsymbol{v}\big)\) and \(\operatorname{Im}\big(\mathrm{e}^{\lambda t}\boldsymbol{v}\big)\), found with Euler's formula.
  • If \(A\) is not diagonalizable, generalized eigenvectors and the Jordan normal form add terms \(t^k\mathrm{e}^{\lambda t}\).
  • Stability (stable: all solutions bounded; asymptotically stable: all solutions converge): \(\boldsymbol{0}\) is asymptotically stable if and only if every eigenvalue of \(A\) has negative real part; it is unstable if some eigenvalue has positive real part. If all real parts are \(\leq0\), the origin is stable exactly when each eigenvalue with zero real part has equal algebraic and geometric multiplicity.
  • If \(A\) is invertible and \(\boldsymbol{b}\) is constant, \(\boldsymbol{x}^*=-A^{-1}\boldsymbol{b}\) and \(\boldsymbol{x}(t)=\boldsymbol{x}^*+\mathrm{e}^{At}(\boldsymbol{x}_0-\boldsymbol{x}^*)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Triangular matrix. \(A=\begin{pmatrix}-2&1\\0&-3\end{pmatrix}\) has eigenvalues \(-2,-3\) with eigenvectors \((1,0)^{\top}\) and \((1,-1)^{\top}\). For \(\boldsymbol{x}_0=(1,2)^{\top}\): \(c_1+c_2=1\), \(-c_2=2\), so \(c_2=-2\), \(c_1=3\) and

\[ \boldsymbol{x}(t)=\begin{pmatrix}3\mathrm{e}^{-2t}-2\mathrm{e}^{-3t}\\2\mathrm{e}^{-3t}\end{pmatrix}. \]

Check: \(x_1'=-6\mathrm{e}^{-2t}+6\mathrm{e}^{-3t}=-2x_1+x_2\). Both eigenvalues are negative, so \(\boldsymbol{x}(t)\to\boldsymbol{0}\).

Rotation. \(A=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\) has eigenvalues \(\pm\mathrm{i}\). The solution \(\boldsymbol{x}(t)=\big(x_1(0)\cos t-x_2(0)\sin t,\ x_1(0)\sin t+x_2(0)\cos t\big)^{\top}\) circles the origin with constant length: stable, not asymptotically stable.

Saddle. \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}\) has eigenvalues \(3\) and \(-1\); the mode \(\mathrm{e}^{3t}(1,1)^{\top}\) grows, so the origin is unstable although one eigenvalue is negative.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a square matrix \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) (or \(\mathbb{C}^{n\times n}\)), the matrix exponential is

\[ \mathrm{e}^{A}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{A^k}{k!} =I+A+\frac{A^2}{2!}+\frac{A^3}{3!}+\cdots, \]

where \(A^0=I\) and powers are matrix products. For a real variable \(t\), \(\mathrm{e}^{At}=\sum_{k\geq0}\frac{t^k}{k!}A^k\). The series converges entrywise for every square matrix.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The definition copies the Taylor series of the scalar exponential function, \(\mathrm{e}^{a}=\sum a^k/k!\). Its purpose is the same as in the scalar case: \(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathrm{e}^{At}=A\mathrm{e}^{At}\), so \(\mathrm{e}^{At}\boldsymbol{x}_0\) solves the linear vector ODE \(\boldsymbol{x}'(t)=A\boldsymbol{x}(t)\) with \(\boldsymbol{x}(0)=\boldsymbol{x}_0\).

The series is rarely summed directly. One computes \(\mathrm{e}^{At}\) through diagonalization or the Jordan normal form, because \((PDP^{-1})^k=PD^kP^{-1}\): the exponential respects a similarity transformation.

The main pitfall: \(\mathrm{e}^{A}\) is not the matrix of entrywise exponentials \((\mathrm{e}^{a_{ij}})\). For a diagonal matrix the rule is "exponentiate the diagonal entries": the off-diagonal zeros stay \(0\) rather than becoming \(\mathrm{e}^0=1\). For a non-diagonal matrix the off-diagonal entries of \(\mathrm{e}^{A}\) have no entrywise formula (see the examples). Also, \(\mathrm{e}^{A+B}=\mathrm{e}^{A}\mathrm{e}^{B}\) can fail when \(AB\neq BA\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathrm{e}^{O}=I\), \(\ \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathrm{e}^{At}=A\mathrm{e}^{At}=\mathrm{e}^{At}A\), and \(\mathrm{e}^{A(s+t)}=\mathrm{e}^{As}\mathrm{e}^{At}\).
  • If \(AB=BA\), then \(\mathrm{e}^{A+B}=\mathrm{e}^{A}\mathrm{e}^{B}\).
  • \(\mathrm{e}^{A}\) is always invertible with \((\mathrm{e}^{A})^{-1}=\mathrm{e}^{-A}\), and \(\det \mathrm{e}^{A}=\mathrm{e}^{\operatorname{tr}A}\) (determinant, trace).
  • If \(A=PDP^{-1}\) with \(D=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)\), then \(\mathrm{e}^{At}=P\operatorname{diag}(\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_1t},\dots,\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_nt})P^{-1}\); the eigenvalues of \(\mathrm{e}^{At}\) are \(\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_it}\).
  • If \(N^m=O\) (nilpotent), the series stops: \(\mathrm{e}^{Nt}=\sum_{k<m}\frac{t^k}{k!}N^k\). For a Jordan block \(\lambda I+N\) this gives \(\mathrm{e}^{(\lambda I+N)t}=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda t}\mathrm{e}^{Nt}\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Diagonal and scalar. \(\mathrm{e}^{\operatorname{diag}(2,-1)t}=\operatorname{diag}(\mathrm{e}^{2t},\mathrm{e}^{-t})\), and \(\mathrm{e}^{\lambda It}=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda t}I\).

Jordan block. \(A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&2\end{pmatrix}=2I+N\) with \(N=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\), \(N^2=O\). Since \(2I\) and \(N\) commute,

\[ \mathrm{e}^{At}=\mathrm{e}^{2t}(I+tN)=\mathrm{e}^{2t}\begin{pmatrix}1&t\\0&1\end{pmatrix}. \]

Check: \(\det \mathrm{e}^{At}=\mathrm{e}^{4t}=\mathrm{e}^{\operatorname{tr}(At)}\).

Diagonalizable. \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}=P\operatorname{diag}(3,-1)P^{-1}\) with \(P=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}\), \(P^{-1}=\tfrac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}\). Then

\[ \mathrm{e}^{At}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}\mathrm{e}^{3t}+\mathrm{e}^{-t}&\mathrm{e}^{3t}-\mathrm{e}^{-t}\\\mathrm{e}^{3t}-\mathrm{e}^{-t}&\mathrm{e}^{3t}+\mathrm{e}^{-t}\end{pmatrix}, \]

which equals \(I\) at \(t=0\).

The figure shows the route taken in this example. Rather than summing the series for \(\mathrm{e}^{At}\) directly (dashed), one passes to eigenvector coordinates with \(P^{-1}\), where the exponential acts as \(\operatorname{diag}(\mathrm{e}^{3t},\mathrm{e}^{-t})\), and returns with \(P\). Both routes give the same \(\boldsymbol{x}(t)=\mathrm{e}^{At}\boldsymbol{x}_0\) because \(\mathrm{e}^{At}=P\operatorname{diag}(\mathrm{e}^{3t},\mathrm{e}^{-t})P^{-1}\).

Move \(t\): the point \(e^{At}\boldsymbol{x}_0\) runs along the solution curve, its coordinates along the eigenvectors multiplied by \(e^{3t}\) and \(e^{-t}\). At \(t=0\) it is \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) itself, since \(e^{O}=I\).

Rotation. For \(A=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\), \(A^2=-I\), and splitting the series into even and odd powers gives \(\mathrm{e}^{At}=\begin{pmatrix}\cos t&-\sin t\\\sin t&\cos t\end{pmatrix}\), the matrix analogue of Euler's formula.

docs.title: Matrix Representation of a Linear Map
Definition
docs.text:
Let \(V\) and \(W\) be finite-dimensional vector spaces over the same field, with an ordered basis \(\mathcal{B}=(\boldsymbol{v}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{v}_n)\) of \(V\) and an ordered basis \(\mathcal{C}=(\boldsymbol{w}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{w}_m)\) of \(W\). For a linear map \(A\colon V\to W\), write each image of a basis vector in the basis \(\mathcal{C}\):

\[ A\boldsymbol{v}_j=\sum_{i=1}^{m}a_{ij}\,\boldsymbol{w}_i,\qquad j=1,\ldots,n. \]

The matrix representation of \(A\) with respect to \(\mathcal{B}\) and \(\mathcal{C}\) is the \(m\times n\) matrix \([A]_{\mathcal{C},\mathcal{B}}=(a_{ij})\). Its \(j\)-th column is the coordinate vector \([A\boldsymbol{v}_j]_{\mathcal{C}}\). When \(V=W\) and \(\mathcal{B}=\mathcal{C}\), one writes \([A]_{\mathcal{B}}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A linear map is fixed by its values on a basis, so the \(n\) columns \([A\boldsymbol{v}_j]_{\mathcal{C}}\) carry all the information about \(A\). The matrix turns the abstract map into arithmetic on coordinates: \([A\boldsymbol{v}]_{\mathcal{C}}=[A]_{\mathcal{C},\mathcal{B}}\,[\boldsymbol{v}]_{\mathcal{B}}\) for every \(\boldsymbol{v}\in V\).

The figure uses the differentiation example below, with \(\mathcal{B}=(1,t,t^2)\) and \(\mathcal{C}=(1,t)\). Going right along the top applies the map \(D\) itself; going down takes coordinates. Both paths from \(p\) to \((b,2c)^{\top}\) agree: differentiating and then taking coordinates gives the same vector as taking coordinates and then multiplying by \([D]\).

The matrix depends on the map and on both chosen bases, including their order. A frequent mistake is to put the coordinates of \(A\boldsymbol{v}_j\) in rows instead of columns, or to write them in the standard basis when \(\mathcal{C}\) is a different basis. For a map \(\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) with the standard bases the representation is the standard matrix from Math II.

The idea matters for eigenvalue problems, which are basis-free questions about a map: choosing a basis of eigenvectors makes the representing matrix diagonal, which is the content of diagonalization.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For fixed bases, \(A\mapsto[A]_{\mathcal{C},\mathcal{B}}\) is a bijective linear map from \(\mathcal{L}(V,W)\) onto the \(m\times n\) matrices; hence \(\dim\mathcal{L}(V,W)=mn\).
  • Composition becomes matrix multiplication: for \(B\colon U\to V\) and basis \(\mathcal{D}\) of \(U\), \([AB]_{\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D}}=[A]_{\mathcal{C},\mathcal{B}}[B]_{\mathcal{B},\mathcal{D}}\) (see product of linear maps).
  • For the identity map on \(V\) and two ordered bases \(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}\) of \(V\), \([I]_{\mathcal{C},\mathcal{B}}\) equals the identity matrix \(I_n\) if and only if \(\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{B}\); otherwise it converts \(\mathcal{B}\)-coordinates into \(\mathcal{C}\)-coordinates (see change of basis).
  • If \(P\) is the invertible matrix whose columns are the \(\mathcal{B}\)-coordinates of a second basis \(\mathcal{B}'\) of \(V\), then \([A]_{\mathcal{B}'}=P^{-1}[A]_{\mathcal{B}}P\). Representations of one operator are therefore similar and share determinant, trace and eigenvalues.
  • An operator on \(V\) is invertible if and only if one (equivalently every) representing matrix is invertible.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
A map \(\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}^3\). For \(A(x,y)=(x,\,y,\,x+y)\) with standard bases, \(A\boldsymbol{e}_1=(1,0,1)^{\top}\) and \(A\boldsymbol{e}_2=(0,1,1)^{\top}\), so

\[ [A]=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}. \]

Differentiation. Let \(D\colon P_2\to P_1\), \(p\mapsto p'\), with bases \((1,t,t^2)\) and \((1,t)\). Then \(D1=0\), \(Dt=1\), \(Dt^2=2t\), so \([D]=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\0&0&2\end{pmatrix}\). Check: \(p=a+bt+ct^2\) has coordinates \((a,b,c)^{\top}\) and \([D]\,(a,b,c)^{\top}=(b,2c)^{\top}\), i.e. \(p'=b+2ct\).

Same operator, two bases. The operator with standard matrix \(A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}\) satisfies \(A(1,1)^{\top}=(3,3)^{\top}\) and \(A(1,-1)^{\top}=(1,-1)^{\top}\). In the basis \(\mathcal{B}'=\big((1,1)^{\top},(1,-1)^{\top}\big)\) its representation is \(\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\): same map, same eigenvalues \(3\) and \(1\), simpler matrix.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(A\) be a real \(m\times n\) matrix. The Moore-Penrose inverse of \(A\) is the \(n\times m\) matrix \(A^+\) satisfying the four Penrose conditions

\[ \reflow \begin{aligned} &\text{(1) }AA^+A=A,\\ &\text{(2) }A^+AA^+=A^+,\\ &\text{(3) }(AA^+)^{\top}=AA^+,\\ &\text{(4) }(A^+A)^{\top}=A^+A. \end{aligned} \]

For every \(A\) exactly one such matrix exists.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Condition (1) alone defines a generalized inverse, of which there are usually many. Condition (2) makes \(A\) in turn a generalized inverse of \(A^+\), and conditions (3) and (4) require the two products to be symmetric. Together they force \(AA^+\) and \(A^+A\) to be orthogonal projections, which pins down a single matrix.

In the figure, \(A\) (blue) carries the row space \(\operatorname{Row}(A)\) onto the column space \(\operatorname{Col}(A)\) and sends \(\operatorname{Null}(A)\) to \(\boldsymbol{0}\). The Moore-Penrose inverse \(A^+\) (red) runs the other way: it undoes \(A\) from \(\operatorname{Col}(A)\) back onto the row space and sends \(\operatorname{Null}(A^{\top})\) to \(\boldsymbol{0}\). This is why \(AA^+\) projects onto \(\operatorname{Col}(A)\) and \(A^+A\) onto \(\operatorname{Row}(A)\).

Geometrically, \(A^+\) inverts \(A\) where it can and sends the rest to zero: it maps \(\operatorname{Col}(A)\) back onto the row space by undoing \(A\), and maps \(\operatorname{Null}(A^{\top})\) to \(\boldsymbol{0}\).

Two cautions. In general \((AB)^+\neq B^+A^+\). And \(A^+\) does not depend continuously on \(A\): for \(\varepsilon\neq0\), \(\operatorname{diag}(1,\varepsilon)^+=\operatorname{diag}(1,1/\varepsilon)\), which explodes as \(\varepsilon\to0\), while \(\operatorname{diag}(1,0)^+=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Via the singular value decomposition \(A=U\Sigma V^{\top}\): \(A^+=V\Sigma^+U^{\top}\), where the \(n\times m\) matrix \(\Sigma^+\) has \(1/\sigma_i\) in place of each positive singular value \(\sigma_i\) and zeros elsewhere.
  • If \(A\) is square and invertible, \(A^+=A^{-1}\). For a scalar, \(a^+=1/a\) if \(a\neq0\) and \(0^+=0\).
  • Full column rank: \(A^+=(A^{\top}A)^{-1}A^{\top}\), a left inverse. Full row rank: \(A^+=A^{\top}(AA^{\top})^{-1}\), a right inverse.
  • \(AA^+\) is the orthogonal projection onto \(\operatorname{Col}(A)\) and \(A^+A\) the orthogonal projection onto the row space \(\operatorname{Row}(A)\).
  • \(\boldsymbol{x}=A^+\boldsymbol{b}\) is the least-squares solution of \(A\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{b}\) of minimum norm; if the system is consistent, it is its minimum-norm solution.
  • \((A^+)^+=A\), \((A^{\top})^+=(A^+)^{\top}\), \(\operatorname{rank}A^+=\operatorname{rank}A\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
A singular matrix. Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}=2\boldsymbol{u}\boldsymbol{u}^{\top}\) with \(\boldsymbol{u}=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1,1)^{\top}\), so its only positive singular value is \(2\). Then

\[ A^+=\tfrac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{u}\boldsymbol{u}^{\top}=\tfrac{1}{4}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}. \]

Check: \(A^2=2A\), so \(AA^+=A^+A=\tfrac{1}{2}A\), which is symmetric, and \(AA^+A=\tfrac{1}{2}A^2=A\), \(A^+AA^+=\tfrac{1}{8}A^2=\tfrac{1}{4}A=A^+\). By contrast the generalized inverse \(G=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\) gives \(AG=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\), which is not symmetric, so condition (3) fails.

A single column. For \(\boldsymbol{a}=(1,2)^{\top}\) (full column rank), \(\boldsymbol{a}^+=(\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{a})^{-1}\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}=\tfrac{1}{5}(1,2)\). For \(\boldsymbol{b}=(1,1)^{\top}\) the least-squares solution of \(\boldsymbol{a}x=\boldsymbol{b}\) is \(x=\boldsymbol{a}^+\boldsymbol{b}=\tfrac{3}{5}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(V\) be a real vector space with an inner product, written \(\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{y}\) (in \(\mathbb{R}^n\): the dot product), and let \(W\subseteq V\). The orthogonal complement of \(W\) is

\[ W^\perp=\{\boldsymbol{v}\in V\colon{}\boldsymbol{v}\cdot\boldsymbol{w}=0\quad \text{for all }\boldsymbol{w}\in W\}, \]

the set of vectors orthogonal to every vector of \(W\). It is read "\(W\) perp". Usually \(W\) is a subspace.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
\(W^\perp\) collects all directions perpendicular to \(W\). In \(\mathbb{R}^3\) the complement of a plane through the origin is its normal line, and the complement of a line through the origin is the plane perpendicular to it.

The figure draws the first example below: \(W=\operatorname{span}\{(1,1,1)^{\top}\}\) is a line, and \(W^\perp\) is the plane \(x_1+x_2+x_3=0\) with basis \((-1,1,0)^{\top},(-1,0,1)^{\top}\). Every vector of the plane is orthogonal to \((1,1,1)^{\top}\), the two meet only in \(\boldsymbol{0}\), and the dimensions add up to \(1+2=3\).

Switch between a line and a plane \(W\) in \(\mathbb R^3\): \(W^\perp\) is the plane or line through \(\boldsymbol{0}\) perpendicular to it, and \(\dim W+\dim W^\perp=3\). Move \(\boldsymbol{b}\) to see it split as \(\boldsymbol{p}+\boldsymbol{e}\) with \(\boldsymbol{p}\in W\) and \(\boldsymbol{e}\in W^\perp\).

"Complement" does not mean set complement: \(V\setminus W\) is never a subspace, as it misses \(\boldsymbol{0}\). Nor is \(W^\perp\) just some subspace \(U\) with \(V=W\oplus U\): such complements are many, but the orthogonal one is unique. It depends on the inner product; with a different inner product on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) the orthogonal complement can change.

To compute it, it suffices to test a spanning set: if \(W=\operatorname{span}\{\boldsymbol{w}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{w}_k\}\), then \(\boldsymbol{v}\in W^\perp\) if and only if \(\boldsymbol{v}\cdot\boldsymbol{w}_i=0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,k\). In \(\mathbb{R}^n\) this is the homogeneous system \(M^{\top}\boldsymbol{v}=\boldsymbol{0}\) with \(M=\begin{pmatrix}\boldsymbol{w}_1&\cdots&\boldsymbol{w}_k\end{pmatrix}\), so \(W^\perp\) is the null space (kernel) of \(M^{\top}\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(W^\perp\) is a subspace for every subset \(W\), and \(W^\perp=(\operatorname{span}W)^\perp\).
  • \(W\cap W^\perp=\{\boldsymbol{0}\}\) for a subspace \(W\), since \(\boldsymbol{w}\cdot\boldsymbol{w}=0\) forces \(\boldsymbol{w}=\boldsymbol{0}\).
  • If \(V\) is finite-dimensional and \(W\) a subspace: \(V=W\oplus W^\perp\) (a direct sum), \(\dim W+\dim W^\perp=\dim V\), and \((W^\perp)^\perp=W\).
  • Inclusions reverse: \(W_1\subseteq W_2\) implies \(W_2^\perp\subseteq W_1^\perp\). Also \((W_1+W_2)^\perp=W_1^\perp\cap W_2^\perp\).
  • \(\{\boldsymbol{0}\}^\perp=V\) and \(V^\perp=\{\boldsymbol{0}\}\).
  • For a real matrix \(A\), \(\operatorname{Null}(A)=\operatorname{Row}(A)^\perp\) and \(\operatorname{Null}(A^{\top})=\operatorname{Col}(A)^\perp\) (Fundamental Theorem of Linear Algebra).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
A line in \(\mathbb{R}^3\). For \(W=\operatorname{span}\{(1,1,1)^{\top}\}\), \(W^\perp=\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon x_1+x_2+x_3=0\}\), with basis \((-1,1,0)^{\top},(-1,0,1)^{\top}\). Dimensions: \(1+2=3\).

A plane in \(\mathbb{R}^3\). For \(W=\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon x_1-2x_2+x_3=0\}\), \(W^\perp=\operatorname{span}\{(1,-2,1)^{\top}\}\): the coefficient vector is the normal vector of the plane.

A plane in \(\mathbb{R}^4\). For \(W=\operatorname{span}\{(1,0,1,0)^{\top},(0,1,0,1)^{\top}\}\), the conditions \(x_1+x_3=0\) and \(x_2+x_4=0\) give

\[ W^\perp=\operatorname{span}\left\{\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\-1\\0\end{pmatrix},\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix}\right\}, \]

and \(2+2=4\). Note that \((1,0,0,0)^{\top}\) is not in \(W\), yet it is not in \(W^\perp\) either: most vectors lie in neither.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A real \(n\times n\) matrix \(Q\) is orthogonal if

\[ Q^{\top}Q=I, \]

where \(I\) is the \(n\times n\) identity matrix. Equivalently, \(Q\) is invertible with \(Q^{-1}=Q^{\top}\), so also \(QQ^{\top}=I\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The \((i,j)\) entry of \(Q^{\top}Q\) is the inner product \(\boldsymbol{q}_i\cdot\boldsymbol{q}_j\) of columns \(i\) and \(j\) of \(Q\). So \(Q^{\top}Q=I\) says exactly that the columns form an orthonormal basis of \(\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(QQ^{\top}=I\) says the same of the rows. The name is traditional: the columns must be orthonormal, not merely orthogonal. The diagonal matrix \(\operatorname{diag}(2,1)\) has orthogonal columns but is not an orthogonal matrix.

Geometrically, \(\boldsymbol{x}\mapsto Q\boldsymbol{x}\) is a rigid motion that fixes the origin: it preserves lengths, angles and distances. In \(\mathbb{R}^2\) every orthogonal matrix is a rotation or a reflection in a line through the origin.

Both panels start from \(\boldsymbol{e}_1,\boldsymbol{e}_2\) (grey); the images \(\boldsymbol{q}_1=Q\boldsymbol{e}_1\) (blue) and \(\boldsymbol{q}_2=Q\boldsymbol{e}_2\) (red) are the columns of \(Q\), and the shaded square is the image of the unit square. On the right \(Q\) is the matrix \(P=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}\) from the Examples, which is \(S_\theta\) with \(\theta=45^\circ\): it reflects in the line at \(22.5^\circ\) (orange) and has \(\det P=-1\). On the left the sign of its second column is swapped, which gives the rotation \(R_{45^\circ}=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\) with determinant \(1\). In both cases the columns stay on the unit circle and at a right angle, so lengths and angles are preserved; only the orientation of the square differs, and that is what the sign of \(\det Q\) records.

Turn \(\theta\) and drag \(\boldsymbol{x}\): under \(R_\theta\) or \(S_\theta\) the unit circle maps onto itself and \(\|Q\boldsymbol{x}\|=\|\boldsymbol{x}\|\), while \(\det Q=-1\) shows up as a mirrored F. Move the length \(k\) of the second column away from \(1\): the columns stay orthogonal, but \(Q^{\top}Q\neq I\), the circle becomes an ellipse and lengths change. Switch on \(Q^{\top}\) to see that it undoes \(Q\) exactly when \(Q\) is orthogonal.

Orthogonal matrices make changes of basis cheap: if the new basis is orthonormal, its transformation matrix \(Q\) is orthogonal and the inverse needed for new coordinates is just the transpose, \(\boldsymbol{y}=Q^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\). This is why they appear in central factorizations. A symmetric matrix can be diagonalized by an orthogonal matrix, \(A=PDP^{\top}\) with orthonormal eigenvectors as the columns of \(P\). In Week 7, the singular value decomposition \(A=U\Sigma V^{\top}\) of an arbitrary matrix also uses orthogonal \(U\) and \(V\).

A rectangular \(n\times k\) matrix \(Q\) with \(k<n\) and orthonormal columns satisfies \(Q^{\top}Q=I_k\) but not \(QQ^{\top}=I_n\); \(QQ^{\top}\) is then the orthogonal projection onto its column space. The word "orthogonal matrix" is reserved for the square case.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(Q\) preserves inner products and lengths: \((Q\boldsymbol{x})\cdot(Q\boldsymbol{y})=\boldsymbol{x}^{\top}Q^{\top}Q\boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{y}\), hence \(\|Q\boldsymbol{x}\|=\|\boldsymbol{x}\|\). Conversely, a square matrix with \(\|Q\boldsymbol{x}\|=\|\boldsymbol{x}\|\) for all \(\boldsymbol{x}\) is orthogonal.
  • \(\det Q=\pm1\), since \((\det Q)^2=\det(Q^{\top}Q)=\det I=1\) by the product rule for the determinant. In \(\mathbb{R}^2\) and \(\mathbb{R}^3\), \(\det Q=1\) gives a rotation and \(\det Q=-1\) includes a reflection. The converse fails: \(\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\) has determinant \(1\) but is not orthogonal, since its second column has length \(\sqrt{2}\).
  • Every (possibly complex) eigenvalue \(\lambda\) of \(Q\) has \(|\lambda|=1\); the only possible real eigenvalues are \(1\) and \(-1\).
  • Products, inverses and transposes of orthogonal matrices are orthogonal: \((Q_1Q_2)^{\top}Q_1Q_2=Q_2^{\top}Q_2=I\). Sums generally are not: \(I+I=2I\) is not orthogonal.
  • A linear system \(Q\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{b}\) with \(Q\) orthogonal is solved by \(\boldsymbol{x}=Q^{\top}\boldsymbol{b}\), without elimination; equivalently, \(x_i=\boldsymbol{q}_i\cdot\boldsymbol{b}\).
  • Every permutation matrix is orthogonal.
  • Applying the Gram-Schmidt algorithm to any basis of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) and placing the resulting vectors as columns produces an orthogonal matrix.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Rotations and reflections in \(\mathbb{R}^2\). For an angle \(\theta\),

\[ \begin{aligned} R_\theta&=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix},\\ S_\theta&=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&\sin\theta\\\sin\theta&-\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}. \end{aligned} \]

Both have orthonormal columns because \(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta=1\). \(R_\theta\) rotates by \(\theta\) and has \(\det R_\theta=1\); \(S_\theta\) reflects in the line at angle \(\theta/2\) and has \(\det S_\theta=-1\).

For example, \(R_{\pi/2}=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\) maps \((3,4)^{\top}\) to \((-4,3)^{\top}\); both vectors have length \(5\), and their dot product \(-12+12=0\) confirms the right angle.

Checking a \(3\times3\) matrix. Let

\[ Q=\frac{1}{3}\begin{pmatrix}1&2&2\\2&1&-2\\2&-2&1\end{pmatrix}. \]

Each column has squared length \(\tfrac{1}{9}(1+4+4)=1\), and the columns are orthogonal, for instance \(\tfrac{1}{9}(1\cdot2+2\cdot1+2\cdot(-2))=0\); so \(Q^{\top}Q=I\) and \(Q^{-1}=Q^{\top}=Q\). Expanding the determinant gives \(\det Q=\tfrac{1}{27}(-27)=-1\). In fact \(Q\boldsymbol{u}=-\boldsymbol{u}\) for \(\boldsymbol{u}=(1,-1,-1)^{\top}\) and \(Q\boldsymbol{w}=\boldsymbol{w}\) for every \(\boldsymbol{w}\perp\boldsymbol{u}\): \(Q\) is the reflection in the plane orthogonal to \(\boldsymbol{u}\).

Diagonalizing a symmetric matrix. For \(A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}\), the eigenvalues are \(3\) and \(1\) with unit eigenvectors \(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1,1)^{\top}\) and \(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1,-1)^{\top}\). With

\[ P=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}, \]

\(P\) is orthogonal and \(A=PDP^{\top}\) with \(D=\operatorname{diag}(3,1)\): no matrix inversion is needed. Here \(\det P=-1\); swapping the sign of one column gives a rotation instead.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(W\) be a subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) (or of a finite-dimensional inner product space \(V\)). Every \(\boldsymbol{b}\) can be written uniquely as

\[ \boldsymbol{b}=\boldsymbol{p}+\boldsymbol{e},\qquad \boldsymbol{p}\in W,\quad \boldsymbol{e}\in W^\perp, \]

where \(W^\perp\) is the orthogonal complement of \(W\). The vector \(\boldsymbol{p}=\operatorname{proj}_W\boldsymbol{b}\) is the orthogonal projection of \(\boldsymbol{b}\) onto \(W\), and \(\boldsymbol{e}=\boldsymbol{b}-\boldsymbol{p}\) is the error. The map \(\boldsymbol{b}\mapsto\operatorname{proj}_W\boldsymbol{b}\) is a linear map; its matrix \(P\) is the orthogonal projection matrix onto \(W\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Drop a perpendicular from \(\boldsymbol{b}\) to \(W\): its foot is \(\boldsymbol{p}\). The error is orthogonal to every vector of \(W\), not just to \(\boldsymbol{p}\); checking \(\boldsymbol{e}\perp\boldsymbol{p}\) alone is not enough.

In the figure, \(\boldsymbol{e}\) stands perpendicular to the whole plane \(W\), not only to \(\boldsymbol{p}\). For any other \(\boldsymbol{w}\in W\) the points \(\boldsymbol{b}\), \(\boldsymbol{p}\), \(\boldsymbol{w}\) form a right triangle with the right angle at \(\boldsymbol{p}\), so the hypotenuse \(\|\boldsymbol{b}-\boldsymbol{w}\|\) is longer than \(\|\boldsymbol{e}\|\). Pythagoras makes this exact: \(\|\boldsymbol{b}-\boldsymbol{w}\|^2=\|\boldsymbol{e}\|^2+\|\boldsymbol{p}-\boldsymbol{w}\|^2\). So orthogonality is what makes \(\boldsymbol{p}\) the closest point of \(W\) to \(\boldsymbol{b}\) in the Euclidean norm; this best-approximation property is the basis of least squares.

Move the entries of \(\boldsymbol{b}\) and switch between a line and a plane \(W\): the error \(\boldsymbol{e}=\boldsymbol{b}-\boldsymbol{p}\) stays perpendicular to \(W\). Switch on the comparison to see that every other \(\boldsymbol{w}\in W\) lies farther from \(\boldsymbol{b}\) than \(\boldsymbol{p}\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Best approximation: \(\|\boldsymbol{b}-\operatorname{proj}_W\boldsymbol{b}\|<\|\boldsymbol{b}-\boldsymbol{w}\|\) for every \(\boldsymbol{w}\in W\) with \(\boldsymbol{w}\neq\operatorname{proj}_W\boldsymbol{b}\).
  • Onto a line spanned by \(\boldsymbol{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}\): \(\boldsymbol{p}=\dfrac{\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{b}}{\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{a}}\,\boldsymbol{a}\) and \(P=\dfrac{\boldsymbol{a}\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}}{\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{a}}\).
  • With an orthonormal basis \(\boldsymbol{q}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{q}_k\) of \(W\) as columns of \(Q\): \(\boldsymbol{p}=\sum_i(\boldsymbol{q}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{b})\boldsymbol{q}_i\) and \(P=QQ^{\top}\).
  • If \(W=\operatorname{Col}(A)\), the column space of an \(n\times k\) matrix \(A\) of full column rank: \(P=A(A^{\top}A)^{-1}A^{\top}\).
  • A square matrix \(P\) is an orthogonal projection matrix if and only if \(P^2=P\) and \(P^{\top}=P\); it then projects onto its column space.
  • Every orthogonal projection matrix is idempotent, but oblique projections are idempotent without being symmetric, so not every idempotent matrix is an orthogonal projection.
  • \(I-P\) is the orthogonal projection onto \(W^\perp\), and \(\|P\boldsymbol{b}\|\le\|\boldsymbol{b}\|\).
  • The eigenvalues of \(P\) lie in \(\{0,1\}\), and \(\operatorname{rank}P=\operatorname{tr}P=\dim W\) (trace).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Onto a line. Project \(\boldsymbol{b}=(1,2,3)^{\top}\) onto the line spanned by \(\boldsymbol{a}=(1,1,1)^{\top}\): \(\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{b}=6\) and \(\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{a}=3\), so \(\boldsymbol{p}=(2,2,2)^{\top}\) and \(\boldsymbol{e}=(-1,0,1)^{\top}\). Check \(\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{e}=0\). The distance from \(\boldsymbol{b}\) to the line is \(\|\boldsymbol{e}\|=\sqrt{2}\).

Onto a plane. Let \(W=\operatorname{Col}(A)\) with \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\boldsymbol{b}=(1,2,5)^{\top}\). Then \(A^{\top}A=\operatorname{diag}(2,1)\), \(A^{\top}\boldsymbol{b}=(6,2)^{\top}\), so the coefficients are \((3,2)^{\top}\) and

\[ \boldsymbol{p}=(3,2,3)^{\top},\qquad \boldsymbol{e}=(-2,0,2)^{\top},\qquad P=\begin{pmatrix}\tfrac{1}{2}&0&\tfrac{1}{2}\\0&1&0\\\tfrac{1}{2}&0&\tfrac{1}{2}\end{pmatrix}. \]

The error is orthogonal to both columns, \(P\) is symmetric with \(P^2=P\), and \(\operatorname{tr}P=2=\dim W\).
