docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In a Bayesian game \(\langle N,\{A_i\},\{\Theta_i\},\{v_i\},p\rangle\), a profile of pure strategies \(s^*=(s_1^*,\dots,s_n^*)\) with \(s_i^*\colon\Theta_i\to A_i\) is a Bayesian Nash equilibrium (BNE) if for every player \(i\), every type \(\theta_i\) with \(p(\theta_i)>0\) and every action \(a_i\in A_i\),

\[ \sum_{\theta_{-i}}p(\theta_{-i}\mid\theta_i)\,v_i\big(s_i^*(\theta_i),s_{-i}^*(\theta_{-i});\theta\big) \ge\sum_{\theta_{-i}}p(\theta_{-i}\mid\theta_i)\,v_i\big(a_i,s_{-i}^*(\theta_{-i});\theta\big). \]

That is, each type's prescribed action is a best response to the other players' type-contingent strategies, given that type's beliefs. Mixed BNE are defined in the same way with mixed actions for each type.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A BNE is a Nash equilibrium in which "player" is replaced by "player-type". Each type maximizes a conditional expectation of her payoff given her own type, and the expectation is taken over the others' types and hence over their type-dependent actions. Players need not know what the others will actually do; they know the others' strategies, the maps from types to actions.

The condition is imposed type by type (interim), but it is equivalent to an ex ante condition: \(s^*\) is a BNE if and only if it is a Nash equilibrium of the normal-form game whose strategies are the maps \(s_i\) and whose payoffs are ex ante expected payoffs \(\sum_\theta p(\theta)v_i(s(\theta);\theta)\), provided every type has positive probability. Maximizing an average with positive weights is the same as maximizing each term.

A common mistake is to check only the type that is "actually realized". Every type must be optimizing, because the other players' incentives depend on what the unrealized types would do.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If every \(\Theta_i\) is a singleton, a BNE is a Nash equilibrium of the underlying game.
  • A finite Bayesian game has at least one BNE, possibly in mixed strategies, by the Nash existence theorem applied to the ex ante game.
  • If an action is strictly dominant for a type that has positive probability, that type plays it in every BNE.
  • In a BNE of a game with a sequential structure, off-path behaviour need not be optimal; sequential versions such as perfect Bayesian equilibrium add this.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Contribution game. Each player \(i\in\{1,2\}\) chooses \(C\) (contribute) or \(D\) (decline); the good (worth 1 to each) is provided if at least one contributes; contributing costs \(\theta_i\in\{\tfrac{1}{4},2\}\), independently low with probability \(q\).

  1. High-cost type: \(C\) gives \(1-2=-1\), \(D\) gives at least 0, so she plays \(D\).
  2. Low-cost type: \(C\) gives \(1-\tfrac{1}{4}=\tfrac{3}{4}\). \(D\) gives 1 times the probability that the other contributes, which is at most \(q\), because the other's high type never contributes.
  3. With \(q=\tfrac{1}{2}\): \(D\) gives at most \(\tfrac{1}{2}<\tfrac{3}{4}\), so the low type contributes.

The unique BNE is \(s_i^*(\tfrac{1}{4})=C\), \(s_i^*(2)=D\) for both players; the good is provided with probability \(1-\tfrac{1}{4}=\tfrac{3}{4}\).

Changing the prior. The profile in step 3 remains a BNE if and only if \(q\le\tfrac{3}{4}\). For \(q>\tfrac{3}{4}\) a low-cost type would rather free-ride on the other's low type; then, for example, "only player 1's low type contributes" is a BNE (player 2's low type gets \(q>\tfrac{3}{4}\) from \(D\), and player 1's low type gets \(\tfrac{3}{4}>0\) from \(C\)).

The figure fixes the other player's strategy at the candidate profile, so that her low type contributes and her high type declines. A low-cost type then gets \(1-\tfrac{1}{4}=\tfrac{3}{4}\) from \(C\) and \(q\) from \(D\). At \(q=\tfrac{1}{2}\) the \(C\) line lies above the \(D\) line, which is step 3; the shaded region \(q\le\tfrac{3}{4}\) is where the profile remains a BNE, and to the right of the threshold declining and free-riding pays more.

Move the prior \(q\) past \(\tfrac34\): declining then pays the low-cost type more than contributing, and the profile stops being a BNE. A lower contribution cost moves the threshold \(1-\theta_i\) to the right.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In a Bertrand duopoly two firms sell an identical (homogeneous) product and simultaneously choose prices \(p_1,p_2\ge0\). Both have the same constant marginal cost \(c>0\), and market demand \(D(p)\) is continuous and nonincreasing with \(D(c)>0\) (for example \(D(p)=\max\{(a-p)/b,0\}\) with \(a>c\)). Consumers buy from the cheaper firm, and split equally at equal prices:

\[ v_1(p_1,p_2) =\begin{cases} (p_1-c)\,D(p_1) & \text{if } p_1<p_2,\\ \tfrac{1}{2}(p_1-c)\,D(p_1) & \text{if } p_1=p_2,\\ 0 & \text{if } p_1>p_2, \end{cases} \]

and symmetrically for firm 2. Prices are continuous, so \(S_i=[0,\infty)\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
With identical products, a slightly lower price captures the whole market. When both firms charge the same price above cost, undercutting by a small amount roughly doubles a firm's sales at almost the same margin. This undercutting pressure drives prices down to marginal cost.

The figure uses the example below, \(D(p)=100-p\) and \(c=10\), and fixes the rival's price at \(p_2=40\). Matching the rival gives firm 1 half the market, a profit of \(900\); any price just below \(40\) gives the whole market and a profit close to \(1800\); any price above \(40\) sells nothing. The open circle at \(1800\) is never reached, which is why no best "just below" price exists, and repeating this argument at every common price above \(c\) pushes the equilibrium down to \(p_1^*=p_2^*=c\).

With \(p_2=40\), move \(p_1\) towards \(40\) from below: the profit approaches \(1800\) but drops to \(900\) at the tie. Lower \(p_2\) towards \(c\) and the gain from undercutting shrinks to nothing.

The result, two firms already pricing as under perfect competition, is called the Bertrand paradox. It contrasts with the Cournot duopoly, where quantity competition gives a price above cost: the choice of strategic variable (price or quantity) changes the prediction. The paradox disappears with differentiated products, capacity limits or repeated interaction (see repeated game, Week 4).

A common error is to look for an equilibrium with a small positive margin, "just below" the rival. With continuous prices there is no best "just below" price, so best responses can fail to exist (see the best-response correspondence).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The unique Nash equilibrium is \(p_1^*=p_2^*=c\); both firms earn zero profit.
  • Proof by cases (the argument for \(p_2<p_1\) is symmetric):
    • \(p_1=p_2=p>c\): either firm gains by undercutting. If \(D(p)>0\), a price slightly below \(p\) raises its profit from \(\tfrac{1}{2}(p-c)D(p)\) to almost \((p-c)D(p)\); if \(D(p)=0\), a price slightly above \(c\) gives a positive profit.
    • \(c<p_1<p_2\): firm 2 earns \(0\) and can earn a positive profit by pricing slightly above \(c\) (and below \(p_1\)).
    • \(c=p_1<p_2\): firm 1 earns \(0\) and can earn a positive profit by pricing slightly above \(c\) but below \(p_2\).
    • \(p_1<c\) with \(p_1\le p_2\): firm 1 makes a loss and gains by raising its price above \(p_2\).
    • \(p_1=p_2=c\): lowering the price gives a loss and raising it gives zero sales; no deviation helps.
  • In equilibrium each firm's strategy is a best response but is not strictly better than every alternative: any \(p_i>c\) also gives zero against \(p_j=c\).
  • With a discrete price grid of step \(h>0\) (for example cents) that contains \(c\), and \(D(c+h)>0\), both \((c,c)\) and \((c+h,c+h)\) are Nash equilibria; the latter because deviating to \(c\) gives \(0<\tfrac{1}{2} h\,D(c+h)\), and every other deviation gives zero or a loss.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Let \(D(p)=100-p\) and \(c=10\).

Undercutting. At \(p_1=p_2=40\), each firm earns \(\tfrac{1}{2}\cdot30\cdot60=900\). Firm 1 deviating to \(39.99\) earns \(29.99\cdot60.01\approx1799.70\), so \((40,40)\) is not an equilibrium.

At cost. At \(p_1=p_2=10\), each earns \(0\). Raising to \(12\) sells nothing and still earns \(0\); lowering to \(9\) earns \((9-10)\cdot91=-91\). Neither firm can gain, so \((10,10)\) is the equilibrium.

Comparison. The Cournot equilibrium with the same demand and cost has price \(40\) and profit \(900\) per firm; Bertrand gives price \(10\) and profit \(0\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The best-response correspondence of player \(i\) assigns to every profile of the other players' strategies \(s_{-i}\in S_{-i}\) the set of player \(i\)'s best responses:

\[ \reflow \begin{aligned} &BR_i(s_{-i})\\ &=\{s_i\in S_i\colon v_i(s_i,s_{-i})\ge v_i(s_i',s_{-i})\\ &\qquad\text{for every } s_i'\in S_i\}\\ &=\arg\max_{s_i\in S_i}v_i(s_i,s_{-i}). \end{aligned} \]

A correspondence is a rule that assigns to each point a set, which may contain several elements or be the empty set. If \(BR_i(s_{-i})\) contains exactly one element for every \(s_{-i}\), the correspondence is an ordinary function, called a best-response function (or reaction function).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The correspondence summarizes all of player \(i\)'s optimal reactions in one object. Several strategies can be optimal against the same \(s_{-i}\) when payoffs tie, which is why a set is used rather than a single value.

The figure draws Example 3 below: above each rival price \(p_2\) it shows the whole set \(BR_1(p_2)\). For \(p_2<c\) the set is the open region above the diagonal, at \(p_2=c\) it is the vertical ray \([c,\infty)\), and for \(p_2>p^m\) it is the single point \(p^m\), where the correspondence behaves like a function. For \(c<p_2\le p^m\) nothing is drawn above the axis, because the set of best responses is empty.

Move the rival price \(p_2\) and read off \(BR_1(p_2)\) above it: a region for \(p_2<c\), a ray at \(p_2=c\), nothing between \(c\) and \(p^m\), and the single point \(p^m\) beyond.

A frequent mistake is to report only one maximizer when several tie; a Nash equilibrium can then be missed. A second is to assume \(BR_i(s_{-i})\) is always nonempty: in games with infinite strategy sets the supremum of the payoff may not be attained.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A profile \(s^*\) is a Nash equilibrium if and only if \(s_i^*\in BR_i(s_{-i}^*)\) for every \(i\in N\).
  • For two players with interval strategy sets, the Nash equilibria are the intersection points of the graphs of \(BR_1\) and \(BR_2\) drawn in the same \((s_1,s_2)\) plane.
  • If \(S_i\) is finite, \(BR_i(s_{-i})\) is nonempty for every \(s_{-i}\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
1. Ties. Suppose player 1 has strategies \(U\), \(M\), \(D\) and, against player 2's strategy \(L\), receives \(1\), \(3\), \(3\). Then \(BR_1(L)=\{M,D\}\), a two-element set.

2. Cournot reaction functions. In a Cournot duopoly with price \(100-q_1-q_2\) and unit cost \(10\),

\[ BR_1(q_2)=\max\Big\{\frac{90-q_2}{2},\,0\Big\},\qquad BR_2(q_1)=\max\Big\{\frac{90-q_1}{2},\,0\Big\}. \]

Both are single-valued. Their intersection solves \(q_1=(90-q_2)/2\) and \(q_2=(90-q_1)/2\), so \(q_1=q_2=30\).

3. Bertrand: an empty set. In a Bertrand duopoly with identical products, unit cost \(c\), demand \(D(p)=\max\{(a-p)/b,0\}\) with \(a>c\), and monopoly price \(p^m=(a+c)/2\):

  • \(BR_1(p_2)=(p_2,\infty)\) if \(p_2<c\) (any price that sells nothing);
  • \(BR_1(p_2)=[c,\infty)\) if \(p_2=c\) (profit is \(0\) at best);
  • \(BR_1(p_2)=\varnothing\) if \(c<p_2\le p^m\): firm 1 wants to price just below \(p_2\), but no largest price below \(p_2\) exists;
  • \(BR_1(p_2)=\{p^m\}\) if \(p_2>p^m\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In a normal-form game \(\langle N,\{S_i\},\{v_i\}\rangle\), fix the other players' strategies \(s_{-i}\in S_{-i}\). A strategy \(s_i\in S_i\) is a best response of player \(i\) to \(s_{-i}\) if, for every \(s_i'\in S_i\),

\[ v_i(s_i,s_{-i})\ge v_i(s_i',s_{-i}). \]

More generally, if player \(i\) holds a belief \(\pi_i\), a probability distribution over \(S_{-i}\) (finite here), then \(s_i\) is a best response to \(\pi_i\) if it maximizes the expected payoff \(\sum_{s_{-i}\in S_{-i}}\pi_i(s_{-i})\,v_i(s_i,s_{-i})\) over \(S_i\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A best response is what a rational agent does once a belief about the others has been formed: the opponents' play is treated as given and the player solves an ordinary maximization problem. With a probabilistic belief this is expected payoff maximization.

The figure uses the matrix of Example 1 below. If player 2's belief puts probability \(\pi_2(T)\) on \(T\), her expected payoffs are \(3-2\pi_2(T)\) from \(L\), \(1+\pi_2(T)\) from \(M\) and \(0\) from \(R\). The best response is the strategy on the highlighted upper envelope: \(L\) while \(\pi_2(T)<\tfrac{2}{3}\) and \(M\) above \(\tfrac{2}{3}\), where the two lines cross, with both optimal at \(\tfrac{2}{3}\); \(R\) is never a best response. At the belief \(0.4\) of Example 2 the comparison is \(2.2\) against \(1.4\).

Move player 2's belief \(\pi_2(T)\): the best response is the strategy on the green upper envelope, switching from \(L\) to \(M\) at \(\tfrac23\). Raise \(R\)'s payoffs to see when it, too, becomes a best response.

A best response is defined relative to \(s_{-i}\); it changes when \(s_{-i}\) changes. If the belief is wrong, the chosen strategy may not be optimal against what is actually played. Nash equilibrium is the situation in which every player best responds to the strategies the others actually use.

Best responses need not be unique: with ties, all maximizers are best responses, collected in the best-response correspondence \(BR_i(s_{-i})\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(S_i\) is finite, a best response exists for every \(s_{-i}\). If \(S_i\) is compact and \(v_i(\cdot,s_{-i})\) is continuous, existence follows from the extreme value theorem on compact sets; otherwise a best response may fail to exist (undercutting in a Bertrand duopoly).
  • A strictly dominated strategy is never a best response, to any \(s_{-i}\) or any belief.
  • A strictly dominant strategy is the unique best response to every \(s_{-i}\).
  • If \(S_i\) is an interval and \(v_i(\cdot,s_{-i})\) is differentiable and concave, every interior point satisfying the first-order condition \(\partial v_i/\partial s_i=0\) is a best response; if no interior point satisfies it, check the endpoints.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
1. Matrix game. Payoffs \((v_1,v_2)\):

\(L\) \(M\) \(R\) \(T\) \(2,1\) \(3,2\) \(0,0\) \(B\) \(1,3\) \(1,1\) \(4,0\)

Player 1 compares down each column: the best response to \(L\) is \(T\) (\(2>1\)), to \(M\) is \(T\) (\(3>1\)), to \(R\) is \(B\) (\(4>0\)). Player 2 compares along each row: the best response to \(T\) is \(M\) (\(2>1>0\)), to \(B\) is \(L\) (\(3>1>0\)).

2. Belief. If player 2 believes player 1 plays \(T\) with probability \(0.4\) and \(B\) with probability \(0.6\), the expected payoffs are \(L\): \(0.4\cdot1+0.6\cdot3=2.2\), \(M\): \(0.4\cdot2+0.6\cdot1=1.4\), \(R\): \(0\). The best response to this belief is \(L\).

3. Cournot. In a Cournot duopoly with price \(100-q_1-q_2\) and unit cost \(10\), firm 1's profit is \((90-q_1-q_2)q_1\). Setting the derivative \(90-2q_1-q_2\) equal to zero gives \(q_1=(90-q_2)/2\); since the second derivative is \(-2<0\), this is a maximum, and against \(q_2=20\) the best response is \(q_1=35\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The chicken game is a symmetric two-player normal-form game in which each player chooses \(S\) (swerve, yield) or \(T\) (go straight, stand firm), and each player's payoffs satisfy

\[ v_i(T,S)>v_i(S,S) >v_i(S,T)>v_i(T,T). \]

Standing firm is best if the other yields, yielding is best if the other stands firm, and mutual standing firm is the worst outcome. A standard numerical version:

\(S\) \(T\) \(S\) \(0,0\) \(-1,1\) \(T\) \(1,-1\) \(-3,-3\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Chicken is an anti-coordination game: each player wants to do the opposite of the other. It models standoffs such as two drivers heading for each other, price wars, or a confrontation in which backing down is costly but collision is disastrous. In biology the same structure is called the hawk–dove game.

In the figure \(p\) and \(q\) are the probabilities with which players 1 and 2 choose \(T\) in the table above. Player 1's best response \(BR_1\) is \(T\) (\(p=1\)) when \(q<\tfrac{1}{3}\), \(S\) (\(p=0\)) when \(q>\tfrac{1}{3}\), and any \(p\) when \(q=\tfrac{1}{3}\); player 2's \(BR_2\) is the mirror image. Because each player wants the opposite of the other, both curves step downwards and cross three times: at the two pure equilibria and at the mixed equilibrium \((\tfrac{1}{3},\tfrac{1}{3})\).

Raise the crash cost \(c\) and watch the mixed equilibrium \(q=w/(w+c-\ell)\) fall towards \(0\); with \(c<\ell\), standing firm becomes dominant and only \((T,T)\) remains.

Compare it with the Prisoner's Dilemma. There, defecting is best whatever the other does, so there is a single equilibrium. In chicken, no action is dominant, \((T,T)\) is worse than being the one who yields, and the game has three equilibria. The theory alone does not say which one is played; the two pure equilibria require the players to know who yields.

Chicken is a standard example for purification: if each player's toughness, that is the payoff from standing firm, is slightly private, the mixed equilibrium can be reinterpreted as pure behaviour by different types, and the game becomes a Bayesian game.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The pure Nash equilibria are \((S,T)\) and \((T,S)\); \((S,S)\) and \((T,T)\) are not equilibria.
  • There is exactly one further Nash equilibrium in mixed strategies, symmetric, in which each player chooses \(T\) with the probability that makes the other indifferent.
  • No action is strictly dominated, so iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies removes nothing.
  • The mixed equilibrium is Pareto-dominated by \((S,S)\), which is not an equilibrium: it is not Pareto efficient.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Mixed equilibrium in the table above. Let the opponent play \(T\) with probability \(q\). By the indifference principle, \(S\) yields \(-q\) and \(T\) yields \((1-q)-3q=1-4q\); equating gives \(q=\tfrac{1}{3}\). By symmetry each player plays \(T\) with probability \(\tfrac{1}{3}\), and each earns \(-\tfrac{1}{3}\).

  • The crash \((T,T)\) occurs with probability \(\tfrac{1}{9}\).
  • Both players get \(0>-\tfrac{1}{3}\) at \((S,S)\), which confirms the Pareto comparison.
  • In the pure equilibria the payoffs are \((-1,1)\) and \((1,-1)\).

General parameters. With \(v_i(S,S)=0\), \(v_i(T,S)=w>0\), \(v_i(S,T)=-\ell<0\) and \(v_i(T,T)=-c\) with \(c>\ell\), indifference gives \(-\ell q=w(1-q)-cq\), so \(q=w/(w+c-\ell)\). A more costly crash (larger \(c\)) lowers the probability of standing firm. The table above has \(w=1\), \(\ell=1\), \(c=3\), so \(q=1/3\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(E\) be a fact (an event) concerning the players \(N=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) of a game. Define the levels of knowledge recursively:

  • \(K^1(E)\): every player knows \(E\) (mutual knowledge);
  • \(K^{m+1}(E)\): every player knows that \(K^m(E)\) holds, for \(m=1,2,\ldots\)

The fact \(E\) is common knowledge among the players if \(K^m(E)\) holds for every \(m\ge1\): everyone knows \(E\), everyone knows that everyone knows \(E\), and so on at every finite level.

Common knowledge of rationality is the case where \(E\) is the statement "every player is a rational agent".

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
In game theory a player's best choice depends on what the others will do, which depends on what they believe, including what they believe about this player. Common knowledge closes this chain of "beliefs about beliefs" by assuming that every level holds.

The figure draws each level as a smaller set of situations: a situation where \(K^2(E)\) holds also satisfies \(K^1(E)\) and \(E\), but not the other way round. Further levels \(K^3(E),K^4(E),\ldots\) would be drawn as more boxes inside \(K^2(E)\); common knowledge is what lies inside all of them. The labels follow Example 1 below: rationality of player 2 alone deletes \(R\), knowing that player 2 is rational lets player 1 delete \(B\), and the second level lets player 2 delete \(L\).

The main misunderstanding is to treat common knowledge as "everyone knows". Mutual knowledge \(K^1(E)\) does not imply \(K^2(E)\): each player may know \(E\) without knowing that the others know it.

Two standard assumptions use the concept. In a static game of complete information the players, strategy sets and payoff functions are common knowledge. Common knowledge of rationality justifies iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies (Key Results).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Common knowledge of \(E\) implies \(K^m(E)\) for every \(m\); no finite level \(K^m(E)\) implies common knowledge.
  • Deleting a strictly dominated strategy in round \(1\) needs only rationality of its owner. A deletion in round \(k\) needs rationality together with \(k-1\) levels of "everyone knows that ..." about rationality. Common knowledge of rationality therefore supports the whole elimination process, for as many rounds as needed.
  • Common knowledge of rationality does not by itself select a Nash equilibrium: in Battle of the Sexes no strategy is eliminated, and players can still fail to coordinate.
  • In a Bayesian game (Week 5) the common prior over types is assumed to be common knowledge.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
1. Levels of rationality. Player 1 chooses \(T\) or \(B\), player 2 chooses \(L\), \(M\) or \(R\); payoffs are \((v_1,v_2)\).

\(L\) \(M\) \(R\) \(T\) \(2,1\) \(3,2\) \(0,0\) \(B\) \(1,3\) \(1,1\) \(4,0\)
  • Player 2 is rational: \(R\) is strictly dominated by \(M\) (\(2>0\) and \(1>0\)), so \(R\) is not played.
  • Player 1 is rational and knows player 2 is rational: without \(R\), \(T\) beats \(B\) \((2>1,\ 3>1)\).
  • Player 2 is rational, knows player 1 is rational, and knows that player 1 knows player 2 is rational: given \(T\), \(M\) beats \(L\) \((2>1)\).

The prediction \((T,M)\) uses rationality plus two levels of knowledge about rationality.

2. Private versus public. Each of two players is told privately that a meeting is at 9:00. Both know the time (\(K^1\)), but neither knows that the other knows. If the time is announced to both together, each sees the other hear it, and the time becomes common knowledge.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In a game with types \(\theta\in\Theta=\Theta_1\times\cdots\times\Theta_n\), a common prior is a single probability distribution \(p\) on \(\Theta\) that is common knowledge among the players and from which every player's beliefs are derived. Player \(i\) of type \(\theta_i\) (with \(p(\theta_i)>0\)) holds the conditional belief

\[ p(\theta_{-i}\mid\theta_i)=\frac{p(\theta_i,\theta_{-i})}{\sum_{\theta'_{-i}}p(\theta_i,\theta'_{-i})}, \]

where \(\theta_{-i}\) denotes the types of the other players. For finite type spaces, \(p\) is a joint probability mass function of the type profile.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The common prior assumption says that players differ in what they know, not in how they interpret the world: any difference in beliefs comes from different private information. Each type's belief is the conditional probability of the others' types given her own, obtained from \(p\) by Bayes' rule.

The figure shows the correlated example below as one table that both players read. Player 1 of type \(a\) knows she is in the outlined row and rescales it by its total \(0.5\), giving \(p(x\mid a)=0.8\); player 2 of type \(x\) knows she is in the dashed column and rescales it by \(0.6\), giving \(p(a\mid x)=\tfrac{2}{3}\). Different types end up with different beliefs only because they condition on different parts of the same \(p\).

This is what lets a Bayesian game be written as one game with Nature moving first, the Harsanyi transformation: Nature draws \(\theta\) from \(p\), and everyone knows that it does.

When types are correlated, a player's own type is informative about the others', so different types of the same player hold different beliefs; using the marginal distribution of \(\theta_{-i}\) in that case is a frequent error. Only independent types give every type the same belief (Key Results).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Beliefs consistent with a common prior satisfy \(p(\theta_i)\,p(\theta_{-i}\mid\theta_i)=p(\theta)\) for all \(i\) and \(\theta\).
  • With independent types, \(p(\theta)=\prod_jp_j(\theta_j)\) and \(p(\theta_{-i}\mid\theta_i)=p(\theta_{-i})\) for every type \(\theta_i\): all types of player \(i\) hold the same belief, the product of the others' marginals.
  • Not every belief system comes from a common prior: two players without private information who assign different probabilities to the same event cannot share one. More generally (Aumann's agreement theorem), under a common prior, posteriors about an event that are common knowledge must be equal.
  • Under a common prior, a type's expected payoff is computed with \(p(\cdot\mid\theta_i)\); the ex ante expected payoff averages these with weights \(p(\theta_i)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Correlated types. Let \(\Theta_1=\{a,b\}\), \(\Theta_2=\{x,y\}\) and

\(x\) \(y\) \(a\) \(0.4\) \(0.1\) \(b\) \(0.2\) \(0.3\)

The entries sum to 1. Type \(a\) has \(p(a)=0.5\) and believes \(p(x\mid a)=0.4/0.5=0.8\); type \(b\) believes \(p(x\mid b)=0.2/0.5=0.4\). Player 2 has \(p(x)=0.6\), \(p(y)=0.4\), so type \(x\) believes \(p(a\mid x)=0.4/0.6=\tfrac{2}{3}\) and type \(y\) believes \(p(a\mid y)=0.1/0.4=\tfrac{1}{4}\).

Independent types. If each \(\theta_i\in\{\tfrac{1}{4},2\}\) with probability \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) independently, \(p(\theta)=\tfrac{1}{4}\) for each of the four profiles and every type believes the other is low-cost with probability \(\tfrac{1}{2}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In a common-value auction the object has the same value \(v\) for every bidder, but no bidder knows \(v\). Each bidder \(i\) privately observes a signal \(\theta_i\) that is informative about \(v\), and her payoff from winning at price \(p\) is \(v-p\). Bidder \(i\)'s expected value therefore depends on the other bidders' signals as well as on her own.

A two-bidder example with this structure has \(v=\theta_1+\theta_2\), where bidder \(i\) observes only her own component \(\theta_i\), and \(\theta_1,\theta_2\) are independent.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The contrast with a private-value auction is about information, not about who values the object more. With private values, learning a rival's signal would not change one's own valuation; with a common value it would. Classic examples are drilling rights to an oil field of unknown size, or a jar of coins whose total is estimated by eye.

Because the value is shared, winning is itself informative: a bidder wins in a symmetric equilibrium when her signal is the highest, which is bad news about the others' signals. A rational bidder therefore bids on the basis of the conditional expectation of \(v\) given her signal and given that she wins (or, in a second-price auction, given that she is just tied). Ignoring this produces the winner's curse.

Truthful bidding results for private values do not carry over directly. In a second-price auction the case argument for bidding "one's value" fails, because one's value is not known; the equilibrium bid must instead be computed as a Bayesian Nash equilibrium.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• In a symmetric equilibrium with increasing bids, \(\mathbb{E}[v\mid\theta_i]\) overstates what a bidder can expect when she wins; the relevant quantity is \(\mathbb{E}[v\mid\theta_i,\ i\text{ wins}]\).
  • For \(v=\theta_1+\theta_2\) with \(\theta_i\) i.i.d. \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\): the symmetric BNE of the second-price auction is \(b(\theta)=2\theta=\mathbb{E}[v\mid\theta_1=\theta_2=\theta]\), and that of the first-price auction is \(b(\theta)=\theta\).
  • In that example both formats give expected revenue \(\frac{2}{3}\).
  • The Dutch–first-price equivalence holds with common values; the English–second-price equivalence can fail with three or more bidders, because drop-out prices reveal signals.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Take \(v=\theta_1+\theta_2\) with \(\theta_1,\theta_2\) independent and uniform on \([0,1]\).

Second-price. Let bidder 2 bid \(2\theta_2\). Bidder 1 with signal \(x\) who bids \(b\le2\) wins when \(\theta_2<b/2\) and pays \(2\theta_2\), so her expected payoff \(\mathbb{E}[u]\) (written \(u\) because \(v\) is the common value) is

\[ \mathbb{E}[u]=\int_0^{b/2}\big(x+y-2y\big)\,\mathrm{d}y =\int_0^{b/2}(x-y)\,\mathrm{d}y. \]

The integrand is positive for \(y<x\) and negative for \(y>x\), so the payoff is maximized at \(b/2=x\), i.e. \(b=2x\). Revenue is \(2\,\mathbb{E}[\min(\theta_1,\theta_2)]=2\cdot\frac{1}{3}=\frac{2}{3}\).

First-price. Let bidder 2 bid \(\theta_2\). Bidder 1 with signal \(x\) bidding \(b\le1\) wins when \(\theta_2<b\), with expected payoff

\[ \mathbb{E}[u]=\int_0^{b}(x+y-b)\,\mathrm{d}y=xb-\tfrac{1}{2}b^2, \]

maximized at \(b=x\). Revenue is \(\mathbb{E}[\max(\theta_1,\theta_2)]=\frac{2}{3}\).

Numbers. With \(x=0.6\), \(\mathbb{E}[v\mid\theta_1=0.6]=1.1\), but \(\mathbb{E}[v\mid\theta_1=0.6,\ \theta_2<0.6]=0.6+0.3=0.9\). The first-price bid \(0.6\) leaves an expected margin of \(0.3\) when winning.

The figure fixes bidder 1's signal at \(x=0.6\), so the value is \(0.6+\theta_2\). Averaged over all \(\theta_2\) it is \(1.1\), but in the first-price equilibrium bidder 1 wins only in the shaded region \(\theta_2<0.6\), where the average value is \(0.9\). A bid computed from \(1.1\) would overpay on average, which is the winner's curse; the equilibrium bid \(0.6\) sits \(0.3\) below the conditional value.

Move the bid \(b\): a winning bid means \(\theta_2<b\), so it buys only the green average value. The naive bid \(1.1\) overpays, while \(b=x=0.6\) maximizes the expected payoff.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In a Cournot duopoly two firms produce a homogeneous good and simultaneously choose quantities \(q_1,q_2\ge0\). In the standard linear version:

  • the market price is given by the inverse demand \(P(q_1+q_2)=\max\{a-b(q_1+q_2),\,0\}\) with \(a>0\), \(b>0\);
  • each firm has constant marginal cost \(c\) with \(0\le c<a\), so its cost is \(c\,q_i\);
  • firm \(i\)'s payoff is its profit \(v_i(q_1,q_2)=\big(P(q_1+q_2)-c\big)q_i\).

This is a static game of complete information with strategy sets \(S_i=[0,\infty)\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Each firm's profit depends on the rival's quantity through the common price: more output by the rival lowers the price and makes one's own output less valuable. A firm's best response therefore falls as the rival's quantity rises.

The figure uses the numbers below (\(a=100\), \(b=1\), \(c=10\)). Firm 1's reaction line \(q_1=(90-q_2)/2\) gives its profit-maximizing output for each \(q_2\), and firm 2's line \(q_2=(90-q_1)/2\) does the same with the roles swapped; both slope downwards because a larger rival output lowers one's own best output. The only point on both lines is \((30,30)\), where each quantity is a best response to the other, so it is the Nash equilibrium.

Drag the profile \(s\): the orange arrows point to each firm's best response to the other's quantity, and they vanish only at \((30,30)\). Change \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\) to move the equilibrium \(q^*=(a-c)/(3b)\).

The equilibrium is found by computing both best responses and solving them together, which is the definition of a Nash equilibrium applied to continuous strategies. Taking the partial derivative of \(v_i\) with respect to the firm's own quantity, holding the rival's fixed, is the key step; differentiating the sum or the rival's quantity is a common error.

The equilibrium lies between monopoly and perfect competition: the firms together produce more than a monopolist, but less than the competitive output at which price equals marginal cost.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Best response (first-order condition \(a-c-2bq_i-bq_j=0\), with \(\partial^2v_i/\partial q_i^2=-2b<0\)):
\[ BR_i(q_j)=\max\Big\{\frac{a-c-bq_j}{2b},\,0\Big\}. \]
  • Unique Nash equilibrium: \(q_1^*=q_2^*=\dfrac{a-c}{3b}\), total output \(Q^*=\dfrac{2(a-c)}{3b}\), price \(P^*=\dfrac{a+2c}{3}\), profit \(\dfrac{(a-c)^2}{9b}\) per firm.
  • A monopolist would produce \(Q^m=\dfrac{a-c}{2b}\); perfect competition gives \(Q^c=\dfrac{a-c}{b}\); so \(Q^m<Q^*<Q^c\).
  • If each firm produced \(\dfrac{a-c}{4b}\) (half the monopoly output), each would earn \(\dfrac{(a-c)^2}{8b}>\dfrac{(a-c)^2}{9b}\), but this is not an equilibrium: each firm's best response to \(\dfrac{a-c}{4b}\) is \(\dfrac{3(a-c)}{8b}\). The equilibrium is not Pareto efficient for the firms.
  • With \(n\) identical firms the symmetric equilibrium is \(q_i^*=\dfrac{a-c}{(n+1)b}\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Numbers. Let \(a=100\), \(b=1\), \(c=10\), so \(P=100-q_1-q_2\) when \(q_1+q_2\le100\) and \(P=0\) otherwise.

  • Profit: \(v_1=(90-q_1-q_2)q_1\); the first-order condition \(90-2q_1-q_2=0\) gives \(BR_1(q_2)=(90-q_2)/2\) for \(q_2\le90\).
  • By symmetry \(q_2=(90-q_1)/2\). Solving this system of linear equations: \(q_1=(90-(90-q_1)/2)/2\), so \(4q_1=90+q_1\) and \(q_1=30\).
  • Hence \(q_1^*=q_2^*=30=(100-10)/3\), \(P^*=40\), profit \(30\cdot30=900\) each.
  • Check: against \(q_2=30\), producing \(31\) gives \((29)(31)=899\) and producing \(29\) gives \((31)(29)=899\), both below \(900\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In a Dutch auction the price starts high and falls continuously (for example on a clock). The first bidder to stop the clock wins the object and pays the current price; the auction then ends. A strategy specifies, for each valuation \(\theta_i\), the price at which the bidder will stop the clock if nobody has stopped it before.

The Dutch auction is strategically equivalent to the first-price auction: the two games have the same strategy sets (a planned stopping price is a bid) and the same mapping from strategy profiles to outcomes (the highest planned price wins and is paid).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The equivalence is easiest to see by writing the Dutch auction as a normal-form game. A strategy in an extensive-form game must say what to do at every point where the bidder could act. But the only information a bidder ever receives before the auction ends is that no one has stopped yet; once someone stops, the auction is over. So a complete plan reduces to one number: the price at which to stop. Bidder \(i\) planning to stop at \(b_i\) wins if and only if \(b_i\) is the highest planned stopping price, and then pays \(b_i\). That is exactly the first-price sealed-bid rule.

In the figure the clock falls from \(1\). Bidder 1, with \(\theta_1=0.8\), plans to stop at \(b_1=\theta_1/2=0.4\), the two-bidder equilibrium of the Examples; bidder 2 plans to stop at \(b_2=\theta_2/2\), drawn here below \(0.4\). The clock reaches the higher planned price first, so bidder 1 wins and pays \(0.4\), and the lower plan is never reached. Read the two dashed lines as sealed bids and the outcome is the same: the highest bid wins and its bidder pays it.

As a result the Dutch auction has the same equilibria as the first-price auction. With values i.i.d. \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\), the symmetric equilibrium stops the clock at \(\frac{n-1}{n}\theta\). The bidder faces the same trade-off as in a sealed first-price bid: waiting lowers the price paid but raises the risk that a rival stops first.

Unlike the English–second-price equivalence, the Dutch–first-price equivalence does not require private values. Because nothing is learnt during a Dutch auction until it ends, the equivalence also holds with common values or risk-averse bidders.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The Dutch and first-price sealed-bid auctions are strategically equivalent under any assumptions on values and risk attitudes.
  • With i.i.d. \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) private values and \(n\) risk-neutral bidders, the symmetric equilibrium stopping price is \(\frac{n-1}{n}\theta\) and expected revenue is \(\frac{n-1}{n+1}\).
  • There is no weakly dominant stopping rule: the best stopping price depends on the rivals' stopping prices.
  • Under the conditions of the revenue equivalence theorem, the Dutch auction gives the same expected revenue as the English and second-price auctions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Two bidders. Values are i.i.d. \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) and both use the first-price equilibrium \(b(\theta)=\theta/2\) as stopping rule. A bidder with \(\theta=0.8\) stops the clock at \(0.4\). She wins if the rival's stopping price \(\theta_2/2\) is below \(0.4\), i.e. with probability \(0.8\), and expects \((0.8-0.4)(0.8)=0.32\).

Waiting longer. If she instead plans to stop at \(0.3\), she wins with probability \(0.6\) and expects \((0.8-0.3)(0.6)=0.30<0.32\). Stopping earlier, at \(0.5\), gives \((0.3)(1)=0.30<0.32\) as well.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: In an English auction the price starts low and rises continuously (for example on a clock). Each bidder is either active or has dropped out, and dropping out is irreversible. The auction ends when only one bidder remains; that bidder wins and pays the price at which the last rival dropped out. A strategy specifies, for each valuation and each history of observed drop-outs, the price at which the bidder quits.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
With private values, a bidder with valuation \(\theta_i\) should stay active while the price is below \(\theta_i\) (winning at that price would be profitable) and quit once the price reaches \(\theta_i\) (winning at a higher price would be a loss). This rule is a weakly dominant strategy, by the same case argument as in the second-price auction: the bidder's quitting point only decides whether she wins, while the price is set by the strongest rival.

The figure uses the three bidders of the Examples. Each bar shows how long a bidder stays active as the price rises; under the dominant strategy each bar ends at the bidder's value. Bidder 1 quits at \(40\) and bidder 2 at \(55\), which ends the auction: bidder 3 wins at the price \(55\), the second-highest value, and keeps the gap \(70-55=15\) up to her own value.

Under these strategies the highest-value bidder wins and pays the second-highest valuation, exactly the outcome of truthful bidding in the second-price sealed-bid auction. This is the sense in which the two formats are equivalent with private values.

The equivalence is weaker than for the Dutch auction and the first-price auction. In an English auction bidders observe when others drop out. With private values this information is irrelevant, because it does not change one's own value. With interdependent or common values and three or more bidders, the drop-out prices reveal information about the object's worth, so the English and second-price auctions can then differ.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• With private values, "stay in until the price reaches \(\theta_i\)" is weakly dominant, whatever the distribution of values and the number of bidders.
  • In that equilibrium the winner is the bidder with the highest value and the price equals the second-highest value (up to the bid increment in a discrete-step auction).
  • With private values the outcome coincides with the truthful equilibrium of the second-price auction; hence expected revenue is \(\mathbb{E}[\theta_{(n-1)}]\), equal to \(\frac{n-1}{n+1}\) for i.i.d. \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) values.
  • Under the conditions of the revenue equivalence theorem, the English auction yields the same expected revenue as the first-price, second-price and Dutch auctions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Three bidders. Valuations are \(40\), \(55\) and \(70\). Bidding by value, bidder 1 drops out at price \(40\) and bidder 2 at \(55\). Bidder 3 wins at price \(55\) and earns \(70-55=15\). In a second-price sealed-bid auction with truthful bids \((40,55,70)\), bidder 3 also wins and pays \(55\).

Why not stay longer? If bidder 2 (value \(55\)) stayed in until \(65\), she would still lose to bidder 3 and gain nothing. If bidder 3's value were \(60\) instead, bidder 2 staying until \(65\) would make her win at \(60\) and earn \(55-60=-5\). Staying past one's value never helps and sometimes hurts.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In an extensive-form game, a strategy profile \(\sigma\), together with Nature's probabilities, determines for every node \(x\) the probability \(\mathbb{P}_\sigma(x)\) that play passes through \(x\). The path of play (or outcome) of \(\sigma\) consists of the nodes and actions reached with positive probability. For a pure-strategy profile without moves of Nature it is a single sequence of nodes from the root \(x_0\) to one terminal node \(z\).

If \(\sigma^*\) is an equilibrium, its path of play is the equilibrium path. An information set \(h\) is on the equilibrium path if it is reached with positive probability,

\[ \mathbb{P}_{\sigma^*}(h)=\sum_{x\in h}\mathbb{P}_{\sigma^*}(x)>0, \]

and off the equilibrium path if \(\mathbb{P}_{\sigma^*}(h)=0\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The path is what an observer would actually see when the equilibrium is played. A strategy says more: it also prescribes what a player would do at information sets that are never reached. That off-path part describes the threats and promises that keep the other players on the path. In the entry game, the incumbent's plan to fight after entry is never carried out when the entrant stays out, yet it is exactly what keeps the entrant out.

Both panels show the entry game from the Examples, with payoffs (entrant, incumbent). Under the Nash equilibrium (Out, \(F\)) on the left, the path is the single thick green branch Out; the incumbent's node (open circle) is never reached, and her planned \(F\) (orange, dashed) is the off-path threat that keeps the entrant out without ever being carried out. Under the SPNE (In, \(A\)) on the right, the same node is on the path In, \(A\). The tree is identical in both panels; only the strategy profile decides which nodes are on the equilibrium path.

Drag the profile \((p,r)\): the entrant enters with probability \(p\) and the incumbent fights with probability \(r\). With \(p=0\) the incumbent's node is off the path, so every \(r\ge\tfrac{1}{2}\) gives a Nash equilibrium with the same path Out and the same payoffs \((0,2)\). As soon as \(p>0\) the node is on the path, fighting costs the incumbent, and only the subgame-perfect equilibrium (In, \(A\)) remains.

Being on or off the path is a property of the profile, not of the tree. The same information set is on the path under one profile and off it under another, and a subgame that is off the path is still a subgame.

Off-path behaviour does not change anyone's payoff under \(\sigma^*\), so Nash equilibrium puts no optimality requirement on it. This is why Nash equilibria can rest on threats that the player would never carry out. A subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium closes this gap by requiring a Nash equilibrium in every subgame, including the subgames off the path. In games with perfect information, backward induction finds it by fixing optimal behaviour at every node, reached or not, before the path is known.

Describing an equilibrium only by its path is a common mistake: an equilibrium is a full profile, and two different equilibria can have the same path. Conversely, the question "is this profile subgame perfect?" cannot be answered from the path alone.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Payoffs depend only on the path: two profiles that induce the same probabilities over terminal nodes give every player the same expected payoffs, whatever they prescribe off the path.
  • If a player changes her strategy only at information sets that are off the path of \(\sigma\), the path and all payoffs stay the same. Hence the Nash conditions never restrict a player's own off-path actions; these matter only through the incentives of the other players.
  • In a Nash equilibrium, every player acts optimally at each of her information sets on the equilibrium path, given the probabilities with which its nodes are reached; non-credible behaviour can occur only off the path.
  • In a Nash equilibrium, the restriction to a subgame reached with positive probability is automatically a Nash equilibrium of that subgame. So a Nash equilibrium is subgame perfect if and only if its restriction to every subgame off the path is a Nash equilibrium as well.
  • The whole game is a subgame that is always on the path. If a game has no proper subgame, every Nash equilibrium is subgame perfect, whatever it prescribes off the path.

Looking ahead:

  • In a multistage game with observed actions (Week 4), a history \(h^t=(a^0,\dots,a^{t-1})\) is on the path if \(\sigma^*\) generates it with positive probability, and the one-stage deviation principle must be checked at every history, including histories off the equilibrium path.
  • A weak perfect Bayesian equilibrium (Week 7) requires sequential rationality at every information set, given a system of beliefs. Bayes' rule determines the beliefs only on the equilibrium path; off the path they may be any probability distribution over the nodes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Entry game. The entrant chooses Out, giving \((0,2)\) to (entrant, incumbent), or In; after In the incumbent chooses Accommodate \((1,1)\) or Fight \((-1,-1)\).

  • In the Nash equilibrium (Out, \(F\)) the path is just Out, and the incumbent's information set is off the path. Her payoff is \(2\) whatever she plans, so \(F\) is a best response.
  • Any incumbent strategy that fights with probability \(r\ge\tfrac{1}{2}\) supports the same path, since In then gives the entrant \((1-r)-r=1-2r\le0\). These are different equilibria with one path.
  • In the subgame after In, \(F\) gives \(-1<1\), so none of them is subgame perfect. The unique SPNE is (In, \(A\)), whose path is In followed by \(A\).

Sequential Battle of the Sexes. Player 1 chooses \(O\) or \(F\); player 2 observes the choice and replies, with the payoffs of the Battle of the Sexes. A strategy of player 2 lists her reply to \(O\), then her reply to \(F\).

  • \((O,OF)\) is the SPNE: the path is \(O\) then \(O\), with payoffs \((2,1)\), and player 2's reply \(F\) to \(F\) is off the path.
  • \((O,OO)\) is a Nash equilibrium with the same path and payoffs. It differs only off the path, where it answers \(F\) with \(O\); that gives player 2 \(0<2\), so it is not subgame perfect.
  • \((F,FF)\) is a Nash equilibrium with path \(F\) then \(F\) and payoffs \((1,2)\). It rests on the off-path threat to answer \(O\) with \(F\), which player 2 would not carry out (\(0<1\)).

Grim trigger in the Prisoner's Dilemma (Week 4). With the Prisoner's Dilemma stage payoffs \(v(C,C)=(3,3)\), \(v(C,D)=(0,5)\), \(v(D,C)=(5,0)\), \(v(D,D)=(1,1)\) and both players using the grim trigger strategy, the equilibrium path is \((C,C)\) in every period, and the on-path histories are \(h^t=((C,C),\dots,(C,C))\). Every history containing a \(D\) is off the path; there the strategies prescribe \((D,D)\) forever. Subgame perfection needs both checks: on the path, cooperation requires \(\delta\ge\tfrac{1}{2}\); off the path, repeating the stage Nash equilibrium \((D,D)\) is optimal for every \(\delta\).

Off-path beliefs in a weak PBE (Week 7). Player 1 chooses Out, giving \((1,3)\), or \(L\) or \(R\). Player 2 sees only that Out was not chosen, so her two nodes form one information set, and she chooses \(u\) or \(d\). Payoffs: \((L,u)=(2,1)\), \((R,d)=(0,1)\), and \((L,d)=(R,u)=(0,0)\). With belief \(\mu\) on the node after \(L\), \(u\) gives player 2 \(\mu\) and \(d\) gives \(1-\mu\), so \(u\) is optimal if and only if \(\mu\ge\tfrac{1}{2}\).

  • Player 1 plays \(L\), player 2 plays \(u\): the information set is on the path, Bayes' rule forces \(\mu=1\), and \(u\) is optimal; player 1 gets \(2>1\).
  • Player 1 plays Out, player 2 plays \(d\): the information set is off the path, so any \(\mu\le\tfrac{1}{2}\) is allowed and makes \(d\) optimal; then \(L\) and \(R\) give player 1 \(0<1\).

Both are weak PBE, and since the game has no proper subgame, both are also subgame perfect. The second is supported only by an off-path belief that puts probability at least \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) on \(R\), although \(R\) is strictly dominated by Out for player 1.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In a decision problem under uncertainty, each action \(a\in A\) induces a probability distribution (a lottery) over the outcome set \(X\), and the decision maker has a payoff \(v(x)\) for each outcome \(x\in X\).

  • If \(X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}\) is finite, action \(a\) gives outcome \(x_k\) with probability \(p(x_k\mid a)\ge0\), where \(\sum_{k}p(x_k\mid a)=1\).
  • If outcomes are continuous, action \(a\) induces a density \(f(x\mid a)\).

The expected payoff of action \(a\) is

\[ \mathbb{E}[v(x)\mid a]=\sum_{k=1}^{m}p(x_k\mid a)\,v(x_k)\quad\text{or}\quad \mathbb{E}[v(x)\mid a]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}v(x)\,f(x\mid a)\,\mathrm{d}x, \]

and expected payoff maximization means choosing \(a^*\in\arg\max_{a\in A}\mathbb{E}[v(x)\mid a]\). A rational agent facing uncertainty is assumed to behave in this way.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The action does not fix the outcome; it changes the distribution of outcomes. The decision maker compares actions through the expectation of the payoff, computed from the probability mass function \(p(\cdot\mid a)\) or the probability density function \(f(\cdot\mid a)\). Computing \(\mathbb{E}[v(x)\mid a]\) from the distribution of \(x\), without first finding the distribution of \(v(x)\), is LOTUS, in the discrete and the continuous case alike.

The figure draws Example 1. Each action leads to a chance node, that is, to a lottery over outcomes: Safe gives \(x=10\) with probability \(1\), Risky gives \(30\) or \(0\) with probabilities \(0.4\) and \(0.6\). The columns on the right are \(\mathbb{E}[v(x)\mid a]\) for two payoff functions, with the larger value in each column shaded: with \(v(x)=x\) Risky is chosen (\(12>10\)), with \(v(x)=\sqrt x\) Safe is chosen (\(3.162>2.191\)).

Here the payoff values are cardinal: differences between payoffs matter, not only their order. A common misunderstanding is that the rule means maximizing expected money. That holds only when \(v(x)=x\). If \(v\) is a strictly concave utility of money, the same rule is maximization of expected utility and describes a risk-averse decision maker (see expected utility and risk aversion).

In games, the uncertainty often comes from the other players: a belief about their choices plays the role of \(p(\cdot\mid a)\), and from Week 2 a mixed strategy creates such uncertainty deliberately.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The expected payoff is linear in the probabilities: for a compound lottery that runs lottery \(L_1\) with probability \(\lambda\) and \(L_2\) with probability \(1-\lambda\), the expected payoff is \(\lambda\,\mathbb{E}_{L_1}[v]+(1-\lambda)\,\mathbb{E}_{L_2}[v]\).
  • Replacing \(v\) by \(\alpha v+\beta\) with \(\alpha>0\) leaves the ranking of actions unchanged; a nonlinear strictly increasing transformation can reverse it (Example 1).
  • If \(A\) is finite, a maximizing action exists.
  • The expected payoff of an action lies between the smallest and largest payoff among the outcomes it can produce.
  • If every action leads to a single outcome with probability \(1\), the rule reduces to choice under certainty.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
1. Safe or risky. Action Safe pays \(10\) for sure. Action Risky pays \(30\) with probability \(0.4\) and \(0\) with probability \(0.6\). With \(v(x)=x\),

\[ \mathbb{E}[v\mid\text{Safe}]=10,\qquad \mathbb{E}[v\mid\text{Risky}]=0.4\cdot30+0.6\cdot0=12, \]

so Risky is chosen. With \(v(x)=\sqrt x\) instead, \(\sqrt{10}\approx3.162\) against \(0.4\sqrt{30}\approx2.191\), so Safe is chosen: the ranking depends on the payoff scale, not only on the order of outcomes.

2. Continuous outcomes. Under action \(a_1\) the outcome has the uniform distribution on \([0,20]\), so \(f(x\mid a_1)=1/20\) and \(\mathbb{E}[x\mid a_1]=10\). Under \(a_2\) the density is \(f(x\mid a_2)=x/200\) on \([0,20]\) (it integrates to \(400/400=1\)), so

\[ \mathbb{E}[x\mid a_2]=\int_0^{20}x\cdot\frac{x}{200}\,\mathrm{d}x =\frac{20^3}{600}=\frac{40}{3}\approx13.33. \]

With \(v(x)=x\) the decision maker chooses \(a_2\), which shifts probability towards high outcomes.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
An extensive-form game (with complete information) specifies:

  1. a finite set of players \(N\);
  2. a game tree, the rooted and directed version of a tree: a set of nodes with a unique root \(x_0\), edges pointing away from the root, and every other node having exactly one immediate predecessor; nodes without successors are terminal nodes, the others are decision nodes;
  3. for every decision node, the player who moves there (possibly Nature, which chooses according to a fixed probability distribution);
  4. for every decision node, the set of actions available there, each action leading to one immediate successor;
  5. for each player, a partition of her decision nodes into information sets, with the same actions available at all nodes in an information set;
  6. a payoff \(v_i(z)\) for every player \(i\) at every terminal node \(z\).

The whole structure is common knowledge. The game has perfect information if every information set is a single node, and imperfect information otherwise.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The normal-form game lists strategies and payoffs; the extensive form adds the order of moves and what each player knows when she moves. Because each terminal node is reached by a unique path from the root, a terminal node is the same thing as a complete play of the game.

On the left is the entry game of the Examples (Acc. = Accommodate): the entrant \(E\) moves at the root \(x_0\), the incumbent \(I\) moves only after In, and each terminal node carries the payoff vector \((v_E,v_I)\). Every information set is a single node, so the game has perfect information. On the right, player 2 does not observe whether player 1 chose \(O\) or \(F\): the dashed line puts her two nodes into one information set \(h_2\) with the same actions at both, and the tree represents the simultaneous Battle of the Sexes.

"Simultaneous" does not need to mean "at the same time": a move counts as simultaneous with an earlier one when it is made without observing it. This is drawn by placing the later mover's nodes in one information set (a dashed line or oval). Hence a static game can be written in extensive form, and the order in which the simultaneous movers are drawn is irrelevant.

The extra structure is what allows one to ask whether threats are credible. The normal form of an extensive-form game keeps the same Nash equilibria but loses the timing, so it cannot distinguish credible from non-credible behaviour.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every extensive-form game has a normal-form representation whose pure strategies are the strategies of the extensive form; different extensive forms can have the same normal form.
  • If player \(i\) has information sets \(h_1,\ldots,h_m\) with \(k_1,\ldots,k_m\) actions, she has \(k_1k_2\cdots k_m\) pure strategies.
  • Nash equilibria of an extensive-form game are defined as those of its normal form.
  • Every finite game of perfect information has a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium, obtained by backward induction (Zermelo, Kuhn).
  • Each decision node with a singleton information set whose successors do not cut an information set starts a subgame.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Entry game. An entrant \(E\) chooses Out, giving payoffs \((0,2)\) to \((E,I)\), or In. After In, the incumbent \(I\) chooses Accommodate, \((1,1)\), or Fight, \((-1,-1)\). The incumbent has one information set with two actions, so the normal form is 2×2:

Accommodate Fight Out \((0,2)\) \((0,2)\) In \((1,1)\) \((-1,-1)\)

Its pure Nash equilibria are (In, Accommodate) and (Out, Fight). In the second, the threat to fight is never tested because entry does not occur.

Sequential Battle of the Sexes. Player 1 chooses \(O\) or \(F\); player 2 observes the choice and then chooses \(O\) or \(F\). Player 2 has two singleton information sets with two actions each, hence \(2\cdot2=4\) strategies, while player 1 has \(2\). If player 2 does not observe player 1's move, her two nodes form one information set and she has only \(2\) strategies: the game becomes the simultaneous Battle of the Sexes.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In a first-price sealed-bid auction, each of \(n\) bidders submits a bid \(b_i\ge0\) simultaneously and without seeing the others' bids. The highest bid wins (ties are broken at random) and the winner pays her own bid; losers pay nothing. In a private-value auction with valuation \(\theta_i\), bidder \(i\)'s payoff is \(\theta_i-b_i\) if she wins and \(0\) otherwise. A strategy is a bidding function \(b_i(\theta_i)\).

Symmetric equilibrium (uniform case). If \(\theta_1,\dots,\theta_n\) are i.i.d. with the uniform distribution on \([0,1]\), the symmetric Bayesian Nash equilibrium with an increasing bidding function is

\[ b(\theta)=\frac{n-1}{n}\,\theta. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Raising the bid has two opposing effects: it raises the probability of winning and lowers the surplus \(\theta_i-b_i\) obtained when winning. Bidding one's value guarantees a payoff of \(0\), so in equilibrium every bidder shades her bid below her value. The amount of shading, \(\theta/n\) in the uniform case, falls as competition increases.

The figure uses the \(n=3\) numbers of the Examples: a bidder with \(\theta=0.9\) whose two rivals bid \(\tfrac{2}{3}\theta_j\) earns the expected payoff \(\mathbb{E}[u]=(0.9-b)(1.5b)^2\) for \(b\le\tfrac{2}{3}\), and \(0.9-b\) for higher bids, which win for sure. Low bids rarely win and high bids leave little surplus, so the curve peaks at the equilibrium bid \(b(0.9)=0.6\) with payoff \(0.243\). The deviations to \(0.5\) and \(0.65\) (orange) give \(0.225\) and \(0.238\), and bidding the value gives \(0\).

Move the bid \(b\): the expected payoff peaks at \(b(\theta)=\tfrac{n-1}{n}\theta\), here \(0.6\) with payoff \(0.243\). Add bidders and the optimal shading \(\theta/n\) shrinks.

Unlike the second-price auction, the first-price auction has no dominant strategy: the best bid depends on what the rivals bid, so a bidder needs beliefs about the rivals' values and strategies. This is why the equilibrium is computed as a BNE rather than by a dominance argument.

A useful reading of the equilibrium bid: a bidder bids the expected highest rival value, conditional on that value being below her own. In the uniform case the highest of \(n-1\) rival values, given that all are below \(\theta\), has expectation \(\frac{n-1}{n}\theta\), which is exactly \(b(\theta)\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• General formula for independent private values (IPV). For i.i.d. values with a continuous cumulative distribution function (CDF) \(F\) on \([0,\overline\theta]\), the symmetric increasing BNE is \(b(\theta)=\theta-\dfrac{\int_0^\theta F(x)^{n-1}\,\mathrm{d}x}{F(\theta)^{n-1}}\) for \(F(\theta)>0\); for \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) values this gives \(\frac{n-1}{n}\theta\).
  • Win probability. Under a symmetric increasing strategy, a bidder of type \(\theta\) wins if and only if she has the highest value, with probability \(F(\theta)^{n-1}\) (\(=\theta^{n-1}\) for \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\)).
  • Expected revenue with \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) values: the winner is the highest order statistic \(\theta_{(n)}\) with \(\mathbb{E}[\theta_{(n)}]=\frac{n}{n+1}\), so revenue is \(\frac{n-1}{n}\cdot\frac{n}{n+1}=\frac{n-1}{n+1}\), the same as in the second-price auction.
  • Interim expected surplus of type \(\theta\) (uniform case): \(\left(\theta-\tfrac{n-1}{n}\theta\right)\theta^{n-1}=\theta^n/n\).
  • Any bid above one's value is weakly dominated by bidding the value, but bidding the value itself is not a best response to the equilibrium bids of the others when \(\theta>0\).
  • The Dutch auction is strategically equivalent to the first-price auction.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Deriving \(b(\theta)\) for \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) values. Suppose the rivals use \(b(\theta)=\beta\theta\) with \(\beta>0\). A bidder with value \(\theta\) who bids \(b\le\beta\) beats a rival \(j\) when \(\beta\theta_j<b\), which has probability \(b/\beta\), so her expected payoff \(\mathbb{E}[u]\) is

\[ \mathbb{E}[u]=(\theta-b)\left(\frac{b}{\beta}\right)^{n-1}. \]

The first-order condition \(-b^{n-1}+(n-1)(\theta-b)b^{n-2}=0\) gives \(b=\frac{n-1}{n}\theta\), independent of \(\beta\). Consistency requires \(\beta=\frac{n-1}{n}\).

Numbers with \(n=3\). A bidder with \(\theta=0.9\) bids \(0.6\), wins with probability \(0.9^2=0.81\) and expects \(0.3\times0.81=0.243\). Deviating to \(0.5\) wins only if both rivals have \(\theta_j<0.75\): payoff \(0.4\times0.5625=0.225\). Deviating to \(0.65\) wins if \(\theta_j<0.975\): payoff \(0.25\times0.950625\approx0.238\). Both deviations do worse. Expected revenue is \(\frac{2}{4}=0.5\).

Two bidders. With \(n=2\) the bid is \(\theta/2\) and expected revenue is \(\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}[\max(\theta_1,\theta_2)]=\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{2}{3}=\frac{1}{3}\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(G=\langle N,\{A_i\},\{v_i\}\rangle\) be a finite stage game and consider its infinite repetition with discount factor \(\delta\in(0,1)\) and average discounted payoffs \((1-\delta)\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\delta^{t}v_i(a^t)\). The set of feasible payoffs is the convex hull, the smallest convex set containing every stage payoff vector,

\[ V=\operatorname{conv}\{v(a)\colon a\in A\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n. \]

Folk theorem. Let \(v^*\) be the payoff vector of a Nash equilibrium of the stage game. For every feasible \(v\in V\) that is strictly larger, \(v_i>v_i^*\) for all \(i\), there is \(\underline\delta<1\) such that for all \(\delta\in(\underline\delta,1)\) the repeated game has a subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium with average payoff \(v\). Past actions are assumed to be observed.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The name records that the result was known informally before anyone published it. Its message: with patient players and observed actions, repetition does not narrow the predictions; almost anything reasonable can be an equilibrium. "Reasonable" has two parts. Feasibility: the payoff must be an average of stage payoffs. Improvement: each player must get strictly more than in the stage Nash equilibrium that serves as the punishment.

The figure draws the Prisoner's Dilemma of the Examples. The whole quadrilateral is the feasible set \(V\), and the dashed lines are the thresholds \(v_i^*=1\), the stage Nash payoffs of \((D,D)\). The green part, where both players get more than \(1\), is the set of payoffs the theorem sustains for \(\delta\) close to \(1\). It contains cooperation \((3,3)\) and the limit \((2.5,2.5)\) of the alternation payoffs, while the corners \((0,5)\) and \((5,0)\) are feasible but give one player less than \(1\).

Drag the target payoff \(v\): the theorem covers the green part of the feasible set, where both players get more than the stage Nash payoff \(1\). Lower \(\delta\) below \(\tfrac12\) and grim trigger can no longer sustain \((3,3)\).

The course version is proved with the grim trigger strategy: play a path that yields \(v\) and revert to the stage Nash equilibrium forever after a deviation.

The theorem says equilibria exist, not which will be played. It covers efficient outcomes (cooperation, collusion) and inefficient ones alike. It also needs \(\delta\) close to 1; for a fixed \(\delta\) the set of equilibrium payoffs may be much smaller.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The repetition of a stage Nash equilibrium is always an equilibrium, so the equilibrium set is nonempty for every \(\delta\).
  • No folk theorem for subgame-perfect equilibria holds under finite repetition of a stage game with a unique Nash equilibrium: the only SPNE repeats that equilibrium in every period.

Beyond the course

Textbooks also state a minmax folk theorem (Fudenberg and Maskin, 1986), in which the stage Nash payoff is replaced by the minmax payoff, the lowest payoff the other players can hold a player to; payoffs above it are called individually rational. The course does not cover this version.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Prisoner's Dilemma. With \(v(C,C)=(3,3)\), \(v(C,D)=(0,5)\), \(v(D,C)=(5,0)\), \(v(D,D)=(1,1)\), \(V\) is the quadrilateral with these corners and the stage Nash payoff is \((1,1)\). The payoff \((3,3)\) needs \(\delta\ge1/2\). Alternating \((C,D)\) and \((D,C)\) under grim trigger gives averages \(5\delta/(1+\delta)\) and \(5/(1+\delta)\), which tend to \((2.5,2.5)\). A player who gets 0 this period earns \(5\delta/(1+\delta)\) from now on, against 1 from deviating, so this path is sustained if and only if \(\delta\ge1/4\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Forward induction is a principle for selecting among equilibria of an extensive-form game. A player who observes an earlier move interprets it as a deliberate choice by a rational opponent: if the move could only have been worthwhile for the mover under some continuations, the observer expects those continuations. In particular, play after a move is not expected to give the mover less than she could have secured by choosing differently earlier.

The course mentions forward induction only briefly, as a minor remark.

Forward induction is an idea rather than a single equilibrium concept. It is used to discard some subgame-perfect Nash equilibria; formal versions include iterated elimination of weakly dominated strategies in the normal form and stable equilibria (Kohlberg–Mertens).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Backward induction evaluates the present by looking at the future: what will be optimal later determines what is optimal now. Forward induction looks at the past to predict the future: what a player already did reveals what she intends to do. The two can point in different directions when a subgame has several equilibria.

The figure draws the outside-option game of the Examples. After In, player 2 cannot see whether player 1 chose \(A\) or \(B\) (dashed information set), and this subgame on its own has several equilibria. Forward induction reads the move In itself: player 1 gave up the sure \(2\) of Out, and \(B\) can give her at most \(1<2\), so she must intend \(A\). Player 2 then plays \(a\), and only the highlighted path to \((3,1)\) survives.

Subgame perfection treats every subgame as if it started afresh, ignoring how play arrived there. Forward induction adds the information carried by the path. It does not reject subgame perfection; it selects among subgame-perfect equilibria.

Claims should be kept modest: different formalizations can select differently in more complicated games, and forward-induction arguments assume that rationality of the earlier mover is believed even after a move that some equilibria treat as a mistake.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A move that gives up a sure payoff \(\bar v\) signals that the mover expects a continuation giving her more than \(\bar v\); continuations in which she cannot get more than \(\bar v\) are ruled out.
  • In the normal form this often appears as a strictly dominated strategy for the mover (an action plan worse than the outside option), followed by weak dominance for the observer.
  • Forward-induction arguments select among existing equilibria (in the examples here, among the SPNE); they do not create new equilibria.
  • In the burning-money game (Battle of the Sexes preceded by player 1's option to publicly destroy one unit of her own payoff), iterated elimination of weakly dominated strategies leaves only the outcome in which player 1 does not burn and the players coordinate on her preferred equilibrium.

Beyond the course

In signalling games, the intuitive criterion (Cho and Kreps) applies the same reasoning to off-path beliefs in a perfect Bayesian equilibrium: after a message that no type sends, beliefs should put no weight on a type that could not gain from it, compared with its equilibrium payoff, whatever the receiver's response. The course does not cover it.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Outside option. Player 1 chooses Out, giving \((2,2)\), or In, after which both play simultaneously: \((A,a)\mapsto(3,1)\), \((B,b)\mapsto(1,3)\), and \((0,0)\) after miscoordination. This game has three SPNE, with outcomes \((3,1)\) via (In \(A\), \(a\)), and \((2,2)\) via (Out \(B\), \(b\)) and via Out with the mixed subgame equilibrium.

Forward induction: if player 2 sees In, she reasons that player 1 gave up \(2\). Playing \(B\) after In gives player 1 at most \(1<2\), while \(A\) can give \(3>2\). So player 1 must intend \(A\), and player 2's best response is \(a\). Only (In \(A\), \(a\)) survives.

The same argument through dominance. In the reduced normal form, where the payoff-equivalent plans (Out, \(A\)) and (Out, \(B\)) are merged into Out, the strategy (In, \(B\)) gives player 1 either \(0\) or \(1\) and is strictly dominated by Out, which gives \(2\). Remove it. Against the remaining strategies (Out, In \(A\)), player 2 gets \(2\) from both \(a\) and \(b\) against Out, while against In \(A\) she gets \(1\) from \(a\) and \(0\) from \(b\), so \(b\) is weakly dominated. Remove \(b\). Now player 1 compares In \(A\) (\(3\)) with Out (\(2\)) and chooses In \(A\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Game theory is the mathematical study of decision making in a strategic environment: a situation with several decision makers, called players, in which the outcome for each player depends not only on his or her own choice but also on the choices of the others.

A game is specified by

  • the set of players \(N=\{1,\ldots,n\}\);
  • the strategies available to each player, a set \(S_i\) for player \(i\in N\);
  • each player's payoff from every combination of choices, a payoff function \(v_i\);
  • the timing of moves and what each player knows when choosing.

Non-cooperative game theory, the approach used here, models every player as a rational agent who chooses individually; there are no binding agreements between players.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A single-person optimization model fixes everything except the decision maker's own choice. In a strategic environment part of the "environment" consists of other optimizers, so the best choice depends on what one expects the others to do, while they reason in the same way about oneself. This interdependence is what distinguishes a game from a decision problem.

The figure arranges the classification in the Key Results. The rows separate static games, in which no player observes another's choice before choosing, from dynamic ones; the columns separate games whose payoffs are common knowledge from games with private information. Each cell names the solution concept used for that class and the weeks of the course that treat it.

"Game" does not mean recreation: markets, auctions, elections and negotiations are games. Conversely, many agents do not by themselves make a situation strategic: a price-taking firm in a large competitive market treats the price as given, so it faces a decision problem, not a game.

A solution concept is a rule that predicts which strategy combinations will be played. Concepts differ in what they assume about rationality, knowledge and beliefs: iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies uses only common knowledge of rationality, whereas Nash equilibrium also requires correct beliefs.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Games are classified by timing (static: no player observes another's choice before choosing; dynamic: some moves are observed) and by information (complete: the game, including all payoffs, is common knowledge, so every player knows it, knows that the others know it, and so on; incomplete: some players hold private information). This gives four classes.
  • Static games of complete information are written as normal-form games and solved by dominance arguments and Nash equilibrium (Weeks 1–2).
  • Dynamic games of complete information use the extensive form and subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium (Weeks 3–4).
  • Static games of incomplete information are Bayesian games solved by Bayesian Nash equilibrium (Weeks 5–6); dynamic games of incomplete information use perfect Bayesian equilibrium (Week 7).
  • Individually rational choices need not give a collectively good outcome: in the Prisoner's Dilemma the unique equilibrium is not Pareto efficient.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Firms. In a Cournot duopoly two firms choose quantities, and the market price depends on total output. Each firm's profit therefore depends on its rival's quantity: a strategic environment, and a static game of complete information when costs and demand are common knowledge.

Classification. Chess is dynamic with complete information: the rules and payoffs are common knowledge, and in addition each player sees every earlier move (perfect information, a stronger property). A sealed-bid auction in which each bidder privately knows her own valuation is static with incomplete information. The market for lemons, in which only the seller knows the quality of the car, is a game of incomplete information.

Not a game. A monopolist choosing output against a known demand curve, with consumers taking the price as given, solves a single optimization problem; no other player's choice enters its profit.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In an infinitely repeated game with discount factor \(\delta\in(0,1)\), fix a target action profile \(a^c\) and a stage-game Nash equilibrium \(a^*\). The grim trigger strategy of player \(i\) is

  • play \(a_i^c\) at \(t=0\) and in every period \(t\) whose history \(h^t\) consists only of \(a^c\);
  • play \(a_i^*\) after every other history, that is, forever once anyone has deviated from \(a^c\).

It is the trigger strategy whose punishment phase never ends.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Among trigger strategies that punish with a given stage equilibrium \(a^*\), grim trigger punishes longest, so it needs the least patience. Its incentive check is short. After any deviation, play is \(a^*\) forever, which is a Nash equilibrium of every such subgame. On the cooperative path, a player compares the stream \(v_i(a^c)\) forever with the best one-period gain followed by \(v_i(a^*)\) forever.

The figure draws this comparison for the Prisoner's Dilemma of the Examples. Cooperating gives \(3\) in every period (blue); deviating gives \(5\), the payoff of defecting against a cooperator, once and then, because the opponent's grim trigger plays \(D\) forever, the mutual-defection payoff \(1\) in every later period (orange). The deviation gains \(2\) now and loses \(2\) in every later period, so it pays only when the future is discounted heavily: cooperation is optimal if and only if \(\delta\ge\tfrac{1}{2}\).

The filled parts of the bars are the discounted payoffs. At \(\delta=0.4\) the one-period gain outweighs the later losses; raise \(\delta\) past \(\tfrac12\) and cooperation becomes optimal.

The profile in which everyone uses grim trigger is a subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium if and only if, for every player \(i\),

\[ v_i(a^c)\ge(1-\delta)\,d_i+\delta\,v_i(a^*),\qquad d_i=\max_{a_i\ne a^c_i}v_i(a_i,a^c_{-i}), \]

that is, \(\delta\ge\big(d_i-v_i(a^c)\big)/\big(d_i-v_i(a^*)\big)\) when \(d_i>v_i(a^*)\).

Grim trigger is unforgiving: a single mistake destroys cooperation forever, even though both players would prefer to restart. This makes it fragile as a description of behaviour, but it is the standard device for showing which outcomes can be sustained at all.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• In a Prisoner's Dilemma, grim trigger sustains \((C,C)\) in every period as a subgame-perfect equilibrium if and only if \(\delta\) is at least the one-period gain from defecting against a cooperator divided by the difference between that defection payoff and the mutual-defection payoff; in the Examples, \(\delta\ge\frac{5-3}{5-1}=\frac{1}{2}\).
  • The threshold lies in \((0,1)\). It rises when the payoff from defecting against a cooperator or the mutual-defection payoff rises, and falls when the mutual-cooperation payoff rises.
  • Off the path, punishment is credible because \(a^*\) is a stage-game Nash equilibrium.
  • Here \(d_i\) is the best payoff from an action other than \(a^c_i\). If \(a^c\) is itself a stage equilibrium, then \(d_i\le v_i(a^c)\), so deviating gains nothing today. The condition then holds for every \(\delta\) if \(v_i(a^c)\ge v_i(a^*)\) for all \(i\) (in particular if \(a^c=a^*\)). If some player strictly prefers the punishment equilibrium, \(v_i(a^*)>v_i(a^c)\), it holds only for \(\delta\le\big(v_i(a^c)-d_i\big)/\big(v_i(a^*)-d_i\big)\): a strict stage equilibrium is sustained for small \(\delta\), and the condition fails for every \(\delta>0\) when some deviation ties, \(d_i=v_i(a^c)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Prisoner's Dilemma. Take \(v(C,C)=(3,3)\), \(v(C,D)=(0,5)\), \(v(D,C)=(5,0)\), \(v(D,D)=(1,1)\). Cooperating forever gives \(3/(1-\delta)\) in total; defecting now gives \(5+\delta\cdot1/(1-\delta)\). Cooperation is optimal if and only if

\[ 3\ge5(1-\delta)+\delta\iff4\delta\ge2 \iff\delta\ge\tfrac{1}{2}=\tfrac{5-3}{5-1}. \]

At \(\delta=0.4\) a defector gets average \(5(0.6)+0.4=3.4>3\), so cooperation fails.

Collusion in a Cournot duopoly. In a Cournot duopoly with inverse demand \(p=a-Q\) and unit cost \(c<a\), write \(m=(a-c)^2\). Producing half the monopoly output, \((a-c)/4\) each, gives profit \(m/8\); the best deviation against it is \(3(a-c)/8\) with profit \(9m/64\); Cournot play gives \(m/9\). Grim trigger sustains collusion if and only if

\[ \delta\ge\frac{9/64-1/8}{9/64-1/9}=\frac{1/64}{17/576} =\frac{9}{17}\approx0.53. \]
