docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The Prisoner's Dilemma is a symmetric two-player normal-form game \(\langle N,\{S_i\},\{v_i\}\rangle\) with \(N=\{1,2\}\) and \(S_1=S_2=\{M,F\}\) (stay Mum, Fink on the other) with two properties:

  1. for each player, \(F\) gives a strictly higher payoff than \(M\) whatever the other player does, so \(F\) is a strictly dominant strategy;
  2. both players get strictly more when both play \(M\) than when both play \(F\).

The story: two suspects are questioned in separate rooms; each can stay mum or fink. A standard numerical version, with payoffs equal to minus the years in prison:

\(M\) \(F\) \(M\) \(-2,-2\) \(-5,-1\) \(F\) \(-1,-5\) \(-4,-4\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The game is the standard example of a conflict between individual and collective rationality. Each player's reasoning is airtight: whatever the other does, finking shortens her own sentence. Yet when both follow it they reach \((F,F)\) with \((-4,-4)\), while \((M,M)\) would give both \(-2\). The unique Nash equilibrium is therefore not Pareto efficient.

Start at mutual silence \((M,M)\) with \(-2\) each. Player 1 alone gains \(1\) by finking (\(-1>-2\), blue arrow), and player 2 alone gains \(1\) in the same way (red arrow); the same gain of \(1\) appears in the other row and column, which is why \(F\) is strictly dominant. When both follow this reasoning they end in the shaded equilibrium \((F,F)\) with \(-4\) each, which is \(2\) worse for each player than the \(-2\) they could have had at \((M,M)\).

The table starts with the payoffs above. Every orange arrow points towards \(F\), so \((F,F)\) is the only equilibrium, although both players prefer \((M,M)\). Change the payoffs and watch the readout: once \(F\) stops being strictly dominant for a player, or \((M,M)\) stops giving both players more than \((F,F)\), the game is no longer a Prisoner's Dilemma.

The same structure appears in price competition (compare the Bertrand duopoly), arms races, contributions to public goods and the overuse of common resources. In those settings \(M\) is usually called cooperate (\(C\)) and \(F\) defect (\(D\)).

The dilemma does not come from a lack of information or of communication. The game is a static game of complete information, so each player knows all payoffs; a promise to stay mum before the game does not change the fact that \(F\) is better afterwards. Changing the outcome requires changing the game, for example through enforceable contracts or, later in the course, through repeated interaction.

The prediction is also unusually robust. Because \(F\) is strictly dominant, a player needs no belief about the other player, and no assumption that the other is rational, to conclude that she should fink. In games such as the Battle of the Sexes, by contrast, each player's best choice depends on what she expects the other to do.

Compare it with the chicken game. There no action is dominant, mutual toughness is the worst outcome, and there are three equilibria. In the Prisoner's Dilemma mutual defection is bad but each player still prefers it to being the only one who cooperates, and there is a single equilibrium.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \((F,F)\) is the unique Nash equilibrium, and it is a strictly dominant strategy equilibrium.
  • Iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies removes \(M\) for both players in the first round, because \(M\) is a strictly dominated strategy.
  • \((F,F)\) is Pareto dominated by \((M,M)\); the other three profiles are Pareto efficient. In the table, \((M,M)\) also has the largest total payoff, \(-4\), against \(-6\) for one-sided finking and \(-8\) for \((F,F)\).
  • Both defining properties are needed. If mutual \(M\) were not better for both than mutual \(F\), the unique equilibrium would be efficient and there would be no dilemma; if \(F\) were not dominant, the game would no longer force \((F,F)\).
  • With mixed strategies (Week 2), \((F,F)\) is still the unique Nash equilibrium in mixed strategies, because a strictly dominated strategy gets probability \(0\) in every equilibrium.

Looking ahead to Week 4: in a finitely repeated game with the Prisoner's Dilemma as stage game, the unique subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium plays \((F,F)\) in every period. In the infinitely repeated game, mutual cooperation can be sustained by the grim trigger strategy if the discount factor \(\delta\) is large enough.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Solving the table above. For player 1,

\[ \begin{aligned} v_1(F,M)&=-1>-2=v_1(M,M),\\ v_1(F,F)&=-4>-5=v_1(M,F), \end{aligned} \]

so \(F\) is strictly dominant, and by symmetry the same holds for player 2. The equilibrium is \((F,F)\) with payoffs \((-4,-4)\), while \((M,M)\) gives \((-2,-2)\).

Against any belief. Let player 1 believe that player 2 plays \(M\) with probability \(q\). By expected payoff maximization she compares

\[ \begin{aligned} v_1(M,\sigma_2)&=-2q-5(1-q)=3q-5,\\ v_1(F,\sigma_2)&=-q-4(1-q)=3q-4, \end{aligned} \]

so \(F\) earns exactly \(1\) more for every \(q\in[0,1]\), and no belief about the other suspect makes staying mum a best response.

Changing the game. Suppose an enforceable agreement adds \(2\) years to the sentence of a suspect who finks. The table becomes \((M,M)=(-2,-2)\), \((M,F)=(-5,-3)\), \((F,M)=(-3,-5)\) and \((F,F)=(-6,-6)\). Now \(M\) is strictly dominant (\(-2>-3\) and \(-5>-6\)), and \((M,M)\) is the unique Nash equilibrium. Any extra penalty above \(1\) year has this effect; a penalty below \(1\) year leaves \(F\) dominant.

The cooperate–defect version (Week 4). The pages on repeated games use \(v(C,C)=(3,3)\), \(v(C,D)=(0,5)\), \(v(D,C)=(5,0)\) and \(v(D,D)=(1,1)\). Defecting is strictly dominant (\(5>3\) and \(1>0\)), and \((3,3)\) beats the equilibrium payoff \((1,1)\). When the game is repeated infinitely with discount factor \(\delta\), cooperating forever against grim trigger gives \(\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\delta^t\cdot3=3/(1-\delta)\), while defecting at once gives \(5+\delta/(1-\delta)\). Cooperation is at least as good if and only if \(3\ge5(1-\delta)+\delta\), that is,

\[ \delta\ge\frac{5-3}{5-1}=\frac{1}{2}. \]

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In a private-value auction, one indivisible object is sold to one of \(n\) bidders. Bidder \(i\) has a valuation \(\theta_i\) for the object that is known only to \(i\) and that does not depend on the information of the other bidders. In a sealed-bid format the bidders simultaneously submit bids \(b_i\ge0\) (open formats such as the English and Dutch auctions work analogously with planned drop-out or stopping prices); the auction rules map the bid profile \((b_1,\dots,b_n)\) to a winner and to payments \(p_i\). Bidder \(i\)'s payoff is

\[ v_i=\begin{cases}\theta_i-p_i & \text{if } i \text{ wins},\\ -p_i & \text{if } i \text{ loses}\end{cases} \]

(in first- and second-price auctions a loser pays \(p_i=0\)). In the independent private-values (IPV) model the valuations \(\theta_1,\dots,\theta_n\) are i.i.d. draws from a cumulative distribution function \(F\) on an interval \([\underline\theta,\overline\theta]\), and \(F\) is common knowledge.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An auction with private values is a Bayesian game: bidder \(i\)'s type is \(\theta_i\), the distribution \(F\) plays the role of the common prior, and a strategy is a bidding function \(b_i(\theta_i)\) giving a bid for every possible valuation. The solution concept is Bayesian Nash equilibrium: every type's bid maximizes its expected payoff given the rivals' bidding functions.

The figure draws the two equilibrium bidding functions of the Examples (\(n=2\), values \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\)). A strategy is the whole line, one bid for every type, not a single number: in the second-price auction each type bids its value, in the first-price auction each type shades its bid to half its value. The type \(\theta_1=0.7\) therefore bids \(0.7\) or \(0.35\), yet both bids give the same interim expected payoff \(0.245\).

Move the type \(\theta\): the two formats prescribe different bids, \(\theta\) and \(\tfrac{n-1}{n}\theta\), yet the same interim payoff \(\theta^n/n\). Add bidders and the first-price line rises towards the diagonal.

"Private" refers to two things: each bidder knows its own value, and learning the rivals' information would not change that value. This is what distinguishes it from a common-value auction, where the rivals' signals are informative about one's own value. A frequent confusion is to think that private values must differ across bidders; they may coincide, the point is only that each value is a matter of personal taste rather than an estimate of a shared quantity.

The format matters for strategy but, under the conditions of the revenue equivalence theorem, not for expected revenue.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• In a second-price auction, bidding \(b_i(\theta_i)=\theta_i\) is weakly dominant for every type.
  • In a first-price auction with IPV values from \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\), the symmetric BNE is \(b(\theta)=\tfrac{n-1}{n}\theta\): bids are shaded below value.
  • With IPV values from \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\), both formats give expected revenue \(\tfrac{n-1}{n+1}\), the expected second-highest valuation.
  • In the standard formats the object goes to the bidder with the highest valuation in the symmetric equilibrium, so the allocation is efficient.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Two bidders, uniform values. Let \(n=2\) and \(\theta_1,\theta_2\sim \operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) independent. In a second-price auction, bidder 1 bids \(\theta_1\). If \(\theta_1=0.7\), she wins with probability \(0.7\) and pays \(\theta_2\) when \(\theta_2<0.7\), so her expected payoff is \(\int_0^{0.7}(0.7-y)\,\mathrm{d}y=0.7^2/2=0.245\).

In a first-price auction the symmetric BNE is \(b(\theta)=\theta/2\). With \(\theta_1=0.7\) she bids \(0.35\), wins with probability \(\mathbb{P}(\theta_2/2<0.35)=0.7\) and gets \((0.7-0.35)(0.7)=0.245\), the same interim expected payoff.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A pure strategy of player \(i\) is a deterministic plan of action: it specifies, without any randomization, which action the player takes in every situation in which he or she may have to move. The set of all pure strategies of player \(i\) is denoted \(S_i\).

A pure-strategy profile is a list \(s=(s_1,\ldots,s_n)\) with \(s_i\in S_i\) for every player \(i\in N=\{1,\ldots,n\}\); the set of all profiles is the Cartesian product \(S=S_1\times\cdots\times S_n\). For player \(i\),

\[ s_{-i}=(s_1,\ldots,s_{i-1},s_{i+1},\ldots,s_n) \in S_{-i}=\prod_{j\ne i}S_j \]

collects the strategies of all other players, and \(s=(s_i,s_{-i})\). Writing \((s_i',s_{-i})\) means that player \(i\) switches to \(s_i'\) while everyone else keeps their strategy.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A strategy is a complete description of how a player will play, detailed enough that someone else could carry it out on the player's behalf. In a static game of complete information nobody observes anything before choosing, so a pure strategy is just one action.

The figure lays out \(S=S_1\times S_2\) for the Prisoner's Dilemma of the Examples: each cell is one profile, \(2\cdot2=4\) in all. In \(s=(F,M)\) we have \(s_1=F\) and \(s_{-1}=M\). A switch by player 1 alone to \(s_1'=M\) moves within the shaded column, because \(s_{-1}\) is held fixed, and lands on \((s_1',s_{-1})=(M,M)\); this is the comparison behind dominance, best responses and Nash equilibrium.

The notation \((s_i',s_{-i})\) is used throughout game theory: strict dominance, best responses and Nash equilibrium all compare \(v_i(s_i,s_{-i})\) with \(v_i(s_i',s_{-i})\) while holding \(s_{-i}\) fixed.

"Pure" contrasts with mixed: a mixed strategy (Week 2) is a probability distribution over pure strategies, and a pure strategy is the special case that puts probability \(1\) on one element of \(S_i\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• With finite strategy sets, the number of pure-strategy profiles is \(|S|=|S_1|\cdot|S_2|\cdots|S_n|\), and \(|S_{-i}|=\prod_{j\ne i}|S_j|\).
  • Strategy sets need not be finite: a firm in a Cournot duopoly chooses \(q_i\in[0,\infty)\), an interval.
  • In a static game, strategies and actions coincide.
  • In a dynamic game (Week 3) a pure strategy is a complete contingent plan with one action at each of the player's information sets, so the number of pure strategies is the product of the numbers of actions over those information sets; see strategy in an extensive-form game.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Prisoner's Dilemma. \(S_1=S_2=\{M,F\}\) (Mum, Fink), so \(S=\{(M,M),(M,F),(F,M),(F,F)\}\) has \(4\) profiles. In the profile \((F,M)\), \(s_1=F\) and \(s_{-1}=s_2=M\).

Three players. If \(|S_1|=2\), \(|S_2|=3\) and \(|S_3|=2\), there are \(2\cdot3\cdot2=12\) profiles, and player 1 faces \(|S_{-1}|=3\cdot2=6\) possible combinations of the others' strategies.

Contingent plan. Player 1 chooses \(L\) or \(R\); player 2 observes this and then chooses \(l\) or \(r\). Player 2 has two actions at each of two decision points, hence \(2\cdot2=4\) pure strategies: \(ll\), \(lr\), \(rl\), \(rr\), where \(lr\) means "\(l\) after \(L\), \(r\) after \(R\)". Two actions per node do not mean two strategies.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A decision problem consists of a set of actions \(A\), a set of outcomes \(X\), a description of how each action leads to an outcome, and the decision maker's preference relation \(\succsim\) over \(X\), where \(x\succsim y\) means "\(x\) is at least as good as \(y\)". The preference relation is assumed to be

  • complete: for all \(x,y\in X\), \(x\succsim y\) or \(y\succsim x\) (or both);
  • transitive: \(x\succsim y\) and \(y\succsim z\) imply \(x\succsim z\).

A payoff function \(v\colon X\to\mathbb{R}\) represents \(\succsim\) if \(v(x)\ge v(y)\) if and only if \(x\succsim y\). Writing \(v(a)\) for the payoff of the outcome that action \(a\) produces, a rational agent (rational player) knows the actions, the outcomes, how actions lead to outcomes and his or her own preferences, and chooses an action \(a^*\in A\) with

\[ v(a^*)\ge v(a)\quad\text{for every } a\in A. \]

When actions lead to outcomes only with some probability, rationality means maximizing expected payoff.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Rationality is a modelling assumption about consistency, not about selfishness or money. The payoff may include altruism, fairness or effort costs; the assumption is only that choices maximize whatever the payoff measures. It turns the choice into an optimization model, which is what makes behaviour predictable.

The figure draws the study-hours example. The rational choice is an action whose payoff is at least that of every other action: the whole graph of \(v(a)=12a-a^2\) on \([0,10]\) lies on or below the line \(v=36\), which it touches only at \(a^*=6\). Replacing \(v\) by \(\mathrm{e}^{v(a)}\) would change the heights but not the location of the maximum, so the choice is the same.

Completeness rules out "cannot compare"; transitivity rules out preference cycles, for which no best element exists.

In a game, the outcome also depends on the other players, so a rational player maximizes given a belief about their choices. Rationality alone does not say which belief is reasonable; that needs further assumptions such as common knowledge of rationality or the correct beliefs built into Nash equilibrium.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• On a finite set \(X\), a complete and transitive preference relation can always be represented by a payoff function.
  • If \(v\) represents \(\succsim\) and \(f\) is strictly increasing, then \(f\circ v\) represents the same preferences and gives the same choice under certainty. Under uncertainty only positive affine transformations \(\alpha v+\beta\), \(\alpha>0\), are guaranteed to preserve choices (see expected payoff maximization).
  • With \(A\) finite an optimal action always exists. With \(A\) infinite it may not: on \(A=[0,1)\) with \(v(a)=a\) the supremum \(1\) is not attained.
  • In a game, a rational player's choice given a belief about the others is a best response to that belief.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Continuous action. A student chooses study hours \(a\in[0,10]\) with payoff \(v(a)=12a-a^2\) (benefit minus effort cost). Since \(v'(a)=12-2a\) is zero at \(a=6\) and \(v''=-2<0\), the rational choice is \(a^*=6\) with \(v(6)=36\). The payoff \(\mathrm{e}^{v(a)}\) represents the same preferences and gives the same \(a^*\).

Cycle. Suppose \(x\succ y\), \(y\succ z\) and \(z\succ x\) (strict preferences). Whichever of the three outcomes is chosen, another is strictly preferred, so no choice is optimal. Transitivity excludes this.

Firm. A firm that believes its rival will produce \(20\) units chooses its own output to maximize profit given that belief; in a Cournot duopoly this choice is its best response.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(G=\langle N,\{A_i\},\{v_i\}\rangle\) be a stage game. The repeated game is the multistage game in which \(G\) is played in every period \(t=0,1,\dots,T-1\) (\(T\) periods; time starts at \(t=0\)), each player observes all past action profiles, and a strategy may condition on the history \(h^t=(a^0,\dots,a^{t-1})\).

  • Finitely repeated (\(T<\infty\)): player \(i\)'s payoff is \(\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\delta^{t}v_i(a^t)\) with \(\delta\in(0,1]\).
  • Infinitely repeated (\(T=\infty\), periods \(t=0,1,2,\dots\)): with discount factor \(\delta\in(0,1)\), player \(i\)'s payoff is \(\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\delta^{t}v_i(a^t)\). When convenient it is normalized to the average discounted payoff
\[ \bar v_i=(1-\delta)\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\delta^{t}v_i(a^t). \]

The factor \((1-\delta)\) only rescales; it does not change any player's preferences over streams, so it is used only where it makes payoffs easier to compare.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Repetition lets today's behaviour be rewarded or punished tomorrow. Whether this matters depends on the horizon. With a known last period, nothing that happens later can influence play in that period, so it must be a stage-game Nash equilibrium; if that equilibrium is unique, the argument unravels backwards to the first period. With an infinite horizon there is no last period, and cooperation can be enforced by threats such as the grim trigger strategy.

The figure plots the two streams of the Examples on the average-payoff scale. Mutual cooperation gives \(3\) for every \(\delta\), while the stream \(5,1,1,\dots\) (defect once, then \((D,D)\) forever) gives \(5-4\delta\), which falls as the future weighs more. The lines cross at \(\delta=\tfrac{1}{2}=(5-3)/(5-1)\): to the right of this threshold the one-period gain of \(2\) no longer pays for the loss of \(2\) in every later period, which is the condition for the grim trigger strategy to sustain cooperation.

Move \(\delta\) across \(\tfrac12\): to the right of the threshold, cooperating forever beats defecting once. Raise the payoff of \((D,C)\), what a defector gets against a cooperator, and the threshold moves to the right.

The discount factor \(\delta\) measures patience. It can also be read as the probability that the relationship continues for another period, so "infinite" means "no known end date", not "literally forever". Large \(\delta\) makes future losses weigh heavily against a one-period gain.

The normalization by \((1-\delta)\) puts repeated-game payoffs on the scale of stage payoffs: by the geometric series \(\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\delta^{t}=1/(1-\delta)\), a constant stream \(v\) has average \(v\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(G\) has a unique Nash equilibrium \(a^*\) and \(T<\infty\), the unique subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium plays \(a^*\) in every period after every history.
  • For any \(T\) and \(\delta\), repeating a fixed stage-game Nash equilibrium regardless of history is subgame perfect.
  • In the infinitely repeated Prisoner's Dilemma of the Examples, mutual cooperation is the outcome of a subgame-perfect equilibrium in grim trigger strategies if and only if \(\delta\ge (5-3)/(5-1)=\tfrac{1}{2}\): the one-period gain from defecting against a cooperator, divided by the difference between that defection payoff and the payoff of mutual defection.
  • The folk theorem: for \(\delta\) close to 1, every feasible payoff vector giving each player strictly more than the payoff of a Nash equilibrium of the stage game is the average payoff of a subgame-perfect equilibrium.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Finite repetition. Take the Prisoner's Dilemma with \(v(C,C)=(3,3)\), \(v(C,D)=(0,5)\), \(v(D,C)=(5,0)\), \(v(D,D)=(1,1)\), played 10 times (\(t=0,\dots,9\)). In the last period, \(t=9\), every subgame is a one-shot game, so both play \(D\). Given that, play at \(t=8\) cannot affect the future and both play \(D\) again, and so on back to \(t=0\): the unique subgame-perfect outcome is \((D,D)\) ten times, an undiscounted total payoff of 10 each.

Average payoffs. With \(\delta=0.9\), the stream \(3,3,3,\dots\) has average 3. The stream \(5,1,1,1,\dots\) has average \((1-\delta)\big(5+\delta/(1-\delta)\big)=5(1-\delta)+\delta=5-4\delta=1.4\). Cooperation (3) beats this one-time defection (1.4); the two are equal at \(\delta=1/2=(5-3)/(5-1)\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Suppose that

  1. \(n\) bidders are risk-neutral;
  2. values are independent private values: \(\theta_1,\dots,\theta_n\) are i.i.d. with a continuous cumulative distribution function (CDF) \(F\) that has a positive density on \([\underline\theta,\overline\theta]\), and each bidder knows only her own value;
  3. two auction formats each have a Bayesian Nash equilibrium in which the object always goes to the bidder with the highest value;
  4. in both equilibria a bidder with the lowest possible value \(\underline\theta\) has expected surplus \(0\).

Then in both equilibria each type \(\theta\) has the same expected payment

\[ m(\theta)=\theta\,G(\theta)-\int_{\underline\theta}^{\theta}G(x)\,\mathrm{d}x,\qquad G(\theta)=F(\theta)^{n-1}, \]

and the seller's expected revenue is the same, namely \(\mathbb{E}[\theta_{(n-1)}]\), the expectation of the second-highest value.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
In equilibrium, a bidder's expected surplus \(U(\theta)=\theta G(\theta)-m(\theta)\) is pinned down by two things only: the probability \(G(\theta)\) of winning, which is fixed by the allocation rule (condition 3), and the surplus of the lowest type (condition 4). An envelope argument gives \(U'(\theta)=G(\theta)\), so \(U(\theta)=U(\underline\theta)+\int_{\underline\theta}^\theta G(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\). Expected payments, and so expected revenue, then cannot differ across formats.

The figure draws the payment formula for \(n=4\) bidders with \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) values, where \(G(x)=x^3\). A type-\(\theta\) bidder wins with probability \(G(\theta)\), so the rectangle \(\theta\,G(\theta)\) is the expected value of the object to her. The area under \(G\) up to \(\theta\) is her surplus \(U(\theta)=\int_0^\theta G(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\), and the rest of the rectangle, above the curve, is the expected payment \(m(\theta)\). Both areas depend only on \(G\), which the allocation rule fixes, and on the zero surplus of the lowest type, which is why the auction format drops out.

Move \(\theta\) and \(n\): the area under \(G\) is the surplus \(U(\theta)\) and the rest of the rectangle is the expected payment \(m(\theta)=\tfrac{n-1}{n}\theta^n\), whatever the auction format.

Each hypothesis matters. With risk-averse bidders the first-price auction yields more revenue than the second-price auction. With a reserve price above \(\underline\theta\), low types never win, so condition 3 fails and revenue can change. With asymmetric value distributions the first-price equilibrium need not allocate to the highest value. With affiliated or common values the formats can rank differently.

A common misunderstanding is that the formats give the same revenue in every realization. They do not: the theorem is about expected revenue. In a second-price auction the price is the realized second-highest value; in a first-price auction it is the winner's bid, which varies differently.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• With i.i.d. \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) values, \(G(\theta)=\theta^{n-1}\) and \(m(\theta)=\frac{n-1}{n}\theta^n\); expected revenue is \(\mathbb{E}[\theta_{(n-1)}]=\frac{n-1}{n+1}\), using the second-highest order statistic.
  • First-price, second-price, English, Dutch and all-pay auctions all satisfy the conditions in their symmetric equilibria with independent private values, so they are revenue-equivalent.
  • Each type's interim expected surplus is also equal across formats: \(U(\theta)=\int_{\underline\theta}^\theta G(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\), which is \(\theta^n/n\) for \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\).
  • The theorem can be used to find equilibrium bids: in a first-price auction a type-\(\theta\) bidder pays \(b(\theta)\) with probability \(G(\theta)\), so \(b(\theta)=m(\theta)/G(\theta)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Two bidders, \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\). Here \(G(\theta)=\theta\) and \(m(\theta)=\theta^2-\theta^2/2=\theta^2/2\).

  • Second-price: the winner pays the rival's value; \(\mathbb{E}[\min(\theta_1,\theta_2)]=\frac{1}{3}\).
  • First-price: bids \(\theta/2\); revenue \(\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}[\max(\theta_1,\theta_2)]=\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{2}{3}=\frac{1}{3}\).
  • All-pay (everyone pays her bid): the symmetric equilibrium bid equals \(m(\theta)=\theta^2/2\), paid by both bidders; revenue \(2\,\mathbb{E}[\theta^2/2]=2\cdot\frac{1}{6}=\frac{1}{3}\).

Recovering a bid. For \(n=4\) and \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) values, \(m(\theta)=\frac{3}{4}\theta^4\) and \(G(\theta)=\theta^3\), so the first-price bid is \(b(\theta)=\frac{3}{4}\theta\) and revenue is \(\frac{3}{5}\).

A violation. With \(n=2\), \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) values and a reserve price \(r=\frac{1}{2}\) in a second-price auction, the object is unsold when both values are below \(\frac{1}{2}\), so condition 3 fails. Expected revenue rises to \(\frac{5}{12}>\frac{1}{3}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: In a second-price sealed-bid auction, each of \(n\) bidders submits a bid \(b_i\ge0\) simultaneously and privately. The highest bidder wins (ties broken at random) and pays the second-highest bid, that is, the highest bid among the other bidders; losers pay nothing. In a private-value auction with valuation \(\theta_i\), bidder \(i\)'s payoff is \(\theta_i-\max_{j\ne i}b_j\) if she wins and \(0\) otherwise.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The winner's own bid decides only whether she wins, not what she pays. Let \(c=\max_{j\ne i}b_j\) be the highest rival bid. Winning is worth \(\theta_i-c\), which is positive exactly when \(c<\theta_i\). Bidding \(b_i=\theta_i\) wins in precisely those cases, so no other bid can do better.

  • Bidding \(b_i>\theta_i\) changes the outcome only when \(\theta_i<c<b_i\): the bidder then wins and pays \(c>\theta_i\), a loss.
  • Bidding \(b_i<\theta_i\) changes the outcome only when \(b_i<c<\theta_i\): the bidder then loses a profitable win.

Hence truthful bidding is a weakly dominant strategy; it is not strictly dominant, because against many rival bids (for instance \(c\) far above or far below \(\theta_i\)) other bids give the same payoff. The argument uses no beliefs about the rivals and no distributional assumptions, but it does rely on private values: with common values, a rival's bid carries information about one's own value.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• With private values, \(b_i(\theta_i)=\theta_i\) is weakly dominant for every type, so the truthful profile is a Bayesian Nash equilibrium for any distribution of values.
  • In the truthful equilibrium the highest-value bidder wins and pays the second-highest valuation.
  • With \(\theta_i\) i.i.d. \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\), expected revenue is the expectation of the second-highest order statistic: \(\mathbb{E}[\theta_{(n-1)}]=\frac{n-1}{n+1}\), the same as in the first-price auction.
  • The truthful equilibrium is not the only BNE: for \(n=2\) with values on \([0,1]\), "bidder 1 bids \(1\), bidder 2 bids \(0\)" is also an equilibrium, but it uses weakly dominated strategies and can give the object to the lower-value bidder.
  • The English auction with private values leads to the same outcome as the truthful second-price equilibrium.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Case check. A bidder values the object at \(10\). Compare bids \(8\), \(10\) and \(12\) against highest rival bid \(c\):

\(c\) bid \(8\) bid \(10\) bid \(12\) \(7\) \(10-7=3\) \(3\) \(3\) \(9\) \(0\) (loses) \(10-9=1\) \(1\) \(11\) \(0\) \(0\) \(10-11=-1\) \(13\) \(0\) \(0\) \(0\)

Bidding \(10\) is never worse than \(8\) or \(12\) and is strictly better against \(c=9\) (versus \(8\)) and \(c=11\) (versus \(12\)).

The figure draws the payoff of the bidder in the case check, value \(10\), as a function of the highest rival bid \(c\). Truthful bidding earns \(\max\{10-c,0\}\). Bidding \(8\) gives the same payoff except for \(8<c<10\), where the bidder loses a profitable win (the shaded area above the axis, e.g. \(1\) at \(c=9\)); bidding \(12\) gives the same payoff except for \(10<c<12\), where she wins and pays more than her value (the shaded area below the axis, e.g. \(-1\) at \(c=11\)). Outside these intervals all three bids earn the same, which is why truthful bidding is weakly but not strictly dominant.

Drag the highest rival bid \(c\) along the axis: bidding \(8\) differs from bidding \(\theta=10\) only for \(8<c<10\), where it gives up a profitable win. Set \(b=12\) to see the loss for \(10<c<12\).

Revenue with three bidders. With \(n=3\) and \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) values, expected revenue is \(\frac{2}{4}=\frac{1}{2}\). For a bidder of type \(\theta\) the expected payment is \(\mathbb{E}[Y;\,Y<\theta]\) with \(Y\) the highest of the two rival values, which has density \(2y\) on \([0,1]\): \(\int_0^\theta y\cdot2y\,\mathrm{d}y=\frac{2}{3}\theta^3\). Averaging over \(\theta\) and summing over the three bidders gives \(3\cdot\frac{2}{3}\cdot\mathbb{E}[\theta^3]=3\cdot\frac{2}{3}\cdot\frac{1}{4}=\frac{1}{2}\), as stated.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In a signalling game, a separating equilibrium is a perfect Bayesian equilibrium in which different types of the sender choose different messages: \(m(\theta)\ne m(\theta')\) whenever \(\theta\ne \theta'\). On the equilibrium path the receiver's beliefs are then degenerate,

\[ \mu\big(\theta\mid m(\theta)\big)=1\qquad\text{for every type } \theta, \]

so after every message that is sent the receiver knows the sender's type and best responds to it.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Separation means the message fully reveals the private information. The beliefs follow from Bayes' rule: if only type \(\theta\) sends \(m\), the posterior puts probability one on \(\theta\).

The figure plots the two incentive constraints of the example below. With acceptance after \(m=1\) and rejection after \(m=0\), type \(H\) is willing to pay for \(m=1\) only if \(c_H\le2\), and type \(L\) refrains from mimicking only if \(c_L\ge2\), so the separating profile in which \(H\) sends \(m=1\) is a PBE exactly in the shaded region. The pair \((c_H,c_L)=(1,3)\) lies inside it, while \((1,1.5)\) lies below the line \(c_L=2\), where \(L\) would mimic. The whole region lies on or above the diagonal \(c_H=c_L\): the signal must be cheaper for the type that wants to be recognized.

Drag the cost pair: separation needs \(c_H\le2\le c_L\). Move it to \((1,1.5)\) and the low type mimics.

The binding conditions are the senders' incentive constraints: each type must prefer its own message, with the receiver's response to it, over imitating any other type's message and receiving the response meant for that type. Separation therefore needs the signal to be relatively cheaper for the type that benefits from being recognized; otherwise the other type mimics. In the example below, type \(H\) must find \(m=1\) cheap enough to be worth being accepted, and type \(L\) must find it expensive enough not to copy \(H\).

Two misconceptions are common. First, a separating equilibrium is not automatically efficient: in the example below the message \(m=1\) produces nothing, and type \(H\) pays \(c_H\) only to be identified. Second, when the message space contains messages that no type sends, off-path beliefs still matter, because they determine whether a type would deviate to an unused message.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• In a separating PBE every on-path belief is \(0\) or \(1\); the receiver plays a complete-information best response to each type.
  • Incentive compatibility: \(v_S\big(\theta,m(\theta),a(m(\theta))\big)\ge v_S\big(\theta,m',a(m')\big)\) for every type \(\theta\) and every message \(m'\), including unused ones.
  • With two types and two messages, a separating PBE leaves no message off the path, so all beliefs are pinned down by the strategies.
  • Separating and pooling equilibria can coexist in the same game.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Two types, two messages. In the signalling game example, now with general costs, type \(H\) (prior \(0.4\)) and type \(L\) send \(m=0\) for free or \(m=1\) at cost \(c_H\) or \(c_L\). The receiver accepts if \(\mathbb{P}(H\mid m)>\tfrac{1}{2}\) and rejects if it is below \(\tfrac{1}{2}\); the sender gets \(2\) if accepted and \(0\) if rejected, minus her cost. In the candidate separating profile, \(H\) sends \(m=1\) and \(L\) sends \(m=0\), so the receiver accepts after \(m=1\) and rejects after \(m=0\). The incentive constraints are

\[ H\colon\ 2-c_H\ge0\iff c_H\le2,\qquad L\colon\ 0\ge2-c_L\iff c_L\ge2. \]

With \(c_H=1\) and \(c_L=3\) both hold: \(H\) gets \(1\) (versus \(0\)) and \(L\) gets \(0\) (versus \(-1\)), so this is a separating PBE.

When separation fails. Keep \(c_H=1\) but let \(c_L=1.5\). Then \(L\) would mimic: \(2-1.5=0.5>0\). No separating PBE with \(H\) sending \(m=1\) exists. The reverse assignment (\(L\) sends \(m=1\), \(H\) sends \(m=0\)) also fails: the receiver would accept after \(m=0\) and reject after \(m=1\), so \(L\) would get \(-1.5\) rather than \(2\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In an extensive-form game, let the other players follow \(\sigma_{-i}\). Player \(i\)'s strategy \(\sigma_i\) is sequentially rational if, at every information set \(h\) at which \(i\) moves, the continuation of \(\sigma_i\) from \(h\) onwards is a best response to \(\sigma_{-i}\), that is, it maximizes \(i\)'s expected payoff from \(h\) onwards. This must hold whether or not \(h\) is reached when \(\sigma\) is played.

If \(h\) is a single node, the expected payoff from \(h\) is well defined. If \(h\) contains several nodes, it is computed with a belief \(\mu(\cdot\mid h)\), a probability distribution over the nodes of \(h\), so sequential rationality is defined relative to these beliefs.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Sequential rationality says a player optimizes whenever she is called upon to move, not only when planning at the start of the game. It formalizes credibility: a threat or promise is credible only if carrying it out would be optimal at the moment it has to be carried out.

The figure draws the entry game of the Examples, with payoffs listed as (entrant, incumbent). In the Nash equilibrium (Out, Fight) the incumbent's node is never reached, so the threat to fight costs her nothing. Sequential rationality asks what she would do if the node were reached: Accommodate gives \(1>-1\), so Fight is not a credible plan, and only the highlighted path (In, Accommodate) survives.

Nash equilibrium does not impose this. In a Nash equilibrium a player must optimize at information sets that are reached with positive probability, but at unreached information sets any action is consistent with ex-ante optimality, because it does not change her payoff. This is the gap through which non-credible threats enter.

Backward induction builds a profile that is sequentially rational at every node of a perfect-information game, and subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium imposes the same requirement subgame by subgame. Where information sets contain several nodes, beliefs are needed; this leads to perfect Bayesian equilibrium.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• In a Nash equilibrium, each player's strategy is optimal at every information set reached with positive probability; off the path it is unrestricted.
  • In a finite game of perfect information, a pure-strategy profile in which every player is sequentially rational at every node is a backward-induction profile, hence an SPNE, and conversely.
  • At a non-singleton information set, the optimal action can change with the belief \(\mu(\cdot\mid h)\).
  • In multistage and repeated games, the one-stage deviation principle reduces the check to single-period deviations.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Entry game. Out gives \((0,2)\) to (entrant, incumbent); after In, Accommodate gives \((1,1)\) and Fight \((-1,-1)\). The profile (Out, Fight) is a Nash equilibrium, but Fight is not sequentially rational: at the incumbent's node, Accommodate gives \(1>-1\). Only (In, Accommodate) is sequentially rational for both players.

Optimality depending on beliefs. An incumbent observes entry but not whether the entrant is ready (\(R\)) or unready (\(U\)); both nodes are in one information set. Her payoffs are: against \(R\), Fight \(-1\) and Accommodate \(1\); against \(U\), Fight \(2\) and Accommodate \(1\). With belief \(\mu\) that the entrant is ready,

\[ \mathbb{E}[\text{Fight}]=-\mu+2(1-\mu)=2-3\mu,\qquad \mathbb{E}[\text{Accommodate}]=1. \]

Fight is sequentially rational if and only if \(2-3\mu\ge1\), that is \(\mu\le\tfrac{1}{3}\); Accommodate is sequentially rational if and only if \(\mu\ge\tfrac{1}{3}\). At \(\mu=\tfrac{1}{3}\) both are.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A signalling game is a two-player dynamic Bayesian game with the following timing:

  1. Nature draws the sender's type \(\theta\in\Theta\) according to a common prior \(p(\theta)\).
  2. The sender observes \(\theta\) and chooses a message (signal) \(m\in M\).
  3. The receiver observes \(m\) but not \(\theta\), and chooses an action \(a\in A\).

Payoffs are \(v_S(\theta,m,a)\) and \(v_R(\theta,m,a)\). A sender strategy is a type-contingent message \(m(\theta)\); a receiver strategy is a response \(a(m)\) to each message; the receiver's beliefs are posteriors \(\mu(\theta\mid m)\), one distribution for each message.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
As an extensive-form game, the receiver has one information set per message, and each contains one node per type. The natural solution concept is therefore perfect Bayesian equilibrium: the receiver needs beliefs after every message, including messages that no type sends.

The figure draws the example below in the usual signalling layout. Nature moves in the centre, the sender knows her type and sends \(m=0\) (left) or \(m=1\) (right), and the receiver observes only \(m\): her two nodes after the same \(m\) form one information set, at which she holds the belief \(\mu(m)=\mathbb{P}(H\mid m)\) and chooses \(A\) or \(R\). The payoffs at the ends, sender first, show why the message \(m=1\) can separate the types: it costs only \(1\) for \(H\) but \(3\) for \(L\).

A message can transmit information only if types behave differently, and types behave differently only if sending a message is more attractive to some types than to others. In the example below, the message \(m=1\) is costly but less costly for type \(H\), so it can separate the types. If a signal is equally costly (or free) for all types, the low type can always imitate the high type.

Equilibria are classified by how much the message reveals: in a separating equilibrium each type sends a different message and the receiver learns the type; in a pooling equilibrium all types send the same message and the receiver learns nothing beyond the prior. Other applications include an entrant whose entry decision signals whether it is competitive or weak, and a research institute sending a message to influence a politician's policy choice.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A sender strategy maps types to messages; a receiver strategy maps messages (not types) to actions.
  • On-path beliefs follow from the sender's strategy by Bayes' rule; beliefs after unsent messages are free in a PBE and determine which deviations are deterred.
  • A signalling game typically has several PBEs, both separating and pooling, supported by different off-path beliefs.
  • With at least two types of positive probability, a signalling game has no proper subgames, because each receiver information set spans several types; subgame perfection alone therefore has no bite.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
A two-type signalling game. The sender is type \(H\) with prior probability \(p=0.4\) or type \(L\) with probability \(0.6\). She sends \(m=0\), which is free, or \(m=1\), which costs \(c_H=1\) to type \(H\) and \(c_L=3\) to type \(L\). The receiver sees \(m\) and accepts (\(A\)) or rejects (\(R\)). Accepting gives the receiver \(1\) if the type is \(H\) and \(-1\) if it is \(L\); rejecting gives her \(0\). The sender gets \(2\) if accepted and \(0\) if rejected, minus her cost of \(m\). With belief \(\mu(m)=\mathbb{P}(H\mid m)\), accepting is worth \(\mu(m)-(1-\mu(m))=2\mu(m)-1\) to the receiver, so she accepts if \(\mu(m)>\tfrac{1}{2}\) and rejects if \(\mu(m)<\tfrac{1}{2}\).

  • Separating (\(H\) sends \(m=1\), \(L\) sends \(m=0\)): \(\mu(1)=1\) and \(\mu(0)=0\), so the receiver accepts after \(m=1\) and rejects after \(m=0\). \(H\) gets \(2-1=1>0\); \(L\) gets \(0>2-3=-1\). Neither deviates: a PBE.
  • Pooling on \(m=0\): \(\mu(0)=0.4<\tfrac{1}{2}\), so the receiver rejects and both types get \(0\). With off-path belief \(\mu(1)=0\) she also rejects after \(m=1\), so deviating gives \(H\) only \(-1<0\) and \(L\) only \(-3<0\): a PBE.
  • Pooling on \(m=1\): \(\mu(1)=0.4\), so the receiver rejects, and \(L\) gets \(-3\), less than the \(0\) or more she gets from \(m=0\) under any belief: not a PBE.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Stackelberg competition is a quantity-setting duopoly with sequential moves. Firm 1 (the leader) chooses \(q_1\ge0\); firm 2 (the follower) observes \(q_1\) and then chooses \(q_2\ge0\). With linear inverse demand \(p=a-b(q_1+q_2)\), constant marginal cost \(c\) and \(a>c\ge0\), \(b>0\), the profits are, for \(i=1,2\),

\[ v_i(q_1,q_2)=\big(a-b(q_1+q_2)-c\big)\,q_i. \]

The leader's strategy is a quantity \(q_1\); the follower's strategy is a function \(s_2\colon[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)\) giving her quantity after every possible \(q_1\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The game is the sequential version of the Cournot duopoly and is solved by backward induction. The follower's best response after observing \(q_1\) follows from the first-order condition \(a-c-bq_1-2bq_2=0\):

\[ BR_2(q_1)=\max\Big\{0,\ \frac{a-c-bq_1}{2b}\Big\}. \]

The leader substitutes this into her own profit. For \(q_1\le(a-c)/b\) this gives \(v_1=\tfrac{1}{2}(a-c-bq_1)\,q_1\), a concave function maximized where \(\tfrac{1}{2}(a-c)-bq_1=0\).

The figure uses the numbers of the Examples (\(a=100\), \(b=1\), \(c=10\)). Because the follower plays \(BR_2\), the leader in effect chooses a point on that line. Her profit is highest where one of her iso-profit curves just touches it: the curve \(v_1=1012.5\) touches at \((q_1,q_2)=(45,22.5)\). The Cournot point \((30,30)\) also lies on \(BR_2\) but gives the leader only \(900\); the difference is the value of commitment.

Move the leader's quantity \(q_1\): the follower answers on \(BR_2\), and the leader's profit peaks at \(q_1=45\), where her iso-profit curve touches \(BR_2\), above the \(900\) she would earn at the Cournot point.

The leader gains because her quantity is a commitment: it is observed and cannot be revised, so she can push the follower to produce less. If the follower could not observe \(q_1\), the game would be strategically simultaneous and the Cournot outcome would result. A frequent error is to report the follower's equilibrium strategy as the number \((a-c)/(4b)\); the strategy is the whole function \(BR_2\), and the number is only its value on the equilibrium path.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium (SPNE): \(q_1^*=\dfrac{a-c}{2b}\) and \(s_2^*=BR_2\), so on the path \(q_2^*=\dfrac{a-c}{4b}\).
  • Total output \(Q=\dfrac{3(a-c)}{4b}\) and price \(p=\dfrac{a+3c}{4}\).
  • Profits \(v_1=\dfrac{(a-c)^2}{8b}\) and \(v_2=\dfrac{(a-c)^2}{16b}\).
  • Compared with Cournot (\(q_i=\tfrac{a-c}{3b}\), \(v_i=\tfrac{(a-c)^2}{9b}\)): the leader produces and earns more, the follower produces and earns less, total output is higher and the price lower.
  • There are Nash equilibria that are not subgame perfect, sustained by a follower strategy that does not best respond off the path.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Numbers. Let \(a=100\), \(b=1\), \(c=10\). The follower plays \(BR_2(q_1)=\max\{0,(90-q_1)/2\}\). The leader maximizes \(\tfrac{1}{2}(90-q_1)q_1\), so \(q_1=45\). Then \(q_2=22.5\), \(Q=67.5\), \(p=32.5\), \(v_1=22.5\cdot45=1012.5=90^2/8\) and \(v_2=22.5\cdot22.5=506.25=90^2/16\). In the Cournot game each firm produces \(30\) at price \(40\) and earns \(900=90^2/9\).

A Nash equilibrium that is not subgame perfect. Let the follower use the constant strategy \(s_2(q_1)=30\) for every \(q_1\), and the leader play \(q_1=30\). The leader's best response to a fixed \(q_2=30\) is \((90-30)/2=30\), and on the path the follower's \(30=BR_2(30)\) is optimal, so this is a Nash equilibrium with the Cournot outcome. It is not subgame perfect: after, say, \(q_1=45\) the follower should produce \(22.5\), not \(30\). The threat to ignore the leader's quantity is not credible.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A stage game is the simultaneous-move normal-form game

\[ G=\big\langle N,\ \{A_i\}_{i\in N},\ \{v_i\}_{i\in N}\big\rangle \]

that is played once in every period of a repeated game, or in one stage of a multistage game. Here \(N=\{1,\dots,n\}\) is the set of players, \(A_i\) is player \(i\)'s set of stage actions, \(A=A_1\times\cdots\times A_n\) is the set of action profiles and \(v_i\colon A\to\mathbb{R}\) is player \(i\)'s stage payoff. A Nash equilibrium of \(G\) (pure or mixed) is called a stage-game Nash equilibrium.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The stage game is the building block; the repeated game adds time, observation of past play and a way of adding up payoffs. A strategy in the stage game is a single action, whereas a strategy in the repeated game is a whole plan that may condition on past play. The two must not be confused: an action profile that is not a stage-game equilibrium (cooperation in the Prisoner's Dilemma) can still be played on the equilibrium path of the repeated game.

The left panel is the Prisoner's Dilemma stage game of the Examples, with \((D,D)\), the unique stage-game Nash equilibrium, shaded. The right panel shows why: if player 2 plays \(C\) with probability \(y\) (a mixed strategy), player 1 earns \(3y\) from \(C\) and \(5y+(1-y)=1+4y\) from \(D\), and \(1+4y>3y\) for every \(y\), so \(D\) is her best response whatever player 2 does.

Stage-game equilibria are always available as credible continuation play, so they serve as rewards or punishments in the repeated game.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Playing a fixed stage-game Nash equilibrium in every period, whatever happened before, is a subgame-perfect equilibrium of the repeated game, finite or infinite, for every discount factor \(\delta\).
  • If \(G\) has a unique Nash equilibrium and is repeated finitely often, that history-independent repetition is the unique subgame-perfect equilibrium.
  • The set of feasible payoffs used in the folk theorem is the set of convex combinations of the stage payoff vectors \(v(a)\), \(a\in A\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Prisoner's Dilemma. With actions \(C\) (cooperate) and \(D\) (defect), take \(v(C,C)=(3,3)\), \(v(C,D)=(0,5)\), \(v(D,C)=(5,0)\), \(v(D,D)=(1,1)\). Since \(5>3\) and \(1>0\), \(D\) is a strictly dominant strategy, so \((D,D)\) is the unique stage-game equilibrium, although both players prefer \((C,C)\); the stage equilibrium is not Pareto efficient.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A static game of complete information is a game in which

  1. each player \(i\in N=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) chooses an action \(s_i\) from a set \(S_i\) simultaneously and independently: no player observes any other player's choice before making his or her own;
  2. given the chosen profile \(s=(s_1,\ldots,s_n)\), each player receives the payoff \(v_i(s)\);
  3. the set of players, the action sets \(S_i\) and the payoff functions \(v_i\) are common knowledge.

Because nothing is observed before choosing, a strategy in such a game is simply an action, and the game is fully described by a normal-form game.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
This is the simplest class in game theory: one round of choices, then payoffs.

The figure draws the Prisoner's Dilemma as if player 1 moved first. Because player 2 does not observe that move, her two nodes lie in one information set and she chooses \(M\) or \(F\) without knowing which node she is at, so her strategy is a single action. The tree then has the same four profiles, with the same payoffs, as the matrix on the right: a sequential game in which later movers do not observe earlier moves is strategically equivalent to a static game.

"Simultaneous" refers to information, not to clock time. Choices made at different times are still simultaneous in this sense if nobody sees the earlier choices, as with sealed envelopes.

"Complete information" means that the structure of the game, including every player's payoffs, is common knowledge. It does not mean that players know what the others will choose; that strategic uncertainty is what solution concepts address. Nor is it the same as perfect information, which is a property of dynamic games in which every player observes all earlier moves.

The assumption fails when some player has private information about payoffs (a Bayesian game) or when some moves are observed before others are made (an extensive-form game).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every static game of complete information can be written as a normal-form game \(\langle N,\{S_i\},\{v_i\}\rangle\); with two players and finite action sets, as a payoff matrix.
  • In a static game the set of pure strategies of player \(i\) equals the action set \(S_i\).
  • Solution concepts for this class include strict dominance, iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies and Nash equilibrium (pure strategies in Week 1, mixed strategies in Week 2).
  • If a player has private information about payoffs, the game becomes a Bayesian game (Week 5). If moves are observed sequentially, it is an extensive-form game (Week 3).
  • A sequential game in which later movers do not observe earlier moves is strategically equivalent to a static game.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Prisoner's Dilemma. Two suspects are questioned in separate rooms and each chooses Mum or Fink without observing the other. The sentences for each pair of choices are known to both: static, complete information.

Cournot duopoly. In a Cournot duopoly two firms choose quantities without seeing each other's choice; demand and both cost functions are common knowledge.

Not in this class.

  • Stackelberg competition: the follower observes the leader's quantity before choosing, so the game is dynamic.
  • A sealed-bid private-value auction, in which each bidder privately knows her own valuation: static, but with incomplete information.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(H_i\) be the collection of player \(i\)'s information sets in an extensive-form game, and \(A_i(h)\) the actions available at \(h\in H_i\). A pure strategy of player \(i\) is a function \(s_i\) that assigns to every \(h\in H_i\) an action \(s_i(h)\in A_i(h)\). It is a complete contingent plan: it specifies what \(i\) does at every information set at which she could move, including information sets that are not reached when the strategy profile is played.

The set of pure strategies is \(S_i=\prod_{h\in H_i}A_i(h)\). A mixed strategy is a probability distribution over \(S_i\); a behavioural strategy instead specifies an independent probability distribution over \(A_i(h)\) at each information set \(h\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A strategy is a full set of instructions that someone could carry out on the player's behalf without consulting her again, whatever happens. It is different from an action (one choice at one information set) and from an outcome (the path actually played).

The figure draws the example of a player who moves twice. Player 1 has two information sets, \(h\) with actions Stop and Continue and \(h'\) with actions \(a\) and \(b\), so \(S_1=\{\text{Stop},\text{Continue}\}\times\{a,b\}\) has \(2\cdot2=4\) elements. The shaded node \(h'\) cannot be reached after Stop, yet every strategy still names an action there: (Stop, \(a\)) and (Stop, \(b\)) produce the same play but are different plans.

The plan must cover information sets that are not reached, and even ones that the player's own earlier choices exclude. The reason is that equilibrium analysis asks what would happen after a deviation: whether the entrant should enter depends on what the incumbent would do after entry, even if entry does not occur. Two profiles can produce the same path and differ only off the path; this is how a non-credible threat can support a Nash equilibrium that is not subgame perfect.

The same idea returns in repeated games, where a strategy assigns an action to every history.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Player \(i\) has \(\prod_{h\in H_i}|A_i(h)|\) pure strategies.
  • A pure-strategy profile determines a unique path from the root to a terminal node (given Nature's moves, a probability distribution over terminal nodes), which yields the normal-form payoffs.
  • The pure strategies of the induced normal-form game are exactly these plans; in a static game, where each player has a single information set, a strategy is just an action.
  • Profiles that agree on the path of play give the same payoffs, whatever they prescribe off the path.
  • Under perfect recall, every mixed strategy has an outcome-equivalent behavioural strategy and vice versa (Kuhn's theorem).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Entry game. The incumbent has one information set (after In) with actions Accommodate and Fight, so her strategies are \(\{A,F\}\). In the profile (Out, \(F\)) the incumbent never moves, yet her strategy \(F\) is what deters entry.

Sequential Battle of the Sexes. Player 2 observes player 1's choice of \(O\) or \(F\). Her strategies are written (reply to \(O\), reply to \(F\)): \(OO\), \(OF\), \(FO\), \(FF\). "Always match" is \(OF\); "always choose \(F\)" is \(FF\).

A player who moves twice. Player 1 chooses Stop or Continue. After Continue, player 2 chooses \(l\) or \(r\); after \(r\), player 1 chooses \(a\) or \(b\). Player 1 has \(2\cdot2=4\) strategies: (Stop, \(a\)), (Stop, \(b\)), (Continue, \(a\)), (Continue, \(b\)). The plans (Stop, \(a\)) and (Stop, \(b\)) produce the same play, but they are different strategies because they differ at an information set that Stop excludes. Player 2 has \(2\) strategies.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In a normal-form game, a strategy \(s_i\in S_i\) is strictly dominant for player \(i\) if, for every \(s_i'\in S_i\setminus\{s_i\}\) and every \(s_{-i}\in S_{-i}\),

\[ v_i(s_i,s_{-i})>v_i(s_i',s_{-i}). \]

Equivalently, \(s_i\) strictly dominates every other strategy of player \(i\), so every other strategy is a strictly dominated strategy.

A profile \(s^D=(s_1^D,\ldots,s_n^D)\) in which every \(s_i^D\) is strictly dominant is a strictly dominant strategy equilibrium.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A strictly dominant strategy is the best choice regardless of what the others do, so a rational player needs no belief about the opponents to choose it. A prediction based on dominant strategies requires only that each player is rational, not that rationality is common knowledge.

In the figure, the blue arrows compare player 1's payoffs within each column: switching from \(M\) to \(F\) raises her payoff from \(-2\) to \(-1\) against \(M\) and from \(-5\) to \(-4\) against \(F\). The red arrows make the same comparison for player 2 within each row. Every arrow points to \(F\) whatever the opponent does, so \(F\) is strictly dominant for both players, and the shaded cell \((F,F)\) is the strictly dominant strategy equilibrium, even though \((M,M)\) would give both players more.

The concept is demanding: the same strategy must be strictly best against every opponent profile. Many games have no strictly dominant strategy for at least one player. A frequent misunderstanding is to treat "best against what the opponent actually does" as dominance; that is only a best response.

Dominant strategies do not guarantee a good outcome. In the Prisoner's Dilemma both players use their dominant strategy, and both would be better off if both deviated.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A player has at most one strictly dominant strategy: if \(s_i\) and \(t_i\ne s_i\) were both strictly dominant, each would give a strictly higher payoff than the other.
  • If \(s_i\) is strictly dominant, then \(s_i\) is the unique best response to every \(s_{-i}\) (and to every belief).
  • A strictly dominant strategy equilibrium, if it exists, is unique, and it is the unique Nash equilibrium of the game.
  • Iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies reaches it in a single round.
  • Existence is not guaranteed: in Battle of the Sexes and in Matching Pennies no player has a strictly dominant strategy.
  • The equilibrium may fail to be Pareto efficient.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
1. Prisoner's Dilemma. With payoffs \((M,M)=(-2,-2)\), \((M,F)=(-5,-1)\), \((F,M)=(-1,-5)\), \((F,F)=(-4,-4)\):

\[ v_1(F,M)=-1>-2=v_1(M,M),\qquad v_1(F,F)=-4>-5=v_1(M,F). \]

So \(F\) is strictly dominant for player 1, and by symmetry for player 2. The strictly dominant strategy equilibrium is \((F,F)\) with payoffs \((-4,-4)\), although \((M,M)\) gives \((-2,-2)\) to both.

2. No dominant strategy.

\(L\) \(M\) \(R\) \(T\) \(2,1\) \(3,2\) \(0,0\) \(B\) \(1,3\) \(1,1\) \(4,0\)

Player 1's best choice is \(T\) against \(L\) and \(M\) but \(B\) against \(R\); player 2's best choice is \(M\) against \(T\) but \(L\) against \(B\). Neither player has a strictly dominant strategy, even though \(R\) is strictly dominated by \(M\).

3. Cournot. In a Cournot duopoly a firm's best quantity falls as the rival's quantity rises, so no single quantity is best against every rival quantity.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In a normal-form game \(\langle N,\{S_i\},\{v_i\}\rangle\), let \(s_i,s_i'\in S_i\) be two strategies of player \(i\). Strategy \(s_i'\) strictly dominates \(s_i\) if, for every \(s_{-i}\in S_{-i}\),

\[ v_i(s_i',s_{-i})>v_i(s_i,s_{-i}). \]

Then \(s_i\) is strictly dominated (by \(s_i'\)). A strategy is strictly dominated if at least one other strategy of the same player strictly dominates it.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A strictly dominated strategy is worse than some alternative whatever the other players do. A rational agent therefore never plays it, and this conclusion needs no knowledge of the other players' rationality or beliefs.

Two conditions must hold together: the comparison is against one fixed alternative \(s_i'\), and the inequality is strict for every \(s_{-i}\). A single tie is enough to break strict dominance; the strategy may then still be weakly dominated, which is a different and weaker notion (see weakly dominant strategy, Week 6).

A common error is to call \(s_i\) dominated because it is never the best choice in any column. Being worse than different strategies in different columns is not strict dominance by a pure strategy (Example 2).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A strictly dominated strategy is never a best response, neither to any \(s_{-i}\) nor to any probabilistic belief about \(s_{-i}\), because the dominating strategy gives a strictly higher payoff in every case and hence a strictly higher expected payoff.
  • Strict dominance is transitive: if \(s_i''\) strictly dominates \(s_i'\) and \(s_i'\) strictly dominates \(s_i\), then \(s_i''\) strictly dominates \(s_i\).
  • Removing strictly dominated strategies never removes a strategy used in a Nash equilibrium; repeating the removal gives iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies.
  • A strategy that is not dominated by any pure strategy can still be strictly dominated by a mixed strategy (Week 2).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
1. Prisoner's Dilemma. With the payoffs of the normal-form game page, for player 1:

\[ v_1(F,M)=-1>-2=v_1(M,M),\qquad v_1(F,F)=-4>-5=v_1(M,F), \]

so Mum is strictly dominated by Fink. By symmetry the same holds for player 2.

2. Not dominated by a pure strategy. Player 1's payoffs (player 2 chooses \(L\) or \(R\)):

\(L\) \(R\) \(U\) \(3\) \(0\) \(M\) \(0\) \(3\) \(D\) \(1\) \(1\)

\(D\) is not dominated by \(U\) (\(1>0\) against \(R\)) nor by \(M\) (\(1>0\) against \(L\)). Yet the mixture "\(U\) and \(M\) with probability \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) each" gives \(1.5>1\) against both columns, so \(D\) is strictly dominated by a mixed strategy.

In the figure, each strategy of player 1 is a point (payoff against \(L\), payoff against \(R\)), and the shaded region contains the points that beat \(D=(1,1)\) in both columns. Neither \(U=(3,0)\) nor \(M=(0,3)\) lies in it, but the segment between them consists of their mixtures, and its midpoint \(\tfrac{1}{2}U+\tfrac{1}{2}M=(1.5,1.5)\) does.

Slide \(\alpha\) along the segment of mixtures of \(U\) and \(M\): the green part beats \(D\) against both columns. Drag \(D\) beyond the segment and no mixture dominates it any more.

3. A tie. If \(v_1(F,F)\) in the Prisoner's Dilemma were changed to \(-5\), then \(F\) and \(M\) would tie against \(F\), and \(M\) would no longer be strictly dominated.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A profile \(\sigma^*=(\sigma_1^*,\ldots,\sigma_n^*)\) of strategies in an extensive-form game \(\Gamma\) is a subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium (SPNE) if, for every subgame \(\Gamma'\) of \(\Gamma\), the restriction of \(\sigma^*\) to \(\Gamma'\) is a Nash equilibrium of \(\Gamma'\).

Since \(\Gamma\) is a subgame of itself, every SPNE is a Nash equilibrium of \(\Gamma\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
SPNE (Selten, 1965) refines Nash equilibrium by removing non-credible threats. In a Nash equilibrium, a player's prescribed behaviour at an unreached information set does not affect her payoff, so it may be irrational there. Subgame perfection requires optimal behaviour in every subgame, on or off the equilibrium path, which is a form of sequential rationality.

In the figure (the entry game below), the incumbent's decision after In is a subgame of its own. There Accommodate gives the incumbent \(1\) and Fight gives \(-1\), so the only Nash equilibrium of the subgame is \(A\), and the threat to play \(F\) is not credible. The profile (Out, \(F\)) is a Nash equilibrium of the whole game but prescribes \(F\) in this subgame, so it is not subgame perfect; the green path is the unique SPNE (In, \(A\)).

An SPNE is a profile of complete strategies, not a path of play. In the plain entry game each player has a single decision node, so (In, \(A\)) is already a complete strategy profile and the SPNE. In larger games, where a player moves at several information sets (as player 1 does in the outside-option example below), writing only the path of play does not specify an SPNE; the answer must state what every player does at every information set, including those off the equilibrium path.

The refinement has bite only when the game has subgames other than itself. When information sets prevent this (for example, an uninformed player moving after a private move), Nash equilibria with implausible behaviour can survive; perfect Bayesian equilibrium addresses this with beliefs.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• SPNE \(\subseteq\) Nash equilibria; the inclusion can be strict.
  • In a finite game of perfect information, the pure-strategy SPNE are exactly the profiles found by backward induction; a pure-strategy SPNE exists, and it is unique if no player has the same payoff at two different terminal nodes.
  • Every finite extensive-form game with perfect recall has an SPNE, possibly in mixed or behavioural strategies: apply the Nash existence theorem to the smallest subgames, replace each by its equilibrium payoffs, and repeat (generalized backward induction).
  • Different equilibria of a subgame can lead to different SPNE of the whole game.
  • If the only subgame is \(\Gamma\) itself, SPNE and Nash equilibrium coincide.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Entry game. Out gives \((0,2)\) to (entrant, incumbent); after In, Accommodate gives \((1,1)\) and Fight \((-1,-1)\). Nash equilibria: (In, \(A\)) and (Out, \(F\)). In the subgame after In, the incumbent's only Nash equilibrium is \(A\) (\(1>-1\)), so (Out, \(F\)) is not subgame perfect: fighting is a non-credible threat. Given \(A\), the entrant prefers In (\(1>0\)). The unique SPNE is (In, \(A\)).

Outside option. Player 1 chooses Out, giving \((2,2)\), or In, after which both play the simultaneous game

\(a\) \(b\) \(A\) \((3,1)\) \((0,0)\) \(B\) \((0,0)\) \((1,3)\)

The subgame has three Nash equilibria: \((A,a)\), \((B,b)\), and a mixed one in which player 2 plays \(a\) with probability \(q=\tfrac{1}{4}\) (from \(3q=1-q\)) and player 1 plays \(A\) with probability \(p=\tfrac{3}{4}\) (from \(p=3(1-p)\)), giving payoffs \((\tfrac{3}{4},\tfrac{3}{4})\). Comparing each with Out's payoff \(2\) for player 1:

  • \((A,a)\): \(3>2\), SPNE (In \(A\), \(a\)), outcome \((3,1)\);
  • \((B,b)\): \(1<2\), SPNE (Out \(B\), \(b\)), outcome \((2,2)\);
  • mixed: \(\tfrac{3}{4}<2\), SPNE (Out with \(p=\tfrac{3}{4}\), \(q=\tfrac{1}{4}\)), outcome \((2,2)\).

Player 1's strategy lists her subgame action even when she chooses Out.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In an extensive-form game \(\Gamma\), a subgame consists of a single decision node \(x\) together with all of its successors, with the property that whenever a node \(x'\) belongs to it, every node in the same information set as \(x'\) also belongs to it. The subgame inherits the players, actions, information sets and payoffs of \(\Gamma\).

Equivalently: a subgame starts at a node \(x\) whose information set is the singleton \(\{x\}\), contains everything that follows \(x\), and does not cut through any information set. The whole game (starting at the root) is always a subgame.

A subgame other than \(\Gamma\) itself is a proper subgame, in the same sense as a proper subset: the whole game is a subgame, but not a proper subgame. When counting, say whether the whole game is included.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A subgame is a part of the game that can be analysed as a game in its own right: once play reaches \(x\), every player knows that it has, and everything relevant for the continuation is contained in the subgame. This is what makes it meaningful to require Nash equilibrium behaviour in it, as subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium does.

In the figure (the outside-option example below), the node after In is a singleton, and the outlined part below it contains both nodes of player 2's information set, so it is a subgame. Neither of player 2's nodes can start a subgame: a part starting there would separate the two nodes of one information set. Together with the whole game, the tree has \(2\) subgames, one of them proper.

Two conditions are often overlooked. First, a node inside a non-singleton information set cannot start a subgame, because the mover there does not know she is at that node. Second, the requirement applies to all successors: a candidate subgame that contains one node of an information set but not another is not a subgame, even if it starts at a singleton.

Subgames are defined by the tree, not by the strategies played: a subgame off the equilibrium path is still a subgame.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every game is a subgame of itself, but not a proper subgame of itself.
  • In a finite game of perfect information, every decision node starts a subgame, so the number of subgames equals the number of decision nodes.
  • A simultaneous-move game written as a tree has no proper subgames.
  • If \(\Gamma\) has no proper subgames, its subgame-perfect equilibria are exactly its Nash equilibria.
  • A profile of strategies of \(\Gamma\) restricts to a strategy profile of every subgame (keep the prescriptions at information sets inside the subgame).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Entry game. The entrant chooses Out or In; after In the incumbent chooses Accommodate or Fight. There are two decision nodes, both singletons, so there are \(2\) subgames: the whole game and the incumbent's decision after In, which is the only proper subgame.

Sequential Battle of the Sexes. Player 1 moves; player 2 observes and moves. Subgames: the whole game and one for each of player 2's two nodes, so \(3\) in total, \(2\) of them proper. In the simultaneous version, player 2's two nodes form one information set, and the only subgame is the whole game.

Outside option followed by a simultaneous game. Player 1 chooses Out (game ends) or In. After In, player 1 chooses \(A\) or \(B\) and player 2, without observing this, chooses \(a\) or \(b\). The node after In is a singleton and all its successors, including both nodes of player 2's information set, lie below it, so it starts a subgame. Player 2's nodes cannot start subgames. The game has \(2\) subgames, one of them proper.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In an extensive-form game, a system of beliefs \(\mu\) assigns to every information set \(h\) a probability distribution over the decision nodes in \(h\):

\[ \mu(x)\in[0,1]\ \text{ for each } x\in h,\qquad \sum_{x\in h}\mu(x)=1. \]

The number \(\mu(x)\) is the probability that the player who moves at \(h\) assigns to being at node \(x\), given that \(h\) has been reached. A strategy profile \(\sigma\) together with a system of beliefs \(\mu\) is called an assessment \((\sigma,\mu)\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
At an information set with several nodes, a player knows that one of them has been reached but not which. To judge whether an action is optimal there, the player needs to weigh the payoffs at the different nodes. Beliefs supply those weights. They make it possible to define sequential rationality at every information set, including information sets that equilibrium play never reaches.

In the figure (the entry example below), the incumbent's information set after entry is reached with probability \(\tfrac{1}{5}\cdot1=0.2\) through the competitive type and \(\tfrac{4}{5}\cdot\tfrac{1}{2}=0.4\) through the weak type. The belief divides these weights by their total \(0.6\), giving \(\mu=\tfrac{1}{3}\) on the competitive node and \(1-\mu=\tfrac{2}{3}\) on the weak one; these are the weights the incumbent uses to compare its actions.

Change the entry probabilities: the beliefs \(\mu\) and \(1-\mu\) are the reach probabilities of the incumbent's two nodes divided by their total. With \(q_C=q_W=0\) the information set is off the path and any belief is allowed.

Beliefs are about past moves that the player did not observe: Nature's choice of a type in a Bayesian game, or an earlier unobserved action of another player. They are a conditional probability of the node given the information set. A singleton information set carries the trivial belief \(\mu(x)=1\), so beliefs only matter at information sets with two or more nodes.

A system of beliefs is part of the description of an equilibrium, not a consequence of payoffs alone. Equilibrium concepts then restrict it: on the equilibrium path, beliefs must follow from the strategies by Bayes' rule; off the path the restriction is weaker, and different beliefs can support different equilibria.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A system of beliefs specifies one distribution per information set; at a two-node information set it reduces to one number \(\mu\in[0,1]\), with \(1-\mu\) on the other node.
  • At an information set reached with positive probability under \(\sigma\), beliefs consistent with \(\sigma\) are uniquely determined by Bayes' rule.
  • At an information set reached with probability \(0\) under \(\sigma\), Bayes' rule does not apply, and a perfect Bayesian equilibrium allows any distribution there.
  • In a signalling game, the receiver has one information set per message, and the beliefs are the posterior probabilities of the sender's types after each message.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Entry with unknown type. Nature makes an entrant competitive with probability \(\frac{1}{5}\) or weak with probability \(\frac{4}{5}\); the incumbent sees entry but not the type. Its information set after entry has two nodes, and a belief is a number \(\mu=\mathbb{P}(\text{competitive}\mid\text{entry})\). If the competitive type always enters and the weak type enters with probability \(\frac{1}{2}\), consistency requires \(\mu=\frac{0.2}{0.2+0.8\cdot0.5}=\frac{1}{3}\).

Signalling with two messages. A sender of type \(H\) or \(L\) sends a message \(m\in\{0,1\}\), and the receiver observes only \(m\). A system of beliefs is a pair \(\big(\mu(H\mid m=0),\ \mu(H\mid m=1)\big)\), for example \((0.4,\,1)\). If both types send \(m=0\), the information set after \(m=1\) is never reached, and any value of \(\mu(H\mid m=1)\in[0,1]\) is admissible as a belief.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: In a repeated game, a trigger strategy for player \(i\) prescribes a target action \(a_i^c\) (the cooperative phase) as long as the history shows no deviation from the target profile \(a^c\) since the cooperative phase began, and switches to a punishment phase once a deviation has occurred. In the punishment phase the players follow a specified punishment path, typically a stage-game Nash equilibrium \(a^*\) played either forever (the grim trigger strategy) or for \(k\) periods, after which play returns to \(a^c\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A trigger strategy turns the future into a hostage: a player who grabs a one-period gain loses the difference between cooperative and punishment payoffs in later periods. Deviation is unprofitable when the discounted future loss exceeds the immediate gain, which requires enough patience \(\delta\) and a punishment that is severe or long enough.

In the figure, \(k=2\) and the payoffs are those of the example below. Deviating at \(t\) raises the payoff from \(3\) to \(5\), a gain of \(2\), but the two punishment periods pay \(1\) instead of \(3\), losses worth \(2\delta\) and \(2\delta^2\) in period-\(t\) terms. The deviation is unprofitable when \(2\delta+2\delta^2\ge2\), which is the condition \(\delta+\delta^2\ge1\) of the example.

With \(k=2\) the deviation is unprofitable from \(\delta\approx0.618\). Set \(k=1\) to see that one period of punishment never deters, then switch to grim trigger for the threshold \(\tfrac12\).

Two separate conditions must hold for a subgame-perfect equilibrium. On the cooperative path, nobody should gain by deviating. In the punishment phase, carrying out the punishment must itself be optimal; a threat to play something that is not a best response once the trigger has been pulled is not credible. Using a stage-game Nash equilibrium as punishment takes care of the second condition.

A trigger strategy reacts to deviations, not to bad luck: it relies on actions being observed. Shorter punishments are more forgiving but weaker, so they need a higher \(\delta\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If the punishment path is a stage-game Nash equilibrium, no player can gain by a deviation during the punishment phase.
  • With \(k\)-period punishment by \(a^*\), a one-period deviation from \(a^c\) is unprofitable if and only if \(\big(v_i(a^c)-v_i(a^*)\big)(\delta+\delta^2+\dots+\delta^k)\ge \max_{a_i\ne a_i^c}v_i(a_i,a_{-i}^c)-v_i(a^c)\) for every \(i\).
  • The left side grows with \(k\) and with \(\delta\); letting \(k\to\infty\) gives the grim trigger condition.
  • With a finite horizon and a unique stage equilibrium, no subgame-perfect equilibrium, in trigger strategies or otherwise, plays anything but that equilibrium.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Short versus long punishment. Prisoner's Dilemma with \(v(C,C)=(3,3)\), \(v(D,C)=(5,0)\), \(v(D,D)=(1,1)\): the gain from defecting is \(5-3=2\) and the per-period loss during punishment is \(3-1=2\). The condition becomes

\[ \delta+\delta^2+\dots+\delta^k\ge1. \]
  • \(k=1\): \(\delta\ge1\), impossible for \(\delta<1\); one period of punishment never deters.
  • \(k=2\): \(\delta^2+\delta-1\ge0\), i.e. \(\delta\ge(\sqrt{5}-1)/2\approx0.618\).
  • \(k=\infty\) (grim trigger): \(\delta/(1-\delta)\ge1\), i.e. \(\delta\ge1/2\).

A deviation during punishment yields \(0\) instead of \(1\) and restarts the punishment, so it never pays.

Collusion. Firms in a repeated Cournot duopoly can produce the joint-monopoly quantities and revert to Cournot quantities after any deviation; the grim version is worked out on the grim trigger page.
