docs.title: Definition
docs.text: In a Bayesian game, a game of incomplete information, player \(i\)'s type \(\theta_i\) is everything payoff-relevant that \(i\) knows privately and the others do not, such as her cost, valuation, quality or preferences. It is drawn from a type space \(\Theta_i\) and observed only by \(i\). A profile of types is \(\theta=(\theta_1,\dots,\theta_n)\), an element of the Cartesian product \(\Theta=\Theta_1\times\cdots\times\Theta_n\), and payoffs \(v_i(a;\theta)\) may depend on the whole profile. From the others' point of view, \(\theta_i\) is a random variable whose distribution is part of the description of the game.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
In a normal-form game every player's payoff function is common knowledge. Types relax exactly this: the structure of the game (players, actions, the type spaces and the distribution of types) remains common knowledge, but the realized type of each player is private. Uncertainty about another player's payoffs becomes uncertainty about which type she is.

In the figure (the private-costs example below), each panel is one pure strategy of neighbour \(i\): arrows assign an action, \(C\) or \(D\), to each cost type \(\theta_i\in\{\tfrac{1}{4},2\}\). Two types with two possible actions each give \(2^2=4\) such maps, the four pure strategies \((C,C)\), \((C,D)\), \((D,C)\) and \((D,D)\), although only one type is realized and only one action is taken.

A type also fixes the player's beliefs. Given a common prior \(p\) over \(\Theta\), type \(\theta_i\) believes the others' types are distributed as \(p(\theta_{-i}\mid\theta_i)\); with independent types this belief does not depend on \(\theta_i\).

The key consequence for strategies: because the other players do not see \(\theta_i\), they must predict what every type of \(i\) would do. A strategy is therefore a type-contingent plan \(s_i\colon\Theta_i\to A_i\), not a single action, even though only one type is realized. Treating each type as a separate "player" who maximizes her own expected payoff is a useful way to think about this.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• With finite \(\Theta_i\) and \(A_i\), player \(i\) has \(|A_i|^{|\Theta_i|}\) pure strategies.
  • A player with a single possible type (\(|\Theta_i|=1\)) has no private information; if all players do, the game reduces to a game of complete information.
  • Types are the moves of Nature in the Harsanyi transformation: Nature draws \(\theta\), and each player observes only her own component.
  • A type can encode information about the state of the world (for example, a signal about a common value), not only preferences.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Private costs. Two neighbours decide whether to contribute to a shared good worth 1 to each if at least one contributes. Contributing costs \(\theta_i\in\Theta_i=\{\tfrac{1}{4},2\}\), known only to \(i\). With actions \(C\) (contribute) and \(D\) (decline), a strategy for \(i\) lists an action for each cost: \((C,C)\), \((C,D)\), \((D,C)\) or \((D,D)\), where the first entry is the action of the low-cost type. That is \(2^2=4\) pure strategies, although each neighbour takes only one action.

Quality. A used-car seller's type is the car's quality \(\theta\in\{L,H\}\). The buyer does not observe it and must form beliefs about it; this is the setting of the market for lemons.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(S_i\) be player \(i\)'s strategy set and \(S_{-i}\) the set of strategy profiles of the other players in a normal-form game with payoffs \(v_i\). A strategy \(s_i\in S_i\) weakly dominates \(s_i'\in S_i\) if, for all \(s_{-i}\in S_{-i}\),

\[ v_i(s_i,s_{-i})\ge v_i(s_i',s_{-i}), \]

with strict inequality for at least one \(s_{-i}\in S_{-i}\). The strategy \(s_i\) is weakly dominant if it weakly dominates every other strategy \(s_i'\ne s_i\) of player \(i\). In a Bayesian game the same definition is applied type by type: for each type, the action must do at least as well against every action profile of the opponents, and strictly better against at least one.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A weakly dominant strategy is never worse than any alternative, whatever the others do, and is strictly better against at least one of their choices. A player who uses it needs no beliefs about the opponents: it is a best response to every \(s_{-i}\).

In the figure (the truthful-bidding example below), a bid that beats the highest rival bid earns \(10\) minus that rival bid, and a losing bid earns \(0\). Bidding \(10\) and bidding \(8\) give the same payoff when the highest rival bid is below \(8\) (for example \(3\) at \(7\)) or above \(10\) (for example \(0\) at \(12\)), and bidding \(10\) is strictly better in between (\(1\) versus \(0\) at \(9\)). That is weak dominance: never worse, and strictly better against some rival bids.

Drag the highest rival bid \(c\): the payoffs of bidding \(10\) and bidding \(8\) coincide except for \(8<c<10\), where bidding \(10\) is strictly better. That single gap is what makes bidding \(10\) weakly, not strictly, dominant.

The difference from a strictly dominant strategy is that ties are allowed. Strict dominance requires a strictly higher payoff against every \(s_{-i}\); weak dominance only requires "never worse, sometimes better". Every strictly dominant strategy is therefore weakly dominant, but not conversely.

Ties have consequences. A weakly dominated strategy can still be a best response to some opponent profile, so it can appear in a Nash equilibrium, and iterated deletion of weakly dominated strategies can give different results depending on the order of deletion. A leading application is the second-price auction, where bidding one's own value is weakly (not strictly) dominant.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Strictly dominant \(\Rightarrow\) weakly dominant; the converse fails (see the example below).
  • Under this definition a player has at most one weakly dominant strategy: two strategies cannot each weakly dominate the other, because each would need a strict inequality the other rules out.
  • If every player has a weakly dominant strategy, the profile of these strategies is a Nash equilibrium. It need not be the only Nash equilibrium.
  • A Nash equilibrium may involve weakly dominated strategies; it can never involve strictly dominated ones.
  • In a second-price sealed-bid auction with private values, bidding \(b_i=\theta_i\) (one's valuation) is weakly dominant; in a first-price auction no bid has this property.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
A weakly but not strictly dominant strategy. Consider

\(L\) \(R\) \(U\) \(1,1\) \(0,0\) \(D\) \(0,0\) \(0,0\)

For the row player, \(U\) gives \(1>0\) against \(L\) and \(0=0\) against \(R\), so \(U\) weakly dominates \(D\) and is weakly dominant, but not strictly dominant. The same holds for \(L\) for the column player. Both \((U,L)\) and \((D,R)\) are Nash equilibria: at \((D,R)\) neither player gains by deviating alone, although both use weakly dominated strategies. Deleting weakly dominated strategies selects \((U,L)\).

Truthful bidding. A bidder with value \(10\) in a second-price auction compares bidding \(10\) with bidding \(8\). If the highest rival bid is \(9\), bidding \(10\) wins and gives \(10-9=1\), while bidding \(8\) loses and gives \(0\). If the highest rival bid is \(7\) or \(12\), both bids give the same payoff (\(3\) and \(0\)). So bidding \(10\) is never worse and sometimes strictly better.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The winner's curse is the systematic overpayment that occurs in a common-value auction when bidders bid on the basis of their naive estimate \(\mathbb{E}[v\mid\theta_i]\) of the common value \(v\), which ignores the information contained in the event of winning. Because a bidder tends to win precisely when her signal \(\theta_i\) is among the most optimistic, the value conditional on winning is lower:

\[ \mathbb{E}[v\mid\theta_i,\ i\text{ wins}]\ <\ \mathbb{E}[v\mid\theta_i] \]

in the usual models, so a naive winner expects to pay more than the object is worth on average.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Each bidder's estimate may be unbiased, yet the winning estimate is biased upwards: the winner is selected as the bidder with the largest estimate, and the largest of several noisy estimates overshoots the truth on average. Winning is bad news about what the other bidders observed.

In the figure (the jar-of-coins example below), each estimate \(\theta_i=100+\varepsilon_i\) is uniform on \([80,120]\) and centred on the true value \(v=100\). The largest of three estimates has density \(3(x-80)^2/40^3\) for \(80\le x\le120\), which piles up near \(120\), and its mean is \(\mathbb{E}[\max_i\theta_i]=110\). A bidder who bids her estimate wins exactly when hers is the largest, so on average she pays \(10\) more than the object is worth.

Add bidders: the largest estimate moves further above the true value, so a naive winner's expected loss \(w(n-1)/(n+1)\) grows. With \(n=1\) there is no curse.

The curse is a mistake of naive bidders, not a feature of equilibrium. A rational bidder computes the conditional expectation of \(v\) given her own signal and the event that she wins, and shades her bid accordingly. In a Bayesian Nash equilibrium of a common-value auction, winners do not lose money on average. The downward adjustment for this effect is larger with more bidders, because winning against many rivals is worse news; stronger competition pushes bids in the other direction, so the net effect of \(n\) on bids depends on the model.

The curse does not arise with private values: a rival's signal then says nothing about one's own value. The same logic of "the event that the trade happens is informative" appears in adverse selection, for example in the market for lemons.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(n\) estimates are \(\theta_i=v+\varepsilon_i\) with i.i.d. errors of mean \(0\), then \(\mathbb{E}[\max_i\theta_i\mid v]=v+\mathbb{E}[\max_i\varepsilon_i]>v\) for \(n\ge2\) (non-degenerate errors), and the bias grows with \(n\).
  • Rational bidding conditions on winning: bid less than \(\mathbb{E}[v\mid\theta_i]\) in a first-price auction; in a second-price auction, bid \(\mathbb{E}[v\mid\theta_i,\ \text{highest rival signal}=\theta_i]\) in the symmetric equilibrium.
  • In equilibrium the winner's expected profit is nonnegative; only bidders who ignore the information in winning suffer the curse.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Jar of coins. The true value is \(v=100\). Each of \(n=3\) bidders observes \(\theta_i=100+\varepsilon_i\) with \(\varepsilon_i\) i.i.d. \(\operatorname{Unif}(-20,20)\), so each estimate is unbiased. The largest error is the maximum order statistic of three uniforms: \(\mathbb{E}[\max\varepsilon_i]=-20+40\cdot\frac{3}{4}=10\). If everybody bids her estimate in a first-price auction, the winner pays \(110\) on average for an object worth \(100\): an expected loss of \(10\).

Two-bidder common value. Let \(v=\theta_1+\theta_2\) with \(\theta_1,\theta_2\) i.i.d. \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\), and bidder 1 observes \(\theta_1=0.6\). Her unconditional estimate is \(\mathbb{E}[v\mid\theta_1=0.6]=0.6+0.5=1.1\). Suppose both bidders naively bid their unconditional estimate \(\theta_i+0.5\) in a first-price auction. Bidder 1 then wins exactly when \(\theta_2<0.6\), and \(\mathbb{E}[v\mid\theta_1=0.6,\ \theta_2<0.6]=0.6+0.3=0.9\). She pays \(1.1\), so she loses \(0.2\) on average whenever she wins. The equilibrium bid in this model is \(b(\theta)=\theta\), here \(0.6\), which leaves an expected margin of \(0.3\) when winning.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For twice differentiable increasing utility with \(u'(w)>0\), the absolute risk aversion coefficient is \(r(w)=-u''(w)/u'(w)\). It measures local curvature relative to marginal utility at wealth \(w\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Curvature determines how much a small uncertain loss matters beyond its mean. The coefficient is unchanged by positive affine transformations of utility.

The figure plots \(r(w)\) for two utilities from the Key Results. Exponential utility with \(\alpha=0.01\), the coefficient of the Example, has the same curvature at every wealth level, so the certainty equivalent of a given small risk lies below \(w\) by about the same amount, \(\tfrac{1}{2}\alpha\varepsilon^2\operatorname{Var}(Z)\), however wealthy the policyholder is. Power utility with \(\gamma=\tfrac{1}{2}\) (chosen for the figure) has \(r(w)=0.5/w\): it is more risk averse than the exponential utility below \(w=50\) and less above, and its aversion to a fixed small risk fades as wealth grows.

Move the wealth \(w\): the exponential \(r(w)=\alpha\) stays flat while the power utility's \(r(w)\) falls with wealth. The approximate premium \(\tfrac12r(w)\operatorname{Var}\) for a small risk of variance 100 is 0.5 at \(\alpha=0.01\).

Expected utility and risk aversion relates concave utility to aversion to uncertain wealth. The higher-order derivative \(u''(w)\) measures that curvature; dividing its negative by marginal utility \(u'(w)\) makes the local coefficient unchanged by positive affine changes of utility.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Exponential utility \(u(w)=-\mathrm{e}^{-\alpha w}\) has constant absolute risk aversion (CARA) \(r(w)=\alpha>0\).
  • Power utility \(u(w)=w^\gamma\), \(0<\gamma<1\), \(w>0\), has \(r(w)=(1-\gamma)/w\).
  • For a small mean-zero risk \(\varepsilon Z\), the certainty equivalent (the sure wealth with the same expected utility as \(w+\varepsilon Z\)) lies below \(w\) by approximately \(\tfrac{1}{2}r(w)\varepsilon^2\operatorname{Var}(Z)\), with smoothness and moment conditions for the Taylor approximation.
  • This local approximation is not an exact formula for arbitrary large losses.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: With exponential coefficient \(\alpha=0.01\) and a sufficiently small centred loss of variance 100, the second-order premium above the mean is approximately \(0.5(0.01)(100)=0.5\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A bonus-malus system (BMS) assigns each policyholder to a rating level, updates that level using claim history, and charges a base premium multiplied by a level-specific premium relativity. It specifies the levels, initial level, transition rules and premium scale.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Claim-free years can earn lower premiums and reported claims can trigger higher premiums. The system uses observed experience to distinguish underlying risks that are not fully captured by initial rating factors.

The figure draws the two-level scheme of the Example. The next level depends only on whether the year's claim count \(N_t\) is zero, not on the current level: a claim-free year (green, probability \(\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda}\) at a fixed rate \(\lambda\)) leads to premium \(c\), and a year with at least one reported claim (red, probability \(1-\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda}\)) leads to \(2c\). The two levels, the arrows of the transition rule and the premium relativities \(1\) and \(2\) are the ingredients the definition lists.

The Poisson distribution models the annual claim count at fixed claim rate \(\lambda\). In particular, its zero-claim probability \(\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda}\) determines how often a claim-free-year bonus applies.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Let \(L_t\) be level in policy year \(t\) and \(r_l\) the premium relativity for level \(l\).
  • With random claim rate \(\Lambda\), the notes model annual claims conditionally as \(N_t\mid\Lambda=\lambda\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)\).
  • A transition rule \(T(l,n)\) maps the current level and reported annual count to next year's level.
  • Conditioning on a fixed claim rate can give a Markov chain. Mixing over unobserved claim rates does not automatically preserve the Markov property.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: A two-level scheme charges \(c\) after a claim-free year and \(2c\) after a year with claims. Its next level depends on whether the reported count is zero.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: At a fixed claim rate \(\lambda\), let \(p_{ij}(\lambda)=\mathbb{P}(L_{t+1}=j\mid L_t=i,\lambda)\). The transition matrix \(\boldsymbol{P}(\lambda)=(p_{ij})\) has nonnegative entries and each row sums to one. For row-vector level probabilities \(\boldsymbol{a}_t\), the next-year distribution is \(\boldsymbol{a}_{t+1}=\boldsymbol{a}_t\boldsymbol{P}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The bonus-malus system supplies the rule assigning next year's class from the current state and claim count. The entries above are conditional probabilities given the current state; the matrix product adds their contributions to the next-year class probabilities.

Each arrow in the figure is one entry of \(\boldsymbol{P}(\lambda)\) from the Example, with \(p=1-\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda}\) and \(q=\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda}\). Red arrows are years with a claim: from every state they lead to state 1, which fills the first column with \(p\). Green arrows are claim-free years: state 1 moves to 2, while states 2 and 3 move to 3. The arrows leaving state \(i\) give row \(i\), and their probabilities sum to \(p+q=1\).

Pick a starting state and move the year \(t\) and the claim rate \(\lambda\): \(\boldsymbol{a}_t=\boldsymbol{a}_0\boldsymbol{P}^t\) reaches the stationary law \((p,pq,q^2)\) after two years from any start. The default \(\lambda=0.2231\approx\log1.25\) gives \(p=0.2\).

The state must store enough history for the transition rule. For a two-year claim-free discount, a simple high/low premium label may omit the information needed for next year.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Under a deterministic rule \(T(i,n)\) and Poisson count, \(\displaystyle p_{ij}(\lambda)=\sum_{n\colon T(i,n)=j}\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda}\lambda^n/n!\).
  • At a fixed rate with independent yearly claims, \(\boldsymbol{a}_t=\boldsymbol{a}_0\boldsymbol{P}^t\).
  • The notes' three states are a claim in the latest year, one claim-free year after a claim, and at least two claim-free years.
  • Matrix orientation must match the row-vector convention. The general Markov chain framework is formalized in Year 3 Stochastic Models; the transition calculation here uses the conditional probabilities defined above.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: With \(p=1-\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda}\) and \(q=\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda}\), the three-state matrix has rows \((p,q,0)\), \((p,0,q)\) and \((p,0,q)\). These rows each sum to one.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Under right censoring at a known cap \(c_i\), an exact continuous loss \(x_i<c_i\) is observed if it is below the cap; otherwise one observes only \(X_i\ge c_i\). With indicator \(\delta_i=1\) for an exact observation, its likelihood contribution is \(f_\theta(x_i)^{\delta_i}\bar F_\theta(c_i)^{1-\delta_i}\) under continuous losses and non-informative censoring (the censoring caps are independent of the losses and carry no information about \(\theta\)).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The policy exists in the sample even when its full loss is unknown. A capped observation gives a tail event, not a point density at the cap.

The curve is the exponential density at the Example's estimate \(\hat\lambda=2/150\). The exact losses 20 and 30 enter the likelihood through the heights \(f_\theta(20)\) and \(f_\theta(30)\); the observation capped at \(c_i=100\) enters through the shaded area \(\bar F_\theta(100)=\mathrm{e}^{-100\lambda}\), which at \(\hat\lambda\) equals \(\mathrm{e}^{-4/3}\approx0.26\). The product \(\lambda^2\mathrm{e}^{-50\lambda}\cdot \mathrm{e}^{-100\lambda}\) has logarithm \(2\log\lambda-150\lambda\), the log-likelihood of the Example.

Move \(\lambda\) and the cap: the capped loss contributes \(\bar F_\theta(100)\), not a density height, so at the default cap \(\hat\lambda=2/150\) rather than the \(3/150\) obtained by treating the cap as an exact loss.

Maximum likelihood estimation maximizes the probability or density of the data actually recorded. A capped observation records a tail event, so its contribution is the survivor function at the cap rather than the density of an exact loss there.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Independent contributions multiply; exact observations contribute log densities and censored observations log survivor probabilities.
  • For a common exponential rate, \(\displaystyle \hat\lambda=r/[\sum_{\mathrm{exact}}x_i+\sum_{\mathrm{censored}}c_i]\), if \(r>0\) is the number of exact losses.
  • If no exact losses occur, an interior maximum need not exist.
  • An atom at the censoring boundary requires careful use of strict or weak tail events.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: For exact losses 20 and 30 plus one observation capped at 100, exponential log-likelihood is \(2\log\lambda-150\lambda\). Thus \(\hat\lambda=2/150\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Under coinsurance, the insurer pays a specified proportion \(a\in[0,1]\) of a covered loss and the insured or another insurer pays the rest. Without other modifications, insurer payment is \(Y=aX\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Both parties share each covered monetary unit. Combining coinsurance with an ordinary deductible or policy limit requires specifying the order of those operations.

The figure splits the Example's loss \(X=1000\), with \(a=0.8\) and deductible \(d=100\), between the insured (blue) and the insurer (red). Applying the deductible first leaves an excess of 900, of which the insurer pays \(0.8(900)=720\) and the insured keeps \(100+180=280\). Sharing first gives the insurer \(aX=800\) before the deductible, so it pays \(700\) and the insured keeps \(100+200=300\). The gap of 20 is \((1-a)d\): sharing after the deductible lowers the insurer's payment below \(aX\) by only \(ad=80\), while deducting after sharing lowers it by the full \(d=100\).

Change the insurer share \(a\), the deductible \(d\) and the loss \(X\): deducting first pays \(a(X-d)_+\), sharing first pays \((aX-d)_+\), and while both are positive they differ by \((1-a)d\). The default \(X=1000\), \(a=0.8\), \(d=100\) gives 720 against 700.

Variance and standard deviation explains why proportional sharing scales the variance quadratically: multiplying each realized loss by \(a\) multiplies its deviation from the mean by \(a\), and its squared deviation by \(a^2\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{E}[aX]=a\mathbb{E}[X]\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(aX)=a^2\operatorname{Var}(X)\) when finite.
  • For \(a>0\), \(F_{aX}(y)=F_X(y/a)\).
  • \(a\min((X-d)_+,u)\) means sharing an already capped excess. It differs from \(\min((aX-d)_+,u)\).
  • In reinsurance, a quota-share treaty applies the same proportional split to the insurer's portfolio losses: the reinsurer pays a fixed share of every loss.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: With \(a=0.8\), \(X=1000\) and deductible 100, sharing after the deductible gives \(0.8(900)=720\). Applying the deductible after sharing gives \(800-100=700\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The collective risk model writes \(\displaystyle S=\sum_{i=1}^NX_i\), where \(N\) is a nonnegative integer claim count and the claim severities \(X_i\) are independent, identically distributed nonnegative variables, independent of \(N\). The sum is zero when \(N=0\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The number of claims is random, and the summands describe actual claims rather than all policies. A policy can generate more than one claim unless the frequency model rules that out.

The figure shows one year of a small portfolio. The policies form a fixed set, but the model sums over the claims they produce: here policy 2 has two claims, policy 4 has one and policies 1, 3 and 5 have none, so \(N=3\) and \(S=X_1+X_2+X_3\). In another year \(N\) could be 0, giving \(S=0\), or exceed the number of policies. In the Example \(N\sim\operatorname{Pois}(5)\), so the portfolio produces five claims on average.

Change \(\lambda\) and the severity mean and standard deviation: \(\mathbb E[S]=\lambda\mu\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(S)=\lambda(\sigma^2+\mu^2)\), so the claim-size mean contributes to the spread of \(S\) even when \(\sigma\) is small.

The individual risk model sums losses over a fixed set of policies; here the summation is over a random number of actual claims. Assuming i.i.d. random variables gives all severities the same law. The independent random variables assumptions ensure that fixing \(N=n\) leaves a sum of \(n\) independent draws from that law.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Conditional on \(N=n\), total loss has the distribution of a sum of \(n\) severities.
  • Mean and variance follow from the random-sum formulas on the compound distribution page.
  • If severities are strictly positive, \(\mathbb{P}(S=0)=\mathbb{P}(N=0)\); otherwise zero severities also matter.
  • Frequency–severity independence is a substantive modelling assumption.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: With \(N\sim\operatorname{Pois}(5)\) and independent severities of mean 100 and variance 400, mean aggregate loss is 500 and variance is \(5(400+100^2)=52000\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A compound Poisson loss is \(\displaystyle S=\sum_{i=1}^NX_i\) with \(N\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)\), \(\lambda\ge0\), and i.i.d. nonnegative severities independent of \(N\). The empty sum is zero.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Poisson frequency makes aggregate losses particularly tractable. Even with continuous positive severities, aggregate loss includes a probability of no claims at all.

The figure plots the Example's loss \(S=2N\) with \(\lambda=3\), so \(\mathbb{P}(S=2k)=\mathrm{e}^{-3}3^k/k!\). The orange bar at zero is the no-claim probability \(\mathbb{P}(S=0)=\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda}=\mathrm{e}^{-3}\approx0.05\), present even though every claim is positive. The mass sits only on even values, and the mean \(6=\lambda\mathbb{E}[X]\) and variance \(12=\lambda\mathbb{E}[X^2]\) follow from the Key Results; a Poisson variable with mean 6 would have variance 6.

Move \(\lambda\) and pick a claim-size law: \(\mathbb E[S]=\lambda\mathbb E[X]\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(S)=\lambda\mathbb E[X^2]\), and the spike at 0 always has height \(e^{-\lambda}\). With claims fixed at 2, \(S=2N\) lives on the even numbers.

This specializes the compound risk distribution by choosing the count from the Poisson distribution. Since its count mean and variance both equal \(\lambda\), the general random-sum variance simplifies to \(\lambda\mathbb{E}[X^2]\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{E}[S]=\lambda\mathbb{E}[X]\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(S)=\lambda\mathbb{E}[X^2]\) when finite.
  • The moment generating function (MGF) satisfies \(M_S(t)=\exp(\lambda(M_X(t)-1))\) where finite.
  • With strictly positive severity, \(\mathbb{P}(S=0)=\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda}\).
  • Claim counts for disjoint severity categories are independent Poisson variables with rates \(\lambda p_j\) (with \(p_j\) the probability that a claim falls in category \(j\)); this uses the Poisson splitting result.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: If each claim is 2 and \(\lambda=3\), then \(S=2N\) has mean 6 and variance 12. Its support is \(0,2,4,\ldots\), so it is not an ordinary Poisson variable.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a Poisson process \(N(t)\) of rate \(\lambda\) and i.i.d. severities \(X_i\ge0\) independent of the entire process, the compound Poisson process is \(\displaystyle S(t)=\sum_{i=1}^{N(t)}X_i\), \(t\ge0\). It records cumulative claims over time.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The path stays constant between claim arrivals and jumps by each arriving claim amount. A compound Poisson distribution describes one time horizon; this process describes all horizons consistently.

The figure shows one possible path for the Example's portfolio (claim rate 2 per year, every claim 100), with claims arriving at the illustrative times 0.35, 0.8, 1.1 and 1.75. The path is flat between arrivals and jumps by the claim amount at each one; a filled dot marks the value at the arrival time, which already includes that claim. The dashed line is the mean \(\mathbb{E}[S(t)]=\lambda t\mathbb{E}[X]=200t\), which equals 100 at \(t=0.5\), as in the Example.

Move \(t\) along the path and draw new paths: \(S(t)\) is flat between arrivals and jumps by one claim at each, while the dashed line is \(\mathbb E[S(t)]=\lambda t\,\mathbb E[X]\). Change \(\lambda\) or switch to exponential claim sizes to see how the jumps change.

The Poisson process supplies both the number and timing of arrivals. Attaching one independent severity to each arrival produces the jumps; its independent increments, together with independent severities, give independent loss increments.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(S(t)\) is compound Poisson with frequency parameter \(\lambda t\).
  • It has stationary independent increments: \(S(t+s)-S(s)\) has the same law as \(S(t)\) for all \(s,t\ge0\), and increments over disjoint intervals are independent.
  • \(\mathbb{E}[S(t)]=\lambda t\mathbb{E}[X]\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(S(t))=\lambda t\mathbb{E}[X^2]\) when finite.
  • The insurer's surplus (its capital) at time \(t\), starting from initial capital \(u\) and collecting premiums at constant rate \(c\), is \(u+ct-S(t)\). Ruin, the event that the surplus becomes negative at some time, is not developed here.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: With claim rate 2 per year and fixed severity 100, \(S(0.5)=100N(0.5)\) and \(N(0.5)\sim\operatorname{Pois}(1)\). Mean half-year loss is 100.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: Let independent compound Poisson losses \(S_j\) have rates \(\lambda_j\ge0\) and severity cumulative distribution functions (CDFs) \(F_j\), for \(j=1,\ldots,m\). If \(\displaystyle \lambda=\sum_j\lambda_j>0\), their sum is compound Poisson with rate \(\lambda\) and severity CDF \(\displaystyle F=\sum_j(\lambda_j/\lambda)F_j\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Pooling portfolios (see Poisson merging) adds their claim-arrival rates. A randomly chosen pooled claim belongs to a portfolio with probability proportional to that portfolio's arrival rate.

The figure uses the Example's portfolios with illustrative arrival times; each bar's height is the claim amount. Pooling keeps every claim, so the pooled stream has rate \(2+3=5\). A pooled claim comes from portfolio 1 and equals 10 with probability \(2/5\), and from portfolio 2 and equals 20 with probability \(3/5\) (in the stretch drawn, 4 of the 10 claims are 10s), so the pooled severity is the mixture \(F=\tfrac{2}{5}F_1+\tfrac{3}{5}F_2\). The mean total loss is \(5(\tfrac{2}{5}\cdot10+\tfrac{3}{5}\cdot20)=80\).

Change the two rates and claim sizes: the pooled compound Poisson law with rate \(\lambda_1+\lambda_2\) and the mixed severity agrees with the convolution of the two portfolio totals at every point.

The pooled severity law is a mixture distribution: first choose the originating portfolio with probability \(\lambda_j/\lambda\), then draw a claim from that portfolio's severity law. Those probabilities are proportional to claim rates, not to portfolio counts.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Pooled severity weights are \(\lambda_j/\lambda\), not equal portfolio weights unless rates are equal.
  • Independent losses have additive means and variances.
  • Multiplying the component moment generating functions (MGFs) yields \(\exp[\lambda(M_X(t)-1)]\) when the MGFs exist.
  • The result also holds without a finite positive MGF, by viewing the pooled claims as one Poisson arrival stream in which each arrival independently carries a portfolio label \(j\) (probability \(\lambda_j/\lambda\)) and a severity from \(F_j\); compare Poisson splitting.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Two portfolios have rates 2 and 3 and fixed claim amounts 10 and 20. Their pooled rate is 5 and severities are 10 with probability \(2/5\) and 20 with probability \(3/5\). Mean total loss is 80.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The distribution of \(\displaystyle S=\sum_{i=1}^NX_i\) is a compound distribution when \(N\) is a nonnegative integer variable and the \(X_i\) are i.i.d. severities independent of \(N\). Let \(\mu=\mathbb{E}[X_1]\) and \(\sigma^2=\operatorname{Var}(X_1)\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Compounding combines uncertainty in the number of claims with uncertainty in their sizes. It differs from mixing a parameter of one distribution.

The figure reads the formula for \(F_S\) as a two-stage experiment. The count is drawn first, with probability \(\mathbb{P}(N=n)\) for each branch; given \(N=n\), the loss is a sum of \(n\) independent severities, whose law is the \(n\)-fold convolution \(F_X^{*n}\) (and \(S=0\) when \(n=0\)). Averaging the branch laws with the branch probabilities gives \(F_S\). In the Bernoulli Example only the branches \(n=0\) and \(n=1\) remain, with weights \(1-q\) and \(q\), which is why the result is a simple mixture.

Pick a claim-count law and move \(\mathbb E[N]\): the count's variance enters \(\operatorname{Var}(S)=\mathbb E[N]\sigma^2+\operatorname{Var}(N)\mu^2\). With a Bernoulli count \(S\) is 0 with probability \(1-q\) and otherwise one severity.

The collective risk model supplies the random-sum assumptions. Given \(N=n\), convolution of independent random variables gives \(F_X^{*n}\), and the probability generating function averages transform powers over the count. Adam’s law: total expectation applied to \(\mathbb{E}[S\mid N]=N\mu\) gives the mean. The conditioning trick for variance combines \(\operatorname{Var}(S\mid N)=N\sigma^2\) with variation in \(N\mu\) to give the two variance terms.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{E}[S]=\mathbb{E}[N]\mu\).
  • \(\operatorname{Var}(S)=\mathbb{E}[N]\sigma^2+\operatorname{Var}(N)\mu^2\), with finite second moments.
  • With moment generating function (MGF) \(M\) and PGF \(G\), \(M_S(t)=G_N(M_X(t))\) where the expression is finite; for integer severities \(G_S(z)=G_N(G_X(z))\).
  • \(\displaystyle F_S(s)=\sum_{n\ge0}\mathbb{P}(N=n)F_X^{*n}(s)\), with \(F_X^{*0}\) the cumulative distribution function of the constant zero.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: If \(N\) is Bernoulli with probability \(q\), then \(S\) is zero with probability \(1-q\) and otherwise has the severity law. Thus a compound Bernoulli model is also a simple mixture.

docs.title: Convex Order and More Dangerous Risks
Definition
docs.text: For integrable losses, convex order \(X\le_{\mathrm{cx}}Y\) means \(\mathbb{E}[h(X)]\le\mathbb{E}[h(Y)]\) for every convex function for which comparison is defined. For nonnegative losses this is equivalent to stop-loss order together with \(\mathbb{E}[X]=\mathbb{E}[Y]\). The course calls the larger risk more dangerous in this equal-mean setting.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Convex order compares dispersion after removing a difference in mean. All risk-averse agents prefer the less dispersed loss when utility expectations are defined.

The figure uses the Example's risks. Both have mean 1, but \(Y\) spreads its mass to 0 and 2. On the right, \(\mathbb{E}[(X-d)_+]=(1-d)_+\) and \(\mathbb{E}[(Y-d)_+]=(2-d)_+/2\) start from the common mean at \(d=0\), and the second is never smaller, so \(X\) precedes \(Y\) in stop-loss order with equal means, which is the characterization of \(X\le_{\mathrm{cx}}Y\) in the definition. The gap between the lines reflects the extra dispersion of \(Y\), which also shows in the variances 0 and 1.

Spread \(X\) and \(Y\) around their common mean 1: both stop-loss transforms start at \(\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[Y]=1\), and the more dispersed risk lies above at every \(d\), so \(X\le_{\mathrm{cx}}Y\) when \(Y\) has the larger spread.

Convexity and concavity determines which test functions enter the comparison. Convex functions penalize dispersion; their negatives are concave, explaining the preference of risk-averse wealth utilities for the less dispersed loss.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The order forces equal means because both \(h(x)=x\) and \(h(x)=-x\) are convex.
  • With finite second moments, \(\operatorname{Var}(X)\le\operatorname{Var}(Y)\); if the distributions differ, this inequality is strict.
  • Variance ordering alone does not imply convex order.
  • Convex order is not preserved by every convex transformation, because equal means can be lost.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: A constant loss of 1 is below the equal-probability loss on \(\{0,2\}\) in convex order. Their variances are 0 and 1.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: If the moment generating function (MGF) \(M_X(t)=\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{e}^{tX}]\) is finite in a neighbourhood of zero, the cumulant generating function is \(K_X(t)=\log M_X(t)\) on that domain. Its derivatives at zero are called cumulants.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Taking logarithms turns products of independent MGFs into sums. This makes cumulants a convenient way to describe aggregate risk.

The figure plots the Example's \(K(t)=\lambda(\mathrm{e}^t-1)\) for independent \(X\sim\operatorname{Pois}(1)\) and \(Y\sim\operatorname{Pois}(2)\) (rates chosen for the figure) and for \(X+Y\sim\operatorname{Pois}(3)\). At every \(t\) the green curve is the sum of the blue and red ones, which is the additivity \(K_{X+Y}=K_X+K_Y\). All three pass through the origin because \(K(0)=\log1=0\), and their slopes there are \(1\), \(2\) and \(3\), the means \(K'(0)=\lambda\).

Change the two Poisson means and move \(t\): \(K_{X+Y}(t)=K_X(t)+K_Y(t)\) at every \(t\), so \(X+Y\) is Poisson with mean \(\lambda_X+\lambda_Y\), and the first two derivatives at 0 both equal the mean.

The MGF of an independent sum is the product of the component MGFs. Taking its logarithm converts that product into addition, which explains the additive cumulant formula.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(K_X'(0)=\mathbb{E}[X]\) and \(K_X''(0)=\operatorname{Var}(X)\).
  • For independent \(X,Y\) with suitable MGFs, \(K_{X+Y}=K_X+K_Y\).
  • \(K_{aX+b}(t)=bt+K_X(at)\) for constants \(a,b\) on the common domain.
  • Existence of ordinary moments does not ensure a finite MGF for positive arguments.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: For \(X\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)\), \(K_X(t)=\lambda(\mathrm{e}^t-1)\). Its first two derivatives at zero both equal \(\lambda\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The expected utility model compares uncertain wealth \(W\) through \(\mathbb{E}[u(W)]\). An increasing concave utility function \(u\) represents risk aversion: for integrable wealth with well-defined utilities, \(\mathbb{E}[u(W)]\le u(\mathbb{E}[W])\). A linear increasing utility represents risk neutrality.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A risk-averse policyholder can prefer a fixed payment to an uncertain loss with the same mean. Utility is applied to final wealth, so larger losses usually reduce utility.

The figure, drawn schematically, takes wealth \(W\) equal to \(w_1\) or \(w_2\) with probability \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) each. The expected utility \(\mathbb{E}[u(W)]\) is the midpoint of the dashed chord, while \(u(\mathbb{E}[W])\) is the height of the curve at the mean; concavity keeps the curve above the chord, so \(\mathbb{E}[u(W)]\le u(\mathbb{E}[W])\). In the Example \(w_1=80\), \(w_2=100\) and \(\mathbb{E}[W]=90\) under logarithmic utility: \([\log100+\log80]/2<\log90\), so the certain loss of 10 is preferred.

Choose a utility and move the wealth \(w\), the loss and its probability: the chord value \(\mathbb E[u(W)]\) stays below \(u(\mathbb E[W])\), and the horizontal gap to the certainty equivalent is the risk premium. The default logarithmic case gives \([\log100+\log80]/2<\log90\).

Convexity and concavity describes the downward curvature of a risk-averse utility. Applying Jensen's inequality to this concave function gives \(\mathbb{E}[u(W)]\le u(\mathbb{E}[W])\), the comparison between uncertain wealth and its certain mean.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Replacing \(u\) by \(au+b\) with \(a>0\) preserves preferences.
  • Concavity gives the Jensen comparison; strict preference requires suitable strict concavity and nondegenerate wealth.
  • Fractional power utility requires positive wealth. Quadratic utility is increasing only on a restricted domain.
  • The expected value of a payoff and expected utility are different criteria.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: At wealth 100, a loss of 0 or 20 with equal probabilities gives expected logarithmic utility \([\log100+\log80]/2\). A certain loss of 10 gives \(\log90\), which is larger.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For integrable loss \(X\ge0\), the expected value principle sets \(\Pi(X)=(1+\theta)\mathbb{E}[X]\), where \(\theta\ge0\) is a fixed loading coefficient: the loading \(\Pi(X)-\mathbb{E}[X]=\theta\mathbb{E}[X]\) is a fixed proportion of the mean, so the principle has nonnegative loading. At \(\theta=0\), it is the net premium principle, \(\Pi(X)=\mathbb{E}[X]\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The loading is a constant proportion of expected loss. Different risks with the same mean receive the same price, regardless of their dispersion.

The figure draws the Examples case \(\theta=0.2\). The premium line \((1+\theta)\mathbb{E}[X]\) is a ray through the origin with slope \(1.2\), so the loading, the vertical gap to the net-premium line \(\mathbb{E}[X]\), grows in proportion to the mean: at \(\mathbb{E}[X]=100\) the premium is 120 and the gap is 20. Only the mean enters, so any two risks with that mean sit at the same point. Adding a certain 10 moves the mean to 110 and the premium to 132, so the certain amount is loaded as well, which is why translation consistency fails.

Move the loading \(\theta\), the expected loss and the certain cost \(c\): \(\Pi(X)=(1+\theta)\mathbb E[X]\), and because the certain cost is loaded too, \(\Pi(X+c)\) exceeds \(\Pi(X)+c\) by \(\theta c\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The principle is proportional and additive for integrable losses, even without independence.
  • It has nonnegative loading and is monotone under stochastic or stop-loss order.
  • For \(\theta>0\), translation consistency fails: adding certain cost \(c\) adds \((1+\theta)c\) to the premium.
  • Iterativity follows from total expectation only in the net case; repeating a positive loading generally applies it twice.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: For expected loss 100 and \(\theta=0.2\), premium is 120. Adding a certain 10 raises the premium to 132, rather than 130.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
An exponential family is a family of probability laws whose mass function or density, relative to a fixed reference measure (counting for a probability mass function, so probabilities are sums; length for a probability density function, so probabilities are integrals), can be written as

\[ f(y;\boldsymbol{\theta})=h(y)\exp\!\left\{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\boldsymbol{T}(y)-A(\boldsymbol{\theta})\right\}. \]

Here \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) is a vector of natural parameters, \(\boldsymbol{T}(y)\) a vector of statistics, \((\cdot)^{\top}\) the transpose (written \((\cdot)^{\top}\) rather than the \((\cdot)^{\top}\) used on the other pages, to avoid a clash with the statistic \(\boldsymbol{T}\)), \(h(y)\) a nonnegative base factor, and \(A\) the log-normalizing function. The parameter domain contains values for which the normalizing sum or integral is finite. The support is fixed across the family in the regular setting used below.

For the one-parameter response families used in generalized linear models, the usual form is

\[ f(y;\theta,\phi)=\exp\!\left\{\frac{y\theta-b(\theta)}{a(\phi)}+c(y,\phi)\right\}. \]

Here \(\theta\) is the scalar natural parameter, \(\phi\) a dispersion parameter, \(a(\phi)>0\) a scale factor, \(b\) the normalizing function, and \(c\) the remaining term. This GLM form is a specialized representation; it does not describe every exponential family with an arbitrary statistic \(\boldsymbol{T}(y)\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The mass function sums to one for a discrete response, whereas the density integrates to one for a continuous response. Their logarithms have the same parameter structure, allowing a common modelling framework for claim counts and continuous responses. An exponential family is a collection of distributions, not just the exponential waiting-time distribution.

The figure takes the Poisson row of the Examples table with \(\lambda=2\), so \(\theta=\log 2\) and \(b(\theta)=\mathrm{e}^\theta\). The slope of \(b\) at that point is \(b'(\theta)=2=\mu\), and its curvature is \(b''(\theta)=2=\operatorname{Var}(Y)\) because \(a(\phi)=1\). Since \(b\) is convex, the slope rises with \(\theta\), so a larger mean comes with a larger variance: the choice of family fixes this mean–variance relationship.

Pick a family and move \(\theta\): \(\mu=b'(\theta)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)=a(\phi)b''(\theta)\), so the convexity of \(b\) fixes how the variance follows the mean. The default Poisson case \(\theta=\log2\) gives \(\mu=\operatorname{Var}(Y)=2\).

The expectation describes the response level and the variance its spread. In the GLM form, both follow from derivatives of \(b\), so choosing a response family also chooses a mean–variance relationship.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
When the support is parameter-independent and differentiation can pass through the normalizing sum or integral, the GLM form gives

\[ \mu=\mathbb{E}[Y]=b'(\theta),\qquad \operatorname{Var}(Y)=a(\phi)b''(\theta). \]

For example, differentiating \(\log f\) with respect to \(\theta\) gives \((y-b'(\theta))/a(\phi)\). The derivative of the normalization condition has expectation zero, yielding the mean identity; differentiating again yields the variance identity. These calculations require the stated regularity, rather than just a visual resemblance to the formula.

The canonical link of a GLM is the link that makes the linear predictor the natural parameter, \(g(\mu)=\theta\), that is \(g=(b')^{-1}\) for the chosen representation. The response family and the link are separate choices; a GLM need not use its canonical link.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Response law Natural parameter \(\theta\) \(b(\theta)\) \(a(\phi)\) Mean and variance Poisson, mean \(\lambda>0\) \(\log\lambda\) \(\mathrm{e}^\theta\) \(1\) Both equal \(\lambda\) Bernoulli, \(0<p<1\) \(\log(p/(1-p))\) \(\log(1+\mathrm{e}^\theta)\) \(1\) \(p\) and \(p(1-p)\) Normal, mean \(\mu\), variance \(\sigma^2>0\) \(\mu\) \(\theta^2/2\) \(\sigma^2\) \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\)

For the Poisson case, \(c(y,\phi)=-\log(y!)\) for integer \(y\ge0\). This gives the log link and variance assumption used by Poisson regression. A count response with variance larger than its mean needs a different variance model; choosing a log link alone does not make its distribution Poisson.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For nonnegative losses, exponential order \(X\le_eY\) means \(\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{e}^{\alpha X}]\le\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{e}^{\alpha Y}]\) for every \(\alpha>0\). Comparisons may use extended values, but a finite exponential premium at a given \(\alpha\) requires the corresponding moment to be finite.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The comparison tests every exponential risk-aversion parameter. It is weaker than agreement among all increasing concave wealth utilities.

The figure plots the two moment generating functions of the Examples case. Both curves start at 1 when \(\alpha=0\) with the same slope, because \(X\) and \(Y\) have the same mean 1; for every \(\alpha>0\) the curve of \(Y\) lies above that of \(X\), which is exactly \(X\le_eY\). The gap widens as \(\alpha\) grows, because a larger risk-aversion parameter weights the outcome 2 of \(Y\) more heavily.

Move \(\alpha\): \(M_X(\alpha)\le M_Y(\alpha)\) at every \(\alpha>0\), so \(X\le_e Y\), and the exponential premium of \(Y\) is the larger one. Shrink the spread \(s\) to 0 and the two curves coincide.

The moment generating function evaluates \(\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{e}^{\alpha X}]\). Exponential order compares these values over positive arguments; finiteness at the chosen argument is needed when turning the comparison into a finite premium.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Stop-loss order implies exponential order, since \(\mathrm{e}^{\alpha x}\) is increasing and convex.
  • For \(u(w)=-\mathrm{e}^{-\alpha w}\), exponential order gives the reverse order of expected utilities of \(w-X\) and \(w-Y\).
  • With equal means and MGFs finite near zero, a Taylor comparison gives \(\operatorname{Var}(X)\le\operatorname{Var}(Y)\).
  • If both positive MGFs are infinite, the comparison can carry little information about finite premiums.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: For \(X=1\) and \(Y\) equal 0 or 2 with probability \(1/2\), \(M_X(\alpha)=\mathrm{e}^\alpha\le(1+\mathrm{e}^{2\alpha})/2=M_Y(\alpha)\) for every positive \(\alpha\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For risk-aversion parameter \(\alpha>0\) and loss \(X\) with \(\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{e}^{\alpha X}]<\infty\), the exponential premium is \(\Pi_\alpha(X)=\alpha^{-1}\log\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{e}^{\alpha X}]=K_X(\alpha)/\alpha\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
This is the indifference price for exponential wealth utility. It gives extra weight to large losses and may be infinite for losses whose positive exponential moments do not exist.

The figure draws the Examples formula with \(\lambda=1\), so \(\mathbb{E}[X]=\operatorname{Var}(X)=1\) and \(\Pi_\alpha(X)=\alpha^{-1}\log[1/(1-\alpha)]\). The premium never falls below \(\mathbb{E}[X]=1\), as Jensen's inequality requires; near \(\alpha=0\) it follows the dotted approximation \(\mathbb{E}[X]+\alpha\operatorname{Var}(X)/2=1+\alpha/2\); and as \(\alpha\) approaches \(\lambda=1\) the moment \(\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{e}^{\alpha X}]\) blows up, so the premium is infinite for \(\alpha\ge\lambda\).

Move \(\alpha\) towards \(\lambda\): \(\Pi_\alpha(X)=\alpha^{-1}\log[\lambda/(\lambda-\alpha)]\) grows without bound and is infinite for \(\alpha\ge\lambda\), while near \(\alpha=0\) it follows \(\mathbb E[X]+\tfrac12\alpha\operatorname{Var}(X)\).

The cumulant generating function is the logarithm of the loss moment generating function (MGF), so \(K_X(\alpha)/\alpha\) expresses the premium compactly. In insurance indifference premiums, substituting exponential wealth utility into the insurer's equation and cancelling the wealth factor gives precisely this formula.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Jensen's inequality gives \(\Pi_\alpha(X)\ge\mathbb{E}[X]\).
  • Translation consistency and independent additivity follow from exponential products.
  • Iterativity follows from the tower property: \(\mathrm{e}^{\alpha\Pi_\alpha(X\mid Y)}=\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{e}^{\alpha X}\mid Y]\).
  • It respects exponential order and hence stop-loss order.
  • For bounded \(X\), \(\Pi_\alpha(X)\le\operatorname{ess\,sup}X\).
  • Near \(\alpha=0\) with sufficient moments and a finite MGF, \(\Pi_\alpha(X)=\mathbb{E}[X]+\alpha\operatorname{Var}(X)/2+o(\alpha)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: For exponential severity of rate \(\lambda\) and \(0<\alpha<\lambda\), premium is \(\alpha^{-1}\log[\lambda/(\lambda-\alpha)]\). At or above \(\lambda\) it is infinite.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For positive exposure \(e_i\) and claim rate \(\lambda_i=\exp(\boldsymbol{x}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta})\), a Poisson frequency model specifies \(N_i\mid \boldsymbol{x}_i,e_i\sim\operatorname{Pois}(e_i\lambda_i)\). Therefore \(\log\mathbb{E}[N_i\mid \boldsymbol{x}_i,e_i]=\log e_i+\boldsymbol{x}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}\). The known term \(\log e_i\) is an offset, with coefficient fixed at one.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A group with twice as much insured time should have twice the expected claim count if its underlying claim rate is unchanged. The offset lets rating coefficients describe rate differences.

The figure draws the Examples case with rate \(\lambda_i=0.2\) per policy-year. On log scales, \(\log\mathbb{E}[N_i]=\log e_i+\boldsymbol{x}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}\) is a straight line whose slope in \(\log e_i\) is fixed at 1 by the offset, while the rating term \(\boldsymbol{x}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\log 0.2\) only sets its height. Multiplying exposure by 10, from 10 to 100, multiplies the expected count by 10, from 2 to 20, so the fitted rate stays 0.2.

Poisson regression relates the logarithm of an expected count to rating predictors. Exposure changes that count mean from \(\lambda_i\) to \(e_i\lambda_i\), so its logarithm adds the known offset \(\log e_i\) without estimating an extra coefficient.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Expected count is \(e_i\lambda_i\); fitted rate is count mean divided by \(e_i\).
  • An offset differs from an estimated covariate coefficient.
  • Exposure must be positive and measured in a consistent unit.
  • A zero-exposure record requires separate treatment; \(\log0\) is undefined.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: At rate 0.2 per policy-year, exposures 10 and 100 have expected counts 2 and 20. Both have the same fitted rate.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: With a franchise deductible \(d\ge0\), the insurer pays the entire loss once it exceeds \(d\): \(Y^L=X\indicator_{\{X>d\}}\). If \(X\le d\), payment is zero. Conditional on a payment, the paid amount has the law of \(X\mid X>d\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The threshold decides whether the insurer pays, but is not deducted from a qualifying loss. This creates a jump in the payment rule at the threshold.

The figure draws the Examples case \(d=100\). Below the threshold both rules pay nothing, so the loss 80 gives payment 0. Above it the franchise payment \(Y^L\) (red) is the whole loss, while the ordinary-deductible payment \((X-d)_+\) (dashed) is \(d\) lower: the loss 150 gives 150 against 50. The open circle at \((100,100)\) marks the jump: under the strict rule a loss of exactly 100 is not paid, and no payment lies strictly between 0 and 100.

Move the loss \(X\) across the threshold \(d\): below it neither rule pays, above it the franchise pays all of \(X\) while the ordinary deductible pays \((X-d)_+\), a gap of exactly \(d\). For an exponential loss \(\mathbb E[Y^L]\) adds \(d\,\mathbb P(X>d)\) to \(\mathbb E[(X-d)_+]\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{E}[Y^L]=\mathbb{E}[(X-d)_+]+d\mathbb{P}(X>d)\) when finite.
  • Payment probability is the same as for an ordinary deductible, but qualifying payments are larger by \(d\).
  • For \(d>0\), there are no payment amounts strictly between zero and \(d\).
  • Whether equality qualifies is a contract convention; here the threshold rule is strict.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: At deductible 100, losses 80 and 150 produce franchise payments 0 and 150. The ordinary deductible would produce 0 and 50.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A generalized linear model (GLM) specifies a conditional response law from an exponential family, a mean \(\mu_i=\mathbb{E}[Y_i\mid \boldsymbol{x}_i]\), and a link \(g\) such that \(g(\mu_i)=\eta_i=\boldsymbol{x}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}\). Here \(\boldsymbol{x}_i\) is the covariate vector, \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) the coefficient vector and \(\eta_i\) the linear predictor. The variance has form \(\phi V(\mu_i)\), where \(V\) is the variance function of the chosen family and \(\phi>0\) is a dispersion parameter (\(\phi=1\) for Poisson and Bernoulli responses).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The predictor is linear in coefficients, while the mean can be nonlinear and the conditional variance can depend on it. This allows count or binary responses without imposing an unconstrained linear mean. The family supplies the conditional response likelihood; maximum likelihood estimation fits the coefficients by maximizing its product over independent observations. The conditional expectation defines the mean being predicted, rather than predicting each observed response exactly.

The diagram separates the three choices in the definition: the linear predictor, the link \(g\) and the response family. Linearity holds only in the first box; the inverse link \(g^{-1}\) turns \(\eta_i\) into the mean, and the family turns the mean into a distribution whose variance \(\phi V(\mu_i)\) may depend on it. The grey row follows the Examples case under a log link: \(\eta_i=\log 2\) gives \(\mu_i=2\), an expected count rather than a guaranteed two claims.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The inverse link gives \(\mu_i=g^{-1}(\boldsymbol{x}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta})\).
  • Poisson regression uses \(g(\mu)=\log\mu\) and variance \(\mu\).
  • A Gaussian identity-link model has conditional mean \(\boldsymbol{x}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}\) and constant variance.
  • A quasi-likelihood model, such as the quasi-Poisson model with variance \(\phi\mu\), specifies a mean–variance relation without necessarily specifying a complete response distribution.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: If \(\eta_i=\log 2\) under a log link, the fitted conditional mean is 2. It is an expected count, not a guarantee of exactly two claims.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Suppose independent losses are observed only as counts \(n_j\) in disjoint intervals \((c_{j-1},c_j]\), \(j=1,\ldots,k\), covering the observation space. Under cumulative distribution function (CDF) \(F_\theta\), interval probability is \(p_j(\theta)=F_\theta(c_j)-F_\theta(c_{j-1})\). The likelihood is proportional to \(\prod_j p_j(\theta)^{n_j}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The observed event is membership in a bin. Replacing each loss by a bin midpoint and using a density discards the actual observation mechanism.

![Exponential density split at c_1=100 into the bins (0,100] and (100,∞), shaded with bin probabilities 0.6 and 0.4 and labelled with the observed counts 6 and 4.](../../assets/svg/grouped-data-likelihood.svg)

The figure draws the Examples case. Only the bin of each loss is recorded, so each observation contributes the area of its bin, \(p_1=1-\mathrm{e}^{-100\lambda}\) or \(p_2=\mathrm{e}^{-100\lambda}\), not a density height, and the likelihood is proportional to \(p_1^{6}p_2^{4}\). Maximizing \(6\log(1-q)+4\log q\) in \(q=\mathrm{e}^{-100\lambda}\) gives \(q=0.4\), that is \(\hat\lambda=\log(2.5)/100\approx0.0092\). The drawn density uses this value, so the shaded areas are 0.6 and 0.4, the observed proportions \(6/10\) and \(4/10\).

Move \(\lambda\), the bin counts and the boundary \(c_1\): each loss contributes the probability of its bin, and at \(\hat\lambda=\log(2.5)/100\) the bin areas equal the observed proportions \(6/10\) and \(4/10\).

Maximum likelihood estimation must use the probability of the recorded bin. Multiplying those bin probabilities, with each raised to its observed count, gives the objective to maximize; point-density likelihoods describe different data.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\displaystyle \ell(\theta)=\sum_jn_j\log p_j(\theta)+C\), where \(C\) is independent of \(\theta\).
  • For multinomial counts, the constant factor is \(n!/\prod_jn_j!\), with \(\displaystyle n=\sum_jn_j\).
  • If the bins omit part of the population, include an outside bin or condition on the sampling region.
  • Grouping can reduce information compared with exact observations.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: If 6 exponential losses are in \((0,100]\) and 4 exceed 100, the likelihood is proportional to \((1-\mathrm{e}^{-100\lambda})^6(\mathrm{e}^{-100\lambda})^4\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Hunger for bonus is a policyholder's incentive not to report a small covered loss when reporting would increase expected future premiums by more than the current reimbursement. It is a behavioural response to a bonus-malus experience-rating rule.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The reported claim record can understate accident experience. The course treats this response as a form of moral hazard (a change in the insured's behaviour caused by the insurance contract itself); it changes the observation process on which rating relies.

The figure draws the Examples comparison. Reporting brings in the reimbursement (red line) but costs the 120 of extra expected discounted future premiums (dashed blue). The lines cross at 120, so a policyholder minimizing expected monetary cost keeps the loss with reimbursement 80 unreported and reports the one with reimbursement 200. The crossing acts as a private reporting threshold, although the contract itself need not have a deductible.

The bonus-malus rule determines how reporting changes the policyholder's current class and subsequent premiums. This decision compares the two future premium streams starting from the current class; it does not require the portfolio to be in its stationary bonus-malus distribution.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A simple decision compares the current payment with the present value of extra future premiums caused by reporting.
  • The relevant future difference depends on current level, transition rules, time horizon and discounting.
  • Observed claim frequency can differ from accident frequency.
  • A reporting threshold need not equal a contractual deductible.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: If reimbursement would be 80 but reporting increases expected discounted future premiums by 120, a policyholder minimizing expected monetary cost prefers not to report. For reimbursement 200, the same comparison favours reporting.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The individual risk model represents total portfolio loss by \(\displaystyle S=\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\), where \(n\) is the fixed number of policies and \(X_i\ge0\) is the loss from policy \(i\), including zero for a claim-free policy. The basic course model assumes independent policy losses, often identically distributed.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The model counts policies first and models the loss outcome of each. Its summands may have an atom at zero even when positive claim amounts are continuous.

The figure draws the Examples portfolio. Each of the 100 policies has an atom at 0 (no claim, probability 0.9) and loses 10 otherwise, so the total \(S\) takes only multiples of 10. Adding the 100 independent policy means and variances gives \(\mathbb{E}[S]=100\cdot0.1\cdot10=100\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(S)=100\cdot0.1\cdot0.9\cdot10^2=900\), a standard deviation of 30.

Change \(n\), the claim probability \(q\) and the fixed claim: the portfolio total has \(\mathbb E[S]=nqb\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(S)=nq(1-q)b^2\). The dots show the compound Poisson approximation with rate \(nq\), whose variance is slightly larger.

An indicator random variable \(I_i\) records whether policy \(i\) claims and switches the claim severity \(B_i\) on in \(X_i=I_iB_i\). Independent random variables allow policy variances to add. Convolution of independent random variables supplies the aggregate distribution by combining the policy-loss laws.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• With independence, \(\displaystyle \mathbb{E}[S]=\sum_i\mathbb{E}[X_i]\) and \(\displaystyle \operatorname{Var}(S)=\sum_i\operatorname{Var}(X_i)\).
  • For \(X_i=I_iB_i\) with independent Bernoulli indicator \(I_i\) of probability \(q_i\) and severity \(B_i\), the mean is \(q_i\mathbb{E}[B_i]\).
  • Its variance is \(q_i\operatorname{Var}(B_i)+q_i(1-q_i)(\mathbb{E}[B_i])^2\).
  • Dependence between policies adds covariance terms to portfolio variance.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: For 100 independent policies with claim probability \(0.1\) and fixed claim 10, \(S=10N\) with \(N\sim\operatorname{Bin}(100,0.1)\). Mean is 100 and variance is 900.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a fitted likelihood model with maximized log-likelihood \(\hat\ell\), \(k\) estimated parameters and sample size \(n\), Akaike's information criterion is \(\operatorname{AIC}=-2\hat\ell+2k\), and Bayesian information criterion is \(\operatorname{BIC}=-2\hat\ell+k\log n\). Smaller values are preferred when models use comparable likelihoods on the same observations.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The fit improvement from extra parameters must compensate for their penalty. Stepwise selection searches neighbouring models and need not find the best model among all possible subsets.

The figure draws the Examples case with \(n=100\); the vertical axis starts at 90. Model B fits better, so its fit term \(-2\hat\ell\) is 4 lower, but it has one more parameter. AIC charges 2 for that parameter, so B wins with 102 against 104; BIC charges \(\log 100\approx4.61\), more than the fit gain of 4, so A wins with 109.21 against 109.82 (B's BIC penalty is \(3\log 100\approx13.82\)).

Change the maximized log-likelihoods \(\hat\ell\), the parameter counts and \(n\): AIC prefers model B here, while BIC, which charges \(\log n\) per parameter, prefers model A once \(n\) exceeds \(e^4\approx54.6\).

Maximum likelihood estimation supplies the maximized log-likelihood \(\hat\ell\). When comparing fitted generalized linear model specifications with different rating predictors on the same observations, an extra coefficient can improve fit but also increases the parameter-count penalty.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Count all estimated likelihood parameters, including an estimated dispersion parameter where applicable.
  • For \(n>\mathrm{e}^2\), BIC penalizes each added parameter more than AIC.
  • AIC and BIC are selection aids, not evidence of causal interpretation or predictive validation.
  • Ordinary likelihood-based AIC is not directly available from a quasi-Poisson mean–variance specification alone.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: With \(n=100\), model A has \(\hat\ell=-50\), \(k=2\), while B has \(\hat\ell=-48\), \(k=3\). AIC values are 104 and 102, favouring B; BIC values are about 109.21 and 109.82, favouring A.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For initial policyholder wealth \(w\), strictly increasing utility \(u\) and full insurance of loss \(X\), the maximum acceptable premium \(P^+\) solves \(u(w-P^+)=\mathbb{E}[u(w-X)]\). For insurer wealth \(W\) and strictly increasing utility \(U\), its minimum acceptable premium \(P^-\) solves \(U(W)=\mathbb{E}[U(W+P^--X)]\), when finite solutions exist.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
One equation compares insured and uninsured wealth for the customer; the other compares taking the contract with taking no risk for the insurer. A trade is acceptable to both when the premium lies between their thresholds.

The figure draws the Examples case with \(\alpha=0.1\). The chord midpoint is the expected utility of the uninsured position, and the wealth on the curve with the same utility is \(w-P^+\), with \(P^+\approx6.20\). Because \(u\) is concave, this point lies to the left of \(w-\mathbb{E}[X]=w-5\). For a risk-neutral insurer \(P^-=\mathbb{E}[X]=5\), so every premium in the green range from 5 to 6.20 is acceptable to both parties.

Move the policyholder's \(\alpha\), the insurer's risk aversion and the loss: any premium between \(P^-\) and \(P^+\) suits both parties. Raise the insurer's risk aversion above the policyholder's and the range closes.

Absolute risk aversion measures the local curvature of the utility used in each indifference equation. For exponential utility it is the constant \(\alpha\), so the example's coefficient specifies how strongly large losses affect the acceptable premium.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Under concavity and well-defined expectations, \(P^+\ge\mathbb{E}[X]\) and \(P^-\ge\mathbb{E}[X]\).
  • A mutually acceptable full-insurance premium exists if \(P^-\le P^+\).
  • A risk-neutral insurer has \(P^-=\mathbb{E}[X]\) in this expense-free model.
  • Exponential utilities with different coefficients produce different thresholds; finiteness requires the respective exponential loss moments.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: For exponential utility parameter \(\alpha\) and loss 0 or 10 with equal probabilities, the indifference premium is \(\alpha^{-1}\log[(1+\mathrm{e}^{10\alpha})/2]\), where \(\log\) is the natural logarithm. At \(\alpha=0.1\) it is about 6.20, above mean loss 5.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a positive differentiable stationary premium \(b(\lambda)\) at claim rate \(\lambda>0\), Loimaranta efficiency is \(e(\lambda)=\lambda b'(\lambda)/b(\lambda)=\mathrm{d}\log b(\lambda)/\mathrm{d}\log\lambda\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The elasticity measures the percentage change in long-run premium produced by a one-percent change in claim rate. A value near one means a proportional response locally, but does not establish accurate individual pricing.

The figure plots the efficiency of the two-level one-year scheme from the Examples, \(b(\lambda)=c(2-\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda})\). At \(\lambda=0.5\) it is about 0.2176: a one-percent rise in claim rate raises the long-run premium by only about 0.22 percent. The curve peaks at about 0.23 near \(\lambda\approx0.77\) and then falls, so at every claim rate this premium responds far less than the proportional premium \(b(\lambda)=k\lambda\) with efficiency 1.

Move \(\lambda\) and switch schemes: \(e(\lambda)=\lambda b'(\lambda)/b(\lambda)\) is the slope of \(\log b\) against \(\log\lambda\), and it stays far below the efficiency 1 of a proportional premium. The default two-level scheme gives \(e(0.5)\approx0.2176\).

Derivative and differentiability gives the local premium response \(b'(\lambda)\). Scaling it by \(\lambda/b(\lambda)\) converts an absolute slope into the relative response of premium to claim rate.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A proportional premium \(b(\lambda)=k\lambda\) has efficiency one.
  • A flat premium has efficiency zero.
  • For the two-year discount scheme, \(e(\lambda)=2\lambda(c-a)\mathrm{e}^{-2\lambda}/[c(1-\mathrm{e}^{-2\lambda})+a\mathrm{e}^{-2\lambda}]\).
  • Numerical evaluation can use nearby log-rate and log-premium differences; check sensitivity to the step size.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: For a two-level one-year scheme, \(b(\lambda)=c(2-\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda})\). At \(\lambda=0.5\), efficiency is \(0.5/(2\mathrm{e}^{0.5}-1)\approx0.2176\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For \(0<\mathbb{E}[X]<\infty\) and ordinary deductible \(d\ge0\), the loss elimination ratio (LER) is

\[ \operatorname{LER}(d)=\frac{\mathbb{E}[X]-\mathbb{E}[(X-d)_+]}{\mathbb{E}[X]} =\frac{\mathbb{E}[\min(X,d)]}{\mathbb{E}[X]}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The ratio measures the share of expected ground-up loss removed from insurer payments. It concerns expected amounts, rather than the fraction of claims receiving no payment.

For \(X\sim\operatorname{Exp}(0.01)\) the whole area under \(\bar F_X(t)=\mathrm{e}^{-0.01t}\) is \(\mathbb{E}[X]=100\). The blue part over \([0,d]\) is \(\mathbb{E}[\min(X,d)]=100(1-\mathrm{e}^{-1})\approx63.2\), the expected amount that the deductible \(d=100\) removes from insurer payments, while the red tail is \(\pi_X(d)=\mathbb{E}[(X-d)_+]=100\mathrm{e}^{-1}\approx36.8\), the expected payment that remains. The loss elimination ratio is the blue share of the total area, \(63.2/100\approx0.632\), as in the example.

Slide \(d\): the area under \(\bar F_X\) to the left of \(d\) is \(\mathbb E[\min(X,d)]\), and dividing it by \(\mathbb E[X]\) gives \(\operatorname{LER}(d)\), which rises towards 1. Compare it with the dashed payment probability \(\mathbb P(X>d)\), which measures something different.

The stop-loss transform and reinsurance gives \(\pi_X(d)=\mathbb{E}[(X-d)_+]\), the expected payment remaining above the deductible. Subtracting this from the ground-up mean and dividing by that mean produces the eliminated share.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(0\le\operatorname{LER}(d)\le1\) and it increases with \(d\).
  • \(\operatorname{LER}(d)=\int_0^d\bar F_X(t)\,\mathrm{d}t/\mathbb{E}[X]\).
  • It is zero at \(d=0\) and tends to one as \(d\to\infty\).
  • A zero or infinite ground-up mean makes this ratio inappropriate without further conventions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: For exponential losses at rate \(0.01\) and deductible 100, LER is \(1-\mathrm{e}^{-1}\approx0.6321\). The payment probability is \(\mathrm{e}^{-1}\approx0.3679\), a different quantity.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For nonnegative i.i.d. severities \(X_i\) independent of count \(N\), the maximum claim is \(M=\max(X_1,\ldots,X_N)\), with \(M=0\) if \(N=0\). Let \(F_X\) be the severity cumulative distribution function (CDF) and \(G_N\) the count probability generating function (PGF).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Aggregate loss and maximum claim measure different exposures. Conditioning on the count reduces the maximum to the probability that every claim is below a chosen threshold.

The figure plots \(\mathbb{P}(M\le z)=G_N(F_X(z))\) for \(N\sim\operatorname{Pois}(5)\) as a function of \(p=F_X(z)\), the probability that a single claim is at most \(z\). In the example a claim exceeds 1000 with probability \(0.1\), so \(p=0.9\) and the probability that no claim exceeds 1000 is \(G_N(0.9)=\mathrm{e}^{-0.5}\approx0.607\). At \(p=0\) the curve starts at \(G_N(0)=\mathbb{P}(N=0)=\mathrm{e}^{-5}\), the chance of no claims at all, and it reaches 1 at \(p=1\). The steep rise near \(p=1\) shows how strongly the maximum depends on the single-claim tail when several claims are expected.

Move \(p=F_X(z)\) and the claim count: \(\mathbb P(M\le z)=G_N(F_X(z))\), which for \(N\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(5)\) and \(p=0.9\) is \(e^{-0.5}\approx0.60653\). The steep rise near \(p=1\) shows how strongly the maximum depends on the single-claim tail.

The collective risk model supplies a random claim count and independent common severities. To study the maximum rather than their sum, condition on the same count: all \(n\) claims are below \(z\) with probability \(F_X(z)^n\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For \(z\ge0\), \(\mathbb{P}(M\le z)=G_N(F_X(z))\).
  • If \(N\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)\), \(\mathbb{P}(M\le z)=\exp[-\lambda(1-F_X(z))]\).
  • With fixed count \(n\ge1\), this becomes \(F_X(z)^n\).
  • The no-claim convention matters at zero and when evaluating moments.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: With Poisson mean 5 and probability \(0.1\) that one claim exceeds 1000, the probability that no claim exceeds 1000 is \(\mathrm{e}^{-0.5}\approx0.60653\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Given a specified family of observation laws indexed by parameter \(\theta\in\Theta\), a maximum likelihood estimate maximizes the likelihood of the observed data. For independent exact observations \(x_i\), \(L(\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^nf(x_i;\theta)\), where \(f\) is the applicable density or mass function.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The parameter varies while the observations remain fixed. Insurance data may report intervals or censoring rather than exact losses, so the likelihood must describe what was actually observed.

As an illustration, take the three exact losses 20, 30 and 100, so \(n=3\) and \(\sum_ix_i=150\). The data stay fixed and the exponential log-likelihood \(\ell(\lambda)=3\log\lambda-150\lambda\) is drawn as a function of the parameter. It is concave, its derivative \(3/\lambda-150\) vanishes at \(\hat\lambda=3/150=0.02\), and that zero is the maximum because \(\ell''(\lambda)=-3/\lambda^2<0\), as in the general example below.

Move \(\lambda\) along the log-likelihood \(\ell(\lambda)=3\log\lambda-\lambda\sum_ix_i\): the slope is positive below \(\hat\lambda=n/\sum_ix_i=0.02\) and negative above it. Change the third loss to move the maximum.

The independent random variables assumption makes the joint observation density or mass function a product. Taking its logarithm then gives the sum of individual log contributions used for estimation.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Maximizing \(L\) is equivalent to maximizing \(\ell=\log L\) where \(L>0\).
  • For independent observations, \(\displaystyle \ell(\theta)=\sum_i\log f(x_i;\theta)\).
  • A zero derivative identifies a candidate, not automatically a maximum. Check the parameter domain, boundaries and curvature or numerical objective.
  • Grouping, censoring and truncation require different observation contributions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: For positive i.i.d. exponential losses with rate \(\lambda\), \(\displaystyle \ell=n\log\lambda-\lambda\sum_i x_i\), so \(\displaystyle \hat\lambda=n/\sum_i x_i\). The second derivative is \(-n/\lambda^2<0\).

docs.title: Mixed Discrete and Continuous Loss Distribution
Definition
docs.text: A mixed discrete and continuous loss has both positive point masses and an absolutely continuous component. Its distribution can be written \(\displaystyle \mathbb{P}(X\in A)=\sum_jp_j\indicator_{\{a_j\in A\}}+\int_A f_c(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\), where \(p_j>0\) and \(\displaystyle \sum_jp_j+\int f_c=1\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A claim can be zero, a normal positive amount, or exactly a policy cap. Jumps of the cumulative distribution function (CDF) record point masses; the ordinary derivative between jumps records only the continuous component. This is a specific distribution structure, while a mixture describes averaging component laws.

The figure shows the example below. The CDF jumps from 0 to \(0.8\) at \(x=0\), and the jump height is the point mass \(\mathbb{P}(X=0)=F_X(0)-F_X(0-)=0.8\). Between 0 and 100 the CDF rises linearly from \(0.8\) to 1 with slope \(0.2/100=0.002\), the continuous component density \(f_c\). No single ordinary density can produce the jump, so both pieces are needed.

A mixture distribution can combine a discrete component and an absolutely continuous component. The component weights give the total atom mass and the total continuous mass; the example mixes a point mass at zero with a uniform positive loss.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{P}(X=a)=F_X(a)-F_X(a-)\).
  • \(\displaystyle \mathbb{E}[h(X)]=\sum_jp_jh(a_j)+\int h(x)f_c(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\) when integrable.
  • A single ordinary density with respect to length cannot represent the atoms.
  • Coverage modifications can introduce atoms even when the original loss is continuous.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: If \(X\) is zero with probability \(0.8\) and otherwise uniform on \((0,100)\), its continuous component density is \(0.002\) on that interval. The mean is \(0.2(50)=10\).
