docs.title: Proposition
docs.text: For random claim rate \(\Lambda\) and stationary class \(L\), the unconstrained class value \(r_l\) minimizing \(\mathbb{E}[(\Lambda-r_L)^2]\) is \(r_l=\mathbb{E}[\Lambda\mid L=l]\), for classes of positive probability and finite second moments. This is on a claim-frequency scale; dimensionless premium relativities require normalization by a base rate.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Each class is priced by the average underlying rate among its members. This minimizes squared prediction error, but can produce an irregular or commercially unsuitable scale.

The figure draws the example below: two equally frequent classes whose members have average claim rates \(\mathbb{E}[\Lambda\mid L=1]=0.1\) and \(\mathbb{E}[\Lambda\mid L=2]=0.3\). These are the optimal class values on the claim-frequency scale (left axis). Their probability-weighted average is \(\tfrac{1}{2}(0.1)+\tfrac{1}{2}(0.3)=0.2=\mathbb{E}[\Lambda]\), in line with \(\mathbb{E}[r_L]=\mathbb{E}[\Lambda]\); dividing by this base rate gives the dimensionless relativities \(0.5\) and \(1.5\) on the right axis.

The stationary bonus-malus distribution and premium supplies the long-run class probabilities used to weight claim rates within each class. Conditional expectation given a random variable minimizes squared prediction error within that class, giving \(r_l=\mathbb{E}[\Lambda\mid L=l]\). Under a linear restriction, covariance measures the joint variation of risk and class, while variance and standard deviation supplies the class spread in the denominator of the regression slope.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If class probability at fixed rate is \(\pi_l(\lambda)\) and rate density is \(f_\Lambda\), then \(r_l=\int\lambda\pi_l(\lambda)f_\Lambda(\lambda)\,\mathrm{d}\lambda/\int\pi_l(\lambda)f_\Lambda(\lambda)\,\mathrm{d}\lambda\).
  • \(\mathbb{E}[r_L]=\mathbb{E}[\Lambda]\).
  • Under a linear restriction \(r_l=a+bl\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(L)>0\), \(b=\operatorname{Cov}(\Lambda,L)/\operatorname{Var}(L)\) and \(a=\mathbb{E}[\Lambda]-b\mathbb{E}[L]\).
  • Refining the same information partition cannot increase unconstrained minimum mean squared error (MSE). Merely changing the number of classes in a different system does not guarantee an improvement.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: If two equally frequent classes have conditional rates 0.1 and 0.3, their optimal frequency-scale values are 0.1 and 0.3. At base rate 0.2, the dimensionless relativities are 0.5 and 1.5.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a nonnegative ground-up loss \(X\) (the full loss before any deductible or limit is applied) and deductible \(d\ge0\), the insurer's per-loss payment is \(Y^L=(X-d)_+=\max(X-d,0)\). The insured retains \(\min(X,d)\). The per-payment distribution is the conditional law of \(X-d\) given \(X>d\) (written \(Y^P\)), defined only when \(\mathbb{P}(X>d)>0\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Every loss is included in the per-loss model, with a zero payment below the deductible. The per-payment model describes only cases generating a positive payment.

For \(X\sim\operatorname{Exp}(0.01)\) and \(d=100\), the blue area is \(\mathbb{P}(Y^L=0)=F_X(d)=1-\mathrm{e}^{-1}\approx0.632\): these losses stay in the per-loss model with payment zero. The red area \(\bar F_X(d)=\mathrm{e}^{-1}\approx0.368\) holds the losses that produce a payment \(X-d\); rescaling that tail by \(1/\bar F_X(d)\) gives the per-payment law \(Y^P\), which here is again exponential with mean 100. Hence \(\mathbb{E}[Y^L]=100\mathrm{e}^{-1}\approx36.79\), as in the example.

Move the deductible \(d\) and the rate \(\lambda\): the blue area \(\mathbb P(Y^L=0)=F_X(d)\) grows with \(d\), while the per-payment mean \(\mathbb E[Y^P]=1/\lambda\) does not move, because the exponential law is memoryless. The default \(d=100\), \(\lambda=0.01\) gives \(\mathbb E[Y^L]=36.79\).

The survivor function \(\bar F_X(d)=\mathbb{P}(X>d)\) gives the probability that the deductible is exceeded. Dividing the shifted tail by this probability normalizes the per-payment law over cases receiving a positive payment.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{P}(Y^L=0)=F_X(d)\) and \(F_{Y^L}(y)=F_X(d+y)\) for \(y\ge0\).
  • For \(y\ge0\), \(\mathbb{P}(Y^P>y)=\bar F_X(d+y)/\bar F_X(d)\).
  • \(\mathbb{E}[Y^L]=\bar F_X(d)\mathbb{E}[Y^P]\) when finite.
  • For continuous \(X\), \(f_{Y^P}(y)=f_X(d+y)/\bar F_X(d)\) for \(y>0\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: For \(X\sim\operatorname{Exp}(0.01)\) and \(d=100\), the probability of payment is \(\mathrm{e}^{-1}\). By the memoryless property, conditional payment has mean 100, so mean payment per loss is \(100\mathrm{e}^{-1}\approx36.79\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A conditional count model is overdispersed relative to Poisson if \(\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid x)>\mathbb{E}[Y\mid x]\). A quasi-Poisson specification uses mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\phi\mu\). A common negative binomial specification has mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\mu+\mu^2/r\), with size parameter \(r>0\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Claims from apparently similar policyholders can still have different underlying rates. A gamma mixture of Poisson rates gives a negative binomial response and an extra variance term.

The figure compares the variance functions of the example below. The grey Poisson line has variance equal to the mean. Quasi-Poisson with \(\phi=1.5\) scales it to \(1.5\mu\), while the negative binomial with \(r=4\) adds the quadratic term \(\mu^2/4\). Both lie above the Poisson line, so both are overdispersed, and both give variance 3 at \(\mu=2\). Away from \(\mu=2\) they differ: the negative binomial excess grows faster for larger means.

Move \(\mu\), \(\phi\) and \(r\): the Poisson variance is \(\mu\), quasi-Poisson scales it to \(\phi\mu\) and the negative binomial adds \(\mu^2/r\). At \(\mu=2\), \(\phi=1.5\) and \(r=4\) both models give variance 3 but only the negative binomial specifies a full law.

Poisson regression assumes equality of conditional mean and variance at fixed predictors. A mixture distribution over unobserved claim rates adds variation between those rates, explaining why a Poisson mixture can have a larger conditional variance.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Quasi-Poisson has overdispersion when \(\phi>1\) and underdispersion when \(0<\phi<1\).
  • Quasi-Poisson is a mean–variance specification, not generally the literal count distribution of \(\phi\operatorname{Pois}(\mu/\phi)\).
  • In the negative binomial model, larger \(r\) reduces excess variance; the Poisson limit is \(r\to\infty\) at fixed \(\mu\).
  • Compare dispersion conditional on predictors and exposure, rather than raw pooled mean and variance alone.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: For \(\mu=2\) and \(r=4\), negative binomial conditional variance is \(2+4/4=3\). A quasi-Poisson fit with \(\phi=1.5\) has the same mean and variance but does not specify the same full law.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The course's Pareto loss model has survivor function \(\bar F_X(x)=[\beta/(\beta+x)]^\alpha\) for \(x\ge0\), shape \(\alpha>0\) and scale \(\beta>0\). It is the Lomax or Pareto type II convention, whose support starts at zero; an unshifted Pareto type I model has a different support.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The polynomial tail allows occasional very large losses. The shape controls which moments are finite, so a valid loss distribution need not have finite variance.

With \(\alpha=2\) and \(\beta=800\), the survivor function falls only like \(x^{-2}\), so a visible share of probability remains far to the right. The total area under \(\bar F_X\) is \(\mathbb{E}[X]=800\). The red area beyond the deductible \(d=300\) is the stop-loss transform \(\pi_X(300)=800^2/1100\approx581.82\), the mean excess per loss; dividing by \(\bar F_X(300)=(8/11)^2\approx0.529\) gives the mean excess per payment, \(1100\). Because the tail is so heavy, part of the red area lies beyond the plotted range.

Change the shape \(\alpha\) and the scale \(\beta\): the mean is infinite for \(\alpha\le1\) and the variance for \(\alpha\le2\). Move \(d\) to see the mean excess \((\beta+d)/(\alpha-1)\) grow linearly in \(d\), unlike the constant mean excess of the dashed exponential.

The ordinary deductible separates per-loss excess \((X-d)_+\) from excess conditional on a payment. The Pareto survivor ratio above \(d\) gives a conditional excess law with scale \(\beta+d\), while integrating the tail gives the expected payment per ground-up loss.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(f_X(x)=\alpha\beta^\alpha/(\beta+x)^{\alpha+1}\) for \(x>0\).
  • \(\mathbb{E}[X]=\beta/(\alpha-1)\) for \(\alpha>1\); variance is \(\beta^2\alpha/[(\alpha-1)^2(\alpha-2)]\) for \(\alpha>2\).
  • For \(\alpha>1\), the stop-loss transform is \(\pi_X(d)=\beta^\alpha(\beta+d)^{1-\alpha}/(\alpha-1)\).
  • Conditional excess over \(d\) is Lomax with the same shape and scale \(\beta+d\).
  • Every positive exponential moment is infinite, so an exponential premium is infinite.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: With \(\alpha=2\), \(\beta=800\) and deductible 300, mean ground-up loss is 800 but variance is infinite. Mean excess per loss is \(800^2/1100\approx581.82\), and mean excess per payment is 1100.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: In Poisson regression, conditionally independent counts satisfy \(Y_i\mid \boldsymbol{x}_i\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\mu_i)\) with \(\log\mu_i=\boldsymbol{x}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}\). Thus \(\mu_i=\exp(\boldsymbol{x}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta})>0\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Y_i\mid \boldsymbol{x}_i)=\mu_i\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The model relates rating factors to expected claim counts through multiplicative effects. It does not directly model claim severity.

The log link turns additive changes in the linear predictor into multiplicative changes in the mean. In the example below, the reference group has \(\boldsymbol{x}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\log0.1\) and mean \(0.1\); switching the binary rating factor on adds its coefficient \(\log1.5\), which multiplies the mean by \(\mathrm{e}^{\log1.5}=1.5\) to give \(0.15\). Because \(\mu_i=\mathrm{e}^{\boldsymbol{x}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}}\) is always positive, no predictor value can produce a negative expected count.

This is a generalized linear model with a logarithmic link and response law from the Poisson distribution. The link enforces a positive mean, while the Poisson law supplies equality of the conditional mean and variance and the stated likelihood.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Increasing covariate \(x_{ij}\) by one multiplies the mean by \(\mathrm{e}^{\beta_j}\) if the model has no relevant interaction.
  • The independent-data log-likelihood is \(\displaystyle \sum_i[y_i \boldsymbol{x}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}-\mathrm{e}^{\boldsymbol{x}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\log(y_i!)]\).
  • Equality of conditional mean and variance is the Poisson assumption; heterogeneity across covariates does not by itself violate it.
  • Different observation durations require exposure adjustment.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: With intercept \(\log0.1\) and a binary rating coefficient \(\log1.5\), the two conditional means are 0.1 and 0.15 at the same exposure.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A policy limit \(u\ge0\) caps the insurer's payment. Without a deductible, payment is \(Y=\min(X,u)\). With an ordinary deductible \(d\) and maximum payment \(u\), it is \(Y=\min((X-d)_+,u)\). A maximum covered ground-up loss is a different convention and must be stated separately.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The cap creates a point mass at the maximum payment whenever losses can reach or exceed it. A deductible controls the bottom of the covered layer (the band of loss amounts from \(d\) to \(d+u\) that the insurer pays); a payment limit controls its width.

With \(d=100\) and \(u=500\), the red payment \(Y=\min((X-d)_+,u)\) is zero below the deductible, rises one-for-one through the covered layer from \(d=100\) to \(d+u=600\), and stays at \(u=500\) for every larger loss; all those losses form the point mass at the maximum payment. A loss of 800 is therefore paid 500. The dashed grey line shows the other convention from the example: capping the ground-up loss at 500 before applying the deductible pays \(500-100=400\).

Move \(X\), \(d\) and \(u\): the payment \(Y=\min((X-d)_+,u)\) rises with slope 1 between \(d\) and \(d+u\) and stays at \(u\) beyond, which differs from capping the ground-up loss first. The readouts give \(\mathbb E[Y]\) and the point mass \(\mathbb P(Y=u)\) for an illustrative exponential loss.

The stop-loss transform and reinsurance values the unbounded layer above a retention \(d\), the amount the insurer keeps. When the transforms are finite, subtracting the transform at \(d+u\) from the transform at \(d\) removes payments beyond the cap. The finite-layer integral below remains valid even when the uncapped transforms are infinite.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{E}[\min(X,u)]=\int_0^u\bar F_X(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\) for nonnegative \(X\).
  • \(\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\min((X-d)_+,u)]=\int_d^{d+u}\bar F_X(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\) for finite \(d,u\ge0\). If \(\mathbb{E}[X]<\infty\), this also equals \(\pi_X(d)-\pi_X(d+u)\).
  • For \(u>0\), the capped excess has mass \(\mathbb{P}(X\ge d+u)\) at \(u\).
  • For \(u>0\), its mass at zero is \(F_X(d)\); at \(u=0\) the entire payment is zero.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: If deductible is 100 and maximum insurer payment is 500, a ground-up loss of 800 gives payment 500. A ground-up coverage cap of 500 instead would give payment 400.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A premium principle is a rule \(\Pi\) assigning a price to a loss law \(X\). The course considers nonnegative loading \(\Pi(X)\ge\mathbb{E}[X]\), no rip-off \(\Pi(X)\le\operatorname{ess\,sup}X\) (the essential supremum, the smallest \(m\) with \(\mathbb{P}(X\le m)=1\), i.e. the largest possible loss), translation consistency \(\Pi(X+c)=\Pi(X)+c\), additivity for independent losses, proportionality \(\Pi(aX)=a\Pi(X)\) and iterativity \(\Pi(X)=\Pi(\Pi(X\mid Y))\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The properties describe how pricing reacts to certain cash flows, rescaling, pooling and conditioning. A plausible-looking formula need not satisfy all of them.

Nonnegative loading and no rip-off together confine a premium to the green band \(\mathbb{E}[X]\le\Pi(X)\le\operatorname{ess\,sup}X\). For the deterministic loss \(X=10\) in the example, both ends equal 10, so the band shrinks to a single point. The expected-value premium \(1.2\,\mathbb{E}[X]=12\) satisfies the loading condition but lies above the largest possible loss, so it violates no rip-off.

Pick a principle and a loss, then move \(\theta\) or \(\alpha\): each readout checks one property on this loss, and a single cross is a counterexample. The default \(\Pi(X)=1.2\mathbb E[X]\) on \(X=10\) charges 12 and violates no rip-off.

Stop-loss order is one way to check whether a pricing rule respects a risk comparison. For example, it orders finite means, so an expected-value premium with fixed nonnegative loading preserves the order. This does not imply that every premium principle has that property.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Iterativity applies the same rule first conditionally and then to the random conditional premium.
  • A universal property needs a proof; one counterexample disproves it.
  • An expected-value loading with positive coefficient fails translation consistency for positive constants.
  • Risk-order compatibility can be checked by expressing a premium in terms of increasing or convex functions.
  • No rip-off is only a finite upper bound when the loss is essentially bounded, that is, \(\operatorname{ess\,sup}X<\infty\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: For \(\Pi(X)=1.2\mathbb{E}[X]\) and deterministic \(X=10\), the premium is 12. It violates no rip-off, since the largest possible loss is only 10.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a nonnegative integer-valued random variable \(N\), its probability generating function (PGF) is \(\displaystyle G_N(z)=\mathbb{E}[z^N]=\sum_{k=0}^\infty\mathbb{P}(N=k)z^k\), at least for \(|z|\le1\). In this power-series definition \(z^0=1\), including at \(z=0\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The coefficient of each power stores a probability. PGFs are especially useful for counting claims and for composing claim frequency with claim severity.

Here \(N\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)\) with \(\lambda=2\), so \(G_N(z)=\mathrm{e}^{2(z-1)}\). The height at \(z=0\) is the constant coefficient, \(G_N(0)=\mathbb{P}(N=0)=\mathrm{e}^{-2}\), and the curve ends at \(G_N(1)=1\) because the probabilities sum to one. The dashed tangent at \(z=1\) has slope \(G_N'(1)=\mathbb{E}[N]=2\), the mean read off by differentiating at one.

Pick a count law and move \(z\): \(G_N(0)=\mathbb P(N=0)\), the slope at \(z=1\) is \(\mathbb E[N]\) and the power-series coefficients are the probabilities shown on the right. The default \(N\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(2)\) gives \(G_N'(1)=2\) and \(G_N''(1)=4\).

For a discrete random variable taking nonnegative integer values, expectation becomes a sum of \(z^k\) weighted by the count probabilities. Substituting \(z=\mathrm{e}^t\) connects the PGF with the moment generating function wherever the transform is finite.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{P}(N=k)=G_N^{(k)}(0)/k!\).
  • \(G_N'(1-)=\mathbb{E}[N]\) and \(G_N''(1-)=\mathbb{E}[N(N-1)]\), allowing infinite values.
  • Independent nonnegative integer-valued sums have product PGFs.
  • For \(z>0\) where finite, \(G_N(z)=M_N(\log z)\). A general real-valued severity need not have a PGF.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: For \(N\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)\), \(G_N(z)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda(z-1)}\). Differentiating at one gives mean \(\lambda\) and second factorial moment \(\lambda^2\).

docs.title: Rating Factors and Interactions in Insurance GLMs
Definition
docs.text: A rating factor is a covariate used in an insurance generalized linear model (GLM) to distinguish expected insured risk. A categorical factor with \(k\) levels can be represented by \(k-1\) indicator variables relative to a reference level when an intercept is included. An interaction allows the effect of one factor to depend on another.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Under a log link, additive predictor terms become multiplicative rate effects. An interaction changes a rate ratio across groups rather than simply adding another independent multiplier.

Each cell is the rate \(\lambda=\exp(\beta_0+\beta_AA+\beta_BB+\beta_{AB}AB)\) for one combination of the binary factors. Moving from \(A=0\) to \(A=1\) multiplies the rate by \(\mathrm{e}^{\beta_A}=1.2\) when \(B=0\), but by \(\mathrm{e}^{\beta_A+\beta_{AB}}=1.2\times1.5=1.8\) when \(B=1\), the values in the example. Without the interaction term the two arrows would carry the same multiplier.

Move \(\beta_A\), \(\beta_B\) and \(\beta_{AB}\): the effect of \(A\) is \(e^{\beta_A}\) when \(B=0\) and \(e^{\beta_A+\beta_{AB}}\) when \(B=1\). Set \(\beta_{AB}=0\) and the effect of \(A\) no longer depends on \(B\).

Poisson regression supplies the log-link interpretation of predictor coefficients as multiplicative count effects. With exposure offset in claim-frequency models, \(\log e_i\) is separated from those rating effects so that the coefficients compare claim rates at equal exposure.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• In \(\log\lambda=\beta_0+\beta_AA+\beta_BB+\beta_{AB}AB\), with binary \(A,B\), the effect of \(A\) is \(\mathrm{e}^{\beta_A+\beta_{AB}B}\).
  • Including all category indicators plus an intercept makes the design redundant: the indicators sum to the intercept column, so the coefficients are not identifiable unless a constraint is imposed, such as dropping a reference level.
  • Reference categories determine coefficient interpretation but do not change fitted means under an equivalent encoding.
  • A fitted association does not establish a causal effect of a rating factor.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: If \(\beta_A=\log1.2\) and \(\beta_{AB}=\log1.5\), the rate ratio for \(A\) is 1.2 when \(B=0\), and 1.8 when \(B=1\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: For independent nonnegative summands, stochastic and stop-loss orders are preserved when adding correspondingly ordered risks. For random sums, suppose i.i.d. nonnegative severities \(X_i\) and \(Y_i\) are independent of their respective counts \(M,N\). If severities and counts are ordered in the same stochastic or stop-loss order, the corresponding aggregate losses inherit that order, subject to required integrability.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
One can compare portfolios through frequency and severity without computing their full aggregate laws. Independence from the count and nonnegative severity are essential to the basic compounding statements.

In the figure, the left column builds the aggregate loss \(\sum_{i=1}^MX_i\) from the severities \(X_i\) and the count \(M\), and the right column builds \(\sum_{i=1}^NY_i\) from \(Y_i\) and \(N\). The two assumed comparisons, severity against severity and count against count, are in the same order (\(\le_{\mathrm{st}}\), \(\le_{\mathrm{sl}}\) or \(\le_e\)); compounding under the independence and nonnegativity assumptions then passes that order on to the aggregate losses, with finite aggregate means needed in the stop-loss case.

This illustrates the Bernoulli-policy result with claim size \(X=1\): change \(\mathbb P(I=1)=q\) and the retention \(d\). The compound sum with \(N\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(q)\) has the same mean as \(IX\) but a stop-loss premium at least as large at every \(d\), because it allows two or more claims.

Stochastic order compares all increasing tests, including indicators of threshold exceedance. The compound risk distribution supplies the random-sum structure: comparing both count and severity laws under its independence assumptions leads to the aggregate comparisons below.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(X_i\le_{\mathrm{st}}Y_i\) and \(M\le_{\mathrm{st}}N\), then \(\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^MX_i\le_{\mathrm{st}}\sum_{i=1}^NY_i\) under the stated model.
  • The analogous result holds for stop-loss order with finite aggregate means.
  • Exponential order also passes to these random sums when the nonnegative severities and counts are exponentially ordered and the required moment generating functions (MGFs) are finite: for \(\displaystyle S_X=\sum_{i=1}^MX_i\) and \(\displaystyle S_Y=\sum_{i=1}^NY_i\), \(M_{S_X}(\alpha)=M_M(\log M_X(\alpha))\le M_N(\log M_Y(\alpha))=M_{S_Y}(\alpha)\). Nonnegative severities ensure the log-MGF arguments are nonnegative.
  • For i.i.d. nonnegative \(X_i\) independent of \(N\), \(\displaystyle X_1\le_{\mathrm{sl}}\sum_{i=1}^NX_i\) when \(\mathbb{E}[N]\ge1\).
  • A Bernoulli-policy loss \(IX\) is below the compound sum in stop-loss order if \(\mathbb{P}(I=1)\le\mathbb{E}[N]\) and the independence assumptions hold.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: An individual policy with claim probability \(q\) and severity \(X\) is stop-loss dominated by a compound Poisson model with rate \(q\) and the same severity. Their means agree, but the Poisson model allows multiple claims.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For nonnegative integrable gain or wealth variables \(X,Y\), \(Y\) has second-order stochastic dominance over \(X\) if \(\int_0^tF_X(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\ge\int_0^tF_Y(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\) for every \(t\ge0\). Equivalently, every increasing concave utility weakly prefers \(Y\) to \(X\), with expectations defined.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
This comparison is stated for favourable outcomes. When the variables denote losses, put the minus sign inside wealth utility. A larger mean alone does not establish second-order dominance.

The figure reads the Examples case as gains: \(X\) is the fair draw of 0 or 2 and \(Y=1\) is certain. Then \(\int_0^tF_X(s)\,\mathrm{d}s=t/2\) for \(0\le t\le2\), while \(\int_0^tF_Y(s)\,\mathrm{d}s=(t-1)_+\) there; the shaded gap shows that the first integral is never below the second, which is the definition of \(Y\) dominating \(X\) in second order. From \(t=2\) on both integrals equal \(t-1\), because once \(t\) exceeds every outcome the integral equals \(t\) minus the mean, and the means are equal.

Move the certain gain \(y\) and the spread of \(X\): while \(y\ge\mathbb E[X]=1\) the integrated CDF of \(X\) is never below that of \(Y=y\), so the certain gain dominates. Push \(y\) below 1 and the curves cross.

Convex order and more dangerous risks compares dispersion at equal means. In that case \(Y\le_{\mathrm{cx}}X\) makes every concave utility prefer the gain \(Y\), explaining the direction of the equal-mean second-order comparison.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• First-order dominance of \(Y\) over \(X\) implies second-order dominance.
  • Dominance requires \(\mathbb{E}[Y]\ge\mathbb{E}[X]\) for integrable variables.
  • At equal means, \(Y\) dominating \(X\) in second order corresponds to \(Y\le_{\mathrm{cx}}X\).
  • For losses, \(X\le_{\mathrm{sl}}Y\) corresponds to preference for wealth \(w-X\) over \(w-Y\) by increasing concave utility.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: As gains, a certain 1 second-order dominates a fair draw of 0 or 2. As losses, the same certain 1 is the less dangerous risk. The preference direction is the same after the outcome meaning is specified.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text: For absolutely continuous laws, suppose \(f_X(t)-f_Y(t)\) is nonnegative before a threshold and nonpositive afterwards, with both densities integrating to one. Then \(F_X(t)\ge F_Y(t)\) for all \(t\), so \(X\le_{\mathrm{st}}Y\). The crossing criterion is sufficient; it is not a necessary requirement for stochastic order.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Integrating the signed density difference accumulates a nonnegative cumulative distribution function (CDF) difference before the crossing and then brings it back to zero. The direction of the signs matters more than merely counting intersections.

The figure draws the Examples case. On the left, \(f_X-f_Y\) is positive before the crossing at \(1/2\) (blue region) and negative after it (red region). On the right, the CDF difference \(F_X(t)-F_Y(t)=2t-2t^2\) accumulates these signed areas: it grows until \(t=1/2\) and then shrinks back to zero at \(t=1\) without becoming negative, so \(F_X\ge F_Y\) everywhere and \(X\le_{\mathrm{st}}Y\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• With equal finite means, the pattern \(f_Y-f_X\ge0\), then \(\le0\), then \(\ge0\) on three consecutive intervals gives the direct thicker-tailed comparison.
  • Multiple density crossings do not by themselves decide stochastic order.
  • Density comparisons are almost-everywhere comparisons; changing a density at one point changes no probabilities.
  • For discrete laws, use cumulative masses rather than derivatives.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: On \((0,1)\), \(f_X(t)=2(1-t)\) and \(f_Y(t)=2t\) cross at \(1/2\). Their CDFs are \(2t-t^2\) and \(t^2\), confirming \(F_X(t)\ge F_Y(t)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a loss with finite second moment, the standard deviation principle sets \(\Pi(X)=\mathbb{E}[X]+\alpha\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)}\), with dimensionless fixed loading \(\alpha>0\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The loading is measured in the same monetary units as loss. Independent pooling generally gives a smaller loading than adding the separate standard deviation loadings.

For independent risks the variances add, so the standard deviations combine like the two legs of a right triangle: in the Examples case the pooled \(\sigma_{X+Y}=\sqrt{2^2+2^2}=\sqrt{8}\approx2.83\) is the hypotenuse, shorter than the path \(\sigma_X+\sigma_Y=4\) along the legs. At \(\alpha=1\) the total loading therefore falls from 4 to about 2.83, and the premium from 24 to about 22.83; this diversification effect is why the principle is not additive.

Change \(\sigma_X\), \(\sigma_Y\) and \(\alpha\): for independent risks the pooled loading \(\alpha\sqrt{\sigma_X^2+\sigma_Y^2}\) is the hypotenuse of the triangle, never longer than the separate loadings \(\alpha(\sigma_X+\sigma_Y)\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• It has nonnegative loading, translation consistency and proportionality for positive scaling.
  • For independent losses, \(\sigma_{X+Y}=\sqrt{\sigma_X^2+\sigma_Y^2}\le\sigma_X+\sigma_Y\).
  • Therefore it is generally not additive, and it rewards diversification.
  • Equal-mean convex order raises the premium when second moments are finite; stochastic order alone need not do so.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Two independent risks each have mean 10 and standard deviation 2. At \(\alpha=1\), separate premiums sum to 24, while the pooled premium is \(20+\sqrt{8}\approx22.83\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A stationary distribution at claim rate \(\lambda\), the general Markov-chain stationary distribution applied to the bonus-malus chain, is a row vector \(\boldsymbol{\pi}(\lambda)\) satisfying \(\boldsymbol{\pi} \boldsymbol{P}=\boldsymbol{\pi}\), \(\pi_l\ge0\) and \(\displaystyle \sum_l\pi_l=1\). With class premiums \(c_l\), the stationary mean premium is \(\displaystyle b(\lambda)=\sum_l\pi_l(\lambda)c_l\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The bonus-malus transition matrix advances the class probabilities by one year. Setting the output equal to the input gives a linear system for the stationary proportions, with a normalization equation ensuring that they sum to one. The stationary distribution leaves class proportions unchanged after another year. Convergence from arbitrary initial proportions is a separate property, not a consequence of solving the stationary equation alone.

The figure uses the Examples numbers. Each class \(l\) is a rectangle of width \(\pi_l\) and height \(c_l\), so its area \(\pi_lc_l\) is that class's contribution to the mean premium: \(40+32+64=136\). The dashed level \(b(\lambda)=136\) is the single premium that would collect the same total from the stationary portfolio; it lies between the bonus premium 100 and the premium 200, closer to 100 because most of the stationary mass sits in the third class.

Move \(\lambda\) and the class premiums: each rectangle has width \(\pi_l\) and height \(c_l\), so the total area is \(b(\lambda)\). The default \(p=0.2\) gives \(\boldsymbol\pi=(0.2,0.16,0.64)\) and \(b(\lambda)=136\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A finite irreducible chain has a unique stationary distribution; aperiodicity additionally guarantees convergence from every initial distribution. These formal properties are covered in Year 3 Stochastic Models; solving the balance equations here does not require a convergence argument.
  • \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\) is a left eigenvector of \(\boldsymbol{P}\) for eigenvalue one, normalized to sum to one.
  • For the three-state two-year scheme, with \(p=1-\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda}\) and \(q=\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda}\) as in the transition-matrix example, \(\boldsymbol{\pi}=(p,pq,q^2)\).
  • If the first two states cost \(c\) and the third costs \(a\), \(b(\lambda)=c(1-\mathrm{e}^{-2\lambda})+a\mathrm{e}^{-2\lambda}\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: With \(p=0.2\) and \(q=0.8\), stationary proportions are \((0.2,0.16,0.64)\). Premiums \((200,200,100)\) give mean premium \(136\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For loss variables \(X,Y\), stochastic order \(X\le_{\mathrm{st}}Y\) means \(F_X(t)\ge F_Y(t)\) for every real threshold \(t\). Equivalently, \(\mathbb{P}(X>t)\le\mathbb{P}(Y>t)\) for every \(t\). Equal laws satisfy the weak order in both directions.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The larger ordered loss has at least as much probability above every threshold. For losses this is an adverse direction; for wealth or gains the same mathematical direction is favourable.

![Step CDFs of X ~ Bernoulli(0.2) and Y ~ Bernoulli(0.4): on 0,1) the CDF of X is 0.8 and that of Y is 0.6, and both are 0 before 0 and 1 from 1 on.

In the figure the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of \(X\) is never below that of \(Y\): the two coincide below 0 and from 1 onwards, and on \([0,1)\) the shaded gap is \(F_X-F_Y=0.8-0.6=0.2\). Equivalently \(\mathbb{P}(Y>t)-\mathbb{P}(X>t)=0.2\) there, so \(Y\) has at least as much probability above every threshold, which is \(X\le_{\mathrm{st}}Y\).

Move \(\mathbb P(X=1)\) and \(\mathbb P(Y=1)\): \(X\le_{\mathrm{st}}Y\) holds exactly when the CDF of \(X\) is never below that of \(Y\), here when \(\mathbb P(X=1)\le\mathbb P(Y=1)\). Swap the order of the two probabilities to see the verdict flip.

The cumulative distribution function gives probability at or below a threshold, while the survivor function gives its complementary upper tail. Their opposite inequality directions express the same comparison of loss sizes.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(X\le_{\mathrm{st}}Y\) if and only if \(\mathbb{E}[h(X)]\le\mathbb{E}[h(Y)]\) for all bounded increasing \(h\).
  • For increasing wealth utility \(u\), \(\mathbb{E}[u(w-X)]\ge\mathbb{E}[u(w-Y)]\) whenever defined.
  • Increasing transformations preserve stochastic order.
  • With finite means, the order implies \(\mathbb{E}[X]\le\mathbb{E}[Y]\); equal means then force equal distributions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: If \(X\sim\operatorname{Bern}(0.2)\) and \(Y\sim\operatorname{Bern}(0.4)\), \(X\le_{\mathrm{st}}Y\). The result compares laws and does not require a specified joint distribution.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For integrable nonnegative losses, stop-loss order \(X\le_{\mathrm{sl}}Y\) means \(\mathbb{E}[(X-d)_+]\le\mathbb{E}[(Y-d)_+]\) for every \(d\ge0\). The course states it for \(d>0\); continuity as \(d\downarrow0\) supplies the mean comparison at zero.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Every excess-loss layer has no larger expected payment for \(X\). This order combines size and dispersion, so it does not require equal means.

The figure takes the Examples case at retention \(d=1\). The payment \((x-1)_+\) is convex, so the expected payment of \(Y\), which is 0 or 2 with equal probabilities, is the midpoint of the chord between \((0,0)\) and \((2,1)\), namely 0.5; the constant \(X=1\) sits at the kink and pays 0. The same chord argument works at every retention, which gives \(\mathbb{E}[(X-d)_+]\le\mathbb{E}[(Y-d)_+]\) for all \(d\ge0\), that is, \(X\le_{\mathrm{sl}}Y\).

Move the retention \(d\) and the spread \(s\) of \(Y\) around 1: \(\pi_X(d)\le\pi_Y(d)\) at every retention, so \(X\le_{\mathrm{sl}}Y\). Raise the constant \(X=m\) above 1 and the order fails already at \(d=0\), where \(\pi_X(0)=\mathbb E[X]\).

The stop-loss transform and reinsurance is the expected payment above each retention. Ordering those transforms yields the definition. Jensen's inequality explains the constant-loss example: \(x\mapsto(x-d)_+\) is convex, so a constant at the mean has no larger expected excess than the original loss.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• It is equivalent to increasing convex order: \(\mathbb{E}[h(X)]\le\mathbb{E}[h(Y)]\) for increasing convex \(h\) whenever the expectations are defined.
  • It implies \(\mathbb{E}[X]\le\mathbb{E}[Y]\) and is transitive.
  • Stochastic order and the equal-mean thicker-tailed comparison each imply stop-loss order.
  • Without equal means, stop-loss order need not imply a variance comparison.
  • Increasing convex transformations preserve the order when the transformed quantities meet the needed integrability conditions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Let \(X=1\) and \(Y\) equal 0 or 2 with equal probabilities. At \(d=1\), expected excesses are 0 and 0.5; their stop-loss transforms are ordered at every retention.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: For nonnegative integrable losses, if \(X\le_{\mathrm{sl}}Z\) and \(\mathbb{E}[X]<\mathbb{E}[Z]\), the separation theorem guarantees a loss law \(Y\) such that \(X\le_{\mathrm{st}}Y\le_{\mathrm{sl}}Z\) and \(\mathbb{E}[Y]=\mathbb{E}[Z]\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The comparison can be separated into an increase in loss size followed by an equal-mean convex-order comparison. The intermediate variable describes a distribution; the theorem does not specify a unique insurance contract.

The figure draws the Examples case. The first arrow moves all the mass of \(X=0\) up to \(Y=1\), an increase in loss size (\(X\le_{\mathrm{st}}Y\)); the second spreads the mass of \(Y\) out to 0 and 2 around the common mean 1 (\(Y\le_{\mathrm{cx}}Z\)). Together the two steps decompose the original comparison \(X\le_{\mathrm{sl}}Z\), in which \(\mathbb{E}[X]=0<\mathbb{E}[Z]=1\).

Stochastic order forms the first comparison, increasing loss size from \(X\) to \(Y\). Stop-loss order forms the second, comparing expected excesses of \(Y\) and \(Z\) at every retention; matching their means turns this second step into a dispersion comparison.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The equal-mean second step is \(Y\le_{\mathrm{cx}}Z\).
  • The theorem gives existence, not uniqueness of \(Y\).
  • Outside the theorem's hypothesis: if \(X\) and \(Z\) already have equal means, then \(X\le_{\mathrm{cx}}Z\) directly, so \(Y=X\) gives the same decomposition.
  • Matching the means alone is insufficient; both order requirements must also hold.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Let \(X=0\) and \(Z\) equal 0 or 2 with equal probabilities. Choosing \(Y=1\) gives \(X\le_{\mathrm{st}}Y\), \(Y\le_{\mathrm{cx}}Z\) and matching means of 1 for \(Y,Z\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a nonnegative integrable loss \(X\), its stop-loss transform at retention \(d\ge0\) is \(\pi_X(d)=\mathbb{E}[(X-d)_+]\). In reinsurance, an insurer passes (cedes) part of its losses to a reinsurer under a contract called a treaty and keeps the rest, its retention. A stop-loss treaty pays the excess of an aggregate loss over its retention; the same positive-part function can describe excess-of-loss cover on an individual claim.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The transform is the expected covered tail beyond a deductible. It distinguishes risks that have the same mean but different upper-tail exposure.

The figure applies the Examples formula with \(\lambda=1/2\), so \(\bar F_X(t)=\mathrm{e}^{-t/2}\) and \(\pi_X(d)=2\mathrm{e}^{-d/2}\). The shaded area under the survivor function beyond \(d=2\) equals \(\pi_X(2)=2\mathrm{e}^{-1}\approx0.74\), the height of the marked point on the right. As the retention grows, the transform falls convexly from \(\pi_X(0)=\mathbb{E}[X]=2\) towards zero, and its slope at \(d\) is \(-\bar F_X(d)\).

Move the retention \(d\): the red area under \(\bar F_X\) to the right of \(d\) is \(\pi_X(d)\), drawn as the point on the right-hand curve, and the tangent there has slope \(-\bar F_X(d)\). Change \(\lambda\) to rescale the curve, which starts at \(\pi_X(0)=\mathbb E[X]=1/\lambda\).

An ordinary deductible produces the payment \((X-d)_+\). Its expectation is therefore the stop-loss transform: the function records the expected ceded payment as the retention changes.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\pi_X(d)=\int_d^\infty\bar F_X(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\).
  • It is nonincreasing and convex in \(d\), with \(\pi_X(0)=\mathbb{E}[X]\) and \(\pi_X(d)\to0\).
  • Its right derivative is \(-\mathbb{P}(X>d)\); its left derivative is \(-\mathbb{P}(X\ge d)\).
  • The retained loss \(\min(X,d)\) plus the ceded excess \((X-d)_+\) equals \(X\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: For exponential loss of rate \(\lambda\), \(\pi_X(d)=\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda d}/\lambda\). This follows by integrating its survivor function from \(d\) onwards.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For integrable losses of equal mean, \(Y\) is directly thicker-tailed than \(X\) if some threshold \(t_0\) satisfies \(F_Y(t)\ge F_X(t)\) for \(t<t_0\) and \(F_Y(t)\le F_X(t)\) for \(t\ge t_0\). This is the course's equal-mean comparison in which the two cumulative distribution functions (CDFs) cross once. At a jump, this convention assigns the crossing point to the upper interval. For continuous CDFs, the two inequalities force \(F_Y(t_0)=F_X(t_0)\); if a CDF jumps at \(t_0\), only \(F_Y(t_0)\le F_X(t_0)\) is required there, not equality.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Probability shifts towards both lower and higher loss values while keeping the mean fixed. This is a relative dispersion comparison; it does not assert a particular asymptotic heavy-tail class.

The figure draws the Examples case. Before \(t_0=1\) the CDF of \(Y\) lies above that of \(X\) (mass moved down to 0); from \(t_0\) up to 2 it lies below (mass moved up to 2), and from 2 on the two agree. The two shaded gaps have the same area \(\tfrac{1}{2}\), which reflects the equal means: for nonnegative losses \(\mathbb{E}[X]-\mathbb{E}[Y]=\int_0^\infty(F_Y(t)-F_X(t))\,\mathrm{d}t\), so the signed gaps must cancel.

Change the two spreads: the CDFs cross once at \(t_0=1\), with \(F_Y\) above \(F_X\) before the crossing and below it after. The two shaded gaps have equal area because the means are equal.

Stochastic order compares CDFs in the same direction at every threshold. Here the CDF direction reverses once, so the relation compares equal-mean dispersion rather than uniformly larger loss size; stochastic order is not the definition.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The direct single-crossing relation is not generally transitive. The notes use its transitive closure when they say indirectly thicker-tailed.
  • The direct comparison implies stop-loss order \(X\le_{\mathrm{sl}}Y\).
  • For \(0\le X\le b\) with mean \(\mu\), the constant \(\mu\) is the least dispersed and the two-point law on \(\{0,b\}\) with upper mass \(\mu/b\) is maximally dispersed in convex order.
  • Unequal means do not meet the definition.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Let \(X=1\) surely and let \(Y\) be 0 or 2 with equal probabilities. Both means are 1. The CDF of \(Y\) is above that of \(X\) below 1 and below it between 1 and 2.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Under left truncation at \(d\), only losses satisfying \(X>d\) enter the dataset. For independent exact observations drawn from that conditional population, the likelihood contribution is \(f_\theta(x_i)/\bar F_\theta(d)\) for \(x_i>d\), provided \(\bar F_\theta(d)>0\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Small losses are absent altogether. The likelihood must renormalize the observed population; this differs from retaining small losses as censored observations.

The figure uses the fitted rate \(2/70\) from the Examples case. The dashed ground-up density \(f_\theta\) puts almost all of its mass below \(d=100\), where nothing is recorded. Dividing by \(\bar F_\theta(100)=\mathrm{e}^{-20/7}\approx0.057\) lifts the part above 100 into a proper density on \(x>100\), and the observations 120 and 150 contribute its heights \(f_\theta(x_i)/\bar F_\theta(d)\) to the likelihood. For the exponential law this conditional density is the original one shifted to start at \(d\), which is why only the excesses 20 and 50 enter the estimate.

Move \(\lambda\) and the truncation point \(d\): dividing by \(\bar F_\theta(d)\) leaves only the excesses over \(d\) in the estimate; at the default \(d=100\), \(\hat\lambda=2/70\) instead of the \(2/270\) obtained by ignoring truncation.

An ordinary deductible produces a dataset of paid claims only when the loss exceeds \(d\). If recorded amounts are excesses, add \(d\) back before evaluating the ground-up density, and divide by the exceedance probability to describe the selected population.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\displaystyle \ell(\theta)=\sum_i\log f_\theta(x_i)-n\log\bar F_\theta(d)\) for a fixed observed sample size.
  • For observation restricted to \((a,b]\), normalize by \(F_\theta(b)-F_\theta(a)\).
  • If a deductible dataset reports excesses \(y_i=X_i-d\), use \(f_\theta(y_i+d)/\bar F_\theta(d)\).
  • Information about the total number of excluded losses would require an additional sampling model.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: For exponential losses observed only above 100, observations 120 and 150 have excesses 20 and 50. The conditional maximum likelihood estimate (MLE) is \(2/(20+50)=2/70\), rather than \(2/270\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a loss with finite second moment, the variance principle is \(\Pi(X)=\mathbb{E}[X]+\alpha\operatorname{Var}(X)\), with fixed coefficient \(\alpha>0\). The coefficient has units inverse to those of the monetary loss.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The loading increases with squared dispersion. Changing the monetary unit requires a corresponding change in the numerical loading coefficient if prices are to describe the same contract.

The figure plots the loading \(\Pi(aX)-a\mathbb{E}[X]=\alpha a^2\operatorname{Var}(X)=0.025a^2\) for the Examples loss. At \(a=1\) it meets the proportional line \(a\cdot0.025\), giving \(\Pi(X)=0.525\); at \(a=2\) the parabola reaches 0.1, twice the proportional 0.05, so \(\Pi(2X)=1.1\) rather than \(2\Pi(X)=1.05\). This quadratic growth is why the principle is not proportional for fixed \(\alpha\).

Move the scale \(a\): the loading \(\alpha a^2\operatorname{Var}(X)\) grows like \(a^2\), so \(\Pi(aX)\) exceeds \(a\Pi(X)\) once \(a>1\). Change \(p\) to vary \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=p(1-p)\) of the Bernoulli loss.

Variance and standard deviation supplies the squared-dispersion measure used in the loading. For independent losses these variances add, explaining additivity; multiplying all losses by \(a\) multiplies this loading by \(a^2\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The principle has nonnegative loading and translation consistency.
  • It is additive for independent losses because their variances add.
  • It is not proportional for fixed \(\alpha\): \(\Pi(aX)=a\mathbb{E}[X]+\alpha a^2\operatorname{Var}(X)\).
  • It preserves equal-mean convex order, but need not preserve stochastic order when means differ.
  • Covariance matters when pricing a dependent portfolio.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: For \(\alpha=0.1\), a Bernoulli loss with probability \(0.5\) has premium \(0.5+0.1(0.25)=0.525\). Doubling the loss gives premium \(1+0.1(1)=1.1\), not \(1.05\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For strictly increasing concave utility \(u\), the zero-utility premium \(\Pi(X)\) solves \(\mathbb{E}[u(\Pi(X)-X)]=u(0)\), when a finite solution exists. It is the insurer's indifference price at reference wealth zero. Utility must be defined on every relevant net outcome.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Premium income offsets the insured loss until expected utility equals the no-contract reference. The name refers to zero change in utility, not necessarily a utility function whose value is zero.

The figure takes \(u(w)=-\mathrm{e}^{-w}\) (so \(\alpha=1\)) and a loss \(X\) equal to 0 or 2 with probability \(1/2\) each, numbers chosen for illustration. The zero-utility premium is then \(\Pi=\log\frac{1+\mathrm{e}^2}{2}\approx1.43\), with net outcomes \(\Pi\) and \(\Pi-2\). Their expected utility, the midpoint of the dashed chord, equals \(u(0)=-1\) and sits above \(w=\Pi-\mathbb{E}[X]\approx0.43\). Because the concave curve lies above its chords, it reaches the level \(u(0)\) already at \(w=0\), so \(\Pi-\mathbb{E}[X]\ge0\): the premium carries a nonnegative loading.

Change \(\alpha\), the loss \(b\) and its probability \(q\): \(\Pi(X)\) is the premium that leaves expected utility equal to \(u(0)\), and it never falls below \(\mathbb E[X]\). Switch to linear utility and the loading vanishes.

Insurance indifference premiums gives the insurer's equation at general reference wealth; setting that wealth to zero gives this equation. Among premium principles and their properties, nonnegative loading follows from concavity: Jensen's inequality gives \(u(\Pi(X)-\mathbb{E}[X])\ge u(0)\), hence \(\Pi(X)\ge\mathbb{E}[X]\) under the stated conditions.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(u\) is strictly increasing, any finite solution is unique.
  • Concavity implies \(\Pi(X)\ge\mathbb{E}[X]\) under the needed integrability conditions.
  • Exponential utility gives the exponential premium principle.
  • For bounded losses, a solution is between the smallest and largest possible loss under suitable continuity and domain conditions.
  • For general utilities, reference wealth affects the indifference price.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: With risk-neutral \(u(w)=w\), the equation is \(\Pi(X)-\mathbb{E}[X]=0\), giving the net premium. With \(u(w)=-\mathrm{e}^{-\alpha w}\) it gives the exponential premium.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a state \(i\) of a homogeneous Markov chain with at least one positive-probability return, its period is

\[ d(i)=\gcd\{n\ge1\colon(\boldsymbol{P}^n)_{ii}>0\}. \]

The state is aperiodic when \(d(i)=1\). An irreducible chain has the same period at every state, so it is enough to check one state. A chain is aperiodic when all its states have period 1.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The powers of the transition matrix identify possible return times. A period greater than one forces returns onto a repeating time grid. Irreducibility allows states to reach one another, which is why they share a period. Aperiodicity removes this cyclic obstruction; it does not require a positive one-step self-transition at every state.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For a finite irreducible aperiodic chain, \(\boldsymbol{\alpha}\boldsymbol{P}^n\to\boldsymbol{\pi}\) for every initial probability row vector \(\boldsymbol{\alpha}\), where \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\) is its unique stationary distribution.
  • In an irreducible chain, a positive self-transition at one state implies period 1 at all states. This is a sufficient condition, not a necessary one.
  • Aperiodicity is not needed merely to solve the stationary equations, nor for uniqueness in a finite irreducible chain.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: For \(\boldsymbol{P}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\), returns occur only at times \(2,4,6,\ldots\), so the period is 2. Replacing the matrix by \(\begin{pmatrix}1/2&1/2\\1/2&1/2\end{pmatrix}\) permits a return after one step and makes the chain aperiodic.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a homogeneous Markov chain, state \(j\) is accessible from state \(i\) if \((\boldsymbol{P}^n)_{ij}>0\) for some integer \(n\ge0\). Two states communicate if each is accessible from the other. The chain is irreducible when every pair of states communicates.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Accessibility uses the multi-step probabilities of the Markov chain. A direct transition can have probability zero while a route through intermediate states has positive probability. Irreducibility says that all states form a single communicating class, that is, a maximal set of states that communicate with each other; it does not require every matrix entry to be positive.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A finite irreducible chain has a unique stationary distribution, with positive probability on every state.
  • Irreducibility alone does not ensure convergence of the distribution at a fixed time: a chain can still be periodic.
  • For a finite chain, draw an arrow \(i\to j\) when \(p_{ij}>0\). Irreducibility is equivalent to a directed path between every ordered pair of states.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: The two-state alternating chain \(\boldsymbol{P}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\) is irreducible: either state reaches the other in one step. It has period 2. By contrast, \(\boldsymbol{P}=\boldsymbol{I}\) with two states is reducible because neither state can reach the other.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A discrete-time Markov chain is a stochastic process \((X_n)_{n\ge0}\) on a finite or countable state space \(S\) whose next-state probabilities depend on the observed past only through the present state. For every history with positive probability,

\[ \mathbb{P}(X_{n+1}=j\mid X_0=i_0,\ldots,X_n=i) =\mathbb{P}(X_{n+1}=j\mid X_n=i). \]

The chain is time-homogeneous when these conditional probabilities do not depend on \(n\). Its transition matrix is \(\boldsymbol{P}=(p_{ij})\), where \(p_{ij}=\mathbb{P}(X_{n+1}=j\mid X_n=i)\), \(p_{ij}\ge0\), and \(\displaystyle\sum_{j\in S}p_{ij}=1\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The state must retain all information from the past needed to predict the next transition. A rating class alone may be insufficient if next year's premium also depends on how many consecutive claim-free years have elapsed; include that count in the state. The property does not say that successive states are independent.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
For a finite homogeneous chain, let \(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_n\) be the row vector of state probabilities. The matrix product sums over possible intermediate states, giving

\[ \boldsymbol{\alpha}_{n+1}=\boldsymbol{\alpha}_n\boldsymbol{P},\qquad \boldsymbol{\alpha}_n=\boldsymbol{\alpha}_0\boldsymbol{P}^n. \]

The entry \((\boldsymbol{P}^n)_{ij}\) is the probability of reaching \(j\) in \(n\) steps when starting at \(i\). These powers require homogeneity; a changing transition rule instead uses the ordered product of the successive matrices.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For \(S=\{0,1\}\) and

\[ \boldsymbol{P}=\begin{pmatrix}0.8&0.2\\0.3&0.7\end{pmatrix}, \]

starting in state 0 gives next-step probabilities \((0.8,0.2)\). After two steps the probability of state 1 is \(0.8(0.2)+0.2(0.7)=0.30\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A stationary distribution for a time-homogeneous Markov chain with transition matrix \(\boldsymbol{P}\) is a probability row vector \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\) such that

\[ \boldsymbol{\pi}\boldsymbol{P}=\boldsymbol{\pi},\qquad \pi_i\ge0,\qquad \displaystyle\sum_i\pi_i=1. \]

Starting the chain with distribution \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\) leaves its distribution unchanged at every subsequent step.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Stationarity describes a distribution that is preserved by a transition. It does not by itself say that the chain approaches this distribution from a different starting point. In a bonus-malus model, stationary class proportions produce a mean premium by weighting each class premium by its stationary probability.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For a finite state space, at least one stationary distribution exists.
  • Finite irreducibility gives uniqueness and strictly positive entries. Additional aperiodicity gives convergence from every initial distribution.
  • To calculate a finite stationary distribution, solve the linear system \(\boldsymbol{\pi}(\boldsymbol{P}-\boldsymbol{I})=\boldsymbol0\) together with the normalization equation. One balance equation can be replaced by the normalization equation when solving the system; always check nonnegativity.
  • A countably infinite irreducible chain need not have a stationary probability distribution; the finite-state conclusion cannot be transferred without further assumptions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For \(\boldsymbol{P}=\begin{pmatrix}0.8&0.2\\0.3&0.7\end{pmatrix}\), the balance equation is \(0.2\pi_0=0.3\pi_1\). Together with \(\pi_0+\pi_1=1\), this gives \(\boldsymbol{\pi}=(0.6,0.4)\).

For the alternating chain \(\boldsymbol{P}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\), \((1/2,1/2)\) is stationary, but a chain started in state 0 alternates forever. A stationary distribution and convergence are different properties.

docs.title: Study abroad
docs.text:
The programme coordinator must approve the foreign minor. Its courses must be postpropaedeutic and must not overlap with courses already taken in the BSc EOR. At most 15 ECTS may fall outside the programme's learning outcomes, including at most one course in the host university's language worth no more than 6 ECTS.

If at least 20 of the approved 30 ECTS are passed, the programme describes a substitution-request route using EOR minor or elective courses. With fewer than 20 ECTS, an entirely different minor is required. Read the official programme for the full conditions before arranging substitutions.

docs.title: Area between two curves and \(\int_0^1\ln x\,\mathrm{d}x\)
docs.text: Math I: Calculus · Mock exam, Question 5(b)–(c) · 14 points · Lectures 11–12

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
• (b) Find the area enclosed by \(2y^2-y=x+2\) and \(y^2=x\text{.}\) [6 points]
  • (c) Evaluate \(\int_0^1\ln x\,\mathrm{d}x\) in two different ways. [8 points]

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Definite integral and the fundamental theorem of calculus, part 2.
  • Improper integral: an integral with an unbounded integrand or interval is a limit of ordinary integrals.
  • Integration by parts.
  • Integration by substitution, type 2: substitute \(x=\varphi(t)\text{.}\)
  • L'Hôpital's rule, for \(\varepsilon\ln\varepsilon\to0\) and \(R\mathrm{e}^{-R}\to0\text{.}\)

docs.title: Plan
docs.text: In (b) both curves are easy to write as \(x\) in terms of \(y\text{,}\) so integrate in \(y\text{:}\) area \(=\int(\text{right}-\text{left})\,\mathrm{d}y\text{.}\) In (c), \(\ln x\) is unbounded near \(0\text{,}\) so this is an improper integral: write it as a limit before integrating. The two methods are integration by parts, and the substitution \(x=\mathrm{e}^{-t}\text{,}\) which turns it into an integral over \([0,\infty)\text{.}\)

docs.title: Step-by-step solution
docs.text:
Try each step yourself before you open it.

(b) Step 1 · Write both curves as functions of y (1 point) \[ x=2y^2-y-2,\quad x=y^2. \] (b) Step 2 · Find the intersections (2 points)

\(y^2=2y^2-y-2\) gives \(y^2-y-2=0\text{,}\) that is \((y-2)(y+1)=0\text{.}\) The curves meet at \(y=-1\) and \(y=2\text{.}\)

(b) Step 3 · Which curve is on the right? (1 point)

For \(-1<y<2\text{,}\)

\[ y^2-(2y^2-y-2)=-(y-2)(y+1)>0, \]

so \(x=y^2\) is the right boundary and \(x=2y^2-y-2\) the left one.

(b) Step 4 · Set up and evaluate (2 points) \[ \begin{aligned} \text{Area}&=\int_{-1}^{2}\left(-y^2+y+2\right)\,\mathrm{d}y\\ &=\left[-\frac{y^3}{3}+\frac{y^2}{2}+2y\right]_{-1}^{2}\\ &=\frac{10}{3}-\left(-\frac{7}{6}\right)=\frac{9}{2}. \end{aligned} \]

Concept: Fundamental theorem of calculus, part 2

(c) Method 1, Step 1 · Write the improper integral as a limit (1 point)

\(\ln x\to-\infty\) as \(x\to0^+\text{,}\) so

\[ \int_0^1\ln x\,\mathrm{d}x=\lim_{\varepsilon\to0^+}\int_{\varepsilon}^{1}\ln x\,\mathrm{d}x. \]

Concept: Improper integral

(c) Method 1, Step 2 · Integrate by parts (1 point)

With \(u=\ln x\) and \(v'=1\text{,}\)

\[ \int_{\varepsilon}^{1}\ln x\,\mathrm{d}x =\big[x\ln x\big]_{\varepsilon}^{1}-\int_{\varepsilon}^{1}1\,\mathrm{d}x =-\varepsilon\ln\varepsilon-(1-\varepsilon). \] (c) Method 1, Step 3 · Take the limit (2 points)

\(\varepsilon\ln\varepsilon\to0\) as \(\varepsilon\to0^+\text{.}\) One way: by L'Hôpital's rule,

\[ \lim_{\varepsilon\to0^+}\frac{\ln\varepsilon}{1/\varepsilon} =\lim_{\varepsilon\to0^+}\frac{1/\varepsilon}{-1/\varepsilon^2} =\lim_{\varepsilon\to0^+}(-\varepsilon)=0. \]

So the integral equals \(0-1=-1\text{.}\)

(c) Method 2, Step 1 · Substitute x = e^(−t) (2 points)

Let \(x=\mathrm{e}^{-t}\text{.}\) Then \(\ln x=-t\) and \(\mathrm{d}x=-\mathrm{e}^{-t}\,\mathrm{d}t\text{;}\) \(x=1\) corresponds to \(t=0\) and \(x\to0^+\) to \(t\to\infty\text{.}\) So

\[ \int_0^1\ln x\,\mathrm{d}x =\int_{\infty}^{0}(-t)\left(-\mathrm{e}^{-t}\right)\,\mathrm{d}t =-\int_0^{\infty}t\mathrm{e}^{-t}\,\mathrm{d}t. \]

The orientation flips because \(x\) decreases as \(t\) increases; keep track of the sign.

Concept: Integration by substitution, type 2

(c) Method 2, Step 2 · Evaluate the new integral (2 points)

On \([0,R]\text{,}\) integration by parts gives

\[ \int_0^R t\mathrm{e}^{-t}\,\mathrm{d}t =\big[-t\mathrm{e}^{-t}\big]_0^R+\int_0^R\mathrm{e}^{-t}\,\mathrm{d}t =-R\mathrm{e}^{-R}+1-\mathrm{e}^{-R}\to1, \]

because \(R\mathrm{e}^{-R}\to0\) and \(\mathrm{e}^{-R}\to0\text{.}\) Hence again \(\int_0^1\ln x\,\mathrm{d}x=-1\text{.}\)

docs.title: Where marks are lost
docs.text:
• Integrating in \(x\) in (b). It can be done, but the region then needs several pieces. Integrating in \(y\) needs one.
  • Treating \(\int_0^1\ln x\,\mathrm{d}x\) as an ordinary integral. Write the limit; the mark for justifying \(\varepsilon\ln\varepsilon\to0\) depends on it.
  • Losing the sign in the substitution. Swapping the limits and the minus sign from \(\mathrm{d}x\) must be done together.
  • Giving the same method twice. "Two different ways" means two genuinely different routes.

docs.title: Continuity of \(1/x^2\) from the \(\varepsilon\)–\(\delta\) definition
docs.text: Math I: Calculus · Mock exam, Question 2(b) · 14 points · Lecture 5

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Use the \(\varepsilon\)–\(\delta\) definition to prove that

\[ f\colon\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}\to\mathbb{R},\quad f(x)=\frac{1}{x^2}, \]

is continuous at every point of its domain.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Continuity: \(f\) is continuous at \(x_0\) if for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there is a \(\delta>0\) such that \(|x-x_0|<\delta\) implies \(|f(x)-f(x_0)|<\varepsilon\text{.}\)
  • Triangle inequality, in both directions: \(|a+b|\leq|a|+|b|\) and \(|a|\geq|b|-|a-b|\text{.}\)
  • Absolute value rules: \(|ab|=|a|\,|b|\) and \(|x^2|=|x|^2\text{.}\)

docs.title: Plan
docs.text: The proof has one idea: write \(|f(x)-f(x_0)|\) as \(|x-x_0|\) times something, then keep that "something" bounded by staying close to \(x_0\text{.}\) Close to \(x_0\) means two things here: \(x\) must stay away from \(0\text{,}\) where \(1/x^2\) blows up, and \(x\) must not be too large. A first restriction \(|x-x_0|<|x_0|/2\) gives both. The final \(\delta\) is the smaller of that restriction and the one that makes the product less than \(\varepsilon\text{.}\)

docs.title: Step-by-step solution
docs.text:
Try each step yourself before you open it.

Step 1 · Fix the point and the tolerance (1 point)

Let \(x_0 eq0\) be arbitrary and let \(\varepsilon>0 ext{.}\) Everything that follows may depend on \(x_0\) and \(\varepsilon ext{,}\) but not on \(x ext{.}\)

Writing "let \(x_0 eq0\) be arbitrary" at the start is what lets you conclude continuity at every point at the end.

Step 2 · Factor the difference (2 points)

For \(x eq0 ext{,}\)

\[ \left| rac{1}{x^2}- rac{1}{x_0^2} ight| = rac{|x_0^2-x^2|}{x^2x_0^2} = rac{|x-x_0|\,|x+x_0|}{x^2x_0^2}. \]

The factor \(|x-x_0|\) is the one we control with \(\delta ext{.}\) The other factor, \(|x+x_0|/(x^2x_0^2) ext{,}\) must be bounded by a constant that depends only on \(x_0 ext{.}\)

Step 3 · Restrict to a neighbourhood that avoids 0 (2 points)

Require first that

\[ |x-x_0|< rac{|x_0|}{2}. \]

Any fixed fraction of \(|x_0|\) smaller than \(1\) works; \(1/2\) keeps the numbers simple. This interval does not contain \(0 ext{,}\) so every such \(x\) lies in the domain.

Step 4 · Bound the denominator from below (2 points)

By the reverse triangle inequality,

\[ |x|\geq|x_0|-|x-x_0|> rac{|x_0|}{2}, \]

so \(x^2>x_0^2/4 ext{.}\) A lower bound on the denominator gives an upper bound on the fraction.

Concept: Triangle inequality

Step 5 · Bound the numerator from above (2 points)

Write \(x+x_0=(x-x_0)+2x_0\) and use the triangle inequality:

\[ |x+x_0|\leq|x-x_0|+2|x_0| < rac{|x_0|}{2}+2|x_0|= rac{5}{2}|x_0|. \] Step 6 · Combine the estimates (2 points)

Put Steps 4 and 5 into Step 2:

\[ |f(x)-f(x_0)| \leq rac{ frac{5}{2}|x_0|}{ frac{1}{4}x_0^2\cdot x_0^2}\,|x-x_0| = rac{10}{|x_0|^3}\,|x-x_0|. \]

This holds for every \(x\) with \(|x-x_0|<|x_0|/2 ext{.}\) The constant \(10/|x_0|^3\) depends on \(x_0\) only, which is allowed.

Write \(\leq\) here, not \(< ext{:}\) the bound on the other factor is strict, but \(|x-x_0|\) can be \(0\) (take \(x=x_0\)), and then both sides are \(0 ext{.}\) The strict inequality comes in Step 7 from \(|x-x_0|<\delta ext{.}\)

Step 7 · Choose δ and verify (2 points)

Take

\[ \delta=\min\left\{ rac{|x_0|}{2},\, rac{\varepsilon|x_0|^3}{10} ight\}. \]

Then \(\delta>0 ext{.}\) If \(|x-x_0|<\delta ext{,}\) the first entry of the minimum makes Step 6 valid, and the second gives

\[ |f(x)-f(x_0)|\leq rac{10}{|x_0|^3}\,|x-x_0| < rac{10}{|x_0|^3}\cdot rac{\varepsilon|x_0|^3}{10}=\varepsilon. \]

Show the verification explicitly; choosing \(\delta\) alone does not earn this mark.

Step 8 · Conclude (1 point)

Since \(x_0 eq0\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) were arbitrary, \(f\) is continuous at every point of \(\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\} ext{.}\)

docs.title: Where marks are lost
docs.text:
• Choosing \(\delta\) that depends on \(x\text{.}\) The value of \(\delta\) may use \(x_0\) and \(\varepsilon\) only.
  • Forgetting the first restriction. Without a bound like \(|x-x_0|<|x_0|/2\text{,}\) the factor \(1/x^2\) is unbounded near \(0\) and Step 6 fails. The minimum in \(\delta\) must contain both restrictions.
  • Bounding \(|x|\) from above instead of below. In the denominator you need a lower bound for \(|x|\text{.}\)
  • Stopping at "choose \(\delta\)". The last three marks need the check that \(|x-x_0|<\delta\) really gives \(|f(x)-f(x_0)|<\varepsilon\) and the conclusion for every \(x_0\text{.}\)

docs.text:
