  • Limit of a sequence from the definition: the same "find a bound, then choose \(N\)" idea for sequences.

Symbols: delta, epsilon, real numbers

docs.title: FTC with a variable limit and a scaled improper integral
docs.text: Math I: Calculus · Week 7 test, open question · 7 points · Lectures 11–12

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
This question consists of two independent parts.

Part A. Define

\[ F(x)=\int_0^{x^2}t^2\mathrm{e}^{-t}\,\mathrm{d}t. \]

Find \(F'(x)\text{.}\) [2 points]

Part B. Let \(a>0\) and define

\[ I(a)=\int_0^{\infty}x^2\mathrm{e}^{-ax}\,\mathrm{d}x. \]
  • (B1) Apply the substitution \(t=ax\) first on \([0,R]\text{,}\) then let \(R\to\infty\text{,}\) to prove that \(I(a)=I(1)/a^3\text{.}\) Justify the transformed upper limit. [2 points]
  • (B2) Evaluate \(I(1)\) by integration by parts and hence find \(I(a)\text{.}\) Justify every boundary limit that occurs. [3 points]

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Fundamental theorem of calculus, part 1: for continuous \(f\text{,}\) \(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}u}\int_0^u f(t)\,\mathrm{d}t=f(u)\text{.}\)
  • Chain rule, because the upper limit is \(x^2\text{,}\) not \(x\text{.}\)
  • Improper integral: \(\int_0^\infty\) means \(\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_0^R\text{.}\)
  • Integration by substitution and integration by parts on a bounded interval.
  • Limits at infinity: \(x^k\mathrm{e}^{-x}\to0\) as \(x\to\infty\text{.}\)

docs.title: Plan
docs.text: Part A is a composition: an integral with a variable upper limit, evaluated at \(x^2\text{.}\) Part B is about doing improper integrals honestly. Every substitution and every integration by parts happens on a bounded interval \([0,R]\text{;}\) only then do you let \(R\to\infty\text{.}\) The gamma function is the general version of \(I(1)\text{.}\)

docs.title: Step-by-step solution
docs.text:
Try each step yourself before you open it.

Part A · FTC and the chain rule (2 points)

The integrand \(f(t)=t^2\mathrm{e}^{-t}\) is continuous, so by FTC part 1 the function

\[ G(u)=\int_0^u t^2\mathrm{e}^{-t}\,\mathrm{d}t \]

is differentiable with \(G'(u)=u^2\mathrm{e}^{-u}\text{.}\) Since \(F(x)=G(x^2)\text{,}\) the chain rule gives

\[ F'(x)=G'(x^2)\cdot2x=2x\,(x^2)^2\mathrm{e}^{-x^2}=2x^5\mathrm{e}^{-x^2}. \]

Concept: Fundamental theorem of calculus, part 1

(B1) Step 1 · Substitute on [0, R] (1 point)

For \(R>0\text{,}\) let \(t=ax\text{.}\) Then \(x=t/a\) and \(\mathrm{d}x=\mathrm{d}t/a\text{;}\) the limits \(x=0\) and \(x=R\) become \(t=0\) and \(t=aR\text{.}\) So

\[ \int_0^R x^2\mathrm{e}^{-ax}\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac{1}{a^3}\int_0^{aR}t^2\mathrm{e}^{-t}\,\mathrm{d}t. \]

Concept: Integration by substitution

(B1) Step 2 · Let R → ∞ (1 point)

Because \(a>0\text{,}\) \(aR\to\infty\) as \(R\to\infty\text{.}\) This is the justification the question asks for: if \(a\) were negative, the upper limit would go to \(-\infty\) instead. Taking limits on both sides,

\[ I(a)=\frac{1}{a^3}\lim_{S\to\infty}\int_0^{S}t^2\mathrm{e}^{-t}\,\mathrm{d}t=\frac{I(1)}{a^3}, \]

where the limit on the right exists because \(I(1)\) converges (B2 computes it).

Concept: Improper integral

(B2) Step 1 · Integrate by parts twice (2 points)

On \([0,R]\text{,}\) with \(u=x^2\) and \(v'=\mathrm{e}^{-x}\text{,}\)

\[ \begin{aligned} \int_0^R x^2\mathrm{e}^{-x}\,\mathrm{d}x &=\left[-x^2\mathrm{e}^{-x}\right]_0^R +2\int_0^R x\mathrm{e}^{-x}\,\mathrm{d}x,\\ \int_0^R x\mathrm{e}^{-x}\,\mathrm{d}x &=\left[-x\mathrm{e}^{-x}\right]_0^R +\int_0^R\mathrm{e}^{-x}\,\mathrm{d}x. \end{aligned} \]

Concept: Integration by parts

(B2) Step 2 · Boundary terms and the answer (1 point)

The boundary terms are \(-R^2\mathrm{e}^{-R}\) and \(-R\mathrm{e}^{-R}\text{,}\) and both tend to \(0\) as \(R\to\infty\text{,}\) because the exponential beats any power. At \(x=0\) both are \(0\text{.}\) Also \(\int_0^R\mathrm{e}^{-x}\,\mathrm{d}x=1-\mathrm{e}^{-R}\to1\text{.}\) Hence

\[ I(1)=2\left(0+1\right)=2,\quad I(a)=\frac{2}{a^3}. \]

Concept: Limit at infinity

docs.title: Where marks are lost
docs.text:
• Forgetting the factor \(2x\) in Part A. The upper limit is \(x^2\text{;}\) FTC alone gives \(G'(u)\text{,}\) and the chain rule supplies \(2x\text{.}\)
  • Substituting directly on \([0,\infty)\text{.}\) The question asks for \([0,R]\) first, and the mark is for saying why \(aR\to\infty\text{.}\)
  • Writing \([-x^2\mathrm{e}^{-x}]_0^{\infty}=0\) without a reason. Each boundary limit needs its own sentence.

docs.title: Try next
docs.text:
• Area between two curves and \(\int_0^1\ln x\,\mathrm{d}x\): another improper integral, this time at an endpoint where the integrand blows up.
  • Gamma function: \(I(1)=\Gamma(3)=2!\text{.}\)

Symbols: gamma, infinity, integral

docs.title: Global extrema of \(x+1/x\) on a closed interval
docs.text: Math I: Calculus · Week 3 test, open question · 7 points · Lectures 5–6

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Let \(f\colon[1/2,3]\to\mathbb{R}\) be defined by \(f(x)=x+1/x\text{.}\)

  1. Explain why \(f\) must attain both a global minimum and a global maximum on \([1/2,3]\text{.}\) [2 points]
  2. Find every stationary point of \(f\) in \((1/2,3)\) and classify each one as a local minimum, a local maximum, or neither. [2 points]
  3. Determine the global minimum and global maximum of \(f\) on \([1/2,3]\text{,}\) including the points where they are attained. [3 points]

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Extreme value theorem: a continuous function on a closed, bounded interval attains a maximum and a minimum.
  • Stationary point and the first-order condition.
  • Local extremum and global extremum.
  • Closed and bounded intervals, whose endpoints are candidates too.

docs.title: Plan
docs.text: The extreme value theorem says the extrema exist, and the first-order condition says where they can be: at an interior stationary point or at an endpoint. So the method is a short list of candidates and a comparison of values.

docs.title: Step-by-step solution
docs.text:
Try each step yourself before you open it.

Part 1 · Existence (2 points)

\(f\) is continuous on \([1/2,3]\) (it is a sum of continuous functions and \(0\notin[1/2,3]\)), and \([1/2,3]\) is closed and bounded. By the extreme value theorem, \(f\) attains a global minimum and a global maximum there.

Both hypotheses must be named. On \((0,3]\) the same formula has no maximum.

Concept: Extreme value theorem

Part 2, Step 1 · Find the stationary points

For \(x\in(1/2,3)\text{,}\)

\[ f'(x)=1-\frac{1}{x^2}. \]

\(f'(x)=0\) means \(x^2=1\text{,}\) and only \(x=1\) lies in the interval.

Part 2, Step 2 · Classify x = 1 (with Step 1: 2 points)

For every \(x>0\text{,}\)

\[ f(x)-f(1)=x+\frac{1}{x}-2=\frac{(x-1)^2}{x}\geq0, \]

with equality only at \(x=1\text{.}\) So \(x=1\) is a strict local minimum.

A second-derivative check works too: \(f''(x)=2/x^3\text{,}\) so \(f''(1)=2>0\text{.}\)

Part 3 · Compare candidates (3 points)

The global extrema can only occur at the stationary point or at the endpoints:

\[ f\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)=\frac{5}{2},\quad f(1)=2,\quad f(3)=\frac{10}{3}. \]

The global minimum is \(2\text{,}\) attained at \(x=1\text{.}\) The global maximum is \(10/3\text{,}\) attained at \(x=3\text{.}\)

Concept: Global extremum

docs.title: Where marks are lost
docs.text:
• Naming the theorem without its hypotheses. Say that \(f\) is continuous and the interval is closed and bounded.
  • Forgetting the endpoints. Here the global maximum is at an endpoint, where \(f'\neq0\text{.}\)
  • Keeping \(x=-1\text{.}\) It solves \(f'(x)=0\) but is outside the domain.

docs.title: Try next
docs.text:
• Stationary points, convexity and an alternating series
  • A function with three local extrema: the same tools with a parameter.

Symbols: element of, real numbers

docs.title: The inverse of \(x+x^3\)
docs.text: Math I: Calculus · Week 5 test, open question · 7 points · Lectures 7–8

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Define \(f\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) by \(f(x)=x+x^3\text{.}\)

  1. Prove that \(f\) is invertible from \(\mathbb{R}\) onto \(\mathbb{R}\text{.}\) [2 points]
  2. Let \(g=f^{-1}\text{.}\) Find \(g'(0)\) and \(g'(2)\text{.}\) [2 points]

  3. Evaluate [3 points]

    \[ \lim_{y\to0}\frac{g(y)-y}{y^3}. \]

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Bijection and inverse function: invertible means injective and surjective.
  • Monotone function: the sign test \(f'>0\Rightarrow f\) strictly increasing.
  • Intermediate value theorem and limits at infinity, for surjectivity.
  • Inverse function theorem: \(g'(y)=1/f'(g(y))\text{.}\)
  • For part 3, any one of: substitution in a limit, the definition of the derivative, or L'Hôpital's rule.

docs.title: Plan
docs.text: There is no formula for \(g\text{,}\) and you do not need one. Everything comes from the relation \(f(g(y))=y\text{.}\) For values of \(g\) at specific points, solve \(f(x)=y\) by inspection. For the limit, either rewrite everything in terms of \(x=g(y)\text{,}\) where it becomes a simple fraction, or use \(g(y)/y\to g'(0)=1\text{.}\)

docs.title: Step-by-step solution
docs.text:
Try each step yourself before you open it.

Part 1, Step 1 · Injective

\(f'(x)=1+3x^2>0\) for every \(x ext{,}\) so \(f\) is strictly increasing by the sign test, hence injective.

Concept: Monotone function

Part 1, Step 2 · Surjective (with Step 1: 2 points)

\(f\) is continuous, \(f(x) o-\infty\) as \(x o-\infty\) and \(f(x) o+\infty\) as \(x o+\infty ext{.}\) For any \(y\in\mathbb{R}\) pick \(a<b\) with \(f(a)<y<f(b) ext{;}\) the intermediate value theorem gives \(x\in(a,b)\) with \(f(x)=y ext{.}\) So the range is all of \(\mathbb{R}\) and \(f\) is invertible.

Concept: Intermediate value theorem

Part 2 · Two derivatives of the inverse (2 points)

Since \(f'(x)=1+3x^2 eq0\) for every \(x ext{,}\) the inverse function theorem applies:

\[ g'(y)= rac{1}{f'(g(y))}= rac{1}{1+3g(y)^2}. \]

Find \(g(0)\) and \(g(2)\) by solving \(f(x)=y ext{:}\) \(f(0)=0\) gives \(g(0)=0 ext{,}\) and \(f(1)=2\) gives \(g(2)=1 ext{.}\) Hence

\[ g'(0)= rac{1}{1}=1,\quad g'(2)= rac{1}{1+3}= rac{1}{4}. \]

Concept: Inverse function theorem

Part 3, Method 1 · Substitute x = g(y) (3 points)

Put \(x=g(y) ext{.}\) Then \(y=f(x)=x+x^3 ext{.}\) Since \(g\) is differentiable by Part 2, it is continuous, and \(g(0)=0 ext{;}\) so \(x o0\) as \(y o0 ext{,}\) and \(x eq0\) when \(y eq0 ext{.}\) So

\[ egin{aligned} rac{g(y)-y}{y^3}&= rac{x-(x+x^3)}{(x+x^3)^3}\ &=- rac{x^3}{x^3(1+x^2)^3}\ &=- rac{1}{(1+x^2)^3} o-1. \end{aligned} \] Part 3, Method 2 · Use g(y)/y → g′(0) (3 points)

From \(f(g(y))=y\) we get \(g(y)+g(y)^3=y ext{,}\) so \(g(y)-y=-g(y)^3 ext{.}\) For \(y eq0 ext{,}\)

\[ rac{g(y)-y}{y^3}=-\left( rac{g(y)}{y} ight)^3. \]

Because \(g(0)=0 ext{,}\) the quotient \(g(y)/y\) is a difference quotient:

\[ \lim_{y o0} rac{g(y)-g(0)}{y-0}=g'(0)=1. \]

So the limit is \(-(1)^3=-1 ext{.}\) Substituting \(y=0\) directly gives \(0/0\) and earns nothing; the justification \(g(y)/y o1\) is the point.

Part 3, Method 3 · L'Hôpital's rule once (3 points)

The quotient is of type \(0/0 ext{.}\) Differentiate numerator and denominator, using Part 2:

\[ rac{g'(y)-1}{3y^2} = rac{1}{3y^2}\left( rac{1}{1+3g(y)^2}-1 ight) =- rac{(g(y)/y)^2}{1+3g(y)^2} o-1, \]

since \(g(y)/y o1\) and \(g(y) o0 ext{.}\) The derivative quotient has a limit, which justifies L'Hôpital's rule, so the original limit is also \(-1 ext{.}\)

Concept: L'Hôpital's rule

Any one of the three methods earns the full 3 points.

docs.title: Where marks are lost
docs.text:
• Showing only injectivity in part 1. Invertible onto \(\mathbb{R}\) also needs the range to be all of \(\mathbb{R}\text{.}\)
  • Writing \(g'(2)=1/f'(2)\text{.}\) The derivative of \(f\) is evaluated at \(g(2)=1\text{,}\) not at \(2\text{.}\)
  • Plugging in \(y=0\) in part 3. The quotient is \(0/0\text{;}\) a limit argument is required.

docs.title: Try next
docs.text:
• Continuity and differentiability of \(x^2\sin(A/x)\)
  • A limit via asymptotic equivalence: more limits of type \(0/0\text{.}\)

Symbols: element of, infinity, real numbers

docs.title: A limit via asymptotic equivalence
docs.text: Math I: Calculus · Mock exam, Question 4(b) · 14 points · Lecture 8

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Define

\[ \begin{aligned} N(x)&=(1+x)^{1/x}+\mathrm{e}^x-\mathrm{e}-1,\\ D(x)&=\ln\left(x+\sqrt{1+x^2}\right). \end{aligned} \]
  • (b1) Prove that \(D(x)\sim x\) as \(x\to0\text{.}\) [4 points]
  • (b2) Evaluate \(\lim_{x\to0}N(x)/D(x)\text{.}\) [10 points]

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Asymptotic equivalence: \(f(x)\sim g(x)\) means \(f(x)/g(x)\to1\text{.}\)
  • Derivative and differentiability: if \(F\) is differentiable at \(0\) and \(F(0)=0\text{,}\) then \(F(x)/x\to F'(0)\text{.}\)
  • Chain rule, logarithm and exponential function.
  • Indeterminate form and L'Hôpital's rule.
  • Euler's number: \((1+x)^{1/x}\to\mathrm{e}\) as \(x\to0\text{.}\)

docs.title: Plan
docs.text: Split the hard limit into pieces that are each a known difference quotient. Part (b1) lets you replace \(D(x)\) by \(x\text{.}\) Then \(N(x)/x\) splits into \([(1+x)^{1/x}-\mathrm{e}]/x\) and \((\mathrm{e}^x-1)/x\text{.}\) The first piece is the only real work: write \((1+x)^{1/x}=\mathrm{e}^{u(x)}\) and use the chain of quotients \(\frac{\mathrm{e}^{u}-\mathrm{e}}{u-1}\cdot\frac{u-1}{x}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Step-by-step solution
docs.text:
Try each step yourself before you open it.

(b1) Step 1 · Connect the limit with D′(0) (1 point)

\(D(0)=\ln1=0 ext{,}\) so

\[ rac{D(x)}{x}= rac{D(x)-D(0)}{x-0} o D'(0). \]

It is enough to show \(D'(0)=1 ext{.}\)

(b1) Step 2 · Differentiate and simplify (2 points)

By the chain rule,

\[ egin{aligned} D'(x)&= rac{1+x/\sqrt{1+x^2}}{x+\sqrt{1+x^2}}\ &= rac{(\sqrt{1+x^2}+x)/\sqrt{1+x^2}}{x+\sqrt{1+x^2}}\ &= rac{1}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}. \end{aligned} \] (b1) Step 3 · Conclude (1 point)

\(D'(0)=1 ext{,}\) so \(D(x)/x o1 ext{,}\) that is, \(D(x)\sim x\) as \(x o0 ext{.}\)

Concept: Asymptotic equivalence

(b2) Step 1 · Rewrite the power (2 points)

Let \(u(x)=\ln(1+x)/x\) for \(x eq0 ext{.}\) Then \((1+x)^{1/x}=\mathrm{e}^{u(x)} ext{,}\) and \(u(x) o1\) because \(\ln(1+x)/x\) is the difference quotient of \(\ln(1+x)\) at \(0 ext{.}\)

(b2) Step 2 · The rate at which u approaches 1 (3 points) \[ egin{aligned} \lim_{x o0} rac{u(x)-1}{x} &=\lim_{x o0} rac{\ln(1+x)-x}{x^2}\ &=\lim_{x o0} rac{1/(1+x)-1}{2x}\ &=\lim_{x o0} rac{-1}{2(1+x)}=- rac{1}{2}. \end{aligned} \]

The second equality is L'Hôpital's rule for the form \(0/0 ext{;}\) it is justified because the last limit exists.

Concept: L'Hôpital's rule

(b2) Step 3 · The first piece of N(x)/x (2 points)

For small \(x eq0 ext{,}\) \(u(x) eq1\) because \(\ln(1+x)<x ext{.}\) So we may write

\[ rac{(1+x)^{1/x}-\mathrm{e}}{x} = rac{\mathrm{e}^{u(x)}-\mathrm{e}}{u(x)-1}\cdot rac{u(x)-1}{x} o\mathrm{e}\cdot\left(- rac{1}{2} ight)=- rac{\mathrm{e}}{2}. \]

The first factor tends to the derivative of \(\mathrm{e}^t\) at \(t=1 ext{,}\) which is \(\mathrm{e} ext{.}\)

(b2) Step 4 · The second piece (1 point)

\(N(x)=\left[(1+x)^{1/x}-\mathrm{e} ight]+\left[\mathrm{e}^x-1 ight] ext{,}\) and \((\mathrm{e}^x-1)/x o1 ext{.}\) Hence

\[ rac{N(x)}{x} o1- rac{\mathrm{e}}{2}. \] (b2) Step 5 · Use (b1) and conclude (2 points)

By (b1), \(x/D(x) o1 ext{.}\) Therefore

\[ rac{N(x)}{D(x)}= rac{N(x)}{x}\cdot rac{x}{D(x)} o1- rac{\mathrm{e}}{2}. \]

docs.title: Where marks are lost
docs.text:
• Applying L'Hôpital's rule to \(N(x)/D(x)\) directly. It is allowed in principle, but the derivative of \((1+x)^{1/x}\) is messy and contains another quotient of type \(0/0\text{.}\) Splitting into known quotients is shorter.
  • Writing \((1+x)^{1/x}\approx\mathrm{e}\) and cancelling. That throws away exactly the term of order \(x\) that the limit depends on.
  • Not citing (b1). The last step uses \(x/D(x)\to1\text{;}\) say so.

docs.title: Try next
docs.text:

  • Area between two curves and \(\int_0^1\ln x\,\mathrm{d}x\)

Symbols: integral, square root

docs.title: Limit of a sequence from the definition, squeeze and bounds
docs.text: Math I: Calculus · Week 2 test, open question · 7 points · Lecture 3

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Define, for \(n\geq1\text{,}\)

\[ a_n=\frac{2(-1)^n}{n^2+n},\quad b_n=\sqrt{2}\cos\left(\frac{1}{n}\right). \]
  • (a) Prove, using the definition, that \((a_n)_{n=1}^{\infty}\) converges to \(0\text{.}\) [2 points]
  • (b) Determine whether the sequence \(a_1b_1,a_2b_2,\dots\) is convergent. If it is, find its limit; if not, justify. [2 points]
  • (c) Evaluate \(\inf_{n\geq1}a_n-\sup_{n\geq1}b_n\) and briefly justify both bounds. [3 points]

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Limit of a sequence: the \(\varepsilon\)–\(N\) definition.
  • Squeeze theorem for sequences.
  • Bounded sequence: a bounded sequence times a sequence tending to \(0\) tends to \(0\text{.}\)
  • Infimum and supremum, and the difference with minimum and maximum.
  • Trigonometric functions: \(|\cos x|\leq1\text{,}\) and \(\cos x<1\) for \(0<x\leq1\text{.}\)

docs.title: Plan
docs.text: In (a), find a simple upper bound for \(|a_n|\) that clearly goes to \(0\text{,}\) and choose \(N\) from it. In (b), do not compute \(\lim b_n\) at all: boundedness of \((b_n)\) is enough. In (c), list the first few terms to see where the extreme values sit, then justify each bound separately. One of them is attained and the other is not.

docs.title: Step-by-step solution
docs.text:
Try each step yourself before you open it.

(a) Step 1 · Bound the distance to the limit and choose N (1 point)

Let \(\varepsilon>0\text{.}\) Since \(n^2+n>n\text{,}\)

\[ |a_n-0|=\frac{2}{n^2+n}<\frac{2}{n}. \]

So it is enough to make \(2/n<\varepsilon\text{.}\) Choose a positive integer \(N>2/\varepsilon\text{.}\)

Concept: Limit of a sequence

(a) Step 2 · Verify for all n ≥ N (1 point)

If \(n\geq N\text{,}\) then

\[ |a_n-0|<\frac{2}{n}\leq\frac{2}{N}<\varepsilon. \]

Since \(\varepsilon>0\) was arbitrary, \(a_n\to0\) by definition.

(b) Step 1 · Bound the second factor (1 point)

Because \(|\cos x|\leq1\) for all \(x\text{,}\) we have \(|b_n|\leq\sqrt{2}\) for every \(n\text{.}\) You do not need the limit of \((b_n)\) here.

(b) Step 2 · Squeeze (1 point)

Then

\[ 0\leq|a_nb_n|\leq\sqrt{2}\,|a_n|\to0. \]

By the squeeze theorem \(|a_nb_n|\to0\text{,}\) so \(a_nb_n\to0\text{.}\) The sequence converges, with limit \(0\text{.}\)

Concept: Squeeze theorem for sequences

(c) Step 1 · The infimum of (a_n) (1 point)

The sign of \(a_n\) alternates: \(a_n>0\) for even \(n\) and \(a_n<0\) for odd \(n\text{.}\) For odd \(n\) the size \(2/(n^2+n)\) decreases as \(n\) grows:

\[ a_1=-1,\quad a_3=-\frac{1}{6},\quad a_5=-\frac{1}{15},\ \dots \]

So every term is at least \(a_1=-1\text{,}\) and \(-1\) is itself a term. Hence \(\inf_{n\geq1}a_n=-1\text{;}\) it is even a minimum.

(c) Step 2 · The supremum of (b_n) (1 point)

For every \(n\text{,}\) \(0<1/n\leq1\text{,}\) so \(\cos(1/n)<1\) and \(b_n<\sqrt{2}\text{.}\) Thus \(\sqrt{2}\) is an upper bound.

It is the least upper bound because \(1/n\to0\) and cosine is continuous, so \(b_n\to\sqrt{2}\text{.}\) For any \(\eta>0\) some \(b_n\) exceeds \(\sqrt{2}-\eta\text{,}\) so no smaller number is an upper bound. Hence \(\sup_{n\geq1}b_n=\sqrt{2}\text{,}\) although no term equals \(\sqrt{2}\text{.}\)

Concept: Supremum

(c) Step 3 · Combine (1 point) \[ \inf_{n\geq1}a_n-\sup_{n\geq1}b_n=-1-\sqrt{2}. \]

docs.title: Where marks are lost
docs.text:
• Choosing \(N\) that depends on \(n\text{.}\) In (a), \(N\) may depend on \(\varepsilon\) only.
  • Trying to compute \(\lim b_n\) in (b) and multiplying limits. That works here, but boundedness is all you need, and the bounded-times-null argument also works when \((b_n)\) has no limit.
  • Saying "the supremum is the largest term". In (c) the supremum \(\sqrt{2}\) is not attained. You must show it is an upper bound and that nothing smaller is.
  • Ignoring the sign of \(a_n\text{.}\) The infimum comes from the negative terms, not from the limit \(0\text{.}\)

docs.title: Try next
docs.text:
• Continuity of \(1/x^2\) from the \(\varepsilon\)–\(\delta\) definition: the same "bound, then choose" idea for functions.
  • Convergence of three series and \(\sum\sin n\): limits of sequences used to decide convergence of series.

Symbols: delta, epsilon, eta, infinity, square root, sum

docs.title: Convergence of three series and \(\sum\sin n\)
docs.text: Math I: Calculus · Mock exam, Question 1(b)–(c) · 14 points · Lecture 10

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
• (b) Determine whether \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\sin n\) converges. Justify your conclusion using a necessary condition for convergence of a series. [4 points]

  • (c) Let \(c_n=1/\sqrt{n}\text{.}\) Determine which of the following series converge and find any accessible sum. [10 points]

    \[ \begin{aligned} S_1&=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{c_n}{3},\\ S_2&=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{c_n}{n^{1/3}},\\ S_3&=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{n^{1/2}c_n}{(-2)^n}. \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Infinite series: if \(\sum b_n\) converges, then \(b_n\to0\) (the term test).
  • Trigonometric functions: \(\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1\) and the addition formula for \(\sin(x+y)\text{.}\)
  • \(p\)-series: \(\sum n^{-p}\) converges exactly when \(p>1\text{.}\)
  • Geometric series: for \(|r|<1\text{,}\) \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}r^n=r/(1-r)\text{.}\)

docs.title: Plan
docs.text: In (b) the term test can only prove divergence, so the work is to show that \(\sin n\) does not tend to \(0\text{.}\) Argue by contradiction with the addition formula. In (c), substitute \(c_n\) first: each series then becomes a standard one you can recognise.

docs.title: Step-by-step solution
docs.text:
Try each step yourself before you open it.

(b) Step 1 · State the necessary condition (1 point)

If \(\sum b_n\) converges, then \(b_n\to0\text{.}\) So if \(\sin n\not\to0\text{,}\) the series diverges.

Concept: Infinite series

(b) Step 2 · Show that sin n does not tend to 0 (2 points)

Suppose, for contradiction, that \(\sin n\to0\text{.}\) Then \(\cos^2n=1-\sin^2n\to1\text{,}\) so \(|\cos n|\to1\text{.}\) The addition formula gives

\[ \sin(n+1)-\sin n\cos1=\cos n\sin1. \]

The left-hand side tends to \(0-0\cdot\cos1=0\text{,}\) because \(\sin(n+1)\to0\) as well. The absolute value of the right-hand side tends to \(|\sin1|>0\text{.}\) This is a contradiction, so \(\sin n\not\to0\text{.}\)

(b) Step 3 · Conclude (1 point)

By the term test, \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\sin n\) diverges.

(c) Step 1 · Rewrite S₁ and S₂ (2 points)

With \(c_n=n^{-1/2}\text{,}\)

\[ S_1=\frac{1}{3}\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}n^{-1/2},\qquad S_2=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}n^{-5/6}, \]

since \(n^{-1/2}n^{-1/3}=n^{-5/6}\text{.}\)

(c) Step 2 · Apply the p-series test (3 points)

\(S_1\) is a constant multiple of the \(p\)-series with \(p=1/2\leq1\text{,}\) which diverges. A nonzero constant factor does not change divergence, so \(S_1\) diverges.

\(S_2\) is the \(p\)-series with \(p=5/6\leq1\text{,}\) so it diverges too.

Concept: \(p\)-series

(c) Step 3 · Recognise S₃ as geometric (2 points)

\(n^{1/2}c_n=1\text{,}\) so

\[ S_3=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{(-2)^n} =\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)^n. \]

This is a geometric series with ratio \(r=-1/2\text{,}\) and \(|r|<1\text{.}\)

(c) Step 4 · Sum it and classify (3 points) \[ S_3=\frac{-1/2}{1-(-1/2)}=\frac{-1/2}{3/2}=-\frac{1}{3}. \]

So \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) diverge, and only \(S_3\) converges, with sum \(-1/3\text{.}\)

Concept: Geometric series

docs.title: Where marks are lost
docs.text:
• Using the term test to prove convergence. \(b_n\to0\) is necessary, not sufficient: \(\sum1/\sqrt{n}\) diverges although \(1/\sqrt{n}\to0\text{.}\)
  • Asserting "\(\sin n\) oscillates" without proof. Part (b) asks for a justification of \(\sin n\not\to0\text{.}\)
  • Starting the geometric sum at \(n=0\text{.}\) The series starts at \(n=1\text{,}\) so the first term is \(-1/2\text{,}\) not \(1\text{.}\)

docs.text:

docs.title: A set identity and a divisibility proof by induction
docs.text: Math I: Calculus · Week 1 test, open question · 7 points · Lecture 1

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
1. Let \(A\) and \(B\) be sets with \(A\subseteq B\text{.}\) Prove that

    \[ B=A\cup(B\setminus A)\quad\text{and}\quad A\cap(B\setminus A)=\varnothing. \]

    [3 points]

  2. Prove by mathematical induction that \(3^{2n}-1\) is divisible by \(8\) for every positive integer \(n\text{.}\) [4 points]

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Subset: two sets are equal exactly when each is a subset of the other.
  • Union, intersection and difference set: what it means for an element to belong to each.
  • Empty set and disjoint sets.
  • Mathematical induction, the induction axiom of the natural numbers: a base case and an inductive step.

docs.title: Plan
docs.text: For part 1, prove the equality by double inclusion: take an element of the left side and show it is in the right side, then the reverse. For part 2, the key is to write the \((k+1)\)-th expression in terms of the \(k\)-th one, so that the induction hypothesis can be used.

docs.title: Step-by-step solution
docs.text:
Try each step yourself before you open it.

Part 1, Step 1 · Show that B is contained in the union

Let \(x\in B ext{.}\) Split into two cases.

  • If \(x\in A ext{,}\) then \(x\in A\cup(B\setminus A) ext{.}\)
  • If \(x otin A ext{,}\) then \(x\in B\) and \(x otin A ext{,}\) so \(x\in B\setminus A\subseteq A\cup(B\setminus A) ext{.}\)

In both cases \(x\in A\cup(B\setminus A) ext{.}\)

Part 1, Step 2 · Show that the union is contained in B (with Step 1: 2 points)

\(A\subseteq B\) is given, and \(B\setminus A\subseteq B\) by the definition of the difference set. A union of two subsets of \(B\) is again a subset of \(B ext{.}\) Together with Step 1, this proves \(B=A\cup(B\setminus A) ext{.}\)

This is the only place where the assumption \(A\subseteq B\) is used. Without it the identity can fail.

Part 1, Step 3 · Show the intersection is empty (1 point)

Suppose some \(x\) lies in \(A\cap(B\setminus A) ext{.}\) Then \(x\in A ext{,}\) and also \(x\in B\setminus A ext{,}\) which means \(x otin A ext{.}\) That is a contradiction, so no such \(x\) exists and \(A\cap(B\setminus A)=\varnothing ext{.}\)

Part 2, Step 1 · Base case (1 point)

For \(n=1 ext{,}\) \(3^{2}-1=8 ext{,}\) which is divisible by \(8 ext{.}\)

Part 2, Step 2 · State the induction hypothesis precisely (1 point)

Assume that for some positive integer \(k ext{,}\) \(3^{2k}-1\) is divisible by \(8 ext{.}\) Write this as an equation:

\[ 3^{2k}-1=8m\quad ext{for some integer }m. \]

Turning "divisible by 8" into an equation is what makes the next step a calculation instead of a sentence.

Part 2, Step 3 · Inductive step (2 points)

Rewrite the next case so that the hypothesis appears:

\[ egin{aligned} 3^{2(k+1)}-1&=9\cdot3^{2k}-1\ &=9(3^{2k}-1)+8\ &=9\cdot8m+8\ &=8(9m+1). \end{aligned} \]

Since \(9m+1\) is an integer, \(3^{2(k+1)}-1\) is divisible by \(8 ext{.}\) By induction the statement holds for every positive integer \(n ext{.}\)

docs.title: Where marks are lost
docs.text:
• Proving only one inclusion in part 1. Equality of sets needs both directions.
  • Checking a few values of \(n\) instead of proving the step. Examples like \(n=2,3\) are not a proof.
  • Assuming what you want to prove. The hypothesis is about a fixed \(k\text{;}\) the step must derive the statement for \(k+1\text{.}\)
  • Leaving "divisible by 8" as words. Without \(3^{2k}-1=8m\) it is hard to show the factor \(8\) in the next case.

docs.title: Try next
docs.text:

Symbols: element of, intersection, subset, union

docs.title: Stationary points, convexity and an alternating series
docs.text: Math I: Calculus · Week 6 test, open question · 7 points · Lectures 9–10

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Consider \(f(x)=x^2(x-2)^2\) for \(x\in\mathbb{R}\text{.}\)

  • (a) Find every stationary point of \(f\) and classify each one as a local maximum or local minimum. [3 points]
  • (b) Find the \(x\)-coordinates of all inflection points. State the intervals on which \(f\) is convex and those on which it is concave. [2 points]

  • (c) Determine whether the series below converges, and justify your conclusion. [2 points]

    \[ \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{n-1}}{\sqrt{n}} \]

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Stationary point and the second-order condition: \(f''(x_0)>0\) gives a local minimum, \(f''(x_0)<0\) a local maximum.
  • Higher-order derivative.
  • Convexity and concavity and inflection point: \(f''\) must change sign, not only vanish.
  • Alternating series test.

docs.title: Plan
docs.text: Factor \(f'\) completely before solving \(f'=0\text{;}\) the factored form shows the three stationary points at once. Then \(f''\) does two jobs: its value at each stationary point classifies it, and its zeros and sign give the inflection points and the convexity intervals. Part (c) is independent: check the two conditions of the alternating series test.

docs.title: Step-by-step solution
docs.text:
Try each step yourself before you open it.

Step 1 · Compute and factor the derivatives (counted in (a) and (b))

By the product rule,

\[ \begin{aligned} f'(x)&=2x(x-2)^2+2x^2(x-2)\\ &=2x(x-2)(2x-2)\\ &=4x(x-1)(x-2). \end{aligned} \]

Expanding \(f'(x)=4x^3-12x^2+8x\) and differentiating again,

\[ f''(x)=12x^2-24x+8. \] (a) · Classify the stationary points (3 points)

\(f'(x)=0\) exactly at \(x=0,1,2\text{.}\) Then

\[ f''(0)=8,\quad f''(1)=-4,\quad f''(2)=8. \]

By the second-order condition, \(x=0\) and \(x=2\) are local minima and \(x=1\) is a local maximum.

Concept: Second-order condition

(b) · Inflection points and convexity (2 points)

\(f''(x)=4(3x^2-6x+2)=0\) gives

\[ x=1\pm\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}. \]

\(f''\) is a parabola opening upwards, so it is positive outside these two roots and negative between them. The sign changes at both roots, so both are inflection points. \(f\) is convex on \((-\infty,1-1/\sqrt{3})\) and on \((1+1/\sqrt{3},\infty)\text{,}\) and concave on \((1-1/\sqrt{3},1+1/\sqrt{3})\text{.}\)

Concept: Inflection point

(c) · The alternating series (2 points)

Write the series as \(\sum(-1)^{n-1}c_n\) with \(c_n=1/\sqrt{n}\text{.}\) The sequence \((c_n)\) is positive, decreasing, and tends to \(0\text{.}\) By the alternating series test, the series converges.

It does not converge absolutely: \(\sum1/\sqrt{n}\) is a \(p\)-series with \(p=1/2\leq1\text{.}\) The question does not ask for this, but it is the reason the alternating series test is needed.

Concept: Alternating series test

docs.title: Where marks are lost
docs.text:
• Calling every zero of \(f''\) an inflection point. Check that \(f''\) changes sign there.
  • Classifying by a picture. State the values of \(f''\) (or the sign change of \(f'\)) at each stationary point.
  • Checking only \(c_n\to0\) in (c). The test also needs \((c_n)\) to be decreasing.

docs.title: A function with three local extrema
docs.text: Math I: Calculus · Mock exam, Question 3(b) · 14 points · Lectures 6–7

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Let

\[ g(x)=\mathrm{e}^{-x}+a\sqrt{x},\quad x\in[0,\infty), \]

with \(a\in\mathbb{R}\text{,}\) and suppose that \(g\) has exactly three local extrema, at \(0=x_0<x_1<x_2\text{.}\)

  • (b1) Find \(g'(x)\) for \(x>0\text{.}\) Determine for which values of \(a\) a finite right derivative exists at \(0\text{.}\) [4 points]
  • (b2) Determine all possible values of \(a\) under the stated assumption of three local extrema. [6 points]
  • (b3) Prove that \(x_2+g(x_1)>3/2\text{.}\) [4 points]

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• One-sided derivative: the right difference quotient at an endpoint.
  • Exponential function: \((\mathrm{e}^{-h}-1)/h\to-1\) as \(h\to0\text{.}\)
  • Stationary point and local extremum, including extrema at an endpoint of the domain.
  • Monotone function: the sign of a derivative gives where a function increases or decreases.

docs.title: Plan
docs.text:
Separate the parameter from \(x\text{.}\) For \(x>0\text{,}\)

\[ g'(x)=\frac{a-2\sqrt{x}\,\mathrm{e}^{-x}}{2\sqrt{x}}, \]

so the sign of \(g'\) is the sign of \(a-h(x)\) with \(h(x)=2\sqrt{x}\,\mathrm{e}^{-x}\text{.}\) Counting stationary points becomes counting how often the horizontal line \(y=a\) meets the graph of \(h\text{.}\) For (b3), use the stationary-point equation to remove \(a\) from \(g(x_1)\text{.}\)

docs.title: Step-by-step solution
docs.text:
Try each step yourself before you open it.

(b1) Step 1 · The derivative for x > 0 (1 point) \[ g'(x)=-\mathrm{e}^{-x}+\frac{a}{2\sqrt{x}}. \] (b1) Step 2 · The right difference quotient at 0 (1 point)

Since \(g(0)=1\text{,}\) for \(h>0\)

\[ \frac{g(h)-g(0)}{h}=\frac{\mathrm{e}^{-h}-1}{h}+\frac{a}{\sqrt{h}}. \]

The formula from Step 1 is not valid at \(x=0\text{;}\) at the endpoint you must use the definition.

(b1) Step 3 · Analyse both terms (2 points)

As \(h\to0^+\text{,}\) the first term tends to \(-1\text{,}\) the derivative of \(\mathrm{e}^{-x}\) at \(0\text{.}\) The second term \(a/\sqrt{h}\) has a finite limit only when \(a=0\text{.}\) So a finite right derivative exists exactly for \(a=0\text{,}\) and then it equals \(-1\text{.}\)

Concept: One-sided derivative

(b2) Step 1 · Separate the parameter (1 point)

For \(x>0\text{,}\) \(g'(x)=0\) is equivalent to

\[ a=h(x):=2\sqrt{x}\,\mathrm{e}^{-x}. \] (b2) Step 2 · Study h (3 points)

Differentiate:

\[ h'(x)=\frac{\mathrm{e}^{-x}}{\sqrt{x}}(1-2x). \]

So \(h\) increases on \((0,1/2)\) and decreases on \((1/2,\infty)\text{.}\) Its maximum is

\[ h\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)=\sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{e}^{-1/2}=\sqrt{2/\mathrm{e}}. \]

Also \(h(x)\to0\) as \(x\to0^+\) and as \(x\to\infty\text{,}\) and \(h>0\text{.}\)

(b2) Step 3 · Count solutions (1 point)

The equation \(h(x)=a\) has exactly two positive solutions precisely when

\[ 0<a<\sqrt{2/\mathrm{e}}. \]

For \(a\leq0\) there is none, for \(a=\sqrt{2/\mathrm{e}}\) only \(x=1/2\text{,}\) and for larger \(a\) none.

(b2) Step 4 · Check that all three are extrema (1 point)

For \(0<a<\sqrt{2/\mathrm{e}}\) the solutions satisfy \(0<x_1<1/2<x_2\text{.}\) Because \(g'(x)\) has the sign of \(a-h(x)\text{,}\) \(g'\) is positive on \((0,x_1)\text{,}\) negative on \((x_1,x_2)\) and positive on \((x_2,\infty)\text{.}\) So \(x_1\) is a local maximum and \(x_2\) a local minimum. At the endpoint, \(g\) increases immediately to the right of \(0\text{,}\) so \(0\) is a local minimum relative to the domain.

The other values of \(a\) fail: for \(a\leq0\text{,}\) \(g'<0\) on \((0,\infty)\text{;}\) for \(a\geq\sqrt{2/\mathrm{e}}\text{,}\) \(g'\geq0\) with at most one zero. In both cases \(0\) is the only local extremum. Hence the possible values are exactly \(0<a<\sqrt{2/\mathrm{e}}\text{.}\)

(b3) Step 1 · Use x₂ > 1/2 (1 point)

From (b2), \(x_2>1/2\text{.}\)

(b3) Step 2 · Remove a from g(x₁) (1 point)

At \(x_1\) the stationary-point relation gives \(a=2\sqrt{x_1}\,\mathrm{e}^{-x_1}\text{,}\) so \(a\sqrt{x_1}=2x_1\mathrm{e}^{-x_1}\) and

\[ g(x_1)=(1+2x_1)\mathrm{e}^{-x_1}. \] (b3) Step 3 · A monotone auxiliary function (1 point)

Let \(q(x)=(1+2x)\mathrm{e}^{-x}\text{.}\) Then

\[ q'(x)=(1-2x)\mathrm{e}^{-x}>0\quad\text{on }(0,\tfrac{1}{2}), \]

so \(q\) is strictly increasing on \([0,1/2]\text{.}\) Since \(0<x_1<1/2\text{,}\) \(g(x_1)=q(x_1)>q(0)=1\text{.}\)

(b3) Step 4 · Combine (1 point) \[ x_2+g(x_1)>\frac{1}{2}+1=\frac{3}{2}. \]

docs.title: Where marks are lost
docs.text:
• Using the formula for \(g'\) at \(x=0\text{.}\) The endpoint needs the difference quotient.
  • Finding \(0<a<\sqrt{2/\mathrm{e}}\) without checking the sign pattern. Two stationary points are not automatically two extrema, and the endpoint extremum must be argued.
  • Leaving \(a\) in \(g(x_1)\text{.}\) The stationary-point equation is what turns (b3) into a one-variable inequality.

docs.text:

docs.title: Continuity and differentiability of \(x^2\sin(A/x)\)
docs.text: Math I: Calculus · Weekly test 2025-26, Week 3, open question · 7 points · Lectures 5–6

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Let \(A,B\in\mathbb{R}\) and define \(f\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) by

\[ f(x)= \begin{cases} x^2\sin(A/x), & x\neq0,\\ B, & x=0. \end{cases} \]
  • (a) Find all \(A,B\) for which \(f\) is continuous at \(0\text{.}\) [2 points]
  • (b) Find all \(A,B\) for which \(f\) is differentiable at \(0\text{,}\) and determine \(f'(0)\text{.}\) [3 points]
  • (c) Find all \(A,B\) for which \(f'\) is continuous at \(0\text{.}\) [2 points]

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Continuity: \(\lim_{x\to0}f(x)=f(0)\text{.}\)
  • Squeeze theorem for functions, with \(|\sin t|\leq1\text{.}\)
  • Derivative and differentiability: the difference quotient at \(0\text{,}\) and the fact that differentiability implies continuity.
  • Chain rule and differentiation rules for \(x\neq0\text{.}\)
  • Limit at a point: if two sequences \(x_k\to0\) and \(y_k\to0\) give different limits of \(f'\text{,}\) then \(\lim_{x\to0}f'(x)\) does not exist.

docs.title: Plan
docs.text: The factor \(x^2\) beats the oscillation of \(\sin(A/x)\) in (a) and (b), so \(A\) never matters there; only \(B\) does. In (c) the derivative for \(x\neq0\) has a term \(-A\cos(A/x)\) with no \(x\) in front, which keeps oscillating. Two sequences that pick out \(\cos=1\) and \(\cos=-1\) show the limit fails unless \(A=0\text{.}\)

docs.title: Step-by-step solution
docs.text:
Try each step yourself before you open it.

(a) · Continuity at 0 (2 points)

For \(x eq0 ext{,}\) \(0\leq|x^2\sin(A/x)|\leq x^2 ext{,}\) and \(x^2 o0 ext{.}\) By the squeeze theorem,

\[ \lim_{x o0}f(x)=0 \]

for every \(A ext{.}\) So \(f\) is continuous at \(0\) exactly when \(f(0)=B=0 ext{,}\) with \(A\) arbitrary.

Concept: Squeeze theorem for functions

(b) Step 1 · Differentiability forces B = 0 (1 point)

A function that is differentiable at a point is continuous there. By (a), \(B=0\) is necessary.

(b) Step 2 · Compute the difference quotient (2 points)

With \(B=0 ext{,}\)

\[ rac{f(x)-f(0)}{x-0}=x\sin\left( rac{A}{x} ight), \]

and \(|x\sin(A/x)|\leq|x| o0 ext{.}\) So \(f'(0)=0\) for every \(A ext{.}\) Hence \(f\) is differentiable at \(0\) exactly when \(B=0 ext{,}\) and then \(f'(0)=0 ext{.}\)

(c) Step 1 · The derivative away from 0

For \(x eq0 ext{,}\) the product rule and chain rule give

\[ f'(x)=2x\sin\left( rac{A}{x} ight) +x^2\cos\left( rac{A}{x} ight)\cdot\left(- rac{A}{x^2} ight) =2x\sin\left( rac{A}{x} ight)-A\cos\left( rac{A}{x} ight). \]

The first term tends to \(0 ext{.}\) The second term has no factor \(x\) to damp it.

(c) Step 2 · If A ≠ 0 the limit of f′ does not exist (with Step 3: 2 points)

Take, for positive integers \(k ext{,}\)

\[ x_k= rac{A}{2\pi k},\quad y_k= rac{A}{(2k+1)\pi}. \]

Both tend to \(0 ext{.}\) At these points \(\sin(A/x)=0 ext{,}\) while \(\cos(A/x_k)=1\) and \(\cos(A/y_k)=-1 ext{.}\) So

\[ f'(x_k)=-A,\quad f'(y_k)=A. \]

Since \(A eq-A\) when \(A eq0 ext{,}\) \(\lim_{x o0}f'(x)\) does not exist, and \(f'\) is not continuous at \(0 ext{.}\)

(c) Step 3 · The remaining case

For \(f'\) to be continuous at \(0\) it must first exist there, so \(B=0\) by (b). If also \(A=0 ext{,}\) then \(f\equiv0 ext{,}\) so \(f'\equiv0 ext{,}\) which is continuous. Therefore \(f'\) is continuous at \(0\) exactly when \(A=B=0 ext{.}\)

docs.title: Where marks are lost
docs.text:
• Using the derivative formula at \(x=0\text{.}\) The formula from (c) Step 1 is only valid for \(x\neq0\text{.}\) At \(0\) you must use the difference quotient.
  • Concluding from "\(\cos(A/x)\) has no limit" without proof. Give two sequences with different limits of \(f'\text{,}\) as above.
  • Forgetting \(B\) in (b) and (c). Differentiability and continuity of \(f'\) both need \(f\) to be continuous at \(0\) first.
